t: Fixed vs working capital → which item is which
text:
## 1. The NCERT definitions (source of the 2024 PYQ)
Fixed capital = tools, machines, buildings that are used in production over many years
Working capital = raw materials and money in hand; used up in one round of production
Item | Category | Why
Farmer's plough | Fixed | Used season after season
Computer, generator, turbine | Fixed | Long-lived machine
Factory building, tractor, tubewell | Fixed | Many years of use
Yarn used by the weaver | Working | Raw material, used up
Clay used by the potter | Working | Raw material
Petrol / diesel for machines | Working | Fuel, consumed in one cycle
Cash to pay wages, seeds, fertiliser | Working | Money in hand / inputs
⚠ The test is life of the asset, not its price: a cheap plough is fixed, costly yarn is working
PYQ 2024: four pairs, "how many correct": plough as working capital (wrong) and yarn as fixed capital (wrong); answer only two

t: Factors of production → land, labour, physical and human capital
text:
## 1. The four requirements (NCERT Class 9, Palampur)
Factor | What it is | Example
Land | Land and natural resources | Water, forests, minerals
Labour | People who do the work | Farm labourer, skilled worker
Physical capital | Inputs at every stage | Fixed + working capital
Human capital | Knowledge and enterprise | Entrepreneur combining the rest
Physical capital = fixed capital + working capital
In Palampur land is fixed: no expansion of cultivated area since 1960; 75% of workers depend on farming
⚠ "Human capital" is a separate factor, not a type of physical capital
⚠ Money in hand counts as working capital, not fixed capital

t: Item → goods class: capital, intermediate, consumer goods
text:
## 1. Use-based classes (IIP product categories, PMF)
Class | Meaning | Examples
Primary goods | Raw materials | Mining products, fuels, electricity, fertilisers
Capital goods | Machinery used in production | Machines, equipment
Intermediate goods | Inputs and semi-finished goods | Yarn, chemicals, steel
Infrastructure goods | Construction materials | Cement, cables, rail materials
Consumer durables | Long-lasting | Vehicles, appliances, electronics
Consumer non-durables | Fast-moving | Food, medicines, toiletries
Capital goods industry = industries that make machine tools used to make consumer articles (NCERT Class 11); colonial India had hardly any
⚠ Same good, two classes: a car bought by a household is a consumer durable; bought by a taxi firm it is a capital good

t: Technical progress → capital-augmenting vs labour-augmenting
text:
## 1. Meaning
Type | What improves | Example
Capital-augmenting | Productivity of a capital good | Steel plough replaces wooden plough
Labour-augmenting | Productivity of workers | Training, better skills
Capital-saving | Same output with less capital | (Beyond your notes)
Labour-saving | Same output with fewer workers | Automation (Beyond your notes)
The plough is still a plough: the capital good becomes more efficient, so it is capital-augmenting
⚠ Not "capital-reducing" (option in 2015) and not labour-augmenting, even though the farmer works faster
PYQ 2015: steel for wooden ploughs = capital-augmenting technological progress

topic: Tangible vs intangible assets and capital vs revenue spending
t: Intangible investments → which assets count
text:
## 1. Meaning (PMF)
Intangible assets = non-physical assets that generate long-term economic value
Include software, data, R&D, brands, design, intellectual property
Asset | Tangible / Intangible
Brand recognition (brand equity) | Intangible
Intellectual property (patents, copyrights, trademarks, trade secrets) | Intangible
Mailing list of clients (customer lists) | Intangible
Software, databases, licences, goodwill, recipes | Intangible
Inventory (stock of goods) | Tangible
Land, buildings, machinery, vehicles, cash | Tangible
⚠ Inventory is the odd one out: it is a physical (tangible, current) asset
PYQ 2023: how many of brand, inventory, IP, client mailing list are intangible → only three

t: Intangible investment → 2025-26 numbers
text:

World Intangible Investment Report 2026: by WIPO and Luiss Business School
Finding | Figure
Global intangible investment | Crossed USD 10 trillion for the first time in 2025

topic: Tangible vs intangible assets and capital vs revenue spending
t: Capital vs revenue expenditure of a firm → which is which
text:
## 1. CAPEX (PMF definition)
Money spent to acquire, upgrade or maintain long-term physical or intangible assets
Spending | Class
Acquiring fixed assets: land, buildings, machinery | Capital
Acquiring new technology, software, patents, licences | Capital
Upgrading existing assets | Capital
Major repairs that extend asset life | Capital
Wages, rent, raw materials, electricity, routine repairs | Revenue
Interest paid on loans | Revenue
Revenue expenditure = recurring, day-to-day, creates no asset
⚠ Loan repayment counts as CAPEX in public finance (reduces liabilities) but interest is revenue expenditure
PYQ 2022: new technology = capital expenditure (correct)

topic: Tangible vs intangible assets and capital vs revenue spending
t: Debt vs equity financing → a financing choice, not an expenditure
text:
## 1. The 2022 trap
 | Debt financing | Equity financing
How | Borrow (bank loan, bonds) | Sell ownership (shares)
Obligation | Repay principal + interest | No repayment; dividends optional
Control | No dilution | Dilutes ownership
Example | Rs 10 lakh bank loan for machinery | Startup sells 20% stake to angel investors
Both are ways of raising funds (sources of capital)
Neither is "capital expenditure" nor "revenue expenditure" (those are uses of funds)
⚠ Statement "debt financing is capital expenditure, equity financing is revenue expenditure" is wrong
PYQ 2022: answer 1 only

t: Activity → sector: primary, secondary, tertiary
text:
## 1. The NCERT rule
Primary: produce a good by exploiting natural resources (depends on nature)
Secondary: natural products changed into other forms by manufacturing (factory, workshop or home)
Tertiary: activities that aid production but do not produce a good; services
Activity | Sector
Agriculture, dairy farm, fishing, forestry, poultry | Primary
Mining, quarrying, mineral exploration | Primary
Weaving cloth, spinning yarn, sugar/gur from cane, bricks from earth | Secondary
Construction, electricity, gas, water supply | Secondary
Storage of agricultural produce (godowns), transport, trade | Tertiary
Banking, communication, marketing, teaching, doctor, barber | Tertiary
Internet cafe, ATM booths, call centres, software firms | Tertiary
⚠ Storage is tertiary, not secondary: nothing is transformed
⚠ Mineral exploration is primary: under NIC-2025 it is a mining support service activity, inside mining and quarrying
PYQ 2024: storage-secondary (wrong), dairy-primary, exploration-tertiary (wrong), weaving-secondary → only two

t: Quaternary and quinary activities → what they are
text:
## 1. Beyond tertiary (PMF Human and Economic Geography)
Sector | Nature | Examples
Quaternary | Knowledge-oriented part of services; R&D, specialised knowledge | Teachers, hospitals, accounting and brokerage firms, software, consulting
Quinary | Creation and interpretation of ideas; evaluation of new technologies; top decision-makers | Senior executives, government officials, research scientists, financial and legal consultants
Quinary = "gold collar" professions
Over half of all workers in developed economies are in the knowledge sector
KPO (R&D, e-learning, IP research, legal, banking) needs highly skilled workers, unlike BPO
⚠ Testbook places scientific research and health/education administration in quinary; PMF puts research and development in quaternary and research scientists in quinary
⚠ Older 3-sector scheme: all of these are simply tertiary

t: Primary, secondary, tertiary activities → further traits
text:
## 1. PMF descriptors
Sector | Trait
Primary | Hunting, gathering, pastoralism, fishing, forestry, agriculture, mining and quarrying
Secondary | Processing, manufacturing and construction; power, mass production, factory labour
Tertiary | Production (services consumed) + exchange (trade, transport, communication)
Tertiary output is measured indirectly, through wages and salaries
Tourism is the world's largest tertiary activity by registered jobs (250 million)
NCERT names: primary = agriculture and related; secondary = industrial; tertiary = service sector
⚠ Construction is secondary, not tertiary; marketing and commerce are tertiary

t: India's sectors → share in GDP and jobs
text:
## 1. Shares
Sector | GDP share (PMF, 2025) | Workforce share (Testbook, 2021-22)
Services | 61.5% | 33.80%

Preview: services 54.35% of nominal GVA in 2025-26 (S.A.E.)

t: Classifying activities → NIC 2025 and new indices
text:
## In news 2025-26
National Industrial Classification (NIC) 2025 released by NSO, MoSPI
Feature | Detail
First NIC | 1962
Aligned with | UN ISIC Rev 5 (up to 4 digits)
Code | 5-digit → 6-digit, about 1,900 subclasses

topic: Real vs financial sector and closed vs open economy
t: Real sector vs financial sector → which activity
text:
## 1. Meaning
Real sector = production of goods and services: farms, factories, non-financial firms, households
Financial sector = financial intermediation: banks, NBFCs, insurers, bond and stock markets
Activity | Sector
Farmers harvesting crops | Real
Textile mills converting cotton into fabric | Real
Steel plant, transport firm, hotel | Real
Bank lending to a trading company | Financial
Corporate issuing rupee bonds overseas (masala bonds) | Financial
Insurance, mutual funds, stock trading | Financial
Monetary statistics: financial sector = money-issuing; real sector = money-holding; government = neither
⚠ Services are not automatically financial: a hotel or transporter is in the real sector
PYQ 2022: real sector = 1 and 2 only

topic: Real vs financial sector and closed vs open economy
t: Sectors of the domestic economy → three-way split
text:
## 1. IMF-style sectorisation (from the 2022 PYQ)
Sector | Contains
Real sector | Non-financial corporations, households, NPISHs
Financial sector | Corporations engaged in financial intermediation
General government | Centre, states, local bodies
Households + NPISHs together = "other resident sectors" in monetary statistics
## 2. Financialisation (PMF)
Raises the weight of the financial sector relative to the real sector
Transfers income from real to financial sector; adds to inequality, wage stagnation, risk of debt deflation

topic: Real vs financial sector and closed vs open economy
t: Closed vs open economy → meaning
text:
## 1. Definitions
 | Closed economy | Open economy
Trade | Neither exports nor imports | Trades with rest of world
Capital flows | None | FDI, FPI, borrowing
GDP identity | C + I + G | C + I + G + (X - M)
Closed: consumers get everything within the economic borders (APPSC Part 1)
Degree of openness = trade (exports + imports) as share of GDP; more open → more exposed to global cycles
⚠ Not "money supply fully controlled", not "deficit financing", not "only exports" (2011 distractors)
PYQ 2011: closed economy = neither exports nor imports take place

topic: Real vs financial sector and closed vs open economy
t: Economic models → two, three and four sectors
text:
## 1. Circular flow (Beyond your notes)
Model | Sectors | Economy type
Two-sector | Households + firms | Closed, no government
Three-sector | + Government | Closed economy
Four-sector | + Rest of the world | Open economy
Household consumption 61.5% of GDP in FY26, highest since 2012 (Economic Survey 2025-26); PMF 2025: 60.34%
⚠ A closed economy can still have a government: closed means no foreign sector
## 2. Economic systems (Testbook)
Capitalist (market decides; USA), socialist (state owns means of production), mixed (India)

topic: Demand: shifters, goods types and elasticity
t: Demand shifters → what raises or lowers demand
text:
## 1. Other things unchanged, demand for good X ...
Change | Effect on demand for X | Type
Price of a substitute rises (coffee for tea) | Rises | Curve shifts right
Price of a complement rises (sugar for tea) | Falls | Curve shifts left
Own price falls | Quantity demanded rises | Movement along curve
Income rises, normal good | Rises | Shift right
Income rises, inferior good | Falls | Shift left
Tastes shift toward X | Rises | Shift right
NCERT: demand for a good moves in the direction of its substitute's price and opposite to its complement's price
⚠ Own price → movement along the curve; everything else → shift of the curve
PYQ 2021: correct = substitute's price up (1) and own price falls (4) → 1 and 4 only

topic: Demand: shifters, goods types and elasticity
t: Normal, inferior and Giffen goods → income and price behaviour
text:
## 1. NCERT definitions
Good | Income rises | Own price falls
Normal | Demand rises | Demand rises
Inferior | Demand falls | Usually rises
Giffen (special inferior) | Demand falls | Demand falls (income effect beats substitution effect)
Inferior examples: low-quality food such as coarse cereals
Same good can be normal at low income, inferior at high income
Law of Demand: if demand moves with income (normal good), demand is inversely related to price
⚠ Every Giffen good is inferior, but not every inferior good is Giffen
## Beyond your notes
Veblen goods: luxury status goods whose demand may rise with price (conspicuous consumption)

topic: Demand: shifters, goods types and elasticity
t: Price effect → substitution and income effects
text:
## 1. Why demand curves slope down
Effect | Meaning
Substitution effect | Good becomes relatively cheaper, consumer substitutes toward it
Income effect | Fall in price raises purchasing power
Normal good: both effects work together → demand rises
Inferior good: effects work opposite; if income effect is stronger → Giffen
Linear demand: d(p) = a - bp; slope -b
⚠ The "income effect" here is a change in purchasing power, not in money income

topic: Demand: shifters, goods types and elasticity
t: Price elasticity of demand → meaning and rules
text:
## 1. NCERT points
Price elasticity = % change in demand ÷ % change in price; a pure number (no units)
Closely linked to total expenditure on the good
Elasticity | Price falls → total expenditure
Elastic (> 1) | Rises
Unitary (= 1) | Unchanged
Inelastic (< 1) | Falls
Monopoly: demand elastic where MR > 0, inelastic where MR < 0
Essentials such as food in the 5% GST slab: inelastic (Sept 2025 GST rationalisation analysis)
Testbook: petrol price up → people switch to public transport → high elasticity example
⚠ Elasticity is a ratio of percentages, not the slope of the curve

topic: Demand: shifters, goods types and elasticity
t: Consumer equilibrium → meaning
text:
## 1. Definition
Consumer is in equilibrium when he fulfils his needs (maximises satisfaction) with a given income
He has no desire to change his basket
Law of equi-marginal utility: MU of good 1 ÷ its price = MU of good 2 ÷ its price
Term | Meaning (NCERT)
Budget set | All bundles affordable at given income and prices
Budget line | Bundles costing exactly the income
Indifference curve | Bundles between which the consumer is indifferent
Monotonic preferences | More of at least one good, no less of other, is preferred
⚠ Not "full comforts", not "new sources of income" (1998 distractors)
PYQ 1998: equilibrium = fulfil needs with a given level of income

topic: Basic concepts: opportunity cost, supply-side, white goods
t: Opportunity cost → meaning and the "free good" trap
text:
## 1. Definition
Opportunity cost = gain foregone from the second-best activity (NCERT); value of the next best alternative (Testbook)
Exists for individuals and society; from scarcity
Case | Opportunity cost
Rs 1,000 put in family business | Interest foregone from the bank
Going to college | Earnings foregone
Govt gives a good free | Not zero: shifts from consumers to the tax-paying public
More of good A on a PPF | Units of good B given up
Normal profit = covers explicit costs + opportunity costs
⚠ "Free" good: cost is transferred to taxpayers, not "zero", not "ignored", not "to the government"
PYQ 2018: answer (c) transferred from consumers to tax-paying public

topic: Basic concepts: opportunity cost, supply-side, white goods
t: Production possibility frontier → scarcity and choice
text:
## 1. NCERT
Production possibility set: all combinations of goods producible with given resources and technology
Its boundary = PPF; moving along it shows opportunity cost
Central problem | Question
What to produce | Which goods, how much
How to produce | Which technique
For whom | Distribution
Unemployment trap: benefits make the opportunity cost of working too high (APPSC Part 1)
PPF shifts outward with better technology or more resources (Beyond your notes)
⚠ A point inside the PPF = unemployed or idle resources

topic: Basic concepts: opportunity cost, supply-side, white goods
t: Supply-side vs demand-side economics → whose view
text:
## 1. Comparison
 | Supply-side | Demand-side (Keynesian)
Focus | Producer, production | Consumer, aggregate demand
Tools | Tax cuts on firms and the rich, deregulation | Govt spending, income tax cuts for consumers
Idea | Savings and investment trickle down | Spending creates output and jobs
2019 corporate tax cut (30% → 22%) = supply-side move; did not lift investment as hoped (weak demand)
Budget 2025-26 income tax cut (about Rs 1 lakh crore) = demand-side course correction; PMF: Rs 1 cut may raise GDP by Rs 1.01
⚠ Supply-side stresses the producer, not consumer, middleman or global economy
PYQ 1998: supply-side economics → producer

topic: Basic concepts: opportunity cost, supply-side, white goods
t: White goods → meaning and current news
text:
## 1. Definition
White goods = large, durable, energy-intensive household appliances: refrigerators, washing machines, ACs, dishwashers
Named because they were first sold only in white
1998 PYQ framing: items purchased for conspicuous consumption; white goods industry delicensed in 1993
Term | Covers
White goods | Fridges, ACs, washing machines, microwave
FMCG | Low-cost, non-durable: toiletries, dairy, bakery
Consumer durables | Long-lasting: vehicles, appliances, electronics
⚠ Automobiles are not FMCG (UPPSC 2012); they are durables
## In news 2025-26
PLI for white goods (ACs and LED lights, from April 2021, 7 years) reopened for applications (Sept 2025); PLI covers 14 sectors
GST 2.0 (from 22 Sept 2025): ACs, refrigerators, large TVs moved 28% → 18%

topic: Basic concepts: opportunity cost, supply-side, white goods
t: Micro vs macro and other one-line terms
text:
## 1. Definitions UPSC has used
Term | Meaning
Microeconomics | Individual consumers, firms, markets
Macroeconomics | Whole economy: GDP, inflation, unemployment
Normal profit | Covers explicit + opportunity costs
Break-even point | Where firm earns only normal profit
Price ceiling | Govt upper limit on price
Very short period market | Supply fixed: flowers, vegetables, fruits
Marginal product is zero when total product is constant (UP 2013)
Increasing returns to scale: output rises more than proportionately to inputs
⚠ Economics (the discipline) ≠ economy (the real system of production, distribution, consumption)

topic: Meaning of national income and its basic terms
t: National income → what it equals (final goods only)
text:
## 1. Definition
National income = money value of final goods and services produced in a country in a given period (usually one year)
Measures the net value of goods and services produced, and includes net earned foreign income (PMF)
It is a flow variable, not a stock
Option UPSC gave (2013) | Why right or wrong
Money value of final goods and services produced | Correct: counts only final output
Total value of goods and services produced by the nationals | Wrong: includes intermediate goods; describes GNP-type output
Sum of total consumption and investment expenditure | Wrong: leaves out G and (X - M)
Sum of personal income of all individuals | Wrong: personal income is derived from NI after taxes and transfers
⚠ Trap: "total value of goods" sounds right, but without the word final it double counts
PYQ 2013: national income asked as a one-liner; the hinge word is final

topic: Meaning of national income and its basic terms
t: Final vs intermediate goods → why only final goods count
text:
## 1. The NCERT wheat-flour-biscuit logic
Value of final goods already includes the value of all intermediate goods used in making them
Counting wheat, then flour, then biscuits separately = counting the same thing three times (double counting)
Sum of production of final goods in the three sectors = GDP (NCERT)
Good | Final or intermediate?
Wheat sold to a flour mill | Intermediate
Flour sold to a biscuit factory | Intermediate
Biscuits bought by a household | Final
Machine bought by a factory (capital good) | Final (investment, not used up in one year)
## 2. Two ways to avoid double counting
Count only final goods, or
Add only the value added at each stage (value of output - value of intermediate inputs)
⚠ A machine bought by a firm is a final good (capital formation), not intermediate
Likely next: "which is not included in GDP" type question on intermediate goods, transfers, second-hand sales

topic: Meaning of national income and its basic terms
t: What is excluded from national income → transfers, second-hand goods
text:
## 1. Factor vs non-factor income
Factor incomes (counted): rent (land), wages/compensation (labour), interest (capital), profit (entrepreneur)
Non-factor / transfer incomes (not counted): received without productive activity
Item | In national income?
Wages, rent, interest, profit | Yes (factor income)
Old-age pension, scholarship, unemployment allowance | No (transfer payment)
Gifts, lottery winnings | No
Sale of second-hand goods (only the dealer's commission counts) | No
Purchase of shares/bonds (financial transfer) | No
Unpaid household work | No (non-market)
Imputed rent of owner-occupied houses | Yes (imputed)
## 2. Problems of measuring NI in India (Preview, state PSC PYQs)
Large non-organised (unorganised) sector without records (the main one asked)
Non-monetised sector, black money, illegal income, double counting, transfer payments, unreliable data
⚠ Transfer payments are part of personal income, not of national income

topic: Meaning of national income and its basic terms
t: Domestic vs national → GDP vs GNP
text:
## 1. The location vs residence split
Basis | GDP | GNP
Measures | Final output within domestic territory | Final output by normal residents (inside + outside)
Basis | Location-based | Residence/nationality-based
Link | GNP = GDP + NFIA | GDP = GNP - NFIA
## 2. Net factor income from abroad (NFIA)
NFIA = factor income earned by residents abroad - factor income earned by non-residents in India
If NFIA is negative (as for India), GNP < GDP
India: GNP 2022-23 ₹261.47 lakh crore vs GDP ₹272.04 lakh crore (Testbook)
Normal resident = person/institution whose centre of economic interest lies in the country (nationality not needed)
⚠ Domestic = location; National = residents. "National" aggregates add NFIA, "domestic" ones do not
Likely next: "GNP of India is less than GDP" (correct, because NFIA is negative)

topic: GDP, GNP, NDP, NNP: market price vs factor cost
t: National income → NNP at factor cost (the formula chain)
text:
## 1. The definition UPSC tests
National Income = NNP at factor cost (NNP-FC)
NI = GNP-MP - depreciation - indirect taxes + subsidies
NI = NNP-MP - net indirect taxes (NIT = indirect taxes - subsidies)
Option (2001) | Equals
GNP-MP - depreciation | NNP at market price (not NI)
GNP-MP - depreciation + NFIA | Wrong: GNP already includes NFIA
GNP-MP - depreciation - indirect taxes + subsidies | National income (NNP-FC)
GNP-MP - NFIA | GDP at market price
Option (1997) | Status
NNP at market price | Wrong
NNP at factor cost | National income
NDP at market price / NDP at factor cost | Wrong (domestic, no NFIA)
⚠ Trap: GNP-MP minus depreciation alone is NNP-MP; NI needs net indirect taxes removed too
PYQ 2001 and 1997: same concept asked twice; also asked by BPSC 2024 ("NNP at factor cost = national income")

topic: GDP, GNP, NDP, NNP: market price vs factor cost
t: Market price vs factor cost → taxes and subsidies
text:
## 1. The two valuations
Basis | Factor cost (FC) | Market price (MP)
Meaning | Cost of production paid to factors | Price paid by the buyer
Indirect taxes | Excluded | Included
Subsidies | Included | Excluded
Link | FC = MP - indirect taxes + subsidies | MP = FC + NIT
## 2. Testbook example
FC ₹100 + sales tax ₹20 = MP ₹120
With a subsidy, MP falls below FC
⚠ PMF wording: factor cost "excludes taxes but includes subsidies"; market price "includes taxes but excludes subsidies"
⚠ Only indirect (product) taxes separate MP and FC; direct taxes (income tax) play no part
Likely next: "NI = NNP-MP - (direct taxes - subsidies)" is a distractor (Chhattisgarh PCS 2023 used it)

topic: GDP, GNP, NDP, NNP: market price vs factor cost
t: Gross vs net → depreciation
text:
## 1. Depreciation (consumption of fixed capital)
Wear and tear of machinery, buildings, equipment during the year
Gross - depreciation = Net (GDP - D = NDP; GNP - D = NNP)
NDP shows how much a country spends just to maintain current output
## 2. The eight aggregates
Aggregate | Formula
GDP-MP | C + I + G + (X - M)
GNP-MP | GDP-MP + NFIA
NDP-MP | GDP-MP - depreciation
NNP-MP | GNP-MP - depreciation
GDP-FC | GDP-MP - NIT
GNP-FC | GNP-MP - NIT
NDP-FC | NDP-MP - NIT (= domestic factor income)
NNP-FC | NNP-MP - NIT = National income
⚠ NNP = GNP - D = GDP + NFIA - D (both forms correct: Uttarakhand PCS 2021)
⚠ NDP = GDP minus depreciation, never plus (Chhattisgarh PCS 2020 trap)

topic: GDP, GNP, NDP, NNP: market price vs factor cost
t: Three adjustments → which one turns which aggregate into which
text:
## 1. Memory grid
Adjustment | Turns | Into
+ NFIA | Domestic | National
- Depreciation | Gross | Net
- NIT (indirect taxes - subsidies) | Market price | Factor cost
National income needs all three: national + net + factor cost
## 2. Related income terms
Per capita income = national income (NNP) / population (Preview); Testbook also uses GDP / population
Personal income = NI - undistributed profits - corporate tax - social security contributions + transfer payments
Personal disposable income = personal income - personal direct taxes
⚠ Per capita income is an average: it hides inequality
Likely next: Statement-I/II on which adjustment converts domestic to national (NFIA, not depreciation)

topic: Nominal vs real: current and constant prices, GDP deflator
t: Current vs constant prices → why real growth is lower
text:
## 1. Two valuations of the same output
Basis | Current price (nominal) | Constant price (real)
Prices used | Prices of the same year | Prices of the base year
Inflation | Included | Removed
Shows | Size of the economy | Actual change in output
Growth in inflation | Higher | Lower
## 2. Testbook example
Year 1: nominal GDP 1,000, price index 100; Year 2: nominal 1,200, index 120
Real GDP in year 2 = 1,200 / 1.20 = 1,000: no real growth at all
Option (2000) | Status
Growth of population | Wrong: both per capita figures divide by the same population
Increase in price level | Correct: constant prices remove it
Growth of money supply / increase in wage rate | Wrong
⚠ Trap: population growth affects both per capita series equally, so it cannot explain the gap
PYQ 2000: per capita income at constant prices grows slower because it removes the rise in price level

topic: Nominal vs real: current and constant prices, GDP deflator
t: Nominal vs real GDP → which is used for what
text:
## 1. PMF rule
Size of the economy uses nominal GDP
International comparisons of growth use real GDP growth, because inflation differs country to country
Gap between real and nominal GDP = effect of inflation
Use | Measure
"$4 trillion economy", debt-to-GDP, fiscal deficit % | Nominal GDP
"Fastest-growing major economy", growth rate | Real GDP
Tax buoyancy, revenue targets | Nominal GDP growth
## 2. Deflation case
If prices fall, real growth can exceed nominal growth
⚠ Nominal GDP can rise steadily even when real growth dips (the 2015 PYQ logic)
## In news 2025-26
Q2 FY26 (Jul-Sep 2025): nominal GDP grew only 8.8% vs real 8.2%, a historically small gap; PMF calls the normal gap 3-4 percentage points (Jan 2026 MCA)
Low nominal growth hurts tax buoyancy and fiscal deficit targets

topic: Nominal vs real: current and constant prices, GDP deflator
t: GDP deflator → formula and how it differs from CPI and WPI
text:
## 1. Definition
GDP deflator = (nominal GDP / real GDP) x 100 (also called implicit price deflator)
Shows how much of GDP increase is due to inflation rather than output
Covers all goods and services produced in the economy: the most comprehensive inflation measure
Available only quarterly (with GDP estimates); CPI and WPI are monthly
Feature | WPI | CPI | GDP deflator
Services | No (goods only) | Yes | Yes
Capital goods | Yes | No | Yes
Imported items | Yes | Yes (consumption basket) | No (domestic output only)
Indirect taxes | Excluded | Included | -
Released by | Office of Economic Adviser (MoCI) | NSO (MoSPI) | NSO (MoSPI)
⚠ PMF infographic: WPI "primarily serves as a GDP deflator" in practice; the deflator itself is economy-wide
⚠ Economic Survey pointer: deflator covers domestically produced goods; CPI covers a consumption basket including imports
Likely next: "GDP deflator is released monthly" (false: quarterly)

topic: Nominal vs real: current and constant prices, GDP deflator
t: Deflators in news → PPI, double deflation, sector terms of trade
text:
## 1. Producer Price Index (PPI)
Ramesh Chand panel (NITI Aayog member): roadmap to move from WPI to PPI; WPI base 2011-12 → 2022-23
PPI = producer's price; excludes indirect taxes, transport, trade margins; can cover services
Two types: Output PPI and Input PPI; PPI gives better national income deflators
New WPI: items 697 → 957; weights on Gross Value of Output; WPI and PPI to run together five years, then WPI phased out
## 2. Double deflation
Separately removes price changes from inputs and outputs, giving truer real GVA (replaces single deflation)
## In news 2025-26
Fact (Economic Survey 2025-26) | Value
Manufacturing deflator / agriculture deflator | 1.29 (FY05) → 0.65 (FY25)
Manufacturing share in nominal GVA | ~14%
Manufacturing share in real GVA | stable ~18% (17-18%)
⚠ Manufacturing's falling nominal share is a relative price effect, not a real decline

topic: Measuring GDP: methods, GVA, NSO and base years
t: Three methods of measuring GDP → what each adds up
text:
## 1. PMF's three approaches
Method | Adds | Components
Expenditure | Spending on final goods and services | C + I + G + (X - M)
Income | Incomes earned | Wages, proprietors' income, rent, corporate profits, net interest (+ indirect taxes, depreciation, payments to RoW)
Product / value-added (output) | Market value of final goods, excluding intermediates | Value added of each sector
Product method ensures consistency with the other two
Open economy: Y = C + I + G + (X - M) (asked in UPSC 2000, as per Preview)
⚠ "Diminishing cost method" is not a GDP method (BPSC 2020 distractor)
## 2. Shares on the demand side (2025-26)
PFCE share in GDP 61.5%, highest since FY12; GFCF share 30.0% (Economic Survey 2025-26)
⚠ PMF's 2025 figure for domestic consumption: 60.34% of GDP

topic: Measuring GDP: methods, GVA, NSO and base years
t: GVA vs GDP → supply side vs demand side
text:
## 1. The link
GDP = GVA + product taxes - product subsidies
GVA = GDP + subsidies on products - taxes on products
GVA = value of output (at basic prices) - intermediate consumption (Economic Survey glossary)
Basis | GDP | GVA
Side | Demand (adds expenditures) | Supply (adds value added by sectors)
Taxes/subsidies | Included | Excluded
Best for | Overall size, cross-country growth | Sector-wise health
## 2. Why they diverge
Rising net tax collection (better compliance) makes GDP grow faster than GVA without more output (Q3 FY24: net taxes up 32%)
PMF: GVA "captures the true momentum"; it avoids tax and subsidy distortion
⚠ If real GDP grows slower than real GVA, subsidies grew faster than taxes (Q1 FY27: GDP 7.8% vs GVA 8.2%)

topic: Measuring GDP: methods, GVA, NSO and base years

text:
## 1. Changes made in 2015 (CSO)
Change | From → To
Base year | 2004-05 → 2011-12
Headline growth measure | GDP at factor cost → GDP at market prices (constant)
Sector value added | Factor cost → GVA at basic prices
Corporate data | Sample surveys → MCA21 database
Coverage | Added financial sector data (SEBI, PFRDA, IRDA), local bodies
## 2. Basic prices
Basic price = factor cost + production taxes - production subsidies
Market price = basic price + product taxes - product subsidies
## 3. Back series debate
New series raised manufacturing's 2004-05 share 11.8% → 15.8%
Arvind Subramanian (former CEA) argued 2011-17 growth was ~4.5%, not ~7%
⚠ Trap: since 2015 the headline is GDP at market prices, not factor cost

topic: Measuring GDP: methods, GVA, NSO and base years
t: Who measures national income → NSO and its history
text:
## 1. Institutions
National income in India is computed by the National Statistical Office (NSO), MoSPI
MoSPI (est. 1999) releases advance, provisional and revised estimates
Advance estimates use the benchmark-indicator method (IIP, listed company results, production data)
Estimate | Meaning
First / Second Advance Estimate (AE) | Before year-end (Jan, Feb)
Provisional Estimate (PE) | End of May, after year-end
First / Second Revised Estimate (RE) | Later years
Final Estimate (FE) | Last revision
## Beyond your notes
First estimate of India's national income: Dadabhai Naoroji (1867-68), in Poverty and Un-British Rule in India
First scientific estimate: V.K.R.V. Rao (1931-32)
National Income Committee (1949): chaired by P.C. Mahalanobis
NSO formed in 2019 by merging CSO and NSSO
⚠ Not RBI, not NITI Aayog, not Finance Ministry: NSO (MoSPI) computes GDP

text:
## 1. NCERT Box 2.4
Usual pattern: agriculture → industry dominant → services dominant at high income
India: agriculture share was over 50% at independence; by 1990 services 40.59%, larger than agriculture or industry
Services share accelerated after 1991
Period | Agriculture | Industry | Services | GDP growth
1980-91 | 3.6 | 7.1 | 6.7 | 5.6

Statement | Verdict | Why
Real GDP growth rate steadily increased in the last decade | Wrong | Fell in 2008-09 (global financial crisis), then later years
GDP at market prices (rupees) steadily increased | Right | Nominal level rises with output + inflation
GDP growth rate steadily increased in last 5 years (2011) | Wrong | Dip in 2008-09

topic: Beyond GDP: limits and alternative measures
t: Limitations of GDP → what it misses
text:
## 1. PMF list
Limitation | Example
Non-market transactions | Unpaid household work, informal work
Standard of living | Per capita income is a better measure
Externalities | Pollution, environmental damage ignored
Income distribution | Inequality hidden by averages
## 2. NCERT Class 10 point
Punjab has higher per capita income than Kerala, yet Kerala has far lower infant mortality
Money cannot buy pollution-free environment or unadulterated medicines: public facilities matter
⚠ Higher per capita real GNP does not mean higher development if poverty and unemployment rise (ROCKET Sheets)

topic: Beyond GDP: limits and alternative measures
t: GNDI and NNDI → income available to the nation
text:
## 1. PMF infographic (June 2026)
GNDI = GNP + net current transfers from abroad (remittances, grants, aid)
NNDI = GNDI - depreciation
Step | Example (₹ lakh crore)
GNP | 300
+ Net current transfers | + 20
= GNDI | 320
- Depreciation | - 40
= NNDI | 280
NNDI = what the nation can actually use for consumption and saving after replacing worn-out capital
⚠ NFIA (factor income) goes into GNP; current transfers (remittances, aid) go into GNDI, not GNP

topic: Beyond GDP: limits and alternative measures
t: GDKP and new indicators → measuring the knowledge economy
text:
## 1. Gross Domestic Knowledge Product (GDKP)
Idea from NITI Aayog (2021); MoSPI reviving it (2025) via a Technical Committee
Measures contribution of knowledge, R&D, innovation, intellectual assets
Now Intellectual Property Products (IPP) are recorded under GFCF
Likely route: a satellite account (like tourism, culture, ocean economy)
## 2. Other new statistics (2025-26)
Indicator | Fact
Index of Service Production (ISP) | Monthly; base 2024-25; uses GSTN data; omits health and education
National Household Income Survey | First pan-India; launch Feb 2026 (MoSPI)
ASUSE 2025 | Calendar year from this round; 7.92 crore establishments; GVA up 10.87%
PMI | S&P Global; >50 = expansion; five sub-indices
Technical recession | Two consecutive quarters of negative real GDP growth
⚠ IMF grade C (Dec 2025) cited outdated base year, no PPI, weak state-level data

topic: Beyond GDP: limits and alternative measures
t: Per capita income → measurement and caveats
text:
## 1. Measurement
Per capita income = national income / population (Preview: NNP / population)
Can be at current or constant prices; constant-price growth is lower in inflation (PYQ 2000)
Year | Real per capita income (₹, NCERT Table 5.1)
1951 | 3,687
1981 | 5,353
1991 | 7,321
2001 | 10,306
## 2. Caveats
An average: hides inequality; ignores regional cost-of-living differences
PCI growth rate fell to 0.8% in 2008-09 (2011-12 prices): not steady (PYQ 2011)
## In news 2025-26
New series: per capita income ₹2,43,180 a year, about ₹20,265 a month (LENS Mar 2026)
PCI growth (2022-23 prices): 6.6% FY24, 6.5% FY25, 6.6% FY26 (2nd AE)
⚠ Per capita income growth = GDP growth minus roughly population growth, so it is lower than GDP growth

topic: Growth vs development and measures of growth
t: Growth vs development → what each means
text:
## 1. The two concepts
Point | Economic growth | Economic development
Nature | Quantitative, narrow | Qualitative + quantitative, broad
Means | Rise in real output (real GDP/GNP, per capita real income) | Growth plus better standard of living, less poverty, jobs, health, education
Measured by | GDP growth rate, per capita real income | HDI, poverty rate, literacy, IMR, MPI
Can occur alone? | Yes, growth without development | No, development needs some growth
Concept type | Positive ("conservative") | Normative
Development = growth with safe drinking water, sanitation, medical care, primary education, less poverty and unemployment (Preview)
⚠ Growth is necessary but not sufficient for development; development is impossible with zero growth over the long run
PYQ 2018: rising real GNP and per capita GNP is not development if poverty and unemployment increase; trap options: industry lagging agriculture, agriculture lagging industry, imports growing faster than exports

topic: Growth vs development and measures of growth
t: Growth without development → the conditions UPSC uses
text:
## 1. When rising GNP is not development
Condition | Why it fails the development test
Poverty rises | Gains go to few; the bottom does not gain
Unemployment rises (jobless growth) | Output grows faster than jobs
Inequality widens | GDP ignores distribution
Environment degraded | GDP ignores externalities
Gains confined to some regions | National average hides disparity
Jobless growth: output expands faster than employment; youth unemployment ~10%, about 3 times the overall rate (PMF, LENS June 2026)
PMF: GDP is "not a measure of quality of life"; ~50% rural and 20% urban people cannot afford two thali meals a day (HCES 2023-24)
⚠ Sectoral imbalance (industry vs agriculture) or a trade deficit is not the textbook reason; the answer is always poverty/unemployment
PYQ 2018: Statement-type trap: "industrial output fails to keep pace with agricultural output" sounds structural but is wrong

topic: Growth vs development and measures of growth
t: Best measure of growth → per capita real income
text:
## 1. Why per capita real income
Measure | Problem as a growth measure
GDP | Ignores population growth; includes depreciation
NDP | Ignores population growth
NNP | Ignores population growth
National income at current prices | Inflated by price rise
Per capita real income | Adjusts for both population and inflation: best
Per capita income = national income ÷ population (NCERT: "average income")
Preview: best measure of growth = "sustained increase in real per capita income" (also called per capita real NNP)
⚠ Growth of per capita income at current prices > at constant prices because constant prices remove the rise in price level (UPSC 2000)
⚠ Total GDP rising with faster population growth can mean falling per capita income
PYQ 2001: options GDP, NDP, NNP, per capita real income; answer per capita real income

topic: Growth vs development and measures of growth
t: Real vs nominal, GDP vs GNP → the definitions behind growth figures
text:
## 1. Key pairs
Pair | Difference
Nominal vs real GDP | Nominal at current prices; real at constant (base-year) prices, inflation removed
GDP deflator | Nominal GDP ÷ real GDP × 100; quarterly only (CPI, WPI are monthly)
GDP vs GNP | GNP = GDP + net factor income from abroad
Gross vs net | Net = gross − depreciation (consumption of fixed capital)
Market price vs factor cost | Market price includes taxes, excludes subsidies; factor cost the reverse
GNDI | GNP + net current transfers from abroad (remittances, aid); NNDI = GNDI − depreciation
In an expanding economy nominal GDP is usually higher than real GDP (PMF)
⚠ GNI and GNP are used interchangeably; HDI uses GNI per capita (PPP), not GDP
## In news 2025-26
National Accounts and IIP rebased to 2022-23 (release Feb 2026, Economic Survey 2025-26)
MoSPI reviving GDKP (Gross Domestic Knowledge Product, proposed by NITI Aayog in 2021) to capture knowledge, R&D and intellectual assets; IPP is now recorded inside GFCF

topic: Growth vs development and measures of growth
t: Income as a development yardstick → strengths and limits
text:
## 1. World Bank vs UNDP criterion
Body | Criterion | Report
World Bank | Per capita income (GNI) only | World Development Report
UNDP | Health + education + income (HDI) | Human Development Report
NCERT: Kerala (lower per capita income) beat Punjab on IMR (11 vs 49), literacy (91 vs 70) and attendance; money cannot buy pollution-free air, unadulterated medicines, good public facilities
Limits of GDP (PMF): misses non-market/unpaid work, externalities, distribution, living standards
⚠ Averages hide inequality; "per capita income is not useful at all" is wrong: it is useful but inadequate
## In news 2025-26
India 6th largest economy by nominal GDP (IMF WEO, ~$4.15 trillion); per capita $2,813, rank 149; by PPP $12,964, rank 119 (PMF 2026)
India is lower-middle income: World Bank band $1,146-$4,515 GNI per capita
FY26 real GDP growth 7.4% (First Advance Estimates, Economic Survey 2025-26)
Likely next: "India ranks 130 in HDI despite being a top-6 GDP economy" (PMF) as a Statement-I/II pair

topic: Measuring development: HDI and other indices
t: HDI → dimensions, indicators, publisher
text:
## 1. Structure
Dimension | Indicator
Long and healthy life | Life expectancy at birth
Knowledge | Mean years of schooling (adults 25+) and Expected years of schooling (children entering school)
Decent standard of living | GNI per capita (PPP $)
3 dimensions, 4 indicators; value 0 to 1; geometric mean of the three dimension indices
Published by UNDP in the Human Development Report; first HDR 1990
Developed by Mahbub-ul-Haq (Pakistan), based on Amartya Sen's capability approach
Four tiers: very high, high, medium (India), low
⚠ HDI uses GNI, not GDP; uses life expectancy, not IMR; uses mean + expected years of schooling, not literacy (literacy and GER were dropped in 2010)
⚠ Not published by World Bank, IMF, UNESCO or UNICEF
Likely next: "how many of the following are HDI indicators" with literacy rate / IMR as distractors

topic: Measuring development: HDI and other indices
t: Other UNDP indices → what each adjusts for
text:
## 1. HDR Office family of indices
Index | What it captures
IHDI (Inequality-adjusted HDI) | HDI discounted for inequality within each dimension
GDI (Gender Development Index) | Ratio of female HDI to male HDI
GII (Gender Inequality Index) | Reproductive health, empowerment, labour market
MPI (Global Multidimensional Poverty Index) | 3 dimensions, 10 indicators; with OPHI since 2010
PHDI (Planetary pressures-adjusted HDI) | HDI adjusted for CO2 emissions and material footprint per capita
India's National MPI is by NITI Aayog: 12 indicators, poor if deprived in at least one-third (weighted)
India GII rank 108 of 166 (HDR 2023-24, PMF)
⚠ GDI is a ratio of HDIs; GII is a loss measure (higher = worse)
## Beyond your notes
IHDI, GII and MPI were introduced in HDR 2010; PHDI in HDR 2020
GII indicators: maternal mortality, adolescent birth rate, parliament seats, secondary education, labour force participation

topic: Measuring development: HDI and other indices
t: Older measures → who devised them and in what order
text:
## 1. Timeline
Measure | By | Year | Components
Per capita income | Simon Kuznets team (US) | 1934 | Income per person
PQLI | Morris D. Morris, for Overseas Development Council | mid-1970s | Basic literacy, IMR, life expectancy at age one (equal weights, 0-100)
HDI | Mahbub-ul-Haq, UNDP | 1990 | Health, education, income
Correct order: per capita income → PQLI → HDI
Best pair for physical quality of life: IMR + literacy
India's first state HDR: Madhya Pradesh, 1995
⚠ PQLI has no income component; HDI has income
⚠ PQLI life expectancy is at age one, HDI at birth

topic: Measuring development: HDI and other indices
t: Growth-development curves → Preston and Kuznets
text:
## 1. Curves to know
Curve | Relates | Shape/claim
Preston curve (Samuel Preston, 1975) | Life expectancy vs per capita income | Rises steeply, then flattens
Kuznets curve (Simon Kuznets) | Inequality vs per capita income/growth | Inverted U: inequality rises, then falls
Environmental Kuznets curve | Environmental degradation vs per capita GDP | Inverted U
Lorenz curve | Cumulative income share vs population | Bows away from 45° line as inequality rises
India: per capita income ~₹9,000 (1947) to ~₹55,000 (2011); life expectancy 32 → 66+ (PMF)
⚠ Laffer curve (tax rate vs revenue) is also inverted U but is not a development curve
Likely next: match curve to the two variables it relates

t: Capital formation → meaning and process
text:
## 1. The chain
Saving → mobilisation (banks, markets) → investment → addition to capital stock
Capital formation = a country does not consume all current income, saves part and invests it to raise future production (Planning Commission: "the real key ... is the growing rate of capital formation")
Term | Meaning
Gross capital formation (GCF) | GFCF + change in stocks + valuables
GFCF | New investment in fixed assets: buildings, machinery, equipment, IPP
Net capital formation | GCF − depreciation
Physical capital | Tangible: factories, machines, infrastructure
Human capital | Intangible: skills, knowledge, health
⚠ "Individuals accumulating more capital" and "tangible wealth" are physical/gross capital formation, not human capital formation (UPSC 2018)
## In news 2025-26
GFCF ~30% of GDP in FY26; GFCF grew 7.6% in H1 FY26, above pre-pandemic average 7.1%, driven by public capex and revival of private investment (Economic Survey 2025-26)
PFCE share 61.5% of GDP, highest since FY12

t: Capital formation → the factor that makes growth happen
text:
## 1. Must-occur vs may-occur
Factor | Does growth in X necessarily follow?
Capital formation in X | Yes: raises productive capacity directly
Technical progress in the world economy | No: X may not adopt it
Population growth in X | No: may lower per capita income
Growth of world trade volume | No: X may not share in it
Main causes of slow per capita income growth in India (UPSC 1993): high capital-output ratio + high population growth (not high capital formation, not fiscal deficit)
⚠ "High rate of capital formation" is a cure, never a cause of slow growth
PYQ 2013: answer capital formation in X; trap: external factors (world technology, world trade) and population growth

t: Capital-output ratio → why high saving may not raise output
text:
## 1. Definition
COR = capital needed to produce one unit of output; ICOR = ΔK / ΔY (extra investment per extra unit of GDP)
Example: invest ₹100, GDP rises ₹10 → ICOR 10
Situation | Effect
High COR | More capital per unit output; low productivity of capital
High COR + high saving | Output may still grow slowly
Low COR | More output from given capital: efficient
Causes of high COR: outdated technology, poor management, inefficiency, underutilised capacity, execution delays
Lower ICOR = more efficient investment
⚠ Weak administration, illiteracy and high population density hurt growth but are not the direct reason why capital formation fails to lift output
PYQ 2018: high-saving economy, capital formation, little output gain → high capital-output ratio

t: Harrod-Domar and Solow → growth models behind the PYQs
text:
## 1. The two models
Model | Key idea
Harrod-Domar (Roy Harrod, Evsey Domar, 1930s-40s) | Growth depends on saving rate (s) and capital-output ratio (k); more investment → more output and jobs
Solow-Swan (Robert Solow, Trevor Swan) | Diminishing returns to capital; technology (exogenous) drives long-run growth; steady state; poorer countries converge
Harrod-Domar assumes a constant capital-output ratio; criticised as too simple
## Beyond your notes
First Five-Year Plan (1951-56) was based on the Harrod-Domar model; the Second Plan on the Mahalanobis model
Harrod-Domar growth rate g = s / k: s = 30%, k = 4 → g = 7.5%; same saving with k = 6 → only 5%
⚠ Testbook writes a "multiplier" form 1/[1−(s/k)]; the standard Prelims form is g = s/k
Likely next: "with a given saving rate, growth falls as ICOR rises" (true)

t: MPI → method and what it measures
text:
## 1. Alkire-Foster method
Both the global MPI and NITI Aayog's national MPI use the Alkire-Foster method
Dual cut-off counting: first a cut-off for each indicator, then a poverty cut-off across indicators
A person is multidimensionally poor if the weighted deprivation score is one-third (33.3%) or more
MPI ranges 0 to 1; higher = more poverty
## 2. What MPI covers and what it does not
Covered (household level) | Not covered
Deprivations in health, education, standard of living (assets, services) | PPP income at national level
Overlapping deprivations of the same person | Budget deficit, GDP growth
 | Income-based "$ a day" extreme poverty
PYQ 2012: only "household deprivation in education, health, assets and services" was correct; trap: PPP and deficit sound like poverty data
## Beyond your notes
Method by Sabina Alkire and James Foster (OPHI); MPI = H (headcount) x A (intensity)

text:

Price levels vary | Correct

PDS quality varies | Wrong
Urban lines are higher than rural because essential goods cost more in cities (NCERT)

t: Total Fertility Rate → what it means, and the distractors
text:
## 1. Definition
TFR = average number of live births a woman would have by the end of her childbearing (reproductive) years, if she followed current age-specific fertility rates
Expressed as births per woman; reproductive age 15-49
Calculated as the sum of age-specific fertility rates (or 5 x the sum for five-year age groups)
Age-specific fertility rate = annual births to women of an age group / women of that age group
## 2. The options UPSC put against it (2024)
Option | What it really is
Children born per 1000 people in a year | Crude Birth Rate
Children born to a couple in their lifetime | Not a standard measure (TFR is per woman)
Birth rate minus death rate | Rate of natural increase (growth rate)
Average live births a woman would have by end of childbearing age | TFR (correct)
⚠ TFR is a per-woman lifetime measure; CBR is per 1,000 population per year
PYQ 2024: TFR "in an economy" defined; trap: CBR and "birth rate minus death rate"

t: Replacement-level fertility → 2.1 and what above or below means
text:
## 1. Meaning
TFR at which a population exactly replaces itself from one generation to the next, without migration
TFR 2.1 = replacement level ("universally set at 2.1"; may vary slightly with mortality)
TFR | Implication
Above 2.1 | Population growth
= 2.1 | Stable over generations (zero population growth)
Below 2.1 | Long-run shrinking and ageing
## 2. Population momentum
Population keeps growing after TFR falls below 2.1 because of a young age structure
UN WPP: India keeps growing till the mid-2060s despite sub-replacement TFR; world peaks mid-2080s
⚠ PMF Mains Magnum once writes "TFR of 2.0 is the replacement rate"; every other PMF page says 2.1
Likely next: zero population growth level per couple = 2.1 (UPPCS 2001, 2020)
## Beyond your notes
The extra 0.1 over 2.0 covers deaths before reproductive age and the excess of boys at birth

topic: Other vital rates and demographic transition
t: Demographic transition → stage and pattern
text:
## 1. Three stages (PMF)
Stage | Birth rate | Death rate | Growth
1 | High | High | Slow
2 | High | Falling/low | Fast (population explosion)
3 | Low | Low | Stable or slow
Order: high-high → high-low → low-low (UPSC 2012)
## 2. India's four phases of growth
Period | Phase
1901-1921 | Stagnant (negative 1911-21)
1921-1951 | Steady growth
1951-1981 | Population explosion (~2.2% a year)
After 1981 | High growth, definite slowdown
India is now in the late stage, with an epidemiological transition: infectious to non-communicable causes of death (Economic Survey glossary)
## Beyond your notes
1921 is called the year of the great divide because growth turned permanently positive after it

topic: Demographic dividend: meaning, window and reaping it
t: Demographic dividend → meaning and age group
text:
## 1. Definition (UNFPA)
Economic growth potential from a shift in age structure, when the working-age share (15-64) is larger than the non-working-age share (0-14 and 65+)
Arises from falling fertility after mortality has fallen: fewer children, bulge of adults
Age group | Role
0-14 | Young dependants
15-64 (UN) / 15-59 (India: SRS, Census) | Working age
65+ (UN) / 60+ (India) | Old dependants
⚠ Dividend comes from a high share aged 15-64, not from a large total population or many children under 15
⚠ Working age is 15-64 in UNFPA and UPSC's answer, 15-59 in SRS, Census and Economic Survey
PYQ 2011: dividend due to high population aged 15-64; distractors below 15, above 65, high total population

topic: Demographic dividend: meaning, window and reaping it

Year / source | 0-14 | Working age | Elderly
1971 (SRS) | 41.2% | 53.4% (15-59) | 6% (60+)

UNFPA SOWP 2025 | - | 68% (15-64) | 7% (65+)
## 2. Dependency ratio
= dependants (children + elderly) per 100 working-age persons; a lower ratio signals a dividend
Testbook: expected to fall from 65% to 54% over the next decade
Old-age dependency ratio = elderly per 100 working-age; Kerala 19.6% (2011) → 26.1% (2021) → 34.3% (2031)

Share 65+ | Label

text:
## 1. Timeline
Marker | Year
Window opens | 2005-06
UN projection: dividend peak, ~65% aged 15-59 | ~2030 (Economic Survey 2025-26)
Working-age share 65% | ~2036 (Social Justice book)
Working-age peak | 2041: 59% aged 20-59 (ES 2018-19); 1,009 million, 65.5% (PMF LENS 2026)

topic: Demographic dividend: meaning, window and reaping it
t: How a young age structure pays → the four channels
text:
## 1. Channels (Testbook)
Channel | How
Labour supply | More workers; ~8 million enter each year
Savings | Earners save; more investment
Human capital | Fewer dependants; healthier, educated women join work
Demand | Rising consumption as incomes grow
## 2. Conditions
Only a potential: needs jobs, skills, health, education; otherwise a liability
Gender dividend: lower TFR frees women for paid work if creches, safe transport exist (Sweden)
India youngest major population: median age 28-29 vs 37 China, US; 45 Japan

Health and education spending

t: Disguised unemployment → what it means
text:
## 1. Meaning
More people are engaged in a task than needed; remove some and total output does not fall
So the marginal productivity of labour (MPL) is zero (the UPSC answer, 2013)
Workers look employed: it is hidden unemployment, not open unemployment
## 2. NCERT example
Farmer with 4 acres needs 2 workers + himself, but employs 5 workers + family: the extra hands are disguisedly unemployed
A late-1950s study found about one-third of agricultural workers in India disguisedly unemployed
NCERT: disguised unemployment is a common form in rural India; most common in agriculture and the informal sector
Option in the 2013 PYQ | Right?
Large number of people remain unemployed | No: that is open unemployment
Alternative employment is not available | No
Marginal productivity of labour is zero | Yes
Productivity of workers is low | No: low is not zero (trap)
⚠ "Low productivity" is the trap; disguised unemployment means the marginal worker adds nothing (MPL = 0), while average productivity can still be positive
⚠ Testbook loosely describes it as "working but not earning enough"; that is underemployment, not the textbook definition UPSC used
PYQ 2013: asked the meaning of disguised unemployment; answer "marginal productivity of labour is zero"

t: Types of unemployment → cause and example
text:
Type | Cause | Example / where
Frictional | Time lost while changing or searching for jobs | Person who quits to find a better job; normal even at full employment
Structural | Mismatch between workers' skills and available jobs (technology, globalisation) | Typist after computers; long-term
Cyclical | Fall in aggregate demand in a recession | Lay-offs in a downturn
Seasonal | Work only in some months | Farm workers in the off-season; migrate to towns, return at monsoon
Disguised | Surplus workers with MPL = 0 | Family farms
Technological | Automation replaces labour | AI, robotics
Educated | Educated people cannot find jobs matching qualifications | Graduates
Open | Willing and able, but no work at all | Registered at employment exchanges
Long-term unemployment: jobless for more than 12 months (Testbook)
India's unemployment is mostly seasonal, disguised and structural; Economic Survey 2022-23: it is turning more structural (skill mismatch)
⚠ Seasonal and disguised are the two NCERT names for rural India; frictional is the only type that exists even at "full employment"

t: Unemployment → related concepts
text:
## 1. Definitions
Unemployment: willing and able to work at the prevailing wage, actively seeking, but no job
NCERT: an unemployed person is one who cannot get work for even one hour in half a day
Full employment does not mean zero unemployment: frictional unemployment remains
Voluntary unemployment: capable person chooses not to seek work
Underemployment: working fewer hours or below skill (Victor who gets 2 hours of work a day, NCERT)
## 2. Phillips curve
Item | Fact
Named after | A.W. Phillips (1958)
Shows | Short-run trade-off between inflation and unemployment
Low unemployment | Higher inflation (firms bid up wages)
High unemployment | Lower inflation
⚠ NCERT: people in India cannot stay fully unemployed for long; poverty forces them into any work, so open unemployment is low but underemployment high
## Beyond your notes
NAIRU: unemployment rate at which inflation does not accelerate; the long-run Phillips curve is vertical at the natural rate

t: Labour Bureau → what it compiles
text:
## 1. About
Set up in 1920; attached office of the Ministry of Labour and Employment (MoLE); offices at Shimla and Chandigarh
Collects, compiles and publishes labour, employment, wage and price statistics
## 2. What it compiles
Data | Notes

CPI-IW (Industrial Workers) | Base 2016 (from Sept 2020; earlier 2001); used for DA of Central Govt employees
CPI-AL (Agricultural Labourers) | MGNREGA / VB-G RAM G wages indexed to it
CPI-RL (Rural Labourers) | Used for the PM-POSHAN cost basket (600 villages, 20 states)
Wage rate indices, earnings, absenteeism, labour turnover | Administrative statistics under labour Acts
Proposed nodal agency for statistical returns under all four Labour Codes
Index | Compiled by
CPI-IW, CPI-AL, CPI-RL | Labour Bureau (MoLE)
CPI-Rural, CPI-Urban, CPI-Combined | NSO (MoSPI)
WPI | Office of Economic Adviser, DPIIT

t: PLFS → activity-status approaches
text:
Approach | Reference period | Counted employed if
Usual Principal Status (UPS) | 365 days | Activity taking the major part of the year
Usual Principal + Subsidiary Status (UPSS) | 365 days | Worked at least 30 days in the year
Current Weekly Status (CWS) | Last 7 days | Worked at least 1 hour on any 1 day of the week
Current Daily Status (CDS) | Each day of the 7 days | 4+ hours a day = employed for the full day; most comprehensive
Usual status = chronic / long-term; CWS = short-term or seasonal
## Key ratios
Ratio | Formula
LFPR | (Employed + seeking/available) / population
WPR | Employed / population
Unemployment rate (UR) | Unemployed / labour force (not population)
⚠ UR is a share of the labour force, LFPR and WPR are shares of the population
⚠ Monthly PLFS estimates use CWS, not usual status
Likely next: "CWS counts a person employed if they worked one hour on any day of the week" (true)

t: Workforce structure → formal vs informal, status of workers
text:
## 1. Formal vs informal (NCERT)
Formal (organised): all public sector establishments + private establishments with 10 or more hired workers
Informal: farmers, agricultural labourers, small enterprises, self-employed without hired workers
Formal workers get PF, gratuity, paid leave, pension; public sector is the biggest formal employer
## 2. Status of employment
Status | Who | Note
Self-employed | Own and run an enterprise (shop owner, farmer) | Largest category, over half
Casual wage labourers | Paid daily for work done | Most vulnerable (NCERT)
Regular salaried | Paid regularly by an employer | Higher in urban areas, more men
About 90% of employment is informal (India Employment Report 2024); agriculture still employs about 46.6%
NEET (youth not in employment, education or training) about 28%; females about five times males
⚠ Casual labour is the second biggest source of work, larger for women than men (NCERT)

topic: Labour laws and the four Labour Codes
t: Casual workers → what the law gives them
text:
2021 statement | Verdict (UPSC key) | Why
All casual workers are entitled to EPF coverage | Wrong | EPF depends on the establishment (size, coverage); not automatic for every casual worker
All casual workers are entitled to regular working hours and overtime | Correct | Minimum Wages Rules 1950; Code on Wages: overtime at least twice the normal rate
Govt can by notification make an establishment pay wages only through bank account | Correct | Payment of Wages (Amendment) Act, 2017: by cheque or bank credit
UPSC answer (b) 2 and 3 only
SC, Pawan Hans v. Aviation Karmachari Sanghatana (Jan 2020): casual workers drawing wages from a company are entitled to PF under the EPF Act
⚠ Preview marks all three correct citing Pawan Hans; follow the UPSC key (b): the word "All" makes statement 1 wrong
⚠ Casual worker = temporary contract, limited benefits, little job security (NCERT: Kamal, the daily-wage shop worker)
PYQ 2021: three statements on casual workers; trap: the absolute "all" in the EPF statement

topic: Labour laws and the four Labour Codes
t: Four Labour Codes → which laws they merged
text:
29 Central labour laws consolidated into 4 Codes; in force from 21 November 2025
Labour is in the Concurrent List (Entries 22-24, 35 of List III): Centre and States both legislate
Code | Year | Laws merged
Code on Wages | 2019 | 4: Payment of Wages 1936, Minimum Wages 1948, Payment of Bonus 1965, Equal Remuneration 1976
Industrial Relations Code | 2020 | 3: Trade Unions Act, Industrial Disputes Act, Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act
Code on Social Security | 2020 | 9: EPF, ESI, gratuity, maternity benefit, unorganised workers' SS Act 2008 and others
OSH and Working Conditions Code | 2020 | 13: factories, mines, contract labour, building and construction, etc.
4 + 3 + 9 + 13 = 29
⚠ Contract Labour (R&A) Act 1970 went into the OSH Code, not the Code on Wages (UPPCS 2021 trap)
⚠ Code on Wages was passed in 2019; the other three in 2020
## In news 2025-26
21 Nov 2025: Centre began implementing all four Codes; Economic Survey 2025-26 lists them among 2025 structural reforms
2026: MoLE notified final Central Rules to operationalise the Codes (below)

topic: Labour laws and the four Labour Codes
t: Code on Wages → key provisions
text:
Provision | Rule
Coverage | All employees, any sector, wage level, industry or gender (earlier only scheduled employments)
National Floor Wage | Set by Centre; State minimum wages cannot be below it
Wage definition | Basic + DA + retaining allowance must be at least 50% of total pay
Working hours | 8-12 hours/day, max 48 hours/week
Overtime | At least 2 times normal wage
Deductions | Cannot exceed 50% of pay
Wage slips | Mandatory for all
Payment deadlines | Daily: end of shift; weekly: before weekly holiday; monthly: within 7 days of next month; on exit: 2 days
## In news 2025-26: Central Rules (2026)
12-hour days allowed within 48 hours/week, enabling a 4-day week
Fixed formula for minimum wages removed
Women may work 7 PM to 6 AM with consent
Establishments with 20+ workers must set up a Grievance Redressal Committee
⚠ Minimum wages are now enforceable under the Code on Wages, 2019 (not the 1948 Act)
## Beyond your notes
The 48-hour week matches the ILO Hours of Work (Industry) Convention 1919

topic: Labour laws and the four Labour Codes
t: Industrial Relations and OSH Codes → thresholds
text:
Item | Earlier | Now
Govt permission for lay-off, retrenchment, closure | 100+ workers | 300+ workers
Factory licence (with power) | 10 workers | 20
Factory licence (without power) | 20 workers | 40
Contract labour provisions apply | contractor with 20 | 50+
Strike notice | Public utilities only | All establishments: notice within 60 days before; no strike within 14 days of notice
Mass casual leave | Not a strike | 50%+ workers on one day = deemed strike
Fixed-term employment formalised: pro-rata benefits equal to permanent workers
Sole negotiating union: one union with 51% membership; else a council of unions with 20%+ each
"Worker" includes supervisory staff earning under ₹18,000/month; excludes apprentices
Safety committees: 500+ factory, 250+ construction, 100+ mine workers
Mandatory appointment letters and annual free health check-ups
⚠ The retrenchment threshold rose to 300, not 200 or 500
⚠ Women may work night shifts only with consent and safety measures

topic: Skill development: PMKVY, RPL and NSQF
t: PMKVY → ministry, agency, components
text:
## 1. Basics
Flagship scheme of MSDE (Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship), not MoLE
Implemented by NSDC; launched July 2015; Central Sector Scheme
Short-term training for school/college dropouts and unemployed; free, with reward on certification
Training is NSQF-aligned and includes soft skills, entrepreneurship, financial and digital literacy
## 2. Components
Component | What
Short-Term Training (STT) | NSQF-aligned classroom + on-the-job training
Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL) | Assess and certify existing informal skills
Special Projects | Marginalised groups, aspirational districts, new job roles
Central and State components: 75% of targets/funds to NSDC, 25% to State Skill Development Missions
2018 statement | Verdict
Flagship scheme of Ministry of Labour | Wrong (MSDE)
Trains soft skills, entrepreneurship, financial and digital literacy | Correct
Aligns competencies of unregulated workforce to NSQF | Correct
⚠ The ministry swap (MSDE vs MoLE) is the trap; NCS and e-Shram are MoLE, PMKVY is MSDE

topic: Skill development: PMKVY, RPL and NSQF
t: Recognition of Prior Learning → what it certifies
text:
RPL = assessing and certifying skills a person already has, acquired through formal, non-formal or informal learning, without a certificate
Introduced in India as a PMKVY component in 2015
Classic case: construction workers who learnt on site through traditional channels
## Objectives of RPL
Align the competencies of the country's unregulated workforce to the NSQF
Raise employability and give alternative routes to higher education
Reduce inequality from privileging some forms of knowledge over others
2017 option | Right?
Certifying skills acquired by construction workers through traditional channels | Yes
Enrolling persons in universities for distance learning | No
Reserving skilled jobs for the poor in PSUs | No
Certifying skills of trainees under the National Skill Development Programme | No: that is fresh training, not prior learning
⚠ RPL recognises skills already acquired; certifying new trainees is STT, not RPL
⚠ PMF: RPL-certified workers earn only 5-10% more, as employer trust is weak
PYQ 2017: answer (a)

topic: Skill development: PMKVY, RPL and NSQF
t: NSQF → levels and expected outcomes
text:
## 1. Basics
National Skills Qualifications Framework, notified December 2013
Competency-based framework: qualifications in 10 levels (1-10) by learning outcomes
Outcomes count whether acquired through formal, non-formal or informal learning
## 2. Expected outcomes
Outcome | 
Mobility between vocational and general education (degrees aligned to NSQF) | the 2017 answer
RPL: move from non-formal to organised job market | 
National quality assurance; standard outcomes across India | 
Global mobility of Indian workers via international equivalence | 
Progressive pathways within and across sectors | 
Approval of NOS/QPs (National Occupational Standards / Qualification Packs) as national standards | 
2017 statement | Verdict
Certification only through formal learning | Wrong
Mobility between vocational and general education | Correct
⚠ "Only formal" is the trap: NSQF covers formal, non-formal and informal learning
PYQ 2017: answer (b) 2 only
## Beyond your notes
NSQF is anchored by NCVET (set up 2018, merged NCVT and NSDA); NSQF revised in 2023 aligned to the National Credit Framework (NCrF) (verify)

t: Public health system → curative bias and who organises services
text:
## 1. Statement-I: curative focus
India's public sector health care largely focuses on curative care, with limited preventive, promotive and rehabilitative care
Cause: historical policy priorities, funding patterns and infrastructure built around hospitals, not the Centre-State division
Correction attempted: Ayushman Bharat HWCs (now Ayushman Arogya Mandirs) move from selective care to comprehensive care: preventive, promotive, curative, rehabilitative, palliative
## 2. Statement-II: decentralised delivery
Under India's decentralised approach, States are primarily responsible for organising health services
Reason: public health and sanitation, hospitals and dispensaries sit in the State List (7th Schedule)
Statement | True? | Why
I: curative bias | Yes | policy, money and infrastructure went to hospitals
II: States organise services | Yes | health is a State subject
II explains I? | No | federal division does not cause the curative tilt
⚠ Both are correct but II is not the explanation of I (answer b). Do not link "State subject" to "curative bias"
PYQ 2023 (Statement-I/II): both true, no causal link; trap: the explanation option (a)

t: Health in the Constitution → which list, which Article
text:
## 1. Seventh Schedule
Subject | List
Public health and sanitation; hospitals and dispensaries | State (Entry 6)
Population control and family planning | Concurrent (Entry 20A, added by 42nd Amendment, 1976)
Economic and social planning, social security, labour welfare | Concurrent
Drugs | Concurrent
## 2. Directive Principles on health
Article | Says
39(e) | protect health and strength of workers, children not abused
42 | just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief
47 | raise level of nutrition and standard of living and improve public health; prohibit intoxicating drinks/drugs
Right to health is read into Art 21 (right to life with dignity) by the Supreme Court
73rd/74th Amendments: panchayats and municipalities empowered for public health (decentralised system)
⚠ Family planning is Concurrent, public health is State: UPSC 1993 asked exactly this pair
## Beyond your notes
Art 47 is the DPSP that names nutrition directly; NFSA is often linked to Art 47 and Art 21

t: Public health infrastructure → tiers and population norms
text:
## 1. The tiers (rural)
Sub-Centre (SC) → Primary Health Centre (PHC) → Community Health Centre (CHC) → Sub-district/District Hospital → medical colleges (tertiary)
SCs and PHCs are being converted into Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (formerly HWCs)
## Beyond your notes
Facility | Plain areas | Hilly/tribal | Staff/role
Sub-Centre | 5,000 people | 3,000 | ANM + male health worker; first contact
PHC | 30,000 | 20,000 | medical officer; refers to CHC; ~6 SCs
CHC | 1,20,000 | 80,000 | 4 specialists (surgeon, physician, gynaecologist, paediatrician); 30 beds; FRU
Norms are the Indian Public Health Standards (IPHS)
⚠ Bed ratio: India about 1.3 beds per 1,000 vs WHO benchmark 3.5 (LENS Sep 2026); rural CHCs face about 80% specialist shortfall

topic: Nutrition and other social sector schemes
t: Food security concepts → definitions
text:
## 1. Three dimensions (NCERT)
Dimension | Meaning
Availability | production + imports + buffer stock
Accessibility | food within reach of every person
Affordability | enough money to buy sufficient, safe, nutritious food
India's system has two components: buffer stock and PDS
Most food insecure: landless/land-poor rural households, casual urban workers, backward and tribal regions
## 2. Hunger types
Chronic hunger: persistently inadequate diet (low income)
Seasonal hunger: tied to crop cycles and casual work
Nutritional security: consistent access to safe, sufficient, nutritious food; extension of food security
⚠ Calorie norm for poverty line: 2,400 kcal rural, 2,100 kcal urban per person per day (NCERT); do not confuse with NFSA's 600 kcal ration

topic: Concept and history of sustainable development
t: Sustainable development → definition and principles
text:
## 1. Brundtland definition
Brundtland Commission = World Commission on Environment and Development (WCED), UN-mandated, set up in the early 1980s
Report: Our Common Future (1987); it popularised the term
Definition: development "meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs"
## 2. NCERT view (Class 11 Economics)
Present generation should hand over the planet "in good order"; leave a stock of quality-of-life assets no less than inherited
Herman Daly's condition | Meaning
Limit population | within the carrying capacity (the "plimsoll line" of a ship)
Technology | input-efficient, not input-consuming
Renewable resources | extraction rate not above regeneration rate
Non-renewable resources | depletion rate not above creation of renewable substitutes
Pollution | inefficiencies from pollution corrected
⚠ The definition is from Brundtland (1987), not from Stockholm (1972) or Rio (1992)
Likely angle: a "how many of the above" on Daly's conditions or on who defined sustainable development

topic: Concept and history of sustainable development
t: Milestones → year, place, outcome
text:
Year | Event | Place | Key outcome
1972 | UN Conference on the Human Environment | Stockholm | Stockholm Declaration (26 principles); World Environment Day, 5 June; UNEP
1987 | Brundtland Report | - | Our Common Future; definition of SD
1992 | UNCED / Earth Summit | Rio de Janeiro | Agenda 21, Rio Declaration, Forest Principles; UNFCCC, CBD, UNCCD; GEF set up on its eve
1997 | Rio+5 | UNGA special session | reviewed Agenda 21
2000 | Millennium Summit | New York | 8 MDGs, target 2015
2002 | Rio+10 / World Summit on SD | Johannesburg | Johannesburg Declaration
2012 | Rio+20 / UN Conference on SD | Rio de Janeiro | "The Future We Want"; SDGs born; PAGE (2013)
2015 | UNGA "2030 Agenda" | New York | 17 SDGs, 169 targets, target 2030
Earth Summit 1992 brought 179 countries, on the 20th anniversary of Stockholm
⚠ Agenda 21 = 1992 Rio, NOT Johannesburg 2002 (UPSC 2016 trap)
⚠ Rio+20 = UN Conference on Sustainable Development; 1992 was UN Conference on Environment and Development
PYQ (Environment head) 2015: Rio+20 is the UN Conference on Sustainable Development; 2018: PAGE emerged from Rio+20

topic: Concept and history of sustainable development
t: Earth Summit 1992 → binding vs non-binding outputs
text:
Output | Nature
UNFCCC | legally binding; led to Kyoto and Paris
CBD | legally binding
UNCCD | legally binding (opened under Earth Summit aegis)
Agenda 21 | non-binding action plan
Rio Declaration | principles (27)
Forest Principles | non-binding
Commission on Sustainable Development (CSD) | body set up to review progress
## 1. HLPF (High-level Political Forum on SD)
Forum under ECOSOC; meets annually under ECOSOC and every 4 years under the UNGA
Reviews Agenda 21, Johannesburg, Rio+20, Barbados Programme (SIDS), LDC-IV outcomes
## 2. NCERT angle
North worried about ozone and global warming; South about development and environment link
Critics: Agenda 21 biased towards growth over ecological conservation

t: 2nd Plan → Mahalanobis strategy
text:
## 1. What the 2nd Plan did
Based on P.C. Mahalanobis model (two-sector, later four-sector); also called the Mahalanobis Plan
Thrust: capital-intensive heavy and basic industries: iron and steel, heavy engineering, machine tools, heavy chemicals
Logic: industry is a pre-condition for agriculture; growth would "trickle down"; heavy industry would spur small-scale units
Industrial Policy Resolution 1956: socialistic pattern of society as goal
From the 2nd Plan: determined thrust towards substitution of basic and capital goods (import substitution industrialisation)
Statement | Verdict
2nd Plan: thrust on basic and capital goods substitution | Correct
3rd Plan introduced import substitution | Wrong: it began with the 2nd
Agriculture got top priority in the 2nd Plan | Wrong: 1st Plan did
PYQ 2019: statement 1 (2nd Plan thrust on basic/capital goods) correct; UPSC 2009 also tested: import substitution was not introduced by the 3rd Plan

topic: Five-Year Plans → objective of each Plan
t: 4th and 5th Plans → equity turn and self-reliance
text:
## 1. Fourth Plan (1969-74)
Twin objectives: growth with stability and progressive achievement of self-reliance (after allies refused supplies in the Indo-Pak war)
Preface: provide a "necessary corrective to the earlier trend" that helped the stronger sections → correcting concentration of wealth and economic power
Growth centre approach for regional disparity; first adopted self-sustaining development
Garibi Hatao was Indira Gandhi's 1971 election slogan (4th Plan period)
## 2. Fifth Plan (1974-79)
Objectives: removal of poverty (Garibi Hatao) and attainment of self-reliance (= zero net foreign aid)
Minimum Needs Programme; Twenty Point Programme (1975, during Emergency)
Terminated in 1978, one year early, by the Janata government
⚠ The 5th Plan did not first make the financial sector an integral part of the Plan (PYQ 2019 statement 3 false)
PYQ 2019: answer "1 and 2 only": 2nd Plan capital goods thrust + 4th Plan correcting wealth concentration
