text:
## 1. Planning Commission
Set up in 1950 with the Prime Minister as Chairperson; five-year plans borrowed from the Soviet Union
Rooted in Industrial Policy Resolution 1948 and the Directive Principles
Plans also had a 20-year perspective plan; goals: growth, modernisation, self-reliance, equity
## 2. Plans before the First Plan
Plan | Year | By
National Planning Committee | 1938 | Indian National Congress
Bombay Plan | 1944 | Industrialists
Gandhian Plan | 1944 | Gandhian thinkers
People's Plan | 1945 | Post-war reconstruction committee of Indian trade unions
Sarvodaya Plan | 1950 | Jayaprakash Narayan
## Beyond your notes
Planning Commission set up on 15 March 1950; NPC chaired by Nehru; Gandhian Plan by S.N. Agarwal; People's Plan by M.N. Roy
Planning Commission and NITI Aayog are both non-constitutional, non-statutory (created by Cabinet resolution); NDC set up 1952
⚠ "Goals of the Plans" in MCQs: growth, modernisation, self-reliance (equity); "Literature" is a classic false item

t: Land reforms → aims and the three measures
text:
## 1. Aims
Equity: transfer land from large landlords to poor and landless ("land to the tiller")
Remove institutional barriers (intermediaries, insecure tenancy); raise farm output
## 2. Measures
Measure | Content
Abolition of intermediaries | Zamindars, jagirdars removed; ~200 lakh tenants came into direct contact with the State
Tenancy reforms | Regulation of rent, security of tenure, ownership to tenants
Ceiling on holdings | Maximum land per person/family; surplus to landless
Consolidation | Successful mainly in Punjab, Haryana, western UP
Guiding report: Kumarappa Committee (Congress Agrarian Reforms Committee, 1949): land belongs to the tiller; no subletting except widows, minors, disabled
PYQ 2019: correct statement = "major aim of land reforms was providing agricultural land to all the landless"

t: Land ceiling → individual, family, exemptions
text:
## 1. How ceilings worked
Ceiling = legally fixed maximum holding; surplus taken (with or without compensation) and given to landless, panchayats or cooperatives
Ceiling laws were put in force mainly during the 3rd Plan
Unit: individual or family holding; family holdings were initially exempt in most states → notional partition among relatives, benami transfers
Exemptions allowed (2nd Plan advice): tea, coffee, rubber plantations, orchards, specialised cattle, dairy, sheep farms; Tamil Nadu reportedly had 26 types
PYQ 2019 option | Verdict
Ceilings aimed at family, not individual holdings | Wrong: both
No exemptions to ceiling | Wrong: many
Made cash crops predominant | Wrong
Aim: land to the landless | Correct
⚠ Cash-crop shift came later from export-oriented policy after the 1991 reforms (NCERT), not from land reforms

t: Tenancy reforms → rent, tenure, ownership
text:
## 1. Three components
Component | Rule
Rent regulation | Max rent not above 1/4 of gross produce in most states (exceptions: AP, Haryana, Punjab); earlier rents were 50-80%
Security of tenure | No ejection except by law; owner may resume only for personal cultivation; tenant keeps a minimum area
Ownership | Tenants given ownership (State pays owner, tenant repays in instalments)
UP alone (with Delhi) gave tenants full security
Result: tenancy fell from 42% (1950-51) to 20-25% by early 1960s; 5.9 million ha given to 7.2 million tenants
⚠ Abolition of zamindari created new intermediaries: superior tenants who sub-leased to sharecroppers

t: Land reforms → outcome and where they worked
text:
## 1. Results
Indicator | Share of cultivated area
Tenancy reforms benefited | ~4% (by 1992)
Land redistributed | ~2%
Total benefit | ~6%
Successful in Kerala and West Bengal (committed governments); partly Andhra Pradesh
Failures: court cases, loopholes, poor land records, benami transfers, weak political will
Phases: institutional (till early 1960s) → technological (Green Revolution, mid-1960s)
## 2. Constitutional cover
1st Amendment 1951: Ninth Schedule, Art 31A, 31B; 4th Amendment 1955 strengthened zamindari abolition
## Beyond your notes
Operation Barga (West Bengal, 1978): registration of sharecroppers (bargadars)

t: 1991 crisis → causes and the IMF route
text:
## 1. Crisis
Forex reserves fell to cover imports for barely two weeks; unable to repay foreign debt; high inflation
Causes: 1980s fiscal deficits, imports outpacing exports, Gulf War oil price spike, rating downgrade
India approached IBRD (World Bank) and IMF; accepted conditions → New Economic Policy (NEP), the Rao-Manmohan reforms
## 2. Two kinds of measures
Type | Horizon | Aim
Stabilisation | Short-term | Fix BoP, control inflation, rebuild reserves
Structural reform | Long-term | Efficiency, competitiveness, remove rigidities
LPG: Liberalisation, Privatisation, Globalisation
⚠ Some liberalisation began in the 1980s (licensing, EXIM, technology); 1991 was more comprehensive

t: Industrial delicensing → the first big step
text:
## 1. New Industrial Policy, 1991
Industrial licensing abolished for almost all products (end of licence raj)
Licensing retained (NCERT list): alcohol, cigarettes, hazardous chemicals, industrial explosives, electronics, aerospace, drugs and pharma
Reserved for public sector (NCERT): defence equipment, atomic energy generation, railway transport
MRTP Act amended: no expansion approval for large firms; SSIs could sell up to 44% equity to large firms
Many SSI items dereserved; market allowed to set prices
Chronology | Policy
1951 | IDR Act (licensing framework)
1956 | Industrial Policy Resolution (public sector dominance)
1991 | New Industrial Policy (delicensing)
PYQ 2000: liberalisation started with substantial changes in industrial licensing; not rupee convertibility, FDI formalities or tax cuts
## Beyond your notes
New Industrial Policy announced 24 July 1991
Today only atomic energy and railway operations remain reserved for the public sector (verify)

t: Financial, tax and forex reforms → what changed
text:
## 1. Reforms by area
Area | 1991 change
Banking | Banks free to set deposit rates; private banks (Indian and foreign); foreign stake in banks ~50%; RBI from regulator to facilitator
Capital market | FIIs (mutual funds, pension funds) allowed
Tax | Steady cut in income and corporate tax; simpler procedures; indirect tax reform toward a common market
Forex | Rupee devalued ~18% (PMF); then market-determined exchange rate
FDI | Cap raised 40% → 51% in priority industries; FIPB created
⚠ Rupee convertibility was not where reform began: current account convertibility came later and gradually
## Beyond your notes
Current account convertibility: August 1994; full capital account convertibility not adopted (as of 2026)

t: Trade policy reforms → QRs, tariffs, WTO
text:
## 1. From import substitution to openness
Before 1991: inward-looking trade, import substitution, high tariffs, quotas
Reforms: (i) dismantle quantitative restrictions (QRs), (ii) cut tariffs, (iii) remove import licensing (kept only for hazardous and environmentally sensitive items)
Fact | Figure / date
Average tariff | ~125% (late 1980s) → ~30% (early 2000s)
QRs on consumer goods and farm products removed | April 2001
Export duties | Removed
WTO member | 1995
First Generation Reforms: 1991-2000
⚠ Tariffs protect domestic firms; quotas fix quantity: both restrict imports

Remittances FY25 | US$135.46 bn, world's largest
India's share in global agricultural exports: 2.2% (1.1% in 2000)
⚠ Survey figure (US$701.4 bn, Jan 2026) differs from PMF's US$785.71 bn (later 2026): follow the latest PMF figure

t: General price rise → what can cause it
text:
## 1. Meaning
Inflation = a sustained, general rise in the price level → purchasing power of money falls
A rise in the price of one or two goods is not inflation (CARE April 2026)
Cause | Channel | Type
More money supply | More money chasing the same goods | Demand-pull (monetary)
Fall in aggregate output | Same demand, less supply | Supply-side / cost-push
Rise in effective demand | Aggregate demand > aggregate supply | Demand-pull
All three raise the general price level
⚠ "How many" trap: a fall in output also causes inflation; it is not only a demand story
PYQ 2013: money supply up, aggregate output down, effective demand up → all three (1, 2 and 3)
## 2. The two sides in one line
Demand side: AD > AS ("too much money chasing too few goods")
Supply side: costs up or supply down while demand is steady

t: Demand-pull vs cost-push → which factor causes which
text:
Factor | Type | Why
Expansionary fiscal/monetary policy | Demand-pull | Raises AD (lower rates, QE, more spending)
Fiscal stimulus (tax cuts, transfers, PM-KISAN, MGNREGA wages) | Demand-pull | More purchasing power
Higher purchasing power | Demand-pull | Consumers buy more
Population growth, rising net exports, forex accumulation (RBI buys dollars, injects rupees) | Demand-pull | More demand or money
Wage hikes (7th Pay Commission), inflation-indexed wages | Cost-push | Higher production cost
Crude oil, raw material, import prices, rupee depreciation | Cost-push | Input cost up
Higher indirect taxes (GST slab 12% → 18%) | Cost-push | Taxes passed to buyer
Higher profit margins of monopolies | Cost-push (profit-push) | Pricing power
Rising interest rates reduce demand → they curb inflation, cause none
⚠ Wage indexation only protects real wages; Preview and the PYQ key treat it as not demand-pull
PYQ 2021: demand-pull from expansionary policies, fiscal stimulus, higher purchasing power → 1, 2 and 4 only; traps: indexing wages, rising interest rates

t: Inflation by rate → creeping to hyperinflation
text:
Type | Speed | Example (as in sources)
Creeping | Slow, steady (~3% a year) | USA in the 1990s
Walking / trotting | Moderate, single digit | (common in developing economies)
Galloping | 10% to several hundred % a year | Argentina 1980s (300% in 1983, 3,079% in 1989)
Hyperinflation | Uncontrolled; usually > 50% per month | Zimbabwe 2008, Weimar Germany 1923, Hungary 1946
Hungary 1946: highest inflation in history; prices doubled every 15 hours (Testbook)
Hyperinflation follows currency collapse, political instability, massive money printing
⚠ Hyperinflation threshold "50% per month" is per month, not per year (CARE October 2025)
## 2. Open vs suppressed
Open inflation (Testbook): driven by outside factors (global prices, exchange rate)
Suppressed inflation: prices held down by controls and rationing

t: Other inflation terms → meaning
text:
Term | Meaning
Structural | Long-term bottlenecks: poor infrastructure, storage, marketing
Bottleneck | Supply-chain disruption in particular goods
Monetary | Rapid rise in money supply (e.g. QE)
Seasonal | Harvest or festival cycles; rises then settles
Imported | Costlier imports or weaker rupee (edible oil, fertiliser, crude)
Skewflation | Price of one good or group rises while overall level stays steady (term from 2009-11)
Stagflation | Inflation + stagnant growth + high unemployment
Wage-price spiral | Prices push wages, wages push prices
Inflation generalisation | Price rises spread across a broad range of the basket (RBI watches it)
⚠ Skewflation is not general inflation; stagflation is not deflation
## In news 2025-26
RBI flagged inflation generalisation (PMF LENS CA, 17 Oct 2026); tracked through CPI diffusion indices and month-on-month momentum

t: Growth and inflation → what usually go together
text:
Economic growth is usually coupled with (moderate) inflation: rising income and demand push prices
Testbook: moderate inflation is "a sign of a healthy, growing economy"
Pairing | Normal?
Growth + moderate inflation | Yes (usual)
Growth + deflation | No
Stagnation + inflation = stagflation | Unusual (oil shocks, tariffs, depreciation)
Low growth + deflation | Recession / depression (1930s)
High growth + low inflation = Goldilocks | "Not too hot, not too cold"
Phillips curve: inverse link between inflation and unemployment
New Keynesian Phillips curve: positive link between output and inflation
Inflationary gap: actual GDP above potential GDP → price pressure
Deflationary gap: actual GDP below potential GDP → risk of deflation
⚠ Stagflation breaks the Phillips curve: high inflation and high unemployment together
PYQ 2011: economic growth is usually coupled with → inflation (not deflation, stagflation or hyperinflation)
## In news 2025-26
RBI called FY26 a "Goldilocks" setting: GDP growth raised to 7.3%, CPI forecast cut to 2.0% (PMF LENS Dec 2025)
PMF: India's flat Phillips curve (2012-2026) means rate hikes cut output without cutting inflation much

t: Food inflation in India → causes
text:
Cause | Valid?
Changing consumption with rising income (protein, fruit, vegetables, milk) | Yes
Structural constraints in the food supply chain (storage, cold chain, marketing) | Yes
Monsoon failure, heatwaves, floods, pests | Yes
Import dependence (edible oil ~50% imported, pulses) | Yes
Foodgrain area fell ~30% in five years | No (exaggerated, false)
Food has the highest weight in CPI, so food shocks drive headline CPI
Repo rate cannot raise crop output: a tool mismatch (PMF)
⚠ The "30% fall in foodgrain area" statement is the trap: no such national decline
PYQ 2011: reasons for high food inflation → 2 and 3 only (income-led diet shift, supply-chain constraints)
## In news 2025-26
Food prices entered deflation (-0.2%) in 2025, first since 2014 (PMF Prelims Magnum Jan 2026)
Economic Survey 2025-26: TOP (tomato, onion, potato) prices fell 20-40%; 30% duty on yellow peas to protect chana farmers; edible oil customs duty raised to 20%, later cut to 10%

topic: Deflation, disinflation, base effect and core inflation
t: Deflation vs disinflation vs reflation → meaning
text:
Term | Meaning | Prices
Deflation | Persistent fall in the general price level (negative inflation) | Falling
Disinflation | Fall in the rate of inflation | Still rising, more slowly
Reflation | Policy to revive demand and lift prices after deflation/slump | Pushed up
Depreciation | Fall in currency value against others | Not deflation
Recession | Fall in output (technical: two quarters of negative real GDP) | Not deflation
Inflation 5% last year → 4% this year = disinflation, prices still up 4%
⚠ Deflation raises purchasing power of money; disinflation only slows its fall
PYQ 2010: deflation = persistent fall in the general price level; traps: currency fall, recession, fall in inflation rate
UPPCS 2017 (Preview): a fall in the inflation rate definitely means only "prices are rising more slowly"

topic: Deflation, disinflation, base effect and core inflation
t: Deflation → causes, spiral and cure
text:
## 1. Causes (PMF)
Weak aggregate demand, productivity-led oversupply, monetary contraction (tight credit, high rates)
Testbook adds: fierce competition, lower money supply, higher propensity to save
## 2. Deflationary spiral
Consumers postpone purchases → profits fall → layoffs → demand falls further
Real debt burden rises: debtors lose, creditors gain
Cure | Type
Cut repo rate, quantitative easing, OMO liquidity | Expansionary monetary
More public spending, tax cuts | Expansionary fiscal
Raise MSP procurement for farmers | Price support
Plus: currency depreciation, subsidies, confidence building
⚠ In deflation creditors gain and debtors lose: the mirror of inflation
## In news 2025-26
Retail inflation fell to a 12-year low of 2.2% in 2025; food inflation -0.2% (PMF LENS Jan 2026)
Concerns: sub-1% CPI prints partly from base effect; crops (soybean, pulses) sold below MSP in Oct-Nov 2025; households perceive inflation at 6.6% (Nov 2025 RBI survey)
Economic Survey: China saw price stagnation/deflation from weak demand and excess capacity

topic: Deflation, disinflation, base effect and core inflation
t: Base effect → how last year's prices move this year's rate
text:
Base effect = impact of the previous year's price level on the calculated inflation rate (year-on-year)
Last year's base | This year's measured inflation
High (prices rose a lot) | Lower, even with similar price rise (favourable / negative base effect)
Low (prices rose little) | Higher, even with a small rise (unfavourable / positive base effect)
Momentum effect = month-on-month price change in the current year
YoY inflation ≈ momentum + base effect
Base effect also distorts GDP growth: a high base makes growth look weaker (PMF Mains Magnum Oct 2025)
⚠ Base effect is a statistical effect: it is not crop failure or a demand surge
PYQ 2011: base effect = impact of the price levels of the previous year on the inflation rate; traps: supply deficiency, demand surge
## In news 2025-26
Economic Survey 2025-26: the base effect dominated the momentum effect in FY26, pulling inflation down
PMF: a future rebound from base effects may force policy reversal after rate cuts

topic: Deflation, disinflation, base effect and core inflation
t: Headline vs core inflation → what each excludes
text:
Feature | Headline | Core
Covers | All items in the basket | Excludes food and fuel
Volatility | More volatile | More stable (underlying trend)
India's target | Headline CPI-Combined | Watched, not targeted
Core is excluded because food and energy move with weather and geopolitics
Second-round effect: food inflation spilling into core and wages (PMF)
⚠ India targets headline, not core, CPI (PMF Prelims Magnum 2026)
## In news 2025-26
Economic Survey 2025-26: core looked sticky at 4.62% (Dec 2025) only because of gold and silver; adjusted core (minus precious metals) = 2.3%
Core eased to 4.1% when headline hit 1.55% (July 2025)
Pronab Sen view: policy should focus on core (CARE Aug 2025)
## Food price measures
CFPI (Consumer Food Price Index): NSO, monthly, base 2012, rural/urban/combined
Oct 2024: CPI 6.21%, CFPI 10.87%; CFPI fell to 0.99% by May 2025 (CARE)

topic: Effects of inflation: gainers and losers
t: Inflation → who gains, who loses
text:
Gains | Loses
Debtors / borrowers (repay in cheaper money) | Creditors / lenders, moneylenders
Producers, traders, farmers (prices rise first) | Fixed-income groups, pensioners
Equity holders (higher profits, dividends) | Bond-holders (fixed nominal coupon)
Government as largest debtor; more tax revenue | Savings-account and FD holders (if rate < inflation)
Holders of real assets (land, gold) | Consumers, wage earners without indexation
Mechanism: real value of fixed money sums falls
Fixed-rate loans make the borrower's gain clearest
⚠ Bond-holders lose: fixed coupons buy less; only inflation-indexed bonds protect them
PYQ 2013: inflation benefits debtors (1 only), not bond-holders
UPPCS 1995 (Preview): who benefits most → debtors
## Deflation reverses it
Creditors and fixed-income earners gain; debtors lose (real debt rises)

topic: Effects of inflation: gainers and losers
t: Inflation → effects on the economy
text:
Area | Effect
Savings | Real return falls; people shift to gold, land
Exports | Less competitive; imports cheaper relative to home goods
Exchange rate | Rupee value tends to fall; it does not improve
Tax revenue | Rises in nominal terms (bracket creep, ad valorem taxes)
Investment | Moderate inflation helps; high inflation creates uncertainty
Distribution | Regressive: poor spend more on food
Fiscal maths | Nominal GDP (= real GDP + inflation) drives tax receipts and deficit ratios
Inflation tax: hidden loss of purchasing power; regressive
Inflation premium: extra return lenders demand for expected inflation
Real interest rate ≈ nominal rate − inflation
⚠ Chhattisgarh PCS 2013 (Preview): inflation raises prices and lowers value of money, but does not improve the exchange rate
## In news 2025-26
Very low inflation hurt nominal GDP: Apr-Jun 2025 real growth 7.8%, nominal only 8.8% vs Budget's 10.1% → slower tax growth (PMF Mains Magnum Oct 2025)
Real wages: 2023 nominal 9.2%, real 2.5% (CARE Aug 2025)

topic: Effects of inflation: gainers and losers
t: Cost Inflation Index → inflation adjustment of capital gains
text:
CII: notified yearly by CBDT under the Income-tax Act, 1961
Purpose: indexation of purchase price to compute long-term capital gains; tax only real gains
FY | CII
2021-22 | 317
2022-23 | 331
2023-24 | 348
2024-25 | 363
2025-26 | 376 (+3.58%)
Taxpayers prefer a higher CII (lower taxable gain)
Long-term holding (P-MCA 2025): 36 months generally; 24 for immovable property and unlisted shares; 12 for listed securities
⚠ CII is issued by CBDT, not RBI or MoSPI
## Beyond your notes
CII base year is 2001-02 = 100
Budget 2024 withdrew indexation for most assets for transfers from 23 July 2024 (land/buildings bought before that date keep an option) (verify)

topic: Deficit financing, money supply and inflation control
t: Financing a budget deficit → which is most inflationary
text:
Method | Effect on money supply | Inflationary?
Creating new money (RBI buys G-secs directly; monetisation) | Adds high-powered money | Most inflationary
Borrowing from banks | Uses bank funds; may expand credit | Moderate
Borrowing from the public (bonds) | Transfers existing money | Least of the three
Repayment of public debt | Returns existing money | Not the most
Money financing of the deficit = printing high-powered money (APPSC book)
New money + no extra output = demand-pull inflation
⚠ Asked twice (2013, 2021) with the same options: answer is always creation of new money
PYQ 2021 and 2013: most inflationary → creating new money to finance a budget deficit

topic: Deficit financing, money supply and inflation control
t: Deficit financing in India → from ad hoc T-bills to WMA
text:
Deficit financing: excess of government expenditure over revenue, covered by borrowing or new money
India used it to fund the Five Year Plans (largest source for the Eighth Plan outlay, APPSC book)
Year | Change
Mid-1950s | Ad hoc Treasury Bills: automatic RBI financing of the Centre's deficit
1 April 1997 | Ad hoc T-bills abolished; replaced by Ways and Means Advances (WMA)
2003 | FRBM Act
WMA = short-term temporary mismatch advances by RBI, not permanent financing
Monetised deficit = RBI's direct purchase of government bonds (Testbook)
⚠ The 1997 change ended automatic monetisation; WMA are temporary, with limits
## Beyond your notes
FRBM Act: RBI barred from subscribing to primary issues of G-secs from 1 April 2006; the 2018 amendment allows it under the escape clause (verify)
Seigniorage: profit from issuing money

topic: Deficit financing, money supply and inflation control
t: Money in circulation → how inflation is controlled
text:
Decreasing money in circulation controls inflation; increasing it fuels inflation
Monetary tool (RBI) | To fight inflation
Repo / bank rate | Raise
CRR, SLR | Raise
OMO | Sell G-secs (absorb liquidity)
LAF, MSS, SDF | Absorb surplus liquidity
Communication | Anchor expectations
Rate hikes reduce demand; tight policy may slow growth (sacrifice ratio)
⚠ Inflation control is shared: RBI (monetary) and the Government (fiscal, supply)
PYQ 2015: correct statement → decreased money circulation helps control inflation; traps: "Government only", "RBI has no role"
## In news 2025-26
RBI raised repo 4% → 6.5% (May 2022-Feb 2023); cut about 125 bps from early 2025 (CARE); repo 5.25% after Dec 2025 cut (PMF)
RBI bought ₹1 lakh crore G-secs via OMO to inject liquidity (Dec 2025)

topic: Deficit financing, money supply and inflation control
t: Fiscal and supply-side measures → the government's role
text:
Measure | Action in inflation | Action in deflation
Public expenditure | Cut | Raise
Taxes (income, corporate, GST) | Raise | Cut
Buffer stocks | Release (OMSS) | Procure
Trade policy | Cut import duty, curb exports | Raise import duty
Administrative | Stock limits, anti-hoarding, price controls | -
Supply | Storage, cold chains, logistics | -
PMGKAY free grain and One Nation One Ration Card help contain food inflation (Testbook, Budget 2023-24)
⚠ Monetary policy cannot fix supply shocks; fiscal and administrative steps are needed
## In news 2025-26
PMF proposes an RBI-Consumer Affairs cell with a food-inflation trigger for buffer release and duty cuts
Govt used edible oil duty changes and yellow peas duty to steer prices (Economic Survey 2025-26)
Crude above $120/barrel on the West Asia conflict (CARE April 2026); India imports ~85% of crude

topic: Deficit financing, money supply and inflation control
t: Sacrifice ratio → cost of cutting inflation
text:
Sacrifice ratio = output (GDP) lost to cut inflation by one percentage point
Country (2022-23 tightening) | Result
USA (Fed: 11 hikes to 5.25-5.50%) | Sacrifice ratio near zero; no recession
UK (Bank of England) | High ratio; recession late 2023; CPI ~3% in Feb 2026 vs 2% target
India | Repo 4% → 6.5%, then cautious easing
Low ratio = disinflation without much job loss
UK weakness: imported-energy dependence, Brexit labour shortages, weak productivity
⚠ A high sacrifice ratio is bad: costly disinflation
## Beyond your notes
The Fed and BoE target 2% inflation (as of 2026)

topic: Price indices: CPI, WPI and other measures
t: CPI types → compiler and base year
text:
Index | Compiled by | Base year
CPI-IW (Industrial Workers) | Labour Bureau, Ministry of Labour and Employment | 2016
CPI-AL (Agricultural Labourers) | Labour Bureau | 1986-87
CPI-RL (Rural Labourers) | Labour Bureau | 1986-87
CPI-Rural / Urban / Combined | NSO, MoSPI | 2012 → 2024 (new series)
WPI | Office of Economic Adviser, DPIIT, Ministry of Commerce and Industry | 2011-12
Three of the four CPIs are Labour Bureau; only CPI R/U/C is NSO
CPI-UNME (Urban Non-Manual Employees) by CSO was discontinued from January 2011
⚠ CPI-IW is not from RBI, DEA, DoPT or NSO: it is the Labour Bureau
PYQ 2015 (and 2010): CPI for Industrial Workers is brought out by → the Labour Bureau
⚠ PMF Infographic Dec 2024 lists CPI-IW base as 2011; PMF P-MCA 2025, Testbook and Preview give 2016: use 2016

topic: Price indices: CPI, WPI and other measures
t: CPI-IW → uses and base-year history
text:
Used to fix dearness allowance (DA) of central and state government and PSU employees
Used for wage indexation of industrial workers
Base year | In force from
1960 = 100 | First all-India series
1982 = 100 | 1988
2001 = 100 | 2006
2016 = 100 | September 2020
Food has a higher weight in CPI-IW than in WPI
Labour Bureau also compiles CPI-AL and CPI-RL (base 1986-87)
⚠ DA is linked to CPI-IW, not WPI or CPI-AL (UPUDA 2001, UPPCS 2008)
## Beyond your notes
Labour Bureau offices: Shimla and Chandigarh
CPI-IW (2016) covers 88 centres; food and beverages weight about 39% (verify)

topic: Price indices: CPI, WPI and other measures
t: CPI-Combined → design and weights
text:
Tracks retail prices of goods and services for a household basket
Formula: Modified Laspeyres fixed-base, base-year expenditure weights
Released monthly; prices collected weekly for perishables, monthly for others
CPI-Combined is the official measure for the inflation target (RBI Act)
Group (old 2012 series) | Weight %
Food and beverages | 45.86
Miscellaneous (services) | 28.32
Housing (all-India; urban 21.67) | 10.07
Fuel and light | 6.84
Clothing and footwear | 6.53
Pan, tobacco, intoxicants | 2.38
Old housing index used HRA of government staff as a rent proxy; urban only
Issues: outdated base, high food weight, substitution bias, quality adjustment
⚠ "Miscellaneous" (28.32%) is mostly services: CPI includes services, WPI does not

topic: Price indices: CPI, WPI and other measures
t: New CPI series (base 2024) → what changed
text:
Feature | Old (2012) | New (2024)
Weights from | 2011-12 survey | HCES 2023-24
Food and beverages | 45.86% | 36.75%
Housing (with utilities) | 10.07% | 17.67%; rural rent included first time
Weighted items | 299 | 358
Classification | - | COICOP 2018, 12 divisions
Rural share in combined | 53.52% | 55.4%
Added: smartphones, OTT subscriptions, international airfare; dropped VCRs, audio cassettes
12 "online markets" track e-commerce prices; PPAC fuel data, online fares used
Employer-provided dwellings excluded; rent collected monthly (was six-monthly)
## In news 2025-26
MoSPI released the first new-series data in Feb 2026: headline 2.75% vs 1.33% (Dec 2025, old series) (PMF LENS Feb 2026)
Transport 8.8% and health 6.1% weights rise
⚠ CARE June 2026 calls it the series "with 2023-24 as base year" (the HCES year); PMF gives base year 2024: use 2024

topic: Price indices: CPI, WPI and other measures
t: WPI → compiler, base, weights, coverage
text:
Measures prices at the first point of bulk sale (wholesale, business to business)
Compiled by Office of Economic Adviser (OEA), DPIIT, Ministry of Commerce and Industry
Released monthly; base 2011-12 (revised from 2004-05 in 2017)
Group | Weight %
Manufactured products | 64.2
Primary articles | 22.6
Fuel and power | 13.1
Goods only, no services; excludes indirect taxes, discounts, transport
Includes capital goods and intermediate goods
Food weight in WPI ≈ 24.4% vs 45.9% in CPI-C (old series)
WPI was the main inflation gauge until RBI moved to CPI in 2014
⚠ WPI comes from Commerce and Industry, not MoSPI; CPI-C comes from NSO (MoSPI)
PYQ 2010: WPI available monthly and gives less weight to food than CPI-IW → both correct

topic: Price indices: CPI, WPI and other measures
t: CPI vs WPI → food weight, services, which RBI uses
text:
Basis | CPI | WPI
Price stage | Retail (consumer) | Wholesale (producer)
Services | Included | Excluded
Food weight | Higher (45.9% old; 36.75% new) | Lower (~24.4%)
Highest weight | Food and beverages | Manufactured products
Indirect taxes | Included | Excluded
Capital goods | Excluded | Included
Compiler | NSO, MoSPI (CPI-C) | OEA, DPIIT
Data collection | Field investigators | Often voluntary reporting
Used by RBI | Yes, since April 2014 | No
⚠ RBI targets CPI-Combined, not WPI (Urjit Patel Committee; adopted 1 April 2014)
PYQ 2020: food weight higher in CPI, WPI excludes services → 1 and 2 only; "RBI adopted WPI" is false

topic: Price indices: CPI, WPI and other measures
t: WPI revision and Producer Price Index → what changes
text:
Feature | Old WPI | New WPI
Base year | 2011-12 | 2022-23
Items | 697 | 957
Weights | Net Traded Value | Gross Value of Output
Fuel and Power | - | Solar, wind, nuclear electricity added; crude and natural gas moved here from Primary Articles
Method | Long-term formula | Chain-based, targeted mean imputation
PPI: prices received by producers; excludes taxes, transport, trade margins (IMF practice)
WPI and PPI run together for five years, then WPI is phased out (DPIIT)
PPI pillar | Frequency
Output PPI (OPPI) | Monthly
Input PPI (IPPI), manufacturing | Monthly (trial)
Service PPI: banking, securities, insurance, pensions, railways, air passenger, telecom | Quarterly
⚠ Unlike WPI, the PPI covers services
## In news 2025-26
DPIIT revision announced (PMF LENS CA 3 June 2026)
New IIP (base 2022-23) deflates with OPPI instead of WPI (PMF LENS CA 30 July 2026)

topic: Price indices: CPI, WPI and other measures
t: GDP deflator vs CPI vs WPI → coverage
text:
GDP deflator = nominal GDP / real GDP (× 100); released by NSO
Feature | WPI | CPI | GDP deflator
Goods | Yes | Yes | Yes
Services | No | Yes | Yes
Capital goods | Yes | No | Yes
Imports | Yes | Yes (consumption basket) | No (domestic output only)
Basket | Fixed | Fixed | Changes with output
Frequency | Monthly | Monthly | Quarterly with GDP
Deflator covers the whole economy and can be split by sector
⚠ Only the deflator reflects changes in the composition of output
## In news 2025-26
Economic Survey 2025-26: ratio of manufacturing deflator to agriculture deflator fell from 1.29 (FY05) to 0.65 (FY25); manufacturing's nominal GVA share ~14%, real ~18%
IMF graded India's national accounts "C", citing old base (2011-12) and no PPI (PMF LENS Dec 2025)

topic: Price indices: CPI, WPI and other measures
t: Other price indices → who publishes
text:
Index | Publisher | Note
CFPI | NSO, MoSPI | Base 2012; monthly; retail food prices
WPI Food Index | OEA, DPIIT | Launched 2017; food articles + food products; producer quotes
FAO Food Price Index | FAO | 5 groups: cereals, vegetable oils, dairy, meat, sugar
CII | CBDT | Capital gains indexation
Index of Eight Core Industries | OEA, DPIIT | 40.27% of IIP (old); new series adds iron ore (nine, 32.88%)
PMI | S&P Global | > 50 = expansion
⚠ CFPI uses retail prices; the WPI food index uses producer prices
## Beyond your notes
CPI data is released on the 12th and WPI on the 14th of each month (verify)

topic: Inflation targeting and who controls inflation
t: Price stability → which authority
text:
Body | Role
RBI | Price stability via monetary policy (RBI Act 1934, amended 2016); MPC sets repo
Government (Finance Ministry) | Sets the target with RBI every five years
Department of Consumer Affairs | Price monitoring of essentials (not inflation targeting)
FSDC | Financial stability and regulator coordination; chaired by the Finance Minister
Expenditure Management Commission | Review of government spending
RBI's chief objective: price stability while keeping growth in mind
⚠ FSDC is about financial stability, not price stability
PYQ 2022: responsible for price stability by controlling inflation → RBI
## Beyond your notes
Expenditure Management Commission (2014) was chaired by Bimal Jalan
Consumer Affairs runs the Price Stabilisation Fund for pulses and onion buffers

topic: Inflation targeting and who controls inflation
t: Inflation targeting → legal provisions
text:
FIT (Flexible Inflation Targeting): central bank publicly commits to a numerical target
Item | Provision
Recommended by | Urjit Patel Committee (2014)
Agreement | Monetary Policy Framework Agreement, 2015 (Govt-RBI)
Statutory basis | RBI Act amended 2016
Who sets target | Central Government, in consultation with RBI, every 5 years (Sec 45ZA)
Target | 4% CPI-Combined, band 2-6%
Failure | Above 6% or below 2% for 3 consecutive quarters (Sec 45ZN): RBI reports reasons, remedies, time to restore
Anchor | Headline CPI (base 2024)
Failure counts both ways: too high or too low
⚠ The Government sets the target; RBI/MPC works to meet it
## In news 2025-26
Government extended the target 4% (2-6%) for 2026-2031 (PMF Prelims Magnum Apr 2026)
PMF: average CPI fell from 6.8% (2012-16) to 4.9% after FIT; volatility 2.3% → 1.5%; food is 37% of the new basket

topic: Inflation targeting and who controls inflation
t: Monetary Policy Committee → composition and voting
text:
Feature | Fact
Members | 6: 3 from RBI + 3 external appointed by Government
RBI side | Governor (ex-officio chair), one Deputy Governor, one RBI officer
External term | 4 years
Decision | Majority vote; Governor has a casting vote on a tie
Meetings | At least 4 a year
Introduced | RBI Act amendment, 2016
MPC decides the policy repo rate to meet the target
⚠ Governor has a casting (second) vote only on a tie, no veto
## Beyond your notes
MPC is under Section 45ZB; quorum is 4 members, including the Governor or the Deputy Governor
MPC meets usually 6 times a year (as of 2026)

topic: Inflation targeting and who controls inflation
t: Monetary policy frameworks → credit planning to FIT
text:
Period | Framework
First two decades after 1947 | No formal framework
1960s-mid-1980s | Credit planning (via SLR and CRR)
Mid-1980s-late 1990s | Monetary targeting with feedback: broad money tied to GDP; inflation range 5-7%
1998-2015 | Multiple indicator approach
2016- | Flexible inflation targeting (4% ± 2%)
Inflation averaged ~7.5% since the 1980s, ~4% in the early 2000s (PMF Infographic)
## Pros and cons
Pros: credibility, anchors expectations, transparency, protects the poor
Cons: policy lags, no cure for supply bottlenecks, may ignore asset bubbles, uniform target ignores regions
## Beyond your notes
Monetary targeting with feedback followed the Sukhamoy Chakravarty Committee (1985)

topic: Money and measures of money supply
t: Monetary aggregates M0 to M4 → what each contains
text:
## 1. RBI's measures (since Second Working Group on Money Supply, 1977)
Measure | Formula | Type
M0 (reserve money) | Currency in circulation + Bankers' deposits with RBI + 'Other' deposits with RBI | Base / high-powered money
M1 | Currency with public + Demand deposits with banks + 'Other' deposits with RBI | Narrow
M2 | M1 + savings deposits of post office savings banks | Narrow
M3 | M1 + net time deposits with banks | Broad (most used)
M4 | M3 + all post office savings deposits (excluding NSCs) | Broad
Liquidity: M1 > M2 > M3 > M4 (decreasing order)
Currency in circulation = currency with public + cash in hand with banks
'Other' deposits with RBI: quasi-government and financial institutions (incl. primary dealers), foreign central banks and governments, international agencies like IMF
⚠ Bankers' deposits with RBI are in M0 only, not in M1 or M3
⚠ APPSC notes write M1 = currency + demand deposits (omit 'other' deposits); the RBI definition and UPSC 1997 include 'other' deposits with RBI

topic: Money and measures of money supply
t: Broad money M3 → what is in it and what is not
text:
## 1. M3 = four components
Component | In M3?
Currency with the public | Yes
Demand deposits with banks (current + savings) | Yes
Time deposits with banks (fixed deposits) | Yes
'Other' deposits with RBI | Yes
Bankers' deposits with RBI | No (only in M0)
Post office deposits | No (M2 / M4)
M3 − M1 = time deposits
Sources of M3 = Net bank credit to Government + Bank credit to commercial sector + Net foreign exchange assets of banking sector + Government's currency liabilities to public − Net non-monetary liabilities of banking sector
PYQ 1997: all four (currency, demand, time, 'other' deposits) form M3; trap: dropping 'other' deposits. PYQ 2002: currency + demand + time deposits, all three are in M3

topic: Money and measures of money supply
t: Liquid assets → order of liquidity
text:
## 1. Decreasing order
Rank | Asset | Why
1 | Currency | Already cash, spent at once
2 | Demand deposits (current a/c) | Withdrawable on demand by cheque
3 | Savings deposits | Some limits on withdrawal frequency
4 | Time deposits (FDs, CDs) | Fixed maturity; penalty on early withdrawal
Liquidity = ease of converting an asset into cash without loss of value
Money is the most liquid asset; near money (time deposits) is less liquid
Same logic for aggregates: M1 (most liquid) > M2 > M3 > M4
PYQ 2013: order 4-1-3-2 (currency > demand > savings > time); trap: putting savings deposits above demand deposits

topic: Money and measures of money supply
t: Transactions → effect on money supply
text:
## 1. Composition change vs creation
Transaction | Effect on M1/M3
Withdraw cash from demand deposit | Unchanged (deposits −, currency +)
Deposit cash into a bank | Unchanged at once (currency −, deposits +)
RBI buys G-secs from public | Increases
Government borrows from RBI | Increases
RBI sells G-secs to public | Decreases
Money supply = money held by the public; shifting between its own forms does not change the total
Banks then lend out new deposits → money supply grows through the multiplier, not by the deposit itself
⚠ PYQ 2012 answer: only RBI's purchase of G-secs and Government's borrowing from RBI raise money supply; Preview ESD calls currency deposit "reducing" money supply, but strictly it only changes composition
PYQ 2020: withdrawing ₹1,00,000 from a demand deposit leaves aggregate money supply unchanged

topic: Money and measures of money supply
t: Legal tender and fiat money → meaning
text:
## 1. Types of money
Term | Meaning
Legal tender | Money a creditor is compelled by law to accept in settlement of claims
Fiat money | Notes and coins with no intrinsic value; value because Government declares it legal tender
Representative money | Claim on a commodity (gold/silver certificates)
Bank money | Cheques, drafts, bills of exchange: not legal tender, can be refused
CBDC (e₹) | Legal tender in digital form, RBI's liability, exchangeable 1:1 with cash
Demonetisation (8 Nov 2016) withdrew legal tender status of old ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes
NCERT: modern currency has no use of its own; it is accepted because it is authorised by the Government; no individual in India can legally refuse a payment made in rupees
NCERT: RBI issues currency notes on behalf of the Central Government; deposits withdrawable on demand = demand deposits (cheque transfers them)
PYQ 2018: legal tender = money a creditor must accept; traps: "money tendered in courts", "cheques and drafts", "metallic money"
## In news 2025-26
e-rupee expansion (Sep 2025): CBDC wallets allow transfers without a bank account and programmable, targeted subsidy delivery
## Beyond your notes
RBI notes are legal tender under Sec 26 of RBI Act, 1934; coins under the Coinage Act, 2011 (coins of ₹1 and above are legal tender only up to ₹1,000 in one payment)

topic: Money and measures of money supply
t: Debt types → financial vs non-financial debt
text:
## 1. Non-financial debt = debt of the non-financial sector
Borrower | Example | Non-financial debt?
Households | Housing loans, credit card dues | Yes
Non-financial firms | Corporate loans and bonds | Yes
Government | Treasury bills, dated G-secs | Yes
Financial firms (banks, NBFCs) | Their own borrowings | No (financial debt)
The test is who owes the debt, not who lent it: a credit card due is owed by a household, so it is non-financial even though a bank lent it
T-bills = short-term debt of the Centre (91, 182, 364 days), issued at a discount
PYQ 2020: housing loans, credit card dues and T-bills, all three are non-financial debt
## Beyond your notes
The BIS tracks "credit to the non-financial sector" in three parts: households, non-financial corporations, general government

t: Money multiplier → what raises it, what lowers it
text:
## 1. Meaning and formula
Money multiplier = M3 / M0 (broad money ÷ reserve money); shows how much money banks create per unit of reserves
Simple form: m = 1 / R (R = reserve ratio); R = 20% → m = 5; R = 10% → m = 10
NCERT: banks keep only a small share of deposits as cash (about 15%) and lend the rest; that is how deposits multiply
## 2. Determinants
Change | Effect on multiplier
Banking habit of people rises (more deposits, less cash) | Rises
CRR raised | Falls
SLR raised | Falls
People hold more cash (festive season, higher cdr) | Falls
Population rises | No direct effect
cdr (currency-deposit ratio) and rdr (reserve-deposit ratio) both lower the multiplier when they rise
⚠ Population growth raises the multiplier only if it brings more deposits
PYQ 2019 and 2021 (repeat): multiplier rises with banking habit; trap options were CRR rise, SLR rise, population rise
## In news 2025-26
Economic Survey 2025-26: money multiplier (M3/M0) rose to 6.21 (31 Dec 2025; 6.0 adjusted for SDF): better financial intermediation
M0 growth looked low (2.9%) because of the CRR cut; adjusted, 9.4%; M3 grew 12.1% on deposits and credit
⚠ A CRR cut slows M0 but raises the multiplier: the 2025 data show both at once
## Beyond your notes
NCERT Class 12 formula (macro text not readable in your files): m = (1 + cdr) / (cdr + rdr)

t: Reserve money (M0) → components and other names
text:
## 1. Reserve money
M0 = Currency in circulation + Bankers' deposits with RBI + 'Other' deposits with RBI
Other names: high-powered money, base money, monetary base, central bank money
It is the base for credit creation by banks; a liability of RBI
## 2. Who creates which money
Money | Created by
Currency (high-powered money) | RBI (and GoI for coins, ₹1 note)
Bank deposits (credit money) | Commercial banks, by lending
Credit creation | Commercial banks; RBI only controls it
RBI changes M0 through OMOs, forex purchases, lending to banks and Government
⚠ A CRR cut lowers M0 (bankers' deposits with RBI fall) but raises the multiplier
⚠ "Credit creation" is a function of commercial banks, not of RBI (UPPSC trap)

t: RBI functions → full list and the non-functions
text:
## 1. Functions
Function | Content
Monetary authority | Formulates and implements monetary policy
Issuer of currency | All notes except ₹1 note
Banker to Government | Centre and States; manages public debt and borrowing programme
Bankers' bank | Holds banks' reserves; lender of last resort
Regulator and supervisor | Banks, NBFCs, credit information companies
Forex manager | Custodian of reserves; under FEMA, 1999
Payment systems | Oversight of payment and settlement systems
Developmental | Set up IDBI, NABARD, SIDBI, Exim Bank, NHB
Acts as Government's agent for India's IMF membership; fiscal agent and adviser to Government
## 2. Not RBI functions
Credit creation (banks), regulating foreign trade (Commerce Ministry), lending to private companies / business families, pension fund management (PFRDA)
NCERT: post-1991 financial sector reforms aim to shift RBI from regulator to facilitator of the financial sector
PYQ 2001: banker to Centre, monetary policy, IMF agent, Government borrowing: all four correct
## In news 2025-26
Payments Regulatory Board (2025): 6 members, chaired by RBI Governor, with 3 Centre nominees; replaces the RBI-only BPSS; powers from PSS Act, 2007

t: Bankers' bank → what it implies
text:
## 1. Three meanings (PYQ 2012: all three correct)
Role | How
Custodian of banks' cash reserves | Banks keep CRR balances with RBI
Lender of last resort | Lends to banks in times of need (repo, MSF)
Adviser | Advises banks on monetary matters
Also: central clearing, settlement and fund transfers between banks
## 2. Lender of last resort (LoLR)
Rescue of a solvent bank with a temporary liquidity problem when no one else lends
⚠ LoLR is not lending to trade and industry, and not financing Government deficits (PYQ 2021: only "liquidity to banks in temporary crisis")
## 3. RBI as regulator of banks controls
Liquidity of assets (CRR, SLR, repo), branch expansion, mergers (with CCI) and winding-up of banks (PYQ 2013: all four)

t: Banker to Government → accounts, debt and WMA
text:
## 1. Centre and States
Item | Detail
Centre | RBI Act requires Centre to entrust all money, remittance, exchange, banking transactions and public debt management to RBI
States | By agreement under Sec 21A of RBI Act: all States + UTs of Puducherry and J&K
Exception | Sikkim: only limited agreement (public debt management)
WMA | Ways and Means Advances: short-term interest-bearing advances for temporary mismatch of receipts and payments
## 2. Government securities
Centre issues T-bills and dated securities; States issue only dated securities (SDLs); no T-bills by States
RBI sells T-bills by auction; tenors 91, 182, 364 days; issued at a discount, redeemed at face value
Cash Management Bills (since 2009): maturity under 91 days, outside WMA limits, SLR-eligible
T-bills were placed under WMA provisions in 1997
## Beyond your notes
WMA (1997) replaced ad hoc Treasury bills, ending automatic monetisation of the deficit; WMA is charged at the repo rate

Statement | Status | Source
Governor appointed by Central Government | Correct | Sec 8(1)(a) RBI Act: Governor + not more than 4 DGs
Centre's power to direct RBI in public interest | In RBI Act Sec 7(1), after consulting Governor | Not in the Constitution

Fact | Detail
Recommended by | Hilton Young Commission (Royal Commission on Indian Currency and Finance), 1926

t: Currency issue → who issues what
text:
## 1. Notes and coins
Item | Issued by | Signature
Notes ₹2 and above | RBI | RBI Governor
₹1 note | Government of India (Ministry of Finance) | Finance Secretary
Coins | Government of India | –
₹1 note reintroduced in 1940 as war measure with status of a coin
Currency notes are liabilities of RBI; backing assets are gold, foreign currencies, G-secs

System | Rule
Proportional Reserve System (till 1956) | 2/5 of assets in gold or sterling (gold at least ₹40 crore)

Item | Income? | Why
Buying and selling Government bonds | Yes | Interest + trading gains on G-secs
Buying and selling foreign currency | Yes | Interest on foreign securities, exchange gains
Lending to banks (LAF, MSF) | Yes | Interest
Managing Government borrowing / transactions | Yes | Commission

topic: Monetary Policy Committee and inflation targeting
t: MPC → composition, chair, votes
text:
## 1. Basics
Statutory body under Sec 45ZB of RBI Act (amended 2016); decides the policy repo rate; decisions binding on RBI
Replaced the earlier Technical Advisory Committee; RBI's Monetary Policy Department assists it
## 2. Composition (6)
Member | Category
RBI Governor | Chairperson, ex officio
Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy | Ex officio
One RBI officer nominated by Central Board | Ex officio
3 external members | Appointed by Central Government, 4-year term
## 3. Procedure
Item | Rule
Meetings | At least 4 a year (in practice 6, bi-monthly)
Quorum | 4 members
Decision | Majority vote; tie → Governor's casting vote
## In news 2025-26
7 Oct 2026: MPC chaired by Governor Sanjay Malhotra voted unanimously (6-0) for a 25 bps hike (LENS: Governor holds a casting vote only in a tie)

topic: Monetary Policy Committee and inflation targeting
t: Inflation targeting → target, band, failure
text:
## 1. Framework
Item | Detail
Recommended by | Urjit Patel Committee (2014): FIT, 4% ± 2%
Agreement | Monetary Policy Framework Agreement, 2015 (GoI-RBI)
Statutory basis | RBI Act amended 2016
Index | CPI-Combined (headline) since April 2014
Target | 4%, band 2-6%
Who sets | Centre in consultation with RBI, every 5 years (Sec 45ZA)
On failure | Sec 45ZN: band breached for 3 consecutive quarters → RBI reports reasons, remedial steps, time to restore
Type: Flexible inflation targeting: price stability while keeping growth in mind
Earlier: credit planning (1960s-80s), monetary targeting with feedback (mid-80s to late 90s)
⚠ Equitable distribution of income is not an objective of monetary policy

First failure letter to Government: Nov 2022

text:

Item | Figure

Inflation volatility | 2.3% → 1.5%
Food and beverages in CPI | 37% of basket
Limits: repo action cannot raise harvests or clear supply bottlenecks; weak transmission; 92% informal workforce blunts wage-price spiral

topic: Monetary Policy Committee and inflation targeting
t: Policy stances → what each signals
text:
## 1. Stances
Stance | Aim | Rate bias
Accommodative | Support growth | Low rates / cuts; more liquidity
Neutral | Balance inflation and growth | Either direction, data-driven
Hawkish | Curb inflation | Hikes
Calibrated tightening | Curb inflation | Hike or pause only; rules out near-term cuts
Dovish | Stimulate activity | Cuts
Withdrawal of accommodation | Gradual tightening | Removing past easing
Stance is announced by the MPC with each policy
⚠ Neutral = move either way; accommodative = favours cuts; calibrated tightening = no cuts, next move a hike or pause
## In news 2025-26
7 Oct 2026: stance neutral → calibrated tightening with the hike to 5.50%: broadening retail inflation, monsoon supply risks, geopolitical tensions, global monetary tightening
Apr 2025: stance neutral → accommodative with the repo cut to 6%
June 2025: back from accommodative to neutral to keep flexibility (Economic Survey 2025-26)
2024: newly reconstituted MPC moved from "withdrawal of accommodation" to "neutral"
## Beyond your notes
External members appointed Oct 2024: Ram Singh, Saugata Bhattacharya, Nagesh Kumar

topic: Monetary Policy Committee and inflation targeting
t: Rate hikes and cuts → why central banks act
text:
## 1. Logic of monetary policy
Central banks assume they can counter rising consumer prices through monetary policy (higher rates → costlier credit → lower demand)
Monetary policy cannot fix supply bottlenecks (supply chains, war in Ukraine); it works on demand
Monetary policy is more effective against inflation, fiscal policy against deflation/depression
Monetary policy acts through two channels: higher repo cuts demand, and steers inflation expectations to the target
2022: World Bank warned that synchronised global hikes, not seen in five decades, risked a global recession
## In news 2025-26
Oct 2026: RBI flagged inflation generalisation (price rises spreading across the CPI basket) and hiked to 5.50%: the same logic as the 2022 global hikes
PYQ 2023 (Statement I-II): many central banks hiked rates post-pandemic (I) because they assume monetary policy can counter consumer prices (II): both correct, II explains I

topic: Policy rates and liquidity adjustment facility
t: Policy rates → who lends to whom
text:
## 1. Rates (as on 7 Oct 2026)
Rate | Direction | Term / collateral | Level
Repo | RBI lends to banks | Short term, against G-secs | 5.50%
Reverse repo (fixed) | RBI borrows from banks | Short term, against G-secs | 3.35%
SDF | Banks park surplus with RBI | No collateral | 5.25%
MSF | Banks borrow from RBI | Overnight, from SLR holdings, penal | 5.75%
Bank Rate | RBI lends to banks | Long term, no collateral | 5.75%
Repo = repurchase agreement: RBI buys securities with an agreement to resell at a set date and price
Repo introduced Dec 1992; reverse repo Nov 1996; term repo April 2014 (Urjit Patel Committee)
Old rule (2011-12): reverse repo fixed 1% below repo; no longer followed
⚠ June 2026 levels were repo 5.25, SDF 5.00, MSF/Bank Rate 5.50; the Oct 2026 hike moved all three by 25 bps
PYQ 2007: repo = rate at which banks borrow from RBI (correct); paired trap: Gini coefficient 1 = perfect inequality, 0 = perfect equality

topic: Policy rates and liquidity adjustment facility
t: LAF corridor → floor, policy rate, ceiling
text:
## 1. Liquidity Adjustment Facility
RBI's window to inject (repo) or absorb (reverse repo / SDF) short-term liquidity
Corridor | Instrument | Oct 2026
Ceiling | MSF (= Bank Rate) | 5.75%
Policy rate | Repo | 5.50%
Floor | SDF | 5.25%
Width: 50 bps, repo in the middle; call money rate moves within it
SDF: banks deposit excess funds without collateral; proposed by RBI in 2015, enabled by Budget 2018-19
SDF fixed at repo − 25 bps (overnight floor); MSF = repo + 25 bps
WACR (weighted average call rate) = RBI's operating target
## In news 2025-26
Sep 2026: surplus liquidity of about ₹10.32 lakh crore pushed WACR below repo
FY26: net LAF on average in surplus; banks used MSF less and parked more in SDF (Economic Survey)
## Beyond your notes
LAF introduced in 2000; SDF operational from April 2022, replacing fixed reverse repo as the floor

topic: Policy rates and liquidity adjustment facility
t: Bank Rate → meaning and uses
text:
## 1. Meaning
Rate at which RBI buys or rediscounts bills of exchange / lends long-term funds to banks; no collateral
Penal rate on CRR/SLR shortfall = Bank Rate + 3% (or + 5%)
Aligned to MSF rate since Feb 2012: moves automatically with MSF
## 2. Effect
Change | Signal
Bank Rate raised | Tight / dear money; credit costlier, money supply falls
Bank Rate cut | More liquidity, cheap money
Quantitative tool | Affects overall credit, not one sector
PYQ 1995: Bank Rate = rate at which RBI discounts bills of exchange; traps: rate RBI pays on banks' deposits, banks' loan rate, bond rate
⚠ Bank Rate = long-term; repo = short-term (BPSC trap swaps them); PLR is fixed by banks, not RBI

topic: Policy rates and liquidity adjustment facility
t: MSF and NDTL → banking-operation terms
text:
## 1. Marginal Standing Facility
Emergency window when inter-bank liquidity dries up; overnight, at a penal rate above repo
Banks dip into their SLR portfolio up to a limit
Raising MSF = tightening (PYQ 2020)
## 2. Net Demand and Time Liabilities
Demand liabilities | Time liabilities
Savings deposits | Fixed deposits
Current deposits | Cash certificates
Demand drafts | Gold deposits
Unclaimed deposits | Staff security deposits
CRR and SLR are calculated on NDTL (excluding inter-bank deposits)
PYQ 2014: MSF rate and NDTL relate to banking operations
## Beyond your notes
MSF introduced in 2011; borrowing limit is a share of NDTL (2% of NDTL, verify)

topic: Policy rates and liquidity adjustment facility
t: VRR and term repo → fine-tuning tools
text:
## 1. Tools beside the fixed repo
Tool | Purpose
Variable Rate Repo (VRR) / term repo | Injects liquidity; rate set by auction; 2-14 days or more
VRRR | Absorbs surplus; competitive auction; RBI gives G-secs as collateral; longer than overnight SDF
LTRO | Longer-term funds (beyond 1 year) against G-secs; lowers long-term rates

## In news 2025-26
Sep 2026: RBI absorbed about ₹6.02 lakh crore through two 3-day VRRR auctions
Jan 2025: deficit peaked at ₹3.15 lakh crore (23 Jan), worst in ~15 years; RBI ran 56-day (₹50,000 crore) and 49-day (₹75,000 crore) VRR auctions
⚠ VRRR rate is set by bidding, not fixed at 25 bps below repo (that is SDF)

t: CRR vs SLR → comparison
text:
## 1. Side by side
Point | CRR | SLR
Kept | With RBI | With the bank itself
Form | Cash only | Cash, gold, approved securities (G-secs, T-bills, SDLs, CMBs)
Interest | None (a cost to banks) | Earns returns
Base | % of NDTL | % of NDTL
Law | RBI Act | Sec 24(2A), Banking Regulation Act, 1949
Level (5 June 2026) | 3.00% | 18.00%
Both are quantitative tools; CRR is the more active liquidity tool
1998 definition: ratio banks must keep between liquid assets (cash, gold, G-secs) and deposits = SLR
PYQ 1998: "ratio between cash in hand and total assets" = SLR; distractors SBR, CBR, CLR do not exist
## Beyond your notes
CRR is under Sec 42 of RBI Act; its 3% floor and 20% ceiling were removed in 2006

t: SLR → credit to Government
text:
## 1. Why SLR finances Government
Banks meet SLR mostly with G-secs (they earn interest) → banks lend to Government by buying its debt
SLR helps Government's debt management programme
## 2. Purposes of statutory reserves
Purpose | Tested?
Let RBI control the amount of advances banks create | Yes (PYQ 2014 answer)
Make deposits safe and liquid | Not the stated purpose (key)
Prevent excessive bank profits | No
Force banks to keep vault cash | No
## 3. Limits and history
2007 amendment removed the 25% floor: RBI can set SLR 0-40%
SLR 38.5% (1991) → 25% (1997) (Narasimham Committee)
PYQ 2010: mechanism by which banks give credit to Government = SLR; traps: LAF, Cash Credit Ratio, Debt Service Obligation
## In news 2025-26
Feb 2025 reform debate: banks hold ~26% of NDTL in SLR securities against the 18% requirement; ~30% of deposits locked in statutory pre-emptions; proposal to review the dual LCR + SLR mandate

t: CRR and SLR changes → effect on lending
text:
## 1. Direction of effects
Change | Effect
CRR raised | Commercial banks have less money to lend; liquidity falls; credit creation falls
CRR cut | More loanable funds, investment, money supply
SLR raised | Less loanable funds; anti-inflation
SLR cut 50 bps | Banks have more funds → SCBs may cut lending rates
1 basis point = 0.01%; 50 bps = 0.5 percentage point
⚠ CRR hike means banks lend less, not RBI or Union Government (PYQ 2010 traps)
PYQ 2015: SLR cut of 50 bps → SCBs may cut lending rates; traps: "GDP rises drastically", "FIIs bring more capital", "liquidity falls drastically"
## 2. Reforms trend and recent levels
June 2025 MPC decision: CRR 4% → 3% in four 25 bps tranches (Sep-Nov 2025); CRR 3%, SLR 18% (June 2026)
Since 1991 both CRR and SLR reduced (CRR 13% in 1996 → 9% in 1999)
## In news 2025-26
Dec 2025: reserve requirements, currency leakage and tax outflows tightened durable liquidity
FY26: CRR cut by 100 bps to 3.0% of NDTL released about ₹2.5 lakh crore by Dec 2025 (Economic Survey)
June 2026: FCNR(B) deposits are exempt from CRR and SLR, which makes them attractive for banks
Dec 2024: CRR cut 50 bps to 4% to ease the liquidity deficit

t: OMO → buy or sell, and the effect
text:
## 1. Open Market Operations
RBI buys or sells Government securities and T-bills in the open market to adjust rupee liquidity
Goal | RBI action | Effect
Curb inflation / excess liquidity | Sells G-secs | Absorbs money; rates up
Ease tight liquidity / recession | Buys G-secs | Injects money; rates down
Outright OMO = permanent (no promise to reverse); repo OMO = temporary, with a resale date and price
OMO is a quantitative monetary tool; trading in securities, not forex or gold auctions
PYQ 2022 (stmt 1): if inflation is too high RBI is likely to sell (not buy) G-secs
## In news 2025-26
Sep 2026: OMO sale auctions of ₹1 lakh crore in three tranches, with T-bill auctions (to absorb surplus)
Dec 2025: OMO purchases of ₹1 lakh crore to inject durable liquidity and steady bond yields
Apr-May 2025: OMO purchases of ₹2.39 lakh crore (Economic Survey)
Jan 2025 deficit: OMO purchases of ₹60,000 crore in three ₹20,000 crore tranches
G-secs: T-bills = under 1 year (Centre only); dated securities = 1 year or more; States issue only SDLs; G-secs are risk-free, gilt-edged

t: Sterilisation → meaning and tools
text:
## 1. Meaning
RBI offsets the effect of its forex operations on domestic money supply
Forex action | Rupee effect | Sterilising step
RBI buys dollars (inflows) | Rupees injected | Sells G-secs (OMO / MSS) to absorb
RBI sells dollars | Rupees withdrawn | Buys G-secs to inject
Classical tool: OMO (selling T-bills and other instruments)
## 2. Market Stabilisation Scheme (MSS)
Introduced April 2004; RBI issues T-bills / G-secs to mop up excess liquidity from capital inflows
Proceeds held in a separate MSS account with RBI; temporary, unwound when liquidity eases
PYQ 2023: sterilisation = conducting OMOs; traps: payment systems oversight, debt and cash management of Governments, regulating NBFCs

t: Forex intervention → when RBI buys or sells dollars
text:
## 1. Rules of thumb (PYQ 2022)
Situation | RBI likely to
Rupee depreciating fast | Sell dollars (raise dollar supply)
Rupee appreciating fast | Buy dollars (inject rupees)
US/EU interest rates fall → FPI inflows → rupee strengthens | Buy dollars
Inflation too high | Sell G-secs (not buy)
Regime: managed float since the 2010s; market sets rate, RBI curbs volatility
⚠ Selling dollars also drains rupee liquidity, so defending the rupee can tighten bank liquidity
PYQ 2022: statements 2 and 3 correct, 1 wrong (answer 2 and 3 only)
## In news 2025-26
Rupee slid from ₹45.56/$ (2010-11) to ₹86.95 (Feb 2025) and later ₹90; reserves fell $51.52 billion in three months of intervention
Forex reserves then hit a record USD 702.28 billion (2025)
Sep 2026: reserves $785.71 billion; India overtook Russia as the 4th largest holder after China, Japan, Switzerland
Reserves = foreign currency assets + gold + SDRs + reserve position in the IMF, managed by RBI
US Fed cut 50 bps: weaker dollar, more inflows into India, rupee strengthening bias

t: Buy-sell swaps and Operation Twist → special liquidity tools
text:
## 1. Tools
Tool | How it works | Aim
Dollar-rupee buy-sell swap | RBI buys dollars now, sells them back later | Long-term rupee liquidity without permanent balance sheet expansion
Operation Twist | Buy long-term G-secs, sell short-term G-secs together | Lower long-term rates, promote long-term investment
MSS | Issue T-bills / G-secs | Absorb surplus
Operation Twist was first used by the US Fed in 1961; it is a special form of OMO
## In news 2025-26
June 2026: special forex swap window for fresh FCNR(B) deposits (min. 3 years), ECBs and overseas borrowings, to draw foreign currency inflows
Terms: a bank may swap once a week, up to FCNR(B) deposits raised the previous week(s), in multiples of $1 million; both legs at the FBIL reference rate (swap at par)
Why: FCNR(B) inflows fell 86% in FY26 ($7.1 billion → $946 million) while rupee NRE/NRO deposits rose
Dec 2025: $5 billion, 3-year buy-sell swap for rupee liquidity
Early 2025: two $10 billion buy-sell swaps during the liquidity crunch
## Beyond your notes
RBI first ran Operation Twist in December 2019

topic: Monetary policy instruments and their effects
t: Quantitative vs qualitative tools → classification
text:
## 1. RBI instruments
Quantitative (general) | Qualitative / selective
Bank Rate | Margin requirements on loans
Open Market Operations | Consumer credit regulation
Repo rate | Issue of directives
Reverse repo rate | Rationing of credit
MSF | Moral suasion and publicity
Variable CRR and SLR | Direct action
Quantitative = overall volume of credit; selective = credit to specific sectors or goods
1991 reforms eliminated most direct/selective credit controls
PYQ 1995: variable cash reserve ratio is not a selective tool; consumer credit regulation, credit rationing and margin requirements are
⚠ RAS 2023: sale of G-secs is not selective; UPPSC 2017: rationing of credit is not quantitative

topic: Monetary policy instruments and their effects
t: Monetary vs fiscal policy → which tool belongs where
text:
## 1. Classification
Monetary (RBI) | Fiscal (Government)
Bank Rate, repo | Public debt
Open market operations | Public revenue (taxes)
CRR, SLR | Public expenditure
Credit control, money supply | Surplus budget
## 2. Inflation control measures
Monetary: raise interest rates, credit control, cut money supply, demonetisation
Fiscal: cut unnecessary spending, raise taxes, raise savings, surplus budget
Monetary policy is complementary to fiscal policy
RBI is responsible for price stability (IAS 2022); decreased money circulation helps control inflation (IAS 2015)
PYQ 2015: Bank Rate and OMO are monetary components; public debt and public revenue are fiscal

topic: Monetary policy instruments and their effects
t: Expansionary vs contractionary → what RBI does
text:
## 1. Dear money vs cheap money
Tool | Contractionary (fight inflation) | Expansionary (fight slowdown)
CRR, SLR | Raise | Cut
Repo, Bank Rate, MSF | Raise | Cut
OMO | Sell G-secs | Buy G-secs
Reverse repo / SDF | Raise (more parking) | Cut
Expansionary policy: more money supply, lower interest rates
Inflation control steps (UPRO 2016): raise Bank Rate, CRR, SLR; buying G-secs raises money supply, so it is not anti-inflation
⚠ Raising MSF makes borrowing costlier: contractionary
Oct 2026 repo hike + calibrated tightening = contractionary; Feb-Dec 2025 cuts + CRR cut + OMO purchases = expansionary
PYQ 2020: in an expansionist policy RBI would not "increase MSF rate" (answer 2 only); cutting SLR, Bank Rate and repo are expansionary

topic: Monetary policy instruments and their effects
t: Interest rate changes → effect on spending and money demand
text:
## 1. Effects
Event | Result
Interest rate cut | Investment expenditure rises (also consumption)
Money demand rises, supply fixed | Interest rate rises
Higher interest rate | Money demanded falls
Larger value of transactions | More money demanded
Reducing interest rate | Not an anti-inflation method
Cheaper borrowing → firms expand, households borrow for homes and cars
PYQ 2014: lower interest raises investment; traps: consumption falls, tax collection rises, savings rise
PYQ 2013: with money supply fixed, higher money demand raises the rate of interest; traps: price fall, income rise

topic: Monetary policy instruments and their effects
t: Monetary transmission → how rate changes reach borrowers
text:
## 1. Lending benchmarks
Benchmark | Basis | Speed of pass-through
Base Rate (2010) | Bank's average cost | Slow
MCLR (1 April 2016) | Marginal cost of funds, tenor-wise | Gradual
External benchmark (EBLR) | Repo rate or T-bill yields | Immediate
MCLR aims at transparency and fairness to borrowers and banks (PYQ 2016)
Savings deposit rates deregulated in Oct 2011: set by banks, not RBI
PLR is fixed by banks, not RBI

Draft RBI (Interest Rates on Loans and Advances) Directions, 2026: floating-rate personal and MSME loans to be linked to an external benchmark; reset at most every 3 months (12 for farm loans); APR ceiling for small loans; from 1 April 2027, old loans migrate by 1 April 2029

FY26: robust pass-through: WALR on fresh loans fell 64 bps (Economic Survey)
## 2. Deflation remedy
Expansionary monetary policy: lower repo, quantitative easing, OMO purchases

t: Bank funding metrics → CASA, CD ratio, minimum balance
text:
Metric | Meaning | Direction
CASA ratio | Share of deposits in low-cost current and savings accounts | Higher = cheaper funds, better margins
CD ratio | Credit / deposits × 100 | Higher = more lending per rupee of deposits

Credit demand from households and industry (raises it)

Tier I (core) | Common equity, retained earnings
Tier II (supplementary) | Subordinated debt, hybrids
Set by RBI (Basel norms), not by each bank
Standard | Minimum CAR
Basel II | 8%
Basel III | 10.5% incl. 2.5% conservation buffer (PMF)
⚠ Testbook gives RBI minimum 9% (PSBs 12%); PMF: 10.5% under Basel III with buffer

## In news 2025-26
Economic Survey 2025-26: SCB CRAR 17.2% (Sept 2025)

topic: Prudential norms: Basel, CAR, lending rates and priority sector
t: Basel accords → what each did
text:
Accord | Year | Focus
Basel I | 1988 | Credit risk; 8% of RWA; risk weights 0-100%
Basel II | 2004 | Measuring capital adequacy; 3 pillars
Basel III | 2010 | Absorb financial and economic stress; better risk management
## Basel II pillars
Minimum capital (credit, market, operational risk); supervisory review; market discipline (disclosure)
## Basel III tools
CET1, leverage ratio, LCR, NSFR, capital conservation buffer, countercyclical buffer
⚠ Basel = Basel Committee on Banking Supervision under BIS; not biodiversity, climate, aviation or doping
PYQ 2015: Basel III → stress absorption; PYQ 2007: Basel II → capital adequacy standards

topic: Prudential norms: Basel, CAR, lending rates and priority sector
t: Basel III in India → buffers and frameworks
text:
Tool | Fact
CCyB | Introduced 2015; trigger: credit-to-GDP gap; not activated
LCR + SLR | India mandates both (most economies only LCR)
Market-risk capital | Simplified Standardised Approach; from 1 April 2027
Exempt from market-risk rules | SFBs, Payments Banks, LABs, RRBs
## In news 2025-26
RBI proposed differentiated risk weights (lower for MSMEs and real estate) aligned with Basel III (Oct 2025)
RBI decided not to activate CCyB after reviewing indicators (PMF 2027 Q2)

topic: Prudential norms: Basel, CAR, lending rates and priority sector
t: MCLR → purpose and features
text:
Introduced 1 April 2016, replacing the base rate
Feature | Detail
Basis | Marginal cost of funds + negative carry on CRR + operating cost + tenor premium
Tenors | Separate MCLR for each tenor; reset periodically
Floor | Minimum rate below which a bank cannot lend (exceptions allowed)
Aim | Transparency in rate-setting; credit at rates fair to borrowers and banks
⚠ Both purposes correct (PYQ 2016) → Both 1 and 2
## In news 2025-26
Draft RBI (Interest Rates on Loans and Advances) Directions, 2026: floating personal and MSME loans to link to an external benchmark (repo, T-bill); credit-risk premium changes only after review; other spread parts fixed 3 years; from 1 April 2027
## Beyond your notes
External benchmark linking for new floating retail and MSE loans began 1 October 2019

topic: Prudential norms: Basel, CAR, lending rates and priority sector
t: Priority sector lending → sectors and targets
text:
Sectors: agriculture, MSMEs, export credit, education, housing, social infrastructure, renewable energy, weaker sections (SC, ST, PwD, minorities)

t: PSL guidelines 2025 → what changed

Item | New limit
Housing loan | ₹50 lakh (city >50 lakh pop.), ₹45 lakh (10-50 lakh), ₹35 lakh (<10 lakh)
Home repair | ₹10-15 lakh

topic: Prudential norms: Basel, CAR, lending rates and priority sector
t: Teaser loans → why a concern
text:
Low initial rate, rises after a fixed period → borrowers may default at higher rates
Point | Fact
Nature | Form of subprime lending (like 2008 crisis)
Segment in India | Mostly housing loans
Provisioning | 2% vs 0.4% for normal home loans
Banned? | No, but higher provisioning
⚠ NOT mainly for inexperienced entrepreneurs or export units
PYQ 2011: teaser loans → 1 only

t: Gold loans → RBI directions 2025-26
text:
Gold loan NPAs rose sharply in 2024; RBI flagged weak loan-to-value (LTV) monitoring
Rule | Detail
Effective | 1 January 2026 (harmonised for all lenders)
LTV cap | 75% for consumption bullet loans; accrued interest counts in LTV
Bullet loans | Tenor capped at 12 months
Valuation | 30-day average of 22-carat gold price
Ownership | No loan on gold of doubtful ownership
Banned | Loans against primary gold/silver and related assets (e.g. ETFs)
Same gold cannot back both a consumption and an income-generating loan
Loans must rest on repayment capacity with end-use records
⚠ LTV = maximum loan as a share of the collateral's appraised value
Economic Survey 2025-26: personal loan growth driven by gold loans

t: Banks Board Bureau → role and successor
text:
Item | Fact
Set up | 2016; idea of P.J. Nayak committee
Chair | A central government nominee (NOT RBI Governor)
Role | Recommend heads/board members of PSBs, PSU insurers, FIs
Also | Help PSBs with strategy and capital-raising plans
Fate | Delhi HC (2021) found it ineffective → replaced by FSIB
FSIB | From 1 July 2022; recommends whole-time directors and non-executive chairpersons
⚠ "RBI Governor chairs BBB" is false → 2 and 3 only
PYQ 2019: PSB chairmen selected by → Banks Board Bureau; PYQ 2022: BBB features

t: PSB recapitalisation → facts and traps
text:
Govt capital infusion into PSBs did not rise steadily over 2007-17; varied year to year
Indradhanush plan: capital infusion into PSBs
4R strategy: Recognition, Resolution, Recapitalisation, Reforms
Asset Quality Review (2015) exposed hidden NPAs

Budget 2026-27: High Level Committee on Banking for Viksit Bharat to review the sector (Economic Survey summary)

t: NPAs → classification and current level
text:
NPA = loan overdue 90 days or more (norm from 2004); agri loans: 1-2 crop seasons
Class | Period as NPA
Sub-standard | Up to 12 months
Doubtful | More than 12 months
Loss | Identified as uncollectible
Year | GNPA / NNPA of SCBs
Sept 2025 | 2.2% (multi-decadal low) / 0.5% (record low)
NPA recovery rate: 13.2% (FY18) → 26.2% (FY25); agri GNPA still 6.0%
## In news 2025-26
Rising gold loan NPAs; RBI gold loan directions (from 1 Jan 2026): LTV 75% for consumption bullet loans; bullet loans max 12 months

t: NPA crisis → causes and response
text:
## 1. Causes (Testbook)
Loan frauds and siphoning of funds
Weak creditworthiness assessment
Slow recovery mechanisms
## 2. Response
By | Measure
RBI | PCA framework (2002); AQR (2015); restructuring schemes like S4A; banks allowed to start insolvency
Government | 4R strategy; Indradhanush recapitalisation; IBC 2016; NARCL (2021-22)
Higher provisioning norms and asset quality reviews
PCA: RBI restricts a weak bank's lending and expansion till capital and asset quality improve
⚠ AQR (2015) was by RBI; 4R and Indradhanush were government steps

t: S4A and Inter-Creditor Agreement → what they were
text:
Scheme | Fact
S4A | RBI, 2016; ended Feb 2018
Aim | Rework finances of large corporates with genuine difficulty
How | Split debt into sustainable and unsustainable parts (by cash flows)
ICA | Signed July 2018 by banks and FIs (also LIC, HUDCO)
Under | Project Sashakt (Sunil Mehta committee)
Covers | Stressed loans ₹50 crore+ under consortium lending
Rule | 66% of lenders by value bind all
⚠ S4A is NOT part of IBC, NOT disinvestment, NOT ecological costing
⚠ ICA is NOT an independent regulator for ₹50 crore loans
PYQ 2017 (S4A) and 2019 (ICA): answer = RBI restructuring scheme; faster resolution of ₹50 crore+ consortium loans

t: IBC 2016 → process and actors
text:
Item | Fact
Applies to | Companies, partnerships, LLPs, individuals, personal guarantors
Regulator | IBBI (statutory; 10 members incl. Finance, Law Ministry, RBI)
Adjudicator | NCLT for companies; DRT for individuals and firms
Who decides | Committee of Creditors = financial creditors
Timeline | 180 days + extension (Testbook); 330-day outer limit, then liquidation (PMF 2026)
Small firms | 90 + 45 days (Testbook)
Liquidation order | Costs → secured creditors and workers → unsecured; govt dues below secured
Moratorium: no legal action against the debtor during resolution
⚠ NCLT does not handle individuals and partnership firms (that is DRT)
⚠ Government dues do not rank above secured creditors
## In news 2025-26
10 years of IBC (PIB 2026): over ₹4 lakh crore realised; 58% of closed cases rescued, 42% liquidated; S&P moved India from Group C to B; average overdue period 344 → 87 days

t: SARFAESI, ARCs and NARCL → powers
text:
Tool | Fact
SARFAESI Act 2002 | Lenders holding 75% of dues send a 60-day notice; then take possession of secured assets or take over management
ARCs | Buy bad loans from banks; set up under SARFAESI; modelled on US practice
NARCL | Announced in Budget 2021-22; takes over about ₹2 lakh crore stressed loans in phases
PCA | RBI framework (2002); limits lending and expansion of weak banks
SARFAESI lets banks act without courts against secured assets; aimed at wilful defaulters
ARC idea came from the Narasimham Committee
⚠ SARFAESI covers secured loans; IBC is the broader insolvency law
⚠ Preview: by 2026 stressed-asset resolution moved from voluntary Sashakt to an RBI-led mandatory framework plus IBC

t: Narasimham Committees → banking reforms
text:
Committee | Key recommendations
I (1991) | Cut CRR to 3-5%, SLR 38.5% → 25%; market-set interest rates; fewer PSBs via mergers; end dual control (RBI + Finance Ministry); ARCs; PSL redefined to 10%
II (1998) | 3-tier structure (2-3 international, 8-10 national, many local banks); CRAR 10%; NNPA below 5% (2000) and 3% (2002); merge strong banks, close weak; depoliticise boards
Outcomes: new private banks (from 1994; first UTI Bank, now Axis), prudential norms, capital adequacy, SARFAESI Act 2002
RRBs were also set up on a Narasimham Working Group report (1975)
⚠ Committee I (1991) is about the financial system; II (1998) about banking sector reforms

t: Interest Coverage Ratio → what it shows
text:
ICR = firm's earnings / interest payable: ability to pay interest from earnings
Statement | Verdict
Shows present risk of a borrower | Correct
Shows emerging risk (a falling ICR warns of trouble) | Correct
Higher ICR = worse debt servicing | Wrong: higher is better
Banks use it in credit appraisal before lending
⚠ Reversal trap: higher ICR = stronger borrower
PYQ 2020: ICR → 1 and 2 only
## Related terms
CASA ratio: share of low-cost current and savings deposits; higher CASA = lower cost of funds

topic: Financial inclusion: meaning and early steps
t: Financial inclusion → meaning, objectives and hindrances
text:
## 1. Definition (C. Rangarajan Committee on Financial Inclusion)
Ensuring access to financial services and timely and adequate credit where needed by vulnerable groups (weaker sections, low-income groups) at an affordable cost
Includes zero/minimum-balance banking for low-income groups (UPPCS 2008)
Objective of FI | Not an objective
Extend financial services to the poor | Shrinking banking infrastructure
Unlock growth potential of weaker sections | Concentrating credit in rich households
Extend financial sector into rural areas | -
Hindrances: low income, illiteracy, lack of bank branches - all three (UPUDA 2013)
NCERT: the poor depend on informal lenders (no collateral, high interest); the aim is cheaper formal credit for all
⚠ FI is about access + usage + quality, not only opening accounts (RBI FI-Index logic)

topic: Financial inclusion: meaning and early steps
t: Bank nationalisation and RRBs → what each did for inclusion
text:
Measure | Key facts
1969 nationalisation | 14 banks, Indira Gandhi govt, 19 July 1969; aim: branch expansion in rural areas, credit to priority sectors
1980 nationalisation | 6 more banks
RRBs | 2 Oct 1975; Narasimham Working Group; for small/marginal farmers, agricultural labourers, rural artisans
RRB ownership | Centre 50% : Sponsor bank 35% : State 15% (PMF)
RRB regulator | Regulated by RBI, supervised by NABARD; supported by sponsor bank
RRB functions (PMF): basic banking, MGNREGA wages and pensions, SHG finance, PMEGP and NRLM credit, UPI/RuPay
⚠ RRBs did not take over the Agricultural Refinance Corporation (that became part of NABARD) (UPPCS 2005)
