Symbol | Fact
National animal | Tiger (Panthera tigris)
National bird | Indian Peacock (Pavo cristatus)
National aquatic animal | Ganges River Dolphin
National river | Ganga (declared 2008)
National flower | Lotus (no formal notification, Govt told Rajya Sabha)
National fruit / tree | Mango / Banyan
National days | 15 Aug, 26 Jan, 2 Oct
Hindi Diwas | 14 September
Constitution Day | 26 November (since 2015)
National Flag, Anthem and Constitution are named in Art 51A(a); the emblem, song, calendar and animals rest on government decisions, not the Constitution
⚠ Only the Flag and Anthem appear in the Constitution's text (51A(a)); "national language" and "national song" do not

topic: Text, components and origin of the Preamble
t: Text of the Preamble → clause by clause
text:
WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC and to secure to all its citizens:
JUSTICE, social, economic and political;
LIBERTY of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship;
EQUALITY of status and of opportunity; and to promote among them all
FRATERNITY assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation;
IN OUR CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949, do HEREBY ADOPT, ENACT AND GIVE TO OURSELVES THIS CONSTITUTION.
Clause | Exact words to remember
Source | We, the people of India
Nature (order) | Sovereign → Socialist → Secular → Democratic → Republic
Objectives (order) | Justice → Liberty → Equality → Fraternity
Beneficiaries | "to secure to all its citizens"
Enacting words | adopt, enact and give to ourselves
⚠ Order trap: "Sovereign, Secular, Socialist" is wrong; Socialist comes before Secular (UP RO/ARO 2023, BPSC 2008)
⚠ Single paragraph; it says "citizens", not "persons" or "people's"

topic: Text, components and origin of the Preamble
t: Components → four things the Preamble reveals
text:
Component | What the Preamble says
Source of authority | We, the People of India (popular sovereignty)
Nature of the State | Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic
Objectives | Justice, Liberty, Equality, Fraternity
Date of adoption | 26 November 1949
Popular sovereignty: authority comes from the people, not from a monarch, legislature or external power (PMF)
NCERT: the Constitution is not "given" by great men; it is made by "We, the people"; people are makers of their own destiny
Testbook: two purposes: (i) the authority behind the Constitution, (ii) the goals it aims at
⚠ "We, the people of India" appears in the Preamble only (MPPSC 2016 option set: DPSP, FR, Citizenship, Preamble)
⚠ "People's sovereignty" because it begins with "We, the People of India" (BPSC 1994), not "Republic of People"

topic: Text, components and origin of the Preamble
t: Date clause → adoption, not commencement
text:
## 1. The dates
Event | Date
Objectives Resolution moved (Nehru) | 13 Dec 1946
Objectives Resolution adopted | 22 Jan 1947
Constitution adopted (date in Preamble) | 26 Nov 1949
Final meeting, signing; anthem, song adopted; Rajendra Prasad elected President | 24 Jan 1950
Constitution came into force | 26 Jan 1950
26 Nov declared Constitution Day (Samvidhan Divas; earlier Law Day) | 2015 (125th birth anniversary year of Ambedkar)
Some provisions (citizenship, elections, provisional Parliament, temporary provisions, short title) came into force on 26 Nov 1949 itself
⚠ The Preamble names 26 November 1949, the date of adoption; 26 Jan 1950 is commencement and is not in the Preamble
⚠ "26 January 1949" and "26 November 1950" are distractor dates
PYQ 1997: "In our Constituent Assembly this 'X' do hereby adopt..." X = twenty-sixth day of November, 1949
## In news 2025-26
Samvidhan Divas, 26 Nov 2025: marked 76 years since adoption (UPSC CA Nov 2025)
Constitution Day (26 Nov) vs Republic Day (26 Jan): Constitution Day is not a public holiday; marked by Preamble reading; Republic Day is a national holiday with the parade

topic: Text, components and origin of the Preamble
t: Objectives → how many types of each
text:
Ideal | Kinds named | Count
Justice | Social, economic, political | 3
Liberty | Thought, expression, belief, faith, worship | 5
Equality | Status, opportunity | 2
Fraternity | assuring (a) dignity of the individual (b) unity and integrity of the Nation | 1 (with 2 assurances)
Count in order J-L-E-F = 3, 5, 2, 1 (UPPSC 2018)
Justice social, economic and political influenced by the Russian Revolution (1917)
Liberty, Equality, Fraternity inspired by the French Revolution
⚠ Justice list has no "legal" justice; equality list has no "equality of income"
⚠ "Dignity of the individual" is in the Preamble (fraternity clause); UP Lower 1998: Preamble secures social and economic justice, liberty of thought and expression, equality of opportunity, dignity of the individual → all four correct

topic: Text, components and origin of the Preamble
t: Liberty clause → the five liberties (and what is missing)
text:
In the Preamble | Not in the Preamble
Liberty of thought | Economic liberty
Liberty of expression | Political liberty / social liberty
Liberty of belief | Liberty of association or movement
Liberty of faith | Liberty of conscience (that word is in Art 25)
Liberty of worship | Liberty of profession (that is Art 19(1)(g))
Detailed freedoms are in Part III: Art 19 (speech, expression), Art 21 (personal liberty), Art 25-28 (religion)
⚠ Economic appears with justice, never with liberty: "economic justice" yes, "economic liberty" no
⚠ "Thought and expression" go together in the Preamble; "conscience" is Art 25's word, not the Preamble's
PYQ 2017: which is not in the Preamble: liberty of thought / economic liberty / liberty of expression / liberty of belief → economic liberty
## In news 2025-26
PMF (75 years of the Constitution, Jan 2025 CA): Preamble "ensures liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship"; Art 19 and Art 21 carry it into enforceable rights

topic: Text, components and origin of the Preamble
t: Words NOT in the Preamble → common distractors
text:
Word/idea | Status
Federal / federation | Not mentioned (Art 1 says "Union of States")
Economic liberty | Not mentioned
People's (People's Republic) | Not mentioned (used in China's constitution)
Welfare State | Not mentioned (an aim read into DPSP)
Integrity | Not in the 1949 original; added 1976
Socialist, Secular | Not in the original; added 1976
Gram Swaraj, "Reliable", "Non-religious" | Never in it
Fundamental Duties | Not mentioned
Words present since 1949: Sovereign, Democratic, Republic, Justice, Liberty, Equality, Fraternity, dignity, unity of the Nation
⚠ UPPSC 2006: word not in the Preamble in 1975 → Integrity
⚠ BPSC 1995 sequence trap: "Sovereign, Socialist, People's, Democratic..." is wrong; correct sequence has no "People's"

topic: Text, components and origin of the Preamble
t: Origin and borrowings → where the Preamble came from
text:
Item | Source
Basis | Objectives Resolution (Nehru, moved 13 Dec 1946, adopted 22 Jan 1947)
Idea of a Preamble | USA (first constitution to begin with a Preamble)
Language | Australian Constitution (ROCKET Sheets)
Justice: social, economic, political | Russian Revolution (1917)
Liberty, Equality, Fraternity | French Revolution
Objectives Resolution envisaged India as an independent sovereign republic, all power derived from the people, safeguards for minorities and backward classes
Testbook: the Preamble was adopted last, after the rest of the Constitution, so it would match the adopted text and fix the date of enactment; in the USA the Preamble came first
⚠ "Objectives Resolution became the Preamble" is true (UPPSC 2009); it was moved by Nehru, not Ambedkar
## Beyond your notes
The motion "that the Preamble stand part of the Constitution" was adopted on 17 October 1949 (verify)

topic: Text, components and origin of the Preamble
t: Descriptions of the Preamble → who said what
text:
Description | By
Identity card of the Constitution | N.A. Palkhivala
Political horoscope | K.M. Munshi
Soul of the Constitution | Pandit Thakur Das Bhargava
"Expresses what we had thought or dreamt so long" | Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar
Constitution is the body, Preamble the soul; building vs foundation stone | Subhash Kashyap
Key to the minds of the makers | Supreme Court, Berubari (1960)
Core soul of the Constitution | SC in Golaknath (1967) (Preview)
NCERT: the best summary of the philosophy of the Constitution is the Preamble
⚠ Art 32 (not the Preamble) is the "heart and soul" of the Constitution per Ambedkar
## Beyond your notes
Ernest Barker called the Preamble the "key-note" of the Constitution; Hidayatullah called it the "soul"

topic: Nature of the State: the five keywords
t: Sovereign → meaning and limits
text:
India is internally supreme and externally independent; not dependent on or subordinate to any State
Membership of the Commonwealth or the UN does not dilute sovereignty
As a sovereign State, India may acquire foreign territory or cede its territory as the Constitution requires
Provision | Link to sovereignty
Art 1 | India, a "Union of States" (indivisible territory)
Art 2 | Parliament may admit/establish new States
Art 51 | Promotes international peace, keeps external discretion
Art 51A(c) | Duty to uphold sovereignty, unity and integrity
Third Schedule | Oaths of office affirm sovereignty
RPA Sec 29A(5) | Parties must affirm allegiance to sovereignty
⚠ "Sovereign" was in the original Preamble; the 42nd Amendment did not add it (UPPSC 2025 code trap)
⚠ India follows constitutional supremacy, not parliamentary sovereignty as in the UK
## Beyond your notes
Berubari (1960) also held that ceding territory needs a constitutional amendment under Art 368 (done by the 9th Amendment, 1960)

topic: Nature of the State: the five keywords
t: Socialist → what kind of socialism
text:
Added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976
Democratic socialism: social and economic justice and reduction of inequalities without communistic/State socialism, complete nationalisation or abolition of private property
Constitution already had a socialist orientation through the DPSP; the 42nd made it explicit
Point | Fact
Model | Mixed economy (public + private)
SC on socialism | Minerva Mills (1980): socialism a guiding principle aligned with Part IV
SC 2024 view | Socialism = commitment to a welfare state, not a rigid economic policy
Older meaning (Testbook) | State ownership of means of production and distribution
⚠ "Socialist" does not mean Marxist or Gandhian socialism alone; Indian socialism is a blend, mainly democratic
⚠ Testbook's "1976 Second Amendment" is a misprint: it is the 42nd (BPSC 2016, MPPSC 2023 answer: 42nd)
## Beyond your notes
D.S. Nakara (1983): SC described Indian socialism as a blend of Marxism and Gandhism leaning to Gandhian socialism; post-1991 LPG reforms diluted the State-led model

topic: Nature of the State: the five keywords
t: Secular → Indian secularism
text:
Added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976; no official State religion; freedom of religion; equal treatment of all religions
Positive secularism: principled State engagement with religion for equality and reform, not strict separation (PMF)
Provision | Secular content
Art 14 | Equality before law, State neutrality
Art 15, 16 | No discrimination on religion; equal opportunity in public jobs
Art 25-28 | Conscience, profess-practise-propagate; religious affairs; no tax for a religion; no religious instruction in State-funded institutions
Art 29, 30 | Minority rights to culture and educational institutions
Kesavananda (1973) | Secularism part of Basic Structure (LENS)
S.R. Bommai (1994) | Secularism part of Basic Structure
⚠ India was secular before 1976; the 42nd only made it explicit (LENS July 2025)
⚠ "Secular" in India = no religion of the State (UPPSC 2005), not "many religions" or "individual will"
⚠ The Preamble (not FRs, 9th Schedule or DPSP) describes India as a Secular State (UPPSC 2005)

topic: Nature of the State: the five keywords
t: Democratic and Republic → meaning
text:
Word | Meaning | Indian feature
Democratic | Authority flows from the people | Representative parliamentary democracy; universal adult franchise, periodic elections
Scope of democracy | Political and social and economic democracy | Founded on Liberty, Equality, Fraternity
Republic | Elected head of State, not hereditary | President, indirectly elected for a fixed term
Republic also means | Popular sovereignty, no hereditary privilege | Public offices open to all citizens
India keeps Commonwealth membership yet is a republic (head of Commonwealth is not India's head of State)
⚠ UK is democratic but not a republic (hereditary monarch); USA is democratic and republic (directly elected executive)
⚠ "Democratic Republic" alone was never India's status; "Sovereign" came first even in 1950

topic: Nature of the State: the five keywords
t: Keyword order and the original vs amended description
text:
Version | Words
Original (26 Jan 1950) | Sovereign Democratic Republic
After 42nd Amendment (1976) | Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic
Fraternity clause, original | dignity of the individual and the unity of the Nation
Fraternity clause, amended | dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation
Added words: exactly three: Socialist, Secular, Integrity
Not added by the 42nd: Sovereign, Democratic, Republic, Fraternity, dignity, Justice
⚠ UPPSC 2025 code question: of Socialist, Secular, Sovereign, Republic, only 1 and 2 were inserted
⚠ "Integrity" was inserted into the fraternity clause, not into the nature-of-State list

topic: Objectives and how the Constitution realises them
t: Economic justice → where it is stated and pursued
text:
Objective | Stated in | Pursued through
Social justice | Preamble | FRs (Art 15, 17) + DPSP (Art 38, 46)
Economic justice | Preamble | DPSP (Art 38, 39, 41, 43)
Political justice | Preamble | Universal adult franchise (Art 326), Art 15-16 equality in office
Art 38: State to secure a social order founded on social, economic and political justice; minimise inequalities in income, status, opportunity
Art 39: adequate livelihood, distribution of material resources (39b), no concentration of wealth (39c), equal pay
Art 39A (42nd CAA 1976): equal justice and free legal aid
⚠ Economic justice is in the Preamble and DPSP, not in Fundamental Rights
⚠ Art 38 is the only DPSP that repeats the Preamble's three justices word for word
PYQ 2013: economic justice is provided in the Preamble and the DPSP (not FRs + DPSP, not Preamble + FRs)

topic: Objectives and how the Constitution realises them
t: Each ideal → its home in the Constitution
text:
Preamble ideal | Main provisions that realise it
Justice (social, economic, political) | Art 38, 39, 39A (DPSP); Art 326 (franchise); Art 17
Liberty (5 kinds) | Art 19, 21, 25-28 (Part III)
Equality of status | Art 14, 15, 17 (untouchability), 18 (titles)
Equality of opportunity | Art 16 (public employment), 15(4)
Fraternity | Single citizenship (Part II), Art 17, Art 51A(e)
Unity and integrity | Art 1, Art 51A(c)
NCERT: the Preamble mentions two things about equality, status and opportunity; Art 16(4) allows reservation to achieve it
⚠ Equality in the Preamble covers status and opportunity, not "equality of income" or "equality of wealth"
⚠ Liberty is not absolute: secured "within constitutional limitations" (reasonable restrictions under Art 19(2)-(6))

topic: Objectives and how the Constitution realises them
t: Fraternity → the two assurances
text:
Fraternity = brotherhood and social harmony; assures (1) dignity of the individual, (2) unity and integrity of the Nation
Ambedkar: liberty, equality, fraternity are an inseparable trinity; "to divorce one from the other is to defeat the very purpose of democracy"
Provision | How it serves fraternity
Part II | Single citizenship (unlike USA)
Art 14-18 | Equality floor; untouchability abolished, titles banned
Art 25 | Inter-faith coexistence
Art 38, 39A | Social order, free legal aid
Art 51A(e) | Duty to promote harmony and common brotherhood
⚠ Fraternity is the only ideal the Preamble says "to promote"; justice, liberty and equality are "to secure"
## In news 2025-26
PMF LENS June 2026: fraternity is "the only constitutional ideal that law alone can neither create nor enforce"; cases cited:
Case | Fraternity holding
Tehseen Poonawalla (2018) | Mob lynching assaults pluralist fabric
Kaushal Kishor (2023) | Public functionaries must restrain speech
Shaheen Abdulla (2023) | Secular harmony a prerequisite
Sec 6A Citizenship case (2024) | "Live and let live" approach
UGC Equity Rules case (2026) | Segregation clauses prima facie "separate but equal", may violate fraternity
PMF LENS Sept 2026: a Uniform Civil Code is argued to further the Preamble's ideal of fraternity through a cohesive civic identity

t: Is the Preamble part of the Constitution → the cases
text:
Case | Year | Holding on the Preamble
In re Berubari Union | 1960 | Not a part of the Constitution; but a key to the minds of the makers and an aid to interpretation
Golaknath | 1967 | Treated as part / "core soul" (ROCKET, Preview)
Kesavananda Bharati | 1973 | Is a part; can be amended under Art 368, subject to Basic Structure
S.R. Bommai | 1994 | Reaffirmed it is a part (Preview, Testbook)
Union Govt v LIC of India | 1995 | Reaffirmed: integral part of the Constitution
Kesavananda overruled Berubari on status; the court noted the Preamble was adopted by the Assembly like other parts
⚠ Berubari was an advisory reference (Art 143); the "not a part" view is overruled, but its "key to the minds" line survives
⚠ LENS cites Berubari as 1961; PMF Indian Polity and all other sources give 1960 → use 1960
⚠ PMF table lists only Berubari, Kesavananda, LIC; Golaknath and Bommai come from lower sources

t: Legal effect → what the Preamble can and cannot do
text:
Question | Answer
Part of the Constitution? | Yes (Kesavananda 1973)
Justiciable / enforceable in court? | No
Independent legal effect? | No; works only with other parts
Source of power to legislature? | No
Limitation on power? | No (not a prohibition on express powers)
Can it override specific provisions? | No
Aid to interpretation? | Yes, where an Article is ambiguous
Can it be amended? | Yes, Art 368, Basic Structure intact
⚠ The trap pair: "part but no legal effect" (wrong) vs "part but no legal effect independently of other parts" (right)
⚠ "Same legal effect as any other part" is wrong: unlike FRs it cannot be enforced by a writ
PYQ 2020: Preamble is a part of the Constitution but has no legal effect independently of other parts (option d)
UPPSC 2009: Objectives Resolution became Preamble, non-justiciable, cannot override specific provisions → true; "cannot be amended" → false

t: Key to the minds of the makers → interpretive guide
text:
Berubari (1960): the Preamble is a key to open the minds of the makers; expresses general purposes and philosophy
Courts use it to understand the purpose of provisions; only where the words are ambiguous or bear more than one meaning
State of Rajasthan v Basant Nahata: where an Article is ambiguous, one may go to the Preamble's goals for guidance; not where the meaning is clear
Document | "Mind of the makers"?
Preamble | Yes (Berubari)
Fundamental Rights | No (enforceable rights)
DPSP | No ("novel feature", fundamental in governance)
Fundamental Duties | No (added 1976, not by the makers)
⚠ FDs (Part IVA) were added by the 42nd Amendment, so they cannot reflect the makers' minds
PYQ 2017: "the mind of the makers of the Constitution is reflected in" → the Preamble

t: Significance → four roles (PMF)
text:
Role | What it means
Constitutional philosophy | Ideals and vision behind the Constitution
Interpretative guide | Courts read provisions in its light; key to makers' minds
Constitutional objectives | Justice, Liberty, Equality, Fraternity direct governance
Constitutional identity | Palkhivala's "identity card"
Kesavananda: the fundamental features in the Preamble (sovereign democratic republic, justice, liberty, equality, fraternity) are part of the Basic Structure
Secularism, democracy, sovereignty, republican form: all listed Basic Structure elements (PMF p.98)
⚠ "Not enforceable" does not mean "not important": it binds the interpretation of every enforceable provision
⚠ The Preamble neither grants a right nor creates a power by itself (ROCKET)

t: 42nd Amendment, 1976 → what changed in the Preamble
text:
Before | After 42nd CAA
Sovereign Democratic Republic | Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic
unity of the Nation | unity and integrity of the Nation
Three words added: Socialist, Secular, Integrity; the only amendment of the Preamble so far
Enacted during the Emergency (1975-77), PM Indira Gandhi; based on the Swaran Singh Committee
Called the "Mini-Constitution"; changed the Preamble, the Seventh Schedule and 53 Articles (NCERT)
Other 42nd changes (not Preamble) | 
Fundamental Duties (Part IVA, Art 51A) | Added
New DPSPs (39A, 43A, 48A) | Added
Art 368(4)-(5) | Barred review of amendments (struck down, Minerva Mills 1980)
Delimitation | Seats frozen
⚠ "Socialist" was added by the 42nd, not 44th, 46th or 52nd; "Secular" also 42nd, not 25th
⚠ The 44th (1978) undid most Emergency changes but retained the Preamble changes

t: Status on 26 January 1950 → the exact words
text:
On commencement India was a Sovereign Democratic Republic
Option UPSC gave | Correct?
A Democratic Republic | No ("Sovereign" missing)
A Sovereign Democratic Republic | Yes
A Sovereign Secular Democratic Republic | No (Secular added 1976)
A Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic | No (status only after 1976)
In the 1949 text: Sovereign, Democratic, Republic, Justice, Liberty, Equality, Fraternity, "unity of the Nation"
⚠ Words absent on 26 Nov 1949 (UPPSC 2009): Socialist, Integrity, Secular; Republic was present
PYQ 2021: exact constitutional status of India on 26 Jan 1950 → a Sovereign Democratic Republic

t: Amendability → Kesavananda and the Basic Structure limit
text:
Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala, judgment 24 April 1973: Preamble is part of the Constitution and can be amended under Art 368
Limit: the basic elements/fundamental features in the Preamble cannot be destroyed (Basic Structure)
Hence the 42nd Amendment's additions were valid: they elaborated, did not destroy, the basic features
Amendable? | Rule
Preamble words | Yes, by Art 368 (special majority)
Basic features in it | No destruction allowed
Number of amendments | One (42nd, 1976)
Cut-off for Basic Structure | Amendments after 24 April 1973 (Waman Rao 1980)
⚠ "Preamble cannot be amended" is false; "Preamble has been amended many times" is false
## Beyond your notes
Kesavananda: 13-judge bench, 7:6 majority

t: Challenge to "socialist" and "secular" → SC 2024 and the debate
text:
SC dismissed petitions challenging the insertion of "socialist" and "secular" by the 42nd Amendment (two-judge bench led by the then CJI, Nov 2024)
Holding | Detail
Retrospective amendment | Parliament's Art 368 power reaches the Preamble even though the adoption date is 26 Nov 1949
Living document | Terms reflect evolving democratic needs
Delay | Petitions filed decades later; terms widely accepted
Secularism | Art 14, 15, 16 bar religious discrimination: State neutrality
Socialism | Welfare State, no rigid economic policy
The terms do not impede legislation or infringe FRs, so long as laws respect the Basic Structure
⚠ The date "26 November 1949" stayed unchanged after 1976; this was the basis of the "retrospective" objection the SC rejected
## In news 2025-26
June 2025: 50th anniversary of the Emergency (from 25 June 1975); Union Cabinet resolution honoured the resistance; the 42nd ("Mini-Constitution") changed "Sovereign Democratic Republic" to "Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic" (Current Care June 2025)
July 2025 (PMF LENS): political debates questioned adding "socialist" and "secular"; experts and SC rulings affirm secularism was always inherent
Republic Day 2026 (77th): CA files recall the 42nd added Socialist and Secular to the Preamble
## Beyond your notes
The 2024 case is Dr Balram Singh v Union of India, decided 25 Nov 2024 by CJI Sanjiv Khanna and Justice Sanjay Kumar (verify)
June 2025 call by RSS general secretary Dattatreya Hosabale to review "socialist" and "secular" triggered the debate (verify)

t: Articles 1-4 → what each says
text:
Article | Provision
Art 1 | Name and territory: "India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States"
Art 2 | Admission or establishment of new States (territory not already part of India)
Art 3 | Formation of new States; alteration of areas, boundaries or names of existing States
Art 4 | Laws under Art 2 and 3 may amend the First and Fourth Schedules; not Art 368 amendments
Part I (Art 1-4) + First Schedule = Union and its territory
"Union of States", not "Federation": (1) federation not the result of an agreement among States; (2) no State can secede
"Indestructible Union of destructible States": Parliament can reorganise States without their consent
Term | Covers
Union of India | States only
Territory of India | States + Union Territories + territories that may be acquired
⚠ "Territory of India" is wider than "Union of India"
⚠ Art 2 = outside territory coming in (e.g. Sikkim); Art 3 = internal reorganisation

t: Art 3 → procedure for a new State or a name change
text:
## 1. What Parliament can do by law
Form a new State (separation, uniting States/parts, uniting territory to a part); increase or diminish area; alter boundaries; alter name
## 2. Procedure
Step | Rule
Introduction | Either House, only on the President's recommendation
Reference | President refers Bill to the affected State Legislature for views within a fixed period (extendable)
Views | Not binding on President or Parliament
Amendments by Parliament | Need no fresh reference to the State
Majority | Simple majority
UTs | "State" includes UT, but no reference to any legislature is needed for a UT
⚠ Constitution requires consultation, not consent of the State
⚠ Bill cannot be introduced on a private member's initiative without the President's recommendation
## In news 2025-26
"Kerala" → "Keralam": Cabinet approval (Feb 2026, PMF LENS); Kerala (Alteration of Name) Bill, 2026 passed by Lok Sabha first, then Rajya Sabha; President Droupadi Murmu assented (Aug 2026, Praveen CA 360); First Schedule amended under Art 3
Kerala Assembly had unanimously supported and sent the proposal in June 2024
A Private Member's Bill proposed a Permanent Framework for State Reorganisation (PMF LENS Feb 2026)

t: New State → First and Fourth Schedule, not Art 368
text:
Art 4: laws under Art 2/3 amend the First Schedule (names and territories of States/UTs) and the Fourth Schedule (Rajya Sabha seats)
Such laws are not deemed constitutional amendments under Art 368 → simple majority
Laws "not deemed amendments under Art 368" | Subject
Art 4 | New States, boundaries, names (Art 2, 3)
Art 169 | Creating/abolishing Legislative Councils
Art 239A | Legislature/CoM for Puducherry
Fifth Schedule para 7, Sixth Schedule para 21 | Amending those Schedules
⚠ New State = law by Parliament under Art 3-4; not an amendment under Art 368, not ratification by half the States
PYQ 2001: creating a new State needs amending the First Schedule by a law under Art 3-4 (Fourth Schedule too, for RS seats)
## Beyond your notes
Art 239AA (Delhi) laws are also "not deemed amendments under Art 368"

t: Cession of territory → Berubari, Maganbhai and the 100th Amendment
text:
Case / Act | Position
Berubari Union (1960) | Art 3 cannot cede Indian territory to a foreign State; cession needs Art 368 amendment
9th Amendment, 1960 | Transferred Berubari areas to Pakistan (East)
Maganbhai Ishwarbhai Patel (1969) | Settlement/demarcation of a boundary (no cession) needs no amendment
100th Amendment, 2015 | India-Bangladesh LBA: exchange of enclaves
⚠ Art 3 = internal change, simple majority; cession to a foreign country = Art 368 amendment
⚠ Kutch (Rann) award was implemented without an amendment because it was demarcation, not cession (Maganbhai)
## Beyond your notes
The 100th Amendment amended the First Schedule entries of Assam, West Bengal, Meghalaya and Tripura

topic: Evolution of States and Union Territories
t: Integration and linguistic reorganisation → commissions and dates
text:
Body / event | Year | Key point
552 princely States | 1947 | 549 joined; Hyderabad, Junagadh, Kashmir later
Junagadh / Hyderabad / J&K | 1947-48 | Plebiscite / Operation Polo (1948) / Instrument of Accession (Oct 1947)
Dhar Commission (S.K. Dhar) | 1948 | Against language as sole basis; administrative convenience
JVP Committee (Nehru, Patel, Pattabhi Sitaramayya) | 1949 | Rejected linguistic States for now
Andhra State | 1953 | First linguistic State after Potti Sriramulu's death
Fazl Ali Commission (H.N. Kunzru, K.M. Panikkar) | 1953 | Language important, not sole basis; rejected "one language, one State"
States Reorganisation Act + 7th Amendment | 1956 | Abolished Part A/B/C/D; 14 States, 6 UTs
1950 classification: Part A, B, C States + Part D territories = 29 units
1956 UTs: A&N, Delhi, Himachal Pradesh, Laccadive-Minicoy-Amindivi, Manipur, Tripura
⚠ JVP = Jawaharlal, Vallabhbhai, Pattabhi (not Jayaprakash)
⚠ Manipur and Tripura were UTs in 1956, became States in 1972

t: Statehood timeline → order of formation
text:
Year | Development

t: Single citizenship → what it means and its limits
text:
Every citizen owes allegiance to the Union; no separate State citizenship (unlike the USA, which has dual citizenship: federal + State)
Promotes national unity, uniform civic status
Exception allowed | Article
Residence as a condition for certain public jobs (law by Parliament) | Art 16(3)
Restrictions on movement/residence to protect Scheduled Tribes | Art 19(5)
Constitution has no permanent code on citizenship: Art 5-11 deal with citizenship at commencement; later matters by Citizenship Act, 1955 (Art 11)
⚠ India: single citizenship + single Constitution for all States (J&K's separate citizenship ended with Art 370 changes in 2019)
⚠ Dual citizenship in the sense of holding a foreign passport is not allowed (Art 9); OCI is not dual citizenship

Art 8 | Persons of Indian origin abroad: registration by Indian diplomatic/consular office
Art 9 | Voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship → ceases to be a citizen

Art 11 | Parliament regulates citizenship by law

Mode | Core rule
Birth | Depends on date of birth (see next page)
Descent | Born outside India to Indian parent(s); register at consulate within 1 year
Registration | PIO / spouse (7 years residence), minors, OCI 5 years + 12 months
Naturalisation | 11 of 14 years + 12 months continuous; renounce foreign citizenship; Eighth Schedule language
Incorporation of territory | Centre notifies by order (e.g. Citizenship (Pondicherry) Order, 1962)

Centre may waive naturalisation conditions for distinguished service to science, philosophy, art, literature, world peace, human progress

topic: Citizenship Act 1955: acquisition, loss, CAA and OCI
t: Loss → renunciation, termination, deprivation
text:
Mode | How | Note
Renunciation | Voluntary declaration by adult | Minor children also lose; may resume within 1 year of majority; may be withheld during war
Termination | Automatic on voluntarily acquiring foreign citizenship | Not during a war India is in
Deprivation | Compulsory order by the Central Government | Only for citizens by registration or naturalisation
Deprivation grounds:
Citizenship obtained by fraud, false representation, concealment
Disloyalty or disaffection to the Constitution
Unlawful trade/communication with enemy during war
Imprisonment 2 years+ within 5 years of registration/naturalisation
7 years continuous ordinary residence abroad (exceptions: students, Govt/international service, annual registration at consulate)
⚠ A citizen by birth is not deprived; deprivation applies to registered/naturalised citizens

topic: Features, Art 12-13 and Who Can Claim FRs
t: Part III at a glance → six rights and their Articles
text:
## 1. Basics
Part III = Articles 12 to 35 (24 Articles); "Magna Carta of India"; inspired by the US Bill of Rights
Demand: Swaraj Bill 1895 → Motilal Nehru Report 1928 → Karachi Session 1931 (presided by Sardar Patel; resolution on FRs and Economic Programme)
Constituent Assembly: Sardar Patel chaired the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, Minorities, Tribal and Excluded Areas
NCERT: ordinary legal rights change by ordinary law; FRs change only by amending the Constitution
Originally 7 FRs, now 6: Right to Property removed by 44th Amdt 1978 (Art 19(1)(f) and 31 repealed → Art 300A)
Right | Articles | No. of Articles
Right to Equality | 14-18 | 5
Right to Freedom | 19-22 (incl. 21A) | 4 (+21A)
Right against Exploitation | 23-24 | 2
Freedom of Religion | 25-28 | 4
Cultural and Educational | 29-30 | 2
Constitutional Remedies | 32 | 1
⚠ Art 31, 33, 34, 35 lie in Part III but are not among the six rights; Art 226 is not in Part III
PYQ 2002: "Right to Equality is granted by five Articles" → 14 to 18; distractors 13-17, 15-19, 16-20

topic: Features, Art 12-13 and Who Can Claim FRs
t: Citizens vs persons → who can claim which FR
text:
Available to | Articles
Citizens only | 15, 16, 19, 29 (+ 30, see ⚠ below)
All persons (citizens + foreigners) | 14, 20, 21, 21A, 22, 23, 24, 25-28
Not to enemy aliens | Art 22 (arrest and detention safeguards)
Art 14 covers even legal persons (companies)
⚠ Sources differ on Art 30: ROCKET Sheets list citizen-only rights as 5 (15, 16, 19, 29, 30); Indian Polity lists 4 (15, 16, 19, 29) and says Art 30 belongs to religious and linguistic minorities, its text not limited to "citizens". In a "how many citizen-only" question, the standard count is 15, 16, 19, 29, 30
Exam shortcut: "all FRs except 15, 16, 19, 29, 30 are available to foreigners"
## In news 2025-26
Oct 2026 (LENS): OCI cardholders get Art 14 and 21 (rights of every person) but not Art 19 (speech, assembly, movement, residence); no vote or legislative office
Louis De Raedt 1991: broad power to expel foreigners; right to reside and settle is for citizens only
PYQ 1999: A British citizen in India cannot claim freedom of trade and profession (Art 19(1)(g)); he can claim equality before law (14), life and liberty (21), freedom of religion (25)

topic: Features, Art 12-13 and Who Can Claim FRs
t: Features of FRs → justiciability, horizontal rights, suspension
text:
Feature | What to remember
Justiciable | Move SC (Art 32) or HC (Art 226) directly
Against State | Most operate only against the State (Art 12)
Also against private persons | Art 15(2), 17, 23, 24
Not absolute | Reasonable restrictions allowed
Amendable | Under Art 368, but not the Basic Structure (Kesavananda 1973)
Saved laws | Operation limited by Art 31A, 31B, 31C, 33, 34
Emergency | Art 358 (Art 19) and Art 359 (others); Art 20 and 21 never suspended (44th Amdt)
Legislation | Art 35: only Parliament legislates to give effect to certain FRs
Some FRs are negative (prohibit the State), some positive (e.g. Art 21A)
Golaknath 1967: Parliament cannot amend FRs → 24th Amdt 1971 affirmed the power

topic: Features, Art 12-13 and Who Can Claim FRs
t: Article 12 → what counts as 'State'
text:
## 1. "State" for Part III includes
Government and Parliament of India
State Governments and State Legislatures
Local authorities: municipalities, panchayats
Other authorities within India or under the control of the Government of India
## 2. Judicial reading
"Other authorities" = statutory and some non-statutory bodies that are an instrumentality or agency of the State
Art 36 adopts the same meaning of "State" for Part IV (DPSPs)
⚠ Because local authorities are "State", municipalities and panchayats are bound by FRs
A private body is not "State", but writs can still reach it if it does a public duty (see Writs)
Zee Telefilms 2005: doing public functions does not make a private body "State" unless the government dominates it financially, functionally and administratively
## In news 2025-26
CIC (LENS May 2026): BCCI is not a "public authority" under RTI Act Sec 2(h), so it is exempt from RTI; consistent with BCCI not being "State" under Art 12

topic: Features, Art 12-13 and Who Can Claim FRs
t: Article 13 → meaning of 'law' and judicial review
text:
## 1. What Art 13 does
Laws inconsistent with or in derogation of FRs are void to the extent of inconsistency: the basis of judicial review
Art 13(1): pre-Constitution laws; Art 13(2): State shall not make laws taking away FRs
## 2. "Law" under Art 13(3)(a) includes
Included | 
Permanent laws of legislatures, ordinances | orders, bye-laws, rules, regulations, notifications
Custom or usage having the force of law | 
## 3. Doctrines
Doctrine | Meaning
Severability | Only the offending part is void; the rest survives
Eclipse | A pre-Constitution law clashing with an FR is dormant, not dead; revives if the bar is removed
Waiver | A citizen cannot waive an FR
⚠ A constitutional amendment is not "law" under Art 13 (Art 13(4) added by 24th Amdt 1971), but it can be struck down if it damages the Basic Structure
PYQ 2026: X said "law" includes ordinances, orders, rules, regulations but not custom; Y said custom or usage is included → only Y is correct

17 | Untouchability abolished; practice in any form forbidden; an offence | All; also against private persons
18 | Abolition of titles (except military and academic) | Citizens and some foreigners
⚠ Untouchability (Art 17) sits under Right to Equality, not under Right against Exploitation or Freedom
⚠ Art 14 says "any person"; Art 15 and 16 say "any citizen"

t: Article 14 → equality before law vs equal protection, arbitrariness
text:
Equality before law | Equal protection of laws
British origin | American origin
Negative concept | Positive concept
No special privileges | Equal treatment in equal circumstances
Equal subjection to ordinary law | Like persons treated alike
Equality before law = Dicey's Rule of Law: absence of arbitrary power, equality before ordinary law, primacy of rights; Rule of Law is Basic Structure
Reasonable classification allowed, class legislation barred: test = intelligible differentia + rational nexus with the object
Anti-arbitrariness: E.P. Royappa 1974 (arbitrariness is antithetical to equality); manifest arbitrariness test; natural justice is part of Art 14
Anwar Ali Sarkar 1952: Special Courts Act 1950 struck down under Art 14
Exceptions: President and Governors (Art 361), MPs/MLAs speech (105, 194), 361A, foreign diplomats, UN agencies
PYQ 2021: a law giving the executive unguided and uncontrolled discretion violates Art 14 (not Art 28, 32 or 44)

## 1. Timeline
Stage | Provision
Original | FR under Art 19(1)(f) and Art 31
1st, 4th, 7th, 25th, 39th, 40th, 42nd Amdts | Curtailed Art 31
44th Amdt 1978 (Janata Party govt, Morarji Desai) | Repealed 19(1)(f) and 31; inserted Art 300A in Part XII
## 2. Status today
Art 300A: "no person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law"
A constitutional/legal right, not an FR; available to any person (citizens and non-citizens)

⚠ Art 301 = freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse, not property

## In news 2025-26
2026: 75 years of the 1st Amendment Act 1951 (assent by President Rajendra Prasad): it added three new grounds to 19(2) (incl. public order, incitement), Art 15(4), Art 31A, 31B and the Ninth Schedule: all four are correct in a "how many" question
## Beyond your notes
Nov 2024, 9-judge bench (Property Owners Association v State of Maharashtra): Art 31C survives as upheld in Kesavananda; not every private resource is a "material resource of the community" under 39(b)
Clause | Ruling to remember
31A | Saves agrarian reform laws from Art 14, 19
31B | Ninth Schedule laws after 24 Apr 1973 reviewable (I.R. Coelho 2007)
31C | Minerva Mills 1980 struck the 42nd Amdt extension to all DPSPs

t: Five writs → meaning and against whom
text:
Writ | Meaning | Purpose | Lies against
Habeas Corpus | "To have the body" | Release from unlawful detention | Public authorities and private individuals
Mandamus | "We command" | Compel a public/statutory duty | Public officials, public bodies, corporations, inferior courts, tribunals, govt
Prohibition | "To forbid" | Stop a lower court exceeding jurisdiction (pending case) | Judicial and quasi-judicial bodies only
Certiorari | "To be certified/informed" | Quash an order or transfer a case | Courts, tribunals; since 1991 also administrative bodies affecting rights
Quo Warranto | "By what authority" | Test legality of claim to public office | Holder of substantive public office of permanent character (statute/Constitution)
Writs are English prerogative writs; issued by SC (Art 32) and HCs (Art 226)
Quo warranto can be sought by any interested person, not only the aggrieved
PYQ 2024: Prohibition = order to a lower court to stop proceedings (not to an officer, legislature or government)

t: Writs → where they do NOT lie
text:
Writ | Not available
Habeas Corpus | Detention lawful; contempt of legislature or court; detention by competent court; outside court's jurisdiction
Mandamus | Private individual/body (unless public duty); departmental instruction without statutory force; discretionary duty; contractual obligation; President/Governors; HC Chief Justice acting judicially
Prohibition | Administrative authorities, legislatures, private bodies
Certiorari | Legislative bodies, private individuals/bodies
Quo Warranto | Ministerial office, private office
⚠ UPSC 2022 key treated "mandamus will not lie against a company even if a Government company" as correct; books say mandamus can issue to public bodies and corporations doing a public duty. In UPSC, follow the 2022 key
## In news 2025-26
Nov 2025, Presidential Reference opinion (5 judges): courts cannot fix deadlines for Governor/President on Bills or deem assent, but may issue a limited mandamus to act within a reasonable time in prolonged, unexplained inaction; Art 361 immunity does not shield the office
PYQ 2022: all three correct: mandamus not against private body without public duty; not against a company; any public-minded person can seek quo warranto

t: Certiorari vs prohibition → preventive or curative
text:
| Prohibition | Certiorari
Stage | While case is pending | After order passed (or to transfer a pending case)
Nature | Preventive | Curative/corrective (books also call it preventive + curative)
Directs | Inactivity | Quash / transfer
Targets | Judicial, quasi-judicial only | Also administrative (since 1991)
Mandamus directs activity; prohibition directs inactivity
Grounds for certiorari: excess of jurisdiction, lack of jurisdiction, error of law
Both are issued by a higher court to a lower court or tribunal
Injunction (from USA, not named in Constitution): mandatory (like mandamus, but against private parties) and preventive (to litigants, not lower courts)

t: Article 32 vs Article 226 → scope and status
text:
| Art 32 (SC) | Art 226 (HC)
Purpose | Only FRs | FRs and any other purpose (legal rights)
Status | Itself an FR | Not an FR (constitutional right)
Discretion | SC cannot refuse if FR violated | Discretionary
Territory | Whole of India | Territorial / cause of action
Emergency | Can be suspended under Art 359 | Not suspended
Ambedkar: Art 32 is the "heart and soul" of the Constitution
Art 32 is Basic Structure (L. Chandra Kumar); powers: original, wide, not exclusive
Art 32(3): Parliament may empower other courts (not HCs) to issue writs
⚠ HC writ power is wider in purpose; SC's is narrower but is itself an FR
PYQ 2002: "heart and soul" = Right to Constitutional Remedies (not religion, property, equality)

t: Approaching the SC → locus standi, res judicata, refusals
text:
Rule | Meaning
Locus standi relaxed | PIL, epistolary (letter/postcard) jurisdiction, suo motu
Res judicata | HC dismissed on merits → no fresh Art 32 petition (only appeal); not if dismissed otherwise
Habeas corpus | Exception to res judicata
Laches | Unexplained delay can bar relief
Other refusals | Malicious petition, suppression of facts, adequate alternative remedy
Art 32(1): right to move SC by "appropriate proceedings"; the SC decides what is appropriate
Romesh Thappar 1950: Art 32 is a "guaranteed" remedy
ADM Jabalpur 1976 ("Habeas Corpus case"): upheld suspension of right to move courts in Emergency; later overruled

t: Articles 33-35 and Emergency → limits on FRs
text:
Article | Content
33 | Parliament (not States) may restrict FRs of armed forces, police/public-order forces, intelligence bodies, their telecom staff
34 | Restrictions while martial law is in force; Parliament may indemnify acts; martial law not defined
35 | Parliament only legislates on 16(3), 32(3), 33, 34 and punishments for Part III offences
358 | Art 19 suspended automatically; only war/external aggression (not armed rebellion)
359 | President suspends enforcement of named FRs; not Art 20, 21
Martial law ≠ National Emergency (Art 352)
Oct 2026: adultery cases in the Army: Joseph Shine (2018) was clarified in 2023 (5 judges) as not affecting the Armed Forces Acts; under Art 33 forces are a distinct class (Army Act 1950 Sec 45, 63)
## In news 2025-26
South Korea: Parliament swiftly reversed a martial law declaration, reviving debate on emergency powers (India: Art 34)
50 years of the 1975 Emergency (25 June 1975 - 21 March 1977): FRs suspended, detentions under MISA, COFEPOSA; 42nd Amdt gave DPSPs primacy via Art 31C
Jul 2026 (LENS) recap of 44th Amdt safeguards: "internal disturbance" → armed rebellion; written Cabinet advice; approval in one month by special majority; Art 20, 21 non-derogable
⚠ After 44th Amdt: Art 358 needs a war/external aggression emergency; Art 20 and 21 survive every emergency

t: Article 37 → enforceable or not, and what it still requires
text:
## 1. The two halves of Art 37
Half of Art 37 | What it says
First half | DPSPs shall not be enforceable by any court (non-justiciable)
Second half | They are fundamental in the governance of the country
Duty | It is the duty of the State to apply them in making laws
So DPSPs are non-justiciable but not meaningless: they guide law-making
Courts cannot compel a government to implement them
Courts may consider a DPSP when judging whether a restriction on Art 14 or 19 is reasonable
⚠ "Fundamental for the governance of the country" = DPSPs only, not FRs, not Fundamental Duties
⚠ "Enforceable by courts" is wrong; "to influence the making of laws" is right
PYQ 2020: Part IV statements → "not enforceable by any court" + "influence the making of laws" = 2 and 3 only
PYQ 2013: which are "fundamental in the governance of the country" → DPSPs (trap: FRs)

t: Purpose of DPSPs → which democracy and which State
text:
## 1. What DPSPs aim at
Part | Democracy it secures | Kind of State
Part III (FRs) | Political democracy | Limits the State
Part IV (DPSPs) | Social and economic democracy | Welfare State
DPSPs seek to turn India from a colonial Police State into a Welfare State
They give content to justice, liberty, equality, fraternity of the Preamble
Testbook: Art 38 and 39 give meaning to "socialist"; Art 44 (UCC) to "secular"
⚠ Purpose is social AND economic democracy, not "social democracy" alone, not "political", not "Gandhian"
⚠ Both statements of PYQ 2015 are true: they spell out socio-economic democracy and are not enforceable
PYQ 2002: purpose of DPSPs → social and economic democracy (distractors: political, social, Gandhian)
PYQ 2015: "spell out socio-economic democracy" + "not enforceable by any court" → both correct

t: DPSPs and the organs of State → limitation or direction
text:
## 1. What DPSPs are and are not
Feature | DPSPs | FRs
Nature | Positive directions to the State | Negative limits on the State
Addressed to | Legislature, executive, administrative authorities | Same State (Art 12)
Limit on legislative function? | No | Yes (Art 13 voids laws)
Limit on executive function? | No | Yes
Remedy | None in court | Art 32 and 226
DPSPs are instructions and recommendations, not restraints
A law that ignores a DPSP is not void; a law that violates an FR is void (Art 13)
⚠ "DPSPs constitute limitations upon legislative and executive function" → neither 1 nor 2
PYQ 2017: DPSPs as limitations on (1) legislative (2) executive function → Neither 1 nor 2

t: Source of DPSPs → borrowed from where
text:
## 1. Origin
Source | Link to DPSPs
Irish Constitution, 1937 | Idea borrowed (Ireland itself drew on the Spanish Constitution)
Instrument of Instructions, GoI Act 1935 | DPSPs resemble them; Ambedkar called DPSPs a new version of them
Sapru Committee, 1945 | Suggested justiciable and non-justiciable rights
B N Rau | Advised the same split of rights
Instrument of Instructions = directions from the British Crown to the Governor-General and Governors
Under the Constitution they became directions to the legislature and executive
⚠ Instrument of Instructions became DPSPs, not FRs, not "extent of executive power", not "conduct of business"
⚠ Ireland gave DPSPs; FRs came from the USA; Fundamental Duties from the USSR
PYQ 2010: Instrument of Instructions (GoI Act 1935) incorporated as → DPSPs

t: Article 36 and the descriptions of DPSPs → who said what
text:
## 1. Art 36
"State" in Part IV has the same meaning as Art 12: Union and State governments and legislatures, local and other authorities
## 2. Descriptions
Person | Description
B R Ambedkar | "Novel feature" of the Constitution
Granville Austin | FRs and DPSPs together = "Conscience of the Constitution"
K T Shah | "Pious superfluities"; a cheque payable at the convenience of the bank
Ivor Jennings | Reflect an older, conservative (Fabian) philosophy
K Santhanam | Can cause friction between Centre and States, President and PM
Nasiruddin | Like "New Year resolutions" (Beyond your notes)
⚠ "Conscience of the Constitution" = FRs and DPSPs together (Austin), not DPSPs alone
## Beyond your notes
"New Year resolutions" (T T Krishnamachari also called them a "veritable dustbin of sentiments")

t: Non-justiciability → why, and what sanction remains
text:
## 1. Why framers kept them non-justiciable
Reason | Detail
Finance | Country lacked resources to implement them
Diversity and backwardness | Would obstruct implementation
Freedom of choice | New State must decide the order, time, place and mode
Separation of powers | Courts interpret law; policy is for legislature
## 2. Sanction
No judicial sanction (Art 37)
Sanction is moral and political: public opinion and elections
Ambedkar: a government based on popular vote cannot ignore them without answering to the electorate
⚠ Sanction behind FRs = legal; behind DPSPs = moral and political

topic: Provision → where it lies (DPSP, FR, Preamble or elsewhere)
t: Welfare State ideal → which Part declares it
text:
## 1. Where the ideal sits
Part | Ideal it embodies
DPSPs (Part IV) | Welfare State, social and economic democracy
Fundamental Rights (Part III) | Political democracy, individual liberty
Preamble | Objectives: justice, liberty, equality, fraternity; "socialist"
Seventh Schedule | Division of subjects (Union, State, Concurrent)
Asked twice with the same four options (2015, 2020)
⚠ Preamble has "socialist" and "justice: social, economic, political", but the Welfare State ideal is in DPSPs
PYQ 2015 and 2020: ideal of the Welfare State → DPSPs (trap: Preamble)

topic: Provision → where it lies (DPSP, FR, Preamble or elsewhere)
t: Separation of judiciary from executive → which provision enjoins it
text:
## 1. Article 50
State shall take steps to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State
It is a Liberal-intellectual DPSP
Implemented by the CrPC 1973 (Beyond your notes): judicial magistrates under the High Court, executive magistrates under the State government
Option UPSC gave | Correct?
Preamble | No
DPSP (Art 50) | Yes
Seventh Schedule | No
Conventional practice | No
⚠ It is enjoined by a DPSP, not a mere convention and not an FR
PYQ 2020: separation of judiciary from executive enjoined by → a DPSP
PYQ 2025 (pairs): Art 50 → DPSP; composite culture → Fundamental Duty; child below 14 in factories → FR: all three correct

topic: Provision → where it lies (DPSP, FR, Preamble or elsewhere)
t: International peace and security → DPSP, Preamble or Duty
text:
## 1. Article 51: four directions
Clause | State shall endeavour to
51(a) | Promote international peace and security
51(b) | Maintain just and honourable relations between nations
51(c) | Foster respect for international law and treaty obligations
51(d) | Encourage settlement of disputes by arbitration
Art 51 (DPSP) and Art 51A (Fundamental Duties, Part IVA) are different Parts
⚠ International peace is not in the Preamble, not a Fundamental Duty, not in the Ninth Schedule
⚠ Art 51 is the last DPSP; Art 51A is the only Article of Part IVA
PYQ 2014: promotion of international peace and security → DPSP
PYQ 2002: which Article deals with international peace → 51 (distractors 48A, 43A, 41)

Subject | Fundamental Right | DPSP
Trafficking and forced labour | Art 23 | -
Intoxicating drinks and drugs | - | Art 47 (except medicinal use)

PYQ 2008: (1) trafficking and forced labour (2) prohibition of intoxicants → 2 only in DPSPs

t: Environment, heritage, panchayats → DPSP, FR, Duty or elsewhere
text:
## 1. Same subject, different Parts
Subject | DPSP | Fundamental Duty (51A) | Other
Environment | Art 48A: protect, improve; forests, wildlife | 51A(g): protect natural environment | Art 21 (courts)
Heritage | Art 49: monuments of national importance | 51A(f): rich heritage of composite culture | -
Village panchayats | Art 40 | - | Part IX (73rd Amdt)
Cooperatives | Art 43B | - | Art 19(1)(c) FR; Part IXB
Education | Art 45 (below 6) | 51A(k): parent to give opportunity 6-14 | Art 21A FR
Scientific temper | - | 51A(h) | -

topic: Provision → where it lies (DPSP, FR, Preamble or elsewhere)
t: Directives outside Part IV and the UDHR → where else
text:
## 1. Non-justiciable directives outside Part IV
Article | Part | Directive
Art 335 | XVI | Claims of SCs and STs in services, consistent with efficiency of administration
Art 350A | XVII | Instruction in mother tongue at primary stage for linguistic minorities
Art 351 | XVII | Development of Hindi as a medium of expression of composite culture
Courts treat these too as non-justiciable, though they lie outside Part IV
## 2. UDHR 1948
Besides FRs, Preamble, DPSPs and Fundamental Duties all reflect UDHR principles (PYQ 2020: 1, 2 and 3)
DPSPs carry UDHR's socio-economic rights: work, wages, education, social security, health
⚠ Art 350A and 351 are not in Part IV but are directive in nature

t: Article 39 → its clauses (a) to (f)
text:
## 1. "Certain principles of policy"
Clause | State shall direct policy towards securing
39(a) | Adequate means of livelihood for all citizens, men and women equally
39(b) | Ownership and control of material resources of the community distributed for the common good
39(c) | Economic system not result in concentration of wealth and means of production
39(d) | Equal pay for equal work for men and women
39(e) | Health and strength of workers and tender age of children not abused
39(f) | Children get opportunities for healthy development in freedom and dignity (42nd Amdt)
⚠ Concentration of wealth violates a DPSP (39(c)), not the Right to Equality, not the Right to Freedom
⚠ Equal pay for equal work = original 39(d), not a 42nd Amendment addition
PYQ 2021: concentration of wealth violates → DPSPs (trap: Right to Equality, "Concept of Welfare")

t: Articles 38, 39A, 41, 42 → social order, legal aid, work, maternity
text:
Article | Content
38(1) | Welfare of people through a social order of social, economic and political justice
38(2) | Minimise inequalities in income, status, facilities, opportunities (44th Amdt, 1978)
39A | Equal justice and free legal aid (42nd Amdt, 1976)
41 | Right to work, education, public assistance in unemployment, old age, sickness, disablement (within economic capacity)
42 | Just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief
38(2) covers inequality among individuals and among groups in different areas or vocations
Art 41 is limited by "economic capacity and development"
MGNREGA 2005 follows Art 41 (right to work); Preview also links it to Art 43
⚠ "Right to work" is a DPSP (Art 41), not an FR; MGNREGA's right is statutory
⚠ Maternity relief = Art 42, not Art 39 or 43
PYQ 2002: 41 = right to work; 48A = environment; 43A = workers' participation; 51 = peace

t: Articles 43, 43A, 43B → wages, management, cooperatives
text:
Article | Content | Added by
43 | Living wage, decent standard of life, full enjoyment of leisure, social and cultural opportunities; cottage industries in rural areas | Original
43A | Participation of workers in management of industries | 42nd, 1976
43B | Voluntary formation, autonomous functioning, democratic control, professional management of cooperative societies | 97th, 2011
Art 43 has two strands: living wage and leisure (Socialist), cottage industries (Gandhian)
"Living wage" is more than minimum or subsistence wage
⚠ Cooperative societies = 43B, not 43A (Preview PYQ: "Cooperatives - Art 43A" is the wrong pair)
⚠ Workers' leisure is in Art 43 but is not Gandhian (PYQ 2012)

t: Articles 44, 45, 46, 47 → UCC, children, weaker sections, nutrition
text:
Article | Content
44 | Uniform Civil Code for citizens throughout India
45 | Early childhood care and education for all children until 6 years
46 | Educational and economic interests of SCs, STs, weaker sections; protect from social injustice
47 | Raise nutrition, standard of living, public health (primary duty); prohibit intoxicating drinks and drugs except medicinal
Art 45 originally: free and compulsory education to 14 years within 10 years; recast by 86th Amdt 2002
Art 47 has a socialist strand (nutrition, health) and a Gandhian one (prohibition)
UCC fields: marriage, divorce, adoption, maintenance, guardianship, inheritance, succession
⚠ Art 45 is now below 6 years; 6-14 years moved to Art 21A (FR)
⚠ Medicinal use is excepted from the Art 47 prohibition

t: Articles 48, 48A, 49, 50, 51 → farming, environment, monuments, judiciary, peace
text:
Article | Content
48 | Agriculture and animal husbandry on modern, scientific lines; preserve breeds; prohibit slaughter of cows, calves, milch and draught cattle
48A | Protect and improve environment; safeguard forests and wildlife (42nd)
49 | Protect monuments, places, objects of artistic or historic interest of national importance
50 | Separate judiciary from executive in public services of the State
51 | International peace, honourable relations, international law, arbitration
Art 49 protects against spoliation, disfigurement, destruction, removal, disposal, export
Monuments "declared by or under law made by Parliament" to be of national importance
⚠ Cow slaughter ban is in Art 48, not Art 47 and not an FR
⚠ Art 48 has two strands: scientific agriculture (Liberal), cow protection (Gandhian)

t: Gandhian principles → which provisions qualify
text:
## 1. The Gandhian list (Testbook, ROCKET)
Article | Gandhian provision
40 | Organise village panchayats as units of self-government
43 | Promote cottage industries on individual or cooperative basis in rural areas
43B | Promote cooperative societies (97th Amdt)
46 | Interests of SCs, STs, weaker sections

Reflect Gandhi's programme of village self-government, cottage industries, welfare of weaker sections

39A | Equal justice, free legal aid

t: Liberal-intellectual principles → which provisions qualify
text:
## 1. The Liberal-intellectual list
Article | Liberal-intellectual provision
44 | Uniform Civil Code
45 | Early childhood care and education (below 6)
48 | Agriculture and animal husbandry on modern, scientific lines
48A | Environment, forests, wildlife

t: Classification → traps and overlaps
text:
## 1. Rules to remember
The Constitution itself does not classify DPSPs; the three-way grouping is conventional
The classification is not watertight
Article | Lists it appears in | Strands
43 | Socialist + Gandhian | Living wage / cottage industries
47 | Socialist + Gandhian | Nutrition, health / prohibition
48 | Gandhian + Liberal | Cow protection / scientific agriculture
## 2. Count check (standard lists)
Socialist 8 (38, 39, 39A, 41, 42, 43, 43A, 47); Gandhian 6 (40, 43, 43B, 46, 47, 48); Liberal 7 (44, 45, 48, 48A, 49, 50, 51)
⚠ A statement "the Constitution classifies DPSPs into three categories" is false
⚠ PMF lists Art 46 under Gandhian; all 42nd Amdt additions (39A, 43A, 48A) are Socialist or Liberal, none Gandhian

t: 42nd Amendment (1976) → which DPSPs it added
text:
## 1. The four changes
Article | Change by 42nd Amendment
39(f) | Recast: opportunities for healthy development of children
39A | New: equal justice and free legal aid to the poor
43A | New: participation of workers in management of industries
48A | New: protect environment, forests and wildlife
Same Amendment added Part IVA (Art 51A, Fundamental Duties) and extended Art 31C to all DPSPs
## 2. Original DPSPs often offered as distractors
Distractor | Article | Status
Equal pay for equal work | 39(d) | Original
Right to work, education, public assistance | 41 | Original
Living wage and humane conditions | 43, 42 | Original
⚠ Only workers' participation in management among the 2017 options was added by the 42nd
PYQ 2017: principle added by 42nd Amendment → participation of workers in management of industries

t: 44th, 86th, 97th Amendments → later changes to Part IV
text:
Amendment | Year | Change
44th | 1978 | Added Art 38(2): minimise inequalities in income, status, facilities, opportunities
86th | 2002 | Recast Art 45: early childhood care below 6; inserted Art 21A (6-14) in Part III; added 51A(k)
97th | 2011 | Added Art 43B: cooperative societies; also Art 19(1)(c) "cooperative societies" and Part IXB
44th also removed the right to property from FRs and created Art 300A (Part XII)
73rd Amdt 1992 gave practical shape to Art 40 (panchayats), but did not amend Art 40
⚠ Art 38(2) came from the 44th, not the 42nd
⚠ 86th made education a Fundamental Right (21A) and narrowed the DPSP in Art 45
## Beyond your notes
Rajendra Shah case (2021): SC struck down parts of Part IXB for State cooperatives (State List subject); Art 43B untouched

topic: FR-DPSP relationship, implementation and DPSPs in news
t: FR vs DPSP → the differences
text:
Feature | Fundamental Rights | DPSPs
Part, Articles | III, Art 12-35 | IV, Art 36-51
Nature | Negative (prohibit the State) | Positive (direct the State)
Justiciable | Yes | No
Sanction | Legal | Moral and political
Democracy | Political | Social and economic
Welfare | Individual | Community
Laws violating them | Void (Art 13) | Not void
Need legislation? | Mostly automatic | Need laws to implement
Available to foreigners? | Some | Directed to the State
⚠ FRs prevail in conflict, except laws protected by Art 31C (39(b), 39(c))

topic: FR-DPSP relationship, implementation and DPSPs in news
t: Conflict between FRs and DPSPs → case and amendment sequence
text:
Year | Case or amendment | Holding
1951 | Champakam Dorairajan | FRs prevail; DPSPs subsidiary → led to 1st Amdt
1967 | Golaknath | Parliament cannot amend FRs to implement DPSPs
1971 | 24th, 25th Amdts | 24th: can amend FRs; 25th: Art 31C for 39(b), (c)
1973 | Kesavananda Bharati | Can amend FRs but not basic structure; struck down 31C's bar on judicial review
1976 | 42nd Amdt | 31C extended to all DPSPs
1980 | Minerva Mills | Extension invalid; harmony and balance between FRs and DPSPs is basic structure
Doctrine of harmonious construction: read FRs and DPSPs together
⚠ After Minerva Mills, 31C protection is only for 39(b) and 39(c)
## Beyond your notes
Property Owners Association v State of Maharashtra (Nov 2024), 9-judge bench: not every private resource is a "material resource of the community" under 39(b); held Art 31C (pre-42nd form) survives (verify)

topic: FR-DPSP relationship, implementation and DPSPs in news
t: Article 31C → what it protects
text:
## 1. The two parts of Art 31C (25th Amdt, 1971)
Part | Content | Status
First | Law implementing 39(b) or 39(c) not void for violating Art 14 or 19 | Valid
Second | Law declaring it gives effect to such policy cannot be questioned in court | Struck down (Kesavananda)
42nd extended the first part to all DPSPs; struck down in Minerva Mills
Courts can still check whether the law genuinely implements 39(b), (c)
Art 31A, 31B, 31C are exceptions to FRs; 31B protects Ninth Schedule laws (I R Coelho 2007: open to basic-structure review)
⚠ 31C shields against Art 14 and 19 only (originally also Art 31), not against Art 21 or 32

topic: FR-DPSP relationship, implementation and DPSPs in news
t: DPSPs → laws and schemes that implement them
text:
DPSP | Implemented by

topic: Origin and Part IVA (42nd and 86th Amendments)
t: Part IVA → origin, amendment, dates
text:
## 1. The gap and how it was filled
Original Constitution (1950): FRs (for individuals) + DPSPs (for the State), no duties for citizens
Gap filled in 1976: 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act inserted Part IVA with a single Article 51A
Recommended by the Sardar Swaran Singh Committee (1976), set up by the Congress Party during the Internal Emergency (1975-77)
Item | Fact
Part | IVA (only one Article: 51A)
Inserted by | 42nd CAA, 1976 ("Mini Constitution")
In force | 3 January 1977
Originally | 10 duties, clauses (a)-(j)
Now | 11 duties: (k) by 86th CAA, 2002 (in force 1 April 2010)
Idea borrowed from | Constitution of erstwhile USSR
⚠ Not in the original Constitution: a question saying FDs were framed in 1949/1950 or by the 41st / 44th Amendment is wrong
⚠ Part IVA sits after Part IV (DPSP), not after Part III (FRs): critics questioned this placement
PYQ angle: state PCS papers ask "which Amendment / which Committee / when": 42nd, Swaran Singh, 1976

Recommendation | Fate

The post-Emergency government (44th Amendment, 1978) reversed many 42nd Amendment changes but did not repeal Fundamental Duties

t: Fundamental Duties → legal status and nature
text:
## 1. Core status
Non-justiciable, like DPSPs: cannot be enforced by courts (no writ to compel a citizen)
Art 51A prescribes no penalty and no legislative process for enforcement
Not correlative to legal duties: they are not the legal counterparts of FRs
Apply only to citizens, not to foreigners
Enjoyment of FRs is not conditional on performing duties (NCERT): FDs did not change the status of FRs
Statement | True / False
A legislative process is provided to enforce FDs | False
FDs are correlative to legal duties | False
FDs can be enforced by writs | False
Parliament may make laws to give effect to particular duties | True
Courts may use FDs to interpret ambiguous statutes | True
⚠ "No procedure in the Constitution" is not "cannot be enforced at all": ordinary laws (PINH Act, WPA) do penalise conduct contrary to certain duties
PYQ 2017: both statements false: no legislative process provided; not correlative to legal duties (answer: neither)

topic: Article 368 and the three modes of amendment
t: Article 368 → what it says and where it sits
text:
## 1. Location and nature
Article 368, Part XX = the only Article on amendment: Parliament's constituent power and the procedure
Parliament may amend any provision by way of addition, variation or repeal (all three)
Limit: cannot alter or destroy the Basic Structure (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973)
Clause of Art 368 | Content
(1) | Constituent power to amend by addition, variation or repeal
(2) | Procedure: bill, special majority, President shall assent; proviso = State ratification list
(3) | Art 13 does not apply to amendments under Art 368
(4), (5) | Inserted by 42nd (1976): no court can question an amendment; no limit on power; struck down in Minerva Mills (1980)
⚠ All three words, addition, variation, repeal, are in Art 368; UPSC 2024 answer = "1, 2 and 3"
PYQ 2024: asked which modes Art 368 permits; trap = picking "1 and 2 only" assuming Parliament cannot repeal a provision
## Beyond your notes
Clause (1), the words "constituent power" and clause (3) were inserted by the 24th Amendment, 1971 (to overturn Golaknath)

topic: Article 368 and the three modes of amendment
t: Modes of amendment → which majority, which provisions
text:
## 1. Three ways, but only two under Art 368
Mode | Majority | Under Art 368? | Covers
Simple majority | Majority of members present and voting | No, outside Art 368 | Art 2, 3, 4, 169, quorum, Fifth/Sixth Schedules...
Special majority | Majority of total membership + two-thirds of present and voting, each House | Yes | Most provisions: FRs, DPSPs, FDs, everything not in other two
Special majority + State ratification | Special majority + not less than one-half of State legislatures (simple majority) | Yes, proviso to Art 368(2) | Federal provisions (Section 3 list)
⚠ Simple-majority changes are not "amendments" for the purposes of Art 368 (Art 4(2), 169(3) say so expressly)
⚠ Fundamental Rights need only special majority, not State ratification
⚠ NCERT Class 11 (p.206) says FR provisions are "also protected" by State ratification; PMF and Testbook put FRs under special majority only: follow PMF
Exam angle: a "how many need State ratification" list usually mixes FRs and Art 3 (neither needs it) with Seventh Schedule items (needs it)

topic: Article 368 and the three modes of amendment
t: Simple majority (outside Art 368) → complete list
text:
## 1. Provisions changed by an ordinary law of Parliament
Group | Provisions
States | Admission/establishment of new States (Art 2); formation, area, boundary, name (Art 3, 4)
Councils | Creation or abolition of State Legislative Councils (Art 169)
Parliament | Quorum; salaries and allowances of MPs; rules of procedure; privileges; use of English in Parliament
Officials | Second Schedule: emoluments, allowances, privileges of President, Governors, Speakers, judges
Supreme Court | Number of puisne judges; conferment of more jurisdiction on SC
Elections | Elections to Parliament and State legislatures; delimitation of constituencies
Others | Citizenship (acquisition, termination); use of official language; Union Territories; Fifth Schedule (Scheduled Areas, STs); Sixth Schedule (tribal areas)
⚠ Art 169: the State Assembly passes a resolution (special majority), then Parliament acts by simple majority; the only way a State starts a constitutional change
⚠ Abolition of a State's Legislative Council does not need ratification (IAS 1995 option trap)
Exam angle: "quorum", "salaries of MPs", "Fifth/Sixth Schedule", "citizenship" are simple-majority items, not Art 368 items

topic: Article 368 and the three modes of amendment
t: Special majority → meaning and arithmetic
text:
## 1. Two conditions, both in each House separately
(i) majority of the total membership of the House (more than 50%, counted irrespective of vacancies or absentees)
(ii) not less than two-thirds of members present and voting
House | Total strength | Condition (i) minimum
Lok Sabha | 543 | 272
Rajya Sabha | 245 | 123
## 2. Worked example (NCERT)
NCERT takes LS = 545, so minimum 273; even if only 300 are present, 273 must vote yes
If 400 vote: need 267 for two-thirds, but 273 for total membership: the higher figure applies
⚠ NCERT's 545 includes the 2 nominated Anglo-Indian seats (abolished by the 104th Amendment, 2020); present LS strength is 543
⚠ Special majority under Art 368 is not the same as Art 249 (RS: two-thirds of present and voting only) or Art 61 impeachment (two-thirds of total membership)
## Beyond your notes
Rajya Sabha figure 245 = 233 elected + 12 nominated (as of 2026)

topic: Article 368 and the three modes of amendment
t: Rigid or flexible → how India compares
text:
## 1. Blend of rigidity and flexibility
Constitution | Amendment | Label
Britain | Ordinary Act of Parliament | Flexible
USA | Two-thirds of Congress + three-fourths of States | Rigid
India | Simple / special / special + half the States | Partly rigid, partly flexible
Indian procedure is more difficult than Britain's but less rigid than the USA's (PMF)
Procedure for amendment borrowed from South Africa (Testbook)
No constituent assembly, convention or referendum needed; only elected representatives decide (NCERT: parliamentary sovereignty as basis)
K C Wheare: Indian procedure strikes a good balance between flexibility and rigidity
⚠ "States cannot initiate, ratification only for federal items, half the States suffice" = why the process is called Parliament-centric
## Beyond your notes
An ordinance (Art 123/213) cannot amend the Constitution

topic: Procedure under Article 368: initiation, passage, assent
t: Initiation → who can introduce, in which House
text:
## 1. The rule
Only by introduction of a bill in either House of Parliament (Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha)
Can be moved by a Minister or a private member
No prior recommendation/permission of the President
Who / where | Can initiate?
Lok Sabha | Yes
Rajya Sabha | Yes
State legislatures | No (only ratify federal amendments; Art 169 resolution is the lone exception)
President | No
Constitution commission / outside body | No
⚠ "Lok Sabha only" is false (2013); "State legislatures" and "President" are false (1999)
⚠ Money Bill = Lok Sabha only + prior recommendation; Constitution Amendment Bill = either House + no recommendation
PYQ 1999: answer "Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha only"; PYQ 2022: "requires prior recommendation of President" is wrong

topic: Procedure under Article 368: initiation, passage, assent
t: Passage → each House separately, no joint sitting
text:
## 1. How the bill is passed
Passed separately by each House by special majority
Both Houses have equal powers; Rajya Sabha can reject it
No joint sitting (Art 108 does not apply) in case of disagreement
If one House rejects, the bill fails / is dropped (UPPCS 2004 answer)
Bill | Majority | Joint sitting?
Ordinary | Simple | Yes (Art 108)
Money | Simple | No (RS only recommends, 14 days)
Constitution Amendment | Special, each House | No
⚠ Testbook (p.165) says a joint sitting "can be called"; PMF, Testbook p.166 and every PYQ: no provision for joint sitting: follow PMF
⚠ A bill cannot be "deemed passed" if LS re-passes it by two-thirds after RS rejection
PYQ 2003: the bill that must be passed by each House separately by special majority = Constitution Amendment Bill, not Money/Finance/Ordinary

topic: Procedure under Article 368: initiation, passage, assent
t: President's assent → obligatory since the 24th Amendment
text:
## 1. Assent
After passage (and ratification where needed) the bill goes to the President, who must give assent
Cannot withhold assent; cannot return for reconsideration: no veto (absolute, suspensive or pocket)
Made mandatory by the 24th Amendment Act, 1971 (words "shall give his assent")
On assent it becomes a Constitution (Amendment) Act and the Constitution stands amended
Bill | President's options
Ordinary | Assent, withhold, or return once
Money | Assent or withhold; cannot return
Constitution Amendment | Must assent
⚠ Testbook (p.165) says the President "has discretion to give or withhold"; PMF, NCERT and PYQ 2022: assent is obligatory: follow PMF
⚠ The 44th Amendment (1978) is about Art 74 reconsideration of Cabinet advice, not about amendment-bill assent (RAS 2013 trap)
PYQ 2022: statements 2 (assent obligatory) and 3 (special majority, no joint sitting) correct; answer "2 and 3 only"

topic: Procedure under Article 368: initiation, passage, assent
t: Ordinary vs Money vs Constitution Amendment Bill → feature grid
text:
## 1. Comparison
Feature | Ordinary Bill | Money Bill | Constitution Amendment Bill
House of origin | Either | Lok Sabha only | Either
President's prior recommendation | Not required | Mandatory | Not required
Rajya Sabha | Equal (amend/reject) | Recommends, 14 days | Equal, passes separately
Majority | Simple | Simple | Special (Art 368)
Joint sitting | Applicable | Not applicable | Not applicable
State role | None | None | Ratification for federal items
President | Assent/withhold/return once | Assent/withhold | Shall assent
⚠ Private member can introduce an amendment bill; private member cannot introduce a Money Bill
Exam angle: "which of these Bills cannot go to a joint sitting" = Money Bill and Constitution Amendment Bill

topic: State ratification: the proviso to Article 368(2)
t: Provisions needing ratification → the complete proviso list
text:
## 1. Proviso to Art 368(2), clauses (a)-(e)
Clause | Provision | Article / Part
(a) | Election of the President and its manner | Art 54, 55
(a) | Extent of executive power of the Union and States | Art 73, 162
(a) | High Courts for Union Territories | Art 241
(a) | GST Council (added by 101st, 2016) | Art 279A
(b) | Union Judiciary (Supreme Court) | Ch IV of Part V
(b) | High Courts in the States | Ch V of Part VI

⚠ UPSC 2025: Union List (c) and extent of State executive power (Art 162, clause a) need ratification; conditions of Governor's office (Art 158) do not: answer "1 and 2 only"
