PYQ 2025: tested by naming a List, an Article-162 subject and a Governor provision; next likely: Art 54 vs Art 58, Art 241 vs Art 239A

topic: State ratification: the proviso to Article 368(2)
t: Ratification → how the States act
text:
## 1. Rules
Legislatures of not less than one-half of the States, not all (2013 trap)
Each State ratifies by simple majority (present and voting), by resolution
Ratification comes after passage by Parliament and before the bill is presented to the President
No time limit for States to ratify
Constitution silent on whether a State can withdraw ratification
States may ratify or reject, but cannot modify the bill
Once half have ratified, process complete; immaterial whether others reject or do nothing
Point | Answer
How many States | At least half
Majority in State House | Simple
Time limit | None
Can States amend the bill? | No
⚠ Testbook (p.166) says "more than half"; the text of Art 368 and PMF say "not less than one-half": follow PMF
PYQ 2013: "ratified by legislature of all the States" is wrong; answer "Neither 1 nor 2"

topic: State ratification: the proviso to Article 368(2)
t: Ratification not needed → traps and look-alikes
text:
## 1. Provisions often mistaken for federal items
Provision | Ratification? | Why
Conditions of Governor's office (Art 158) | No | Not named in proviso (2025)
Qualifications of President (Art 58) | No | Only election and manner (Art 54, 55) are listed
Conditions of office of President (Art 59) | No | Not listed
Tenure of President (Art 56) | No | Not listed (CGPSC 2017)
Fundamental Rights | No | Special majority only
DPSPs, FDs | No | Special majority only
New States / boundaries (Art 2-4) | No | Simple majority
Legislative Council (Art 169) | No | Simple majority
Union Territories (Art 239A) | No | Not listed; only Art 241 (HCs for UTs) is
⚠ President's election = ratification; President's qualifications, conditions, tenure = no ratification (ROCKET sheet trap)
Exam angle: UPSC pairs one listed and one look-alike item: Art 54 vs Art 58, Art 241 vs Art 239A, Art 162 vs Art 158

topic: State ratification: the proviso to Article 368(2)
t: Ratified amendments → examples and firsts
text:
## 1. Examples
Amendment | Why ratification
3rd, 1954 | First amendment ratified under the proviso; re-enacted Entry 33, Concurrent List
101st, 2016 (GST) | Changed Seventh Schedule; added Art 279A to the proviso; inserted Art 246A
17th, 1964 | Challenged (Sajjan Singh) as unratified; held valid 3:2 as it did not affect Art 226
Seventh Schedule today (PMF): Union 100, State 61, Concurrent 52 subjects
⚠ Testbook (p.261) gives the original 97 / 47 for Union / Concurrent; PMF's current count is 100 / 61 / 52
## Beyond your notes
97th Amendment, 2011 (cooperative societies, Part IXB): SC in 2021 (Union of India v Rajendra Shah) struck down the Part IXB provisions for State co-operatives because they were not ratified by half the States

t: Amendment Bills of 2024-26 → majority and ratification needed

Bill | Content | Ratification?
129th Amendment Bill, 2024 (ONOE) | Simultaneous LS and Assembly polls; new Art 82A (appointed date) | No (Kovind panel)

topic: Evolution of the amending power: cases and amendments
t: Amending power → case and amendment timeline
text:
## 1. From Shankari Prasad to Waman Rao
Year | Case / Amendment | Position
1951 | Shankari Prasad | Parliament can amend FRs; amendment is not "law" under Art 13
1965 | Sajjan Singh | Reaffirmed; J R Mudholkar first asked about "basic features"
1967 | Golaknath | Parliament cannot amend FRs; amendment is "law" under Art 13
1971 | 24th Amendment | Power to amend any part incl. FRs; assent mandatory
1973 | Kesavananda Bharati | Can amend any part, not the Basic Structure
1975 | Indira Gandhi v Raj Narain | Applied doctrine; struck Art 329A(4)
1976 | 42nd Amendment | Art 368(4),(5): unlimited power, no judicial review
1980 | Minerva Mills | Struck 368(4),(5); limited amending power and judicial review = basic structure
1980 | Waman Rao | Doctrine applies to amendments after 24 April 1973
⚠ Golaknath is the only case holding FRs unamendable; Kesavananda overruled it
Exam angle: match case → principle; Shankari Prasad and Sajjan Singh (amend FRs) vs Golaknath (cannot)

topic: Evolution of the amending power: cases and amendments
t: 24th and 42nd Amendments → what they did to Art 13 and 368
text:
## 1. Parliament's replies to the Court
Amendment | Change | Fate
24th, 1971 | Amended Art 13 and 368: amendment under Art 368 is not law under Art 13; power to abridge/take away FRs; President shall assent | Upheld in Kesavananda
25th, 1971 | "Compensation" replaced by "amount"; Art 31C | Part excluding judicial review struck in Kesavananda
42nd, 1976 | Art 368(4): no amendment can be questioned in any court; 368(5): no limit on constituent power | Struck down, Minerva Mills 1980
42nd also: "secular" (and socialist, integrity) in Preamble, Fundamental Duties, LS term 5 to 6 years, changes to 53 Articles and the Seventh Schedule (NCERT)
⚠ The 24th is still in force: assent mandatory; Art 13(4)
## Beyond your notes
42nd also extended Art 31C to all DPSPs; that extension too was struck in Minerva Mills

topic: Evolution of the amending power: cases and amendments
t: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) → key facts
text:
## 1. The judgment
Point | Fact
Bench | 13 judges, the largest Constitution Bench
Majority | 7 : 6
Date | 24 April 1973: the cut-off date for the doctrine
Held | Parliament can amend any part incl. FRs, but cannot alter or destroy Basic Structure
Also held | Preamble is part of the Constitution (overruling Berubari 1960 on this)
Key judge | H R Khanna propounded the major features (Testbook)
Elements named in the case (Testbook): supremacy of Constitution, republican and democratic government, secular character, separation of powers, federal character, sovereignty and unity, freedom and dignity of individual, parliamentary system, welfare state
⚠ Doctrine first suggested by Justice Mudholkar in Sajjan Singh (1965), but propounded in Kesavananda
⚠ Kesavananda upheld the 24th Amendment

topic: Evolution of the amending power: cases and amendments
t: Emergency amendments → 38th, 39th, 42nd and the 43rd/44th repair
text:
## 1. Who did what
Amendment | What it did
38th, 1975 | Made National Emergency proclamation immune from judicial review
39th, 1975 | Inserted Art 329A: election disputes of PM and Speaker beyond courts
42nd, 1976 | Restricted judicial review; Art 368(4),(5)
43rd, 1977 | Undid many 42nd changes on courts' powers
44th, 1978 | Removed 38th immunity; omitted Art 329A; deleted Art 19(1)(f) and 31 (property), added Art 300A
Indira Gandhi v Raj Narain (1975) ("Election Case"): clause 4 of Art 329A struck as violating free and fair elections, rule of law, equality
⚠ 39th put the PM's election beyond judicial review; 44th did the opposite (UPSC 2019 statement 1 is false)
Exam angle: 38th = Emergency immune, 39th = PM's election immune, 44th = restored both

topic: Basic structure: nature, elements, Ninth Schedule
t: Basic structure → legal status (not defined, judicial creation)
text:
## 1. Status
The Constitution does not define Basic Structure; the word does not appear in it
A judicial creation: Kesavananda Bharati, 1973
SC has given no exhaustive list; elements added case by case
Constitution does not expressly use the term "judicial review"; the power is grounded in Art 13, 32, 226 etc.
Statement | True?
Constitution defines basic structure as federalism, secularism, FRs, democracy | False
Constitution expressly "provides for judicial review" | False (as worded in 2020)
SC has listed all basic features | False
Parliament can amend all parts except basic structure | True
⚠ NCERT Q: "Constitution specifies the basic tenets" = incorrect; "judiciary has defined" all aspects = incorrect
PYQ 2020: both statements false: answer "Neither 1 nor 2"; trap = federalism, secularism are basic features, but judicially, not textually

topic: Basic structure: nature, elements, Ninth Schedule
t: Elements of basic structure → feature and case
text:
## 1. PMF table (not exhaustive)
Group | Elements
Framework | Supremacy of Constitution, federal character, separation of powers, unity and integrity, limited amending power
Democratic order | Sovereign, democratic, republican polity, parliamentary system, free and fair elections, secular character
Rights and justice | Freedom and dignity, equality, welfare state, principles behind FRs, harmony of FRs and DPSPs
Judicial safeguards | Judicial review, independence of judiciary, access to justice, SC powers (Art 32, 136, 141, 142), HC powers (Art 226, 227), rule of law
## 2. Case that added the element
Element | Case
Free and fair elections, rule of law, equality | Indira Gandhi v Raj Narain, 1975
Limited amending power, judicial review, FR-DPSP balance | Minerva Mills, 1980
Judicial review under Art 226/227 and 32 | L Chandra Kumar, 1997
Independence of judiciary | Fourth Judges Case, 2015
## Beyond your notes
S R Bommai (1994): federalism and secularism as basic features

topic: Basic structure: nature, elements, Ninth Schedule
t: Ninth Schedule and basic structure → Waman Rao, I R Coelho
text:
## 1. Immunity is not absolute
Art 31B + Ninth Schedule: inserted by the 1st Amendment, 1951; protects listed laws from FR challenge (land reform, zamindari abolition)
Case | Held
Waman Rao, 1980 | Laws put in Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 valid only if they do not damage basic structure
I R Coelho, 2007 | Post-24 April 1973 Ninth Schedule laws subject to judicial review; judicial review is a basic feature
⚠ Laws added before 24 April 1973 keep the protection; after = testable on basic structure
⚠ Ninth Schedule came by the 1st Amendment (Art 31B); Art 31A also by the 1st
## Beyond your notes
I R Coelho was decided by a 9-judge bench

topic: Basic structure: nature, elements, Ninth Schedule
t: Basic structure doctrine → significance and criticism
text:
## 1. Both sides
Significance | Criticism
Preserves identity and supremacy of Constitution | No textual basis; no precise definition
Check on majoritarianism | Gives judiciary wide power: judicial overreach, subjectivity
Balance of flexibility and stability | Debate over Parliament's constituent power vs judicial review
Amendment = power to change, not to destroy (PMF)
India described as "quasi-federal" (K C Wheare); SC treats federalism as basic structure
Judicial review is part of the basic structure: cannot be amended away (PMF Mains Magnum 2025)
⚠ The doctrine limits constitutional amendments; ordinary laws are tested against the whole Constitution, not just the basic structure
Exam angle: NCERT asks whether the doctrine "increased the powers of the judiciary and came to be accepted by parties and government": true

topic: Judicial review of amendments and laws
t: Amendments struck down → case, ground
text:
## 1. Amendments invalidated by the Supreme Court
Amendment | Provision struck | Case | Ground
39th, 1975 | Art 329A(4) (PM/Speaker election) | Indira Gandhi v Raj Narain, 1975 | Free and fair elections
42nd, 1976 | Art 368(4), (5) | Minerva Mills, 1980 | Limited amending power, judicial review
99th, 2014 | NJAC + NJAC Act | Fourth Judges Case, 2015 | Independence of judiciary
52nd, 1985 | Para 7, Tenth Schedule | Kihoto Hollohan | No State ratification
NJAC (99th): CJI, two senior-most SC judges, Union Law Minister, two eminent persons; struck down, collegium restored
⚠ UPSC 2019: 99th struck down for violating independence of judiciary = true; 44th placing PM's election beyond review = false
⚠ ROCKET sheet dates Kihoto Hollohan 1993; it is usually cited as 1992 (verify)
## Beyond your notes
NJAC verdict: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v Union of India, October 2015, majority 4:1
97th (Part IXB, co-operatives) partly struck, 2021, for lack of ratification

topic: Judicial review of amendments and laws
t: Amendments upheld → do not mark as struck down
text:
## 1. Challenged but valid
Amendment | Case | Result
1st, 1951 | Shankari Prasad, 1951 | Upheld
17th, 1964 | Sajjan Singh, 1965 | Upheld (3:2; no ratification needed)
24th, 1971 | Kesavananda, 1973 | Upheld
103rd, 2019 (10% EWS) | Janhit Abhiyan, 2022 | Upheld; 50% cap applies to backward classes, not EWS
52nd (rest of Tenth Schedule) | Kihoto Hollohan | Upheld; Speaker's decision open to judicial review
⚠ 52nd Amendment: Tenth Schedule upheld, only Para 7 struck: "struck down" vs "upheld" both partly true
Exam angle: "SC struck down the 99th / 103rd Amendment" → 99th yes, 103rd no

topic: Judicial review of amendments and laws
t: Judicial review → who, under which Articles
text:
## 1. Constitutional basis
Article | Role
13 | Laws violating FRs void: base of judicial review
32 | SC writs for FRs; "heart and soul" (Ambedkar); itself a FR
226 | HC writs for FRs and other legal rights (wider than 32)
131-136 | Original, appellate, special leave jurisdiction
141, 142 | SC law binding; complete justice
245 | Legislative power subject to the Constitution
High Courts can declare central laws unconstitutional under Art 226 (UPSC 2019 statement 1 false)
SC can examine constitutional amendments on the basic structure test (statement 2 false)
Term "judicial review" not used in Constitution; idea from Marbury v Madison (USA, 1803) (Testbook)
⚠ India = "procedure established by law": narrower review than US "due process"
## Beyond your notes
42nd Amendment inserted Art 226A, 228A (and 32A, 131A) curbing courts on central laws; 43rd (1977) repealed them
PYQ 2019: answer "Neither 1 nor 2"

topic: Judicial review of amendments and laws
t: Judicial review vs judicial activism → distinction
text:
## 1. Terms
Term | Meaning
Judicial review | Constitutional process: tests validity of laws, executive acts, amendments
Judicial activism | Broad intervention beyond the traditional role, may shape public policy
Judicial overreach / "despotism" | Entering policy or administration; weak accountability
PIL expanded locus standi after the Emergency (PMF Mains Magnum 2025)
Art 142 used for "complete justice" (Babri, irretrievable breakdown of marriage, Tamil Nadu Governor bills)
## In news 2025-26
State of Tamil Nadu v Governor (April 2025): SC used Art 142 to deem 10 re-passed Bills assented (PMF Prelims Magnum 2026)
Presidential Reference (5-judge bench, 2025): no fixed judicial timelines for Governor/President under Art 200, 201; deemed assent rejected (PMF Prelims Magnum 2026)
⚠ These are Art 200/201 rulings, not amendments; they show the Court's review power over constitutional functionaries
Exam angle: judicial review of amendments rests on basic structure, not on Art 13 (Art 368(3) excludes Art 13)

topic: Emergency provisions at a glance and Art 355
t: Art 355 → duty of the Union to protect every State
text:
## 1. What Art 355 says
"It shall be the duty of the Union to protect every State against external aggression and internal disturbance"
and to ensure that the government of every State is carried on in accordance with the Constitution
Article | Nature | Role
355 | Duty of the Union | Basis for the Union to act
356 | Power of the President | Means to make Art 355 effective
365 | Deeming clause | State's failure to obey Union directions can count as breakdown
⚠ Art 355 still says "internal disturbance"; only Art 352 had that phrase replaced by "armed rebellion" (44th Amdt)
⚠ Distractors used: Art 215 (HC court of record), 275 (grants-in-aid), 325 (no exclusion from electoral roll)
PYQ 2003: the words "duty of the Union to protect every State against external aggression and internal disturbance" = Art 355

topic: Emergency provisions at a glance and Art 355
t: Part XVIII → Articles 352-360 and what each says
text:
## 1. Articles at a glance
Article | Provision
352 | Proclamation of National Emergency
353 | Effect of the proclamation (Union directions, Parliament's power)
354 | President may modify distribution of revenues
355 | Duty of the Union to protect States
356 | Failure of constitutional machinery in States (President's Rule)
357 | Exercise of legislative powers under an Art 356 proclamation
358 | Suspension of Art 19 during Emergency
359 | Suspension of enforcement of Part III rights
359A | Application to Punjab (repealed)
360 | Financial Emergency
⚠ Art 365 (Union directions) is in Part XIX, outside Part XVIII; Art 239AB gives a 356-type power for Delhi
Emergency makes the federation unitary without any formal amendment

topic: Emergency provisions at a glance and Art 355
t: Three emergencies → grounds and common names
text:
## 1. Three types
Type | Article | Ground | Also called
National | 352 | War, external aggression, armed rebellion | External (war/aggression) or Internal (armed rebellion) Emergency
President's Rule | 356 | Failure of constitutional machinery in a State | State Emergency, Constitutional Emergency
Financial | 360 | Threat to financial stability or credit of India or any part | —
⚠ The Constitution never uses the word "Emergency" for Art 356
## 2. Views
Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar: "very life-breath of the Constitution"; Mahabir Tyagi: "safety-valve"
K.M. Nambiar: "fraud on the Constitution"; Ambedkar hoped Art 356 would remain a "dead letter"
Art 356 derives from Section 93, GoI Act 1935

t: Art 352 → grounds and who decides
text:
## 1. Grounds
Item | Rule
Grounds | War, external aggression, armed rebellion
Timing | Can be proclaimed before actual occurrence if imminent danger
Extent | Whole of India or a part (part allowed by 42nd Amdt 1976)
Advice | Only on written recommendation of the Union Cabinet (44th Amdt 1978)
Multiple | Different proclamations on different grounds may run simultaneously
⚠ "Internal disturbance" was replaced by "armed rebellion" by the 44th (not 42nd) Amendment
⚠ Cabinet advice must be written and collective, not the PM's alone
Judicial review: barred by 38th Amdt 1975, restored by 44th; Minerva Mills (1980): challengeable if mala fide or on wholly extraneous, absurd, perverse grounds
⚠ Testbook says the 42nd Amdt widened "internal disturbance" to include armed rebellion: follow PMF, the 44th made the swap

t: National Emergency → approval, majority, duration, revocation
text:
## 1. Parliament's control
Step | Rule
Approval | Both Houses within 1 month (was 2 months before 44th)
Majority | Special: majority of total membership + two-thirds present and voting, in each House
LS dissolved | Survives on Rajya Sabha approval till 30 days from first sitting of new LS
Duration | 6 months, extendable indefinitely by fresh approval every 6 months
Revocation by President | Any time, no parliamentary approval
Revocation forced by LS | LS resolution of disapproval by simple majority
Special sitting | Notice by 1/10 of total LS members → sitting within 14 days
⚠ Continuation needs both Houses + special majority; disapproval needs only Lok Sabha + simple majority
⚠ Rajya Sabha has no role in disapproval
## Beyond your notes
The 1/10 notice goes to the Speaker if the House is in session, to the President if not

t: National Emergency → effects on Centre-State relations
text:
## 1. Executive, legislative, financial
Sphere | Effect
Executive | Union can direct any State on any matter; State government continues
Legislative | Parliament can legislate on State List; State Legislature not suspended
Ordinances | President can issue ordinances on State List subjects
Laws' life | Parliament's State-List laws lapse 6 months after Emergency ends
Financial (Art 354) | President may modify revenue distribution; lasts till end of the financial year in which Emergency ends; order laid before Parliament
⚠ Under National Emergency the State government and Legislature continue; under President's Rule the CoM is dismissed
Provisions on division of taxes (Art 268-281) can be modified during National, not Financial, Emergency (Chhattisgarh PCS)
## Beyond your notes
Parliament's State-List power in emergency comes from Art 250

t: National Emergency → effect on term of legislatures
text:
## 1. Extension of term
House | Rule
Lok Sabha | Extended by law of Parliament, 1 year at a time, any number of times (Art 83(2))
State Assembly | Parliament may extend similarly, 1 year at a time
Outer limit | Not beyond 6 months after Emergency ceases
Example: Fifth Lok Sabha (1971-77) was extended
⚠ Extension is by law of Parliament, not by Presidential order
⚠ Rajya Sabha is permanent: nothing to extend
## Beyond your notes
State Assembly term extension: Art 172(1)

t: 44th Amendment 1978 → safeguards added after 1975
text:
## 1. Complete list
Before 44th | After 44th
"Internal disturbance" | "Armed rebellion"
PM's advice enough | Written Cabinet recommendation
Approval within 2 months | Within 1 month
Simple majority | Special majority
Once approved, ran as long as executive wished | Fresh approval every 6 months
No LS power to end it | LS can force revocation (1/10 notice, 14 days)
Art 358 for all emergencies | Art 358 only for war/external aggression
Art 20, 21 could be suspended | Art 20, 21 enforcement never suspended
Judicial review barred (38th) | Judicial review restored
Also capped President's Rule beyond 1 year with two conditions (Section on Art 356)
⚠ The 42nd Amdt (1976) allowed Emergency in part of India; the 44th undid most other 42nd changes

t: National Emergencies → the three proclamations
text:
## 1. Instances
Year | Ground | Note
Oct 1962 | External aggression (China) | Not revoked even after the ceasefire
Dec 1971 | External aggression (Pakistan, Bangladesh war) | Bangladesh Liberation War
Jun 25, 1975 | Internal disturbance | Declared under Indira Gandhi; 21 months, ended Mar 1977
1975-77: press censorship, MISA arrests, ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla (habeas corpus suspended); Shah Commission found it unjustified
1977 polls: Janata Party, first non-Congress government (Morarji Desai), revoked the Emergency
## In news 2025-26
25 Jun 2025: 50 years of the 1975 Emergency; Union Cabinet passed a resolution; marked as Samvidhan Hatya Diwas
⚠ PMF Mains Magnum dates the 50-year mark to 2024; 1975 + 50 = 2025 (P-MCA 2025, CARE)
Jan 2025 (PMF): India's Emergency compared with South Korea's martial law: in India the Army does not take over, Parliament must approve, courts can review

t: Art 358 vs Art 359 → what each suspends
text:
## 1. Comparison
Basis | Art 358 | Art 359
Rights | Only Art 19 | Rights named in Presidential Order (never 20, 21)
Operation | Automatic on proclamation | Needs a Presidential Order
Ground | War or external aggression only | Emergency on any ground (incl. armed rebellion)
Duration | Whole Emergency | Period in the Order
Extent | Whole country | Whole or any part
Effect | Art 19 limits on State power relaxed | Right to move courts suspended, rights themselves remain
⚠ Art 358 does not operate in an Emergency of armed rebellion
⚠ Art 359 suspends enforcement, not the rights themselves
⚠ Testbook says Art 359 also applies under Art 356/360: follow PMF, both Articles work only in National Emergency

t: Emergency and FRs → 44th Amendment protections
text:
## 1. After 1978
Protection | Detail
Art 20 and 21 | Enforcement cannot be suspended even in Emergency
Art 358 immunity | Only for laws with a recital linking them to the Emergency, and executive action under them
Art 358 ground | War / external aggression only
Laws made under Art 358 or 359 cannot be challenged during Emergency; they lapse when it ends to the extent inconsistent
Likely angle: "which FR enforcement can never be suspended": Art 20 (conviction safeguards) and Art 21 (life, liberty)
⚠ Some CA notes claim Art 14 stays protected: it does not by itself; only 20 and 21 are guaranteed
## Beyond your notes
ADM Jabalpur (1976) upheld suspension of habeas corpus; overruled in Puttaswamy (2017); the 44th Amdt's Art 21 shield is the constitutional answer

t: FRs in other emergencies → what does NOT happen
text:
## 1. No automatic effect
Emergency | Effect on FRs
National (war/aggression) | Art 358 automatic + Art 359 by order
National (armed rebellion) | Only Art 359 by order
President's Rule (356) | None: Art 19 not suspended
Financial (360) | None
⚠ PYQ 2018 option "Art 19 is suspended in that State" under Art 356 is false
The Army does not assume governance; any deployment is under laws such as AFSPA

t: Art 356 → what the President can and cannot do
text:
## 1. Contents of the proclamation
President may | President may NOT
Assume all or any functions of the State government and Governor | Assume powers of the High Court
Declare that State Legislature's powers are exercisable by or under Parliament | Suspend constitutional provisions on the High Court
Make incidental provisions, suspend other constitutional provisions on State bodies | Himself make laws for the State (unless Parliament delegates)
⚠ It is Parliament, not the President, that gets the State's legislative power
⚠ Proclamation on Governor's report "or otherwise": the report is not mandatory
PYQ 2018: answer "powers of the Legislature exercisable by or under the authority of Parliament"; traps: Assembly automatically dissolved, Art 19 suspended, President makes laws

t: President's Rule → consequences: necessary or not
text:
## 1. Must, may, does not
Consequence | Necessarily?
Council of Ministers (CM) dismissed | Yes, always
Governor runs State on behalf of President (with Chief Secretary, advisers) | Yes
Parliament passes State bills and budget | Yes
Assembly dissolved | No: may be dissolved or kept in suspended animation
Local bodies dissolved | No
High Court affected | No: status and powers unchanged
Art 19 suspended | No

## 1. Parliament's control
Step | Rule
Approval | Both Houses within 2 months
Majority | Simple majority
LS dissolved | Survives on RS approval till 30 days from first sitting of new LS
Duration | 6 months at a time, maximum 3 years

Condition | Detail
1 | National Emergency in operation in whole of India or whole/part of the State
2 | Election Commission certifies that Assembly elections cannot be held

## 1. Holdings
Holding | Effect
Proclamation is subject to judicial review | Satisfaction must rest on relevant material
Majority doubts → floor test in the Assembly | Not the Governor's private assessment
Unconstitutional proclamation | Court can restore the dismissed government and Assembly

topic: Meaning and principle of parliamentary government
t: Parliamentary system → what defines it
text:
## 1. Definition (PMF)
The real executive emerges from the legislature and remains collectively responsible to it
Council of Ministers stays in office only as long as it enjoys the confidence of the Lower House (Lok Sabha)
So the government is responsible to Parliament and can be removed by it (no-confidence)
Option type UPSC gives | Correct? | Why
Govt responsible to Parliament, removable by it | Yes | Defining feature
All parties in Parliament represented in govt | No | That is a national/all-party govt
Govt elected by and removable by the people | No | People elect the House, not the govt
Chosen by Parliament, not removable before a fixed term | No | That is Swiss-type fixed executive
⚠ "Removable by the people" is the trap: removal is by the Lok Sabha, not by voters
PYQ 2020: asked what a parliamentary system is; answer: government responsible to Parliament and removable by it

topic: Meaning and principle of parliamentary government
t: Parliamentary government → its other names
text:
## 1. Same system, four names
Name | Stresses
Cabinet government | Cabinet is the real centre of power
Responsible government | Executive answerable to the legislature
Westminster model | Named after the seat of the British Parliament
Prime-ministerial government | Modern dominance of the PM (Crossman, Mackintosh)
Prevalent in Britain, Japan, Canada, India; also Germany, Italy, Portugal (NCERT)
First emerged in Great Britain (UPPCS 2018: birthplace of parliamentary government)
India adopted it at both Union and State levels
⚠ "Cabinet government" = "responsible government" = parliamentary system: not three different systems
PYQ 2017: the principle underlying the Cabinet form = collective responsibility of the government to the people (through the Lok Sabha)

topic: Meaning and principle of parliamentary government
t: Cabinet government → its underlying principle
text:
## 1. Collective responsibility (Art 75(3))
Council of Ministers collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha; ministers "swim or sink together"
No-confidence passed → entire Council resigns, including ministers from the Rajya Sabha
Cabinet decisions bind all ministers; a minister who disagrees must accept or resign
NCERT: the ministry is an executive committee of Parliament; a no-confidence vote even against a single minister brings down the whole Council
2017 option | Verdict
Minimising criticism of government | Wrong
Speeding up government activity | Wrong
Ensuring collective responsibility of govt to the people | Correct
Strengthening the head of government | Wrong
⚠ Responsibility runs to the Lok Sabha only, never to the Rajya Sabha
PYQ 2017 (main advantage): the executive remains responsible to the legislature; "continuity of policy / more efficient" is the presidential-system trap

topic: Meaning and principle of parliamentary government
t: India is parliamentary → right and wrong reasons
text:
## 1. The reason
India has a parliamentary system because the Council of Ministers is responsible to the Lok Sabha (Art 75(3))
## 2. Distractors that are true but irrelevant
2015 option | True? | Makes India parliamentary?
Lok Sabha directly elected | Yes | No: presidential USA also has an elected House
Parliament can amend the Constitution | Yes | No: a constituent power, any system
Rajya Sabha cannot be dissolved | Yes | No: a bicameral feature
CoM responsible to Lok Sabha | Yes | Yes
⚠ "True statement" is not the same as "the reason": pick the one about executive responsibility
UPPCS 2025 (A-R): A = India parliamentary; R = executive responsible to legislature → both true, R explains A
PYQ 2015: answer d; trap: three true-but-unrelated facts

topic: Meaning and principle of parliamentary government
t: Constitutional basis → Articles 74, 75, 163, 164
text:
## 1. Union and State provisions
Article | Level | Says
74 | Union | CoM headed by PM aids and advises the President; advice binding
75 | Union | PM appointed by President; others on PM's advice; 75(3) collective responsibility to LS; 75(5) six-month rule
163 | State | CoM headed by CM aids and advises Governor, except in discretion
164 | State | CM appointed by Governor; 164(2) collective responsibility to Legislative Assembly; 164(4) six-month rule
Art 78: PM communicates all CoM decisions to the President
Art 88: ministers may speak in both Houses but vote only in their own
Advice tendered to President/Governor cannot be inquired into by any court (Art 74(2), 163(3))
⚠ Governor has constitutional discretion (Art 163); the President has no such express clause
## Beyond your notes
42nd Amendment (1976) made advice binding; 44th (1978) allowed the President to return it once for reconsideration

topic: Features of the parliamentary system in India
t: Features of parliamentary government → the full list
text:
## 1. Nine features (PMF; BPSC 2019 list)
# | Feature | Hinge
1 | Nominal and real executive | President vs PM + CoM (Art 74)
2 | Majority party rule | Majority in Lok Sabha forms govt
3 | Collective responsibility | Art 75(3), to Lok Sabha
4 | Political homogeneity | Same party / coalition consensus
5 | Double membership | Ministers in both executive and legislature
6 | Leadership of the PM | Heads CoM, House, party
7 | Dissolution of the Lower House | President, on PM's advice
8 | Secrecy | Oath of secrecy
9 | No strict separation of powers | Fusion of executive and legislature
⚠ Not features: fixed tenure, judicial review, federalism, bicameralism (all exist outside parliamentary systems)

topic: Features of the parliamentary system in India
t: Parliamentary principles → which are implied institutionally
text:
## 1. The 2013 statements
Statement | Verdict | Reason
Members of the Cabinet are Members of Parliament | Correct | Double membership (non-member must enter within 6 months)
Ministers hold office while they enjoy confidence | Correct | Bedrock principle, Art 75(3)
Cabinet is headed by the Head of the State | Wrong | Headed by the PM, Head of Government

PYQ 2013: answer "1 and 2 only"; trap: statement 3 swaps Head of State with Head of Government

topic: Features of the parliamentary system in India
t: Nominal and real executive → who is which
text:
## 1. Two executives
 | President | Prime Minister + CoM
Executive type | Nominal / de jure / titular | Real / de facto
Head of | State | Government
Chosen | Indirectly elected, 5 years | Leader of LS majority
Removal | Impeachment (violation of Constitution) | Loss of LS confidence
Art 52: "there shall be a President": office never vacant
Nehru: a head that "neither reigns nor governs"; a great figurehead
President's real discretion: choosing PM in a hung House, returning advice once, pocket veto
⚠ 1998 hung House: President K.R. Narayanan asked Vajpayee for support letters and a confidence vote within ten days

topic: Features of the parliamentary system in India
t: Double membership → the six-month rule
text:
## 1. Rules
Minister must be an MP; a non-member may be appointed but must enter either House within six consecutive months, else ceases to be minister (Art 75(5); States 164(4))
PM may be from Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha (UK PM: by convention, House of Commons)
CM in a bicameral State: Assembly or Council; responsible only to the Assembly
Point | India | UK
Non-MP as minister | Up to 6 months | Conventionally must be sitting MPs
PM's House | Either | Commons
Responsible to | Lok Sabha | House of Commons
⚠ "Ministers must be MPs at appointment" is false: membership can follow within 6 months
Limitation (PMF): limited scope for experts, as ministers come mainly from Parliament
## Beyond your notes
SC (S.R. Chaudhuri, 2001): a non-member cannot be re-appointed after six months without getting elected (verify)

topic: Features of the parliamentary system in India
t: Leadership of the PM → his place in the system
text:
## 1. Descriptions
Who | Called the PM
Lord Morley | Primus inter pares; "keystone of the Cabinet arch"
H.J. Laski | Central to the formation, life and death of the CoM
Nehru | "Linchpin of Government"
CoM exists only after the PM takes oath; PM's death or resignation dissolves the whole CoM
A minister's death or exit only creates a vacancy
PM: leader of the Council, of the Lok Sabha, of the ruling party
Constitution does not prescribe a fixed term for the PM; holds office while LS confidence lasts
⚠ Constitution does not classify ministers into Cabinet / MoS / Deputy: that is convention
CoM size: max 15% of Lok Sabha strength (91st Amendment, 2003); States 15% of Assembly, minimum 12

topic: Features of the parliamentary system in India
t: Collective, individual and legal responsibility → who answers to whom
text:
## 1. Three kinds
Type | Basis | Meaning
Collective | Art 75(3) | Whole CoM to Lok Sabha; resign together
Individual | Art 75(2) | Minister holds office during pleasure of President; removed on PM's advice
Legal | None in India | No countersignature by a minister needed for President's orders
President's orders authenticated under rules of Art 77; court cannot question them on the ground of not being made by the President
⚠ UK has legal responsibility (minister countersigns the Crown's acts); India does not
Likely-next: "Indian ministers bear legal responsibility for the President's acts" is false

topic: Features of the parliamentary system in India
t: Council of Ministers vs Cabinet → how they differ
text:
## 1. Comparison (PMF)
Council of Ministers | Cabinet
Larger body: Cabinet ministers, MoS, Deputy ministers | Smaller, nucleus: PM + Cabinet-rank ministers
Does not meet as a body | Meets regularly, deliberates collectively
Implements Cabinet decisions | Principal policy-making body
Constitutional body, Art 74-75 | Word inserted only in Art 352 (by 44th Amendment, 1978)
Collective responsibility is of the Council, though decided in the Cabinet
⚠ The original Constitution did not mention the "Cabinet"; Art 352 was the insertion

t: Parliamentary vs presidential → feature by feature
text:
## 1. Comparison (PMF)
Parliamentary | Presidential
Dual executive (nominal + real) | Single executive: President is real
Executive drawn from legislature | Executive separate from legislature
Collective responsibility to Lower House | Not responsible to legislature
Ministers are legislators | Secretaries need not be (cannot be) legislators
Depends on confidence | Fixed tenure
Lower House can be dissolved | President cannot dissolve it
Fusion of powers | Separation of powers
Greater accountability | Greater stability
⚠ Ambedkar: parliamentary = more responsibility, less stability; presidential = more stability, less responsibility
Likely-next: "fixed term and separation of powers" describes the USA, not India

t: Presidential system → features of the US model
text:
## 1. Features
J.W. Garner: executive constitutionally independent of the legislature in tenure and not responsible to it for policies
President = Head of State + Head of Government; all executive powers vested in him (UPPCS 2005)
Elected separately from Congress; fixed four-year term
22nd Amendment: max two terms (8 years)
Veto over legislation; appoints key officials
Country | Presidential term rule (PMF 2026)
USA | Max 2 terms (22nd Amendment)
Brazil | 2 consecutive, then a break
South Korea | Single 5-year term, no re-election
Indonesia | Max 2 terms
Other presidential states: Argentina, Mexico, Chile, Colombia, Philippines, Maldives, Ghana, Kenya (Testbook)
⚠ Testbook lists Russia and Sri Lanka as presidential; NCERT classes them semi-presidential: follow NCERT

t: Types of executive → which country has which
text:
## 1. Classification (NCERT)
System | Countries | Key point
Parliamentary | UK, India, Germany, Italy, Japan, Portugal, Canada | PM real; monarch/president nominal
Presidential | USA, Brazil, most of Latin America | President is head of State and Govt
Semi-presidential | France, Russia, Sri Lanka | President has real day-to-day powers + PM
Germany: ceremonial President; real head = Chancellor
Japan: Emperor (head of State) + PM; Canada: monarch + PM
France: President appoints PM and ministers but cannot dismiss them (responsible to parliament)
Sri Lanka: Executive Presidency since 1978; President directly elected for 6 years
⚠ "A country with a president is presidential" is false: India, Germany, Italy have Presidents but are parliamentary
## Beyond your notes
Switzerland: collegial executive (Federal Council) elected by the legislature for a fixed term: neither model

t: Parliamentary system → merits and limitations
text:
## 1. PMF list
Merits | Limitations
Responsible government: questions, debates, no-confidence | Political instability: coalition breakdowns, defections
Harmony of legislature and executive | Lack of policy continuity
Prevents concentration of power (collective CoM) | Executive / Cabinet dominance with big majority
Alternative government without immediate polls | Fusion of powers dilutes separation
Wide representation of regions, communities | Limited scope for experts
Testbook adds: ministers overburdened with double functions; government inefficiency debate
⚠ "Continuity of policy" and "efficiency" are presidential merits; in 2017 they were the wrong option

t: Why India chose the parliamentary system → the framers' reasons
text:
## 1. Reasons (PMF, NCERT, Testbook)
Reason | Hinge
Familiarity | Worked it under the Acts of 1919 and 1935
Responsibility over stability | Ambedkar preferred accountability
Avoid deadlock | Presidential separation could cause legislature-executive conflict
Diverse society | Executive can represent regions, communities
Avoid personality cult | Presidential system concentrates power in one person (NCERT)
Adopted for both the Union and the States
Some CA members (e.g. Begum Aziz Rasul) wanted a Swiss-type executive elected by the legislature by STV: rejected
⚠ Framers wanted a strong executive with safeguards, not a weak one
Likely-next: Ambedkar's "more responsibility, less stability" line as a Statement-I/II pair

t: India vs UK → features common to both
text:
## 1. Shared (not differences)
Feature | India | UK
Nominal + real executive | President + PM | Monarch + PM
Collective responsibility | To Lok Sabha | To Commons
Bicameralism | LS + RS | Commons + Lords
Majority party rule | LS majority | Commons majority
Dissolution of Lower House | Yes | Yes
PM leadership, secrecy, double membership | Yes | Yes
## 2. The difference
Judicial review: Indian courts can strike down unconstitutional laws; UK courts cannot override Acts of Parliament
India took judicial review from the US Constitution
⚠ 1998 options a, b, c are common to both; only judicial review differs
PYQ 1998: "Indian system differs from British in having...": answer judicial review

t: Parliamentary sovereignty vs constitutional supremacy → 2021 angle
text:
## 1. The two doctrines
 | UK | India
Doctrine | Parliamentary sovereignty | Constitutional supremacy
Law-making | Can make or repeal any law | Limited by the Constitution
Courts | Cannot ordinarily override Acts | Judicial review
Binding future Parliaments | No Parliament binds its successor | Bound by Basic Structure
Indian Parliament is limited by: written Constitution, federal division of powers, Fundamental Rights, judicial review
Amends under Art 368, but cannot destroy Basic Structure (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973)
PMF: India is a synthesis of parliamentary sovereignty and judicial supremacy
## 2. Constitution Bench
Art 145(3): at least five judges for a substantial question of law on interpreting the Constitution and for every Art 143 reference
CJI constitutes the bench; larger benches are odd-numbered (7, 9, 11, 13)
PYQ 2021: both statements correct; trap: assuming Indian Parliament is as sovereign as Britain's

t: India vs UK → full difference table
text:
## 1. PMF 2026 comparison
Feature | India | UK
Supremacy | Constitutional | Parliamentary sovereignty
Head of State | Indirectly elected President, 5 years | Hereditary monarch
Structure | Federal | Unitary
PM | Either House; removed by LS confidence loss | Commons; party can replace PM mid-term
Ministers' liability | Not legally liable for President's acts | Countersign, legal responsibility
Anti-defection | Tenth Schedule disqualification | Lose whip, keep seat
Shadow cabinet | None institutionalised | Institutionalised
Speaker | Usually keeps party membership | Resigns from party

t: India's departures → Westminster features not adopted

## 1. What India changed
Feature | UK | India
Constitution | Unwritten / uncodified | Written, lengthiest
State form | Monarchy | Republic
Legal sovereignty | Parliament | Constitution
Courts | No judicial review of Acts | SC and HCs review laws
Polity | Unitary | Federal, strong Union
Legal responsibility of ministers | Yes | No
PMF: India "not a replica": adapted to a written Constitution, republican character and federal structure
⚠ India borrowed parliamentary government, rule of law, single citizenship, legislative procedure, CAG, writs, bicameralism from the UK, but not sovereignty of Parliament
## In news 2025-26
22 June 2026: UK PM Keir Starmer announced resignation as PM and Labour leader (in office since 5 July 2024) after internal party pressure; shows a UK party replacing its PM mid-term without an election

topic: Separation of powers in a parliamentary system
t: Separation of powers → how far India follows it
text:
## 1. Functional separation with checks
Link | How
Executive ↔ Legislature | Fusion: ministers sit in Parliament; CoM responsible (Art 75(3))
Legislature → Executive | Delegated legislation within limits
Judiciary → both | Judicial review
Legislature → Judiciary | Removal of SC/HC judges
DPSP | Art 50: separate judiciary from executive
## 2. Cases
Ram Jawaya Kapur v. Punjab (1955): no rigid separation, but functions sufficiently differentiated
Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975): separation of powers stressed; later held part of Basic Structure
⚠ India has no strict separation (USA has it); Testbook's "India maintains separation of powers" means functional separation
Likely-next: "Parliamentary system involves strict separation of executive and legislature" is false

topic: Separation of powers in a parliamentary system
t: Parliamentary control of executive → the devices
text:
## 1. Tools of accountability
Questions, supplementaries, Zero Hour (informal, Indian innovation)
Debates and motions; approval of budget and taxes
No-confidence motion: only in the Lok Sabha; removes whole CoM
Committees scrutinise government
Device | House | Effect
No-confidence motion | Lok Sabha only | Entire CoM resigns
Questions / motions | Both Houses | Political accountability
Money Bills / taxation | Lok Sabha decisive | Financial control
⚠ Rajya Sabha cannot remove the government
## Beyond your notes
No-confidence motion is not in the Constitution; it is under Lok Sabha Rule 198, needs support of 50 members
Governments lost confidence votes: V.P. Singh (1990), Deve Gowda (1997), Vajpayee (1999, by one vote)

t: Executive tenure without limits → PM's term debate
text:
## In news 2025-26
PM Narendra Modi became India's longest-serving (continuous) PM; debate on executive term limits (PMF LENS April 2026)
⚠ Praveen Sir CA 360: on 10 June 2026 he completed 4,399 consecutive days (since 26 May 2014), surpassing Nehru's uninterrupted tenure (from 1952); PMF says "longest-serving" without the "continuous" qualifier
## 1. Constitutional position
No fixed term for the PM; holds office while he has Lok Sabha confidence (Art 75)
Ambedkar: continuous accountability (questions, debates, no-confidence) better than term limits
President: only an informal convention of two terms; Constitution has no limit
Weakening factor | Effect

Weak intra-party democracy | No leadership challenge

Constitution (130th Amendment) Bill, 2025 referred to a Joint Parliamentary Committee
Amends Art 75 (Union), 164 (States), 239AA (Delhi)

Trigger | Result

t: Article 74 advice → 42nd vs 44th Amendment
text:
## 1. How binding is ministerial advice
Stage | Position
Original Art 74 | CoM to aid and advise; binding nature only by convention
42nd Amdt, 1976 | Advice made binding on the President
44th Amdt, 1978 | President may require CoM to reconsider advice once; bound by advice tendered after reconsideration
Proviso added to Art 74(1) by the 44th Amendment
K.R. Narayanan returned the Cabinet's recommendation for President's Rule in UP (1997) and Bihar (1998)
⚠ 39th and 40th Amendments have nothing to do with it; the 42nd binds, the 44th allows one return
⚠ After reconsideration the President must act on the same advice: no second return
PYQ 2002: asked which amendment lets the President send back a matter for reconsideration; answer 44th, trap option 42nd

t: Situational discretion → when the President acts alone
text:
## 1. No constitutional discretion, only situational
NCERT: send back advice once, suspensive / pocket veto, choosing PM in a hung House
Situation | What the President decides
No party has clear majority in LS | Whom to appoint PM
PM dies suddenly, no obvious successor | Appointment of PM
CoM cannot prove confidence of LS | Dismissal of CoM
CoM has lost majority | Dissolution of LS
President = nominal / de jure executive; PM + CoM = real / de facto executive
President = Head of State; PM = Head of Government
CoM is collectively responsible to Lok Sabha (Art 75)
⚠ The Constitution gives the President no express discretion (unlike the Governor, Art 163)

t: Article 77 conduct of business → in whose name
text:
## 1. Article 77 clauses
Clause | Content
77(1) | All executive action of GoI expressed to be taken in the name of the President
77(2) | Orders authenticated as per rules made by the President; validity cannot be questioned on the ground that the President did not make it
77(3) | President makes rules for more convenient transaction of business and allocation among Ministers
State parallel: Art 166 (in the name of the Governor)
Art 78: PM communicates all decisions of CoM to the President and furnishes information asked
President may require a matter decided by one Minister to be placed before the whole CoM
⚠ Executive action is in the name of the President, never the PM
PYQ 2014: statement "executive action in the name of the Prime Minister" was the trap; only the rules-of-business statement was correct

t: Articles 59 and 79 → President is part of Parliament but not a member
text:
## 1. Two Articles UPSC paired
Article | Says
79 | Parliament = President + Council of States + House of the People
59(1) | President shall not be a member of either House or of a State Legislature; seat deemed vacant on entering office
59(2) | Shall not hold any other office of profit
59(3) | Rent-free official residence; emoluments fixed by Parliament
59(4) | Emoluments cannot be diminished during term
President is an integral part of Parliament: summons, prorogues, dissolves LS, addresses, assents
Same for States: Governor is part of the State Legislature (Art 168) but not a member
⚠ "Part of Parliament" (Art 79) and "not a member" (Art 59) are both true
PYQ 1997: both statements correct; trap was to think one excludes the other

t: Electoral college → who votes and who does not
text:
## 1. Article 54
Members | Presidential election | Impeachment
Elected MPs (LS + RS) | Yes | Yes
Nominated MPs | No | Yes
Elected MLAs (States, Delhi, Puducherry) | Yes | No
Nominated MLAs | No | No
MLCs (elected or nominated) | No | No
Delhi and Puducherry added by the 70th Amendment, 1992 (Explanation to Art 54)
If an Assembly is dissolved, its former members cannot vote, and the election is not postponed
Parties cannot issue whips for the Presidential election; voting is by secret ballot
⚠ Nominated members of either House or of any Assembly are out
⚠ Legislative Councils have no role in election or impeachment
PYQ 2023: statement that nominated members are in the electoral college was false

t: Value of votes → the formula
text:
## 1. Article 55: uniformity among States, parity with Union
Elector | Value of one vote
MLA | Population of State ÷ elected MLAs ÷ 1000
MP | Total value of all MLAs' votes ÷ total elected MPs (LS + RS)
Population used: 1971 Census (freeze till the first Census after 2026)
Value depends on the ratio population / seats, not on number of seats
Every MP (LS or RS) has the same value
⚠ "More Assembly seats = higher MLA value" is false
⚠ LS MP's vote is not worth more than an RS MP's vote
PYQ 2018: MLA value varies State to State (true); LS MP vote > RS MP vote (false)

t: Vote value examples → which State weighs more
text:
## 1. Figures (1971 population, ECI 2022)
State/UT | Seats | MLA vote value
Uttar Pradesh | 403 | 208 (highest)
Kerala | 140 | 152
Andhra Pradesh | 175 | 159
Madhya Pradesh | 230 | 131
