Appropriation Bill must be passed by both Houses | Not correct (answer)
No withdrawal from CFI except under Appropriation Act | Correct
No Money Bill except on President's recommendation | Correct
Finance Bill for new taxes; no new bill for existing rates | Treated as correct by key
⚠ Appropriation Bill does not need RS passage; Rajya Sabha cannot block it
PYQ 2004: odd one out = "must be passed by both Houses"

t: Finance Bill → taxes and the 75-day rule
text:
Introduced every year to give effect to the tax proposals for the next year
Usually a Money Bill (Art 110); can be Financial Bill I if it carries other matters
Unlike the Appropriation Bill, amendments to reject or reduce a tax may be moved
## Beyond your notes
Provisional Collection of Taxes Act, 1931: new duties take effect immediately; Finance Bill must be enacted within 75 days
Art 265: no tax levied or collected except by authority of law
Bill | Deals with | Amendment to cut amount?
Appropriation Bill | Expenditure | No
Finance Bill | Receipts / taxes | Yes (reduce or reject tax)
Finance Bill 2025 created a dedicated HSN code for popped makhana (PMF LENS-CA Aug 2026): a tariff change made through the Finance Bill

t: Other grants (Art 115-116) → when each is used
text:
Grant | Article | When
Supplementary | 115 | Amount for a service insufficient in the year
Additional | 115 | New service not in the Budget
Excess | 115 | Spending exceeded the grant; voted after the year (after PAC approval)
Vote on account | 116 | Advance for part of the year
Vote of credit | 116 | Unexpected demand of indefinite character; a blank cheque
Exceptional | 116 | Special purpose, no part of current service
Token | (practice) | New service met by reappropriation; token sum voted
All need an Appropriation Act, like the regular Budget
## Beyond your notes
Excess grants go first to the Public Accounts Committee before LS votes them
⚠ Vote of credit is for an indefinite demand; exceptional grant is outside current service

t: Vote on account versus interim budget → difference
text:
Feature | Vote on account | Interim budget
Basis | Art 116 | Convention; no article
Covers | Expenditure only | Receipts and expenditure
Period | Usually 2 months (about 1/6 of estimates); can be longer | Transitional period, until full budget
Tax changes | None | Normally none
Used by | Any government | Usually outgoing government in election year
Vote on account is passed within the interim budget framework
R.K. Shanmukham Chetty presented independent India's first vote on account (1948) and the first budget (26 Nov 1947)
⚠ 2011 statement 1 false: vote on account is not only for a regular government and interim budget is not only for a caretaker
PYQ 2011: only statement 2 (vote on account = expenditure; interim = both)

t: Parliamentary financial control → methods and limits
text:
Method | Present in India?
Annual Financial Statement before Parliament | Yes
Withdrawal from CFI only after Appropriation Bill | Yes
Supplementary grants, vote on account | Yes
Finance Bill | Yes
Mid-year review by a Parliamentary Budget Office | No PBO in India
PAC, Estimates Committee, COPU | Yes (post-facto)
Limits: post-facto scrutiny, guillotine, lack of time and expertise, executive dominance
Estimates Committee: 30, all LS; largest financial committee
PAC: 22 (15 LS + 7 RS), 1 year, examines CAG reports; chair usually Opposition
⚠ India has no Parliamentary Budget Office (2012 trap, option 4)
PYQ 2012: 1, 2, 3 and 5
## In news 2025-26
PAC 2026-27 chaired by K.C. Venugopal (Praveen Sir CA, Mar 2026)

t: Budget rejected by Lok Sabha → consequence
text:
Budget (Appropriation / Finance Bill) defeat in LS = loss of confidence
Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to LS (Art 75(3)) → PM submits resignation of the whole Council
Defeat of a cut motion, Motion of Thanks or a Money Bill has the same effect
Wrong option (2011) | Why wrong
Budget modified and re-presented | No such procedure
Referred to Rajya Sabha | RS has no vote on demands
Finance Minister alone resigns | Responsibility is collective
Government defeat on a Private Member's Bill does not imply loss of confidence
PYQ 2011: PM submits resignation of the Council of Ministers

t: Budget history and practice → facts and in news
text:
Fact | Detail
First budget (British India) | 1860, James Wilson
First budget of independent India | 26 Nov 1947, R.K. Shanmukham Chetty
First budget of Republic | John Mathai
Most budgets | Morarji Desai (10)
Date shift to 1 February | 2017 (Arun Jaitley)
Railway Budget merged | 2017 (separate since 1924)
Time 5 pm → 11 am | 1999 (Yashwant Sinha)
First paperless budget | 2021-22
First woman to present | Indira Gandhi (1970-71)
⚠ PMF infographic says Art 112 requires presentation on 1 February: the date is practice, not in the Constitution
## In news 2025-26
Union Budget 2026-27: Nirmala Sitharaman's 9th (most by a woman FM); 6th digital; first prepared at Kartavya Bhavan; built on "three Kartavyas"
Halwa ceremony marks start of budget printing (North Block press since 1980)

t: Consolidated Fund of India (Art 266(1)) → what goes in, how money comes out
text:
Credited: all revenues of the Union, all loans raised (treasury bills, loans, ways and means advances), money received in repayment of loans
Withdrawal only with Parliament's authorisation by law (Appropriation Act, Art 114), except charged items which are not voted but still appropriated
States have their own Consolidated Fund of the State (Art 266(1))
Question | Answer
Where are tax revenues credited? | CFI (2011)
Who authorises withdrawal? | Parliament (2011), not President, PM or FM
Who issues money? | Under appropriation by Parliament
Audit | CAG
⚠ CFI withdrawal needs Parliament; Public Account withdrawal does not (2015)
## In news 2025-26
Health Security se National Security Cess (replacing GST compensation cess on sin goods): proceeds go to the CFI and are not shared with States

t: Charged expenditure (Art 112(3)) → full list
text:
Charged on CFI | Note
President: emoluments, allowances, office expenditure | 
Chairman, Deputy Chairman of RS; Speaker, Deputy Speaker of LS: salaries | 
Supreme Court judges: salaries, allowances, pensions | 
High Court judges: pensions only | HC salaries are on the State fund
CAG: salary, allowances, pension | 
Debt charges of GoI | Interest, sinking fund
Sums for any court judgment, decree, arbitral award | 
Any other expenditure declared by Constitution or Parliament by law | e.g. UPSC members' expenses
Not voted by LS but can be discussed in both Houses
Election Commission salaries are not in the constitutional list (UPPCS trap)
⚠ Parliament cannot vote on charged items, but it can discuss them
## In news 2025-26
SC (Anoop Baranwal, 2023) urged that Election Commission expenditure be charged on the CFI (CARE May 2026)

t: Public Account and Contingency Fund → nature and control
text:
Feature | Public Account (Art 266(2)) | Contingency Fund (Art 267)
Money | All other public money: PF, small savings, deposits, remittances | Fixed corpus set by Parliament by law
Government's role | Banker / trustee | For unforeseen expenditure
Withdrawal | No parliamentary appropriation needed; executive action | By President, pending Parliament's approval
Recoupment | Not applicable | Recouped from CFI after Parliament approves
## Beyond your notes
Operated by the Finance Secretary (Department of Economic Affairs) on the President's behalf
Contingency Fund of India Act, 1950; corpus raised from Rs 500 crore to Rs 30,000 crore (Finance Act 2021; as of 2026)
Each State has its own Contingency Fund (Art 267(2)) at the Governor's disposal
⚠ "All disbursements from Public Account need Parliament's authorisation" is false (2015)
⚠ Appropriation from the Contingency Fund is not a Money Bill matter (only custody is)

t: Budget-related offices → who prepares and audits
text:
Task | Body
Prepares Union Budget | Budget Division, Department of Economic Affairs (Ministry of Finance)
Tax revenue administration | Department of Revenue (CBDT, CBIC)
Accounts of CFI, Public Account | Controller General of Accounts
Audit of Union and States | CAG (Art 148-151)
Examines CAG reports | PAC
Examines estimates | Estimates Committee
Constitutes Finance Commission | President (Art 280)
Budget documents include AFS, Demands for Grants, Finance Bill, Budget at a Glance, Receipt and Expenditure Budgets, FRBM statements (Macro-Economic Framework, Medium-Term Fiscal Policy cum Fiscal Policy Strategy)
⚠ The Department of Revenue does not prepare the Budget (2015 statement 1 false)
PYQ 2015: only statement 2 correct (CFI needs Parliament; Revenue Dept and Public Account statements false)

topic: Questions, Question Hour and Zero Hour
t: Types of questions → oral or written, supplementaries allowed?
text:
## 1. The four types (PMF)
Type | Answer | Supplementaries | Note
Starred | Oral (on the floor) | Allowed | Max 20 listed for oral answer per day (Rocket)
Unstarred | Written (laid on the table) | Not allowed | Answered in writing, so no follow-up
Short notice | Oral | Allowed (Rocket) | Urgent public importance; notice shorter than 10 clear days
Question to a private member | - | - | Only on a Bill, resolution or other business that member is responsible for
## 2. Memory hook
Starred = star speaker = spoken (oral) answer + supplementaries
Unstarred = written, no supplementaries
⚠ 2026 trap: the statements swapped the two definitions ("unstarred = oral", "starred = written"); only "no supplementary on unstarred" was right
PYQ 2026: "how many correct" on starred vs unstarred; answer: only one statement (no supplementary on unstarred) correct

topic: Questions, Question Hour and Zero Hour
t: Question Hour → timing, purpose, control over the executive
text:
## 1. What it is
First hour of a sitting is generally devoted to questions (PMF): members seek information from Ministers and exercise parliamentary control over the executive
NCERT: Question Hour is perhaps the most effective method of keeping vigil on the executive; maximum attendance is recorded in it
## 2. Timings (Rocket Sheets)
House | Question Hour | Zero Hour
Lok Sabha | 11:00 AM - 12:00 Noon | Immediately after, 12 Noon onwards
Rajya Sabha | 12:00 Noon - 1:00 PM (shifted after 2014) | Begins the day (11 AM)
Questions are submitted in advance; Ministers of the department answer (Testbook)
⚠ Question Hour is in the Rules of Procedure; Zero Hour is not in the Rules
## Beyond your notes
In Rajya Sabha, Zero Hour is taken at 11 AM, before Question Hour (since 2014 shift)
Question Hour was suspended in the Monsoon Session 2020 (COVID); written questions continued

topic: Questions, Question Hour and Zero Hour
t: Supplementary questions and the control triangle
text:
## 1. Supplementaries
Asked orally after the answer to a starred or short notice question, to probe the Minister further
Not possible on an unstarred question (the answer is written)
## 2. The "accountability triangle" (Rocket Sheets)
Device | Why it controls the CoM
Question Hour | Daily questioning of Ministers on their departments
Supplementary questions | On-the-spot follow-up; Minister must reply orally
Adjournment motion | Interrupts business; element of censure on the government
All three are tools of Art 75(3) collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha
⚠ A follow-up on an answer already given (matter of fact) can also be taken as a half-an-hour discussion: no formal motion, no voting
PYQ 2017: Parliament controls the CoM through adjournment motion, Question Hour and supplementary questions; answer "1, 2 and 3"

topic: Questions, Question Hour and Zero Hour
t: Zero Hour vs Question Hour → status, timing, notice
text:
Feature | Question Hour | Zero Hour
Timing (LS) | First hour (11-12) | Immediately after Question Hour (12 Noon)
Origin | Formal procedure under the Rules | Indian innovation, early 1960s (1962)
Status | In the Rules of Procedure | Not in the Constitution, not in the Rules: informal convention
Duration | 1 hour | Up to 1 hour, not fixed in Rules
Notice | Advance notice of each question | Matters raised without prior notice (Mains Magnum)
Minister's reply | Must answer | Not bound to reply (NCERT)
UK has no direct equivalent of Zero Hour; parliamentary questions there need advance notice (PMF Mains Magnum)
⚠ "Zero Hour is mentioned in the Rules of Procedure" is wrong; "Zero Hour is an Indian innovation" is right
⚠ Rule 377 and the Zero Hour convention let MPs raise matters of public importance (LENS Aug 2026)

topic: Questions, Question Hour and Zero Hour
t: Question Hour in news 2025-26
text:
## In news 2025-26
Session | Fact (PMF LENS)
Monsoon 2025 | LS functioned 29% and RS 34% of scheduled time; only 23% (LS) and 6% (RS) of Question Hour questions answered
Monsoon 2026 | Question Hour ran just 1% of scheduled time in LS and 12% in RS; estimated loss Rs 175 crore
Trend | Annual sittings fell from 121 days (1952-70) to about 68 days since 2000; Constitution prescribes no minimum sitting days
Frequent adjournments weaken Question Hour, Parliament's primary oversight mechanism (accountability vacuum)
Reform ideas: statutory minimum 100-120 sitting days, fixed calendar (Australia model)
LENS Apr 2026: a larger Lok Sabha (proposed 850 seats) would cut each MP's chance to speak in Question Hour and Zero Hour
Exam angle: a statement "the Constitution fixes minimum sitting days" is false; only a gap of not more than 6 months between sessions (Art 85)

topic: Adjournment Motion and Other Discussion Devices
t: Adjournment motion → purpose, support, house
text:
## 1. Core facts
Introduced only in Lok Sabha to draw attention to a definite matter of urgent public importance (PMF)
Interrupts the normal business of the House: an extraordinary device
Involves an element of censure against the Government, so Rajya Sabha cannot use it
Item | Rule
Support to admit | 50 members
Discussion | Not less than 2 hours 30 minutes
Per sitting | Only one adjournment motion
Consent | Presiding officer (Speaker)
⚠ Option traps in 2012: "reduce a specific amount in a demand" = cut motion; "collect information from Ministers" = questions; "postpone proceedings due to disorder" = the Speaker's adjournment of the House, not an adjournment motion
PYQ 2012: purpose of adjournment motion = discussion on a definite matter of urgent public importance

topic: Adjournment Motion and Other Discussion Devices
t: Adjournment motion → conditions of admissibility
text:
## 1. The matter must (PYQ explanation, Rocket)
Be definite, factual, urgent and of public importance
Cover only one matter
Be a specific matter of recent occurrence, not framed in general terms
## 2. It must not
Raise a question of privilege
Revive discussion on a matter already discussed in the same session
Deal with a matter that is under adjudication by a court (sub judice)
Raise a question that can be raised on a distinct motion
Device | Censure element? | House
Adjournment motion | Yes | Lok Sabha only
Calling attention | No | Both
⚠ Testbook says the Chairman in Rajya Sabha may accept an adjournment motion; PMF and the PYQ explanations: RS cannot use it (follow PMF)

topic: Adjournment Motion and Other Discussion Devices
t: Calling attention → Indian innovation without censure
text:
## 1. Procedure (PMF)
A member, with the permission of the presiding officer, calls the attention of a Minister to a matter of urgent public importance
The Minister makes a statement on it; questions/clarifications may follow (Preview)
An Indian innovation in parliamentary procedure (like Zero Hour)
## 2. Compared
Feature | Calling attention | Adjournment motion
Censure | None | Yes
House | Either House | LS only
Business | Not interrupted | Normal business set aside
Voting | No | Yes
Calling attention notices historically restricted the scope of adjournment motions (not Question Hour or Zero Hour) (Rocket)
## Beyond your notes
In operation since 1954; Lok Sabha Rule 197
⚠ "Both Zero Hour and Calling Attention are Indian innovations": correct

topic: Adjournment Motion and Other Discussion Devices
t: Discussion without voting → half-an-hour, short duration, special mention
text:
Device | Purpose | Motion / vote
Half-an-hour discussion | Further clarification on a matter of fact from an answer already given | No formal motion, no voting
Short duration discussion | Matter of urgent public importance | No formal motion, no voting
Special Mention (RS) | Matter of public importance that cannot be raised by other devices | Mention only
Rule 377 (LS) | LS equivalent of Special Mention | Written notice + Speaker's consent
Rule 184 (LS) | Discussion on a matter followed by voting | Yes, political cost to govt
Rule 377: matters per day raised from 20 to 30 in 2015 (Rocket)
⚠ Rule 184 = discussion with voting; short duration discussion = without voting
## Beyond your notes
Short duration discussion = "two-hour discussion": LS Rule 193, RS Rule 176
Rajya Sabha Rule 267: suspension of the day's business to discuss a matter; notices are frequent, admission rare

topic: Adjournment Motion and Other Discussion Devices
t: Which device in which House → complete list
text:
Device | Lok Sabha | Rajya Sabha
Question Hour, supplementaries, short notice questions | Yes | Yes
Zero Hour, calling attention, half-an-hour discussion | Yes | Yes
Privilege motion, point of order, closure | Yes | Yes
Adjournment motion | Yes | No
No-confidence motion | Yes | No
Censure motion (Rocket) | Yes | No
Cut motions (Demands for Grants) | Yes | No
Special Mention | Rule 377 instead | Yes
Logic: devices that test or censure the government sit only in the House to which the CoM is collectively responsible (Art 75(3))
⚠ RS can discuss the budget but cannot vote Demands for Grants, so no cut motions there
Exam angle: "Rajya Sabha can entertain an adjournment motion / no-confidence motion" is the standard wrong statement

t: No-confidence motion → source, house, support, grounds, time limit
text:
## 1. The facts UPSC tests
Point | Rule
In the Constitution? | No; neither confidence nor no-confidence motion is mentioned
Basis | Art 75(3): CoM collectively responsible to Lok Sabha; procedure in LS Rule 198
House | Lok Sabha only; RS cannot entertain it
Notice | Written notice to the Secretary-General of Lok Sabha
Support for leave | At least 50 members
Grounds | Need not state reasons
Taken up | Within 10 days of leave being granted
Against | Entire CoM, not an individual minister
Passed by | Simple majority of members present and voting
If passed | CoM must resign
⚠ 2004 trap: "no-confidence motion has to set out the grounds" = wrong (that is the censure motion)
PYQ 2014: not in the Constitution + only in Lok Sabha: both correct

t: No-confidence vs censure vs confidence motion
text:
Feature | No-confidence | Censure | Confidence
Moved by | Opposition (any LS member with 50 supporters) | Members | Government / CoM
Reasons | Need not be stated | Must be stated | -
Against | Entire CoM only | Individual minister, group, or entire CoM | -
Purpose | Test whether CoM enjoys confidence | Disapprove specific policies/actions | Prove majority on the floor
If passed / lost | CoM must resign | No forced resignation | If lost, govt falls
House | LS only | LS (Rocket) | LS only
Censure shows political weakness but does not oblige resignation (Rocket)
⚠ "Censure motion can be moved only against the whole CoM" = wrong

t: No-confidence and confidence motions → history
text:
## 1. From your notes
First no-confidence motion: 1963, 3rd Lok Sabha, Acharya J.B. Kripalani against Nehru govt
Till 15 Aug 2023: 28 no-confidence motions (28th on Manipur, 2023) and 11 confidence motions discussed (Preview)
Half of the no-confidence motions (14 of 28) came in 1965-75; 12 against Indira Gandhi governments
NCERT: after 1989 several governments resigned for losing Lok Sabha's confidence because coalition partners withdrew support
⚠ Preview's own question cites 27 no-confidence / 9 confidence motions; its explanation gives 28 / 11: use 28 / 11
## Beyond your notes
Year | Government | Outcome
1979 | Morarji Desai | Resigned during a no-confidence debate
1990 | V.P. Singh | Lost confidence vote
1997 | H.D. Deve Gowda | Lost confidence vote
1999 | A.B. Vajpayee | Lost confidence vote by one vote
2018 and 2023 no-confidence motions against the Modi govt were defeated

t: Motion of Thanks → President's Address as a confidence test
text:
## 1. Constitutional base
Art 86: President may address either House or both (not mandatory); no address under Art 86 since 1950
Art 87: special address at the first session after each general election and the first session of every year
Discussion under Rules (Art 87(2)); like Britain's "speech from the Throne"
## 2. The motion
Point | Fact
Moved by | A member, seconded by another (selected by the PM)
Discussion | About 3 days, then voting
Scope | Any matter of national or international importance
Defeat in LS | Serious loss of confidence = defeat of the government
Motion of Thanks is a substantive motion that needs seconding (exception; most do not)
⚠ Address is drafted by the government; the President only reads it
## Beyond your notes
Members may move amendments to the Motion of Thanks

t: "No-confidence motion" against the Speaker → really a removal resolution
text:
## In news 2025-26
10 Feb 2026: Opposition (notice by Congress chief whip K. Suresh, for Congress, SP, DMK) moved a "no-confidence motion" against Speaker Om Birla, alleging partiality
Point | Rule
Basis | Art 94(c): resolution passed by a majority of all the then members (effective majority)
Notice | At least 14 days
Leave | 50 members must stand up; fewer = motion fails
Rules | LS Rules 200-203; Rule 200A: charges must be specific
Taken up | Within 10 days of leave
Speaker during it | Cannot preside (Art 96); may speak and vote in the first instance, but no casting vote
Earlier attempts 1954 (G.V. Mavalankar), 1966 (Hukam Singh), 1987 (Balram Jakhar): all failed
⚠ It is not a Rule 198 no-confidence motion against the CoM; it needs an effective majority, not a simple one

topic: Motions, Closure, Privilege and Cut Motions
t: Kinds of motions → substantive, substitute, subsidiary
text:
Kind | Meaning
Substantive | Independent, self-contained proposal on an important matter; put to vote
Substitute | Moved in place of an original motion; proposes an alternative
Subsidiary | No independent meaning; depends on another motion or proceeding
## 1. Substantive motion examples
Motion of Thanks, adjournment motion, confidence / no-confidence motions, resolutions for removal of Speaker / Deputy Speaker, motions on vacancy, suspension or expulsion of members
Discussion of the Speaker's conduct (and of a judge's conduct under Art 121) only on a substantive motion
## In news 2025-26
Feb 2026: notice of a substantive motion filed against Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi for "unethical conduct" in speeches (PMF Prelims Magnum)
⚠ Most substantive motions need no seconding; exceptions: Speaker / Deputy Speaker election and Motion of Thanks

topic: Motions, Closure, Privilege and Cut Motions
t: Substantive motion vs resolution → rules
text:
## 1. Procedure (PMF LENS Feb 2026)
Notice mandatory; moved only by the member who gave notice (a minister may move for another minister)
Mover has a right of reply; proceeds only if the Chair admits it
## 2. Restrictions
Rule of anticipation: inadmissible if it anticipates a matter already scheduled in the same session
Sub judice: not on a matter under active judicial consideration
Cannot be withdrawn if an amendment to it is pending
Point | Resolution | Substantive motion
Relation | All resolutions are substantive motions | Not all are resolutions
Repeat bar | One year on same subject | Generally within the same session
Vote | Always put to vote | Some concluded without a vote
## 3. Types of resolution (PMF)
Type | Moved by
Private Member's | A member who is not a Minister
Government | A Minister
Statutory | Minister or private member, under the Constitution or an Act

topic: Motions, Closure, Privilege and Cut Motions
t: Closure motions → four forms
text:
## 1. Closure = cut short a debate and put the matter to vote (PMF)
Form | What happens
Simple closure | Matter declared sufficiently discussed, put to vote
Closure by compartments | Clauses/parts grouped and voted together
Kangaroo closure | Only important clauses debated and voted; rest treated as passed
Guillotine | When allotted time ends, all remaining clauses or demands voted, discussed or not
Guillotine on the last day of voting on Demands for Grants: Speaker puts all remaining demands to vote
⚠ Kangaroo = jumps over unimportant clauses; Guillotine = time runs out
Exam angle: LENS Aug 2026 lists guillotine as a cause of weak fiscal scrutiny

topic: Motions, Closure, Privilege and Cut Motions
t: Privilege motion → breach of privilege, procedure
text:
## 1. What it is
Concerned with a breach of parliamentary privilege by a Minister or member (or outsider), including misleading the House (PMF)
Can be moved by any member of either House
## 2. Procedure (PMF Prelims Magnum 2026)
Step | Detail
Notice | LS Rule 222; RS Rule 187
Timing | Usually after Question Hour; urgent cases any time
First scrutiny | Speaker / Chairman: decides or refers
Examination | Privileges Committee: summons witnesses, evidence
Decision | The House (committee only recommends)
Committee | LS 15 members (Speaker nominates; Speaker-appointed chair); RS 10 (Chairman nominates; chaired by Deputy Chairman)
## In news 2025-26
Mar 2026: LS Privileges Committee constituted for the first time in the 18th LS; chair Ravi Shankar Prasad + 14 MPs (Praveen Sir)
Privilege notice against comedian Kunal Kamra: summoned by Maharashtra Legislative Council's Privileges Committee (LENS Feb 2026)
⚠ Privileges extend to Ministers and the Attorney General, not the President

topic: Motions, Closure, Privilege and Cut Motions
t: Cut motions → three types and the Rs 1 / Rs 100 numbers
text:
Type | Amount | Purpose
Policy cut | Demand reduced to Rs 1 | Disapproval of policy behind the demand
Economy cut | Reduced by a specified amount | Economy in expenditure
Token cut | Reduced by Rs 100 | Ventilate a specific grievance
Moved only in Lok Sabha on Demands for Grants
Passage = serious expression of lack of confidence; Rocket: obliges the government to resign
⚠ 2012 distractor: "reduction of a specific amount in demand for grant" = cut motion, not adjournment motion
⚠ PMF: passage is a "serious expression of lack of confidence"; Rocket goes further ("obliges resignation"): follow PMF wording
Exam angle: Rs 1 = policy (Policy, one rupee); Rs 100 = Token

topic: Motions, Closure, Privilege and Cut Motions
t: Point of order, no-day-yet-named motion and other procedural terms
text:
Term | Meaning
Point of order | Raised when proceedings do not conform to Rules or the Constitution; decided by presiding officer; ordinarily no debate
No-day-yet-named motion | Admitted by Speaker but no date fixed for discussion
Lame-duck session | Last session of the old LS after a new LS is elected; defeated members = lame ducks
Quorum | One-tenth of total members (Art 100)
Casting vote | Presiding officer does not vote in the first instance; votes only in a tie
Raised by any member; the presiding officer's ruling is final
⚠ A point of order suspends the business only until the presiding officer rules on it

t: Floor terms → meaning (the 1996 option set)
text:
Term | Meaning
Yielding the floor | Speaker asks a speaking member to stop and let another member speak
Crossing the floor | Member changes party allegiance: leaves one party, joins another or turns independent
Interpellation | Procedure of demanding that the government explain an act or policy (formal questioning)
Decorum | Members enter and leave the chamber without disturbing proceedings; proper conduct
Cross-voting | Voting for a party one does not belong to (e.g. RS elections)
Speaker or Chairman can prohibit one member and allow another to speak: yielding the floor (Preview)
⚠ "Crossing the floor" is not about moving to another seat to speak; it means defection
PYQ 1996: Speaker asks a member to stop and let another speak = yielding the floor; asked again in State PSC papers

t: Disorder on the floor → walkout, well, suspension
text:
## 1. NCERT
Heated Question Hour: members raise their voice, walk to the well of the House or walk out in protest
These are political techniques to gain concessions and force accountability, but cost legislative time
Term | Meaning
Walkout | Members leave the House in protest
Well of the House | Space in front of the presiding officer's chair; entering it = protest
Suspension of a member | Presiding officer names a member and the House suspends him/her for disorder
## In news 2025-26
Opposition cited mass suspensions (100 Opposition MPs in Dec 2023; 8 MPs in 2026) in the Feb 2026 notice against the Speaker (CARE, Praveen Sir)
LENS Aug 2026: limited Opposition space turns disruption into standard tactics
⚠ The Speaker's adjournment of the House for disorder is not an "adjournment motion"

t: Adjournment, adjournment sine die, prorogation, dissolution
text:
Act | By whom | Effect
Adjournment | Presiding officer | Suspends sitting for hours, days or weeks; session continues
Adjournment sine die | Presiding officer | Ends sitting without a day fixed for the next
Prorogation | President | Ends the session; does not dissolve the House
Dissolution | President | Ends the life of Lok Sabha; RS is never dissolved
Speaker also adjourns or suspends a sitting for lack of quorum (PMF)
Max 6 months between two sessions (Art 85)
## Beyond your notes
Pending notices (except of Bills) lapse on prorogation; Bills lapse on dissolution subject to Art 107 rules
⚠ 2012 option (d) "postpone proceedings to check violent behaviour" describes the Speaker's adjournment power, not the adjournment motion

t: Rule numbers → device (Lok Sabha unless marked)
text:
Rule | Device
184 | Discussion with voting
198 | No-confidence motion
200-203 | Removal of Speaker (resolution under Art 94(c))
222 | Privilege notice (RS 187)
377 | Special mention-type matters (30 a day since 2015)
8(1) | Election of Deputy Speaker (date fixed by Speaker)
## Beyond your notes
Rule | Device
56 | Adjournment motion
193 | Short duration discussion (RS 176)
197 | Calling attention (RS 180)
267 (RS) | Suspension of business
⚠ The Constitution has no Article for no-confidence, Zero Hour or Rule 377 devices: they come from Rules or conventions

t: Parliamentary control over administration → through committees
text:
## 1. Why committees
Parliament has limited time; detailed scrutiny of Bills, expenditure and administration is done in committees
NCERT calls committees "miniature legislatures"; much of the discussion on Bills happens there
Testbook: effective parliamentary control over the administration is "primarily exercised through a system of parliamentary committees", chiefly the 3 financial committees and 24 DRSCs
## 2. What makes a committee "parliamentary" (PMF)
Test | Requirement
Formation | Appointed or elected by the House, or nominated by Speaker/Chairman
Direction | Works under the Presiding Officer
Report | Presents report to the House or the Presiding Officer
Staff | Secretariat of Lok Sabha / Rajya Sabha
Authority from Article 105 (privileges of Parliament and its committees), Article 118 (Rules of Procedure), and conventions
⚠ Committees are not created by the Constitution by name; they come from the Rules of Procedure
PYQ 2001: how Parliament controls the administration; answer through Parliamentary Committees, not Consultative Committees, periodic reports or writs

text:

Type | Nature | Examples
Standing | Permanent, constituted every year or periodically | Financial committees, DRSCs, Petitions, Privileges, BAC, Rules
Ad hoc | Temporary, end after report | Inquiry committees; Advisory (Select/Joint Committees on Bills)
## 2. Six groups of standing committees (PMF / Preview)
Group | Members
Financial | PAC, Estimates, COPU
DRSCs | 24
To inquire | Petitions, Privileges, Ethics
To scrutinise and control | Govt Assurances, Subordinate Legislation, Papers Laid, SC/ST Welfare, Empowerment of Women, Offices of Profit

House-keeping | General Purposes, House, Library, Salaries and Allowances
Other ad hoc examples (Testbook): Railway Convention Committee, committees on Draft Five Year Plans, Hindi Equivalents
⚠ Ad hoc OBC Welfare Committee is called "ad hoc" in Testbook though reconstituted every year

Rule | Fact

Feature | Parliamentary committee | Consultative committee
Constituted by | House / Presiding Officer | Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs
Attached to | Parliament | Ministries

t: Lok Sabha Ethics Committee → origin and complaint rules
text:
## 1. Origin
Year | Step
Oct 1996 | Presiding Officers' Conference (New Delhi) urged legislatures to explore ethics committees
1997 | Rajya Sabha Ethics Committee, first in any Indian legislature (Chairman K.R. Narayanan)
16 May 2000 | First Lok Sabha Ethics Committee, ad hoc, by Speaker G.M.C. Balayogi (13th LS), on Privileges Committee's recommendation
2015 | Made permanent: rules added to LS Rules of Procedure
## 2. Complaint procedure (LS Rule 233A, Chapter XXA)
Any person or member may complain; a complaint by a person must be forwarded through an LS member
Complainant gives evidence and an affidavit that it is not false, frivolous or vexatious (not needed if an MP complains)
Speaker may also refer complaints
No sub judice matters; Committee's view on sub judice is final
No complaints based only on media reports; makes a prima facie inquiry first
Report goes to the Speaker; half-hour discussion possible
⚠ Not "only an MP can complain": any person can, through an MP
PYQ 2024: ad hoc at first (correct); only MPs complain (wrong); no sub judice (correct); answer 1 and 3 only

House | Members | Chair
Lok Sabha | 15, nominated by Speaker | Appointed by Speaker
Rajya Sabha | 10, nominated by Chairman | Usually the Deputy Chairman
State legislatures | Nominated per House rules | -
## 2. Powers and procedure
Semi-/quasi-judicial: can summon members and outsiders, call for documents, record evidence
Recommends action (reprimand, suspension, expulsion, imprisonment during session); House decides
Notice raised under LS Rule 222 / RS Rule 187; presiding officer is the first level of scrutiny and may refer it to the committee
Privileges rest on Articles 105 and 194; cases: Searchlight (1958), JMM bribery (1998)
⚠ The Committee cannot itself punish; only the House can

t: Strength of the Supreme Court → who decides
text:
## 1. Article 124(1)
SC = CJI + such number of other judges as Parliament may by law prescribe
Fixed by the SC (Number of Judges) Act, 1956; changed by an ordinary law (simple majority), not a constitutional amendment
Year | Strength (incl. CJI)
1950 (inaugurated 28 Jan 1950) | 8 (CJI + 7)
2009 Amendment Act | 31
2019 Amendment Act | 34 (33 + 1)
2026 Amendment Act | 38 (37 + 1)
⚠ The power to raise the number lies with Parliament, not the President or the CJI
⚠ SC succeeded the Federal Court (GoI Act 1935, set up 1937) and replaced the Privy Council as the final appeal court
## In news 2026
May 2026: Cabinet approved the SC (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026: 34 → 38
June 2026: first done by Ordinance (Art 123), criticised as misuse of ordinance power; replacing Bill introduced in Lok Sabha (July 2026)

topic: Supreme Court: Composition, Appointment and Collegium
t: SC judges → appointment, qualifications, oath, tenure
text:
## 1. Appointment (Art 124(2))
By the President by warrant under hand and seal; in practice on Collegium recommendation
## 2. Qualifications (Art 124(3)): citizen of India + any one
Route | Requirement
Judge | of a High Court (or HCs in succession) for 5 years
Advocate | of a High Court (or HCs in succession) for 10 years
Jurist | distinguished jurist in the President's opinion
⚠ No minimum age; no fixed tenure: holds office till 65
⚠ "Distinguished jurist" is not defined; the route has stayed unused for 76+ years (PMF 2026)
## 3. Oath and tenure
Item | Rule
Oath | before the President or a person appointed by him (Third Schedule)
Retirement | 65 years
Age dispute | decided by authority and manner Parliament provides
Resignation | in writing to the President (Art 124(2)(a))
Removal | President's order after Parliament's address (Art 124(4))
⚠ A judge vacates office on resignation, removal or reaching 65; there is no term in years

topic: Supreme Court: Composition, Appointment and Collegium
t: Chief Justice of India → appointment convention and role
text:
## 1. How the CJI is appointed
Office mandated by Art 124(1), appointed under Art 124(2); no separate procedure in the Constitution
Convention: senior-most judge by length of service in the SC, not age
Steps: outgoing CJI recommends → Law Minister → PM → President
Doubt about fitness: other SC judges consulted (Art 124(2)); process follows the MoP
Eligibility same as any SC judge (5 / 10 years / jurist)
⚠ Convention broken: 1973 A.N. Ray (superseded 3 seniors), 1977 M.H. Beg (superseded H.R. Khanna)
## 2. Role of the CJI
Power | Detail
Master of the roster | allocates cases, composes Benches
Collegium head | SC and HC appointments, transfers
Administrative | staff (Art 146), ad hoc judges (Art 127)
Status | first among equals: no superior judicial power
2019: SC held the office of the CJI is under the RTI Act, 2005
## In news 2025-26
Sanjiv Khanna 51st CJI (Nov 2024); B.R. Gavai 52nd CJI (14 May 2025)
Surya Kant sworn in as 53rd CJI (24 Nov 2025)

t: Judges Cases → what each held
text:
Case | Year | Held
First (S.P. Gupta) | 1981 | "Consultation" ≠ concurrence: executive primacy
Second (SC AOR Assn) | 1993 | Consultation = concurrence; Collegium born; judicial primacy
Third (Presidential reference, Art 143) | 1998 | Collegium = CJI + 4 senior-most judges for SC
Fourth (NJAC) | 2015 | 99th Amendment + NJAC Act 2014 struck down; Collegium restored
## 1. NJAC (struck down)
Members: CJI, 2 senior-most SC judges, Union Law Minister, 2 eminent persons
Ground: violated independence of judiciary (basic structure)
⚠ The Third Judges Case came through an Art 143 reference, not a regular appeal

text:
## 1. Composition
For | Members

HC appointments (SC Collegium) | CJI + 2 senior-most SC judges
HC Collegium (initiates) | HC Chief Justice + 2 senior-most HC judges
Transfer of HC Chief Justice | CJI + 4
## 2. Process rules
Proposal for SC: initiated by CJI; for HC: by the HC Chief Justice
Names from HC Collegium go with Government's views to the SC Collegium
Government may return a name once; if reiterated, must appoint
MoP: framed after NJAC was struck down; criteria: experience, integrity, judicial temperament, regional and community representation; Government must give reasons for rejecting a name
⚠ Collegium is not in the Constitution or any Act; formalised by the Third Judges Case (1998)
Criticism: lack of transparency, favouring kin of sitting judges; demands for regional SC benches

topic: Supreme Court: Composition, Appointment and Collegium
t: Acting, ad hoc and retired judges → Articles 126-128
text:
Article | Who | Appointed/requested by | Condition
126 Acting CJI | an SC judge | President | CJI office vacant, CJI absent/unable
127 Ad hoc judge | a qualified HC judge | CJI with previous consent of President after consulting the HC Chief Justice | lack of quorum
128 Retired judge | retired SC judge (or eligible retired HC judge) | CJI with previous consent of President + consent of the person | any time
Art 127 and 128 judges enjoy the jurisdiction, powers and privileges of an SC judge while sitting; Art 128 judge is not deemed an SC judge otherwise
⚠ Art 127 needs quorum shortage; Art 128 has no such condition
⚠ Constitution's ad hoc judges are for the SC only (Art 127); HCs use Art 224A (retired judges)
⚠ Ad hoc judge of the SC must leave HC duties: SC work has priority
PYQ 2021: retired SC judge can be called back by CJI with President's prior permission (Art 128) true; "HC can review its own judgment like SC" was marked false by UPSC's key
⚠ PMF: HCs as courts of record do have limited review power; follow UPSC's key (answer: 1 only)

topic: Supreme Court: Composition, Appointment and Collegium
t: Seat, Benches and procedure → Articles 130 and 145
text:
Item | Rule
Seat (Art 130) | Delhi; CJI may appoint other place(s) with the President's approval
Nature of Art 130 | enabling, not mandatory: no regional bench yet
Rules (Art 145) | SC frames rules of practice and procedure with President's approval
Constitution Bench | at least 5 judges for substantial questions of constitutional interpretation and Art 143 references
Judgment | in open court, by majority; dissent allowed
Smaller vs larger Bench | a smaller Bench cannot overrule a larger Bench
⚠ The Government does not choose the seat: it is the CJI with President's approval
⚠ The "approval of the President" (not Parliament) is needed for both Art 130 and Art 145

topic: Removal, Independence and Accountability of Judges
t: Removal of judges → procedure under the Judges (Inquiry) Act 1968
text:
## 1. Grounds: Art 124(4) (SC), Art 217(1)(b) / Art 218 (HC)
Only proved misbehaviour or incapacity; neither term defined in the Constitution
SC has read misbehaviour to include corruption, wilful misconduct, moral turpitude
Procedure laid down by the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968, made under Art 124(5)
## 2. Steps
Step | Detail
Motion | signed by 100 LS or 50 RS members
Admission | Speaker/Chairman may admit or refuse; no time limit, no reasons needed
Inquiry committee | SC judge or CJI + HC Chief Justice + distinguished jurist
Report | not guilty → motion ends; guilty → taken up
Voting | each House separately, special majority: majority of total membership + 2/3 present and voting, same session
Order | President issues removal order
⚠ Constitution says "removal", not "impeachment" (impeachment is for the President)
⚠ Motion does not lapse on dissolution of Lok Sabha (Testbook)
⚠ State Legislature has no role in removing an HC judge
Notices in both Houses on the same day: Speaker and Chairman form one joint committee
PYQ 2019: Speaker can reject the motion: true; misbehaviour defined in Constitution: false; procedure in the Act: true; special majority in each House: true

topic: Removal, Independence and Accountability of Judges
t: Removal cases → names and outcome
text:
Case | Outcome
V. Ramaswami (SC, 1991-93) | first motion; got 2/3 of present but not majority of total (Congress abstained): not removed
Soumitra Sen (Calcutta HC, 2011) | RS passed motion; resigned before LS vote
S.N. Shukla (Allahabad HC, 2022) | guilty in in-house inquiry; not impeached
Yashwant Varma (2025-26) | cash found after fire (14 Mar 2025); motions in both Houses 21 July 2025
⚠ No judge has ever been removed through the full process
## In news 2025-26
Jan 2026: SC dismissed Justice Varma's plea against the Speaker's 3-member committee; rejection in one House does not void the other; Deputy Chairman can act for Chairman (Art 91)
July 2026: Speaker decided to table the committee report despite Varma's resignation; the 1968 Act is silent on inquiries after resignation and has no pension-forfeiture provision
Resignation is a unilateral right, needs no acceptance by the President (Gopal Chandra Misra, 1978)

topic: Removal, Independence and Accountability of Judges
t: In-house procedure → misconduct below removal threshold
text:
Item | Detail
Origin | C. Ravichandran Iyer v. A.M. Bhattacharjee (1995); 5-member committee 1997; adopted 1999
Refined | 2014, seven-step framework
Complaint to | CJI or concerned HC Chief Justice
Panel for HC judge | 2 HC Chief Justices + 1 HC judge
Panel for SC judge | 3 sitting SC judges
Outcomes | minor: advised to resign; serious: CJI may recommend removal; baseless: dropped
Refusal to resign | judicial work withdrawn; matter sent for removal
⚠ It is not statutory: no Act backs it
Judicial Standards and Accountability Bill, 2010: proposed oversight committee; lapsed, not passed
## In news 2025
CJI ordered a 3-member in-house inquiry into Justice Varma; he was transferred Delhi HC → Allahabad HC

topic: Removal, Independence and Accountability of Judges
t: Independence of the Supreme Court → constitutional safeguards
text:
Safeguard | Provision
Appointment | President consults judiciary (Collegium)
Tenure | not at pleasure of the President; removal only by Parliament's address
Service conditions | cannot be varied to disadvantage except in Financial Emergency (Art 360)
Expenses | salaries, pensions, admin expenses charged on CFI (non-votable)
Conduct | cannot be discussed in Parliament/State Legislature except in a removal motion (Art 121, 211)
Post-retirement | retired SC judge cannot plead in any court or authority in India
Contempt | power to punish for its contempt (Art 129)
Staff | CJI appoints officers and servants (Art 146)
Jurisdiction | Parliament can enlarge but not curtail
⚠ Removal: Parliament + President, never the CJI; staff: CJI, not Government
Independence of judiciary and judicial review are parts of the basic structure
Art 50 (DPSP): separate judiciary from executive in public services
PYQ 2012: autonomy safeguards: President consults CJI and salaries on CFI true; removal by CJI and staff by Government false

topic: Removal, Independence and Accountability of Judges
t: Supreme Court's constitutional role → guardian and federal court
text:
Role | Basis
Guardian/custodian of the Constitution | judicial review, final interpreter
Protector of Fundamental Rights | Art 32 writs
Federal court | Art 131 disputes
Highest court of appeal | Art 132-136
Final interpreter | Art 141: law binding on all courts
Adviser | Art 143
Keeps the balance among Legislature, Executive, Judiciary, Union and States
India: an integrated judiciary: one SC on top of HCs and subordinate courts
⚠ Not the President (protects Constitution through oath), not Parliament: SC is the "guardian"
PYQ 2015: custodian/guardian of the Constitution = Supreme Court

t: Original jurisdiction (Art 131) → which disputes are covered
text:
## 1. Covered: federal disputes only
Dispute | Under Art 131?
Union vs one or more States | Yes
Union + State(s) vs other State(s) | Yes
State vs State | Yes
Election disputes of MPs/MLAs | No: High Court
Union vs Union Territory | No (UT is not a State)
Pre-Constitution treaties, covenants | No
Inter-State river water disputes | No, if Parliament excludes (Art 262; ISRWD Act 1956)
Private citizen vs Union | No (writ/suit route)
Original = case starts in SC; exclusive = no other court can hear it
Dispute must involve a legal right (question of law or fact), not a political one
⚠ Art 32 writ jurisdiction is also original but not exclusive (HCs share it under Art 226)
PYQ 1996, 2014: Centre-State disputes = original jurisdiction (not advisory, appellate or writ)
PYQ 2012: trap options added election disputes and Centre vs UT: both outside Art 131

t: Advisory jurisdiction (Art 143) → when and how binding
text:
Clause | Subject | Is SC bound to answer?
143(1) | question of law or fact of public importance, arisen or likely | No, may decline
143(2) | disputes from pre-Constitution treaties, covenants | Yes, must report
Only on reference by the President: never suo motu, and not limited to Fundamental Rights
Opinion is not binding on the President
Decided by a Bench of at least 5 judges (Art 145(3))
⚠ USA's Supreme Court has no advisory jurisdiction
## 1. Famous references
Reference | Subject
Kerala Education Bill (1958) | first big reference
Berubari (1960) | cession of territory needs amendment
Ayodhya (1993) | SC declined to answer
Third Judges Case (1998) | Collegium
2002 | EC deferring Gujarat elections
2025 | Governor/President timelines on Bills
PYQ 2010: SC advises only on the President's reference; PYQ 2003: Gujarat reference was under Art 143

t: Presidential Reference 2025 → Governors, timelines and Art 142
text:
Date | Event
April 2025 | 2-judge Bench (Tamil Nadu Governor case) set timelines and used Art 142 for "deemed assent" to TN Bills
May 2025 | President made an Art 143(1) reference (14 questions)
Nov 2025 | 5-judge Bench's opinion
## 1. What the opinion said
No judicial timelines for Governor/President on Bills
No "deemed assent": Art 142 cannot replace the Governor's/President's constitutional role
Only limited mandamus against prolonged, unexplained inaction
⚠ The April 2025 judgment was a regular case; the Nov 2025 one was advisory (not binding on the President)
⚠ Advisory opinion came from a Constitution Bench of 5, as Art 145(3) requires

t: Appellate jurisdiction → Articles 132-136
text:
Article | Appeal in | Condition
132 | Constitutional cases | HC certifies a substantial question of constitutional interpretation
133 | Civil cases | HC certifies a substantial question of law of general importance
134 | Criminal cases | HC reverses acquittal to death, or withdraws a case and sentences to death, or certifies
134A | Certificate | HC grants certificate (44th Am 1978)
136 | Special Leave | discretionary, from any court/tribunal
⚠ Art 133 money limit removed by the 30th Amendment, 1972
⚠ Art 136 excludes courts/tribunals of the armed forces
Special Leave is an extraordinary discretionary power, not a right of appeal
Parliament can widen criminal appeals (it did by the Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction Act, 1970)
## Beyond your notes
Art 135: SC gets Federal Court's jurisdiction on matters not covered by 133-134

t: Articles 129-146 → what each provides
text:
Article | Provision
129 | Court of Record; power to punish contempt of itself
130 | Seat at Delhi (enabling other places)
131 | Original jurisdiction
137 | Review of its own judgments
138 | Parliament may enlarge jurisdiction on Union List matters
139 | Parliament may give power to issue writs for other purposes
139A | Transfer of cases between HCs or to itself
140 | Ancillary powers by Parliament
141 | Law declared binding on all courts
142 | Complete justice decrees, enforceable throughout India
143 | Advisory
144 | All civil and judicial authorities act in aid of SC
145 | Rules of procedure (with President's approval)
146 | Officers and servants: appointed by CJI; expenses on CFI
⚠ Art 141 binds courts, not Parliament; SC itself may reconsider its precedents

t: Review and curative petition → Article 137 and beyond
text:
Remedy | Basis | When
Review petition | Art 137 + rules under Art 145 | against SC's own judgment
Curative petition | judge-made, Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002) | after review is dismissed
Special Leave | Art 136 | against any court/tribunal order
Curative aim: prevent gross miscarriage of justice and abuse of process
Curative is based on interpretation of Art 137 and Art 142
## 1. Court of Record (Art 129)
Judgments recorded for perpetual memory, have evidentiary value, cannot be questioned in any court
Power to punish contempt of itself
⚠ Review is not "judicial review": the latter tests laws and executive action
PYQ 2025: subordinate courts are not courts of record (SC: Art 129, HC: Art 215)

t: Article 142 → complete justice and its limits
text:
## 1. What it gives
142(1): any decree/order necessary for complete justice in any matter pending before it, enforceable throughout India
142(2): secure attendance of persons, production of documents, punish contempt (subject to law of Parliament)
Ordinary laws cannot limit Art 142; but it cannot override fundamental constitutional limits or basic structure
Only the SC has it; HCs (Art 226) do not
Case | Point
Prem Chand Garg (1963) | cannot contravene Fundamental Rights
SC Bar Association (1998) | cannot supplant substantive law
Union Carbide (1991) | Bhopal settlement
Used in Ayodhya (2019), divorce on irretrievable breakdown (Shilpa Sailesh, 2023)
## Beyond your notes
Union Carbide, Ayodhya and Shilpa Sailesh uses of Art 142 are from general knowledge
PYQ 2019: "ordinary laws cannot limit Art 142" means SC is not constrained by laws made by Parliament

t: Parliament and SC jurisdiction → can and cannot
text:
Parliament can | Parliament cannot
Increase judges (Art 124(1)) | curtail constitutionally given jurisdiction
Enlarge jurisdiction on Union List (Art 138(1)) | reduce judges' service conditions (except Financial Emergency)
confer extra writ powers (Art 139) | discuss judges' conduct (except removal)
supplementary powers (Art 140) | abolish judicial review (basic structure)
exclude river water disputes (Art 262) | 
⚠ Enlarging jurisdiction on other matters needs a special agreement of Centre and the State (Art 138(2))
⚠ The President, CJI or Law Ministry cannot enlarge jurisdiction: only Parliament
PYQ 2003: enlarging SC jurisdiction on Union List matters rests with Parliament
PYQ 2005: Parliament can enlarge SC jurisdiction: true

t: Other powers and India vs USA → comparison
text:
## 1. Other powers (PMF list)
Decides President and Vice-President election disputes (original, exclusive)
Transfers cases between HCs or to itself (Art 139A)
Inquires into conduct of UPSC/SPSC Chairman/members on President's reference
Aided by all authorities (Art 144)
## 2. Indian vs American SC
India | USA
Integrated judicial system | Dual (federal + state)
Special Leave (Art 136) | no equivalent
Advisory jurisdiction (Art 143) | none
Procedure established by law | Due process of law
narrower judicial review | wider judicial review
Parliament can enlarge jurisdiction | jurisdiction limited by the Constitution
⚠ India: neither British parliamentary supremacy nor American judicial supremacy

topic: Judicial Review and Public Interest Litigation
t: Judicial review → meaning and what it is not
text:
## 1. Meaning
Power to examine the constitutional validity of laws and executive orders and declare them void
Tests constitutionality, not the wisdom of a law
Option UPSC gave | Judicial review?
pronounce on constitutionality of laws and executive orders | Yes
question the wisdom of laws | No
review bills before assent | No
review its own judgments | No: that is Art 137 review
Both SC and HCs exercise it
⚠ In India judicial review is narrower than in the USA: "procedure established by law"
PYQ 2017: judicial review = pronouncing on constitutionality; trap: "wisdom" and "own judgments"

topic: Judicial Review and Public Interest Litigation
t: Judicial review → basis and landmark cases
text:
No single Article titled "judicial review"; flows from Art 13, 32, 131-136, 143, 226, 227, 245, 246, 372
Covers constitutional amendments, central/state laws, subordinate legislation, executive action
Origin: Marbury v. Madison (1803), USA
Case | Point
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) | basic structure; amendments reviewable
Minerva Mills (1980) | judicial review part of basic structure
L. Chandra Kumar (1997) | review under Art 32 and 226/227 is basic structure
I.R. Coelho (2007) | Ninth Schedule laws after 24 April 1973 reviewable
NJAC (2015) | amendment struck down for judicial independence
⚠ The Constitution does not define "basic structure": it is judge-made
Grounds: violation of FRs, lack of legislative competence, violation of other constitutional provisions

topic: Judicial Review and Public Interest Litigation
t: Public Interest Litigation → origin and pioneers
text:
Fact | Answer
Origin | USA, 1960s
In India | early 1980s (judicial activism from mid-1970s)
Pioneers | Justice P.N. Bhagwati and Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer
CJI when introduced | P.N. Bhagwati (CJI 1985-86)
Also called | Social Action Litigation
Filed under | Art 32 (SC) and Art 226 (HC)
⚠ V.R. Krishna Iyer was never CJI (SC judge 1973-80), but is a progenitor of PIL
⚠ PIL is not mentioned in the Constitution or any Act: judge-made
PYQ 2006: CJI when PIL came = P.N. Bhagwati; PYQ 2008: Krishna Iyer as CJI false; PYQ 1997: PIL originated in USA

topic: Judicial Review and Public Interest Litigation
t: PIL features and early cases → how it works
text:
## 1. Features
Relaxes locus standi: any public-spirited person can file for the disadvantaged
Epistolary jurisdiction: letters/telegrams treated as writ petitions
Non-adversarial; court may appoint commissions to gather facts
Cannot be filed in subordinate courts: only SC and HCs
## 2. Early PILs
Case | Issue
Hussainara Khatoon v. Bihar (1979) | undertrial prisoners; speedy trial
Sunil Batra (1980) | letter by a prisoner to Krishna Iyer
S.P. Gupta (1981) | locus standi widened (First Judges Case)
Bandhua Mukti Morcha (1984) | bonded labour
⚠ "Judicial activism" term coined by Arthur Schlesinger Jr. (1947)
Criticism: judicial overreach, frivolous PILs; courts now impose costs for misuse
## Beyond your notes
PIL guidelines in State of Uttaranchal v. Balwant Singh Chaufal (2010)

t: Contempt of Court → Constitution vs Act
text:
## 1. Where the power sits
Item | Source
SC power to punish contempt of itself | Art 129 (Court of Record)
HC power to punish contempt of itself | Art 215
Civil / criminal contempt defined in | Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, not the Constitution
Law-making power on contempt | Parliament (Union List entry 77 for SC; Concurrent List entry 14 for others)
Act based on | H.N. Sanyal Committee (report 1963)
⚠ Constitution only recognises the power; the Act defines and regulates it
⚠ Contempt is a reasonable restriction on free speech under Art 19(2)
PYQ 2022: statements 1, 2, 4 correct; trap: Constitution defines civil and criminal contempt is false
## Beyond your notes
List entries: Union List 77 (SC), Concurrent List 14 (contempt other than SC)

t: Contempt types → civil vs criminal, punishment
text:
## 1. Two types (Act of 1971)
Type | Meaning
Civil | wilful disobedience of a judgment, order, writ, or wilful breach of an undertaking
Criminal | publication or act that scandalises/lowers authority of a court, prejudices proceedings or obstructs justice
## 2. Punishment
Simple imprisonment up to 6 months or fine up to Rs 2,000 or both (Testbook)
Apology may discharge the contemnor if bona fide
⚠ Subordinate courts are not courts of record: HC punishes contempt of them
⚠ History: Act of 1926 → Act of 1952 → Act of 1971
Purpose: secure public respect and confidence in the judicial process
PYQ 1997: contempt punishable under the Act; purpose: public confidence (A and R true, R explains A)

t: Contempt defences and reform → what is not contempt
text:
Not contempt | Basis
Fair and accurate report of judicial proceedings | Act of 1971
Fair criticism of a judgment after decision | Ashwini Kumar Ghosh (1952)
Truth as defence, if in public interest and bona fide | 2006 amendment
Innocent publication without knowledge of pending case | Act of 1971
## In news 2025-26
Nov 2025: remarks against the CJI revived debate; PMF: fair criticism of judgments is not contempt
PMF way forward: amend the 1971 Act as per Law Commission 274th Report (2018) to restrict criminal contempt to clear obstruction of justice
Henderson doctrine invoked in a contempt petition (Celir LLP v. Sumati Prasad Bafna, 2024) to curb repetitive litigation
⚠ UK abolished "scandalising the court" in 2013
## Beyond your notes
UK abolition (2013) and the 2006 truth defence are from general knowledge

topic: High Courts: Judges, Appointment and Service
t: HC judges → appointment and qualifications
text:
## 1. Appointment (Art 217)
Judge | President consults
Chief Justice | CJI + Governor
Other judges | CJI + Governor + HC Chief Justice
HC strength not fixed by the Constitution (Art 216): President decides
## 2. Qualifications (Art 217(2)): citizen +
10 years in a judicial office in India, or
10 years as advocate of an HC (or HCs in succession)
⚠ Not 5 years: 5 years as HC judge is an SC qualification
⚠ No distinguished jurist route for HCs (added by 42nd Am 1976, in force Jan 1977, omitted by 44th Am 1978)
Item | HC rule
Minimum age | none
Retirement | 62
Oath | before Governor (Art 219)
Resignation | to the President
PYQ 2006: HC judge needs 10 years (not 5); retired HC judge can plead in SC and other HCs

topic: High Courts: Judges, Appointment and Service
t: HC Chief Justice → appointment under the MoP
text:
## 1. Procedure
Art 217(1): appointment; Art 222: transfer of a sitting Chief Justice
CJI initiates, finalises with 2 senior-most SC judges
HC Chief Justices come from outside their parent HC
Law Minister gets State Government's views through the Governor
Law Minister → PM → President issues warrant
⚠ Executive is consulted but has no veto (Second 1993, Third 1998 Judges Cases)
Step | Who
Initiates | CJI
State's view | via Governor
Advises President | PM
Appoints | President
## In news 2026
Sep 2026: Chief Justices appointed to eight HCs on SC Collegium advice (e.g. Kameswar Rao → Patna, Ravindra Ghuge → Calcutta, M.C. Tripathi → Bombay)
Punjab Cabinet objected to Justice Ashwani Kumar Mishra as P&H HC CJ, saying State consultation was bypassed

topic: High Courts: Judges, Appointment and Service
t: SC vs HC judges → salary, pension, removal, practice
text:
Item | SC judge | HC judge
Salary, allowances | CFI | Consolidated Fund of the State
Pension | CFI | CFI (not State)
Admin expenses | CFI | State Consolidated Fund
Retirement | 65 | 62
Removal | Parliament's address, President | same procedure and grounds
Practice after retirement | barred in all courts | allowed in SC and other HCs (Art 220)
Staff appointed by | CJI | HC Chief Justice (Art 229)
Oath before | President | Governor
⚠ HC expenses are not votable in the State Legislature, but are charged on the State fund, not CFI
⚠ Age dispute of an HC judge: decided by President after consulting the CJI; decision final
PYQ 2002: HC judges' salaries charged on State Consolidated Fund
PYQ 2005: HC staff appointed by HC Chief Justice; expenses on State fund; Parliament can enlarge SC jurisdiction

topic: High Courts: Judges, Appointment and Service
t: Independence of High Courts → safeguards and removal
text:
Safeguard | Provision
Appointment | consultative, judiciary-led
Tenure | till 62; not at pleasure
Service conditions | fixed by Parliament (Art 221); no change to disadvantage except Financial Emergency
Conduct | not discussed in Parliament/State Legislature except removal motion in Parliament
Practice | retired permanent judge: only SC and other HCs (Art 220)
Contempt | Art 215
Jurisdiction | neither Parliament nor State Legislature can cut constitutional powers
HC judge removed exactly like an SC judge: same grounds, Parliament's special majority, President's order
⚠ State Legislature has no role in removal
PYQ 2007: HC judge removed like SC judge: true; retired permanent HC judge can plead in SC and other HCs: true

topic: High Courts: Judges, Appointment and Service
t: HC transfer, acting, additional and retired judges → Articles 222-224A

224(2) | Acting judge | President

Jan 2026: a year after the SC (25 Jan 2025) allowed ad hoc retired judges under Art 224A (cap 10% of sanctioned strength), none of the 25 HCs had recommended any

topic: High Courts: Number, Common HCs and Jurisdiction

Art 214: an HC for each State

Art 231: Parliament may set up a common HC for 2+ States or States + UT (7th Amendment 1956)
Fact | Answer

Total now | 25

Meghalaya, Manipur, Tripura HCs set up in March 2013

topic: High Courts: Number, Common HCs and Jurisdiction
t: Pendency and judicial reforms → 2025-26 numbers
text:
Level | Pending (2025-26)
All courts | over 5 crore cases
District and subordinate courts | over 4.6 crore
Supreme Court | over 70,000
High Courts carry large vacancy rates; ad hoc judges (Art 224A) unused
Reforms discussed: more judges, ADR, case management, eCourts (mission mode project from 2007), All India Judicial Service (42nd Am 1976 amended Art 312)
Law Commission 245th Report: pendency = cases unresolved whatever their filing date
2025: SC restored 3 years' minimum practice for entry to judicial service (reversed 2002 Shetty Commission view)
## In news 2025-26
9 Oct 2025: 5-judge Bench (CJI Gavai) held serving judicial officers eligible for direct recruitment as district judge, overruling Dheeraj Mor (2020)
⚠ Subordinate courts in detail belong to the Subordinate Courts topic

t: District Judge → appointment, eligibility, who consults whom
text:
## 1. Article 233: appointment of District Judges
Appointment, posting and promotion of District Judges: by the Governor in consultation with the High Court
Direct recruit (a person not already in Union/State service): must be an advocate or pleader for at least 7 years AND recommended by the High Court
The State PSC has no role in appointing District Judges
Post | Appointed by | Consultation / rules
District Judge (Art 233) | Governor | High Court only
Other judicial officers (Art 234) | Governor | Rules after consulting State PSC + High Court
High Court judge (Art 217) | President | CJI + Governor (+ HC Chief Justice)
⚠ District Judge → Governor + HC (no PSC); Civil Judge / Magistrate → Governor + PSC + HC
⚠ The District Judge is appointed by the Governor, not the President and not the High Court
PYQ 2004: all four statements correct: District and Sessions Judge is the highest criminal court of the district; appointed by Governor in consultation with HC; 7 years as advocate/pleader or a judicial officer; death sentence needs HC confirmation

t: Articles 233-237 → what each says
text:
## 1. Part VI, Chapter VI: Subordinate Courts
Article | Provision
233 | Appointment, posting, promotion of District Judges: Governor + HC; 7 years' practice for direct recruits
233A | Validation of certain District Judge appointments and their judgments (20th Amendment, 1966)
234 | Recruitment of other judicial officers: Governor, rules after consulting State PSC and HC
235 | Control over district courts and subordinate courts vested in the High Court (posting, promotion, leave of officers below District Judge)
236 | Definitions: "district judge" and "judicial service"
237 | Governor may by public notification apply these provisions to any class of magistrates (with exceptions/modifications)
Structure, jurisdiction and nomenclature vary from State to State
⚠ Art 233A came by the 20th Amendment (1966), not the 42nd
⚠ Art 237 extends the provisions to magistrates by Governor's notification, not by Parliament's law
PYQ angle: "How many of Art 233-237 deal with the High Court's control?" Only Art 235 vests control; 233 and 234 give the HC a consultative role

t: Article 236 → who counts as a "district judge"
text:
## 1. "District judge" includes (Art 236(a))
Included | Side
Judge of a City Civil Court | Civil
Additional / Joint / Assistant District Judge | Civil
Chief Judge of a Small Cause Court | Civil
Chief Presidency Magistrate and Additional Chief Presidency Magistrate | Criminal
Sessions Judge, Additional Sessions Judge, Assistant Sessions Judge | Criminal
⚠ Not included: a Tribunal judge; also not a Chief Judicial Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate (they are not in the list)
## 2. "Judicial service" (Art 236(b))
A service consisting exclusively of persons intended to fill the post of District Judge and other civil judicial posts inferior to District Judge
PYQ 1996: asked which is NOT a "district judge"; answer tribunal judge; trap: Chief Presidency Magistrate (a criminal-side post) IS included

t: Structure of subordinate courts → civil and criminal ladders
text:
## 1. Three tiers below the High Court
Level | Civil side | Criminal side
District | District Judge | Sessions Judge
Intermediate | Civil Judge (Senior Division) / Subordinate Judge | Chief Judicial Magistrate
Lower | Civil Judge (Junior Division) / Munsiff | Judicial Magistrate (First / Second Class)
The same officer is District Judge on the civil side and Sessions Judge on the criminal side
Civil Judge (Senior Division) / Subordinate Judge: unlimited pecuniary jurisdiction; Munsiff: limited
Metropolitan areas: City Civil Courts (civil) and Metropolitan Magistrates (criminal); Small Causes Courts decide low-value civil cases summarily (final, subject to HC revision)
Some States have Panchayat courts: Nyaya Panchayat, Gram Kutchery, Adalati Panchayat, Panchayat Adalat
⚠ Per Current Care: CJM tries offences punishable up to 7 years; Judicial Magistrate up to 3 years
## Beyond your notes
Under the BNSS 2023 (as under the CrPC), a CJM may pass any sentence except death, life imprisonment or imprisonment above 7 years; a JMFC up to 3 years (as of 2026)

t: Sessions Judge → powers, death sentence, appeals
text:
## 1. District and Sessions Judge
Highest judicial authority of the district; both judicial and administrative powers; supervises all subordinate courts in the district
Original and appellate jurisdiction in civil and criminal matters; appeals from it lie to the High Court
Can impose any sentence, including life imprisonment and death
Point | Rule
Death sentence by Sessions Court | Must be confirmed by the High Court before execution
If the convict does not appeal | Confirmation still required
Appeals from Magistrates | Lie to the Sessions Court
Appeals from Sessions Court | Lie to the High Court
⚠ HC confirmation is needed whether or not the convict appeals
⚠ Testbook describes Additional and Assistant Sessions Judges as posted by the High Court; the District Judge post itself is filled by the Governor under Art 233
PYQ 2004 tested the "highest criminal court of the district" and the HC confirmation of a death sentence

t: High Court's hold over subordinate courts → Art 227, 228, 235, 50
text:
## 1. Instruments of control
Provision | What it gives the High Court
Art 227 | Superintendence over all courts and tribunals in its territory (administrative + judicial, even suo motu)
Art 228 | Withdraw a case from a subordinate court if it involves a substantial question of constitutional interpretation
Art 235 | Administrative control: posting, promotion, leave, transfer, discipline below District Judge
Art 233 / 234 | Consultation in appointment of District Judges and other judicial officers
Art 50 (DPSP) | State to separate judiciary from executive in public services
Under Art 228 the HC may decide the whole case or decide only the constitutional question and return the case
Law declared by a HC binds all subordinate courts in its territory
⚠ Art 227 superintendence does not extend to courts/tribunals under Armed Forces laws
⚠ Separation of judiciary from executive is a DPSP (Art 50), not a Fundamental Right

Route to District Judge | Share

topic: Legal Services Authorities and Lok Adalats
t: Legal aid framework → Art 39A, LSAA 1987, NALSA tiers
text:
## 1. Basis
Art 39A (DPSP, added by 42nd Amendment): equal justice and free legal aid
Free legal aid also read into Art 21 and Art 14 (Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar, 1979)
Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987: came into force in 1995; NALSA set up 1995 (HQ New Delhi)
## 2. Four-tier structure
Level | Body | Head
National | NALSA | CJI = Patron-in-Chief; Executive Chairman: an SC judge
Supreme Court | SC Legal Services Committee (Sec 3A) | Sitting SC judge as Chairman + up to 9 members, nominated by CJI
State | SLSA | HC Chief Justice = Patron-in-Chief; Executive Chairman: senior-most HC judge after CJ
District | DLSA | District Judge (ex officio Chairman)
Taluk | Taluk Legal Services Committee | Senior Civil Judge
⚠ NALSA Executive Chairman: "serving/retired SC judge nominated by President in consultation with CJI" (P-MCA); Current Care says the second senior-most SC judge (the convention)
⚠ SLSA Executive Chairman is appointed by the Governor on the HC Chief Justice's recommendation

topic: Legal Services Authorities and Lok Adalats
t: Free legal aid → who is eligible

## 1. Eligible regardless of income
Category | Note
Women and children | All, no income test
Members of SC/ST | All
Industrial workmen | All
Victims of trafficking / begar | All
Persons with disability | All

topic: Legal Services Authorities and Lok Adalats
t: Lok Adalat → what it can take up (stage and nature of case)
text:
## 1. Basics
"People's Court"; statutory ADR body under the LSAA 1987, based on compromise
First Lok Adalat: Una, Junagadh district, Gujarat, 1982 (before the Act)
## 2. Jurisdiction
Question | Answer
Pending court cases? | Yes (by consent of both, application of one, or court's own referral)
Pre-litigation disputes? | Yes (on application of either party to SLSA/DLSA)
Civil matters? | Yes
Criminal matters? | Only compoundable offences
Non-compoundable offences? | No jurisdiction
Matrimonial / family disputes? | Yes (maintenance, property, custody settlements)
⚠ Testbook: no jurisdiction over divorce itself or non-compoundable offences; but family/matrimonial disputes are covered
PYQ 2010: all three statements wrong (pending + pre-litigation; civil + compoundable criminal; members not only judicial officers) → "None of the above"

topic: Legal Services Authorities and Lok Adalats
t: Lok Adalat → which disputes are typically settled
text:
## 1. Common categories (National and State Lok Adalats)
Category | Examples
Motor accident claims (MACT) | Compensation cases
Telecom / mobile company disputes | Billing disputes (pre-litigation)
Service matters | Pension, pay, retiral dues
Bank recovery | Loan defaults, cheque bounce (Sec 138 NI Act)
Public utility bills | Electricity, water
Family | Maintenance, matrimonial settlements
Labour | Wage disputes
Land acquisition | Compensation
Compoundable criminal | Minor offences settled by parties
PYQ 2005: Lok Adalats are held for all three: mobile company disputes, motor accident cases, pension cases
## 2. Levels and forms
Organised at taluk, district, State, HC and SC level by the legal services bodies
National Lok Adalat: held on one day across the country for mass settlement
Mobile Lok Adalat: travels place to place
Banks: Lok Adalats gave about 3% of bank recoveries in FY 2023-24 (IBC 48%, SARFAESI 32%, DRTs 17%)

topic: Legal Services Authorities and Lok Adalats
t: Lok Adalat → composition and procedure
text:
## 1. Bench composition (Testbook)
Level | Bench
State | Sitting/retired HC judge or sitting/retired judicial officer + one or both: lawyer, social worker
High Court | Sitting/retired HC judge + one or both: lawyer, social worker
District / Taluk | Sitting/retired judicial officer + one or both: lawyer, social worker / para-legal (preferably a woman)
Usual pattern (Preview): judicial officer as Chairman + lawyer + social worker (composition not fixed)
⚠ Lok Adalat members are not only serving/retired judicial officers: lawyers and social workers sit too (2010 trap)
## 2. Procedure
Consent of both parties is essential; no compulsion to settle
No strict application of procedural laws or the Evidence Act
Parties may speak to the judge directly, even if represented
If no settlement, the case returns to the court (ordinary Lok Adalat cannot decide on merits)

topic: Legal Services Authorities and Lok Adalats
t: Lok Adalat award → status, appeal, court fee
text:
## 1. Award
Feature | Rule
Legal status | Deemed a decree of a civil court
Binding? | Final and binding on all parties
Appeal | No appeal lies to any court
Court fee | None payable
Fee already paid in a referred case | Refunded on settlement
Since it rests on compromise, no party can walk away once the award is made
## Beyond your notes
Award provision: Sec 21 LSAA; organisation of Lok Adalats: Sec 19; aggrieved party's only remedy is a writ (Art 226/227) on limited grounds
9 November (Act's commencement, 1995) is observed as National Legal Services Day
⚠ "No appeal" does not mean no writ: HC writ jurisdiction survives
PYQ 2009: award deemed civil decree, no appeal → correct; "matrimonial/family disputes not covered" → wrong

topic: Legal Services Authorities and Lok Adalats
t: Permanent Lok Adalat → public utility services
text:
## 1. Permanent Lok Adalat (PLA)
Added by the 2002 amendment to the LSAA; set up under Section 22B
Chairman + 2 members; a pre-litigation forum
Pecuniary limit: disputes up to ₹1 crore
No jurisdiction over non-compoundable offences
First tries conciliation; if that fails, may decide on merits (unlike an ordinary Lok Adalat)
Award final, binding, deemed civil decree
## 2. Public Utility Services (list)
Covered | Covered
Transport (air, road, water) | Postal, telegraph, telephone
Supply of power, light, water | Public conservancy / sanitation
Hospital or dispensary | Insurance
Other services may be notified
## Beyond your notes
Any one party may move a PLA (Sec 22C); once moved, neither party can take the same dispute to a court
⚠ A PLA can proceed without the other party's consent; an ordinary Lok Adalat needs consent to settle

topic: Legal Services Authorities and Lok Adalats
t: Lok Adalat vs Permanent Lok Adalat → comparison
text:
Basis | Lok Adalat | Permanent Lok Adalat
Nature | Organised periodically | Permanent body
Stage | Pending + pre-litigation | Pre-litigation only
Subject | Any matter capable of settlement | Public Utility Services
Role | Conciliation only | Conciliation, then adjudication
If settlement fails | Cannot decide on merits | May decide on merits
Value limit | No fixed limit | ₹1 crore
Award | Final, binding, civil decree | Final, binding, civil decree
Appeal | No appeal | No statutory appeal
Key hinge: ordinary Lok Adalat depends on settlement; PLA can adjudicate
Likely next: "A Permanent Lok Adalat can decide a dispute even if the parties fail to agree" → correct

t: Gram Nyayalayas Act 2008 → establishment and Nyayadhikari
text:
## 1. Origin and status
Suggested by the Law Commission, 114th Report (1986)
Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008; in force 2 October 2009
Deemed a Court of Judicial Magistrate of the First Class, with civil and criminal jurisdiction for petty village disputes
## 2. Set-up
Point | Rule
Where | Intermediate Panchayat level, or a group of contiguous intermediate Panchayats; group of contiguous Panchayats where no intermediate tier
Established by | State Government in consultation with the High Court
Mandatory? | No
Headquarters | Intermediate Panchayat HQ or place notified by State
Presiding officer | Nyayadhikari: qualified to be a JMFC; appointed by State Govt in consultation with HC
Status of Nyayadhikari | Full judicial officer, same salary and powers as First Class Magistrates
Central support | Non-recurring cost up to ₹18 lakh per Gram Nyayalaya
⚠ Nyayadhikari is a judicial officer, not an elected panchayat member
⚠ Setting up Gram Nyayalayas is not mandatory for States

topic: Gram Nyayalayas, Family Courts and Other Special Courts
t: Gram Nyayalaya → jurisdiction, conciliation, appeals
text:
## 1. Powers and procedure
Exercises powers of both Criminal and Civil Courts over cases in the Act's First and Second Schedules
Both Centre and States can amend the Schedules (as per legislative competence)
A mobile court: holds sittings in villages
Tries to settle disputes by conciliation, using appointed conciliators (social workers allowed)
Summary procedure in criminal trials; judgment deemed a decree, executed summarily
Not bound by the Indian Evidence Act; guided by natural justice and HC rules
Accused may apply for plea bargaining
Language: an official language of the State other than English
## 2. Appeals
Case | Appeal to | Time limit
Criminal | Court of Session | Disposal within 6 months
Civil | District Court | Disposal within 6 months
⚠ Gram Nyayalayas hear civil AND criminal cases (2016 trap: "only civil")
PYQ 2016: statement 1 ("only civil, not criminal") wrong; statement 2 (local social activists as mediators/conciliators) right → answer 2 only
## 3. Problems
No separate Nyayadhikari cadre; poor funding; lukewarm Bar and police; regular Taluk-level courts reduce the need
