topic: Legal Profession: Advocates Act and Bar Councils
t: Advocates Act 1961 → who is an advocate
text:
## 1. Single class of practitioners
Old categories (vakils, barristers, pleaders, mukhtars) merged into one class: "advocates"
An enrolled advocate may practise in all courts in India
Sets up autonomous Bar Councils: one for India (BCI) and one for each State
Person | Advocate?
Government law officers (enrolled) | Yes
Corporate lawyers (enrolled) | Not excluded per se
Patent attorneys (enrolled) | Not excluded per se
Law firm as an entity | No: only individuals enrol

topic: Legal Profession: Advocates Act and Bar Councils
t: Bar Council of India → composition and leadership
text:
## 1. Status
Statutory body under Section 4, Advocates Act 1961
Recommended by the All-India Bar Committee (1953), chaired by Justice S.R. Das
## 2. Composition
Member | How
Attorney General of India | Ex officio
Solicitor General of India | Ex officio
One member from each State Bar Council | Elected by that SBC, for its term
Chairman and Vice-Chairman | Elected by the Council for 2 years
Ministry of Law has no representative or bureaucrat on the BCI
Rule 15 of BCI Rules: Chairman has general oversight, subject to Council resolutions
⚠ The Law Minister/Ministry does not sit on the BCI; the AG and SG do
⚠ The BCI Chairman is elected, not appointed by the CJI or the Government

Class | Rule
Senior Advocate | Designated by the SC or a HC, with his consent, for ability, standing or special knowledge
Advocate-on-Record | Only class that can file matters/documents in the SC
Other advocates | On a State roll; can argue in the SC but cannot file

Cannot file a vakalatnama, draft pleadings or affidavits, advise on evidence, or do conveyancing

t: State Executive → Articles 153-167 and who is in it
text:
## 1. Members of the State Executive
Part VI, Articles 153-167: the State Executive
Members: Governor, Chief Minister, Council of Ministers, Advocate General
No State counterpart of the Vice-President
Article | What it says
153 | A Governor for each State; 7th CAA 1956: same person for two or more States
154 | Executive power of the State vested in the Governor
155 | Appointed by the President by warrant under hand and seal
156 | Term: pleasure of the President; 5 years
157 | Qualifications: citizen, 35 years
158 | Conditions of office
159 | Oath
160 | President provides for contingencies
161 | Pardoning power
163 | CoM to aid and advise; discretion
164 | CM and Ministers
165 | Advocate General
166 | Conduct of business
167 | Duties of CM to Governor
Dual role: constitutional head of the State + link between Union and State

t: Appointment → appointed, not elected (and why)
text:
## 1. Mode of appointment
Neither directly elected nor indirectly elected (unlike the President): appointed by the President (Art 155)
In practice: President acts on advice of Union Council of Ministers
Hargovind Pant v. Raghukul Tilak (1979): Governor's office is an independent constitutional office, not subordinate to the Union; Governor is not a government servant
## 2. Why the Constituent Assembly dropped election
Reason | Meaning
Parliamentary system | Elected Governor could rival the CM
Neutrality | Election would politicise the office
Cost/effort | Would mean another election
Unity and stability | Keep Governor as Union-State link
Model: Canadian (appointment by Centre); American model of elected Governor rejected
⚠ Draft Constitution originally had elected Governors; dropped
## 3. Conventions (not in the Constitution)
Governor should be an outsider to the State
Consult the CM before appointment
⚠ Constitution does not require consulting the CM for appointment or removal (PMF)

t: Qualifications and conditions → Articles 157-158
text:
## 1. Qualifications (Art 157): only two
Citizen of India
Completed 35 years of age
No educational, residential or prior-office qualification
## 2. Conditions of office (Art 158)
Condition | Detail
Not a legislator | Not a member of Parliament or a State Legislature; seat vacated on entering office
Office of profit | Cannot hold any other office of profit
Residence | Official residence rent-free
Emoluments | Fixed by Parliament by law; cannot be diminished during term (Art 158(4))
Two States | Emoluments allocated among the States in proportion fixed by the President (Art 158(3A))
## 3. Which fund pays
Emoluments charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State (Art 202(3)(a))
⚠ Testbook says "charged upon Consolidated Fund of India": wrong; Preview and ROCKET give State Consolidated Fund
PYQ 2018: "emoluments not diminished during term" is correct (Art 158(4)); it is paired with immunity under Art 361

t: Oath and firsts → Article 159
text:
## 1. Oath (Art 159)
Administered by the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court; in absence, senior-most available HC judge
Swears to: faithfully execute the office; preserve, protect and defend the Constitution and the law; devote to service and well-being of the people of the State
## 2. Comparison of oath
Office | Oath administered by
President | Chief Justice of India
Governor | Chief Justice of the State High Court
CM and State Ministers | Governor
## 3. Firsts and facts
Sarojini Naidu: first woman Governor (United Provinces/UP, 15 Aug 1947 - 2 Mar 1949)
Governor may be reappointed and transferred from one State to another
Governor of Punjab is also the Administrator of Chandigarh
⚠ LG/Administrator of a UT is appointed under Art 239, not Art 155

t: Governor appointments → 2025-26 changes
text:
## In news 2025-26
July 2025: Ashim Kumar Ghosh (Haryana) and P. Ashok Gajapathi Raju (Goa) appointed Governors; Kavinder Gupta LG of Ladakh
Mar 2026: 9 appointments after West Bengal Governor C.V. Ananda Bose resigned: R.N. Ravi Tamil Nadu → West Bengal; Rajendra Arlekar (Kerala) given additional charge of Tamil Nadu; Syed Ata Hasnain Governor of Bihar; Shiv Pratap Shukla to Telangana; Jishnu Dev Varma Telangana → Maharashtra (5 transfers, 1 additional charge, 3 fresh)
Oct 2026: President reshuffled Governors across six States
⚠ Appointment, transfer and additional charge are all by the President (Art 155-156); LGs under Art 239
Likely angle: "one person can hold two States" (additional charge) and "Governor can be transferred": both true

topic: Term, Removal and Order of Precedence
t: Article 156 → what each clause says about term
text:
## 1. The four parts of Art 156
Clause | Provision
156(1) | Holds office during the pleasure of the President
156(2) | May resign by writing to the President
156(3) | Term of five years from entering office, subject to the above
Proviso | Continues after 5 years until successor enters office
## 2. What follows
Can be removed before 5 years (pleasure)
Can continue beyond 5 years (no interregnum)
5-year term is customary, not legally binding
⚠ Both statements "cannot be removed before 5 years" and "cannot continue beyond 5 years" are false
PYQ 1995: Art 156 statements; answer "neither"; trap: the 5-year term is subject to presidential pleasure and the successor proviso

topic: Term, Removal and Order of Precedence
t: Removal → no procedure, no grounds, pleasure doctrine
text:
## 1. Removal
No impeachment and no procedure or grounds for removal in the Constitution
Removed by the President (on Union Cabinet advice) at any time
State Legislature has no power to remove the Governor
## 2. Courts on the pleasure doctrine
Case | Holding
Surya Narain | President's pleasure under Art 156 is non-justiciable
B.P. Singhal (2010) | Removal cannot be arbitrary, capricious or unreasonable, not merely because the Centre's government changed; limited judicial review; no reasons or hearing needed
## 3. Compare with other offices
Office | Removal
President | Impeachment (Art 61) for "violation of the Constitution"
Governor | Pleasure of President; no procedure
SC/HC judge | Address by Parliament, special majority
⚠ Removal "on a resolution of the State Legislature" is wrong; it is a reform proposal only (Kurian Joseph Committee)
PYQ 2013: correct option was "no procedure laid down for removal of a Governor"

topic: Term, Removal and Order of Precedence
t: One person, two States → 7th Amendment and Art 160
text:
## 1. Multiplicity of office
7th CAA 1956 added to Art 153: same person can be Governor of two or more States
Emoluments then shared as the President determines (Art 158(3A))
Additional charge is common (e.g., Kerala Governor holding Tamil Nadu, 2026)
## 2. Contingencies (Art 160)
President may make provision for discharging the Governor's functions in any contingency not provided in the Constitution
In practice the Chief Justice of the HC may be sworn in as acting Governor
## 3. 2013 PYQ: the three wrong options
Option | Why wrong
Same person cannot be Governor of two States | 7th CAA allows it
HC judges appointed by Governor | Appointed by President (Governor only consulted, Art 217)
CM of a UT with legislature appointed by LG | Appointed by President (Delhi: Art 239AA)
⚠ Governor does not appoint HC judges; he appoints district judges (Art 233)

topic: Term, Removal and Order of Precedence
t: Order of Precedence → where the Governor ranks
text:
## 1. The top of the list
Rank | Holders
1 | President
2 | Vice-President
3 | Prime Minister
4 | Governors within their States
5 | Former Presidents
5A | Deputy Prime Minister
6 | Chief Justice of India, Speaker of Lok Sabha
7 | Union Cabinet Ministers; CMs within their States; Vice-Chairperson NITI Aayog; former PMs; Leaders of Opposition in both Houses
7A | Bharat Ratna holders
8 | Ambassadors; CMs outside their States; Governors outside their States
9 | Judges of the Supreme Court
9A | Chairperson UPSC, CEC, CAG
## 2. Lower ranks often asked
Rank | Holders
11 | Attorney General, Cabinet Secretary, LGs within UTs
14 | Speakers of State Legislatures and HC Chief Justices within their States
21 | Members of Parliament
23 | Chief Secretaries within their States
25 | Advocate Generals of States
List kept by MHA; for ceremonial use only, no role in day-to-day government (notified 26 July 1979)
⚠ A Governor outside his State drops to rank 8
PYQ 2003: Governor within his State ranks above Former President, Deputy PM and Speaker

t: Article 361 → the four immunities of President and Governor
text:
## 1. What Art 361 gives
Clause | Immunity
361(1) | Not answerable to any court for exercise of powers and duties of office
361(2) | No criminal proceedings instituted or continued during term (even for personal acts)
361(3) | No process for arrest or imprisonment during term
361(4) | Civil proceedings for personal acts allowed during term only after two months' written notice
## 2. Limits of the immunity
Personal to the office-holder; the action itself stays open to judicial review
Bars naming the Governor as accused or even investigating; police may act only after he leaves office
Rameshwar Prasad (2006): immunity holds even against allegations of personal mala fides
2025 Presidential Reference: Art 361 does not shield the office from review of prolonged inaction
President's conduct can be reviewed by a body designated by Parliament for an impeachment charge (Art 61)
⚠ "President or Governor cannot be sued for any act" is false: civil suits for personal acts lie after 2 months' notice
PYQ 2025: all three correct: Art 361(1), 361(2) for Governor, and Art 194 for MLAs

t: Immunity → who has it and who does not
text:
## 1. Comparison
Functionary | Art 361 immunity?
President | Yes
Governor | Yes
Prime Minister | No
Chief Minister | No (Kejriwal: first serving CM arrested, 2024)
Lt Governor / Administrator of UT | No
MPs / MLAs | No Art 361 immunity; only speech-and-vote privilege (Art 105/194)
## 2. Other protections of the Governor's office
Emoluments cannot be diminished during term (Art 158(4))
Section 135A CPC: legislators exempt from civil arrest during sessions and 40 days before and after; no exemption from criminal arrest
⚠ Art 361 protects only the President and Governors; not ministers, not LGs
## In news 2025-26
Aug 2026 (PMF LENS): Art 361 cited as giving President and Governors absolute immunity from criminal proceedings and arrest during tenure
Telangana HC: Art 361 immunity is personal in nature

t: Article 194 → privileges of State legislators
text:
## 1. Art 194 (State) = Art 105 (Union)
Clause | Privilege
194(1) | Freedom of speech in the Legislature
194(2) | No court proceedings for anything said or any vote given in the House or committees; nor for publication under House authority
194(3) | Other privileges as defined by law of the Legislature (till then, as before 44th CAA)
194(4) | Extends to non-members with right to speak: Ministers and the Advocate General
## 2. Key points
Advocate General enjoys Art 194 privileges while taking part in proceedings (Art 177)
Speech outside the House is not protected
## Beyond your notes
Sita Soren v. Union of India (2024): privilege under Art 105/194 does not protect a legislator taking a bribe for a vote or speech (overruled P.V. Narasimha Rao 1998)
⚠ Art 194 immunity is for speech or vote in the House, not for bribery linked to it

t: Executive powers → whom the Governor appoints, who removes them
text:
## 1. Executive powers
All executive action taken in the Governor's name (Art 166); makes rules of business and authentication rules
Executive power extends to matters on which State Legislature can make laws (Art 162)
May seek information from CM (Art 167); may recommend President's Rule (Art 356)
## 2. Appointments
Governor appoints | Removed by
Chief Minister; other Ministers on CM's advice (Art 164) | Hold office at Governor's pleasure (in practice, confidence of Assembly)
Advocate General (Art 165) | Pleasure of Governor
State Election Commissioner | Only like a HC judge
Chairman and members of SPSC | Only by the President
District judges (Art 233, with HC) | -
Vice-Chancellors (as Chancellor, under State law) | -
Tribal welfare minister compulsory in Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha (Art 164(1)); Bihar dropped by 94th CAA 2006
⚠ Governor appoints SPSC members but cannot remove them; only the President can
⚠ Chancellor role is statutory (State law), not constitutional
⚠ Testbook lists 14 States for the tribal minister: outdated; PMF's four States are correct

t: Legislative powers → Articles 168, 174-176, 192
text:
## 1. Governor is part of the Legislature (Art 168)
Power | Article
Summon, prorogue; dissolve the Assembly | 174
Address and send messages to House(s) at any time | 175
Special address: first session after each general election and first session of each year | 176
Nominates 1/6 of Legislative Council (literature, science, art, co-operative movement, social service) | 171(3)(e)
Decides disqualification of MLAs on Election Commission's opinion (binding) | 192
Recommends Money Bills and certain Bills | 207
Appoints a member to preside if Speaker and Deputy both vacant | -
Anglo-Indian nomination to Assembly ended by 104th CAA 2019 (from 25 Jan 2020)
⚠ Governor nominates 1/6 to the Council; President nominates 12 to Rajya Sabha
⚠ Under Art 174 he acts on Cabinet advice: Nabam Rebia (2016): cannot summon the House on his own
## In news 2025-26
Jan 2026: Governors' walkouts during special addresses sparked debate: Governor has no authority to refuse or alter the Art 176 address; it reflects the elected government's policy
Motion of Thanks (Art 176(2)): its defeat = loss of confidence
Kurian Joseph Committee (TN, 2026) proposed deleting Art 176

t: Ordinance power → Article 213
text:
## 1. Conditions
Only when the Assembly (or, in a bicameral State, either House) is not in session and immediate action is needed
Same force as an Act; ceases six weeks after reassembly (later date if Houses reassemble on different dates)
Can be withdrawn any time; cannot exceed State legislative competence
## 2. President's instructions needed when a Bill on the same matter would
Case | 
1 | Need President's previous sanction to introduce
2 | Be reserved by the Governor for the President
3 | Be invalid without President's assent
D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987): repeated re-promulgation is unconstitutional
## Beyond your notes
Maximum life: 6 months + 6 weeks; Krishna Kumar Singh (2017): re-promulgation is a fraud on the Constitution; ordinance not immune from judicial review
⚠ Ordinance power is the Governor's "most important legislative power" (Testbook), but exercised on CoM advice

t: Financial powers → budget, money bills, funds
text:
## 1. Financial powers
Power | Detail
Budget | Causes Annual Financial Statement to be laid before the Legislature
Money Bill | Introduced only on Governor's recommendation
Grants | No demand for grant except on his recommendation
Contingency Fund | Makes advances from the Contingency Fund of the State
State Finance Commission | Constitutes it every five years (Art 243-I, 243Y) for Panchayats and Municipalities
Reports | Lays reports of SFC, SPSC and CAG (State accounts) before Legislature
Supplementary, additional and excess grants also routed through the Governor
⚠ The Finance Commission (Art 280) is constituted by the President; the State Finance Commission by the Governor

t: Pardoning power → Art 161 versus Art 72
text:
## 1. Comparison
Point | President (Art 72) | Governor (Art 161)
Scope | Offences against Union law | Offences against State law
Death sentence | Can pardon | Cannot pardon; can suspend, remit, commute
Court martial | Can grant clemency | No power
Forms | Pardon, reprieve, respite, remission, suspend, remit, commute | Same five forms
## 2. Judicial review and advice
Epuru Sudhakar (2006): pardoning power subject to limited judicial review
Perarivalan (2022): Governor is a formal head, bound by Cabinet advice in purely executive matters
⚠ "Governor can pardon a death sentence" is false (UPPSC 2005 asked this)
## In news 2025-26
2026: Madras HC held that under Art 161 the Governor is bound by State Cabinet advice on remission; cannot act independently
The "bias exception" of M.P. Special Police Establishment (2004) (Governor may sanction prosecution of a minister against advice) does not apply to Art 161
Governor may only return a mercy petition to the Cabinet for reconsideration if facts were missed

t: Judicial and other powers → courts, Governor vs President
text:
## 1. Judicial appointments
Power | Article
Consulted by President on appointing HC judges | 217
Appoints, posts, promotes district judges with HC | 233
Appoints State judicial service (other than district judges) with SPSC and HC | 234
## 2. Powers the Governor lacks (vs President)
No diplomatic, military or emergency powers
Cannot pardon death sentence or court-martial sentence
Pocket veto: none (Testbook: Governor has absolute and suspensive veto, not pocket veto)
⚠ The Governor has no emergency powers; he only reports under Art 356

t: Article 200 → the Governor's options on a State Bill
text:
## 1. Options when a Bill is presented
Option | Note
Assent | Bill becomes law
Withhold assent | Bill fails
Return for reconsideration | Not for a Money Bill; only once
Reserve for the President | Mandatory in one case; optional in others
Re-passed Bill (with or without amendment): Governor cannot withhold assent again
Money Bill: assent, withhold or reserve; cannot be returned
⚠ Sources count three options (assent, withhold-with-return, reserve) or four (return separately); same content
⚠ Only the Governor reserves a State Bill; the President cannot reserve it on his own
PYQ 2025: "President can, of his own, reserve a State Bill" is false: reservation is the Governor's act under Art 200

t: Reservation → mandatory and optional grounds
text:
## 1. Mandatory reservation (only one)
Bill that would derogate from the powers of the High Court so as to endanger its position
## 2. Optional reservation (Governor's discretion)
Ground | 
1 | Ultra vires (against the Constitution)
2 | Opposed to DPSP
3 | Against the larger interest of the country
4 | Of grave national importance
5 | Compulsory acquisition of property under Art 31A
## 3. Re-passed Bill and reservation
PMF book (2025 Reference): after re-passage, Governor cannot withhold, but reservation may still be available in appropriate cases
⚠ LENS Apr 2026 and Prelims Magnum 2027: "must sign a re-passed Bill, cannot refer it to the President" (April 2025 TN ruling); the Nov 2025 Reference is the later word, follow the PMF book

t: Article 201 → the President's options on a reserved Bill
text:
## 1. President's options
Option | Note
Assent | Law
Withhold | No reasons needed; not judicially reviewable on merits
Direct return to the State Legislature | Non-Money Bill only
## 2. After return
Legislature must reconsider within six months
Re-passed Bill goes again to the President
President is not obliged to assent even then
## 3. Compare with Art 111 (Union Bills)
Point | Art 111 (Union) | Art 201 (reserved State Bill)
Return | President returns for reconsideration | President directs the Governor to return
After re-passage | Must assent | Not obliged to assent
Time limit | None | None (pocket veto possible)
⚠ The President acts on Union Cabinet advice under Art 201, not independently

t: State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor of TN (April 2025) → what it held
text:
## 1. Facts
10 Bills (mostly Vice-Chancellor appointments in State universities) pending with Governor R.N. Ravi (sent Jan 2020 - Apr 2023)
After TN moved SC (Nov 2023), Governor withheld 10, referred 2 to the President
Bench: Justices J.B. Pardiwala and R. Mahadevan (two judges)
## 2. Holdings
Invoked Art 142 to declare the 10 re-enacted Bills deemed assented
No absolute veto or pocket veto; "as soon as possible" means urgency
Governor must act on CoM advice; cannot re-refer re-enacted Bills to the President
## 3. Timelines set (PMF)
Action | Time
Assent or reserve on CoM advice | 1 month
Withhold against CoM advice | 3 months
Assent to re-passed Bill | 1 month
Reserve (max) | 3 months
⚠ CARE summary gives: withhold or reserve 3 months; President 3 months on reserved Bills; follow PMF for Governor timelines
First time SC set a time limit for Governors; later overturned in effect by the Nov 2025 Reference

t: Presidential Reference No. 1 of 2025 → the Nov 2025 opinion
text:
## 1. The reference
May 2025, under Art 143(1); five-judge Constitution Bench headed by CJI B.R. Gavai
Opinion delivered 20 November 2025
## 2. What the Court said
Question | Answer
Fixed timelines for Governor/President? | No; courts cannot impose them
Deemed assent? | Rejected; a Bill needs explicit assent
Governor bound by CoM advice in choosing among Art 200 options? | No; it is his discretion
Judicial review of Art 200 decision? | Not on merits; only limited mandamus against prolonged, unexplained inaction
Review of President's Art 201 decision? | Not on merits
Must President consult SC (Art 143) for every reserved Bill? | No
Can SC use Art 142 to substitute Governor's role? | No
Judicial review applies to laws, not Bills
⚠ The "advice binding" line of April 2025 versus "discretion in choosing options" of Nov 2025: a likely Statement I/II trap

t: Reform proposals on assent → timelines suggested by commissions
text:
## 1. Who proposed what
Body | Proposal
Sarkaria (1988) | Discretion only in rare cases of unconstitutionality; President to dispose reserved Bills in 6 months
Punchhi (2010) | Governor to decide on Bills within 6 months
Kurian Joseph Committee (TN, 2026) | State List Bills approved or returned in 15 days; re-passed Bills in 15 days; reasons for reserved Bills in 60 days; amend Arts 200, 201
Constitution itself: no time limit, only "as soon as possible" (proviso to Art 200)

t: Article 163 → explicit discretion and its three clauses
text:
## 1. What Art 163 says
Clause | Provision
163(1) | CoM headed by CM to aid and advise the Governor, except where he is required to act in his discretion
163(2) | If a question arises whether a matter is discretionary, Governor's decision is final; validity cannot be questioned on that ground
163(3) | Courts cannot inquire into what advice ministers gave
## 2. Governor vs President
Point | President | Governor
Discretion in text | None explicit | Explicit in Art 163
Advice binding | 42nd CAA 1976 (binding); 44th CAA: can return advice once | Binding except discretionary matters
Shamsher Singh (1974): Governor ordinarily acts on advice; discretion is the exception
Discretion beyond constitutional limits is reviewable (Nabam Rebia 2016)
PYQ 2025: "Constitution explicitly mentions that in certain spheres the Governor acts in his discretion": correct (Art 163)

t: Discretion → constitutional versus situational (complete list)
text:
## 1. Constitutional discretion
Power | Article
Reserving a Bill for the President | 200
Report recommending President's Rule | 356
Acting as Administrator of an adjoining UT (additional charge) | 239(2)
Fixing mineral royalty share of Autonomous District Councils (Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram) | Sixth Schedule
Seeking information from CM on administrative and legislative matters | 167
## 2. Situational (hidden) discretion
Appointing CM in a hung Assembly or when a CM dies with no obvious successor
Dismissing a ministry that has lost confidence and refuses to resign
Dissolving the Assembly when the ministry has lost majority
## 3. Not discretionary
Function | Why not
Appointing Ministers | On CM's advice (Art 164(1))
Making rules of business | Art 166(3), on advice
Summoning the House (Art 174) | On advice (Nabam Rebia)
Pardon / remission (Art 161) | On advice (Perarivalan; Madras HC 2026)
PYQ 2014: discretionary = report for President's Rule + reserving Bills; trap: appointing ministers and business rules are on advice

t: Special responsibilities → Articles 371-371J
text:
## 1. Special responsibility of Governors (individual judgment)
Article | State | Responsibility
371(2) | Maharashtra, Gujarat | Separate development boards (Vidarbha, Marathwada; Saurashtra, Kutch)
371A | Nagaland | Law and order
371C | Manipur | Hill Areas committee
371F | Sikkim | Peace and social and economic advancement
371H | Arunachal Pradesh | Law and order
371J | Karnataka | Development board for Hyderabad-Karnataka (Kalyana Karnataka) region
In these matters the Governor acts in individual judgment after consulting the CoM; his decision is final
⚠ Law and order special responsibility: Nagaland and Arunachal only (PMF)
## Beyond your notes
State-wise mapping of Arts 371, 371C, 371F, 371J above is standard text; PMF names only Nagaland and Arunachal

t: Hung Assembly and floor test → what the Governor must do
text:
## 1. Order of invitation (Sarkaria / Punchhi)
Priority | Claimant
1 | Pre-poll alliance with majority
2 | Single largest party with support of others
3 | Post-poll coalition (all partners join government)
4 | Post-poll alliance with outside support
## 2. Floor test rules
Majority to be tested on the floor of the House, not by Governor's subjective view (S.R. Bommai 1994)
Subhash Desai (2023): Governor needs objective material before calling a floor test; intra-party differences not enough
Rameshwar Prasad (2006): Governor's personal opinion cannot justify dissolution or President's Rule
## In news 2025-26
May 2026: Tamil Nadu: TVK single largest party but short of majority: hung Assembly
May 2026: West Bengal CM refused to resign after poll defeat; CM continues only while enjoying confidence; once a new CM is sworn in, incumbent ceases
⚠ Constitution does not expressly require a defeated CM to resign; majority principle makes it unavoidable

topic: Chief Minister, Council of Ministers and Chief Secretary
t: Chief Secretary → who chooses, tenure, rank
text:
## 1. Key facts
Point | Fact
Post | Senior-most cadre post in State administration; head of State Secretariat
Appointment | Chosen by the CM through executive action taken in the name of the Governor
Tenure | No fixed tenure; excluded from the tenure system
Precedence | 23rd (within the State); maintained by MHA
Not constitutional | Office is not in the Constitution
## 2. Where there is none
UTs governed by Administrators: no Chief Secretary; an Adviser appointed by the Union
Delhi, J&K, Puducherry (with legislatures) have Chief Secretaries
During President's Rule, Governor runs the State with the Chief Secretary and advisers
## 3. Reform
2nd ARC (15th Report): fixed tenure of at least two years for Chief Secretary; a State Civil Services Authority to handle senior appointments
⚠ Preview's key marks 2016 as "(a) 1 only"; UPSC's answer is (d) neither: the CM chooses, the Governor does not appoint on his own
PYQ 2016: "appointed by Governor" and "has fixed tenure" are both wrong
## In news 2025-26
2026: Sanjay Jaju appointed Chief Secretary of Telangana, succeeding K. Ramakrishna Rao (retired 30 June 2026)

topic: Chief Minister, Council of Ministers and Chief Secretary
t: Chief Minister → appointment under Article 164
text:
## 1. Appointment
Appointed by the Governor; other ministers on CM's advice (Art 164(1))
Normally the leader of the majority in the Assembly; hung Assembly: limited discretion
Need not be a member at appointment; must become an MLA/MLC within six consecutive months (Art 164(4))
May be from either House in a bicameral State
## 2. Council of Ministers (Art 164)
Rule | Source
Size max 15% of Assembly, min 12 (incl. CM) | 91st CAA 2003
Defector disqualified from being minister | 91st CAA 2003
Collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly | 164(2)
Oaths of office and secrecy by Governor (Third Schedule) | 164(3)
Salaries fixed by State Legislature | 164(5)
No fixed tenure for CM; ministers hold office at the Governor's pleasure
⚠ Ministers from the Council also resign on a no-confidence vote in the Assembly

topic: Chief Minister, Council of Ministers and Chief Secretary
t: Article 167 and 166 → duties of CM, conduct of business
text:
## 1. Art 167: duties of the CM
Duty | 
1 | Communicate all CoM decisions on administration and legislative proposals to the Governor
2 | Furnish information the Governor calls for
3 | Place before the CoM, if Governor requires, a matter decided by one minister but not considered by the Council
## 2. Art 166: conduct of business
All executive action expressed in the Governor's name
Orders authenticated per Governor's rules; validity cannot be questioned on ground that Governor did not make them
Governor makes rules for transaction and allocation of business, except discretionary matters
## 3. Art 177
Ministers and Advocate General can speak in both Houses and committees but cannot vote (by this Article)
⚠ Seeking information under Art 167 is a constitutional discretion (PMF lists it); making business rules is not

topic: Chief Minister, Council of Ministers and Chief Secretary
t: Advocate General → Article 165
text:
## 1. Key facts
Point | Advocate General (Art 165) | Attorney General (Art 76)
Appointed by | Governor | President
Qualification | Qualified to be HC judge | Qualified to be SC judge
Tenure | Pleasure of Governor; no fixed term | Pleasure of President
Remuneration | Fixed by Governor | Fixed by President
Rights in Legislature | Art 177 (no vote) | Art 88 (no vote)
By convention resigns when the government changes; not constitutionally required
Rank 25 in order of precedence
⚠ "Advocate General appointed by the President on Governor's recommendation" is false (UPSC 2009)

topic: Reforms, Commissions and Key Judgments on the Governor
t: Commissions → who recommended what on the Governor
text:
## 1. Recommendations
Body | Key recommendations
Rajamannar Committee (1969, TN) | Abolish Art 356; permanent Inter-State Council (Art 263); never implemented
Sarkaria Commission (1983-88) | Eminent, outsider, not recently active in politics; consult the CM; 5-year tenure not disturbed; Art 356 as last resort
Venkatachaliah / NCRWC (2002) | Appoint Governor on recommendation of a committee (PM, Home Minister, LS Speaker, CM)
Punchhi Commission (2007-10) | Stop treating Governors as "political footballs"; fixed tenure; two-year cooling-off for politicians; drop Chancellor role
Justice Kurian Joseph Committee (TN, Apr 2025) | State proposes 3 names approved by Assembly; removal by Assembly resolution; fixed 5 years; HC CJ to act in vacancy
⚠ PMF infographic credits the PM-HM-Speaker-CM collegium to Punchhi; Testbook credits a committee of the same members to NCRWC
NCERT: Sarkaria (set up 1983, report 1988) wanted Governor appointments strictly non-partisan
## In news 2025-26
18 Feb 2026: first part of Kurian Joseph Committee report tabled in TN Assembly: amend Arts 155, 156, 200, 201; delete Art 176; Governor not to have held political or profit office in previous 5 years
June 2026 (PMF): Punchhi call to divest Governors of Chancellorship revived amid VC appointment deadlocks

topic: Reforms, Commissions and Key Judgments on the Governor
t: Supreme Court judgments → case and holding
text:
## 1. Judgments in sequence
Case | Holding
Shamsher Singh (1974) | Governor acts on aid and advice; discretion is exception
Hargovind Pant (1979) | Independent constitutional office, not subordinate to Union
D.C. Wadhwa (1987) | Re-promulgation of ordinances unconstitutional
S.R. Bommai (1994) | Floor test; Art 356 judicially reviewable
Rameshwar Prasad (2006) | Governor's report cannot justify unconstitutional dissolution (Bihar)
Epuru Sudhakar (2006) | Art 161 pardons: limited judicial review
B.P. Singhal (2010) | Removal not arbitrary; limited review
Nabam Rebia (2016) | Discretion limited; cannot summon House on own (Arunachal)
Subhash Desai (2023) | Objective material before floor test (Maharashtra)
State of Punjab v. Governor (2023) | Governor must act "as soon as possible", cannot sit on Bills
State of TN v. Governor (Apr 2025) | Art 142 deemed assent; timelines
Presidential Reference No. 1 (Nov 2025) | No timelines, no deemed assent; limited mandamus
⚠ Nabam Rebia is the Arunachal case; Subhash Desai is the Maharashtra case

topic: Reforms, Commissions and Key Judgments on the Governor
t: Governor's office → recent controversies and issues
text:
## 1. Issues in functioning
Issue | Constitutional position
CM appointment (hung Assembly) | Government that can prove majority on the floor
Dismissal of ministry | Loss of majority to be shown on the floor
President's Rule report | Proclamation subject to judicial review
Assent delays | Arts 200-201; 2025 Reference
Chancellor role | Statutory, from State law
## 2. Recent controversies (2024-26)
Kerala: HC quashed Governor-appointed interim VCs (UGC norms)
Karnataka: Governor Thawar Chand Gehlot sanctioned prosecution of CM Siddaramaiah
Punjab (2023): Governor refused to summon Budget Session
Mizoram (2024): Governor imposed direct rule over the Chakma Autonomous District Council
Puducherry: LG bypassed CM on appointments
⚠ Governor can sanction prosecution of a CM (Sec 197 CrPC / Sec 19 PCA) against Cabinet advice where bias is apparent (M.P. Special Police Establishment, 2004)

Article | Subject

⚠ The Governor is part of the State Legislature (Art 168), as the President is part of Parliament

t: Legislative Assembly → strength, election, exceptions
text:
## 1. Article 170
Item | Fact
Maximum | 500
Minimum | 60
Election | Direct, territorial constituencies (FPTP)
Seat ratio | Population-to-seat ratio same throughout the State, as far as practicable
Readjustment | After each Census; freeze until first Census after 2026
## 2. Exceptions to the minimum of 60 (special provisions)
State | Constitutional minimum (PMF) | Actual seats (ROCKET)
Sikkim | 30 | 32 (smallest State Assembly)
Goa | 30 | 40
Mizoram | 40 | 40
Arunachal Pradesh | 30 | 60
Largest: Uttar Pradesh 403; Bihar 243; Puducherry (UT) 33 = 30 elected + 3 nominated
104th CAA 2019 ended nomination of Anglo-Indians to Assemblies (Art 333)
SC/ST seats reserved in proportion to population (Art 332)
⚠ The ceiling is 500, not 450; 450 is the trap from PYQ 2008
PYQ 2008: "not more than 450 members" wrong; "minimum age 25" right

t: Legislative Council → size and who elects whom
text:
## 1. Size (Art 171)
Maximum = 1/3 of Assembly; minimum = 40 (ordinarily)
Actual strength fixed by Parliament by law
So a Council can never exceed half of its Assembly
## 2. Composition
Share | Elected / chosen by
1/3 | Members of local authorities (municipalities, district boards)
1/12 | Graduates of 3 years' standing residing in State
1/12 | Teachers of 3 years' standing (secondary school or higher)
1/3 | MLAs, from among persons who are not MLAs
1/6 | Nominated by Governor
First four categories: PR by single transferable vote, secret ballot
Governor nominates from literature, science, art, co-operative movement, social service
⚠ Co-operative movement is a ground for Council nomination, not for Rajya Sabha (Art 80); "industrialists" fits neither
⚠ Council Chairman is elected by the Council from its members, not nominated by the Governor
PYQ 2015: both statements wrong: Council larger than half of Assembly (no: max 1/3); Governor nominates Chairman (no: elected)

t: Councils → how created or abolished (Art 169)
text:
## 1. Procedure
Step | Requirement
1. Assembly resolution | Special majority: majority of total membership + 2/3 of members present and voting
2. Parliament law | Simple majority
Status of law | Not an amendment under Art 368, though it amends the Constitution
Assembly only initiates; Parliament decides; resolution does not bind Parliament to act
No ratification by States or President's prior recommendation is required in the Constitution
## 2. States with Councils now (6)
State | Council seats
Uttar Pradesh | 100 (largest)
Maharashtra | 78
Bihar | 75
Karnataka | 75
Andhra Pradesh | 58
Telangana | 40 (= minimum)
J&K had a 36-member Council, abolished 2019 (Reorganisation Act); UT of J&K is unicameral
⚠ Tamil Nadu, West Bengal, Odisha, Rajasthan, Assam do not have Councils
## Beyond your notes
Andhra Pradesh Assembly passed a resolution to abolish its Council in 2020 and withdrew it in 2021; Councils of Odisha, Rajasthan and Assam remain proposals

t: Council vs Rajya Sabha → where they differ
text:
Feature | Rajya Sabha | Legislative Council
Existence | Mandatory | Optional (Art 169)
Ordinary bill | Equal; joint sitting on deadlock | Only delay (3 + 1 months); no joint sitting
Money bill | Recommend, 14 days | Recommend, 14 days
Electors | MLAs (elected) | Local bodies, graduates, teachers, MLAs + nominated
Nomination | 12, by President | 1/6, by Governor
Presidential election | Elected members vote | No role
Special powers | Art 249, 312 | None
Presiding officer | Vice-President (non-member) | Chairman elected from members
Both are permanent Houses: 1/3 retire every 2 years, 6-year term
Ministers are collectively responsible only to the Assembly (Art 164(2))
⚠ MLCs do not vote in the President's election or Rajya Sabha elections

t: Duration → Assembly vs Council (Art 172)
text:
House | Term | Ends by
Assembly | 5 years from date of first meeting | Expiry or earlier dissolution by Governor
Council | Permanent, never dissolved | 1/3 members retire every second year; member's term 6 years
National Emergency: Parliament may extend Assembly term by law one year at a time, not beyond 6 months after the Emergency ends
⚠ Only the Assembly can be dissolved; the Council is a continuing House

t: Qualifications and disqualifications → who can sit (Art 173, 191, 192)
text:
## 1. Qualifications (Art 173)
Item | Assembly | Council
Citizenship | Indian citizen | Indian citizen
Minimum age | 25 | 30
Oath | Before Governor or his appointee | Same
Other | As Parliament prescribes (RPA 1951) | Same
## 2. Disqualifications (Art 191)
Office of profit under Union/State (unless exempted by law)
Unsound mind declared by court; undischarged insolvent
Not a citizen / acquired foreign citizenship / allegiance to foreign State
Disqualified by law of Parliament; or under Tenth Schedule (defection)
## 3. Who decides (Art 192)
Ground | Decided by
Art 191(1) grounds | Governor, bound by Election Commission's opinion
Defection (Tenth Schedule) | Speaker / Chairman, subject to judicial review
⚠ Governor decides ordinary disqualification on EC's binding opinion, not on CM's advice

t: Vacation of seats → five ways (Art 190)
text:
Ground | Rule
Double membership | Cannot be member of both Houses, or of Parliament and State
Disqualification | Seat vacant from disqualification
Resignation | To Speaker / Chairman; may be refused if not voluntary
Absence | 60 days from all meetings without permission
Others | Election void, expulsion, elected President/VP, appointed Governor
Sitting or voting before oath or while disqualified: Rs 500 per day penalty (Art 193)
Members' salaries fixed by State Legislature by law (Art 195)
## In news 2025-26
Telangana HC (18 Sep 2026) set aside Speaker's order and disqualified Khairatabad MLA Danam Nagender under Para 2(1)(a) Tenth Schedule; seat declared vacant
SC in Padi Kaushik Reddy v. Telangana (2025) called for timely, impartial defection decisions; Keisham Meghachandra (2020): decide within 3 months

t: Assembly Speaker → when the office is vacated (Art 179)
text:
## 1. Vacates office if
# | Ground
1 | Ceases to be a member of the Assembly
2 | Resigns in writing to the Deputy Speaker
3 | Removed by resolution of majority of all the then members (effective majority), after 14 days' notice
## 2. Dissolution rule
On dissolution, the Speaker does not vacate; continues until immediately before the first meeting of the new Assembly
⚠ Speaker vacates on ceasing to be a member, but not on dissolution
PYQ 2018: statement 1 right; statement 2 ("vacates immediately on dissolution") wrong
## 3. Election
Elected by the Assembly from among its members (Art 178); same for Deputy Speaker
Salary fixed by State Legislature, charged on Consolidated Fund of State (Art 186)

t: Speaker under removal → what he may and may not do
text:
During removal resolution | Speaker
Preside | No (Art 181)
Speak, take part | Yes
Vote | First instance only
Casting vote | No
Removal needs effective majority = majority of total membership excluding vacancies
The same rules apply to the Lok Sabha Speaker under Art 94-96
## In news 2025-26
Opposition moved a removal notice against Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla (10 Feb 2026)
Procedure: written notice to Secretary-General, 14 days, 50 members must rise for leave; Lok Sabha Rules 200-203
Earlier motions: Mavalankar 1954, Hukam Singh 1966, Balram Jakhar 1987; no Speaker ever removed
Nabam Rebia (2016): Speaker facing a removal notice cannot decide disqualification petitions

t: Speaker → powers in the Assembly
text:
Maintains order, interprets rules, adjourns for want of quorum
Casting vote only in a tie; does not vote in first instance
Certifies Money Bills: decision final (Chairman of Council has no such power)
Decides defection cases (Tenth Schedule): subject to judicial review (Kihoto Hollohan 1992)
Nominates Panel of Chairpersons; Chairman nominates Panel of Vice-Chairpersons
Officer | Resigns to | Removed by
Speaker | Deputy Speaker | Assembly, effective majority
Deputy Speaker | Speaker | Assembly, effective majority
Chairman | Deputy Chairman | Council, effective majority
Deputy Chairman | Chairman | Council, effective majority
⚠ All four removals need 14 days' notice

t: Chairman of Council → how it differs from RS Chairman
text:
Feature | Council Chairman | Rajya Sabha Chairman
Who | Elected by Council from its members (Art 182) | Vice-President, ex officio
Member of House | Yes | No
Removal | By Council, effective majority | Only by removal as Vice-President
Money Bill certification | No | No
Powers otherwise like Speaker's (order, casting vote, defection decisions)
Governor's only role: nominates 1/6 members, not the Chairman
## Beyond your notes
Speaker pro tem of a new Assembly is appointed by the Governor (usually the senior-most member), who administers his oath; he swears in members and conducts the Speaker's election

topic: Sessions, Governor's address and rules of procedure
t: Governor's address → Art 175 vs Art 176
text:
Feature | Art 175 (discretionary) | Art 176 (special address)
When | Any time | Start of first session after each general election + first session of each year
Nature | Optional; also sends messages on Bills | Mandatory
To whom | Either House or both together | Assembly, or both Houses assembled together
Art 176 address tells the Legislature the causes of its summons
Address = policy of the Council of Ministers; Governor cannot refuse or alter it
Art 176(2): rules must allot time for discussion: Motion of Thanks; its defeat = loss of confidence
Messages under Art 175(2) to be considered with "all convenient dispatch"
⚠ Customary address is at the first session of the year, not at every session
PYQ 2019: both statements correct: address at first session of the year; where a State has no rule, it follows the Lok Sabha rule
## In news 2025-26
Governors' walkouts and omission of Cabinet-approved text at inaugural sessions (Jan 2026) revived the Art 176 debate
Justice Kurian Joseph Committee (Tamil Nadu, report Feb 2026) suggested deleting Art 176
Cases: Shamsher Singh (1974), Nabam Rebia (2016), State of TN v. Governor of TN (2024): Art 175/176 functions on ministerial advice

topic: Sessions, Governor's address and rules of procedure
t: Sessions → summoning, prorogation, dissolution (Art 174)
text:
Act | By | Effect
Summoning | Governor | Gap between sessions max 6 months: so at least 2 sessions a year
Adjournment | Presiding officer | Suspends a sitting
Adjournment sine die | Presiding officer | Ends sitting, no date fixed
Prorogation | Governor | Ends session; Bills do not lapse
Dissolution | Governor | Ends Assembly; Council cannot be dissolved
Governor acts on CM's advice in summoning (Nabam Rebia: no independent discretion under Art 174)

topic: Sessions, Governor's address and rules of procedure
t: Bills on dissolution → which lapse
text:
Status of Bill | Effect
Pending in Assembly | Lapses
Passed by Assembly, pending in Council | Lapses
Pending in Council, not passed by Assembly | Does not lapse
Pending Governor's / President's assent | Does not lapse
Returned by President for reconsideration | Does not lapse
⚠ Unlike Parliament, there is no joint sitting row: States have no joint sitting at all

topic: Sessions, Governor's address and rules of procedure
t: Rules, quorum, language → House procedure
text:
Item | State Legislature
Quorum | 10 members or 1/10 of total membership, whichever is greater
Voting | Majority of present and voting; presiding officer has casting vote
Language (Art 210) | Official language(s) of State, Hindi or English; mother tongue with permission
Ministers + Advocate General (Art 177) | May speak in either House, but vote only where a member
No State rule on a matter: Lok Sabha rule followed (PYQ 2019, UPPCS 2022)
## Beyond your notes
Art 208: each House makes its own rules of procedure; until then, the pre-1950 provincial rules applied
Art 211: no discussion on conduct of SC/HC judges; Art 212: courts cannot question proceedings for procedural irregularity

t: Ordinary Bills → Council's delaying power (Art 196-197)
text:
## 1. Bill from the Assembly
Round | Council's options | Max delay
1st | Pass, reject, amend, or no action | 3 months
Assembly re-passes | - | -
2nd | Same | 1 month
Result | Deemed passed in the form the Assembly passed the second time | Total ~4 months
## 2. Bill from the Council
If the Assembly rejects it, the Bill ends
No joint sitting in State Legislatures
⚠ Council can only delay, never veto; the Assembly has the final say
⚠ Contrast: Rajya Sabha can hold an ordinary Bill till a joint sitting; Council cannot

t: Money Bills → Assembly vs Council (Art 198-199, 207)
text:
Feature | Ordinary Bill | Money Bill
Introduced in | Either House | Assembly only
Governor's prior recommendation | Not needed | Required (Art 207)
Council's power | Delay | Recommend only
Max Council delay | ~4 months | 14 days
Certified by | - | Speaker (final)
Joint sitting | None | None
Council cannot reject or amend; Assembly may accept or reject its recommendations
Not returned in 14 days: deemed passed in the Assembly's form
Demands for grants go only to the Assembly; no demand without Governor's recommendation
Budget (Annual Financial Statement) laid by Governor under Art 202

t: Assent → Governor's and President's options (Art 200-201)
text:
Authority | Options
Governor (Art 200) | Assent; withhold; return (not a Money Bill) for reconsideration; reserve for President
President (Art 201) | Assent; withhold; direct Governor to return (not a Money Bill)
Re-passed Bill: Governor must assent; President is not bound to assent
Returned by President: House(s) to reconsider within 6 months
## In news 2025-26
SC (TN v. Governor, Apr 2025): Governor to act within 1 month (on advice) / 3 months (against advice); President within 3 months under Art 201; re-passed Bill: assent within 1 month
Presidential Reference (5-judge bench, Nov 2025): decisions under Art 200-201 not justiciable before enactment; but limited mandamus for prolonged inaction
Kurian Joseph Committee: State List Bills to be assented or returned within 15 days
⚠ Detailed Governor powers are in the Governor and State Executive topic

t: Grants and votes → which exist in States
text:
Device | Article
Annual Financial Statement | 202
Appropriation Bill | 204
Supplementary / additional / excess grants | 205
Vote on account, vote of credit, exceptional grants | 206
Financial Bills | 207
Expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State is not voted (e.g. Speaker's and Governor's emoluments)
No withdrawal from State Consolidated Fund except by appropriation law
⚠ Council cannot vote on demands for grants; only discussion of the budget

t: Federal features → what makes India federal
text:
## 1. The defining feature
Constitutional division of powers between two levels of government is the core; other features reinforce it
## 2. Federal features of the Constitution (PMF list)
Feature | How it shows
Dual polity | Union and State govts, each in its own sphere
Written Constitution | Defines organisation and powers of both levels
Division of powers | Art 246 + Seventh Schedule (3 Lists); residuary Art 248
Supremacy of Constitution | Both levels derive authority from it
Partly rigid | Federal provisions need special majority + half the States
Independent judiciary | SC settles Centre-State and inter-State disputes (Art 131)
Bicameralism | Rajya Sabha represents the States
⚠ The essential federal feature is an independent judiciary that umpires the division of powers; elected representatives from units, regional-party ministers or justiciable FRs are not marks of federalism
PYQ 2021: asked the "essential feature that indicates federal character"; answer: independence of judiciary is safeguarded. Trap: "FRs enforceable by courts" is a rights feature, not a federal one

t: "Union of States" → why India is not a federation by agreement
text:
## 1. Article 1
Art 1(1): "India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States"; the word Federation is not used anywhere in the Constitution
Dr B.R. Ambedkar: "Union" means (1) the federation is not the result of an agreement among States, and (2) no State has the right to secede; the Union is indestructible
## 2. Holding together vs coming together
Type | How formed | Examples
Coming together | Independent States voluntarily unite | USA, Switzerland, Australia
Holding together | Large country distributes power to units | India, Canada, Spain, Belgium
India resembles the Canadian model: holding-together, the term "Union", strong Centre, residuary power with the Centre
⚠ "Result of an agreement among the federating units" is not a feature of Indian federalism; independent judiciary, clear division of powers and unequal RS representation are features
PYQ 2017: "which is NOT a feature of Indian federalism"; answer: result of an agreement among the federating units

t: Unitary features → the strong-Centre list
text:
Unitary feature | Provision
Strong Centre | Important subjects + residuary power + Union law prevails in Concurrent conflicts
States destructible | Art 3: Parliament alters area, boundaries, names; State's views not binding
Single Constitution, single citizenship | Arts 5-11 citizenship for all
Flexible Constitution | Most provisions amended without States; amendment Bills only in Parliament
Unequal RS representation | By population, unlike equal US Senate
Integrated institutions | Single judiciary, CAG, Election Commission
All India Services | Art 312
Governor | Appointed by President (Art 155), holds office at pleasure (Art 156)
Emergency provisions | Federal balance shifts to Union
Control over State legislation | Arts 249-253; reservation of Bills (Arts 200, 201)
India = "indestructible Union of destructible States"
⚠ There is no division of judicial power: one integrated judiciary administers both Union and State laws

t: Scholars → how they described Indian federalism
text:
Scholar | Description
K.C. Wheare | Quasi-federal (federal with strong centralising bias)
Granville Austin | Cooperative federalism
Morris Jones | Bargaining federalism
Ivor Jennings | Federation with a strong centralising tendency
Alexandrowicz | Sui generis (unique)
Ambedkar | "Union of States", not "federation of States"; not an agreement
## Beyond your notes
Paul Appleby: "extremely federal"; Ambedkar also said the Constitution can be both unitary and federal according to time and circumstances
⚠ Wheare = quasi-federal, Austin = cooperative, Morris Jones = bargaining: the classic match-the-pairs swap
Likely next: match scholar to phrase; "Federation" not used in the Constitution

t: Types of federalism → meaning and example
text:
Type | Meaning | Example / institution
Cooperative | Union and States jointly pursue goals | Inter-State Council, Finance Commission, GST Council, NITI Aayog
Competitive | States compete for investment, better services | NITI Aayog rankings
Asymmetrical | Differentiated arrangements for some regions | Arts 371-371J, Fifth and Sixth Schedules
Fiscal | Division of taxing and spending powers | Art 280 FC, Art 279A GST Council
Horizontal | State-to-State relations and disputes | Cauvery, Mahadayi, Assam-Mizoram border
Federal vs unitary: federal = dual government, written, supreme Constitution, rigid on federal matters, independent judiciary essential, generally bicameral; unitary = single government, may be unwritten, unicameral or bicameral
⚠ The GST Council's recommendations are not binding (Mohit Minerals, 2022): persuasive value only

t: Federalism and the courts → key judgments
text:
Case | Holding
State of West Bengal v Union (1962) | India has a quasi-federal structure; Union strong for unity
S.R. Bommai v Union (1994) | Federalism is part of the Basic Structure; Art 356 proclamations open to judicial review
Mohit Minerals (2022) | GST Council recommendations persuasive, not binding
State of Punjab v Principal Secy to Governor (2023) | Governor cannot indefinitely sit on Bills; pocket veto weakens democracy
⚠ PMF and CARE give Bommai (1994) as the case that made federalism basic structure; Current Care Sept 2025 credits Kesavananda (1973), which listed federal character among basic features. For "which case" questions, Bommai is the safer answer
Parliament may modify the distribution of powers but cannot destroy the federal character

t: Amendments needing State ratification → federal provisions
text:
## 1. Rule (Art 368(2) proviso)
Special majority of Parliament + ratification by at least half the State Legislatures (simple majority) before Presidential assent
## 2. Provisions covered (PMF + Beyond your notes)
Covered (needs States) | Not covered
Any List of the Seventh Schedule | Conditions of the Governor's office
Extent of executive power of Union and States | Creation of new States (Art 3, simple majority)
Distribution of legislative powers (Part XI Ch I) | Citizenship, FRs, DPSPs
SC and High Courts | Quorum, salaries of MPs
Election of the President; representation of States in Parliament | 
Art 368 itself; GST Council (Art 279A) | 
⚠ Amendment Bills can be introduced only in Parliament; States cannot initiate
PYQ 2025 (outside this set): of "Union List", "extent of executive power of a State", "conditions of Governor's office", only the first two need ratification
## In news 2025-26
J&K statehood (Sept 2025): plea in Zahoor Ahmed Bhat v UT of J&K; SC (11 Dec 2023) upheld abrogation of Art 370 and directed restoration of statehood; 90-member Assembly elected Oct 2024 but J&K remains a UT
Structural reset debate (Feb 2026, PMF): cesses outside the divisible pool, uniform CSS rules, BSF jurisdiction in Punjab beyond 15 km cited as centralisation

topic: Seventh Schedule and Distribution of Legislative Powers
t: Three Lists → who legislates, how many subjects
text:
List | Legislates | Subjects now (originally) | Typical subjects
List I Union | Parliament exclusively, Art 246(1) | 100 (97) | Defence, foreign affairs, currency, banking, railways, inter-State trade
List II State | State Legislature exclusively, Art 246(3) | 61 (66) | Public order, police, public health, agriculture, prisons, local government
List III Concurrent | Both, Art 246(2) | 52 (47) | Criminal law, marriage, education, forests, electricity
Counts from Testbook; entries keep their original numbering with letter suffixes (17A, 20A)
Union List: national matters needing uniformity; State List: regional/local matters; Concurrent: uniformity desirable but not essential
Model: GoI Act 1935 three lists: Federal 59, Provincial 54, Concurrent 36; residuary power then with the Governor-General
⚠ In 1935 residuary power lay with the Governor-General; in 1950 it went to Parliament (Art 248)

topic: Seventh Schedule and Distribution of Legislative Powers
t: Residuary power → who holds it
text:
Art 248: Parliament has exclusive power on matters not in the State or Concurrent List, including residuary taxes
Examples: space research, cyber law (Rocket)
Country | Residuary power with
India, Canada | Centre
USA, Australia | States
GoI Act 1935 | Governor-General
Art 246A (101st Amdt 2016): Parliament and States both legislate on GST; Parliament alone for inter-State supply
Art 269A: GST on inter-State supplies levied by Union, apportioned
⚠ Sarkaria: residuary power on taxation should stay with the Union; some States demanded residuary powers go to States
Likely next: "residuary powers in India lie with" (Parliament), with USA/Canada as distractors

topic: Seventh Schedule and Distribution of Legislative Powers
t: Predominance and repugnancy → whose law prevails
text:
## 1. Overlap between Lists
Union vs State List → Union prevails; Union vs Concurrent → Union; Concurrent vs State → Concurrent
## 2. Art 254 (Concurrent List conflict)
Situation | Result
Central and State law inconsistent | Central law prevails; State law void to the extent of repugnancy
State law reserved and assented by President (254(2)) | State law prevails in that State
Parliament later legislates on same matter | Can still add to, amend or repeal that State law
Doctrine of occupied field: Union law excludes a State law if Parliament intended to occupy the whole field (Deep Chand case)
⚠ Presidential assent gives precedence within that State only, not immunity from future Parliamentary law

topic: Seventh Schedule and Distribution of Legislative Powers
t: Territorial extent → Art 245 and its limits
text:
Legislature | Territorial reach
Parliament | Whole or any part of India; only it can make extra-territorial laws
State Legislature | Whole or part of the State; outside only on territorial nexus
## 1. Restrictions on Parliament
President's regulations for specified UTs: same force as an Act, may repeal Parliamentary laws there
Governor may exclude or modify Acts of Parliament for Scheduled Areas (Fifth Schedule)
Governor of Assam may do the same for autonomous districts (Sixth Schedule)
## 2. Doctrines of interpretation
Pith and substance; colourable legislation (cannot do indirectly what cannot be done directly); reading down
⚠ Extra-territorial law: Parliament only; State laws need sufficient nexus

topic: Parliament's Power over the State List
t: Five circumstances → Parliament legislates on State List
text:
Article | Trigger | Key limit
249 | Rajya Sabha resolution, 2/3 of members present and voting, national interest | Resolution 1 year, renewable; law lapses 6 months after
250 | National Emergency (Art 352) in operation | Law lapses 6 months after Emergency ends
252 | Two or more States pass resolutions | Applies only to those States; others may adopt
253 | Implementing international treaties, agreements, conventions | No State consent needed
356 | President's Rule in a State | Parliament exercises State Legislature's powers
⚠ Only Art 249 needs a Rajya Sabha resolution; Art 253 needs nothing from States or RS
Likely next: match Article to circumstance (249 national interest, 250 emergency, 252 consent, 253 treaty)

topic: Parliament's Power over the State List
t: Article 249 → national interest resolution
text:
## 1. Procedure
Rajya Sabha declares it necessary in the national interest
Majority: two-thirds of members present and voting (not total membership, not Lok Sabha)
Resolution in force max 1 year; renewable any number of times, one year at a time
Law ceases 6 months after resolution ceases (except things done)
## 2. Effect on the State
State keeps its power on the same matter; in inconsistency, Parliament's law prevails
Rajya Sabha special powers (same majority) | Article
Parliament legislates on State List | 249
Create new All India Services | 312
Removal of Vice-President initiated only in RS | 67
⚠ Sarkaria: States' fears about Art 249 are baseless
PYQ 2016: options mixed Lok Sabha/Rajya Sabha and total/present-and-voting; answer: Rajya Sabha, 2/3 present and voting

topic: Parliament's Power over the State List
t: Article 250 → legislation during National Emergency
text:
While a National Emergency (Art 352) operates, Parliament can legislate on any State List matter
Law ceases 6 months after the Emergency ends (past actions saved)
State Legislature's power not suspended; in conflict, Parliament's law prevails
Emergency | Effect on Centre-State relations
National (352) | Union directions on any matter; Parliament legislates on State List; Art 354 lets President modify revenue distribution (Arts 268-279)
President's Rule (356) | President takes State executive; Parliament exercises State legislative power
Financial (360) | Directions on financial propriety; cut salaries; reserve Money Bills for President
⚠ State governments are not suspended merely because a National Emergency is in operation

topic: Parliament's Power over the State List
t: Article 252 → laws by consent of two or more States
text:
Two or more State Legislatures pass resolutions requesting Parliament
Law applies only to the requesting States; others may adopt later by resolution
Can be amended or repealed only by Parliament, not by the State Legislatures
The requesting State ceases to have power on that matter
Examples of Art 252 laws (Testbook)
Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972
Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976
Transplantation of Human Organs Act, 1994
Clinical Establishments Act, 2010 (Sikkim, Mizoram, Arunachal, Himachal)
⚠ Under 249 and 250 the State keeps its power; under 252 it loses it for that matter

topic: Parliament's Power over the State List
t: Article 253 → laws to implement treaties
text:
Parliament can make laws on any subject, including the State List, for any part of India, to implement treaties, agreements, conventions or decisions of international conferences
No consent of any State required
Examples (Testbook)
United Nations (Privileges and Immunities) Act, 1947
Geneva Conventions Act, 1960
Anti-Hijacking Act
## Beyond your notes
Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and Air Act, 1981 were enacted after the Stockholm Conference (1972) using Art 253
⚠ Punchhi Commission: treaties impinging on State List should be negotiated with greater State involvement
PYQ 2013: "Parliament can legislate for any part of India to implement international treaties": with or without consent of any State; Art 253

topic: Finance Commission: Constitution, Mandate and Grants (Art 275, 280-282)

text:
## 1. Article 280(3): the duties of the Finance Commission
Clause | FC recommends
280(3)(a) | Distribution of net proceeds of shareable taxes between Union and States (vertical) and allocation of the States' share among States (horizontal)
280(3)(b) | Principles governing grants-in-aid to States out of the Consolidated Fund of India (Art 275)
280(3)(bb) | Measures to augment a State's Consolidated Fund to supplement Panchayat resources (on SFC recommendations)
280(3)(c) | Same for Municipalities
280(3)(d) | Any other matter referred by the President in the interests of sound finance
## 2. What the FC does NOT do (UPSC distractors)
Does not authorise withdrawal from the CFI (that is Parliament via Appropriation Act)
Does not supervise whether governments levy taxes per the budget (Finance Ministry / CAG)
Does not handle foreign capital inflow, PSU finances or "transparency in financial administration"
⚠ FC recommends; it does not levy, collect or release money

topic: Finance Commission: Constitution, Mandate and Grants (Art 275, 280-282)
t: Finance Commission → composition, qualifications, term
text:
## 1. Constitution
Art 280(1): President constitutes it within two years of the Constitution's commencement and then every fifth year or earlier
Chairman + 4 other members, all appointed by the President
Qualifications fixed by Parliament: Finance Commission (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1951
## 2. Qualifications
Post | Who
Chairman | Person with experience in public affairs
Member | High Court judge or qualified to be one
Member | Special knowledge of government finance and accounts
Member | Wide experience in financial matters and administration
Member | Special knowledge of economics
## 3. Tenure and disqualification
Term as fixed in the President's order; eligible for reappointment; resigns in writing to the President
Disqualified if of unsound mind, undischarged insolvent, convicted of moral turpitude, or has a prejudicial interest
⚠ Qualifications are in a 1951 Act of Parliament, not in Art 280 itself

Constitutional body (Art 280); described as quasi-judicial

Point | Fact
Report submitted to | President
Laid before | Parliament (not State legislatures)
Binding? | No: advisory, not legally binding on the Union
Implemented by | President's order (Art 270 share) and Parliament's law (Art 275 grants)

Planning Commission (extra-constitutional) gave plan grants, overlapping with the FC

text:
Article | Levied by | Collected / kept by | Examples
268 | Union | Collected and appropriated by States | Stamp duties on bills of exchange, cheques, promissory notes, insurance, share transfers
269 | Union | Collected by Union, assigned to States | Taxes on inter-State sale/consignment of goods (other than newspapers)
269A | Union (IGST) | Apportioned between Union and States | GST on inter-State supplies
270 | Union | Shared (divisible pool) on FC recommendation | Income tax, corporation tax, CGST, Centre's share of IGST

topic: Distribution of Taxing Powers and Tax Revenues (Art 265-293)
t: Taxes of the States → State List and pre-GST sales tax
text:
## 1. Taxes levied, collected and retained by States (State List: 18)
Group | Taxes
Land | Land revenue; taxes on agricultural income; succession/estate duty on agricultural land; taxes on lands and buildings
Goods | Sales tax (other than newspapers); excise on alcoholic liquor for human consumption and narcotics; entry tax
Services/others | Taxes on professions (max ₹2,500/yr, Art 276); road vehicles; luxuries, entertainment, betting; electricity; tolls; capitation tax
Duties | Stamp duty on documents (except Union List ones); fees (except court fees)
## 2. Pre-GST sales tax
Sales tax on a toothpaste was imposed and collected by the State Government; each State had its own law and rates (VAT)
⚠ Inter-State sale tax (CST) fell under Art 269: levied by Union, assigned to States: do not confuse with intra-State sales tax

topic: Distribution of Taxing Powers and Tax Revenues (Art 265-293)
t: Divisible pool → cess and surcharge exclusions
text:
## 1. What is outside the pool
Item | Why
Cess | Tax for a specific purpose (e.g. Krishi Kalyan cess, road and infrastructure cess); excluded by Art 270
Surcharge | Art 271; e.g. on income above ₹50 lakh; no specific purpose
Cost of collection | Deducted from gross tax revenue
Art 268, 269 taxes | Go wholly to States
## 2. Shrinking pool
Cess: 6% of gross tax revenue (2011) → 18% (2021); cess + surcharge now about 22-25%
Divisible pool: 89.1% of GTR (2014-15) → 74-80% (2020-24)
CAG (2018-19): about ₹1 lakh crore cess kept in the CFI instead of reserve funds
⚠ Actual transfers fall below the 41% headline because cesses and surcharges are not shareable

topic: Distribution of Taxing Powers and Tax Revenues (Art 265-293)

text:
Article | Provision
265 | No tax without authority of law
274 | Bill affecting taxes in which States are interested, or defining agricultural income, needs President's prior recommendation
279 | Net proceeds ascertained and certified by CAG
285 | Union property exempt from State taxes (unless Parliament provides)
289 | State property and income exempt from Union tax; State trade/business can be taxed
286 | States cannot tax supplies outside the State or in import/export
292 | Union borrows on security of the CFI, within limits set by Parliament

Date from which GST applies to petroleum crude, HSD, petrol, natural gas, ATF
Sets up a dispute adjudication mechanism

topic: Fiscal Federalism: Transfers, Imbalances and Debates
t: Fiscal federalism → issues and evolution
text:
## 1. Issues
Issue | Fact
Vertical imbalance | Union has buoyant taxes; States bear health, education, agriculture
Cess/surcharge | Outside divisible pool; about 22-25% of GTR
GST | States surrendered taxes; compensation ended June 2022
Own revenue | States' own tax revenue about 7% of GSDP
Southern States | "Penalised" for population control; demand 50% share
## 2. Evolution (Testbook)
Montford Reforms (1919) separated revenue heads; Meston Award (1920); GoI Act 1935 allowed sharing of income tax; 1st FC 1951
## 3. Bodies on Centre-State relations
Rajamannar Committee (1969, Tamil Nadu): abolish Planning Commission, revitalise FC; Sarkaria (1983-88); Punchhi (2007-10)
Next-likely: Sarkaria and Punchhi were Union commissions; Rajamannar was set up by Tamil Nadu

topic: Fiscal Federalism: Transfers, Imbalances and Debates

text:
## 1. Why GSDP
Argument | Fact
Fixes "headquarters (PAN) bias" | Direct tax booked where firms are registered, not where production occurs
Correlation with direct taxes | 0.75 (2023-24)
Correlation with GST | 0.91
Gainers | Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Gujarat
Relative losers | Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh
## 2. Against
Rewards already-rich States; contradicts income distance (equalisation)
## 3. Outcome
16th FC added contribution to GDP (10%)
## In news 2025-26

topic: Legal status: constitutional, statutory or executive

## 1. The three-way classification
Body | Status | Source of creation
Inter-State Council | Constitutional | Article 263; set up by Presidential Order, 28 May 1990
Zonal Councils (5) | Statutory | States Reorganisation Act, 1956 (Part III, Section 15)

t: Article 263 → what it permits and who sets the Council up
text:
## 1. Article 263
President may establish an Inter-State Council "if it appears that public interest would be served"; President fixes its organisation, procedure and duties
Clause | Function
263(a) | Inquire into and advise on disputes between States
263(b) | Investigate and discuss subjects of common interest (States, or Centre and States)
263(c) | Recommend better coordination of policy and action
The 1990 Order gives the ISC only (b) and (c), not dispute inquiry under (a)
## 2. Establishment
Sarkaria Commission (1983-88): permanent ISC under Art 263, to be called "Inter-Governmental Council"
Presidential Order, 28 May 1990; first ISC constituted December 1990
⚠ The ISC is set up by the President, not Parliament or the PM (UPPSC 2017, CGPSC 2019)
⚠ ISC discusses legal and non-legal issues and recommends; the Supreme Court (Art 131) decides legal disputes with binding effect
## Beyond your notes
Other bodies set up under Art 263: Central Council of Health, Central Council of Local Government (and similar councils for specific sectors)

t: Zonal Councils → legal basis and nature
text:
## 1. Status
Statutory, not constitutional: States Reorganisation Act, 1956 (Part III; Section 15)
Mooted by PM Jawaharlal Nehru in 1956 during the debate on linguistic reorganisation of States
Deliberative and advisory: recommendations not binding
## 2. Factors used to draw the zones
Factor | Why
Natural divisions | Geographical continuity
River systems, communications | Water and transport cooperation
Cultural and linguistic affinity | Social and administrative coordination
Economic development, security, law and order | Balanced growth
## 3. Objectives
National and emotional integration; curb State consciousness, regionalism, linguistic particularism; remove after-effects of reorganisation
Matters: economic and social planning, linguistic minorities, border disputes, inter-State transport
Called "sub-federal links" of the federal system (CGPSC 2019)

Point | Fact

Member | In NDC?

topic: Planning Commission and National Development Council
t: National Development Council → status, objectives and functions
text:
## 1. Status
Set up 6 August 1952 by executive resolution: neither constitutional nor statutory
"Highest body below Parliament" for planning policy; recommendations not binding; to meet at least twice a year
Not an organ of the Planning Commission: a separate forum of the Centre and States that approved the Five-Year Plans drafted by the Commission
⚠ Testbook calls the NDC an "advisory body to the Planning Commission", but UPSC 2013 marked "organ of the Planning Commission" false
## 2. Objectives and functions
Objectives | Functions
Secure cooperation of States in executing the plan | Guidelines for formulating the national plan
Mobilise national effort and resources | Consider the plan formulated by the Planning Commission
Promote common economic policies | Assess resources, suggest how to augment them
Balanced and rapid development of all regions | Review working of the plan
Sarkaria: give it constitutional status under Art 263, rename it National Economic and Development Council
⚠ PMF: NITI's Governing Council is not the NDC under a new name
## Beyond your notes
The NDC has not met since the Planning Commission was wound up (last meeting approved the 12th Plan, Dec 2012) (verify)

topic: Planning Commission and National Development Council

Provision | What it says
Concurrent List, Entry 20 | "Economic and social planning": both Union and States can legislate
Art 243G + Eleventh Schedule (29 subjects) | State Legislature may empower Panchayats to prepare plans for economic development and social justice
Art 243W + Twelfth Schedule (18 subjects) | Same for Municipalities
Art 243ZD | District Planning Committee consolidates panchayat and municipal plans
Art 243ZE | Metropolitan Planning Committee
So the Constitution plans from below but names no central planning body
⚠ Statement 1 (NDC an organ of the Planning Commission) false; answer "2 and 3 only"
