topic: Concept and Objectives of Panchayati Raj
t: Local self-government → what it best explains
text:
## 1. Meaning
Panchayati Raj = system of rural local self-government aimed at democratic decentralisation and people's participation in governance and development at the grassroots (PMF)
Decentralisation (NCERT): power taken away from Central and State governments and given to local government
Local government is "the best way to realise one important principle of democracy, namely local self-government" (NCERT Class 10)
Option UPSC gave (2017) | Fits? | Why
Democratic decentralisation | Yes | Power devolved to elected grassroots bodies
Federalism | No | Federalism = Union-State division by the Constitution
Administrative delegation | No | Delegation keeps power with the officer above; no elected body
Direct democracy | No | Only the Gram Sabha is close to direct democracy; PRIs are representative
⚠ Trap: "administrative delegation" sounds close, but local self-government transfers power to elected bodies, not to officials
PYQ 2017: local self-government is best explained as an exercise in democratic decentralisation

topic: Concept and Objectives of Panchayati Raj
t: Fundamental object of Panchayati Raj → what UPSC accepts
text:
## 1. The two fundamental objects
People's participation in development
Democratic decentralisation
Item | Fundamental object?
People's participation in development | Yes
Democratic decentralisation | Yes
Political accountability | No (an associated effect only)
Financial mobilisation | No (an associated effect only)
## 2. Why decentralisation (NCERT)
Many problems are best settled at the local level; people know local needs and where to spend money
Local level allows people to directly participate in decision making; builds a habit of democratic participation
73rd Amendment shifts India from representative to participatory democracy (Testbook)
⚠ PYQ 2015 answer was 1 and 3 only: political accountability and financial mobilisation are not the fundamental objects
PYQ 2015: picked 2 of 4 objects; trap: every option sounds positive, only participation and decentralisation are the core

topic: Concept and Objectives of Panchayati Raj
t: Article 40 and local government before 1992 → constitutional status
text:
## 1. Original Constitution
Article 40 (DPSP): State shall organise village panchayats and endow them with powers to function as units of self-government
Local government was a State subject (State List entry 5); DPSP = non-justiciable
73rd Amendment gave practical effect to Article 40 and brought PRIs into the justiciable part of the Constitution
## 2. Why it got little space in 1950 (NCERT)
Person | View
Nehru | Extreme localism a threat to unity and integration
B.R. Ambedkar | Faction- and caste-ridden village society would defeat local government
Mahatma Gandhi | "Every village will be a republic"; pyramid sustained by the bottom
K. Santhanam (Gandhian) | Pushed decentralisation in the CA; led to Article 40
Ananthasayanam Ayyangar | Villages should be trained in the art of self-government
## 3. Pre-independence base
Lord Mayo's resolution 1870, Lord Ripon's resolution 1882 (father of local self-government), Royal Commission on Decentralisation 1909
Early rural experiments: Sriniketan (Tagore, 1922), Marthandam (Tamil Nadu)
⚠ Article 40 is a DPSP, not part of Part IX; Part IX (Art 243-243O) came only in 1992
## Beyond your notes
Local government is entry 5 of the State List (Seventh Schedule)

topic: Evolution: Committees and First Panchayati Raj
t: First Panchayati Raj → where, when, by whom
text:
## 1. The 1959 launch
Rajasthan = first State to establish Panchayati Raj
Inaugurated by PM Jawaharlal Nehru on 2 October 1959 at Nagaur district
Followed the Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957)
Andhra Pradesh followed soon after (PMF)
Fact | Answer
First State | Rajasthan
Place | Nagaur
Date | 2 Oct 1959 (Gandhi Jayanti)
Inaugurated by | Nehru
Second State | Andhra Pradesh
"Architect of Panchayati Raj" | Balwant Rai Mehta
Other early adopters of elected local bodies around 1960: Gujarat, Maharashtra (NCERT)
⚠ Trap options 1998: Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka; Kerala/Karnataka are today's top devolution States, not the first
PYQ 1998: Panchayati Raj first introduced in October 1959 in Rajasthan
## Beyond your notes
Andhra Pradesh launched on 1 November 1959 (verify)

topic: Evolution: Committees and First Panchayati Raj
t: Committees on Panchayati Raj → year and key recommendation
text:
Committee | Year | Key recommendation
Balwant Rai Mehta | 1957 | Three-tier: Gram Panchayat, Panchayat Samiti, Zila Parishad; "democratic decentralisation"
Ashok Mehta | 1977 | Two-tier: Zila Parishad + Mandal Panchayat; political parties in elections
Dantwala | 1978 | Block-level planning
Hanumantha Rao | 1984 | District planning
G.V.K. Rao | 1985 | Zila Parishad pivotal; post of District Development Commissioner
L.M. Singhvi | 1986 | Constitutional recognition; Gram Sabha base; Nyaya Panchayats
P.K. Thungon | 1988 | Constitutional recognition, 3 tiers, 5-year term, State Finance Commission
V.N. Gadgil | 1988 | Constitutional status, direct elections, SFC and SEC
⚠ NCERT dates Thungon to 1989; PMF and Testbook say 1988: follow 1988
⚠ April 2025 news summary dates Hanumantha Rao to 1983; Testbook says 1984
Background: Community Development Programme (1952) and National Extension Service (1953), examined by Balwant Rai Mehta

topic: Evolution: Committees and First Panchayati Raj
t: Balwant Rai Mehta vs Ashok Mehta → three-tier vs two-tier
text:
Feature | Balwant Rai Mehta (1957) | Ashok Mehta (1977)
Tiers | Three | Two (Zila Parishad, Mandal Panchayat)
Executive body | Panchayat Samiti | Zila Parishad
Zila Parishad role | Advisory, coordinating; chaired by Collector | Executive; district = first point of decentralisation
Elections | Village panchayat direct; Samiti and ZP indirect | Political parties participate officially
Other | Genuine transfer of power and resources | Compulsory taxation powers; social audit; Nyaya Panchayats separate, under a judge
Ashok Mehta Mandal Panchayat = group of villages of 15,000-20,000 population
Ashok Mehta: elections within six months of supersession; constitutional recognition; Minister for PR in State cabinet
Janata Government fell, so no Central action; West Bengal, Karnataka, AP adopted its ideas ("second generation panchayats")
⚠ "Two-tier" = Ashok Mehta; "three-tier" = Balwant Rai Mehta and the 73rd Amendment

topic: Evolution: Committees and First Panchayati Raj
t: G.V.K. Rao, Singhvi, Thungon, Gadgil → road to constitutional status
text:
## 1. G.V.K. Rao (1985)
Reviewed administrative arrangements for rural development and poverty alleviation
Zila Parishad of pivotal importance; District Development Commissioner as CEO of ZP
Called PRIs "grass without roots" as development got bureaucratised (Testbook)
## 2. L.M. Singhvi (1986)
Concept paper on "Revitalisation of PRIs for Democracy and Development"
Constitutional recognition with a new chapter; Gram Sabha = embodiment of direct democracy
Nyaya Panchayats for a cluster of villages; judicial tribunals for election disputes
## 3. Thungon (1988) and Gadgil (1988)
Point | Thungon | Gadgil
Constitutional status | Yes | Yes
Tiers | Three | Three
Term | Five years; supersession max 6 months | Five years
Key body | State Finance Commission; ZP CEO = Collector | SFC + State Election Commission
Elections | n/a | Direct at all three levels
⚠ First to recommend constitutional recognition in this run: Singhvi (1986); Ashok Mehta (1977) had already suggested some constitutional provision (Preview)

topic: Evolution: Committees and First Panchayati Raj
t: Constitutionalisation → bills and governments
text:
Step | Year | Government | Result
64th Amendment Bill | 1989 | Rajiv Gandhi | Passed Lok Sabha, defeated in Rajya Sabha
New Bill | 1990 | V.P. Singh | Lapsed on fall of government
Modified Bill | 1991 | P.V. Narasimha Rao | Became 73rd Amendment Act, 1992
In force | 24 April 1993 | n/a | National Panchayati Raj Day
73rd (rural, Part IX) and 74th (urban, Part IXA) both came into force in 1993
States got one year to bring laws in conformity (Art 243N)
⚠ Testbook says the 64th Bill "emerged as" the 73rd Act; PMF is precise: the 1991 modified Bill became the 73rd Act

topic: 73rd Amendment: Structure, Gram Sabha and Composition
t: Three-tier system → village, intermediate, district (Art 243B)
text:
## 1. The rule
Panchayats at village, intermediate and district levels in every State (Art 243B(1))
20-lakh exception: intermediate level need not be constituted in a State with population not exceeding 20 lakh (Art 243B(2))
Tier | Common name | Other names
Village | Gram Panchayat | Sarpanch/Pradhan heads it
Intermediate | Panchayat Samiti | Block, Mandal, Taluka Panchayat
District | Zila Parishad | Zilla Panchayat
⚠ 2025 trap: "intermediate panchayats exist in all States" is wrong; small States (pop. ≤ 20 lakh) may skip them
⚠ Not "25 lakh", "30 lakh" or "35 lakh": the figure is 20 lakh
PYQ 1996: Panchayati Raj set-up is a three-tier structure at village, block and district levels (not two-tier or four-tier with State)
## Beyond your notes
States/UTs using the exemption include Goa, Sikkim and small UTs (as of 2026, verify)

topic: 73rd Amendment: Structure, Gram Sabha and Composition
t: Articles 243-243O → what each says
text:
Article | Content
243 | Definitions (243(b) Gram Sabha)
243A | Gram Sabha powers: as State Legislature decides
243B | Constitution of Panchayats: three tiers, 20-lakh exception
243C | Composition: by State Legislature; direct election; chairpersons
243D | Reservation: SC/ST, one-third women, OBC optional
243E | Duration: 5 years; election within 6 months of dissolution
243F | Disqualifications: minimum age 21
243G | Powers, Eleventh Schedule (29 subjects)
243H | Powers to impose taxes; funds
243I | State Finance Commission (by Governor, every 5 years)
243J | Audit of accounts (by State law)
243K | State Election Commission
243L | Application to UTs
243M | Exempted areas
243N | Continuance of existing laws (1 year)
243O | Bar on court interference in electoral matters
73rd Amendment added 16 articles (243-243O) + Eleventh Schedule (Preview)
⚠ 243ZD (District Planning Committee) is in Part IXA (74th), not Part IX

topic: 73rd Amendment: Structure, Gram Sabha and Composition
t: Gram Sabha vs Gram Panchayat → who is who (Art 243A, 243(b))
text:
Feature | Gram Sabha | Gram Panchayat
Who | All persons registered in the electoral rolls of the village | Elected ward members (panch) + sarpanch
Nature | Village assembly; direct democracy | Executive, representative body
Defined in | Art 243(b); powers under 243A | Art 243B, 243C
Powers | As the State Legislature decides | As State law + 243G
NCERT: Gram Sabha meets at least twice or thrice a year to approve GP budget and review performance
Gram Sabha is a compulsory provision; its powers are voluntary (State decides)
⚠ Gram Sabha is not "all persons living in the village": only those registered as voters (UPPCS 2019 trap)
⚠ Testbook calls the Gram Sabha "not mandatory": wrong; PMF lists it as compulsory
## In news 2025-26
July 2026: NITI Aayog released the NIRD&PR study "Low Participation in Gram Sabha" for MoPR: low procedural literacy, under-representation of women, youth and migrants, "participation fatigue", trust deficit

topic: 73rd Amendment: Structure, Gram Sabha and Composition
t: Composition and election → members and chairpersons (Art 243C)
text:
## 1. Who decides and how chosen
State Legislature makes provisions on composition (Art 243C(1)), not Governor, Parliament or President
Office | Mode of election
Members, all three levels | Direct election from territorial constituencies
Chairperson, village level | As the State Legislature decides
Chairperson, intermediate and district | Indirect: by and from among elected members
## 2. Optional representation (State law may provide)
Chairpersons of village panchayats in intermediate panchayats
Chairpersons of intermediate panchayats in district panchayats
MPs, MLAs (and MLCs, Rajya Sabha MPs registered in the area)
⚠ Before 1992 many States had indirect elections to district bodies (NCERT); now members at all levels are directly elected
⚠ Chairperson of a village panchayat is not constitutionally indirect: the State decides

topic: 73rd Amendment: Structure, Gram Sabha and Composition
t: Compulsory vs voluntary provisions → which is which
text:
Compulsory | Voluntary (State's choice)
Organisation of Gram Sabha | Powers and functions of Gram Sabha
Three tiers (subject to 20 lakh) | Representation of MPs, MLAs
Direct election of all members | Manner of electing village chairperson
Indirect election of intermediate/district chairpersons | Reservation for backward classes
SC/ST reservation | Devolution of powers (29 subjects)
At least one-third women | Financial powers (taxes, tolls, fees)
Five-year term; election within 6 months | Grants-in-aid, Panchayat funds
State Election Commission | Maintenance and audit of accounts
State Finance Commission every 5 years | n/a
Minimum age 21 | n/a
⚠ Testbook p.516 calls the SEC and Gram Sabha "voluntary": wrong; PMF (and Testbook p.517 table) list both as compulsory
⚠ OBC reservation is voluntary; transfer of the 29 subjects is voluntary (only 20% States transfer all 29)

t: Reservation in Panchayats → SC/ST, women, OBC (Art 243D)
text:
Group | Seats | Chairperson offices
SC/ST | In proportion to their population in the Panchayat area; all three levels | As State law provides
Women | Not less than one-third of directly elected seats (incl. SC/ST women) | Not less than one-third at each level
SC/ST women | At least one-third of SC/ST seats | n/a
Backward classes | Optional (State law) | Optional
Women's quota is horizontal: cuts across General, SC and ST (CARE)
Reserved seats are allotted by rotation among constituencies
One-third is a minimum: States may go to 50%
Seats 243D(3); chairpersons 243D(4) (Preview)
⚠ "Fifty percent seats for SC/ST women" is wrong: it is one-third of SC/ST seats
⚠ OBC reservation is not mandated by Part IX
## Beyond your notes
Bihar was the first State to give 50% women reservation in PRIs (2006) (verify)
SC (K. Krishna Murthy 2010; Vikas Kishanrao Gawali 2021): OBC quota in local bodies needs the triple test and total reservation within 50% (verify)

t: Women in Panchayats → numbers and 2025-26 news
text:
Figure | Value | Source
States with 50% women reservation | 19 States/UTs (2026) | CARE April 2026
Women share of elected PRI members | 49.7% (12.14 lakh of 24.41 lakh) | CARE April 2026
Women representation, national average | 46.44% (2024); 7 States below 50% incl. Haryana, Punjab, Tripura | PMF, PDI 2024
Elected women representatives | 14 lakh | PMF LENS Feb 2025
⚠ PMF (Feb 2025) gives 14 lakh EWRs; CARE (April 2026) gives 12.14 lakh: follow PMF, note the other
## In news 2025-26
April 2026: Centre said women increasingly win unreserved seats; came after a Constitution Amendment Bill for immediate women's reservation in legislatures was defeated
Proxy leadership ("sarpanch pati"): SC in Mundona Rural Development Foundation v. UoI (2023) directed MoPR to form an advisory committee; it recommended exemplary penalties, public oath in Gram Sabha, helplines; Haryana-type Class 8 education rule not adopted
Women's reservation in legislatures: 106th Amendment, 2023 (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam); municipalities use Art 243T

t: Duration and elections → five years, six months (Art 243E)
text:
## 1. The term
Every Panchayat continues for five years from the date appointed for its first meeting (not date of result or oath)
Can be dissolved earlier under State law
## 2. Elections
Situation | Election must be completed
Normal expiry | Before expiry of 5 years
Premature dissolution | Within six months of dissolution
Remainder of term < 6 months | No election needed for that period
A Panchayat formed after premature dissolution serves only the remainder of the original term, not a fresh 5 years
Purpose (NCERT): ensures elected local bodies always exist; earlier States postponed elections for years
⚠ 2009 options 1 month / 3 months / 1 year: answer 6 months
⚠ 2016 trap: the reconstituted Panchayat does not get a full five-year term
PYQ 2009: dissolved Panchayat → elections within six months; PYQ 2016: reconstituted Panchayat serves the remainder period

t: Disqualification and minimum age → 21, not 25 (Art 243F)
text:
## 1. Grounds
Disqualified under (a) any law for elections to the State Legislature, or (b) any law made by the State Legislature
Proviso: no one disqualified for being under 25 if he has attained 21
Disputes on disqualification decided by the authority the State Legislature prescribes
Body | Minimum age
Panchayat (all levels) | 21
Municipality (Art 243V) | 21
State Legislative Assembly | 25
Legislative Council / Rajya Sabha | 30
⚠ 2016 trap: 25 years; 2025 trap: 30 years for intermediate level. Correct answer both times: 21, same at every tier
PYQ 2025: "member of intermediate Panchayat must be 30" is wrong; age is 21

t: Exempted areas → where Part IX does not apply (Art 243M)
text:
Area | Status
Nagaland, Meghalaya, Mizoram | Part IX does not apply
Scheduled Areas (Fifth Schedule) | Not automatic; extended by PESA 1996 with modifications
Tribal Areas (Sixth Schedule) | Not applicable
Union Territories (243L) | Applies with modifications by the President
PESA, 1996: ST seats not less than one-half; all chairperson offices reserved for STs; Gram Sabha consent on land acquisition and minor minerals (details in the PESA topic)
⚠ PESA does not create autonomous tribal regions (PYQ 2013, PESA topic)
## Beyond your notes
Also exempt: hill areas of Manipur with District Councils and Darjeeling district (for the Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council)
Parliament may extend Part IX to Scheduled/Tribal Areas by law (Art 243M(4)(b))

topic: Finances, SFC, SEC and Eleventh Schedule
t: State Finance Commission → who constitutes, what it recommends (Art 243I)
text:
## 1. Constitution
Constituted by the Governor every five years to review the financial position of Panchayats
Composition, qualifications and selection: by State Legislature
## 2. Recommends to the Governor the principles governing
Item | Example
Distribution State ↔ Panchayats | Net proceeds of State taxes, duties, tolls, fees; shares among levels
Assignment | Taxes, duties, tolls, fees assigned to / appropriated by Panchayats
Grants-in-aid | From the Consolidated Fund of the State
Improvement | Measures to improve Panchayat finances
Reference | Any matter the Governor refers
Governor lays the report + action-taken memorandum before the State Legislature
Same SFC also reviews Municipalities (Art 243Y)
⚠ 2025 trap: the Chief Minister does not constitute it; 2010 traps: DPC, State Finance Ministry, State PR Ministry
PYQ 2010: the State Finance Commission recommends to the Governor the principles for taxes Panchayats may appropriate

topic: Finances, SFC, SEC and Eleventh Schedule
t: Panchayat finances → taxes, funds and the Finance Commission
text:
Provision | Content
Art 243H | State law may let Panchayats levy, collect, appropriate taxes, duties, tolls, fees; assign State revenue; grants-in-aid
Art 243I | SFC every 5 years
Art 243J | Accounts and audit by State Legislature law (not Parliament, CAG or Collector)
Art 280(3)(bb) | Union Finance Commission suggests measures to augment a State's Consolidated Fund for Panchayats, on SFC recommendations
## In news 2025-26
Own Source Revenue (OSR) only ~1% of PRI revenue in 2022-23; revenue mix: 80% central grants, 15% State grants, 1% own tax (PMF)
Untied grants fell from 85% (13th FC) to 60% (15th FC)
OSR sources: property tax, professional tax, building licence fees (tax); water charges, market fees (non-tax)
⚠ Audit of Panchayat accounts is provided by State law under 243J (BPSC 2024 trap)

topic: Finances, SFC, SEC and Eleventh Schedule
t: State Election Commission → powers and removal (Art 243K)
text:
Feature | Provision
Powers | Superintendence, direction, control of electoral rolls and all Panchayat elections
Appointed by | Governor
Removal | Only like a High Court judge (same manner and grounds)
Service conditions | Cannot be varied to his disadvantage after appointment
Link with ECI | Independent; not under the Election Commission of India
Same SEC conducts municipal elections (Art 243ZA)
Earlier, State administration ran local polls (NCERT)
⚠ Appointed by the Governor, but not removable by the Governor: removal like an HC judge
⚠ Do not confuse: CEC also removed like an SC judge; SEC like an HC judge
## Beyond your notes
Art 243O(b): Panchayat elections can be questioned only by an election petition under State law

topic: Finances, SFC, SEC and Eleventh Schedule
t: 73rd vs 74th Amendment → which body comes from where
text:
Body / feature | 73rd (Part IX, Panchayats) | 74th (Part IXA, Municipalities)
Schedule | Eleventh, 29 subjects (243G) | Twelfth, 18 subjects (243W)
SFC | 243I | 243Y (same SFC)
SEC | 243K | 243ZA
Audit | 243J | 243Z
Reservation | 243D | 243T
Duration | 243E | 243U
District Planning Committee | n/a | 243ZD
Metropolitan Planning Committee | n/a | 243ZE
DPC consolidates plans of Panchayats and Municipalities and prepares a draft district plan
⚠ 2011 answer was all three (DPC, SEC, SFC): UPSC treated DPC as part of the scheme, though Art 243ZD came with the 74th; read the question's wording
⚠ PDI 2024: DPCs exist but lack proper implementation
PYQ 2011: 73rd Amendment provides for DPCs, State Election Commissions and State Finance Commissions (1, 2 and 3)

topic: Finances, SFC, SEC and Eleventh Schedule
t: Eleventh Schedule → the 29 subjects (Art 243G)
text:
Area | Subjects
Agriculture and resources | Agriculture and extension; land improvement; minor irrigation, watershed; animal husbandry; fisheries; social/farm forestry; minor forest produce
Rural economy | Small-scale industries; khadi and village industries; rural housing; drinking water; fuel and fodder; roads, culverts; rural electrification; non-conventional energy
Development and welfare | Poverty alleviation; education (primary and secondary); technical/vocational; adult and non-formal; libraries; cultural activities; markets and fairs
Health and social | Health and sanitation (PHCs, dispensaries); family welfare; women and child development; social welfare; welfare of weaker sections (SC/ST)
Distribution and assets | Public distribution system; maintenance of community assets
Subjects came from the State List; actual transfer depends on State law
⚠ Not in the list: public order, police, judicial functions (ROCKET trap)
⚠ Twelfth Schedule (urban) has 18 subjects; Eleventh has 29
## In news 2025-26
Only 20% States have transferred all 29 subjects (PMF, Feb 2025)

topic: Finances, SFC, SEC and Eleventh Schedule
t: Articles 243L, 243N, 243O → UTs, old laws and courts
text:
Article | Rule
243L | Part IX applies to UTs, with exceptions/modifications by the President
243N | Inconsistent State Panchayat laws continue for max one year after commencement (till 24 April 1994)
243O(a) | Courts cannot question laws on delimitation or allotment of seats
243O(b) | Panchayat election challenged only by election petition before the authority State law sets
NCERT: all States passed conforming laws; most held at least two rounds of elections by 2004
⚠ 243O bars courts on delimitation/seat allotment, not on everything; election disputes still go via election petition

t: Rashtriya Gram Swaraj Abhiyan (RGSA) → period, objective, funding
text:
Feature | Fact
Type | Centrally Sponsored Scheme, Ministry of Panchayati Raj
Launched | 2018
Revamped period | 1 April 2022 - 31 March 2026 (co-terminus with 15th FC)
Key objective | Strengthen PRI governance to deliver the SDGs (LSDGs)
Coverage | All States/UTs; ~3 lakh Panchayats (incl. traditional bodies)
Funding | 60:40 general States; 90:10 NE and hilly; 100% central only for UTs
## 1. Objectives and components
Strengthen Gram Sabhas; institutional capacity; OSR (own source revenue)
Central component: incentivisation, e-Panchayat (e-Gram Swaraj, PRIASoft), ICT
State component: capacity building, HR, Gram Sabha engagement
⚠ 2026 traps: period from 2021 (wrong: 2022); 100% central for all (wrong)
PYQ 2026: only "enhance PRIs to deliver on SDGs" was correct (2 only)
## In news 2025-26
Economic Survey 2025-26: RGSA trained 35 lakh+ participants in FY25
Budget 2026-27: RGSA ₹1,142 crore (BE); 2025-26 RE ₹850 crore
Training of Trainers (2025) under RGSA to raise OSR; master trainers nominated by States

t: PM Viksit Gram Swaraj Yojana (2026) → RGSA's successor
text:
Feature | Fact
Approved | Union Cabinet, October 2026
Type | Centrally Sponsored Scheme; nodal: MoPR
Period | 2026-27 to 2030-31 (co-terminus with 16th FC)
Outlay | ₹7,395.55 crore (Centre ₹4,869.48 cr; State ₹2,526.07 cr)
Reach | ~32 lakh representatives and functionaries; 2.55 lakh Panchayats
2.55 lakh integrated GPDPs a year on eGramSwaraj; 2.55 lakh online audit plans via AuditOnline
Each awareness campaign to reach 1 crore people; capacity building for localised SDGs
No permanent jobs; contractual staff at State, district, block level
⚠ Like RGSA, it is shared Centre-State funding, not 100% central
⚠ Notes say "successor": inferred from timing (RGSA ended March 2026); verify the official link

t: Digital and participation tools → which does what
text:
Tool / initiative | What it does
e-Gram Swaraj (2020) | Single window: GP profile, planning, accounting, monitoring; 2.54 lakh GPDPs FY25
SVAMITVA | Drone mapping of rural inhabited land; property cards; property-tax base (3.28 lakh villages done by Dec 2025)
SabhaSaar | AI minutes of Gram Sabha meetings; linked to Bhashini, 13 languages; Tripura first
Model Youth Gram Sabha | Classes 9-12 hold mock Gram Sabhas; MoPR + Education + Tribal Affairs; 600 JNVs + 200 EMRS
Atmanirbhar Panchayat Program | Challenge under RGSA; GP OSR ≥ ₹50 lakh, Block ≥ ₹1 crore; Gram Sabha consent mandatory
AuditOnline | Online audit of Panchayat accounts
SabhaSaar: about 1 lakh GPs held 1.38 lakh Gram Sabhas with auto minutes (Nov 2025)
Atmanirbhar: 50 projects in Year 1, 100 a year in Years 2-4; max 10 per State (Year 1), 20 (Years 2-4)
## Beyond your notes
SVAMITVA and e-Gram Swaraj launched on 24 April 2020 (National PR Day)

t: Panchayat indices → PDI and PAI

Index | By | Measures | Key result

t: Ministry, Panchayati Raj Day and awards → dates and names

Item | Fact

t: Issues and 3Fs → what weakens Panchayats
text:
Issue | Detail
3Fs not devolved | Functions, Funds, Functionaries depend on State will
Fiscal dependence | OSR ~1%; untied grants 85% → 60%
Parallel bodies | Development agencies bypass PRIs
DBT/JAM | Reduce PRI role in beneficiary selection

Reservation rotation | Disrupts leadership continuity
Capacity | Staff shortage; only 7 States/UTs have 100% pucca Panchayat offices

t: First municipal bodies → place and year
text:
Year | Event
1688 | First Municipal Corporation of India at Madras (29 Sept 1688; now Greater Chennai Corporation)
1726 | Municipal Corporations at Bombay and Calcutta
1765 | First cantonment at Barrackpore (after Plassey, 1757)
Order to remember: Madras (1688) → Bombay and Calcutta (1726)
⚠ First corporation was Madras, not Calcutta, Bombay or Delhi
⚠ Testbook writes "1687-88" for Madras; PMF and the PYQ key give 1688
PYQ 2009: "first Municipal Corporation was set up in" Calcutta / Madras / Bombay / Delhi; answer Madras
Only the Presidency towns (Calcutta, Madras, Bombay) had local bodies that worked as real self-government; elsewhere they were like Government departments

t: British-era resolutions and Acts → what each did
text:
Year | Measure | What it did
1870 | Lord Mayo's Resolution | Financial decentralisation; transferred some resources and duties to local bodies
1882 | Lord Ripon's Resolution | Magna Carta of local self-government; Ripon = Father of Local Self-Government
1907-09 | Royal Commission on Decentralisation | Set up 1907, report 1909; urged stronger local bodies
1919 | GoI Act (Montagu-Chelmsford) | Local self-government a transferred provincial subject under dyarchy
1924 | Cantonments Act | Passed by the Central legislature
1935 | GoI Act | Local self-government a provincial subject under provincial autonomy
## Ripon's 1882 provisions
Majority non-officials; non-officials elected where possible; a non-official could be Chairman
Limits: elected members a minority in most bodies; narrow franchise; Government could suspend or supersede bodies
⚠ PMF Polity and Testbook call Mayo's 1870 resolution "financial decentralisation"; PMF Prelims Magnum says it "introduced the idea of elected representation in municipalities"
⚠ Under 1919 dyarchy local government was transferred but finance was reserved, so Indian ministers lacked funds
## Beyond your notes
The Royal Commission on Decentralisation was chaired by C.E.H. Hobhouse

t: After 1950 → path to the 74th Amendment
text:
Year | Step
1950 | Local government placed in the State List (Entry 5)
1953 | UP sets up corporations in KAVAL towns: Kanpur, Agra, Varanasi, Allahabad, Lucknow; UP Act 1959
1963-66 | Rural-Urban Relationship Committee (A.P. Jain): merge small town area committees with PRIs
Aug 1989 | 65th Amendment Bill (Nagarpalika Bill, Rajiv Gandhi): passed LS, defeated in RS (Oct 1989)
Sept 1990 | V.P. Singh's revised Bill: lapsed on dissolution of LS
Sept 1991 | P.V. Narasimha Rao's modified Municipalities Bill
1992 | 74th Constitutional Amendment Act
1 June 1993 | 74th Amendment in force
⚠ 65th Bill (1989) = Nagarpalika (urban); 64th Bill (1989) = Panchayats; both failed in the Rajya Sabha
⚠ 74th came into force on 1 June 1993; 73rd on 24 April 1993 (National Panchayati Raj Day)
Article 40 (DPSP) speaks only of village panchayats; there is no DPSP for municipalities

t: 73rd vs 74th Amendment → Part, Articles, Schedule
text:
Feature | 73rd (1992) | 74th (1992)
Domain | Rural: Panchayats | Urban: Municipalities
Part | Part IX | Part IX-A
Articles | 243 to 243-O | 243P to 243ZG
Schedule | Eleventh: 29 subjects | Twelfth: 18 subjects
In force | 24 April 1993 | 1 June 1993
Tiers | Village, intermediate, district | Nagar Panchayat, Municipal Council, Municipal Corporation
Planning body | (uses DPC) | DPC (243ZD) and MPC (243ZE)
Elections | SEC 243K | SEC 243ZA
Finance Commission | 243-I | 243Y (same SFC reviews)
PYQ 2005: statement 1 (Part IX, Panchayats, 73rd Amendment) correct; statement 2 (243Q envisages two types) wrong: three types
⚠ Panchayats are three-tier by level; municipalities are three types by area, not a hierarchy

t: Part IX-A Articles → what each says
text:
Article | Subject
243P | Definitions (Metropolitan area, Municipal area, Committee...)
243Q | Constitution of Municipalities: three types
243R | Composition: direct election from wards
243S | Wards Committees (3 lakh+ population)
243T | Reservation of seats (SC, ST, women; BCs optional)
243U | Duration: five years
243V | Disqualifications
243W | Powers and functions (Twelfth Schedule)
243X | Power to impose taxes; funds
243Y | Finance Commission (SFC under 243-I)
243Z | Audit of accounts
243ZA | Elections: State Election Commission
243ZB | Application to Union Territories

243ZE | Metropolitan Planning Committee

243ZG | Bar to interference by courts
⚠ DPC (243ZD) sits in Part IX-A (74th), even though it plans for Panchayats too

t: Art 243Q → three types of municipalities
text:
Type | Area | Common names
Nagar Panchayat | Transitional area (rural to urban) | Notified Area Council, City Council
Municipal Council | Smaller urban area | Municipality, Municipal Board / Committee
Municipal Corporation | Larger urban area | Nagar Nigam, Mahanagar Palika
## 1. Who decides and how
Governor specifies the area by public notification, considering: population, density, revenue for local administration, % non-agricultural employment, economic importance, other factors
## 2. Industrial township exception
A municipality need not be constituted where municipal services are provided by an industrial establishment; the Governor may specify it as an industrial township
⚠ Three types, not two; the Nagar Panchayat is a municipality under Part IX-A, not a Panchayat under Part IX
CA Oct 2026: AP announced reservations in 106 municipalities; ULBs = Municipal Corporations, Municipal Councils and Nagar Panchayats

t: Arts 243R-243S → composition, chairperson, wards committees
text:
## 1. Composition (243R)
All seats filled by direct election from wards
State law may add: persons with special knowledge of municipal administration (no right to vote); MPs and MLAs of the area; RS members and MLCs registered as electors there; chairpersons of committees (other than wards committees)
Chairperson: manner of election decided by State Legislature
## 2. Wards Committees (243S)
Point | Fact
Where compulsory | Municipality with population 3 lakh or more
Consists of | One or more wards
Composition and area | Fixed by State law
⚠ Nominated experts sit but cannot vote; this is the voting trap of 243R
⚠ Wards Committees need 3 lakh; a metropolitan area (MPC) needs 10 lakh
## Beyond your notes
Chairperson of a one-ward committee is the member representing that ward; for multi-ward committees, one of the members elected by the committee (Art 243S)
243S also lets the State constitute other committees in addition to Wards Committees

t: Art 243T → reservation in municipalities
text:
Category | Rule
SC / ST | Seats in proportion to population in the municipal area; may rotate
Women | Not less than one-third of directly elected seats (includes SC/ST women)
SC/ST women | Not less than one-third of SC/ST seats
Chairpersons | Reserved for SC, ST, women as State law provides
Backward classes | Optional: State Legislature may provide
SC/ST reservation (other than women's) ends with the period in Art 334 (as for legislatures)
Women's reservation is horizontal; one-third is a minimum, so States can go to 50%
⚠ BC reservation is not mandatory under 243T; only SC/ST and women are
## In news 2025-26
Aug 2026: Andhra Pradesh approved 33.33% BC reservation for ULB polls under the AP Municipal Corporations Act 1994 and AP Municipalities Act 1965; AP has 123 ULBs (100 voted in 2021)
Oct 2026: AP notified reservations in 106 municipalities (e.g. BC General 18, BC Women 18, General Women 27)

t: Arts 243U, 243V, 243ZA → term, disqualification, elections
text:
Point | Rule
Term | 5 years from the date of first meeting
Before dissolution | Municipality must get a reasonable opportunity of being heard
Change of law | Cannot dissolve a functioning municipality before its term ends
Election after dissolution | Within 6 months; not needed if remainder is under 6 months
Reconstituted body | Serves only the remainder of the term
Disqualification | Laws for State Legislature elections or a State law
Minimum age | 21 years (not 25)
Disputes on disqualification | Authority fixed by State law
Electoral rolls and polls | State Election Commission (243ZA)
⚠ Age 21 applies even though MLAs need 25; the Constitution says a 21-year-old cannot be disqualified for being under 25

t: Contesting municipal elections → who can stand
text:
Nomination requires the candidate's name in the voters' list (electoral roll) of the area
Not required: party membership, college permission, separate oath of allegiance at nomination
Voters choose councillors directly; in UP the municipal chairman is elected by voters on the electoral list (Preview PYQ UPPSC 2010)
PYQ 2000: college student contesting Municipal Council; valid nomination depends on his name being in the voters' list
⚠ Independent candidates can contest; party membership is not a condition
## Beyond your notes
State Municipal Acts make being a registered elector of the municipality a qualification for a councillor; the SEC conducts polls on that roll
Gram Sabha (Part IX) = persons registered in the electoral roll of a village; there is no "Nagar Sabha" in Part IX-A (some States created Area Sabhas by law)

t: 74th Amendment → compulsory vs voluntary provisions
text:
Compulsory (must) | Voluntary (State may)
Three types of municipalities | Representation of MPs, MLAs, experts
Direct elections to all seats | Manner of electing the Chairperson
Wards Committees (3 lakh+) | Other committees
SC/ST and one-third women reservation | BC reservation
5-year term, poll within 6 months | Devolution of Twelfth Schedule powers
SEC and SFC | Taxes, assigned revenues, grants (243X)
Minimum age 21 | Audit provisions (243Z)
DPC and MPC | Composition of DPC/MPC (within limits)
The Act constitutionalises municipalities but leaves powers and functions to State law ("permissive devolution")
⚠ Twelfth Schedule functions are not automatically transferred; Art 243W says the State Legislature may endow them

topic: Powers, finances and the Twelfth Schedule
t: Twelfth Schedule → the 18 functions
text:
Group | Functions
Planning | 1 Urban planning incl. town planning; 2 Regulation of land use and buildings; 3 Planning for economic and social development
Infrastructure | 4 Roads and bridges; 5 Water supply (domestic, industrial, commercial)
Health and services | 6 Public health, sanitation, conservancy, solid waste management; 7 Fire services
Environment and welfare | 8 Urban forestry, environment, ecology; 9 Weaker sections incl. disabled; 10 Slum improvement; 11 Urban poverty alleviation
Amenities | 12 Parks, gardens, playgrounds; 13 Cultural, educational, aesthetic aspects; 14 Burials, cremation grounds, electric crematoriums
Civic administration | 15 Cattle pounds, prevention of cruelty to animals; 16 Vital statistics (births and deaths); 17 Street lighting, parking, bus stops, public conveniences; 18 Slaughterhouses and tanneries
⚠ Not in the Twelfth Schedule: police, primary education, electricity distribution, public transport; fire services is in it
⚠ 18 urban subjects (Twelfth) vs 29 rural subjects (Eleventh)

topic: Powers, finances and the Twelfth Schedule
t: Arts 243W-243Z → powers and money
text:
Article | State Legislature may
243W | Endow powers to work as institutions of self-government; plans and schemes for economic development and social justice, incl. Twelfth Schedule matters
243X | Authorise taxes, duties, tolls, fees; assign State taxes; grants-in-aid from State Consolidated Fund; constitute municipal funds
243Y | SFC (constituted under 243-I by the Governor every 5 years) also reviews municipal finances
243Z | Provide for maintenance and audit of accounts
## Finance Commission links
Art 280(3)(c): Union Finance Commission recommends measures to augment a State's Consolidated Fund to supplement municipal resources (on the basis of SFC recommendations)
Governor lays SFC report with an action-taken memorandum before the State Legislature
⚠ One SFC serves both Panchayats (243-I) and municipalities (243Y); there is no separate municipal finance commission
## In news 2025-26
16th Finance Commission (Chair Arvind Panagariya, 2026-31): local body grants released only if States hold local body elections and constitute the SFC (e.g. AP Panchayats got Rs 16,627 crore)
PMF LENS (Aug 2026): urges "three-tier fiscal federalism" through regularly constituted SFCs

topic: Powers, finances and the Twelfth Schedule
t: Arts 243ZB-243ZG → where Part IX-A applies and court bar
text:
Article | Rule
243ZB | Applies to UTs with exceptions and modifications by the President
243ZC | Not applicable to Scheduled Areas and tribal areas (Art 244); Parliament may extend it; does not affect the Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council
243ZF | Inconsistent State municipal laws could continue for one year only
243ZG | Delimitation and seat allotment laws cannot be questioned in court; election disputes only by election petition
Similar court bar exists for Parliament and Legislatures in Art 329
⚠ Part IX-A extends to UTs by President's order, but to Scheduled Areas only by Parliament's law
## Beyond your notes
Part IX (Panchayats) excludes Nagaland, Meghalaya, Mizoram and hill areas of Manipur under Art 243M; PESA (1996) extended Part IX to Fifth Schedule areas; no equivalent municipal extension law has been passed (verify)

t: Constitutional bodies created by 73rd and 74th → which Article
text:
Body | Article | Amendment
State Election Commission (Panchayats) | 243K | 73rd
State Finance Commission | 243-I | 73rd
SEC for municipalities | 243ZA | 74th
SFC for municipalities | 243Y | 74th
District Planning Committee | 243ZD | 74th

Not created: State Property Tax Valuation Board (Preview PYQ UP 2010)
IAS 2011 PYQ (Preview): the 73rd Amendment provides for SEC elections and SFCs, but not DPCs, which come from the 74th
## Beyond your notes
SEC is appointed by the Governor and removed only like a High Court judge (Art 243K)

t: Metropolitan Planning Committee → status, composition, job
text:
Point | Fact
Basis | Constitutional: Art 243ZE, 74th Amendment
Where | Every metropolitan area
Metropolitan area | 10 lakh+ population; one or more districts; two or more municipalities/panchayats; specified by Governor
Elected share | Not less than two-thirds elected by elected municipal members and Panchayat chairpersons of the area
Proportion | Ratio of municipal and panchayat populations
Job | Prepare a draft development plan for the whole metropolitan area
Plan goes to | State Government via its Chairperson
Considers: municipal and panchayat plans; common interests (spatial planning, water and resources, integrated infrastructure, environment); Centre and State objectives; investments by agencies
⚠ MPC prepares a draft plan; it does not have sole responsibility for implementing government schemes
PYQ 2011: MPC is constitutional (correct) and prepares draft plans (correct); "sole responsibility for implementing schemes" is wrong; answer 1 and 2 only

t: District Planning Committee → composition and job
text:
Point | Fact
Article | 243ZD
Where | Every district (compulsory)
Job | Consolidate Panchayat and municipal plans; prepare draft development plan for the district
Elected share | Not less than four-fifths elected by elected members of district panchayat and municipalities
Proportion | Rural-urban population ratio of the district
Plan goes to | State Government via Chairperson
State law decides | Composition, election of members, functions, Chairperson
Considers spatial planning, sharing of water and natural resources, integrated infrastructure, environmental conservation
Preview PYQ (RAS 2024): in Rajasthan the DPC chairperson is the Zila Pramukh (Zila Parishad head) under the Rajasthan PR Act 1994
⚠ DPC Chairperson is not fixed by the Constitution; it varies by State (Zila Pramukh, minister, or Collector)

t: DPC vs MPC → the comparison traps
text:
Basis | DPC | MPC
Article | 243ZD | 243ZE
Area | District | Metropolitan area (10 lakh+)
Purpose | Consolidate plans | Draft plan for the metro area
Elected component | ≥ 4/5 | ≥ 2/3
Who elects | Elected members of district panchayat + municipalities | Elected municipal members + panchayat chairpersons
Representation | Rural : urban population | Municipal : panchayat population
Plan to | State Government | State Government
Both are constitutional, both advisory/planning bodies; neither implements schemes
⚠ Fractions: DPC four-fifths, MPC two-thirds; do not swap
## In news 2025-26
Nov 2026: PMF LENS on a National Urbanisation Policy: expand regional planning through DPCs and MPCs; 52% of statutory towns and 76% of census towns lack a master plan; nine States keep planning laws older than the 74th Amendment
LENS (May 2026): DPCs should align public capital spending with local needs ("allocative efficiency")
## Beyond your notes
Most States have not constituted functional MPCs; Kolkata (KMPC) is the oft-cited working example (verify)

topic: Types of urban bodies and municipal administration
t: Eight types of urban local bodies → what each is
text:
Body | Set up for | Key feature
Municipal Corporation | Big cities | State Act (UTs: Act of Parliament)
Municipality | Towns and smaller cities | Also called municipal council / board / committee
Notified Area Committee | Fast-developing or not-yet-qualified town | Created by gazette notification; wholly nominated; neither elected nor statutory
Town Area Committee | Small town | Semi-municipal; limited functions (drainage, roads, lighting); separate State Act
Cantonment Board | Cantonment area | Under Union / MoD; elected + nominated
Township | Staff colonies of large public enterprises | Town Administrator appointed by the enterprise; no elected body
Port Trust / Port Authority | Port areas | Port administration plus civic tasks
Special Purpose Agency | One function (housing, water, transport) | Single-purpose, e.g. development authorities
⚠ A Notified Area Committee is entirely nominated (including chairman); a Township has no elected members at all
⚠ Preview notes Port Trusts are now Major Port Authorities

topic: Types of urban bodies and municipal administration
t: Cantonment Boards → law, ministry, classes
text:
Point | Fact
Constitutional entry | Union List, Entry 3
Law | Cantonments Act, 2006 (earlier 1924)
Ministry | Ministry of Defence
Nature | Statutory local authority
Classes | Four (Class I to IV) by area and population
Members | Elected civilians + nominated/ex-officio military members
First cantonment Barrackpore (1765); set up by the East India Company after Plassey
⚠ Cantonment Boards are the only urban bodies under the Union (MoD), not the State
## In news 2025-26
Oct 2025: Centre drafting a roadmap to modernise cantonments: renewable energy for net-zero, e-Chhawani 2.0 for online civic services, lighter penalties under the Jan Vishwas Act
## Beyond your notes
India has about 62 notified cantonments (as of 2026, verify); the President of a Cantonment Board is the Station Commander

topic: Types of urban bodies and municipal administration
t: Municipal corporation → council, standing committees, commissioner
text:
Authority | Role
Council | Deliberative and legislative wing; elected councillors + nominated experts; headed by Mayor
Standing committees | Public works, education, health, taxation, finance
Municipal Commissioner | Chief executive; appointed by State Government, usually IAS
## Mayor
Ceremonial head and first citizen of the city; presides over council meetings; assisted by a Deputy Mayor
Term often one year, renewable (Testbook); election method fixed by State law
## Municipality (council)
Headed by a President/Chairman who, unlike the Mayor, is the pivot of administration with executive powers; a Chief Executive Officer (State-appointed) runs daily work
⚠ Executive power of a corporation is with the Commissioner, not the Mayor; in a municipal council the Chairman has real executive role
## In news 2025-26
SC upheld the Delhi L-G's power to nominate aldermen to the MCD without aid and advice of the Delhi Council of Ministers, because the DMC Act gives it explicitly (P-MCA 2025)
A private member's Bill sought direct election of Mayors

topic: Types of urban bodies and municipal administration
t: Urban area → statutory vs census definition, ministries
text:
## 1. Two definitions
Type | Test
Statutory town | Declared by law: municipality, corporation, cantonment, notified area
Census town | 5,000+ population; density 400+/sq km; 75%+ of (male) workers in non-farm work: all three together
⚠ Testbook says "75% of the working population"; the Census criterion uses the male main working population
## 2. Union ministries for urban local government
Ministry | Handles
Urban Development (separate since 1985; now MoHUA) | Municipalities in general
Defence | Cantonment boards
Home Affairs | Urban bodies of Union Territories
Local government is a State List subject (Entry 5); Union ministries only guide and fund
## Beyond your notes
MoHUA was formed in 2017 by merging Urban Development and Housing and Urban Poverty Alleviation

topic: Urban governance in practice: finance, missions, 2025-26
t: Urban local bodies → problems and fixes
text:
Problem | Detail
Incomplete 3Fs | Funds, Functions, Functionaries not fully devolved
Fiscal starvation | Own-Source Revenue only about 0.3% of GDP; old property-tax registers
Parastatals | Development authorities, Jal Boards, SPVs bypass elected ULBs
Credit exclusion | Weak accounts, no accrual accounting: few investment-grade ratings for municipal bonds
Capacity | Few trained staff, poor data and planning
## Fixes in use
15th Finance Commission: performance-linked grants; ULBs must publish audited accounts and notify property-tax floor rates
AMRUT 2.0: rewards property-tax reform and municipal bond issues; NUDM (National Urban Digital Mission) for shared digital infrastructure
⚠ Urban water and sanitation are Twelfth Schedule (ULB) functions, but States often hand them to parastatal Jal Boards

Mission | Launch | Key facts
AMRUT | June 2015 | 500 cities; ~60% of urban people; ULBs execute; ran to March 2021
AMRUT 2.0 | 2021 (to 2026) | ~4,900 statutory towns, ~10.5 crore people; City Water Balance Plans; universal water and sewerage

⚠ PMF Magnum gives AMRUT 2.0 cover as ~4,900 statutory towns; PMF LENS (June 2026) says 4,378 statutory towns for universal tap coverage

t: Urban Challenge Fund → funding and design (2026)
text:
Point | Fact
Size | Rs 1 lakh crore; expected to draw about Rs 4 lakh crore investment
Funding | Centre 25%, States 25%, 50% from market
Selection | Challenge mode; release tied to reforms and outcomes
Verticals | Cities as Growth Hubs, Creative Redevelopment of Cities, Water and Sanitation

Ministry | MoHUA (est. 1952 as a ministry; Minister Manohar Lal)
Marks a shift from grants to market-linked, results-based urban finance

t: Article 244 → which Schedule applies where
text:
## 1. The three clauses
Provision | Deals with | Applies to
Art 244(1) + Fifth Schedule | Administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes | Every State other than Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram
Art 244(2) + Sixth Schedule | Administration of Tribal Areas | Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram only
Art 244A | Parliament may create an autonomous State within Assam (own Legislature and/or Council of Ministers) | Assam only
Art 244 sits in Part X (Scheduled and Tribal Areas)
Sixth Schedule rests on Art 244(2) and Art 275(1) (grants for ST welfare and Scheduled Area administration)
⚠ Memory hook AMTM (Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram): never Manipur, Nagaland, Arunachal, Sikkim
PYQ 2008: which Schedule has special provisions for administration and control of Scheduled Areas in several States: Fifth (traps: Third, Seventh, Ninth)

t: Fifth vs Sixth Schedule → purpose and key differences
text:
## 1. Both protect Scheduled Tribes
Purpose of both Schedules: protect the interests of Scheduled Tribes (not State boundaries, not Panchayat powers, not border States)
Basis | Fifth Schedule | Sixth Schedule
Article | 244(1) | 244(2) and 275(1)
Unit | Scheduled Areas (declared by President) | Autonomous Districts/Regions (organised by Governor)
Main institution | Tribes Advisory Council (advisory only) | District and Regional Councils (elected)
Nature | Protective administration via Governor | Greater tribal self-government
Law-making | Governor's regulations | Councils legislate on listed subjects
Judicial power | None comparable | Village councils/courts
Finance | Through State framework | Councils levy taxes, collect land revenue
⚠ Fifth Schedule = Governor + TAC; Sixth = elected Councils. "Creates a local self-governing body" is a Sixth Schedule effect, not Fifth
PYQ 2015: Fifth and Sixth Schedules are made to protect the interests of STs; trap options: State boundaries, Panchayat powers (that is the Eleventh Schedule)

t: Tribal provisions → where each sits in the Constitution
text:
## 1. Schedules and Parts
Item | Location
Fifth Schedule | Art 244 (PMF infographic); administration of Scheduled Areas and STs
Sixth Schedule | Art 244 and 275
Eleventh Schedule (29 subjects) | Art 243G, Panchayats (73rd Amendment 1992)
Part IX not applied to Scheduled/Tribal Areas | Art 243M
Part IXA not applied to them | Art 243ZC
Art 243M(4)(b): Parliament may extend Part IX to Fifth Schedule areas with exceptions; such law is not an amendment under Art 368 → this is the basis of PESA 1996
Part IX does not apply to Nagaland, Meghalaya, Mizoram (own customary bodies)
⚠ Sixth Schedule's origin: Gopinath Bordoloi sub-committee on North-East tribal areas of the Constituent Assembly
## Beyond your notes

Notified Order of the President, after consultation with the State Government

Union executive power extends to giving directions to the State on their administration
Claim | True/false

Point | Fact

73rd Amendment (1992) left Fifth Schedule Areas outside Part IX (Art 243M); Parliament extended Part IX to them under Art 243M(4)(b)
Based on the Bhuria Committee (set up 1994, recommendations 1995)
Objective | In PESA?
Tribal self-governance / self-rule | Yes
Recognise traditional/customary rights and practices | Yes
Free tribals from exploitation | Yes
Gram Sabha as nucleus of activities | Yes
Create autonomous regions in tribal areas | No (that is the Sixth Schedule)

Right | Nature | Basis
Right to vote | Constitutional right (UPSC 2017 key) | Art 326 adult suffrage + RPA 1950/1951
Right to vote (court view) | Statutory right | Kuldip Nayar v. UoI (2006): right under RPA 1951
Right to contest | Statutory | RPA 1951 (no FR, no constitutional right)

Right to vote is not a Fundamental Right; it is not in Part III

topic: Right to Vote and Constitutional Framework (Art 324-329)
t: Right to vote → age, 61st Amendment, who cannot vote
text:
## 1. Adult suffrage
Art 326: elections to Lok Sabha and State Assemblies on adult suffrage
Voting age 21 → 18 by the 61st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1988 (in force 28 March 1989)
Only citizens aged 18+ on the qualifying date can be enrolled (Sec 16 RPA 1950 bars non-citizens)
## 2. Qualifying dates and restrictions
Point | Rule
Qualifying dates | 1 January, 1 April, 1 July, 1 October (four dates)
Prisoners / police custody | Cannot vote (Sec 62(5) RPA 1951)
Preventive detention | Can vote (the exception)
Prisoner contesting | Not barred merely by the voting bar
Overseas Indian (not foreign citizen) | Can register at passport address
Aadhaar | Voluntary; refusal cannot by itself deny enrolment
⚠ A person in jail cannot vote but can contest unless disqualified on conviction
⚠ 61st Amendment was 1988, effective 1989; NCERT writes "1989 amendment"

topic: Right to Vote and Constitutional Framework (Art 324-329)
t: Articles 324-329 (Part XV) → what each says
text:
## 1. The six Articles of Part XV
Article | Content
324 | Superintendence, direction and control of elections vested in ECI (rolls + conduct of elections to Parliament, State Legislatures, President and VP)
325 | One general electoral roll per territorial constituency; no exclusion on religion, race, caste, sex alone
326 | Adult suffrage for Lok Sabha and Assemblies (18 years)
327 | Parliament may make laws on elections to legislatures
328 | State Legislature may make election laws (subject to Parliament's law)
329 | Bar on courts interfering in electoral matters; delimitation laws not questionable; election challenged only by election petition
Art 324 does not cover Panchayat/Municipal polls → State Election Commissions (Art 243K, 243ZA)
⚠ Art 325 lists 4 grounds (religion, race, caste, sex); "place of birth" and "descent" are not in it
⚠ Art 329(b): no judicial interference during an election; petition only after results

topic: Right to Vote and Constitutional Framework (Art 324-329)
t: Election laws → RPA 1950 vs RPA 1951 and rules
text:
## 1. Which law does what
Law | Main content
RPA 1950 | Allocation of seats, delimitation, electoral rolls, voter registration (Sec 16, 21(3), 22, 24)
RPA 1951 | Conduct of elections, qualifications and disqualifications, party registration (Sec 29A), corrupt practices, election disputes
Registration of Electors Rules, 1960 | Detailed electoral roll rules; Form 6 (enrolment), Form 7 (deletion)
Conduct of Elections Rules, 1961 | Polling, counting, postal ballot (Rule 27A, 54A)
Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968 | Party recognition and symbols
RPA 1950 linked Articles: 81, 82, 170, 171, 325, 326; RPA 1951: 84, 102, 173, 191, 324, 329
⚠ Electoral rolls come under RPA 1950, not 1951; disqualification under RPA 1951
