Provision | Content
Sec 21(3) RPA 1950 | ECI may order special revision of rolls in any manner it thinks fit
Sec 22 | ERO deletes names after inquiry (death, shifted, duplicate)
Sec 16 | Non-citizens cannot be registered
Lal Babu Hussain (1995) | Burden of proving citizenship on fresh applicants, not existing voters
## In news 2025-26
Nationwide SIR (Special Intensive Revision) of rolls under Sec 21(3) RPA 1950: first nationwide revision in 20 years (Bihar first, 2025)
ADR v. ECI (2026): SC upheld SIR; ECI may examine citizenship (Sec 16 RPA 1950) but existing voters enjoy presumption of citizenship; doubtful cases referred to Centre under Citizenship Act 1955
ECI told SC: Aadhaar and ration card are not proof of citizenship (2025); SC later allowed Aadhaar as an identity document
Voting as FR debate (2026): two ECs objected to CEC's roll changes; 97 Goa voters excluded via ECINet software

topic: Election Commission of India: Composition, Appointment, Removal and Functions
t: ECI → composition and multi-member history
text:
## 1. Composition (Art 324(2))
CEC + such number of ECs as the President fixes; at present three-member (1 CEC + 2 ECs)
Permanent, all-India, constitutional, quasi-judicial body, set up 1950 (25 January 1950)
Date | Strength
1950 - 15 Oct 1989 | Single member (CEC only)
16 Oct 1989 - 1 Jan 1990 | First 2 ECs added; posts abolished soon after
1 Oct 1993 onward | Multi-member again (CEC + 2 ECs)
T.N. Seshan v. UoI (1995): CEC has no superiority over ECs; decisions by majority
CEC chairs but has no overriding/casting vote; work done unanimously as far as possible, else majority (Sec 18, 2023 Act)
⚠ ECI is three-member, not five; number is fixed by the President, not by the Constitution
⚠ Constitution allows a single-member ECI: appointing more ECs is not mandatory (NCERT exercise)
PYQ 2017: "ECI is a five-member body" → false; also "MHA decides election schedule" → false (ECI does)

topic: Election Commission of India: Composition, Appointment, Removal and Functions
t: CEC and ECs → appointment (2023 Act, Anoop Baranwal)
text:
## 1. Before and after 2023
Stage | Appointing method
Till 2023 | President on advice of PM / Council of Ministers
Anoop Baranwal v. UoI (March 2023) | Interim panel: PM + LoP (Lok Sabha) + CJI until Parliament legislates
CEC and Other ECs Act, 2023 | Search Committee → Selection Committee → President
## 2. Committees under the 2023 Act
Committee | Members | Task
Search | Law Minister (head) + 2 Secretary-rank officers | Panel of 5 names
Selection (Sec 7) | PM (chair) + LoP in Lok Sabha (or leader of largest opposition party) + Union Cabinet Minister nominated by PM | Recommends to President
Selection Committee may pick a name outside the panel; a vacancy does not invalidate its recommendation
Eligibility: holds/held post equal to Secretary to GoI + election management experience
Sec 16: courts barred from civil/criminal proceedings against serving/former CEC/ECs for official acts
⚠ CJI is not a member of the statutory committee (he was only in the Baranwal interim panel)
⚠ Constitution itself prescribes no qualifications for ECs; the 2023 Act does

topic: Election Commission of India: Composition, Appointment, Removal and Functions
t: CEC appointment → 2025-26 challenges to the 2023 Act
text:
## 1. Points of contention
Issue | Criticism
Selection panel | 2 of 3 members from the executive
Search Committee | Headed by Law Minister with Secretaries
Elevation EC → CEC | No seniority rule
EC removal | ECs lack CEC's judge-like protection
Reform asks: CJI in place of Cabinet Minister (Law Commission 255th), post-retirement bar (Dinesh Goswami 1990)
## In news 2025-26
SC split verdict (Sept 2026) on Centre's plea to refer challenges to the 2023 Act to a Constitution Bench
Critics: 2:1 executive majority; LoP got a 6-name shortlist 10 minutes before the March 2024 meeting

topic: Election Commission of India: Composition, Appointment, Removal and Functions
t: CEC and ECs → term, salary and removal
text:
## 1. Service conditions
Feature | CEC | Other ECs
Term | 6 years or 65 years, whichever earlier | Same
Salary, status | Equal to SC judge | Equal to CEC (same as SC judge)
Powers | Equal (first among equals) | Equal
Reappointment | Not eligible | Not eligible; EC-then-CEC total tenure max 6 years
Removal | Like an SC judge: special majority in both Houses, proved misbehaviour or incapacity | By President on recommendation of CEC; Constitution gives no grounds
Service conditions | Cannot be varied to disadvantage after appointment | No such express protection
Resignation | To the President | To the President
CEC does not hold office at the pleasure of the President
Constitution does not bar later government jobs for retired CEC/ECs
⚠ Term is 6 years / 65 years, not 5 years / 62 years (UPSC 2002 trap)
⚠ Salaries are equal, not unequal; CEC removal protection is not extended to ECs
PYQ 2002: correct = CEC salary of SC judge + CEC removed like SC judge; wrong = unequal salaries, 5 yrs/62 yrs

topic: Election Commission of India: Composition, Appointment, Removal and Functions
t: CEC removal → process (2026 news angle)
text:
## 1. Steps (Art 324(5), Sec 11(2) of 2023 Act)
Step | Rule
Notice | Signed by 100 Lok Sabha or 50 Rajya Sabha members
Admission | Speaker/Chairman may admit or refuse
Inquiry | 3-member committee: CJI or SC judge + HC Chief Justice + distinguished jurist
Voting | Each House: majority of total membership + two-thirds present and voting
Session | Both Houses in the same session; then President orders removal
Motion does not lapse on prorogation or Lok Sabha dissolution during inquiry
No CEC has ever been removed
N. Gopalaswamy (CEC) recommended removal of EC Navin Chawla; Government refused, showing CEC's recommendation is not self-executing
## In news 2025-26
March 2026: opposition moved to initiate removal motion against CEC Gyanesh Kumar: first against a CEC appointed under the 2023 Act
Sept 2026: two ECs filed 14 objections in 10 months against roll decisions taken without collegial consensus

topic: Election Commission of India: Composition, Appointment, Removal and Functions
t: ECI functions → administrative, advisory, quasi-judicial
text:
## 1. Administrative
Delimitation work under Delimitation Acts (with the Delimitation Commission)
Prepare and revise electoral rolls, register voters
Notify election schedule for general and bye-elections; scrutiny of nominations by Returning Officers
Register parties, grant national/State party recognition, allot symbols (Symbols Order 1968)
Model Code of Conduct; observers; cancel polls / order re-poll for booth capturing, violence
Request staff: Art 324(6) President/Governor must provide
## 2. Advisory and quasi-judicial
Type | Function
Advisory | Opinion to President (Art 103) on MP disqualification; to Governor (Art 192) on MLA disqualification
Advisory | Whether elections can be held to extend President's Rule beyond 1 year
Advisory | Opinion on persons found guilty of corrupt practices
Quasi-judicial | Disputes on recognition, splits/mergers of recognised parties and symbols
Quasi-judicial | Disqualify a candidate for 3 years for not lodging election expenses; remove/reduce disqualification period
PYQ 2004: functions = superintendence, rolls, party recognition and symbols; NOT "final verdict in election disputes"

topic: Election Commission of India: Composition, Appointment, Removal and Functions
t: ECI → what it does NOT do (traps)
text:
## 1. Not ECI's job
Task | Who does it
Final verdict on election disputes | High Court (election petition); appeal to SC
Disputes on President/VP election | Supreme Court only
Panchayat and Municipal elections | State Election Commission
Decide Tenth Schedule disqualification | Speaker/Chairman
Decide Art 102 disqualification | President (on ECI's binding opinion)
Nominate candidates | Political parties
Deregister a party generally | Not ECI (INC v. Institute of Social Welfare, 2002); only for fraud, loss of allegiance, unlawful
Change election rules/forms | Union Government (Sec 28 RPA 1950)
Once results are declared, ECI cannot review any result on its own
ECI decisions are subject to judicial review by HC and SC
⚠ ECI rules on a party split/symbol dispute, but that does not settle a defection case
PYQ 2017: ECI (not MHA) fixes election schedule; ECI resolves split/merger disputes of recognised parties → only statement 3 correct

topic: Election Commission of India: Composition, Appointment, Removal and Functions
t: Political parties → registration and recognition criteria
text:
## 1. Registration
Registered under Sec 29A RPA 1951; 97% of registered parties are RUPPs (unrecognised)
RUPP privileges: contest as registered party, common symbol (conditions), 100% tax exemption (Sec 13A IT Act)
## 2. Recognition (Symbols Order 1968): any one condition
State party | National party
6% votes in Assembly poll + 2 Assembly seats | 6% votes in LS/Assembly polls in 4+ States + 4 LS seats
6% votes in LS poll + 1 LS seat from State | 2% of LS seats (11 of 543) from 3+ States
3% of Assembly seats or 3 seats, whichever greater | Recognised as State party in 4+ States
1 LS seat per 25 allotted to State | 
8% votes in State (LS or Assembly), even with no seat | 
⚠ The word "political party" entered the Constitution through the Tenth Schedule (52nd Amdt, 1985)
## In news 2025-26
ADR (2026): 223% surge in declared income of RUPPs; ~2,800 RUPPs flagged as letterhead fronts

topic: Election Commission of India: Composition, Appointment, Removal and Functions
t: ECI vs SEC vs Chief Electoral Officer
text:
## 1. Comparison
Feature | ECI | State Election Commission | Chief Electoral Officer
Basis | Art 324 | Art 243K / 243ZA | Statutory (Sec 13A RPA 1950)
Elections | Parliament, State Legislatures, President, VP | Panchayats, Municipalities | Supervises ECI's work in a State/UT
Head removal | Like SC judge | Like HC judge | Under ECI control
Appointed by | President | Governor | ECI in consultation with State Govt
District: District Election Officer (Collector); constituency: Returning Officer; booth: Presiding Officer; rolls: ERO
⚠ CEO is not the State Election Commissioner; SECs work independently of ECI
## Beyond your notes
25 January (ECI founding day) is observed as National Voters' Day (since 2011); first CEC: Sukumar Sen

topic: Candidates: Qualification, Nomination, Disqualification and Disputes
t: Contesting → qualifications (Constitution + RPA)
text:
## 1. Qualifications for Parliament (Art 84)
Requirement | Lok Sabha | Rajya Sabha
Citizenship | Citizen of India | Citizen
Oath | Before person authorised by ECI (Art 84(a)) | Same
Minimum age | 25 years | 30 years
RPA 1951 | Elector in any parliamentary constituency (Sec 4(d)) | Elector in any constituency in India (since 2003)
Reserved seat | Must be SC/ST (can also contest general seats) | –
Lok Sabha candidate need not be a resident of the constituency
2003 Amendment: Rajya Sabha domicile (elector in that State) requirement removed; upheld in Kuldip Nayar (2006)
⚠ Nomination can be filed by any citizen whose name is in the electoral roll of any constituency; not "anyone residing in India", not "any citizen"
PYQ 2017: nomination for Lok Sabha → option (c) "any citizen of India whose name appears in the electoral roll of a constituency"
## Beyond your notes
State Legislature (Art 173): 25 years for Assembly, 30 years for Council; Assembly candidate must be an elector in that State

topic: Candidates: Qualification, Nomination, Disqualification and Disputes
t: Nomination → proposers, two seats, by-elections
text:
## 1. Rules
Point | Rule
Proposers (recognised party candidate) | 1 proposer
Proposers (independent / RUPP) | 10 proposers from the constituency
Max constituencies | Two (Sec 33(7), since 1996; after Devi Lal contested 3 in 1991)
Elected from two | Must vacate one
Death of candidate | Poll no longer countermanded automatically (1996); recognised party may nominate replacement
Campaign silence | 48 hours before close of poll (Sec 126)
Casual vacancy | By-election within 6 months unless remainder <1 year or ECI+Centre certify difficulty
## Beyond your notes
Security deposit: Rs 25,000 Lok Sabha, Rs 10,000 Assembly (half for SC/ST) (as of 2026); forfeited below 1/6 of valid votes

topic: Candidates: Qualification, Nomination, Disqualification and Disputes
t: Disqualification → Art 102 vs RPA vs Tenth Schedule: who decides
text:
## 1. Constitutional grounds (Art 102 / 191)
Office of profit (unless exempted by law), unsound mind (declared by court), undischarged insolvent, not a citizen / foreign allegiance, disqualified by law of Parliament
## 2. Deciding authority
Disqualification | Decided by | Consultation
General, MP (Art 102(1)) | President (Art 103) | ECI opinion, binding
General, MLA (Art 191(1)) | Governor (Art 192) | ECI opinion, binding
Defection (Art 102(2), 191(2)) | Speaker / Chairman | No ECI role; judicial review
RPA grounds: corrupt practices, conviction, not lodging expenses (3 yrs), interest in govt contracts, office in corporation with 25%+ govt share, dismissal for corruption/disloyalty
Preventive detention is not a disqualification
⚠ President acts on ECI's opinion (Art 103), not on Council of Ministers' advice
⚠ Absence 60 days without permission → House may declare seat vacant (vacation, not disqualification)

topic: Candidates: Qualification, Nomination, Disqualification and Disputes
t: RPA Sec 8 → disqualification on conviction
text:
## 1. Section 8 ladder
Sub-section | Rule
8(1) | Specified offences (e.g. enmity between groups, bribery, untouchability, sati, dowry etc.): disqualified regardless of sentence, + 6 years after release
8(3) | Any offence with sentence 2 years or more: disqualified from date of conviction + 6 years after release
8(4) | 3-month appeal protection for sitting legislators: struck down in Lily Thomas (2013)
Sec 11 | ECI may remove or reduce the disqualification period
Disqualification is not permanent/lifetime: it lasts sentence period + 6 years
Related: ADR v. UoI (2002) and PUCL (2004) made disclosure of criminal cases, assets, education mandatory (affidavits)
Public Interest Foundation (2018): parties must publicise candidates' criminal records
⚠ Five-year sentence ≠ permanent ban (UPSC 2020): after release, bar lasts 6 more years
## In news 2025-26
SC hearing PIL for lifetime ban on convicted MPs/MLAs (2025); Law Commission 255th Report (2015) had proposed disqualification on framing of charges (offence punishable with 5+ years, charges framed 1 year before scrutiny)

topic: Candidates: Qualification, Nomination, Disqualification and Disputes
t: Non-member minister → six-month rule (2020 angle)
text:
## 1. Art 75(5) and Art 164(4)
Level | Rule
Union minister | Non-member must become MP within 6 months (Art 75(5))
State minister | Non-member must become MLA/MLC within 6 months (Art 164(4)) or cease
Test | Must be qualified to be elected (25 years for Assembly), not merely eligible to vote (18)
Disqualified defector | Cannot be minister till term ends or re-election (Art 75(1B), 164(1B), 91st Amdt)
91st Amdt caps State ministry at 15% of Assembly, minimum 12
⚠ Constitution has no "eligible to vote" test for ministers (UPSC 2020 statement 1 false)
PYQ 2020: both statements false: "eligible to vote → minister for 6 months" and "5-year sentence → permanently disqualified"

topic: Candidates: Qualification, Nomination, Disqualification and Disputes
t: Election disputes → election petition
text:
## 1. Where disputes go
Election | Forum | Time limit
Parliament / State Legislature | High Court (election petition) | 45 days from result
Appeal | Supreme Court | As per law
President / Vice-President | Supreme Court only | –
Local bodies | As per State law | –
Art 329(b): no court interference during the electoral process
Corrupt practices: bribery, undue influence, etc. (RPA 1951) decided through legal process
⚠ ECI cannot give final verdict on election disputes (UPSC 2004)
## In news 2025-26
Telangana HC (18 Sept 2026) disqualified MLA Danam Nagender under para 2(1)(a) of Tenth Schedule, setting aside the Speaker's dismissal; seat declared vacant from April 2024 (Art 226 review)

topic: Electoral Systems: FPTP and Proportional Representation
t: FPTP → how the winner is decided
text:
## 1. First-Past-the-Post (plurality system)
Each territorial constituency elects one representative
Candidate with most valid votes wins: plurality, not majority; 50% not needed
Used for Lok Sabha and State Assemblies (method prescribed by the Constitution)
Feature | FPTP
Winner needs | More votes than any other candidate
Votes for losers | "Wasted": can give a party more seats than vote share
Voter-MP link | Clear: one MP per constituency
Stability | Favours single-party majorities
NOTA: even if NOTA gets most votes, highest-polling candidate wins
⚠ Winning candidate need not get 50% of votes polled (UPSC 2017 statement 1 false)
PYQ 2017: also tested "Speaker to majority, Deputy Speaker to opposition is in the Constitution" → false, it is only a convention

topic: Electoral Systems: FPTP and Proportional Representation
t: Speaker and Deputy Speaker → constitutional or convention?
text:
## 1. What the Constitution says
Point | Status
Speaker and Deputy Speaker elected by Lok Sabha from among members (Art 93) | Constitutional
Speaker's election date fixed by President; Deputy Speaker's by Speaker | Constitutional/rules
Speaker to ruling party, Deputy to opposition | Convention only (not always followed)
Speaker resigns to Deputy Speaker | Constitutional
Removal: effective majority (majority of all then members), 14 days' notice | Constitutional
While removal resolution is pending, Speaker cannot preside but may speak and vote in the first instance (no casting vote)
⚠ The Constitution does not allot posts by party; the Deputy Speaker post to opposition is convention

topic: Electoral Systems: FPTP and Proportional Representation
t: PR → when needed and its types
text:
## 1. Proportional Representation
Party gets seats in proportion to its vote share; seats filled from a pre-declared list (Israel, Netherlands: whole country one constituency)
Point | FPTP | PR
Constituency | Single-member | Large / multi-member
Voter votes for | Candidate | Party (list) or preferences
Seat-vote match | Distorted | Close match
Suited for | Two-party systems, clear accountability | Multi-party, minorities spread out
PR is not necessary where a two-party system has developed (distortion is minimal, e.g. UK)
⚠ Reserved constituencies, FPTP prevalence, fusion of systems are not reasons PR becomes unnecessary
PYQ 1997: "PR is NOT necessary in a country where ..." → a two-party system has developed

topic: Electoral Systems: FPTP and Proportional Representation
t: Indian elections → which use which system
text:
## 1. Election-wise method
Election | System | Voting
Lok Sabha | FPTP | Secret ballot, direct
State Assemblies | FPTP | Secret, direct
Rajya Sabha | PR by single transferable vote (STV) | Elected MLAs; open ballot (party agent sees) since 2003
Legislative Council | PR-STV (partly) | Indirect
President | PR-STV | Secret; MPs + MLAs (elected)
Vice-President | PR-STV | Secret; all MPs (elected + nominated)
Rajya Sabha voters (MLAs) mark a preference order; Lok Sabha voters mark one candidate
⚠ "FPTP is followed for all elections in India" is false (NCERT exercise)
⚠ Anti-defection law does not apply to Presidential poll (no whip)

t: Delimitation Commission → composition and legal finality
text:
## 1. Basis and composition
Delimitation = redrawing Lok Sabha and Assembly boundaries; principle "one person, one vote, one value"
Art 82 (Lok Sabha) and Art 170 (Assemblies): readjustment after every census
Statutory body under a Delimitation Act of Parliament; appointed by the President; works with ECI
Member | Role
Retired/serving SC judge | Chairperson
Chief Election Commissioner (or EC nominated) | Ex officio member
State Election Commissioner of the State | Ex officio member
Up to 10 associate members (MPs, MLAs) per State | No voting rights
## 2. Finality of orders
Orders have the force of law; cannot be challenged in any court (Art 329(a))
Laid before Lok Sabha and Assemblies, which cannot modify them; no parliamentary approval needed
Takes effect on a date notified by the President
⚠ Both statements true in UPSC 2012: no court challenge and no legislative modification
PYQ 2012: Delimitation orders cannot be challenged in court and cannot be modified by Lok Sabha/Assembly → both correct

t: Delimitation Commissions → years and seat freeze
text:
## 1. Four commissions
Commission | Act | Census used
1952 | Delimitation Commission Act 1952 | 1951
1963 | Act 1962 | 1961
1973 | Act 1972 | 1971
2002 | Act 2002 (completed 2008) | 2001 (boundaries only)
## 2. Freeze amendments
Amendment | Effect
42nd (1976) | Froze inter-State seats at 1971 census till 2000
84th (2001) | Extended freeze till first census after 2026
87th (2003) | Boundaries redrawn on 2001 census (was 1991); seat totals still 1971
Lok Sabha: 543 seats; ceiling 550 (530 States + 20 UTs); 84 SC, 47 ST seats
⚠ Four commissions constituted by GoI (UPSC 2024); a separate 2020 J&K delimitation panel is counted as fifth by Preview: follow PMF/UPSC four
PYQ 2024: Delimitation Commissions constituted till Dec 2023 → Four

t: Delimitation → SC/ST reservation and women's quota
text:
## 1. Reservation work
Art 330 (Lok Sabha) and Art 332 (Assemblies): seats reserved for SC/ST in proportion to population
ST seats: constituencies with highest ST proportion
SC seats: high SC proportion and spread across regions; may rotate with each delimitation
No reservation in LS/Assemblies for OBCs
## 2. Women's reservation (106th Amendment Act, 2023)
Point | Fact
Quota | One-third seats in Lok Sabha (Art 330A) and Assemblies (Art 332A), incl. SC/ST women
Start | Only after census + delimitation
Validity | 15 years
Notified in force | 16 April 2026
## In news 2025-26
Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026 + Delimitation Bill, 2026: Lok Sabha 543 → 850 (815 States, 35 UTs), early delimitation on 2011 census, amend Art 81, 82, 334A
Bill defeated in Lok Sabha (298 for, 230 against; needed 326: special majority under Art 368)
Census 2027 to trigger delimitation; southern States fear "demographic penalty"

t: Tenth Schedule → origin and amended Articles
text:
## 1. Origin
Point | Fact
Inserted by | 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985
Articles amended | 101, 102, 190, 191
Strengthened by | 91st Amendment Act, 2003
Applies to | Parliament and State Legislatures (both Houses)
Not applicable | Presidential election (no whip)
Aim: curb defections of the 1960s-70s ("Aaya Ram Gaya Ram"), ensure stability
The term "political party" appears in the Constitution through this Schedule
⚠ UPSC 2025: "No mention of 'political party' in the Constitution" → false (Tenth Schedule mentions it, since 1985)

t: Tenth Schedule → grounds of disqualification
text:
## 1. Para 2 grounds
Member | Disqualified if
Party member | Voluntarily gives up party membership (conduct enough; no formal resignation needed)
Party member | Votes or abstains against party direction without permission and not condoned within 15 days
Independent | Joins any party after election
Nominated | Joins a party after 6 months of taking seat
Nominated member may join a party within 6 months
Expulsion from party does not make a member independent (G. Viswanathan, 1996)
Ravi S. Naik (1994): giving up membership can be inferred from conduct
⚠ UPSC 2022: "nominated legislator cannot join any party within six months" → false; he can join within 6 months, not after
PYQ 2022: statement 2 (no time limit for presiding officer) correct → answer 2 only

t: Tenth Schedule → exceptions (merger, split, presiding officer)
text:
## 1. What protects a member
Situation | Status now
Merger (Para 4): original party merges, 2/3 of legislature party agree | Protected (both who merge and who stay out)
Split by 1/3 of legislature party (old Para 3) | Deleted by 91st Amdt (2003): no protection
Elected Speaker/Deputy Speaker/Chairman/Deputy Chairman gives up party | Protected; may rejoin after leaving office
The 2/3 rule is not a licence to leave and form a new party
⚠ Split exception no longer exists; only merger survives
## In news 2025-26
April 2026: 7 of 10 AAP Rajya Sabha MPs (incl. Raghav Chadha) merged with BJP, claiming merger (exactly two-thirds); Chairman to decide
2026: merger of 20 TMC MPs with NPCI revived the Tenth Schedule debate
ADR (2026): 111 sitting MPs/MLAs elected 2022-26 changed parties mid-term

t: Defection cases → who decides, time limit, judicial review
text:
## 1. Deciding authority (Para 6)
Speaker (Lok Sabha/Assembly) or Chairman (Rajya Sabha/Council) decides; acts as a tribunal
If the question concerns the presiding officer → member elected by the House
Not the President/Governor, not the ECI, not on Council of Ministers' advice
## 2. Key judgments
Case | Ruling
Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992) | Law valid; Speaker's decision subject to judicial review (para 7 bar struck)
Nabam Rebia (2016) | Speaker facing removal notice cannot decide disqualification
Keisham Meghachandra Singh (2020) | Decide within 3 months ordinarily (judicial standard)
Subhash Desai (2023) | Speaker must set a clear timeline
Padi Kaushik Reddy (2025) | SC again urged timely decisions
⚠ The Schedule itself fixes no time limit; 3 months is a court standard
⚠ UPSC 2025: "President decides on CoM advice" → false; Speaker decides

t: Defection → consequences and 91st Amendment package
text:
## 1. Consequences
Item | Rule
Seat | Lost
Minister post | Barred till term ends or re-election (whichever earlier)
Remunerative political post | Barred for same period
Rules | Speaker/Chairman frames; House may modify
## 2. 91st Amendment (2003): four changes
Deleted split provision
Union Council of Ministers ≤ 15% of Lok Sabha; State ≤ 15% of Assembly, minimum 12
Defectors barred from ministerial and remunerative political posts
These size caps are not disqualification grounds
## 3. Reform suggestions
Shift power to ECI/President/Governor on ECI's binding advice (Dinesh Goswami, Law Commission 170th); limit whip to confidence/money votes; independent tribunal (Keisham)

topic: Electoral Reforms, Committees and Election Management
t: Electoral reform committees → what each dealt with
text:
## 1. Committees
Committee / report | Year | Subject
Dinesh Goswami Committee | 1990 | Electoral reforms: musclemen, booth capturing, EVMs, state funding, post-retirement bar on CEC/ECs; led to 1996 RPA amendments
Indrajit Gupta Committee | 1998 | State funding of elections: partial, in kind, for recognised parties
Law Commission 170th Report | 1999 | Reform of electoral laws, party regulation
Law Commission 255th Report | 2015 | Electoral reforms; CJI on CEC panel; disqualification on framing of charges
Ram Nath Kovind High-Level Committee | 2023-24 | One Nation, One Election
Full State funding is not in force (only indirect support: free rolls, broadcast time)
⚠ Dinesh Goswami was not about banks, insurgency or Chakmas
PYQ 1995: Dinesh Goswami Committee concerned with → electoral reforms
## Beyond your notes
Tarkunde Committee (1974-75): electoral reforms (JP); Vohra Committee (1993): criminal-politician nexus

topic: Electoral Reforms, Committees and Election Management
t: Reform milestones → EVM, VVPAT, NOTA, disclosure
text:
## 1. Timeline
Reform | Fact
61st Amdt 1988 | Voting age 18
Affidavits | Criminal cases, assets, liabilities, education (ADR 2002, PUCL 2003)
NOTA | PUCL v. UoI (2013); does not change the result
VVPAT | Printed slip shown briefly, falls into sealed box
Rajya Sabha open ballot | 2003 (against cross-voting)
Electoral Bonds | Struck down, ADR v. UoI (Feb 2024): donor info is an Art 19(1)(a) right
Postal ballot from home | Age raised 80 → 85 (Rule 27A, March 2024); also 40%+ disabled
EPIC (voter ID) | 1993; ERONET since 2017; now ECINet
Corporate donation: Sec 182 Companies Act; parties report donations above Rs 20,000 (Sec 29C)
## Beyond your notes
First EVM use: Paravur (Kerala), 1982; VVPAT first: Noksen (Nagaland), 2013 (verify)

topic: Electoral Reforms, Committees and Election Management
t: Model Code of Conduct and expenditure → legal status
text:
## 1. Key facts
Item | Status
MCC | ECI guideline, not a law; applies from announcement of schedule
Breach of MCC | Not automatically a crime
Candidate spending | Ceiling fixed (Rule 90)
Party spending | No ceiling
Failure to file accounts | 3-year disqualification by ECI (Sec 10A)
Campaign silence | 48 hours (Sec 126)
Common Cause (1996): parties cannot disguise candidate spending as party expenditure
⚠ Candidate ceiling is not a ceiling on party spending

topic: Electoral Reforms, Committees and Election Management
t: One Nation, One Election → proposal and amendments
text:
## 1. ONOE
Simultaneous polls held in 1951-52 to 1967; cycle broke after 1968-69 dissolutions and 1970 Lok Sabha dissolution
Point | Fact
Committee | Ram Nath Kovind High-Level Committee (2023-24)
Phase 1 | Lok Sabha + State Assemblies together
Phase 2 | Local bodies within 100 days
Bill | Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill, 2024; new Art 82A (President notifies "appointed date")
Articles to amend | 83, 85, 172, 174 (and 356 per Preview)
Status | Referred to JPC (31 members per PMF: 21 LS + 10 RS)
⚠ A "fresh House" after mid-term dissolution serves only the remaining term

topic: Electoral Reforms, Committees and Election Management
t: Election management → 2025-26 developments
text:
## 1. ECI digital and roll measures
Development | What changes

t: CAG duties → what it audits and what it does NOT do
text:
## 1. What the CAG audits (Art 149 + CAG Act 1971)
Account / body | Audited by CAG?
Consolidated Fund of India, of each State, of each UT with a legislature | Yes
Contingency Funds and Public Accounts of Union and States | Yes
Departmental trading, manufacturing, profit and loss accounts, balance sheets, stores and stock | Yes
Union and State receipts (checks on assessment, collection, allocation of revenue) | Yes
Bodies substantially financed from government revenue; grants and loans for specified purposes | Yes
Any other body on request of President or Governor (e.g. local bodies) | Yes, on request
Control of receipt and issue of public money (exchequer control) | No
⚠ The British C&AG controls issue of money; India's CAG is only an auditor, not a comptroller
Audit is after expenditure; the CAG does not approve withdrawals beforehand
PYQ 2001: which duty is NOT performed: "control receipt and issue of public money and lodge revenue in the exchequer"; the three audit options (CFI, Contingency Funds and Public Accounts, trading accounts) are all genuine duties

t: CAG → appointment, tenure, removal
text:
## 1. Office
Art 148: independent office; head of the Indian Audit and Accounts Department; "guardian of the public purse"
Feature | Rule
Appointment | President, by warrant under hand and seal
Oath | Before the President or person appointed by him (form in Third Schedule)
Tenure | 6 years or age 65, whichever earlier (fixed by CAG Act 1971, not the Constitution)
Resignation | In writing to the President
Removal | Like a Supreme Court judge: address by both Houses with special majority, on proved misbehaviour or incapacity
Reappointment / later office | Not eligible for any further office under GoI or a State
Qualification | None laid down in the Constitution
⚠ CAG is appointed by the President but does not hold office at his pleasure
⚠ "6 years" is in the 1971 Act; the Constitution (Art 148(3)) leaves service conditions to Parliament
K. Sanjay Murthy is the 15th CAG (appointed 2024); G.C. Murmu was the 14th

t: CAG independence → the complete list of safeguards
text:
## 1. Safeguards (six)
Safeguard | Detail
Security of tenure | Removed only like an SC judge
No further office | Barred from office under Union or State after leaving
Salary by Parliament | Equal to an SC judge (Second Schedule Part E; CAG Act 1971)
No variation to disadvantage | Salary, leave, pension, retirement age
Staff rules | Made by President after consulting the CAG
Charged expenditure | Office expenses incl. staff salaries and pensions charged on CFI (not voted)
No minister can represent the CAG in Parliament (either House); no minister answers for his actions
⚠ Expenses are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India, not on the Public Account
LENS Nov 2025 practice: "holds office at the pleasure of the President" is the planted false statement

Appropriation accounts; finance accounts; public undertakings
CAG = "guide, friend and philosopher" of the PAC

CAG reports are discussed by the PAC | Yes
Investigating agencies (CBI, ED) can use CAG findings to press charges | Yes

## 1. Duties
Advise GoI on legal matters referred by the President; other legal duties assigned by him or by law
Appear for GoI in all SC cases concerning the Union; in Art 143 presidential references; in HCs when required
## 2. Limitations
AG should not... | Without
Advise or hold brief against GoI | Never
Advise in a case where he must appear for GoI | Never
Defend an accused in a criminal prosecution | GoI permission
Become a company director | GoI permission

⚠ Acid attack victims, Parkinson's, thalassemia, haemophilia, sickle cell and SLD were added in 2016; they were not in the 1995 list of 7
## Beyond your notes
The 1995 list of 7: blindness, low vision, leprosy-cured, hearing impairment, locomotor disability, mental retardation, mental illness
The Central Government can notify more categories

topic: Disability Rights: RPwD Act, Sugamya Bharat and Institutions
t: RPwD Act → benefits, reservation and duties of the State
text:
## 1. Entitlements (persons with benchmark disability)
Benefit | Provision
Free education | Every child with benchmark disability aged 6-18 years, in a neighbourhood school or a special school of choice (Sec 31)
Higher education | Govt and govt-aided HEIs reserve not less than 5% seats
Public jobs | Not less than 4% of vacancies, spread over visual, hearing, locomotor and intellectual/multiple disabilities
Land and housing | 5% reservation in allotment of agricultural land and housing, and land at concessional rates for business, occupation, enterprise; priority to women with benchmark disability
Poverty alleviation schemes | 5% allotment
Accessibility | Barrier-free environment, ramps; existing public buildings made accessible within 5 years of the rules (Sec 45)
Also: reasonable accommodation, non-discrimination, access to justice, inclusive education in govt-funded/recognised institutions
⚠ PYQ 2011: free schooling till 18, preferential land allotment and ramps were all correct (answer: 1, 2 and 3); the 1995 Act already required ramps in public places
⚠ Reservation in jobs and education is in addition to SC/ST reservation (horizontal)
PYQ 2011: "benefits under the law" for PwDs; trap: thinking free education stops at 14 (that is RTE; RPwD extends it to 18)

topic: Disability Rights: RPwD Act, Sugamya Bharat and Institutions
t: RPwD Act → bodies and enforcement
text:
## 1. Statutory machinery
Body | Role
Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities | Regulatory and grievance redressal at Centre; monitors implementation
State Commissioners for PwD | Same role in States
Central Advisory Board on Disability | Statutory body to advise GoI (State Advisory Boards for States)
National and State Funds | Financial support to PwDs
Special Court in each district | Speedy trial of offences under the Act
Benchmark disability = at least 40%; certified by a medical authority, now via UDID
## Beyond your notes
Penalty for contravening the Act: up to Rs 10,000 first time; Rs 50,000 to Rs 5 lakh for later contraventions
Atrocities against PwDs (insulting, assaulting, denying food) punishable with 6 months to 5 years and fine
⚠ The Chief Commissioner is a statutory office under the 2016 Act, not a constitutional one

topic: Disability Rights: RPwD Act, Sugamya Bharat and Institutions
t: Sugamya Bharat Abhiyan → three domains and the agency
text:
## 1. Accessible India Campaign
Launched by the PM on 3 December 2015, the International Day of Persons with Disabilities
Implementing agency: Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities (DEPwD), Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment
Aim: universal accessibility, a barrier-free environment for Divyangjan
Domain (three key domains) | Example
Built environment | Accessible public buildings, spaces
Transportation system | Airports, railway stations, buses
Information and Communication Technology (ICT) ecosystem | Accessible govt websites, Sugamya Bharat app, sign language on TV
Added component: sign language access (interpreter training, media support)
Sugamya Bharat App (DEPwD): users report accessibility problems in buildings, transport, infrastructure
⚠ Three domains: built, transport, ICT; not health, education or employment
⚠ 3 December was fixed by a UNGA resolution of 1992
## Beyond your notes
Harmonised Accessibility Guidelines 2021 set building norms (as listed in the AUGUST-2025 CA file)

topic: Disability Rights: RPwD Act, Sugamya Bharat and Institutions
t: Disability institutions and schemes → which ministry, what they do
text:
## 1. Nodal ministry: Social Justice and Empowerment (DEPwD)
Body / scheme | What it does
NDFDC (National Divyangjan Finance and Development Corporation) | Concessional loans for self-employment of PwDs
UDID (Unique Disability ID) | Single national digital disability card / certificate
ADIP scheme | Free aids/appliances (income below Rs 22,500/month), subsidised up to Rs 30,000
DDRS (Deendayal Disabled Rehabilitation Scheme) | Grants to NGOs for rehabilitation, vocational training
Niramaya | Health insurance up to Rs 1 lakh/yr for autism, cerebral palsy, intellectual and multiple disabilities
Composite Regional Centres; 9 National Institutes | Rehabilitation, research, HRD
IGNDPS (pension) | Under Rural Development (NSAP): Rs 300/month central share to severely disabled BPL persons
⚠ NDFDC is under Social Justice and Empowerment, not Corporate Affairs (PYQ 2026 trap)
⚠ IGNDPS is the exception: it is part of NSAP under the Ministry of Rural Development
## Beyond your notes
NDFDC was set up in 1997 as a not-for-profit company (Sec 25 of Companies Act 1956), wholly owned by GoI under MoSJE
National Trust Act 1999 covers 4 disabilities (autism, cerebral palsy, mental retardation, multiple disabilities); RCI Act 1992 regulates rehabilitation professionals

topic: Disability Rights: RPwD Act, Sugamya Bharat and Institutions
t: Disability → Constitution, other laws and data
text:
## 1. Constitutional base
Provision | Content
Art 41 (DPSP) | Public assistance in cases of disablement, old age, sickness, unemployment
State List | "Relief of the disabled and unemployable"
Art 15, 16, 21 | Equality, non-discrimination, dignity
## 2. Other disability laws
Rehabilitation Council of India Act, 1992; National Trust Act, 1999; Mental Healthcare Act, 2017
National Policy for Persons with Disabilities 2006 (under revision)
## 3. Data
Census 2011: 2.68 crore PwDs (2.21%); NFHS-5: 4.52%; WHO estimate ~15%
Only about 1 crore UDID cards issued since 2015; private sector only 0.4% disabled employees (ILO 2021)

topic: Maternity Benefit and Women's Workplace Laws
t: Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act 2017 → leave, creche, eligibility
text:
## 1. Applicability
Amends the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961; applies to establishments with 10 or more employees
Not for self-employed women
Eligibility: worked at least 80 days in the 12 months before expected delivery
## 2. Entitlements
Case | Leave
1st and 2nd child | 26 weeks paid; up to 8 weeks may be taken before delivery
3rd child onwards (two or more surviving children) | 12 weeks (6 before delivery)
Adopting a child below 3 months / commissioning mother | 12 weeks from the date the child is handed over
Miscarriage / medical termination | 6 weeks after the event
Creche: mandatory in establishments with 50 or more employees; mother may visit 4 times a day (including rest interval)
Work from home after the leave, if the work allows, by mutual agreement
No employment of a woman in the 6 weeks immediately after delivery or miscarriage
⚠ Leave is 26 weeks, not "3 months + 3 months"; creche visits are four, not six; women with two children do get reduced leave (12 weeks): PYQ 2019 answer "3 only"
⚠ Commissioning mother = biological mother who uses her egg to create an embryo implanted in another woman (surrogacy)

topic: Maternity Benefit and Women's Workplace Laws
t: Maternity → 1961 Act vs 2017 Amendment vs Code on Social Security 2020
text:
## 1. Comparison
Feature | MB Act 1961 (original) | 2017 Amendment | Code on Social Security 2020
Paid leave | 12 weeks | 26 weeks (first two children) | 26 weeks (first two)
3rd child | 12 weeks | 12 weeks | 12 weeks
Adoptive / commissioning | none | 12 weeks (child below 3 months) | 12 weeks; age limit struck down in 2026
Creche | none | 50+ employees, 4 visits | 50+ employees
The Code on Social Security 2020 consolidates maternity benefits and replaces the 1961 Act (one of 9 laws merged)
ESI Act 1948: maternity cash benefit to women in ESI-covered establishments (employer-employee contributions)
## 2. Constitutional and international base
Art 42 (DPSP): just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief
Art 21: maternity leave is part of reproductive rights (Umadevi 2025); Suchita Srivastava (2009): reproductive autonomy under Art 21
ILO Maternity Protection Conventions (1919, revised 2000); UDHR Art 25: special care for motherhood
⚠ There is no universal paternity leave law; central govt employees get 15 days paternity leave (service rules)
## Beyond your notes
ILO Convention 183 (2000) sets a minimum of 14 weeks; India has not ratified it

topic: Maternity Benefit and Women's Workplace Laws
t: Maternity rights → In news 2025-26
text:
## In news 2025-26
Date | Case / event | What it held
May 2025 | K. Umadevi v. Govt of Tamil Nadu | Maternity leave for a third child cannot be denied; it is a reproductive right under Art 21; State rules yield to central law under Art 254; population policy cannot override rights
17 Mar 2026 | Hamsanandini Nanduri v. Union of India (Pardiwala, Mahadevan JJ) | Struck down Sec 60(4) of the Code on Social Security 2020; all adoptive mothers get 12 weeks irrespective of the child's age; violated Art 14 and 21; urged paternity leave
Mar 2026 | SC on menstrual leave | Making it legally mandatory may hurt women's hiring; suggested policy and sensitisation instead
Data: FLFPR 37% (PLFS 2022-23); only about 10% of women (formal sector) covered (LENS Jun 2025)
⚠ Sec 60(4) had limited adoptive leave to children below 3 months; that limit is now gone

topic: Maternity Benefit and Women's Workplace Laws
t: Women-protection laws → year and key provision
text:
## 1. Statutes UPSC confuses by year
Act | Year | Key provision
Dowry Prohibition Act | 1961 | Giving/taking dowry punishable: 5 years and fine of at least Rs 15,000 or dowry value
Equal Remuneration Act | 1976 | Equal pay for equal work; now merged in Code on Wages 2019
Commission of Sati (Prevention) Act | 1987 | Bans sati and its glorification; DM can seize property
PCPNDT Act | 1994 | Bans sex determination; regulates ultrasound clinics
Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act | 2005 | Civil law; Right to residence (Sec 17); Protection Officers; decision within 60 days
POSH Act (Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace) | 2013 | Internal Committee where 10 or more employees; Local Committee at district
Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act | 2019 | Instant talaq-e-biddat void; up to 3 years jail
106th Amendment (Nari Shakti Vandan) | 2023 | 33% seats for women in LS, State Assemblies, Delhi
⚠ CDI file says dowry punishment is "up to five years"; the Act says not less than five years
⚠ DV Act gives civil protection; marital rape is still an exception under Sec 63 BNS (except wife below 18)
## Beyond your notes
POSH: complaint within 3 months; inquiry within 90 days; grew out of Vishaka v. Rajasthan (1997)
DV Act reliefs: protection, residence, monetary, custody, compensation orders

topic: Labour Laws, Labour Codes and Child Labour
t: Standing Orders Amendment Rules 2018 → fixed-term employment
text:
## 1. Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Central (Amendment) Rules, 2018
Fixed-term employment workman: engaged on a written contract for a fixed period
Extended fixed-term employment to all sectors
Point | Rule
Wages, hours, allowances | Same as a permanent workman
Statutory benefits | Proportionate to period served, even below the qualifying period
End of contract (expiry / non-renewal) | No notice or pay in lieu of notice
Temporary workman (monthly, weekly, piece-rated), probationers, badli workmen | No notice of termination necessary
Effect: easier for firms to hire and fire (lay off); smaller role of middlemen/contractors
⚠ Both statements of PYQ 2019 were correct: fixed-term rules make lay-offs easier, and no notice is needed for a temporary workman
PYQ 2019: Statement pair on the 2018 Rules; trap: assuming fixed-term workers get notice pay or fewer wages (they get parity but no notice)
## Beyond your notes
Parent law: Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946; it is now merged in the Industrial Relations Code 2020

topic: Labour Laws, Labour Codes and Child Labour
t: Four Labour Codes → laws merged and main changes
text:
## 1. The codes (29 central laws merged)
Code | Laws merged | Key changes
Code on Wages, 2019 | 4 | Single definition of wage (basic + DA + retaining allowance); minimum wage for all workers; National Floor Wage; no gender pay discrimination
Industrial Relations Code, 2020 | 3 (ID Act 1947, Trade Unions Act 1926, Standing Orders Act 1946) | Prior approval for layoff/closure: 100 → 300 workers; fixed-term employment with parity and gratuity after 1 year; strike notice extended; mass casual leave by over half the workforce counts as strike; worker includes those earning below Rs 18,000
Code on Social Security, 2020 | 9 | First legal definition of gig and platform workers; Aadhaar-linked portal; wider EPFO/ESIC cover; maternity benefit
OSH and Working Conditions Code, 2020 | 13 | Covers workplaces with 10+ workers, all mines and docks; free annual health check-up at 40+; women in night shifts with consent
Implemented nationwide in November 2025 (enacted 2019-20)
⚠ 4 + 3 + 9 + 13 = 29 laws; the Code on Wages merges 4 laws (Testbook says 29, which is the total of all four codes)
## Beyond your notes
Code on Wages merged: Payment of Wages Act 1936, Minimum Wages Act 1948, Payment of Bonus Act 1965, Equal Remuneration Act 1976
The codes came into force on 21 November 2025 (verify)

topic: Labour Laws, Labour Codes and Child Labour
t: Child labour → age limits in each law
text:
## 1. Ages
Law / provision | Rule
Art 24 | No child below 14 in factory, mine or hazardous work
Art 21A | Free, compulsory education 6-14
Art 39(e), 39(f) | Children not abused; develop in freedom and dignity
Factories Act 1948 | No child below 14 in factories
Mines Act 1952 | No one below 18 in mines
Child and Adolescent Labour (P&R) Act 1986, amended 2016 | Below 14: banned in all occupations; 14-18 (adolescents): banned in hazardous work
2016 exceptions for children: family enterprises (after school hours) and audio-visual entertainment (not circus), without affecting studies
Hazardous list for adolescents cut to mines, inflammable substances, explosives
Punishment: 6 months-2 years and Rs 20,000-50,000; stricter for repeat; Rehabilitation Fund
⚠ Mines Act bar is 18, Factories Act bar is 14
⚠ Art 24 does not ban children in non-hazardous work; the 2016 Act goes further
## 2. Schemes and international
NCLP (Labour Ministry; merged with Samagra Shiksha 2016); PENCIL portal (2017)
ILO 138 (minimum age) and ILO 182 (worst forms); SDG 8.7: end child labour by 2025
Gurupadswamy Committee (1979); National Policy on Child Labour (1987)
Census 2011: 1.01 crore child labourers (5-14), 3.9% of child population

topic: Right to Education (RTE) Act and Teacher Standards
t: RTE Act 2009 → main provisions
text:
## 1. Base
Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 operationalises Art 21A (free, compulsory education 6-14)
Art 21A was inserted by the 86th Amendment, 2002
Provision | Content
Govt schools | Free education for all children
Aided schools | Free seats in proportion to aid
Private unaided schools | 25% of entry-level seats for disadvantaged groups, State reimburses (Sec 12(1)(c))
Banned | Capitation fee, screening, corporal punishment and mental harassment
Norms | Pupil-teacher ratio, teacher qualifications (TET), infrastructure (toilets, boundary wall, library, playground)
Monitoring | NCPCR and SCPCRs review RTE safeguards and complaints
## Beyond your notes
In force 1 April 2010; PTR 30:1 (primary), 35:1 (upper primary)
2019 amendment: ended blanket no-detention; States may hold exams in classes 5 and 8 and detain after a re-exam
School Management Committees: three-fourths members parents
⚠ 86th Amendment also changed Art 45 (early childhood care, below 6) and added Art 51A(k) (parents' duty)

topic: Right to Education (RTE) Act and Teacher Standards
t: RTE → who sets teacher qualifications (NCTE, TET)
text:
## 1. Teacher standards
Statement | Correct position
Minimum qualifications for teachers | Laid down by the academic authority notified by the Centre: the NCTE, not a State Council
Teacher Eligibility Test (TET) | Required for primary teachers; conducted per NCTE guidelines
Teacher education institutions | Mostly private; not 90% under State govts
NCTE: statutory apex regulator of teacher education under the NCTE Act, 1993; prescribes norms for training institutions
Supporting bodies: SCERTs (State) design training; DIETs (district) give pre- and in-service training
NEP 2020: four-year integrated B.Ed.
⚠ PYQ 2018: only statement 2 (TET per NCTE guidelines) was correct; trap 1: "State Council of Teacher Education"; trap 3: "90% under State govts"
PYQ 2018: RTE teacher norms; trap: the qualifying authority is national (NCTE), even for State teachers
## Beyond your notes
CTET is conducted by CBSE; State TETs follow NCTE norms
NCTE was formed in 1995 under the Ministry of Education

topic: Right to Education (RTE) Act and Teacher Standards
t: RTE and minorities → In news 2025-26
text:
## 1. Case trail
Case | Year | Holding
Society for Unaided Private Schools of Rajasthan | 2012 | RTE valid as reasonable restriction; unaided minority schools exempt
Pramati Educational & Cultural Trust | 2014 | All minority schools (aided and unaided) exempt, including the 25% quota
## In news 2025-26
Sep 2025: a two-judge SC bench questioned the blanket minority exemption and referred Pramati (2014) to a larger bench
May 2026: SC held education in the mother tongue is a fundamental right (Rajasthani in teacher-recruitment syllabus case); Art 350A: primary education in mother tongue for linguistic minorities; NEP 2020 favours it

t: Consumer law → rights and who can file a complaint
text:
## 1. Consumer Protection Act, 2019
Replaced the Consumer Protection Act, 1986; three-tier District, State, National Commissions
## 2. Who can complain
Complainant | Allowed?
The consumer | Yes
Legal heir or representative of a deceased consumer | Yes
Parent/guardian of a minor consumer | Yes
Registered voluntary consumer association | Yes
Central or State Government; CCPA | Yes
One or more consumers with the same interest (class complaint) | Yes
Food samples: a consumer can get food samples tested (food law allows a purchaser to have food analysed by a Food Analyst)
Fees: not always free; fee depends on the value of goods/services (no fee for small claims)
⚠ PYQ 2012 answer "1 and 3": samples and legal heirs are correct; "no fee is required" is wrong
## Beyond your notes
Six consumer rights: safety, information, choice, to be heard, to seek redressal, consumer education
No fee for claims up to Rs 5 lakh (2020 Rules); e-filing allowed; complaint where the complainant resides or works
Purchaser's right to food analysis: Sec 40, Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006
National Consumer Day 24 December; World Consumer Rights Day 15 March

t: Consumer Commissions → pecuniary limits and appeals
text:
## 1. Jurisdiction (2021 Rules, by value of goods/services paid)
Commission | Pecuniary limit | Head | Appeal goes to
District (DCDRC) | Up to Rs 50 lakh | Serving/former District Judge + at least 2 members | State Commission, 45 days
State (SCDRC) | Rs 50 lakh-2 crore | Serving/former HC Judge + at least 4 members | National Commission, 30 days
National (NCDRC) | Above Rs 2 crore | Sitting/retired SC Judge or HC Chief Justice + at least 4 members | Supreme Court, 30 days
NCDRC: set up 1988 under the 1986 Act; statutory, quasi-judicial; original, appellate, revisional jurisdiction; civil court powers
Also hears appeals against specified CCPA orders; can declare unfair contract terms void
⚠ Limit is based on consideration paid, not compensation claimed (the 1986 Act used claim value)
⚠ NCDRC is not a constitutional body (PYQ 2023 trap)
## Beyond your notes
The 2019 Act originally set Rs 1 crore and Rs 10 crore; the 2021 Rules cut them to Rs 50 lakh and Rs 2 crore

t: CCPA → powers and status
text:
## 1. Central Consumer Protection Authority
Statutory regulator set up in 2020 under the CPA 2019; HQ New Delhi
Under the Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution
Power | Detail
Investigate | Violations of consumer rights, unfair trade practices, misleading ads
Recall | Order recall of unsafe goods / withdrawal of services
Refund | Reimbursement of prices for recalled goods
Discontinue | Unfair practices; false or misleading advertisements
Other | Bans surrogate advertising; acts against influencers promoting illegal betting
⚠ CCPA protects consumers as a class (regulator); NCDRC adjudicates disputes; they are distinct
## Beyond your notes
CCPA can fine a manufacturer or endorser up to Rs 10 lakh (up to Rs 50 lakh for repeat) for misleading ads, and bar an endorser for up to 1 year
New in the 2019 Act: product liability, mediation, e-commerce rules (2020), dark patterns guidelines (2023)

topic: Child Rights: UNCRC, POCSO, JJ Act and Child Marriage
t: UNCRC → the rights it contains
text:
## 1. The Convention
UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, adopted 1989; India acceded in 1992
Child = person below 18
Covers children's civil, political, economic, social, health and cultural rights
Right | UNCRC Article
Best interests of the child | Art 3
Life, survival and development | Art 6
Right to be heard (views) | Art 12
Freedom of expression | Art 13
Freedom of association | Art 15
Rest, leisure, play and recreation | Art 31
⚠ Development, expression and recreation are all UNCRC rights (PYQ 2010 answer: 1, 2 and 3)
PYQ 2010: which are rights of the child under UNCRC; trap: treating "development" as only a State goal, or recreation as not a right
## Beyond your notes
Adopted 20 November 1989 (World Children's Day); in force 1990; 54 articles; monitored by the Committee on the Rights of the Child
Four general principles: non-discrimination (Art 2), best interests (Art 3), life, survival and development (Art 6), respect for views (Art 12)
Four rights groups: survival, development, protection, participation
Two Optional Protocols (2000): children in armed conflict; sale of children, child prostitution and pornography (India ratified both, 2005)
Most widely ratified rights treaty; the USA has not ratified it

topic: Child Rights: UNCRC, POCSO, JJ Act and Child Marriage
t: POCSO Act 2012 → key provisions
text:
## 1. Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act
Feature | Provision
Who is protected | Children below 18
Nature | Gender-neutral; consent of a minor is immaterial (strict liability)
Courts | A Sessions Court in each district designated Special Court (State, with HC Chief Justice)
Time limit | Case to be disposed of within one year of reporting
Penalty | Up to life or death in aggravated cases
2019 amendment | Raised penalties; criminalised child pornography
Monitoring | NCPCR and SCPCRs
Child offender | Tried under the JJ Act 2015
Scheme for Care and Support to Victims under Sec 4 and 6 of POCSO (Ministry of WCD)
⚠ POCSO is gender-neutral for victims and offenders; it is not limited to girls
## Beyond your notes
Mandatory reporting: failure to report is an offence; the child's evidence is to be recorded within 30 days

topic: Child Rights: UNCRC, POCSO, JJ Act and Child Marriage
t: JJ Act 2015 and adoption → provisions
text:
## 1. Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 (amended 2021)
Aligns with UNCRC; covers children in conflict with law and in need of care and protection
Item | Provision
Offence classes | Petty (up to 3 yrs), serious (3-7 yrs), heinous (7 yrs or more)
Age 16-18 | JJB assesses whether the child is tried as an adult in the Children's Court
JJB | Every district; Principal Magistrate + 2 social workers (at least 1 woman); child produced within 24 hours
CWC | Child Welfare Committee for children needing care
2021 amendment | DMs/ADMs issue adoption orders
## 2. CARA
Est. 1990; statutory under the JJ Act 2015; Ministry of WCD; runs CARINGS
Central Authority under the Hague Convention on inter-country adoption
Surrendered child: two-month reconsideration period for biological parents
⚠ PMF lists 16-18 adult trial for serious offences in one place and ROCKET for heinous; the Act applies it to heinous offences

topic: Child Rights: UNCRC, POCSO, JJ Act and Child Marriage
t: Child marriage and NCPCR → age, body, scheme
text:
## 1. Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006
Child: girl below 18, boy below 21
Punishes the adult male who marries a child, those who conduct or promote it: up to 2 years RI and fine up to Rs 1 lakh
## 2. NCPCR
Item | Detail
Law | Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005; set up 2007
Status | Statutory, under Ministry of WCD
Composition | Chairperson + 6 members (at least 2 women)
Tenure | 3 years, max two terms; age limit 65 (chair) / 60 (members)
Monitors | RTE 2009, POCSO 2012, JJ Act 2015
First chair Shantha Sinha
## In news 2025-26
Bal Vivah Mukt Bharat (MWCD, 2024): target prevalence below 5% by 2029; 100-day campaign (Dec 2025) on its first anniversary; Child Marriage Free Bharat Portal; 7 high-burden States incl. Andhra Pradesh
Prevalence 47.4% (NFHS-3) to 23.3% (NFHS-5); WB 41.6%, Bihar 40.8%, AP 29.3%, J&K lowest 4.5% (May 2026 survey)
## Beyond your notes
A child marriage is voidable at the option of the party who was a child (petition within 2 years of majority)

t: SC/ST Atrocities Act 1989 and PCR Act 1955 → provisions
text:
## 1. Comparison
Feature | Protection of Civil Rights Act | SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act
Year | 1955 (renamed 1976 from Untouchability (Offences) Act) | 1989 (Rules 1995)
Purpose | Enforces Art 17; penalises practising untouchability | Defines atrocities; protection, relief, rehabilitation
Bail | Normal | No anticipatory bail (Sec 18); Sec 18A (2018): no preliminary inquiry or prior sanction before arrest
Courts | Ordinary | Special Courts (Sessions), Special Public Prosecutors
Offences only by non-SC/ST persons against SC/ST members; penalties 6 months to life, death in some cases; property confiscation
PCR Act offences: barring temple entry, denying shops/hotels/hospitals, refusing goods or services, preaching untouchability
⚠ A person who converts out of Hinduism, Sikhism or Buddhism loses SC status and Atrocities Act protection (SC, 2026; Para 3, Constitution (SC) Order 1950)

topic: FIR, Arrest and Custody under BNSS
t: Zero FIR → what BNSS Section 173 allows
text:
## 1. FIR basics
FIR: first official record of a cognizable offence; can be filed by the victim, a witness or any person aware of it
Police cannot refuse an FIR over jurisdiction: they must register a Zero FIR and transfer it to the competent station (Sec 173 BNSS)
Zero FIR idea: Justice Verma Committee after the Nirbhaya case (2012)
Point | Rule
Offences covered | Cognizable only
Where | Any police station, regardless of where the offence occurred
Modes | Oral, written or electronic
e-FIR | Must be signed by the informant within 3 days
Electronic mode | Optional, one permitted mode, not compulsory
⚠ Zero FIR is not for non-cognizable offences (2026 trap: "cognizable/non-cognizable")
⚠ Giving information electronically is not obligatory (2026 trap)
FIR is a public document under the BSA 2023; Sikkim HC (2026): media may name the accused while reporting an FIR

topic: FIR, Arrest and Custody under BNSS
t: Preliminary enquiry → offences punishable 3 to 7 years
text:
## 1. Section 173(3) BNSS
Feature | Rule
Offences | Cognizable, punishable 3 years or more but less than 7 years
Permission | Prior permission of an officer not below DSP
Time limit | Preliminary enquiry within 14 days
Purpose | Check whether a prima facie case exists
Option | Or proceed directly to investigation if a prima facie case exists
Below 3 years and 7 years or more: no such preliminary-enquiry window
PYQ 2026: only statement 2 correct (Officer-in-Charge may, with competent authority's permission, start a preliminary enquiry); traps: Zero FIR for non-cognizable offences and compulsory e-filing
## 2. Other BNSS investigation rules
Forensic investigation mandatory for offences punishable with 7 years or more (use another State's lab if none)
Videography of searches (Sec 185), crime scenes (Sec 176) and property seizure (Sec 105); app eSakshya (NIC)
Medical report in rape cases to the IO within 7 days; POCSO investigation within 2 months; informant told of progress within 90 days
Sanction to prosecute a public servant: decide within 120 days, else deemed granted; no sanction for sexual offences, trafficking

topic: FIR, Arrest and Custody under BNSS
t: Police custody vs judicial custody → where held, who can question
text:
## 1. Comparison
Basis | Police custody | Judicial custody
Physical custody | Police | Magistrate
Kept in | Police station lock-up | Jail (central/state prison)
Interrogation | Police may interrogate | Only with court's permission
Maximum | 15 days in all | Rest of the remand period
Death in custody | During interrogation | Due to prison conditions/violence
⚠ Judicial custody means jail, not the police station (2021 trap)
⚠ Mere interrogation in jail with Magistrate's permission does not turn judicial custody into police custody (Gian Singh v. State, 1981)
PYQ 2021: statement 1 (judicial custody = police station) wrong; statement 2 (no interrogation without court approval) right
## 2. Remand under BNSS
Sec 187(2): police custody capped at 15 days, but may be split across the first 40 or 60 days of detention
Sec 58: produce the arrested person before a magistrate within 24 hours
## Beyond your notes
Default bail if charge-sheet not filed within 90 days (offences punishable with death, life or 10+ years) or 60 days (others); 40-day window applies to 60-day cases, 60-day window to 90-day cases

topic: FIR, Arrest and Custody under BNSS
t: Arrest safeguards → Article 22 and BNSS sections
text:
## 1. Constitution
Clause | Safeguard
Art 22(1) | Told grounds of arrest; right to consult a lawyer of choice
Art 22(2) | Produced before nearest magistrate within 24 hours (excluding journey)
Art 22(3) | Above do not apply to enemy aliens and preventive detainees
Art 22(5) | Detenu told grounds; earliest chance to represent
Art 22(7) | Parliament prescribes maximum detention period
## 2. BNSS
Section | Rule
35 | Arrest without warrant for cognizable offences; reasons recorded for offences below 7 years
35(7) | DSP's permission to arrest an infirm or over-60 person for offence below 3 years
37 | Arrested persons' details displayed (physically and digitally) at police stations
38 | Meet an advocate during interrogation (not throughout)
43(5) | No arrest of women after sunset/before sunrise, except with Judicial Magistrate's prior permission
47 | Inform grounds of arrest and right to bail
48 | Inform a nominated relative/friend
53 | Medical examination by a government medical officer
D.K. Basu (1997): 11 arrest requirements; Arnesh Kumar (2014): no automatic arrest for offences up to 7 years; Joginder Kumar (1994): arrest not arbitrary

text:
## 1. Replacement table
New law (2023) | Replaced | Nature
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) | Indian Penal Code, 1860 | Substantive offences
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) | CrPC, 1973 | Procedure: arrest, bail, trial
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA) | Indian Evidence Act, 1872 | Evidence
All three in force from 1 July 2024

## 2. BNS points
Sec 113: terrorist act as a distinct offence; an officer not below SP decides whether to book under BNS or UAPA
Age-specific rape classes; sex by false promise/deceit punished
⚠ Criticism: marital rape exception retained; male and transgender victims not covered

topic: New Criminal Laws: BNS, BNSS, BSA 2023
t: BNSS → key procedural changes
text:
## 1. Changes over CrPC
Area | CrPC | BNSS
Undertrial release at half the maximum sentence | Not for death-punishable offences | Also not for life imprisonment offences and persons facing multiple cases
Medical exam of accused | On request of Sub-Inspector or above | Any police officer
Specimen samples | Signatures/handwriting | Adds finger impressions and voice samples; even from a person not arrested
Metropolitan areas | Metropolitan Magistrates | Classification removed
"Judicial Magistrate" | Term used | Replaced by "Magistrate"
Arms in processions (Sec 144A) | DM could prohibit | Not mentioned in BNSS
Trial in absentia | Only record evidence | Full trial and verdict allowed
Whole process from FIR to judgment to be digitised; trial including cross-examination by video conferencing
Police may detain/remove persons resisting lawful directions in preventive action (Sec 172)

t: Prisons → constitutional entry and governing law
text:
## 1. Framework
Item | Fact
Constitutional entry | Prisons: State List, Entry 4, Seventh Schedule
Main law | Prisons Act, 1894 + State Prison Manuals
Other law | Prisoners Act, 1900
Day-to-day management | State Home Departments
Advisory | BPR&D issues reform guidelines
Oversight | Courts, NHRC inspections
The Prisons Act 1894 vested Provincial Governments (now States) with power to make prison rules
⚠ Prisons are a State subject; the Centre only issues model laws and manuals
PYQ 2023: Statement I (States manage prisons with own rules) and Statement II (Prisons Act 1894 kept prisons with Provincial Governments) both correct; II explains I
## Beyond your notes
Entry 4 of the State List reads "Prisons, reformatories, Borstal institutions and other institutions of a like nature, and persons detained therein"; Police is Entry 2 and public order Entry 1 of the State List

t: Model prison laws → Manual 2016 and Act 2023
text:
## 1. Central guidance
Instrument | Point
Model Prison Manual, 2016 | Uniform standards: classification, medical care, vocational training; aligned with Nelson Mandela Rules
Model Prisons and Correctional Services Act, 2023 | Finalised by MHA to replace the colonial approach; reformation and rehabilitation; a guiding document for States
E-Prisons Project | Digital inmate records; prevents detention beyond sentence
Support to Poor Prisoners Scheme | MHA funds bail/fine of poor prisoners via district Empowered Committee
Open prisons | Semi-open facilities for low-risk prisoners
Nelson Mandela Rules = UN Standard Minimum Rules for treatment of prisoners
⚠ The Model Prisons Act 2023 is not binding: States must adopt it
## 2. Caste in prisons
SC (2024) asked States to remove caste-based work allocation in prison manuals; colonial Prisons Act 1894 practices blamed

t: Parole vs furlough → who grants, does it count, is it a right
text:
## 1. Comparison
Basis | Parole | Furlough
For | Short-term need (illness, death or wedding in family) | Long-term prisoners, to break monotony
Reason needed? | Yes, specific reason | No reason needed
Right? | Not a right; can be denied even if a case is made out | Treated as a matter of right (periodic)
Duration | Up to 1 month (extendable) | Up to 14 days
Counts toward sentence? | No | Yes
Granted by | Divisional Commissioner | DIG of Prisons
Frequency | Multiple times | Multiple times
Exempted from parole: crimes against the State / threat to national security; murder, child rape (unless authority decides otherwise)
⚠ Parole is not a right (2021 trap); furlough is
PYQ 2021: statement 1 (parole becomes a right once a sufficient case is made) wrong; statement 2 (States have own parole rules) right

t: Parole and furlough → legal basis and limits
text:
## 1. Law
No specific provision on parole or furlough in the Prisons Act 1894 or Prisoners Act 1900
Sec 59, Prisons Act: States make rules, including shortening sentences for good conduct
Hence each State has its own Prisoners Release on Parole Rules
Suspension of sentence is distinct from furlough
K.M. Nanavati (1960): the Governor under Art 161 cannot suspend a sentence while an appeal is pending
## 2. Delhi Prison Rules 2018
Rule 1224: no furlough while an appeal is pending in HC/SC; Delhi HC read it as only the appellate court can grant furlough then
## In news 2025-26
Delhi HC (2025) heard a challenge that denying furlough despite good conduct violates Art 14 and 21

topic: Special Laws: Official Secrets, Arms, Benami and UAPA
t: Official Secrets Act 1923 → which act falls under which section
text:
## 1. Basics
Enacted 1923 (British rule), modelled on the British OSA 1911; retained after Independence
Applies to government servants, citizens and foreigners
Does not define "secret" or "official secret"
Section | Offence
3 | Spying; access to prohibited places/sensitive data (up to 14 yrs defence-related, else 3 yrs)
4 | Contact with foreign agents (guilt presumed without valid reason)
5 | Wrongful communication of secrets, intentional or negligent
6 | Unauthorised use of police/military uniforms, falsified reports, forgery, personation
7 | Obstructing, misleading or interfering with police/armed forces on duty near a prohibited place

Rule | Source
RTI Act prevails over OSA in conflict | Sec 22, RTI Act
OSA-covered information may be disclosed if public interest outweighs harm | Sec 8(2), RTI Act
Exempt grounds (security, strategic, foreign relations) | Sec 8(1)

text:
## 1. Arms Act 1959
Governs manufacture, sale, possession and use of arms; licence needed for most firearms
Arms Rules 2016 (replacing 1962 Rules)
## 2. Arms (Amendment) Act 2019: new offences
Offence | Punishment
Celebratory gunfire endangering life/personal safety (public gatherings, religious places, weddings) | Up to 2 years, fine up to ₹1 lakh, or both
Rash or negligent use of firearm endangering others | Same as above
Snatching firearm from police/armed forces | 10 years to life + fine
## Beyond your notes
2019 amendment cut the number of licensed firearms per person from 3 to 2, raised licence validity from 3 to 5 years, and raised punishment for illegal manufacture/sale to 7 years to life (verify)
## In news 2025-26

topic: Special Laws: Official Secrets, Arms, Benami and UAPA
t: Benami law → what counts as benami
text:
## 1. Act
Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988; renamed Prohibition of Benami Property Transactions (PBPT) Act by the 2016 amendment, in force 1 November 2016
## 2. A transaction is benami if
Limb | Example
Property held by one person (not as fiduciary) for another who paid | Proxy owner
Held in a fictitious name | Fake name
Owner is unaware of or denies ownership | Unwitting name-lender
Person who financed it is not traceable | Untraceable source
⚠ Owner's unawareness does not save it: that is itself a benami limb (2017 trap)
## Beyond your notes
Not benami: property held by a Karta for an HUF; in the name of spouse/child paid from known sources; jointly with a sibling or lineal ascendant/descendant from known sources; held in a fiduciary capacity

topic: Special Laws: Official Secrets, Arms, Benami and UAPA
t: Benami law → authorities, appeal, penalties
text:
## 1. Machinery and penalties
Feature | Rule
Confiscation | Benami property liable to confiscation by the Government, without compensation
Attachment | Provisional attachment, then confiscation
Punishment | RI 1 to 7 years + fine
Adjudication | Adjudicating Authority
Appeal | Appellate Tribunal
Benami transactions are a scheduled offence under the Fugitive Economic Offenders Act, 2018 (crime value ₹100 crore+)
⚠ The Act does have an appellate mechanism (2017 trap: "no appellate mechanism")
PYQ 2017: only statement 2 (confiscation) correct
## Beyond your notes
Investigating authorities: Initiating Officer, Approving Authority, Administrator; Adjudicating Authority decides; appeal to Appellate Tribunal, then High Court
SC (2022, Ganpati Dealcom): 2016 amendment is prospective; struck down Sec 3(2) of the 1988 Act

topic: Special Laws: Official Secrets, Arms, Benami and UAPA
t: UAPA → bail bar and its limits
text:
## 1. Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967
Provision | Rule
Sec 43D(5) (2008 amendment) | Bail denied if accusation is prima facie true
Sec 43D(4) | No anticipatory bail
Investigation period | Up to 180 days (vs 60-90 under CrPC)
2019 amendment | Individuals can be designated terrorists; NIA needs only DG NIA sanction for property seizure (no State DGP approval)
Sec 15 | Defines terrorist act
Validity from reasonable restrictions under Art 19(2), (3), (4)
Zahoor Ahmad Shah Watali (2019): accept prosecution material at face value; K.A. Najeeb (2021): 43D(5) cannot override speedy trial (Art 21)
## In news 2025-26
2026: SC reaffirmed bail is the rule, jail the exception even under UAPA
Gulfisha Fatima ruling (PMF, Jan 2026): SC widened Sec 15 to include organised preparatory/conspiratorial acts; "hierarchy of participation" for bail

topic: Bureaucracy, good governance and administrative ethics in practice
t: Bureaucracy → role in India
text:
## 1. What UPSC wants
Bureaucracy (civil service) = agency for the implementation of public policy
It assists ministers in policy formulation, then implements; works under the political executive
Politically neutral, permanent, hierarchical, rule-bound (Weber's rational-legal model)
Option type | Verdict
Implementation of public policy | Correct characteristic
Widening parliamentary democracy | Role of Parliament / parties
Strengthening federalism | Constitution, Inter-State Council
Political stability and growth | Outcome, not defining trait
⚠ Bureaucracy does not take political decisions; ministers do
PYQ 2020: "characteristic appropriate for bureaucracy" → implementation of public policy
## 2. Constitutional anchors (Beyond your notes)
Art 309 (recruitment and conditions), Art 310 (doctrine of pleasure), Art 311 (safeguards: no dismissal by authority lower than appointing one; inquiry)
Art 312: All-India Services created by Parliament on a Rajya Sabha resolution (two-thirds)
⚠ 2nd ARC suggested deleting Art 311 and protecting civil servants by a law under Art 309 (PMF)

topic: Bureaucracy, good governance and administrative ethics in practice
t: Principles of public administration → which one an action shows
text:
Principle | Meaning | Example action
Accountability | Officials answerable for actions and outcomes | Report defaulting vendor to vigilance, halt contract
Transparency | Criteria, processes, decisions open | Proactive disclosure (RTI Sec 4)
Due process | No penalty on unproven allegations | Verify before blacklisting
Equity | Fair, just treatment | Targeted benefits to the poor
Esprit de corps | Team spirit among staff (Fayol) | Building unit morale
Delegation | Passing authority down | Assigning tasks to subordinates
Responsiveness | Prompt reply to citizens' needs | Time-bound grievance redress
Participation | Citizens in decisions | Public consultations, social audit
⚠ A whistle-blowing + contract-halting act = accountability, not equity or esprit de corps
PYQ 2026: vaccine distributor compromising quality; officer reports to vigilance → accountability

topic: Bureaucracy, good governance and administrative ethics in practice
t: Transparency vs due process → the "limited disclosure" logic
text:
## 1. The 2026 case
Official holds confidential, unproven adverse information on a shortlisted contractor; boss says hide it
Option | Verdict | Why
Disclose immediately to committee and public | Wrong | Breaches confidentiality, due process
Remove contractor from shortlist | Wrong | Misconduct not established
Limited disclosure to an oversight committee | Right | Balances transparency with confidentiality
⚠ Answer pattern: neither suppress nor broadcast; route to the competent oversight body
## 2. Transparency tools (PMF)
RTI 2005; proactive disclosure (Sec 4); e-governance (UMANG); Open Government Data platform; CAG audits; GeM e-procurement (cf. South Korea's KONEPS)
Limits: Sec 8 RTI exemptions; DPDP Act 2023 limits personal data disclosure; information overload; digital divide

topic: Bureaucracy, good governance and administrative ethics in practice
t: Conflict resolution with stakeholders → participatory answer
text:
## 1. The 2026 case
Waste-management plant on land a tribal community calls sacred; urban residents and industry support it
Step | Verdict
Acknowledge cultural and emotional concerns of the tribal community | Helps

t: Janani Suraksha Yojana → objective and features
text:
## 1. What JSY is
Safe motherhood intervention under the National (Rural) Health Mission – not of the State Health Departments
Launched April 2005, replacing the National Maternity Benefit Scheme (NMBS)
Centrally sponsored; implemented by States
Conditional cash transfer that promotes institutional delivery among poor pregnant women
Objective: reduce maternal AND neonatal mortality (not maternal only, not infant only)
Cash is given irrespective of age of mother and number of children for delivery in a government or accredited private facility
Special dispensation for States with low institutional delivery rates
ASHA is the link between government and pregnant women
## 2. Cash assistance (CDI Indian Society)
Delivery | Cash to mother
Institutional, rural | Rs 1,400
Institutional, urban | Rs 1,000
Home delivery (BPL) | Rs 500
⚠ JSY gives money to meet the cost of delivery; it does NOT compensate wage loss – that is PMMVY
⚠ JSY does NOT give free treatment to sick infants up to one year – that is JSSK
PYQ 2023: how many of four JSY statements are correct – only two (reduce maternal/neonatal mortality; promote institutional delivery); trap: "State Health Department intervention" and "sick infants up to one year"

## 1. Four schemes UPSC mixes up
Scheme | Year | Ministry | Core benefit
JSY | 2005 | MoHFW (NHM) | Cash for institutional delivery
JSSK | 1 June 2011 | MoHFW (NHM) | Free, cashless delivery incl. C-section, drugs, diagnostics, diet, blood, transport
PMSMA | 2016 | MoHFW (NHM) | Free antenatal check-up by specialists on the 9th of every month
PMMVY | 2017 | MoWCD | Rs 5,000 maternity benefit; partial compensation for wage loss
## 2. JSSK details
Eliminates out-of-pocket expenses for pregnant women and sick newborns/infants in public health institutions
Covers normal and caesarean deliveries; free transport home to facility, between facilities on referral, and drop-back
Exemption from all user charges
Sick newborn originally up to 30 days; extended to sick infants up to 1 year
⚠ "Free treatment for sick infants" → JSSK; "cash for delivery" → JSY; "wage loss" → PMMVY
⚠ PMMVY is under Women and Child Development, the other three under Health and Family Welfare
