t: PMSMA → what it guarantees and who provides it
text:
## 1. Core features (PMF)
Launched 9 June 2016; flagship of MoHFW; under RMNCAH+N strategy of NHM
Assured, comprehensive, quality antenatal care (ANC) free of cost, especially in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters
Fixed day: the 9th of every month at government health facilities (PHC/CHC/DH, rural and urban)
Eligibility: all pregnant women, especially unregistered, adolescent, early and high-risk pregnancies; missed/dropped-out ANC cases
Principle: every pregnant woman gets at least one check-up by a physician/specialist in the 2nd or 3rd trimester
## 2. Minimum service package
Item | Included
Clinical examination, blood and urine tests | Yes
One ultrasound | Yes
Iron-folic acid AND calcium supplements | Yes
Risk marking | Green sticker = no risk; Red sticker = high-risk
Six months post-delivery care | No
## 3. Private sector
OBGY specialists, radiologists, physicians in the private sector volunteer at government facilities where public specialists are unavailable
Doctors pledge one day a month (12 days a year); IPledgeFor9 awards; national portal and mobile app
⚠ PMSMA does give calcium (unlike Anaemia Mukt Bharat); but it does NOT guarantee post-delivery care

text:
## 1. Basics
Launched 2018; MoHFW; life-cycle approach
Target: cut anaemia by 3 percentage points a year in children, adolescents, women
6 beneficiaries x 6 interventions x 6 institutional mechanisms
## 2. The six interventions
# | Intervention
1 | Prophylactic iron-folic acid (IFA) supplementation
2 | Periodic deworming of children and adolescents
3 | Year-round behaviour change campaign – incl. delayed cord clamping (3 minutes)
4 | Testing and treatment – digital methods, point-of-care
5 | IFA-fortified foods in government programmes
6 | Non-nutritional causes in endemic pockets – malaria, haemoglobinopathies, fluorosis
⚠ No calcium – AMB gives iron-folic acid, not calcium (calcium is in PMSMA)

Who | Adult members of any rural household willing to do unskilled manual work (citizens, 18+)
Days | At least 100 days per household per year (Section 3(1))
Extra days | 150 days in drought/calamity areas and for ST households with FRA rights; States may give more at own cost
Women | At least one-third of beneficiaries
Time limit | Work within 15 days of demand, else unemployment allowance
Distance | Within 5 km, else 10% extra wages
⚠ Not limited to BPL, SC/ST or backward households: any rural household
⚠ The guarantee is per household, not per person
PYQ 2011: answer = adult members of any household

topic: Political Parties and the Party System
t: Political party → meaning, components, functions
text:
## 1. Meaning (NCERT)
A group of people who come together to contest elections and hold power in the government
Parties are about a part of society, so they involve partisanship
## 2. Three components
Component | Role
Leaders | Decide policy, pick candidates
Active members | Run the organisation
Followers | Support the party
## 3. Seven functions (NCERT)
Contest elections; put forward policies and programmes; make laws; form and run governments; play opposition; shape public opinion; give people access to government machinery and welfare schemes
⚠ In the USA, members and supporters choose candidates (primaries); in India, top party leaders choose them
⚠ Inner-party democracy = periodical elections within the party to elect office-bearers. It does not mean a coalition government

topic: Political Parties and the Party System
t: Party systems → one-party, two-party, multi-party
text:
System | Meaning | Example
One-party | Only one party allowed to control government | China (Communist Party)
Two-party | Power usually alternates between two main parties | USA, UK
Multi-party | More than two parties have a reasonable chance of power, alone or in alliance | India
Alliance or front: several parties join hands to contest elections and win power. 2004 examples: NDA, UPA, Left Front
NCERT: a one-party system is not a democratic option, because a democracy must allow at least two parties to compete
NCERT: a party system evolves from a society's social and regional divisions, its political history and its electoral system. A country does not choose it
⚠ India's multi-party system comes from its social, linguistic and regional diversity (PMF), not just from "too many parties"
Likely angle: matching country to party system; trap: UK and USA are two-party even though other parties exist and win some seats

topic: Political Parties and the Party System
t: Party system in India → phases and features
text:
## 1. Phases (PMF)
Phase | Feature
One-party dominance | INC dominated for decades: the "Congress system" (Rajni Kothari)
Competitive politics | National and regional parties grew; a party may be strong at Union level, in some States, or both
Coalitions | Two or more parties govern together. Since 1996, nearly every State party has been part of a national coalition (NCERT)
## 2. Markers
1989 Lok Sabha election ended the "Congress system". INC was still the single largest party (197 seats); V.P. Singh's National Front formed the government with outside support from BJP and the Left
NCERT: coalitions have strengthened federalism
PMF internal challenges: personality or family-centred leadership, factionalism, weak internal elections, opaque funding
NCERT's four challenges: lack of internal democracy, dynastic succession, money and muscle power, no meaningful choice between parties
⚠ Rajni Kothari, not Myron Weiner, called it the one-party dominant system (State PCS PYQ)

topic: Political Parties and the Party System

text:
Source | What it gives parties
Art 19(1)(c) | Right to form associations, including political parties
Tenth Schedule (52nd Amendment, 1985) | First constitutional recognition of parties; uses the term "political party"
Sec 29A, RP Act 1951 | Registration by the ECI
Symbols Order, 1968 | Recognition as National or State party, and reserved symbols
Art 324 | ECI's power of superintendence, under which it registers parties
52nd Amendment Bill was passed on 15 Feb 1985 and came into force on 1 March 1985
The word "political party" is not in the original Constitution; it entered through the Tenth Schedule
⚠ "The Constitution does not mention 'political party'" is false: the Tenth Schedule uses it
PYQ 2025 (IAS Pre): two statements: "President decides Tenth Schedule disqualification on the Council of Ministers' advice" and "no mention of 'political party' in the Constitution". Answer: neither. The Speaker or Chairman decides; the Tenth Schedule names parties
PYQ (UPPCS 2010): parties first got constitutional recognition in 1985

topic: Political Parties and the Party System
t: Party founders → Ambedkar, Swatantra and movement-born parties
text:
## 1. Ambedkar's parties
Independent Labour Party (1936), Scheduled Castes Federation (1942). Not the Peasants and Workers Party (1948)
## 2. Other founders
Swatantra Party: C. Rajagopalachari. Socialist Party: JP, Lohia, Acharya Narendra Dev
Movement-born parties (NCERT): Asom Gana Parishad came out of the Assam students' movement; DMK and AIADMK go back to the social reform movement of the 1930s-40s
PYQ 2012: Ambedkar founded the ILP and the SC Federation, not the PWP. PYQ 2024: of four party-leader pairs, only BJS-Mookerjee and CFD-Jagjivan Ram were correct (only two)
PYQ 1995: Muslim League, RSP, Forward Bloc and PWP: none is a national party

topic: Registration and Recognition of Parties by the ECI
t: Registration → law, conditions, benefits
text:
## 1. Law
Sec 29A, RP Act 1951: the ECI registers parties, using its power under Art 324
Apply within 30 days of formation, with: the party constitution, affidavits from 100 members, a non-refundable fee of ₹10,000
The party constitution must pledge allegiance to the Constitution and to socialism, secularism, democracy, and to the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India
## 2. Registration vs recognition
Step | Law | Gives
Registration | Sec 29A, RPA 1951 | Can contest as a party, tax exemption, donations, common symbol on conditions
Recognition | Symbols Order, 1968 | National or State status, reserved symbol
⚠ Registration does not automatically give National or State status
⚠ PMF 2027: registration is not mandatory (registered parties get preference over independents for free symbols). ! NCERT says "every party has to register". Follow PMF
Over 2,800 registered parties (2025); 97% are unrecognised (ADR)

topic: Registration and Recognition of Parties by the ECI
t: National party → three alternative criteria and the six parties
text:
## 1. Criteria (any ONE, last general election)
No. | Votes | Seats
1 | 6% valid votes in 4 or more States (LS or Assembly) | + 4 Lok Sabha seats
2 | none | 2% of LS seats (11 of 543) from at least 3 States
3 | Recognised as a State party in 4 States | none
## 2. Recognised national parties: six
AAP, BSP, BJP, CPI(M), INC, NPP
⚠ Not national parties now: CPI, NCP, AITC (AITC got national status on 2 Sept 2016, now lost), Samajwadi Party, TDP, Akali Dal
⚠ Option traps: "5% votes", "10% in four States", "6% in more than half the States", "state party in three States": all wrong
## Beyond your notes
ECI withdrew national status from CPI, NCP and AITC and granted it to AAP in April 2023; NPP became a national party in 2019 (first from the North-East)

topic: Registration and Recognition of Parties by the ECI
t: State party → five alternative criteria
text:
No. | Election | Votes | Seats
1 | Assembly | 6% | + 2 Assembly seats
2 | Lok Sabha | 6% in the State | + 1 LS seat from it
3 | Assembly | none | 3% of seats or 3 seats, whichever is more
4 | Lok Sabha | none | 1 LS seat per 25 (or fraction) allotted to the State
5 | LS or Assembly | 8% | no seat needed
Status applies only in the State(s) where criteria are met; the party may still contest anywhere
Of the major parties, those outside the six national ones are classed as State parties (regional parties), even if some (SP, RJD) have national-level organisation (NCERT)
⚠ 8% votes with zero seats is enough for State status (criterion 5)
⚠ NCERT gives only criterion 1 (6% + 2 seats) and the old national rule (6% in 4 States + 4 LS seats): incomplete
Likely angle: "How many of the following entitle a party to State status?" Count all five

topic: Registration and Recognition of Parties by the ECI
t: RUPPs → benefits, duties, deregistration
text:
## 1. What
Registered under Sec 29A, but not yet recognised as State or National party
## 2. Benefits and duties
Benefits | Compliance
Tax exemption on donations (Sec 13A, IT Act 1961) | Apply within 30 days of formation
Common symbol if it contests 2 LS seats or 5% of Assembly seats | Report donations above ₹20,000 annually
20 star campaigners (travel outside candidate expenditure ceiling) | Take donations above ₹2,000 only by cheque or bank transfer
Can receive donations | Contest at least one election every 6 years

topic: Registration and Recognition of Parties by the ECI
t: RUPPs → deregistration vs delisting, and 2025-26 news
text:
## 1. Deregistration
INC v. Institute of Social Welfare (2002): ECI has no general power to deregister. Only for (1) fraud in registration, (2) disavowing allegiance to the Constitution, (3) being declared unlawful by government
Delisting (removal from the ECI list after show-cause and hearing) is different from deregistration
Law Commission 255th Report (2015): let ECI deregister parties that do not contest for 10 consecutive years; ECI memo 2016 agreed. 170th and 255th Reports: law on internal democracy
## In news 2025-26
July 2025: ECI began delisting 345 RUPPs that had not contested in 6 years and had no traceable office
Sept 2026: only about 750 of 2,800+ RUPPs contested the 2024 general election
Sept 2026 (ADR): RUPPs' declared income jumped 223%
⚠ PMF Sept 2026 gives the tax exemption as "Section 12 of the Income Tax Act, 2025"; older PMF pages give Sec 13A, IT Act 1961

topic: Registration and Recognition of Parties by the ECI
t: Election symbols → reserved, free and disputed
text:
Type | Who gets it | Scope
Reserved | National party | All India
Reserved | State party | Only in the State(s) where it is recognised
Free | RUPP candidates and independents | Chosen from the free list; not guaranteed
Common symbol | RUPP meeting conditions | For one election
Symbols Order, 1968 governs allotment; ECI decides rival claims to a recognised party's name and symbol after a split, subject to judicial review
A symbol decision does not decide Tenth Schedule disqualification; that is decided separately by the Speaker or Chairman
Two recognised parties in different States may hold the same symbol
No animal symbols since the 1990s; BSP's elephant is a grandfathered exception
## In news 2025-26
Free symbols list (May 2025): 184 symbols
2026: satirical "Cockroach Janta Party" (a youth pressure group, not registered). Even if registered it would be unrecognised and could not get an animal symbol
## Beyond your notes
Sadiq Ali v. ECI (1971) upheld the Symbols Order and the ECI's power to decide splits

topic: Party Funding, Transparency and Internal Democracy
t: Party funding → limits and rules
text:
Rule | Figure | Law
Report contributions above | ₹20,000 (per person or company) | Sec 29C, RPA
Cash donation limit for tax exemption | ₹2,000 | Income Tax Act
Tax exemption on contributions | 100% | Sec 13A, IT Act 1961
Who may donate | Individuals and non-government companies; no govt-owned entities | Sec 29B, RPA
Corporate donations | Board approval, party-wise disclosure; 7.5% profit cap restored after 2024 ruling | Sec 182, Companies Act 2013
Electoral trusts | Must pass at least 95% of collections to registered parties | CBDT-approved
⚠ The ₹20,000 disclosure and ₹2,000 cash limit are separate requirements
⚠ Candidates have spending caps (Rule 90); parties have no limit on total election expenditure

topic: Party Funding, Transparency and Internal Democracy
t: Electoral bonds and foreign funding of parties
text:
## 1. Electoral bonds
ADR v. Union of India (2024): SC struck down the Electoral Bond Scheme; voters' right to know donors is part of Art 19(1)(a); it also struck down unlimited corporate donations. Bonds are no longer operative
## 2. Foreign funding
FCRA amended retrospectively (2016): Indian subsidiaries of foreign companies (over 50% foreign shareholding) can fund parties; Delhi HC (2014) had found BJP and INC in breach over Vedanta donations
## In news 2025-26
22 parties had ₹18,742.31 crore available in the 2024 election (ADR, Sept 2026)

topic: Party Funding, Transparency and Internal Democracy
t: Parties under RTI and other judgments
text:
## 1. RTI
CIC (2013) declared six national parties "public authorities" under Sec 2(h) of the RTI Act; parties resisted and compliance remains disputed
RTI Amendment Bill 2013 to exclude parties did not pass
Reasons given (Testbook): free airtime on DD and AIR, cheap office space, LoP sits on selection panels (CIC, Lokpal, CBI, CVC)
## 2. Judgments
Case | Held
Common Cause v. UoI (1996) | No blanket exemption from disclosing poll expenses
INC v. Institute of Social Welfare (2002) | ECI cannot generally deregister parties
ADR v. UoI (2024) | Electoral bonds struck down
Subhash Desai v. Governor of Maharashtra (2023) | Whip is appointed by the political party, not the legislature party
⚠ Testbook says an SC 2018 verdict made parties disclose income "under RTI": no PMF source confirms; treat as unverified

topic: Party Funding, Transparency and Internal Democracy
t: Reforms → committees on parties and funding
text:
Body | Recommendation
Indrajit Gupta Committee | Partial state funding, mainly in kind
Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990) | Electoral reforms
Law Commission 170th (1999), 255th (2015) | Internal democracy law; ECI power to deregister
2nd ARC (Ethics in Governance) | Partial state funding; defection cases to President or Governor on ECI advice
NCRWC | Defer state funding until party regulation improves
Election and Other Related Laws (Amendment) Act, 2003 | 100% tax exemption, disclosure above ₹20,000, indirect public funding (free electoral rolls, media time)
NCERT suggestions: law on internal party affairs, one-third tickets to women, state funding in kind or cash; the ECI already makes parties hold organisational elections and file income tax returns
PMF reforms: independent CAG-empanelled auditors (amend Sec 29C), end anonymous cash under ₹2,000, spending caps on parties
⚠ Indrajit Gupta Committee year: 1998 (PMF); ! 2nd ARC report says 1999
Likely angle: matching committee to recommendation; trap: Indrajit Gupta = state funding, not anti-defection

topic: Party Funding, Transparency and Internal Democracy
t: Tenth Schedule → how it treats political parties
text:
52nd Amendment (1985) inserted the Tenth Schedule and amended Arts 101, 102, 190, 191; 91st Amendment (2003) removed the one-third split exception
Ground | Rule
Voluntarily gives up party membership | Disqualified (can be inferred from conduct: Ravi S. Naik 1994)
Votes or abstains against party whip | Disqualified unless the party condones within 15 days
Independent joins a party | Disqualified
Nominated member joins a party | Disqualified only after 6 months
Merger (para 4) | Protected if two-thirds of the legislature party agree
No whip for Rajya Sabha or Presidential elections (ECI 2017); RS uses open ballot (Kuldip Nayar 2006)
⚠ Details of the Tenth Schedule belong to the Elections and Anti-defection topic

topic: Party Funding, Transparency and Internal Democracy
t: Defections and party mergers → 2025-26 cases
text:
Merger test: two-thirds of the legislature party; the Speaker or Chairman decides, subject to judicial review (Kihoto Hollohan 1992); petitions ordinarily within 3 months (Keisham Meghachandra 2020)
## In news 2025-26
April 2026: 7 of AAP's 10 RS MPs (exactly two-thirds) claimed merger with BJP; Chairman to decide
June 2026: merger of 20 TMC MPs with the National People's Congress of India (NPCI)
Sept 2026 (ADR): 111 sitting legislators switched parties in 2022-26 (26 LS MPs, 7 RS MPs, 78 MLAs); Nagaland highest (32), then West Bengal (20), Telangana (9)
18 Sept 2026: Telangana HC disqualified MLA Danam Nagender (BRS to Congress) under para 2(1)(a), setting aside the Speaker's decision

t: Pressure groups vs political parties → the distinguishing feature
text:
Point | Pressure group | Political party
Aim | Influence government policy | Win and hold power
Elections | Does not put up candidates | Contests elections
Accountability | Not answerable to voters | Faces people in elections
Political stance | Takes positions on issues | Takes positions on issues
Base | Common occupation, interest or opinion | Broad programme for society
NCERT definition: organisations that attempt to influence government policies but do not aim to directly control or share political power
Also called interest groups or lobby groups
⚠ Both take political stances; the only distinguishing feature is that pressure groups do not seek power
⚠ "All pressure groups are political parties": false
Likely angle: "Which may be a pressure group?" Answer type: members of a trade union; not MPs, panchayat members or the Cabinet (State PCS PYQ)

t: Types → sectional, public interest and movements
text:
Type | Feature | Examples
Sectional interest group | Betterment of its own members | Trade unions, business associations, professional bodies (lawyers, doctors, teachers), fertiliser dealers' association
Public interest (promotional) group | Collective good; members may not benefit | Group against bonded labour, FEDECOR (Bolivia), BAMCEF (both)
Single-issue movement | One goal, short time frame; clear leadership | Narmada Bachao Andolan, Nepal democracy movement
Long-term (generic) movement | Many issues, no single controlling organisation | Women's movement, environmental movement
Umbrella body | Organisation of organisations | NAPM
Movements: loose organisation, informal decisions, depend on spontaneous mass participation
BAMCEF: mostly government employees; campaigns against caste discrimination for all society
## Beyond your notes
Almond and Powell's four types: institutional (e.g. civil servants' associations), associational (trade unions), anomic (riots, spontaneous protests), non-associational (kinship, caste, religion groups)
Likely angle: matching (NCERT model): pressure group = fertiliser dealers' association; single-issue = NBA; long-term = women's movement; party = Asom Gana Parishad

t: Techniques → how pressure groups influence politics
text:
## 1. Methods (NCERT)
Information campaigns, meetings, petitions; win media attention
Protest: strikes, disrupting government programmes (workers, employees, movements)
Lobbying and expensive advertisements (business groups)
Members sit on official advisory bodies
## 2. Relationship with parties
Form | Example
Formed or led by party leaders; extended arms | Most trade unions and student bodies
Party grows out of a movement | AGP (Assam movement), DMK/AIADMK
Separate but in dialogue | Movements raise new issues that parties take up
## 3. Trade unions and their parties
Union | Party
BMS | BJP
INTUC | INC
AITUC | CPI
UTUC | RSP
Mewat case (NCERT): civil groups forced INC and INLD to back a new district (created July 2005)
## In news 2025-26
Nari Adalats (Mission Shakti, Sambal sub-scheme): no legal status; function as a pressure group; 7-11 Nyaya Sakhis

topic: Civil Society, NGOs and Self-Help Groups
t: Civil society → meaning and roles
text:
Organisations and groups that work independently of the government and the private sector (Testbook)
Role | Example
Advocacy | Human rights, gender, environment
Service delivery | Health, education, disaster relief
Watchdog | Transparency International India
Policy influence | RTI Act grew from civil society campaigns
## National Policy on the Voluntary Sector, 2007
Covers voluntary organisations (VOs): community-based organisations, NGDOs, charities, support organisations, networks, professional associations
Four aims: an enabling environment that keeps VOs autonomous; let VOs raise funds from India and abroad; find ways for government and VOs to work together; make VOs adopt transparent, accountable governance
Term "NGO" was coined in the UN Charter (1945)
World Bank definition: private organisations that relieve suffering, promote the poor's interests, protect the environment, provide basic services or undertake community development

topic: Civil Society, NGOs and Self-Help Groups
t: NGOs → laws under which they register
text:
Law | Form of NGO
Societies Registration Act, 1860 | Society (memorandum of association)
Indian Trusts Act, 1882 | Public charitable trust (trust deed)
Companies Act, 2013 | Section 8 company (not for profit)
FCRA, 2010 | Needed only to receive foreign contribution
Income Tax Act, 1961 | Tax exemption under 12A and 80G
State laws | e.g. Maharashtra Public Trusts Act, 1950
Some international donors (Ford Foundation, UK's DFID) were registered under FEMA, not FCRA (Testbook)
⚠ FCRA is not a registration law for all NGOs; it applies only to those taking foreign funds
## Beyond your notes
NGO Darpan (NITI Aayog portal) gives NGOs a unique ID to apply for government grants

topic: Civil Society, NGOs and Self-Help Groups
t: Self-Help Groups → definition and evolution
text:
NABARD: "a homogeneous group of rural poor voluntarily formed to save whatever amount they can conveniently save... and mutually agree to contribute to a common fund" for emergent credit needs
Principle: "Savings first, credit later"; internal lending; collective guarantee for bank loans; mostly women
Year | Milestone
1954 | Textile Labour Association (TLA), Ahmedabad: women's wing, first organised effort
1975 | Muhammad Yunus (Chittagong University), Bangladesh
1980s | MYRADA (Karnataka NGO)
1986-87 | First SHG credit through NABARD
1991-92 | SHGs linked with banks (main push)
South India (AP, TN, Karnataka, Kerala) holds about 44% of bank-linked SHGs
## In news 2025-26: DAY-NRLM (Nov 2025)
Ministry of Rural Development; launched 2011 (restructured SGSY), renamed 2016
Centrally Sponsored, 75:25 (Centre:State); 90:10 for NE and special category States
Over 10 crore women in 90 lakh SHGs; ₹11 lakh crore collateral-free loans; repayment over 98%
⚠ DAY-NRLM is not a Central Sector scheme and not under the Agriculture Ministry

t: FCRA → evolution and key provisions
text:
Year | Change
1976 | Enacted during the Emergency over fear of foreign interference
2010 | FCRA 2010 replaced it; bars use of foreign funds for activities detrimental to national interest
2016 | Retrospective change: Indian subsidiaries of foreign firms not "foreign source"
2018 | Further amendment
2020 | Aadhaar of office-bearers; admin expenses capped at 20%; designated SBI account, New Delhi; no transfer to other NGOs
2023 | No intimation for gifts below ₹10 lakh from relatives abroad
Nodal ministry: MHA; Intelligence Bureau does background checks
Two routes: FCRA registration or prior permission (specific donor, amount, project)
⚠ FCRA was enacted in 1976, not 2010; 2010 is the replacement Act
## Beyond your notes
The 2020 amendment cut the admin expense ceiling from 50% to 20% and added public servants to the barred list

t: Who cannot receive foreign contribution → the full list
text:
Barred category
Election candidates
Political parties and their office-bearers
Members of legislatures
Judges
Government servants
Journalists
Newspaper and broadcast-media companies
Organisations of a political nature
Reason (PMF): keep institutional neutrality and democratic integrity
⚠ NGOs are not barred; they must register or get prior permission
Likely angle (PMF practice 2025): "How many of the following cannot receive foreign contribution: candidates, judges, civil servants, parties, media?" Answer: all five

t: FCRA registration → validity, renewal, cancellation
text:
Item | Rule
MHA decision on application | Within 90 days
Validity | 5 years
Renewal application | Within 6 months before expiry
Suspension during inquiry | Up to 180 days, with funds frozen
Ban after cancellation | 3 years on re-registration
Report of receipt (Testbook) | Within 30 days
Appeal | Orders can be challenged in High Court
Eligibility: no forced conversion activity, no communal disharmony, no diversion of funds, not against national interest
Cancellation grounds: false statements, violations, no activity for 2 consecutive years, defunct NGO, misuse of funds, public interest; notice and hearing first
Testbook: about 20,000 NGO licences revoked in two years

t: FCRA → In news 2025-26
text:
## In news 2025-26
Oct 2025: MHA cancelled FCRA registration of Sonam Wangchuk's SECMOL (Ladakh protests)
April 2026: FCRA Amendment Bill, 2026
Proposal | What it changes
Designated authority | Manages or disposes of assets made with foreign funds when registration is cancelled, surrendered or expires
Wider "key functionary" | Directors, trustees, partners, governing members
Officials liable | Unless they prove due diligence
Prior Central approval | Before State agencies start FCRA probes
Automatic cancellation | On non-renewal or expiry
Penalty | Max jail cut from 5 years to 1 year
June 2026: FCRA Rules amended (MHA): state activities and States/UTs of operation; foreign citizens (except PIOs) as key functionaries make an NGO ineligible; spend at least ₹10 lakh in 2 years to renew; prior-permission holders use 75% of an instalment before the next; proselytisation cannot be funded (religious education can); disclose social-media accounts and original donors
⚠ The prison cut (5 to 1 year) is in the Bill, not the Rules

t: 97th Amendment (2011) → three changes
text:
Change | Where
Right to form cooperative societies | Art 19(1)(c) (FR), with associations and unions
State to promote voluntary formation, autonomous functioning, democratic control, professional management | New Art 43B (DPSP)
Framework for cooperatives | New Part IXB, Arts 243ZH to 243ZT (after Part IXA)
Legislative entry | Body
Entry 32, State List | State cooperatives: State Acts, State Registrar
Entry 44, Union List | Multi-State cooperatives: MSCS Act 2002, Central Registrar
⚠ Part IXB is Part IX-B, not IX-A (IX-A is Municipalities)
⚠ It is Art 43B, not 43A (43A = workers in management)

t: Part IXB → numbers to remember
text:
Provision | Rule
Board size | Up to 21 directors
Co-opted members | Up to 2 (expertise); cannot vote in elections or be office-bearers
Reservation on board | 1 SC/ST seat, 2 women seats
Term | 5 years
Supersession | Not more than 6 months; not if no govt shareholding, loan or guarantee
Audit | Once a year, within 6 months of year end
AGM and returns | Within 6 months of year end
Elections | By the body named in the law, not the ECI
⚠ Board elections are not conducted by the ECI
Supersession grounds: persistent default, negligence, acts against the society, stalemate, failure to hold elections

t: Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (2021) → scope of Part IXB
text:
SC: Part IXB cannot apply to State cooperatives, because the 97th Amendment touched a State subject and was not ratified by half the States
Survives: Part IXB for multi-State cooperatives and those in UTs; Art 19(1)(c) and Art 43B stay intact
Cooperative banks: registered under cooperative law, banking functions regulated by RBI (BR Act 1949); NABARD supervises rural cooperative banks
Urban Cooperative Banks: under the BR Act since 1966; can issue equity and preference shares
⚠ Struck down only for State cooperatives; not the whole Amendment
PYQ 2021: UCBs are not regulated by State-set local boards; statements 2 and 3 correct (shares; BR Act from 1966)

t: Cooperatives → evolution and 2025-26 news
text:
Year | Event
1904 | Cooperative Credit Societies Act
1915 | Maclagan Committee
1919 | Montagu-Chelmsford reforms: cooperation a provincial subject
2002 | MSCS Act; National Policy on Cooperatives
2011 | 97th Amendment
2021 | Ministry of Cooperation ("Sahkar se Samriddhi")
2023 | MSCS (Amendment) Act: Cooperative Election Authority, Cooperative Ombudsman
Nehru: cooperatives, panchayats and schools are three pillars of democracy
⚠ Ministry of Cooperation (2021) did not shift State cooperatives to Parliament
## In news 2025-26
2025: International Year of Cooperatives (UNGA); launched at the ICA Global Conference hosted by India; host body COPAC (Geneva)
National Cooperative Policy 2025 (July 2025): 3rd national policy; Suresh Prabhu Committee; one cooperative in every village; 30% more cooperatives by 2030; triple GDP share by 2034; 6 pillars
Tribhuvan Sahkari University: India's first cooperative university
White Revolution 2.0: milk procurement up 50% in 5 years through 20,000+ new dairy cooperatives
Jan 2026: one-third of PACS inactive in MP and UP audits

t: Site → what it is famous for (the 2021 and 2024 pairs)
text:
Site | State | Famous for
Burzahom | Kashmir (16 km NW of Srinagar) | Neolithic pit dwellings, bone tools, dogs buried with masters
Ganeshwar | Sikar, Rajasthan (near Khetri) | Copper artefacts (over 1,000); pre-Harappan chalcolithic
Daimabad | Ahmednagar, Maharashtra (Pravara) | Bronze hoard: chariot, elephant, rhino, buffalo
Chandraketugarh | West Bengal (35 km NE of Kolkata, Bidyadhari) | Terracotta art; port town, pre-Mauryan to Pala-Sena
Inamgaon | Pune, Maharashtra (Ghod, tributary of Bhima) | Chalcolithic (Malwa, Jorwe phases)
Mangadu | Kerala | Megalithic burials
Salihundam | AP (Vamsadhara) | Buddhist stupa site, not a rock-cut shrine
⚠ Burzahom is not known for rock-cut shrines; Chandraketugarh is in WB, not Odisha
PYQ 2021: Burzahom-rock-cut shrines (wrong), Chandraketugarh-terracotta, Ganeshwar-copper: answer 2 and 3
PYQ 2024 (other topic): only Inamgaon-chalcolithic and Mangadu-megalithic rows were right

t: Neolithic sites → region, crop and feature
text:
Site | Region | Grain / feature
Mehrgarh | Baluchistan | Earliest farming (7000 BCE); wheat, barley; mud-brick houses; goats in burials
Burzahom, Gufkral | Kashmir | Wheat, lentil; pit dwellings; no microliths
Koldihwa, Mahagara | Belan valley, UP | Rice; Mahagara cattle hoof marks
Chirand | Bihar | Many bone tools; wheat, barley
Daojali Hading | Assam | Jadeite (from China), fossil-wood tools, mortars
Hallur, Maski, Brahmagiri | Karnataka | Millet; cattle (southern neolithic)
Utnur (Telangana), Paiyampalli (TN), Nagarjunakonda (AP) | South | Ash mounds, black gram
Axe types: NW rectangular, curved edge; South oval sides, pointed butt; NE polished, shouldered hoes
Gordon Childe coined "Neolithic Revolution"
⚠ Lahuradeva (Sant Kabir Nagar, UP) has early rice; PMF: if it is an option for "earliest farming", pick it, else Mehrgarh
⚠ Belan valley sites grew out of a mesolithic base (Chopani-Mando); Mehrgarh had no mesolithic phase

t: Chalcolithic cultures → region and hallmark
text:
Culture | Region / sites | Hallmark
Ahar (Banas) | SE Rajasthan: Ahar (Tambavati), Balathal, Gilund | Copper smelting; no microliths; Gilund burnt bricks
Kayatha | Ujjain, MP | Sequence Kayatha → Ahar → Malwa
Malwa | MP; also Navdatoli, Daimabad, Inamgaon | Malwa ware, richest chalcolithic pottery
Jorwe | Maharashtra (Pravara-Godavari core), 1400-700 BCE | Black-on-red matt ware; gold only here; Daimabad, Inamgaon near urban
Prabhas, Rangpur | Gujarat | Lustrous Red Ware
Ganeshwar-Jodhpura | NE Rajasthan, 2800-2000 BCE | Copper supplier to Harappa; OCP pottery
Chalcolithic people: no plough or hoe in central/west India; did not milk animals; no horse; copper from Khetri
Technologically pre-Harappan though mostly post-Harappan in date: no bronze, no writing, no cities
Burials: Maharashtra north-south in urns under house floors; South India east-west
⚠ Jorwe covers all Maharashtra except Konkan (and parts of Vidarbha); no shifting agriculture (CDS 2024)

t: Daimabad and Inamgaon → phases and finds
text:
## 1. Daimabad (largest Jorwe site, about 20 ha)
Period | Culture
I (2300-2100 BCE) | Savalda
II (2100-1800 BCE) | Late Harappan
III | Daimabad
IV | Malwa
V (1400-1000 BCE) | Jorwe
Southernmost Late Harappan site
Bronze hoard: elephant, rhinoceros, buffalo and the Daimabad man on a two-wheeled chariot drawn by two yoked oxen, a dog on the pole
⚠ Daimabad chariot is drawn by oxen (bulls), not horses; PMF infographic says "horses": follow the main text
## 2. Inamgaon and social signs
Female figurines (Inamgaon, Nevasa): fertility goddesses
Chief in rectangular houses, others in round huts; child burials with copper necklaces at Chandoli, Nevasa → inequality
High infant mortality (child burials in western Maharashtra)

t: Megalithic sites → state
text:
State | Sites
Karnataka | Maski, Hallur, Piklihal, Hanamsagar, Brahmagiri

Megaliths are mostly iron age, some late neolithic/chalcolithic: "megalithic cultures" (plural)

## Beyond your notes
Bhimbetka (MP): rock shelters with paintings, UNESCO 2003; Bagor (Rajasthan): mesolithic

Site | Region | Finding

t: Odd one out → Harappan or not (2019)
text:
Place | Harappan? | Fact
Chanhudaro | Yes | Sindh craft town
Kot Diji | Yes | Early Harappan, Sindh
Desalpur | Yes | Gujarat (Kutch)
Sohgaura | No | Gorakhpur, UP: Mauryan plate on famine relief

Twin record: Mahasthan inscription (Bangladesh), famine relief with gandaka coins

PYQ 2019: "not a Harappan site": Sohgaura
## Likely next: Gujarat and Baluchistan sites

t: Dholavira → water management and other firsts
text:
Feature | Fact
Location | Khadir bet, Great Rann of Kutch (Kachchh Desert WLS); locally Kotada Timba
Water | 16 reservoirs fed by Manhar and Mansar rivulets; dams and channels; largest reservoir 73 m
Layout | Three parts: citadel, middle town, lower town
Material | Stone (sandstone) fortifications, polished limestone pillars
Inscription | Ten large signs ("signboard")
Stadium | Open ground with stepped stands (R.S. Bisht: earliest stadium)
UNESCO | 2021: first IVC site in India; India's 40th WHS, Gujarat's 4th
Other finds: bronze mirror, chisel, stone gameboard, tumulus burials like stupas
Polished pillars push monumental stone art back from the Mauryas to the 3rd millennium BCE
PYQ 2021: dams + channels + connected reservoirs = Dholavira, not Kalibangan, Rakhigarhi or Ropar

t: Lothal and Rakhigarhi → port and largest site
text:
## 1. Lothal
"Mound of the dead" (Gujarati) like Mohenjodaro (Sindhi); on Bhogava, a tributary of Sabarmati
Dockyard (one of earliest tidal docks), storehouse with seals, citadel not walled off
Mud-brick houses, burnt-brick drains; copper dog and bird
Other ports: Khirsara, Kuntasi (India), Sutkagendor, Balakot (Pakistan)
## 2. Rakhigarhi
Hisar, Haryana; largest Harappan site; Early to Mature phases
Seven-chamber granary, fire altars, gold foundry, gemstone factory, chert weights
Cylindrical steatite seal with alligator motif; only site with ancient DNA: no "Steppe" gene
⚠ River: PMF book says Sarasvati, PMF CA 2026 says Drishadvati, P-MCA says near Ghaggar
## In news 2025-26
June 2026: ASI sent Rakhigarhi skeletons (Mound 7) to the Anthropological Survey of India, Kolkata
Aug 2026: India-Singapore MoU on maritime heritage around the National Maritime Heritage Complex, Lothal (Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways)

t: Discovery and phases → who, when, how long
text:
Site | Discoverer / excavator | Year
Harappa | Daya Ram Sahni | 1921
Mohenjodaro | R.D. Banerji | 1922

John Marshall announced the "Indus civilisation" in the Illustrated London News, 1924
Phases: Early (Kot Diji) c.2800-2600, Mature 2600-1900 BCE, Late (Cemetery H) to 1300 BCE
One phase: Sothi (early), Mohenjodaro (mature), Daimabad (late); two: Kalibangan, Lothal; all three: Harappa, Banawali, Dholavira, Rakhigarhi
About two-thirds of sites in the Sarasvati (Ghaggar-Hakra) basin
⚠ Harappa's bricks were looted for the Lahore-Multan railway (Cunningham: about 100 miles)

t: Evidence → what can be inferred (2026 format)
text:
Evidence | Valid inference | Wrong inference
Spindle-whorls in houses, no spinning wheel | Spinning was laborious and done at home | -
Weights and scales with graduations | Extent of scientific knowledge | -
Large baked-brick houses, spacious courtyards, own wells, baths | Private wealth, social differences | Common property system
Uniform bricks, seals, weights | Central authority making complex decisions | Proof of a priest ruler
Terracotta plough, Kalibangan field | Plough agriculture | Iron ploughs
Granaries | Surplus, grain as tax/wages | -
Seals with holes | Amulets, belief in evil forces | -
⚠ Uniform textile thickness hints at spinning wheels, but no wheel has been found
PYQ 2026: answer 1 and 2 only; trap: big private houses suggest inequality, not common property

t: Town planning → features and exceptions
text:
Feature | Fact
Layout | Grid: streets at right angles; drains laid out first
Parts | Small high western citadel + larger lower eastern lower town
Bricks | Burnt bricks, ratio 1:2:4 (houses 7.5x15x30 cm; walls 10x20x40 cm)
Drains | Covered, gentle slope, manholes, sump/cesspit
Privacy | No ground-level windows facing streets; entrance hides courtyard
Wells | Mohenjodaro about 700 wells
Houses | Courtyard-centred; mostly single-storey
## Exceptions
Site | Variation
Chanhudaro | Only city without a citadel
Dholavira | Three divisions, stone built
Lothal, Surkotada | Citadel inside the main settlement, not walled off
⚠ Egypt used mainly dried bricks, Mesopotamia baked; Harappans used burnt bricks on a large scale

t: Agriculture and animals → what they had and lacked
text:
Had | Lacked / doubtful
Wheat, barley, millets, pulses, sesamum, mustard | Iron (totally unknown)
Rice (husk at Lothal, Rangpur: earliest in South Asia) | Horse (only a superficial level at Mohenjodaro, doubtful Lothal figurine, doubtful Surkotada bones)
Cotton: among the earliest; Greeks called it sindon | Horse-drawn chariots
Wooden plough (Banawali, Cholistan models) | Metal money (barter only)
Oxen, buffalo, goat, sheep, elephant, dog, cat, pig; humped bull favoured | Canals in Punjab/Sindh (only Shortughai)
Granaries: Harappa, Mohenjodaro, Rakhigarhi, Kalibangan
⚠ "IVC used cotton for textiles" is correct (2011); "used iron ploughs" is wrong (JKPSC 2024)

t: Crafts and craft centres → where each was made
text:
Centre | Craft
Chanhudaro | Beads, shell-cutting, metal, seals, weights (craft town)
Lothal | Stone, shell, beads, metal
Nageshwar, Balakot | Shell bangles, ladles, inlays
Kalibangan | Black terracotta bangles (name means black bangles)
Sukkur and Rohri hills | Chert blades and limestone
Khetri (Ganeshwar) | Copper supply
Pure copper objects far outnumber bronze; tin was scarce
Silver more common than gold; beads of carnelian, steatite, amethyst, gold
Lapis lazuli (Shortughai/Afghanistan) and carnelian point to long-distance trade
⚠ Weaving was a cottage industry; actual cotton cloth survives from Mohenjodaro

t: Trade, weights and script → key facts
text:
Item | Fact
Trade | Internal and external; barter, no metal money; sea trade with Mesopotamia, Oman (Harappan jar)
Weights | Usually chert, cubical, no markings; binary then decimal ratios
Script | Undeciphered; pictographic, not alphabetic; 375-400 signs
Direction | Right to left; some long seals boustrophedon
Longest text | About 26 signs
Why undeciphered | No bilingual inscription
Games: dice with 1 opposite 2, 3 opposite 4, 5 opposite 6; seashell buttons; pitthu-like discs; Karanpura whistle
⚠ P-MCA gives 400-600 symbols; PMF book gives 375-400
## Beyond your notes
Mesopotamian texts call the Indus region Meluhha

topic: Harappan art: seals, sculpture and terracotta

On seals | Absent from seals
Unicorn (most common) | Cow
Humped bull (finest art) | Horse
Bull, buffalo, bison | Lion

Gharial, snake, goat, antelope | -

topic: Harappan art: seals, sculpture and terracotta

Feature | Fact
Site | Mohenjodaro, steatite
Figure | Three faces, horned headdress, seated cross-legged in yogic posture
Right side | Elephant, tiger
Left side | Rhinoceros, buffalo
Below seat | Two antelopes (deer)

Sculpture | Material | Site

text:
Item | Fact
Found | 1926, Ernest Mackay (under John Marshall), Mohenjodaro
Named by | John Marshall
Size | About 10.5 cm (PMF book: about 4 inches)

2023: International Museum Expo mascot was a modern Dancing Girl

topic: Harappan art: seals, sculpture and terracotta
t: Terracotta and pottery → features
text:
Item | Fact
Terracotta | Crude, common people's; women figures more common
Main figurine | Mother Goddess: jewelled, fan-shaped headdress
Others | Toy carts, rattles, whistles, birds, monkeys; horned-god mask (Kalibangan, Gujarat)
Pottery | Wheel-made, red slip, black painted designs; plain more common than painted
Polychrome | Rare
Paintings | No wall paintings survive; painting only on pottery
⚠ Seals and metal images were elite goods; terracotta was for common people

topic: Religion, polity and the Harappan-Vedic contrast
t: Religion → what they worshipped and where
text:
Evidence | Meaning
Mother Goddess figurines | Female deity
Pashupati seal | Male deity (proto-Shiva)
Fire altars | Lothal, Kalibangan, Banawali, Rakhigarhi
Great Bath (Mohenjodaro citadel) | Ritual bathing; bitumen-sealed
Trees, animals (unicorn, humped bull) | Nature and animal worship
Amulets | Belief in evil spirits
No temple found anywhere: worship likely outdoors, under trees
Religion present but not dominant: predominantly secular
⚠ They worshipped both male and female deities: correct (2013)
PYQ 2013: only "male and female deities" was right; no palaces or temples, no horse-drawn chariots
PYQ 2011: both statements correct: secular civilisation and cotton textiles

topic: Religion, polity and the Harappan-Vedic contrast
t: Polity → who ruled (and the traps)
text:
Uniform bricks, seals, weights, planned towns: complex decisions were taken, but by whom is unknown
No palaces, no royal tombs, few weapons: peaceful society
Theory | Status
No rulers, all equal | Possible
Several city rulers | Possible
One state | Most plausible (PMF)
Merchant rule | Suggested
Priest rule | Unlikely: no temples; "priest-king" label borrowed from Mesopotamia
Assembly hall (Mohenjodaro, 27x27 m, 20 pillars) hints at collective decisions
JKPSC 2025: "granary is the largest building at Harappa" marked wrong; Great Bath lies within the citadel (right)
⚠ "Possessed great palaces and temples" is wrong

topic: Religion, polity and the Harappan-Vedic contrast
t: Harappan vs Vedic → the contrast table
text:
Point | Harappan | Rigvedic
Settlement | Urban, planned cities | Rural
Metals | Gold, silver, copper, bronze; no iron | Later Vedic knew iron
Horse | Not known | Domesticated, chariots
Writing | Script (undeciphered) | Oral tradition
War | Peaceful, few weapons | Glorified war, chariots, mail
Religion | Secular; Mother Goddess, Pashupati; idols | Nature gods (Indra, Agni); no idols early
Economy | Trade, surplus, specialised crafts | Pastoral, then agrarian
⚠ The cow is central to Vedic life but absent from Harappan seals
Sarasvati: Naditama, Devitama, Matetama in the Rig Veda; mentioned far more than the Ganga
Rakhigarhi aDNA: no Steppe pastoralist gene → indigenous continuity

t: Decline → when and why
text:
Item | Fact
Mature phase | 2600-1900 BCE
Abandoned by c.1900 BCE | Harappa, Mohenjodaro, Cholistan
Mohenjodaro | Decline from 2200 BCE, ended by 2000 BCE
Lingered | Degenerate form in Gujarat, Rajasthan, Haryana, western UP
Sarasvati | Dried up about 1900 BCE; today Ghaggar (India), Hakra (Pakistan)
Causes debated: climate change (weaker monsoon), river shifts, tectonics, overuse of resources, invasion (least accepted)
Decline was not uniform across sites
## In news 2025-26
July 2026: pollen from Deoria Tal (Uttarakhand), dated by AMS radiocarbon of Trapa seeds: the 4.2 ka event weakened the monsoon → drought, eastward migration
High oak pollen = warm, humid; rising pine = cool, dry
⚠ The 4.2 ka event is about 2200 BCE, matching Mohenjodaro's decline

t: Recent finds → what each changes
text:
Find | Fact
Bhirrana dating (Feb 2026) | Oldest sample 8.35 ± 0.14 ka BP (about 8,000 years): settled life before Egypt's dynasties (3100 BCE)
Padta Bet (Kutch) | 3200-2600 BCE; sandstone structures, carnelian/agate beads, spindle whorls
Juna Khatiya (Kutch) | Largest Harappan burial site in India (about 197 burials); no nearby habitation; Rajesh S.V. won Shanghai Archaeology Forum award
Lakhapar (Kutch, June 2025) | Settlement 1.5 km from Juna Khatiya; Pre-Prabhas Ware in a burial (first); Rohri chert
Rakhigarhi | Iconic site in Budget 2020 with Hastinapur, Shivsagar, Dholavira, Adichanallur
"BP" = Before Present, with present fixed at 1950 CE
⚠ Bhirrana's early date is for settlement, not the mature urban phase (still 2600-1900 BCE)
P-MCA says Rakhigarhi "dates back about 6500 BCE": settlement roots, not the city

topic: Who were the Aryans: language, homeland, sources
t: 'Aryan' → a language label, not a race
text:
## 1. What the term means
Aryans = speakers of the Indo-Aryan language (Sanskrit), part of the Indo-European family
'Indo-European' and 'Indo-Aryan' are language labels; 19th-century writers shortened "Indo-Aryan-speaking people" to "Aryan", later misused as a racial term
'Arya' occurs 36 times in the Rig Veda: a cultural community speaking an Indo-Aryan language
Rig Veda (~1500 BCE) calls its people Arya; Avesta (~1400 BCE, Iran) says Airiia
Option in 1999 | Verdict
Ethnic group | No
Nomadic people | No (they were pastoral, but the term does not mean this)
Speech group | Yes
Superior race | No
⚠ In classical Sanskrit 'arya' also came to mean "noble man" (Preview); the historical sense is still linguistic
PYQ 1999: 'Aryan' denotes a speech group; trap: "superior race" (19th-century misuse)

topic: Who were the Aryans: language, homeland, sources
t: Indo-European languages → members and earliest records
text:
Family member | Examples
Indian | Sanskrit, Hindi, Assamese, Gujarati, Kashmiri, Sindhi, Bengali, Urdu
Asian | Persian
European | English, French, German, Greek, Italian, Spanish
Common words for horse, goat, dog, pine, maple; few common words for mountains
Sir William Jones (18th c.) noted Sanskrit-Latin-Greek similarity
Earliest Indo-European record | Place | Date
Hittite inscriptions | Turkey | 19th c. BCE
Kassite inscriptions | Iraq | 1600 BCE
Mitanni inscriptions | Syria | 14th c. BCE
Boghaz Koi (Hittite-Mitanni treaty) | Asia Minor | 1380 BCE
Boghaz Koi names Indara (Indra), Uruvanass (Varuna), Mitras (Mitra), Nasatia (Ashvins)
⚠ Earliest Indo-European inscriptions are found outside India; Boghaz Koi gives four Rigvedic gods (not Agni)
⚠ PMF places Boghaz Koi in "north-eastern Syria"; Preview says Asia Minor (Turkiye): the site is in Turkey

topic: Who were the Aryans: language, homeland, sources
t: Vedic period → phases, texts and region
text:
Phase | Date | Main source | Core region
Early (Rig) Vedic | 1500-1000 BCE | Rig Veda Books II-VII (family books) | Saptasindhu (E Afghanistan, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Punjab, fringe of W UP)
Later Vedic | 1000-600 BCE | Rig Veda Books I, VIII-X; Yajur, Sama, Atharva; Brahmanas, Aranyakas, Upanishads | Upper Gangetic basin, Kuru-Panchala
No cities, monuments or inscriptions from the Vedic period: history rests on texts plus pots and tools
After 1000 BCE moved into W UP; by 6th c. BCE eastern UP and north Bihar (Aryavarta)
Oldest surviving Indian manuscripts are not older than 4th c. BCE (Central Asia)
⚠ Preview dates Later Vedic as 1000-600 BCE; Testbook says 1000-500 BCE: PMF uses 600 BCE

t: Most mentioned vs most sacred river → Sindhu vs Saraswati
text:
River | Status in Rig Veda

t: Vedic regions → names and later expansion
text:
Term | Meaning

topic: Rigvedic material life and comparison with the Harappans
t: Well irrigation and draught power → what the evidence supports (2026)
text:
Evidence offered | Supports well irrigation / animal-drawn water?
Ashma chakra (stone pulley wheel) and ahava (strapped wooden pails) to draw water | Yes, both statements
Implements parashu/kulisha (axe), datra/srini (sickle) | No: shows forest clearing and harvesting, not irrigation
Ox used even before the Rig Veda for ploughing and carts | Yes: draught power existed
Claim tested: wells let farming spread away from flood plains into Punjab-Haryana plains with high groundwater
Rig Vedic plough names: phala, langala, sira; plough drawn by oxen
⚠ Evidence-support format: a true fact (axe, sickle) can still be irrelevant to the claim
PYQ 2026: answer 1 and 3 only
## Beyond your notes
Ashma chakra and ahava appear only in the PYQ explanation, not in your books; treat as "Rig Veda mentions wells with stone pulley and pails" (verify)

Term | Meaning
vap / krish | To sow / to cultivate
phala, langala, sira | Plough (three words)
khanitra | Hoe
datra / srini | Sickle
parashu / kulisha | Axe

Kshetrapati (lord of the field) first in the Rig Veda; kshetra-patni first in the Atharva Veda
Wooden ploughshare; fire used to clear forest; subsistence farming, agriculture secondary to cattle
⚠ Later Vedic names: barley yava, wheat godhuma, rice vrihi; Rig Veda knows mostly barley, not rice
UPSC CDS 2024: cereal terms in Rig Veda = yava and dhanya

topic: Rigvedic material life and comparison with the Harappans
t: Cattle economy → key Rigvedic words
text:
Word | Meaning
Gavishti | War ("search for cows")
Gomat | Rich man with many cattle
Duhitri | Daughter ("one who milks")
Goghna | Guest (one fed on cattle)
Aghanya | Cow, "not to be killed"
Ayas | Copper or bronze
Nishka | Gold ornament (necklace); later a coin
Bali | Voluntary offering to chief or god
Cow = chief wealth; beef eaten on special occasions
Mentions: asva (horse) 215, go (cow) 176, vrsabha (bull) 170: horse most mentioned animal
Barter; no coins; no regular trade; land not private property
⚠ Nishka = neck ornament in Rig Veda, coin later (UPSC 1993); ayas = copper/bronze, iron = krishna/shyama ayas (later)

topic: Rigvedic material life and comparison with the Harappans
t: Rigvedic Aryans vs Harappans → the differences UPSC tests
text:
Feature | Harappans | Rig Vedic Aryans
Settlement | Urban, planned cities | Rural, no towns
Metals | Gold, silver, copper, bronze; no iron | Gold, silver, copper, bronze (iron only later)
Horse | No clear evidence | Domesticated, glorified
Warfare | Peaceful, no armour evidence | Horse chariots, coat of mail (varman), helmet
Script | Undeciphered script | Oral tradition
Economy | Trade, surplus | Pastoral, barter
Dead | Burial | Cremation
Religion | Mother Goddess, Pashupati, idols | Nature gods, no idols
⚠ "Indus people knew iron" is false: statement 2 wrong
⚠ Preview argues statement 3 is also wrong (horse bones at Surkotada, Lothal figurine, Bhagwanpura) and gives answer 1 only; follow PMF/UPSC key: 1 and 3
PYQ 2017: answer 1 and 3 only

topic: Rigvedic material life and comparison with the Harappans
t: Aryan cultural traits → horse, spoked wheel, cremation, fire cult
text:
Trait | Detail
Horse | Domesticated in Central Asia (steppe burials ~5,000 yrs ago); entered India after Harappan collapse
Spoked wheel | First in Caucasus ~2300 BCE; Harappan toy carts had solid wheels
Cremation | Vedic and Avesta texts; Harappans buried
Fire and soma cult | Only Iranian and Vedic peoples; vedi = fire altar
Animal sacrifice | Incl. horse sacrifice; all Indo-Europeans
Banawali spoked wheel is post-Harappan; Lothal and Kalibangan "fire altars" are doubtful
Surkotada (Kutch) bones: horse or wild ass, debated
## In news 2025-26
Rakhigarhi: DNA of a 4,600-year-old woman matched neither Steppe nor Iranian people → "Harappans indigenous"; NCERT Class 12 added this; fire altars found there revive the Vedic-Harappan link debate (PMF Mains Magnum 2025)

t: Rigvedic social units → kula to jana
text:
Unit | Head | Note
Kula (family) | Kulapa | Joint family over three generations
Grama | Gramani | Kin group; clash = samgrama (war); later "village"
Vish (clan) | Vishayapati | Gives the word vaishya
Jana (tribe) | Rajan | Highest unit; loyalty to tribe
Jana appears ~275 times in the Rig Veda; janapada not even once
Society patriarchal, patrilineal, patrilocal; monogamy usual
⚠ Janapada (territory, rashtra) first appears in later Vedic texts: tribe → territory is the later Vedic shift

t: Assemblies → sabha, samiti, vidatha, gana
text:
Assembly | Nature | Women? | Later Vedic fate
Sabha | Smaller, elite | Yes (Rig Vedic) | Survives, dominated by nobles; women excluded
Samiti | One member per household; chose the Rajan | No | Survives, noble-dominated
Vidatha | Oldest; deliberative, religious, military | Yes | Disappears
Gana | Tribal assembly / militia unit |  | 
Rajan's role: protect cattle, lead in war, pray for the tribe; not hereditary at first
Atharva Veda: sabha and samiti are twin daughters of Prajapati (Testbook)
⚠ The assembly that vanished is vidatha; the one that elected the chief is samiti

t: Officials and tax → early vs later Vedic
text:
Official | Function | Phase
Purohita | Chief priest, adviser (most important) | Both
Senani | Army commander | Both
Vrajapati | Head of pasture land; led kulapas, gramanis | Early
Sangrahitri | Treasurer / tribute collector | Later
Bhagadugha | Revenue collector | Later
Akshavapa | Accountant | Later
Suta | Charioteer | Later
Palagala | Messenger | Later
Bali: voluntary in Rig Veda, obligatory in later Vedic; vaishyas the only tribute payers
No standing army in either phase (militias: vrata, gana, grama, sardha)
Rig Vedic priests: Vasishtha (conservative), Vishvamitra (liberal)
⚠ No regular tax, no army, no bureaucracy = no state even in later Vedic times
UPPCS 2023: Bhagadugha = revenue collector

t: Battle of Ten Kings → sides and result
text:
Item | Fact
Winner | Sudas, king of the Bharatas (Tritsu clan; priest Vasishtha)
Coalition | Ten chiefs: five Aryan (Puru, Yadu, Turvasa, Anu, Druhyu) + five non-Aryan (Alina, Pakhta, Bhalanas, Sivas, Vishanin)
River | Parushni (Ravi)
Text | 7th Mandala of Rig Veda
Outcome | Bharatas + Purus → Kurus; Kurus + Panchalas dominate the doab
Five Aryan tribes = panchajana
Bharatavarsha named after the Bharata tribe, first named in the Rig Veda
Dasas (softly treated, in Iranian texts; later "slave") vs Dasyus (hostile; dasyuhatya; chief Trasadasyu)
Indra Purandara (fort-breaker): forts were not Harappan; fights likely in Indo-Iranian borderland

t: Varna → from occupation to birth
text:
Phase | Basis | Groups
Early Rig Veda | Occupation, flexible | Brahmin, Kshatriya; vaishya and shudra absent
Late Rig Veda | Purusha Sukta (Book X) | Four varnas named first time
Later Vedic | Birth, rigid | Shudra disabilities; untouchables (Chandala, Nishada)
'Varna' in Rig Veda = colour (arya varna vs dasa varna), not caste
Purusha Sukta: Brahmana from mouth, Kshatriya shoulders/arms, Vaishya thighs, Shudra feet
Later Vedic: gotra exogamy appears; dwija (upanayana) for three higher varnas; rathakara still had sacred thread
Ashramas: first three in Chhandogya Upanishad; all four first in Dharmasutras (PMF)
⚠ Testbook says all four ashramas in the Jabala Upanishad; follow PMF (Dharmasutras)
⚠ Slaves (war, debt) were domestic, not used in farming; gifts to priests were cows and women slaves, never land

t: Women in the Rig Veda → seers and status
text:
Woman | Role
Lopamudra | Brahmavadini, composed Rig Vedic hymns; wife of Agastya
Ghosha | Rig Vedic seer; example of an unmarried woman
Apala | Seer; tended her father's fields
Vishvavara | Seer
Vishpala | Warrior, lost a leg in battle
Sikta, Nivavari | Brahmavadinis (Preview)
Rights: attend sabha and vidatha, education, choose husband, stay unmarried, widow remarriage, levirate; no child marriage, no sati
But no women priests; sacrifice only with husband; prayers for sons, not daughters
Not a Rig Vedic seer | Who she is
Gargi | Upanishadic philosopher; debated Yajnavalkya (Brihadaranyaka)
Maitreyi | Upanishadic thinker
Leelavati | Mathematics text (Bhaskara II)
⚠ Gargi is later Vedic / Upanishadic, not Rig Vedic (BPSC 71st: odd one out)
PYQ 1995: Brahmavadini who composed Vedic hymns; answer Lopamudra

t: Women in later Vedic period → what changed
text:
Right | Rig Vedic | Later Vedic
Attend assemblies | Yes | No
Study Vedas | Yes | No
Choose husband | Yes | No
Child marriage | No | Common
Birth of girl | Not unwelcome | Unwelcome (Aitareya Brahmana: "source of misery")
Rituals | With husband | Excluded (queens at coronation only)
Shatapatha Brahmana: good wife "pleases husband, bears sons, never talks back"
Anuloma (high man, low woman) tolerated; pratiloma disapproved
Sati only symbolic; widows remarried (levirate)
⚠ Women were often grouped with Shudras in later Vedic texts

t: Early Vedic religion → nature worship and yajna
text:
Feature | Early Vedic
Object of worship | Personified forces of nature (rain, fire, sun, wind)
Main mode | Prayers, with yajnas (milk, ghee, grain into fire; sometimes animals)
Temples, idols | None
Aim | Praja (sons), pashu (cattle), food, wealth, health
Type | Naturalistic polytheism; henotheism (god of the hymn is supreme for that hymn)
Sacrifice held at the yajamana's house (patron), not the priest's
Simple domestic sacrifices by householders; complex ones need specialist priests
⚠ Bhakti and image worship are absent in early Vedic religion: both 2012 distractors
PYQ 2012: religion of early Vedic Aryans = worship of nature and yajnas
UPSC CDS 2015: Rig Vedic religion naturalistic polytheism, similar to Avesta; yajamana is the patron, not the priest

t: Rigvedic gods → domain and rank
text:
God | Domain | Note
Indra | Rain, war | Most important, ~250 hymns; Purandara
Agni | Fire | Second, ~200 hymns; intermediary between gods and men
Varuna | Water, cosmic order | Third; upholds rita (Ritasyagopa)
Soma | Plants, sacred drink | Whole 9th Mandala
Mitra | With Varuna, guards rita | 
Rudra | Archer, disease, destruction | Maruts are his sons
Maruts | Storms | 
Ashvins (Nasatyas) | Twins, war and fertility | 
Surya, Savitri | Sun | Gayatri addressed to Savitr
Pushan | Paths, herds | Later god of Shudras
Vishnu | Rarely mentioned | Rises later
Brihaspati | Priest of the gods | 
⚠ Soma (divine sacrificial drink) vs sura (mundane drink)

t: Rigvedic goddesses → what each grants
text:
Goddess | Domain
Usha | Dawn; invoked for wealth
Aditi | Freedom; protects from sickness, harm, evil; mother of gods
Sinivali | Grants children
Raka | Bounty
Vach | Speech
Prithvi | Earth
Saraswati | River goddess
Male gods dominate (patriarchy)
⚠ Classic swap: Usha = dawn (not Aditi); Aditi = freedom from sickness (not Usha); Vach = speech (not Raka)
UPSC CDS 2025: correct statement was Sinivali bestows children

t: Rita and dharma → meaning and who guards them
text:
Concept | Meaning | Guardian / phase
Rita | Cosmic, ritual and moral order governing the universe and all in it; an impersonal law | Varuna and Mitra; central in Rig Veda
Dharma | Obligations; discharge of duties to oneself and others; personal actions that keep the order | Minor in Rig Veda; dominant in later Vedic
Rita covers nature, gods, human conduct and yajna
Later: rita declines, dharma rises (later the basis of law and varna duties)
⚠ Both 2011 statements are correct; rita = natural law (Chhattisgarh PSC 2016)
PYQ 2011: dharma = duties; rita = fundamental moral law of the universe; answer both 1 and 2

t: Later Vedic religion → what changed
text:
Aspect | Early Vedic | Later Vedic
Top gods | Indra, Agni | Prajapati (creator, supreme), Vishnu (protector), Rudra (destroyer)
Worship | Prayers dominant | Sacrifices dominant; prayers decline
Idols | None | Signs of idolatry appear
Shudra god |  | Pushan
Priests | Few | Brahmanas dominate; 16 priest classes
Sacrifices public (king + community) and private; success depends on correct words (formulae)
Rajasuya dakshina could reach 2,40,000 cows; land grants as fee not established
Reaction: Upanishads (Panchala, Videha) stress knowledge, Atman-Brahman; Kshatriya kings (Janaka of Videha, Ashvapati of Kekaya) taught
⚠ Moksha is not in the Vedas; first discussed in the Upanishads (Preview)

t: Four Vedas → content and priest
text:
Veda | Content | Priest | Upaveda
Rig | Hymns praising gods; oldest (~1500 BCE) | Hotri (recites) | Ayurveda
Yajur | Ritual formulas, rules of sacrifice; prose + verse | Adhvaryu (performs) | Dhanurveda
Sama | Rig hymns set to tune; shortest; origin of Indian music | Udgatri (chants) | Gandharvaveda
Atharva | Charms, magic spells, healing, herbs; latest | Brahman | Arthashastra (or Shilpa Veda)
Rig + Yajur + Sama = Trayi; Atharva not used in public rituals
Yajur: Krishna (black: mantra and brahmana mixed; Taittiriya, Kathaka, Kapishthala, Maitrayani) vs Shukla (white: separated; Madhyandina, Kanva)
Atharva Samhitas: Shaunaka, Paippalada
⚠ Ayurveda: PMF lists it as Upaveda of Rig Veda but says it originates in the Atharva Veda
PYQ 2004: Veda with magical charms and spells = Atharva Veda
## Beyond your notes
Udgatri (Sama) and Brahman (Atharva) priests are standard but not named in your books

t: Atharva Veda → distinctive content
text:
Content | Example
Charms and spells | Ward off evil, disease, snake bites, insects
Agriculture | Protect crops from drought and lightning; kshetra-patni (mistress of the field)
Medicine | Herbs and healing → origin of Ayurveda
Society | Sabha and samiti = daughters of Prajapati; gotra first named (Testbook)
Non-Aryan life | Beliefs and practices of non-Aryans
Not used in public (shrauta) rituals; hence some exclude it from the "Trayi"
Brahmana: Gopatha; no Aranyaka; Upanishads Mundaka, Mandukya, Prashna
⚠ Kshetrapati = Rig Veda; kshetra-patni = Atharva Veda (not Rig Veda, Ashtadhyayi, Arthashastra)
PYQ 2026: kshetra-patni originates in the Atharva Veda

t: Rig Veda → structure, mandalas and famous suktas
text:
Unit | Number
Mandalas | 10
Anuvakas | 85
Suktas (hymns) | 1028
Mantras (riks) | 10,552
Part | Fact
Books II-VII | Oldest, family books (Gritsamada II, Vishvamitra III, Vamadeva IV, Atri V, Bharadvaja VI, Vasishtha VII)
Books I and X | Latest
Book III | Gayatri mantra (Vishvamitra; to Savitr)
Book VII | Battle of Ten Kings
Book IX | All hymns to Soma
Book X | Purusha Sukta (90th), Nasadiya Sukta (129th, creation), Surya Sukta (85th, marriage)
UNESCO: Rig Veda in Memory of the World (2007); Vedic chanting intangible heritage (2008)
'Gamester's Lament' = secular poem in Rig Veda
⚠ Testbook calls Mandalas 2-8 "Saptarishi Mandalas"; PMF: family books = II-VII
## Beyond your notes
Family-book seers for IV-VII (Vamadeva, Atri, Bharadvaja, Vasishtha) are standard but not listed in your books; Tandya is also called Panchavimsha Brahmana

t: Brahmanas, Aranyakas, Upanishads → which Veda
text:
Veda | Brahmana | Aranyaka | Principal Upanishads
Rig | Aitareya, Kaushitaki | Aitareya, Kaushitaki | Aitareya, Kaushitaki
Krishna Yajur | Taittiriya | Taittiriya, Maitrayaniya | Taittiriya, Katha, Shvetashvatara, Maitrayaniya
Shukla Yajur | Shatapatha | Brihadaranyaka | Brihadaranyaka, Isha
Sama | Tandya (Panchavimsha), Samavidhana | Jaiminiya, Chandogya | Chandogya, Kena
Atharva | Gopatha | None | Mundaka, Mandukya, Prashna
Order: Samhita → Brahmana → Aranyaka → Upanishad; Karma-kanda (Samhita, Brahmana) vs Jnana-kanda (Aranyaka, Upanishad)
Aranyakas (~700 BCE): forest books, secret rites; Upanishads (~600 BCE, Panchala, Videha) = Vedanta
Muktika lists 108 Upanishads; 'Upanishad' = sitting near the teacher
Nachiketa-Yama: Katha; Gargi-Yajnavalkya: Brihadaranyaka; Shvetaketu "tat tvam asi": Chandogya
⚠ Atharva Veda has no Aranyaka; Shatapatha Brahmana tells Videgha Mathava and the Great Flood

t: Famous mottos and concepts → source text
text:
Motto / concept | Source
Satyameva Jayate | Mundaka Upanishad
Yato dharmastato jayah (Supreme Court) | Mahabharata
Gayatri mantra | Rig Veda Book III
Asato ma sadgamaya, tamaso ma jyotirgamaya | Brihadaranyaka Upanishad
Four varnas, Shudra first named | Purusha Sukta (Rig Veda X)
Origin of universe | Nasadiya Sukta (Rig Veda X)
First three ashramas | Chhandogya Upanishad
Transmigration (samsara) | Brihadaranyaka Upanishad (Testbook)
Trimurti | Maitrayani Upanishad (Testbook)
Mahavakyas | Prajnanam Brahma (Rig), Aham Brahmasmi (Yajur), Tat tvam asi (Sama), Ayam Atma Brahma (Atharva)
⚠ Testbook prints Satyameva Jayate from the Mandukya; PMF says Mundaka (correct)

t: Shruti, Smriti and Vedangas → classification
text:
Class | Meaning | Texts
Shruti | "Heard", revealed, apaurusheya | Four Vedas, Brahmanas, Aranyakas, Upanishads
Smriti | "Remembered", human authorship | Six Vedangas, epics, Puranas, Manusmriti
Vedanga | Subject | Famous text
Shiksha | Phonetics | Shiksha-sutras
Kalpa | Ritual | Shrauta, Shulba (altar measures), Grihya, Dharma sutras
Vyakarana | Grammar | Panini's Ashtadhyayi
Nirukta | Etymology | Yaska
Chhandas | Metre | Pingala
Jyotisha | Astronomy | Timing of rituals
Vedangas c. 500-200 BCE; Vedic Sanskrit differs from classical Sanskrit
⚠ Upanishads are Shruti, epics and Puranas are Smriti; Upanishads predate Puranas and do contain parables (UPSC 2024)

topic: Later Vedic economy, polity and pottery
t: Iron and crops in the later Vedic period → evidence
text:
Item | Fact
Iron first | Dharwar (Karnataka) ~1000 BCE; also E Punjab, W UP, MP, Rajasthan
Iron weapons in W UP | ~800 BCE
Name | Shyama / Krishna ayas; first in Yajur Veda
Iron ploughshare | Only one, Jakhera, end of period
Rice remains | Hastinapur and Atranjikhera (8th c. BCE)
New crops | Rice (vrihi), wheat (godhuma), lentils
Agriculture primary; wooden ploughshare still common; ploughs pulled by up to 24 oxen
Kings ploughed: Janaka (Videha); Balarama = Haladhar
Proto-urban sites at the end: Hastinapur, Kaushambi; term nagara appears
⚠ Rig Veda has no iron; iron came with the later Vedic expansion into the doab

topic: Later Vedic economy, polity and pottery
t: Doab pottery sequence → OCP to NBPW
text:
Culture | Date | Phase | Key sites
OCP (Ochre Coloured) | 2000-1500 BCE | Chalcolithic | Jodhpura, Siswal, Hastinapur, Atranjikhera
BRW (Black and Red) | 1450-1200 BCE | Chalcolithic | Atranjikhera, Noh, Jodhpura
PGW (Painted Grey) | 1200-500 BCE | Early iron / later Vedic | Ahichchhatra (first found 1940), Hastinapur, Bhagwanpura, Ropar, Noh
NBPW (N Black Polished) | 700-100 BCE | Second urbanisation | Ganga valley; punch-marked coins
PGW: fine grey tableware with black geometric designs; ~700 sites; earliest PGW (Ghaggar-Hakra, Bhagwanpura) has no iron
Bhagwanpura (Haryana): 13-room mud house, horse bones, PGW with late Harappan pottery
Later Vedic potteries (four): red ware (most popular), black-slipped, BRW, PGW (most distinctive)
⚠ Order: OCP → BRW → PGW → NBPW (JKPSC 2024); at Hastinapur and Ahichchhatra OCP is followed by a break, then PGW

topic: Later Vedic economy, polity and pottery
t: Royal rituals and kingship → later Vedic
text:
Ritual | Purpose
Rajasuya | Consecration; confers supreme power
Ashvamedha | Horse wanders; unquestioned control over area it crosses
Vajapeya | Chariot race won against kinsmen
Kingship becomes hereditary (primogeniture); raja of a janapada, not a jana
Sabha advisory; king final authority; wars for territory
King ate from the same plate as the vish before war (ritual)
⚠ Aitareya Brahmana gives Kshatriya precedence over Brahmanas (Testbook)

topic: Later Vedic economy, polity and pottery
t: Early vs later Vedic → one-line contrasts
text:
Aspect | Early Vedic | Later Vedic
Economy | Pastoral, cattle wealth | Agriculture, land matters
Metal | Copper, bronze (ayas) | Iron (krishna ayas)
Polity | Jana; elected Rajan; vidatha alive | Janapada; hereditary king; vidatha gone
Tax | Voluntary bali | Obligatory tribute (Sangrahitri, Bhagadugha)
Society | Occupational, egalitarian | Birth-based varna, gotra
Women | Assemblies, education | Excluded
Gods | Indra, Agni, Varuna | Prajapati, Vishnu, Rudra
Worship | Prayer | Sacrifice; idolatry signs
Region | Saptasindhu | Ganga-Yamuna doab
Three big changes: territorial kingdoms, agricultural society, varna-divided society
⚠ Neither phase had a standing army or regular tax system

t: Mahajanapada → river flowing in it
text:
## 1. The four pairs UPSC gave (2025)
Pair | Verdict | Why
Asmaka - Godavari | Correct | Lay along the Godavari (between Godavari and Manjira); capital Potana on the Godavari
Kamboja - Vipas (Beas) | Wrong | Kamboja was in the far north-west (Rajouri-Hazara, NWFP, Afghanistan); Beas flows in Punjab

Answer: only two pairs correct

⚠ Vipas = Beas = Greek Hyphasis: the river where Alexander's army stopped

text:
## 1. Sources of the list
Text | Tradition | List
Anguttara Nikaya | Buddhist | 16 (standard list)

## In news 2025-26
Rajghat (Ganga-Varuna confluence): capital of the Kashi janapada; 22 boxes of 10,000+ artefacts opened (2026); urban origins of Varanasi to ~800 BCE
