t: Monarchies vs ganas → how they differed
text:
## 1. PMF comparison
Feature | Monarchy | Gana / Sangha
Location | Mostly Gangetic plain | North-west and Himalayan foothills
Ruler | One hereditary raja | Many rajas, under an assembly
Revenue | King alone | Each raja
Army | Standing army; no private arms | Each raja's own small army
Brahmanas | Great influence | No place
Examples | Kosala, Magadha | Vajji, Malla, Shakya
Vajji: confederacy of 8 clans (Lichchhavi strongest, Videha, Jnatrika); Malla: 9 clans
Lichchhavis had 7,707 rajas (Buddhist text)
Women, dasas and kammakaras were excluded from assemblies
Last ganas conquered by the Guptas
⚠ Buddha (Shakya) and Mahavira (Jnatrika, Vajji) came from ganas
## 2. Revenue and officials
Tax on crops = 1/6 (bhaga); traders paid customs; craftsmen paid in labour
High officials: mahamatras; village headman: gramabhojaka / gramini
Punch-marked coins (mostly silver, symbols only, no text) from ~6th century BCE

topic: Rise of Magadha, the Nandas and Alexander
t: Magadhan dynasties → rulers and conquests
text:
## 1. Sequence and dates (PMF)
Dynasty | Period (BCE) | Key rulers
Haryanka | 545-413 | Bimbisara (545-493), Ajatashatru (493-462), Udayin (462-444)
Shishunaga | 413-345 | Shishunaga, Kalashoka
Nanda | 345-321 | Mahapadma Nanda, Dhana Nanda
Maurya | 321-185 | Chandragupta, Bindusara, Ashoka
## 2. Who annexed what
Ruler | Annexed
Bimbisara | Anga (defeated Brahmadatta); Kashi as dowry
Ajatashatru | Kosala and Vajji (16-year war; used Mahashilakantaka, Rathamusala)
Shishunaga | Avanti and Vatsa
Mahapadma Nanda | Kalinga (Hathigumpha inscription)
Bimbisara's wives: Mahakosala (Kosala), Chellana (Lichchhavi), Khema (Madra)
Bimbisara's physician Jivaka treated Pradyota of Avanti
⚠ Avanti was Magadha's most serious rival; took ~100 years to subdue Ujjain

topic: Rise of Magadha, the Nandas and Alexander
t: Magadha's capitals → who shifted them
text:
## 1. Seats of power
Ruler | Capital
Bimbisara | Rajgir (Girivraja), ringed by five hills
Ajatashatru | Fortified Pataligrama, built Pataliputra (base against Vaishali)
Udayin | Shifted capital Rajgir → Pataliputra
Shishunaga | Temporarily Vaishali
Kalashoka | Back to Pataliputra; held Second Buddhist Council at Vaishali (383 BCE)
Pataliputra at Ganga-Son confluence = a jaladurga (water fort)
⚠ Ajatashatru built/fortified Pataliputra; Udayin made it the capital (PMF; NDA 2023 key said Ajatashatru)
## 2. Councils linked to Magadhan kings
First Buddhist Council at Rajgir under Ajatashatru; Second at Vaishali under Kalashoka; Third at Pataliputra under Ashoka

topic: Rise of Magadha, the Nandas and Alexander
t: Causes of Magadha's success → the factors
text:
## 1. PMF's seven factors
Factor | Detail
Ambitious rulers | Bimbisara, Ajatashatru, Mahapadma Nanda and their ministers
Natural forts | Rajgir (five hills), Pataliputra (water fort)
Iron mines | In present Jharkhand: tools and weapons
Ganga | Cheap transport, fertile land
Productive agriculture | Alluvial soil, heavy rain, iron ploughshare
Forests / elephants | First state to use elephants on a large scale
Unorthodox society | Kiratas and Magadhas; recently Vedicised, keen to expand
⚠ Not a cause: "superior cavalry", "gold mines", "republican government" (EPFO 2023 distractors)
⚠ Avanti also had iron (eastern MP), which made it Magadha's main competitor

topic: Rise of Magadha, the Nandas and Alexander
t: Nanda dynasty → first empire builders
text:
## 1. Mahapadma Nanda
Murdered Mahanandin (last Shishunaga); born of a Shudra mother
Titles: Ekarat (sole monarch), Sarvakshatrantak (destroyer of all Kshatriyas, Puranas)
Called the first empire builder of India; conquered Kalinga, built a canal there (Hathigumpha)
Nau Nand Dehra (Nanded) on the Godavari may mark Nanda reach into the Deccan
## 2. Army and fall
Fact | Value
Army | 200,000 infantry, 60,000 cavalry, 3,000-6,000 elephants
Kings | Mahapadma + eight sons (9 Nandas)
Last king | Dhana Nanda (329-321 BCE)
Overthrown by | Chandragupta Maurya with Chanakya, 321 BCE
Dhana Nanda's oppressive taxes made him unpopular
PYQ 2000: dynasty ruling North India at Alexander's invasion = Nanda (not Maurya, Sunga, Kanva)

topic: Rise of Magadha, the Nandas and Alexander
t: Persian and Macedonian invasions → key facts
text:
## 1. Achaemenid (Persian) phase
Cyrus II: first to invade; took Gandhara and Kamboja
Darius I (516 BCE): Sindh and Punjab west of the Indus; 20th satrapy (Hindush) paid 360 talents of gold
Effects: Kharoshthi from Aramaic (right to left); "lipi" in Ashoka like Darius's "dipi"
## 2. Alexander (327-325 BCE)
Event | Fact
Crossed Indus | 326 BCE
Ambhi of Taxila | Submitted
Porus (Jhelum-Chenab) | Fought at Hydaspes (Jhelum); lost but kingdom restored
Furthest point | Hyphasis (Beas): army refused to go on
Left India | 325 BCE; died at Babylon 323 BCE
Army refused partly for fear of the Nanda army
Resisted by ganas: Malloi (Malavas), Oxydrakai (Kshudrakas), queen Cleophis of Massaga
"Sandrokottas" in Greek sources = Chandragupta: the sheet anchor of Indian chronology
⚠ Alexander never crossed the Hyphasis (NDA 2022)

topic: The Mauryas: sources, rulers and the Kalinga war
t: Sources of Mauryan history → author and content
text:
## 1. Literary and archaeological sources
Source | Author / type | Content
Arthashastra | Kautilya (Chanakya, Vishnugupta) | Statecraft: 15 books, 180 chapters; Saptanga theory
Indica | Megasthenes (envoy of Seleucus) | Pataliputra administration, army; original lost
Mudrarakshasa | Vishakhadatta (Gupta age) | Chandragupta and Kautilya overthrow the Nandas
Dipavamsa, Mahavamsa | Sri Lankan chronicles | Ashoka and Buddhism in Sri Lanka
Sohgaura copper plate | Gorakhpur, UP | Granaries, famine relief; oldest copper plate
Junagadh inscription | Rudradaman | Pushyagupta, Sudarshana lake under Chandragupta
Arthashastra found 1905; published by R. Shamasastry (text 1909, translation 1915)
Indica fragments compiled by Schwanbeck (1846), translated by McCrindle (1877)
Saptanga: Swami, Amatya, Durga, Danda, Janapada, Kosha, Mitra
⚠ Arthashastra never names the Mauryas or Pataliputra; many scholars date it post-Maurya, but treat it as Mauryan for exams
## In news 2025-26
Arthashastra's rain gauge: a clay bowl at granaries, rainfall measured in drona (~13.2 kg of water) (May 2026)

topic: The Mauryas: sources, rulers and the Kalinga war
t: Chandragupta and Bindusara → key facts
text:
## 1. Chandragupta Maurya (321-297 BCE)
Met Chanakya at Taxila; overthrew Dhana Nanda; capital Pataliputra
305 BCE: defeated Seleucus Nicator; got eastern Afghanistan, Baluchistan, area west of Indus + marriage; gave 500 elephants
Seleucus sent Megasthenes
End: became Jain, went with Bhadrabahu to Shravanabelagola (Chandragiri hill), fasted to death
## 2. Bindusara (297-272 BCE)
Fact | Detail
Title | Amitraghata (slayer of enemies); Greek Amitrochates
Conquest | Deccan up to Mysore
Not conquered | Kalinga, Cholas, Pandyas, Cheras
Greek envoy | Deimachus from Antiochus I
Sect | Supported the Ajivikas
⚠ Bindusara asked Antiochus for sweet wine, figs and a sophist; the sophist was refused
## In news 2025-26
Samrat Samprati Museum, Koba (Gujarat) for Jain heritage (2026); Samprati = Ashoka's grandson, ruled ~230-215 BCE

topic: The Mauryas: sources, rulers and the Kalinga war
t: Ashoka's accession → succession and Buddhism
text:
## 1. Accession
Governor (Kumara) of Taxila and Ujjayini under Bindusara
Accession 272 BCE, coronation 268 BCE (4-year gap = succession struggle)
Bindusara wanted Susima; minister Radhagupta backed Ashoka (Divyavadana)
Sri Lankan legend: killed 99 brothers (likely exaggerated)
## 2. Turn to Buddhism
Fact | Detail
Guide | Monk Upagupta
Pace | Gradual: upasaka first, bhikkhu 2.5 years later (Minor Rock Edict I)
Third Council | Pataliputra, c. 250 BCE, president Moggaliputta Tissa
Sri Lanka mission | Mahendra and Sanghamitra; met King Devanampiya Tissa (Anuradhapura)
Pilgrimage | Lumbini, Sarnath, Sravasti, Kusinagara; first dhamma yatra to Bodh Gaya
⚠ Minor Rock Edict I shows a gradual, not sudden, conversion (CDS 2022)

topic: The Mauryas: sources, rulers and the Kalinga war
t: Kalinga war → why Ashoka annexed Kalinga
text:
## 1. The Assertion-Reason (2000)
Statement | Verdict
A: Ashoka annexed Kalinga to the Mauryan Empire | True
R: Kalinga controlled the land and sea routes to South India | True, and explains A
Kalinga was a bridge between north and south; dominated eastern sea trade and land routes from the Ganga valley to the Deccan (Preview)
## 2. The war (Major Rock Edict XIII)
Eight years after coronation, c. 261/260 BCE
1 lakh killed, 1.5 lakh deported/captured
Shift from Bherighosha (sound of war drums) to Dhammaghosha
Kalinga was retained; army not disbanded
Edict | Kalinga link
Major Rock Edict XIII | Describes the war and remorse
Dhauli, Jaugada | Omit XI, XII, XIII; carry Separate Kalinga Edicts
⚠ Dhauli and Jaugada (in Kalinga itself) do not carry Edict XIII
PYQ 2000: A and R both true, R explains A; trap: assuming the reason was religious

t: District officers → Pradeshika, Rajuka, Yukta
text:
## 1. The 2025 question
Ashokan inscriptions show Pradeshika, Rajuka and Yukta were district-level officers
Officer | Role
Pradeshika | Overall in charge of the district, like a collector
Rajuka | Survey and assessment of land; judicial powers (Pillar Edict IV)
Yukta | Subordinate officials; assisted Rajukas, kept accounts/revenue
Major Rock Edict III: Yuktas, Rajukas, Pradeshikas toured every five years to spread dhamma (12 years after coronation)
⚠ Not village, not provincial, not central (2025 options)
⚠ Preview compares Pradeshika to a divisional commissioner; PMF (higher source) to a collector
PYQ 2025: officer trio placed at district level; mnemonic PRIYA (Pradeshika, Rajuka, Yukta)

t: Local administration → village and city
text:
## 1. Levels below the province
Level | Officials
District (Vishaya / Ahara) | Pradeshika, Rajuka, Yukta
Group of 10-15 villages | Gopa
Village | Gramani
City (Pataliputra) | Municipal board of 30: six committees of five
## 2. Megasthenes' six city committees
Industrial arts; foreigners; registration of births and deaths; trade and commerce; supervision of manufactures; collection of tax on sales
Census was a permanent institution: castes, occupations, even animals counted
⚠ The 30-member, six-committee scheme is from Megasthenes, not Ashoka's edicts (JKPSC 2024 trap)

t: Central administration → key officers
text:
## 1. King and council
King supreme; advised by Mantriparishad
Highest functionaries (tirthas): mantrin, purohita, senapati, yuvaraja
Departments headed by Adhyakshas (Testbook: 26 departments)
Officer | Duty
Samaharta | Chief of revenue: assessment and collection
Sannidhata | Treasury and storehouse
Senapati | Commander-in-chief
Dharmadhikarin | Chief justice
Dhamma Mahamatras | Spread dhamma (from 13th year, Rock Edict V)
Pativedakas | Reporters: bring public affairs to the king any time (Rock Edict VI)
⚠ Samaharta = collects; Sannidhata = stores
Elaborate espionage system watched enemies and officials

t: Provinces → capitals
text:
## 1. Five political centres (PMF)
Centre | Province | Present state
Pataliputra | Imperial capital | Bihar
Taxila | North | Pakistan
Ujjayini | West | Madhya Pradesh
Tosali | East (Kalinga) | Odisha
Suvarnagiri | South | Karnataka (gold mines)
Governors = Kumaras (royal princes); assisted by mahamatyas
Taxila and Ujjayini lay on long-distance trade routes
⚠ Testbook names four provinces as Uttarapatha, Avantipatha, Dakshinapatha, Magadha
⚠ PMF: Tosali more likely Sisupalgarh than Dhauli

t: Revenue, army and justice → the numbers
text:
## 1. Revenue
Land revenue = one-sixth of produce; irrigation charged
State monopolies: mining, liquor sale, arms
Imperial currency: punch-marked silver coins (peacock, hill, crescent)
## 2. Army
Fact | Value
Size (Greek accounts) | 6,00,000 infantry, 30,000 cavalry, 9,000 elephants, 8,000 chariots
Control | Board of 30, six sub-committees of five
Wings | Infantry, cavalry, elephants, chariots, navy, transport
## 3. Justice
Supreme court at capital; town cases: Nagaravyavaharika Mahamatra; village: Gramavriddha
Ashoka asked Dhamma Mahamatras to act against unjust imprisonment
⚠ Lumbini: Ashoka cut the bhaga from 1/6 to 1/8 and exempted bali (Rummindei pillar)

t: Major Rock Edicts I-XIV → content of each
text:
## 1. PMF list
Edict | Content
I | Ban on animal slaughter and festive gatherings
II | Medical care for humans and animals; names Cholas, Pandyas, Satiyaputras, Keralaputras
III | Generosity; Yuktas, Rajukas, Pradeshikas tour every 5 years
IV | Dhammaghosha over Bherighosha
V | Dhamma Mahamatras appointed (13th year); slaves
VI | King wants reports any time (pativedakas); welfare
VII | Tolerance for all sects
VIII | First dhamma yatra to Bodh Gaya
IX | Condemns useless ceremonies
X | Condemns desire for fame and glory
XI | No gift like the gift of dhamma
XII | Religious tolerance: do not praise own sect or blame others
XIII | Kalinga war, remorse, dhamma-vijaya over five Greek kings and southern kingdoms
XIV | On the engraving of the edicts
⚠ Tolerance appears in VII and XII; XII is "completely devoted" to it (UPPSC 2008)

t: Southern kingdoms in the edicts → Rock Edicts II and XIII
text:
## 1. The 1998 answer
Rock Edicts II and XIII name the Sangam-age kingdoms outside the empire
Edict | Neighbours named
II | Cholas, Pandyas, Satiyaputras, Keralaputras, Tamraparni, Yavana king Antiyoka
XIII | Cholas, Pandyas, Tamraparni + five Greek kings
Only the Satiyaputras are not clearly identified
Megasthenes first mentions the Pandyas (pearls, ruled by a woman)
## 2. Five Hellenistic kings (XIII)
Edict name | King | Kingdom
Antiyoka | Antiochus II | Syria
Turamaya | Ptolemy II Philadelphus | Egypt
Antikini | Antigonus Gonatas | Macedonia
Maka | Magas | Cyrene (N Africa)
Alikasudara | Alexander | Epirus / Corinth
⚠ Options I and X, I and XI, II and XIV are distractors; Kerala and Tamil Nadu were outside the empire
PYQ 1998: Sangam kingdoms = Rock Edicts II and XIII

t: Rock Edict XII → the tolerance text (2020)
text:
## 1. The quoted lines
"Whosoever praises his religious sect or blames other sects out of excessive devotion ... injures his own sect very severely"
Answer: Ashoka (not Samudragupta, Harshavardhana, Krishnadeva Raya)
PMF wording: dhamma grows through restraint in speech; learn and respect other faiths' main ideas
Ruler in options | Known record
Ashoka | Rock Edict XII (tolerance)
Samudragupta | Allahabad Prashasti (Harishena)
Harshavardhana | Banskhera, Madhuban plates
Krishnadeva Raya | Amuktamalyada (Telugu work)
⚠ Ashoka made gifts to non-Buddhist sects too: Barabar caves to Ajivikas
PYQ 2020: identify the ruler from the quote; the hinge is "blames other sects"

t: Edicts naming Ashoka → Maski and three others
text:
## 1. Personal name "Asoka"
Most edicts call him Devanampiya (beloved of the gods) Piyadasi (one who looks kindly)
Site | State | Wording
Maski | Karnataka (Raichur) | Devanampiya Asoka
Gujarra | MP (Datia) | Devanampiya Piyadasi Asoka
Nittur | Karnataka (Ballari) | Name Asoka
Udegolam | Karnataka (Ballari) | Name Asoka
Kanaganahalli | Karnataka | "Ranyo Asoko" on a stone portrait (only inscribed portrait)
All four are copies of Minor Rock Edict I
Maski found 1915 fixed Piyadasi = Ashoka; George Turnour linked the title via Dipavamsa
⚠ Kalsi, Rummindei, Special Kalinga Edict do not give the name (1997 options)
PYQ 1997: Maski; likely next: Gujarra, Nittur, Udegolam, Kanaganahalli (CSE 2019)

t: Edict classification → rock, pillar, cave
text:
## 1. PMF scheme
Type | Number | Notes
Major Rock Edicts | 14 at 10 sites | Moral and political
Minor Rock Edicts | 3 at 18 sites | Earliest; religious; densest in Andhra-Karnataka
Separate Rock Edicts | 2 | Dhauli, Jaugada ("All men are my children")
Major Pillar Edicts | 7 at 7 pillars | Latest; only Delhi-Topra has all seven
Minor Pillar Edicts | 4 | Schism, Queen's (Karuvaki), Rummindei, Nigali Sagar
Cave inscriptions | 3 | Barabar hills (Ajivikas)
Order: minor rock → major rock → pillar edicts
Language mostly Prakrit in Brahmi; Kharoshthi in NW; Greek and Aramaic in Afghanistan
Deciphered by James Prinsep (1837)
⚠ Nigali Sagar has the earliest known record of the word "stupa"

t: Major Rock Edict sites → state and script
text:
## 1. Ten sites
Site | Location | Script
Kandahar | Afghanistan | Greek
Shahbazgarhi | Pakistan | Kharoshthi
Mansehra | Pakistan | Kharoshthi
Kalsi | Uttarakhand | Brahmi
Girnar | Gujarat | Brahmi
Sopara | Maharashtra | Brahmi
Dhauli | Odisha | Brahmi
Jaugada | Odisha | Brahmi
Sannati | Karnataka | Brahmi
Yerragudi | Andhra Pradesh | Brahmi
Girnar rock also has Rudradaman and Skandagupta inscriptions
⚠ CSE 2022 pairs: Dhauli-Odisha, Erragudi-AP correct; Jaugada is Odisha (not MP), Kalsi Uttarakhand (not Karnataka)
## 2. Pillar sites
Delhi-Topra, Delhi-Meerut (both moved by Firoz Shah Tughlaq), Allahabad-Kausambi, Lauriya Araraj, Lauriya Nandangarh, Rampurva, Kandahar
Allahabad pillar also carries Samudragupta and Jahangir inscriptions

t: Dhamma → social ethics, not a religion
text:
## 1. The 1998 Assertion-Reason
Statement | Verdict
A: In Ashoka's edicts, social harmony mattered more than religious devotion | True
R: He spread ideas of equity instead of promoting a religion | True, explains A
Dhamma involved no god, no sacrifice: a code of conduct for all
Testbook: Ashoka saw dhamma not as piety but as conformity to a social ethic
Inspired by the Buddhist upasaka code, but Buddhism stayed his personal faith
⚠ Greek and Aramaic versions do not mention the Buddha; edicts never name the Four Noble Truths, Eightfold Path or Nibbana
PYQ 1998: both true, R explains A; trap: calling dhamma "spreading Buddhism"

t: Dhamma → what it asked of people
text:
## 1. Contents (PMF)
Principle | Edict link
Respect elders, parents, teachers | RE III, IX, XI
Generosity to Brahmanas and Shramanas | RE III, IX
Kind treatment of slaves and servants | RE V, IX
Tolerance of all sects | RE VII, XII
No animal sacrifice, no festive gatherings | RE I
Avoid costly, meaningless rituals | RE IX
Conquest by dhamma, not war | RE XIII
Killing of certain animals banned; slaughter prohibited in the capital
⚠ "Honouring the king" was not part of dhamma (NDA 2021); respecting Brahmanas was
## 2. Motive
Practical: reduce family and sect conflict, keep social order in a diverse empire
Paternal kingship: "All men are my children" (Separate Kalinga Edict I)

t: Spreading Dhamma → officials, tours, missions
text:
## 1. Means
Means | Detail
Dhamma Mahamatras | Appointed 13 years after coronation (RE V)
Specialised mahamatras | Anta (frontiers), Nagara (cities), Stryadhyaksha (women)
Dhamma yatras | Replaced royal hunts; 256 nights on tour
Edicts | On highways and pilgrim routes; read aloud to the unlettered
Welfare | Roads, wells, rest houses, shade trees, medical care for humans and animals (RE II)
Missions abroad | Sri Lanka, Burma, Gandhara, Kashmir, Greek kingdoms
Message to tribes: follow dhamma, but warned of consequences if they disturbed order
⚠ Ashoka was the first Indian king to speak directly to people through inscriptions

t: Ashoka's place in history → assessment
text:
## 1. Achievements (PMF)
Political unification: one dhamma, one language, practically one script (Brahmi)
Religious tolerance: gifts to non-Buddhist and even anti-Buddhist sects
Only king to give up conquest after winning a war
Spread Gangetic material culture to tribal and peninsular areas; Tamil chiefs adopted "dear to the gods"
## 2. Criticism and limits
View | PMF verdict
Pacifism ruined the empire | Not true: kept Kalinga, kept the army
Neglected the north-west | True: no defence like China's Great Wall (~220 BCE)
Grants drained the treasury | Part of the financial-crisis explanation
⚠ Kautilya advised physical conquest; Ashoka followed the reverse policy

topic: Mauryan art and the end of the empire
t: Mauryan pillars and caves → features
text:
## 1. Pillars
Monolithic, Chunar sandstone, no base, mirror polish, carved in the round
Seven surviving capitals: Sarnath (4 lions), Sanchi (4 lions), Rampurva bull, Rampurva lion, Vaishali lion, Sankissa elephant, Lauriya Nandangarh lion
Sarnath abacus: elephant, horse, bull, lion + 24-spoke wheels; adopted as State Emblem 26 Jan 1950 (bell lotus dropped)
Mauryan pillar | Persian pillar
Monolith | Built in pieces
No base | With base
Smooth polished shaft | Polished but fluted
## 2. Caves and sculpture
Barabar caves (Lomas Rishi) by Ashoka, Nagarjuni caves by Dasharatha, for Ajivikas: oldest rock-cut caves
Dhauli elephant, Didarganj Yakshi, Kumrahar 80-pillar hall
## In news 2025-26
Barabar caves spotlighted (May 2026): 4 Barabar + 3 Nagarjuni caves = "Satghar"
Sanchi relics of Sariputta and Mahamoggallana taken to Mongolia (June 2026)
Vaishya Tekri, Ujjain: Mauryan stupa, ~350 ft wide, larger than Sanchi; excavation to resume after ~90 years (Aug 2026)

topic: Mauryan art and the end of the empire
t: Decline of the Mauryas → causes and the end
text:
## 1. End
Ashoka died 232 BCE; last king Brihadratha killed by general Pushyamitra Shunga, 185 BCE
⚠ Testbook gives 187 BCE; PMF (higher source) gives 185 BCE
## 2. Causes (PMF)
Cause | Point
Brahmanical reaction | Ban on sacrifices cut Brahmana income; Shungas, Kanvas, Satavahanas were Brahmanas
Financial crisis | Army, bureaucracy, grants to monks; gold images melted
Oppressive provinces | Taxila revolts under Bindusara and Ashoka
Spread of material culture | Iron and techniques reached outer areas: new kingdoms (Shungas, Chedis, Satavahanas)
Neglect of NW frontier | Bactrian Greeks invaded first
⚠ Empire never covered Kerala, Tamil Nadu or the Brahmaputra valley (CDS 2025)

t: Succession after the Mauryas → who killed or deposed whom
text:
Event | Killer / successor | Date
Last Maurya Brihadratha killed | His commander-in-chief Pushyamitra Sunga | 185 BCE
Last Sunga Devabhuti killed | His Brahmana minister (amatya) Vasudeva Kanva | c. 75 BCE
Last Kanva Susharman deposed | The Andhras (Satavahanas); Vayu Purana names Simuka | c. 30 BCE
Chain in the Gangetic valley: Maurya → Sunga → Kanva; in the Deccan the Satavahanas succeeded the Kanvas
Sungas: 10 kings, ~112 years; Kanvas: ~45 years, confined to Magadha
PMF: in the north the Kanvas gave way to the Mitras (c. 30 BCE); Samudragupta ended the Mitras of Kosambi
⚠ All three statements of the 2003 question are true: Sunga killed Maurya, Kanva killed Sunga, Andhras deposed Kanva
⚠ Pushyamitra was senapati (commander), Vasudeva was minister: do not swap roles
PYQ 2003: Brihadratha-Pushyamitra, Devabhuti-Vasudeva Kanva, last Kanva-Andhras → 1, 2 and 3

t: Sungas → rulers, wars and sources
text:
Item | Fact
Pushyamitra | Founder 185 BCE; staunch Brahmanist; two Ashvamedhas; repelled the Indo-Greeks
Agnimitra | Son; viceroy at Vidisha; hero of Kalidasa's Malavikagnimitra
Vasumitra | Grandson; beat the Yavanas on the Sindhu while guarding the sacrificial horse
Bhagabhadra | 5th/9th king; received Heliodorus
Devabhuti | Last king; killed by Vasudeva Kanva
Patanjali (Mahabhashya on Panini; Yoga Sutra) lived in this age; mentions Yavanas at Saketa and Madhyamika and sacrifices for Pushyamitra
Buddhist Divyavadana calls Pushyamitra a persecutor; yet Bharhut railings/toranas and Sanchi were enlarged in Sunga times
Besnagar (Heliodorus) pillar: Greek envoy of Antialcidas (Taxila) set up a Garuda pillar to Vasudeva; Prakrit, Brahmi; earliest record of a foreign convert to Vaishnavism
⚠ Malavikagnimitra (love story of the son of the Sunga founder) is by Kalidasa (Gupta age), not a Sunga writer
## In news 2025-26
Sanchi Great Stupa (PMF LENS June 2026): Ashokan brick core cased in sandstone and doubled in Sunga times; Satavahanas added the four toranas

t: Satavahanas → rulers and inscriptions
text:
Ruler | Known for
Simuka | Founder; son of a Mauryan feudatory Satavahana
Satakarni I | Naneghat inscription of Queen Naganika: 2 Ashvamedhas, 1 Rajasuya
Hala (17th king) | Gathasaptashati, 700 verses, Maharashtri Prakrit
Gautamiputra Satakarni (106-130 CE) | Destroyed Shakas, Yavanas, Pahlavas; beat Nahapana (Kshaharata); Nasik inscription by mother Gautami Balashri
Vashishtaputra Pulumavi (130-154) | Capital Paithan; first to rule Andhra; twice beaten by Rudradaman but spared (marriage ties)
Yajna Sri Satakarni (165-194) | Last great king; ship on coins; regained North Konkan, Malwa
Puranas call them Andhras; the word Andhra is not in Satavahana inscriptions
Metronymics (Gautamiputra, Vashishtiputra) but patrilineal succession
Successors after the 3rd century: Vakatakas, Abhiras, Ikshvakus, Kadambas, Western Gangas
⚠ Nasik inscription was issued by the mother (Gautami Balashri), not by Gautamiputra himself

t: Satavahana economy → land grants, coins, ports
text:
First rulers to grant tax-free villages to Brahmanas and Buddhist monks (more grants to monks)
Nasik inscriptions (Satavahana and Western Kshatrapa, 1st century CE): earliest epigraphic records of land grants
Feature | Satavahana practice
Coins | Mainly lead; also potin, copper, bronze, silver; no gold
Commonest coin | Elephant-type potin
Silver | Began with Gautamiputra over-striking Nahapana's coins
Ports | Kalyani (west); Gandakasela (Ghantasala) and Ganjam (east)
Officials | Amatya, mahamatra, district ahara; senapati as governor; gaulmika in villages
Feudatories | Raja (could coin), Mahabhoja, Senapati
Military camps: kataka, skandhavara
⚠ Land grants began with the Satavahanas, not the Guptas; Guptas made them common
## In news 2025-26
Circular stone labyrinth, Boramani grasslands, Solapur (PMF LENS Jan 2026): ~2,000 years old, linked to the Satavahana period; largest such labyrinth in India
Gudimallam linga (near Tirupati), among the oldest Shiva lingas, dated to the Satavahana period (PMF LENS CA 25 June 2026)

t: Kalinga and the republics → Kharavela, Yaudheyas
text:
## 1. Kharavela of Kalinga
Chedi-Mahameghavahana dynasty, 3rd ruler; Jain ("bhikshu-raja")
Hathigumpha inscription (Udayagiri, Bhubaneswar): Prakrit, Brahmi, 17 lines, undated; year-wise to his 13th year
Claims wins over Satakarni, Magadha (brought back the Kalinga Jina image), Indo-Greeks, Tamil states; built canals
## 2. Republics (ganas)
Republic | Region
Yaudheyas | Punjab, Haryana; copper coins with six-headed Kartikeya and peacock
Malavas | Rajasthan
Arjunayanas | Rajasthan
Audumbaras, Kunindas | North-west
Madrakas | Punjab
Absorbed by Indo-Greeks and Kushanas; finally crushed by Samudragupta
⚠ Yaudheyas were a republican tribe, not a Buddhist or Jain sect (CDS 2015)

t: Order of the invaders → who came first
text:
Order | Invader | Period | Origin
1 | Indo-Greeks (Bactrian Greeks) | 2nd-1st century BCE (~100 years) | Bactria
2 | Shakas (Scythians) | 1st century BCE-4th century CE | Central Asia
3 | Parthians (Pahlavas) | From c. 20 BCE | Iran
4 | Kushanas (Yuezhi) | 1st-3rd century CE | North-central Asia near China
5 | Hunas | Late 5th-6th century CE | Central Asia (Gupta age)
Chain reaction: Great Wall (c. 220 BCE) pushed the Yuezhi west → they pushed the Shakas → Shakas pressed the Bactrian Greeks into India
Series of invasions began c. 200 BCE; some ruled side by side (Shaka-Pahlavas)
⚠ Order is Greeks → Shakas → Kushans; Parthians fit between Shakas and Kushans
PYQ 2006: chronological order of invaders → Greeks, Sakas, Kushans

t: Indo-Greeks → rulers and firsts
text:
Ruler / item | Fact
Diodotus | Bactrian governor who broke from the Seleucids (mid-3rd century BCE)
Demetrius | First to cross the Hindu Kush into Punjab
Menander (Milinda) (165-145 BCE) | Capital Sakala/Sagala (Sialkot); converted by Nagasena; Milindapanho (Pali)
Agathocles | Coins with Balarama and Vasudeva-Krishna (Ai-Khanoum): first known Krishna image
Antialcidas | Sent Heliodorus to the Sunga court
Firsts | First gold coins in India; first coins with names and images of kings; military governorship
Coins: Greek on obverse, Kharoshthi/Prakrit on reverse; mostly silver
Menander is the only Indo-Greek king named in Indian sources
Brought Hellenistic art → Gandhara school
⚠ Indo-Greeks issued the first gold coins; Kushanas issued gold on a large scale

t: Rule of the foreigners → military governors, satraps, dual rule
text:
Practice | Introduced by
Military governorship (strategos) | Indo-Greeks
Mahakshatrapa / kshatrapa provinces (Achaemenid model) | Shakas
Satrap system; hereditary dual rule (two kings at once) | Kushanas
Title Maharajadhiraja; divine titles ("son of god") | Kushanas
Military governors held down the conquered people for the new rulers
Result: less centralisation, a feudatory order of tribute-paying princes
⚠ Military governorship = Greeks, not Shakas, Parthians or Mughals
PYQ 2000: military governorship first introduced by → the Greeks (strategos)

t: Shakas and Western Kshatrapas → Rudradaman and Junagadh
text:
First Shaka king: Maues (Moga), c. 85 BCE, in Gandhara; Azes ended the last Indo-Greeks
Five branches: Afghanistan, Taxila, Mathura, Western India (Western Kshatrapas), upper Deccan
Western Kshatrapa line | Kings
Kshaharata | Abhiraka, Bhumaka, Nahapana (silver at Nashik)
Kardamaka | Chashtana (c. 78 CE), Rudradaman I (130-150 CE)
Rudradaman I: Junagadh (Girnar) rock inscription, Shaka era 72 (150 CE): first long inscription in chaste Sanskrit; earliest kavya specimen
Repaired Sudarshana lake with own funds, no new tax; lake begun by Pushyagupta (Chandragupta Maurya), finished by Tushaspha (Ashoka)
Same rock: Ashoka, Rudradaman, Skandagupta (governor Parnadatta repaired the lake again)
Ended by Chandragupta II (defeated Rudrasimha III) → title Sakari
⚠ Western Kshatrapas were the first to put dates on coins (Shaka era)
Parthian king Gondophernes: St Thomas came in his reign

t: Kushanas → rulers, Kanishka, Silk Road
text:
Ruler | Fact
Kujula Kadphises | United the 5 Yuezhi clans; copper coins imitating Roman coins
Vima Kadphises | Expanded east of Indus; first Kushana gold coins; Shiva devotee
Kanishka (c. 78 CE) | Shaka era 78 CE; capitals Purushapura (Peshawar), Mathura; 4th Buddhist Council, Kashmir, president Vasumitra
Huvishka | Successor
Vasudeva | Last "Great Kushan"; first with an Indian name; Vishnu worship
Kanishka's court: Ashvaghosha (Buddhacharita), Vasumitra, Charaka; Patanjali was not there
Rabatak inscription (Bactrian, Greek script): Kanishka's genealogy back to Kujula
Controlled the Silk Route; tolls built the empire; Sassanians replaced them by mid-3rd century
⚠ Kanishka's coins carry Buddha (BODDO) and Shiva (Oesho); he ended Greek-Kharoshthi coins and used Bactrian
## In news 2025-26
Zehanpora (J&K) Buddhist complex, ~10 acres, Kushan period, Gandharan style, on a Silk Route corridor (PMF LENS Jan 2026; Praveen CA 360 Jan 2026)

t: Coins of the age → which dynasty did what first
text:
Dynasty | Coin fact
Indo-Greeks | First gold coins; first with king's name and image
Shakas (Western Kshatrapas) | First dated coins; much silver
Kushanas | Gold on a large scale; purer than Gupta gold; weight equal to Roman coins
Satavahanas | Lead, potin, copper; no gold
Yaudheyas | Copper with Kartikeya
Guptas | Largest number of gold coins (dinara); silver rupaka
Mauryas | Punch-marked silver (karshapana, pana)
Everyday trade used lead, potin, copper; Roman gold and silver for big deals
⚠ Kushana gold was not different in weight from Roman coins (CAPF 2023 trap)

t: Foreigners and religion → why many took Buddhism
text:
Buddhism was more accessible: Vaishnavism and Shaivism were tied to birth and caste
Buddhists welcomed foreign followers, even non-vegetarians → Mahayana
Foreigner | Faith
Menander | Buddhism
Kanishka | Mahayana Buddhism
Vima Kadphises | Shiva
Vasudeva (Kushan) | Vishnu
Heliodorus | Vasudeva Krishna (Bhagavata)
Foreigners entered society as Kshatriyas (e.g. Shakas through marriage with Satavahanas)
Jain split into Digambara and Shvetambara c. 300 CE
⚠ Reason given by the key: easier access to Indian society, not "Buddhism was in the ascendant"
PYQ 1998: Greeks, Kushanas, Shakas chose Buddhism because → it gave easier access to Indian society

t: Eras of the period → who started which
text:
Era | Start | Founder
Vikrama Samvat | 58-57 BCE | King of Ujjain after expelling the Shakas (some link it to Azes I)
Shaka era | 78 CE | Kanishka
Gupta era | 319-20 CE | Chandragupta I
Harsha era | 606 CE | Harsha
Vikram Samvat is ~57 years ahead of the Gregorian calendar
National calendar = Shaka era, adopted 22 March 1957; 1 Chaitra = 22 March (21 in leap year)
⚠ Testbook prints the Vikram era as "58 CE"; PMF gives 58-57 BCE
## In news 2025-26
PMF LENS Jan 2025 and Infographics Jan 2025 recalled the Shaka national calendar (Kanishka, 78 CE) and the Vikram Samvat (57 BCE)

t: Allahabad Pillar → whose record, which contents
text:
Ashokan pillar, first at Kausambi, moved to Allahabad fort (Akbar)
Inscription on it | Ruler | Language
Ashokan edicts | Ashoka | Prakrit, Brahmi
Prayaga Prashasti (33 lines) | Samudragupta, by court poet Harisena | Sanskrit (prose + verse)
Persian record | Jahangir | Persian
Three languages, three millennia on one pillar
Harisena's titles: Sandhivigrahika, Kumaramatya, Mahadandanayaka
Praises him as Kaviraja, musician (puts Tumburu, Narada to shame), equal to Kubera, Varuna, Indra, Yama
⚠ Script: PMF Modern history page says Nagari; PMF Art & Culture and Testbook say Brahmi (Gupta Brahmi)
⚠ Prashasti does not praise him as a sculptor (CDS 2016)
PYQ 2006: Allahabad Pillar inscription associated with → Samudragupta; trap: Ashoka (his edicts are on it too)

t: Samudragupta's campaigns → policy towards four kinds of rulers
text:
Category | Policy | Examples
Aryavarta (9 kings, mostly Nagas) | Extermination, annexed | North Indian rulers
Frontier states and ganas | Subordination, tribute | Samatata, Davaka, Kamarupa, Nepala; Malavas, Yaudheyas, Arjunayanas, Madrakas, Abhiras
Dakshinapatha (12 kings) | Captured and released (grahana-moksha-anugraha) | Vishnugopa of Kanchi
Outlying powers | Submission, gifts, daughters | Kushan and Shaka heirs, Sri Lanka
Atavika (forest) states made servants
Meghavarman of Sri Lanka asked leave to build a monastery at Gaya
Performed Ashvamedha ("restorer of the Ashvamedha" coins); veena coin type; "Napoleon of India"
⚠ Southern kings were released, not annexed

t: Gupta rulers → title and achievement
text:
Ruler | Years | Key facts
Sri Gupta | — | Founder; Maharaja
Ghatotkacha | — | Maharaja
Chandragupta I | 319/20-334 | Maharajadhiraja; Gupta era 319-20; married Kumaradevi (Lichchhavi)
Samudragupta | 335-380 | Conquests; Lichchhavi-dauhitra
(Ramagupta) | — | Disputed; Devichandraguptam story
Chandragupta II | 380-412 | Sakari, Vikramaditya; beat Rudrasimha III; Ujjain 2nd capital; Fa Xian
Kumaragupta I (Shakraditya) | 415-455 | Nalanda; Kartikeya coins; Ashvamedha
Skandagupta | 455-467 | Repelled the Hunas; last great Gupta
Guptas were probably Vaishyas and Kushana feudatories in UP; base Prayag; capital Pataliputra
Learned saddle, reins, trousers, boots from the Kushans: cavalry over chariots and elephants
⚠ Fa Xian came under Chandragupta II (UPSC 2025) and never named him
## In news 2025-26
Gupta-era bathing ghat (~1,600 years) found at Pansokhar Pokhar, near Nalanda with a Gupta copper coin (Praveen CA 360 June 2026)
Udayagiri Caves (Gupta, Vidisha) added to India's UNESCO Tentative List (CA 22 Oct 2026)

t: Inscriptions of the age → ruler and content
text:
Inscription | Ruler | Content
Allahabad (Prayag) Prashasti | Samudragupta | Conquests, by Harisena
Mehrauli Iron Pillar | Chandragupta II | Vishnu pillar; moved to Qutb complex (Anangpal Tomar)
Udayagiri caves 6 and 8 | Chandragupta II | Western victory; minister Virasena
Bhitari pillar | Skandagupta | Genealogy; defeat of Pushyamitras and Hunas
Junagadh/Girnar | Ashoka, Rudradaman, Skandagupta | Sudarshana lake
Eran (Airana) | Bhanugupta (510 CE) | Earliest evidence of sati (Testbook)
Nasik | Gautamiputra Satakarni (by Gautami Balashri) | Conquests, land grants
Naneghat | Satakarni I (by Naganika) | Sacrifices
Hathigumpha | Kharavela | Campaigns, Jainism
Besnagar | Heliodorus (Sunga age) | Vasudeva worship
Rabatak | Kanishka | Kushan genealogy
Junagadh inscription names both Chandragupta Maurya and Ashoka (Preview)
Gupta copper plates (tamrapatra) record land grants: donor, donee, gift
⚠ Mehrauli pillar = Chandragupta II; Bhitari = Skandagupta

t: Chandragupta II → alliances, court, Fa Xian
text:
Daughter Prabhavati Gupta married Vakataka Rudrasena II; ruled as regent → indirect hold on the Vakatakas
Conquest of western Malwa and Gujarat → western ports, Roman gold, silver coinage
Navaratna | Field
Kalidasa | Poet, dramatist
Amarasimha | Lexicographer (Amarakosha)
Varahamihira | Astronomer
Dhanvantari | Physician
Vararuchi | Grammarian
Shanku | Architect
Ghatakarna, Kshapanaka, Vetalabhatta | Others
## Fa Xian (c. 400-410 CE)
Six of nine years in the Gupta empire; 3 years at Pataliputra
Gangetic valley = "land of Brahmanism"; mild government, no spies, fines common, cowries for daily trade
Noted the plight of the chandalas
⚠ UPSC 2020: Kalidasa ↔ Chandragupta II is right; Amarasimha is not Harsha's, Panini is not Pushyamitra's

topic: Gupta administration, revenue and land grants
t: Gupta units → officer in charge
text:
Unit | Officer
Empire | King (Maharajadhiraja, Paramabhattaraka, Parameshvara)
Bhukti (province) | Uparika
Vishaya (district) | Vishayapati
Vithi (eastern India) | —
Grama (village) | Gramika / village headman with elders
Key officials: kumaramatyas (paid in cash), sandhivigrahika, mahadandanayaka
Mantri parishad advised the king; succession not by primogeniture
Town boards of artisans, merchants, scribes; their consent needed for land deals
⚠ Gupta rule was decentralised and feudal, unlike the Mauryas
## Beyond your notes
Urban board (Damodarpur plates): nagarashreshthi (chief banker), sarthavaha (caravan leader), prathama kulika (chief artisan), prathama kayastha (chief scribe)

topic: Gupta administration, revenue and land grants
t: Gupta revenue → taxes and forced labour
text:
Levy | Meaning
Land tax | 1/4 to 1/6 of produce
Uparikara | New tax, probably on temporary tenants
Udranga | New tax, unclear: water tax or police tax
Vata-bhuta | Cess for rites to winds and spirits
Halivakara | Probably a plough tax
Vishti | Forced labour for the army and officials
Supplies | Feed passing army; animals, grain, furniture for officers
Land taxes rose, trade taxes (shulka, tolls) fell
Vishti was found in central and western India (Madhya Pradesh, Kathiawar)
Vishti statement (2019) | Status
Source of income for the State, a tax paid by the people | Correct
Totally absent in MP and Kathiawar | Wrong: it existed there
Labourer got weekly wages | Wrong: unpaid
Eldest son was sent | Wrong
PYQ 2019: vishti → a source of income for the State, a sort of tax paid by the people

topic: Gupta administration, revenue and land grants
t: Land grants and feudalism → origin and growth
text:
Grants to Brahmanas, temples and officials: first by the Satavahanas, common under the Guptas
Grants were tax-free forever; royal agents could not enter; grantees collected taxes and punished criminals
Samantas got land, paid homage, gave troops; strong samantas could become kings
Debate (PMF) | View
Expansion view | Grants extended farming into new areas
Weakness view | Kings losing control bought allies with land
Effect | Priestly landlords (esp. MP); tribal peasants lowered; forced labour
Assertion-Reason 2000 | Status
A: origin of feudalism traced to military campaigns | Taken as true by the key (conquest → land to officers)
R: feudalism expanded in the Gupta period | True
Link | R is a chronological fact, not the cause → R does not explain A
⚠ The engine of feudalism is the land grant; campaigns only made more land to grant
PYQ 2000: feudal origin in military campaigns; expansion under Guptas → both true, R not the explanation
Feudal system essentials (UPSC 2015): land-based administration and lord-vassal ties; not a strong centre

topic: Gupta administration, revenue and land grants
t: Weak centre → why the Gupta empire fell
text:
Cause | Detail
Huna invasions | Toramana, Mihirakula; Skandagupta resisted; Yashodharman (Aulikara, Mandsaur) beat Mihirakula
Rise of feudatories | Later Guptas (Magadha), Maukharis (Kanauj), Valabhi, Thanesar princes
Loss of western India | No Gupta coin in Saurashtra after 467 CE
Land grants | Lower revenue, hard to keep a standing army
Trade decline | Silk weavers left Gujarat for Mandasor (473 CE)
Debased gold | Less pure gold in later dinaras
Bihar and UP were out of Gupta hands by about 550 CE
⚠ Hunas later became one of the 36 Rajput clans

t: Land measures → kulyavapa, dronavapa, nivartana
text:
Unit | Meaning | Size (PMF)
Kulyavapa | Area sown with one kulya of seed | 12-16 acres
Dronavapa | Area sown with one drona of seed | 1.5-2 acres
Nivartana | Land unit in other regions | —
These terms appear in Gupta land-grant inscriptions, used for assessing land tax
⚠ PMF says kulyavapa was used in the west and dronavapa in the north; Prelims GS PYQs places both in Bengal inscriptions
⚠ They are land measures, not coins, not urban land classes, not rituals
PYQ 2020: kulyavapa and dronavapa denote → measurement of land
## Beyond your notes
Kulyavapa and dronavapa occur in the Paharpur and Damodarpur copper plates of Bengal
## In news 2025-26
PMF LENS June 2026 (practice question): drona was also a volumetric unit for grain, used in Mauryan rainfall measurement

t: Land categories → term and meaning
text:
Term | Meaning
Kshetra | Cultivated land
Khila | Uncultivated / waste land
Aprahata | Jungle / forest land
Vasti (vastu) | Habitable land
Gopata sarah | Pasture land
Testbook groups uncultivated land as khila or aprahata
Landowning class: mahattaras, gramikas, kutumbikas
⚠ Kshetra = cultivated; khila = not cultivated: the commonest swap
Statement-type trap: these are rural land classes in inscriptions, not "classification of urban land"

t: Grant terms → who received what
text:
Term | Meaning
Agrahara | Land to a Brahmana, free of revenue; right to collect dues
Brahmadeya | Land gifted to Brahmanas (Testbook pairs it with agrahara)
Devagrahara / devadana | Land to temples
Samanta | Feudatory chief holding land
Taniyur | Big brahmadeya treated as a separate unit (south, early medieval)
Vishti | Forced labour, a tax in labour
Gupta grants were mostly to Brahmanas and religious bodies; tax-free land also to officials later
⚠ Tax-free farmland in the Gupta age went to Brahmins (MPPSC 2014), not to court scholars or soldiers
## Beyond your notes
Fiscal terms of the age: bhaga (king's share of produce), bhoga (periodic supplies), hiranya (tax in cash)

t: Gupta coins → metal and name
text:
Metal | Name | Note
Gold | Dinara (dinar) | Largest number of gold coins in ancient India; Roman-influenced name
Silver | Rupaka | After the conquest of Gujarat; for local trade
Copper | — | Very few
Coins: king on obverse, deity on reverse; Indian deities, Brahmi legends; Lakshmi as Vishnu's wife
Gupta gold was less pure than Kushana gold; used to pay officers and buy land
Biggest Gupta hoard: Bayana (Bharatpur, Rajasthan)
Other coin names | Era
Karshapana, pana | Mauryan silver
Nishka | Vedic gold
Tanka, jital | Delhi Sultanate (Iltutmish)
⚠ Rupaka = silver, dinara = gold; karshapana and pana are Mauryan
⚠ Copper was the smallest, not the largest, Gupta issue (CDS 2020)
PYQ 1997: Gupta silver coins → rupaka

t: Gupta coin types → which king
text:
King | Coin type
Chandragupta I / Samudragupta | Chandragupta-Kumaradevi (Lichchhavi) type
Samudragupta | Veena-player, Ashvamedha; probably first Gupta issuer
Chandragupta II | Silver rupaka after beating the Shakas; many gold types
Kumaragupta I | Kartikeya on coins
Chandragupta II, Kumaragupta I, Skandagupta, Budhagupta | Issued silver
Gupta coinage began by imitating Kushan weight and design
⚠ ROCKET credits Chandragupta I as first issuer; PMF Art & Culture thinks Samudragupta struck the Kumaradevi coins

t: Ports → which coast and age
text:
Port | Location | Note
Tamralipti (Tamluk) | Bengal | Main port for North Indian trade in Gupta times; SE Asia, China
Ghantasala (Kontakossylla) | Andhra coast | Gupta-era foreign trade
Kadura | Andhra coast | Gupta-era foreign trade
Chaul | Konkan (south of Mumbai) | Gupta-era foreign trade
Broach (Bharukachchha) | Gujarat | Chief post-Mauryan western port
Sopara, Kalyan | Maharashtra | Post-Mauryan / Satavahana
Arikamedu | Puducherry | Roman trade

⚠ Kalyan and Broach were western ports; north Indian goods went out by Tamralipti
PYQ 2020: Ghantasala, Kadura, Chaul → ports handling foreign trade
PYQ 1999: port for North Indian trade in Gupta times → Tamralipti
## In news 2025-26
Baliyatra (Cuttack, Kartika Purnima) honours Sadhabas who sailed from Tamralipti, Manikpatna, Palur, Pithunda (PMF LENS Nov 2025)
Tamluk (Tamralipti), on the Rupnarayan, noted as a capital of Suhma (PMF Prelims Magnum 2025)
## Beyond your notes
Fa Xian sailed home from Tamralipti via Sri Lanka

t: Trade and towns → decline in the Gupta age
text:
Period | Trade picture
Post-Mauryan (200 BCE-300 CE) | Boom: Roman trade; India a gainer; guilds (shrenis)
Gupta | Decline in long-distance trade
Causes: less demand for Indian silk; Byzantines learnt silk from China (mid-6th century); Huna disruption of the north-west route
Silk weavers' guild left Gujarat for Mandasor and changed jobs (5th century)
Gold coin finds fall after the 6th century: crisis or less hoarding (debate)
Guilds kept their own laws and immunities
Roman trade (PMF Infographics) | Items
Indian exports | Pepper, pearls, ivory, diamonds, malabathrum, spikenard
Imports | Gold and silver coins, wine, glass, copper, tin
⚠ Gupta age is a "golden age" of culture, not of trade: towns and trade declined

topic: Kingdoms between the Guptas and Harsha
t: Post-Gupta kingdoms → capital and founder
text:
Kingdom | Capital / region | Facts
Later Guptas of Magadha | Magadha (Bihar) | No link to the imperial Guptas; ousted by the Maukharis; Narasimhagupta beat Mihirakula
Maukharis | Kanauj | Founder Yajnavarman; Grihavarman married Rajyashri, Harsha's sister
Pushyabhutis (Vardhanas) | Thanesar (Haryana) | Founder Pushyabhuti; Prabhakaravardhana first big king

Aulikaras | Dashapura (Mandsaur) | Yashodharman beat Mihirakula
Hunas | Malwa, Punjab, Kashmir | Toramana, Mihirakula

PYQ 2021: power between Gupta decline and Harsha → Guptas of Magadha, Pushyabhutis, Maukharis, Maitrakas (1, 3, 4, 6)

topic: Kingdoms between the Guptas and Harsha

text:
Dynasty | Period | Note
Paramaras of Malwa | ~10th-13th century | Bhoja (1010-1055), capital Dhar

Yadava capital Devagiri was raided by Alauddin Khalji (1296) and annexed under Mubarak Shah Khalji (1317-18)

topic: Kingdoms between the Guptas and Harsha
t: Kanauj rises → why power moved from Pataliputra
text:
Pataliputra lived on trade and tolls; as trade fell and grants replaced cash, it declined
Kanauj: on high ground (easy to fortify) and central in the doab (land and river routes)
Military camps (skandhavaras) became seats of power
Event | Year
Maukharis independent at Kanauj | mid-6th century
Prabhakaravardhana rules Thanesar | 580
Grihavarman killed by Devagupta (Malwa) with Shashanka | 605-06
Harsha accedes; Harsha era | 606
Harsha moves capital to Kanauj | after driving out Shashanka
After Harsha came the tripartite struggle for Kanauj (Palas, Pratiharas, Rashtrakutas)
⚠ Kanauj was the Maukhari capital before it was Harsha's

t: Harsha → his southern defeat and other wars
text:
## 1. Harsha vs Pulakesin II
Pulakesin II (Chalukya of Badami/Vatapi) defeated Harsha on the Narmada and stopped his march into the Deccan
Harsha's only defeat; treaty made the Narmada his southern border
Pulakesin II then took the title Parameshvara
Recorded by Hiuen Tsang and the Aihole inscription (by Ravikirti)
## 2. Harsha's other wars
Opponent | Result
Shashanka of Gauda (Bengal) | Driven out of Kanauj; Magadha and Bengal taken after his death

t: Harsha → the Kanauj and Prayag assemblies
text:
## 1. Two assemblies, two purposes
Feature | Kanauj assembly | Prayag assembly
Purpose | Honour Hiuen Tsang; publicise Mahayana | Charity to all sects, held once in five years
Attendees | Hiuen Tsang, 20 rulers (incl. Bhaskaravarman), Buddhist, Jain and Vedic scholars | Shramanas, Brahmanas and all sects
Events | No one refuted Hiuen Tsang for 5 days; attempt on Harsha's life | Harsha emptied the treasury, gave away even his clothes and jewels
Prayag = confluence of Ganga and Yamuna; some call it the first recorded Kumbh Mela
Harsha: early Shaiva, later Mahayana Buddhist (Hiuen Tsang's influence); honoured Buddha, Surya, Shiva at Prayag
⚠ Popularising only Mahayana was the aim of Kanauj, not Prayag
PYQ 2001: A - Harsha convened the Prayag Assembly (true); R - to popularise only Mahayana (false) → A true, R false

t: Harsha → sources and literature
text:

Source | Author | Note

Kadambari | Banabhatta (finished by son Bhushanabhatta) | Romance
Si-Yu-Ki | Hiuen Tsang (in India 630-645) | Richer and more reliable than Fa Xian
Ratnavali, Priyadarsika, Nagananda | Harsha himself | Nagananda shows his charity

## 2. Inscriptions
Inscription | Content
Madhuban copper plate (UP) | Land grants; genealogy for 4 generations
Banskhera copper plate (UP) | Bears Harsha's signature
Sonpat (Haryana) | Harsha-era record
Aihole (Karnataka) | Pulakesin II's prashasti; Harsha "no longer Harsha"

t: Harsha → administration and society (Hiuen Tsang)
text:
## 1. State
More feudal and decentralised than the Guptas; officers paid in land → few coins
Army: 1,00,000 horses, 60,000 elephants (feudatories contributed)
Land tax one-sixth; new grazing and pond taxes; duties at ferries and barrier stations
## 2. Law and society
Hiuen Tsang noted | Detail
Roads unsafe | He himself was robbed
Ordeals | By fire, water, poison
Robbery | Right hand cut off; later life imprisonment
Shudras | Practised agriculture
Untouchables | Lived outside villages; announced their entry
Women | No widow remarriage (higher castes), dowry, sati
Patronised Nalanda; brick Lakshmana temple, Sirpur assigned to his age
PYQ 2013: roads were NOT immune from robbery; ordeals and ferry duties were correct

t: Pali coin terms + punch-marked coins → what they prove
text:
## 1. The 6th century BCE package
Pali texts give the first definite references to coins: kahapana, nikkha, kamsa, kakanika
Corroborated by punch-marked coins from many sites, mostly silver
Both point to: emergence of urban life (second urbanisation) + transition to money economy
Evidence | What it shows
Early Vedic nishka, nishka-griva, hiranya-pinda | Gold / gold ornaments / gold globules, not coins
Later Vedic nishka, satamana, suvarna, pada | Metal pieces of definite weight / prestige objects, possibly not coins
Pali kahapana, nikkha | First definite coin names
Silver punch-marked finds | Money economy, trade, towns
⚠ Vedic nishka = gold ornament, not a coin; Stone Age, Chalcolithic and Harappan people used barter
Testbook: Mahajani system (money lending, banking) recognised in Buddhism and Jainism
PYQ 2026: two statements on Pali coin terms linked to urban life and money economy; answer both. Expect more source → inference pairs

t: Coin types → first, largest, purest
text:
## 1. Sequence of Indian coinage
Coin / ruler | The "first" fact
Punch-marked (6th c BCE) | Earliest coins; silver/copper; symbols only, no text; rectangular/square/round
Uninscribed cast | Copper alloys, poured into moulds; everywhere except the far south
Uninscribed die-struck | From 4th c BCE; copper, rarely silver; Taxila, Ujjain
Indo-Greeks | First inscribed coins, first with king's name and image, first gold, bilingual
Western Kshatrapas (Shakas) | First dated coins (Saka era)
Kushanas | First gold coins on a large scale; purer than Gupta gold (22-23 carat)
Satavahanas | Lead, potin, copper, bronze; ship motif
Guptas | Largest number of gold coins (dinara); king obverse, deity reverse
⚠ Kushan gold is purer; Gupta gold is more numerous. Mauryan imperial currency: silver punch-marked (karshapana/pana) with peacock, hill, crescent
⚠ Punch-marked coins were mostly issued by states, some by guilds, merchants, bankers; they circulated till the early centuries CE

text:
## 1. Inferences UPSC can pair with a coin fact
Coin evidence | Inference
Wide circulation of Kushana coins | Thriving trade
Roman coins in south India | Indo-Roman trade, favourable balance
Ship on Satavahana coins | Maritime trade of the Deccan
Debased later Gupta gold | Economic / fiscal decline
Largest number of coins post-Mauryan | Trade flourished
Guild coins (merchants, goldsmiths) | Issued with the ruler's permission
Many Indo-Greek kings | Known only through coins
Dated coins (Kshatrapa Saka era, Gupta regnal years) fix chronology; any coin helps date excavation layers
⚠ Post-6th c fall in gold coins: one view = Western Roman collapse cut trade; other view = new towns and networks, coins still mentioned in texts (fewer hoards, not less circulation)

t: Guilds (shreni) → powers and features
text:
## 1. What a shreni did
From ~6th c BCE: traders, craftsmen, moneylenders, agriculturists in shrenis under elected headmen
Feature | Fact
Rules | Own internal laws; king did not interfere, but royal recognition
Economic | Fixed wages, rules of work, standards, prices; training, raw material, sale
Judicial | Judicial powers over own members; punished breaches of guild custom
Banking | Took deposits; interest funded monks (Nasik 2nd c CE) and feeding Brahmins (Mathura)
Number | At least two dozen guilds (post-Mauryan, Mathura and western Deccan)
Coins | Some guilds issued coins with ruler's permission
⚠ Guilds were not registered with a central authority, and the king was not their chief administrator
Testbook: merchant guilds called sartha; Gupta silk-weavers' guild moved Gujarat → Mandasor (473 CE) and left weaving
Ivory workers financed part of a Sanchi gateway
PYQ 2012: statements 2 and 3 correct; trap: "registered with the State" is wrong

t: Bay of Bengal → why contacts with Southeast Asia
text:
## 1. The monsoon factor
Monsoon winds (pattern known ~1st c CE) made voyages predictable: out with the SW monsoon, back with the NE monsoon
Ships waited at Indian and SE Asian ports for winds; direct China-West Asia voyages were rare
Tamralipti = Pala port for China and SE Asia; India exported sandalwood, camphor, spices; imported silk, porcelain
Monument | Builder / fact
Angkor Wat (Cambodia) | Suryavarman II, Khmer, 12th c; originally Vishnu temple
Borobudur (Java) | Buddhist (Sailendras)
Prambanan (Java) | Hindu; India-Indonesia conservation project
⚠ Ship-building or royal patronage is not the "most convincing" reason; geography (monsoon) is
PYQ 2011: monsoon winds; PYQ 2006: Angkor Vat built under Suryavarman II
## In news 2025-26
Two 2,000-year-old gold rings, one with a Brahmi inscription ("Pusharakitsava"), at Don Yee Thong, Phetchaburi, Thailand (Praveen CA, July 2026)
## Beyond your notes

text:
## 1. Observations (PMF)
Buddhism flourishing in north-west India, neglected in the Gangetic valley, which he called the "land of Brahmanism"
Holy places Kapilavastu and Kusinagara in an unsatisfactory state
Empire prosperous; tiered money: cowrie shells for daily trade, gold coins (dinara/suvarna) for big purchases
A free hospital at Pataliputra, endowed by citizens, gave food and medicine to the poor (Preview)
Not interested in politics; saw everything from the Buddhist angle; social picture exaggerated

## Beyond your notes
Came overland via Central Asia; returned by sea via Sri Lanka and Java
Noted Chandalas living outside towns; criminals mostly fined, no death penalty; people avoided meat, onion, garlic and liquor

## 1. Law and order (the 2013 question)
Statement | Hiuen Tsang's record
Roads and river routes safe? | No: roads unsafe from robbers; he himself was robbed
How was guilt decided? | Ordeals by fire, water and poison
Duties on traders? | Yes: duties at ferries and barrier stations
Punishment for robbery | treated as second treason: right hand cut off; later softened to life imprisonment under Buddhist influence
## 2. Society and economy
Shudras practised agriculture (earlier texts made them servants of the three upper varnas)
Untouchables (scavengers, executioners) lived outside villages, ate garlic and onion, shouted to announce entry into town
Land tax one-sixth of produce; trade declining (fewer coins, weaker guilds)
Mathura famous for cotton cloth; Thanesar prosperous from trade

t: Qutbuddin Aibak (1206-1210) → works and death

Item | Fact
Origin | Turkish slave bought by Muhammad Ghori at Ghazni
Capital | Lahore
Title | Lakh Baksh (giver of lakhs)
Mosques | Quwwat-ul-Islam (Delhi), Adhai Din Ka Jhopra (Ajmer)

t: Iltutmish (1211-1236) → consolidation measures
text:
Measure | Detail
Capital | shifted Lahore → Delhi
Coins | silver tanka and copper jital: the two basic Sultanate coins
Iqta | started the iqta system in India
Nobility | Chahalgani ("the Forty") Turkish nobles
Legitimacy | Letter of investiture (1229) from Abbasid Caliph Al-Mustansir
Mongols | refused asylum to Jalaluddin Mangbarni; saved India from Chengiz Khan
Buildings | completed Qutub Minar; Hauz-i-Sultani; own tomb (1235)
Scholar | Minhaj-i-Siraj (Tabaqat-i-Nasiri)
"Slave of a slave"; real founder/consolidator of the Sultanate
Annexed Sind and Multan; recovered Ranthambhor, Jalor, Ajmer, Gwalior
⚠ Iltutmish was the first to issue independent Sultanate coins; Ghori's gold coins imitated Lakshmi-type Dehliwal coins

t: Raziya and the Forty → struggle of crown vs nobles
text:
Iltutmish nominated his daughter Raziya; nobles first enthroned Ruknuddin Firuz (mother Shah Turkan ruled)
Raziya (1236-1240): first and only woman ruler of the Sultanate
Act | Reaction
gave up purdah, wore kuba (coat) and kulah (cap) | Turkish nobles offended
made Abyssinian Yaqut Khan Amir-i-Akhur (master of horses) | charge of favouring a non-Turk
fought Altunia of Tabarhinda (Bathinda) | captured; married him; killed 1240
After her: Bahram Shah, Masud Shah (puppets); Nasiruddin Mahmud (1246-66) with Balban as Naib
⚠ Raziya's quote "not of the right sex" is from Minhaj-i-Siraj, not Barani (PPSC 2025 trap)
⚠ "Nasiruddin Mahmud" of the Slave dynasty is not the last Tughlaq Nasiruddin Mahmud Shah

t: Balban (1266-1287) → theory of kingship and military reforms
text:
## 1. Kingship
Feature | Detail
Title | Zil-i-Ilahi (Shadow of God)
Theory | Sultan's power from God, not nobles or people (divine right)
Court customs | sijda (prostration), paibos (kissing feet)
Festival | Persian Nauroz
Nobles | broke the Forty; spies; excluded non-nobles and Indian Muslims
## 2. Administration and army
Created separate military department Diwan-i-Arz (first time)
Policy of consolidation, not expansion; crushed Mewatis; blood and iron
Revolt of Tughril Khan (Bengal, 1279) crushed; son Prince Mahmud killed by Mongols
His tomb (Mehrauli): first true arch (and true dome, PMF)
⚠ Other titles: Tuti-i-Hind = Amir Khusrau; Din-i-Ilahi = Akbar; Kaisar-i-Hind = British medal

⚠ Barani's reason is not the non-Muslim majority (that was Jalaluddin's argument)
PYQ 2002: Barani: Sultan framed his own regulations to supplement Muslim law

t: Iqta system → features and officials
text:
Feature | Detail
Meaning | territorial revenue assignment in lieu of salary/service
Holder | iqtadar / muqti / wali
Origin | Arabic, early Islamic/Caliphate institution, not indigenous
In India | started by Iltutmish
Transfer | muqtis rotated every 3-4 years
Hereditary? | No, until Firuz made it hereditary
Control | accountants checked; tightest under Alauddin and MbT
Muqti paid soldiers, sent a fixed sum to the treasury, kept the balance
Fawazil = surplus revenue the iqtadar paid to the exchequer after his expenses
Early Turkish rule was essentially military: land parcelled into iqtas among military leaders
⚠ Iqta gave no ownership right in land
PYQ 1998: fawazil = excess paid to the exchequer by iqtadars; A-R on military administration: both true, R explains A

t: Local units and officials → who headed what

Unit | Head
Iqta (province, later suba) | muqti / wali
Shiq | shiqdar
Pargana | amil and chaudhri
Village | muqaddam and khot; accountant patwari
Amil (ummal) = officer in charge of revenue collection (UPSC 2019)
Royal household: wakil-i-dar (household), amir-i-hajib (ceremonies, petitions)
Chief judge: qazi-ul-mumalik (qazi-ul-quzzat); Hindus under panchayats and personal law
⚠ BPSC: muqaddam/chaudhuri = village headmen (rural aristocracy)
PYQ 2019: amil = revenue in-charge true; iqta indigenous false; Mir Bakshi under Khaljis false

t: Society and nobility → who held power
text:
Group | Position
Turks | top; monopolised high office till 1290
Persians (Tajiks), Afghans | next; excluded under Balban
Indian Muslims (converts) | lowest among Muslims; rose under Khaljis, Tughlaqs
Hindus | dominated trade, lower administration, rural aristocracy (khots, muqaddams, chaudhuris)
Bandagan: military slaves made governors, esp. by Iltutmish; loyal to master, not to heirs
Khaljis and Tughlaqs raised men of humble origin: tawarikh writers attacked "low-born" appointments
Noble birth stayed the key qualification; nobility broadened only under the Tughlaqs
⚠ Each new Sultan brought his own slaves and clients: old vs new nobility conflict on every accession
Zimmis: protected non-Muslims who paid jizya; Brahmans exempt until Firuz

t: Founding of Vijayanagara → who, where, in whose name
text:
## 1. Founders
1336: brothers Harihara I (Hakka) and Bukka (Bukkaraya), two of five sons of Sangama (hence Sangama dynasty)
Earlier feudatories of the Kakatiyas of Warangal, then ministers of Kampili; captured by Muhammad bin Tughlaq, converted to Islam, reconverted under guru Vidyaranya (a Shaiva saint; with Sayana, the Vedic commentator)
## 2. The city and the deity
Point | Fact
New city | Vijayanagara ("City of Victory") on the south bank of the Tungabhadra
Tungabhadra is | a tributary of the Krishna
Ruled as | Agent of Virupaksha (form of Shiva), to whom all land south of the Krishna belonged
First capital | Anegundi, on the north bank
Clan (Testbook) | Kuruba / cowherd, claimed Yadava ancestry
⚠ Distractors in 2015: Amoghavarsha I (Rashtrakuta, Manyakheta), Ballala II (Hoysala), Prataparudra II (last Kakatiya)
PYQ 2015: "new city on the south bank of a tributary of the Krishna, ruled as agent of a deity" = Harihara I

t: Vijayanagara → capitals, insignia and Hampi
text:
## 1. Capitals in order
No. | Capital | When
1 | Anegundi (north bank, Tungabhadra) | Earliest
2 | Vijayanagara / Hampi (south bank) | 1336-1565
3 | Penukonda | After Talikota, under Tirumala (Aravidu)
4 | Chandragiri | Under Venkata II
## 2. Identity
Royal insignia: Sun, Moon, Dagger, Boar (Varaha); Varaha = 3rd avatar of Vishnu
Name Hampi from local goddess Pampadevi; city sacked in 1565 and deserted
Ruins brought to light in 1800 by Colin Mackenzie (first Surveyor General of India, 1815)
Hampi = UNESCO World Heritage Site (1986); natural defence of craggy hills and the Tungabhadra on the north
Empire also called the Karnata kingdom
⚠ Penukonda came before Chandragiri; Anegundi is on the north bank, Hampi on the south

t: Vijayanagara vs neighbours → rivals and zones of conflict
text:
## 1. Rivals by frontier
Frontier | Rival
North | Bahmani Sultanate (later the five Deccan Sultanates)
East | Gajapatis of Orissa; Reddis (upper Krishna-Godavari delta); Kakatiyas/Velamas of Warangal
South | Hoysalas; Madurai Sultanate
## 2. Three zones of clash with the Bahmanis
Zone | Why
Raichur Doab (between Krishna and Tungabhadra) | Wealth, fertile land
Krishna-Godavari delta | Fertile land, many ports
Marathwada / Konkan | Fertile Konkan and the port of Goa, gateway for horses from Iran and Iraq
⚠ Good horses were not bred in India: control of western ports (Goa, Bhatkal) = control of cavalry
Next-likely: "Raichur Doab lies between Krishna and Godavari" (false: Krishna and Tungabhadra)

t: Early Sangama rulers → Harihara I to Harihara II
text:
Ruler | Reign | Key facts
Harihara I | 1336-1356 | Fort at Barkur (west coast); absorbed Hoysala lands after Vira Ballala III was killed by the Madurai Sultan (1343); whole Hoysala kingdom by 1346
Bukka I | 1356-1377 | Embassy to China; patron of Telugu poet Nachana Soma
Kumara Kampana (Bukka's son) | - | Ended the Madurai Sultanate (1370s; 1378 in PMF timeline); empire up to Rameswaram
Harihara II | 1377-1404 | Took Belgaum and Goa from the Bahmanis; titles Maharajadhiraja, Vaidikamarga Sthapanacharya; patron of Jain poet Madhura
## 1. Literary source
Madhura Vijayam (Sanskrit) by Gangadevi, wife of Kumara Kampana: his conquest of Madurai
⚠ PMF prints Harihara's coronation as "1136": read 1336
⚠ Bahmani-Warangal alliance blocked Harihara II in the Tungabhadra doab
Next-likely: "first Vijayanagara ruler to capture Goa from the Bahmanis" = Harihara II

t: Deva Raya I (1406-1422) → irrigation, wars, court
text:
## 1. Irrigation works (PYQ 2023)
Work | Purpose
Dam across the Tungabhadra | Bring water into the city
Canal-cum-aqueduct (about 24 km, c. 1410) to the capital | Relieve water shortage; canals raised revenue by 3,50,000 pardaos
Dam on the Haridra river | Irrigation
## 2. Wars
Defeated by Bahmani Firuz Shah: paid 10 lakh huns, married his daughter to the Sultan, ceded Bankapur as dowry
Later, allied with Warangal, defeated Firuz Shah, annexed Reddi land to the Krishna mouth; defeated the Gajapatis
## 3. Army and court
Better cavalry, Turkic archers, horses from Arabia and Persia; about 10,000 Muslims in army, built a mosque
Nicolo de Conti (Italian) visited in 1420
⚠ Testbook credits the Hazara Rama temple to Deva Raya I; PMF credits it to Krishnadeva Raya
## In news 2025-26
Copper plates of Deva Raya I's coronation (PMF 2026): grant of Gudipalli village; image of Vamana, not the usual Varaha
PYQ 2023: dam on Tungabhadra + aqueduct to capital = Devaraya I; distractors Mallikarjuna, Vira Vijaya, Virupaksha were later Sangama kings

t: Deva Raya II (1424-1446) → army, literature, envoys
text:
## 1. Titles
Greatest Sangama ruler; called Immadi Devaraya, Praudha Devaraya; inscriptions: Gajabetekara ("elephant hunter")
## 2. Army
Enlisted 2,000 Muslim cavalrymen, gave them jagirs, made Hindu soldiers learn archery from them
Tribute from Quilon, Sri Lanka, Pulicat, Pegu, Tenasserim (per Nuniz)
## 3. Literature
Person | Role
Deva Raya II (author) | Sobagina Sone, Amaruka (Kannada); Mahanataka Sudhanidhi (Sanskrit)
Chamarasa, Kumara Vyasa | Kannada poets
Gunda Dimdima | Sanskrit poet
Srinatha | Telugu; title Kavisarvabhauma; wrote Haravilasam
Parameshvara | Kerala school of astronomy-mathematics
## 4. Envoy
Abdur Razzaq, envoy of Timurid Shah Rukh (Persia), 1443-44: "three hundred ports", troops "eleven lakhs"
⚠ Virupaksha temple was expanded by Lakkan Dandesha, a chieftain under Deva Raya II

Order | Ruler | Reign

2 | Bukka I | 1356-1377

topic: Dynasties, Usurpations and the End of the Empire
t: Four dynasties → founder and period
text:
Dynasty | Period | Founder | Note
Sangama | 1336-1485 | Harihara I (with Bukka) | Shaiva; deity Virupaksha
Saluva | 1485-1505 | Saluva Narasimha | First usurpation
Tuluva | 1505-1570 | Vira (Veer) Narasimha | Second usurpation; Krishnadeva Raya
Aravidu | 1570-1646 (PMF) | Tirumala Deva Raya | Penukonda, then Chandragiri
Order: Sangama → Saluva → Tuluva → Aravidu (mnemonic S-S-T-A)
Later dynasties leaned to Vaishnavism; worship of Shiva continued
⚠ Aravidu end: PMF 1646 (last ruler Sri Ranga III, 1642-46); Preview gives 1672
Next-likely: order questions; "Saluva preceded Sangama" or "Tuluva followed Aravidu" are false

topic: Dynasties, Usurpations and the End of the Empire
t: First usurpation (1485) → Saluva Narasimha and why
text:
## 1. The event
Weak successors of Deva Raya II; civil wars; feudatories independent; Bahmani and Gajapati pressure
Saluva Narasimha, governor/feudal lord of Chandragiri, the powerful Mahanayakacharya, deposed the last Sangama king in 1485
## 2. Saluva dynasty rulers
Ruler | Reign
Saluva Narasimha Deva Raya | 1485-1491
Thimma Bhupala | 1491
Narasimha Raya II (Immadi Narasimha) | 1491-1505
## 3. Reason (Assertion-Reason, 2003)
He took the royal title to save the kingdom from further degeneration and disintegration; recovered Konkan and coastal areas
⚠ Last Sangama king deposed: Praudha Raya (PMF table, Preview); some accounts name Virupaksha Raya II
PYQ 2003: A (Saluva Narasimha ended the old dynasty) and R (to save it from degeneration) both true, R explains A

topic: Dynasties, Usurpations and the End of the Empire
t: Second usurpation (1505) → Tuluva succession
text:
Year | Event
1505 | Vira Narasimha (son of Tuluva Narasa Nayaka) deposed Immadi Narasimha, last Saluva: Tuluva dynasty
1505 | Vira Narasimha let Portuguese viceroy Francisco de Almeida build a factory at Anjediva
1509 | His younger (half-)brother Krishnadeva Raya succeeded
1529 | KDR succeeded by half-brother Achyuta Deva Raya (chosen by KDR)
## 1. Relationships to remember
Vira Narasimha = elder half-brother of Krishnadeva Raya (PMF)
Achyuta = younger half-brother of Krishnadeva Raya
⚠ Testbook calls Achyuta "younger brother"; PMF and the 2004 key say half-brother
⚠ Anjediva (1505, Vira Narasimha) vs Bhatkal (1510, Krishnadeva Raya)
PYQ 2004: all four statements correct: Saluva ends Sangama; Vira Narasimha deposes last Saluva; KDR succeeds his brother; Achyuta (half-brother) succeeds KDR

topic: Dynasties, Usurpations and the End of the Empire
t: After Krishnadeva Raya → Achyuta to Sadashiva and Rama Raya
text:
Ruler | Reign | Facts
Achyuta Deva Raya | 1529-1542 | Fernao Nuniz visited; Achyutaraya (Tiruvengalanatha) temple; patron of Purandaradasa (father of Carnatic music)
Venkata I | 1542 | Achyuta's son; killed within about six months
Sadashiva Raya | 1542/43-1570 | Last Tuluva ruler; a figurehead
Aliya Rama Raya (regent) | 1543-1565 | Son-in-law of KDR; real power; played the Sultanates against each other
"Aliya" = son-in-law; Rama Raya and brothers Tirumala and Venkatadri belonged to the Aravidu family
## In news 2025-26
June 2026: ASI found three trilingual (Telugu, Tamil, Kannada) rock inscriptions of 1554 at Sadasivakona, Seshachalam forest, Tirupati: Sadashiva Raya's holy bath; taxes (Kaanika) from Gudimallam temple lands moved to the new Sadasivakona temple
⚠ Gudimallam has one of the oldest Shiva lingas (2nd-1st c. BCE, Satavahana period)

topic: Dynasties, Usurpations and the End of the Empire
t: Battle of Talikota (1565) → who fought and what followed
text:
## 1. Sides
Point | Fact
Date | January 1565
Other names | Rakshasa-Tangadi, Bannihatti
Allies | Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda, Bidar
Not in alliance | Berar
Vijayanagara king | Sadashiva Raya (figurehead)
Commander | Rama Raya: captured and executed (by Hussain Nizam Shah, Preview)
## 2. Result
Capital destroyed, looted, deserted; conventionally the end of the empire
Kingdom survived under the Aravidu dynasty at Penukonda / Chandragiri for about a century
Caesar Frederick (Venetian) saw the ruined capital in 1567
⚠ "Talikota" is Ferishta's name; the fighting was between villages Rakshasi and Tangadi
⚠ Talikota is not a battle against the "Bahmani kingdom", which had already broken up

topic: Dynasties, Usurpations and the End of the Empire
t: Aravidu dynasty and the rise of Mysore → who ruled when
text:
## 1. Rulers
Ruler | Facts
Tirumala Deva Raya | Brother of Rama Raya; dethroned Sadashiva, founded Aravidu (1570); capital to Penukonda
Sri Ranga I | Tirumala's eldest son
Venkata II | Capital Chandragiri; one of the greatest later kings; Queen Eraivi let the Dutch set up a factory at Pulicat (1609)
Venkata III | Under him Damarla Venkatapathy Nayak granted land for Fort St. George, Madras (1639)
Sri Ranga III | Last ruler, 1642-1646
## 2. Mysore Wodeyars
Raja Wodeyar founded the kingdom of Mysore while Venkata II ruled Vijayanagara
⚠ Dates differ: Preview 1612; PMF: Mysore line from Yaduraya Wodeyar, 1399, substantially independent 1612-13; the 2006 key gives 1578/1610 (Raja Wodeyar took Srirangapatna in 1610, Beyond)
PYQ 2006: options Sadashiva, Tirumala, Ranga II, Venkata II: answer Venkata II

t: Krishnadeva Raya → campaigns and titles
text:
## 1. Against the Deccan Sultanates
Defeated the Muslim armies (battle of Diwani, Testbook); took the Raichur Doab; captured Raichur fort (1520) from Ismail Adil Khan of Bijapur
Freed Bahmani Sultan Mahmud Shah, restored him at Bidar: title Yavanarajya Sthapanacharya ("restorer of the Yavana kingdom")
Defeated Sultan Quli Qutb Shah of Golconda (battle of Golconda)
## 2. Against Orissa
Early campaign against Gajapati Prataparudra: took Udayagiri fort; Jaya Stambha at Simhachalam; Vijaya Mahal at the capital
Prataparudra gave his daughter in marriage; KDR returned lands north of the Krishna
## 3. Titles
Title | Meaning
Andhra Bhoja, Abhinava Bhoja | Patron of letters
Andhra Pitamaha | Telugu literature
Yavanarajya Sthapanacharya | Restored the Bahmani Sultan
Babur called him the most powerful ruler of India
NDA 2024 (in PMF): marched first against Orissa; Raichur 1520; restored Mahmud Shah: all correct

t: Krishnadeva Raya and the Portuguese → Bhatkal, Goa, horses
text:
## 1. Relations (PYQ 2024)
Point | Fact
Portuguese governor | Afonso de Albuquerque sent ambassadors
1510 | KDR permitted the Portuguese to build a factory/fort at Bhatkal (Uttara Kannada, Arabian Sea coast)
1510 | Albuquerque took Goa from Bijapur with Vijayanagara's help
Horses | KDR got a monopoly on horses supplied by the Portuguese
Portuguese offer | Help to recover Goa from Bijapur + horse monopoly, to buy his neutrality
## 2. Two factors behind the friendship
Common enmity with Bijapur
Supply of imported horses (and guns)
## 3. Bhatkal
Main port of Vijayanagara: horses and weapons in; sugar, pepper, spices, fine rice out
⚠ Distractors 2024: Narasimha Saluva; Muhammad Shah III (Bahmani, Mahmud Gawan's master); Yusuf Adil Shah (founder of Bijapur, lost Goa)
⚠ Anjediva factory was Vira Narasimha's permission to Almeida (1505)
PYQ 2024: fort at Bhatkal = Krishnadevaraya

t: Krishnadeva Raya → literature and the Ashtadiggajas
text:
## 1. His own works
Work | Language | Theme
Amuktamalyada | Telugu | Story of Tamil saint Andal; one of the five great Telugu kavyas
Jambavati Kalyanam | Sanskrit | Drama
Ushaparinayam | Sanskrit | Drama
## 2. Ashtadiggajas: eight Telugu poets at his court
Poet | Known for
Allasani Peddana | Foremost; Manucharitramu, Harikathasaramu
Tenali Ramakrishna | Panduranga Mahatmyam (a great kavya)
Golden age of Telugu literature; also patronised Kannada and Tamil poets
## Beyond your notes
Other Ashtadiggajas: Nandi Timmana, Dhurjati, Madayyagari Mallana, Ayyalaraju Ramabhadrudu, Pingali Surana, Ramarajabhushana
Amuktamalyada also sets out his views on statecraft
⚠ Ashtadiggajas = eight Telugu poets, not ministers, warriors or advisers
Mains 2016 asked KDR as scholar and patron: Prelims may ask author-work pairs

t: Krishnadeva Raya → temples, towns and tanks
text:
Work | Fact
Vitthala (Vijaya Vitthala) temple | Built by KDR, continued under Achyuta; stone chariot
Hazara Rama temple | Credited to KDR (PMF, Preview); Testbook: Deva Raya I
Krishnaswamy temple | Hampi
Virupaksha temple | KDR built the hall (Ranga Mandapa, 1510) in front of the shrine to mark accession, and the eastern gopuram
Nagalapuram | New town near the capital, named after mother Nagala Devi
Irrigation | Enormous tank, tanks and reservoirs for rainwater
Donations to Tirupati, Srisailam, Kalahasti, Kanchipuram, Tiruvannamalai, Chidambaram
A Vaishnava who respected all religions
Domingo Paes (c. 1520): KDR's routine, sesame oil, wrestling, riding
⚠ Krishnadeva Raya's tank and Nagalapuram are his; the Tungabhadra dam is Deva Raya I

t: Taxation under Krishnadeva Raya → land tax and other taxes
text:
## 1. Land revenue
Main income; land surveyed and classified: wet land, dry land, orchards, woods
Rate varied with land quality, crop, soil, irrigation: usually one-sixth, up to one-fourth; paid in cash and kind
Crop / land (inscription) | Share
Kuruvai rice (winter) | One-third
Sesame, ragi, horsegram | One-fourth
Millet etc. on dry land | One-sixth
Brahmans / temples | 1/20 / 1/30
Main tax Shist (Rai-rekha); revenue department Athavane
## 2. Other taxes
Industry tax on private owners of workshops; professional taxes on shopkeepers, farm-servants, shepherds, washermen, potters, shoemakers, musicians
Property, grazing, house, marriage taxes; tax on sale of produce; military contribution in distress
Transit dues: sthaladayam, margadayam, manudadayam; port customs; tribute from vassals
PYQ 2016: land tax by quality of land and industry tax on workshop owners: both correct

t: Land tenure → bhandaravada, manya, amara
text:
Tenure | What it was | Size
Bhandaravada | Crown villages; part of income kept the forts | Smallest
Manya | Tax-free villages for Brahmans, temples, mathas | -
Amara | Villages given to amara-nayakas for military service | Largest: about three-quarters of villages
Amara holders had no proprietary right in land, only a share of its income
Amara income was residual: shared out after deductions for Brahmans and forts
⚠ The largest category is amara, not crown land

t: Amara-nayaka system → features
text:
## 1. What it was
Major political innovation; many features likely from the Delhi Sultanate iqta
Amara-nayakas (Nayaks, Palaiyagars/Poligars) were military commanders given territory (amaram) by the Raya
## 2. Duties
Duty | Detail
Collect taxes | From peasants, craftspersons, traders
Pay tribute | Annually to the king; appear at court with gifts
Keep troops | A fixed contingent of horses and elephants
Maintain | Temples and irrigation works
## 3. Control and outcome
Kings transferred nayakas to assert control
By the 17th century nayakas of Tanjore, Madurai (and others) became independent; weakened the empire
## Beyond your notes
Historians also call it the nayankara system
⚠ Nayakas had no ownership of land, and posts tended to become hereditary

t: Administrative units and village system → names
text:
## 1. Hierarchy
Unit | Head
Mandalam (province) | Mandaleswara / Nayak
Nadu (district) | -
Sthala (sub-district) | -
Grama (village) | Ayagars
## 2. Ayagar system: village functionaries
Post | Local names
Headman | Reddy, Gauda, Maniyam
Accountant | Karnam, Senabhova
Watchman | Talaiyari
## 3. King and justice
Raya had absolute executive, judicial, legislative power; council of ministers; highest court of appeal
Harsh punishments: mutilation, throwing to elephants
Provincial governors (earlier princes) had own courts and armies: state looked like a confederacy
⚠ Hereditary nayakships weakened Chola-style village self-government

t: Army and firearms → organisation
text:
Point | Fact
Wings | Cavalry, infantry, artillery, elephants
Horses | Imported from Arabia and Persia/Gulf via west-coast ports
Officers | Nayaks / Poligars, paid in land; soldiers paid in cash
Firearms | Trained by Turkish and Portuguese experts; cannons on bullock carts or elephants
Forts | Gun holes, parapets for cannon
Deva Raya I: Turkic archers; Deva Raya II: 2,000 Muslim horsemen with jagirs
Ferishta (Deva Raya II): 80,000 cavalry, 2,00,000 infantry, 60,000 archers
⚠ Abdur Razzaq's "eleven lakh troops" is a traveller's figure, not an official count

t: Economy, trade and coins → what and where
text:
## 1. Production
Agriculture main; tanks, dams, canals built; guilds of craftsmen; diamond mines in Kurnool and Anantapur
## 2. Trade
Item | Goods

## 1. The four battles
Battle | Year | Opponent | Outcome
Panipat I | 21 April 1526 | Ibrahim Lodi | Delhi, Agra won; Mughal rule begins
Khanwa (near Agra, Rajasthan) | 1527 | Rana Sanga of Mewar | Babur declared jihad, took title Ghazi; Delhi-Agra secured

topic: Babur and the founding of the empire (1526-1530)

text:
## 1. Who invited Babur
Person | Identity
