Alam Khan | Uncle of Ibrahim Lodi, pretender to Delhi throne
Rana Sanga | King of Mewar (likely invitation)
## 2. Tactics
Tulughma: army split into left, right, centre (with forward and rear) to encircle the enemy
Araba: carts tied with ropes, cannons behind them (Rumi/Ottoman method)
Army about 12,000 vs Ibrahim's much larger force (about 100,000 per Testbook)
## 3. Arrival of Babur led to
Claim | Verdict
Timurid dynasty established | Yes
Gunpowder introduced | No: Bahmanis, Vijayanagara used firearms earlier
Arch and dome introduced | No: came with the Sultanate
⚠ LENS (2026) calls Panipat the "first major use of field artillery" in India; still, Babur did not introduce gunpowder

Ruler of Farghana at 12 (1494); twice took and lost Samarqand to Uzbek Shaibani Khan

Strategy | Kabul and Qandahar joined to north India (first since Kushanas)
Gardens | Chahar bagh (four-part Persian garden)
Memoir | Tuzuk-i-Baburi (Baburnama) in Turki; Persian translation by Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khanan
Mosques | Kabuli Bagh (Panipat), Sambhal; Babri Masjid (1528) by Mir Baqi
Died Agra 1530; reburied at Bagh-e Babur, Kabul
⚠ Baburnama is in Turki, not Persian (Persian versions came under Akbar)

Sirhind Fateh Diwas (12-14 May): Banda Bahadur took Sirhind in 1710; Farrukhsiyar's forces defeated him (1715), executed 1716

t: Decline of the Mughal Empire → causes and historians
text:
## 1. Causes
Cause | Detail
Aurangzeb's policies | Over-expansion; jizya 1679; Deccan ulcer (27 years)
Jagir crisis | Too many mansabdars, too few jagirs; peasants squeezed
Weak successors, wars of succession | No primogeniture
Noble factions | Turani vs Hindustani parties; kingmakers
Regional states | Hyderabad (Nizam-ul-Mulk), Awadh, Bengal
Invasions | Nadir Shah 1739, Abdali 1748-67
Europeans | British advantage of economy and technology
## 2. Historians' views
Historian | Main cause
Irfan Habib | Exploitative agrarian system → peasant revolts
Satish Chandra | Crisis of the jagirdari system
New Cambridge History | Decline from the system's success; rich zamindars rebelled
Company stopped coining in the emperor's name in 1835 (Akbar Shah II); last emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar, exiled to Rangoon

t: Central offices → department each headed
text:
## 1. Ministers
Office | Department
Wazir | Highest rank; finance powers removed by Akbar
Diwan-i-Kul | Revenue and finance; seal needed on revenue papers
Mir Bakhshi | Military: mansabdar appointments, salary papers, dagh, chehra
Mir Saman | Royal karkhanas and household
Sadr-us-Sudur | Religious affairs, charity grants (madad-i-maash)
Qazi-ul-Quzzat | Justice (separated from Sadr under Aurangzeb)
Mir Bakhshi = Sultanate Mir-i-Arz renamed; stood on emperor's right; supervised waqia nawis (news writers)
⚠ Mir Bakhshi was military, not revenue (Diwan) or household (Mir Saman)
PYQ 1997: head of the military department under Akbar = Mir Bakhshi

t: Administrative units → order and officers
text:
## 1. Units (largest to smallest)
Unit | Officers
Suba (province) | Subadar/Nizam, Diwan, Bakhshi, Sadr
Sarkar (district) | Faujdar, Amalguzar
Pargana | Shiqdar, Amil; semi-hereditary qanungo, chaudhuri, qazi
Grama (village) | Muqaddam, Patwari
Subas: 12 in 1580, 15 under Akbar, 22 under Aurangzeb
Land types: Khalisa (Crown), Jagir, Inam
⚠ Provincial Diwan was an independent officer answerable to the Centre, not to the subadar
PYQ 2021: ascending order = Pargana - Sarkar - Suba

t: Jagirdar vs zamindar → the 2019 trap
text:
## 1. Comparison
Point | Jagirdar | Zamindar
Basis | Revenue assignment in lieu of salary for state service | Hereditary claim to share of produce
Hereditary? | No (except watan jagir) | Yes; could buy, sell, divide
Transfer | Transferable (tankha every 3-4 yrs) | Not transferable
Duties | Mansab military and state service | Revenue collection + law and order, troops, forts
Allowance | Jagir income | Nankar (10%) + milkiyat land
## 2. Types of jagir
Type | Feature
Tankha | In lieu of salary; transferable
Mashrut | On conditions
Inam | No service obligation
Watan | To zamindars; hereditary, non-transferable
⚠ Testbook says jagirdars "did have inherited rights"; PMF and the UPSC key: not hereditary
PYQ 2019: both statements wrong (Neither 1 nor 2)

t: Mansabdari → zat, sawar and the 10-20 rule
text:
## 1. Features
Introduced by Akbar (zat-sawar dual rank in his 40th regnal year, 1591-95 per Preview)
Zat = personal rank and salary; Sawar = number of horsemen to maintain
Ranks 10 to 5000; later 7000 (Mirza Aziz Koka, Raja Man Singh)
Salary in cash, paid in cash or jagir; mansab not hereditary
Class | Sawar vs zat
First | Sawar = zat
Second | Sawar half or more of zat
Third | Sawar less than half
## 2. Horses
20 horses for every 10 sawars: horses rested on march, replacements in war
Sawar with one horse = half a sawar
Du-aspa sih-aspa (Jahangir): double troopers without raising zat
PYQ 1999: 20 horses per 10 cavalrymen (A and R both true, R explains A)

t: Ahadis and the army → who they were
text:
## 1. Ahadis
Gentleman troopers recruited singly by the emperor; not under any mansabdar
Own muster-master; 8-10 horses; about Rs 800 a month
Compared to knights of medieval Europe
Troop type | Recruited by | Served under
Ahadi | Emperor | Emperor directly
Dakhili | Emperor | Mansabdars
Tabinan | Mansabdar | Mansabdar
⚠ Ahadis were not attached to any chief or noble
PYQ 1998: ahadis = troopers who offered services singly, under the emperor
## Beyond your notes
Tabinan were troopers recruited and paid by the mansabdar himself

t: Mansabdar grades and the jagir crisis → names and numbers
text:
## 1. Grades by zat
Zat rank | Called
Below 500 | Mansabdar
500 to below 2500 | Amir
2500 and above | Amir-i-umda / Umda-i-azam
## 2. Appointment
Mir Bakhshi presented candidates; or a noble's tajwiz (recommendation)
Diwan and bakhshi processed; farman under the wazir's seal; emperor alone appointed, promoted, dismissed
## 3. Pay
Mughal mansabdars = highest-paid service in the world (Satish Chandra); a sawar averaged Rs 20/month
Contingents mixed (Mughal, Pathan, Hindustani, Rajput) to curb tribalism
## 4. Jagir crisis
Akbar matched jagir income to salary; by Aurangzeb, collections fell short and mansabdars multiplied → long delays in allotment
Jagirdars squeezed peasants while they held a jagir
Shah Jahan: noble kept only one-third (sometimes one-fourth) of sawar rank
⚠ Mansab = rank; jagir = revenue assignment; neither was hereditary

t: Zamindars → rights, troops and role
text:
## 1. Rights
Hereditary claim to a share of produce, not land ownership; could be bought, sold, inherited, divided
Rights predated the Mughals; state recognised them, used zamindars as revenue agents
Nankar: 10% of revenue as allowance (even if state collected directly)
Milkiyat: personal lands, tilled with hired or servile labour
Emperor could remove a zamindar only for sedition or non-payment
## 2. Military strength (Ain-i-Akbari)
Item | Number
Cavalry | 3,84,558
Infantry | 42,77,057
Elephants | 1,863
Cannons | 4,260
Boats | 4,500
Forts (qilachas) and armed contingents
Term used from Akbar's time for anyone with a hereditary claim on produce (pre-Mughal: chief of a territory)
PYQ 2019 angle: zamindars had duties beyond revenue (troops, order), and their rights were hereditary

t: Land revenue → zabt, dahsala, land classes
text:
## 1. Akbar's revenue system
Todar Mal surveyed yields and prices for 10 years (1570-80) → cash rate per crop (dahsala, Ain-i-Dahsala)
Zabt: measurement-based; Lahore to Allahabad, Malwa, Gujarat (not Bengal)
State share: one-third of average produce
Land | Fallow
Polaj | Never
Parauti | Briefly
Chachar | 3-4 years
Banjar | 5+ years
Other systems: batai/ghalla-bakhshi (crop sharing); jama = assessed, hasil = collected
Ijarah (revenue farming): used by Sultans, dropped by Sher Shah and Akbar, revived under Jahangir, spread under Jahandar Shah
## 2. Currency
Rupaya (silver, base), Mohur (gold), Dam (copper)

t: Chronicles → author, emperor, language
text:
## 1. Table
Work | Author | Reign covered | Language
Tuzuk-i-Baburi | Babur | Babur | Turki
Humayun Nama | Gulbadan Begum | Babur, Humayun | Persian
Akbar Nama (3 vols; 3rd = Ain-i-Akbari) | Abul Fazl (1589-1602) | Akbar | Persian
Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri | Jahangir | Jahangir | Persian
Padshahnama/Badshah Nama | Abdul Hamid Lahori (vols 1-2, 1627-47); Waris (vol 3) | Shah Jahan | Persian
Alamgir Nama | Muhammad Kazim | Aurangzeb's first 10 yrs | Persian
Padshahnama modelled on the Akbar Nama; 3 daftars of 10 lunar years each; revised by wazir Sadullah Khan
⚠ Lahori could not finish vol 3 (old age): Waris wrote it
PYQ 2006: official historian of Shah Jahan = Abdul Hamid Lahori

t: Abul Fazl and the Ain → contents and facts
text:
## 1. Ain-i-Akbari: five books
Book | Subject
Manzil-abadi | Imperial household
Sipah-abadi | Military and civil administration, mansabdars
Mulk-abadi | Fiscal; "Account of the Twelve Provinces"
4 and 5 | Religion, literature, culture; Akbar's sayings
## 2. Abul Fazl
Son of Shaikh Mubarak, brother of Faizi; spokesman of sulh-i-kul
Referred to the discovery of America (not Amir Khusrau, Jaisi or Raskhan)
Murdered 1602 by Bir Singh Bundela at Prince Salim's instance
Ain translated by Blochmann (vol 1, 1873) and Jarrett (vols 2-3)
PYQ 1997: medieval writer referring to the discovery of America = Abul Fazl

t: Ashtapradhan → the eight ministers and their portfolios
text:
## 1. Council of eight ministers (Shivaji, fixed at the 1674 coronation)
Sanskrit title | Earlier (Persian) title | Portfolio
Peshwa (Mukhya Pradhan) | - | Prime Minister, head of general administration
Amatya | Majumdar | Finance, accounts, treasury
Mantri | Waqianavis | Interior: intelligence, espionage, posts, royal household
Sachiv | Surnavis / Chitnis / Shurunavis | Royal correspondence; drafted royal orders (Secretary)
Sumant | Dabir | Foreign affairs, envoys; master of ceremonies
Senapati | Sar-i-Naubat | Commander-in-chief (army organisation, supply)
Nyayadhish (Nyayadhyaksha) | - | Chief Justice
Panditrao | - | Religious affairs, charitable grants (High Priest)
⚠ Sumant = foreign affairs (PYQ 1998); not Peshwa, not Sachiv, not Panditrao
⚠ PMF (Ancient & Medieval) labels Sachiv as "Land Revenue Minister"; PMF LENS, Preview, Satish Chandra and the PYQ key give Sachiv = correspondence: use correspondence
⚠ Mantri handled intelligence (not foreign affairs, which is Sumant)
PYQ 1998: "member of the Ashtapradhan who looked after foreign affairs"; trap: Sachiv sounds like "secretary of state"

t: Ashtapradhan → nature, and the dynasties it is confused with
text:
## 1. Nature of the body
Ashtapradhan = Maratha (Shivaji's) council of eight ministers (PYQ 1995; also asked by BPSC, UPPCS)
Functions were advisory; each minister was directly responsible to the king (Satish Chandra: "not in the nature of a council of ministers")
Shivaji abolished hereditary offices, paid officials cash salaries, transferred them periodically
Most important posts: Peshwa and Senapati (Senapati usually a leading Maratha chief)
Sambhaji upheld the Ashtapradhan system after Shivaji (PMF LENS 2025)
⚠ Ashtapradhan reached eight members only by 1674 (Preview)
## Beyond your notes
Distractor in PYQ 1995 | What that regime is known for instead
Gupta | Kumaramatyas (officials), feudatory samantas
Chola | Village assemblies (Ur, Sabha), Nadu
Vijayanagara | Nayankara and Ayagar systems
Maratha | Ashtapradhan (correct)
Shivaji's first Peshwa was Moropant Trimbak Pingle
All ministers except the Panditrao and Nyayadhish could be asked to lead military campaigns
Shivaji had the Rajya Vyavahar Kosh compiled to replace Persian official terms with Sanskrit ones

t: Shivaji's revenue → chauth, sardeshmukhi and land terms
text:
## 1. Swarajya revenue
Lands surveyed and assessed; state demand 30% of gross produce (later 40%), in cash or kind
Famine relief: money and grain advanced, repaid in instalments
System patterned on Malik Ambar's; new assessment by Annaji Datto (1679)
## 2. Levies outside Swarajya
Term | Meaning
Chauth | One-fourth (25%) of the revenue of a district; "revenue for protection" from Mughalai areas not directly ruled
Sardeshmukhi | Additional 10%, claimed as hereditary Sardeshmukh (chief deshmukh)
Saranjam | Revenue grant to chiefs for maintaining troops/forts (feudal-military grant)
Mokasa | Jagir assigned to officials
Deshmukhi | Zamindari right; Shivaji did not abolish it but supervised it
Mirasdar | Holder of hereditary rights in land, strictly supervised
⚠ Chauth is 25%, sardeshmukhi 10%; do not swap them
⚠ Saranjam is a land grant, not a tax (BPSC 1994: "land revenue system of the Marathas")
## 3. Mughal grants of these rights
1711: Daud Khan Panni / Zulfiqar Khan agreement: chauth and sardeshmukhi of the Deccan (collected by Mughal officials)
Saiyid brothers' pact: Swarajya + chauth and sardeshmukhi of the six Deccan provinces

t: Shivaji's military → army, forts and navy
text:
## 1. Army
Category | Feature
Bargirs | Horses and equipment provided by the State
Shiledars (Silahdars) | Maintained their own horses and equipment
Paga | Regular cavalry (30,000-40,000) under havaldars on fixed salary
Strict discipline: no women or dancing girls with the army; plunder accounted for
## 2. Forts and navy
Forts were the mainstay; three men of equal rank guarded each fort against treachery
Ramchandrapant Amatya's Adnyapatra (Royal Edict) stresses forts
Built a navy: "Father of the Indian Navy"; ships traded to Mocha, Muscat, Malacca
Guerrilla warfare against Mughals
18th century: Marathas adopted European-style infantry and artillery; Mahadji Shinde built a European-trained army (French officers)
⚠ Bargir = state-equipped; shiledar = self-equipped

t: Shivaji's career → events, treaties and dates
text:
## 1. Chronology
Year | Event
1630 | Born at Shivneri fort (near Pune) to Shahaji Bhosale and Jijabai
1648 | Victory at Chakan fort
1659 | Afzal Khan (Bijapur, Adil Shah II) killed; Pratapgarh battle
1660 | Siddi Jauhar besieged Panhala; Shiva Kashid's sacrifice; Bajiprabhu at Ghodkhind

1665 | Treaty of Purandar with Jai Singh: 23 of 35 forts surrendered; Sambhaji to serve Mughals
1666 | Agra visit; house arrest; escape in fruit baskets
1672 | Salher: first large-scale victory over Mughals
1674 | Coronation at Raigad; title Chhatrapati; Rajyabhisheka shaka era; Gagabhatta officiated
1677-78 | Karnataka expedition (Dakshina Digvijaya); Jinji (Gingee) base
1680 | Died 3 April
⚠ Preview gives Shivaji's birth as "1627 or 1630"; PMF gives 1630
⚠ Guru: Samarth Ramdas (Dasbodh); Shahaji first conceived Swarajya (PMF)
## Beyond your notes
Coronation date 6 June 1674 (Shivrajyabhishek Day); a second (Tantric) coronation followed later in 1674

text:

Date | Event | Detail

Mar 2025 | First Shivaji Maharaj temple in Maharashtra, Bhiwandi | Second in India after Srisailam

## 2. The 12 forts
State | Forts
Maharashtra (11) | Salher, Shivneri, Lohgad, Khanderi, Raigad, Rajgad, Pratapgad, Suvarnadurg, Panhala, Vijaydurg, Sindhudurg

topic: Successors of Shivaji: Sambhaji to Shahu
t: Chhatrapatis after Shivaji → order and key event
text:
## 1. Order of rulers
Ruler | Years | Key point
Sambhaji | 1680-89 | Elder son; resisted Aurangzeb; captured at Sangameshwar, executed at Tulapur (11 Mar 1689)
Rajaram | 1689-1700 | Second son; fled to Gingee (Jinji), carrying the war into the South
Shivaji II | 1700-07 | Minor son of Rajaram; Tarabai regent
Shahu | 1707/08-49 | Son of Sambhaji; Mughal prisoner from 1689, released 1707
At Aurangzeb's death (1707) Maratha leadership was with Tarabai (UPPCS)
Tarabai led the war from 1700; retook Sinhagad, Raigad, Satara
⚠ Order: Sambhaji → Rajaram → Shivaji II → Shahu (UPPCS 2025 sequence)
⚠ Shahu is Shivaji's grandson (Sambhaji's son), not Rajaram's son

topic: Successors of Shivaji: Sambhaji to Shahu
t: Sambhaji → campaigns and legacy
text:
## 1. Life
Born 14 May 1657, Purandar fort; mother Saibai; sent to Mughal court at nine under the Treaty of Purandar
Briefly joined Mughal general Diler Khan, then returned; crowned 20 July 1680 at Raigad
Rivalry with stepmother Soyarabai, who backed Rajaram
Aurangzeb came to the Deccan after his rebel son Akbar sided with Sambhaji
Campaign | Year | Note
Burhanpur raid | 1681 | Mughal trade centre
Siege of Ramsej | 1682-88 | Held out six years
Konkan campaign | 1683-84 | vs Siddis and Portuguese
Battle of Wai | 1687 | Won; lost Senapati Hambirrao Mohite
Title "Dharamveer" (refused to convert); upheld the Ashtapradhan
## In news 2025-26
Mar 2025: Sambhaji's life in the news (PMF LENS, Prelims Magnum); PMF infographic on his campaigns
⚠ Aurangzeb conquered Bijapur (1686) and Golconda (1687) before capturing Sambhaji

topic: Successors of Shivaji: Sambhaji to Shahu
t: Shahu vs Tarabai → civil war and the two seats
text:
## 1. Split of the Maratha state
Event | Year | Detail
Shahu released | 1707 | After Aurangzeb's death; civil war with Tarabai
Two principalities | c. 1710 | Satara (Shahu) and Kolhapur (Tarabai's line)
Treaty of Warna | 1731 | Confirmed the Satara-Kolhapur division
Balaji Vishwanath made Peshwa | 1713 | For rallying sardars to Shahu
Saiyid pact; Farrukh Siyar deposed | 1719 | Swarajya and Deccan chauth/sardeshmukhi
Kolhapur stayed a princely state of the Bhonsles until merged with Bombay in 1949
## In news 2025-26
Jul 2025: PMF LENS notes the samadhi of Maharani Tarabai at Satara lies neglected, though she fought the Mughals for about 30 years
## Beyond your notes
Shahu defeated Tarabai's forces at the Battle of Khed (1707)

t: Peshwas → order, tenure and landmark
text:
## 1. The eight Peshwas (Bhat family, Chitpavan Brahmins)
Peshwa | Tenure | Landmark
Balaji Vishwanath | 1713-20 | Appointed by Shahu; first Peshwa of the Maratha state; streamlined administration
Baji Rao I | 1720-40 | Greatest Peshwa; confederacy; Palkhed, Bhopal; office became hereditary
Balaji Baji Rao (Nana Saheb) | 1740-61 | Zenith; capital Poona; Panipat III
Madhav Rao I | 1761-72 | Recovery after Panipat; Delhi retaken 1771

t: Balaji Vishwanath → what he did (1713-20)
text:
## 1. Rise
Began as a small revenue official; helped Shahu win sardars against Tarabai
Made Peshwa (Mukhya Pradhan) by Shahu in 1713 (November)
## 2. Achievements
Area | Work
Administration | Streamlined Maratha administration after Sambhaji; made it "easy and convenient"; power shifted from Chhatrapati to Peshwa
Mughal pact | With Saiyid brothers: Swarajya + chauth and sardeshmukhi of six Deccan provinces
Delhi politics | Helped Saiyids depose and kill Farrukh Siyar (1719)
Revenue assignment | Gave separate areas to sardars to collect chauth/sardeshmukhi; Raja's share = sardeshmukhi + 34% of chauth
Effect: Peshwa's patronage grew; sardars conquered with private armies; in the long run sardars became autonomous (seed of the confederacy's weakness)
⚠ PYQ 2000: "Who streamlined Maratha administration after Sambhaji?" Balaji Vishwanath; distractors Rajaram, Ganga Bai, Nanaji Deshmukh
⚠ The office was not hereditary under him; it became hereditary when Baji Rao I succeeded in 1720 (Testbook says Balaji Vishwanath made it hereditary)
PYQ 2000: person → role; trap: Rajaram ruled after Sambhaji but did not reorganise the state
## Beyond your notes
Richard Temple called the 1719 Mughal grants the "Magna Carta" of the Maratha empire

t: Baji Rao I → campaigns and the confederacy (1720-40)
text:
## 1. Campaigns
Campaign | Year | Result
Palkhed (near Aurangabad) | 1728 | Defeated Nizam; chauth and sardeshmukhi of Deccan confirmed
Bhopal | 1737 | Defeated Nizam-led Mughal army; got Malwa
vs Portuguese (by brother Chimaji Appa) | 1739 | Took Bassein and Salsette
By 1740: Malwa, Gujarat, parts of Bundelkhand; turned a Maharashtra kingdom into an empire
"Greatest exponent of guerrilla tactics after Shivaji"; led campaigns himself
Weakness: little attention to administration of conquests; feud with the Nizam
## 2. Confederacy
Assigned each chief a sphere of influence to conquer and rule in Shahu's name; partly to appease the kshatriya section led by Senapati Dabhade (Dabodi)
Houses that rose: Gaekwad, Holkar, Sindhia, Bhonsle
⚠ Bassein was taken by Chimaji Appa, not Baji Rao himself
## Beyond your notes
Raided Delhi (1737); died 1740 at Raverkhedi on the Narmada

t: Balaji Baji Rao → the zenith (1740-61)
text:
## 1. Power passes to the Peshwa
Shahu died 1749; by his will the Peshwa took charge; government shifted to Poona
Sangola agreement (1750): Peshwa became real head of the confederacy; king a non-entity
## 2. Expansion
Direction | Gain
East | Repeated Bengal raids (under Raghoji Bhonsle); Alivardi Khan ceded Orissa (1751)
South | Mysore paid tribute; Nizam defeated at Udgir (1760): territory worth Rs 62 lakh a year
North | Made Imad-ul-Mulk wazir (1752); de facto masters of Delhi
## 3. Treaty of April 1752 with the Mughal emperor
Marathas to protect the empire against Rohillas, Jats, Rajputs, Afghans
In return: Rs 50 lakh, chauth of Punjab, Sindh, Multan, Rajputana, Rohilkhand, governorship of Ajmer and Agra
⚠ UPPCS 2007: the king became a non-entity from the time of Balaji Baji Rao, not Balaji Vishwanath
⚠ Sought British help against the Angre navy; this let the British dominate the west coast

t: Later Peshwas → Madhav Rao I to Baji Rao II
text:
## 1. Recovery and decline
Event | Year | Detail
Madhav Rao I | 1761-72 | Fought Nizam (1763) and Haidar Ali (1765-72); restored northern control
Delhi retaken | 1771 | Under Mahadji Shinde; Shah Alam II returned to Delhi; Marathas got Kora and Allahabad
Madhav Rao I dies | 1772 | End of the dream to replace the Mughals
Narayan Rao murdered | 1773 | By Raghunath Rao's faction
Sawai Madhav Rao | 1774 | Posthumous son; proclaimed on the 40th day of birth
Battle of Kharda | 1795 | All chiefs (Peshwa, Sindhia, Holkar, Bhonsle, Gaekwad) beat the Nizam: last united action; Nizam ceded Daulatabad
Mahadji dies / Nana dies | 1794 / 1800 | Decline sets in
Nana Phadnis ran the state ~30 years and refused subsidiary alliance
The Nizam, fearing the Marathas, accepted subsidiary alliance (1 Sept 1798)
⚠ John Shore stayed non-interventionist at Kharda although the Nizam was a British ally

t: Confederacy houses → seat of each family
text:
## 1. The five houses (spheres assigned under Baji Rao I)
House | Seat | Note
Gaekwad | Baroda (Vadodara) | Gujarat
Bhonsle | Nagpur | Raids into Bengal, Bihar, Orissa (Raghoji Bhonsle, 1727-55)
Holkar | Indore (capital later Maheshwar under Ahilyabai) | Malwa
Sindhia (Scindia) | Gwalior | Mahadji controlled Delhi
Peshwa | Poona (Pune) | Head of the confederacy
Sardars ran Mughal-pattern administrations with own armies; loyalty to the Peshwa became symbolic
Worked well from Baji Rao I to Madhav Rao I; weakened after Panipat and 1772
⚠ Holkar → Indore, Sindhia → Gwalior: the usual swap trap
## Beyond your notes
Founders: Pilaji Gaekwad, Parsoji/Raghoji Bhonsle, Malhar Rao Holkar, Ranoji Sindhia

t: Mahadji Sindhia → role in the North
text:
## 1. Career
Leading Maratha chief of the North after Panipat; retook Delhi (1771)
Escorted Shah Alam II from Allahabad to Delhi
Mediator of the Treaty of Salbai (1782)
Built a strong army with French officers
1784: Shah Alam gave him management of Delhi and Agra; got the Peshwa made the emperor's Naib-i-Munaib (deputy), Mahadji acting for him
Mahadji ran the North; Nana Phadnis ran the South
Died 1794
⚠ An Afghan, Ghulam Qadir, blinded Shah Alam II while Mahadji was away from Delhi
Date | Maratha hold on Delhi
1757 | Raghunath Rao expelled Najib; Antaji Mankeshwar governor
1771 | Mahadji retook Delhi
1803 | British (Lord Lake) took Delhi in the Second Anglo-Maratha War
PMF: the British took India "from the Marathas rather than from the Mughals"

t: Ahilyabai Holkar → administration and In news 2025-26
text:
## 1. The ruler
Maratha queen of Malwa (Holkar house) from 1767; capital Maheshwar on the Narmada
Ran civil administration and finances herself; Tukoji Rao Holkar commanded the army
Area | Work
Temples | Rebuilt Kashi Vishwanath (Varanasi), restored Somnath
Public works | Ghats, wells, roads, dharmashalas from Kedarnath to Rameswaram
Economy | Maheshwari saree industry
Social | Opposed forced sati; widows' inheritance rights
Tribes | Bhil and Gond given highway-protection rights (Bhil-Kaur)

t: Road to Panipat → Abdali's invasions and the immediate cause
text:
## 1. Background
Nadir Shah (Persia): Karnal, 13 Feb 1739; took Koh-i-Noor and Peacock Throne
Ahmad Shah Abdali (Durrani), Nadir's general, ruler of Afghanistan: invaded eight times, 1748-67
Year | Event
1751-52 | Mughals ceded Punjab to Abdali
1757 | Abdali took Delhi; kept Alamgir II; Najib-ud-Daulah (Rohilla) as Mir Bakshi/his agent
1758 | Raghunath Rao expelled Najib from Delhi and captured Punjab, driving Abdali's son and viceroy Timur Shah out of Lahore
1759 | Abdali returned to take revenge
14 Jan 1761 | Third Battle of Panipat
⚠ Immediate cause (PYQ 2010): Marathas expelled Timur Shah from Lahore; not Adina Beg's invitation, not Chahar Mahal revenue, not a plan to annex Punjab up to Delhi
⚠ Najib-ud-Daulah also invited Abdali, unable to bear Maratha supremacy (a background cause)
PYQ 2010: immediate reason for Panipat III; trap: Adina Beg Khan, the Jalandhar governor, had brought the Marathas into Punjab; he was not the reason Abdali came in 1759
## Beyond your notes
Lahore was taken in 1758 by Raghunath Rao with Malhar Rao Holkar, helped by Adina Beg Khan

t: Third Battle of Panipat → sides, commanders, allies
text:
## 1. The two sides
Side | Leaders | Allies
Marathas | Sadashiv Rao Bhau (Peshwa's cousin, real commander); Vishwas Rao (Peshwa's son, nominal commander) | Only limited help from Imad-ul-Mulk
Afghans | Ahmad Shah Abdali | Najib-ud-Daulah (Rohilkhand), Shuja-ud-Daulah (Awadh)
Peshwa at the time: Balaji Baji Rao; he died in June 1761 on hearing the news
Mughal emperor in 1761: Shah Alam II (Panipat and Buxar both fell in his reign; Buxar 1764)
About 28,000 died, including Vishwas Rao and Bhau
## 2. Why the North did not help
Jats and Rajputs alienated by Maratha conquests; Mughal nobles beaten in the power game
Northern rulers saw southern Marathas as rivals; resented interference at Delhi
⚠ Shuja-ud-Daulah of Awadh joined Abdali, though his father Safdar Jang had allied with the Marathas
Eyewitness historian: Kashiraj Pandit (Chhattisgarh PCS 2003)
## Beyond your notes
Maratha artillery was led by Ibrahim Khan Gardi (French-trained); the Jat Suraj Mal left the Maratha camp before the battle

t: Panipat → why the Marathas lost, and what it changed
text:
## 1. Battle factors (Testbook)
Factor | Detail
Artillery | Abdali's mobile artillery (camel-mounted swivel guns)
Tactics | Feigned water-fetching from the Yamuna to break Maratha formation; rumours of retreat
Elephants | Maratha elephants panicked under fire
Supplies | Marathas fortified with carts and wagons; ran short of food
## 2. Outcome
Marathas lost the cream of their army and prestige; ended their bid to replace the Mughals
Helped the English EIC consolidate (Plassey 1757, Buxar 1764)
Abdali gained nothing lasting: went home; Afghans never returned, could not hold Punjab
PMF: Panipat decided "not who was to rule India, but who was not"
Marathas recovered within a decade (Delhi 1771, Madhav Rao I)
⚠ Merchant's message to the Peshwa: "Two pearls dissolved, 27 gold mohurs lost, silver and copper cannot be cast up"; Preview prints "22 gold coins"

t: Three battles of Panipat → who fought whom
text:
## 1. Comparison
Battle | Year | Victor | Defeated | Result
First | 1526 | Babur | Ibrahim Lodi | Mughal rule founded
Second | 1556 | Akbar (Bairam Khan) | Hemu | Mughal rule restored
Third | 1761 | Ahmad Shah Abdali | Marathas (Sadashiv Rao Bhau) | Maratha northern bid ended
Panipat lies in Haryana, on the Delhi-Lahore route, open plain for cavalry (UPSC Mains 2014 asked why so many battles were fought there)
⚠ Karnal (1739) is a different battle (Nadir Shah vs Muhammad Shah), also in Haryana

t: Marathas → strongest native power, but not a "nation"
text:
## 1. Assertion-Reason (PYQ 2003)
Claim | Verdict
Marathas emerged as the strongest native power after the Mughal decline | True
Marathas were the first to have a clear concept of a united Indian nation | False
Answer: A true, R false
## 2. Why R is false
Maratha sardars lacked unity, outlook and programme for an all-India empire (PMF)
Rise was a regional reaction to Mughal centralisation and upward mobility of peasant castes seeking Kshatriya status
Expansion was military and revenue-driven (chauth), not nationalist; northern rulers saw them as rivals
Raids (e.g. ten-year Bengal campaign) caused hardship to locals
⚠ PMF also says the Marathas fought Panipat with a "India is for Indians" outlook (Bhau's appeal to northern rulers); that is not a modern concept of a united nation
PYQ 2003: A-R on Maratha power; trap: reading Bhau's appeal or Hindavi Swarajya as a pan-Indian national idea
## 3. Reasons for the Maratha rise (Preview)
People of Maharashtra united by regional identity, religious toleration, geography (hills, forts), leadership of Shivaji

t: First Anglo-Maratha War (1775-82) → treaties
text:
## 1. Treaties in order
Treaty | Year | Between | Terms
Surat | 1775 | Bombay govt and Raghunath Rao | Bassein and Salsette to the English; 2,500 soldiers for Raghoba
Purandar | 1776 | Calcutta (Warren Hastings via Col. Upton) and Nana Phadnis | Madhav Rao II accepted; Raghoba pensioned (Rs 25,000/month); British keep Salsette
Convention of Wadgaon | (1779) | Marathas (after Talegaon-Wadgaon win) and Bombay | English give up gains since 1773 and Raghoba's cause; rejected by Hastings
Salbai | 1782 | British and Marathas, mediated by Mahadji Scindia | Madhav Rao II Peshwa; Raghoba pensioned; Salsette to British; Bassein back to Marathas; Marathas to help against Haidar Ali
Salbai gave the British 20 years of peace with the strongest Indian power
⚠ Salbai = Salsette to British, Bassein restored to Marathas; Bassein (1802) is a different treaty (Second war)
⚠ Testbook says the British returned areas "per the Purandar Treaty" after the war; PMF ties the final terms to Salbai

t: Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05) → Bassein and the treaty with each house
text:
## 1. Trigger
Nana Phadnis died 1800; Holkar beat Peshwa and Sindhia (25 Oct 1802)
Baji Rao II fled to the British: Treaty of Bassein, 31 Dec 1802 (subsidiary alliance)
## 2. Treaty of Bassein terms
Subsidiary force of 6,000 infantry; territory yielding Rs 26 lakh ceded
Company controls Peshwa's foreign relations; arbitrates with Nizam and Gaekwad; no Europeans employed
## 3. Treaty with each house
House | Treaty | Year
Peshwa | Bassein | 1802
Bhonsle | Deogaon (ceded Balasore, Cuttack) | 1803
Sindhia | Surji-Arjungaon (Doab, Delhi-Agra, Broach) | 1803
Sindhia | Burhanpur (subsidiary alliance) | 1804
Holkar | Rajghat | 1805-06
Richard Wellesley (GG 1798-1805) declared war; Arthur Wellesley in the Deccan, Lord Lake took Delhi and Shah Alam II
⚠ Testbook pairs Surji-Arjungaon with Bhonsle and Rajghat with Scindia; PMF: Surji-Arjungaon = Sindhia, Rajghat = Holkar
## Beyond your notes
Battles: Assaye (Sept 1803, Arthur Wellesley vs Sindhia-Bhonsle), Laswari (Nov 1803, Lake vs Sindhia)

t: Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817-19) → outcome and end of the Peshwai
text:
## 1. Run-up
Treaty of Pandharpur (1812): British protection to Southern Jagirdars, undercutting the Peshwa
Gangadhar Shastri (Gaekwad's minister) murdered at Nasik (1815), blamed on Trimbakji
Treaty of Poona (13 June 1817) forced on Baji Rao II by Elphinstone
5 Nov 1817: Peshwa attacked the Poona Residency; Appa Sahib (Nagpur) and Holkar rose; GG Lord Hastings crushed them
## 2. Result
Outcome | Detail
Peshwaship | Abolished; Baji Rao II to Bithur (near Kanpur), pension Rs 8 lakh
Peshwa's lands | Annexed to an enlarged Bombay Presidency
Satara | Small kingdom for Pratap Singh (descendant of Shivaji); annexed 1848 by lapse
Chiefs | All accepted subsidiary alliance; Holkar last (1818)
Treaties of this war: Poona, Gwalior, Mandasor (PMF)
## Beyond your notes
Battles: Khadki (Kirkee) and Sitabuldi (Nov 1817), Mahidpur (Dec 1817, Holkar), Koregaon (1 Jan 1818)

t: Maratha decline → causes of defeat by the British
text:
## 1. Causes (PMF)
Cause | Detail
Leadership | Later Peshwas, esp. Baji Rao II, could not unite the sardars
Autonomous sardars | Chiefs joined enemies when the centre pressed them
Economy | Lived on chauth/sardeshmukhi; neglected trade, industry
Military | European-trained armies depended on foreign officers; weak artillery
Diplomacy | Misjudged British strength; poor relations with other Indian powers
Administration | No sound rule outside Maharashtra; dominion by force alone
Science | Did not encourage science and technology
British used Maratha-Mysore rivalry and divided the sardars, defeating them in separate battles
⚠ Marathas were the British chief rivals in the late 18th century; after Tipu (1799) they were the only major power left

t: Araghatta → what the device was
text:
## 1. Meaning
Araghatta = Persian water wheel, a water-lifting device for irrigation
Build: a large wheel with earthen pots tied to the outer ends of its spokes (a garland of pots)
Worked by animal (bullock) power through a gear; pots lift water from open wells in succession
PMF: used for irrigation in the Chola period (early medieval)
Option UPSC gave | What it really describes
Leather bag pulled over a pulley | Charas / mot (not araghatta)
Wheel with pots on spokes | Araghatta ✔
Bonded labour (2016 option) | Vishti / vetti, not araghatta
Land grant to military officers | Iqta / jagir, not araghatta
⚠ The trap is the leather bag over a pulley: that is the charas, a bucket device; araghatta is always a wheel with pots
⚠ Satish Chandra calls the improved rahat "miscalled the Persian wheel"; it lifted water from a deeper level (14th century)
PYQ 2025: asked the build of araghatta (wheel with pots); PYQ 2016: asked its use (waterwheel for irrigation)

t: Water-lifting devices → how each works
text:
## 1. The four devices UPSC can list
Device | How it lifts water | Power
Araghatta / rahat | Chain of pots on a wheel | Bullocks (geared)
Charas / mot | Large leather bag pulled over a pulley | Bullocks walking down a ramp
Dhenkuli / dhekli | Bucket on a lever with a counterweight (shaduf type) | One person
Hand bucket and rope | Rope pulled directly by hand | Hand
## 2. Context
Turks spread improved crafts: rahat, paper-making, glass-making, spinning wheel, improved loom, superior mortar
⚠ Do not mix: charas = bag + pulley; dhenkuli = lever; araghatta = wheel + pots
## Beyond your notes
Dhenkuli and charas are named in Babur's description of irrigation in north India (Baburnama); Babur also describes the wheel (verify wording)

t: Hundi → what it was
text:
## 1. Meaning
Hundi = a bill of exchange: written promise to pay a fixed sum at a particular place, at once or after a set period
Issued by bankers: sarrafs (shroffs), mahajans, sahukars
Type | Feature
Darshani hundi | Payable on sight
Miyadi hundi | Payable after a fixed period
Hundi for money transfer | Deposit in one city, cash in another, no need to carry coin
Hundi for credit | Used to borrow
⚠ Not a royal advisory, not a daily diary, not a feudal lord's order: these were the 2020 distractors
⚠ Satish Chandra: hundi often included insurance, rate by goods, destination and route; cashed at a discount
PYQ 2020: "hundi in post-Harsha sources" = bill of exchange

t: Banjaras → who they were
text:
## 1. The trader-nomads
Banjaras = the most important trader-nomads of medieval India (PYQ 2016 options: agriculturists, warriors, weavers, traders)
Caravan = tanda; owned their oxen; bought grain cheap, sold dear
Source | What it says on Banjaras
Alauddin Khalji | Used them to carry grain to city markets
Jahangir (Tuzuk) | Carried grain on bullocks; supplied Mughal army
Peter Mundy (English, Shah Jahan) | A tanda of 14,000 oxen; families travel along; 6-7 miles a day

topic: Village officials, feudalism and revenue assignments
t: Feudalism → its essential elements
text:
## 1. What feudalism is
Essential: administration based on control and possession of land; lord-vassal relationship
Not essential: a very strong centre with weak local authority (feudalism is decentralised)
Feature | Feudal?
Land-based administrative structure | Yes
Lord-vassal ties (samanta and overlord) | Yes
Strong central authority | No
Hereditary revenue officials (Pratiharas) | Yes, sign of decentralisation
Europe: serfdom and the manor; India had no serfdom or manor as such, but samantas held feudal powers (Satish Chandra)
Cavalry warfare and the iron stirrup helped feudalism grow
⚠ PYQ 2015 answer: 2 and 3 only; statement 1 (strong centre) is the opposite of feudalism

topic: Village officials, feudalism and revenue assignments
t: Samantas and land grants → feudal features
text:
## 1. How Indian feudalism grew
Samantas: given land; paid homage and military support; strong samantas could become kings
Land grants began with Satavahanas in the Deccan, common under Guptas
Feature of grants | Detail
Tax | Tax-free forever; grantee collected the taxes
Royal agents | Could not enter granted villages
Justice | Grantee could punish criminals
Agrahara | Land to a Brahmana, exempt from revenue
Recorded on | Stone in Prakrit first; later copper plates in Sanskrit
Western Gangas gave land mostly to Jainas; Pallavas mainly to Brahmanas
Kings took the title dharma-maharaja (Vakataka, Pallava, Kadamba, Western Ganga)
⚠ Feudatory chiefs like Deshmukhs, Deshpandes gained power under the Pratiharas (Testbook)

topic: Village officials, feudalism and revenue assignments
t: Iqta system → features over time
text:
## 1. Iqta
Started in India by Iltutmish: officials assigned land revenue instead of cash salary
Firoz Tughlaq revived it and made iqta hereditary (son, then son-in-law, then slave)
Ruler | Iqta change
Iltutmish | Introduced
Firoz Tughlaq | Revived, hereditary, soldiers paid in land
Mughals (modified form) | Became jagir under mansabdari
Effect of hereditary iqta: no noble revolts under Firoz, but fewer competent men recruited
## Beyond your notes
Alauddin Khalji paid soldiers in cash and resumed many iqtas (verify)
⚠ Provinces in the Sultanate were also called iqtas under muqtis/walis

topic: Village officials, feudalism and revenue assignments
t: Amara-nayaka and other assignments → features
text:
## 1. Amara-nayaka (Vijayanagara)
Major political innovation; likely derived from the iqta
Military commanders given territory (amaram); collected taxes; sent annual tribute to the raya; kept troops and horses for him; funded temples and irrigation
By the 17th century Nayakas of Tanjore and Madurai became independent
## 2. Other revenue terms
Term | Meaning
Jagir | Mughal land whose revenue went to the jagirdar, not the state
Mokasa | Maratha jagir
Chauth | Maratha levy of one-fourth
Sardeshmukhi | Additional one-tenth
Jizya | Tax on non-Muslims
⚠ Shivaji did not abolish deshmukhi and did award mokasa (Satish Chandra)

topic: Tamil and Kannada roots of Bhakti
t: Tamil Siddhas and Lingayats → what they believed
text:
## 1. Siddhas (Sittars) of the Tamil region
Monotheistic; condemned idolatry, rituals and caste
"Siddha" = one who has attained siddhi (perfection), as distinct from a bhakta still seeking God
Mystical movement within Shaivism, 16th-17th c; practised yoga, Tantra, control of body and mind
Thayumanavar (18th c, Tamil Nadu): Saiva Siddhanta; his Sittar poetry protested temple abuses and caste
## 2. Lingayats / Virashaivas of the Kannada region
Belief | Lingayat position
Rebirth | Questioned it; devotee unites with Shiva at death, does not return
Caste | Rejected caste hierarchy and Brahmanical treatment of women
Ritual, idols | Against all ritual and idol worship
Dharmashastra practice | Allowed post-puberty marriage, widow remarriage
Dead | Buried, not cremated
⚠ Both statements of 2016 are correct: Siddhas = monotheistic + anti-idol; Lingayats = question rebirth + reject caste
PYQ 2016: two-statement question on Siddhas and Lingayats; answer "both"; trap is to assume Lingayats, being Shaiva, accepted rebirth

Movement was a reaction to the Tamil Bhakti link with temple worship

t: Ramanuja → teaching and the Statue of Equality
text:
## 1. Life
Born 11th c (1017-1137) at Sriperumbudur (TN) under the Cholas; taught at Srirangam
Deeply influenced by the Alvars; chief exponent of Sri Vaishnavism
Converted Hoysala king Vishnuvardhana from Jainism to Vaishnavism
## 2. Teaching: Vishishtadvaita (qualified non-dualism)
Soul even when united with God remains distinct; world is real, not maya; universe is Vishnu's body
Best means of salvation = intense devotion (bhakti) to Vishnu, with God's grace (kripa) and surrender
Moksha = eternal communion with Vishnu in Vaikuntha, not dissolution
Follower Ramananda carried his teachings to North India
Option in 2022 | Whose idea
Devotion best means of salvation | Ramanuja (answer)
Vedas eternal, self-existent, wholly authoritative | Mimamsa
Logical argument for highest bliss | Nyaya
Salvation through meditation | Yoga

1498: reached Calicut (Kozhikode) with 3 ships, guided by Gujarati pilot Abdul Majid

text:
In Bengal the Portuguese turned to piracy, smuggling, kidnapping and the slave trade

topic: The Portuguese: Calicut to Goa and Diu
t: Cartaz and Cafila → Portuguese trade controls
text:
System | What it was
Cartaz | Licence/pass every Asian ship had to buy; introduced by Vasco da Gama (1502); ship without it seized
Cafila | Convoy of small local merchant ships escorted by a Portuguese fleet; earned customs revenue
Banned cargo on passes (Portuguese monopoly items): pepper, horses, ginger, coir, ship pitch, sulphur, lead, cinnamon
Albuquerque used the cartaz to dominate from Hormuz to Malacca and the Spice Islands
Kunjali Marakkars: admirals of the Zamorin; four of them fought the Portuguese 1520-1600; credited with the first naval defence of the Indian coast
⚠ First time in Indian history a group of merchants demanded exclusive trading rights
## Significance (PMF)
First commercial treaties with Indian rulers; farming became market-oriented
Their infantry drill was adopted by the French, English, Marathas and Sikhs
Alphonso mango is named after a Portuguese Afonso (Albuquerque or priest Nicolau Afonso)

topic: Anglo-French struggle: Carnatic wars and Dupleix
t: Dupleix → first European to meddle in princes' quarrels
text:
## 1. Dupleix's method
Joseph Dupleix, French Governor-General at Pondicherry (1742-54)
After the First Carnatic War he saw that a small disciplined army could decide any quarrel between Indian princes
Strategy: back one prince against another and take commercial, territorial or money rewards from the winner
He also pioneered the subsidiary system: paid French troops for the Nizam and Carnatic princes (late 1740s); Clive copied it after 1757; Wellesley gave it final shape
Claimant backed | Rival backed by English | Outcome
Chanda Sahib (Carnatic) | Muhammad Ali (son of Anwaruddin) | Chanda Sahib killed after siege of Arcot
Muzaffar Jang (Hyderabad) | Nasir Jang | Muzaffar Jang became Nizam; French got Masulipatam
⚠ Not Clive, Albuquerque or Warren Hastings: Dupleix began the policy; Clive only perfected it in Bengal
PYQ 1996: first European to take part in quarrels of Indian princes to acquire territory = Dupleix

topic: Anglo-French struggle: Carnatic wars and Dupleix
t: Carnatic wars → European war, battle, treaty
text:
## 1. Three wars (1746-63)
War | European cause | Key battle | Treaty
First (1746-48) | Austrian Succession | Adyar / St Thome (1746): French beat Nawab's army | Aix-la-Chapelle (1748): Madras returned to English
Second (1749-54) | None (Indian succession disputes) | Ambur (1749): Anwaruddin killed; siege of Arcot (1751) by Clive | Pondicherry (1754): no interference in princes' quarrels
Third (1756-63) | Seven Years' War | Wandiwash (22 Jan 1760): Eyre Coote beat Count de Lally | Paris (1763): French factories unfortified, trade only
Second war had no European war behind it: purely Indian succession quarrels exploited by both companies
Godeheu replaced Dupleix (1 Aug 1754) and signed the Treaty of Pondicherry
⚠ Adyar showed a small European-trained force (230 Europeans + 700 sepoys) could rout 10,000 Mughal troops
⚠ PMF table writes "Third Carnatic War (1758-63)"; text says 1756-63: use 1756-63

topic: Anglo-French struggle: Carnatic wars and Dupleix
t: Wandiwash and after → end of French power
text:
## 1. Sequence 1758-1763
English secured Masulipatam and the Northern Sarkars from the Nizam
Wandiwash (1760): decisive; English General Eyre Coote vs French Count de Lally
1761: Pondicherry captured and destroyed; French lost almost all possessions
Paris (1763): factories restored but could not be fortified; French lived under British protection
Bengal's revenue after Plassey (1757) paid for the English army in the Third war

Misuse of dastaks (Farrukhsiyar's farman of 1717) for servants' private trade
Fortification of Calcutta without permission; refuge to Krishna Das; Nawab refused them a mint

## 1. Battle of Buxar (22 Oct 1764)
Mir Qasim + Shuja-ud-Daulah (Nawab of Awadh) + Shah Alam II (Mughal emperor) vs English under Major Hector Munro
More decisive than Plassey: beat the combined armies of two major Indian powers

topic: Subsidiary alliance, Doctrine of Lapse and Awadh
t: Awadh after annexation → taluqdars and Summary Settlement
text:
## 1. British policy in 1856
Taluqdars were disarmed and their forts destroyed immediately after annexation
Summary Settlement (1856) assumed taluqdars were interlopers/outsiders who held land by force and fraud
Estates of most taluqdars confiscated; British aimed to take revenue directly from peasants
Indicator | Before British | After Summary Settlement
Villages held by taluqdars | 67% | 38%
## 2. Chain of grievances in 1857
Prince (Nawab exiled), court dependants jobless, taluqdars dispossessed, peasants faced over-assessment, sepoys (many from Awadh) angry
Taluqdars joined Begum Hazrat Mahal at Lucknow
⚠ Taluqdars were dispossessed and disarmed: "allowed to retain arms and forts" is false

Ring-fence | Warren Hastings | Defend neighbours' frontiers to guard Company lands (Awadh as buffer)
Subsidiary alliance | Wellesley (pioneer Dupleix) | Paid British force, Resident, loss of foreign policy
Paramountcy | Lord Hastings | Company supreme; may annex any state
Doctrine of Lapse | Dalhousie | No natural heir → annexation
Annexation also by misgovernment (Mysore 1831, Coorg 1834, Awadh 1856) and by war (Bengal, Mysore, Marathas, Sindh, Punjab)
⚠ British success: Bengal's revenue, regular pay for sepoys, artillery, able second-line leaders, Indian disunity and absence of nationalism

topic: Titles: Governor of Bengal to Viceroy
t: Title changes → which Act, first and last holder
text:
## 1. Four titles, four Acts
Title | Created by | First holder | Last holder
Governor of Bengal | Company rule after Plassey | Robert Clive (1757-60, 1765-67) | Warren Hastings (1772-73)
Governor-General of Bengal | Regulating Act 1773 | Warren Hastings (1773-85) | William Bentinck
Governor-General of India | Charter Act 1833 | William Bentinck | Canning (last GG under the EIC)
Viceroy and GG of India | GoI Act 1858 | Canning (1858) | Mountbatten (1947)
Viceroy = Crown's representative; formally "Viceroy and Governor-General of India"
Indian Independence Act 1947 abolished the office of Viceroy; each Dominion got a Governor-General
⚠ Clive was Governor of Bengal, never Governor-General: the first GG of Bengal is Warren Hastings
⚠ Bentinck is both the last GG of Bengal and the first GG of India; Hastings is both the last Governor and the first GG of Bengal
PYQ 2007: "Clive first GG of Bengal; Bentinck first GG of India" - only statement 2 correct. PYQ 2023 (Acts topic): the GG of Bengal became GG of India by the Charter Act 1833, not the Regulating Act or Pitt's India Act

t: Wellesley → subsidiary alliance: the terms
text:
## 1. What the Indian ruler accepted
Permanent stationing of a British force in his territory + a subsidy for its upkeep
Unable to pay → cede territory (Nizam ceded land instead of cash, 1800)
Keep a British Resident at court; disband his own army
Employ no Europeans without British approval (aimed at the French)
No negotiation with any other Indian ruler without the GG
## 2. What the British gave
Defence against domestic and foreign enemies; promise of non-interference in internal affairs (broken by the Resident)
Lost by the ruler | Gained by the British
Right of self-defence | Army maintained at the states' expense
Diplomatic relations | Wars fought far from own territory
Right to employ foreign experts | Tribute in the name of protection
Settling disputes with neighbours | Paramountcy; easy annexation
⚠ System was old (pioneered by French Dupleix, late 1740s; used by Clive after 1757); Wellesley only gave it a definite shape

t: Subsidiary alliance → its aims (and what it was not)
text:
## 1. Aims UPSC accepts
Maintain a large standing army at others' expense
Keep India safe from the Napoleonic/French danger
Establish British paramountcy over Indian states
Check the threat of Zaman Shah of Kabul (pretext for the Awadh treaty, 1801)
## 2. Not an aim
To secure a fixed income for the Company - the goal was military-political dominance, not stable revenue
Effect on people | Detail
Unemployed soldiers | Disbanded armies joined the Pindaris
Misgovernment | Protected rulers no longer feared their subjects
PYQ 2018: which does NOT apply to Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance - "to secure a fixed income for the Company"; trap: "army at others' expense" sounds financial but is a real aim
PYQ 1999: the GG who "kept the British flag flying" while Europe fell to Napoleon = Wellesley, not Warren Hastings, Cornwallis or Lord Hastings

text:
## 1. Expansion (1798-1805)

Event | Detail

## 1. Step by step
Act | Effect on centralisation

Feature | Detail

## 1. Facts
Royal Commission on Indian Currency and Finance, 1926
Fixed rupee at 1 shilling 6 pence - an overvalued rate
Motive: aid remittances to Britain (Home Charges: pensions, interest, military costs, dividends) and keep India's creditworthiness
Hurt Indian exports; helped importers (not the motive)
Nationalists wanted 1s 4d: Gandhi's 11 demands (1930) asked to reduce ratio to 1s 4d
Recommended a central bank → RBI Act 1934 → RBI 1 April 1935, Calcutta
Ambedkar's ideas (The Problem of the Rupee, 1923) fed the RBI concept

Remittances + creditworthiness | Correct
Support importers / cotton exports / gold value | Wrong

Bentinck | 1831 | Provincial appeal and circuit courts abolished; Indians as Deputy Magistrates, Principal Sadar Amins
High Courts | 1862 | Calcutta, Madras, Bombay
Federal Court | 1937 | Under 1935 Act
## 2. Police
Cornwallis set up the regular police: thanas under an Indian Daroga; zamindars relieved of police duty; later District SP
## 3. Codes (Law Commission under Macaulay)
Civil Procedure Code 1859, IPC 1860, CrPC 1861
⚠ Regular police = Cornwallis, not Warren Hastings
PYQ 2005: SC Calcutta by Regulating Act and IPC 1860 correct; Hastings-police wrong
## Beyond your notes
IPC was enacted 1860 but came into force 1 January 1862

topic: Civil services, judiciary, police and local bodies
t: District Collector → 1793 and 1831 changes
text:
## 1. Evolution
Period | Collector's role
1786 | District made the unit; Collector = revenue + judge + magistrate
1793 Regulation (Cornwallis) | Collector only collects revenue; Judge-Magistrate does civil justice and order
1831 (Bentinck) | Civil justice to a Civil Judge; Collector gets revenue + order + lower criminal justice

PYQ 2010: reason = concentration of power undesirable (not efficiency, not "Europeans only")

topic: Civil services, judiciary, police and local bodies
t: Ilbert Bill 1883 → racial parity in courts
text:
## 1. Facts
Viceroy Ripon, 1883; Law Member Ilbert
Aim: let Indian district magistrates and sessions judges try Europeans in criminal cases
Fierce European agitation; government bowed and diluted the Bill
Lesson for Indians: racial discrimination; spurred organised nationalism
Point | Status before Bill
Civil cases | Since 1836 British subjects tried in same courts as Indians
Criminal cases | Indian judge could not try a European

Compromise of 1884: a European could claim a jury of which half were Europeans

topic: EIC trade, free trade and deindustrialisation
t: Bengal exports in mid-18th century → what the EIC bought
text:
## 1. The staple exports
Bengal = richest, most fertile province; EIC bought goods with Bengal's own revenue after Diwani (1765) = "Investments"
Source | Exports from Bengal
PMF | Cotton textiles, silk, indigo, saltpetre
UPSC 2018 key | Cotton, silk, saltpetre, opium
Preview | Cotton cloth, opium, saltpetre, sugar, silk

topic: EIC trade, free trade and deindustrialisation
t: Stages of colonialism → form of exploitation
text:
## 1. Three stages (Bipan Chandra frame, in PMF)
Stage | Period | Surplus taken by
1. Monopoly trade and revenue | 1757-1813 | Monopoly over traders + direct seizure of revenue (Diwani)
2. Free trade / exploitation through trade | After 1813 | India = market for British goods + raw-material supplier
3. Foreign investment | From ~1860s | British capital in railways, plantations, mines, banks
Stage 1: Indian textile exports rose; weavers ruined by Company monopoly, not by British imports
Stage 2: free trade, English replaced Persian, modern education, liberal imperialism
Stage 3: reactionary imperialism (Lytton, Dufferin, Lansdowne, Curzon); faster railways
⚠ Weavers were ruined before machine imports by forced contracts: buy raw cotton dear, sell cloth cheap

topic: EIC trade, free trade and deindustrialisation
t: One-way free trade after 1813 → how it worked
text:
## 1. The Charter Act 1813 turn
British manufacturers campaigned against EIC; 1813 ended its monopoly of Indian trade (except tea and China)
Direction | Policy
British goods into India | Free or nominal duty
Indian goods into Britain | Heavy duties; prohibitive by 1820
India's role | Consumer of manufactures, supplier of raw cotton, raw silk, indigo, tea, grain
Calico Act 1720: banned printed cotton (chintz) in England
1769: Court of Directors ordered discouragement of Bengal silk manufacture
By 1880s two-thirds of cotton cloth worn in India was British
⚠ NCERT: India became exporter of primary products and importer of consumer goods and light capital goods; Suez Canal (1869) tightened British control
Marx (1853): India, "great workshop of cotton manufacture", was inundated with English cotton at nominal duty

topic: EIC trade, free trade and deindustrialisation
t: Deindustrialisation → causes
text:
## 1. Why handicrafts collapsed
Cause | Detail
Industrial Revolution | Machine goods cheaper (Kay's flying shuttle, Hargreaves' jenny, Arkwright's water frame, Watt's engine)
One-way free trade | After 1813
EIC oppression | Forced low prices, ban on working for Indian merchants
Loss of patrons | Indian rulers and courts disappeared
Railways | British goods reached remote villages
Raw-material export | Dearer raw cotton for weavers
Shipbuilding crushed: 1813 law barred ships under 350 tonnes on India-Britain route; 1814 Indian ships not "British-registered"
Iron smelting declined: forest laws + British steel imports
⚠ Industrial Revolution was driven by manufacturers seeking markets, not by the inventions alone (PMF)
PYQ 2020: first-half-19th c impact = handicrafts ruined; not machines in Indian mills, not railways, not heavy duties on British goods

topic: EIC trade, free trade and deindustrialisation
t: Deindustrialisation → consequences
text:
## 1. What followed
Consequence | Detail
Ruralisation | Artisans became tenants and agricultural labourers
Overcrowding of land | Main cause of poverty
Village economy broken | Union of agriculture and domestic industry (spinning) separated
Share of world economy | ~23% (early 18th c) → ~3% (1947)
Textile exports | Testbook: 27% of world (1700) → 2% (1800)
India reverted to exporting cotton yarn, not cloth (NCERT)
Decline of handicrafts was not offset by modern industry
⚠ British conquest differed from earlier ones by: disrupting the village economy + drain of wealth
## In news 2025-26
History of Swadeshi (IE explainer, Aug 2025): Samachar Chandrika (1822) urged Indian goods; Gopal Hari Deshmukh, Rajnarayan Basu; Ranade preferred Indian goods even if costlier; Naoroji's drain and Dutt's deindustrialisation turned swadeshi into economic critique

topic: EIC trade, free trade and deindustrialisation

Term | Meaning
Muslin | Fine cotton, from Mosul (Iraq) where Europeans met it; Dacca malmal
Calico | From Calicut; general name for cotton cloth
Chintz | Printed cotton
Bandanna | Bright printed neck/head scarf
Rangrez | Dyer

t: Commercial crops → why the EIC pushed them
text:
## 1. Crop → use
Crop | Use
Raw silk | British weavers
Cotton | British weavers; sold to China
Indigo | Dye for Western textiles
Opium | Smuggled into China to pay for tea
Tea | Assam from 1840s to end dependence on China
Also | Pepper, tobacco, sugar
Rule: none competed with British products; all high value per kg
China wanted silver for tea; Indian opium, cotton, ivory replaced silver
PYQ 2018: a 19th c economic result of British rule = commercialisation of agriculture; not handicraft exports, not Indian-owned factories, not rapid urbanisation

t: Commercialisation → effects on the peasant
text:
## 1. Effects
Effect | Detail
Forced sale | Sold right after harvest to pay revenue, rent, debt
Merchant-moneylender gained | Bought low
Instability | London prices decided Indian incomes
Food security | Food crops displaced; grain exported
Drain | Exports earned no matching imports
Rebellion | Cotton price fall (late 1860s) → Deccan riots
NCERT: higher cash-crop yields in some areas, but farmers did not gain
⚠ Commercialisation was forced, not a sign of prosperity (PMF)

t: Indigo → rise, revolt and decline
text:
## 1. Timeline
Year | Event
End of 18th c | Indigo manufacture begins in Bengal and Bihar
1859-60 | Indigo Revolt (Bengal); planters' gomasthas beaten
1860 | Neel Darpan by Dinabandhu Mitra
1917 | Champaran Satyagraha against tinkathia
1918 | Tinkathia abolished
Tinkathia: indigo on 3 of every 20 parts of land (Praveen CA: 3 of 20 bighas)
Decline cause: synthetic dye made natural indigo unprofitable in the world market
⚠ 2020 trap: not peasant resistance, not national leaders, not government control
PYQ 2020: indigo declined due to unprofitability from new inventions (synthetic dye)
## In news 2025-26
108th anniversary of Champaran Satyagraha (10 April 2026): begun 10 April 1917, invited by Rajkumar Shukla; Gandhi's first satyagraha in India; inquiry committee with Gandhi as member
## Beyond your notes
Synthetic indigo commercialised by BASF (Germany), 1897 (verify)

t: Plantations and the cotton boom → key facts
text:
## 1. Plantations
Fact | Detail
Assam Tea Company | 1839; first tea plantation company; Royal Charter 1845; Dwarkanath Tagore a founding director
Owners | Indigo, tea, coffee = exclusively European
Downsides | Foreign equipment, staff, markets; Britain used the forex
## 2. Cotton boom (Deccan)
American Civil War (1861): US cotton to Britain fell below 3% of normal; by 1862 over 90% of British cotton imports came from India
1865: war ends, demand collapses; 1867 revenue raised >50%
12 May 1875: riots begin at Supa (Pune); bonds and bahi khatas burnt
⚠ Sahukar = moneylender-cum-trader; Marwari = Gujarati moneylender (PMF)

Motive | Detail
Export | Raw materials and food grains to ports
Import | Market for British manufactures
Capital | Outlet for British surplus capital
Capital goods | Market for British rails, engines, wagons
Military | Move troops against rebellion / invasion
Freight rates favoured ports, hurt internal trade
⚠ Railways helped ruin handicrafts by reaching remote villages

Capital | Over Rs 350 crore, almost all British
Paid by | Indian taxpayer when lines lost money (first 50 years)
By 1869 | Over 4,000 miles by guaranteed companies
From 1869 | State railways; after 1880 both

t: Modern industry → firsts and owners

Industry | First

t: Industrial backwardness → main reason
text:
## 1. Why no independent industrialisation
Factor | Detail
No heavy / capital-goods industry | No machine-making, little steel: key reason
No tariff protection | Refused till 1920s-30s; then discriminatory
Railway freight | Favoured imports
Credit | Banks British-dominated
Technical education | 7 engineering colleges in 1939
Regional imbalance | Few cities only
Discriminating protection: match (foreign) protected; cement, steel, glass (Indian) denied or under-protected
New classes: industrial capitalists and modern working class
⚠ UPSC 1999 key (PMF): absence of heavy industries; Preview prints "preference of the rich to invest in land": follow PMF
PYQ 1999: no independent industrial development = absence of heavy (capital goods) industries

topic: Drain of wealth and the economic critique
t: Drain of wealth → meaning and components
text:
## 1. Definition
Wealth sent to Britain for which India got no adequate economic or material return; peculiar to British rule (Mughals settled and spent here)
Visible drain (to 1813) | Invisible drain (after 1813)
Gifts and bribes from Bengal rulers | Salaries, allowances, pensions of British officials
Private trade profits via misused dastak | Salary and pension of Secretary of State and India Office
Investments (goods bought from Bengal revenue) | Interest on foreign loans (incl. railway guarantees)
Unfair trade practices | Profits on foreign capital; shipping, banking, insurance payments
Size: ~9% of national income (end 18th c); ~6% (end 19th c)
After 1813: drain took the form of unrequited exports (export surplus)
⚠ Naoroji called drain the "evil of all evils"; INC adopted drain theory at Calcutta, 1896

topic: Drain of wealth and the economic critique
t: Home Charges → what was included
text:
## 1. Spent in England by the Secretary of State for India
Included | Not included
India Office establishment in London | Wars outside India
Salaries and pensions of British personnel (retired civil servants) | 
Interest on public debt raised abroad | 
Interest on railway capital | 
Military stores purchased in England | 
Non-effective army charges; EIC dividends | 
⚠ Florence Nightingale: famine money diverted to the Afghan war (1878-80); but wars abroad are not in the 2011 Home Charges list
PYQ 2011: Home Charges = 1 and 2 only (India Office + salaries/pensions)

topic: Drain of wealth and the economic critique
t: Dadabhai Naoroji → works and firsts
text:
## 1. The "Grand Old Man"
Fact | Detail
Poverty and Un-British Rule in India | Drain theory book; the "Un-British" phrase
England's Duties to India | First drain lecture, East India Association, London, 2 May 1867
The Wants and Means of India (1870), Poverty of India (1876) | Poverty papers
Per capita income | Rs 20 (1867-68): first estimate
Organisations | East India Association (1866); London Indian Society (1865, with W.C. Bonnerjee)
House of Commons | First Indian MP, Liberal, 1892
Welby Commission | First Indian member
Journals | Rast Goftar (1851), Voice of India (1883)
INC | Demanded swaraj at Calcutta 1906
⚠ Main contribution (2012 key) = exposing economic exploitation; not reinterpreting texts, not "social reform first"
PYQ 2008: "Un-British"; PYQ 2000: first per-capita estimate = Naoroji

topic: Drain of wealth and the economic critique

text:

Book | Author

PYQ 2015: Naoroji, G. Subramania Iyer and R.C. Dutt all critics (1, 2 and 3)

topic: Drain of wealth and the economic critique
t: Drain theory → who believed, who did not
text:
## 1. Supporters vs rejecter
Leader | Position
Naoroji, R.C. Dutt, Ranade, Tilak, Gokhale | Accepted drain
Forerunners (1840s): Bhaskar Pandurang Tarkhadkar, Bhau Mahajan (G.V. Kunte), Ramkrishna Vishwanath | Attacked drain before Naoroji
Sir Syed Ahmed Khan | Rejected: saw British rule as modernising; loyal
1840s forerunners attacked: ruin of handicrafts, no-tariff policy, curbs on industry, wars charged to India

PYQ 1996: Syed Ahmed Khan did not believe in drain theory

topic: Drain of wealth and the economic critique
t: Nationalist critique → tariffs, finance, agriculture
text:
## 1. What the early nationalists demanded
Area | Critique / demand
Trade | Imperial preference and free trade ruined industry; demand tariff protection
Capital | Opposed foreign capital in railways, plantations
Finance | Abolish salt tax, cut land revenue, cut military spending
Services | Indianisation: Europeans costly and sent pay home (drain)
Agriculture | Long fixed tenure for peasants, not Bengal-type zamindari
Remedy | Swadeshi, boycott, government aid to industry
Imperial preference: empire-wide preferential tariff: British imports into India at nominal duty; Indian exports taxed heavily in Britain
⚠ Imperial preference ≠ racial discrimination or preference to British political agents
PYQ 1999: imperial preference = special privileges on British imports in India

t: Three settlements → founder, area, owner
text:
## 1. Comparison
Feature | Permanent | Ryotwari | Mahalwari
Year | 1793 | 1820 | 1822
By | Cornwallis | Alexander Read, Thomas Munro | Holt Mackenzie
Area | Bengal, Bihar, Orissa, Varanasi, N Madras | Madras, Bombay, Assam, Coorg, Burma | NW Provinces, Punjab, Ganga valley, C India
Share of British India | ~19% | ~51% | ~30%
Revenue | Fixed for ever | Revised 20-30 yrs | Revised periodically
Pays | Zamindar | Ryot directly | Village headman
Owner | Zamindar | Ryot | Village community
Survey | No | Yes | Yes
PYQ 2017: Ryotwari = Read and Munro (2 and 3 only); Cornwallis = Permanent

t: Land tenures → granted to whom
text:
## 1. The 2000 match
Tenure | Land / rights given to
Jagirdari | Big feudal lords (Mughal assignment)
Zamindari | Revenue farmers / rent collectors
Ryotwari | Each peasant, with right to sublet, sell, mortgage
Mahalwari | Village as a unit (mahal)
Talukdari | Big landowners of Oudh and Bengal
Malguzari | Central Provinces; Maratha revenue farmers made owners
Permanent Settlement also called Istimrari, Malguzari, Bishwedari (Preview)
Temporary zamindari: parts of Central India and Avadh
PYQ 2000: Jagirdari-feudal lords, Zamindari-revenue farmers, Ryotwari-peasant, Mahalwari-village

t: Permanent Settlement → features
text:
## 1. How it worked
Steps: Hastings' five-year farming (1772) → annual → Cornwallis' decennial (1789) → permanent (1793); John Shore, James Grant consulted
Feature | Fact
Zamindar's status | Owner, right hereditary and transferable
Share | 10/11 to Company, 1/11 kept
Revenue | Fixed permanently
Sunset Law | Unpaid by sunset of due date → estate auctioned
Cultivators | Reduced to tenants
Aims | Steady revenue; zamindars to invest in land
Jotedars (haoladars, gantidars, mandals): rich peasants who bought auctioned estates
Jama = revenue demand; Amlah = zamindar's collecting officer
Zamindars were to issue pattas but many did not: no official check (IAS 2001)

t: Permanent Settlement → effects and the litigation trap
text:
## 1. Effects
Group | Effect
Old zamindars | By 1815 nearly half of Bengal's landed property sold to merchants
Company | Easy collection, stable income; but no share in rising land value
Cultivators | High rents, insecure, evictions
Structure | Subinfeudation, absentee landlords
Rarely extended because: prices rose after 1810, Ricardo's rent theory, and the state preferred settling directly with ryots
Bengal Tenancy Act 1885: rights of tenants in Bengal and Bihar
⚠ 2011 trap: increased litigation is not traced to stronger zamindars, EIC overlordship or efficient courts → answer none
PYQ 2011: answer (d) none of (a), (b), (c)

t: Ryotwari → what the system did
text:
## 1. Features (2012 statements)
Feature | Fact
Payment | Rent paid directly by peasants to government
Title | Ryots registered and given pattas
Assessment | Land surveyed and assessed before tax
Rights | Sell, lease, mortgage, transfer
Revision | Every 20-30 years, usually raised
Rate | 1/3 to 1/2 of produce; Read-Munro fixed 50% in Baramahal
Reality: "one giant zamindar" (the state); putcut assessment (no survey); cultivation compelled
1855: only 14.5 m acres cultivated, 18 m acres waste in Madras
⚠ It did not create true peasant ownership; CAPF 2016: Madras and Bombay, not Bengal
PYQ 2012: all three statements correct

t: Thomas Munro and Bombay ryotwari → career facts
text:
## 1. Munro's path
Year | Post
1792-99 | Baramahal (Salem) with Captain Alexander Read: first ryotwari trial
1799 | West Kanara
1801-07 | Collector, Ceded Districts (from Nizam); conceived ryotwari; opposed Cornwallis' plan
1820-27 | Governor of Madras; enforced ryotwari; died of cholera at Pattikonda (1827)
## 2. Bombay Deccan
After Peshwa's fall (1818): Elphinstone introduced ryotwari
Pringle's survey on Ricardo's rent theory: too high, peasants fled to Nizam's land
Wingate and Goldsmid (from 1836): moderate, soil-and-location based
⚠ Testbook dates Munro's governorship 1819-26; PMF 1820-27

t: Mahalwari → features
text:
## 1. Holt Mackenzie's village settlement
Feature | Fact
Introduced | 1822, NW Provinces of Bengal Presidency (now UP)
Unit | Mahal = village or group of villages
Collector | Village headman (lambardar)
Ownership | Village community jointly
Revenue | Sum of plot estimates; revised periodically
Spread | Punjab (village system), Ganga valley, Central India, MP
1833: William Bentinck made it more flexible; promoted in Agra and Awadh
Problems: faulty surveys, high demand, deserted villages, collection costs > revenue at times
## Beyond your notes
1833 revision under Bentinck carried out by R.M. Bird and James Thomason (Regulation IX of 1833)

t: Pre-British revenue → what the English did not introduce
text:
## 1. 2012 statements
Item | Actually introduced by
Revenue by soil and crop quality | Alauddin, Sher Shah, Akbar (Todar Mal)
Mobile cannons | Babur / Mughals
Tobacco, red chillies | Portuguese
Tipu and Haidar: removed intermediaries; ijara (fixed rent) and hissa (share) land; nationalised tobacco, sandalwood
⚠ "Introduced by the English" = none of the three
PYQ 2012: answer (d) none

t: Private property in land → debt trap
text:
## 1. Land as a commodity
Before British | After British
Moneylender subordinate to village | Could seize land
Could take jewellery, standing crop | Land saleable, mortgageable, alienable
Why: protect revenue (land can be auctioned) + motive to improve land
Chain: over-assessment → arrears → debt → land sales → peasant revolts
## In news 2025-26
Kolhan (Ho): Permanent Settlement let zamindars encroach on Ho land → Ho (1821-22), Kol (1831-32) revolts; Wilkinson's Rules (31 rules, 1837) recognised Manki-Munda system (CARE, Sept 2025)
Glossary of Revenue Terms (Jan 2026): DoLR with CoE-LAM, YASHADA Pune, harmonises terms from Todar Mal, ryotwari, mahalwari (under DILRMP)

t: Impoverishment of peasants → causes
text:
## 1. Why peasants sank
Cause | Detail
High revenue | Clive and Hastings maximised; ryotwari/mahalwari 1/3-1/2 of produce
Rigid collection | Pay on due date even after crop failure
Overcrowding | Ruined artisans pushed onto land
Landlord exactions | Illegal dues, forced labour
Moneylenders | Land transfers
New landlordism: absentee, urban, ruthless; subinfeudation (chains of intermediaries)
Stagnation: no investment by cultivator, landlord or state; 6 agriculture colleges in 1939
⚠ Landlords became political supporters of British rule

t: Colonial poverty → man-made, not natural
text:
## 1. The nationalist and NCERT view
Point | Fact
Pre-British Bengal | Bernier: "richer than Egypt"; exported cottons, silks, rice, sugar, butter
Growth (first half 20th c) | Aggregate output < 2%, per capita ~0.5% a year (NCERT)
Dependence on agriculture | ~85% lived in villages (NCERT); ~80% (PMF)
Paradox | Poor people in a rich country
Causes | Exploitation, deindustrialisation, drain, landlord-moneylender squeeze, high taxes
Britain's goals (NCERT): market for British exports, India to service debt, manpower for imperial armies
Poverty was not a Mughal legacy or a matter of geography (PMF)
⚠ Colonial government never officially estimated national income; only individual estimates (Naoroji to R.C. Desai)

t: Famines → year and region
text:

topic: Early Company institutions and the Orientalist phase (1781-1813)
t: Early institutions → founder, year and purpose
text:
## 1. The three "exceptions" to non-intervention
Institution | Year | Founder | Purpose
Calcutta Madrasa | 1781 | Warren Hastings | Teach Muslim law
Sanskrit College, Banaras | 1791 | Jonathan Duncan (Resident at Banaras) | Study Hindu law and philosophy
College of Fort William, Calcutta | 1800 | Lord (Richard) Wellesley | Train young civil service recruits
First two: to supply qualified Indians to help administer law in Company courts
Third: to educate British civil servants, not Indians
⚠ Sanskrit College = Jonathan Duncan, not William Jones (Jones founded the Asiatic Society, 1784)
⚠ Fort William = Richard Wellesley (Governor-General), not Arthur Wellesley (his brother, later Duke of Wellington)
⚠ Preview gives the Madrasa as 1780 (first principal Mulla Majduddin); PMF and Testbook give 1781
PYQ 2018: only Calcutta Madrasa-Warren Hastings correct (answer: 2 only)

topic: Early Company institutions and the Orientalist phase (1781-1813)
t: Fort William College → why Wellesley set it up
text:
## 1. Purpose and working
Founded 1800 (formally 10 July / 24 Nov 1800 in the sources) at Calcutta
Young civil servants came from England untrained, without Indian languages, laws or customs
Taught Indian languages, law, history; William Carey headed its Bengali department (1801) and wrote Bengali textbooks
2020 option | Correct?
Ordered by the Court of Directors | No: Wellesley's own initiative
To revive oriental learning | No (that was the Madrasa/Sanskrit College aim)
To employ William Carey and associates | No (Carey was hired later, 1801)
To train British civilians for administration | Yes
⚠ Training shifted to East India College, Haileybury (England) by 1806; Testbook says the college "closed in 1802"
## In news 2025-26
Civil Services Day (21 April 2025) coverage (PMF LENS) recalled Fort William College as the first civil service training centre, replaced by Haileybury
## Beyond your notes
The college lingered as a language and translation centre until 1854 (verify)
