topic: Early Company institutions and the Orientalist phase (1781-1813)
t: Missionaries and Serampore → role before and after 1813
text:
## 1. Missionaries
Believed modern education would draw Indians to Christianity; pressed the Company for English education
1783 Act: missionaries barred from India without a licence
Charter Act 1813 permitted missionaries to do religious and educational work
After 1857, the Government hesitated to back missionary schools directly
## 2. Serampore Mission
Fact | Detail
Founded | 1800, at Serampore, in Danish territory
Serampore Trio | William Carey, Joshua Marshman, William Ward
Press | Printing press 1800
College | Serampore College 1818
Carey | Baptist Missionary Society (1792); Bible into Bengali and other languages
Gangakishore Bhattacharya, first Bengali printer, began at the Serampore Press
⚠ Serampore was Danish, which is why the missionaries settled there (the Company opposed them until 1813)

t: Charter Act 1813 → what it provided for education
text:
## 1. Provisions
Real beginning of Western education in India
Governor-General in Council to spend at least Rs 1 lakh a year on education
"for the revival and improvement of literature and the encouragement of learned natives, and the introduction and promotion of knowledge of the sciences"
First time the Company accepted state responsibility for education
Missionaries allowed to come and preach/teach
Myth | Fact
Fixed English as medium | No: said nothing on medium or type of institutions
Money spent at once | No: unspent till 1823
⚠ "Real beginning of Western education" = Charter Act 1813, not Macaulay 1835 or Charter Act 1793
PYQ 2018: Charter Act 1813, GCPI 1823 and the Orientalist-Anglicist controversy all led to English education (answer: 1, 2 and 3)

t: GCPI and Orientalist-Anglicist controversy → the two camps
text:
## 1. General Committee of Public Instruction (1823)
Set up 1823 to oversee education; most members Orientalists at first
Replaced by a Council of Education in 1841
## 2. The two camps
 | Orientalists | Anglicists
Wanted | Sanskrit, Arabic, Persian learning expanded | Western knowledge
Medium | Classical / Indian languages | English (one faction wanted vernaculars)
Leaders | Early Company officials (most GCPI members) | Macaulay, backed by Bentinck
Educated Indians led by Raja Rammohan Roy backed Western learning
Despatch of the Court of Directors 1824 already favoured Western education
⚠ Even the Anglicists were split on medium: English vs vernacular (Spectrum)
## Beyond your notes
Rammohan Roy's 1823 letter to Lord Amherst protested the plan for a new Sanskrit college in Calcutta

t: Macaulay's Minute 1835 → what it decided and what followed
text:
## 1. The Minute
Macaulay: Law Member and President of the GCPI; settled the controversy for the Anglicists
"A single shelf of a good European library was worth the whole native literature of India and Arabia"
Class "Indian in blood and colour, but English in taste, in opinions, in morals and in intellect"
Bentinck accepted it on 7 March 1835: European literature and science through English; stop promoting Calcutta Madrasa and Banaras Sanskrit College
## 2. What followed
Year | Step
1835 | Bentinck announces end of Persian as court language
1837 | English replaces Persian as official language (administration, higher courts)
1841 | Council of Education replaces GCPI
1844 | Hardinge: Western-educated get government jobs
⚠ Macaulay's Minute is not the "Magna Carta of English education": that is Wood's Despatch (1854)
## Beyond your notes
Minute dated 2 February 1835

t: Downward Filtration Theory → meaning and abandonment
text:
## 1. Meaning
Educate a few from the upper and middle classes; knowledge would filter down to the masses
Reason: funds too small to teach many
Government opened a few English schools and colleges instead of many elementary schools
## 2. Abandoned (on paper) in 1854
Reason | Detail
Jobs | English-educated got government posts and did not teach others
Gulf | Created a "separate caste" of English scholars cut off from the people
Wood's Despatch (1854) rejected it on paper; in practice it lasted till the end of British rule
Modern ideas did filter down, but through parties, press, pamphlets, platforms, not as rulers wished
⚠ Wood's Despatch repudiated downward filtration; Macaulay's Minute put faith in it

t: Hindu College and individual efforts → founder and place
text:
## 1. Hindu College, Calcutta (1817)
India's first Western-style secular college; later Presidency College
Founded by David Hare (Scottish watchmaker) with the Bengali elite; linked with Raja Rammohan Roy
Spectrum: "Calcutta College" set up in 1817 by educated Bengalis got a government grant
2009 option | Correct?
Raja Rammohan Roy | Yes (UPSC key)
H.L.V. Derozio | No: he taught at Hindu College (Young Bengal)
Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar | No
Keshab Chandra Sen | No
Rammohan also ran an English school (1817) and Vedanta College (1825)
## 2. Bombay and Madras
Bombay: Native School Book and School Society (1822, Elphinstone; with Jagannath Shankarseth, Jamsetji Jejeebhoy) → Bombay Native Education Society; Elphinstone College (resolution 1827, constituted 1835, separate 1856)
Madras: Christian College 1837, Presidency College 1853
## Beyond your notes
Alexander Duff reached Calcutta only in 1830 (General Assembly's Institution, now Scottish Church College): the 2009 question's "with Duff" is loose

t: Adam's Reports and vernacular schemes → findings
text:
## 1. William Adam (Scottish missionary, appointed by Bentinck)
Reports 1835, 1836, 1838 on vernacular schools of Bengal and Bihar
Found over 1 lakh pathshalas, each with no more than 20 pupils
Flexible: no fixed fee, no fixed syllabus, no building, no printed books, no exams, no timetable; closed at harvest
Proposed vernacular medium and revival of indigenous schools: Bentinck rejected it
## 2. Other vernacular steps
Year | Step
1843-53 | James Thomson, Lt-Governor NW Provinces: village schools in vernacular (mensuration, agriculture)
1853 | Dalhousie's Minute backs vernacular education
1854 | Wood's Despatch: vernacular standards, supervision, normal schools
Indigenous system: Madrasas, Maktabs (Muslims); Tols, Pathshalas (Hindus)
⚠ Spectrum calls the NWP Lt-Governor "James Jonathan" in one list and "James Thomson" elsewhere: the man is Thomson

t: Wood's Despatch → its recommendations
text:
## 1. Who and what
1854, Court of Directors to the Governor-General; issued by Charles Wood, President of the Board of Control
"Magna Carta of English Education in India"; first comprehensive plan for education
## 2. Recommendations
No. | Recommendation
1 | State to take responsibility for education of masses and women
2 | Universities at Calcutta, Bombay, Madras on the London University model
3 | Department of Education in each of the five provinces
4 | Grants-in-aid to encourage private enterprise
5 | Vocational education; technical schools and colleges
6 | Teachers' training (English model)
7 | Graded system: primary → middle → high school → college → university
8 | Vernacular schools for elementary education
9 | Education in government institutions to be secular
PYQ 2018: grants-in-aid and universities right; "English at all levels" wrong (answer: 1 and 2 only)

t: Wood's Despatch → medium of instruction (the trap)
text:
## 1. Level-wise medium
Level | Medium
Primary / elementary (school) | Vernacular
Secondary | English and modern Indian languages
Higher (college, university) | English
Modern Indian languages to be built up as media of higher education over time
Hierarchy: vernacular primary schools in villages → Anglo-Vernacular High Schools → affiliated college (district) → affiliating universities (presidency towns)
⚠ "English as medium at all levels" is false: English only at the higher stage
⚠ Hunter (1882) later favoured English for secondary; Wardha (1937) wanted mother tongue and English only after class VIII

t: Wood's Despatch → aim and motives
text:
## 1. Aim
Stressed practical benefits of European learning as against oriental knowledge: the spread of Western culture/knowledge
2003 option | Correct?
Jobs for native Indians | No
Spread of Western culture | Yes
Literacy through English medium | No (vernacular at lower levels)
Scientific research and rationalism | No
## 2. Motives (PMF)
Motive | Logic
Economic | European tastes → demand for British goods
Administrative | Cheap supply of educated Indians for lower posts
Political | Reconcile Indians to British rule
Missionaries attacked "practical" education; wanted Christian moral education
PYQ 2003: aim = spread of Western culture in India

t: After Wood's Despatch → what was set up
text:
## 1. Developments
Year | Development
1857 | Universities of Calcutta, Bombay, Madras
1858 | Bankim Chandra Chatterjee among the first two graduates of Calcutta University
After 1854 | Departments of education in all provinces
1849 → | Bethune School brought under grants-in-aid and inspection
Later | Agriculture Institute, Pusa (Bihar); Engineering Institute, Roorkee
Schools: about 10,000 (1854) → about 76,000 (1882) (Testbook)
Five decades of Wood's model: rapid Westernisation, European heads of institutions
## 2. Weak points (PMF assessment)
Mass and women's education neglected; literary bias; heavy spending on higher education
By 1857 only three medical colleges and one good engineering college (Roorkee)
⚠ Wood's Despatch asked for women's education, but officials did little: female clerks were not employable, and orthodoxy might be upset

topic: Commissions and plans under the Crown (1882-1944)
t: Hunter Commission 1882 → why and what it recommended
text:
## 1. Set-up
1882-83; chairman W.W. Hunter; appointed under Lord Ripon; first education commission; 8 Indian members
To review progress since Wood's Despatch (1854); mostly on primary and secondary education
Background: education shifted to provinces in 1870, hurting primary schooling
## 2. Recommendations
Area | Recommendation
Primary | State's special responsibility; through vernacular
Control | Primary schools to district and municipal boards (may levy cess)
Secondary | Two streams: literary (to university) and vocational (commercial)
Private effort | Liberalise grants-in-aid; aided schools equal to government ones
Women | Noted poor female education outside presidency towns
Followed by Punjab University (1882), Allahabad University (1887)
⚠ Hunter endorsed Wood's Despatch with more stress on primary education; it did not overrule it

topic: Commissions and plans under the Crown (1882-1944)
t: Raleigh Commission and Universities Act 1904 → what changed
text:
## 1. Raleigh Commission (1902)
Appointed by Curzon; head Sir Thomas Raleigh; on universities only (barred from primary and secondary)
## 2. Indian Universities Act 1904
Change | Detail
Research | Universities to focus on study and research; appoint professors
Senate | Fellows fewer, shorter terms, mostly nominated by Government
Control | Government could veto/amend Senate regulations
Affiliation | Stricter conditions for private colleges
Money | Rs 5 lakh a year for 5 years
Nationalists saw it as control after political unrest; Gokhale: "retrograde measure"
Sadler later said 1904 made Indian universities among the most government-controlled in the world

Year | Event

1906 | Baroda makes primary education compulsory statewide (first Indian ruler)
1911 | Gokhale's bill for free compulsory primary education defeated

text:
## 1. Set-up
Calcutta University Commission; chairman Michael Sadler (VC, Leeds); Indian members Ashutosh Mukherjee and Zia-ud-din Ahmad; report 1919
View: improving secondary education is a precondition for better universities
## 2. Recommendations
Recommendation | Detail
School course | 12 years; enter university after intermediate, not matric
Degree | 3 years
Board | Separate Board of Secondary and Intermediate Education
Universities | Unitary, residential, teaching bodies, not scattered affiliating ones
Others | Honours courses; women's education; teachers' training
1916-21: seven new universities: Mysore, Patna, Banaras, Aligarh, Dacca, Lucknow, Osmania
## 3. Under Dyarchy
1919 Act: education a transferred subject; to Indian ministers in 1921

topic: Commissions and plans under the Crown (1882-1944)
t: Hartog, Wardha and Sargent → 1929, 1937, 1944
text:
## 1. Three later plans
Plan | Year | Key point
Hartog Committee | 1929 (set 1928 by Simon Commission) | Consolidation, not diffusion of primary education; restrict university admissions
Wardha Scheme (Nai Talim) | 1937 | Learning through a handicraft; 7 years free compulsory; mother tongue
Sargent Plan | 1944 | CABE's Post-War Plan; parity with England in 40 years
## 2. Wardha details
Based on Gandhi's articles in Harijan; Wardha conference Oct 1937 (Gandhi presided)
Zakir Hussain Committee report March 1938; adopted at Haripura (Feb 1938)
No English in curriculum (Spectrum: English only after class VIII); no religious education (League objected)
Faded with WW2 and Congress ministries' resignation (Oct 1939)
## 3. Sargent details
Pre-primary 3-6; free compulsory 6-11; high school 11-17 (academic and technical types)
Abolish intermediate; 3-year degree; adult illiteracy ended in 20 years
⚠ Spelling in UPSC 1997: "Sargeant"; John Sargent was educational adviser to the Government

topic: Rammohun Roy, Brahmo Samaj and Young Bengal
t: Rammohun Roy → ideas (East-West synthesis, reason, equality)
text:
## 1. What he stood for
Criticised | Argued for
Idolatry, polytheism, meaningless rituals, priestly exploitation | Monotheism (Advaita / Vedanta; Quranic Tauhid)
Sati, polygamy, child marriage, subjugation of women | Widow remarriage, women's inheritance and property rights
Blind reliance on the past, rigidity of caste | Rational and scientific approach, human dignity, social equality of men and women
Supersession of Hinduism by Christianity | Modern education for men and women; unity of Indians
Synthesis of East and West: great love and respect for the traditional philosophic systems of the East + belief that modern culture alone would regenerate India
Learn from the West without imposing Western culture; one may depart from scripture if reason demands
Applied reason to Christianity too (Precepts of Jesus angered missionaries)
First to link social-religious reform with political upliftment; "Father of Indian Renaissance", "Father of Modern India"
⚠ UPSC 2025: both statements true: love for Eastern philosophy and rational-scientific approach, human dignity, equality
PYQ 2025: Rammohun respected Eastern philosophy and wanted rational approach, dignity, equality → Both 1 and 2

text:

Year | Body
1815 (Prelims Magnum: 1814) | Atmiya Sabha (Society of Friends), Calcutta
1817 | Helped David Hare found Hindu College; English school
1821 | Calcutta Unitarian Committee (with William Adam)

20 Aug 1828 | Brahma Sabha → Brahmo Samaj
## 2. Writings and journals
Work | Note
Tuhfat-ul-Muwahhidin (1803/1809) | Persian; Gift to Monotheists
Precepts of Jesus (1820) | Morals of Christ, not miracles
Bengali translation of Vedas + 5 Upanishads | To prove monotheism
Gaudiya Vyakaran | Bengali grammar
Sambad Kaumudi (1821) | Bengali weekly
Mirat-ul-Akhbar (1822) | Persian; closed after 1823 Adams press ordinance
Campaign against sati from 1818 → Bentinck's Regulation, 1829
Title "Raja" from Mughal Akbar II (1830); died Bristol, 1833

topic: Rammohun Roy, Brahmo Samaj and Young Bengal
t: Brahmo Samaj → beliefs (what it did and did not hold)
text:
## 1. Twin pillars: Reason + Vedas and Upanishads
Brahmo Samaj | Status
Opposed idolatry | Yes
Denied need of a priestly class to interpret texts | Yes
Worship of one formless God; best of other religions | Yes
Opposed sati, polygamy, caste rigidity; female education | Yes
Vedas infallible | No: rejected infallibility (that is Arya Samaj)
Human reason as final test | Yes
A reformist (not revivalist) movement, influenced by Western rationalism
⚠ Statement "popularised doctrine that Vedas are infallible" is false for Brahmo Samaj
PYQ 2012: Brahmo Samaj opposed idolatry and denied priestly class; did not hold Vedas infallible → 1 and 2 only

## 2. Native Marriage Act, 1872 (Act III of 1872)
Result of Keshab's 1868 petition for legal Brahmo marriages
Civil marriage without religious rites; min age 14 (bride), 18 (groom); polygamy an offence; inter-caste allowed
Only for those declaring they profess no Indian religion (self-excommunication clause)
Under Keshab, Brahmo Samaj campaigned for women's education (UPSC 2001: true)
⚠ Keshab founded Tabernacle of New Dispensation and Indian Reform Association; not Calcutta Unitarian Committee

topic: Rammohun Roy, Brahmo Samaj and Young Bengal

text:
## 1. Derozio and his group
Point | Fact
Founder | Henry Vivian Derozio (1809-1831), Anglo-Indian teacher at Hindu College (1826)
Inspiration | French Revolution; free thought, question all authority
Members | Dakshinaranjan Mukherjee, Ram Gopal Ghose, Krishna Mohan Banerji

Called the first nationalist poet of modern India ("To India - My Native Land")
Failed: radicalism bookish, no link with peasants/masses
⚠ More radical than Brahmo Samaj, but created no mass movement

Point | Fact

topic: Western India: Prarthana Samaj, Ranade and the Rakhmabai Case

text:
## 1. Four methods (PMF)
Method | Reformers
Reform from within (tracts, debates) | Rammohun (sati), Vidyasagar (widow pamphlets), B.M. Malabari (age of consent)
Reform through legislation | Keshab Chandra Sen (Bengal), M.G. Ranade (Maharashtra), Veerasalingam (Andhra)
Symbols of change (non-conformist acts) | Young Bengal / Derozians
Social work | Vidyasagar, Arya Samaj, Ramakrishna Mission
Weakness of legislation route: law in a colonial society lacked popular sanction
After 1858, reform broadened; earlier it was a few individuals
⚠ Ranade = legislation method; Derozians = symbols of change

text:
## 1. Dadaji Bhikaji v. Rukhmabai
Point | Fact
Parties | Rukhmabai (married at 11) v. husband Dadaji Bhikaji (19)
Husband's suit | Restitution of conjugal rights
Her plea | Marriage not binding: no consent as a child
Court (Mar 1887) | Live with husband or 6 months' jail
End | Wrote to Queen Victoria; settled July 1888 (Rs 2,000 compensation)
Result | Fuelled Age of Consent Act, 1891
Rukhmabai became one of the first women doctors of British India
⚠ Case revolved around age of consent and restitution of conjugal rights, not women's right to education
⚠ Year: UPSC says 1884 (suit filed); PMF heads it 1885/1887 (hearings, verdict)

## 1. Swami Dayanand Saraswati (1824-1883)
Point | Fact
Founded | 1875 (April), Bombay
Ten principles finalised | 1877, Lahore
Book | Satyarth Prakash (1875, Hindi; revised 1882)
Born | Morbi, Gujarat (Mool Shankar)

Vedas infallible; Puranas full of false teachings; but Vedas open to interpretation by reason

## 1. Two streams
Reformist (Western rationalism) | Revivalist (glorious past)
Brahmo Samaj | Arya Samaj
Prarthana Samaj | Deoband movement
Aligarh movement | Theosophical Society
Young Bengal | Vivekananda's Vedantic superiority
Revivalists were not anti-reform; Arya Samaj reforms were rational in content

## 2. Ramakrishna Mission
Ramakrishna Paramahansa: priest at Dakshineshwar; all religions = paths to one goal
Vivekananda: Ramakrishna Mission (1897), Belur Math (1898); Chicago, 1893; Neo-Vedanta; social service, not personal salvation

## 1. Phule (1827-1890), Mali caste, Pune
Point | Fact
Satyashodhak Samaj | 24 Sept 1873: organise lower classes, end Brahmin/priestly domination
Region | Maharashtra: an anti-caste movement

topic: Tribal revolts: causes, features and colonial response
t: 19th-century tribal revolts → the common factor
text:
## 1. The one-line answer
Tribal movements = resentment against British policies that disrupted the old agrarian order of tribal communities
Cause (PMF list) | How it hit the tribals
Land revenue system | Land auctioned when rent unpaid; tribals made tenants
Moneylenders, traders | High interest, land lost on debt
Encroachment on land | Outsiders (dikus) settled tribal land
Forest laws (forest policy 1884) | Ended customary rights, jhum, hunting
Intrusion in tribal polity | Chiefs lost power, paid tribute
## 2. Why the other options fail
New revenue system, missionaries, moneylenders as middlemen = parts of the disruption, not the common factor
⚠ The answer is the complete disruption of the old agrarian order; each other option is only one local cause
PYQ 2011: asked the common factor of 19th-century tribal insurrections; trap: "new land revenue system" and "moneylenders as middlemen" are true but partial

topic: Tribal revolts: causes, features and colonial response
t: Tribal movements → features and three phases
text:
## 1. Salient features
Attack on outsiders (dikus): landlords, traders, officials hit first
Negative consciousness: identifying the enemy mattered more than class identity
Messiah leaders: chiefs claimed authority from God (Sidhu-Kanhu's Thakur, Birsa as Bhagwan)
Unequal conflict: bows, arrows, axes against modern guns
## 2. Three phases (PMF)
Phase | Years | Nature
First | 1795-1860 | Primary resistance against moneylenders, zamindars, officials
Second | 1860-1920 | Complex: agrarian + religious + political
Third | 1920-1947 | Linked to Gandhian national movement; land-forest revival; tribal middle class seeking autonomy/statehood
⚠ Andhra tribal forest agitation merged with Non-Cooperation = third-phase example

t: Santhal Hul → background and causes
text:
## 1. How Santhals reached Rajmahal hills
British failed to settle the Paharias as farmers → turned to Santhals
Santhals arrived in Bengal c.1780s (after the 1770 famine), entered Rajmahal hills c.1800
1832: area demarcated as Damin-i-Koh (land of the Santhals), with a promise of non-interference
## 2. Causes
Cause | Detail
Dikus | Zamindars, moneylenders, merchants, officials (Diku = exploiting outsider)
Leasing | Rajas of Maheshpur and Pakur leased Santhal villages to zamindars
Permanent Settlement 1793 | Land auctioned when rent unpaid
Cash rent | Barter economy → borrowing at high interest
Interest | Up to 500% (Testbook)
⚠ Damin-i-Koh was for Santhals, not Mundas, Oraons or Saoras

t: Santhal Hul → leaders, events and outcome
text:
## 1. The revolt
Began 30 June 1855 at Bhognadih (PMF book: Bhaganidihi) village, now Jharkhand
Leaders: brothers Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu, with Chand, Bhairav and sisters Phulo and Jhano
Claimed a call from Thakur (God); declared independence, set up a parallel government
United 32+ tribal and backward communities; martial law; crushed by 1856
## 2. Outcome
Measure | Detail
Santhal Parganas | ~5,500 sq miles from Bhagalpur and Birbhum
Santhal Pargana Tenancy Act 1876 | Land of Santhal/Adivasi cannot go to non-Santhals; only inherited
⚠ Deaths: PMF over 10,000; Testbook about 20,000
⚠ Not treated leniently; not the only mid-19th-century rebellion (1857 followed)

t: Indigo revolt 1859-60 → cause and course
text:
## 1. The system
System | Share of indigo land | Feature
Nij | under 25% | Planter's own land, hired labour
Ryoti | 75% | Ryot signs contract, takes advance, grows indigo on 25% of holding
Act XI of 1860 made breach of contract a crime: used to oppress ryots
## 2. The revolt
March 1859, Nadia district (Govindpur village), leaders Digambar Biswas and Bishnu Biswas
Ryots refused advances, contracts and rent; attacked factories; boycotted planters' men; even women fought
Zamindars and missionaries backed the ryots; indigo gone from Bengal by end of 1860
⚠ Planters then moved to Bihar (→ Champaran 1917)

t: Indigo revolt → Neel Darpan and the Indigo Commission
text:
## 1. Writers and press
Person | Role
Dinabandhu Mitra | Play Neel Darpan (written 1858-59, published 1860)
Michael Madhusudan Dutt | English translation
Rev. James Long | Published it; jailed 1 month, fined Rs 1,000
Shishir Kumar Ghosh (Amrit Bazar Patrika) | Called it "the blueprint for India's national liberty movement"
## 2. Indigo Commission (March 1860)
Ryots must finish existing contracts but could refuse indigo in future
Found the advance system oppressive; suggested one-year contracts
⚠ Indigo declined by the 20th century because of synthetic dyes, not peasant resistance (UPSC 2020)
⚠ Translator = Madhusudan Dutt, not James Long (Long only published)

t: Pabna agrarian league 1873-85 → features and outcome
text:
## 1. Course
Act of 1859 gave occupancy rights; zamindars evaded them by illegal rent hikes, evictions
May 1873: agrarian league in Yusufshahi pargana, Pabna (East Bengal)
Methods: legal battles, non-payment of rent; rarely violent
Wanted to be "Queen's ryots": loyal to the Crown, no demand to end zamindari
## 2. Key points
Item | Fact
Leaders | Keshab Chandra Roy, Shambhunath Pal (both Hindus)
Supporters | Bankim, Surendranath Banerjee, Anand Mohan Bose, Dwarkanath Ganguli
Unity | Hindu-Muslim unity, though most ryots Muslim, zamindars Hindu
Result | Bengal Tenancy Act 1885
⚠ Act of 1885 created powerful jotedars
⚠ Testbook wrongly ties Pabna to indigo; Pabna was against zamindars' rent hikes

t: Deccan riots 1875 → cause and outcome
text:
## 1. Background
Ryotwari in Bombay Deccan; revenue fixed for 30 years; first settlement 1820s
American Civil War (1861-65) → cotton boom → easy credit; by 1862 India gave 90% of Britain's cotton imports
1865 boom ends; 1867 revenue raised by over 50%; Sahukars/Marwaris refuse credit
## 2. The riots
Item | Fact
Start | 12 May 1875, Supa, Poona
Spread | Ahmednagar
Acts | Bahi khatas (account books) and debt bonds burnt
Support | Poona Sarvajanik Sabha
Enquiry | Deccan Riots Commission, report to Parliament 1878
Law | Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act 1879
1879 Act: no jail for debt; restricted sale of land to outsiders; Ranade welcomed it
⚠ Commission blamed moneylenders, not government revenue
⚠ Immediate cause (practice MCQ) = high land revenue rates

Support | Bengali intellectuals | Bengali intellectuals | Bombay educated Indians
Gain | Ryots need not grow indigo | Bengal Tenancy Act 1885 | Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act 1879
All three: early nationalists and middle class helped, but Congress later avoided anti-landlord stands
Educated Indians: Gokhale in Bombay; Lajpat Rai, Ajit Singh in Punjab

t: UP Kisan Sabha 1918 → founders and split
text:
## 1. Background in Awadh
After 1857, land returned to taluqdars → high rents, evictions
Illegal dues: nazarana (gift/renewal fee), bedakhli (eviction), rasad (supplies), begar/hari (unpaid labour)
## 2. Founding

Awadh Kisan Sabha | October 1920 | Baba Ramchandra (ex-Fiji labourer)
UP Kisan Sabha had 450 branches by June 1919
Split: Malaviya preferred the constitutional path; others joined Non-Cooperation
Ended mid-1921: repression + Awadh Rent (Amendment) Act
⚠ Nehru was not a founder; he toured Awadh villages only in 1920 through Baba Ramchandra

t: Eka movement 1921-22 → leader, area and cause
text:
## 1. Course
Began late 1921 in Hardoi, Bahraich, Sitapur (Preview adds Barabanki), Awadh
Started by Congress and Khilafat leaders; then led by Madari Pasi (low-caste radical)
Pledge in holy water: obey no illegal orders of landlords, no forced labour, abide by panchayats, help no criminals
Turned violent → Congress withdrew → crushed by March 1922
## 2. What it opposed
Grievance | Detail
Rent | About 50% above the recorded rent
Rent in kind | Wanted rent turned into cash
Forced labour | Begar
Eka included small zamindars angry at high revenue; Kisan Sabha was mainly tenants
⚠ Leader = Madari Pasi, not taluqdars; area = north Awadh, not Varanasi-Mirzapur

Gandhi and Shaukat Ali at Calicut, 18 Aug 1920: merged with Khilafat-NCM

text:
## 1. Founding
April 1936, Lucknow (with the Congress session): All India Kisan Congress, later All India Kisan Sabha
First president Swami Sahajanand Saraswati; general secretary N.G. Ranga
Indulal Yagnik edited the Kisan Bulletin; All India Kisan Day = 1 September (from 1936)
Session | Year | Place | President
First | April 1936 | Lucknow | Sahajanand Saraswati
Second | Dec 1936 | Faizpur | N.G. Ranga
Third | 1938 | Comilla | Sahajanand
Fourth | 1939 | Gaya | Narendra Dev
Sixth | 1942 | Patna | Indulal Yagnik
Eighth | 1944 | Vijayawada | Sahajanand
Tenth | 1947 | Secunderabad | Karyanand Sharma
⚠ By May 1942 the CPI controlled the Sabha; it kept away from Quit India; Ranga, Yagnik, Sahajanand left

topic: Kisan Sabha and peasant struggles of the 1930s-40s
t: Kisan Sabha → aims and the Congress link
text:
## 1. Kisan manifesto demands
Demand | Detail
Zamindari | Abolition; occupancy rights for all tenants
Revenue | 50% cut
Begar | Abolition
Labour | Living/minimum wages
Unions | Recognition of peasant unions
## 2. With the Congress
Faizpur (Dec 1936): Congress adopted an Agrarian Programme
1937 ministries: debt relief; UP occupancy status; Bihar Bakasht land partly restored; Maharashtra grazing fees abolished
Haripura (Feb 1938): Congressmen barred from Kisan Sabha membership
⚠ Bihar Congress ministry took a pro-landlord line
Sahajanand's papers: Hunkar (Hindi weekly, Patna), Lok Sangraha (Preview)

topic: Kisan Sabha and peasant struggles of the 1930s-40s
t: 1930s peasant revolts → no-tax, no-rent, Bakasht
text:
## 1. Early provincial bodies
Body | Year | Founder
Andhra Provincial Ryots Association | 1928 | N.G. Ranga
Bihar Provincial Kisan Sabha | 1929 | Sahajanand Saraswati
Zamindari abolition demand | 1935 | Kisan Sabha
## 2. Two kinds of campaign
Campaign | Against | Who stops paying
No-tax (UP 1930) | Government | Zamindars stop revenue
No-rent (UP winter 1931) | Landlords | Tenants stop rent
Bengal and Bihar: no-tax only, no no-rent
Bakasht = tenant land taken by landlords for unpaid rent; movement in Bihar led by Karyanand Sharma
⚠ Match: Bakasht-Karyanand Sharma, Eka-Madari Pasi, Mappila-Kunjahammad Haji, Awadh Kisan Sabha-Baba Ramchandra

topic: Kisan Sabha and peasant struggles of the 1930s-40s
t: Tebhaga movement 1946 → demand and outcome
text:
## 1. Background
Jotedars held big lands, gave them to sharecroppers (adhiars, bargadars) for half the crop
Depression, war inflation and the 1943 famine turned many cultivators into sharecroppers
## 2. The movement
Item | Fact
Call | Bengal Provincial Kisan Sabha, September 1946
Meaning | Tebhaga = "three shares"
Demand | Landlord's share cut from one-half to one-third; sharecropper keeps two-thirds
Backing | Floud Commission had recommended two-thirds to the sharecropper
Spread | 19 districts, ~6 million peasants, many Muslims
Leaders | Communists (Kisan Samitis)
End | Bargadari Bill (Muslim League govt), repression, communal riots
⚠ Demand was not land ownership, end of zamindari or debt write-off
PYQ 2013: Tebhaga demand = reduce landlord's share from one-half to one-third

topic: Kisan Sabha and peasant struggles of the 1930s-40s
t: Telangana and Punnapra-Vayalar → features
text:
Feature | Telangana (1946-51) | Punnapra-Vayalar (1946)
State | Hyderabad (Nizam) | Travancore
Against | Landlords, moneylenders, Nizam's officials, forced labour | Jenmis, the Diwan
Political issue | Nizam's bid to stay independent; Razakars | Diwan C.P. Ramaswamy Aiyar's "independent Travancore" plan
Leaders | Communists; Praja Mandal link | Communists; coir workers, toddy tappers, fishermen
End | Went on after police action (1948); withdrawn Oct 1951 | Vayalar camp stormed; ~800 killed
Most militant 1940s movements were in princely states
⚠ Telangana continued after Independence and was put down by the Indian government

topic: Kisan Sabha and peasant struggles of the 1930s-40s
t: Post-war peasant movements → leaders and region
text:
Movement | Year | Region | Leadership
Tebhaga | 1946 | Bengal | Communists, Bengal Kisan Sabha
Telangana | 1946-51 | Hyderabad | Communists
Punnapra-Vayalar | 1946 | Travancore | Communists
Warli | 1945-47 | Thana, Bombay | Maharashtra Kisan Sabha, Godavari Parulekar
Nationalism gave local peasant movements an all-India character; peasants gave Congress its mass base
Congress avoided anti-landlord class struggle for all-class unity (except UP)
## In news 2025-26
Dec 2025: Communist movement centenary (Kanpur 1925): Tebhaga (crop share) and Telangana (land redistribution) listed as its main mass movements
Mar 2025: Punjab unit of AIKS dates from 1943 (farm unions history)
⚠ CPI dates itself from Kanpur 1925; CPI(M) from Tashkent 1920

t: Causes → which section was hurt, and how
text:
## 1. Every section had a grievance
Revolt = accumulated grievances of a century of Company rule, not only sepoy anger
Section | Grievance
Rulers (nawabs, rajas) | Residents at court, armies disbanded, annexation (Doctrine of Lapse)
Taluqdars of Awadh | Estates confiscated by the Summary Settlement (1856)
Peasants | High revenue, rigid collection, loss of land to moneylenders
Artisans | One-way free trade; loss of royal patrons
Religious preachers | Loss of patronage of Indian rulers; spread hatred of foreign rule
Sepoys | Low pay, no promotion above subedar, loss of batta, religious fears
## 2. Religious and social fears
Sati abolished (1829), widow remarriage permitted, Western education (Bentinck)
1850 law: a convert to Christianity could inherit ancestral property
Missionaries attacked Hinduism and Islam in public
⚠ The foreign, racially arrogant character of rule is itself listed as a cause

t: Sepoy grievances and earlier mutinies → year and place
text:
## 1. Grievances of the sepoy
Paid far less than a British soldier; could not rise above subedar
No foreign service allowance (batta) when serving in Sindh or Punjab
Banned from caste marks, beards, turbans
General Service Enlistment Act, 1856 (Canning): new recruits must serve overseas if ordered; crossing the sea = loss of caste
Spectrum: the sepoy was a "peasant in uniform"
## 2. Earlier sepoy mutinies
Year | Place | Issue
1764 | Bengal | Sepoy mutiny
1806 | Vellore | Sepoy mutiny
1824 | Barrackpore (47th Regiment) | Refused to go to Burma by sea; regiment disbanded, men fired upon
1844 | Seven battalions | Salaries and batta
⚠ Spectrum dates the Barrackpore mutiny 1825; PMF gives 1824
Saiyid Ahmad Khan: "The Causes of the Indian Mutiny"

t: Annexations → which leader became an enemy
text:
## 1. Doctrine of Lapse and annexation (Dalhousie)
Ruler | What the British did | Result in 1857
Nana Saheb | Refused pension of adopted father Baji Rao II (last Peshwa) | Led Kanpur
Rani Lakshmibai | Adopted son not recognised; Jhansi annexed (Lapse) | Led Jhansi
Wajid Ali Shah (Awadh) | Awadh annexed 1856, Nawab exiled to Calcutta | Begum led Lucknow
Bahadur Shah Zafar | Name off coins; 1849 Dalhousie: family to leave Red Fort; 1856 Canning: he would be the last king | Symbolic head at Delhi
## 2. Awadh, the core of the revolt
Subsidiary Alliance on Awadh in 1801; annexed 1856 on charge of misrule
Awadh = "nursery of the Bengal Army": most Bengal sepoys came from Awadh and NWP
Summary Settlement: taluqdar share of Awadh villages fell from 67% to 38%
⚠ Doctrine of Lapse annexed Jhansi, Satara, Nagpur; Awadh was annexed for misrule, not by Lapse

t: Immediate cause → greased cartridges, rumours, prophecies
text:
## 1. The spark
Enfield rifle cartridge had to be bitten; grease said to be cow and pig fat
Rumour of bone dust of cows and pigs in atta
Both fed the fear of forced conversion to Christianity
⚠ PMF links the Enfield to Henry Hardinge; he was not Governor-General in 1857 (Canning was)
## 2. Prophecies and signs
Sign | Detail
Plassey prophecy | British rule to end on the centenary of Plassey, 23 June 1857
Ahmadullah Shah of Faizabad | Prophesied the end of British rule
Chapattis | Passed village to village at night; meaning still unknown
Red lotuses, sanyasis, fakirs | Cited as evidence of a planned conspiracy
## 3. British invincibility shaken by
First Afghan War (1838-42), Punjab Wars (1845-49), Crimean War (1854-56), Santhal rebellion (1855-56)
⚠ PMF practice MCQ: "end of Kali Yuga and return of Ram Rajya" was not a cause

t: Outbreak → date, place, unit
text:
## 1. Before Meerut
Date (1857) | Event
Feb, disbanded March | 19th NI at Berhampore refused the Enfield
29 March | Mangal Pandey (34th NI) attacked officers at Barrackpore
8 April | Mangal Pandey hanged
3 May | 7th Awadh Regiment defied officers
24 April | 90 men of 3rd Native Cavalry at Meerut refused cartridges
9 May | 85 dismissed, 10 years' jail
10 May | Meerut mutiny; comrades freed, officers killed
11 May | Sepoys reach Delhi; Bahadur Shah proclaimed Shahenshah-e-Hindustan
⚠ PMF (book) writes "Mangat Pande hanged on 29 March"; Spectrum, Testbook and PMF LENS give attack 29 March, hanging 8 April
Proclaiming the Mughal turned a mutiny into a revolutionary war
## In news 2025-26
July 2026: PM paid tribute to Mangal Pandey on his birth anniversary (19 July 1827); attacked Lt Baugh and Sgt-Major James Hewson (PMF LENS)

t: Governor-General during the revolt → Canning
text:
## 1. Lord Canning
Governor-General 1856-58, then first Viceroy (1858-62)
Passed General Service Enlistment Act, 1856; ruled Bahadur Shah would be the last Mughal king
Announced Queen's Proclamation at Allahabad, 1 Nov 1858; declared peace 8 July 1858
Said loyal princes acted as "breakwaters to the storm"
Universities of Calcutta, Bombay, Madras (1857) came in his time
GG | Link to 1857
Dalhousie (1848-56) | Doctrine of Lapse, annexed Jhansi and Awadh
Canning (1856-62) | GG during the revolt; last GG, first Viceroy
Hardinge (1844-48) | Not GG in 1857
Lytton (1876-80) | Much later (Vernacular Press Act)
⚠ Trap: Dalhousie caused the grievances, Canning faced the revolt
PYQ 2006: who was GG during the Revolt of 1857; options Canning, Dalhousie, Hardinge, Lytton; answer Canning

t: Spread month by month → where the revolt reached
text:
## 1. Timeline
Month | Spread
May 1857 | Meerut, Delhi; Ferozpur, Aligarh, Etawah, Bulandshahr, Nasirabad, Bareilly, Moradabad
June 1857 | Gwalior, Bharatpur, Allahabad, Jhansi, Faizabad, Sultanpur, Lucknow (4 June)
July 1857 | Indore, Mhow, Sagar, Jhelum, Sialkot
Sept 1857 | Delhi recaptured (20 Sept)
Dec 1857 | Campbell wins at Kanpur
March 1858 | Lucknow recaptured
April 1858 | Jhansi recaptured
May 1858 | Bareilly, Jagdishpur, Kalpi recaptured
Spread from Punjab to the Narmada, and from Bihar to Rajputana
Almost every Bengal cantonment rose; only the Madras army stayed loyal

t: Places affected and not affected → storm centres vs untouched
text:
## 1. Storm centres (PMF)
Delhi, Kanpur, Lucknow, Bareilly, Jhansi, Arrah (Bihar); Testbook adds Gwalior
Also: Meerut, Faizabad, Allahabad, Banaras, Kalpi, Jagdishpur, Danapur, Baghpat, Mandla
## 2. Not affected
Not affected | Note
Chittor | Not a centre (UPSC 2005 answer)
Agra | Not a centre (PMF practice MCQ); Sindhia took refuge there
Munger (Bihar) | Only part of Bihar unaffected (BPSC)
South, east, west India | "More or less unaffected" (Spectrum)
Punjab (mostly), Sindh, Rajputana states | Rulers loyal
Spectrum: at most one-fourth of the area and one-tenth of the population affected
PYQ 2005: which territory was not affected; options Jhansi, Chittor, Jagdishpur, Lucknow; trap: Jagdishpur (Kunwar Singh) sounds obscure but was a centre
## Beyond your notes
Chittor could mean Chittorgarh (Rajasthan) or Chittoor (Andhra Pradesh): neither was a centre

t: Centre → rebel leader → British officer
text:
## 1. Master table
Centre | Rebel leader | British officer
Delhi | Bahadur Shah II; real command Bakht Khan | John Nicholson, Hudson, Willoughby
Kanpur | Nana Saheb, Tantia Tope, Azimullah | Hugh Wheeler surrendered; Colin Campbell
Lucknow | Begum Hazrat Mahal (son Birjis Qadir) | Henry Lawrence (killed), Havelock, Outram, Inglis, Campbell
Jhansi | Rani Lakshmibai | Hugh Rose
Bareilly | Khan Bahadur Khan | Colin Campbell
Bihar (Jagdishpur, Arrah) | Kunwar Singh | William Taylor, Vincent Eyre
Faizabad | Maulvi Ahmadullah | -
Allahabad | Maulvi Liyaqat Ali | Colonel Neill
Banaras | - | Colonel James Neill
Baghpat | Shah Mal | Dunlap
Mandla (MP) | Rani Avantibai Lodhi | Waddington
⚠ Testbook pairs Lucknow only with Henry Lawrence; he defended and died, Campbell recaptured it

t: Kunwar Singh → Jagdishpur, Bihar
text:
## 1. Facts
Ruined zamindar of Jagdishpur, near Arrah (Shahabad district), Bihar; a Rajput
Nearly 80 years old; PMF calls him perhaps the most outstanding military leader and strategist
Took command of sepoys who revolted at Danapur (25 July 1857); occupied Arrah two days later
Vincent Eyre relieved Arrah (Aug 1857) and destroyed Jagdishpur
Fought also in Avadh and Central India; joined Nana Saheb's forces; took Azamgarh (March 1858)
Won near Jagdishpur (23 April 1858, over Le Grand); died of wounds in Jagdishpur
Brother Amar Singh continued the fight (Shahabad), joined rebels in Nepal Terai (1859)
Point | PMF | Preview
Death | 27 April 1858 | 26 April 1858
⚠ Kunwar Singh = Bihar, not UP or MP; Jagdishpur is in Bhojpur/Shahabad, Bihar
PYQ 2005: Kunwar Singh belonged to which place; answer Bihar; trap options MP, Rajasthan, UP

t: Tantia Tope → betrayed, captured, hanged
text:
## 1. Facts
Real name Ramachandra Pandurang Tope; born Yeola (Maharashtra), raised at Bithur
General of Nana Saheb; carried the chief burden of fighting at Kanpur
Defeated by Campbell at Kanpur (Dec 1857); defeated by Hugh Rose when relieving Jhansi
With Lakshmibai and Rao Sahib captured Gwalior (June 1858)
Guerrilla war in central India with tribal support; allied with Raja Bhabhut Singh (Gond)
Betrayed by friend Man Singh, captured asleep (forest of Paron), tried, hanged at Shivpuri
Point | PMF | Preview
Hanged | 15 April 1859 | 18 April 1859
## 2. How the other leaders ended
Leader | Fate
Nana Saheb | Escaped to Nepal (early 1859), never heard of
Begum Hazrat Mahal | Hid in Nepal after Lucknow fell
Bahadur Shah | Exiled to Rangoon, died 1862
Lakshmibai | Died fighting, June 1858
Kunwar Singh | Died of wounds at home
Bakht Khan | Killed in battle, 13 May 1859
⚠ Only Tantia Tope was betrayed by a friend and executed
PYQ 2006: betrayed by a friend, captured, put to death; options Nana Sahib, Kunwar Singh, Khan Bahadur Khan, Tantia Tope
## Beyond your notes
Man Singh was the Raja of Narwar

t: Delhi and Kanpur → who led, who advised
text:
## 1. Delhi
Bahadur Shah Zafar: nominal, symbolic head
Real command: Court of Soldiers under General Bakht Khan (led Bareilly troops to Delhi)
Court = 10 members: 6 army + 4 civilian
After Delhi fell (20 Sept 1857) Bakht Khan fought on at Lucknow
Princes shot by Lt Hudson; Nicholson led the siege and died of wounds
Emperor tried, sent with Zinat Mahal to Rangoon (Oct 1858), died Nov 1862
## 2. Kanpur
Person | Role
Nana Saheb | Proclaimed himself Peshwa; Bahadur Shah's governor
Tantia Tope | Commander-in-chief, fought from Bithur
Azimullah Khan | Political adviser, secretary; "Krantidoot"
Rao Sahib | Nana's brother (Spectrum); at Gwalior
Hugh Wheeler surrendered 27 June 1857; Campbell took Kanpur 6 Dec 1857
⚠ Azimullah's role was political, not military

t: Lucknow and Awadh → Begum, Maulvi, Chinhat
text:
## 1. Begum Hazrat Mahal
Wife of Wajid Ali Shah; proclaimed son Birjis Qadir Nawab
Revolt at Lucknow from 4 June 1857; offices shared by Hindus and Muslims
Residency besieged; Henry Lawrence (Chief Commissioner) killed; Inglis held on
Havelock and Outram failed; Campbell evacuated (Gorkhas), recaptured Lucknow March 1858
## 2. Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah
From Faizabad (native of Madras, Spectrum); preached jihad
Called "Danka Shah": rode a palanquin with drummers
Fought at Chinhat
Battle of Chinhat | Detail
Date | 30 June 1857
British | Henry Lawrence, defeated
Rebels | Led by Barkat Ahmad
⚠ Ahmadullah was not killed by Henry Lawrence's troops (PMF practice MCQ trap)
Taluqdars and peasants fought together; ~1,00,000 of 1,50,000 dead in Awadh were civilians

t: Jhansi, Gwalior and Central India → Rani and allies
text:
## 1. Rani Lakshmibai
Widow of Raja Gangadhar Rao; Jhansi annexed by Lapse (1854); born Kashi
Cry: "Main apni Jhansi nahin doongi"
Hugh Rose besieged Jhansi 23 March 1858; she fled to Gwalior
Took Gwalior with Tantia Tope and Afghan guards; Sindhia fled to Agra
Hugh Rose: "the only man among the rebels"; samadhi at Gwalior
Point | PMF | Preview
Death | 17 June 1858 | 18 June 1858
## 2. Rani Avantibai Lodhi (Ramgarh, now Dindori, MP)
Husband Vikramaditya Singh; British sent an administrator (Lapse)
Led 4,000 in the Mandla region; Battle of Kheri over Waddington
Chose death when surrounded, 20 March 1858
## In news 2025-26
Aug-Sep 2026: Avantibai remembered on martyrdom day (PMF LENS; LENS prints "1931" for 1831)

t: Local, Dalit and tribal leaders → place and deed
text:
## 1. Table
Leader | Place | Deed
Shah Mal | Baraut, Baghpat (Meerut) | Raised 84 villages; broke Yamuna bridge of boats; bungalow as "hall of justice"; killed July 1857
Khan Bahadur Khan | Bareilly (Rohilkhand) | Grandson of Hafiz Rahmat Khan; own government, army of 40,000
Liyaqat Ali | Allahabad | Took Khusro Bagh; crushed by Neill
Raja Bhabhut Singh | Narmadapuram, MP (Gond) | Satpura guerrilla, ally of Tantia Tope; "Shivaji of Narmadanchal"
Veer Narayan Singh | Sonakhan, Chhattisgarh (Binjhwar) | Hanged Raipur, 10 Dec 1857; Chhattisgarh's first martyr
Veera Pasi | Raebareli, UP (Pasi, Dalit) | Lieutenant of Rana Beni Madhav Baksh Singh; rescued him
## In news 2025-26
Pachmarhi WLS renamed after Raja Bhabhut Singh by MP government (PMF Magnum 2026)
May 2026: statue of Veera Pasi unveiled in Raebareli (PMF LENS)
⚠ PMF lists only Khan Bahadur for Bareilly; Bakht Khan led the Bareilly troops to Delhi

t: British commanders → where each fought
text:
## 1. Officers
Officer | Linked to
John Nicholson | Delhi siege, died of wounds
Hudson | Shot the Mughal princes
Hugh Wheeler | Surrendered Kanpur
Colin Campbell | C-in-C; Kanpur (Dec 1857), Lucknow (March 1858)
Henry Lawrence | Chief Commissioner of Awadh; killed at Lucknow
Havelock, Outram | Relief of Lucknow
Hugh Rose | Jhansi, Gwalior
James Neill | Banaras, Allahabad
Vincent Eyre | Relieved Arrah
John Lawrence | Punjab; "had a single leader of ability arisen ... we must have been lost"
⚠ Henry Lawrence = Lucknow; John Lawrence = Punjab

t: Hindu-Muslim unity → Aitchison's remark
text:
## 1. Evidence of unity
Hindu sepoys of Meerut marched to Delhi to make a Muslim emperor their leader
Cow slaughter banned wherever the revolt succeeded
Hindus and Muslims equally represented in leadership (Nana Saheb with Azimullah; Rani with Afghan guards)
Proclamation in Bahadur Shah's name: fight under the standards of Muhammad and Mahavir
## 2. Who said what
Speaker | Remark
Aitchison (British official) | "In this instance we could not play off the Mohammedans against the Hindus"
Maulana Azad | Unity of Hindus and Muslims, and loyalty to the Mughal Crown
James Outram | "A Mohammedan conspiracy making capital of Hindu grievances"
⚠ After 1858 the British repressed Muslims; after 1870 they courted them against nationalism
PYQ 2000: Aitchison's remark related to the Revolt of 1857, not Champaran, Khilafat-NCM or the August (Quit India) Movement

t: Azamgarh Proclamation → promises to each group
text:
## 1. Facts
Dated 25 August 1857, in the name of Bahadur Shah; mostly written by Firoz Shah (his grandson)
Urged Hindus and Muslims to unite behind the Badshahi government
Group | Promise
Zamindars | Lighter jumas (revenue)
Merchants | End of British trade monopoly
Public servants | Better pay, higher posts
Artisans | Jobs lost to European goods restored
Pundits, fakirs | Guardians of both religions in holy war
⚠ PMF practice MCQ keys "Hindu-Muslim divide" as its stress; read it as the divide the proclamation sought to overcome
Rebels attacked moneylenders' account books, courts, tehsils, thanas: a glimpse of an egalitarian vision

t: Why the revolt failed → who stayed away
text:
## 1. Groups that did not join
Group | Why
Princes (< 1% of chiefs joined) | Fear of British might
Awadh taluqdars | Left once estates were promised back
Moneylenders, big merchants | Targets of rebels; profits from British trade
Educated Indians | Saw rebels as backward-looking
## 2. Rulers who helped the British
Sindhia (Gwalior), Holkar (Indore), Nizam (Hyderabad), Nawab of Bhopal, Kashmir, Ranas of Nepal, Patiala and other Sikh chiefs
Gwalior's 20,000 troops still went to Tantia Tope and the Rani
## 3. Other causes
Weak Bahadur Shah (old, vacillating; Zinat Mahal and sons intrigued)
No common plan, central leadership, or forward-looking programme
Swords and pikes vs Enfield and the telegraph
Modern nationalism not yet born
⚠ Almost half the Indian soldiers fought for the British

t: Nature of the revolt → historian and view
text:
## 1. Views
Historian | View
V.D. Savarkar | "Indian War of Independence" (1909): planned national war
R.C. Majumdar | Neither first, nor national, nor war of independence
S.N. Sen | Began as a fight for religion, ended as war of independence
S.B. Chaudhuri | First combined attempt of many classes
Nehru | Mainly feudal uprising with nationalist elements
M.N. Roy | Last stand of feudalism against commercial capitalism
John Seeley, Lawrence | Mere sepoy mutiny
T.R. Holmes | Civilisation vs barbarism
L.E.R. Rees | War of fanatic religionists against Christians
Eric Stokes | Elitist in character
Stanley Wolpert | More than a mutiny, less than a war of independence
K. Datta | Mainly military outbreak used by princes, landlords
Marxists | Soldier-peasant democratic combine
## In news 2025-26
Feb 2025: Savarkar's book recalled: 1857 as planned, national, with Hindu-Muslim unity; banned by the British (PMF LENS)

t: Act of 1858 and Queen's Proclamation → what changed
text:
## 1. Government of India Act, 1858 (passed 2 Aug 1858)
Company rule ended; power to the Crown
Secretary of State for India (Cabinet member) + India Council of 15
Replaced Board of Control and Court of Directors
GG also titled Viceroy; Canning first Viceroy
## 2. Queen's Proclamation (Allahabad, 1 Nov 1858)
Promise | Detail
No annexation | Doctrine of Lapse ended; adoption allowed
Princes | Accept the Queen as Sovereign Paramount
Religion | No interference, no forced conversion
Services | Open on merit, regardless of race or creed
Customs | Old rights and practices respected in law
⚠ The Act is sometimes called the "Magna Carta of Indian Liberty" (Testbook)

t: Army and policy after 1857 → division and counterpoise
text:
## 1. Army
Fewer Indian, more European soldiers
Recruits from Gurkhas, Sikhs, Pathans ("martial races"), not Awadh, Bihar
Units by caste/community/region: "division and counterpoise"
Indian artillery abolished except a few mountain batteries
Army Amalgamation Scheme, 1861; White Mutiny of Company's European troops over lost batta
## 2. Policy
Area | Change
Landlords | Protected, rights secured
Social reform | Era of reform ended; customs respected
Muslims | Lands confiscated, treated with suspicion
Educated Indians | Praised in 1857, later called "babus"
Law | IPC 1860, CrPC 1861, High Courts Act 1861, Indian Councils Act 1861
⚠ Worst legacy: racial hatred; divide and rule began in earnest

t: Associations → founder, year and region (master table)
text:
## 1. Before 1858 (loyalist, landlord-led, petitioned Parliament on the Charter)
Association | Year | Region | Founder / leaders
Bangabhasha Prakasika Sabha | 1836 | Bengal | Associates of Rammohun Roy
Landholders' Society (Zamindari Association) | 1837 | Bengal | Radhakant Deb, Dwarkanath Tagore, Prasanna Kumar Tagore
Bengal British India Society | 1843 | Bengal | (Calcutta; broader public interest)
British Indian Association | 1851 | Bengal | Pres. Radhakant Deb, Secy. Debendranath Tagore
Madras Native Association | 1852 | Madras | Gazulu Lakshminarasu Chetty
Bombay Association | 1852 | Bombay | Jagannath Shankar Sheth
## 2. After 1858 (middle-class, educated)
Association | Year | Region | Founder / leaders
East India Association | 1866 | London | Dadabhai Naoroji
Poona Sarvajanik Sabha | 1870 | Bombay Pres. | M.G. Ranade, G.V. Joshi, S.H. Chiplunkar
India League | 1875 | Bengal | Sisir Kumar Ghosh, Sambhu Charan Mukherjee
Indian Association | 1876 | Bengal | Surendranath Banerjee, Ananda Mohan Bose
Madras Mahajana Sabha | 1884 | Madras | M. Veeraraghavachariar, G. Subramania Iyer, P. Anandacharlu
Bombay Presidency Association | 1885 | Bombay | Pherozeshah Mehta, K.T. Telang, Badruddin Tyabji
⚠ Chetty founded the Madras Native Association (1852), NOT the Madras Mahajana Sabha (1884)
PYQ 2017: three pairs; Radhakant Deb (BIA) and S.N. Banerjee (Indian Association) correct, Chetty-Mahajana Sabha wrong

t: British Indian Association and the pre-1858 bodies → features
text:
## 1. Landholders' Society / Zamindari Association (1837)
First political association of modern India; landlords of Bengal, Bihar, Orissa
Aim: landlord class interests; wanted Permanent Settlement extended all over India
## 2. Bengal British India Society (1843)
Loyalist, but aimed at general public interest (not only landlords)
## 3. British Indian Association (1851)
Formed by merging the Zamindari Association + Bengal British India Society
First President Raja Radhakant Deb; Secretary Debendranath Tagore
1859: refused to back indigo planters against Act X of 1859; supported the ryots
## 4. Common petitions before the Charter Act of 1853
Demand | Outcome
Indians in legislative bodies | Charter Act 1853 separated legislative and executive functions; 6 legislative members added
End Company's salt and indigo monopoly | Partly conceded
Bigger share in administration, better peasant conditions | Partly conceded

t: Rise of nationalism → factors and immediate triggers
text:
## 1. Factors (PMF list of 8)
Foreign domination; administrative and economic unification; Western education; socio-religious reform; press and literature; rediscovery of India's past; racial discrimination; Lytton's regime and Ilbert Bill
## 2. Lytton (1876-80): immediate irritants
Measure | Why resented
Vernacular Press Act, Arms Act (1878) | Discriminatory; Europeans exempt from arms licence fee
ICS age 21 to 19 (1878) | Kept Indians out
Delhi Durbar 1877 during famine | Rulers indifferent
Import duties on British textiles removed; 2nd Afghan War | Economic drain
## 3. Ilbert Bill (1883, Lord Ripon)
Let Indian magistrates and judges try Europeans in criminal cases
European agitation forced amendment; Indians learned to organise nationally

text:
Head | Demands
Constitutional | Expand/reform Legislative Councils; Indian majority; budget control; "No taxation without representation"; later self-govt within Empire (Gokhale 1905, Naoroji 1906)
Economic | Drain theory; abolish salt tax; cut land revenue and military expenditure; tariff protection for industry; swadeshi
Administrative | Indianisation of services; simultaneous ICS exam in England and India; separate judiciary from executive; primary and technical education; agricultural banks; irrigation; better treatment of Indian labour abroad; police reform; repeal discriminatory Arms Act
Civil rights | Freedom of speech, press, thought, association

t: Moderates vs Extremists → how they differed
text:
Basis | Moderates (1885-1905) | Extremists (1905-1920)
View of British rule | Believed in British justice and fair play; rule could be reformed | Did not trust British goodness; rule meant exploitation
Goal | Constitutional reforms, more Indians in services; later self-government within Empire | Swaraj (self-rule; for some, complete independence)
Method | Prayer, petition, protest within the law | Passive resistance, Swadeshi, boycott, national education
Inspiration | Western liberalism | Indian history, culture, religion
Masses | Little faith in masses | Faith in masses; demanded self-sacrifice from youth
Social base | Zamindars, upper middle class | Educated lower middle class
Leaders | Naoroji, Surendranath Banerjea, Gokhale, Pherozeshah Mehta | Tilak, Lajpat Rai, B.C. Pal, Aurobindo

topic: Rise of Extremism: causes, ideology and leaders
t: Extremist ideology → methods they advocated
text:
## 1. Core idea
Self-government (Swaraj) to be won by aggressive means, not petitions
Struggle against foreign rule a full-time activity
## 2. Programme (PMF list)
Plank | What it meant
Swadeshi + boycott of foreign goods | Boost indigenous industry
Non-cooperation with bureaucracy | Boycott government services, courts, councils, titles
National education | Schools in Indian languages, pride in heritage
Passive resistance | Non-payment of taxes; parallel indigenous institutions in villages, talukas, districts
Used symbols: Shivaji, Ganapati, Kali, "Mother India" as Shakti
Rejected violence and political murder, but sympathised with revolutionaries' motives
⚠ Extremists' "Dharma" meant universal moral law; they used religious symbols but claimed not to mix religion with politics
PYQ 1998: Extremist ideology = self-government by aggressive means in place of petitions and constitutional ways

topic: Rise of Extremism: causes, ideology and leaders
t: Causes of militant nationalism → the seven factors
text:
Factor | Example
Failure of Moderate politics | No major demand accepted
True nature of British rule realised | Councils Act 1892 a disappointment; Natu brothers deported 1897; Tilak jailed 1897; sedition law 1898
Education and unemployment | Low-paid, jobless educated youth
Self-respect and self-confidence | Tilak, Pal preached self-reliance
Militant school of thought | Rajnarain Bose, Ashwini Kumar Dutt, Vishnu Shastri Chiplunkar
International events | Ethiopia beat Italy (Adwa, 1896); Boer War (1899-1902); Japan beat Russia (1905)
Curzon's administration | Partition of Bengal and other measures
Japan's win "exploded the myth of European superiority"
Militancy had been growing slowly since 1857: it did not appear suddenly in 1905
⚠ The Boer War reverses, not a British victory, inspired Indians
Exam angle: "Extremism arose only because of the partition" is incomplete: partition was the immediate trigger

topic: Rise of Extremism: causes, ideology and leaders
t: Curzon's measures → why nationalists were angered
text:
Measure | Year | Effect
Calcutta Corporation (Municipal Amendment) Act | 1899 | Cut number of elected members
Indian Universities Act | 1904 | Fewer elected senate members; official control over affiliation and grants
Official Secrets (Amendment) Act | 1904 | Curbed press freedom
Ancient Monuments Act | 1904 | Protection of monuments (not a grievance)
Partition of Bengal | announced July 1905 | Seen as a bid to divide Bengalis
Curzon (Viceroy 1899-1905) believed in despotic imperialism
Successor Lord Minto II (1905-10): Swadeshi, Muslim League, Surat split, Morley-Minto reforms
Lord Hardinge II (1910-16): Delhi Durbar 1911, annulment, capital to Delhi
⚠ Universities Act 1904 followed the Raleigh Commission (1902): it is a Curzon measure, not Minto's
Exam angle: viceroy matching: partition = Curzon; annulment = Hardinge II; separate electorates = Minto II

text:

B.G. Tilak | Maharashtra | Kesari (Marathi), Mahratta (English), 1881; Gita Rahasya (Mandalay jail); "Swaraj is my birthright"
Lala Lajpat Rai | Punjab | Punjab Kesari; deported to Mandalay with Ajit Singh, May 1907
Bipin Chandra Pal | Bengal | New India (1901), Bande Mataram (1906); jailed 6 months for refusing to testify against Aurobindo
Aurobindo Ghose | Bengal | Editor Bande Mataram; first principal Bengal National College; New Lamps for Old
Lal-Bal-Pal = Lajpat Rai, Tilak (Bal), Pal; add Aurobindo for the four

Valentine Chirol called Tilak "Father of Indian Unrest"
⚠ Kesari is Marathi, Mahratta is English
## In news 2025-26

topic: Rise of Extremism: causes, ideology and leaders
t: Religion and nationalism → festivals and reinterpretations
text:
Who | What

Aurobindo | Reinterpreted Vedanta; national work = God's work, done as Karma Yoga

Aurobindo's New Lamps for Old (Indu Prakash) attacked Moderates' prayer-petition politics

t: Partition timeline → key dates
text:
Date | Event
December 1903 | Proposal to divide Bengal made public: protests begin under Moderates
19 July 1905 | Curzon's order dividing Bengal (Preview: 20 July)
7 August 1905 | Calcutta Town Hall meeting: Boycott resolution, formal launch of Swadeshi
16 October 1905 | Partition takes effect: day of mourning
Dec 1905 | Benaras Congress (Gokhale) condemns partition
Dec 1906 | Calcutta Congress (Naoroji): four resolutions
Dec 1907 | Surat split
12 December 1911 | Delhi Durbar: George V annuls partition, capital to Delhi
⚠ 7 August = launch of Swadeshi (Town Hall); 16 October = partition came into effect: UPSC swapped them in 2009
PYQ 2009: 16 October 1905 is known because partition took effect; not Town Hall proclamation, not Naoroji's Swaraj, not Tilak in Poona
PYQ 2010: immediate cause of Swadeshi = partition by Curzon (not Tilak's sentence, not Lajpat Rai's deportation, not Chapekar sentence)

t: Partition → official reason vs real motive
text:
## 1. The division
New province | Population
Eastern Bengal and Assam (capital Dacca) | 31 million (Muslim majority)
Rest of Bengal (Western Bengal, Bihar, Orissa) | 54 million: 18 million Bengalis, 36 million Biharis and Oriyas
## 2. Official reason
Bengal (about 80 million) too big to administer; partition would help develop Assam
## 3. Real motive (nationalist view)
Make Bengalis a minority in their own province
Divide Hindus and Muslims: Curzon at Dacca promised Muslims a unity "not enjoyed since the old Mussalman Viceroys"
Weaken Calcutta, the nerve centre of nationalism
Nationalists said efficiency needed separating Hindi-speaking Bihar and Oriya-speaking Orissa, not splitting Bengali speakers
⚠ Partition split Bengal on religious lines in effect, though justified on administrative grounds

t: 16 October 1905 → how Bengal observed it
text:
Practice | Meaning
Fasting, hartal in Calcutta, hearths unlit | National mourning
Bath in the Ganga, barefoot processions | Mass participation
Singing Bande Mataram | Became the movement's theme song
Tagore's Amar Sonar Bangla | Sung in streets; now Bangladesh's national anthem
Raksha Bandhan: Hindus and Muslims tied rakhis | Unity of Bengalis and both halves of Bengal
Federation Hall foundation (Surendranath Banerjea, Ananda Mohan Bose) | Indestructible unity of Bengal; crowd of 50,000+
Tagore called for the Raksha Bandhan observance and set up swadeshi stores (Spectrum)
Partition, meant to divide, united Bengalis
⚠ Testbook says Surendranath and Ananda Mohan Bose raised Rs 50,000; PMF says they addressed a crowd of over 50,000

t: Delhi Durbars → which one did what
text:
Durbar | Occasion | Key point
1877 | Queen Victoria as Empress of India (title 1876) | Viceroy Lytton; Imperial Assemblage, 1 Jan 1877
1903 | Succession of Edward VII | Attended by Duke of Connaught; Viceroy Curzon
1911 | Succession of George V | Only Durbar attended by the sovereign; Viceroy Hardinge II
## 1911 decisions
Capital shifted from Calcutta to Delhi
Partition of Bengal annulled
Jana Gana Mana first sung at the Calcutta Congress, 27 December 1911
⚠ The annulment was announced by the King-Emperor, not by an Act of Parliament or the Viceroy alone
PYQ 2014: partition lasted until George V abrogated it at the Delhi Durbar 1911: not WWI, not Civil Disobedience, not 1947

t: Annulment of 1911 → what changed and why
text:
## 1. New arrangement
Unit | After 1911
Bengal | Reunited (Bengali-speaking districts)
Bihar and Orissa | Separated from Bengal as a new province
Assam | A separate province again
Capital | Delhi (from Calcutta)
## 2. Why annulled
To curb the menace of revolutionary nationalism in Bengal
## 3. Reactions
Rude shock to the loyalist Muslim elite who backed partition
Capital moved to Delhi partly to appease Muslims (associated with Muslim glory); they were not pleased
Muslim estrangement grew: annulment 1911, Aligarh university refused (1912), British stance on Turkey in Balkan wars
⚠ Odisha became a separate province only in 1936 (Utkala Dibasa, 1 April); in 1911 it was joined with Bihar

t: Launch of Swadeshi → 7 August 1905, Calcutta Town Hall
text:
Massive anti-partition meeting in Calcutta Town Hall: Boycott resolution passed, formal proclamation of Swadeshi
Boycott idea first suggested by Krishna Kumar Mitra (Preview), editor of Sanjivani
Delegates spread the pledge across Bengal: boycott of Manchester cloth and Liverpool salt
Swadeshi and boycott adopted as methods of struggle for the first time
Date commemorated | Day
7 August | National Handloom Day (first observed 2015, Ministry of Textiles)
⚠ Swadeshi and boycott predate Gandhi: first used in 1905, not in Non-Cooperation (1920) or Home Rule (1916)
PYQ 2023: National Handloom Day (7 Aug) commemorates the Swadeshi Movement of 1905
PYQ 2016: Swadeshi and boycott first adopted in the agitation against partition of Bengal
## In news 2025-26
12th National Handloom Day, 7 Aug 2026: President gave 22 awards (3 Sant Kabir, 19 National Handloom Awards) under the NHDP; theme "Celebrating Weavers, Renewing Traditions, Expanding Horizons"

t: Two phases → Moderate-led vs Extremist-led
text:
Phase | Leaders | Methods
1903-1905 (Moderates) | Surendranath Banerjea, K.K. Mitra, Prithwishchandra Ray | Petitions, public meetings, memoranda, pamphlets, press (The Bengalee, Sanjivani)
After 1905 (Extremists) | Tilak, B.C. Pal, Aurobindo, Lajpat Rai | Passive resistance; boycott of schools, courts, services, councils; Swaraj
## Why leadership passed to Extremists
Moderate protests failed to stop partition
Repression: ban on shouting Bande Mataram in East Bengal streets; press curbs; police assault on the Barisal conference (April 1906)
Aim of Extremists: make administration impossible by organised refusal (Aurobindo)
Partition became secondary; India's freedom became the central question
⚠ The anti-partition movement was the work of the whole Bengal leadership: Moderates led its first stage

t: Forms of struggle → what the movement used
text:
Form | Example
Boycott of foreign goods | Cloth burnt, shops picketed; washermen, priests refused foreign goods: most successful form
Public meetings, processions | Main tools of mass mobilisation
Samitis (volunteer corps) | Swadesh Bandhab Samiti (Barisal, Ashwini Kumar Dutt); Swadeshi Sangam (Tirunelveli, V.O. Chidambaram Pillai, Subramania Siva)
Festivals and melas | Tilak's Ganapati, Shivaji festivals; jatras
Atmashakti (self-reliance) | Swadeshi enterprises, social reform
National education | National Council of Education
Samitis did famine relief, physical training, crafts, national schools, arbitration courts, magic-lantern lectures
Social campaigns against caste oppression, early marriage, dowry, alcohol
⚠ Women refused foreign bangles; priests refused offerings with foreign sugar
Exam angle: the movement anticipated Gandhian methods: passive resistance, non-cooperation, constructive work

t: Participation, repression and decline → limits of the movement
text:
## 1. Who joined
Group | Role
Students | Picketing; fined, expelled, beaten
Women | Urban middle-class women joined processions: first time
Muslims | Many stayed away; Nawab of Dacca (Rs 14 lakh loan) backed partition
Peasants, workers | Largely untouched (Barisal the exception)
## 2. Repression

## 3. Why it declined by mid-1908

t: Calcutta 1906 → the four resolutions
text:
Resolution | Note
Swaraj | Self-government like the UK or the colonies (Australia, Canada)
Swadeshi | Indigenous goods
Boycott of foreign goods | Moderates wanted it limited to goods and Bengal
National Education | Parallel schools and colleges
Passed under Extremist pressure (they had a majority of support)

Extremists called for boycott of schools, councils, municipalities, courts

topic: Congress 1905-1907: Calcutta resolutions and Surat split
t: Surat split 1907 → causes
text:
## 1. What each side wanted
Issue | Extremists | Moderates
Venue | Nagpur (Central Provinces) | Surat (Bombay Presidency)
President | Tilak or Lajpat Rai | Rash Behari Ghosh
Calcutta resolutions | Retain all four | Drop them
Rule: a leader from the host province could not preside: Surat (Tilak's home province) kept Tilak out
Session on 26 December 1907: chairs broken, shoes and sticks; Moderates captured the party machinery
## 2. Deeper cause
Extremists' lack of faith in the Moderates' capacity to negotiate with the British
Swadeshi movement's scope (Bengal only vs all India; goods only vs all associations)
⚠ PYQ 2016 wrong options: Minto's communalism, Muslim League's founding, Aurobindo's failure to become president
PYQ 2015: movement that led to the Moderate-Extremist split = Swadeshi (not Quit India, NCM, CDM)

topic: Congress 1905-1907: Calcutta resolutions and Surat split
t: After Surat → carrot and stick
text:
## 1. Government's three-pronged policy
Step | Action
1 | Mildly repress Extremists to frighten Moderates
2 | Conciliate Moderates with concessions if they disown Extremists
3 | Crush Extremists fully, then ignore Moderates
Concession: Indian Councils Act 1909; repression: jailing leaders, Newspapers Act 1908
## 2. Results
Moderates lost public support; politically aware Indians sided (passively) with Tilak
National movement weakened till reunion at Lucknow 1916
Split helped neither side: British divide and rule
⚠ PYQ 1998 (A-R): "partition ended the Moderates' role" is false; "Surat 1907 separated Extremists from Moderates" is true: answer (d)
Exam angle: Moderates failed to see the state negotiated with them out of fear of Extremists; Extremists failed to see Moderates as their outer defence

topic: Muslim League and the Morley-Minto Reforms
t: Muslim League → founding and early politics
text:
Fact | Detail
Simla Deputation | October 1906, Muslim leaders met Viceroy Minto: representation by numbers and "political importance"
Founded | 1906, Dacca
Leaders | Aga Khan (first president), Nawab Salimullah of Dacca, Nawab Mohsin-ul-Mulk
Character | Loyalist, communal, conservative; did not criticise colonialism
Stand | Supported partition; sought safeguards in services
London Muslim League | Syed Ameer Ali, 1908
Jinnah joined | 1913 (while still in Congress)

Al-Hilal (Abul Kalam Azad): no conflict between Islam and nationalism
## Beyond your notes
League founded on 30 December 1906 at the All India Muhammadan Educational Conference, Dacca
⚠ Punjab Hindu Sabha 1909; All India Hindu Mahasabha 1915 (Madan Mohan Malaviya)
## In news 2025-26
AIML completed 118 years (Prelims Magnum 2025)

topic: Muslim League and the Morley-Minto Reforms
t: Morley-Minto Reforms 1909 → provisions
text:
Provision | Detail
Separate electorates | Muslims elected by Muslim voters only: first time
Weightage | More seats than population share
Indirect elections | Introduced for the first time
Central council | Additional members raised to 60 (from 16); official majority kept
Provincial councils | 30-50 additional members; non-official majority
Functions | Supplementary questions; vote on part of budget; move resolutions
Executive council | One Indian: Satyendra Prasanna Sinha (Law member, 1909)
Morley (Secretary of State, Liberal) and Minto (Viceroy)
Minto = "Father of communal electorate"
Two Indians in the India Council (1907): K.G. Gupta, Syed Hussain Bilgrami
⚠ Councils stayed advisory; Morley said reforms were not meant to lead to self-government
Exam angle: first resolution under the new rules: Gokhale, 25 Feb 1910, against indentured labour for Natal

topic: Muslim League and the Morley-Minto Reforms
t: Morley-Minto → aims and effects
text:
## 1. Aims (nationalist reading)
Rally the Moderates, isolate the Extremists
Divide nationalist ranks; check Hindu-Muslim unity
## 2. Central council (1909)
Category | Number
Ex-officio | 9
Nominated officials | 28
Nominated non-officials | 5
Elected (indirectly) | 27
Of the 27: provincial councils 13, landholders 6, Muslims 5 (+1 Muslim landholders alternately), chambers of commerce 2
## 3. Effects
Separate electorates bred communalism and separatism
Moderates cooperated and lost respect
Jinnah unhappy with separate electorates at the 1909 Lahore Congress
⚠ Official majority was abolished in provincial councils (on Gokhale's and R.C. Dutt's advice), not at the centre

topic: Reunion, Lucknow Pact and Home Rule (1914-1918)
t: Reunion of Congress → steps 1914-1916
text:
Year | Step
1914 | Annie Besant urges Moderates to readmit Extremists; Tilak released (June 1914); re-entry fails in Dec 1914
1915 | Pherozeshah Mehta dies: Bombay Moderates' opposition weakens; Bombay session (S.P. Sinha) changes constitution to admit Extremists
1916 | Lucknow session (A.C. Mazumdar): Moderates and Extremists reunite

topic: Reunion, Lucknow Pact and Home Rule (1914-1918)
t: Lucknow Pact 1916 → terms and significance
text:
Point | Detail
Signed | December 1916, joint sessions at Lucknow
Architects | Tilak and Jinnah; Annie Besant helped
Demand | Further reforms as a step to self-government
Executive councils | Half the members to be Indians
Legislatures | More Indians, elected members
Separate electorates | Accepted by Congress

topic: Reunion, Lucknow Pact and Home Rule (1914-1918)
t: Home Rule movement → repression, Montagu declaration, decline
text:
## 1. Repression backfired
June 1917: Besant, Arundale, Wadia interned: nationwide protest
S. Subramania Aiyar renounced knighthood; Jinnah, Surendranath, Malaviya joined
Tilak urged passive resistance; Gandhi suggested a march of 1,000 volunteers
## 2. Montagu Declaration (20 August 1917)
Goal: "gradual development of self-governing institutions" leading to responsible government
Home Rule no longer seditious; Besant released Sept 1917, Congress president Dec 1917
## 3. Decline (1918)
Moderates satisfied by promised reforms; Besant vacillated; Tilak went to England (libel case against Valentine Chirol)
## 4. End
1920: Gandhi became president of All India Home Rule League, renamed it Swarajya Sabha
PYQ 2018: body renamed Swarajya Sabha in 1920 = All India Home Rule League
⚠ Montagu's 1917 statement was a clear advance on Morley's 1909 denial of self-government

Role | Person
Persuaded Gandhi (Lucknow Congress, Dec 1916) | Raj Kumar Shukla, a peasant
Accompanied Gandhi | Rajendra Prasad, Mazhar-ul-Huq, J.B. Kripalani, Narhari Parikh, Mahadev Desai
## 3. Outcome
Gandhi defied the order to leave (civil disobedience); govt set up Champaran Agrarian Committee with Gandhi a member
Tinkathia abolished; 25% refund of illegal dues; planters soon left
⚠ Rajendra Prasad did NOT invite Gandhi: he joined as a colleague
PYQ 2018: significance = joining peasant unrest to the national movement (not all-India participation, not Dalit/tribal involvement)
## In news 2025-26
April 2026: Champaran Satyagraha anniversary marked: first satyagraha, ended tinkathia (Praveen Sir CA 360)

Follower | Fact

t: Ahmedabad mill strike 1918 → issue, leaders, result
text:
## 1. Facts (PMF)
1917 plague: owners paid plague bonus (up to 75% of wages), then withdrew it; workers wanted 50% hike, owners offered 20%
Gandhi asked workers to demand 35% and stay non-violent
15 March 1918: Gandhi's fast unto death (his first); owners relented on day 4; tribunal awarded 35%
Person | Role
Anasuya (Anusuya) Sarabhai | Gandhi's chief lieutenant; sister of mill-owner Ambalal
Ambalal Sarabhai | President, Ahmedabad Mill Owners Association
25 Feb 1920: Anasuya founded Ahmedabad Textile Labour Association (Majoor Mahajan Sangh)
⚠ Morarji Desai had no role (he was entering provincial civil service in 1918)

t: Kheda 1918 → why the satyagraha, who led it
text:
## 1. Cause
Revenue Code: full remission if crop below 25% of normal; 1918 crop was below one-fourth
Govt did not suspend revenue collection, seized property of non-payers
Local leaders Mohanlal Pandya, Shankarlal Parikh began no-revenue campaign (Nov 1917); approached Gandhi via Gujarat Sabha (Gandhi its president 1918-19)
## 2. Course
Point | Fact
Gandhi's stand | Suspension is a legal right, not grace
Nadiad meeting | 22 March 1918, about 5,000 peasants
Assisted by | Vallabhbhai Patel, Indulal Yajnik
End | Revenue to be recovered only from those able to pay
⚠ There was no proposal of Permanent Settlement in Gujarat (it was Bengal, Bihar, Odisha)
PYQ 2011: only statement 1 (revenue not suspended despite drought) correct

Statement | Verdict

At Chelmsford's War Conference he opposed recruiting Indians | False: he supported recruitment

## 1. Facts (PMF)
Point | Fact
