topic: Montford, Rowlatt Act and Rowlatt Satyagraha (1918-19)
t: Rowlatt Act 1919 → origin and provisions
text:
## 1. Origin
Sedition Committee under Justice Sydney Rowlatt probed "revolutionary crime"
Two bills in Imperial Legislative Council, 6 Feb 1919; one dropped, other passed March 1919 (LENS: 10 March 1919)
Official name: Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act, 1919; replaced wartime Defence of India Act (1915) with a permanent law
## 2. Provisions
Provision | Meaning
Detention without trial | Up to 2 years
Special court | 3 High Court judges, no appeal
Evidence | Inadmissible under Evidence Act allowed
Arrest without warrant | Search and arrest
Habeas corpus | Could be suspended
Called "Black Act" (Gandhi); "lawless law" (Jinnah)
⚠ Aim was imprisonment without trial and summary trials, not press curbs, war funds or suppressing Khilafat
PYQ 2012, 2009: why indignation = imprisonment without trial; PYQ 1996: ARC Act = Rowlatt Act
## In news 2025-26
2026: LENS on preventive detention: today's laws "echo Regulation III of 1818 and the Rowlatt Act"

topic: Montford, Rowlatt Act and Rowlatt Satyagraha (1918-19)
t: Rowlatt Act in the Council → who opposed, who resigned
text:
## 1. Council vote
Every Indian member of the Imperial Legislative Council opposed it; official majority passed it
Resigned in protest | Note
M.A. Jinnah | "Lawless law"
Madan Mohan Malaviya | Spoke 2.5 hours on the bill
Mazhar-ul-Haq | Also a Champaran colleague
⚠ Mohammad Ali and Azad did not resign in 1916: they were interned in the war years
PYQ 2003: A false (1916 resignation), R true (all Indian members opposed): answer "A false, R true"

topic: Montford, Rowlatt Act and Rowlatt Satyagraha (1918-19)
t: Rowlatt Satyagraha → features and significance
text:
## 1. Features
Satyagraha Sabha, Bombay, 24 Feb 1919: pledge to disobey and court arrest
Members: young radicals of the Home Rule Leagues, pan-Islamists (Abdul Bari)
Methods: hartal (called for 6 April 1919), fasting, prayer, sale of banned books (Hind Swaraj)
Gandhi article "Satyagrahi" (7 April 1919); withdrew 18 April 1919 after violence; "Himalayan blunder"
## 2. Significance
Point | Fact
Scale | First all-India struggle (first mass strike)
Gandhi | Emerged as all-India leader
Limits | Congress hardly involved; urban more than rural
Opposed by Liberals (Wacha, Surendranath, Sapru, Sastri) and Annie Besant
⚠ Simon Commission protests were 1928, not with Rowlatt Satyagraha
PYQ 2015: Sedition Committee (true), Home Rule League used (true), Simon coincided (false)
PYQ 1999: first all-India venture = Rowlatt Satyagraha (Champaran, Kheda, Ahmedabad were local)

topic: Montford, Rowlatt Act and Rowlatt Satyagraha (1918-19)
t: Montford reforms → Congress reaction and the Liberal exit
text:
## 1. Timeline
Date | Event
20 Aug 1917 | Montagu Declaration: gradual self-governing institutions, "responsible government"
July 1918 | Montagu-Chelmsford (Montford) Report
Aug 1918 | Special Bombay Congress (Hasan Imam): reforms "disappointing and unsatisfactory"
1919 | Moderates form Indian National Liberal Federation
1920 | Congress boycotted first elections
INLF founders: Surendranath Banerjee, Tej Bahadur Sapru, V.S. Srinivasa Sastri, M.R. Jayakar
⚠ Not the Swaraj Party (1923) or "Independence Federation"; Liberals played a minor role afterwards
⚠ Govt's "carrot and stick": Montford = carrot, Rowlatt = stick
PYQ 2003: moderates who left over Montford formed the Indian Liberal Federation

t: Jallianwala Bagh, 13 April 1919 → sequence of events
text:
## 1. Build-up
Date | Event
6 Apr | Rowlatt hartal
9-10 Apr | Arrest of Dr Saifuddin Kitchlew and Dr Satyapal; firing at DC's house; mob violence
13 Apr | Baisakhi gathering at the Bagh
## 2. The massacre
Brig-Gen Reginald Dyer banned assembly of more than three; blocked the only exit; fired without warning
1,650 rounds, 10-15 minutes, until ammunition ran out
Lt Governor Michael O'Dwyer backed Dyer; Viceroy Chelmsford; martial law in Punjab
## 3. Death toll
Source | Killed
Official (PMF book, Spectrum, Praveen Sir) | 379
Congress Punjab Inquiry (PMF) | about 1,200 (3,600 wounded)
⚠ PMF LENS gives "291 per British reports" and over 500 per the Malaviya committee; Spectrum gives Congress estimate about 1,000
PYQ 2007: the Act behind the indignation = Rowlatt Act (not Arms, Public Safety, Vernacular Press)

t: Jallianwala reactions → who protested and how
text:
## 1. Protests
Person | Reaction
Rabindranath Tagore | Renounced knighthood (31 May 1919); "great moral outrage"
C. Sankaran Nair | Resigned from Viceroy's Executive Council
Montagu (Secretary of State) | Called it "preventive murder"
Churchill | "Monstrous"
Gandhi | Cooperation with a "satanic regime" impossible
Dyer hailed by House of Lords, Rudyard Kipling; Morning Post fund raised £28,000
Golden Temple's Arur Singh gave Dyer a siropa: triggered Gurdwara reform

PYQ 2004: returned knighthood over 1919 Punjab atrocities = Tagore; PYQ 1998: "preventive murder" = Jallianwala

t: Hunter Commission and Congress inquiry → members and findings

## 1. Hunter Commission
Disorders Inquiry Committee, set up 14 Oct 1919; 8 members, 3 Indian
Indian member | Background
Chimanlal Setalvad | VC, Bombay University
Jagat Narayan | Lawyer
Sultan Ahmed Khan | Lawyer

Congress non-official inquiry (drafted by Gandhi; C.R. Das, Abbas Tyabji, M.R. Jayakar; Praveen Sir lists Motilal Nehru)
Amritsar Congress 1919 (Motilal Nehru): demanded Chelmsford's recall, action on O'Dwyer and Dyer, boycott of Hunter Commission

## Beyond your notes
Chaired by Lord William Hunter, Scottish judge

topic: Khilafat and the road to Non-Cooperation (1919-20)
t: Khilafat issue → demands, leaders, significance
text:
## 1. Issue
Indian Muslims saw the Ottoman Sultan as Khalifa; Britain dismembered Turkey (Treaty of Sevres, May 1920)
Demands: Khalifa keeps control of Muslim holy places and enough territory to defend the faith
## 2. Leaders
Body | Leaders / fact
Khilafat Committee, Bombay 1919 | Ali brothers (Shaukat, Muhammad), Azad, Hakim Ajmal Khan, Hasrat Mohani
All-India Khilafat Conference | Delhi, Nov 1919; advocated non-cooperation; Gandhi its president
31 Aug 1920: Khilafat Committee launched non-cooperation; Gandhi first to join
## 3. Significance
Brought urban Muslims into the national movement; anti-imperialism common to both
⚠ Kemal Pasha abolished the Caliphate in 1924: no protest in India, showing wider anti-imperialist motive
PYQ 1998: A true, R true, R explains A

topic: Khilafat and the road to Non-Cooperation (1919-20)
t: Khilafat → end and assessment (1922-24)
text:
## 1. End of the issue (PMF)
Date | Event in Turkey
Nov 1922 | Mustafa Kemal Pasha stripped the Sultan of political power
1924 | Caliphate abolished; Islam removed from the Constitution
Kemal also secularised education, gave women rights, adopted European legal codes
## 2. Assessment
Criticism | Defence
Mixed religion with politics; strengthened communal forces later | Expressed wider anti-imperialist feeling of Muslims
 | No protest in India when the Caliphate was abolished (1924)
## 3. Contribution of Khilafat-NCM (PMF list)
Hindu-Muslim unity; urban Muslims brought in
Students, women, peasants participated in large numbers
Politicised artisans, urban poor, traders; nationalism reached every corner
Attack on untouchability, caste barriers
⚠ In many places two-thirds of those arrested were Muslims (Spectrum): never seen before or after
PYQ 1998: Khilafat brought urban Muslims in (A); anti-imperialism common to both (R): both true, R explains A

1920 | Gandhi became President, renamed it Swarajya Sabha

⚠ Do not confuse with Swaraj Party (C.R. Das, Motilal Nehru, 1923)

topic: Khilafat and the road to Non-Cooperation (1919-20)

text:
## 1. Creed and plan
President C. Vijayaraghavachariar; NCM resolution moved by C.R. Das
Creed changed: from self-government by constitutional means to Swaraj by peaceful and legitimate means
Staged: boycotts first; civil disobedience and non-payment of taxes next, if Swaraj not in a year and repression came
Gandhi: Swaraj within a year
## 2. Organisation
Change | Detail

AICC | 350 members
PCCs | On linguistic basis
Membership | 4 annas, age 21 (18 in 1921)

Defence at Allahabad HC | Madan Mohan Malaviya, aided by Krishna Kant

Gorakhpur sessions court | 170 sentenced to death

topic: NCM programme, spread and Chauri Chaura (1920-22)
t: Government response 1921 → talks, repression, Prince of Wales
text:
## 1. Sequence (Spectrum, PMF)
Date | Event
May 1921 | Gandhi-Reading talks broke down: Viceroy wanted Gandhi to make the Ali brothers drop violent passages
May / July 1921 | Khilafat Committee: no Muslim to serve in the army
Sept 1921 | Ali brothers arrested; Gandhi had the resolution repeated at hundreds of meetings
Nov 1921 | Prince of Wales visit met with hartal, strikes, demonstrations
Dec 1921 | Volunteer corps banned, meetings banned, press gagged; all leaders except Gandhi jailed
Congress let provincial committees start civil disobedience, including no-tax, if people were ready
Congress volunteer corps acted as a parallel police
⚠ Gandhi refused to split from the Khilafat leaders: he saw a wedge strategy
⚠ PMF dates the army resolution May 1921; Spectrum says the Ali brothers' call was July 1921
## Beyond your notes
Prince of Wales landed at Bombay, 17 Nov 1921; riots in Bombay made Gandhi fast

topic: NCM programme, spread and Chauri Chaura (1920-22)
t: Why NCM was withdrawn → causes and the debate
text:
## 1. Causes (PMF)
Cause | Detail
Non-violence not learnt | Chauri Chaura showed workers not ready
Violence invites repression | British could crush a violent movement
Fatigue | High intensity cannot last
Drift to no-rent | Turning against zamindars; local movements out of control
No talks | Govt not ready to negotiate
## 2. Bardoli resolution (12 Feb 1922)
Stopped all law-breaking; constructive work: khadi, national schools, temperance, Hindu-Muslim unity, removal of untouchability
Gandhi began a 5-day fast as penance (12 Feb)
## 3. Gains of NCM (PMF)
Self-confidence and self-esteem; textile industry gained from boycott
Congress could no longer be called a "microscopic minority" (Dufferin, 1888)
⚠ Withdrawal by the CWC at Bardoli, not by a full Congress session
PYQ 1998: Gandhi withdrew NCM (Feb 1922) because of the violence at Chauri Chaura

topic: NCM programme, spread and Chauri Chaura (1920-22)
t: After the withdrawal → reactions, arrest, legacy
text:
## 1. Reactions and arrest
Leader | Reaction
Subhas Bose | "National calamity"
Jawaharlal Nehru | "Amazement and consternation"
C.R. Das, Motilal Nehru | Resented it
Gandhi arrested 10 March 1922: 6 years; "non-cooperation with evil is as much a duty as cooperation with good"
Gaya 1922 (C.R. Das): Das and Motilal resigned; Congress-Khilafat Swaraj Party formed
## 2. Legacy
Hindu-Muslim unity; nationalism reached peasants, workers, women
Viceroy Dufferin's "microscopic minority" jibe (1888) could no longer be made
## In news 2025-26
Aug 2025: centenary of Vithalbhai Patel as first Indian President of Central Legislative Assembly (1925); he opposed the 1922 suspension and co-founded the Swaraj Party
July 2026 (LENS): K. Kamaraj joined the freedom struggle after Jallianwala and took part in NCM

t: Simon Commission → why boycotted
text:
## 1. Appointment
Act of 1919 provided a review Commission after 10 years; appointed early, on 8 November 1927, by Lord Birkenhead (Secretary of State); chairman Sir John Simon
Official name: Indian Statutory Commission; 7 members from Conservative, Liberal and Labour parties
Why early: Conservatives feared a Labour win in 1929; communal tension high in 1927
## 2. Why boycotted
No Indian member (an "all-white" commission); seen as an insult to self-respect
Madras Congress 1927 (President M.A. Ansari): boycott "at every stage and in every form"
Landed at Bombay 3 February 1928: all-India hartal, black flags, slogan "Simon Go Back" (coined by Yusuf Meherally)
⚠ Answer is always "no Indian member", NOT "it recommended abolition of dyarchy" or "it suggested partition"
PYQ 2013 and 1998: asked why Indians boycotted it; both times the key was the absence of any Indian member

t: Simon Commission → who supported, who opposed
text:
Opposed (boycotted) | Did NOT oppose
Congress | Muslim League faction of Muhammad Shafi
League faction of Jinnah | Justice Party (Madras)
Hindu Mahasabha, Liberal Federation | Unionists (Punjab), Central Sikh Sangh
Revolutionaries (Bhagat Singh) | Ambedkar's Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha, All India Achut Federation
## Repression
Lucknow: Nehru and G.B. Pant beaten
Lahore: Lala Lajpat Rai lathi-charged, died; HSRA (Bhagat Singh) killed Saunders in revenge
Commission visited twice (Feb-Mar 1928; Oct 1928-Apr 1929); youth leagues under Nehru and Bose
## In news 2025-26
G.B. Pant birth anniversary (Sept 2026, PMF Prelims Magnum): organised the Simon protest in Lucknow (1928) and the UP salt campaign (1930); Premier of UP 1937-39

t: Simon Commission Report → what it recommended
text:
Published May 1930; rejected by almost all Indian parties; later basis of the GoI Act 1935
Recommendation | Detail
Provinces | Abolish dyarchy; responsible government in the provinces
Electorates | Retain separate electorates
Depressed classes | Reserved seats (not separate electorate)
Structure | Ultimate character to be federal
Territory | Separate Burma from India, Sindh from Bombay
Centre | No responsible government at the Centre (later)
⚠ It did NOT recommend responsible government at the Centre, inter-provincial council or abolition of central bicameralism
PYQ 2010: correct option = replacement of dyarchy with responsible government in the provinces

t: Nehru Report → what it recommended
text:
## 1. Background
Birkenhead's challenge (1925): frame a constitution all Indians agree on
All Parties Conference, Bombay, May 1928 set up committee: chairman Motilal Nehru; Jawaharlal Nehru secretary; members incl. Tej Bahadur Sapru, Subhas Bose, Ali Imam, M.R. Jayakar, N.M. Joshi
Report placed at Lucknow, August 1928
## 2. Recommendations
Asked | Nehru Report said
Goal | Dominion Status as next step (not complete independence)
Electorate | Joint electorates, adult suffrage; no separate electorates
Minorities | Reserved seats for Muslims where minority (not Punjab, Bengal); minorities for 10 years
Rights | 19 fundamental rights, equal rights for women, unions, secular state
Structure | Federal with residuary powers at Centre; bicameral; linguistic provinces
⚠ Statement "complete independence" is wrong; correct answer 2011 = 2 and 3 only

t: Nehru Report → who rejected it, and the Independence for India League
text:
## 1. Rejection
Muslim League and Hindu Mahasabha did not accept; All Party Convention, Calcutta, Dec 1928, failed to pass it
Jinnah's 3 amendments rejected (1/3 seats at Centre; reservation in Punjab-Bengal by population; residuary powers to provinces) → Fourteen Points, March 1929
## 2. Independence for India League (1928)
Feature | Detail
Founders | Jawaharlal Nehru, Subhas Bose, S. Srinivasa Iyengar
President | Srinivasa Iyengar; Nehru and Bose secretaries
Opposed | Nehru Report's Dominion Status
Aim | Complete independence; republic on socialist lines
A pressure group within Congress
⚠ It opposed the Nehru Report, NOT the Gandhi-Irwin Pact or Montford Reforms
PYQ 1995: the radical wing founded the League "in opposition to" the Nehru Report

t: Jinnah's Fourteen Points (March 1929) → key demands
text:
Area | Demand
Electorate | Separate electorates to continue
Structure | Federal constitution, residuary powers with provinces
Provinces | Provincial autonomy; Sindh separated from Bombay; reforms in NWFP, Baluchistan
Centre | One-third Muslim seats in central legislature; one-third Muslim ministers
Majorities | No redistribution to reduce Muslim majority in Punjab, Bengal, NWFP
Veto | No bill if three-fourths of a community's members oppose it
Safeguards | Religion, culture, education, language, personal law; services quota
Background: Delhi Proposals (1927) offered joint electorates for 1/3 central seats etc.; Jinnah's amendments rejected at Calcutta (Dec 1928) → he rejoined the Shafi faction
⚠ Nehru Report wanted residuary powers at the Centre; Jinnah wanted them with provinces

t: Calcutta 1928 and the road to Lahore → dates and outcomes
text:
Event | Date | Outcome
Delhi Proposals | 20 Mar 1927 | Muslim leaders accept joint electorates with conditions
Madras session (Ansari) | Dec 1927 | Boycott Simon; first independence resolution (J. Nehru)
Calcutta session (Motilal Nehru) | Dec 1928 | Approved Nehru Report; one-year ultimatum for Dominion Status by 31 Dec 1929; All India Youth Congress formed
Irwin's Deepavali Declaration | 31 Oct 1929 | Dominion Status as goal, no timeline; promised an RTC
Delhi Manifesto | 2 Nov 1929 | RTC to plan implementation of Dominion Status; Congress majority; amnesty
Irwin rejected the Delhi Manifesto (Dec 1929) → Lahore
⚠ Two years for Dominion Status was Gandhi's proposal; younger leaders cut it to one year

t: Lahore 1929 → president and resolutions
text:
## 1. Session
44th session, Lahore, 29 Dec 1929 - 1 Jan 1930; President Jawaharlal Nehru (backed by Gandhi; only 3 of 18 PCCs supported him); succeeded father Motilal (1928)
## 2. Decisions
Decision | Detail
Goal | Poorna Swaraj (complete independence)
Nehru Report | Declared lapsed
RTC | Boycott
Civil disobedience | Working Committee authorised to launch it, incl. non-payment of taxes
Legislators | Asked to resign
Independence Day | 26 January 1930, to be observed annually
Midnight 31 Dec 1929: Nehru hoisted the tricolour on the Ravi
⚠ Lahore did NOT reunite moderates and extremists (that was Lucknow 1916) and passed nothing on the two-nation theory
PYQ 2014, 2012, 2006, 2005: Lahore = Purna Swaraj (not "self-government"), presided by Jawaharlal (not Motilal), and authorised the CWC to start civil disobedience

t: Purna Swaraj Day → pledge and flag
text:
26 January 1930: flag hoisting; independence pledge drafted by Nehru: "inalienable right... to have freedom"; right to alter or abolish an oppressive government
Gandhi's instruction: spend the day on constructive work (spinning, service of untouchables, Hindu-Muslim unity, prohibition)
Swaraj flag: saffron-white-green, ratio 2:3, charkha in centre
Srinivasa Iyengar and Bose walked out; formed Congress Democratic Party (1930)
No Congress session in 1930; Nehru continued as president
⚠ The Lahore "Purna Swaraj resolution" (1929) is different from the Muslim League's Lahore Resolution (1940)
## In news 2025-26
77th Republic Day (26 Jan 2026): 26 January chosen in 1950 to honour Purna Swaraj Day 1930 (PMF Prelims Magnum Feb 2026); theme "150 Years of Vande Mataram" (other CA)

Year | Venue | President | Remember

t: Gandhi's Eleven Demands → what they asked
text:
Viceroy's speech 25 Jan 1930 ruled out early Dominion Status → Gandhi's letter to Irwin, 31 Jan 1930; deadline 11 March
Area | Demand
Currency | Rupee-sterling ratio to 1s 4d
Land | Halve land revenue, legislative control
Salt | Abolish salt tax and govt monopoly
Expenditure | Halve top salaries and military spending
Prisoners | Release all political prisoners
Trade | Customs duty on foreign cloth; coastal shipping for Indians
Others | Prohibition; reform CID; Postal Reservation Bill; arms licences for self-defence
Nehru saw them as a step back from Purna Swaraj
CWC at Sabarmati (Feb 1930) entrusted Gandhi to launch the movement

t: Dandi March → route, dates, numbers
text:
Item | Fact
Start | 12 March 1930, Sabarmati Ashram (Ahmedabad)
Marchers | 78 followers
Distance | 240 miles (~390 km), 24 days
Reached Dandi | 5 April 1930 (Navsari district, near Surat)
Salt law broken | Morning of 6 April 1930
Gandhi arrested | 5 May 1930
Why salt: used by rich and poor; tax sometimes 14 times the salt's value; govt monopoly under Salt law 1882
Joined at Dandi: Sarojini Naidu, Mithuben Petit, Abbas Tyabji
⚠ Started from Sabarmati, NOT Sevagram, Wardha or Dandi
⚠ PMF PYQ book says "nearly 200 miles"; PMF main text gives 240 miles
PYQ 2009 and 1995: Dandi began the Civil Disobedience Movement (not NCM or Quit India) and it started from Sabarmati

t: "Sedition has become my religion" → when Gandhi said it
text:
## 1. The quote
Said when publicly violating the Salt Law at Dandi (1930), at the launch of the CDM
Full line: British rule caused "moral, material, cultural and spiritual ruination"; "I regard this rule as a curse... Sedition has become my religion. Ours is a non-violent battle"
## 2. Do not confuse
Quote | Occasion
"Sedition has become my religion" | Dandi, 1930
British rule a "curse" | Also in letter to Irwin, 2 March 1930
"I want world sympathy in this battle of Right against Might" | Dandi, to journalists
⚠ NOT Champaran, NOT Second RTC, NOT Quit India
PYQ 2025: asked the occasion of this quote; trap options were Champaran and Second RTC
## Beyond your notes
"Do or Die" = Quit India, August 1942 (not CDM)

t: Vedaranyam march → details

Rajaji began the satyagraha on 13 April 1930 (PMF CA)
Marching song "Kathiyindri, rathamindri, yudham ondru varugudhu" by Namakkal V. Ramalingam Pillai

t: Khudai Khidmatgars and Peshawar → aims and events
text:
Item | Fact
Founder | Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan (Badshah Khan, Frontier Gandhi)
Name | "Servants of God", Red Shirts
Who | Pathans of NWFP
Aim | Pathan regional unity + non-violent struggle against colonialism
Arrest | 23 April 1930 → Peshawar in crowds' hands for over a week
Garhwal Rifles: soldiers under Chandra Singh Garhwali refused to fire on unarmed crowds → nationalism entering the army
Sholapur: textile strike, parallel government for a few days
⚠ They did NOT seek union with Afghanistan, terrorist methods or communist revolution
PYQ 2002: Red Shirts called for Pathan regional nationalist unity and a struggle against colonialism

t: CDM → spread, social groups, end
text:
## 1. After Gandhi's arrest the CWC sanctioned
No land revenue in ryotwari areas; no-chaukidari tax in zamindari areas; forest laws broken in Central Provinces
UP: no-revenue, no-rent campaign became a no-rent struggle
## 2. Participation
Group | Compared with NCM
Women | Higher; first large-scale participation (Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay persuaded Gandhi)
Muslims | Lower (except NWFP)
Peasants | Massive
Arrests | 90,000+, about 3 times NCM
Method | Break laws (NCM: refuse cooperation)
## 3. End
Resumed 4 Jan 1932; suspended May 1933, withdrawn April 1934

topic: Gandhi-Irwin Pact, Karachi 1931 and the Round Table Conferences
t: Truce attempts in 1930 → who tried what
text:
Date | Attempt | Outcome
July 1930 | Irwin offers RTC; Tej Bahadur Sapru and M.R. Jayakar allowed to explore peace | Failed
August 1930 | Motilal and Jawaharlal taken to Yeravada to meet Gandhi | Failed
25 Jan 1931 | Gandhi and CWC released unconditionally | Talks open
14 Feb - 5 Mar 1931 | Gandhi-Irwin talks | Delhi Pact
Congress demands at Yeravada: right of secession from Britain; national government controlling defence and finance; independent tribunal on Britain's financial claims
First RTC without Congress was like "Ramlila without Rama"
⚠ Sapru and Jayakar were Liberals acting as mediators, not Congress negotiators

topic: Gandhi-Irwin Pact, Karachi 1931 and the Round Table Conferences
t: Gandhi-Irwin Pact → what each side gave
text:
Talks from 14 Feb 1931; signed 5 March 1931 (Delhi Pact)
Government agreed | Congress agreed
Release prisoners not convicted of violence | Suspend the CDM
Remit penalties not yet collected | Attend the Second RTC
Return confiscated land not yet sold | 
Salt for consumption in coastal villages | 
Peaceful picketing of liquor and foreign cloth | 
Leniency to employees who resigned | 
NOT conceded | 
Public inquiry into police excesses | 
Commutation of Bhagat Singh's death sentence | 
⚠ UPSC's 2020 question on its terms was dropped; know: invitation to RTC and release of non-violent prisoners were in it, police-excess inquiry was not
Left-wing youth opposed it; Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev, Rajguru hanged 23 March 1931

topic: Gandhi-Irwin Pact, Karachi 1931 and the Round Table Conferences
t: Karachi session 1931 → president and resolutions
text:
March 1931, President Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel; six days after the executions; Gandhi met black flags en route
Item | Fact
Pact | Endorsed the Gandhi-Irwin Pact
RTC | Gandhi authorised as Congress's representative
Goal | Reiterated Purna Swaraj
Key resolution | Fundamental Rights and National Economic Programme
Drafted by | Jawaharlal Nehru, revised by Gandhi
First time Congress defined what Swaraj means for the masses: "political freedom must include real economic freedom of the starving millions"
⚠ Karachi did NOT oppose the pact; other 2003 options were true: Bose formed the Forward Bloc, Bhagat Singh co-founded the HSRA
PYQ 2010 and 2005: drafter = Nehru (not Patel, Prasad or Ambedkar); Patel only presided

topic: Gandhi-Irwin Pact, Karachi 1931 and the Round Table Conferences
t: Karachi Resolution → rights and economic programme
text:
Head | Promised
Civil rights | Free speech, press, assembly
Equality | Before law, irrespective of caste, creed, gender
Religion | State neutrality
Education | Free and compulsory primary
Franchise | Universal adult franchise
Peasants | Reduce rent and revenue; exempt uneconomic holdings; curb moneylending
Workers | Living wage, limited hours, women's protection, unions
Industry | State ownership or control of key industries, mines, transport
Reflected the growth of socialist ideas (cited by PMF as a left-wing gain)
Showed Congress commitment to civil, political and economic rights of the people together

topic: Gandhi-Irwin Pact, Karachi 1931 and the Round Table Conferences
t: Round Table Conferences → dates, viceroy, who attended
text:
RTC | Dates | Viceroy | Congress
First | Nov 1930 - Jan 1931 | Irwin | Boycotted (CDM on)
Second | 7 Sep - 1 Dec 1931 | Willingdon | Gandhi sole representative
Third | 17 Nov - 24 Dec 1932 | Willingdon | Absent (Labour Party too)
British PM throughout: Ramsay MacDonald (Labour, then National Govt from Aug 1931)
First RTC: 74 Indian delegates (58 British India + 16 states); recommended All-India Federation and responsible govt at Centre with safeguards
Attended all three: Ambedkar, Jayakar, Aga Khan, Sapru, N.M. Joshi; Jinnah not invited to the Third
⚠ Technically one conference in three sessions, not three conferences
PYQ 1996: "incorrect to call them First, Second and Third RTC" because it was one conference in three sessions

topic: Gandhi-Irwin Pact, Karachi 1931 and the Round Table Conferences
t: Why the CDM was suspended in 1931 → reasons
text:
Gandhi's satyagraha gives the opponent a chance to change heart; a mass movement must be short (people's capacity to sacrifice is limited)
Late-1930 problem | Detail
Militancy | Peasant and tribal violence rising
Traders | Urban traders losing enthusiasm, selling foreign goods
Rich peasants | Property seizures cooled their ardour
Leadership | Almost all leaders in jail
Gain: Gandhi negotiated with the Viceroy on equal terms, raising Congress's prestige
Lord Willingdon (Viceroy from April 1931) saw the truce as a mistake; arrested Nehru and Ghaffar Khan (Dec 1931)
⚠ PMF calls the suspension a practical step, not a retreat

topic: Gandhi-Irwin Pact, Karachi 1931 and the Round Table Conferences
t: Second RTC → why it failed
text:
Gandhi claimed Congress spoke for all India; challenged by Muslim League, Princes and Ambedkar (for the lowest castes)
Deadlock on separate electorates (demanded by Muslims, depressed classes, Christians, Anglo-Indians); Gandhi opposed one for depressed classes
New faces: Iqbal, Malaviya, Sarojini Naidu (women), G.D. Birla, S.K. Datta
MacDonald announced NWFP and Sindh as Muslim-majority provinces and warned of a unilateral Communal Award
Gandhi back 28 Dec 1931; CDM resumed 4 Jan 1932; Congress banned

topic: Gandhi-Irwin Pact, Karachi 1931 and the Round Table Conferences
t: RTCs to the Act of 1935 → steps
text:
Step | Date
White Paper on RTC recommendations | March 1933
Joint Parliamentary Committee report | 22 Nov 1934
Bill passed | 2 Aug 1935
Act provided an All-India Federation of provinces and princely states (never formed: states did not join)
Provincial autonomy, dyarchy at Centre, Federal Court (1937)
⚠ Both 2009 statements correct: Third RTC discussions led to the 1935 Act; Act provided the All-India Federation
⚠ Under the 1935 Act defence and foreign affairs were outside the federal legislature's control (PYQ 2024 trap)

topic: Gandhi-Irwin Pact, Karachi 1931 and the Round Table Conferences
t: Government of India Act 1935 → main provisions
text:
Level | Provision
Federation | All-India Federation of provinces and princely states (states optional, via Instrument of Accession); never formed
Federation condition | States filling 52 of 104 Council of State seats and half the states' population
Centre | Dyarchy at Centre (reserved: defence, foreign affairs, tribal areas)
Legislature | Federal Assembly 375, Council of State 260; states nominated 33% / 40%
Provinces | Dyarchy abolished; provincial autonomy in 11 provinces
Lists | Federal 59, Provincial 54, Concurrent 36; residuary powers with Governor-General
Others | Federal Court (1937), RBI, Burma and Sindh separated, Orissa formed
Franchise only about 14%; separate electorates extended to women, depressed classes, labour; Council of India abolished
⚠ Residuary powers went to the Governor-General, not the federal or provincial legislature (PYQ 2018)

topic: Communal Award, Poona Pact and the Harijan campaign
t: Communal Award → what it gave
text:
Announced 16 August 1932 by PM Ramsay MacDonald after the Second RTC deadlock
Provision | Detail
Depressed classes | Declared a minority → separate electorate
Double vote | Vote in general seats + extra vote in 71 special seats, for 20 years
Separate electorates | Muslims, Sikhs, Christians, Anglo-Indians, Europeans, Marathas (Bombay, 7 seats)
Women | 3% seats within communities (except NWFP)
Seats | Provincial seats doubled
Background: 1909 Muslims; 1919 Sikhs, Christians, Anglo-Indians, Europeans; Lothian Franchise Committee (1932) recommended no electorate
⚠ Award covered provincial legislatures only

topic: Communal Award, Poona Pact and the Harijan campaign
t: Gandhi's 1932 fast → why and where
text:
Date (1932) | Event
18 Aug | Gandhi writes to MacDonald: will fast unto death
20 Sep | Fast begins in Yerwada Jail, Poona
24 Sep | Poona Pact signed
26 Sep | Fast ends in presence of Tagore
Gandhi: separate electorate would permanently split depressed classes from Hindu society
Ambedkar: "political stunt"; needed political power against organised oppression
Rajaji exchanged pens with Ambedkar
⚠ The fast was against the Communal Award, NOT the RTC failure or Congress-League differences
PYQ 2012: reason for the 1932 fast unto death = MacDonald's Communal Award

topic: Communal Award, Poona Pact and the Harijan campaign
t: Poona Pact → terms
text:
Term | Communal Award | Poona Pact
Electorate | Separate for depressed classes | Joint
Provincial seats | 71 | 148 reserved
Central legislature | none | 18% of general seats
Duration | 20 years | Decided later by mutual agreement
Signed by Hindu and depressed class leaders; Ambedkar agreed as it gave more seats than the Award
Gandhi had backed adequate representation but at first opposed reserved seats under either electorate (PMF)
To Ambedkar, Depressed Classes' rights came before political independence; Gandhi fought for independence and Hindu unity together
Gandhi accepted reserved seats within a joint electorate; Ambedkar gave up the separate electorate
⚠ No provision for local bodies or civil services (PYQ 2005 trap)
PYQ 1997: Poona Pact = joint electorate with reserved seats for depressed classes

topic: Communal Award, Poona Pact and the Harijan campaign
t: After the Poona Pact → Harijan campaign
text:
Gandhi made Harijan upliftment part of his political and social programme
Step | Date
Harijan Sevak Sangh (All-India Anti-Untouchability League) | 30 Sep 1932
Harijan weekly | 11 Feb 1933
Country-wide Harijan tour (12,500 miles, 9 months) | From 7 Nov 1933
Gandhi leaves Congress (village industries, Harijan work) | 30 Oct 1934
"Harijan" = children of God
⚠ It followed the Poona Pact, NOT the Gandhi-Irwin Pact, Quit India or the 1935 Act

topic: Communist movement: Comintern, M.N. Roy, Tashkent to Kanpur
t: CPI's two births → Tashkent 1920 vs Kanpur 1925
text:
Point | Tashkent CPI | Kanpur (Cawnpore) conference
Date | 17 October 1920 | 26 December 1925
Place | Tashkent (Soviet Turkistan), outside India | Kanpur, UP: first all-India communist meet on Indian soil
Leader | M.N. Roy | organised by Satyabhakta; presided by Singaravelu Chettiar
Others | Abani Mukherji, M.P.T. Acharya, Mohammad Ali, Mohammad Shafiq, Evelyn Roy-Trent, Rosa Fitingov | Muzaffar Ahmad, Nalini Gupta; joint secretaries S.V. Ghate, J.P. Bagerhatta
Backing | under the Comintern | coincided with the INC annual session
Weakness | no mass base, members arrested on return | went on to work inside the Congress
Kanpur line: members to join the Congress and build a strong left wing inside it
⚠ CPI counts Kanpur 1925 as its founding; CPI(M) traces itself to Tashkent 1920
⚠ The 2005 options also offered P.C. Joshi (who led the CPI only from 1935) and M.C. Chagla (a jurist, not a communist)
PYQ 2005: who headed the Indians at Tashkent who set up the CPI in Oct 1920 → M.N. Roy

topic: Communist movement: Comintern, M.N. Roy, Tashkent to Kanpur
t: M.N. Roy → life and contribution
text:
Stage | Fact
Real name | Narendranath Bhattacharya; took "Manabendra Nath Roy" in the USA
WWI | tried to get German arms for a revolt (Zimmermann Plan)
Mexico | met Comintern agent Michael Borodin; helped found the Communist Party of Mexico
1920 Moscow | Second Congress of Comintern; first Indian in Comintern leadership
Oct 1920 | founded CPI at Tashkent and a military school for frontier tribes and Muhajirs
1922 | edited Vanguard (of Indian Independence), the émigré CPI organ
1940 | founded the Radical Democratic Party
## Roy-Lenin debate (1920)
Lenin | Roy
communists in colonies should back bourgeois nationalist movements | bourgeois nationalists are reactionary; communists should fight independently through workers' and peasants' parties
Compromise: back the "revolutionary national bourgeoisie" but keep an independent workers-peasants struggle
⚠ Roy was not a CSP leader (2015-type pairing trap "CSP: M.N. Roy" = wrong match)
PYQ 1995: émigré communist journal of M.N. Roy → Vanguard (traps: The Worker, Kisan Sabha, Anushilan)
## Beyond your notes
Roy also wrote India in Transition (1922); he was later expelled from the Comintern (1929) and his followers were called Royists

topic: Congress Socialist Party and the left within the Congress
t: CSP programme → what it did and did not stand for
text:
## 1. Four founding ideas
Freedom first: nationalism is a stage on the way to socialism
Work inside the INC, the main national organisation
Give the Congress a socialist direction
Organise workers and peasants
## 2. Programme vs non-programme
Advocated | Did not advocate
abolition of zamindari, land to the tiller | dictatorship of the proletariat
state ownership of land, nationalisation of industries and banks | separate electorates for minorities or depressed classes
redistribution of land; minimum wages | tax evasion, boycott as its programme
democratic, parliamentary path; decentralised socialism | allegiance to the Comintern
JP's book: Why Socialism? (1936)

topic: Early labour: Lokhande, Factories Acts, nationalists
t: First efforts for workers → who did what
text:
Person | Year | Work
Sasipada Banerjee (Brahmo) | 1870 | Workingmen's Club, Bengal; journal Bharat Sramjeebi
S.S. Bengalee | 1878 | failed Bill in Bombay Council to limit working hours

topic: Early labour: Lokhande, Factories Acts, nationalists
t: Factories Acts → provisions year by year
text:
Act | Main provisions
1881 | child labour: no child below 7; ages 7-12 max 9 hours; 4 holidays a month; fencing of dangerous machinery
1891 | women 11 hours; no child below 9; ages 9-14 max 7 hours; weekly holiday for all
1911 | adult males: max 12 hours a day
1922 | hours cut to 11
1948 | 48 hours a week; safety, ventilation, sanitation
Limits of 1881 and 1891: covered only women and children, not plantations, weak enforcement
Pushers: Lancashire cotton interests, Bengalee and Lokhande
⚠ 1881 Act did not fix wages and did not allow trade unions (unions became legal only in 1926)
PYQ 2017: "Factories Act 1881 aimed to fix wages and allow trade unions" → incorrect

topic: Early labour: Lokhande, Factories Acts, nationalists
t: Early nationalists and labour → why aloof, when involved
text:
## 1. Why aloof (1880s-1900)
Reason | Detail
Fear of division | Dadabhai Naoroji (2nd INC session): Congress should take up only all-nation questions
Fear for Indian industry | saw British textile lobby behind hours regulation, so opposed factory laws
Backed workers only against British-owned firms or the government, not Indian mill-owners
## 2. Swadeshi phase (1905-08)
Strikes and hartals on 16 Oct 1905 (Bengal partition day)
Bengal: Aswini Coomar Banerjee, Prabhat Kumar Roy Chowdhuri; Punjab: Lajpat Rai, Ajit Singh; Tamil Nadu: V.O. Chidambaram Pillai, Subramaniya Siva (foreign-owned cotton mills, Tuticorin)
G. Subramania Iyer (1903) urged workers to form their own organisations
⚠ Labour moved from purely economic to political issues in the Swadeshi period, but no lasting unions formed

t: Ahmedabad mill strike 1918 → events
text:
Step | Fact
Cause | mill-owners withdrew the plague bonus (up to 75% of wages) after the 1917 plague
Demand | workers sought 50%; owners offered 20%
Gandhi | studied mill finances, asked for 35%; insisted on non-violence
Mill-owners' leader | Ambalal Sarabhai (Ahmedabad Mill Owners' Association)
Workers' side | his sister Anasuya Sarabhai
Turning point | Gandhi's first fast, 15 March 1918; settled 18 March by arbitration
Result | award of 35% raise
4 Dec 1917 wage win under Anasuya is kept as "Majoor Din" in Ahmedabad
Mahadev Desai's book on it: A Righteous Struggle
⚠ This was Gandhi's first hunger strike in India; same year as Kheda (1918)

Phase | Labour's role

t: Trade Disputes Act 1929 → what it did
text:
Passed 11 April 1929 (Lord Irwin) to curb communist-led strikes
Provision | Fact
Disputes | tribunals (courts of inquiry, boards of conciliation)
Strikes | practically banned strikes that "coerced" the government or caused hardship to the public
Twin measure: Public Safety Bill (deport "undesirable foreigners", detain without trial up to 2 years); rejected by the Assembly, issued as an Ordinance, 13 Apr 1929
8 April 1929: Bhagat Singh and B.K. Dutt bombed the Central Assembly against both bills, just as Vithalbhai Patel was to rule on the Public Safety Bill
⚠ TDA 1929 gave no worker participation in management, no arbitrary powers to management, no British-court intervention
PYQ 2017: Trade Disputes Act 1929 provided for → a system of tribunals and a ban on strikes

t: Colonial labour laws → year and purpose
text:
Law | Year | Purpose
Workmen's Breach of Contract Act | 1860 | punished workers leaving jobs (plantations)
Factories Acts | 1881, 1891, 1911, 1922 | hours, child and women labour
Trade Unions Act | 1926 | registration and regulation of unions; rights and immunities
Trade Disputes Act | 1929 | tribunals, curbs on strikes
Payment of Wages Act | 1936 | timely, full wages; permitted deductions
Bombay Industrial Disputes Act | 1938 | Congress ministry; curbed strikes and lockouts
## Beyond your notes
Workmen's Compensation Act 1923 gave compensation for injury at work
The Trade Unions Act 1926 first gave registered unions legal status and immunity from civil and criminal liability for bona fide union work
⚠ Unions became legal only with the 1926 Act, long after Lokhande (1890) and Wadia (1918)

t: Royal Commission on Labour 1929 → members and remit
text:
Point | Fact
Appointed | 1929
Chairman | J.H. Whitley
Indian members | N.M. Joshi, Diwan Chaman Lal
Remit | conditions in factories and plantations: health, efficiency, living standards, employer-worker relations
Report | 1931, progressive but not implemented at once
Its boycott was a split issue at the 1929 Nagpur AITUC session
⚠ Whitley Commission = labour; do not confuse with the Simon Commission (constitutional, 1927) or the Royal Commission on Agriculture (Linlithgow, 1926)

t: Congress ministries and labour 1937-39 → promises and practice
text:
## 1. 1937 Labour Committee programme (adopted by AICC)
Holidays with pay, sickness leave with pay, employment insurance, minimum wages, recognition of peaceful unions
## 2. Practice
Bombay alone passed labour law: the Industrial Disputes Act (1938), aimed at preventing strikes and lockouts
Opposed by the Congress left; workers struck, ~20 killed in police firing
Ministries often treated union struggles as law and order: Section 144, arrests of union and kisan leaders
⚠ Unions doubled in 1936-39 thanks to the freer climate, even as ministries curbed strikes

t: Post-1947 labour laws and the four Labour Codes → what changed
text:
## 1. Early independent India
Law | Year | Purpose
Industrial Disputes Act | 1947 | conciliation, arbitration; notice before strike or lockout
Factories Act | 1948 | 48-hour week, safety
Minimum Wages Act | 1948 | state fixes minimum wages
ESI Act | 1948 | medical, sickness, maternity, injury benefits
## 2. Four Labour Codes (29 laws merged)
Code | Year | Key change
Code on Wages | 2019 | one definition of wages; National Floor Wage; minimum wage for all workers; no gender pay gap
Industrial Relations Code | 2020 | merges ID Act 1947, Trade Unions Act 1926, Standing Orders Act 1946; layoff approval threshold 100 → 300; fixed-term employment; wider strike notice
Code on Social Security | 2020 | merges 9 laws; first legal definition of gig and platform workers
OSH and Working Conditions Code | 2020 | safety, health, working conditions
Labour is in the Concurrent List
## In news 2025-26
Centre began implementing the four Labour Codes from 21 Nov 2025; unions object to hire-and-fire, retrenchment and strike limits
Nine-judge SC bench (CJI Surya Kant, 6:3, 2026) refined the "industry" definition of Bangalore Water Supply v. A. Rajappa (1978), seven judges led by V.R. Krishna Iyer, "triple test": systematic activity, employer-employee cooperation, goods or services for human wants; new ruling is prospective and tied to the IR Code 2020

topic: War outbreak and the resignation of ministries (1939)
t: Congress ministries resign → why and when
text:
## 1. Sequence of 1939
Date | Event
1 Sep 1939 | Germany invades Poland; Britain declares war on 3 Sep
Sep 1939 | Viceroy Linlithgow joins India to the war without consulting Congress or the elected central legislature
10-14 Sep | CWC at Wardha debates its stand
13 Oct | Gandhi meets Linlithgow; talks fail
17 Oct | Viceroy's statement: a consultative committee now; 1935 Act to be modified after the war
23 Oct | CWC rejects the statement, refuses war support, asks ministers to resign
Oct-Nov 1939 | Ministries in the seven Congress provinces resign after 28 months of rule
## 2. The reason
India was made a party to the war without consultation; Congress would not fight for democracy abroad while it was denied at home
⚠ Not because Congress failed to form ministries in the other 4 provinces, not a left-wing split, not communal riots
⚠ Testbook's timeline says the ministers resigned "in 1942": wrong; PMF and all PYQs give Oct-Nov 1939
PYQ 2012: reason = "none of the above" (Viceroy made India a belligerent unilaterally); PYQ 2008: A and R both true, R explains A

topic: War outbreak and the resignation of ministries (1939)
t: CWC at Wardha (Sep 1939) → each leader's stand
text:
## 1. Three views
Leader(s) | Stand on the war
Subhas Bose, socialists Narendra Dev, JP | War is imperialist on both sides: seize the chance, resist war mobilisation, launch a mass struggle
Nehru | Justice lay with Britain, France, Poland but they were imperialists: no participation till freedom, yet no struggle exploiting Britain's difficulty
Gandhi | Critical of Hitler; unconditional support to Britain, not to exploit its trouble; later backed Nehru
CWC adopted Nehru's line: India cannot join a war for democratic freedom while that freedom is denied to India
## 2. Congress's two conditions for full cooperation
Responsible government at the Centre immediately
A Constituent Assembly to frame free India's constitution after the war
⚠ Gandhi's own first position was unconditional support; the CWC resolution was Nehru's conditional line

topic: War outbreak and the resignation of ministries (1939)
t: Day of Deliverance and the war-time line-up → who stood where
text:
## 1. Reactions to the resignations
Party | Reaction
Muslim League | Jinnah (on 2 Dec) declared 22 Dec 1939 "Day of Deliverance" and thanksgiving
Nationalists | Backed the Congress decision
CPI | Backed Bose's radical line in 1939; after Germany attacked the USSR (22 Jun 1941), the "People's War" line
Princes, landlords | Supported the war effort
## 2. Viceroy and his era
Linlithgow (1936-43): the longest-serving Viceroy; his term saw the 1937 ministries, Tripuri, resignations, August Offer, Individual Satyagraha, Lahore Resolution, Cripps, Quit India
Wavell (Oct 1943-1947): C.R. Formula, Gandhi-Jinnah talks, Desai-Liaquat pact, Simla Conference
⚠ Testbook dates the Day of Deliverance to "September 1939": PMF's PYQ explanation gives 22 December 1939
## In news 2025-26
Dec 2025 (CPI centenary coverage): CPI stayed active in the freedom movement except 1942-45, when it put the global anti-fascist struggle above Quit India

topic: Tripuri crisis, Forward Bloc and Bose's war strategy (1939-40)
t: Tripuri crisis (1939) → sequence of events
text:
## 1. From election to resignation
Step | Fact
Jan 1939 election | First contested election; Bose beat Pattabhi Sitaramayya, Gandhi's candidate, 1580-1377
Gandhi | "Pattabhi's defeat is more mine than his"
CWC | Bose called the right wing compromisers on federation; CWC members resigned in protest (Nehru did not join them)
Tripuri, 8-12 Mar 1939 | Jabalpur district (MP); Bose ill, Azad conducted sittings; Gandhi fasting at Rajkot
Pant resolution | G.B. Pant: Bose to appoint the CWC as Gandhi wishes; passed by an overwhelming majority
Apr 1939 | Bose resigned; Rajendra Prasad became president
May 1939 | Forward Bloc formed (3 May)
Tripuri also ended non-interference in the princely states' struggles
⚠ Bose presided over Haripura 1938 (Gujarat) and Tripuri 1939 (MP); Gandhi refused to impose a CWC on him
PYQ 2026 builds on this chain: why did a newly re-elected president quit within weeks?

topic: Tripuri crisis, Forward Bloc and Bose's war strategy (1939-40)
t: Forward Bloc (1939) → why Bose formed it
text:
## 1. The 2026 factors
Statement | Verdict
Bose failed to win Gandhi's confidence | Correct
Congress Left disunited, did not back him on Pant's resolution | Correct: the CSP, which backed him in the election, abstained
Communists did not support Bose | Wrong: they were sympathetic at this stage
Royists (M.N. Roy) and socialists like JP chose Congress unity | Correct
The Left saw that a rival leadership would split the movement; the masses moved only under Gandhi
## 2. The party
Formed within the Congress to unite radical-left elements; All India Forward Bloc (1939-41)
After a 9 Jul 1939 protest call, Bose was removed as Bengal PCC president and barred from Congress office for 3 years
⚠ Founded 1939, not 1938; not "Indian Freedom Party", "Revolutionary Front" or Azad Hind Fauj
PYQ 2026: answer 1, 2 and 4; PYQ 2005: party founded by Bose in 1939 = Forward Bloc

topic: Tripuri crisis, Forward Bloc and Bose's war strategy (1939-40)
t: Left groups in 1939 → where each stood
text:
## 1. Who was who on the Congress Left
Group | Leaders | 1939-42 stand
Congress Socialist Party (1934) | Narendra Dev, JP, Achyut Patwardhan, Lohia | Backed Bose in the poll, not against Pant's resolution; led Quit India underground
CPI | S.A. Dange, Muzaffar Ahmad, Singaravelu | Sympathetic to Bose; "People's War" from 1941, opposed Quit India
Royists | M.N. Roy (back in India 1930) | Preferred Congress unity to backing Bose
Forward Bloc | Subhas Bose | Anti-compromise; with Kisan Sabha at Ramgarh
Kisan Sabha (1936) | Sahajanand, N.G. Ranga | Joined Anti-Compromise Conference
Left commanded nearly one-third of AICC votes; Nehru 1936-37 and Bose 1938-39 presidents
⚠ The CSP had opened its doors to Communists and Royists in 1935; they drifted apart by 1940
Bipan Chandra: the Left fought the right wing on methods and tactics, not ideology, and was isolated when it came to the crunch

topic: Tripuri crisis, Forward Bloc and Bose's war strategy (1939-40)
t: Bose's war strategy → "godsent opportunity"
text:
## 1. Bose on the coming war
Year | Position
1938 | Predicted a European war; urged a six-month ultimatum to Britain, then mass civil disobedience for Poorna Swaraj
10 Mar 1939 | Repeated it in the Tripuri presidential address
Sep 1939 | At Wardha: war is imperialist, exploit Britain's difficulty
Mar 1940 | Anti-Compromise Conference at Ramgarh
1941 onwards | Sought help from USSR, then Germany and Japan
## 2. Who held the opposite view
Nehru and Gandhi: refused to exploit Britain's difficulty
Rajaji: urged support for the war, stayed out of Quit India
Jinnah: used the war to press the League's claims
⚠ Bose believed in force and modern technology; Gandhi in non-violence, yet Bose called him "Father of the Nation" (1944)
PYQ 1999: leader who saw an Anglo-German war as a godsent opportunity = Bose (not Rajaji, Jinnah, Nehru)

topic: Tripuri crisis, Forward Bloc and Bose's war strategy (1939-40)
t: Anti-Compromise Conference and Holwell agitation → Bose in 1940
text:
## 1. Two campaigns
Campaign | Facts
Anti-Compromise Conference, Ramgarh, Mar 1940 | Joint auspices of Forward Bloc and Kisan Sabha; urged people not to help the war effort
Holwell Monument agitation, Calcutta, Jul 1940 | Bose allied with the Muslim League to remove the 1760 monument to the Black Hole victims
## 2. Holwell details
J.Z. Holwell claimed 146 prisoners were shut in Fort William in June 1756, over 100 suffocated; nationalists held it exaggerated
3 Jul 1940 meeting: homage to Siraj-ud-Daulah, demand to delete slurs from textbooks; satyagraha set for 16 Jul
British arrested Bose a day before, fearing joint Hindu-Muslim action
⚠ The Holwell campaign shows Bose's Hindu-Muslim unity strategy in Bengal, not a communal issue
## In news 2025-26
Aug 2025: centenary of Vithalbhai Patel becoming first Indian President of the Central Legislative Assembly (1925); in the 1930s he aligned with Bose and willed his estate to Bose's political work (family won the court case)

t: Ramgarh session (Mar 1940) → what it decided
text:
## 1. Gandhi's reasons for delaying civil disobedience
Indiscipline and differences within Congress
Masses not ready
No Hindu-Muslim unity; fear of communal riots
Bose, socialists, communists argued differences would vanish once a movement began
## 2. The session
Item | Fact
Session | 53rd, Ramgarh (now Jharkhand), Mar 1940
President | Maulana Azad (stayed president till 1946: no session 1941-45)
Resolution | Nothing short of complete independence
Civil disobedience | To start when the organisation is ready; left to Gandhi
⚠ Two Ramgarh meetings in March 1940: Congress session (Azad) and Anti-Compromise Conference (Bose)

t: August Offer (8 Aug 1940) → provisions
text:
## 1. Provisions (Linlithgow, at Simla)
Provision | Detail
Dominion status | After the war (first explicit offer)
Executive Council | Expanded, with an Indian majority
Constituent assembly | After the war, to frame a new constitution
War Advisory Council | To meet regularly; incl. Indian States' representatives
Minorities | Full weight; no constitution without their consent
## 2. Significance
First time the Indians' right to frame their own constitution was accepted
Constituent Assembly idea: M.N. Roy (1934) → INC demand (1935) → accepted in principle by the August Offer
⚠ Do not confuse: War Advisory Council = August Offer 1940; constitution body elected by provincial assemblies = Cripps 1942

t: August Offer → who rejected it and why
text:
## 1. Responses
Party | Response
Congress | Rejected: no national government; it encouraged the League
Muslim League | Rejected (PMF): wanted a clear promise of Pakistan
Viceroy's pledge | No constitution or government without the League's and minorities' support: a minority veto
## 2. Follow-up (1941)
22 Jul 1941: Executive Council of 12, 8 Indians: Indians outnumber Britons for the first time
But defence, finance, home stayed British
30-member National Defence Council to coordinate Centre, provinces, states
Ambedkar joined the Council as labour member (1942)
⚠ Testbook and Spectrum say the League endorsed the August Offer; PMF says both Congress and League rejected it: follow PMF

t: Individual Satyagraha (1940-41) → who and why
text:
## 1. Facts
Item | Fact
Start | 17 Oct 1940, by Gandhi
Issue | "Freedom of speech", not "freedom of India"
1st satyagrahi | Vinoba Bhave
2nd | Jawaharlal Nehru
3rd | Brahma Dutt
Aim | Disprove the British claim that India backed the war wholeheartedly
Why limited | Not to embarrass Britain's war effort by a mass upheaval
Trigger: ordinances curbing free speech; arrests of socialists, labour and youth leaders
⚠ The order is the trap: Vinoba first, Nehru second; not Rajendra Prasad, Rajaji or Patel
PYQ 2009: Vinoba first, second = Nehru

t: Individual Satyagraha → method, course, end
text:
## 1. Method and course
Step | Detail
Act | Satyagrahi made an anti-war declaration in public
If not arrested | Repeat it, go to villages, march towards Delhi: "Delhi Chalo" movement
15 May 1941 | Over 25,000 satyagrahis jailed
Dec 1941 | CWC suspended it
## 2. Vinoba Bhave (1895-1982)
Born Gondia (Maharashtra), 11 Sep 1895; translated the Gita into Marathi (Geetai)
Sent by Gandhi to Wardha in 1921; later Sarvodaya Samaj (1948), Bhoodan (1951, Pochampally), Gramdan
⚠ "Delhi Chalo" first appears in the 1940 satyagraha plan; Bose's INA made it famous in 1943-44
## In news 2025-26
Sep 2026: Vinoba's birth anniversary; PMF recap: first Individual Satyagrahi (1940), Nehru second; Nagpur Flag Satyagraha (1923), Quit India (1942)

t: Lahore Resolution (1940) and 1941 turning points
text:
## 1. The Pakistan demand
Item | Fact
Date | 23 Mar 1940, League's Lahore session
Demand | Autonomy for Muslim-majority areas of NW and NE
Word "Pakistan" | Not used; no mention of partition
Drafter | Sikandar Hayat Khan (Unionist): later rejected "Muslim Raj here, Hindu Raj elsewhere"
Name "Pakistan" | Choudhry Rehmat Ali, Cambridge, pamphlets 1933, 1935
Earlier idea | Iqbal, League address 1930: NW Muslim state within a loose federation
Pakistan marks 23 March as its National Day
## 2. War reaches India
22 Jun 1941 Germany attacks USSR; 7 Dec 1941 Pearl Harbour; Japan takes Rangoon, Mar 1942
15 Jan 1941 (AICC): Gandhi named Nehru, "not C. Rajagopalachari", his successor
⚠ League's "Divide and Quit" slogan came later, at Karachi, 1944

t: Cripps proposals → what they offered
text:
## 1. Draft Declaration
Proposal | Detail
Status | Indian Union with dominion status immediately after the war, right to secede from the Commonwealth
Constitution body | After the war; members elected by provincial assemblies, nominated by rulers for princely states
Provinces | Any province could stay out, have a separate constitution / union, sign a separate agreement with Britain
Princely states | Could keep pre-existing relations with the Crown
Meanwhile | Defence and military operations stay with Britain
Minorities | A treaty between the constitution body and Britain to protect them
⚠ Not full independence; not a partition into two; not a republic; no immediate transfer of power
⚠ 2022 trap: Assembly "nominated by Provincial Assemblies" is wrong: provinces elect, states' rulers nominate
PYQ 2022: "2 only"; PYQ 2009: constitution body yes, full independence no; PYQ 2016 and 2003: dominion status very soon after the war

t: Cripps Mission → background, who sent it, who negotiated
text:
## 1. Why March 1942
Japan overran Philippines, Indonesia, Malaya, Burma; Rangoon fell (Mar 1942): war at India's door
Allied pressure (USA, China) on Britain to win Indian cooperation
Congress offered to cooperate if power was transferred now and independence promised after the war
## 2. People
Role | Person
Sent by | PM Winston Churchill (Conservative; a diehard imperialist who tried to thwart it)
Head | Sir Stafford Cripps, cabinet minister (Labour members of the all-party government were sympathetic)
Congress negotiators | Nehru and Maulana Azad
Viceroy | Linlithgow
⚠ Not MacDonald, Baldwin or Chamberlain; negotiators not Gandhi-Patel, Kripalani-Rajaji or Prasad-Kidwai
PYQ 2009: Churchill sent it; PYQ 2010: Nehru and Azad negotiated

t: Rejection of Cripps → each party's objection
text:
## 1. Objections
Party | Objection
Congress | Dominion not Purna Swaraj; provinces' right to secede; no immediate transfer of power; states represented by rulers' nominees
Muslim League | Opposed a single union; wanted a definite Pakistan declaration
Hindu Mahasabha, Liberals | Provinces' right to secede
Depressed Classes, Sikhs, Christians, Anglo-Indians | More safeguards
## 2. Why talks broke down (Testbook)
Deadlock over the Viceroy's veto in the interim period
Cripps's "take it or leave it" attitude; could not go beyond the Draft Declaration
Accession by a legislature resolution weighed against Hindus of Bengal and Punjab
⚠ The mission was all-white, but that was not why Congress rejected it
PYQ 1998: A true, R true, R not the explanation

t: Cripps → comments, quotes and links
text:
## 1. Who said what
Remark | By
"Post-dated cheque on a tottering (crashing) bank" | Gandhi
Present structure and autocratic powers would remain | Nehru
Book "Mystery of Sir Stafford Cripps" | Ram Manohar Lohia
## 2. Cripps after 1942
Cripps returned in 1946 in the Cabinet Mission with Pethick-Lawrence and A.V. Alexander
Cripps's failure left an angry public: "time for a final assault" → Quit India
⚠ Some books print "post-dated cheque on a crashing/falling bank": same remark, always Gandhi (not Nehru, Kripalani, JP)

t: August Offer vs Cripps vs Cabinet Mission → constitution-making body
text:
## 1. Comparison
Plan | Year | Constitution body | Status offered
August Offer | 1940 | Representative body after the war (no method) | Dominion, after the war
Cripps | 1942 | Elected by provincial assemblies + rulers' nominees | Dominion immediately after the war, may secede
Cabinet Mission | 1946 | 389 members: 292 provinces, 4 chief commissioners' provinces, 93 states; indirect election by STV | Independence; Union of provinces and states
## 2. Lines to remember
Only Cripps let a province opt out and form its own union: seen as a seed of Pakistan
Cabinet Mission gave the actual scheme the Assembly was built on (Nov 1946)
⚠ "Right to frame own constitution" first accepted in 1940 (August Offer), not 1942

topic: Quit India: causes, resolution and Gandhi's call (1942)
t: Quit India → causes
text:
## 1. PMF's five causes
Cause | Effect
Failure of Cripps | No real constitutional advance on offer
Rising prices, food shortages | Popular discontent
British evacuation of Malaya and Burma | Faith in British rule shaken
Japanese armies on India's borders | Fear of Japanese occupation
Gandhi more militant | Would address the people directly if Congress did not agree
## 2. Opinions in Congress
Nehru first opposed a mass movement (anti-fascist war), then backed it and moved the resolution
Rajaji urged support for the war; with Bhulabhai Desai resigned from the AICC (Jul 1942), stayed out
⚠ Launched after the Cripps failure, not the Cabinet Mission (1946), Wavell Plan (1945) or Simon Report (1930)
PYQ 2013: Quit India launched in response to the Cripps proposals

topic: Quit India: causes, resolution and Gandhi's call (1942)
t: Quit India resolution → dates, places, people
text:
## 1. Steps
Date / place | Step
May 1942 | Gandhi drafts resolution: British withdrawal, non-violent non-cooperation against any Japanese invasion
14 Jul 1942, Wardha | CWC adopts it (Preview: meeting 5-14 Jul, Azad presiding)
7-8 Aug 1942, Gowalia Tank, Bombay | AICC ratifies it on 8 Aug: immediate end of British rule
Moved / seconded | Nehru / Sardar Patel
Congress president | Maulana Azad
9 Aug 1942 | Movement begins; "August Kranti"
## 2. What else the resolution said
Free India would defend itself against fascism and imperialism; a provisional government after the British leave
Mass struggle on non-violent lines under Gandhi; every participant to act "within the four corners of the general instructions"
⚠ 8 Aug 1942 is not the Council expansion (1941), the ministries' resignation (1939) or Cripps' offer (1942)
PYQ 2021: 8 Aug 1942 = AICC adopted the Quit India Resolution

topic: Quit India: causes, resolution and Gandhi's call (1942)
t: "Do or Die" speech (8 Aug 1942) → what Gandhi said
text:
## 1. The speech
"I want freedom immediately, this very night, before dawn"
No bargain with the Viceroy "for ministries and the like"; nothing short of complete freedom
The mantra: "Do or Die": free India or die trying; not live to see slavery perpetuated
## 2. Slogans and their movements
Slogan | Movement / person
Do or Die | Quit India, Gandhi, 1942
Delhi Chalo, Jai Hind | Bose / INA
Give me blood, I will give you freedom | Bose
Divide and Quit | Muslim League, Karachi 1944
Pattabhi Sitaramayya: Gandhi spoke that day "with the power of an Avatar and Paigambar"
⚠ "Do or Die" is not Swadeshi, Non-Cooperation or Civil Disobedience
PYQ 2009: "Do or Die" = Quit India Movement
## In news 2025-26
8 Aug 2026: Quit India / August Kranti Day observed; resolution adopted at the Bombay AICC on 8 Aug 1942

topic: Quit India: causes, resolution and Gandhi's call (1942)
t: Gandhi's instructions → each group
text:
## 1. Instructions in the 8 Aug speech
Group | Instruction
Government servants | Do not resign; openly declare allegiance to Congress
Soldiers | Do not leave posts; refuse to fire on Indians
Princes | Accept the sovereignty of their people; stop homage to foreign power
People of states | Declare themselves part of the Indian nation; follow princes only if they side with the people
Students | Give up studies only if firm till independence
Peasants | The brave may refuse land revenue; land belongs to the tiller
Zamindari areas | Pay a pro-people zamindar by agreement; pay nothing to a pro-government one
Never formally issued: preventive arrests came first
⚠ "Servants to resign" and "soldiers to leave posts" are both false
PYQ 2005: only the princes statement correct: "3 only"

topic: Quit India: causes, resolution and Gandhi's call (1942)
t: Arrests of 9 Aug 1942 → who was jailed where
text:
## 1. Operation Zero Hour
Leader(s) | Jail
Gandhi, Sarojini Naidu | Aga Khan Palace, Poona
Nehru, Azad, Patel, Pant, Kripalani, Pattabhi + others (CWC) | Ahmednagar Fort
Rajendra Prasad | Bankipur jail, Patna
JP | Hazaribagh jail (escaped 9 Nov 1942)
Congress, AICC, CWC and PCCs declared illegal
Aruna Asaf Ali presided over the rest of the session and hoisted the flag at Gowalia Tank on 9 Aug
## 2. Gandhi in jail
10 Feb 1943: 21-day fast at Aga Khan Palace against the charge that Congress caused the violence
Operation Rubicon: secret British plan if Gandhi died during the fast
Released on health grounds: PMF June 1944; Preview 6 May 1944
⚠ Gandhi was in jail from day one: Quit India was not led by Gandhi in practice

topic: Quit India: course, underground and parallel governments
t: Course of Quit India → spontaneous, leaderless, violent
text:
## 1. Features
Feature | Fact
Leadership | Leaderless after arrests: students and Congress socialists led locally
Spontaneity | More spontaneous than earlier movements, but within the AICC's broad framework
Violence | Began non-violent; repression provoked attacks on police stations, rail, post, telegraph
Gandhi | Refused to condemn people's violence; blamed the state's bigger violence
Labour | Strikes in factories, but labour as a whole not drawn in (CPI line)
Duration | Mass phase crushed in 6-7 weeks
Strongest in Bihar and eastern UP (Ballia, Azamgarh, Gorakhpur; Saran, Champaran, Gaya), Bombay, Bengal, Orissa
⚠ Of "non-violent / led by Gandhi / spontaneous / did not attract labour in general", the false one is "led by Gandhi"
PYQ 2011: not true = "It was led by Mahatma Gandhi"

topic: Quit India: course, underground and parallel governments
t: Repression and Linlithgow's verdict → "most serious rebellion since 1857"
text:
## 1. Repression
Measure | Fact
Firing | Crowds machine-gunned, even bombed from the air
Deaths | Over 10,000 in police and military firing
Press | Completely muzzled
Legal tool | Armed Forces (Special Powers) Ordinance, 1942
Repression not seen since 1857
## 2. Linlithgow
Telegram to Churchill: "by far the most serious rebellion since 1857"
Reason: massive peasant upsurge (peasants farmed by day, raided by night)
Linlithgow also called Gandhi's movements "political blackmail"
Wavell was Commander-in-Chief in 1942; Viceroy from Oct 1943
PYQ 1999: A and R true, R explains A (peasant upsurge)
## In news 2025-26
Oct 2026: MHA extended AFSPA, 1958 for six months in parts of Manipur, Nagaland, Arunachal; PMF: AFSPA traces to the 1942 ordinance used to suppress Quit India

topic: Quit India: course, underground and parallel governments
t: Sumit Sarkar's three phases → character of each
text:
## 1. Phases ("Modern India, 1885-1947")
Phase | When | Character
1 | From 9 Aug | Urban revolt: strikes, boycotts, picketing; students and urban middle class lead; quickly crushed
2 | Mid-Aug 1942 | Peasant rebellion in the countryside; communications destroyed; national governments set up
3 | End Sep 1942 onwards | Longest, least formidable: sabotage by educated youth, propaganda, Usha Mehta's radio
## 2. Was it spontaneous or organised?
Spontaneity was greater than before, but not total: Congress gave the broad framework
As in 1930 (Dandi gave the frame, locals chose actions), local initiative was built into the plan
Quit India demanded immediate independence: after it, talks could only be on how power would pass
⚠ The peasant (second) phase, not the urban phase, is what made Linlithgow invoke 1857

topic: Quit India: course, underground and parallel governments
t: Underground leaders → who did what
text:
## 1. Three streams (PMF)
Stream | Leader | Method
Radical | Jayaprakash Narayan | Guerrilla bands on the India-Nepal border; "Azad Dasta"
Centrist | Aruna Asaf Ali (Congress Socialists) | Volunteers for sabotage across India
Gandhian | Sucheta Kripalani | Non-violent action, constructive work
## 2. Others underground
Achyut Patwardhan (helped by Sumati Morarjee), Ram Manohar Lohia, Biju Patnaik, Chhotubhai Puranik, R.P. Goenka
Work: blowing bridges, cutting wires, derailing trains, keeping up morale
⚠ Aruna Asaf Ali was a Quit India underground organiser, not of Civil Disobedience, NCM or Swadeshi
PYQ 2009: Aruna Asaf Ali = woman organiser of underground activity in Quit India

No. | Provision

topic: Wavell Plan, Simla, INA trials and RIN revolt (1945-46)
t: Wavell Plan (June 1945) → main provisions
text:
## 1. What the plan offered
Announced June 1945 by the British government and Viceroy Lord Wavell for an interim settlement
Provision | Detail
Executive Council | Reconstituted at once, members increased
Who is Indian | All members Indian except the Viceroy and the Commander-in-Chief
Communal balance | Balanced representation; equal numbers of caste Hindus and Muslims (parity)
Legal frame | Works within GoI Act 1935; not responsible to the legislature
Viceroy | Keeps the veto
Nature | Temporary, until a new constitution; talks on it after the war
Nominations | Parties to give a joint list; separate lists if none
All portfolios, including External Affairs, to Indians; only Defence/War stayed with the C-in-C
⚠ Parity was between caste Hindus and Muslims, not Hindus-Muslims-Sikhs
⚠ The plan aimed to break the deadlock, not to avoid partition (2007 Reason was false)

topic: Wavell Plan, Simla, INA trials and RIN revolt (1945-46)
t: Simla Conference (25 June 1945) → who attended, why it failed
text:
## 1. The conference
Convened by Wavell at Simla on 25 June 1945; Congress leaders released from jail to attend
Maulana Azad (Congress president) led the Congress; Jinnah led the League
Gandhi attended to advise the Viceroy, not as Congress representative (held no office)
## 2. Why it broke down
Issue | Stand
Muslim seats | 6 of 14 seats Muslim; League wanted to nominate all six
Congress | Represents all communities, so it must nominate Muslims too
Unionist Party (Punjab) | Its Muslim claim ignored by Jinnah
Communal veto | League wanted a two-thirds majority on Muslim issues
Wavell announced the breakdown instead of bypassing the League: gave the League a virtual veto
⚠ The Viceroy was Wavell, not Mountbatten (Mountbatten came only in March 1947)
PYQ 2008: the body that proposed all portfolios, including War, to Indian leaders = Simla Conference
PYQ 2005: "Mountbatten was Viceroy at Simla" was the false statement

Release of INA prisoners and political prisoners | CPI: only party to support
Withdraw troops from Indonesia (Java) and China | Congress and League: condemned
Better food, equal pay with British sailors | Gandhi: condemned
Civilised treatment | Aruna Asaf Ali: one of few leaders to back it

t: Cabinet Mission Plan → recommendations
text:
## 1. Structure
United India: British India + princely states; Pakistan rejected
Loose three-tier federation: Union → groups of provinces → provinces
Section | Provinces
A (Hindu-majority) | Madras, Bombay, UP, Bihar, CP, Orissa
B (Muslim NW) | Punjab, NWFP, Sind
C (Muslim NE) | Bengal, Assam
Weak Centre: only foreign affairs, defence, communications; residuary powers to provinces
Province could leave a group (not the Union) after first elections; review after 10 years
Communal veto: major communal issues need majorities of both General and Muslim members
Constituent Assembly of 389 by indirect election; interim government from it
Paramountcy to end; princes free to deal with successor government
⚠ It did nothing on Indian courts or ICS (2015 statements 2 and 3 false)

League | Grouping compulsory (B, C as future Pakistan) | Withdrew acceptance 29 July 1946; called Direct Action

The plan never said whether grouping was compulsory or voluntary
After this, partition was seen as inevitable; only Gandhi and Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan held out
⚠ Testbook says Congress accepted the proposals; PMF: both first accepted the long-term plan, then rejected it

## 1. Attlee's statement, 20 February 1947
British to leave by 30 June 1948
Mountbatten to replace Wavell as Viceroy
Power to more than one central government if the Constituent Assembly was not fully representative
## 2. Mountbatten's mandate
Item | Fact
Arrived | March 1947, last Viceroy

Explore till | Unity and division options until October 1947

## 1. The two sites
Site | State | Faith | Date

t: Ajanta caves → number, phases, patrons
text:
## 1. Basic facts
30 rock-cut caves incl. unfinished 5, 24, 29 (PMF); cliff above the Waghora river, horseshoe-shaped gorge
5 chaityas (9, 10, 19, 26, 29); the rest viharas
Rediscovered 1819 by Captain John Smith (tiger hunt); UNESCO World Heritage Site
⚠ Testbook and PYQ keys say 29 caves (25 viharas + 4 chaityas); PMF counts 30 with 5 chaityas: follow PMF, accept 29 if options demand
## 2. Two phases
Phase | Period | Sect | Caves | Buddha shown as
First | 2nd-1st c. BCE, Satavahana | Hinayana | 8, 9, 10, 12, 13, 15A | symbols
Second | 5th-6th c. CE, Vakataka-Gupta | Mahayana | remaining 24 | human (idol) form
## 3. Patrons (second phase)
Cave | Patron
16 | Varahadeva, PM of Vakataka king Harishena
17-20 | Upendragupta, local feudatory of Harishena
4 | Mathuradasa
26 | Buddhabhadra
⚠ Murals of caves 9 and 10 are the oldest (Shunga-Satavahana age); the rest are Gupta-Vakataka

t: Ajanta paintings → technique, colours, themes
text:
## 1. Technique
Tempera / fresco-secco ("dry fresco"): pigment with water-soluble binder applied after the plaster dried (PMF)
Outlines first drawn in red, then filled; shading gives three-dimensional volume
⚠ Testbook and the PYQ keys call Ajanta "fresco" (wet plaster); PMF: Ajanta is not true fresco but tempera. Statement "Ajanta paintings are true frescoes" → treat as incorrect
## 2. Colours (five of the Shilpa Sutra)
Colour | Source
Red ochre (geru) | local
Yellow ochre (pilimitti) | local
Black (kajal, lampblack) | local
White (lime, khadia) | local
Lapis lazuli (blue) | imported from Afghanistan
Different skin colours suggest a multi-coloured population
## 3. Themes
Life of the Buddha, Jatakas (previous births) and Avadanas; detailed jewellery, clothing, birds and animals; largely religious
Likely next: "all colours were local" is wrong; lapis lazuli alone came from Afghanistan

t: Ajanta famous paintings → which cave
text:
## 1. Bodhisattva Padmapani (Avalokiteshvara)
Cave 1, 5th c. CE; stands in tribhanga pose, blue lotus (padma) in right hand, big crown, eyes downcast = calm meditation
Painted beside Vajrapani (holding a vajra); both are shrine guardians
Padmapani = Bodhisattva of compassion
## 2. Other paintings
Painting | Cave
Padmapani, Vajrapani | 1 (best preserved)
Dying Princess | 16
"Picture gallery" (many Jataka panels) | 17
Mahabhinishkramana (Great Departure) | Vakataka-age caves
Apsara with cymbal-like instrument | Ajanta
⚠ Padmapani is not at Badami, Bagh or Ellora (2017 options); Badami murals show Kirtivarman's palace dance, Bagh shows dance and elephant processions
PYQ 2017: Padmapani painting → Ajanta
## In news 2025-26
INSV Kaundinya (Navy stitched-sail ship) is recreated from a ship in a 5th-c. Ajanta mural; maiden voyage Porbandar → Muscat (Dec 2025)
Padmapani Award of the Ajanta-Ellora International Film Festival given to Ilaiyaraaja (Jan-Feb 2026, Chhatrapati Sambhaji Nagar)
Telangana Heritage Dept and Iran's Noor International Microfilm Centre restore early-20th-c. copies of Ajanta murals (by Christiana Herringham, Nandalal Bose, Syed Ahmad) at the Telangana State Museum (2025)

t: Bagh caves → location, Rang Mahal, Hallisalasya
text:
## 1. Location and date
9 Buddhist rock-cut caves, southern slopes of the Vindhyas, on the Baghini (Baghni) river, a tributary of the Narmada, Dhar district, MP
Excavated 4th-6th c. CE (Gupta); sandstone; style same as Ajanta
⚠ Testbook places Bagh in "Hoshangabad"; PMF and LENS: Dhar district
## 2. Paintings
Feature | Fact
Technique | tempera on dry, lime-primed mud plaster
Largest cave | Cave 4 = Rang Mahal ("Palace of Colours")
Hallisalasya | joyous folk dance: group of women dancing round a man
Dancing panel (5th c.) | dancers with heavy jewellery, one playing drum
Other famous panel | procession of elephants
Bagh figures: sharper contours, more earthly, human, secular in tone than Ajanta (Testbook)
Hallisaka (PMF dance chapter) = circle dance with joined hands round a youth acting as Krishna
⚠ Hallisalasya is not Buddha in meditation, not Shiva-Parvati on Kailasa (that is an Ellora sculpture theme), not Samudramanthan
PYQ 2026: Hallisalasya painting at Bagh represents → a joyous folk dance
## In news 2025-26
Bagh Cave Paintings added to India's UNESCO Tentative List (Sept-Oct 2026) with Chambal Valley temples, Udayagiri caves, Ginnorgarh (MP) and transnational "Sites of Satyagraha" (India-South Africa); India's Tentative List = 78, WHS = 45 (LENS)

t: Ajanta, Ellora and Bagh → compared
text:
Point | Ajanta | Ellora | Bagh
State | Maharashtra | Maharashtra (Charanandri hills) | MP (Dhar)
Faith | Buddhist only | Hindu 17, Buddhist 12, Jain 5 | Buddhist
Period of paintings | 2nd c. BCE-7th c. CE | 7th-12th c. CE | 4th-6th c. CE
Dynasty | Satavahana, Vakataka | Rashtrakuta (Hindu, Buddhist), Yadava (Jain) | Gupta age
Preserved paintings | best preserved | only in Kailasa temple | sparse, damaged
Ellora paintings: Vishnu and Lakshmi on Garuda through clouds, Shiva, apsaras
Ellora was never lost: visited by Al-Masudi, Firishta, Thevenot, Manucci; Ajanta was lost until 1819
⚠ "Ajanta and Ellora paintings both include Buddhist themes" → correct (PMF quiz); "both are only Buddhist" → wrong

topic: Early miniatures: Pala, Jain, early Rajput, Sultanate
t: Miniature schools before the Mughals → region, faith, text
text:
## 1. What a miniature is
Small paintings on vellum, palm leaf, paper, cloth, ivory, copper, made for books or albums
## 2. Pre-Mughal schools
School | Region, period | Faith | Hinge fact
Pala | Eastern India (Bengal-Bihar), 8th-12th c. | Buddhist | earliest extant: Astasahasrika Prajnaparamita (Mahipala, 10th c.); subdued colours, Ajanta-like curves
Jain / Western Indian / Apabhramsa | Gujarat, 10th-15th c. | Jain | Kalpasutra (Bhadrabahu) most illustrated; protruding far eye, pointed nose; palm-leaf "punthis"
Early Rajput | 15th c. | Hindu | Bhagavata Purana; Chaurapanchasika (Bilhana)
Sultanate | Malwa (Mandu), late 15th c. | Persian court | Nimatnama = cookbook of Ghiyath Shah
⚠ Pala disappeared by the late 13th c. after monasteries were destroyed; Jain painting moved to Rajasthan, Malwa and grew into Rajput painting
⚠ Jain painting used gold and lapis lazuli (Jaunpur Kalpasutra, 1465) and was patronised by merchants
Likely next: Pala → Eastern India, Buddhism; Nimatnama → cookery (PMF quiz)

topic: Early miniatures: Pala, Jain, early Rajput, Sultanate
t: Jain and Chaurapanchasika styles → features
text:
Feature | Jain (Western Indian) | Chaurapanchasika (early Rajput)
Colours | bright, gold, lapis lazuli | vibrant, transparent drapery
Figure | far eye protruding, angular | broad-chested men, narrow waists
Symbols | textile patterns | every object a mood (fire = passion)
Patron | Chalukya (Solanki) Kumarapala, merchants | Hindu courts
Kumarapala (12th c.) distributed hundreds of Kalpasutra copies
Paper reached Jain painting only in the 14th c.

t: Mughal emperors → contribution to painting
text:
Ruler | Contribution
Babur | names Behzad, Shah Muzaffar in Tuzuk-i-Baburi; no painting of his own
Humayun | founder: brought Mir Sayyid Ali, Abdus Samad from Persia; Nigar Khana workshop; began Hamzanama
Akbar | Tasvir Khana (Fatehpur Sikri), 100+ painters; completed Hamzanama (1400 miniatures); illustrated manuscripts
Jahangir | zenith; albums (muraqqa), portraits, birds and animals; himself a painter
Shah Jahan | architecture first; portraits, bright colours, stylisation; Padshahnama
Dara Shikoh | album of 40 paintings
Aurangzeb | opposed painting; artists moved to Deccan and Rajput courts
Muhammad Shah "Rangeela" | brief revival (1719-48)
⚠ Painting began to decline under Shah Jahan (PMF), not Aurangzeb; Aurangzeb's withdrawal only scattered the artists
PYQ 1996: Mughal painting reached its zenith under → Jahangir (traps Akbar, Shah Jahan)

t: Akbar vs Jahangir → the shift to albums and portraits
text:
Aspect | Akbar | Jahangir
Themes | grand political, religious, battles, narrative | nature, realism, aristocracy, court portraits
Production | mass, teams of artists per painting | fewer, high-quality, often one master
Format | illustrated manuscripts | albums (muraqqa) of individual paintings
Margins | plain | gold-illuminated hashiya with flora, fauna
Jahangir: peacock blue and red, 3-D effect, halo behind the emperor, European and Christian motifs
