t: Mughal miniature → features and illustrated texts
text:
## 1. Features
Persian + Indian fusion; court art for the emperor's circle; almost secular; realism, profile portraits
Women minimal; teamwork (outline, colour, faces by different artists)
Brushes of a single squirrel hair for fine detail (NCERT)
## 2. Illustrated manuscripts under Akbar
Text | What
Hamzanama | adventures of Amir Hamza; begun under Humayun
Tutinama | Tales of a Parrot
Razmnama | Mahabharata in Persian
Anwar-i-Suhaili | Persian Panchatantra
Baburnama, Akbarnama | chronicles
Tarikh-i-Khandan-i-Timuriyah | chronicle of Timur's line; listed by LENS (Apr 2025) among India's earlier UNESCO Memory of the World entries

t: Deccan painting → courts and contrast with Mughal
text:
Sultanates after the Bahmani break-up: Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar, Bidar, Berar; peak late 16th-mid 17th c., revival around Hyderabad
Works: Ragamala, Lady with the Myna (Yogini), Lady Smoking Hookah, Composite Horse; Ibrahim Adil Shah II of Bijapur himself painted Ragamala
Point | Mughal | Deccan
Colour | naturalistic | more brilliant
Realism | high | less; mystic, fantastic
Themes | court, history, hunts | mythology, nature, Hindu touches
Women | few | tall women, small heads, in saris
⚠ Deccan painting predates the 18th c. (PMF quiz: Company, Bazar, Patna Kalam came later)

t: Rajput painting → features and Mughal link
text:
Hindu kingdoms of Rajasthan and the hills, late 16th-mid 19th c.; term coined by Ananda Coomaraswamy (1916)
Painted on wasli (layered handmade paper); themes from Bhakti: Gita Govinda, Rasikapriya, Rasamanjari, Ragamala, Bhagavata Purana
Colours mean moods: yellow = passion, white = purity, red = joy
Influenced by Mughal painting | Not Mughal-derived
Rajasthani (Bikaner, Bundi, Amber, Marwar) | Kalighat (Bengal folk, 19th c.)
Pahari incl. Kangra (Kashmiri painters trained in Mughal style) | Warli, Madhubani and other folk forms
Deccan | Pala, Jain (earlier than Mughals)
Mughal link of Rajput states began with Raja Bharmal of Amber giving his daughter to Akbar (1562)
PYQ 1995: which was not influenced by Mughal painting → Kalighat; Pahari, Rajasthani and Kangra were

t: Stupa → origin, purpose and parts
text:
## 1. Origin and purpose
Stupa (Sanskrit: heap) = mound holding relics of the Buddha or monks
Tradition is pre-Buddhist: Vedic-era burial mounds over remains of kings and nobles
Buddhism adopted it; Ashoka (Ashokavadana) distributed relics and raised stupas everywhere
Types: relic, commemorative (events of Buddha's life), votive (fulfilment of a vow)
## 2. Parts
Part | What it is
Anda | Solid hemispherical dome; relics buried inside; cannot be entered
Harmika | Square railing on top of the dome
Chhatri | Triple umbrella = Buddha, Dharma, Sangha
Medhi | Raised circular terrace for circumambulation
Vedika | Railing (horizontals = suchi)
Torana | Gateways at the four cardinal points
⚠ Stupa is not Buddhist in origin, but it is a relic repository and a votive/commemorative structure
PYQ 2023: how many of three statements correct; answer two; trap: "concept of stupa is Buddhist in origin" is false

t: Chaitya vs vihara → worship hall vs dwelling

Feature | Chaitya | Vihara
Meaning | Sacred spot; prayer / congregation hall | Monastery, residence of monks
Plan | Vaulted hall, apsidal end, stupa at far end | Central hall, verandah, cells around
Roof | Semicircular, horseshoe vault | Flat
Examples | Karla (largest rock-cut chaitya), Bhaja (one of earliest, 2nd c BCE), Ajanta caves 9, 10, 19, 26, 29 | Nasik (inscriptions of Nahapana, Gautamiputra), Ajanta, Kanheri, Bagh
Chaitya possibly from chita = funeral pyre
Post-Mauryan rock-cut caves = these two types
⚠ Chaitya is the place of worship; vihara is the dwelling; options swap them

⚠ Praveen CA (Jul 2026, Telugu Mahotsavam held there) calls Undavalli originally a Buddhist vihara, 4th-5th c, Vishnukundina; follow PMF (Jain origin) but know both
Kailasa, Ellora (NCERT Heritage Crafts): whole temple cut from one hill, carved from the top downwards; granite at Mahabalipuram vs sandstone at Khajuraho
Bagh caves and Udayagiri caves added to India's UNESCO Tentative List (LENS-CA 30 Sep 2026)

t: Three temple styles → defining features
text:
Feature | Nagara (North) | Dravida (South) | Vesara (Deccan)
Tower | Curvilinear shikhara | Pyramidal stepped vimana | Blend of both
Gateway | Usually no boundary wall/gateway | Tall gopuram, often taller than vimana | Varies
Top | Amalaka + kalasha | "Shikhara" = crowning stupika | 
Plan | Square; often on jagati | Prakaras, tanks, big complex | Square, star-shaped
Doorway | River goddesses Ganga, Yamuna | Dvarapalas | 
Examples | Khajuraho, Lingaraja, Modhera | Thanjavur, Kanchi Kailasanatha | Badami Chalukya, Hoysala
Nagara sub-types: Latina/rekha-prasada (common), Phamsana (broad, slabbed), Valabhi (wagon-vault)
Nagara regional schools: Kalinga, Chandela, Solanki
Vesara developed by Badami Chalukyas; culminated under Rashtrakutas and Hoysalas
⚠ Nagara, Dravida, Vesara are temple styles, not racial, linguistic or musical groups
PYQ 2012 and 1995: same direct question on what the three terms are

t: Gupta temples → evolution from flat roof to shikhara
text:
## 1. From your notes
Temple | Place | Why it matters
Bhitargaon (5th-6th c) | Kanpur, UP | Brick; oldest Hindu shrine with a roof and a high shikhara
Dashavatara (6th c) | Deogarh, Lalitpur, UP | High jagati, steps on all four sides; Vishnu panels (Sheshashayi, Gajendramoksha); early Nagara
Parvati temple | Nachna (Panna, MP) | Covered ambulatory, upper storey
Tigawa | Jabalpur, MP | Flat-roofed square shrine + pillared porch
Sanchi Temple 17 | Sanchi, MP | Earliest flat-roofed stone shrine
By the 7th c the main temple features were fixed and codified in texts (Shilpa Shastra)
## Beyond your notes
Five-stage scheme often taught: (1) flat-roofed square + shallow porch (Sanchi 17, Tigawa); (2) adds ambulatory and upper storey (Nachna); (3) low square shikhara (Deogarh, Bhitargaon); (4) rectangular shrine (Ter, Maharashtra); (5) circular shrine (Maniyar Math, Rajgir)
⚠ Bhitargaon is brick, Deogarh is stone; both Gupta, both UP
Likely next: earliest shikhara temple; Gupta temple ↔ state

t: Regional styles → Solanki, Bengal, Gadag
text:
Style | Region, dynasty | Hallmarks | Example
Solanki / Maru-Gurjara | Gujarat, Rajasthan; Chaulukyas, 11th-13th c | Walls with many projections and recesses; ornate curvilinear shikhara; adopted by Jains | Modhera, Dilwara, Rani-ki-Vav
Bengal (Malla) | Bishnupur Malla kings | Terracotta / brick; hut-like curved roofs | Bishnupur temples
Gadag (Western/Kalyani Chalukya) | Tungabhadra-Krishna doab, 11th-13th c | Ornate pillars; sub-type of Vesara; link between Badami Chalukya and Hoysala | Lakkundi (temples + stepwells)
## 1. Bengal roof types
Type | Shape
Chala | Hut-like curved roof and cornices (do-chala, char-chala, at-chala)
Jor-Bangla | Two huts joined: porch + shrine; "Bengal's most distinctive contribution"
Ratna | Curved roof with pinnacles: eka-ratna (1), pancha-ratna (5)
Dalan | Flat roof, heavy cornices on S-curved brackets
⚠ Gadag style is Western (Kalyani) Chalukya, not Badami Chalukya; Pattadakal-Aihole-Badami are clustered, Gadag temples are dispersed

t: Sultanate architecture → phase and feature
text:
Phase | Feature
Early (Slave) | Temple materials; lintel-slab; Quwwat-ul-Islam, Qutub Minar
Balban's tomb | First true arch
Khalji | Alai Darwaza (1311): first true dome; red sandstone + marble
Tughlaq | Rubble, battered (sloping) walls, high platform, arch-beam, encaustic tiles, octagonal tombs
Lodi | Double dome (Sikandar Lodi's tomb); tombs in gardens

t: Indo-Islamic terms → meaning
text:
Term | Meaning | First / best example
True arch | Voussoirs locked by a keystone | Balban's tomb
True dome | Dome on squinches over a square | Alai Darwaza
Double dome | Inner + outer shell, more height | Sikandar Lodi's tomb
Arch-beam | Four-centred arch + supporting beam | Tughlaq hallmark
Pietra dura | Semi-precious stones inlaid in marble | Itmad-ud-Daula, Taj
Jali | Lattice screen cut from one slab | Sidi Sayyid mosque, Ahmedabad
Charbagh | Fourfold garden with water channels | Humayun's tomb, Taj
Encaustic tiles | Coloured tiles with inlaid pattern | Tughlaq buildings
Chunam | Lime plaster over rubble | Sultanate walls
Decoration: calligraphy, geometry, arabesque (no human figures)
Three streams: Imperial (Delhi Sultans), Mughal, regional (provincial) styles
Early mosques reused temple material: Quwwat-ul-Islam (Delhi, 1198; 27 temples) and Adhai Din ka Jhonpra (Ajmer)
⚠ Before the Turks, Indian builders used trabeate (beam and lintel) and corbelled arches; true arch came with the Turks
Likely next: firsts (arch, dome, double dome, white marble building)

topic: Hindustani music: styles, gharanas and maestros
t: Hindustani vocal styles → defining feature
text:
## 1. Background
Hindustani and Carnatic split by the 13th century; Hindustani = Indo-Turko-Persian blend of north, east, central India
Amir Khusrau fused Indian and Persian systems; Hindu exponent = Pandit, Muslim = Ustad
Style | Hinge feature
Dhrupad | Oldest surviving style; devotional; tambura + pakhawaj
Dhamar | Lighter Dhrupad, sung at Holi
Khyal | "Thought/imagination"; most common today; credited to Amir Khusrau; popularised by Muhammad Shah's Sadarang, Adarang
Tarana | Fast, uses bols; end of concert; = Carnatic Tillana
Thumri | Semi-classical; court of Wajid Ali Shah; Braj, Awadhi, Bhojpuri; Radha-Krishna love; linked to Kathak
Tappa | From folk songs of camel riders of Rajasthan; Muhammad Shah's court
Ghazal | Arabic origin (7th c), came via Sufis; Mir, Ghalib popularised
Qawwali | Sufi; Amir Khusrau = father of qawwali; session = Mehfil-e-Sama
⚠ Tambura is an instrument, not a singing style (PMF practice MCQ)
⚠ Alap (slow, no rhythm) = Carnatic Alapana; Tarana = Tillana

topic: Hindustani music: styles, gharanas and maestros
t: Dhrupad → origin, nature and banis
text:
## 1. What UPSC tested (2012)
Primarily devotional and spiritual: praise of deities; Vishnu-themed Dhrupad = Vishnupad
Alap uses syllables like "Nom Tom", Ri, Na, Num, drawn from Sanskrit mantras (e.g. Hari Om Ananta Narayan)
Roots older than Mughal rule: from Prabandha / Dhruvapada and Sama Veda chanting; Natya Shastra mention
Flourished at Raja Man Singh Tomar of Gwalior (PMF: "inventor", moved Dhruvapada from Sanskrit into Hindi) and Akbar's court (Tansen, Swami Haridas, Baiju Bawra)
Declined in the 18th century as Khyal rose; sung often by duos of male vocalists
## 2. Four banis (vanis)
Bani | Note
Dagar | Dagar family (Muslims singing Hindu texts); Gundecha Brothers
Gauhar (Gaurhar) | Tansen's Kalpadruma dhrupads are in this bani
Khandar | Darbhanga, Talwandi gharanas
Nauhar | Bettiah gharana
Gundecha Brothers (Umakant and Ramakant) = Dhrupad vocalists, Dagar bani
⚠ Art_&_Culture calls them "Gundecha Brothers of Jaipur"; they run the Dhrupad Sansthan, Bhopal (see Beyond)
⚠ Dhrupad did not originate in Mughal-era Rajput courts; it only flourished there
PYQ 2012: statements 2 and 3 correct; trap: "originated in Rajput kingdoms in Mughal period"
PYQ 2009: Gundechas are Dhrupad vocalists, not Kathak, sarod or tabla
## Beyond your notes
Gundechas trained under Zia Mohiuddin and Zia Fariduddin Dagar; Padma Shri 2012; Ramakant died 2019

topic: Hindustani music: styles, gharanas and maestros
t: Tansen → names, patrons, contributions
text:
Item | Fact
Birth name | Ramtanu Pandey, Gaur Brahmin, Gwalior
Guru | Swami Haridas (Vrindavan); Sufi master Muhammad Ghaus
Patrons | Raja Man Singh Tomar (Gwalior), Raja Ramchandra of Rewa, then Akbar (c.1562, at ~60)
Title "Tansen" | From Raja Vikramjit of Gwalior
Title "Mian" | From Akbar ("learned man"); one of the Navaratnas
Ragas created | Miyan ki Todi, Miyan ki Malhar, Darbari Kanada (Mian ki Sarang)
Works | Dhrupads in Braj on Ganesha, Shiva, Vishnu, Saraswati, Surya; songs on patrons; Sri Ganesh Stotra, Sangita Sara
Legacy | Founding figure of Gwalior gharana; refined the rabab
Death | Buried near Muhammad Ghaus, Gwalior; Tansen Samaroh each December
⚠ "Tansen was the title given by Akbar" is false: Akbar gave Mian (2019)
⚠ Death year: PMF book 1589; PMF LENS / Magnum 1586
PYQ 2019: "not correct" statement = title by Akbar; he did compose dhrupads on gods, songs on patrons, new ragas
## In news 2025-26
MP High Court rejected a plea for religious activities at Muhammad Ghaus's tomb, Gwalior (LENS Jul 2025)

topic: Ragas: time theory and Carnatic-Hindustani equivalents
t: Raga → time of performance
text:
## 1. Samay theory
Day split into Poorva Bhaag (morning, daytime: Poorva ragas) and Uttar Bhaag (afternoon to night: Uttar ragas)
Hindustani ties ragas to time and season more strongly than Carnatic
Time | Ragas (PMF list)
Morning | Todi, Bhairav, Ahir Bhairav, Bilawal, Bhatiyar, Basant, Hindol, Bilaskhani Todi, Bhoopali Todi
Afternoon | Vrindavani Sarang, Shuddh Sarang, Poorvi
Evening | Bhoopali, Yaman, Hansdhwani, Khamaj, Shyam Kalyan, Shree
Night | Darbari, Malkauns, Malhar, Kirwani, Durga, Nand, Chandani Kedar
Any time | Bhairavi
⚠ Todi = morning; Darbari = night; Bhoopali = evening (2000)
⚠ Bhairav is a morning raga, but Bhairavi can be sung any time
PYQ 2000: early-morning raga among Todi, Darbari, Bhopali, Bhimpalasi → Todi
## Beyond your notes
Bhimpalasi = afternoon raga (Kafi thaat); Mian ki Sarang = midday

topic: Ragas: time theory and Carnatic-Hindustani equivalents
t: Raga → season and rasa
text:
Raga | Season
Malkaus | Shishir (winter)
Hindol | Vasant (spring)
Deepak | Grishma (summer)
Megh | Varsha (monsoon)
Bhairav | Sharad (autumn)
Shree | Hemant (pre-winter)
Legends: Tansen lit lamps with Deepak, brought rain with Megh Malhar; Tana-Riri (Vadnagar) cured his burns with Malhar
Raga classes by notes: Audav (5), Shadav (6), Sampurna (7)
Shruti = microtone; 22 shrutis; 7 svaras Sa Re Ga Ma Pa Dha Ni
Talas: Teentaal 16 beats, Ektaal 12
Nine rasas: Shringara, Hasya, Karuna, Raudra, Vira, Bhayanaka, Bibhatsa, Adbhuta, Shanta (added later)
⚠ Raga Bhairav: morning and Sharad season; Raga Bhairav evokes devotion (PMF)

topic: Ragas: time theory and Carnatic-Hindustani equivalents
t: Thaat and melakarta → Bilawal = Dheera Shankarabharanam
text:
## 1. Two systems
Feature | Hindustani Thaat | Carnatic Melakarta
Number | 10 | 72
Codified by | V.N. Bhatkhande | Concept in Chaturdandi Prakashika (Venkatamakhin)
Role | Parent scale of ragas | Parent (janaka) scales
Ten thaats: Bilawal, Khamaj, Kafi, Asavari, Bhairavi, Bhairav, Kalyan, Marwa, Poorvi, Todi
## 2. Equivalents
Hindustani | Carnatic
Bilawal | Dheera Shankarabharanam
Asavari | Natabhairavi
Bhairavi thaat | Hanumatodi (Carnatic "Todi")
Puriya Dhanashri (Poorvi) | Kamavardhini (Pantuvarali)
⚠ Carnatic Todi (Hanumatodi) = Hindustani Bhairavi, not Hindustani Todi
⚠ Jana Gana Mana is set in Shankarabharanam (Bilawal); Shankarabharanam = "ornament of Shiva"
PYQ 2026: Carnatic raga similar to Bilawal; options Nat Bhairavi, Kamavardhini, Hanumatodi, Dheera Shankarabharanam
## Beyond your notes
Hindustani | Carnatic
Kalyan / Yaman | Mechakalyani (Kalyani)
Khamaj | Harikambhoji
Kafi | Kharaharapriya
Bhairav | Mayamalavagowla (first scale taught, per Purandara Dasa)
Todi thaat | Shubhapantuvarali
Bhoopali | Mohanam
Malkauns | Hindolam

topic: Ragas: time theory and Carnatic-Hindustani equivalents
t: Hindustani vs Carnatic → similarities and differences
text:
Point | Hindustani | Carnatic
Region | North, east, central | South
Influence | Hindu + Persian-Muslim | Largely Hindu, devotional
Focus | Improvisation, long alap | Composition (kriti)
Tempo | Slow unfolding; vilambit-madhya-drut | Faster, structured
Instruments | Tabla, sitar, sarod, harmonium, sarangi | Mridangam, veena, ghatam, violin
Languages | Hindi, Urdu, Braj, Awadhi | Telugu (dominant), Sanskrit, Tamil, Kannada
Time theory | Strong | Weak
Sub-schools | Gharanas | Composer lineages
Common: raga and tala, Natya Shastra and Sangita Ratnakara roots, flute and violin in both, voice as ideal instrument
Sangita Ratnakara: 13th c, Sarangadeva, court of Yadava Simhana (Devagiri); authority for both systems
Jugalbandi: duet of two soloists; Jasrangi (Pandit Jasraj): male and female sing two ragas at once
⚠ Alap ≈ Alapana and Tarana ≈ Tillana: pairs across the two systems

Annamacharya (Annamayya) | 1408-1503, Tallapaka (AP) | 32,000 samkirtanas on Venkateswara | Andhra Pada Kavita Pitamaha
Annamacharya: earliest to compose samkirtanas; songs Adhyatma and Sringara; found 1922 on copper plates at Tirumala
Opposed untouchability: Brahmam Okkate
Annamacharya and Purandara Dasa were contemporaries (met c.1500 at Tirumala)
⚠ Annamacharya (15th c) and Tyagaraja (1767-1847) are not contemporaries (2018)
⚠ Pitamaha of Carnatic music = Purandara Dasa, not Dikshitar or Swati Tirunal
PYQ 2018: correct = Tyagaraja created new ragas + Annamacharya sang of Venkateshwara

Muthuswami Dikshitar | 1776-1835 | Sanskrit, Manipravalam | Guruguha | 500+ kritis on gods and temples; travelled north, Hindustani influence
All three born in Tiruvarur, Tamil Nadu; flourished at Thanjavur

topic: Classical dances: canon and the southern forms
t: Natya Shastra concepts → meaning
text:
Term | Meaning
Nritta | Pure dance; no emotion or story
Nritya | Expressive: mood via face, hands
Natya | Dramatic: imitation of character
Angika | Abhinaya by body, gestures
Vachika | By song, words
Aharya | By costume, make-up
Sattvika | By inner emotion
Lasya / Tandava | Feminine grace / vigorous
Natanabheda = Nritta, Nritya, Natya
Natya Shastra: Bharata, 200 BCE-200 CE, ~6,000 verses; rasa theory; four regional styles Avanti, Dakshinatya, Panchali, Odra-Magadhi
Abhinavabharati: commentary by Abhinavagupta (10th c)
Abhinaya Darpanam: Nandikeshwara (~1000 CE)
Nritta Ratnavali: Jayapa, general of Kakatiya Ganapati Deva (13th c)
⚠ Nritta = no expression; Nritya = with expression

topic: Classical dances: canon and the southern forms
t: Bharatanatyam → origin, features, revival
text:
## 1. Facts
From devadasi Sadir / Dasi Attam; renamed 1932 by E. Krishna Iyer and Rukmini Devi Arundale
Bha-Ra-Ta = bhava, raga, tala; Chidambaram gopuram has 108 karanas
Thanjavur Quartet (Ponniah, Chinniah, Sivanandam, Vadivelu), court of Serfoji II: codified adavus and the margam
Features: fixed torso, aramandi (half-sit), intricate adavus; Carnatic music; nattuvanar with cymbals
Margam order | Item
1 | Alarippu (invocation)
2 | Jatiswaram (pure dance)
3 | Shabdam (first expression)
4 | Varnam (longest; nritta + nritya + natya)
5 | Padam
6 | Thillana (climax)
7 | Shlokam / Mangalam
Banis: Pandanallur, Kalakshetra (Rukmini Devi, 1936), Vazhuvoor, Mysore
Muthulakshmi Reddy: bill (1928) → Act 1929 freeing devadasis
⚠ Bharatanatyam is first refashioned as theatre art; state dance of TN
## Beyond your notes
Exponents: Priyadarsini Govind, Leela Samson, Geeta Chandran, Alarmel Valli, Malavika Sarukkai

topic: Classical dances: canon and the southern forms
t: Kuchipudi vs Bharatanatyam → how to tell them apart
text:
Feature | Kuchipudi | Bharatanatyam
Origin | Bhagavatulu troupes, village dance-drama | Temple devadasis, courts
Traditional dancers | Male Brahmins | Women
Dialogue / singing by dancer | Yes (dance-drama; Daruvu) | No
Brass-plate dance | Tarangam: on plate rim, water pot on head | No
Style | Fluid, rounded, theatrical | Linear, geometric, sharp
Ancestor | Natya Mela | Nattuva Mela
Kuchipudi: Kavutvams = acrobatics; Bhama Kalapam by Siddhendra Yogi; Tirtha Narayana Yati
Patrons: Krishnadevaraya; Abul Hassan Tana Shah (1675) gifted the village
Revival: Vedantam Lakshminarayana Sastri; Vempati Chinna Satyam codified; Yamini Krishnamurthy
⚠ Brass plate is Kuchipudi's, not Bharatanatyam's (2012)
PYQ 2012: answer 1 only: dialogue is Kuchipudi's; statement 2 flips the brass plate

text:
"Story play", Kerala, 17th c; from Krishnanattam via Ramanattam (Kottarakkara Thampuran)
Grew in courts and theatres, unlike temple dances; uses Kalaripayattu moves
Lit by Kalivilakku oil lamp; dusk to dawn; actors are speechless, use mudras of Hastalakshana Deepika
Text: Aattakatha; music Sopanam, language Manipravalam
Drums: Maddalam, Chenda, Idakka; centre: Kerala Kalamandalam (Thrissur)

Pacha (green) | Noble heroes
Kathi (knife) | Villains
Thadi (beard) | Hanuman-type
Kari (black) | Demons
Minukku (radiant) | Women, sages
⚠ Kathakali dancers do not speak; contrast Kuchipudi

topic: Classical dances: Kathak, Odissi, Manipuri, Sattriya and dancers
t: Odissi → poses: Tribhanga, Abhanga, Samabhanga
text:
Pose | Meaning
Tribhanga | Triple bend at neck, torso, knees: "S" shape; one leg bent, body curved oppositely at waist and neck; feminine
Abhanga | Weight on one leg; meditation
Samabhanga | Upright, perfect balance
Chowk | Square, masculine stance
Odissi: maharis of Jagannath, Puri; Gita Govinda ashtapadis; Udayagiri Rani Gumpha and Hathigumpha (Kharavela) evidence
Streams: Mahari (temple), Gotipua (boys as girls), Nartaki (court)

Repertoire ends with Moksha; music: Odissi (Hindustani + Carnatic); drum mardala
Exponents: Kelucharan Mahapatra, Sonal Mansingh, Sanjukta Panigrahi, Madhavi Mudgal

t: Sattriya → Sankardeva's Assam tradition
text:
Born in sattras (Vaishnavite monasteries) of Assam; created by Sankardeva (15th-16th c)
Music + dance + drama; part of one-act Ankiya Nat / Bhaona
Performed by male monks (bhokots); now women too; confined to sattras (mostly Majuli) till mid-20th c
Base: Mati-Akhora; styles Paurashik (male) and Prakriti (female) bhangi
Music: Borgeets of Sankardeva and Madhavdeva; khol drum; Gayan-Bayan interlude
Themes: Krishna, Rama; Brajavali language
Statement (2014) | Verdict
Music, dance, drama | Correct
Living tradition of Vaishnavites of Assam | Correct
Based on songs of Tulsidas, Kabir, Mirabai | Wrong: Sankardeva's borgeets
⚠ Sattriya is Assam's Ekasarana (neo-Vaishnav) art, not north Indian Bhakti songs

Playwright | Plays | Hinge

## 2. Bhasa details
Kalidasa names Bhasa in the prologue of Malavikagnimitram, so Bhasa is earlier
Urubhanga and Karnabhara = the only tragic Sanskrit plays of ancient India

## 1. Features
Feature | Fact
Language | Sanskrit + Prakrit in one play; verse and prose mixed
Who speaks Sanskrit | King and most Brahmins
Who speaks Prakrit | Women and common men / sudras (often Shauraseni Prakrit)
Vidushaka | Stock comic character, always a misshapen Brahmana
Sutradhara | "Holder of strings", coordinates the stage
Ending | Tragedy rejected; plays end happily
Themes from | Mahabharata and Ramayana
Survival | Koodiyattam (Kerala) keeps Sanskrit theatre alive
Kalidasa's Shakuntalam uses Maharashtri Prakrit too
⚠ In Gupta plays women speak Prakrit even if high-born; do not assume queens speak Sanskrit
⚠ Vidushaka is a Brahmana, not a shudra (UPSC 1994)

t: Kingdoms in the Buddha's life → Kosala and Magadha
text:
## 1. Where each event happened
Event | Place | Polity

## 2. Rulers who became disciples
Bimbisara, Ajatashatru (Magadha), Prasenjit (Kosala), Udayana (Vatsa, Kaushambi), Chanda Pradyota (Avanti)

t: Life of the Buddha → ages, family, first disciples
text:
## 1. Family
Father Suddhodana (chief of Shakya gana); mother Mahamaya / Mayadevi, a Koliya princess; raised by aunt Mahaprajapati Gautami
Married Yashodhara at 16; son Rahula
## 2. Milestones
Age | Event | Term / symbol
29 | Four Sights (old man, sick man, corpse, ascetic) | —
29 | Left on horse Kanthaka with charioteer Chhandaka | Mahabhinishkramana (horse)
29-35 | Six years of austerities, then gave them up | —
35 | Enlightenment under peepal, 49th day | Nirvana (Bodhi tree)
35 | First sermon to five disciples | Dhammachakkapavattana (wheel)
80 | Death; last sermon to Subhadda | Mahaparinirvana (stupa)
Five first disciples: Kaundinya (first arhat), Bhaddiya, Vappa, Mahanama, Assaji
First lay followers: merchants Tapassu and Bhallika
Relics split into 8 shares → 8 stupas (+ ashes and urn stupas)

t: Four Noble Truths and Eightfold Path → names and order
text:
## 1. Four Noble Truths (Arya Satya)
# | Truth | Pali term
1 | Life is suffering | Dukkha
2 | Cause of suffering is desire (tanha); some texts say ignorance (avidya) | Samudaya
3 | Suffering ends when desire ends | Nirodha
4 | The way is the Eightfold Path | Magga
## 2. Eightfold Path (Ashtangika Marga) in three groups
Group | Steps
Prajna (wisdom) | Right view (observation), Right intention (determination)
Sila (ethics) | Right speech, Right action, Right livelihood
Samadhi (mind) | Right effort (exercise), Right mindfulness (memory), Right concentration (meditation)
The path is the middle path between luxury and severe penance
Taught first at Sarnath; recorded in the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta
⚠ Order asked in state PYQs: suffering → cause → cessation → path
Panchasheel (for laity): no killing, no lying, no stealing, no misconduct, no intoxicants
Buddhist Triratna = Buddha, Dhamma, Sangha (Jain Triratna = right faith, knowledge, conduct)

t: Core doctrines → nirvana, anicca, anatta, dependent origination
text:
Term | Meaning
Nirvana / Nibbana | "blowing out": extinction of the flame of desire (lust, hatred, delusion); summum bonum; reachable in this life
Parinirvana | final release of an arhat at death
Anicca | impermanence; later the doctrine of momentariness (kshanabhangavada)
Anatta | no permanent self (anatmavada)
Patichcha-samuppada | dependent origination: 12 links (nidanas), starting with avidya
Avyakta | metaphysical questions the Buddha refused to answer
Karma | accepted: actions shape this life and the next
No god and no eternal soul (atman); rebirth and karma accepted
Taught in Prakrit/Pali, the people's language; rationalist; stressed karuna (compassion)
⚠ Nirvana is not "complete annihilation of self" nor "a state beyond comprehension": it is the dying out of passion
PYQ 2013: best description of Nirvana → the extinction of the flame of desire

t: Vassa and Pavarana → what the ceremony was
text:
## 1. Terms
Vassa: three-month rains retreat; monks stay in viharas instead of wandering
Pavarana ("inviting admonition"): held at the end of Vassa; monks invite peers to point out faults and confess offences
## 2. The 2002 options decoded
Option | What it really describes
(a) elect Sanghaparinayaka and two speakers, on Dhamma and on Vinaya | UPSC key answer
(b) confession of offences committed during the rainy-season stay | textbook meaning of Pavarana (Indian Art & Culture)
(c) initiation: head shaved, yellow robes | Pravrajya
(d) gathering after Ashadha full moon to take a fixed abode | start of Vassa
⚠ Sources disagree: the key gives (a), while Indian Art & Culture describes Pavarana as option (b); answer (a) in the exam, but know Pavarana = end of Vassa
PYQ 2002: Pavarana → key (a)
## In news 2025-26
International Abhidhamma Divas (Culture Ministry with IBC; PMF Magnum 2025): marks the Buddha's descent from Tavatimsa heaven to Sankassa (Sankisa, UP); falls at the end of Vassa, on Pavarana

t: Sthaviravadins vs Mahasanghikas → beliefs and offshoots
text:
Point | Sthaviravadins | Mahasanghikas
Rules | strict original Vinaya | relaxed, modified rules
Buddha | human; won nirvana by own effort | divine, transcendent; many Buddhas everywhere
Images | — | first to show the Buddha in human form

Offshoots | Sammitiya, Sarvastivada, Vibhajyavada, Vatsiputriya | Lokottaravada, Ekavyavaharika, Kaukkutika, Prajnaptivada, Caitika
Stronghold | — | Dhanyakataka / Amaravati (Andhra)

t: Early schools → hinge doctrine of each
text:
School | Branch | Hinge doctrine
Sarvastivada | Sthaviravada | "sarvam asti": dharmas exist in past, present, future; not wholly momentary, exist forever in latent form
Vaibhasika | Hinayana sub-sect | (with Sautrantika, the main Hinayana sub-sects)
Sautrantika | Hinayana sub-sect | Buddhist, not Jain
Sammitiya | Sthaviravada offshoot | Buddhist, not Jain
Lokottaravada | Mahasanghika | Buddha supramundane; text Mahavastu

## Beyond your notes
Sautrantika = "those who rely on the suttas", rejecting Abhidharma as final authority
Sammitiya = the main Pudgalavada school: held that a "person" (pudgala) exists

t: Hinayana vs Mahayana → features
text:
Aspect | Hinayana (Theravada) | Mahayana
Buddha | human teacher | deified, worshipped as god
Worship | symbols only, no images | image worship and rituals
Goal | Arhat, own salvation, monks only | Bodhisattva, salvation of all, laity too
Language | Pali | Sanskrit
Canon | Pali Tripitaka | adds Mahayana sutras (Lotus, Prajnaparamita)
Patron | Ashoka | Kanishka
Today | Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia | China, Japan, Korea, Vietnam, Nepal, Sikkim
Sub-sects | Vaibhasika, Sautrantika | Madhyamaka, Yogachara
Mahayana arose c. 1st c BCE in Andhra, became a recognised form under Kanishka; Nagarjuna its leading exponent
Hinayana ("lesser vehicle") is the Mahayanists' label; the old school called itself Theravada (path of the Theras)
⚠ The Bodhisattva concept is central to Mahayana, not Hinayana
PYQ 2019: deification, Bodhisattva path, image worship and rituals → all three are Mahayana
PYQ 2016: Bodhisattva statements → 2 and 3 only

t: Bodhisattva and paramitas → meaning
text:
## 1. Bodhisattva
Being (sattva) seeking enlightenment (bodhi); compassionate; postpones own nirvana to help all beings
Passes 10 bhumis (stages) to Buddhahood; the Buddha in past births was a Bodhisattva
Idea known earlier, but central only in Mahayana

Paramita | Meaning
Dana | generosity
Sila | ethical conduct
Kshanti | patience
Virya | diligence
Dhyana | meditation
Prajna | wisdom

t: Jain doctrine → soul, karma and Universal Law
text:
The world is not created or run by a god; it is eternal and works by Universal Law
Soul (jiva) in everything: animals, plants, even stones, rocks, running water (hylozoism)
Six dravyas: jiva + five ajiva: pudgala (matter), dharma (motion), adharma (rest), akasha (space), kala (time)
Karma = fine matter clinging to the soul; the bane of the soul; removed by penance
Term | Meaning
Asrava | influx of karma
Bandha | bondage of karma
Samvara | stopping the influx
Nirjara | shedding karma (by penance)
Moksha / Kaivalya | liberation / omniscience
Siddha | fully liberated soul
Gods exist but rank below the Jina; Mahavira held birth-varna came from past karma
⚠ PYQ 2011 options Universal Truth, Faith, Soul are wrong: Universal Law
PYQ 2013: penance annihilates karma; every particle has a soul; karma is the bane of the soul → all three Jain
PYQ 2023: souls in rocks and running water → Jainism

t: Forms of existence → the four gatis
text:

Deva | gods
Manushya | humans
Naraki | hell beings
Tiryancha | animals and plants
Tiryancha are graded by the number of senses
Lowest: ekendriya (one sense, touch): tiny nigodas and sthavara (immobile earth, water, fire, air and plant bodies)
Hence Jain practice: no digging earth, no lighting or putting out fire, no needless disturbing of water or air
Strict vegetarianism; even naturally dead animals not eaten (breeding ground for nigodas)
Soul has four infinities: knowledge, perception, bliss, energy
⚠ Yaksha (demi-god) is not one of the four forms
PYQ 2026: not among the four forms of existence → Yaksha

t: Ahimsa and occupation → why Jains became traders
text:
Jainism prohibited war and agriculture: ploughing and tilling kill insects and pests
Farmers found the rules hard → Jainism confined to traders
Lay followers were told to avoid agriculture
Today Jains of Malwa, Gujarat, Rajasthan are mainly in trade and commerce
Monks: walk only by day, sweep the path, pull out hair by hand, beg for food
Point | Jainism | Buddhism
Ahimsa | extreme; even elements | milder; monks ate what was offered
Vegetarianism | strict | not required
Caste of followers | traders, merchants | all groups; merchants prominent
Merchants backed both faiths: non-violence helped trade; money-lending not condemned
⚠ Ahimsa in Buddhism did not necessarily mean vegetarianism

40-day fast of the Sindhis to please Jhulelal, patron deity of Sindhi Hindus, incarnation of Varuna (water god)

t: Motion of Earth or Moon → the phenomenon it causes
text:
## 1. Cause → effect (PMF's master table)
Motion | Causes
Rotation of Earth on its axis | Day and night
Revolution on a tilted axis | Seasons = change in length of day and night season to season
Revolution in an elliptical orbit | Perihelion and aphelion
Revolution of Moon around Earth | Phases of the Moon
Moon's revolution in an elliptical orbit | Perigee and apogee
Moon's revolution on a tilted orbital plane | Solar and lunar eclipses
Tilted plane + elliptical orbit | Different apparent size of the Moon in different solar eclipses
## 2. What does NOT cause seasons
Latitude decides how much sunlight a place gets, not the seasonal change
Elliptical orbit (distance from Sun) only gives perihelion/aphelion
⚠ Seasons = revolution + tilt together; rotation alone gives only day and night
PYQ 2013: variation in day and night length season to season is due to revolution of the Earth on a tilted axis; traps: rotation, elliptical revolution, latitudinal position

t: Rotation → direction, period, axis and tilt
text:
## 1. Key numbers
Feature | Value
Direction | West to east (anticlockwise seen from above the North Pole)
One rotation (sidereal day) | 23 h 56 min 4 s (~24 h)
Axis tilt from the normal to orbital plane | 23.5°
Axis angle with the orbital (ecliptic) plane | 66.5°
Line dividing day from night | Circle of illumination
Axis is antipodal: passes through North Pole, Earth's centre and South Pole
Because Earth rotates west to east, the Sun rises in the east and places to the east are ahead in time
⚠ "Tilted 23.5°" is from the perpendicular; the angle with the plane is 66.5°; both figures appear as options
## 2. Consequences of rotation
Day and night; Coriolis force (deflects winds and currents); equatorial bulge (geoid shape)
Gravity is greater at the poles, less at the equator (bulge + higher centrifugal force at the equator)
## Beyond your notes
Solar day (Sun to Sun, 24 h) is ~4 min longer than the sidereal day because Earth also moves along its orbit
Rotation speed at the equator ~1,670 km/h, zero at the poles

t: Revolution → year, leap year and orbit
text:
## 1. Revolution basics
Orbit plane = ecliptic; one revolution = 365¼ days (365 days 6 h)
Extra ~6 h a year → one day every 4 years → 29 February; 366-day year = leap year
## 2. Perihelion and aphelion
Position | Date (approx.) | Distance from Sun
Perihelion (closest) | ~3 January (2 weeks after December solstice) | 147.3 million km
Aphelion (farthest) | ~4 July (2 weeks after June solstice) | 152.1 million km
Average | - | ~150 million km (150 x 10^6 km)
Dates are not fixed; orbit shifts between near-circular and elliptical roughly every 100,000 years
⚠ Earth is closest to the Sun in January (northern winter): distance does not make seasons
PYQ 2007: average Sun-Earth distance asked; answer 150 x 10^6 km

t: Elliptical orbit → effect on energy and on season length
text:
## 1. Energy received
Solar constant changes very little through the year: eccentricity of Earth's orbit is very small (circle = 0)
Southern Hemisphere's small gain at perihelion is offset by its higher water-to-land ratio
## 2. Length of seasons (Kepler's 2nd law)
Fact | Detail
Orbital speed | Fastest at perihelion, slowest at aphelion
NH summer (June solstice to Sept equinox side) | ~92 days
NH winter | ~89 days
So in the Northern Hemisphere summer is slightly longer than winter
Kepler's 2nd law: line joining planet and Sun sweeps equal areas in equal times
⚠ PMF LENS 2025: it is the constant axial tilt, not distance from the Sun, that determines equinoxes and solstices
Likely next: "Earth is nearest the Sun in July" (false); "elliptical orbit causes seasons" (false)

text:
## 1. June (summer) solstice: NH tilted towards the Sun
Latitude | On 21 June
Tropic of Cancer (23.5°N) | Sun vertically overhead at noon; day >12 h
Arctic Circle (66.5°N) | Sun does not set (24 h daylight for one day)
North Pole | Continuous daylight (polar day, ~6 months)
Equator | ~12 h day (not overhead)
Tropic of Capricorn | Day <12 h: its shortest day
Antarctic Circle | Sun does not rise (24 h night)
Whole NH has longest day, shortest night; whole Arctic region is inside the circle of illumination
In the SH it is the winter solstice
⚠ Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer, not the Equator; it is the Arctic, not the Antarctic, circle that has no sunset

text:
## 1. What happens
Feature | March equinox | September equinox
Date | 20/21 March | 22/23 September
NH season | Spring (vernal) | Autumn
SH season | Autumn | Spring
Sun's onward movement | Northward → June solstice | Southward → December solstice
Other name | Northward equinox | Southward equinox

topic: Solstices, equinoxes and length of day
t: Day length rules → by latitude and season
text:
## 1. Rules
Place / period | Day length
Equator | ~12 h all year (no winter; only wet and dry)
Summer hemisphere | >12 h, rising towards the pole
Winter hemisphere | <12 h
21 March to 23 September | NH gets >12 h of daylight
23 September to 21 March | SH gets >12 h; South Pole has 6-month day
## 2. Days slightly longer than nights at the equator
Cause: atmospheric refraction bends slanting morning/evening rays → Sun visible while still below the horizon
With no atmosphere, day and night at the equator would be near equal
## 3. Midnight sun
At the polar circle: Sun stays up for one day at the solstice; ~100 km poleward for weeks; at the pole for six months
Opposite: polar night in winter
⚠ "Day and night equal throughout the year" → Equator (state PYQ); "equal everywhere" → only on equinoxes

text:
## 1. Latitudinal heat zones
Zone | Between | Feature
Torrid | Tropic of Cancer and Tropic of Capricorn | Noon Sun overhead at least once a year; maximum heat
Temperate (2) | Tropics and polar circles | Sun never overhead; moderate temperatures
Frigid (2) | Beyond Arctic and Antarctic circles | Sun low, rays always slanting; very cold
## 2. Zero Shadow Day
Occurs twice a year only between 23.5°N and 23.5°S; never beyond the tropics
Condition: Sun's declination = latitude of the place → rays perpendicular, shadow under the object
Once between December and June solstice, once between June and December solstice
⚠ Exactly at the Tropics the Sun is overhead only once (on the solstice)

## 1. Normal rotation (west to east)

## 1. Basics
Feature | Fact
Base line | 180° meridian, through the Pacific Ocean
Time on either side | 24 h apart (GMT+12 vs GMT-12)
Crossing east → west (America → Asia) | Lose a day: date jumps ahead (Monday → Tuesday)
Crossing west → east (Asia → America) | Gain a day: date repeats (Tuesday → Monday)
Shape | Zig-zag
## 2. Why zig-zag
Bends at the Bering Strait and around Polynesia, Melanesia, Micronesia (and Aleutians) so that one island country or group keeps one date
Some areas keep Asiatic/NZ time, others the American date
⚠ The western (Asian) side is always one day ahead

t: Declination, dip and magnetic equator → definitions and values
text:
## 1. Terms
Term | Meaning | Values
Declination | Angle between magnetic north and true north | Larger at high latitudes; small in India
Dip (inclination) | Angle of field lines with the horizontal | 0° at magnetic equator, 90° at magnetic poles; ~18° in southern India
Magnetic equator | Irregular line of zero dip | Passes Thumba (Kerala); not fixed
Deviation | Compass error from nearby metal | -
At the true North Pole a compass points to the magnetic north pole
Dip poles: compass needle points straight down at north magnetic pole, straight up at south

text:
## 1. Origin
Generated by convection of molten iron and nickel in the outer core + Coriolis effect = self-sustaining geodynamo
Outer core 4,400°C (outer) to 6,000°C (near inner core)
## 2. Reversal
Feature | Earth | Sun
Reversal | Not periodic: gap 10,000 years to 25 million years | Every 11 years
Average (last 20 Myr) | ~200,000-300,000 years | -
Evidence | Palaeomagnetism in rocks | Sunspot cycle
Last full reversal: Brunhes-Matuyama, ~780,000 years ago; Laschamps excursion ~41,000 years ago = temporary weakening, no full flip
⚠ Laschamps was an excursion, not a reversal
## In news 2025-26
PMF LENS May 2025 ("Magnetic flip-flop"): field weakened ~10% in 200 years; North Magnetic Pole moving to Siberia at ~35 km/year; risk to aviation, satellites, NavIC
⚠ PMF Physical Geography gives the drift as ~10 km/yr historically, ~40 km/yr lately; LENS gives ~35 km/yr

text:
## 1. Leap second
Earth's rotation is gradually slowing (tidal friction of Moon and Sun) → atomic time (UTC) drifts ahead
Leap second (one-second "stop" in UTC) added periodically since 1972
## 2. Related findings
Finding | Effect
Inner core slowed since 2010 (rotates slower than surface) | Tiny day-length change; fewer leap seconds needed
Polar ice melt (Greenland, Antarctica) | Water moves towards the equator → alters rotation and axis
Inner core: solid iron-nickel, radius ~1,220 km, ~5,200°C
PYQ 2025 (Statement I-II-III): axis/rotation shift is real; statements on solar flares and ice melt both correct, but only ice melt moving water to the equator explains it
## In news 2025-26
PMF LENS Feb 2025 / Geo Magnum 2026: study confirms inner core slowing, linked to outer-core turbulence and mantle gravity

## 1. Layers (PMF)
Layer | Depth | State / composition
Crust | ~8 km under oceans, ~30 km under continents (to Moho) | Continental: felsic, granite (sial); oceanic: mafic, basalt (sima)
Asthenosphere | Below lithosphere to 80-200 km | Viscous, weak, ductile; main source of magma
Outer core | 2,900-5,100 km | Liquid iron-nickel; convection → magnetic field (dynamo)
Inner core | 5,100 km to centre | Solid iron (~80%) + nickel (NiFe); ~6,000 °C
## 2. Discontinuities
Discontinuity | Separates
Conrad | Upper and lower continental crust
Mohorovicic (Moho) | Crust and mantle
Gutenberg | Mantle and outer core
Lehmann | Outer and inner core
Core = ~16% of Earth's volume but ~33% of its mass

## 1. Share of volume and mass (PMF)
Part | Volume | Mass | Key facts
Crust | ~1% | <1% | Temperature rises ~30 °C per km in upper crust
Mantle | ~83% | ~67% | Moho to 2,900 km; 45% O, 23% Mg, 21% Si; ~200 °C to ~4,000 °C
Core | ~16% | ~33% | Iron-nickel; outer liquid, inner solid
## 2. Rigid vs weak layers
Layer | Made of | Behaviour
Lithosphere (10-200 km) | Crust + upper mantle | Rigid; broken into tectonic plates
Asthenosphere (to 80-200 km) | Upper mantle | Weak, ductile; plates glide on it; isostasy
Lower mantle | Solid silicates | Density 3.3-5.7 g/cm3

t: P, S and surface waves → nature and order of arrival
text:
## 1. Body and surface waves (PMF)
Wave | Nature | Medium | Order / damage
P (primary) | Longitudinal: particles vibrate to and fro along propagation | Solid, liquid, gas | Fastest (~1.7x S), recorded first, least destructive
S (secondary) | Transverse: particles vibrate at right angles | Solids only | Second
Love | Surface, side to side | Surface | Fastest surface wave
Rayleigh | Surface, rolling | Surface | Most damage
Surface (L) waves are slowest, recorded last, most destructive
## 2. Shadow zones
S-wave shadow: beyond 103° from epicentre → proof of liquid outer core
P-wave shadow: band 103°-142° (refraction at mantle-core boundary)
⚠ P waves also travel through liquids; only S waves stop
PYQ 2023: both statements correct (P first; P longitudinal, S transverse)

t: Shadow zones → what they reveal
text:
## 1. Zones by angular distance from the epicentre (PMF)
Distance from epicentre | Waves received | Inference
0°-103° | Both P and S | Crust and mantle are solid
103°-142° | Neither (shadow for both) | Refraction at mantle-core boundary
Beyond 142° | P only, no S | S cannot cross liquid outer core
## 2. Why velocity changes
Seismic velocity rises with elasticity and density; waves reflect/refract at boundaries
Sudden velocity jumps mark discontinuities: Moho (crust-mantle), Gutenberg (mantle-core)
P-wave velocity: <6 km/s in crust, ~13.5 km/s in lower mantle, ~11 km/s in inner core
Early warning: detect fast, harmless P waves; up to 60-90 s before destructive waves
⚠ The S-wave shadow (beyond 103°) is the proof of a liquid outer core; P shadow is a band only
PYQ 2023 angle: arrival order on a seismograph is P → S → surface (L)

text:
## 1. Seafloor spreading (Harry Hess, 1960)
At mid-ocean ridges basaltic magma rises, cools and forms new ocean floor; older floor moves away
Driven by mantle convection (Arthur Holmes, 1930s): rising limbs push plates apart, falling limbs pull them together
## 2. Evidence (PMF)
Evidence | Observation
Magnetic striping | Alternate normal/reversed polarity stripes, symmetric on both sides of ridges
Age of floor | Youngest at ridge, oldest near trenches; ocean floor far younger than continents
Sediment thickness | Thin near ridges, thicker away
Heat flow, quakes | High at ridges
Palaeomagnetism = magnetism locked in rocks at formation; it revived Wegener's idea

Process | How
Exfoliation (unloading / sheeting) | Overburden removed → outer sheets peel off granite domes
Thermal stress | Day-night heating and cooling; dry, high places
Granular disintegration | Dark grains expand more than light grains
Frost wedging, freeze-thaw | Water in cracks freezes (+9% volume)
Block disintegration | Splitting along joints into blocks
Salt crystallisation, wetting-drying | Arid coasts
## 2. Rock cycle
Igneous → (weathering) → sedimentary → (heat, pressure) → metamorphic → (melting via subduction) → magma → igneous
Any rock can become metamorphic; crustal rocks return to the mantle by subduction

Fold (young) | Compression at convergent edges | Himalaya, Alps, Andes, Rockies, Atlas
Fold (old) | Pre-Pangaea collision | Appalachians, Urals
Block | Faulting: horst (up) and graben (down) | Vosges (France), Black Forest (Germany), Vindhya, Satpura, Sierra Nevada
Volcanic | Accumulation | Kilimanjaro, Fuji, Cascades, Mauna Kea
Residual | Denudation of old mountains | Aravallis, Urals
Rhine Valley = graben between Vosges and Black Forest horsts
Orogenies: Caledonian (Appalachians, Aravallis), Hercynian (Vosges, Black Forest, Urals), Alpine (Himalaya, Alps, Rockies, Atlas)
⚠ Vosges is a block mountain in Europe, not a fold mountain in Central Asia
⚠ Alps are fold, not block
PYQ 2024: rows 3 (Appalachians fold) and 4 (Andes fold) right → only two

t: Mountains by orogeny → age and examples
text:
## 1. Orogenies (PMF)
Orogeny | Period | Examples
Precambrian | Before 541 mya | Laurentian, Algoman (residual)
Caledonian | ~430-380 mya | Appalachians, Aravallis, Mahadeo; Scottish Highlands

Location | Examples

t: Fold and block mountains → features
text:
## 1. Fold mountains (PMF)
Youngest, longest but narrow; marine fossils in sedimentary rock; granite intrusions
Formed at C-C (Himalaya, Alps, Atlas, Urals, Appalachians) or C-O convergence (Rockies, Andes)
Simple folds vs complex folds; detached recumbent folds = nappe (Himalaya)
No volcanoes in Himalaya (C-C, thick crust); volcanoes in Andes (C-O)
## 2. Block mountains
Term | Meaning | Example
Horst | Uplifted block | Vosges, Black Forest
Graben | Down-dropped block | Rhine Valley, East African Rift, Narmada valley
Tilted block | One steep, one gentle side | Sierra Nevada
Lifted block | Flat top, steep sides | 
Andes = longest range; Himalaya still rising (~5-10 cm/yr per PMF)

topic: Earth's dynamic system: forces, magnetism, rotation
t: Forces → endogenic or exogenic
text:
## 1. Forces that change the surface
Force | Type | Acts through
Geothermal energy (radioactive decay ~50% of heat) | Endogenic | Convection → plate movement, folding, faulting
Plate movement | Endogenic | Diastrophism, quakes, volcanoes
Gravity | Both | Pressure gradients; mass wasting
Electromagnetic (solar) radiation | Exogenic | Weather → weathering, erosion
Rotation | Both | Coriolis steers convection, winds, currents
Revolution | Exogenic | Seasons
Diastrophism: orogenic (mountain building: folding, faulting) and epeirogenic (continent-forming: uplift, subsidence)
Denudation = weathering + erosion (exogenic)
PYQ 2013: all six are responsible → 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6

topic: Earth's dynamic system: forces, magnetism, rotation
t: Endogenic movements → diastrophism types
text:
## 1. Classification (PMF)
Movement | Speed | Type | Result
Orogenic | Slow | Diastrophic: mountain building | Folding, faulting along narrow belts
Epeirogenic | Slow | Diastrophic: continent building | Uplift, subsidence, warping of large areas
Earthquakes | Sudden | Sudden movement | Local displacement
Volcanism | Sudden | Sudden movement | Eruptions, intrusions
Energy source: radioactive decay + gravity (pressure gradients) → mantle convection → plate movement
Exogenic: weathering, mass wasting, erosion, deposition (denudation) powered by the Sun
Earthquakes can uplift or sink land: New Zealand 1885 (+3 m), Japan 1891 (-6 m)
⚠ Folding results from orogenic (compressional) force, not epeirogenic

topic: Earth's dynamic system: forces, magnetism, rotation
t: Evolution and mass extinctions → geological drivers
text:
## 1. Drift, ice ages and life
Continental drift shifts climate zones and separates populations (Glossopteris, Mesosaurus, lemurs)
Glacial cycles: Gondwana's drift to South Pole → Ordovician glaciation → first mass extinction
Extinction | Linked geological cause (PMF)
Ordovician-Silurian | Glaciation, sea-level fall
Late Devonian | Sea-level change, ocean anoxia, cooling
Permian-Triassic (largest, ~250 mya) | Siberian Traps flood basalt
Cretaceous-Paleogene (~66 mya) | Chicxulub meteor + Deccan Traps (Reunion hotspot)
Stromatolites (cyanobacteria) drove the Great Oxidation Event ~2.4 billion years ago; Chambaghat (HP) site in news 2025 (CARE)
PYQ 2014 angle: both drift and glacial cycles shaped evolution

topic: Earth's dynamic system: forces, magnetism, rotation
t: Magnetic field and early atmosphere → facts
text:
## 1. Geomagnetic reversal (PMF)
Field comes from convection in liquid outer core (geodynamo)
Poles flipped roughly every 200,000-300,000 years over the last 20 million years; not periodic (10,000 years to 25 million years)
North Magnetic Pole near Ellesmere Island, drifting towards Siberia (~40 km/yr)
## 2. Early atmosphere (PMF)
Stage | Composition
Hadean | Volcanic outgassing: CO2, N2, water vapour, almost no oxygen
Archean | No oxygen; cyanobacteria begin photosynthesis
~2.4 billion yrs ago | Great Oxidation Event: free oxygen appears
~280 million yrs ago | Oxygen peaked ~30%; today 21%
⚠ Early Earth had no free oxygen: "54% oxygen and no CO2" is false
PYQ 2018: statements 1 (reversals) and 3 (life modified atmosphere) → 1 and 3 only
## In news 2025-26
Study: magnetic reversals may last much longer than thought (PMF Prelims Magnum 2027 Q1)

topic: Earth's dynamic system: forces, magnetism, rotation
t: Earth's axis and rotation → what shifts them
text:
## 1. Mass redistribution moves the axis
Cause | Effect
Polar ice melt (Greenland, Antarctica) → water moves to equator | Axis shifts; day lengthens slightly
2004 Sumatra quake | North Pole shifted ~2.5 cm; day shortened 2.68 microseconds (PMF)
Tidal friction (Moon) | Rotation slows ~1.4 ms per 100 years (PMF)
Solar flares / CMEs | Energy hits upper atmosphere only: not a cause of axis shift
Earth's axis tilt 23.5°; Moon stabilises it
⚠ 2025: Statements II and III are both true, but only III explains I → (b)
PYQ 2025: polar ice melt moving water to the equator explains the axis shift
## Beyond your notes
Large-scale groundwater pumping also measurably shifted Earth's rotational pole (2023 study, verify)
Melting ice also loads/unloads crust and can trigger seismicity (CARE, July 2025)

topic: Composition: gases, water vapour and dust
t: Water vapour → where it is maximum and how it varies
text:
## 1. Distribution
Feature | Fact
Share of air volume | 0.02% (cold, dry) to 4% (humid tropics): the most variable gas
With altitude | Decreases: 90% of moisture lies within 6 km of the surface
With latitude | Decreases from equator towards poles (maximum in equatorial/tropical belt)
Upper limit | Found only up to about 90 km (PMF)
## 2. Role
Absorbs long-wave terrestrial radiation AND part of incoming short-wave (visible, UV)
Only water vapour and ozone absorb both incoming and outgoing radiation; CO2 is transparent to incoming solar radiation
Source of clouds and precipitation; condensation releases latent heat, the driving force of storms
⚠ PYQ 2024: "percentage maximum at the poles" is false: cold polar air holds the least vapour
PYQ 2024: two statements: decreases with altitude (correct), maximum at poles (wrong); answer 1 only
PYQ 2003 (A-R): moisture varies with latitude because the capacity to hold vapour depends on temperature

topic: Composition: gases, water vapour and dust
t: Dust and solid particles → where more and why
text:
## 1. Sources and role
Sand (weathered rock), volcanic ash, pollen, small organisms, soot, sea salt, burnt meteor fragments
Concentrated in the lower atmosphere; convection lifts some higher
Hygroscopic dust and salt act as condensation nuclei for clouds, fog, rain, hail
Absorb, reflect and scatter radiation: red and orange sunrise/sunset, length of dawn and twilight
## 2. Latitudinal distribution
Belt | Dust load | Why
Subtropical and temperate | More | Dry winds, deserts, little rain to wash dust out
Equatorial | Less | High humidity and daily rain suppress and wash out dust
Polar | Less | Surface under snow and ice, few dust sources
⚠ PYQ 2025: Statement II said subtropical belts have "less dry winds": false; dust is more because of dry winds (answer c)
⚠ PMF credits the blue sky to selective scattering by dust; physics texts credit scattering of short blue wavelengths by gas molecules
## In news 2025-26
Urban aerosols add condensation nuclei: monsoon rain disproportionately high over cities, low over rural areas (PMF)

topic: Composition: gases, water vapour and dust
t: Permanent gases → share by volume and order
text:
## 1. Composition of dry air
Gas | PMF % | Preview %
Nitrogen | 78.08 | 78.084
Oxygen | 20.95 | 20.947

Order: N2 > O2 > Ar > CO2 > Ne > He; N2 + O2 = about 99%
Permanent gases (fixed proportion): N2, O2, Ar; CO2, ozone, water vapour vary
⚠ CO2 0.036% in PMF is an old figure; today it is about 0.042% (424 ppm): Preview's figure matches current data
⚠ Argon, not CO2, is the third most abundant gas

topic: Composition: gases, water vapour and dust
t: Major constituents → role and height limit
text:
Constituent | Key fact
Oxygen | Needed for respiration and combustion; negligible above 120 km
Nitrogen | Inert; dilutes oxygen and controls combustion; fixed by bacteria and lightning
CO2 | Transparent to incoming, opaque to outgoing radiation; key to heat budget
Ozone | <0.00005% of volume; maximum at 20-30 km (lower stratosphere); absorbs UV
Water vapour | 0-4%; absorbs both radiations; source of latent heat
Solid particles | Condensation nuclei; scattering
Heavier gases (N2, O2) stay near the bottom; lighter gases rise higher
CO2 and water vapour only up to 90 km (PMF)
⚠ Preview gives a different height table: CO2 up to 20 km, O2 and N2 up to 100 km, H2 up to 125 km; follow PMF in a PMF-style question
Uses: N2 in chips packets (prevents rancidity); argon/nitrogen in bulbs (protect filament)

topic: Composition: gases, water vapour and dust
t: Evolution of the atmosphere → stages
text:
Stage | Atmosphere
First | Gases of solar nebula, mainly hydrogen and helium (lost to space)
Hadean | Volcanic outgassing: heavy CO2, N2, water vapour; almost no oxygen
After oceans form | Most CO2 dissolved in oceans, some locked as carbonates
Late Archean | Cyanobacteria begin photosynthetic oxygen
~2.4 billion years ago | Free oxygen appears (Great Oxidation)
~280 mya | Oxygen peaked near 30%; today 21%
Light gases (H, He) still escape from the exosphere (atmospheric escape); Earth's magnetic field limits it
PYQ 2018: "54% oxygen and no CO2 at Earth's creation" is false; living organisms did modify the early atmosphere

t: Layers upward → height and temperature trend
text:
Layer (upward) | Height (PMF) | Temperature with height
Troposphere | 0-12 km (8 poles, 18 equator) | Falls 6.5°C/km
Tropopause | boundary | Constant
Stratosphere | 12-50 km | Constant, then rises to 0°C (ozone)
Mesosphere | 50-80 km | Falls to about -85°C (mesopause)
Thermosphere (ionosphere 80-400 km) | 80-700 km | Rises rapidly
Exosphere | above 700 km | Rises gradually
Mnemonic order: T-S-M-T-E; ionosphere is part of the thermosphere
⚠ Heights differ by source: Preview: troposphere to 15 km, ionosphere 80-640 km, exosphere above 640 km; PMF exosphere 700 to 1,000 (or 10,000) km
PYQ 1998: order upward = troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, ionosphere; trap options put ionosphere below mesosphere
Speed of sound follows the temperature profile

t: Troposphere → why thicker at the equator
text:
## 1. Thickness
Place | Height of tropopause | Temperature at tropopause
Equator | ~18 km | -80°C (colder: thicker layer)
Poles | ~8 km | -45°C
Average | ~12-13 km | 
## 2. Cause
High insolation at the equator heats the surface; strong convection currents carry heat to great heights
Weak heating and weak convection at the poles: thin troposphere
Troposphere also thicker in summer than in winter (same logic)
⚠ The tropopause is coldest over the equator, not the poles, because the air has risen higher
PYQ 2024 (Statement I-II) and PYQ 2004 (A-R): thickness greater at equator and convection explains it; answer (a) both times
## In news 2025-26
Weather balloons (LENS May 2025): Teisserenc de Bort (balloons from 1896) discovered the tropopause and stratosphere; India has 56 radiosonde stations; launches at 0000 and 1200 UTC (5:30 AM/PM IST); balloons reach about 35 km

t: Troposphere → features
text:
Contains almost all water vapour and dust: all weather (clouds, rain, fog, hail, cyclones)
Convective region: all convection stops at the tropopause
Normal lapse rate 6.5°C per km (1°C per ~165 m)
Marked by turbulence, eddies and local temperature inversions
Holds about 90% of the atmosphere's mass (90% below 16 km)
Boundary | Feature
Tropopause | Constant temperature; lapse rate zero
Stratopause | ~50 km, about 0°C
Mesopause | ~80 km, coldest level
Jet streams blow just below the tropopause: polar jet 6-9 km, subtropical jet 10-16 km (troposphere is higher in low latitudes)
⚠ "Ozone layer lies in the troposphere" is a common distractor: it is in the stratosphere
Exam angle: "most weather activity occurs in" = troposphere, not ozonosphere or ionosphere

t: Stratosphere → why jet aircraft fly in it
text:
## 1. Features
From tropopause to 50 km; temperature constant at first, then rises (negative lapse rate) to 0°C at 50 km
Rise caused by ozone absorbing UV
Very dry: little water vapour, so almost no clouds or weather
Warm air above cold air: stable, no vertical (convective) winds
## 2. Why jets fly here
Reason | True?
No clouds or water vapour | Yes (almost)
No vertical winds/turbulence | Yes
Ozone reduces fuel use | No
Constant temperature helps engines | No
⚠ Exceptions: cirrus in lower stratosphere and Polar Stratospheric (nacreous) Clouds, 15-25 km, polar winter
PYQ 2011: official answer both 1 and 2; PMF notes "no clouds" is absolute, so (b) was arguable
Aircraft fly in the lower stratosphere or upper troposphere

t: Ozone layer → where it is and what it does
text:
Feature | Fact
Ozonosphere | 20-55 km (stratosphere + lower mesosphere)
Ozone layer (max concentration) | 20-30 km (PMF)
Heating | Temperature rises about 5°C/km through it
Other name | Chemosphere (O2 split by UV, O + O2 → O3)
Destroyers | Chlorine, bromine radicals from CFCs, halons; one radical breaks 100,000+ O3
PSCs (water, nitric acid, sulphuric acid) give surfaces that turn reservoir halogens into reactive forms: Antarctic ozone hole in spring
Methane is not an ODS (no halogen)
⚠ Height varies: PMF 20-30 km; Preview and PMF Environment 15-35 km
## In news 2025-26
Antarctic ozone hole (CAMS, Sept 2026): expanded to about 25 million sq km, ~5 million above average; extreme cold formed more PSCs; ozone hole = total column ozone below 220 Dobson Units; called short-term polar-vortex variability, not a failure of ODS phase-out
Ozone hole and GHGs strengthened westerlies, driving Antarctic sea-ice loss since 2015 (May 2026)

t: Mesosphere → meteors and the coldest level
text:
## 1. Facts
50-80 km; temperature falls with height
Mesopause: coldest place in the atmosphere, about -85°C (PMF)
Meteors burn up here: enough gas for friction (thermosphere and exosphere too thin)
Noctilucent clouds: polar-mesospheric ice-crystal clouds, 76-85 km: the highest clouds, seen at sunset/sunrise
Highest clouds | Layer | Height
Noctilucent | Mesosphere | 76-85 km
Nacreous (PSCs) | Lower stratosphere | 15-25 km
Cirrus | Upper troposphere | 8-12 km
⚠ "Meteors burn in the thermosphere/ionosphere" is the trap: they burn in the mesosphere
## In news 2025-26
Geminid meteor shower (Dec 2025): debris of asteroid 3200 Phaethon; meteors burn in the mesosphere
Super Typhoon Sinlaku (June 2026): latent heat from eyewall towers generated atmospheric gravity waves reaching the mesosphere (80-100 km)

t: Thermosphere and ionosphere → radio waves, auroras, satellites
text:
## 1. Thermosphere (80-700 km)
Temperature rises rapidly (solar radiation) but air so thin that no heat is felt
ISS and many satellites orbit here; auroras in its lower part
Kármán line, 100 km: boundary of space; crossing it makes one an astronaut
## 2. Ionosphere (80-400 km, part of thermosphere)
Feature | Fact
Formed by | EUV and X-rays ionising gases: layer of free electrons
Use | Reflects radio waves (HF skywaves): long-distance communication
Not reflected | Frequencies above critical frequency; microwaves absorbed
Auroras | Borealis (north), Australis (south)
⚠ PYQ 2011: ionosphere reflects radio waves because of free electrons, not ozone, and not simply because of long wavelength: answer neither
PYQ 1996: layer that deflects radio waves = ionosphere
## In news 2025-26
Indian researchers built the first method to reconstruct the topside ionosphere over India (PIB, July 2026); LENS: ionosphere 60 to 1,000+ km, expands by day, shrinks at night, disrupted by solar flares
SMILE (ESA + Chinese Academy of Sciences, Vega-C, 2026): solar wind-magnetosphere-ionosphere link

t: Exosphere and mass of the atmosphere → key numbers
text:
## 1. Exosphere
Uppermost layer, above ~700 km (Preview: above 640 km); extremely rarefied; temperature rises slowly
Atmospheric escape: hydrogen and helium lost to space
Medium and high Earth orbit satellites lie here (little drag)
## 2. Mass distribution
Height | Share of mass below it
5.6 km | 50%
16 km | 90%
100 km (Kármán line) | 99.99997%
## 3. Importance of the atmosphere
Life-giving gases; regulates entry of solar radiation; blocks UV, solar wind, cosmic rays
Temperature balance: without it, extreme day-night contrasts
Burns meteors (mesosphere); pressure allows liquid water on the surface
⚠ Preview says communication satellites lie in the exosphere (geostationary ~36,000 km); PMF places ISS and LEO satellites in the thermosphere

t: Insolation → wavelengths and who absorbs what
text:
## 1. Insolation
Incoming solar radiation: received as short waves (UV, visible, near-infrared)
Measured per sq cm per minute; Earth's surface re-emits long-wave infrared (terrestrial radiation)
Solar constant: energy received at the top of the atmosphere, nearly constant
## 2. Absorption in the atmosphere
Radiation | Absorbed by
UV (incoming) | Ozone in the stratosphere
Near-infrared (incoming) | Water vapour, ozone, other gases in the troposphere
Visible (incoming) | Mostly passes through (atmosphere transparent)
Long-wave infrared (outgoing) | Water vapour, CO2, other GHGs
⚠ PYQ 2023: infrared is not visible; it lies beyond red
⚠ PYQ 2023: infrared is not two-thirds of insolation (roughly half)
PYQ 2023: correct statement: infrared is largely absorbed by water vapour concentrated in the lower atmosphere

t: Insolation by latitude → equator vs poles
text:
Fact | Value
Equator vs pole insolation | About 2.4-2.5 times, not 10 times
Highest temperatures | Around 20°N (subtropical deserts), not the equator
Thermal equator | North of geographical equator (more land in NH)
Perihelion (3 Jan) | 147.3 million km: insolation slightly more
Aphelion (4 July) | 152.1 million km: effect masked by land-sea and tilt
Insolation falls polewards as rays become slanting and pass through more atmosphere
Equator gets less than subtropics because of heavy cloud cover
## Beyond your notes
Solar constant about 1.94 calories per sq cm per minute; Earth intercepts about one two-billionth of the Sun's output
Spectrum: UV small share, visible a little under half, infrared about half (sources vary)
⚠ PYQ 2023 trap: "equator gets 10 times the poles": false
Preview (UPPSC 2002, MPPSC 2010): "zone of maximum temperature lies along the equator" is false: it is near 20°N

t: Heat transfer → radiation, conduction, convection, advection
text:
Mode | How | Atmospheric example
Radiation | No medium needed | Sun to Earth; Earth's long-wave radiation
Conduction | Molecule to molecule, no movement | Lowest air layers warmed by ground contact
Convection | Vertical movement of matter | Rising warm air; limited to troposphere
Advection | Horizontal transfer by wind | Loo; warm/cold air masses
Air is a bad conductor: conduction heats only the lowest layers
Denser materials (iron, water) conduct better
## Beyond your notes
In middle latitudes most day-to-night variation is due to advection; in tropics (northern India in summer) the loo is an advection product
⚠ The atmosphere is heated indirectly: Sun → surface (short-wave) → air (long-wave, conduction, convection)
Exam angle: "atmosphere receives most heat directly from the Sun" is false (UPPSC 1997 A-R: true is "indirectly from the Sun, directly from Earth's surface")

t: Factors of temperature distribution → list
text:
Factor | Effect
Angle of incidence | Vertical rays heat more (equator); slanting rays less
Duration of sunshine | Long summer days: more heat
Transparency | Dust, clouds, vapour scatter, reflect, absorb
Albedo | Snow reflects 70-90%: cold stays cold
Land-sea differential | Land heats/cools fast; sea slow
Prevailing winds | Carry heat between latitudes, land and sea
Aspect of slope | Sun-facing slopes warmer and drier
Ocean currents | Warm North Atlantic Drift keeps UK mild
Altitude | ~1°C fall per 150-165 m in troposphere
Scattering when wavelength > particle size (gas); reflection when wavelength < particle size (dust)
Mountains: Himalaya shields India from Siberian cold; Rockies and Andes block oceanic influence
## In news 2025-26
2022 South Asian heatwaves study (April 2025): dry soil left little energy for evaporation, so incoming radiation heated the air; March heat from Rossby wave amplification, April from soil-moisture loss

t: Albedo → descending order of surfaces
text:
Surface | Albedo
Fresh snow | 80-90%
Thick cloud | 70-80%
Old snow | 45-50%
Concrete | 40-50%
Desert | 30-45%
Thin cloud | 25-35%
Grass, soil, crops | 10-25%
Forest | 10-20%
Oceans | 6-10%
Asphalt | 5%
Land albedo > water; 0 = black body, 1 = perfect reflector
Planets: Venus 0.84 highest; Mercury 0.14
⚠ Earth's albedo: PMF 0.37, Preview 30%, NCERT heat budget 35 units
PYQ 2002: decreasing albedo Tundra > Taiga > Tropical deciduous > Tropical evergreen; PYQ 2010: fresh snow reflects most; PYQ 2008: Mercury's albedo is lower than Earth's
## In news 2025-26
Elevation-dependent warming (LENS July 2026): high Kashmir stations warm faster, driven by surface-albedo feedback; HKH warms about 3 times the global average

t: Atmosphere heated from below → terrestrial radiation
text:
## 1. Mechanism
Atmosphere is mostly transparent to incoming short waves
Surface absorbs them and re-radiates long waves (infrared)
GHGs (CO2, water vapour) absorb long waves: lower air warms
Statement | Truth
Heated more by incoming solar than terrestrial radiation | False
GHGs are good absorbers of long-wave radiation | True
Atmosphere heated indirectly by the Sun | True
Cloudy nights warmer than clear nights | True: clouds absorb and return long waves
⚠ PYQ 2024 trap: Statement I reversed the source of heat: answer (d) Statement I incorrect, II correct
Mountain climbers get colder though closer to the Sun: heat comes from the ground

t: Heat budget → the 100-unit balance
text:
## Beyond your notes (NCERT Fundamentals of Physical Geography)
Of 100 units of insolation | Units
Reflected by clouds | 27
Reflected by snow and ice | 2
Scattered back to space | 6
Total albedo | 35
Absorbed by atmosphere directly | 14
Absorbed by surface | 51
Surface → space directly | 17
Surface → atmosphere | 34 (6 absorption, 9 convection, 19 latent heat)
Atmosphere → space | 48 (14 + 34)
Outgoing 17 + 48 = 65 = absorbed 65: Earth neither warms nor cools overall
PMF: Earth takes in short waves and returns long waves; this give-and-take keeps temperature constant
⚠ Latent heat (19) is the largest of the surface-to-air transfers
Planetary albedo here = 35%

t: Latitudinal heat balance → surplus and deficit zones
text:
Zone | Balance | Why
Equator to 40° N and S | Surplus | Abundant, near-vertical sun
Beyond 40° | Deficit | Slant rays, high polar albedo
30-50° (mid-latitudes) | Main transfer belt | Jet streams, temperate cyclones
Tropics do not keep heating up because winds and ocean currents carry surplus heat poleward
Without this, only mid-latitudes would be habitable
## In news 2025-26
2024 the warmest year on record (WMO State of Climate in Asia, Prelims Magnum 2026): 1991-2024 warming in Asia double the 1961-1990 rate; 23 of 24 monitored Himalayan and Tian Shan glaciers lost mass
⚠ Exam angle: "most heat transfer occurs across the equator" is false: it is across the mid-latitudes

t: Greenhouse effect → why Earth is not frozen
text:
## 1. Natural greenhouse effect
Average surface temperature ~15°C; without it about -18°C (well below freezing)
Water aerosols (vapour, ice, fog, sea-salt droplets) give over 95% of greenhouse warming
CO2 second after water vapour; near the surface CO2 matters more (denser than air)
GHG | Note
Water vapour | Strongest and most abundant
CO2 | Transparent to incoming, opaque to outgoing
Methane | 20-year GWP 84; ~30% of warming since pre-industrial (UNEP)
Nitrous oxide | Long-lived
CFCs, ozone | Also trap infrared
⚠ PYQ 2025: all three statements correct: no atmosphere → below freezing; trapped heat keeps average; CO2 good absorber
PYQ 2012: CO2 warms air because it absorbs the infrared part (outgoing), not UV, not all radiation
Greenhouse analogy: glass passes visible light, blocks outgoing infrared

t: Clouds → which cool and which warm
text:
Cloud | Albedo | Net effect
Low, thick (stratus) | 70-80% | Cooling: reflect sunlight; emit IR to space nearly as much as to surface
High, thin (cirrus) | 25-30% | Warming: let sunlight in, trap outgoing IR
Low clouds are now commoner than high clouds: net cooling today
Warming may bring more high, fewer low clouds: cloud feedback turns warming
Aerosols act as condensation nuclei: more, brighter clouds, more cooling (indirect effect)
⚠ PYQ 2022: both statements reversed (high clouds "cool", low clouds "warm"): answer neither
## In news 2025-26
EarthCARE (JAXA + ESA, on Falcon 9): studies clouds, aerosols and radiation; four instruments: ATLID (lidar), CPR (radar), MSI, BBR; sun-synchronous orbit ~393 km

text:

WMO Greenhouse Gas Bulletin 2025 (Oct 2025), values for 2024 | Figure
CO2 | 423.9 ppm, up 3.5 ppm: largest rise since 1957
CO2 vs pre-industrial | 152%
Methane | 1942 ppb (266%); ~16% of radiative forcing
Nitrous oxide | 338 ppb (125%)

CARE: CO2 rose from 377.1 ppm (2004), a 12.5% rise in 20 years
