Hunga Tonga (2022, P-MCA 2025): underwater eruption sent water vapour into the stratosphere: no cooling; vapour is a potent GHG and aids ozone loss

t: Stratospheric aerosol injection → how it cools
text:
## In news 2025-26
Solar geoengineering (Solar Radiation Management): inject SO2 into the stratosphere
SO2 + water vapour → sulphate aerosols reflect sunlight: raises albedo
Copies the cooling after big volcanic eruptions
2025 study | Figure
12 million tonnes SO2 a year at 13 km | ~0.6°C cooling
For 1°C cooling | 21 million tonnes
Higher aerosols stay longer (months to years), especially near the equator where the stratosphere is higher
Risks: disrupted monsoon, delayed ozone recovery, acid rain, more cooling at poles than tropics, masks warming
⚠ SAI is Solar Radiation Management, not Carbon Dioxide Removal

topic: Vertical distribution: lapse rate and inversion
t: Temperature falls with height → the reasons
text:
Reason | Valid?
Atmosphere heated from the surface upward | Yes
Air less dense above (holds less heat; expands and cools) | Yes
GHGs (CO2, vapour) concentrated near surface | Yes
More moisture in upper air | No: moisture decreases upward
Closer to the Sun so should be warmer | Irrelevant
Falling pressure lets rising air expand and cool (adiabatic)
Applies only to the troposphere
⚠ PYQ 2012 trap: "more moisture in the upper atmosphere" is false: answer 1 and 3 only
PMF CA 2025: heat from conduction and long-wave radiation weakens with height; convection makes rising air expand and cool

topic: Vertical distribution: lapse rate and inversion
t: Lapse rates → normal, dry and wet values
text:
Rate | Value | Applies to
Normal / environmental | 6.5°C/km (1°C per ~165 m) | Still air of troposphere
Dry adiabatic (DALR) | 9.8°C/km | Rising unsaturated air
Wet adiabatic (WALR) | ~4°C/km (variable) | Rising saturated air
Adiabatic: no heat exchange; change only from pressure/volume
Rising air expands and cools; sinking air is compressed and warms
WALR is lower because condensation releases latent heat
Lapse rate sign | Layer
Positive (falls with height) | Troposphere
Zero | Tropopause
Negative (rises with height) | Stratosphere; inversions
⚠ PMF gives the normal rate as 1°C per 150-155 m in one place and 153-165 m in another: use 6-6.5°C/km
Katabatic wind: air warming adiabatically as it descends a slope

topic: Vertical distribution: lapse rate and inversion
t: Atmospheric stability → comparing lapse rates
text:
Condition | Rule | Weather
Absolute stability | Rising parcel cools faster than the air around (PMF: parcel's rate > DALR) | Little moisture: no rain
Conditional stability | Rate lies between WALR and DALR | Normal moisture: may or may not rain
Absolute instability | Rising parcel cools slower than the air around (PMF: rate < WALR) | Excess moisture: thunderstorms
Comparison of lapse rates guides forecasts of clouds, thunderstorms, turbulence
Moist air: more condensation, more latent heat, parcel stays warmer than surroundings and keeps rising
⚠ In textbook terms (environmental lapse rate): below WALR = absolutely stable; above DALR = absolutely unstable
⚠ Wet air cools slower than dry air as it rises: WALR < DALR
Exam angle: DALR is associated with stable, WALR with unstable conditions (PMF)

topic: Vertical distribution: lapse rate and inversion
t: Latent heat → absorbed or released
text:
Phase change | Latent heat
Ice → water (fusion) | Absorbed
Water → vapour (evaporation) | Absorbed
Vapour → water (condensation) | Released
Water → ice (solidification) | Released
Temperature stays constant during a phase change (boiling water stays at 100°C)
Latent heat of condensation powers cumulonimbus, thunderstorms and tropical cyclones
Cyclones weaken on landfall: moisture and latent heat supply cut off
Evaporation from oceans moves heat from surface to air (19 of 100 units in heat budget)
⚠ Condensation warms the air; evaporation cools the surface
## In news 2025-26
Super Typhoon Sinlaku (2026): latent heat in eyewall "hot towers" launched gravity waves into the mesosphere

topic: Vertical distribution: lapse rate and inversion
t: Temperature inversion → conditions and types
text:
## 1. Ideal conditions
Long nights (outgoing > incoming radiation), clear skies, calm and stable air
## 2. Types
Type | How it forms | Where
Ground/surface (radiation) | Ground cools fast on clear nights, chills air above | Higher latitudes; destroyed by day in tropics
Air drainage (valley) | Cold dense air slides down slopes, pools in valley | Mountains, deep valleys
Subsidence (upper) | Sinking air compressed and warmed | Under high-pressure centres, subtropical oceans
Frontal (advectional) | Cold air mass undercuts warm air | Fronts; sloping, unstable
⚠ Subsidence inversion is called upper surface inversion; frontal inversion is the only sloping one

topic: Vertical distribution: lapse rate and inversion
t: Temperature inversion → effects and 2025-26 news
text:
## 1. Effects
Effect | Why
Convection inhibited | Inversion acts as a lid; rainfall below normal
Fog | Surface air cooled below dew point
Smog, pollution trapped | No vertical mixing
Stable, calm weather | Warm air above cold air
## Beyond your notes
Valley floors get frost; settlements and plantations prefer upper slopes
## In news 2025-26
North India winter smog (Dec 2025): cold air under warm air forms an "atmospheric lid" over the IGP; summer pollution (June 2026) is driven by PM10 dust and ground-level ozone instead
WiFEX (Winter Fog Experiment, since 2015 at IGI Airport, IITM Pune/MoES): inversion layers trap fog
Heat dome (Western Europe, 2026): stalled high pressure acts as a lid; sinking air compressed and heated

topic: Horizontal distribution: isotherms and land-sea contrast
t: Land-sea contrast → why continental interiors have a big range
text:
## 1. Why land and water differ
Property | Land | Water
Specific heat | Low | 2.5 times higher
Sunlight penetration | ~1 m | ~20 m
Mixing | None | Convection, currents spread heat
Heats and cools | Fast | Slow
## 2. Result
Continentality: diurnal and annual ranges highest in interiors; least over oceans
NH (40% land) warmer and with bigger anomalies than SH (20% land)
Ocean diurnal range barely 1°C; ocean maximum in August, minimum in February (lag)
⚠ PYQ 2013: only thermal difference between land and water is a reason; altitude, strong winds and heavy rain in interior are not (answer 1 only)
PYQ 2007: annual range greater in NH than SH (true); greater in Pacific than Atlantic (false: smaller ocean, larger range)

topic: Horizontal distribution: isotherms and land-sea contrast
t: January isotherms → bends over land and ocean
text:
## 1. Northern Hemisphere (winter)
Over | Bend | Why
Continents | Equatorward (south) | Land colder; polar winds penetrate interiors
Oceans | Poleward (north) | Oceans warmer; Gulf Stream, North Atlantic Drift
Western margins warmer than eastern (westerlies bring ocean warmth)
Isotherms closer on eastern margins (less ocean moderation)
Coldest: northern Siberia and Greenland
## 2. Southern Hemisphere (summer)
Isotherms regular, nearly parallel to latitudes
Hottest belt around 30°S; thermal equator south of geographical equator
⚠ PYQ 2025: Statement II (oceans warmer than land in January) explains Statement I: answer (a)
⚠ Preview inference question: Gulf Stream and NAD are warm currents; saying "cold currents make the North Atlantic colder" is false
Deviation from parallels is greater in January than July, and in the NH (more land)

topic: Horizontal distribution: isotherms and land-sea contrast
t: July isotherms → bends reverse
text:
## 1. Northern Hemisphere (summer)
Over | Bend | Why
Continents | Poleward | Land overheated; hot tropical air goes far north
Oceans | Equatorward | Oceans cooler, carry moderating effect
Thermal equator north of the geographical equator
Equatorial oceans >27°C; subtropical Asia along 30°N >30°C
Hottest belt: N Africa, West Asia, NW India, SE USA; coldest: Greenland
## 2. Southern Hemisphere (winter)
Regular; slight equatorward bend at continental edges
Season | NH land | NH ocean
January | Equatorward | Poleward
July | Poleward | Equatorward
⚠ Rule: isotherms bend towards the pole over whatever is warmer

topic: Horizontal distribution: isotherms and land-sea contrast
t: Isotherms → general rules
text:
Isotherm: line joining places of equal temperature, reduced to sea level (altitude ignored)
Roughly follow parallels (same latitude, same insolation)
Irregular in NH (land-sea contrast); regular in SH
Sudden bends at land-ocean boundaries
Spacing | Meaning
Close | High thermal gradient (rapid change)
Wide | Low gradient
Region | Gradient
Tropics | Low (sun overhead all year)
Mid and high latitudes | High
Eastern margins of continents | Low: warm currents
Western margins | High: cold currents
Warm currents push isotherms poleward (Gulf Stream, NAD, Kuroshio)
⚠ Thermal equator lies north of the geographical equator on the annual average

topic: Horizontal distribution: isotherms and land-sea contrast
t: Temperature extremes and anomaly → key values
text:
Fact | Value
Highest annual range | >60°C over Siberia (continentality)
Least annual range | ~3°C between 20°S and 15°N
Highest temperatures | Tropics and subtropics (around 20°N, hot deserts)
Lowest | Polar and subpolar continental interiors
Temperature (thermal) anomaly: mean of a place minus mean of its latitude
Largest anomalies in NH (more land); smallest in SH (oceans)
Hemispheres: NH ~40% land / 60% water; SH ~20% land / 80% water
⚠ Siberia's large range is due to continentality, not altitude
Exam angle: the hot belt of the world is not on the equator: it runs through N Africa, West Asia and NW India

t: Pressure belts → latitude, origin, nature
text:
## 1. The seven belts
Belt | Latitude | Pressure | Origin
Equatorial low (Doldrums) | 10° N - 10° S | Low | Thermal (intense heating)
Sub-tropical high (Horse latitudes) | Tropics to ~35° N and S (along 30°) | High | Dynamic (subsidence)
Sub-polar low | 45° to 66.5° N and S (along 60°) | Low | Dynamic (convergence, Coriolis)
Polar high | 80-90° N and S | High | Thermal (cold, heavy air)
Seven belts: all except the equatorial low form matching pairs in both hemispheres
Belts shift with the sun: north in NH summer (July), south in NH winter (January)
Shift is smaller in the SH because of the predominance of water
⚠ Two belts are thermal (equatorial low, polar high); two are dynamic (sub-tropical high, sub-polar low)

t: Horse latitudes → pressure, weather, name
text:
## 1. Sub-tropical high-pressure belt
Air that rose at the equator loses moisture, turns dry and cold aloft; Coriolis blocking makes it subside at about 30° N and S
Subsiding air is warm and dry (compressional heating): calm, anticyclonic weather, feeble winds
Most hot deserts lie along this belt in both hemispheres (on western sides of continents)
Feeds the trade winds (equatorward) and westerlies (poleward)
Feature | Fact
Latitude | 30-35° N and S
Pressure | HIGH
Winds | Calm, feeble
Name | Sailing ships becalmed; horses thrown overboard when fodder ran out
⚠ Horse latitudes are high-pressure, not low-pressure belts
PYQ 2007: (1) belts at 30-35° N and S over oceans are horse latitudes: correct; (2) they are low-pressure belts: wrong. Answer: 1 only.

t: Doldrums and the ITCZ → features
text:
## 1. Equatorial low-pressure belt
10° N - 10° S; moves seasonally between 5° N-S and 20° N-S
Zone where NE and SE trades converge: the ITCZ
Calm at the surface (only vertical currents): hence "doldrums"
Rising moist air gives cumulonimbus and convectional rain
Question | Answer
Surface winds? | Almost absent
Rainfall type? | Convectional, afternoon thunderstorms
Cyclones within 5° of equator? | No: Coriolis negligible
The monsoon trough over India is the ITCZ shifted north in summer
⚠ "Extremely low pressure yet calm weather": doldrums are calm, not stormy

t: Sub-polar lows and polar highs → seasonal behaviour
text:
## 1. Sub-polar low (60° N and S)
Formed by convergence of westerlies and polar easterlies and Coriolis blocking
NH winter: broken into two cells: Aleutian Low (N Pacific) and Icelandic Low (Iceland-Greenland)
Mainly over oceans; SH belt poorly differentiated
Contrast of air masses here produces the polar front jet (~60°)
## 2. Polar high (80-90°)
Small in area; cold heavy air subsides
Belt | Winter cells / feature
Sub-polar low (NH) | Aleutian and Icelandic lows
Polar high | Source of polar easterlies

t: Three-cell circulation → which cell, which wind
text:
## 1. General circulation
Cell | Latitude | Origin | Surface wind
Hadley | 0-30° | Thermal (convection) | Trades (easterlies)
Ferrel | 30-60° | Dynamic (Coriolis, blocking) | Westerlies
Polar | 60-90° | Thermal | Polar easterlies
Hadley air rises to ~14 km at the equator, moves poleward, sinks near 30°
Heat transfer from low to high latitudes maintains the circulation
⚠ Ferrel cell is dynamic; Hadley and Polar cells are thermal

topic: Forces on wind and the Coriolis effect
t: Coriolis force → what controls its size
text:
## 1. Formula and behaviour
Magnitude = 2 v ω sin φ (v = wind speed, ω = Earth's angular velocity, φ = latitude)
Variable | Effect on Coriolis
Wind velocity rises | Coriolis rises
Latitude rises | Coriolis rises
Equator (φ = 0°) | Zero
Poles (φ = 90°) | Maximum
Air at rest | None: acts only once air moves
Acts perpendicular to the direction of motion; changes direction, not speed
A plane flying along the equator shows no deflection
⚠ Coriolis is equal in both hemispheres at the same latitude; only the direction of deflection differs
PYQ 2024: (1) increases with wind velocity; (2) maximum at poles, absent at equator: both correct.

topic: Forces on wind and the Coriolis effect
t: Direction of deflection → Ferrel's law
text:
## 1. Right in NH, left in SH
Winds are deflected to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere (Ferrel's law)
Cause: rotation of the Earth (west to east)
Option in PYQ 2010 | Verdict
Temperature | Wrong
Magnetic field | Wrong
Rotation of the Earth | Correct
Pressure | Wrong
Applies to winds, ocean currents, aircraft, missiles
⚠ Myth: Coriolis does not decide the swirl of water in a sink; container shape does
PYQ 2010: wind deflects left in SH because of the Earth's rotation.

topic: Forces on wind and the Coriolis effect
t: Pressure systems → rotation in each hemisphere
text:
## 1. Cyclone vs anticyclone
System | Centre | NH | SH
Cyclone | Low | Anticlockwise | Clockwise
Anticyclone | High | Clockwise | Anticlockwise
Cyclone: converging, rising air, unstable weather
Anticyclone: sinking, diverging air, stable clear weather
Surface circulation is matched by the opposite circulation aloft
⚠ PYQ 2005 (A-R): "wind patterns are clockwise in NH": false for cyclones; Coriolis governs direction (R true)
Sudden fall in barometer = stormy weather (PYQ 2011)

topic: Forces on wind and the Coriolis effect
t: Forces acting on wind → what each does
text:
## 1. Six factors
Force | Role
Pressure gradient | Starts motion high → low; closer isobars = stronger wind
Friction | Slows surface wind; up to 1-3 km; least over sea
Coriolis | Deflects (right NH, left SH)
Centripetal acceleration | Inward force making circular flow round centres
Buoyant force | Air rises in lows, sinks in highs
Gravity | Balances vertical pressure gradient
Surface winds cross isobars at an angle (friction); in the upper air they blow parallel to isobars: geostrophic wind (pressure gradient = Coriolis)
Why no cyclones at the equator: low pressure gets filled instead of spiralling (zero Coriolis)
⚠ Coriolis at 5° latitude is enough to start a vortex; between 0-5° cyclones do not form

topic: Planetary winds: trades, westerlies, Roaring Forties
t: Planetary winds → from where to where, direction
text:
## 1. Three permanent winds
Wind | From → To | NH direction | SH direction
Trade winds | Sub-tropical high → equatorial low | NE trades | SE trades
Westerlies | Sub-tropical high → sub-polar low | SW → NE | NW → SE
Polar easterlies | Polar high → sub-polar low | NE → SW | SE → NW
Trades: 30° N - 30° S; stable at origin, humid and warm near equator; eastern parts drier (cool currents)
Winds are named by the direction they come from
⚠ Westerlies in the SH blow from the north-west, not the south-west

topic: Planetary winds: trades, westerlies, Roaring Forties

text:
## 1. Facts
Blow between 30° and 60° latitude in each hemisphere separately (30-60° N and 30-60° S)
Bring wet spells and variable weather; poleward boundary fluctuates
Western disturbances (Mediterranean-origin temperate cyclones) that give winter rain to NW India travel within the westerlies
Statement (PYQ 2015) | Verdict
Westerlies blow between 30° N and 60° S | Wrong: separate belts in each hemisphere
Moist air masses giving NW India winter rain are part of westerlies | Correct
⚠ "30° N to 60° S" spans the whole tropics: a deliberate trap

text:

SH westerlies are stronger and persistent because of the vast expanse of water (less land, less friction)
NH westerlies are irregular because of uneven relief of large landmasses
Reason offered | Verdict
SH has less landmass | Correct
Coriolis is higher in SH | Wrong: same at equal latitudes

text:
## 1. The foehn mechanism
Moist air rises on the windward side, cools, drops rain (orographic)
Dry air descends the leeward side and warms by compression
Wind | Benefit / harm

t: Jet streams → features
text:
## 1. What they are
Circumpolar, narrow (50-150 km), upper-tropospheric, westerly, geostrophic streams of fast wind
Form from temperature/pressure contrast between air masses plus Coriolis
Occur in both hemispheres; NH jets stronger (greater temperature gradient)
Feature | Fact
Speed | ~120 kmph winter, ~50 kmph summer; core up to 400 kmph
Direction | West → east in both hemispheres
Meanders | Rossby waves (when contrast is weak)

t: Permanent jets → polar vs subtropical
text:
## 1. Two permanent jets
Feature | Polar front jet (PFJ) | Subtropical jet (STJ)
Height | 6-9 km | 10-16 km
Between | Polar and temperate air | Temperate and tropical air
Strength | Strongest, more variable | Weaker
Role | Steers temperate cyclones (~60°) | Linked to Indian and African monsoons
Season | Strong, continuous in winter | All year in SH; intermittent in NH summer

Jet | Where | Role

Tropical Easterly Jet (TEJ) | 5-20° N, S Asia and N Africa; June-Oct | Easterly; upper-level vent for SW monsoon; from heating of Tibet
TEJ has shown a decreasing trend (bad for monsoon)
⚠ The TEJ is easterly; all other major jets are westerly

t: STJ and the Indian monsoon → winter vs summer

Season | STJ position | Effect
Winter | Splits at Himalaya/Tibet: southern branch along 25° N, south of Himalaya | High pressure, dry offshore winds over N India
Early June | Jumps north of the Himalaya | Onset (burst) of monsoon
Withdrawal | Returns south | Monsoon withdraws

Phenomenon | Cause

text:

Large sea surface with temperature above 27 °C (warm layer 60-70 m deep)
Enough Coriolis force (so not within 5° of the equator)
A pre-existing low or low-level circulation (easterly wave)
Low vertical wind shear
Upper-level divergence
Driver | Fact
Energy source | Latent heat of condensation
Season (NH) | Late summer: Aug to mid-Nov (oceans warmest in August)
Most active belt | 10-20° latitude (~65% of activity)
Weaken on landfall: moisture supply cut off

t: Humidity → absolute, relative, specific
text:
## 1. Three measures
Measure | What it is | Unit | Changes with temperature?
Absolute humidity | Actual water vapour per unit volume of air | g/m³ | Yes (volume changes)
Relative humidity (RH) | Actual vapour ÷ maximum capacity at that temperature × 100 | % | Yes: falls as air warms
Specific humidity | Vapour per unit weight of air | g/kg | No: changed only by adding/removing moisture
Water vapour: 0-4% of air by volume (average ~2%); measured by hygrometer
Warm air holds more moisture than cold air
Saturated air: RH = 100%; evaporation suppressed
Absolute and relative humidity are greatest over oceans, least over continents
⚠ Specific humidity is not affected by pressure or temperature; relative humidity is
PYQ 2003 (A-R): moisture related to latitude because capacity depends on temperature → both true, R explains A

t: Relative humidity → how it rises and falls
text:
## 1. Two ways to change RH
Change | Effect on RH
Add moisture (evaporation) | RH rises
Cool the air (capacity falls) | RH rises
Remove moisture (precipitation) | RH falls
Warm the air (capacity rises) | RH falls
## 2. Worked example (PMF)
1 m³ holds 0.2 kg; saturates at 0.5 kg → RH = 40%
Cool by 2 °C (capacity falls 0.1 kg per °C) → saturation at 0.3 kg → only 0.1 kg more needed
## 3. Dew point
Dew point = temperature at which air becomes saturated (RH = 100%)
RH decides the amount and rate of evaporation: an important climatic factor
⚠ At night RH rises even with no new moisture, because air cools
## In news 2025-26
Heat Index (apparent temperature): how hot it feels once humidity is counted; high humidity stops sweat evaporating (heat stress)

t: Evaporation → factors and where it is highest
text:
## 1. Factors that raise evaporation
Factor | Effect
Temperature | Higher → more
Low relative humidity | Dry air has room → more
Wind | Replaces saturated layer → more
Low air pressure | More
Larger surface area, more water | More
Salinity | Higher → less (sea water ~5% slower than fresh)
Oceans give 84% of annual evaporation, continents 16%
Maximum: sub-tropical western North Atlantic and North Pacific (Gulf Stream, Kuroshio); land maximum in the equatorial region
Plants lose water faster than bare land
⚠ Evaporation is inversely related to salinity

t: Condensation → how air is cooled to dew point
text:
## 1. When condensation occurs
Air cooled to dew point at constant volume; or volume and temperature both reduced; or moisture added
Needs hygroscopic condensation nuclei: dust, smoke, pollen, sea salt
Releases latent heat of condensation (fuel for storms)
Vapour straight to solid = desublimation; solid straight to gas = sublimation
## 2. Cooling processes
Process | How | Produces
Adiabatic | Rising air expands and cools (no heat removed) | Clouds, substantial precipitation
Non-adiabatic | Radiation, conduction, mixing | Only dew, fog, frost
## 3. Forms of condensation
Dew point | Forms
Above freezing | Dew, fog, clouds
Below freezing | White frost, snow, hail, cirrus
At the surface: dew, frost, fog, mist; in free air: clouds
⚠ Non-adiabatic cooling cannot give heavy rain; rain needs rising air
## 4. Lapse rates and stability
Condition | Weather
Absolute stability: ALR > DALR | No clouds, no thunderstorm
Conditional stability: WALR < ALR < DALR | May or may not rain
Absolute instability: ALR < WALR | Thunderstorms
WALR ~4 °C/km (latent heat slows cooling); normal lapse rate ~6 °C/km; DALR > 6 °C/km
## Beyond your notes
DALR is ~10 °C/km; the normal (environmental) lapse rate is usually quoted as 6.5 °C/km

topic: Dew, frost, fog and cloudy nights
t: Cloudy nights → warmer, and no dew
text:
## 1. Why
Earth radiates long-wave (infrared) heat at night
Clouds reflect and re-radiate this terrestrial radiation back to the surface (a blanket / greenhouse effect)
Surface does not cool to dew point → no dew; night stays warmer
## 2. Day vs night
Sky | Day | Night
Cloudy | Less sunlight in → cooler day | Less heat lost → warmer night
Clear | More solar heating | Rapid cooling → dew, frost, fog, inversion
Cloudy days and nights → small diurnal range (e.g., equatorial climate)
⚠ 2019 answer: clouds reflect back Earth's radiation, not "clouds absorb the radiation" and not "surface is colder on cloudy nights"
⚠ 2001 answer: clouds reflect back heat given off by Earth; they do not produce heat, nor stop "cold waves from the sky"
PYQ 2019 and 2001: same idea asked twice; traps are "absorb", "produce heat", "deflect wind"

topic: Dew, frost, fog and cloudy nights
t: Dew and white frost → ideal conditions
text:
## 1. Dew
Water droplets on cool solid surfaces (grass, leaves, stones), not on nuclei in the air
Dew point must be above freezing
## 2. Ideal conditions (same for both)
Condition | Why
Clear sky | Surface loses infrared heat fast
Calm air | No mixing with warmer air
High relative humidity | Little cooling needed to saturate
Cold, long nights | Time to cool
## 3. White frost
Dew point at or below 0 °C; moisture deposits as ice crystals, not droplets
⚠ Frost needs the same conditions as dew plus temperature ≤ 0 °C
⚠ Any one of cloud, wind or dry air stops dew

Feature | Fog | Mist | Haze | Smog
Condensation? | Yes | Yes | No (dry particles) | Yes
Visibility | < 1 km | 1-2 km | Often > 1 km | Variable
Moisture | Less than mist | More per nucleus | None needed | Fog + pollutants
Typical | Winter IGP mornings | Mountains | Dust in Rajasthan, smoke | Delhi-NCR winter

Mist forms when drizzle evaporates before reaching ground; also on mountain slopes

Type | Formation | Character

Frontal (precipitation) fog | Rain from warm air falls into cold air at a front | At air-mass boundary

text:
## 1. Basic types
Cloud | Height | Look | Made of
Cirrus | High: 8,000-12,000 m | Thin, detached, feathery (fibrous), always white | Ice crystals
Cumulus | 4,000-7,000 m (vertical growth) | Cotton wool, flat base, dome/cauliflower top, in patches | Water droplets
Stratus | Low | Layered, cover large sky; from heat loss or mixing of air masses | Droplets
Nimbus | Middle or near surface | Black/dark grey, thick, opaque; rain-bearing | Droplets
Clouds are formed mainly by adiabatic cooling of air below dew point

Family | Clouds | Note
High | Cirrus, cirrostratus, cirrocumulus | Thin; ice; halo
Middle | Altostratus, altocumulus | "Alto-" = middle
Low | Stratocumulus, nimbostratus (and stratus) | Nimbostratus: long-duration rain; rain bands of tropical cyclones

Cloud | Association

t: Why clouds float → low density, tiny droplets
text:
## 1. The 1995 answer
Clouds float because of their low density (answer); not low temperature, velocity or pressure
Droplets/ice crystals are extremely small → very low terminal velocity
Gentle updrafts keep them suspended; cloud air is buoyant
## 2. When they fall
Continuous condensation makes droplets grow; when air resistance can no longer hold them against gravity, they fall as precipitation
Langmuir effect: droplets coalesce until gravity beats updrafts (sudden downpour, cloudbursts)
⚠ Clouds are the result of condensation, not evaporation (state PSC trap)
PYQ 1995: clouds float due to low density

t: Clouds and radiation → which cloud warms, which cools
text:
## 1. High vs low clouds
Feature | High, thin (cirrus) | Low, thick
Albedo | 25-30% | 70-80%
Incoming sunlight | Lets most through | Reflects most
Outgoing infrared | Traps it | Absorbs some, re-emits to space
Net effect | Warming | Cooling
Today low clouds dominate → clouds cool the climate overall; warming may bring more high clouds (reversal)
Aerosols act as cloud condensation nuclei: more aerosols → more, brighter clouds → cooling (indirect effect)
Water vapour and clouds give the bulk of the natural greenhouse effect
⚠ PYQ 2022 (other topic): "high clouds reflect sunlight and cool; low clouds absorb IR and warm" → neither is correct

text:
## 1. Mechanism
Intense heating → air rises in convection currents → expands, cools → condenses → cumulus/cumulonimbus

Heavy, short, highly localised; little cloudiness otherwise

## 2. Equatorial rain: the A-R pair (asked twice)
Item | Fact
Assertion | Areas 5-8° either side of equator get rain throughout the year

t: Thermal thunderstorm → three stages
text:
## 1. Stages
Stage | What happens
1. Cumulus | Intense ground heating → warm humid air rises → low pressure → air rushes in → towering cloud
2. Mature | Latent heat → stronger updraft; downdraft brings cool gust and rain; anvil top forms
3. Dissipating | Cloud reaches subzero heights → hail; heavy rain; storm dies in minutes
Anvil cumulonimbus = mature stage (top hits stratospheric stability)
Isolated storms move ~20 km/h; supercells 65-80 km/h; path erratic
## 2. Downbursts
Type | Size | Winds

Type | Fact

## 2. Pre-monsoon thunderstorms of India
Name | Region
Mango showers | Kerala (single-cell)

Bordoisila | Assam
Norwesters: March-May, from heating over Chhotanagpur; moist Bay air below, dry NW air above; can become derechos; help jute, paddy, tea
⚠ Kalbaisakhi = "calamity of Baisakh"; Norwesters are mesoscale convective systems

t: Lightning → charge separation in cumulonimbus
text:
## 1. How it forms
Rising vapour forms ice crystals; small ones go up, big ones come down; collisions of ice crystals, droplets and hailstones strip electrons
Cloud top becomes positive; middle and bottom negative
Potential difference 10⁹-10¹⁰ volts; current 10⁵-10⁶ amperes
Earth is relatively positive to the cloud base → 15-20% of discharges go cloud-to-ground
Near the ground (~80-100 m) lightning turns to tall objects (hence lightning rods)
## 2. Where most
Lake Maracaibo, Venezuela: most lightning on Earth (warm water, mountains on three sides)
⚠ Most victims are hit by ground currents, not direct strikes; sheltering under trees or lying flat raises risk

t: Thunder → what produces it
text:
## 1. The mechanism
Lightning heats its channel to ~30,000 °C (plasma, ionised gas)
Channel pressure far exceeds surroundings → supersonic expansion → shock wave
Shock wave decays to the speed of sound → heard as thunder
Thunderbolt = lightning flash with a crash of thunder
## 2. The 2014 options
Option | Verdict
Meeting of cumulonimbus clouds | Wrong
Lightning that separates nimbus clouds | Wrong
Violent upward movement of air and water particles | Wrong (that causes charge, not sound)
None of the above | Correct
⚠ Thunder comes from lightning heating and expanding air, not clouds colliding
PYQ 2014: answer (d) none of the above produces thunder (Preview tags it IAS 2013)
## Beyond your notes
Light travels far faster than sound, so the flash is seen before the thunder is heard

t: Lightning in India → deaths and response
text:
## 1. Scale
Fact | Figure
Deaths 1975-2024 | Over 1.02 lakh
Share of natural-hazard deaths (2024) | 35.7%: India's leading weather killer

1 °C warming → ~10% more lightning
## 2. Response

t: Hailstorm → conditions and formation
text:
## 1. Favourable conditions
Strong updraft; high liquid water content; great vertical extent of cumulonimbus; much of cloud below 0 °C; high surface temperature
## 2. Formation
Droplets freeze on nuclei; updrafts (~180 km/h) carry them up repeatedly through supercooled water → new opaque layers
Falls when updraft can no longer hold it; layers alternate clear and opaque
Fact | Detail
Size | Up to 15 cm, > 0.5 kg
Frequency | Less common in tropics despite more thunderstorms (warm atmosphere to great height)
Damage | Crops, windshields, livestock
⚠ Hail needs high surface temperature, not cold surfaces; it is a mid-latitude-favoured hazard

t: Tornado and waterspout → born of supercells
text:
## 1. Facts
Feature | Tornado | Waterspout
Where | Over land, mid-latitudes, spring-summer | Over water
Cloud | Cumulonimbus, mesocyclone | Cumulus or cumulonimbus
Winds | Strongest on Earth: 480-500 km/h | Mostly weak
Funnel | Condensation, dust, debris | Condensed vapour, not sucked-up sea water
Cause: warm humid air meets cold air → vertical wind shear → rotating updraft
Most violent tornadoes: USA; second most: Canada; in the subcontinent: Bangladesh
Tornadoes on all continents except Antarctica
## In news 2025-26
Waterspouts (PMF infographic, Sept 2026): tornadic vs fair-weather types; seen over Arabian Sea, Bay of Bengal, Brahmaputra
⚠ A waterspout's visible funnel is condensed water droplets, not water pulled up from the sea

topic: Koppen scheme and identifying a climate
t: Koppen's groups → defining criterion
text:
V. Koppen: empirical scheme linking vegetation to temperature and precipitation values
Five major groups: four on temperature (A, C, D, E = humid), one on precipitation (B = dry)
Group | Criterion
A Tropical humid | Coldest month 18 °C or more
B Dry | Potential evaporation > precipitation
C Warm temperate (mid-latitude) | Coldest month between -3 °C and 18 °C
D Cold snow-forest | Coldest month -3 °C or below
E Cold (polar) | All months below 10 °C
H Highland | Highland with snow cover (later addition)
Koppen-Geiger = most recently updated version
⚠ B is the only group defined by moisture; the rest by temperature
⚠ A, C, D, E are humid; B is dry

topic: Koppen scheme and identifying a climate
t: Koppen letters → meaning
text:
Letter | Meaning
f | No dry season
m | Monsoon (short dry season)
w | Winter dry season
s | Summer dry season
a, b, c, d | Severity of temperature (a hot summer ... d very cold winter)
h / k | Low latitude (hot) / high latitude (cold)
S / W | Steppe (semi-arid) / Desert (arid)
Main types and their hinge:
Code | Climate | Hinge
Af | Tropical rainforest | No seasons; every month > 6 cm rain
Am | Tropical monsoon | Seasonal reversal of winds
Aw | Savanna | Distinct wet and dry seasons
BWh / BWk | Hot / cold desert | Rain < 25 cm
BSh / BSk | Hot / cold steppe | Semi-arid
Cs | Mediterranean | Dry summer, 35-90 cm
Cfa | Humid subtropical (China type) | Rain all year, summer max
Cfb | Marine west coast (British type) | Rain all year, winter max
Dfb | Humid continental (Laurentian) | Severe winter
Dfc | Subarctic (taiga) | Highest annual range
ET / EF | Tundra / ice cap | No true summer / perennial ice
⚠ Cs = summer dry (Mediterranean); Cw / Aw = winter dry

topic: Koppen scheme and identifying a climate
t: Four-statement check (2002) → seasons by climate
text:
Statement | Verdict | Why
Equatorial year has four seasons | Wrong | No seasons: uniform heat and rain
Mediterranean: summer gets more rain | Wrong | Rain in winter (on-shore westerlies)

Vertical zonation in tropical highlands (Andes, East Africa): hot lowlands → temperate → cold → snow with altitude; e.g. Quito near the equator is mild

topic: Equatorial climate and the tropical rainforest
t: Equatorial climate → temperature and rainfall
text:
Feature | Fact
Location | 5° N to 5° S mostly; Amazon, Congo, Malaysia, Indonesia
Temperature | ~27 °C all year; very small annual and diurnal range; no winter
Rain | > 150 cm (up to 250-300 cm); no dry month; > 6 cm each month
Pattern | Convectional: clear morning, sea breeze, afternoon cumulonimbus thunderstorm, rain soon over
Peaks | Two maxima at equinoxes (April, October) as ITCZ passes; least at solstices
Cyclones | None: little Coriolis force near the equator
Double rain peak at equinoxes is unique to equatorial climate
⚠ The 2015 passage ("each day is more or less the same ... rain with thunder ... soon over") = equatorial, not monsoon or savanna
PYQ 2015: answer Equatorial
PMF-listed PYQ 2003 (A-R): rain all year near equator, explained by afternoon convection: both true, R explains A

topic: Equatorial climate and the tropical rainforest
t: Rainforest structure → canopy, epiphytes, diversity
text:
## 1. Features
Tall, closely set trees (up to ~50 m); crowns form a continuous canopy; Amazon forest = selvas
Layered structure: emergents, canopy, lower trees; plants struggle upward for light
Sparse undergrowth: little light reaches the floor; soil surface almost bare
Epiphytes (on trees, take moisture from air: commensalism) and climbers / lianas abound
Huge species diversity; trees in mixed, not pure, stands
Hardwoods: mahogany, ebony, dyewoods; mangroves in brackish coasts
No seasonal rhythm: seeding, flowering, decay all year
Statement (2013) | Verdict
Tall trees, continuous canopy | Correct
Many species coexist | Correct
Numerous epiphytes | Correct
⚠ 2021 description (fastest litter decay, bare floor, climbers and epiphytes) = tropical rainforest, not coniferous, dry deciduous or mangrove
PYQ 2013: answer 1, 2 and 3; PYQ 2021: answer tropical rain forest
## Beyond your notes
Rainforests hold roughly half of known species (PMF Environment); timber trade hard: mixed stands and heavy logs that do not float

topic: Equatorial climate and the tropical rainforest
t: Rainforest soil → poor despite fast decomposition
text:
Statement | Verdict
Rainforest soil is rich in nutrients | Wrong: leached, nutrient-poor
Heat and moisture decompose litter fast | Correct
Cleared rainforest gives farmland for intensive farming for years without fertiliser | Wrong: fertility gone after 2-3 crops
Primary productivity of rainforest is very high | Correct
Leaching: torrential rain washes nutrients out of topsoil; laterite-type soils
Nutrients sit in the living plants, not the soil; released nutrients are re-absorbed at once
Cleared plots: lalang grass and thick undergrowth choke regrowth; forest does not regenerate quickly
Exception: Java: fertile volcanic ash
Fire: rainforest species are fire-sensitive; a burn permanently removes stored nutrients
⚠ Fast decomposition does not make the soil rich: the trap in 2023 and 2003
PYQ 2023: Statement-I wrong, II right → (d); PYQ 2003: A false, R true → (d)
PMF-listed PYQ 2011: rainforest regenerates slowly because the soil is deficient in nutrients

topic: Equatorial climate and the tropical rainforest
t: Amazon and tropical forests → 2025-26 news
text:
## In news 2025-26
Amazon tipping point: a Nature study says self-driven collapse could begin at 1.5-1.9 °C warming; ~17-18% already lost (LENS May 2026)
Amazon makes ~50% of its own rain by evapotranspiration; tree loss breaks this recycling
Study: Amazon frequently releases more CO2 than it absorbs (carbon source) due to deforestation, drought, fire, El Nino (LENS Nov 2026)
Amazon spread: Brazil 60%, Peru 13%, Colombia 10%; 9 countries; ~10% of known species
Beyond ~2 °C, parts of the Amazon could turn to savanna (LENS Jun 2026)
Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF): launched by Brazil at COP30, Belem; ~1.2 bn ha in 70+ countries; 20% funds for Indigenous peoples; India joined as Observer (LENS Nov 2025)
ESA BIOMASS satellite: radar (SAR) to map tropical and boreal forest biomass (LENS Apr 2025)
⚠ "Lungs of the Earth" is a misconception: rainforest oxygen is almost all re-used by respiration; ~half of Earth's oxygen comes from ocean plankton (PMF)

text:
Feature | Fact

t: Savanna vegetation → why so few trees
text:
Factor (2021) | Checks tree growth?
Fire | Yes: kills seedlings and seeds
Grazing herbivores | Yes: eat and trample saplings
Seasonal rainfall | Yes: long dry season, dry grass fuels fires
Burrowing animals, termites | Not the answer
Soil properties | Not the answer

text:
## 1. Causes of aridity (BWh)
On western coasts of continents between 15° and 30° N and S
Subtropical high-pressure cells: descending, warming, drying air (Hadley cell)
Off-shore trade winds (hence trade-wind deserts)
Cold ocean currents: chill and stabilise coastal air, no rain (fog only)
Rain shadow in places
Statement | Verdict
African-Eurasian deserts lie in subtropical high-pressure cells | Correct (2011)
They are under warm ocean currents | Wrong: currents off desert coasts are cold
Tropical deserts on western margins in the trade-wind belt | Correct (2009)
⚠ Warm currents add moisture; deserts pair with cold currents

## Beyond your notes
Desert | Cold current

Namib, Kalahari | Benguela

Sonoran, Mojave | California
Great Australian | West Australian

Industry | Ruhr, Yorkshire, Manchester
NW Europe is a net food importer (wheat); climate called best for human output
⚠ In NZ the west is wet (orographic); Canterbury in the east is the rain-shadow sheep land

t: Laurentian (cool temperate eastern margin) → features
text:
Feature | Fact
Nature | Intermediate between British (moderate) and taiga (extreme)
Regions | NE North America (E Canada, NE USA, Newfoundland); E Asia (E Siberia, N China, Manchuria, Korea, N Japan)
Hemisphere | Northern only: SH has little land south of 40° S (Patagonia is rain shadow)
Winter | Dry, below freezing, snow
Summer | Warm (~25 °C), wet
Rain | 75-150 cm, all year, summer maximum
Fog: Gulf Stream + Labrador current meet off Newfoundland; Kuroshio + Oyashio off N Japan
Forest: conifers north of 50° N, deciduous (oak, beech, maple, birch) to the south
Economy: lumber, pulp (E Canada), Annapolis Valley apples, Grand Banks fishing
⚠ Laurentian type is absent in the southern hemisphere

t: Taiga (boreal, Siberian) climate → features
text:
Feature | Fact
Belt | 50°-70° N; Canada, Scandinavia, Russia; northern hemisphere only
Summer | Brief, warm (20-25 °C)
Winter | Long, -30 to -40 °C; Verkhoyansk -67 °C
Annual range | Greatest of all climates (50-60 °C in Siberia): continentality
Rain | 38-63 cm, summer max (convection); winter snow
Winds | Blizzard (Canada), buran (Eurasia)
Borders: tundra poleward, steppe equatorward
Absent in SH: narrow land, strong ocean influence
## In news 2025-26
Smew, a duck that breeds in the Eurasian taiga, was recorded at Kaziranga (LENS Mar 2026)

t: Coniferous forest → features and world share
text:
## 1. Features
Evergreen conifers: pine, fir, spruce, larch; same leaf stays up to 5 years
Conical shape sheds snow; needle, thick leaves cut transpiration; thick bark
Pure stands, few species → easy lumbering of softwood (pulp, paper, newsprint: Canada ~half)
Soil: podzol: thin, leached, acidic, low humus; slow decay; negligible undergrowth
Lowest productivity of all forest biomes
Statement (2003) | Answer
Highest share of world forest area | Temperate coniferous (boreal) forests
Not tropical rain, tropical monsoon or temperate deciduous | Decoys
⚠ Taiga has lowest productivity but largest coniferous area; do not confuse area with productivity
PYQ 2003: answer (a) temperate coniferous
## Beyond your notes
By FAO climatic domain (FRA 2020): tropical ~45%, boreal ~27%, temperate ~16%, subtropical ~11% (verify); the 2003 question compared forest types
## In news 2025-26
FAO State of the World's Forests 2026: global forest 4.14 bn ha = 32% of land (LENS Oct 2026)
FAO Global Forest Resources Assessment 2025: India 9th in forest area, 3rd in net annual gain (LENS Sep 2026)

t: Tundra and ice cap → features
text:
Feature | Tundra (ET) | Ice cap (EF)
Temperature | Not more than 4 months above 0 °C | No month above 0 °C
Vegetation | No trees: mosses, lichens, reindeer moss, berries in summer | None
Where | Arctic coasts of Eurasia, N Canada, Alaska, Greenland coast | Greenland, Antarctica
Alpine tundra: above the tree line on high mountains (Himalaya, Andes, Alps)
No trees because of permafrost (frozen at least two years running)
Animals: reindeer, musk-ox, arctic fox, lemming, arctic hare, polar bear; penguins only in Antarctica
Mammals: large bodies, short tails and ears; reptiles and amphibians almost absent
Arctic willow lives 150-230 years
People: Eskimos (Inuit); igloos; seals, walrus
Minerals: iron at Kiruna, Gallivare (Sweden), Labrador; oil in Alaska (Kenai)
⚠ Precipitation mostly snow; convectional rain absent

t: Biome → soil, decomposition, productivity
text:
Biome | Decomposition | Soil | Hinge
Tropical rainforest | Fastest | Leached, poor | Nutrients in plants
Savanna | Seasonal | Lateritic, poor | Fire-maintained
Tropical deciduous | Moderate | Varied | Leaves shed in dry season
Mediterranean | Slow in dry summer | Thin | Fire-prone, xerophytic
Temperate deciduous | Moderate | Podzolic, deep | Leaves shed in autumn
Steppe | Moderate | Chernozem (rich) | Treeless
Taiga | Slow | Podzol, acidic | Lowest forest productivity
Tundra | Very slow | Permafrost | Treeless
Desert | Very slow (dry) | Saline, low humus | Xerophytes
Biome: large community of flora and fauna over a major habitat; one biome spans many habitats
Ecotone: transition zone between biomes (e.g. mangrove, grassland between forest and desert)
Temperate rainforest: NW North America (California to Alaska), S Chile, NZ: Douglas fir, Sitka spruce, red cedar
⚠ Fast decay → poor soil (rainforest); slow decay → acidic, humus-poor soil (taiga): both infertile for opposite reasons

topic: Ocean currents: forces, types and counter-currents
t: Forces → what sets ocean currents moving
text:
## 1. Primary forces (start the movement)
Force | How it acts
Solar heating | Water expands; equatorial sea level ~8 cm higher than mid-latitudes; gravity pulls it down the slope
Wind | Friction drags surface water: sets speed and direction; monsoon reverses Indian Ocean currents
Gravity | Levels the water piles
Coriolis force (Earth's rotation) | Deflects water right in NH, left in SH
## 2. Secondary forces
Temperature and salinity → density differences → vertical and horizontal flow; cold, salty water sinks
## 3. What does not drive currents
Revolution of the Earth: only an indirect effect (seasons shift pressure belts)
Ocean configuration (coastline shape) steers currents: it is a modifier
⚠ 2012 trap: "revolution" looks like rotation; only rotation, wind/pressure, density were correct
PYQ 2012: answer (b) 1, 2 and 3

topic: Ocean currents: forces, types and counter-currents
t: Ocean currents → statements that are true or false
text:
Statement | Verdict | Why
Currents are only slow surface movements | False | Can reach 5 knots (~9 km/h); deep and subsurface currents exist
Currents help maintain Earth's heat balance | True | Move heat poleward, cold water equatorward
Set in motion primarily by prevailing winds | True | Wind friction drives surface flow
Affected by configuration of the ocean | True | Coasts and basins steer them
Surface currents hold most ocean water | False | Surface layer (top 400 m) = only ~10% of ocean water
Deep currents are wind-driven | False | Driven by density and gravity (thermohaline)
Speeds: strongest near surface (>5 knots); deep currents <0.5 knot; 1 knot ≈ 1.8 km/h
Gulf Stream = the fastest current in the world ocean (PMF)
⚠ The word "only" or "slow" usually makes a current statement false
PYQ 2002: answer (b) 2, 3 and 4

topic: Ocean currents: forces, types and counter-currents
t: Warm vs cold currents → which coast gets which
text:
Latitude band | East coast of continents | West coast of continents
Low and middle latitudes | Warm currents | Cold currents
High latitudes | Cold currents | Warm currents
Reason: clockwise gyres in NH, anticlockwise in SH around subtropical highs
Warm currents flow from the equator, on the surface; cold currents start as polar water that sinks and creeps equatorward
Convergence: warm and cold currents meet; divergence: one current splits
## 1. Quick test pairs
West coast, tropics: Peru, Benguela, Canary, California, West Australian (all cold)
East coast, tropics: Brazil, Kuroshio, Gulf Stream, East Australian, Agulhas (all warm)
High-latitude west coast: North Atlantic Drift, Norwegian, Alaska (warm)
⚠ Exception to watch: Labrador, Oyashio, East Greenland are cold currents on eastern sides of high-latitude continents

topic: Ocean currents: forces, types and counter-currents
t: Equatorial counter-current → why it flows east
text:
Trade winds push the North and South Equatorial Currents westward (Pacific: ~14,500 km)
Water piles up in the west (Indonesia-Australia; north of Brazil's bulge; SE of Horn of Africa)
The piled-up water flows back east between the two currents = counter-current
Factor | Role
Convergence/piling of the two equatorial currents | UPSC key (b)
Doldrums (belt of calm) | Calm belt lets water flow back; PMF argues this is the main cause
Earth's rotation | Coriolis does not create counter-currents
Salinity difference | Mainly vertical currents: ruled out
⚠ The official key is (b) convergence of the two equatorial currents; PMF's explanation picks (d) doldrums. Mark (b) in the exam
In El Nino years the counter-current carries warm water to Peru-Ecuador
In the North Indian Ocean in summer there is no north equatorial current and no counter-current
PYQ 2015: eastward flow explained by convergence of equatorial currents

topic: Ocean currents: forces, types and counter-currents
t: Gyres and the Sargasso Sea → circulation loops
text:
Gyres: large circular currents around subtropical highs (anticyclonic); higher latitudes follow cyclonic loops
North Atlantic Gyre: Gulf Stream (W), North Atlantic Drift (N), Canary (E), North Equatorial Current (S)
Feature | Fact
Sargasso Sea | Only sea with no coastline; inside the North Atlantic Gyre
Named for | Floating Sargassum seaweed carried in by the currents
Bottom water | Warm: high insolation, little mixing (like Red Sea, Mediterranean)
## Beyond your notes
Five main subtropical gyres: North and South Pacific, North and South Atlantic, Indian Ocean; plastic "garbage patches" collect in them, the largest in the North Pacific (verify)
⚠ Sargasso is bounded by currents, not land: a favourite "sea without shore" question

topic: Ocean currents: forces, types and counter-currents
t: Thermohaline circulation and AMOC → deep ocean conveyor
text:
Thermohaline: deep currents driven by density = temperature (thermo) + salinity (haline); winds drive only the top ~100 m
Also called the global/ocean conveyor belt; bottom relief shapes it
## 1. AMOC (Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation)
Warm, salty water flows north in the upper Atlantic, cools, gets saltier by evaporation, sinks, returns south at depth
Effect of AMOC weakening | Detail
Europe | Colder NW Europe winters, more sea ice
Monsoons | ITCZ shifts south: weaker monsoons in India, West Africa, Amazon
Sahel | Droughts
US east coast | Regional sea-level rise
Carbon | Ocean absorbs less CO₂
Atlantic | Fewer tropical cyclones; lower North Atlantic productivity
Cause: warming surface + Greenland/Arctic meltwater (fresh, less dense, does not sink)
## In news 2025-26
PMF (July 2025): AMOC is a potential climate tipping point; a 2021 study found it weakest in over 1,600 years
⚠ Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Drift are the surface limb of AMOC

topic: Currents of the Pacific, Atlantic and Indian Oceans
t: Pacific Ocean currents → warm or cold, where
text:
Current | Type | Course
North and South Equatorial | Warm | East → west under trade winds
Equatorial counter-current | Warm | West → east between them
Kuroshio | Warm | North off Philippines → Japan ("Japan current")
Oyashio | Cold | Kamchatka → meets Kuroshio off Hokkaido
Okhotsk | Cold | Past Sakhalin → joins Oyashio
North Pacific | Warm | Japan → North America under westerlies
Alaska | Warm | Northern branch, anticlockwise along BC-Alaska
California | Cold | Southern branch along US west coast
East Australian | Warm | South along E Australia to Tasmania
Peru (Humboldt) | Cold | North along Chile-Peru; feeds S Equatorial
South Pacific / West Wind Drift | Cold | West → east in high southern latitudes
Kuroshio-Oyashio meeting = fog and mist; north Japan is "a second Newfoundland" and a top fishing zone
⚠ Alaska current is warm (relative to its surroundings) though it is in high latitudes

topic: Currents of the Pacific, Atlantic and Indian Oceans
t: Atlantic Ocean currents → warm or cold, where
text:
Current | Type | Course
North and South Equatorial | Warm | East → west from West Africa
Antilles | Warm | East of West Indies
Florida → Gulf Stream | Warm | Florida Strait → Cape Hatteras → Gulf Stream
North Atlantic Drift | Warm | Grand Banks → British Isles, under westerlies
Norwegian | Warm | Keeps north Norway ports ice-free; Russia's Barents Sea cargo route
Labrador | Cold | Arctic → east coast of Canada
East Greenland | Cold | Arctic → Atlantic
Canary | Cold | Between Spain and Azores → joins N Equatorial
Brazil | Warm | South along Brazil from Cape São Roque
Falkland | Cold | Off Argentina; meets Brazil current
Benguela | Cold | Up the west coast of southern Africa
## Beyond your notes
Guinea current: warm, flows east along the Gulf of Guinea coast (fed by the counter-current)
⚠ Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Drift are warm, not cold (PYQ 2024 trap)
⚠ UPSC 1999 map pair: Benguela and Falkland (both cold, South Atlantic)

topic: Currents of the Pacific, Atlantic and Indian Oceans
t: Indian Ocean currents → seasonal reversal by monsoon
text:
Indian Ocean is "half an ocean" (mostly in the SH); North Indian Ocean currents reverse with the monsoon
Season | North Indian Ocean circulation
Winter (NE monsoon) | N and S Equatorial currents flow east → west; counter-current present; Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea circulate anticlockwise
Summer (SW monsoon) | Strong west → east SW Monsoon Drift; N Equatorial current obliterated; no counter-current; circulation clockwise
## 1. Southern Indian Ocean (little seasonal change)
South Equatorial (warm) → splits at Madagascar into Agulhas (east of it) and Mozambique (channel) → rejoins as Agulhas, warm till West Wind Drift
West Australian: cold, north along W Australia, feeds S Equatorial
1997 option | Verdict
Half an ocean | True fact, not the cause
Monsoon drift | Correct: wind reversal reverses currents
Land-locked ocean | Wrong
Greater salinity variation | Wrong
## Beyond your notes
Somali current: flows north along Somalia in summer (strong upwelling) and south in winter (verify)
PYQ 1997: monsoon drift changes Indian Ocean current direction

topic: Currents of the Pacific, Atlantic and Indian Oceans
t: Antarctic Circumpolar Current → the only global loop
text:
Fact | Detail
Other name | West Wind Drift
Rank | Largest wind-driven current on Earth
Unique | Only current that circles the globe; links Atlantic, Pacific, Indian Oceans
Direction | West → east (clockwise seen from the South Pole)
Role | Thermally isolates Antarctica; heat, CO₂ exchange; upwells nutrients
Branches | Feeds Peru, Benguela, Falkland, West Australian cold currents
Brazil current swings east at ~35°S to join it
⚠ ACC is a cold current; it keeps the Southern Ocean separate from northern oceans

topic: Currents of the Pacific, Atlantic and Indian Oceans
t: Water masses vs currents → how they differ
text:
Water mass: ocean water with shared temperature, salinity, density from a common origin; moves slowly
Aspect | Ocean current | Water mass
Speed | Fast, defined path | Slow
Mainly affects | Sea surface temperature, coastal climate | Benthic (bottom) zone
Example | Gulf Stream | Antarctic bottom water; Mediterranean water
Mediterranean water: warm, salty (evaporation), sinks and spills over the Gibraltar sill as a westward sub-surface current
Water masses carry oxygen to deep habitats via thermohaline flow
Upwelling (mostly tropical, trade winds push surface water away) → cold, nutrient-rich water → high productivity
Downwelling (polar, anticyclonic zones) → low productivity
⚠ Cold water masses moving into the tropics can damage coral reefs

topic: Effects of currents: fishing grounds, deserts, El Nino
t: Fishing grounds → where and why
text:
Richest grounds lie where warm and cold ocean currents meet: mixing replenishes oxygen and nutrients → plankton → fish
Fishing ground | What meets / why
Grand Banks (Newfoundland) | Warm Gulf Stream + cold Labrador; "richest fishing grounds on Earth"
NE Japan | Warm Kuroshio + cold Oyashio
Peru coast | Cold upwelling (Humboldt); hit in El Nino years
Falkland/Argentina | Wide shelf + cold Falkland meets warm Brazil
Dogger Bank (North Sea) | Shallow bank on the shelf
## 1. Other conditions
Shallow continental shelves (sunlight + river nutrients): almost all marine food comes from shelves
Cold high-latitude water (<20°C) favours plankton; warm tropical water inhibits it
Indented coasts give ports; cold climate cuts fish-preservation cost
⚠ Option (a) "atmospheric currents meet" is the trap; PMF's printed key for 2013 shows (a), a misprint: the answer is (c) oceanic currents
PYQ 2013: warm and cold oceanic currents meet

topic: Effects of currents: fishing grounds, deserts, El Nino
t: Cold currents → west-coast deserts and fog
text:
Major hot deserts lie at 20-30° latitude on the western sides of continents
Reason | How
Subtropical high (horse latitudes) | Descending air, no rain
Offshore trade winds | Rain-bearing winds blow away from land ("trade wind deserts")
Cold currents offshore | Chill air → fog and temperature inversion → no convection
## 1. Desert → cold current beside it
Desert | Cold current alongside
Atacama (rain <1.3 cm/yr) | Peru/Humboldt
Namib, Kalahari | Benguela
Sahara (west) | Canary
Sonoran/Baja | California
Great Australian (west) | West Australian
⚠ PYQ 2011: African-Eurasian desert belt is due to subtropical high cells (true), not warm currents
## In news 2025-26
A strong Antarctic polar anticyclone brought snowfall to the Atacama for the first time in over a decade (PMF, July 2025)

topic: Effects of currents: fishing grounds, deserts, El Nino
t: Currents → climate, rain, fog and navigation
text:
Effect | Example
Moderate winters | North Atlantic Drift warms Britain and Norway (ports never frozen)
Cooling | Canary cools Spain, Portugal
Rain on east coasts | Warm currents along tropical east coasts (Florida, Natal)
Fog and drizzle | Mixing zones: Newfoundland gets more drizzle than anywhere
Cyclones | Warm water piled in the west of oceans breeds them
Navigation | Mexico → Philippines on the N Equatorial Drift; back along the counter-current
Isotherms bend poleward over warm currents (Gulf Stream, Kuroshio)
Bomb cyclones of the western North Atlantic draw extra energy from the warm Gulf Stream (CARE, Jan 2026)
⚠ Tropical cyclones form on the western margins of oceans (warm currents), rarely on eastern margins (cold currents) except in strong El Nino years

topic: Effects of currents: fishing grounds, deserts, El Nino
t: El Nino and upwelling → ocean-atmosphere link
text:
Condition | East Pacific (Peru) | West Pacific (Indonesia)
Normal | High pressure; cold upwelling; good fishing | Low pressure; warm water; rain
El Nino | Warm water; thermocline drops, upwelling cut; fishing hit; rain | Cold water; drought
La Nina | Stronger normal: extra cooling | Extra rain
Walker cell weakens or reverses in El Nino; counter-current piles warm water off Peru
El Nino Modoki: warming in the central Pacific, cooling east and west
## In news 2025-26
IMD flagged possible El Nino in the 2026 monsoon; El Nino recurs every 2-7 years, lasts 9-12 months, weakens the Indian monsoon, cuts upwelling and causes coral bleaching (CARE, May 2026)
⚠ Normal El Nino forms in the eastern Pacific; Modoki in the central Pacific (PYQ 2010)

t: Land-sea contrast → why winter shows the bigger gap
text:
Specific heat of water is ~2.5 times that of land; sunlight penetrates water ~20 m, land ≤1 m; water mixes by convection
So land heats and cools faster; oceans keep small diurnal and annual ranges
Season | Land | Ocean | Contrast
Summer | Hot | Warm | Smaller (both warm)
Winter | Very cold | Stays mild | Greater
## 1. The 2023 statements
Statement (2023) | Verdict
Contrast greater in summer than winter | False
Specific heat of water > land | True
Interiors of continents have the highest ranges (Siberia >60°C): continentality, not altitude (PYQ 2013)
⚠ Statement-I/II answer was (d): I false, II true
PYQ 2023: land-ocean contrast is greater in winter

t: January isotherms → where they bend
text:
Isotherms join places of equal sea-level temperature; they roughly follow latitudes
January (NH winter) | Bend
Over oceans | Poleward (north): warm Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Drift carry heat north
Over continents | Equatorward (south): cold polar air penetrates interiors
Coldest | N Siberia, Greenland
Thermal equator | South of geographical equator
SH | Isotherms regular, nearly parallel
## 1. July for contrast
July (NH summer) | Bend
Over continents | Poleward: land overheated
Over oceans | Equatorward: oceans cooler
Hottest belt | N Africa, West Asia, NW India, SE USA
Isotherms are close on western margins (cold currents) and wide on eastern margins (warm currents), low-mid latitudes
⚠ 2024 statement 2 was false because it called the Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Drift cold
PYQ 2024: only statement 1 correct

t: East vs west sections of oceans → which is warmer
text:
Zone | Warmer section | Why
Tropical | Western sections | Trade winds pile warm water west; cold currents on eastern side
Temperate | Eastern sections | Westerlies carry warm water east (North Atlantic Drift to Europe)
Mean equatorial surface temperature ~27°C; falls ~0.5°C per degree of latitude
Cyclones need >27°C water, 60-70 m deep: found on western margins of tropical oceans
⚠ UPSC key for 2021 = both statements correct; PMF argues only statement 1 (eastern temperate sections are warmed but cold currents keep them below western ones). Mark (c) in the exam
PYQ 2021: answer (c) both

t: Annual range of ocean temperature → which is larger
text:
Rule: more water → smaller annual range
Comparison | Larger range | Why
NH vs SH | Northern Hemisphere | ~40% land (SH ~20%)
Atlantic vs Pacific | Atlantic | Narrower, more land influence
North vs south parts of Pacific/Atlantic | Northern parts | Weaker winds; southern parts have more extensive currents
Open ocean vs interiors | Continental interiors | Continentality
Daily range in oceans ≈ 1°C; surface max ~2 pm, min ~5 am
Ocean annual max in August, min in February (lag behind land)
Largest temperature anomalies are in the NH (more land)
⚠ 2007 statement 1 reversed the truth: the Atlantic, not the Pacific, has the larger range
PYQ 2007: only statement 2 (NH > SH) correct

t: Vertical temperature → layers, thermocline, pycnocline
text:
Layer (low-mid latitudes) | Depth | Temperature
Warm surface layer | Top ~500 m | 20-25°C; year-round in tropics, summer-only in mid-latitudes
Thermocline | Starts ~100-400 m, 500-1,000 m thick | Rapid fall with depth
Deep cold layer | To the floor | Near 0°C, stable
~90% of ocean water lies below the thermocline
Pycnocline: density boundary (100-1,000 m) that blocks vertical mixing; almost absent in polar seas (cold water sinks)
Halocline: rapid salinity change; photic zone to ~200 m
Polar oceans: one cold layer, surface to bottom
⚠ Fall of temperature with depth is greater at the equator than at the poles

t: Factors affecting ocean temperature → what raises or lowers it
text:
Factor | Effect
Insolation | Main heat source; interior heat and friction negligible
Heat loss | Back radiation, exchange with air, evaporation
Enclosed seas | Low latitudes warmer (Red Sea, Mediterranean); high latitudes colder than open sea
Sills | Bab-el-Mandeb sill (~366 m): Red Sea subsurface water ~20°C warmer than Indian Ocean at same depth
Offshore winds | Push warm water away → upwelling of cold water (Peru, normal years)
Onshore winds | Pile warm water (Peru in El Nino)
Currents | Gulf Stream warms; Labrador cools Newfoundland
Land share | NH oceans get more heat
Deep-sea life survives on chemosynthetic bacteria using Earth's interior heat
Equatorial surface water can be cooler and less salty than the layer below (heavy rain)
⚠ Enclosed seas of both low and high latitudes have warmer bottom water

t: Salinity → definition and composition
text:
Salinity = grams of dissolved salt per 1,000 g of seawater, in ppt (‰)
24.7‰ = upper limit of brackish water; open ocean 33-37‰; average ~35‰
Salt | Share
Sodium chloride | 77.7%
Magnesium chloride | 10.9%
Magnesium sulphate | 4.7%
Calcium sulphate | 3.6%
Potassium sulphate | 2.5%
Top ions by weight: chlorine (18.97 g/kg) > sodium (10.47) > sulphate > magnesium > calcium > potassium
## 1. What controls surface salinity
Evaporation (raises) vs precipitation (lowers)
River inflow (coasts), freezing/thawing of ice (poles)
Winds and currents move salty water around
⚠ Higher salinity raises the boiling point and so reduces evaporation

t: Salinity distribution → high and low seas
text:
Water body | Salinity (‰) | Why
Lake Van (Turkey) | 330 | Inland, evaporation
Dead Sea | 238 | Inland
Great Salt Lake (Utah) | 220 | Inland
Red Sea | ~41 | Landlocked, hot, dry
Mediterranean | 38+ | High evaporation
Subtropical highs (20-30°N, 20-60°W Atlantic) | ~37 | Dry sinking air
Equator | ~35 | Heavy rain, doldrums
Arabian Sea | Higher than Bay | High evaporation, little river water
Bay of Bengal | Lower | Ganga, Brahmaputra inflow
North Sea | Fairly high | Salty North Atlantic Drift water
Baltic, Black Sea | Low | Huge river inflow
Polar seas | 20-32 | Meltwater, little evaporation
Atlantic average 36-37; Indian Ocean 35
Highest open-ocean salinity is in the subtropics, not at the equator
⚠ The North Sea is saltier than its latitude suggests; the Baltic is the classic low-salinity sea

t: Vertical salinity → change with depth and latitude
text:
Latitude | With depth
High latitudes | Salinity increases with depth
Middle latitudes | Rises to ~35 m, then falls
Equator | Sub-surface salinity lower
Generally salinity rises with depth; the sharp-change zone is the halocline
Dense, salty water sinks below fresher water: stratification by salinity
Salinity and temperature together set density: the engine of thermohaline circulation
## 1. Why salinity matters
Controls compressibility, thermal expansion, density, absorption of insolation, evaporation; shapes fish distribution
Mixing zones of cold and warm water: NH western parts drop from 35 to ~31 (Arctic meltwater)
⚠ Meltwater freshening of the North Atlantic is what weakens AMOC

t: Tides → causes and the two bulges
text:
Tide: periodic rise and fall of sea level, once or twice a day
Cause | Role
Moon's gravity | Main cause (Moon's pull > twice the Sun's)
Sun's gravity | Lesser cause
Centrifugal force (Earth-Moon rotation) | Acts opposite to gravity; creates the far-side bulge
Near side: Moon's pull > centrifugal force → bulge towards the Moon
Far side: centrifugal force dominates → bulge away from the Moon
Tide-generating force = gravity minus centrifugal force
## 1. What controls tide size
Moon's movement relative to Earth; Sun-Moon positions; uneven water distribution; configuration of the ocean
⚠ 2015 answer was all three (Sun, Moon, centrifugal force): leaving out the Sun is the trap
PYQ 2015: tides from Sun, Moon and Earth's centrifugal force

t: Spring vs neap tides → alignment and moon phase
text:
Feature | Spring tide | Neap tide
Sun-Earth-Moon | Straight line | Right angles
Moon phase | New moon and full moon | First and third quarter
High tide | Higher than usual | Lower than usual
Low tide | Lower than usual | Higher than usual
Tidal range | Maximum | Minimum
Frequency | Twice a month | Twice a month
Spring and neap tides are ~7 days apart
Kerala tidal (king tide, "sunny day") flooding peaks at full and new moon
⚠ Neap tides do not occur at new moon: the 2001 reason was false
PYQ 2001: A true (lower highs, higher lows), R false (neap is at quarter moons)
## In news 2025-26
Kerala declared tidal flooding a state-specific disaster for the first time; relief from the SDRF (Praveen CA, Feb 2026)

t: Tides by frequency → semi-diurnal, diurnal, mixed
text:
Type | Pattern | Where
Semi-diurnal | 2 high + 2 low a day, similar heights | Most common
Diurnal | 1 high + 1 low a day | Gulf of Mexico
Mixed | 2 highs and 2 lows of different heights | West coast of North America, Pacific islands
Interval between high tides = 12 h 25 min (Moon moves east each day)
Ebb: falling water (high → low); flood/flow: rising water
Southampton: tides 6-8 times a day (North Sea + English Channel)
⚠ Two high tides a day are not exactly 12 hours apart

t: Tidal range → perigee, perihelion, funnel bays
text:
Situation | Tidal range
Perigee (Moon closest) | Greater than normal
Apogee (Moon farthest) | Smaller
Perihelion (~3 Jan) | Greater
Aphelion (~4 July) | Smaller
Wide continental shelf | Higher bulge (barrier effect)
Mid-ocean islands | Low tides (no barrier)
Funnel-shaped bays | Magnified
Bay of Fundy (Nova Scotia, Canada): highest tidal range, 15-16 m
Horizontal forces (barriers, funnelling) matter more than vertical forces for bulge height
⚠ Perihelion falls in January: tidal ranges are largest then, though it is NH winter

t: Tidal bores and tidal ports → where and why
text:
Tidal bore: wall of water rushing upstream when a strong tide enters a narrow, shallow estuary
Fact | Detail
When | Flood tide only; almost never at neap tide
Needs | Tidal range typically >6 m
India | Hooghly
World's strongest | Qiantang (China)

Latitude | 30°N-30°S, tropical
Temperature | Warm, narrow daily and annual range (around 20°C+)
Depth | Shallow: ideal 45-55 m, needs sunlight

text:
## 1. Why "young" (PMF)
Young, weak, flexible structure: the most unstable landmass of India; still faulting, folding, thrusting
Rivers in youthful stage: gorges, V-shaped valleys, rapids, waterfalls
Evidence | Why it shows youth
Deep gorges | Rapid uplift; rivers cut down faster than they widen
U-turn river courses | Rivers bend round rising ranges and syntaxial bends; past glaciation
Parallel ranges | Folding and compression, ridges not yet eroded
Steep gradients, landslides | Still rising; unstable slopes
Folds asymmetrical: steep south slopes, gentle north slopes (hogback topography)
⚠ All four statements were evidence of youth (answer: 1, 2, 3 and 4)
⚠ V-shaped young gorges belong to the Himalaya, not the Peninsular block (PYQ 2026)

topic: The Himalaya: origin, ranges and peaks
t: Formation of the Himalaya → plates, Tethys and the plain
text:
## 1. Sequence (PMF)
Stage | Event
~250 mya | Pangaea surrounded by Panthalassa
~150 mya | Split into Laurasia (Angaraland) and Gondwanaland; Tethys Sea between them
~150 mya on | Indian Plate drifts north from Gondwana
Eocene (~60 mya) | Collision with Eurasian Plate begins
Oligocene-Lower Miocene | Uplift of Tibetan Plateau; Himalaya emerge
Shiwalik (14-0.2 mya) | Foreland sediments form the Shiwaliks
Tethys geosyncline sediments compressed → Himalaya + Indo-Gangetic-Brahmaputra trough to the south
Trough filled by Himalayan rivers → aggradational plain
Tectonic lines: Indus-Tsangpo Suture Zone, Main Central Thrust
⚠ Tertiary = the most significant period: the Himalaya were born (PMF)
⚠ The Himalaya are continent-continent convergence; theoretically they include Purvanchal, Arakan Yoma and the Andaman-Nicobar islands

## 1. Character (PMF)
Tableland of Archaean gneisses and schists (~4 billion years); part of Gondwana: oldest, most stable landmass

Parts of the west coast submerged: narrow plain, natural harbours
Most rivers flow west to east; Narmada, Tapi flow west in rift valleys

t: Rann of Kutch → origin and features
text:
## 1. Origin
Was a shallow arm of the Arabian Sea; repeated falls in sea level and geological uplift closed off the sea
Indus sediment filled the sea and lagoons around the then island of Kutch
Now a seasonal salt marsh: flooded in monsoon, dry white salt crust in summer
Part | Location
Great Rann | Salt plain north of Kutch
Little Rann | Southern continuation, south-east of Kachchh
Luni (Thar's largest river) is endorheic and ends in the Rann
## 2. Related places
Place | Fact
Sir Creek | 96-km tidal estuary, India (Gujarat)-Pakistan (Sindh) dispute; India wants Thalweg line
Banni grassland / Chhari-Dhand | Seasonal desert wetland; Gujarat's first Conservation Reserve (2008)
Guneri inland mangrove | 45 km from sea, no seawater inflow; one of 8 inland mangroves worldwide
⚠ Not: Bhitarkanika (mangroves, Odisha), Marakkanam (salt pans, TN), Naupada (swamp, AP)
PYQ 2023: best example of marshland from repeated sea-level falls → Rann of Kutch

t: Coral reefs → growth conditions and types
text:
## 1. Conditions
Need | Range
Latitude | 30°N-30°S tropical waters
Temperature | ~20°C or above, small range
Depth | Shallow, sunlit: ideal 45-55 m
Water | Clear salt water; fresh or very saline water harmful
Food | Plankton: corals grow more on the seaward side
Absent on west coasts of tropical continents (cold currents)
Corals = calcareous skeletons of polyps (phylum Cnidaria) with symbiotic algae
## 2. Types
Type | Fact

topic: Himalayan drainage: nature, origin and river shifts
t: Antecedent rivers → which and why
text:
## 1. What antecedent means
River older than the mountains it crosses: as the land rose, the river kept its course by cutting down (vertical erosion) → deep gorges
Also called inconsequent drainage; a type of discordant drainage
River | Antecedent gorge / evidence
Indus | Gorge near Nanga Parbat (western syntaxis)
Sutlej | Cuts the Himalaya at Shipki La; gorge in Naina Devi Dhar (Bhakra)
Brahmaputra | Gorge round Namcha Barwa (eastern syntaxis)
Subansiri | Rises in Tibet, cuts across to Arunachal
Arun (Kosi system) | Rises in Tibet, cuts across Nepal Himalaya (Beyond your notes)
## 2. The contrast
Type | Meaning | Examples
Antecedent | Older than the uplift; cuts through new landform | Indus, Sutlej, Brahmaputra
Superimposed | Pattern inherited from a cover rock now eroded | Damodar, Subarnarekha, Chambal, Banas, Rewa plateau rivers
⚠ PYQ 2026: "antecedent + three countries + Tibetan source + irrigation + no distributaries" = Sutlej (Indus and Brahmaputra form deltas/distributaries; Teesta rises in India)

topic: Himalayan drainage: nature, origin and river shifts
t: Himalayan vs Peninsular rivers → how they differ
text:
Aspect | Himalayan | Peninsular
Source | Glaciers and snowmelt | Plateaus and hills
Flow | Perennial (snow + rain) | Mostly seasonal, rain-fed
Age | Young | Older, graded shallow valleys
Upper course | Gorges, V-valleys, rapids, waterfalls | Broad mature valleys
Lower course | Meanders, ox-bows, braided channels, frequent course changes | Fixed course, few meanders
Silt | Heavy load | Low
Length, discharge | Longer, larger | Shorter, smaller
Hydropower potential | High (steep gradient) | Lower
Himalayan drainage = Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra basins
Peninsular rivers of the Ganga system: Chambal, Sind, Betwa, Ken, Son (rise in the north of the peninsula)
⚠ Narmada and Tapi are peninsular yet meandering and perennial: they flow in rift valleys
Kosi = classic Himalayan course-changer (shifts westward)

text:
## 1. The idea (PYQ 2026)
In the Pleistocene, either the Yamuna flowed into the Indus, or the Sutlej flowed into the Yamuna: a major tributary switched between the Ganga and Indus systems
## 2. Which evidence counts
Proposed basis | Valid? | Why
Same dolphin species in Indus and Ganga systems | Yes | Freshwater dolphins cannot cross the sea: the two systems must once have been connected (headstream capture between Sutlej and Yamuna)
Nadi-Sukta of the Rigveda | No | Lists rivers of the Vedic period; no Pleistocene evidence
Robert Bruce Foote | No | Geologist of prehistoric (Stone Age) archaeology; not a Sutlej-Yamuna explorer
The Ghaggar (successor of the legendary Saraswati) is the only river between the Yamuna and Sutlej; the Haryana tract is the water divide
⚠ Answer 2026: 3 only
## In news 2025-26
First dolphin survey (2025): only 3 Indus river dolphins in India, all in the Beas (Punjab); Project Dolphin (2020) under the Wildlife Institute of India

t: Peninsular vs Himalayan rivers → how they differ
text:
## 1. Comparison (PMF)
Aspect | Himalayan | Peninsular
Age | Young | Older: broad, graded, shallow valleys; mature rivers
Source | Glaciers, snowmelt | Plateaus and hills (mostly Western Ghats)
Flow | Perennial | Seasonal, monsoon-fed (exceptions below)
Course | Meanders, shifts course (Kosi) | Fixed course, few meanders
Silt, discharge | High | Lower
Hydel potential | High (steep) | Lower (gentler gradients)
## 2. Lines to remember
Western Ghats = main water divide of the Peninsula
Chambal, Sind, Betwa, Ken, Son rise in the north of the Peninsula but belong to the Ganga system
77% of India's drainage goes to the Bay of Bengal; Arabian Sea and Bay drainages are split by Delhi Ridge, Aravallis, Western Ghats
⚠ Narmada and Tapi are the exceptions: meandering, perennial, because they run in rift valleys

topic: Peninsular drainage: slope, rift valleys, estuaries
t: Why most rivers flow east → slope of the Deccan
text:
## 1. The slope
Deccan Plateau is higher on its western edge and slopes gently east to the Bay of Bengal
Hence Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Cauvery flow east: consequent rivers (follow the slope)
West-flowing rivers off the Ghats are short, swift streams
## 2. East-flowing vs west-flowing (PMF)
Feature | East-flowing | West-flowing
Origin | Eastern slopes of Western Ghats | Western slopes of Ghats (or rift valleys)
Length, basin | Long, large | Short, small
Tributaries | Well-developed dendritic system | Few
Mouth | Large deltas (Mahanadi, Krishna) | Estuaries (Narmada, Tapi)
⚠ Kalinadi (Uttara Kannada, 184 km) rises in the Western Ghats and flows west to the Arabian Sea
⚠ Kerala has east-flowing rivers (Kabini from Wayanad); MP has west-flowing ones (Narmada, Tapi)

River | Rift / trough | Flows
Narmada | Between Vindhyas (N) and Satpuras (S) | West to Gulf of Khambhat
Tapi | South of the Satpuras | West

## 2. Why Narmada flows west (2013 logic)
Correct: it occupies a linear rift valley: the rift itself tilts west
Flanking Vindhyas and Satpuras are a product of the same faulting, not the cause
"Land slopes west from Central India" is wrong: the Deccan slopes east
⚠ Only rift rivers buck the eastward slope; Damodar is the east-flowing rift river
