t: Southwest monsoon → why the winds blow in
text:
## 1. The summer pressure pattern
Summer heating → thermal low over north-west India and the subcontinent (heat-low acts as a suction pump)
Higher pressure over the Indian Ocean (Mascarene High, east-northeast of Madagascar)
Air moves high → low; south-east trades cross the equator and are deflected by Coriolis to blow from the south-west
Season | Pressure over land | Pressure over sea | Wind
Summer | Low (Tibet, NW India) | High | SW monsoon, sea → land, wet
Winter | High (Tibet, Siberia) | Low | NE monsoon, land → sea, dry
Monsoon = seasonal reversal of winds; word from Arabic mausim ("season")
⚠ Option traps: south-east monsoon, trade winds, westerlies: the in-blowing summer wind is the south-west monsoon
PYQ 1996: low pressure over the subcontinent draws in the south-west monsoon; PYQ 2014: seasonal reversal of winds = monsoon climate

t: Monsoon factors → formation, onset and intensity
text:
## 1. PMF's three lists
Role | Factors
Formation (SW) | Intense heating of Tibetan Plateau; permanent Mascarene High
Onset | Above + STJ shift, Tropical Easterly Jet, ITCZ
Intensity | Tibet low vs Indian Ocean high, Somali (Findlater) Jet, Somali Current, Indian Ocean branch of Walker cell, IOD
NE monsoon formation | Highs over Tibet and Siberia; Mascarene High weakens westward; ITCZ moves south of India
## 2. Snow over Tibet
Thick, widespread Tibetan snow → easterly jet fails to form → weak monsoon
Lower Eurasian snow cover → stronger monsoon (PMF 2026)
⚠ Findlater Current upwelling near the Horn of Africa has little impact on Indian monsoon (zone too small), unlike IOD

t: Monsoon theories → classical vs modern
text:
## 1. Classical (thermal) theory
Sir Edmund Halley (17th century): differential heating of land and sea; monsoon = land and sea breeze on a large scale
First study: Arab traders; Al Masudi (10th century) described reversal of winds and currents
Fails to explain sudden burst, delayed onset, uneven development
## 2. Modern explanations
Theory | Key idea
Air mass / ITCZ | ITCZ shifts north to the Ganga plain (monsoon trough); SE trades cross equator, become SW
Jet stream | STJ leaves south of Himalayas → TEJ forms → burst
Tibet heating | Tibet as elevated heat source drives TEJ
Also matter: shape of continents, orography, upper-troposphere circulation
⚠ Halley's theory is "classical", not modern; the modern view adds jet streams and upper-air circulation

t: Jet streams and the monsoon → STJ, TEJ, Somali Jet
text:
## 1. Roles
Jet | Season and position | Effect
STJ (westerly) | Winter: south of Himalayas, ~25°N; southern branch ~240 km/h | Divergence, high pressure, dry; steers western disturbances
STJ shift | 25 May-10 June north of Himalayas; ~40°N by June | First indication of onset
TEJ (easterly) | First week of June to late October | Upper anticyclone, surface low → burst
Somali / Findlater Jet | Low-level, from Mauritius/N Madagascar, crosses Kenya coast ~3°S | Carries moisture to west coast
STJ returns south of the Himalayas in mid-October → withdrawal
Somali Jet splits over Arabian Sea; northern branch meets west coast near 17°N
⚠ Northward jump of the STJ (not TEJ) is the first sign of onset; TEJ forms after it
## In news 2025-26
Weak Somali Jet listed among causes of the June 2026 monsoon slowdown (PMF LENS 19 Oct 2026)

Whole country covered by mid-July (Kashmir last)

⚠ Advance is a sudden burst; withdrawal is gradual

t: Monsoon branches → Arabian Sea vs Bay of Bengal
text:
## 1. Two branches
 | Arabian Sea branch | Bay of Bengal branch
Strength | More powerful (bigger sea; whole current enters India) | Weaker (part goes to Myanmar, Thailand)
Streams | 3: Western Ghats; Narmada-Tapi trough; along Aravalli | 2: Meghalaya (Garo-Khasi); along Himalayan foothills
Big rain | West coast 250+ cm; windward Ghats 400-500 cm | Mawsynram 1,221 cm, Cherrapunji 1,102 cm
Dry zone | Rajasthan (Aravalli parallel to wind); Mount Abu ~170 cm | -
Branches merge near Delhi
Tamil Nadu dry in SW monsoon: Ghats rain shadow + Bay current parallel to coast
Bay advance is faster than Arabian Sea advance
Bhojpur calls the monsoon "Purvaiya" (easterly) as the Bay branch arrives from the east
⚠ Aravalli lies parallel to the wind, so Rajasthan stays dry

t: Break in monsoon → causes and pattern
text:
## 1. What happens
Monsoon trough shifts north to the Himalayan foothills → rain falls in sub-Himalaya, NE India, SE peninsula; rest of India dry
Core zone hit: Gujarat to West Bengal/Odisha
Declared when rainfall anomaly index over core zone < -1 for 3+ days
1-2 breaks a year, in 85 of 100 years; mostly second week of August
Temperature rises during a break
## 2. Causes (PMF)
Cause | How
El Nino | Weaker monsoon, longer breaks
Negative IOD | Cooler western Indian Ocean
Arabian Sea cyclone | Sucks moisture; worse if it turns to Yemen
Suppressed MJO | 30-60 day eastward convection pulse in dry phase
⚠ During a break the Himalayan foothills get more rain, not less
Most monsoon rain in central/north India comes from depressions (3-4/month) from the Bay, entering via river deltas

t: Retreating monsoon → October-November weather
text:
## 1. Features
Season: mid-September to November; monsoon trough weakens, moves south; onset of NE monsoon not clearly defined
Most destructive cyclones: Bay of Bengal, peak October-first half of November; ~55% hit Indian coast
Tamil Nadu: Oct-Nov is the main rainy season; NE winds pick up moisture over the Bay of Bengal; secondary rains in Kerala
Region | Main rain season
Most of India | June-September (SW)
Coromandel / TN | October-December (NE/retreating)
Bengaluru | Both SW and NE
⚠ NE monsoon is dry land wind over most of India; it is wet only after crossing the Bay of Bengal
## Beyond your notes
"October heat" is the standard NCERT term for the humid post-monsoon heat

topic: ENSO, IOD and other monsoon drivers
t: El Nino and ENSO → effect on the monsoon
text:
## 1. What they are
El Nino: abnormal warming of central and eastern Pacific (off Peru-Ecuador); every 2-7 years; trade winds weaken, Walker cell weakens/shifts east
Southern Oscillation: see-saw of pressure between east and west tropical Pacific (atmospheric part)
ENSO = El Nino (ocean) + SO (atmosphere), coupled
Phase | Pacific | India
El Nino | Warm east, low pressure east | Weak monsoon, droughts; good for Arabian Sea cyclogenesis
La Nina | Cold east, strong trades | Strong monsoon, floods; Bay cyclogenesis up
Neutral | Normal | -
ENSO and monsoon are inversely related
⚠ Not every El Nino causes drought: 1997 strong El Nino, no drought (IOD); 2002 moderate El Nino, severe drought
PYQ 2002: event linked to occasional weak monsoon = El Nino and Southern Oscillation; La Nina and jet streams were traps

topic: ENSO, IOD and other monsoon drivers
t: Southern Oscillation Index → how it signals monsoon
text:
## 1. SOI (PMF)
SOI = pressure at Tahiti minus pressure at Port Darwin (N Australia)
SOI | Pressure | India
Positive | Tahiti > Darwin | Good monsoon
Negative | Darwin > Tahiti | Bad monsoon (El Nino-like)
## 2. Related terms
El Nino Modoki: warming in central Pacific, cooling east and west; two-cell Walker circulation
Super El Nino: SST anomaly above +2.0°C in central Pacific
Bjerknes feedback: warming weakens trades further, sustaining El Nino
⚠ PMF's labels for Tahiti/Darwin as "eastern/western Pacific" are loose: Tahiti is central Pacific, Darwin western

topic: ENSO, IOD and other monsoon drivers
t: Indian Ocean Dipole → definition and phases
text:
## 1. Definition
SST difference between a western pole (Arabian Sea, western Indian Ocean) and an eastern pole (eastern Indian Ocean south of Indonesia)
Discovered 1999; develops April-May, peaks October; measured by Dipole Mode Index
Atmospheric part: EQUINOO (Equatorial Indian Ocean Oscillation): pressure see-saw between Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea
Phase | West Indian Ocean | East (Indonesia) | Indian monsoon
Positive | Warmer | Cooler, dry | Good
Negative | Cooler | Warmer, rainy | Weak
Positive IOD often coincides with El Nino; negative with La Nina; can also arise independently
⚠ IOD is Indian Ocean west vs east, not Western Indian Ocean vs Eastern Pacific
PYQ 2017: statement 1 (Pacific) wrong, statement 2 (IOD can modify El Nino's impact) right → 2 only

topic: ENSO, IOD and other monsoon drivers
t: El Nino with IOD → combined outcomes
text:
## 1. Combinations
Combination | Monsoon outcome | Example
El Nino + positive IOD | Damage partly offset | 1997 (no drought); 2019 strong IOD
El Nino + negative IOD | Severe weakening | 2002, 2015
La Nina + positive IOD | Strong monsoon | -
## 2. Other drivers (PMF)
MJO: eastward tropical convection pulse, cycle 30-60 days, found 1971 (Madden and Julian); intra-seasonal (ENSO is seasonal)
Atlantic Nino (Atlantic Zonal Mode), aerosols, Asian desert dust, Eurasian snow cover
Low-pressure systems from the Bay carry rain inland to NW India and Himalayan foothills
## In news 2025-26
Nov 2026 (PMF LENS 2 Nov): analysis shows a strong El Nino need not mean a deficient monsoon; positive IOD can partly offset it
⚠ Monsoon outcome = ENSO + IOD + MJO + regional factors together

Category | Rainfall
Deficient | < 90%
Below normal | 90-96%
Normal | 96-104%
Above normal | 104-110%
Excess | > 110%

60% of 14 stations record ≥ 2.5 mm for 2 consecutive days
Westerlies up to 600 hPa; 15-20 knots at 925 hPa; OLR < 200 W/m²
Declared on the second day after conditions are met

t: Winter season → western disturbances and Tamil Nadu rain
text:
## 1. Western disturbances
Residual frontal (temperate) cyclones from the Mediterranean, pick up moisture over Caspian and Black Sea; steered by southern branch of STJ
4-6 reach NW India October-April; rain up to Patna; snow in Himalayas; cold waves and fog after
Vital for rabi crops: wheat, barley, mustard, gram
## 2. Winter (Nov-March) facts
Point | Fact
Coldest month | January
20°C isotherm | Roughly parallel to Tropic of Cancer
Winter rain in south | Tamil Nadu, S Andhra, SE Karnataka, SE Kerala (NE monsoon, Nov)
Coldest place | Dras, -45°C (1908)
Himalayas keep north India 3-8°C warmer in winter than same latitudes
⚠ Winter rain in north India is from westerlies (western disturbances), not the NE monsoon
## In news 2025-26
May 2026: IMD forecast a fresh western disturbance over north India (11-13 May), showing WDs now also act in early summer (CARE May 2026)

t: 18°C January isotherm → tropical vs subtropical India
text:
## 1. Stamp's division
L.D. Stamp used the 18°C mean January isotherm to split India
North: temperate / continental (subtropical) zone; south: tropical zone
The line follows roughly the base of the peninsula, near/parallel to the Tropic of Cancer (Tapi estuary in west to Mahanadi delta in east, per PYQ key)
Zone | Sub-regions
Temperate (5) | Himalayan; North-western; Arid lowland; Moderate rainfall; Transitional
Tropical (6) | Very heavy rain; Heavy rain; Moderate rain; Konkan; Malabar; Tamil Nadu
Total 11 regions
⚠ Distractors 21°C, 15°C, 12°C: the answer is 18°C; do not confuse with the 20°C January isotherm parallel to the Tropic of Cancer
PYQ 1997: January isotherm dividing tropical and subtropical India = 18°C

## 1. The classification
H.G. Champion (1935); revised with S.K. Seth (1968); national standard
Treats each forest type as an ecosystem; 5 climate-based major groups, 16 type groups
Major group | Type groups
A. Moist Tropical | Wet evergreen; semi-evergreen; moist deciduous; littoral and swamp
B. Dry Tropical | Dry evergreen; dry deciduous; thorn
C. Montane Sub-Tropical | Broad-leaved hill; moist hill (pine); dry evergreen

E. Alpine | Sub-alpine; moist alpine scrub; dry alpine scrub

Rainfall | Type
>250 cm (Preview: >200 cm) | Wet evergreen
200-250 cm | Semi-evergreen

## 1. Distribution
Region | Wet evergreen?
Western side of Western Ghats (500-1370 m): Kerala, Karnataka, TN | Yes
North-East: Arunachal, Assam, Meghalaya (Khasi-Jaintia), Mizoram, Nagaland, Tripura | Yes
Andaman and Nicobar Islands | Yes

## 2. Characteristics
Rain >250 cm, 25-27 °C, very short dry season
Trees 45-60 m, multi-layered canopy, mesophytic, sparse undergrowth (bamboo, ferns, climbers, orchids)

Juniper (dry alpine) | Mahogany (tropical; native to Central/South America)
Silver fir, spruce (temperate/sub-alpine) | Sandalwood (south peninsula)
Deodar, blue pine, chir pine | Teak (central and south India)
Oak, rhododendron, birch, hemlock | Red sanders (Eastern Ghats)
Taxus (yew; anti-cancer taxol) | Rosewood, mesua (Western Ghats evergreen)
Birch bark (bhojpatra) was used for writing scriptures
PYQ 2008: mahogany is not Himalayan; juniper, silver fir, spruce are
PYQ 2014: oak and rhododendron grow naturally in the Himalaya; sandalwood does not

Feature | Eastern Himalaya | Western Himalaya

text:
## 1. Definitions (Forest Survey of India)
Term | Meaning
Recorded Forest Area (RFA) | Land legally notified/recorded as forest (Reserved, Protected; Indian Forest Act 1927); may have no trees
Forest cover | Land ≥1 ha with canopy >10%, any ownership or land use; includes plantations
Very Dense Forest | Canopy ≥70%
Moderately Dense | 40-70%
Open Forest | 10-40%
Tree cover | Tree patches <1 ha outside RFA, any density
Trees Outside Forests (TOF) | All trees outside RFA, any size; tree cover is a subset
Forest + tree cover is measured against the National Forest Policy goal of 33%
Deemed forests ≈ 1% of forest land; States define RFA criteria since 1996
⚠ Forest cover counts plantations and orchards: a criticism of the ISFR ("anything green is a forest")

t: Parent rock → soil it gives
text:
## 1. Six parent-material groups of India (PMF)
Parent rock | Nature | Soil on weathering
Ancient crystalline and metamorphic (granite, gneiss, schist) | Oldest, pre-Cambrian; Basement Complex of the Peninsula; rich in ferromagnesian minerals | Red soils (iron oxide)
Cuddapah and Vindhyan | Ancient sedimentary, ~4000 m thick | Calcareous and argillaceous (clayey) soils, devoid of metals
Gondwana | Younger sedimentary | Less mature, low fertility, uniform
Deccan basalts | Lava from fissures over ~10 lakh sq km; rich in titanium, magnetite, aluminium, magnesium | Dark soils → regur / black cotton soil
Tertiary and Mesozoic sedimentary (extra-Peninsula) | Young | Immature alluvial soils (little relation to parent rock)
Recent and sub-recent | River deposits | Alluvium
Basic rocks (basalt, gabbro; ~40% silica) are dark and weather easily; acid rocks (granite; up to 80% silica) are light and resist weathering
⚠ The same parent rock can give different soils in different climates, and different rocks can give the same soil: climate can override parent rock

t: Climate and relief → which soil forms
text:
## 1. Climate → soil
Climate | Soil result
Heavy rain + high temperature, alternate wet and dry | Red / lateritic: leaching, then iron and aluminium oxides drawn up by capillary action
Hot summer, low rain (parts of Tamil Nadu) | Black soil irrespective of parent rock
Arid (Rajasthan) | Sandy soil from both granite and sandstone
Arid and semi-arid (evaporation > precipitation) | Light colour, low humus, lime-accumulating = pedocal
Cold Himalaya | Slow decay of vegetation → acidic soils
Crystalline granite → laterite in moist monsoon areas, non-laterite in drier areas
## 2. Relief and vegetation
Steep slopes: erosion hinders soil formation (Chambal ravines, bare upper Himalaya)
Gentle slopes / low relief: deposition, deep soils (Indo-Gangetic plain)
Dense forests give some of the best soils: leaf litter adds humus
Soil-forming factors: active = climate, organisms; passive = parent material, relief, time (PMF Indian Agriculture)

t: Texture → sandy, clayey and loamy soils
text:
## 1. Classified by particle size
Soil | Particles | Water and air
Sandy | Mostly big particles | Drains fast; light colour, well aerated, dry
Clayey | Mostly fine particles, packed tight | Holds most water, little air, heavy
Loamy | Sand + clay + silt in near-equal share, with humus | Right water-holding capacity; ideal topsoil
Silt particle size lies between sand and clay; occurs as riverbed deposit
## 2. Texture → crop (PMF)
Crop | Best soil
Wheat, gram | Clayey and loamy
Paddy | Clay rich in organic matter, good water retention
Lentils (masoor), pulses | Loamy, drains easily
Cotton | Sandy loam or loam, drains well, holds air
Loam typically 40% sand, 18% clay, 42% silt (Preview)
⚠ Alluvial sand soil has the minimum water retention; clayey soils the most (Uttarakhand PCS 2003)

t: Soil profile → horizons from top to bedrock
text:
## 1. Horizons (PMF)
Horizon | Name | Key feature
O | Organic layer | Litter (leaves, twigs, moss) and humus
A | Topsoil | Organic + mineral; dark, soft, porous, rich in life; loses iron, clay, Al downward
E | Eluviated layer | Leached of clay, iron, Al oxides; quartz left; between A and B in older soils
B | Subsoil | Illuviation: accumulates leached iron, clay, Al; highest clay content
C | Parent material | Weathered rock lumps; transition to bedrock
R | Bedrock | Continuous hard rock; source of parent material
Eluviation = removal of material from a horizon by percolating water; illuviation = its deposition in a lower horizon
Pedology = study of soils; pedogenesis = soil formation (weathering, leaching, calcification)
⚠ Leaching removes from A/E; accumulation is in B, not C

t: Peninsular vs extra-Peninsular soils → sedentary or transported
text:
## 1. Comparison
Feature | Peninsular soils | Extra-Peninsular soils
Formation | In situ decomposition of underlying rock | Deposition by rivers and wind
Name | Sedentary soils | Transported / azonal soils
Depth | Shallower, coarse-grained | Very deep
Maturity / fertility | More mature, less fertile | Immature, very fertile (silt, clay, Himalayan replenishment)
Example | Black, red, laterite | Alluvial
## 2. ICAR's eight major soil groups and their share (PMF)
Group | Area | % of India
Alluvial | ~15 lakh sq km | 45.6% (largest)
Black | 5.46 lakh sq km | 16.6%
Red | ~3.5 lakh sq km | 10.6%
Forest / mountain | 2.85 lakh sq km | 8.67%
Laterite | 2.48 lakh sq km | -
Arid / desert | 1.42 lakh sq km | 4.32%
Saline / alkaline | 68,000 sq km | -
Peaty / marshy | small patches | -
⚠ Order by area: alluvial > black > red > forest > laterite > desert > saline; red soils "with minor groups" are also called one of the largest groups

topic: Soil properties: organic matter, nutrients and fertility
t: Organic matter and humus → water-holding capacity
text:
## 1. Humus
Dark organic matter from decayed plants and animals; holds water and nutrients; natural fertiliser
High organic matter increases water-holding capacity (does NOT reduce it)
## 2. Soil Organic Carbon (SOC) (PMF LENS Nov 2025)
Fact | Value / rule
SOC | Carbon part of soil organic matter (SOM), as % of soil weight
Healthy soils | 1-6% SOC
Carbon share of SOM | 50-60%
Forms | Fresh residues, humus, living microbes
Higher SOC | Cooler climates, higher elevation, clay soils, grasslands, flat low land, topsoil
Lower SOC | Tropics (fast decay), arid or flooded soils, sandy soils, steep slopes
Benefits: aggregates soil, cuts erosion, feeds microbes, raises cation exchange, stores moisture, carbon sink
⚠ Forests lose SOC faster than grasslands (surface litter decays quickly); hill regions hold more SOC than plains
⚠ PMF Statement-I/II practice: "healthy soils contain 50-60% SOC" is wrong: 50-60% is carbon's share of SOM; SOC is 1-6%
PYQ 2018: "high organic matter drastically reduces water-holding capacity" is false; only statement 3 (irrigation can salinise land) was correct
## In news 2025-26
ICAR study (Nov 2025): climate change and unbalanced fertiliser use are speeding SOC decline; Haryana, Punjab, western UP show high loss from prolonged urea and phosphorus use
PIB (Jul 2026): average SOC reportedly fell from 1% to 0.3% over 70 years

topic: Soil properties: organic matter, nutrients and fertility
t: Soil and nutrient cycles → sulphur cycle
text:
## 1. Sulphur cycle (mostly sedimentary)
Stored in organic (coal, oil, peat) and inorganic (pyrite) deposits; released by rock weathering, runoff, decomposition
Sulphates taken up by plants from soil → sulphur amino acids → food chain → back to soil and sediments by excretion and decay
Gaseous only as H2S and SO2; SO2 returns as weak sulphuric acid (acid rain)
## 2. Which cycles are sedimentary
Cycle | Type | Main reservoir
Phosphorus | Sedimentary | Rocks (weathering is main source)
Sulphur | Mostly sedimentary | Rocks, soil, sediments
Carbon, nitrogen | Gaseous | Atmosphere
⚠ "Soil plays no role in the sulphur cycle" is false (UPSC 2018)
PYQ 2021 (Environment): weathering of rocks is the main nutrient source for the phosphorus cycle

topic: Soil properties: organic matter, nutrients and fertility
t: Fertility status → what each soil lacks and has
text:
## 1. Deficiencies (PMF Indian Agriculture)
Soil | Deficient in | Rich in
Alluvial | Nitrogen, organic matter | Phosphoric acid, potash
Black | Organic carbon, N, S, P | Lime, calcium
Red | N, phosphate, lime, humus | Iron, potash
Laterite | N, P, calcium | Iron and aluminium oxides
Arid | Organic matter, nitrogen | Phosphate, calcium carbonate
Saline-alkaline | Calcium, nitrogen | Soluble salts
Forest | Potash, phosphorus, lime | Humus
Peaty | Potash, phosphate | Organic matter
India: 58% soils deficient in N, 49% in P, 48% in K
Nitrogen is low in almost every Indian soil group: the common answer in "rich in N" traps
Desirable NPK ratio 4:2:1; actual ratio skewed to nitrogen → micronutrient deficiency, alkalinity, salinity

text:

Scheme | Key fact
Soil Health Card (2015) | Tests soil on 12 parameters; plot-wise balanced fertiliser advice
Neem Coated Urea | Slows nitrogen release
Sulphur Coated Urea (Urea Gold) | Also fixes sulphur deficiency
Nano Urea, Nano DAP | Better absorption, precision use
PM-PRANAM | Cut chemical fertiliser use by states
NMNF (Nov 2024) | Natural farming; ₹4,000/acre/yr for 2 years
RAD (2014, under NMSA) | Integrated farming to control erosion in rainfed areas
## In news 2025-26
PIB (Jul 2026): 25.89 crore Soil Health Cards issued; NMNF 18,786 clusters, 8.80 lakh ha, 18.19 lakh farmers
Khet Bachao Abhiyan (2026): soil-management outreach, 1.07 crore farmers reached
Aadi programme (Sep 2026): India's first soil-carbon payments to 2,550 farmers in Punjab and Haryana (Grow Indigo, ICAR guidance; Verra VM0042 methodology; DSR, reduced tillage)

## Beyond your notes
World Soil Day is 5 December (FAO; observed since 2014)

t: Alluvial soil → origin, properties and distribution
text:
## 1. Key facts
Silt of the Indus-Ganga-Brahmaputra; Himalayan rocks are parent material; coastal ones by wave action
Largest group: ~15 lakh sq km, 45.6%; supports >40% of population
Immature, weak profile (recent origin); mostly loamy, porous, well drained; kankar beds on terraces
## 2. Chemistry
Low | Adequate
Nitrogen (generally low), humus | Potash, phosphoric acid, alkalis (lime)
## 3. Where
Type | Region
Indo-Gangetic-Brahmaputra plains | Punjab to Assam (except desert-sand cover)
Deltaic / coastal alluvium | Deltas of Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Cauvery
Others | Narmada and Tapi valleys, north Gujarat
Crops: rice, wheat, sugarcane, tobacco, cotton, jute, maize, oilseeds; respond well to canal and tube-well irrigation
West Bengal delta soils renewed by floods yearly: ideal for jute
Chhattisgarh PCS 2020: alluvial soil is rich in phosphoric acid; Reh, Thur, Chopan are names of saline soils, not alluvium

t: Khadar, bhangar and other plain belts → which is which
text:
## 1. Belts of the northern plain
Belt | Nature
Bhabar | 8-10 km, Shiwalik foothills; pebbles, porous; streams disappear
Tarai | 10-20 km; streams re-emerge; marshy; soil rich in N and organic matter, poor in phosphate
Bhangar | Older alluvium, above flood level, terrace-like; clayey, dark; kankar (lime nodules); fossils
Khadar | Newer alluvium of floodplains; renewed yearly; very fertile; sandy clays and loams, less calcareous
Bhur | Wind-blown sand mounds of the upper Ganga-Yamuna doab
Barind | Bhangar variant in Bengal delta; reddish-yellow clay
Reh / Kollar | Saline efflorescence in drier Haryana; spread with irrigation (capillary action)
⚠ Kankar is in bhangar, not khadar; khadar = new + flooded, bhangar = old + above floods
⚠ Rarh = ancient alluvium at higher level (Preview); Barind and Bhur are regional bhangar forms

t: Black cotton soil → parent rock and origin
text:
## 1. Origin
Weathering of Deccan Trap basalt: lava that flowed out of fissures (fissure eruption, not central-vent) over ~10 lakh sq km
Basalt is a basic, extrusive igneous rock, rich in titanium, magnetite, Al, Mg → dark soil
Exception: in Tamil Nadu (and parts of AP) black soil comes from gneisses and schists; also formed by hot, dry climate irrespective of rock
Option in PYQ 2021 | Reality
Brown forest soil | Not a parent rock of regur
Fissure volcanic rock | Correct: Deccan basalt
Granite and schist | Parent of red soils (schist only for TN black soils)
Shale and limestone | Sedimentary; not regur
Names: regur (Telugu "reguda"), black cotton soil, tropical chernozem
PYQ 2021: black cotton soil formed by weathering of fissure volcanic rock; trap: "granite and schist" (red soil parent)

t: Black soil → properties and colour
text:
## 1. Physical
Highly argillaceous: clay 62% or more → retains moisture long
Summer: shrinks, deep wide cracks → air reaches depth = self-ploughing
Rains: swells, very sticky → hard to plough
Upland black soils of low fertility; valley ones very fertile
## 2. Colour and chemistry (PMF)
Item | Fact
Colour | Titaniferous magnetite / iron and black parent constituents (not humus)
Composition | ~10% alumina, 10% iron oxide, 6-8% lime and magnesium carbonates
Low | Phosphates, nitrogen, humus; potash variable (<0.5%)
Rich | Lime, calcium, iron, magnesia
⚠ Assertion "regur is black because rich in humus" is false (UPPCS 1999): black soils are low in humus
⚠ PMF Indian Agriculture calls black soil "rich in potash"; PMF Indian Physical Geography gives potash as variable, <0.5%: follow the latter, note the former

t: Black soil → distribution and crops
text:
## 1. Where
5.46 lakh sq km (16.6%): Maharashtra (most widespread), MP, Gujarat (Saurashtra), Malwa, Karnataka, Telangana, AP, Chhattisgarh, Tamil Nadu; along Godavari and Krishna valleys
Typical of hot, low-rainfall parts of the Peninsula
## 2. Crops
Group | Crops
Best | Cotton (hence "black cotton")
Others | Wheat, jowar, linseed, Virginia tobacco, castor, sunflower, millets
With irrigation | Rice, sugarcane
Cultivated for centuries without fertiliser with little sign of exhaustion
⚠ Black soil is not found in the Himalaya (UPPCS 2018)
## In news 2025-26
PMF (Sep 2026): national cotton output fell to 290.91 lakh bales in 2025-26; northern belt acreage down 23.2%; India a net importer of raw cotton for the first time in decades
Causes include soil degradation: cotton monocropping and urea-skewed NPK depleted SOC in central and western tracts
Mission for Cotton Productivity (2026-31): lint yield ~440 → 755 kg/ha, 140 districts (LENS Jun 2026)

t: Red soil → why it is red
text:
## 1. Cause of colour
Iron oxide (ferric oxide, Fe3+), from oxidation of iron in crystalline and metamorphic rocks
Colour from wide diffusion of iron, not a high percentage of it
Looks yellow when the iron is hydrated → "red and yellow soils"
Under waterlogging (reduction) red iron turns greenish or bluish grey
PYQ 2010 option | Correct?
Abundance of magnesium | No
Accumulated humus | No (humus darkens; red soils are poor in humus)
Presence of ferric oxide | Yes
Abundance of phosphates | No (red soils are poor in phosphate)
PYQ 2010: red soil colour = ferric oxide; traps: humus, phosphates (both actually deficient)

t: Red soil → parent rock, chemistry, distribution and crops
text:
## 1. Properties
Parent: acid granites, gneisses, quartzites (crystalline, metamorphic)
Texture sand to clay, mostly loams; uplands poor, gravelly; lowlands deep, dark, fertile
Acidic; poor in lime, magnesia, phosphates, nitrogen, humus; fairly rich in potash
## 2. Where and what grows
Item | Detail
Area | ~3.5 lakh sq km (10.6%)
Rainfall | Mostly low-rainfall regions
Main | Almost all Tamil Nadu; Karnataka, SE Maharashtra, Telangana, AP, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Chota Nagpur, eastern Rajasthan, NE
Crops (with fertiliser, irrigation) | Cotton, wheat, rice, pulses, millets, groundnut, tobacco, potato, fruits
Loamy → cannot retain water like black soil
⚠ Preview says red soils are "more leached than laterite"; PMF links heavy leaching to laterite: follow PMF

t: Laterite soil → how it forms
text:
## 1. Formation
End product of weathering; high temperature + heavy rainfall + alternate wet and dry seasons
Heavy rain leaches lime and silica; oxides of iron and aluminium remain
"Later" = brick (Latin); hardens like iron on drying (Buchanan-Hamilton studied it, 1807)
Red due to iron oxides (PMF also: little clay, more gravel of red sandstone)
## 2. Chemistry
Poor in | Rich in
Lime, magnesia, potash, nitrogen; phosphorus, calcium | Iron and aluminium oxides (bauxite)
Phosphate may be high as iron phosphate; humus higher in wetter places
Acidic, porous, poor water-holding (not "large clay factor")
⚠ "Rich in nitrogen and potash" is false; laterite is rendered infertile by excess iron (UPSC 1994)
⚠ PMF Indian Agriculture: laterites under forests are "rich in humus"; PMF Indian Physical Geography: humus only higher in wetter places; rich in lime is false

t: Laterite soil → where it is found and what grows
text:
## 1. Distribution
2.48 lakh sq km; summits of Western Ghats (1000-1500 m), Eastern Ghats, Rajmahal hills, Vindhyas, Satpuras, Malwa plateau
Well developed in south Maharashtra, Karnataka, Kerala (Malabar), Odisha, West Bengal, Jharkhand, Assam, Meghalaya
Not in Rajasthan, UP, Punjab, HP (low rainfall)
## 2. Use
Use | Detail
Crops (manured, irrigated) | Tea, coffee, rubber, cinchona, coconut, arecanut
Tolerant crops | Cashew, tapioca (tolerate acidic, low-nutrient soil; deep roots)
Others | Grazing grounds, scrub forests
Building material | Cut into blocks, hardens in air, durable
Cashew = "Gold Mine of Waste Land": grows on poor soils, checks erosion
PYQ 2013: laterites are red (1) and suit tapioca and cashew (4); traps: "rich in N and potash" (2) and "well developed in Rajasthan and UP" (3) → answer 1 and 4
## In news 2025-26
LENS (Mar 2025, coffee exports): coffee does best in gravelly laterite and red clay loam, not sandy or calcareous soils

t: Black vs red vs laterite → one-glance comparison
text:
Feature | Black | Red | Laterite
Parent / process | Fissure basalt | Granite, gneiss | Intense leaching
Rainfall | Low, hot | Low | Heavy, wet-dry
Colour from | Titaniferous magnetite | Ferric oxide diffusion | Iron, Al oxides
Water holding | Very high (clay) | Low (loamy) | Low (porous)
Rich in | Lime, iron, magnesia | Potash | Iron, aluminium
Poor in | N, P, humus | N, P, lime, humus | N, K, lime
Signature crop | Cotton | Millets, groundnut | Cashew, tea, coffee
⚠ The nitrogen deficiency is common to all three: a "rich in nitrogen" statement is almost always wrong

topic: Forest, desert, saline and peaty soils
t: Forest and mountain soils → properties and slope
text:
## 1. Facts
2.85 lakh sq km (8.67%); heterogeneous; formed by organic matter from forests
Himalaya: in valleys, gentle and north-facing slopes; south-facing slopes steep, denuded, little soil
Loamy, silty on valley sides; coarse on upper slopes; acidic, low humus in snow-covered areas
Rich | Deficient
Humus | Potash, phosphorus, lime
Region | Crops
Peninsula (W and E Ghats) | Tea, coffee, spices, tropical fruits
Himalaya | Wheat, maize, barley, temperate fruits
Darjeeling hill soils: humus, iron, potash, phosphorus → tea

topic: Forest, desert, saline and peaty soils
t: Arid and desert soils → properties and crops
text:
## 1. Facts
Aeolian sand 90-95%, clay 5-10%; 1.42 lakh sq km (4.32%)
Rajasthan, Punjab, Haryana; sand blown from Indus basin and coast by SW monsoon winds; coastal sandy soils of Odisha, TN, Kerala
Low | High
Organic matter, nitrogen (some as nitrates) | Phosphate (as high as alluvium), calcium carbonate (subsoil 10x more)
Some are alkaline; fertile wherever water is available (phosphates + nitrates)
Crops: drought and salt-tolerant barley, cotton, millets, maize, pulses
⚠ Desert soils are rich in phosphate, unlike red and laterite soils

topic: Forest, desert, saline and peaty soils
t: Saline and alkaline soils → where and why
text:
## 1. Formation
Topsoil covered with salt efflorescence (Na, Mg, Ca salts, sulphurous acid)
Poor drainage → salts left as water evaporates; high water table → capillary action lifts salts in dry season
Saline = chlorides and sulphates of Na, Ca, Mg; alkaline = sodium carbonate dominant, pH > 8.5
## 2. Where (PMF)
Cause | Areas
Canal irrigation, high water table | Punjab, Haryana, UP, Bihar, Rajasthan, Maharashtra, AP, Telangana, Karnataka
Sea tides | Gulf of Khambhat: estuaries of Narmada, Tapi, Mahi, Sabarmati
Storm surges | Low-lying coastal AP and Tamil Nadu
Local names: Reh, Kallar, Usar, Thur, Chopan, Rakar, Karl
⚠ Area: PMF Indian Physical Geography 68,000 sq km; PMF Environment ~6.7-6.75 million ha, with UP most affected

topic: Forest, desert, saline and peaty soils
t: Peaty and marshy soils → where they occur
text:
## 1. Facts
Very high organic matter + soluble salts; most humid regions
Black, heavy, highly acidic; deficient in potash and phosphate
Under water in rains; then put under paddy
State | Area
Kerala | Kottayam and Alappuzha
Odisha, Tamil Nadu | Coastal areas
West Bengal | Sundarbans
Others | Bihar; Almora (Uttarakhand)
⚠ Peaty soils are black but acidic and humus-rich; black regur is low in humus and alkaline-calcareous
## Beyond your notes
Kerala's acidic peaty paddy soils are locally called Kari soils (verify)

t: Irrigation → salinisation and its remedies
text:
## 1. How irrigation salinises land
Over-irrigation in canal commands raises the water table; salts rise by capillary action and form white efflorescence on evaporation
Hot dry climate concentrates salts; poor drainage worsens it; waterlogging is a chief cause of salinity
Indira Gandhi Canal boosted farming but triggered wide salinity in Rajasthan
## 2. Reclamation
Measure | How
Gypsum (liberal) | Converts alkalis to soluble compounds (for alkaline/sodic soils)
Sulphur, pyrite, sulphuric acid | Neutralise alkali
Rice husk, straw | Decompose into mild acid
Drainage outlets, canal lining | Lower water table, stop seepage
Flushing with water | Leach salts out
Salt-tolerant crops | Cotton, barley
⚠ Gypsum (not lime) reclaims alkaline usar soil; lime is for acidic soils
PYQ 2018: "irrigation over time can salinise some agricultural lands" was the only correct statement

t: Deforestation and other causes → soil erosion
text:
## 1. Causes of land degradation (PMF)
Cause | How it erodes
Deforestation | Roots no longer bind soil; fast runoff (Shiwaliks, Chos of Punjab, Chambal ravines)
Shifting cultivation | Bare hill slopes lose topsoil
Overgrazing | Hooves pulverise soil, grass torn out
Ploughing along the slope | Water runs unchecked
Monocropping | Exhausts soil, easily eroded
Mining, dams, urbanisation | Expose and destabilise land
Degradation types: physical (erosion), chemical (salinity, alkalinity), biological (pollution, vegetation loss)
PYQ 2014: soil erosion in India linked to deforestation; terrace cultivation reduces it (does not cause it)
## In news 2025-26
LENS (Jun 2026): extreme rainfall bursts exceed absorption → runoff, moisture loss and nitrogen washout; N loss accelerates above 700 mm annual rain

t: Water and wind erosion → types and landforms
text:
## 1. Water erosion sequence
Stage | Feature
Splash / raindrop | Drops (~5 mm, 32 km/h) break soil structure
Sheet | Thin uniform removal; can create peneplain
Rill | Finger-like channels
Gully | Enlarged rills → badlands (Chambal)
Ravine → canyon | Deepened gully bed (>30 m) → canyon (Grand Canyon)
Also streambank, landslide, coastal (32% of India's coast eroded, 1990-2018, NCCR), glacial
## 2. Wind erosion (arid lands)
Process | Particles
Saltation | Fine and medium sand in bounds
Suspension | Dust, carried far
Surface creep | Coarse sand rolled
Leftover coarse surface = desert pavement; deflation hollows begin oasis formation

t: Soil conservation → method and where it is used
text:
## 1. Methods
Method | How it helps
Terracing | Steps on steep slopes; cut runoff and erosion
Contour ploughing | Across slope; cuts erosion 10-50%
Contour bunding / barriers | Banks along contours; terrace effect
Strip cropping | Alternate strips; tall crops as windbreaks
Shelterbelts | Tree rows in dry and coastal areas (Casuarina)
Mulching | Covers bare soil; holds moisture
Crop rotation, legumes | Restore nutrients
Afforestation; checking grazing and shifting cultivation | Bind soil
Gully plugging, rock dams | Stop gully growth
Geotextiles | Jute, coir (PMGSY roads allowed 2020)
Forest target: 33% (20% plains, 60% hills)
⚠ Terracing and contour bunding are for hill slopes (water erosion); shelterbelts and sand fences for wind erosion

t: Desertification and waterlogging → extent and remedies
text:
## 1. Facts
Desertification = desert-like conditions spreading in dry areas from human action or climate change; worst between the Indus and the Aravallis
Thar advancing ~0.5 km per year; causes: overgrazing, tree felling, population
Waterlogged soils ~12 million ha (half coastal); remedies: surface and vertical drainage
Remedies: tree belts in transition zones, dune mulching, grazing control, alternative fuels; NAPCD in India; SDG 15
## In news 2025-26
FAO Status of the World's Soil Resources 2026 (Global Soil Partnership; ITPS; 75 countries): loss of soil biodiversity is the 4th of seven threats after erosion, SOC loss, nutrient mismanagement; sustainable practices deteriorating in 58% of regions
Global Soil Partnership set up 2012
PMF (2025-26): Aravalli 100 m definition could open dust corridors for Thar sand into the Indo-Gangetic plain
## Beyond your notes
UNCCD (1994) is the desertification convention; 17 June is Desertification and Drought Day; India hosted COP14 (2019) and targets restoring 26 million ha by 2030

text:
Stage | Birth rate | Death rate | Growth | Example
1 | High | High | Slow | Pre-industrial, agrarian
2 | High (falls later) | Low (sanitation, health) | Very high (gap) | Developing countries

t: Rural settlement types in India → where each is found
text:
## 1. Four types
Type | Form | Found in
Clustered / nucleated | Compact built-up area, distinct from fields | Fertile alluvial plains, north-eastern states; for defence in Bundelkhand, Nagaland
Semi-clustered / fragmented | Main cluster + segregated outer sections (dominant caste in centre, lower strata on flanks) | Gujarat plain, parts of Rajasthan
Hamleted | Village split into physically separate units with one name: panna, para, palli, nagla, dhani, faliya | Middle and lower Ganga plain, Chhattisgarh, lower Himalayan valleys
Dispersed / isolated | Isolated huts in jungles or on hills | Meghalaya, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, Kerala
Dispersion is caused by fragmented terrain and scattered land resources
Hamleting is motivated by social and ethnic factors
⚠ Kerala and Meghalaya = dispersed; Ganga plain = clustered/hamleted; Gujarat plain = semi-clustered

## 1. Patterns by shape
Pattern | Forms where
Linear | Along a road, railway, river, canal edge or levee
Rectangular | Plains, wide intermontane valleys; streets cross at right angles
Circular | Around lakes, tanks; open centre to keep animals safe
Star-like | Several roads converge

Water supply (rivers, lakes, springs), fertile land, flood-free upland (terraces, levees; stilt houses in marshes)

## 1. Census of India definition
Category | Criterion
Statutory town | Any place with a municipality, corporation, cantonment board or notified town area committee, whatever its population
Census town (all three needed) | Population ≥ 5,000; ≥ 75% of male main workers in non-agricultural work; density ≥ 400 persons/sq km
A census town is administratively a village but meets the three demographic criteria
Criteria unchanged since 1981; RGI will retain them for Census 2027
## 2. Thresholds elsewhere
Country | Minimum population for urban
Denmark, Sweden, Finland | 250
Iceland | 300
Canada, Venezuela | 1,000
Colombia | 1,500
Argentina, Portugal | 2,000
USA, Thailand | 2,500
India | 5,000 (+ density + occupation)
Japan | 30,000
Brazil, Bolivia: any administrative centre is urban
⚠ The 75% criterion counts male workers only (criticised as gender-biased)
⚠ Census town population is 5,000, not 10,000; density 400, not 200 (LENS Sept 2026 practice MCQ trap)

## 1. Slums
Slum population 27.9 million (1981) → 65.5 million (2011), 17.37% of urban population (Census 2011)
Mains Magnum (Feb 2026, on ES 2025-26): ~24% of urban population now in slums
UN slum: lacks one or more of secure tenure, durable housing, sufficient space, improved water, sanitation
One in five slum residents is SC
158 million Indian slum dwellers live in floodplains, most in the Ganga delta (July 2025 study)
## 2. Urban heat island causes
Cause | How
Lack of vegetation | No shading or evapotranspiration
Low albedo | Dark asphalt absorbs heat
Anthropogenic heat | Vehicles, factories, ACs
Urban canyons | Tall buildings trap long-wave radiation, block breezes
Male-selective migration distorts the sex ratio of cities
⚠ Slum share is 17.37% by Census 2011; newer figures differ

topic: Chemical fertilisers: types, inputs, pricing and reforms
t: Fertiliser raw materials → where each comes from
text:
## 1. Raw material chain
Fertiliser | Key raw material | Source of that input
Ammonia (base of all N-fertilisers) | Hydrogen + N₂ (Haber-Bosch) | Natural gas (methane) gives the hydrogen
Urea CO(NH₂)₂ | Ammonia + CO₂ | Gas-based plants (India shifted from naphtha/fuel oil)
Phosphoric acid / DAP / SSP | Rock phosphate + sulphuric acid | Sulphur = by-product of oil refineries
MOP (KCl) | Potash ore | 100% imported
## 2. Facts that hinge
Urea manufacture consumes CO₂ (not SO₂, not chlorine)
About 90% of global sulphur comes from petroleum refining and natural-gas processing
India imports 78% of natural gas for urea, ~90% of phosphatic inputs, all potash (PMF)
⚠ The 2020 PYQ "sulphur is a by-product of oil refineries" is true; "ammonia from natural gas" is true
PYQ 2020: three statements on fertilisers; only the pricing one ("market-driven") was false. Answer: 2 and 3 only

topic: Chemical fertilisers: types, inputs, pricing and reforms
t: Fertiliser pricing → administered or market-driven
text:
## 1. Who fixes the price
Fertiliser | Price regime | Subsidy
Urea | MRP statutorily fixed by Centre: ₹242 per 45 kg bag (excl. neem coating, taxes) | Covers gap between cost and fixed MRP
P&K (DAP, MOP, NPK, SSP) | MRP set by companies, but under "reasonableness of MRP" guidelines | Nutrient Based Subsidy (NBS) from 1 April 2010 on N, P, K, S content
## 2. Control instruments
Fertiliser Control Order (FCO) 1985, under the Essential Commodities Act 1955: quality, price, distribution
Fertiliser Movement Control Order 1973: Dept of Fertilisers decides rail "rake" destinations
Fertiliser subsidy = second-largest subsidy after food
⚠ "Retail price is market-driven and not administered" is false: urea is fully controlled; even P&K are monitored
⚠ Urea is outside NBS (NBS 2010 excluded urea); that exclusion is why urea is overused
Urea bag cut from 50 kg to 45 kg in March 2018

topic: Chemical fertilisers: types, inputs, pricing and reforms
t: Neem-coated urea → why the government promotes it
text:
## 1. Policy
Neem-Coated Urea Policy 2015 (from May 2015): 100% of subsidised agricultural urea, domestic and imported (coated at port), must be neem-coated
## 2. Two purposes
Purpose | How
Slow release of N | Neem oil is a nitrification inhibitor: slows urea → ammonium → nitrite → nitrate, N available longer, higher N-use efficiency
Stop diversion | Coated urea is useless for plywood, resins, dyes, cattle feed, synthetic milk
## 3. Traps in the 2016 options
⚠ Neem oil does not increase nitrogen fixation by microbes
⚠ It does not stop N₂O emission "at all"; it only reduces losses
⚠ It is not a weedicide-fertiliser combination
Urea consumption fell in 2016-17 and 2017-18, then rose again: record 35.8 mt in 2023-24
Next step: Sulphur Coated Urea "Urea Gold": tackles sulphur deficiency, cheaper per unit nutrient
PYQ 2016: answer "neem coating slows down the rate of dissolution/distribution of urea in the soil"

Neem-coated urea | 2015 | 100% coating
DBT in fertilisers | - | 100% subsidy to companies after Aadhaar-authenticated PoS sale
One Nation One Fertiliser (PM Bhartiya Jan Urvarak Pariyojana) | 2022 | Single brand "Bharat" for urea, DAP, MOP, NPK; cuts cross-movement and freight subsidy
PM-PRANAM | 2023 | States get 50% of subsidy saved by cutting chemical fertiliser use
⚠ Under DBT the subsidy still goes to the company, not to the farmer's account

t: Excess nitrogenous fertiliser → what happens and what does not
text:
## 1. Effects
Statement | True/False | Why
Soil acidity increases | True | Nitrification of ammonium releases H⁺
Nitrate leaches to groundwater | True | Nitrate is highly soluble; leads to eutrophication, blue-baby risk
N-fixing microbes proliferate | False | Abundant mineral N suppresses biological N fixation; Rhizobium activity declines
## 2. Other effects
Lower soil organic matter, micronutrient depletion, weaker soil structure
Lodging and delayed maturity of crops; more pest attack
N₂O (potent GHG) from fields; ammonia volatilisation
⚠ Excess N also speeds microbial decomposition of organic carbon: Punjab, Haryana, west UP show high SOC loss

topic: Irrigation methods and water conservation practices
t: Drip irrigation → advantages and the salinity trap
text:
## 1. Method
Trickle irrigation: water to root zone via emitters at 2-20 litres/hour
Efficiency ~90% vs 35-40% for flood irrigation; productivity up 20-90%; energy use down 10-17%
## 2. Advantage or not (2016 PYQ)
Claim | Verdict | Why
Reduces weeds | Yes | Only root zone wetted; inter-row soil stays dry
Reduces soil erosion | Yes | No surface runoff
Reduces soil salinity | No | Salts accumulate at the wetting-front edge; needs leaching/flushing
## 3. Other features
Advantage | Disadvantage
Water and labour saving | High initial cost (so mainly high-value row crops, orchards, vines)
Easy fertigation, chemigation | Emitter clogging
Suits all soils, slopes | Tubes damaged by UV, rodents
PYQ 2016: answer "1 and 3 only"

Efficient use of rock phosphate and all phosphatic fertilisers | No: rock phosphate is insoluble; P fertilisers can precipitate and clog emitters
Increased nutrient availability | Yes
Less leaching of nutrients | Yes
## 3. Limits
Needs soluble fertilisers and corrosion-proof equipment; risk of backflow into water source
Chemigation = any agrochemical (pesticide, herbicide, fungicide) through irrigation water

t: Conservation Agriculture → its three principles (what is and is not CA)
text:
## 1. Definition
Farming system that prevents loss of arable land while regenerating degraded land; raises water and nutrient use efficiency
## 2. The three core principles
Principle | What the farmer does
Minimum soil disturbance | Zero/minimum tillage; seed sown directly into residues of previous crop
Permanent soil cover | Soil always covered by cover crops or dead residue/mulch
Crop diversification | Rotation/sequencing or intercropping, ideally with at least one legume
Preview: keep at least 30% of soil covered by crop residue
⚠ CA does not mean "avoiding plantation crops" and is not framed as "avoiding monoculture"; UPSC's key took only minimum tillage, residue cover, crop rotation
PYQ 2018: five options; answer 2, 4 and 5 (minimum tillage, residue cover, spatial and temporal crop sequencing); trap: "avoid monoculture" and "avoid plantation crops" sound green but are not CA principles

t: Zero tillage → advantages UPSC counts
text:
## 1. What it is
Crop seed sown with a drill directly into untilled soil where previous crop stubble is present; also called no-till
Residue retained on the surface
## 2. Advantages (all three correct in 2020)
Advantage | Why
Wheat sown without burning paddy residue | Drill sows through stubble; cuts stubble burning and air pollution
Direct seeding of paddy, no nursery | Avoids nursery and transplanting; saves water and labour
Soil carbon sequestration | Undisturbed soil keeps Soil Organic Carbon (SOC)
Also: less erosion, more soil moisture, lower fuel and labour cost, faster sowing
⚠ Zero tillage conserves water: UPSC 2017 counted zero tillage, gypsum before irrigation, residue left in field all as water-conserving
PYQ 2020: answer 1, 2 and 3; trap: carbon sequestration looks unrelated but is a key benefit

t: Zero-till wheat and Direct Seeded Rice → how they work
text:
## 1. 'FreeHit' Zero Tillage (wheat)
Standing paddy stubble cut and mixed in soil; wheat sown with a seed-cum-fertiliser drill; herbicide at about 25 days
Varieties 'Goal' and 'Mukut' (Mahyco) tolerate herbicide Imazethapyr; Metribuzin also used for weeds
## 2. Direct Seeded Rice (DSR, 'Tar-wattar')
Feature | DSR | Transplanted rice
Nursery | None | Needed
Plants per sq m | 35-40 ('FullPage') | 15-20
Weed control | Herbicide (Imazethapyr) | Standing water
Best soils | Heavy/medium-heavy | All
Promoted by Punjab; hybrids 'Sava 134', 'Sava 127'
⚠ DSR should be avoided in light-textured soils (need irrigation every 2-3 days, cancelling water saving)
Majha and Doaba (Punjab) have heavy soils; Malwa has mixed pockets
## Beyond your notes
Happy Seeder: tractor-mounted machine that cuts and lifts paddy straw and sows wheat in one pass (ICAR-PAU)

t: Tillage, residue and soil carbon → why zero tillage stores carbon
text:
## 1. Soil Organic Carbon (SOC)
Carbon part of soil organic matter; 50-60% of SOM is carbon; healthy soils hold 1-6% SOC
## 2. Factors that lower SOC
Factor | Effect
Repeated ploughing | Exposes buried organic matter to air, breaks carbon bonds
Excess nitrogen fertiliser | Speeds microbial decomposition, raises acidity
Burning/removing residue | Removes main source of new carbon
Land conversion, warming, erosion | Lose carbon-rich topsoil
SOC higher in cool, hilly, clayey, grassland soils; lower in hot plains, arid and sandy soils
ICAR study (Nov 2025): Haryana, Punjab, western UP show high SOC loss (prolonged urea and phosphatic fertiliser)
Exam angle: "carbon sequestration in soil" is a benefit of zero tillage, residue retention, biochar, agroforestry, cover crops

t: Regenerative agriculture → principles and types
text:
## 1. Definition
WEF: farming that uses soil conservation as the entry point to regenerate provisioning, regulating and supporting services
Goes beyond organic: restores the whole ecosystem, not only cuts chemicals
## 2. Core principles (PIB 2026)
Minimise soil disturbance, protect living roots of perennials, continuous soil cover, integrate livestock
Type | Key idea
No-till and pasture cropping | Drillers plant while grasses kept for grazing
Annual organic cropping | No synthetic chemicals
Compost tea | Liquid extract of compost microbes
Biochar and Terra Preta | Black carbon; carbon sequestration up to 70 times
Perennial cropping | No yearly replanting, deep roots
Ecological aquaculture | Aquatic life with organic matter and trees
## In news 2025-26

t: Organic farming → what it avoids, what it uses
text:
## 1. Avoids
Synthetic fertilisers, pesticides, growth regulators, livestock feed additives
## 2. Relies on
Crop rotation, crop residues, animal manure, legumes, green manure, off-farm organic waste, biofertilisers, biological pest control

## 3. Eco-friendly vs not (1999)

Organic farming | Yes
Shifting cultivation (jhum, slash-and-burn) | No: burns forest
High-yielding varieties | No: need heavy fertiliser, water, pesticide
Glasshouse cultivation | No: energy-intensive

topic: Organic farming, natural farming and certification
t: Zero Budget Natural Farming → components
text:
## 1. Origin
Natural farming: Masanobu Fukuoka, 'The One-Straw Revolution' (1975), "do-nothing farming"
ZBNF in India: Subhash Palekar (Padma Shri 2016); in Budget 2019-20
"Zero budget": intercrop income offsets main-crop cost; neither chemical nor organic
## 2. The four pillars and pest preparations
Component | Meaning
Jeevamrutha | Fermented microbial culture: cow dung, urine, jaggery, pulse flour
Bijamrita | Seed treatment against fungus, soil- and seed-borne disease
Acchadana | Mulching
Whapasa | Soil with both air and water; noon-only irrigation in alternate furrows
Agniastra, Brahmastra, Neemastra | Pest management from cow urine, chilli, garlic, neem, tobacco
Promotes soil aeration, minimal watering, intercropping, bunds
⚠ ZBNF opposes vermicompost and deep ploughing; revives local deep-soil earthworms

topic: Organic farming, natural farming and certification
t: Organic vs natural farming → differences
text:
Point | Organic farming | Natural farming / ZBNF
Inputs | Bulk organic manure, compost, vermicompost | Only on-farm cow dung-urine preparations
Ploughing, tilling, weeding | Allowed | Avoided
Cost | Can be capital-intensive, certification cost | Extremely low (near zero)
Philosophy | Holistic system optimising agroecosystem | "Do-nothing", natural way
Common: both avoid synthetic fertilisers and pesticides, use local seeds
⚠ Challenge: Sikkim saw yield decline after going organic; some farmers reverted
Benefits of natural farming: low cost, chemical-free food, efficient soil moisture use; Central Water Commission: agriculture uses over 83% of water

t: Permaculture vs conventional chemical farming → four statements
text:
## 1. Meaning
Coined 1970s by Australians Bill Mollison and David Holmgren: "permanent agriculture" + "permanent culture"
Planned system of farming and habitation that emulates natural ecosystems
## 2. The 2021 statements
Statement | Verdict
Permaculture discourages monoculture; chemical farming monoculture-dominated | Correct
Chemical farming raises soil salinity; not seen in permaculture | Correct
Permaculture not easily possible in semi-arid regions | Wrong: effective in dry, semi-arid areas
Mulching very important in permaculture | Correct
## 3. Practices
Integration of crops, trees, livestock; mulching and permanent cover; composting; rainwater harvesting; minimum or no tillage; native species; biological pest management
PYQ 2021: answer 1, 2 and 4; trap: statement 3 assumes permaculture needs rich water

t: Eco-friendly agriculture → what counts (2020)
text:
Practice | Meaning | Counted?
Crop diversification | Adding new crops; moves away from monoculture and water-guzzling crops | Yes
Legume intensification | Legumes fix atmospheric nitrogen, cut urea | Yes
Tensiometer use | Sealed water tube + ceramic porous cup + vacuum gauge; measures soil moisture to time irrigation | Yes
Vertical farming | Indoor stacked layers, artificial light | No (official key)
⚠ Preview book prints answer (d), counting vertical farming too; the UPSC key is (a) 1, 2 and 3 only
PYQ 2020: trap: vertical farming uses less water but is energy- and capital-intensive

t: Soilless and controlled farming → hydroponics, aeroponics, aquaponics
text:
Term | Meaning
Vertical farming | Indoors, stacked layers, uses soilless systems
Hydroponics | Plants grown without soil in water with mineral nutrients
Aeroponics | Roots suspended in air, sprayed with nutrient mist
Aquaponics | Aquaculture (fish) + hydroponics; fish waste feeds plants
Protected agriculture | Controlled temperature, humidity, light: greenhouse, polyhouse, net house, shade-net, plastic tunnel
⚠ Glasshouse/greenhouse farming is not treated as eco-friendly (1999 option)
Agrivoltaics: crops under solar panels; PM-KUSUM does not yet include APVs

t: Other farming systems → term and meaning
text:
Term | Meaning
Biodynamic farming | Farm as a living organism; biodynamic calendar by moon and stars
Precision farming | Location-specific inputs using GIS, GPS, remote sensing
Regenerative agriculture | Restores soil, biodiversity, stores carbon
Conservation agriculture | Min tillage + soil cover + diversification
Natural farming | Minimal intervention, no external inputs (Fukuoka)
High-density planting | Dense dwarf fruit trees; mechanised; automated fertigation
Integrated Pest Management | Keep pests below economic threshold; biological first, chemicals last
Precision-farming tools: fertigation, greenhouse, soil and leaf nutrient tests, mulching, micropropagation, drip
Exam angle: "name → category" questions pair a term with its idea; learn one hinge word per system

t: Crop rotation and legumes → rules and benefits
text:
## 1. Benefits
Controls insects and diseases, raises fertility, cuts erosion
Monocropping exhausts some nutrients, leaves others unused: imbalance, pests
## 2. Best practice rules (PMF)
Rule | Example
Legume before non-legume | Green gram, then wheat
Less-water crop after more-water crop | Rice, then pulses
Less-manure crop after more-manure crop | Sugarcane, then pulses
⚠ CARE June 2026 words it as "a legume should follow a non-legume"; PMF says legumes precede non-legumes; follow PMF
Sequences: green gram-wheat-moong; groundnut-wheat-moong; paddy-wheat-moong
Green manure: sun hemp (sanai) gives most N (86-129 kg/ha), Dhaincha 84-105, Guar 68-85

topic: Mixed farming, integrated systems and agroforestry
t: Mixed farming vs mixed cropping vs intercropping → definitions
text:
Term | Meaning
Mixed farming | Crops + livestock on the same farm
Mixed cropping | Two or more crops grown together in the same field (risk cover)
Intercropping | Crops in definite rows/pattern together, e.g. cereal + legume
Polyvarietal cultivation | Several varieties of the same crop
Polyculture | Plants maturing at different times grown together
Multiple cropping | Two or three crops in succession in a year
Strip farming | Main crop in wide rows, gaps filled with another crop to cut erosion
⚠ Mixed farming is not "two crops in one field" (that is mixed cropping) and not "cash + food crops"
PYQ 2012: chief characteristic of mixed farming = rearing animals and cultivating crops together

topic: Mixed farming, integrated systems and agroforestry
t: Mixed farming → advantages
text:
Pasture and leguminous forage in rotation improve soil and cut erosion
Livestock manure returns fertility; crops on level land, pasture on slopes
Livestock eat crop residue in low-rainfall years: buffers crop failure
Flexible feeding and marketing: cushions price fluctuations, uses labour all year
Mixed cropping advantage | Why
Lower fertiliser and water need | Crops differ in requirements
Natural pest control | Predators find habitats
Higher yield per hectare than monoculture | Resource complementarity
Usually a long-duration crop with a short-duration one; often a legume with the main crop

topic: Mixed farming, integrated systems and agroforestry
t: Integrated Farming System → components and support
text:
## 1. Meaning
Combines crops, livestock, poultry, fisheries, horticulture, agroforestry (and apiculture) on the same land synergistically
Waste of one enterprise is input of another: income stability, year-round family employment
Component | Examples
Crops | Monocropping, intercropping, mixed, multi-tier cropping
Livestock | Milch cows, goats, sheep, poultry, bees
Trees | Fuel, timber, fodder, fruit
Suits India's 86% small and marginal farmers (<2 ha, Agriculture Census 2015-16)
## In news 2025-26

Agrihorticulture | Fruit trees + seasonal crops
Apisilviculture | Flowering trees + beekeeping

Plantation | Large estate, one cash crop, for sale: tea, coffee, rubber, banana, spices
Commercial | Produce sold; HYV, chemicals, irrigation
Shifting (jhum) | Slash-and-burn, swidden; plot abandoned to regenerate
Dry farming | Rainfall below 750 mm

t: Micro-irrigation → benefits and the "only means" trap
text:
## 1. Meaning
Water via drippers, sprinklers, foggers or emitters, on or below soil; low-pressure, low-flow, direct to root zone
## 2. The 2011 statements
Statement | Verdict
Fertiliser/nutrient loss reduced | Correct: fertigation at root zone, less leaching
Only means of irrigation in dryland farming | Wrong: also contour bunds, check dams, farm ponds, surface irrigation
Checks receding groundwater table | Correct: less pumping
## 3. Efficiency figures
Surface irrigation 35-40% efficient; well-run drip about 90%
Yield up 20-90%; energy use down 10-17%
PYQ 2011: answer 1 and 3 only; trap: absolute word "only"

t: Drip vs sprinkler irrigation → features
text:
Feature | Drip (trickle) | Sprinkler
How | Small pipes with emitters, 2-20 litres/hour at root | Sprays water like rain
Best for | Row crops, trees, vines, high-value crops | Closely spaced dense crops
Soils | Most soils and slopes | All except heavy clay
Fertigation | Easy | Soluble fertilisers possible
Drawbacks | High cost, emitter clogging, UV/rodent damage | Wind drift, evaporation, wet foliage disease
No land levelling needed for sprinkler
⚠ UPSC 2016: drip reduces weeds and soil erosion, but not soil salinity (answer 1 and 3)
Fertigation (UPSC 2020): controls alkalinity, raises nutrient availability, cuts leaching; not for rock phosphate/superphosphate (precipitates)

t: Dryland farming → water-saving methods beyond micro-irrigation
text:
Method | How it saves water
Contour bunding, terracing | Holds runoff on slopes
Check dams, farm ponds | Store runoff for protective irrigation
Mulching (Acchadana) | Cuts evaporation
Zero tillage + residue cover | Keeps soil moisture
Tensiometer | Irrigate only when soil is dry
Alternate Wetting and Drying (rice) | Re-flood when water falls ~15 cm below surface; cuts methane
Drought-tolerant crops | Millets, pulses, oilseeds
~52% of India's net sown area is rainfed (LENS Jan 2026)
Exam angle: options with "only", "all", "cannot" in sustainable-farming questions are usually wrong

PMKSY | 'Har Khet Ko Paani'; micro-irrigation under Per Drop More Crop

NMSA micro-irrigation subsidy | Up to 55%, capped at 5 ha

t: Vegetative propagation → method and plant
text:
## 1. Meaning
Asexual; one parent; offspring genetically identical (clone); keeps purity of variety
⚠ Vegetative propagation can also transmit plant viruses
## 2. Method → plant (sources)
Method | Plants
Stem cutting | Bougainvillea, carnation, cocoa, grapes, sugarcane, rose, duranta
Grafting | Sweet orange
Layering | Jasmine
Air layering (gootee) | Pomegranate (also cuttings)
Suckers, rhizomes, peepers, tissue culture | Banana
Seeds | Mango, cotton (generally)
⚠ Cocoa is also popularly raised from seed, yet UPSC 2002 counted it under stem cuttings: answer all four
PYQ 2002: answer 1, 2, 3 and 4; UPSC 2009: sweet orange by grafting and jasmine by layering, both correct

t: Vegetative organs → crops raised from them
text:
Organ used | Crops
Stem cutting (setts) | Sugarcane
Stem tuber | Potato
Rhizome | Ginger, turmeric, banana
Bulb/cloves | Garlic
Budding | Rose, citrus
## Beyond your notes
Potato by tubers, ginger and turmeric by rhizomes, garlic by cloves
Budding (e.g. T-budding) common in rose and citrus; mango commercially by grafting (veneer, softwood, inarching)
Onion is a bulb crop but is raised from seed (nursery, then transplanting)
Exam angle: older PYQs ask "which is propagated by X"; learn both the method list and the exceptions

t: Transplanting vs direct sowing → which crops
text:
## 1. Transplanting
Seeds raised in a nursery; seedlings moved to main field (onion after 4-8 weeks)
Gives better survival, spacing, uniform growth
## 2. Crops
Raised by transplanting | Sown directly
Onion | Maize
Rice (traditional) | Sorghum
Tomato, brinjal, chilli | Soybean
Cabbage, cauliflower | Wheat, pulses, groundnut
Rice methods: transplantation, broadcasting, drilling; DSR now promoted
⚠ DSR removes the nursery: same question angle as zero tillage 2020
## Beyond your notes
Tomato, brinjal, chilli, cabbage, cauliflower and tobacco are nursery-transplanted crops
PYQ 1997: answer onion; trap: maize, sorghum, soybean are all direct-seeded

t: Micropropagation and tissue culture → meaning and use
text:
Micropropagation: rapid multiplication of a selected plant into many progeny using plant tissue culture
Feature | Detail
Product | Disease-free, uniform planting material
Common crops | Banana, sugarcane, potato, ornamentals
Part of | Precision farming toolkit (PMF)
Advantage | Large numbers in short time, true to type
Banana farmers increasingly use tissue-culture seedlings instead of suckers
Seed village concept: trained farmer group produces seeds for own and neighbouring villages
Exam angle: tissue culture and cuttings are both asexual; seedlings from seed are sexual propagation

t: Kharif, rabi, zaid → which crop goes where
text:
## 1. The three seasons
Season | Sown | Harvested | Major crops
Kharif | With monsoon, June-July | Sept-Oct | Paddy, maize, jowar, bajra, tur, moong, urad, cotton, jute, niger, groundnut, soybean
Rabi | Winter, Oct-Dec | Summer, April-June | Wheat, barley, peas, gram, rapeseed-mustard
Zaid | Between rabi and kharif, March-June | Short summer season | Moong, urad, watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, vegetables, fodder
Rabi crops depend on residual soil moisture and irrigation; western disturbances (winter rain) help wheat, mustard, barley
Principal kharif cereal = rice; principal rabi cereal = wheat
⚠ Cotton and groundnut are kharif; mustard, rapeseed and gram are rabi (CISF AC 2025: only cotton was kharif among cotton, gram, mustard, rapeseed)
⚠ Zaid crops are grown mainly under irrigation (moong and urad)
PYQ 2013 and 2004: "which are kharif" - cotton, groundnut, rice, maize = kharif; trap options slipped in wheat (2013) and mustard (2004), both rabi

t: Crops grown in both seasons → the exceptions
text:
## 1. Season-flexible crops (the trap list)
Crop | Seasons
Rice | Kharif in north; three crops (kharif, rabi, summer) in deltas of WB, Krishna-Godavari, parts of UP-Bihar
Jowar | Kharif (36.6%: Rajasthan, UP, Haryana, MP) and rabi (63.4%: Maharashtra, Karnataka, TN, AP)
Urad, moong, cowpea (lobia) | Pulses grown in both seasons
Sesame | Kharif in north, rabi/summer in south
Sunflower, castor | Both rabi and kharif
Groundnut | Kharif, rabi, summer - but ~90% area kharif
Maize | Year-round; 85% kharif
Tobacco | India is the only country growing it in two seasons
## 2. Bengal rice seasons
Season | Sown | Harvested
Aus (autumn) | May-June | Sept-Oct
Aman (winter) | June-July | Nov-Dec
Boro (spring) | Dec-Jan | March-April
⚠ Rabi pulses: gram, lentil, pea, rajmash; kharif pulses: arhar, urad, moong, lobia, kulthi

Class | Feature | Examples

text:

Type | Examples
Annual | Maize, rice, millet, cowpea, groundnut, soybean

Perennial | Cocoa, oil palm, rubber, mango, coffee, cassava, ginger, sugarcane

topic: Legumes, nitrogen fixers and green manure
t: Nitrogen-fixing plants → legume or not
text:
## 1. How legumes fix nitrogen
Pulses fix atmospheric nitrogen through root nodules with Rhizobium; so they are grown in rotation with cereals
Nitrogen fixation = atmospheric N converted to ammonia/organic N by bacteria and cyanobacteria
## 2. The 2022 list
Plant | Family | N-fixer?
Alfalfa (lucerne) | Legume | Yes
Chickpea (gram) | Legume | Yes
Clover | Legume | Yes
Amaranth | Amaranthaceae | No
Purslane (kulfa) | Portulacaceae | No
Spinach | Amaranthaceae | No
⚠ Leafy vegetables (amaranth, spinach, purslane) are not legumes; the test is the pea/bean family
Other legume N-fixers: tur, urad, moong, cowpea, groundnut, soybean, dhaincha, sunn hemp
PYQ 2022: picked alfalfa, chickpea, clover (1, 3, 4 only); trap = leafy greens that look "soil-friendly"
## Beyond your notes
Alfalfa and clover are fodder legumes; amaranth and spinach are in Amaranthaceae, purslane in Portulacaceae

topic: Legumes, nitrogen fixers and green manure
t: Pulse, fodder and green manure → which legume does all three
text:
## 1. Multi-use legumes
Crop | Pulse | Fodder | Green manure
Cowpea (lobia) | Yes | Yes | Yes
Green gram (moong) | Yes | Yes | Yes
Urad | Yes | Yes (also silage) | Yes
Pigeon pea (tur) | Yes | Residues only | No - a long-duration pulse, not ploughed in
PMF: "Cowpea and green pea are also used for fodder and green manure"
Tur = second pulse after gram; deep-rooted, drought-hardy, intercropped with cotton, sorghum, bajra, maize, soybean, groundnut
Legume rule of rotation: a legume should follow a non-legume (e.g., paddy-wheat-moong) (UPSC CARE June 2026)
⚠ Tur fixes nitrogen but is not a green manure crop
PYQ 2012: cowpea and green gram (1 and 2 only); trap = pigeon pea

topic: Legumes, nitrogen fixers and green manure
t: Major pulses → climate, soil, top states
text:
## 1. Pulse profiles
Pulse | Season | Climate/soil | Top states
Gram (~40-42% of pulses) | Rabi, rainfed | 20-25°C, 600-1000 mm; deep loam | Maharashtra, MP, Rajasthan
Tur/arhar | Kharif | Tropical semi-arid; black cotton soil | Maharashtra, Karnataka, Jharkhand
Urad ("King of Pulses", 24-26% protein) | Kharif + rabi + zaid | Hot humid; not on alkaline/saline soil | MP, AP, UP, Maharashtra
Gram + arhar = ~50% of pulse area, 60% of output
India: largest producer, consumer and importer of pulses; ~80% of pulse output is rainfed
Top pulse states: MP, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, UP, Karnataka

text:
## 1. SRI (Madagascar method)
Practice | Benefit
Young single seedlings, wide spacing | Seed only 5-6 kg/ha - less seed
Wet-dry cycle (AWD) instead of flooding | 35-40% water saving, less electricity for pumping
Fewer anaerobic days | Less methane
Strong tillers, roots | Resists lodging, higher yield
Fits any variety (local, HYV, hybrid); ~1000 mm rain + irrigation, pH 5.5-7
## 2. Other methods
AWD: re-irrigate when water drops ~15 cm below the soil; cuts methane but can raise nitrous oxide (GWP CH4 ~28, N2O ~265)
DSR: seed drilled, no nursery or transplanting; first irrigation 21 days after sowing; PAU Lucky Seed Drill
Puddling cuts percolation; Japanese method = HYV + heavy manuring, 3-4 seedlings/spot
⚠ SRI needs lower, not higher, seed rate
PYQ 2022: SRI with AWD → less seed, less methane, less electricity - all correct
## In news 2025-26

Feature | South India | North India

Yield | 70-80 t/ha | 50-60 t/ha
Crushing | 7-8 months | 4-5 months
Sucrose recovery | 10-11% | 9-10%
Area | Smaller | Much larger - dominates

t: Sugarcane planting practices → what saves seed
text:
## 1. The 2020 statements
Statement | Verdict
Bud-chip settlings raised in nursery, transplanted | Correct - big saving in seed cane
Single-budded setts germinate better than multi-bud setts (direct planting) | Wrong
Single-bud setts survive better in bad weather than large setts | Wrong
Tissue-culture settlings can be used | Correct
## 2. Other practices
Ratooning: next crop from stubble/roots of first crop (Sugarcane Breeding Institute, Coimbatore); cuts cost ~25%, matures a month earlier
By-products: bagasse (fuel, paper), molasses (ethanol), press mud (manure), wax
Sustainable Sugarcane Initiative (SSI): bud-chip nursery, wide spacing, drip, intercropping
## Beyond your notes
Conventional planting uses 2-3 bud setts; single-bud setts dry out and give poorer germination and survival when planted directly

t: Rare earth elements → what they are and why "rare"
text:
## 1. The 17 REEs
Group | Members
15 lanthanides | Lanthanum (La) to lutetium (Lu): cerium, neodymium, praseodymium, samarium, europium, gadolinium, terbium, dysprosium...
+ 2 | Scandium (Sc) and yttrium (Y) (same deposits, similar chemistry)
Light REEs dominate India's deposits; heavy REEs (dysprosium, terbium) in non-extractable amounts
## 2. Why "rare"
Not geologically scarce: cerium is as abundant as copper; most REEs more abundant than silver, gold, platinum
Rare economically: low concentration, mixed together, chemically alike, so separation is hard
Main ores: monazite, bastnasite; processing leaves radioactive (thorium, uranium) and acid waste

topic: Coal types, quality and coking coal
t: Coal ranks → carbon content (peat to anthracite)
text:
## 1. Coalification order (oldest = best)
Plants → peat → lignite → sub-bituminous → bituminous → anthracite
With time, oxygen, nitrogen and moisture fall; the proportion of carbon rises (the quantity does not)
Rank | Carbon (PMF Geography) | Moisture / volatiles | Key feature
Peat | below 40-55% | very high | Burns like wood, much smoke and ash
Lignite (brown coal) | 40-55% | over 35% moisture | Spontaneous combustion (mine fires)
Bituminous (black coal) | 40-80% | 15-40% volatiles | Most widely used; coke, power, steel
Anthracite | 80-95% | very little | Best, hardest; short blue flame
Meta-anthracite: beyond anthracite, graphitic, not mined commercially in India
⚠ Carbon ladder goes on past coal: peat < lignite < bituminous < anthracite < graphite < diamond
⚠ Books differ on the % bands (PMF S&T: peat 50-60, lignite 60-70, bituminous 70-85, anthracite 85-95; Preview: anthracite 90-95); the order never changes
PYQ 1999: which coal has the highest carbon; answer anthracite (options were bituminous, lignite, peat)

topic: Coal types, quality and coking coal
t: Coal ranks → calorific value, uses and Indian distribution
text:
## 1. Properties that rise with rank
Calorific value, hardness, density rise from peat to anthracite; moisture and smoke fall
Rank | Where in India | Largest producer
Lignite | Rajasthan, Lakhimpur (Assam), TN, Gujarat, J&K | Tamil Nadu (Neyveli), then Rajasthan, Gujarat
Bituminous | Jharkhand, Odisha, WB, Chhattisgarh, MP | Odisha, then Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand
Anthracite | Only limited: Damodar valley, Kalakot (Jammu) | negligible
Peat | Nilgiri hills, Kashmir valley (Jhelum alluvium) | negligible
Anthracite ignites slowly, little heat loss, least common, most efficient (PMF S&T)
Bituminous: most widely used coal in India; name from the liquid bitumen
⚠ Anthracite is generally absent in Gondwana coalfields; India's reserves are mostly bituminous and sub-bituminous
⚠ Coal is a sedimentary rock of biotic origin (Preview), not metamorphic

topic: Coal types, quality and coking coal
t: Indian coal → high ash, low sulphur, high ash-fusion temperature
text:
## 1. The three properties UPSC paired
Property | Indian coal | Consequence
Ash content | High, 35-45% (about triple global average) | Low calorific value, fly-ash, pollution
Sulphur | Low compared to world coal | Less SO2 per tonne burnt
Ash fusion temperature (AFT) | High, about 1500°C | Ash melts late; problem for gasifiers
AFT = temperature at which coal ash starts to melt and agglomerate
Other traits: low calorific value; Gondwana coal has sulphur and phosphorus, ash ~30%, carbon rarely above 60%
⚠ Trap: "low ash fusion temperature" is wrong; Indian coal has high AFT (that is why gasifiers clog and need flux)
⚠ Exception: Tertiary/NE coal (Assam) has low ash but high sulphur, the reverse of Gondwana coal
PYQ 2013: high ash and low sulphur correct, low AFT wrong; answer 1 and 2 only
## In news 2025-26
LENS May 2026 (coal gasification): 35-45% ash and high AFT listed as the main challenges; fix proposed: Circulating Fluidised Bed reactors

text:
Feature | Coking / metallurgical | Non-coking / thermal / steaming

Use | Heated without air → coke for blast furnace (steel) | Power generation

Top producers | China, Australia, US | India, China, US
Top exporters | Australia, US, Canada | Indonesia, Australia

Over 90% of coking coal reserves in Jharkhand (Jharia); minor in WB and MP

text:
## 1. The figures
Gondwana fields hold about 98% of coal reserves and 99% of coal production of India
Damuda series (Lower Gondwana) = most productive (about 80% of production)
Gondwana system named after Gond tribes; laid in synclinal troughs from the Permian (~250 million years ago)
Coal age | Age | Quality | In India
Carboniferous | ~350 mn yrs | Best (oldest) | Almost absent
Gondwana | ~250 mn yrs | Medium; ash ~30%, carbon < 60% | 98% reserves
Tertiary | 60-15 mn yrs | Low carbon, high moisture and sulphur | NE, lignite belts
Gondwana rocks also have iron ore, copper, uranium, antimony, sandstone, slate
⚠ Gondwana coal is younger than Carboniferous coal (Ruhr, UK, Great Lakes), hence poorer
⚠ Preview calls Gondwana coal "high quality, low ash"; follow PMF: ash ~30%, poorer than Carboniferous

t: Uranium isotopes and enrichment → which level for what
text:
Grade | U-235 share | Use
Natural uranium | ~0.7% (U-238 ~99.3%) | PHWR fuel (no enrichment)
LEU (low-enriched) | below 20%; power reactors 3.5-5% | PWR/BWR power
HALEU | about 5-20% | Advanced reactors, ANEEL fuel
HEU | 20% or more | Research, naval
Weapons grade | ≥90% | Bombs
Only U-235 is fissile; U-238 is fertile (becomes Pu-239)
Enrichment methods: gaseous diffusion, gas centrifuge, laser separation
⚠ "At least 60% enrichment needed for electricity" is false: 3-5% suffices (60% is Iran-type near-weapons level)
PYQ 2023 (Statement I/II): India relies on coal despite uranium (true); 60% enrichment needed (false); answer (c)

t: Thorium vs uranium → advantages
text:
Claim | Correct? | Reason
Thorium more abundant | Yes | 3-4 times uranium in crust (0.0006% vs 0.00018%)
More energy per mined mass | Yes | Natural U is only 0.7% fissile; Th breeds U-233 from almost all of it
Less harmful waste | Yes | Fewer long-lived transuranics (Pu, Am, Cm)
Proliferation | Better | U-233 more proliferation resistant
Catch: Th-232 is fertile, not fissile; needs U-235 or Pu-239 to start, then becomes U-233
Thorium cycle allows thermal breeders (Preview)
⚠ Thorium cannot run a reactor on its own: a likely Statement-II trap
PYQ 2012: all three advantages correct; answer 1, 2 and 3

t: Three-stage nuclear programme → reactor, fuel, output
text:
Stage | Reactor | Fuel | Produces | Status
I | PHWR | Natural uranium | Power + Pu-239 | Mature, commercial
II | Fast breeder (sodium-cooled, no moderator) | MOX (Pu-239 + U-238) | More Pu than used; U-233 from Th blanket | PFBR Kalpakkam
III | AHWR / thorium reactors | Th-232 + U-233 | Power + U-233 | Design (BARC)
Designed by Homi J. Bhabha (1950s); logic: limited uranium, abundant thorium
First reactor Apsara (1956); KAMINI = first reactor on U-233; CIRUS (1960) natural U, heavy water
PFBR built by BHAVINI (DAE PSU); India follows a closed fuel cycle (reprocessing at Trombay, Tarapur, Kalpakkam)
## In news 2025-26
2026: PFBR (500 MWe) at Kalpakkam attained first criticality → formal entry into Stage II; India 2nd after Russia with a commercial-scale FBR
Feb 2026 (IE): PHWR scale-up (50-75 GWe by 2047) to irradiate thorium and build U-233 faster; 19 PHWRs operating
March 2026: BARC found HALEU-thorium (ANEEL) fuel may not fit well India's programme

t: Industrial inertia and policy → why industries stay or move
text:
## 1. Industrial inertia
Firm stays in its original location after initial advantages are lost
Reasons: established transport and economic links, skilled labour pool, high relocation cost, government incentives, easier to modernise
Examples: Ruhr (Germany), Pittsburgh (USA), Lancashire (UK)
## 2. Other shifting forces
Force | Example
Strategic dispersal after WWII | US steel moved west; USSR moved industry east
Technology (BOF, scrap) | Steel freed from coalfields
Regional policy | Bhilai, Rourkela; Vizag, Vijayanagar (Hospet), Salem plants of the 4th Plan, away from main raw-material belt
Agglomeration economies | Savings from linked industries nearby
Industry classes: agro-based (cotton, jute, sugar), mineral-based (steel), chemical, forest, animal-based (leather, woollen); basic (steel, aluminium smelting) vs consumer goods
⚠ Salem steel plant location was influenced politically (then TN CM M. Karunanidhi): a policy factor, not raw material
