## 1. Black Sea
Marginal sea of the Atlantic; between Europe, Caucasus and Anatolia; Pontic Mts (S), Caucasus (E), Crimean Mts (N)
Linked: Bosporus → Sea of Marmara → Dardanelles → Aegean; Kerch Strait → Sea of Azov (north)
Meromictic: upper and lower layers rarely mix, deep water oxygen-poor; fed by Danube, Dnieper, Dniester
⚠ Croatia and Syria do not touch the Black Sea (Croatia is Adriatic; Syria is Mediterranean)
## 2. Sea of Azov
Between Ukraine and Russia; shallowest sea (average ~7 m); fed by Don and Donets, so low salinity; ports Mariupol, Berdyansk
## In news 2025-26
Aug 2026: attack on merchant ship MV OMORFI in the Black Sea killed an Indian crew member (LENS)
June 2026: Ukraine says it struck five vessels in the Sea of Azov (LENS)
Apr 2026: drone hit a tanker with Russian crude near the Bosporus (LENS)
Kerch Strait: tanker split in a storm, oil spill; it is the only direct link Russia-Crimea (Magnum)
## 3. Salinity and the Turkish Straits (Magnum Aug 2026)
Danube, Dnieper, Dniester inflow keeps surface salinity ~17-18 ppt, about half the ocean average
Montreux Convention (1936): gives Turkey control of the Bosporus and Dardanelles; limits passage and tonnage of warships of non-Black Sea states

text:
## 1. Shape and links
~1,930 km from Suez to Bab-el-Mandeb; a rift valley / axial trough (African and Arabian plates parting)
North end splits into Gulf of Suez (shallow) and Gulf of Aqaba (deep)
Israel (Eilat) and Jordan (Aqaba) reach it only via the Gulf of Aqaba
## 2. Why it is special
Very little rain (often <100 mm a year) and no permanent river enters it
So evaporation > precipitation + runoff: negative water balance, high salinity
⚠ Syria is not on the Red Sea (Mediterranean coast only)

t: Ecosystem → the best definition
text:
## 1. Term → meaning (the four options of PYQ 2015)
Description | Term
Community of organisms interacting with one another | Ecological community
Part of the Earth inhabited by living organisms | Biosphere
Community of organisms + the environment in which they live | Ecosystem
Flora and fauna of a geographical area | Biodiversity
Ecosystem = functional unit of nature: producers, consumers, decomposers interacting among themselves and with the physical environment
Term coined by A G Tansley, 1935 (ROCKET); an ecosystem is an open system
Can be any size: a pond, a forest, an aquarium, a crop field (human-made)
⚠ A community alone is not an ecosystem: the abiotic environment must be included
PYQ 2015: best description of ecosystem → community of organisms together with the environment

t: Environment, habitat, ecosystem, ecology, biosphere → how they differ
text:
Term | Meaning
Environment | Everything around, living or not; any size
Habitat | Area where an organism lives (its address)
Ecosystem | Producers, consumers, decomposers and their relations: functional unit
Ecology | Study of interactions in an ecosystem
Biome | Large natural community over a major climate zone (rainforest, tundra, taiga)
Biosphere | Life-supporting part of Earth: lithosphere + hydrosphere + atmosphere
A habitat always has life; an environment need not: all habitats are environments, not all environments are habitats
Biosphere is absent at the poles' extremes, highest peaks, deepest oceans
Spores above 8,000 m are dormant, not active life
⚠ A biome can hold many habitats; biome ≠ habitat

t: Components of an ecosystem → biotic, abiotic, limiting factor
text:
## 1. Biotic components
Group | Members
Producers (autotrophs) | Green plants, cyanobacteria, certain bacteria; phytoplankton in water
Macro-consumers | Herbivores (sheep), carnivores (wolf, snake), omnivores (humans, bears, pigs)
Saprotrophs / decomposers | Bacteria and fungi (mushrooms)
Detritivores | Earthworms, nematodes, millipedes, woodlice
## 2. Abiotic and limiting factors
Abiotic: light, rainfall, temperature, atmosphere, soil, salinity, pH, altitude
Limiting factor = the single factor that limits an organism's range
Rainforest: leached surface soil limits seed germination; shade limits saplings
Nitrogen is the limiting nutrient for natural and farm ecosystems
⚠ Eurythermal / euryhaline = wide tolerance; stenothermal / stenohaline = narrow

t: Ecological niche → space plus functional role
text:
## 1. Niche vs habitat vs ecotone vs home range
Term | Meaning
Ecological niche | Physical space + functional role ("lifestyle and profession")
Habitat | Physical surroundings only (the "address")
Ecotone | Transition zone between two ecosystems
Home range | Area an animal moves in daily or periodically (bigger than habitat)
## 2. Kinds of niche
Habitat niche (where it lives), food niche (what it eats, competes with), reproductive niche (how, when), physical-chemical niche (temperature, soil, humidity)
A niche is unique to a species; many species share a habitat
No two species in a habitat can hold the same niche for long (competition displaces one)
Niche concept: Grinnell (ROCKET)
⚠ "Physical space AND functional role" = niche, not habitat
PYQ 2013: term covering physical space and functional role → ecological niche (traps: ecotone, habitat, home range)

t: Ecotone, edge effect and ecocline → transition zones
text:
Feature | Ecotone | Ecocline
What | Transition zone between two distinct ecosystems | Gradual change along a gradient
Boundary | Sharp | No sharp boundary
Diversity | High | Changes gradually
Examples | Mangroves, estuaries, grassland (forest-desert), riverbank, marsh | Vertical zonation on mountains; thermocline, halocline
Ecotone = zone of tension; may be narrow (grassland-forest) or wide (forest-desert)
Edge effect: species richness and density higher in the ecotone than in either community
Edge species: kingfishers, river turtles (estuary); birds, deer (chital, sambar) in grassland ecotone
Ecotones (mangroves, wetlands, estuaries) have greater productivity than forest, ocean, pond, desert
⚠ Mudskippers on mudflats: organisms found only in a well-developed ecotone

Found within the population of one species | False: species sit at different trophic levels
Shows the numbers of each organism eaten | False: not quantified (food web / pyramids deal with this)
Example: Grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle
Energy flow along a chain is unidirectional
Usually not more than 4 (PMF) trophic levels, as energy runs out
⚠ Testbook says "4 to 5" levels; PMF says usually not more than four
PYQ 2013: food chain statements → 1 only (order of feeding)

topic: Food chains, food webs and trophic levels
t: Ocean primary producers → which organisms qualify
text:
## 1. Producers vs consumers in the sea
Organism | What it is | Role
Diatoms | Unicellular algae | Producer
Cyanobacteria | Prokaryotic "blue-green algae" (Synechococcus, Prochlorococcus) | Producer
Coccolithophores | Unicellular eukaryotic protists | Producer
Dinoflagellates | Flagellated protists | Producer
Copepods | Small crustaceans (zooplankton) | Consumer
Foraminifera | Amoeboid protists | Consumer
Krill | Shrimp-like crustaceans | Consumer (eat phytoplankton)
Phytoplankton = "grass of the sea"; almost all ocean biomass derives from them
⚠ Cyanobacteria are bacteria, not algae, yet photosynthetic producers
PYQ 2021: copepods, cyanobacteria, diatoms, foraminifera → producers = 2 and 3

topic: Food chains, food webs and trophic levels
t: Marine food chain → correct sequence
text:
## 1. The chain
Level | Organism
Producer | Diatoms (phytoplankton)
Primary consumer | Crustaceans (copepods, krill, shrimp)
Secondary consumer | Herrings (fish eat crustaceans)
Aquatic grazing chain: phytoplankton → zooplankton → fish → pelicans
Terrestrial grazing chain: grass → caterpillar → lizard → snake
A chain always starts with a producer and ends with a top consumer
⚠ Any option starting with crustaceans or herrings is wrong: producers come first
PYQ 2014: correct food chain → Diatoms - Crustaceans - Herrings
## In news 2025-26
Antarctic krill: record industrial harvest forced an early fishery shutdown (PMF LENS Aug 2025); krill = keystone species; Antarctic krill IUCN Least Concern

topic: Food chains, food webs and trophic levels
t: Decomposers vs detritivores → who breaks down dead matter
text:
Organism | Role | Why
Fungi | Decomposer | Enzymes break detritus to inorganic matter
Bacteria | Decomposer | Same (catabolism)
Virus | Not a decomposer | Metabolically inactive outside a host; parasite
Earthworm, millipede, woodlice | Detritivore | Feed on detritus, speed decomposition
Jellyfish, seahorse | Not detritivores | Marine predators
Slime moulds | Grow on dead matter | Some protists act so
Decomposition: humification (forms humus) and mineralisation (releases nutrients)
Warm, wet conditions speed decomposition; cold and anaerobic conditions slow it (taiga: acidic soils)
⚠ Viruses are not decomposers; Paramecium and Euglena are not decomposers either
PYQ 2013: virus, fungi, bacteria → decomposers = 2 and 3 only
PYQ 2021: detritivores among earthworm, jellyfish, millipede, seahorse, woodlice → 1, 3 and 5

topic: Food chains, food webs and trophic levels
t: Grazing vs detritus food chain → where energy mainly flows
text:
Feature | Grazing chain | Detritus chain
Starts with | Living plants (producers) | Dead organic matter (detritus)
First consumer | Herbivore | Detritivore / decomposer
Main pathway in | Aquatic ecosystems | Terrestrial ecosystems
Example | Phytoplankton → zooplankton → fish | Leaf litter → earthworm → bird
Lakes: grazing pathway dominant; wetlands: detritus pathway dominant (PMF)
⚠ PMF: on land a much larger share of energy flows through the detritus chain; one lower source says the reverse
Food web = interlinked food chains; gives organisms alternative foods, raising survival

topic: Food chains, food webs and trophic levels
t: Trophic levels → who sits where
text:
Level | Organism | Type
1st | Green plants, phytoplankton | Producers (autotrophs)
2nd | Herbivores | Primary consumers
3rd | Carnivores | Secondary consumers
4th | Top carnivores | Tertiary / quaternary consumers
"Trophe" = nourishment; trophic level = position in a food chain
Energy decreases upward (heat loss at each level)
Omnivores (humans) can occupy more than one level
## Aquatic organisms by zone
Group | Meaning | Example
Neuston | Air-water interface | Floating plants
Periphyton | Attached to stems of rooted plants | Sessile algae
Plankton | Drift with currents | Phytoplankton, zooplankton
Nekton | Strong swimmers | Fish, squid, marine mammals
Benthos | Bottom-dwelling | Molluscs, crustaceans
⚠ Plankton cannot overcome currents; nekton can

topic: Food chains, food webs and trophic levels
t: Biotic interactions in a food web → effect on each species
text:
Interaction | Sp 1 | Sp 2 | Example
Mutualism | + | + | Hermit crab and sea anemone; coral and zooxanthellae (symbiosis)
Commensalism | + | 0 | Suckerfish on shark; epiphytes on trees
Predation | + | - | Tiger and deer
Parasitism | + | - | Tapeworm, Plasmodium (mosquito is a vector, not a parasite)
Competition | - | - | Two species for a scarce resource
Amensalism | - | 0 | Penicillium inhibits bacteria (antibiosis); big tree shading a small plant
Neutralism | 0 | 0 | Very unlikely in nature
Lichens = algae (or cyanobacteria) + fungi; termites and gut protozoa = mutualism
⚠ Goat and beetle sharing food where only the beetle suffers = amensalism, not competition

t: Ecological pyramids → upright or inverted
text:
Pyramid | Measures | Shape
Numbers | Individuals at each level | Upright (grassland, pond); inverted (a tree ecosystem)
Biomass | Dry weight (standing crop) | Upright on land; inverted in oceans and ponds
Energy | Energy at each level | Always upright
Producers form the base, top carnivore the tip
Ocean biomass pyramid is inverted because phytoplankton are tiny and reproduce fast: at any instant consumer biomass exceeds producer biomass
Aquatic pyramid of numbers is upright even where the biomass pyramid is inverted
⚠ The energy pyramid can never be inverted
⚠ Pond biomass: inverted (ROCKET); forest and grassland biomass: upright

t: Energy flow → the 10 per cent law
text:
## 1. Ecological efficiency
Only about 10% of energy passes from one trophic level to the next: Lindeman's 10% law (1942)
Example (PMF): 1,000 cal of sunlight → plants store 100 → deer stores 10 → lion gets less
Energy lost because (1) respiration and metabolism at each level, (2) loss at each transfer (heat)
Point | Fact
Direction of energy flow | Unidirectional (sun → producers → consumers)
Nutrients | Cyclic (biogeochemical cycles)
Limit on chain length | Energy loss: usually ≤ 4 levels
Pyramid best for comparing functional roles | Energy pyramid
⚠ Energy flows, nutrients cycle: do not swap
The energy pyramid also explains biomagnification (see next section)

t: Ecological pyramids → limitations
text:
## 1. What pyramids leave out
Do not account for the same species at two or more levels (omnivores)
Assume a simple food chain; cannot show a food web
Saprophytes / decomposers are not included, though vital
Pyramid of numbers hard to use: counting all organisms is difficult; ignores size
Pyramid | Main weakness
Numbers | Ignores size (one tree vs many insects)
Biomass | A snapshot (standing crop), ignores turnover rate
Energy | Needs data over time; hardest to measure
## Beyond your notes
Standing crop = biomass present at one time; it differs from productivity (rate of production)

t: Biomagnification → which organism carries the most
text:
## 1. Rule: the highest trophic level in the options
PYQ chain or options | Highest level | Answer
Food crop → rat → snake → hawk | 4th | Hawk
Grasshopper, toad, snake, cattle | Snake (above toad) | Snake
Grasshopper and cattle = primary consumers; toad = secondary; snake = tertiary
Pesticide named: chlorinated hydrocarbon (DDT family)
⚠ Do not pick the biggest animal (cattle): pick the highest trophic level
⚠ The food crop has the lowest concentration, though it was sprayed
PYQ 2010: chlorinated hydrocarbon on a crop → highest in the hawk
PYQ 1997: highest DDT among grasshopper, toad, snake, cattle → snake

t: Bioaccumulation vs biomagnification → the difference
text:
Feature | Bioaccumulation | Biomagnification
Scale | Within one organism over time | Across trophic levels of a food chain
Cause | Intake faster than excretion / breakdown | Progressive bioaccumulation at each level
Result | Chronic poisoning of the individual | Top predators carry the highest concentration
## 1. Conditions for biomagnification
Pollutant must be persistent (long biological half-life)
Fat-soluble, not water-soluble (water-soluble ones are excreted)
Measured in fatty tissue (fish) and milk of mammals
⚠ A water-soluble pollutant does not biomagnify
Non-degradable pollutants cannot be broken down by detritivores; they persist in a level

t: Pollutants that biomagnify → examples
text:
Pollutant | Type | Note
DDT | Chlorinated hydrocarbon (organochlorine) | Thin eggshells in raptors (Beyond your notes)
Aldrin | Organochlorine insecticide, POP | Banned in India in the 1990s (Insecticides Act 1968)
Dioxins, furans | POPs from incineration | Bioaccumulate in fat, biomagnify
Mercury (methylmercury) | Heavy metal | Minamata disease, Japan (Beyond your notes)
PCBs | Industrial organochlorines | Beyond your notes
POPs are regulated under the Stockholm Convention; India's POP Rules, 2018
## In news 2025-26
Aldrin confirmed (NGT joint committee) as cause of mugger crocodile deaths in the Chandraloi river, Kota, Rajasthan; Chandraloi = right-bank tributary of the Chambal (PMF Prelims Magnum 2026-07)
Mugger: IUCN Vulnerable, CITES Appendix I, WPA Schedule I; an apex predator (top level, hence most exposed)

t: Ecosystems → order of decreasing productivity
text:
## 1. PYQ order
Mangroves > grasslands > lakes > oceans (open ocean least per unit area)
## 2. Full PMF order (per unit area per unit time)
Rank | Ecosystem
1 | Estuaries
2 | Swamps and marshes (wetlands, mangroves)
3 | Coral reefs
4 | Tropical rainforests
5-6 | Temperate forests > boreal (taiga) forests
7-8 | Grasslands > tundra
9-10 | Open ocean > deserts
Productivity = production per unit area per unit time; depends on number and diversity of producers
Open ocean: low per unit area, but large total output (vast area)
Lakes slightly above oceans (photosynthetic plants in photic zone)
⚠ Deserts are even less productive than the open ocean
PYQ 2013: decreasing productivity → mangroves, grasslands, lakes, oceans

t: Productivity → terms and units
text:
Term | Meaning
Primary productivity | Rate of organic matter made by autotrophs
Gross primary productivity (GPP) | Total photosynthesis (Beyond your notes)
Net primary productivity (NPP) | GPP minus respiration loss (Beyond your notes)
Secondary productivity | Rate of new organic matter formed by consumers
Standing crop | Biomass present at a given time
Ecotones (mangroves, estuaries) are the most productive because species of both sides mix
Lake vs wetland (PMF): lake = phytoplankton, grazing pathway, low productivity, oligotrophic; wetland = macrophytes, detritus pathway, high productivity, eutrophic
⚠ Grasslands are high only when narrow and transitional; vast steppe and savanna are low

t: Marine upwelling → why it raises productivity
text:
## 1. Mechanism
Winds push surface water away; cold, nutrient-rich deep water rises to replace it
Nutrients (nitrate, phosphate) reach the sunlit photic zone → phytoplankton bloom → rich fisheries
Statement (PYQ 2011) | Correct?
Brings decomposer microorganisms up | No
Brings nutrients up | Yes
Brings bottom-dwelling organisms up | No
## 2. Where
Peru coast (cold Humboldt current); current convergence zones (Grand Banks); high latitudes (Iceland)
Tropical oceans: surface nutrients used up → low productivity; downwelling zones low
⚠ Upwelling brings up nutrients, not organisms
PYQ 2011: upwelling raises productivity by bringing → 2 only (nutrients)

t: Phytoplankton loss → what would happen
text:
Effect (PYQ 2012) | Happens? | Why
Ocean as carbon sink weakened | Yes | They fix CO₂ by photosynthesis
Food chains disrupted | Yes | They are the base of marine food chains
Density of ocean water drops sharply | No | Density depends on temperature and salinity
Phytoplankton produce more than half of the oxygen we breathe (PMF)
Chlorophyll c is in diatoms, dinoflagellates, brown algae; chlorophyll a in all algae and cyanobacteria
⚠ Eliminate density first: biology does not set seawater density
PYQ 2012: complete loss of phytoplankton → 1 and 2 only
PYQ 2025 (PMF): marine phytoplankton and photosynthetic bacteria make about 50% of world oxygen

t: Ocean productivity in news → darkening, warming, browning
text:
## In news 2025-26
Event | Fact | Link to productivity
Ocean darkening (study, June 2025) | 21% of global oceans darkened, 2003-2022 | Photic zone (up to 200 m, base of ~90% marine life) shrinks; less phytoplankton
Record ocean heat, 2025 | Oceans absorbed +23 ZJ (2024: +16 ZJ), top 2,000 m | Stronger stratification blocks mixing → less upwelling of nutrients
Water browning (July 2026) | More dissolved organic carbon and iron | Blocks sunlight, cuts primary productivity
Darkening most marked in the Arctic, Antarctic, Gulf Stream; threatens Calanus copepods
Warming: sea-surface temperature 2025 ~0.5°C above 1981-2010 (third-highest)
⚠ Stratification = warm, light surface layer floating on dense water: mixing stops

t: Grasslands → why trees do not replace grasses
text:
## 1. The two reasons (PYQ 2013)
Reason | How it works
Water limits | Grasslands occur where rainfall is scant; tree growth limited
Fire | Dry grass ignites in the dry season; fire kills other plants and seeds
In grasslands, grasses are the climax community (in most ecosystems it is forest)
Once deforestation in dry areas turns land to grass, the change is almost irreversible
Fire here is a grass-driven (autogenic) mechanism (PMF)
⚠ "Limited sunlight and paucity of nutrients" and "insects and fungi" are wrong
PYQ 2013: trees do not replace grasses because of → water limits and fire
## In news 2025-26
UN: 2026 = International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists; grasslands ~40% of land, 20-24% of India; store ~90% of carbon underground; Banni (Gujarat) = Asia's largest tropical grassland (PMF Mains Magnum Jan 2026)

t: Ecological succession → stages and terms
text:
Term | Meaning
Succession | Directional replacement of communities over time
Pioneer community | First colonisers (microbes, lichens, mosses)
Sere / seral stage | Each transitional community
Climax community | Final, stable, mature, complex
Succession raises productivity, diversity, and food-web complexity
Faster in the middle of a continent (seeds arrive quickly)
Lichens = algae + fungi (PYQ 2014); lichens and mosses survive without soil (PYQ 2021: lichen, moss)
⚠ Mushrooms (fungi) and ferns need organic soil or substrate; not pioneers on bare rock

t: Primary vs secondary succession → where and how fast
text:
Feature | Primary | Secondary
Starts on | Area never colonised | Area where community was destroyed
Soil | None at start | Already present
Speed | Slow | Faster
Examples | Bare rock, new volcanic island, lava flow, sand dune, new delta, glacial moraine | Abandoned farm, burnt or cleared forest, after flood
Pioneers | Lichens, mosses | Hardy grasses
Secondary on abandoned land: grasses → tall grasses, herbs → trees → forest
⚠ Landslide-exposed slopes and lava flows = primary, not secondary
## In news 2025-26
Delhi Central Ridge restoration (Sept 2026): remove invasive Vilayati Keekar (Prosopis juliflora), eucalyptus, babool; native planting to allow natural succession (PMF LENS CA)

t: Types of succession → hydrarch, xerarch, autogenic, allogenic
text:
Type | Meaning
Hydrarch (hydrosere) | Starts in water: phytoplankton → floating plants → rooted hydrophytes → sedges, grasses → trees
Xerarch (xerosere) | Starts on dry land: lichens → mosses → herbs → shrubs → trees
Autogenic | Driven by the community itself (biotic)
Allogenic | Driven by outside / abiotic forces (fire, flood)
Autotrophic | Photosynthetic species dominate early (bare rock)
Heterotrophic | Heterotrophs dominate (dead wood: bacteria, fungi → insects)
Both hydrarch and xerarch end in a mesic (moderate-moisture) climax
Pioneer in hydrarch = phytoplankton; in xerarch = lichens
⚠ Xerophytes: cactus, acacia, Prosopis; hydrophytes: water hyacinth, lotus; mesophytes: banana, rice

t: Rainforest regeneration → why it is slow
text:
## 1. Options of PYQ 2011
Option | PMF verdict
Soil deficient in nutrients | True (answer)
Propagules have poor viability | True but minor
Rainforest species slow-growing | False: they grow fast to reach light
Exotic species invade fertile soil | False: topsoil is not fertile
## 2. Mechanism
Near-daily rain → leaching: nutrients washed from topsoil
Nutrients are locked in biomass, not soil (Beyond your notes)
Seeds do not germinate for years; layer beneath topsoil is fertile
⚠ Answer is the soil, not the species
PYQ 2011: rainforest regenerates slowly → soil deficient in nutrients

t: Millennium Ecosystem Assessment → service categories
text:
Category | Examples
Supporting | Nutrient cycling, soil formation, primary production
Provisioning | Food, water, timber, fibre, genetic resources, medicinal herbs, biomass energy
Regulating | Climate control, disease control, water purification, flood control, carbon sequestration
Cultural | Recreation, tourism, spiritual, aesthetic
Supporting services are the basis of all other services
The four MEA categories: supporting, provisioning, regulating, cultural ("preserving" in the question is the odd one)
⚠ PMF PYQ book: pollination is a regulating service in the MA framework; the option was right because of nutrient cycling
PYQ 2012: supporting service → nutrient cycling and crop pollination (food/water = provisioning; climate/disease = regulating)
## Beyond your notes
MEA was released in 2005, called by UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan (2000)

t: Ecosystem services and valuation → TEEB and goods
text:
## 1. Services vs goods
Ecosystem services: benefits from healthy ecosystems
Ecosystem goods: harvested products: wild fruit, forage, timber, game, fibres, medicines
PMF lists: cultural, provisioning, economic, regulating (carbon sequestration, decomposition, detoxification, climate stabilisation), ecological (nutrient cycling, flood protection, soil renewal)
## 2. Valuation
Item | Fact
Ecosystem valuation | Puts economic value on services for cost-benefit decisions
TEEB | Global initiative on the economic benefits of biodiversity; hosted by UNEP (not IMF, not WEF)
Net Present Value | Fee for loss of ecosystem services when forest land is diverted
⚠ TEEB 2016 PYQ: "hosted by UNEP, IMF and WEF" is false
## In news 2025-26
Aravalli Green Wall Project: 5 km buffer green belt over 6.45 mha; restore 8 lakh ha in 29 districts of 4 states; Green India Mission aims to enhance services such as carbon sequestration and groundwater recharge (Current Care Prelims Summary June 2025)

t: Homeostasis → how ecosystems self-regulate
text:
## 1. Mechanism
Homeostasis = an ecosystem's capacity to self-regulate and resist change
Driven by negative feedback from a limiting resource
Pond: zooplankton rise → eat more phytoplankton → food scarce → zooplankton fall → phytoplankton recover
Capacity is not unlimited
Ecosystem functions (PMF)
1. Homeostasis (cybernetic feedback control)
2. Ecological succession
3. Energy flow through food chains
4. Nutrient cycling
## 2. Organisms facing stress
Response | Example
Regulate | Birds, mammals: thermoregulation
Conform | Most animals and nearly all plants
Migrate | Siberian birds to Keoladeo (Bharatpur)
Suspend | Spores, seeds, hibernation (polar bear), aestivation (snails, fish), diapause (zooplankton)
⚠ Very small animals are rare in polar regions: high surface area to volume loses heat

t: Species strategies and keystone roles → likely-next terms
text:
Term | Meaning
Keystone species | Effect far larger than its numbers; e.g., krill in polar seas (PMF LENS)
Apex predator | Top of the food chain; e.g., big cats, mugger crocodile
Umbrella species | Protecting it protects many others (big cats)
Carrying capacity | Maximum population an environment can sustain (ROCKET)
## Beyond your notes
Strategy | Traits | Examples
r-selected | Many offspring, little care, fast growth, unstable habitats | Insects, weeds, rodents
K-selected | Few offspring, much care, long life, stable habitats near carrying capacity | Elephants, whales, humans
⚠ Big cats are apex predators and umbrella species, which regulate herbivores (CARE May 2026)

t: Interaction types → effect on each partner (+, -, 0)
text:
Interaction | Species 1 | Species 2 | Example
Mutualism | + | + | Coral and zooxanthellae; lichen; mycorrhiza
Commensalism | + | 0 | Suckerfish (remora) on shark; epiphytes on trees
Parasitism | + | - | Tapeworm, Plasmodium, Cuscuta
Predation | + | - | Tiger and deer
Competition | - | - | Two species sharing a scarce resource
Amensalism | - | 0 | Large tree shading a small plant; Penicillium inhibiting bacteria
Neutralism | 0 | 0 | Extremely unlikely in nature
Symbiosis = very intimate mutualism where partners can no longer live apart (coral and zooxanthellae)
⚠ If only one is harmed and the other is unaffected it is amensalism, not competition (goat grazing beside a beetle)
⚠ Parasitism and predation are both +/-: a parasite lives in or on the host, a predator kills and eats

t: Symbiosis → which groups have symbiotic species
text:
## 1. The 2021 list: all three form symbioses
Group | Symbiosis | Partner gets
Cnidarians (corals, sea anemones, jellyfish, hydra) | Corals with zooxanthellae (dinoflagellates, genus Symbiodinium) | Coral: fixed carbon and colour; alga: shelter and CO2
Fungi | Lichen (with algae/cyanobacteria); mycorrhiza (with roots) | Fungus: food; partner: water, minerals, shelter
Protozoa | Termite gut flagellates | Termite: wood (cellulose) digestion; protozoa: food and lodging
## 2. Other classic mutualisms
Rhizobium + legume: nitrogen fixed in root nodules
Fig + fig wasp: one-to-one pollination; wasp larvae eat some seeds
Ant + fungus: ants cultivate fungus as food
Sea anemone + hermit crab: anemone gets transport and food, crab gets camouflage and protection
⚠ Most protozoa are predators or parasites; only a few are symbiotic, but that is enough to tick "protozoa"
PYQ 2021: "which have species that can establish symbiotic relationship": cnidarians, fungi, protozoa; answer all three

t: Commensalism and amensalism → examples
text:
Commensal (+) | Host (0) | Benefit
Remora / suckerfish | Shark | Protection, free ride, leftovers
Epiphytes (orchids, ferns, mosses) | Trees | Support and access to light
Barnacles | Whales | Transport
Cattle egret | Grazing cattle | Insects stirred up
Kinds of commensalism (Preview): inquilinism (living in host's dwelling), metabiosis (using something the host made), phoresy (transport)
## Amensalism
Antibiosis: one organism releases a substance that harms another: Penicillium makes penicillin
## Beyond your notes
NCERT examples: orchid on a mango branch; clownfish among sea anemone tentacles (commensalism in NCERT)
⚠ Epiphyte-tree = commensalism, not parasitism and not mutualism

t: Parasitism → kinds and examples
text:
Kind | Meaning | Example
Ectoparasite | Lives on the body surface | Lice, ticks, leeches, Cuscuta
Endoparasite | Lives inside the host | Tapeworm, roundworm, Plasmodium
Total stem parasite | No chlorophyll, draws all food | Cuscuta (dodder)
Hyperparasite | Parasite whose host is itself a parasite | Wasp-waisted Hymenoptera, flies, beetles
Parasitoid | Larvae develop in and finally kill the host insect | Parasitoid wasps
Viral parasite | Obligate intracellular | Herpes simplex in human cells
Common human parasites: tapeworms, roundworms, malarial parasite, many bacteria, fungi, viruses
⚠ The female mosquito is not a parasite: it feeds on blood but does not live on the host; it is a vector of Plasmodium (Rocket calls it an ectoparasitic blood feeder: follow PMF)
## Beyond your notes
Brood parasitism: cuckoo lays eggs in the crow's nest; partial (hemi) parasite mistletoe (Loranthus) has chlorophyll but takes water from host
NCERT exemplar: Cuscuta, lice, tapeworm share the parasitic mode of nutrition

t: Predation and keystone roles → what they do for the community
text:
Predators (leopards, tigers, cheetahs) keep diversity high by reducing competition among prey species
Keystone species: loss changes at least one other species sharply; all top predators, elephants, corals and pollinators are keystone
Keystone | Why
Bats | Ebony, Indian laurel depend on bats for pollination
Elephants | Seed dispersal, habitat engineering
Pollinators | Coevolved plant-pollinator pairs go extinct together (co-extinction)
Co-extinction: when a host fish goes extinct its unique parasites also vanish
⚠ Coevolved mutualists (fig and its wasp) face co-extinction: losing one dooms the other

t: Lichens → partners and roles
text:
Partner | Name | Role
Alga (green alga or cyanobacterium) | Phycobiont | Photosynthesis: makes food
Fungus | Mycobiont | Shelter, absorbs water and minerals
Nature: mutualism (symbiotic association of algae and fungi)
Pioneers of primary succession on bare rock; their organic acids weather rock (biological weathering)
Pollution indicators: do not grow in polluted (SO2-rich) air
Not placed in Whittaker's five kingdoms (with viruses, viroids, prions)
⚠ Lichen = algae + fungi, not "algae + bacteria" or "fungi + mosses" (PYQ 2014)
## In news 2025-26
Five new Allographa species (script lichens, lichen-forming fungi) from the Western Ghats (July 2026)
Buellia maharajensis, new lichen from Mathikettan Shola NP, Kerala (Sept 2026)
BSI Plant Discoveries 2024 (July 2025): 63 lichens, 156 fungi, 15 bryophytes, 4 pteridophytes among 433 taxa; Kerala led

t: Mycorrhiza → what the fungus does for the plant
text:
Mycorrhiza = symbiotic association of a fungus with plant roots (mutualism)
Fungus gives the plant | Plant gives the fungus
Phosphorus (dissolves P roots cannot absorb), N, zinc | Sugars (carbohydrates)
Water: hyphae increase absorptive area | Nitrogen compounds
Drought resistance | 
Tolerance to extreme pH, salinity, heat, heavy metals | 
Disease resistance (barrier to root pathogens) | 
Found on roots of about 90% of land plants (LENS); some plants like Pinus cannot grow without it
Used to rehabilitate degraded sites and as biofertiliser (phosphorus-mobilising)
⚠ 2013 PYQ: drought resistance + absorptive area, pH tolerance and disease resistance: all three correct
PYQ 1999: mycorrhiza = symbiotic fungus-root association; the trap options were fungus-algae (lichen) and bacteria-root (Rhizobium)

t: Mycorrhiza types → and in news
text:
Type | Feature | Example
Ectomycorrhiza | Hyphae sheath the root, stay outside cells | Oak, pine; bolete mushrooms
Arbuscular (AM / VAM) | Hyphae enter root cells, form arbuscules | Most crops; vermicompost carries VAM fungi
## Beyond your notes
AM fungi genus Glomus; orchid seeds need mycorrhizal fungi to germinate
## In news 2025-26
Tyler Prize 2026 ("Nobel for the Environment", est. 1973, run by USC) to Dr Toby Kiers for research on mycorrhizal fungal networks; first Indian winner M.S. Swaminathan (1991)
New ectomycorrhizal bolete from oak forests of Bageshwar, Uttarakhand (Feb 2026): first record of the group in India
⚠ Mushrooms (Agaricus) are saprophytic, not biofertilisers; Plaited Ink Cap (Parasola plicatilis, Arunachal, Jan 2026) is a saprophytic fungus

t: Nitrogen fixers → symbiotic, associative, free-living
text:
Type | Organism | Host / habitat
Symbiotic (nodules) | Rhizobium | Legumes (peas, beans, lentils, clover)
Symbiotic (nodules) | Frankia | Non-legumes, e.g. Alnus
Symbiotic | Anabaena in Azolla (water fern) | Rice fields
Associative (no nodules) | Azospirillum | Cereals, grasses
Free-living aerobic | Azotobacter, Beijerinckia | Soil
Free-living anaerobic | Clostridium, Rhodospirillum | Soil
Free-living cyanobacteria | Nostoc, Anabaena | Paddy fields (heterocysts)
Enzyme nitrogenase occurs only in prokaryotes
Rhizobium-legume is mutualism: plant gives organic acids (carbon), bacteria give ammonia
⚠ Excess nitrogen fertiliser reduces N-fixers (plants stop feeding them), raises soil acidity, leaches nitrate (2015)
Likely next: which pairs are symbiotic: Rhizobium-legume, Frankia-Alnus, Anabaena-Azolla (yes); Azotobacter (no, free-living)

t: Biofertilisers → which organism does what
text:
Biofertiliser | Function
Rhizobium, Azotobacter, Azospirillum | Nitrogen fixation
Nostoc, Anabaena (blue-green algae) | N fixation in flooded rice
Azolla-Anabaena | N + biomass in rice; Azolla 2-3% N when wet
PSB: Pseudomonas, Bacillus, Penicillium, Aspergillus | Phosphate solubilising
Arbuscular mycorrhiza | Phosphate mobilising
Cellulolytic microbes | Organic matter decomposers
⚠ 2013 PYQ: Nostoc only is a biofertiliser; Agaricus (mushroom) and Spirogyra (green alga, no N fixation) are not
Limits: slow action, sensitive to temperature, moisture, pH, short shelf life

t: Surviving without soil → lichens and mosses yes, ferns and mushrooms no
text:
Organism | Grows on bare surface? | Why
Lichen | Yes | Fungus anchors, alga photosynthesises; weathers rock
Moss | Yes | Rhizoids (no true roots), no vascular tissue
Fern | No (generally) | Vascular plant; needs soil for anchorage and nutrients
Mushroom | No | Fruiting body of fungus whose mycelium grows in organic substrate
⚠ Some epiphytic ferns grow on trees, but ferns as a group need soil: UPSC's answer was lichen and moss only
PYQ 2021: "found surviving on a surface without soil": fern, lichen, moss, mushroom; answer 2 and 3 (lichen, moss)

t: Primary succession → pioneers to climax
text:
Primary succession: where no community existed: bare rock, new deltas, sand dunes, volcanic islands, lava flows, glacial moraines, landslide slopes
Pioneers: microbes, lichens, mosses; organic acids weather rock, debris forms soil pockets
Sere | Sequence
Xerosere (bare rock) | Lichens → mosses → herbs → shrubs → trees
Hydrosere (pond) | Phytoplankton → floating plants → rooted hydrophytes → sedges, grasses → trees
Heterotrophic (dead wood) | Bacteria, fungi → termites, beetles → mosses → soil
Both xerarch and hydrarch end in a mesic (mesophytic) climax
Secondary succession starts on existing soil: faster
⚠ In grasslands trees do not replace grasses because of water limits and fire (2013): grass is the climax there

t: Bryophytes, pteridophytes, fungi → body and habitat
text:
Feature | Bryophytes (mosses, liverworts) | Pteridophytes (ferns, horsetails) | Fungi
Roots | Rhizoids only | True roots, stems, leaves | Hyphae / mycelium
Vascular tissue | Absent | Present (first land plants with it) | Absent
Nutrition | Autotroph | Autotroph | Heterotroph (saprophyte, parasite, symbiont)
Dominant phase | Gametophyte | Sporophyte | -
Cell wall | Cellulose | Cellulose | Chitin
Sphagnum moss gives peat; mosses form mats that check soil erosion; called amphibians of the plant kingdom (Beyond)
## In news 2025-26
Utricularia kumtensis, a lithophytic (rock-growing) bladderwort, new from Karnataka (Oct 2025)
Tardigrades ("water bears", "moss piglets") live in thin water films on mosses and lichens (June 2025)

topic: Detritivores, Decomposers and Modes of Nutrition
t: Detritivores → which animals eat detritus
text:
Organism | Group | Role
Earthworm | Annelid | Detritivore
Millipede | Arthropod (myriapod) | Detritivore (leaf litter)
Woodlouse | Arthropod (crustacean, isopod) | Detritivore
Dung beetle | Insect | Detritivore
Jellyfish | Cnidarian | Predator (stinging tentacles)
Seahorse | Fish | Predator (small crustaceans)
Detritivores ingest dead organic matter (internal digestion); saprotrophs (fungi, bacteria) secrete enzymes and absorb externally
⚠ The 2021 trap: jellyfish and seahorses are marine predators, not detritivores
PYQ 2021: earthworms, jellyfish, millipedes, seahorses, woodlice; answer 1, 3 and 5
## In news 2025-26
Green pill millipede (Western Ghats endemic, Apr 2026): detritivore of leaf litter; rolls into a ball, water-repelling exoskeleton

topic: Detritivores, Decomposers and Modes of Nutrition
t: Decomposers → who decomposes, who does not
text:
Organism | Decomposer? | Note
Bacteria | Yes | Enzymes break detritus (catabolism)
Fungi | Yes | Main decomposers; mushrooms are fruiting bodies
Viruses | No | Metabolically inactive outside a host
Slime moulds (protists) | Yes, on dead matter | Paramecium, Euglena are not decomposers
Processes: fragmentation (detritivores) → leaching → catabolism (bacteria, fungi) → humification → mineralisation (Beyond on stage names)
⚠ 2013 PYQ: decomposers = fungi and bacteria only; virus is the trap

topic: Detritivores, Decomposers and Modes of Nutrition
t: Grazing vs detritus food chain → where energy flows
text:
Feature | Grazing food chain | Detritus food chain
Starts with | Living plants | Dead organic matter
First consumers | Herbivores | Detritivores, decomposers
Main energy route in | Aquatic ecosystems | Terrestrial ecosystems (larger share)
Example | Grass → caterpillar → lizard → snake | Leaf litter → earthworm → bird
Ocean primary producers: diatoms, cyanobacteria, coccolithophores, dinoflagellates; copepods (crustaceans) and foraminifera (protists) are not producers (2021)
⚠ In land ecosystems more energy flows through the detritus chain than the grazing chain

topic: Detritivores, Decomposers and Modes of Nutrition
t: Modes of nutrition → classify the organism
text:
Mode | Meaning | Examples
Photoautotroph | Sunlight | Plants, algae, cyanobacteria
Chemoautotroph | Chemical energy | Sulphur- and iron-oxidising bacteria
Detritivore | Eats dead matter | Earthworm, dung beetle
Saprotroph | External digestion of dead matter | Fungi (yeast, bread mould, mushroom), bacteria
Parasite | Food from living host | Tapeworm, ticks, Cuscuta, lice
Insectivorous plant | Photosynthesises but traps insects for nitrogen | Pitcher plant (Nepenthes), bladderwort, Drosera, Venus flytrap
⚠ NCERT: food broken down outside the body and absorbed = yeast, mushroom, bread mould
⚠ Insectivorous plants are autotrophs that grow in nitrogen-poor soil, not heterotrophs

t: Epiphytes → what they take from the host
text:
Epiphyte: grows harmlessly on another plant and takes moisture and nutrients from air, rain and debris around it
Takes from host | Does not take
Mechanical support (a perch near light) | Food
 | Water from host tissues
Examples: orchids, epiphytic ferns, mosses and lichens (temperate rainforest), bromeliads (Beyond)
Relation with tree: commensalism (+/0)
⚠ An epiphyte is not a parasite: it neither taps the host's vascular tissue nor harms it
PYQ 2001: epiphytes use other plants only for support, not for food or water

t: Plant life-forms → how each uses another plant or surface
text:
Life-form | Relation | Example
Epiphyte | On a plant, support only | Orchids, epiphytic ferns
Total parasite | Takes all food, no chlorophyll | Cuscuta
Partial parasite | Takes water/minerals, has chlorophyll | Mistletoe (Loranthus) (Beyond)
Lithophyte | On rock | Utricularia kumtensis, mosses, lichens
Climber / liana | Uses tree for support, rooted in soil | Rainforest lianas
Hemi-epiphyte / strangler | Starts as epiphyte, roots reach ground | Banyan (Ficus)
Saprophyte | Lives on dead matter | Fungi
Banyan usually begins as an epiphyte on another tree, sends down aerial roots that become prop trunks (LENS July 2026)

t: Epiphytes and biomes → where they abound
text:
Biome | Epiphyte feature
Tropical rainforest | Numerous epiphytes; plants climb or perch to reach canopy light; litter decomposes fastest, soil surface almost bare
Temperate rainforest (Pacific NW) | Mosses and lichens as epiphytes
Tropical evergreen (Western Ghats, A&N) | Undergrowth of ferns, climbers, orchids
2013 PYQ: tall closely set trees, coexistence of many species and numerous epiphytes are all features of equatorial forests
2021 PYQ: "plants reach canopy by climbing or as epiphytes, litter decomposes fastest" = tropical rainforest
## In news 2025-26
New epiphytic orchids: Gastrochilus pechei (Sept 2025), Oberonia marnkuliensis (Karnataka, Oct 2025); Hoya nagaensis, climbing epiphytic vine (Nagaland, Feb 2026)
Arunachal Pradesh, "Orchid State", has ~60% of India's orchid varieties

t: Agents of pollination → term and example
text:
Agent | Term | Flower traits | Examples
Wind | Anemophily | Small, dull, light dry pollen, exposed stamens | Grasses, wheat, maize, pine
Water | Hydrophily | Aquatic | Vallisneria, seagrasses
Insects | Entomophily | Bright, scented, nectar | Sunflower, rose, orchids
Birds | Ornithophily | Bright, tubular, nectar | Hibiscus, fuchsia (hummingbirds, sunbirds)
Bats | Chiropterophily | Large, fragrant, night-blooming | Baobab, agave
Other animals | Zoophily | Ground-level flowers | Small mammals, lizards
Insect pollinators: bees, butterflies, moths, beetles, flies
⚠ Bats, bees and birds are all pollinators (2012); bats are nocturnal pollinators
PYQ 2012: asked which of bats, bees, birds are pollinators; answer all three

t: Specialised pollination → coevolved pairs
text:
Plant | Pollinator | Note
Fig | Fig wasp | One fig species, one wasp species; wasp lays eggs in fruit, larvae eat some seeds
Ebony, Indian laurel | Bats | Depend exclusively on bats
Baobab, agave | Bats | Night flowers
## Beyond your notes
Yucca and yucca moth; Ophrys orchid uses sexual deceit (petal mimics female bee); Amorphophallus gives a carrion smell for flies
Mahua flowers are bat-pollinated; Rafflesia is fly-pollinated and parasitic
⚠ Coevolution: fig's flower and its wasp's evolution are linked; extinction of one leads to co-extinction of the other
PYQ 2024 (outside this set): tree with a coevolved insect that alone pollinates it: fig (not mahua, sandalwood, silk cotton)

t: Pollinators → value and threats
text:
About one-third of world food crops depend on pollination (Praveen)
$235-577 billion of global crop output a year at risk from pollinator loss
Pollinators count as keystone species
Threat | Example
Pesticides | Pollinator deaths in Himachal Pradesh (WII)
Varroa mite | Millions of bees culled in Australia (2022)
Habitat loss, climate change | Solitary bee decline
Solitary bees = ~75% of all bee species; nest alone, no honey, ground-nesting aerates soil
## In news 2025-26
NHAI "Bee Corridors" (Feb 2026): India's first; flowering clusters every 500 m-1 km along highways
Two new ground-nesting solitary bees of subfamily Anthophorinae (incl. one named after the Adi community, July 2026)
India's lepidoptera checklist (Aug 2026): 13,703 species (~8.25% of world): 1,417 butterflies, 12,286 moths; Geometroidea moths are nocturnal pollinators

topic: Adaptations to Desert, Saline, Aquatic and Cold Habitats
t: Desert plant leaves → how each cuts water loss
text:
Leaf feature | How it reduces transpiration
Hard, waxy (thick cuticle) leaves | Waterproof layer blocks evaporation
Tiny leaves / few leaves | Less surface area
Thorns / spines instead of leaves | Leaf surface almost eliminated
Sunken stomata (in pits) | Still air around pores
Succulent (fleshy) leaves | Store water
Hairy, leathery or needle-shaped foliage | Less evaporation
When leaves become spines, flattened green stems do photosynthesis: phylloclade of Opuntia; fleshy stems of Euphorbia
⚠ All three 2013/2018 options (hard waxy leaves, tiny leaves, thorns) are correct: "all of the above"
PYQ 2018 and 2013: desert-plant leaf modifications; every listed feature reduces transpiration

topic: Adaptations to Desert, Saline, Aquatic and Cold Habitats
t: Xerophytes → features beyond the leaf
text:
Feature | Example
Long, deep roots; plants widely spaced | Desert shrubs reach groundwater
Phreatophytes: roots ~20-30 m to the water table | Prosopis (Beyond on species)
Water storage in swollen stems, leaves, roots | Cactus, aloe
Thick, tough seed coats; seeds dormant for years | Desert grasses, herbs
Dieback (tip-to-base death, roots survive) | Sal, red sanders, silk-cotton
Xerophyte examples: cactus, aloe vera, acacia, Prosopis juliflora, casuarina, calotropis, pineapple
## Beyond your notes
CAM plants (cactus, pineapple) open stomata at night to save water
⚠ Vegetation pairs (PMF): sloping branches + needle leaves = taiga; deep roots, waxy stem, no leaves = desert; canopy = tropical forest
⚠ Mediterranean plants are also xerophytic (small leathery leaves, thick bark) against summer drought

topic: Adaptations to Desert, Saline, Aquatic and Cold Habitats
t: Halophytes → mangrove adaptations to salt and anoxia
text:
Problem | Adaptation
Anoxic mud | Pneumatophores (Avicennia), breathing roots
Soft unstable mud | Stilt / prop roots (Rhizophora), buttresses
Salty water kills seeds | Vivipary: seeds germinate on the tree
Excess salt | Root-level exclusion; salt glands on leaves; salt stored in old leaves that drop; sequestration in vacuoles
Water loss | Succulent leaves, sunken stomata
Mangroves need high solar energy for salt filtration: confined to tropics/subtropics (about 24°N-38°S)
Halophytes also grow in saline semi-deserts, marshes, seashores
⚠ Vivipary is the classic mangrove answer; pneumatophores = Avicennia, stilt roots = Rhizophora

topic: Adaptations to Desert, Saline, Aquatic and Cold Habitats
t: Hydrophytes and mesophytes → water-plant adaptations
text:
Group | Habitat | Examples
Xerophytes | Dry (xeric) | Cactus, acacia, aloe
Hydrophytes | Water / saturated soil | Water hyacinth, lotus, water lily, pondweed
Mesophytes | Moderate moisture | Banana, rice, sugarcane, jamun, eucalyptus
Halophytes | Saline | Mangroves
Hydrophyte key adaptation: aerenchyma (air-filled tissue for buoyancy and oxygen)
## Beyond your notes
Hydrophytes: reduced roots and xylem, thin or absent cuticle, stomata on upper leaf surface in floating leaves, finely dissected submerged leaves
⚠ Cuticle is thicker in desert plants and absent in roots (PMF)

topic: Adaptations to Desert, Saline, Aquatic and Cold Habitats
t: Animal adaptations → physiological and behavioural
text:
Type | Example
Physiological | Kangaroo rat (N. American desert) makes water by fat oxidation, concentrates urine
Physiological | Acclimatisation at altitude: more RBC and haemoglobin, faster breathing
Behavioural | Desert lizards bask and shade-seek; rodents burrow
Behavioural | Great Migration (wildebeest, zebra, gazelle) Serengeti-Masai Mara, clockwise
Morphological | Allen's Rule: cold-climate endotherms have shorter limbs and ears
Elephants do not sweat: they flap huge ears to lose heat
## Beyond your notes
Bergmann's Rule: endotherms in colder climates have larger body size
⚠ Very small animals (shrews, hummingbirds) are rare in polar regions: high surface-to-volume ratio loses heat fast

topic: Adaptations to Desert, Saline, Aquatic and Cold Habitats
t: Escaping stress → hibernation, aestivation, diapause, spores
text:
Strategy | Against | Examples
Hibernation (winter sleep) | Cold, food shortage | Bats, ground squirrels, hedgehogs, chipmunks, polar bears
Aestivation (summer sleep) | Heat, drought | African lungfish (mucus cocoon), snails, earthworms, frogs, toads, crocodiles
Diapause | Unfavourable season | Zooplankton in lakes and ponds
Spores, seeds | Any stress | Bacteria, fungi, lower plants; seeds in higher plants
Migration | Seasonal stress | Siberian birds at Keoladeo (Bharatpur)
Regulators (all birds and mammals) keep body temperature constant; most animals and nearly all plants are conformers
⚠ Hibernation = cold, aestivation = heat/drought: the classic swap

topic: Adaptations to Desert, Saline, Aquatic and Cold Habitats
t: Extremophiles → organisms of extreme habitats
text:
Extremophile | Habitat | Example
Hyperthermophile | Above boiling point | Pyrolobus fumarii at 113 °C
Cold-tolerant | Below freezing | Nematode Panagrolaimus davidi (Antarctica)
Acidophile | pH below 3 | Extreme acidophiles
Halophile | Very salty | Archaea
Thermoacidophile | Hot and acidic | Archaea
Archaebacteria survive extremes thanks to special lipid-linked membranes; eubacteria and cyanobacteria cannot
⚠ 2023 PYQ: microbes growing above boiling, below freezing and below pH 3: all three statements correct

t: Gaseous vs sedimentary cycles → which cycle has which reservoir
text:
Type | Reservoir | Cycles
Gaseous | Atmosphere or hydrosphere | Water, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, methane
Sedimentary | Earth's crust (rocks, soil, sediments) | Phosphorus, sulphur, calcium, magnesium
Mixed | Crust and air | Sulphur (gas phase only H2S, SO2)
Gaseous cycles are global and near "perfect" (nutrients replaced as fast as used)
Sedimentary cycles are "imperfect": nutrients get locked in sediments for long periods
Mineral cycles have two phases: rock phase and salt solution phase; weathering releases, sedimentation returns
⚠ Phosphorus has no significant gaseous phase; sulphur is "mostly" sedimentary but has gases
Likely next: "which cycles are sedimentary" - phosphorus, sulphur, calcium (yes); carbon, nitrogen (no)

t: Elements of life → share and role
text:
Element | % of human body | Role
Oxygen | ~65 | Water, all biomolecules
Carbon | ~18 | Backbone of organic molecules
Hydrogen | ~10 | Water, organic molecules
Nitrogen | ~3 | Amino acids, DNA, RNA
Calcium | ~1.5 | Bones, teeth, nerves
Phosphorus | ~1 | DNA, RNA, ATP, membranes
Sulphur | ~0.3 | Some amino acids, vitamins
O, C, H, N = ~96% of body mass; with P and S = ~97%
For most organisms C, H, O, N, P, S make up >95% of biomass
⚠ Oxygen, not carbon, is the most abundant element in the body by mass

t: Plant nutrients → source of each
text:
Group | Elements | Source
Macronutrients (9) | C, H, O | Air (CO2) and water
 | N, P, K, Ca, S, Mg | Soil minerals
Micronutrients | Fe, Mn, Cu, Mo, Zn, B, Cl, Ni | Soil (trace)
Beneficial | Na, Si, Co, Se | Soil
17 essential elements; NPK most significant
Most soil nutrients come from weathered rocks; soil also hosts N-fixers, holds water and air
⚠ Plants do not take C from soil; it comes from CO2 in air

topic: Carbon cycle: sources and sinks of CO2
t: What adds and what removes CO2 → the PYQ list
text:
Process | Effect on atmospheric CO2
Respiration | Adds
Decay / decomposition of organic matter | Adds
Volcanic action | Adds (from Earth's interior)
Burning fossil fuels, biomass, forest fires | Adds
Cement making, deforestation | Adds
Photosynthesis | Removes
Ocean uptake, rock weathering (carbonation), burial | Removes
⚠ Photosynthesis is the only option that removes CO2 - the trap in both PYQs
PYQ 2011 and 2014: volcanic action, respiration, decay add CO2 - answer "2, 3 and 4" (2011) / "1, 2 and 4" (2014)
Undecomposed organic matter stores carbon in soil (peat, carbonates) instead of releasing it

topic: Carbon cycle: sources and sinks of CO2
t: Short-term vs long-term carbon cycle → where carbon goes
text:
## 1. Short-term (biological)
Air CO2 → photosynthesis (plants, phytoplankton) → animals → back by respiration and decomposition
Carbon is only ~0.04% of air, yet anchors all organic matter
## 2. Long-term (geological)
Store | How carbon gets there | How it returns
Peat (marshy soils) | Undecomposed organic matter | Drainage, fire
Fossil fuels | Buried before decay (peat → lignite → bituminous → anthracite) | Combustion
Carbonate rocks, deep-sea sediments | Insoluble carbonates | Uplift and erosion
Photosynthesis converts free energy (sunlight) into potential energy (carbohydrates); respiration oxidises food to CO2 + water
⚠ Coal forms in anaerobic swamps: absence of oxygen stops full decay

topic: Carbon cycle: sources and sinks of CO2
t: Carbon sinks → ocean, forest, soil
text:
Sink | Fact
Ocean | Largest active sink: absorbs ~25-30% of human CO2 each year; uptake acidifies water
Blue carbon | Carbon in seagrass, mangroves, salt marshes; sequester faster than forests
Forests | Sink when growing; source when degraded; tropical forests absorb ~18% of fossil CO2
Soils | Boreal forests keep up to 80% of carbon in soil (peat)
A sink absorbs more carbon than it releases; a source releases more
Seagrass stores ~3x tropical forest carbon per unit area (PMF)
⚠ Unlike other sinks, the ocean sink causes acidification, threatening corals
## Beyond your notes
Ocean "biological pump": phytoplankton fix CO2, dead matter sinks to the deep sea; "solubility pump": cold water dissolves more CO2 and sinks

topic: Carbon cycle: sources and sinks of CO2
t: Enhanced rock weathering and carbon removal → how each works
text:
Method | Mechanism
Natural weathering | CO2 + rain → carbonic acid → dissolves rock → stored as bicarbonate, then limestone
Enhanced Rock Weathering | Spread crushed basalt on farms to speed weathering
Ocean fertilisation | Add iron to trigger phytoplankton blooms
BECCS | Burn biomass for energy, capture the CO2
DACCS | Machines pull CO2 from air, store underground
ERW co-benefits: higher soil alkalinity and fertility; Brazil issued the first verified ERW credits
Carbonation is faster in cold water (more dissolved CO2)
## In news 2025-26
India's Mati Carbon won the $50 million XPRIZE Carbon Removal grand prize for ERW
⚠ ERW is a geological (weathering) route; ocean fertilisation is a biological one

topic: Carbon cycle: sources and sinks of CO2
t: Methane in the carbon cycle → sources and sinks
text:
Natural sources | Human sources
Wetlands (~80% of natural) | Agriculture (~40%): ruminants, rice
Termites | Fossil fuels (~35%): leaks, coal-bed methane
Oceans | Waste (~20-25%): landfills, sewage
Methane hydrates | Biomass burning
Made by methanogens (archaea) in low-oxygen conditions; ruminants release it mainly by belching
Sinks: hydroxyl radical (OH) in the troposphere ("cleanser of the atmosphere"); methanotrophic bacteria in well-aerated soils
⚠ Human > natural; natural order wetlands > termites > oceans > hydrates
PYQ 2022 (linked): rice is the main crop source of both methane and nitrous oxide
## In news 2025-26
WMO Greenhouse Gas Bulletin (Oct 2025): CO2 423.9 ppm in 2024; +3.5 ppm jump, largest since 1957; N2O 338 ppb
El Nino 2024 cut land and ocean sink efficiency (droughts, fires)

t: What adds nitrogen to soil → the PYQ list
text:
Input | Adds N to soil?
Excretion of urea / uric acid | Yes: ammonification → ammonia → nitrate
Death of vegetation and animals | Yes: decomposition releases N compounds
N-fixing bacteria, legumes | Yes
Lightning | Yes, a little (nitrate in rain)
Fertilisers (urea, ammonium salts) | Yes
Burning coal | No directly: releases NOx to the air (smog, acid rain)
⚠ Coal burning puts nitrogen in the air; PMF notes it reaches soil only indirectly via acid rain ("debatable c/d"); the key is "1 and 3 only"
PYQ 2013: urea excretion and death of vegetation add soil N - answer "1 and 3 only"

t: Nitrogen fixation → who fixes and how
text:
N2 has a triple bond: most organisms cannot use it; must be fixed to ammonia / ammonium
Three routes: N-fixing microbes, industry (Haber-Bosch), lightning (limited)
Fixer type | Examples
Free-living aerobic | Azotobacter, Beijerinckia
Free-living anaerobic | Clostridium, Rhodospirillum
Symbiotic (legume nodules) | Rhizobium
Cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) | Nostoc, Anabaena, Spirulina
Enzyme nitrogenase: found only in prokaryotes; needs anaerobic conditions
Leghaemoglobin in nodules (pink) protects nitrogenase from oxygen; ~8 ATP per NH3
⚠ Human fixation (fertilisers, combustion) now exceeds natural terrestrial fixation, making N a pollutant

t: Nitrification, ammonification, denitrification → step and organism
text:
Step | Change | Organisms
Fixation | N2 → NH3 / NH4+ | Rhizobium, Azotobacter, cyanobacteria
Ammonification | Urea, uric acid, dead matter → NH3 | Decomposer bacteria
Nitrification 1 | NH4+ → nitrite (NO2-) | Nitrosomonas, Nitrosococcus
Nitrification 2 | Nitrite → nitrate (NO3-) | Nitrobacter, Nitrospira
Denitrification | Nitrate → N2 gas | Pseudomonas, Thiobacillus
Nitrifiers are chemoautotrophs (energy from oxidising N compounds, carbon from CO2); nitrification is aerobic
Denitrification is anaerobic; used with nitrification to strip N from sewage
Plants absorb NH4+ and NO3-; nitrate is reduced to ammonia in leaves to make amino acids
⚠ "Nitroso-" bacteria make nitrite; "Nitro-bacter" makes nitrate; Pseudomonas returns N to the air

t: Excess nitrogen fertiliser → effects
text:
Effect | Why
Soil acidity rises | Nitrification releases H+
Nitrate leaching to groundwater | Nitrate is highly water-soluble
N-fixers decline (not proliferate) | Plants stop feeding symbiotic fixers
Acid rain, N2O emission | Microbes turn excess N into NO, N2O
Eutrophication | Runoff feeds algal blooms
Urea has the highest N content of solid fertilisers; breaks down to ammonium in soil
PYQ 2015 (linked): excess N fertiliser raises acidity and leaches nitrate; does not increase N-fixers - "2 and 3 only"
## In news 2025-26
Kharif 2025: rice and maize area rose, soybean and pulses (natural N-fixers) fell - urea and DAP shortage
DAP = 18% N + 46% P2O5; substandard APS and TSP samples flagged (2026)

t: Phosphorus cycle → source and path
text:
Reservoir: phosphate rocks; released by weathering, erosion, leaching and mining
Path: rock → soil solution → plant roots → herbivores → wastes, dead bodies → phosphate-solubilising bacteria → soil
In the sea, phosphate settles on continental shelves; returns to land only by tectonic uplift over millions of years
Feature | Phosphorus | Carbon / Nitrogen
Main reservoir | Rocks | Atmosphere
Gas phase | None significant | Yes (CO2, N2)
Respiratory release | No | CO2 yes
Entry route | Weathering of rocks | Fixation, photosynthesis
⚠ Weathering of rocks is the main source for phosphorus - not carbon, nitrogen or sulphur
PYQ 2021: answer phosphorus cycle

t: Phosphorus in living things and water → role
text:
Role | Detail
Biomolecules | DNA, RNA, ATP, membrane phospholipids
Animals | Shells, bones, teeth
Plants | Root growth, early maturity, legume N-fixation
Lakes | Limiting nutrient: drives eutrophication and phytoplankton blooms
Fertiliser: superphosphate = rock phosphate + sulphuric acid; all manures contain P
Only a small fraction of soil P is available to plants
Mycorrhizal fungi and phosphate-solubilising bacteria (biofertilisers) free soil P
⚠ Phosphorus, not nitrogen, is usually the trigger of freshwater algal blooms (PMF)

t: Sulphur cycle → sources, path and role of soil
text:
## 1. Stores and release
Stored in organic (coal, oil, peat) and inorganic (pyrite, sulphur rock) deposits as sulphates, sulphides
Released by rock weathering, runoff and decomposition
## 2. Sources of atmospheric sulphur
Source | Form
Volcanic eruptions | SO2
Fossil fuel burning (coal, diesel) | SO2
Ocean surface (algae) | Dimethyl sulphide (DMS)
Decomposition | H2S (oxidised to SO2)
SO2 returns as weak sulphuric acid (acid rain)
Plants take up sulphates → sulphur amino acids (proteins) → food chain → back to soil by excretion and decay
⚠ Soil plays a central role in the sulphur cycle - the false statement in PYQ 2018
DMS is the main source of marine sulphate aerosols
## In news 2025-26
Flue Gas Desulphurisation (FGD, removes SO2 from coal plants): blanket mandate reviewed (2025)

topic: Oxygen: ocean production and dissolved oxygen
t: Who produces Earth's oxygen → oceans vs rainforests
text:
Producer | Share / fact
Ocean (phytoplankton, cyanobacteria, kelp) | ~50% of Earth's oxygen (PYQ key: 50-80% with seaweeds)
Prochlorococcus | Ocean's most abundant photosynthetic cyanobacterium; ~20% alone (PYQ key)
Rainforests | Large gross output, but net ~zero: recycled by respiration and decay in the same forest
Ocean primary producers: diatoms, coccolithophores, cyanobacteria (Synechococcus, Prochlorococcus), dinoflagellates
Calling rainforests "lungs of the Earth" is a misconception (PMF)
⚠ Rainforests do not produce more oxygen than oceans
PYQ 2025: only statement 2 correct - answer "2 only"

topic: Oxygen: ocean production and dissolved oxygen
t: Dissolved oxygen vs air → how much less
text:
Medium | Oxygen
Air | ~209,000 ppm; ~270-300 mg per litre
Well-oxygenated fresh water | ~8-10 mg/L (8-10 ppm)
Ratio per litre | Air holds ~25-35 times more
Ratio in ppm | Air ~20,000-26,000 times higher
O2 enters water at the air-water interface and by aquatic photosynthesis; leaves by respiration and decay
Fish die when DO falls below ~3-5 ppm; fish use dissolved O2 because they cannot absorb gaseous oxygen (NCERT)
⚠ "Surface water holds several-fold more oxygen than air" is false: water holds far less
⚠ PYQ explanation uses ~210,000 mg/L for air and 8-14 mg/L for water; PMF gives 270-300 mg/L air vs 8-10 mg/L water - both mean water holds far less

topic: Oxygen: ocean production and dissolved oxygen
t: Why oxygen in water falls → causes
text:
Cause | Mechanism
Warming | O2 less soluble in warm water; faster decay
Stratification | Melt water forms a light layer that blocks mixing
Eutrophication | Algal blooms consume O2 at night and on decay → dead zones
Winterkill | Ice cuts light, photosynthesis stops, respiration continues
Plastics | Leachates impair Prochlorococcus photosynthesis
IUCN: ocean O2 fell ~2% between 1960 and 2010
Anaerobic water favours Clostridium botulinum toxins
⚠ Algal blooms reduce oxygen overall, though algae photosynthesise by day

topic: Oxygen: ocean production and dissolved oxygen
t: Plants: respiration vs photosynthesis → gas exchange
text:
Time | Net gas exchange of green plant
Day | Photosynthesis > respiration → O2 released
Night | Only respiration → CO2 released
Plants respire day and night; respiratory CO2 by day is reused in photosynthesis
Gas exchange through stomata and lenticels; no special respiratory organs
⚠ "Plants respire only at night" is false

t: Soil organic matter → effect on water and fertility
text:
Property | Effect of high organic matter (humus)
Water-holding capacity | Increases
Soil structure | Binds particles into stable aggregates
Infiltration | Increases; less surface crusting and erosion
Nutrients | Slow-release N, P, S; higher cation exchange capacity
pH | Buffers pH
Microbes | Feeds beneficial microbes
Humus: dark, decayed plant and animal matter; most in the topsoil (A-horizon); O-horizon is the organic layer
Organic matter is only 2-10% of most soils' mass; ~50-60% of it is carbon; healthy soils have 1-6% SOC
⚠ High organic matter raises, not reduces, water-holding capacity
PYQ 2018: statements 1 and 2 false, 3 true - answer "3 only"

t: Soil organic carbon → what raises and lowers it
text:
Raises SOC | Lowers SOC
Cool climate (slow decay) | Heat: tropical soils lose carbon fast
Clay texture | Sandy soil (leaching)
Grasslands (deep roots) | Repeated tillage
Moderate rainfall, high elevation | Excess N fertiliser, residue burning
Mulching, green manure, biochar | Erosion, forest-to-farm conversion
Biochar: porous carbon from pyrolysis (heating biomass with little oxygen); improves structure, holds carbon long-term
## In news 2025-26
ICAR study (Nov 2025): SOC falling fastest in Haryana, Punjab, western UP from prolonged urea and phosphate use; SOC rises with elevation, falls with temperature
Over half of Karnataka's farmland low in SOC; black soil "Eremannu" worst (2025); PASCI model predicts SOC

t: Irrigation and salinisation → how and where
text:
## 1. Mechanism
Canal irrigation raises the water table; in the dry season capillary action lifts salts to the surface
Salts of sodium, calcium, magnesium form a white efflorescence; soil becomes infertile
Poor drainage: stagnant salty water evaporates and leaves salts in the topsoil
## 2. Where in India
Cause | Areas
Canal irrigation | Punjab, Haryana, UP; Rajasthan; Maharashtra, Gujarat, AP, Telangana, Karnataka
Sea tides | Gulf of Khambhat; estuaries of Narmada, Tapi, Mahi, Sabarmati
Storm surges | Coastal AP and Tamil Nadu
Saline and alkaline soils cover ~68,000 sq km
⚠ Irrigation can salinise soil - the one true statement of PYQ 2018
## Beyond your notes
Saline-alkaline soils are called reh, kallar, usar; reclaimed with gypsum, drainage and salt-tolerant crops

t: Indian soils linked to the cycles → organic matter and salts
text:
Soil | Feature
Peaty / marshy | Very high organic matter, highly acidic; Kottayam, Alappuzha, Sundarbans; poor in potash, phosphate
Saline / alkaline | Salt efflorescence; canal areas, coasts
Loamy | Has humus; right water-holding capacity
Red (crystalline rocks) | Iron oxide; low humus
Black (Deccan basalt) | Dark; holds moisture
Salt-tolerant crops on such land: barley, cotton, millets
⚠ Peaty soils are acidic and organic-rich; saline soils are alkaline and salt-rich
Freshwater salinisation syndrome: rising salt in rivers from road salt, mining, faster weathering and sea-water intrusion

t: Wetland functions → which metaphor fits which function
text:
## 1. "Kidneys of the Earth" = water purification
Aquatic plants absorb heavy metals and excess nutrients; wetlands trap sediments, detoxify pollutants, reduce BOD
Kidneys filter toxins out of blood; wetland plants filter toxins out of water
Metaphor | Function it stands for | Example
Kidneys | Filtering nutrients, heavy metals, sediments | East Kolkata Wetlands treat Kolkata's sewage
Sponges | Store floodwater, release it slowly, recharge aquifers | Floodplains; Bhoj Wetland buffers monsoon floods
Lungs (not wetlands) | Rainforests, tropical forests | Amazon
Bio-shields | Cut storm surge and wave energy | Mangroves, lagoons, mudflats
⚠ The 2022 distractors were all true facts about wetlands (water cycle, algae as nutrient base, sediment balance) but only heavy-metal and nutrient absorption matches "kidneys"
PYQ 2022: matched the "kidneys" quote to a function; trap: picking a true but non-filtering function

t: Wetland definition → Ramsar and the 2017 Rules
text:
## 1. The common definition
Area of marsh, fen, peatland or water; natural or artificial; permanent or temporary; water static or flowing; fresh, brackish or salt
Includes marine water up to 6 m deep at low tide
## 2. What counts as a wetland (Ramsar sense)
All lakes and rivers, lake littorals, floodplains, underground aquifers, swamps, marshes, wet grasslands, peatlands, oases, estuaries, deltas, tidal flats, mangroves, coral reefs
Human-made sites: fishponds, rice paddies, reservoirs, salt pans
## 3. Wetland as an ecotone
Feature | What it means
Hydric soils | Waterlogged long enough to turn anaerobic
Hydrophytes | Plants adapted to waterlogged soil
Periodic flooding | From adjacent deep-water habitats
⚠ The 2017 Rules use the same words but exclude river channels, paddy fields and many human-made water bodies (see Wetland laws section)
⚠ The figure is 6 m at low tide, not high tide

t: Wetland vs lake → depth, producers, nutrient status
text:
NLCP treats a lake as standing water ≥3 m deep, usually >10 ha, little aquatic vegetation
Wetlands are generally <3 m deep, nutrient-rich, full of macrophytes
Aspect | Lake | Wetland (shallow lake)
Depth | Shallow or deep | Shallow
Thermal stratification | Yes | No
Vertical mixing | Thermally regulated | Wind regulated
Dominant producers | Phytoplankton | Macrophytes (hydrilla, lotus)
Food chain | Grazing pathway | Detritus pathway
Productivity | Low | High
Trophic status | Oligotrophic | Mostly eutrophic
Flood control, waste treatment | Minor | Significant
Example of a shallow fluvial wetland-lake: Kolleru (AP)
⚠ Too many submerged/floating macrophytes harm water quality, but marginal vegetation is desirable (checks erosion, gives habitat)

t: Wetland types → service each provides
text:
Type | Key services (PMF)
Lake littorals, swamps, marshes | Fish nursery; riparian buffer; shoreline protection
Floodplains | Natural sponges cut flood peaks; fertile soils; recharge
Deltas | Fertile farmland; dissipate storm waves
Tidal flats | Feeding ground for migratory shorebirds
Mangroves | Storm defence; fish/crab/prawn nursery; blue carbon
Salt pans | Salt livelihoods; flamingo habitat (Rann of Kutch)
Wet grasslands | Pastoralism: Terai, phumdis of Loktak, Banni
Peatlands | Among the biggest carbon stores on Earth
Estuaries | "Fish factories", the most productive water bodies
## 1. Other wetland terms
Marsh: herbaceous (non-woody) plants; swamp: trees and shrubs
Bog: acidic, built by peat moss; fen: alkaline, fed by groundwater seepage
⚠ Bog = acidic, fen = alkaline: an easy pair to swap

t: Estuary vs delta vs lagoon → how to tell them apart
text:
Aspect | Estuary | Delta | Lagoon
Core idea | River-sea mixing zone | Depositional landform | Coastal water cut off by a barrier
Tide | Strong | Weak | Restricted exchange
Salinity | Gradient fresh → marine | Mostly fresh | Often hypersaline; varies
Channels | Single main channel | Many distributaries | Few inlets
India | West-flowing: Narmada, Tapi, Periyar | East-flowing: Ganga-Brahmaputra, Mahanadi, Godavari | Chilika, Pulicat, Vembanad
Estuary salinity: 0-35 ppt; ~60% of humanity lives along estuaries and coasts
A delta can hold estuarine reaches near its mouth (Godavari's Gautami branch)
Ports sit on estuaries: Shanghai (Yangtze), Rotterdam (Rhine), London (Thames), Mormugao (Zuari)
⚠ Estuaries, not reefs or rainforests, top the productivity order: estuaries > swamps/marshes > coral reefs > tropical rainforests > ... > open ocean > deserts

t: Wetland threats and fixes → by wetland type
text:
Wetland | Main threat (PMF) | Example
Lakes | Sewage → eutrophication; encroachment; water hyacinth | Bhoj (urbanisation)
Swamps, marshes | Drainage for farms; pesticides | Kolleru
Wet grasslands | Invasives: Prosopis juliflora ("mad tree") | Banni
Peatlands | Drainage, peat extraction | Congo, SE Asia
Estuaries, deltas | Upstream dams cut sediment; dredging | Hooghly
Mangroves | Shrimp ponds, salt pans, timber | Mumbai Coastal Road
Invasive spread | Water hyacinth cuts oxygen and light | Vembanad
Weak enforcement | Pollution, illegal land use | East Kolkata Wetlands
Fixes: STPs before discharge; catchment afforestation; GIS geofencing; floodplain zoning ("room for the river"); reopening blocked tidal creeks
HYDRAA (Telangana) removes encroachments on public assets
## In news 2025-26
Global Wetland Outlook 2025 (Ramsar Secretariat): 22% of world wetlands lost since 1970; wetlands are ~6% of Earth's surface but give ~7.5% of global GDP; worst degradation in Africa, Latin America, Caribbean

topic: Wetlands of India: extent, superlatives, river links
t: India's wetland area → inland vs coastal, top state
text:
## 1. National Wetlands Atlas 2024 (SAC-ISRO)
16.89 million ha (1,68,900 km²) = ~5.12% of India's area
~70% of this is paddy (human-made)
Inland wetlands = 69.22%: far more than coastal

t: Mangroves as bio-shields → the mechanism
text:
## 1. Why they protect coasts
Complex roots (prop/stilt roots, pneumatophores) anchor trees in soft mud: they are not uprooted by storms and tides
Roots dissipate wave energy: protect from tsunamis, storm surges, erosion
Slow water flow → sediment deposition → land accretion, shoreline stabilised
Moderate tidal floods, reduce inundation of lowlands
Statement type | Verdict
Roots keep trees from being uprooted | Correct (2011)
Bio-shield + biomass livelihood base | Correct (2026)
Store freshwater, ideal for paddy | Wrong
Salt-sensitive roots make freshwater aquaculture zones | Wrong: they are salt-tolerant
Tall dense canopies serve as cyclone shelter | Wrong: mostly shrubs/small trees
Wide no-go zone between people and sea | Wrong
⚠ Aquaculture (shrimp ponds) is the biggest threat to mangroves, not a service
PYQ 2026: rationale for mangroves in climate resilience; only "bio-shield + livelihood" was right

t: Mangroves → definition and assertion-reason logic
text:
Halophytic (salt-tolerant) evergreen shrubs or small trees; littoral forest below the high-water mark of spring tides
Best on sheltered, low-energy coasts: estuaries, mudflats, creeks, backwaters, lagoons; brackish water, regular tidal flushing, silt
Assertion-reason (1996) | Verdict
A: specialised forests of tropical/subtropical coasts | True
R: stabilise shoreline, bulwark against sea | True
Does R explain A? | No: R is a service, not the reason they are specialised
They are specialised because of adaptations to salinity, anoxic mud and tides
⚠ India's coast is mostly high-energy: so mangroves are patchy, confined to deltas, estuaries, lagoons, creeks
PYQ 1996: both true, R not the explanation

t: Mangrove adaptations → organ and job
text:
Adaptation | What it does | Example
Pneumatophores | Upright "breathing roots" from buried laterals | Avicennia
Prop roots | Arise from horizontal branches | Rhizophora
Stilt roots | Arise from basal stem nodes | Rhizophora
Buttresses | Wide support for shallow roots | 
Vivipary | Seed germinates on the parent tree | Most mangroves
Salt exclusion | Blocks salt at root level | 
Salt glands | Leaves excrete salt | 
Sacrificial leaves | Salt stored in leaves that drop off | 
Succulence, sunken stomata | Save water | 
## 1. Why not beyond the subtropics
Salt filtration is energy-intensive and needs high solar radiation: so mangroves stay between about 24°N and 38°S
⚠ Vivipary = germination while attached; it beats the problem of germinating in saline water

t: Mangrove services → blue carbon and productivity
text:
Service | Detail
Coastal defence | Tsunami, surge, cyclone, erosion
Nursery | Breeding and rearing of fish, crabs, prawns
Filter | Trap sediment and heavy metals; recycle nutrients
Livelihood | Honey, tannin, wax, firewood, fodder, fish

t: Peatlands → what they are and why they matter
text:
Terrestrial wetlands where waterlogging stops plant matter from fully decomposing → peat accumulates
Among the biggest carbon stores on Earth; carbon also locked in "peaty layers of marshy soil" (carbon cycle)

Acidic peatland | Bog (peat moss, rain-fed)
Alkaline peatland | Fen (groundwater-fed)

Coal series | Peat → lignite → bituminous → anthracite

CARE (Feb 2026): mangroves and peatlands are powerful carbon sinks supporting India's NDCs
⚠ Peat is the first stage of coal formation, lowest in carbon

text:
Item | Fact
Adopted | 2 February 1971, Ramsar, Iran (Caspian shore)
In force | 1975
World Wetlands Day | 2 February

Parties | 172

topic: Ramsar Convention, Montreux Record and partners
t: Ramsar obligations → what is binding, what is not
text:
Obligation | Status
Designate at least one wetland on accession (Art 2) | Required
Maintain ecological character of listed sites | Expected, not enforced by sanctions
Promote wise use of all wetlands in territory | Commitment ("shall formulate planning")
Set up nature reserves on wetlands (listed or not), train staff | Commitment
National report every 3 years (at COP) | Required
Protect and conserve every wetland in India | Not mandatory
Penalties for default | None: non-regulatory, non-punitive
Deletion: a Party may delete or shrink a site for urgent national interest but must compensate elsewhere; no site has ever been deleted this way
Transboundary Ramsar Sites: managed jointly across borders
⚠ Binding in international law as a treaty, yet no punitive sanctions
PYQ 2019: "mandatory to protect all wetlands" was false

topic: Ramsar Convention, Montreux Record and partners
t: Wise use → Ramsar's central idea
text:
Wise use = maintaining ecological character within sustainable development
In practice: conserve through an ecosystem approach and allow simultaneous sustainable use
Option (2010) | Verdict
Keep all sites inaccessible to people | Wrong: no "hands-off" rule
Ecosystem approach, only tourism and recreation | Wrong: too narrow
Conserve for a period with no use, then allow use | Wrong: use is simultaneous
Ecosystem approach + simultaneous sustainable use | Correct
## 1. Three pillars of the Convention
Wise use of all wetlands
Designation and conservation of Ramsar Sites
International cooperation on shared wetlands, species, water
The 2017 Wetland Rules also adopt wise use; the State Wetland Authority decides what is wise use for each wetland
PYQ 2010: "simultaneous sustainable use" is the key word

topic: Ramsar Convention, Montreux Record and partners
t: Montreux Record → meaning and Indian sites
text:
Register of Ramsar sites where ecological character has changed, is changing or is likely to change due to human interference (pollution, development, technology)
Adopted 1990 at Montreux, Switzerland; triggers technical help and priority attention
Ramsar Advisory Missions: expert teams sent on request
Indian site | On record | Reason
Keoladeo NP (Rajasthan) | 1990 to date | Water shortage, unbalanced grazing; invasive Paspalum distichum
Loktak Lake (Manipur) | 1993 to date | Catchment deforestation, water hyacinth, pollution
Chilika (Odisha) | 1993-2002 | Siltation; removed after restoration
## 1. Reading the 2014 options
Option (2014) | Verdict
Ecological change due to human interference | Correct
Law banning activity within 5 km | Wrong
Survival depends on community culture | Wrong
Gets World Heritage status | Wrong
⚠ Keoladeo is both Montreux-listed and a UNESCO World Heritage Site: the two lists are different
PYQ 2014: Montreux Record = threatened Ramsar sites

topic: Ramsar Convention, Montreux Record and partners
t: Ramsar site criteria → what qualifies a wetland
text:
Nine criteria in all (LENS Oct 2026); PMF's grouping:
Criterion | Test
Uniqueness | Rare or unique natural wetland type
Species at risk | Supports VU, EN or CR species
Biodiversity | Populations important for regional diversity
Waterbirds | Regularly 20,000 or more waterbirds, or 1% of a population of one species
Fish | Food source, spawning ground or migration path for fish
## 1. Benefits of designation
Easier grants: World Bank, GEF, donors; latest scientific guidance; eco-tourism and local pride
## 2. Partner conventions and bodies
CBD (joint work plan 2024-30), CMS, CITES, UNCCD, World Heritage Convention; UNEP/UNDP implement GEF projects
⚠ Waterbird threshold is 20,000, not 10,000; the 1% rule is for one species
