topic: Wetland laws and schemes of India
t: Wetland Rules 2010 vs 2017 → who regulates, what is covered
text:
Feature | Rules 2010 | Rules 2017
Parent law | EPA 1986 | EPA 1986
Apex body | Central Wetland Regulatory Authority (Secretary, MoEF) | CWRA abolished; National Wetland Committee (advisory)
State role | No mandatory state authority | State Wetland Authority in every State/UT, headed by state Environment Minister
Catchment | Covered: drainage/catchment as determined by authority | Focus on notified wetland; wise use set by SWA
Coverage gaps | Small jheels, tanks left out | Excludes river channels, paddy, human-made water bodies
Origin | Framed voluntarily by India | Replaced 2010 rules
EPA backing: violations punishable up to 5 years jail plus fines
⚠ 2010 Rules were not framed on Ramsar's recommendation, but they did include the catchment
PYQ 2019: answer "3 only" (catchment covered); statements 1 and 2 false

topic: Wetland laws and schemes of India
t: Wetland Rules 2017 → coverage, exclusions, prohibitions
text:
## 1. Applies to
Ramsar sites + wetlands notified by Centre or State/UT
## 2. Excluded
River channels, paddy fields, water bodies built for drinking water, aquaculture, salt production, recreation, irrigation
Areas under Indian Forest Act 1927, FCA 1980, WPA 1972, CRZ 2019 cannot be notified under these Rules
## 3. Prohibited in notified wetlands
Prohibited | Allowed exception
Conversion to non-wetland use | 
New industry or expansion | 
Hazardous substances, C&D waste | 
Solid waste dumping; untreated effluents | 
Encroachment, poaching, permanent construction | Boat jetties
## 4. SWA deadlines
List all wetlands: 3 months; list to be notified: 6 months; digital inventory: 1 year, updated every 10 years
⚠ ESZ around a protected wetland is generally up to 10 km
## In news 2025-26
Supreme Court (2026) agreed to examine whether the 2017 Rules weaken protection: the petition says excluding human-made wetlands violates Ramsar, and that removing CWRA diluted limits on reclamation and construction
SC late 2024: states to finish ground-truthing (boundary demarcation) of wetlands; 2026: 10-km no-mining zone around Wetland Conservation Reserves (Praveen CA)

topic: Coral reefs: biology and growth conditions
t: Coral polyps → what builds a reef
text:
## 1. Builders
Reefs = calcareous (CaCO₃) skeletons of tiny marine animals, coral polyps
Polyps belong to phylum Cnidaria, with sea anemones and jellyfish
Polyps extract calcium salts from seawater; calcareous algae also deposit CaCO₃
Dead polyps leave skeletons; new polyps grow on them: layers build up over millions of years
Organism | Group
Coral polyps, sea anemones, jellyfish | Cnidaria (animals)
Zooxanthellae | Dinoflagellata (single-celled photosynthetic algae; e.g. *Symbiodinium*)
Scleractinian corals | Stony / hard, reef-building corals
Giant clams | Bivalve molluscs that also host zooxanthellae
⚠ Corals are animals, not plants; the photosynthesis is done by the algae inside them
Adjacent PYQ 2021: cnidarians can form symbiotic relationships (corals + zooxanthellae, anemone + clownfish)

topic: Coral reefs: biology and growth conditions
t: Corals and zooxanthellae → the symbiosis
text:
## 1. Two ways corals feed
By night: capture plankton with tentacles (stinging cells, nematocysts)
By day: sugars from photosynthesis of zooxanthellae living in polyp tissue
Coral gives algae | Algae give coral
Protected home | Fixed carbon (energy), up to most of its food
Steady CO₂ and nutrients from digestion | Enhanced calcification
Well-lit platform | Colour (coral tissue is itself clear)
Type: mutualism (both benefit); lets slow-growing corals compete with faster algae
Very high productivity and diversity: "Tropical Rainforests of the Oceans"
⚠ Colour of coral comes from the algae's pigments, not from the coral tissue
## Beyond your notes
Deep, cold-water corals (e.g. *Lophelia*) live without zooxanthellae and without sunlight: the light rules below apply to warm-water reef-building corals

topic: Coral reefs: biology and growth conditions
t: Ideal conditions → where corals grow and where they do not
text:
## 1. Six conditions (PMF)
Condition | Requirement
Temperature | Warm tropical water, about 20°C, narrow daily and annual range
Latitude | 30°N to 30°S
Depth | Shallow: ideal 45-55 m; needs sunlight
Water | Clear salt water; fresh water and very saline water harmful
Food | Abundant plankton and oxygen: so reefs grow faster on the seaward side
Pollution | Little or none; very sensitive
⚠ No reefs on west coasts of tropical continents: cold ocean currents
⚠ No reefs near river mouths: fresh water and sediment (e.g. few reefs along India's mainland coasts)
Likely next: "corals grow faster on the landward side of the reef": false (plankton richer seaward)

t: Reef types → fringing, barrier, atoll
text:
## 1. Three relief forms
Type | Key features | Examples
Fringing (shore) reef | Grows directly from shore, narrow (1-2 km); shallow lagoon; most common type | South Florida, New Hebrides; Gulf of Mannar, Gulf of Kutch, A&N
Barrier reef | Parallel to shore, separated by a wide, deep lagoon; largest in size, least common | Great Barrier Reef (2,300 km)
Atoll | Ring/horseshoe reef round a central lagoon (80-150 m deep), far from land, on submerged island or volcanic cone | Lakshadweep, Maldives (Addu), Chagos, Fiji, Marshall Islands
Atolls are most common in the Pacific
Atoll forms: true atoll (no island), atoll with island, coral island (atoll island)
⚠ Barrier reefs are largest in size, not in distribution; fringing reefs are the most common

t: Darwin's subsidence theory → how an atoll forms
text:
## 1. Three stages (Charles Darwin)
Step | What happens | Result
1 | Reef grows in shallow water close to a tropical island | Fringing reef
2 | Island subsides, reef grows upward and outward, lagoon widens | Barrier reef
3 | Island fully submerged, ring of reef remains | Atoll
Lakshadweep: atolls on the Reunion hotspot volcanic chain; no recent volcanism; flat, highly vulnerable to sea-level rise
## 2. Microatolls
Flat, disc-shaped corals whose upward growth stops at lowest-tide level, then grow sideways
Used as a natural tide gauge: Maldives microatolls show central Indian Ocean rose ~0.3 m (1930-2019)
⚠ Lakshadweep = coral (atoll) islands; Andaman and Nicobar = tectonic islands (continuation of Arakan Yoma) fringed by reefs

t: Coral bleaching → what it is and what it is not
text:
## 1. Mechanism
Stressed corals expel zooxanthellae (or algal pigment falls): tissue turns transparent, white CaCO₃ skeleton shows
Corals commonly lose 60-90% of their zooxanthellae
Bleached ≠ dead: weakened, at risk of starvation, disease and death
Mild, short stress: algae regained in weeks to months; prolonged stress: coral dies
Recovery from large-scale bleaching can take >15 years
Statement | True / False
Bleached corals are dead | False
Bleaching can occur in cold snaps too | True (sudden drops, upwelling, cold-air outbreaks)
Eutrophication directly expels zooxanthellae | False (it can even raise their density; harms indirectly)
Repeated mild stress may build resistance | True (research cited by PMF)
⚠ White skeleton from coral disease (tissue sloughing) is not bleaching

t: Causes of bleaching → the full list
text:
## 1. Triggers (PMF)
Cause | Detail
High temperature | ~1°C above normal maximum for weeks, or 3-4°C jump over days
Marine heatwaves | Now the strongest global driver
UV / solar radiation | Low wind, clear skies, calm seas, low turbidity
Low temperature | Upwelling, cold-air outbreaks
Subaerial exposure | Extreme low tides, ENSO sea-level drop, tectonic uplift
Xenobiotics | Copper, herbicides, oil
Sediment, freshwater, salinity change | River plumes cut sunlight
Crown-of-thorns starfish, epizootics | Predation, disease
Degree Heating Week (DHW): heat stress accumulated over 12 weeks; >4°C-weeks = significant bleaching
## 2. Ocean acidification
Ocean absorbs ~25-30% of human CO₂ → carbonic acid → fewer carbonate ions → harder to build CaCO₃
Surface pH ~8.1 now vs ~8.2 pre-industrial: "less alkaline", not acidic
⚠ Acidification reduces calcification; it does not directly cause bleaching (it lowers resilience)
Adjacent PYQ 2012: acidification harms calcareous phytoplankton, coral reefs, animals with planktonic larvae, and cloud formation (less DMS): all four
Adjacent PYQ 2014: above 3°C warming → widespread coral mortality

t: Global bleaching events → years and scale
text:
## 1. Four global events
Event | Years | Scale
1st | 1998 | 
2nd | 2010 | 
3rd | 2014-2017 | 68.2% of reef area under bleaching-level heat stress (PMF)
4th | 2023-2025 (ongoing per NOAA) | ~84% of reefs; at least 83 countries/territories
Confirmed by NOAA with the International Coral Reef Initiative (ICRI)
⚠ GCRMN dates the events 1998-99, 2010-11, 2016-17, 2023-25; PMF book uses 1998, 2010, 2014-17
⚠ An earlier PMF CA figure (2024) said 77% of reefs, beating the 2014-17 record of 66%: the 84% figure is the later count
## In news 2025-26
7th Status of Coral Reefs of the World (GCRMN, est. 1995, under ICRI): hard coral cover down 9.5% vs 1980-2009; 87% of reefs under heat stress in 2024; disturbances now every 4-6 years (earlier once a decade)
IUCN Red List of Ecosystems (2026): ~96% of shallow-water reef ecosystems face severe collapse risk by 2075; most rated Critically Endangered
Global Tipping Points Report 2025: warm-water reefs near irreversible decline at ~1.4°C

text:
## 1. Facts
Item | Fact

t: India's reefs in news → bleaching, discovery, restoration
text:
## 1. Indian bleaching record
Gulf of Mannar: 85% of corals bleached after the 2020 marine heatwave
Lakshadweep Sea: 1°C above normal since Oct 2023, DHW crossed 4°C-weeks (ICAR-CMFRI)
Western Indian Ocean: largest rise in marine heatwaves (~1.5 events/decade); north Bay of Bengal ~0.5
## 2. Restoration tools
Tool | Fact
Biorock | Low current through steel frame: CaCO₃ deposits at cathode; ZSI tried it in Gulf of Kachchh
Coral translocation | Moving live colonies; done earlier in Gulf of Kachchh and Lakshadweep
Coral gardening, artificial reefs | Way-forward measures
## In news 2025-26
Feb 2026: healthy continuous reef found near Kalpeni Island, Lakshadweep, despite 4th global event (thermal buffering, water flushing, heat-tolerant species)
Jun 2026: ZSI identified 4 sites on west coast of Great Nicobar to translocate corals and giant clams (both Schedule I) for the Great Nicobar project
2026: new reef crab *Galathea balasubramaniani* (~3 mm squat lobster) found near Agatti, Lakshadweep

t: Seagrass → biology, India, value
text:
## 1. What seagrass is
Flowering plants (angiosperms) of shallow marine and brackish water; roots, rhizomes, leaves
Depth limited by light (turbidity); tropics to temperate (even sub-Arctic)
India: abundant in Palk Strait/Palk Bay and Gulf of Mannar; also A&N, Lakshadweep, Gulf of Kutch
Value | Fact
Blue carbon | ~3x carbon per area of tropical rainforest; >10% of ocean carbon burial on 0.2% of area
Ecosystem engineer | Food for dugong, nursery for fish
Coastal protection | Stabilise sediment, damp waves
Water quality | Trap sediment, absorb N and P
Decline 1-2% a year: eutrophication (epiphytic algae raise turbidity), dredging, overfishing, storms
⚠ Seagrass is not seaweed and not algae: it is a vascular flowering plant

t: Open ocean → zones and productivity
text:
## 1. Light zones and life forms
Term | Meaning
Photic zone | Surface down to 1% of surface light: all photosynthesis here
Aphotic zone | Below photic zone: no photosynthesis
Plankton | Drifters (phyto = producers, zoo = consumers)
Nekton | Strong swimmers (fish, squid, whales)
Benthos | Bottom dwellers
Neuston | Air-water interface
## 2. Productivity
Open ocean has low productivity per area: sunlight (surface) and nutrients (deep) are separated; high only at upwelling zones
Order: estuaries > wetlands/mangroves > coral reefs > tropical rainforests > ... > tundra > open ocean > deserts
Marine phytoplankton produce about half of world's oxygen
⚠ Coral reefs are highly productive despite nutrient-poor water: tight recycling + symbiosis

t: Levels of biodiversity → what each means
text:
## 1. Three levels
Level | Meaning | Example
Genetic diversity | Variation within a species | Humans: Chinese, Indian, African populations
Species diversity | Variety of species in a community; combines richness + evenness | Tropical rainforest, coral reef
Ecological (ecosystem) diversity | Variety of habitats/ecosystems | India (deserts, rainforests, mangroves, reefs, alpine meadows) > Norway
Genetic diversity lets a species adapt to change and carry desirable genes
Species diversity generally falls from the equator to the poles (few exceptions)
WHO: biodiversity spans genes to cultural diversity; measured by species richness and species evenness
⚠ India has greater ecosystem diversity than a Scandinavian country: the comparison is about habitats, not species count

t: Richness, evenness and alpha-beta-gamma → meaning
text:
## 1. Two measures
Measure | Meaning
Species richness | Number of species in a community (highest: tropical rainforests on land, coral reefs in sea)
Species evenness | Relative abundance of each species; low evenness = a few species dominate
PMF example: forest A (2 tigers, 6 deer, 7 rabbits) and forest B (1, 6, 8) have the same richness (3) and same count (15); A is more even
## 2. Scale of diversity
Type | Scale
Alpha (α) | Within one habitat/community (usually species richness)
Beta (β) | Between habitats/ecosystems: rate of species change across them
Gamma (γ) | Overall diversity of a whole region/landscape
⚠ Beta compares two ecosystems; gamma is the regional total. They are not the same thing
## Beyond your notes
Terms come from R.H. Whittaker

t: Endemism, bioprospecting, biopiracy → meaning
text:
## 1. Terms
Term | Meaning
Endemism | Species found only in a defined area (island, country, habitat)
Cosmopolitan distribution | Opposite of endemism: found widely
Bioprospecting | Exploring biodiversity for commercially valuable genes and biochemicals
Biopiracy | Taking genetic resources or traditional knowledge without prior informed consent or benefit-sharing
A native species is not endemic if it also occurs elsewhere
Nagoya Protocol (CBD) deals with access on Prior Informed Consent (PIC) and Mutually Agreed Terms (MAT) and fair benefit-sharing
⚠ Indigenous ≠ endemic: indigenous only means native

topic: Value of biodiversity and keystone species
t: Keystone species → meaning and examples
text:
## 1. Definition (2000)
Keystone species determine the ability of many other species to persist in a community
Adding or removing one changes the occurrence of at least one other species; losing it degrades the ecosystem
Examples (PMF) | Why
Top predators: tiger, lion, crocodile | Regulate prey populations
Elephants, corals | Shape habitat
Pollinators, e.g. bats | Ebony and Indian laurel depend on bats
Snow leopard | Apex predator; ecosystem engineer
Indian wolf | Keystone in Panna-Satpura corridor forest
## 2. The distractors
Term | Meaning
Allopatric species | Occupy different geographic areas
Sympatric species | Occupy the same area
Threatened species | IUCN CR, EN or VU
PYQ 2000: answer keystone species; allopatric/sympatric describe ranges, not roles
## Beyond your notes
Flagship = charismatic species for public support (tiger); umbrella = protecting it protects many (tiger); indicator = signals ecosystem health (lichens, butterflies)

topic: Value of biodiversity and keystone species
t: Loss of a species → cascading consequences
text:
## 1. Butterflies fall (2017)
Consequence | Likely?
Pollination of some plants affected | Yes
Fall in wasps, spiders, birds that eat butterflies/larvae | Yes
Sharp rise in fungal infections of crops | No: butterflies do not control fungi
PYQ 2017: answer 1 and 3 only
## 2. Co-extinction
When a species dies out, species tied to it obligately also die out
Host fish lost → its unique parasites lost; coevolved plant-pollinator mutualism: one goes, the other goes
Invasive species that displace a keystone species set off cascades
⚠ The 2017 trap was a plausible-sounding disease link with no ecological basis

## 1. Tested pair (2011): both correct
Gradient | Rule
Latitude | Diversity greater at lower latitudes (tropics) than higher latitudes
Altitude | Diversity greater at lower altitudes than higher ones along mountain slopes
Altitude mimics latitude: temperature and oxygen fall, conditions harsher

Why tropics are richer (NCERT hypotheses) |

t: Species-area relationship → meaning
text:
## Beyond your notes
Within a region, species richness rises with explored area, but only up to a limit
Described by Alexander von Humboldt
Item | Value
Equation | log S = log C + Z log A
Z (small areas) | 0.1 to 0.2 regardless of taxon or region
Z (whole continents) | 0.6 to 1.2 (steeper)
This explains why habitat loss cuts species numbers and why large reserves hold more species
⚠ Z is steeper for whole continents than for small areas within a region
Rivet popper hypothesis (Paul Ehrlich): each lost species is a rivet popped from a plane; losing key "rivets" (keystone species) is most dangerous
David Tilman: plots with more species are more stable and productive

t: In-situ vs ex-situ → which site is which
text:
In-situ (on-site, whole ecosystem) | Ex-situ (off-site, special care)
Biosphere reserves | Botanical gardens
National parks | Zoological parks, wildlife safari parks
Wildlife sanctuaries | Seed banks, gene banks
Conservation and community reserves | Cryopreservation of gametes, tissues
Reserved and protected forests | Tissue culture, in-vitro fertilisation
Sacred groves, tiger reserves | Captive breeding centres
In-situ protects all three levels (genetic, species, ecosystem): "protect the forest to protect the tiger"
Ex-situ is preferred when a species needs urgent rescue from extinction
⚠ A botanical garden is ex-situ even though plants grow in soil: they are taken out of their natural habitat
PYQ 2011: "not an in-situ site" → botanical garden; trap: biosphere reserve sounds like a "collection" but is in-situ

t: In-situ categories → law and level of protection
text:
Category | Declared by / law
Reserved / protected forest | State, Indian Forest Act 1927
Wildlife sanctuary, national park | Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972
Conservation reserve | State, on government land next to PAs (2002 amendment)
Community reserve | State, on private/community land volunteered
Biosphere reserve | Nominated by India, designated under UNESCO MAB; no change in legal status
Eco-sensitive zone | MoEF under Environment (Protection) Act 1986
Protection order: National Park > Sanctuary > Reserved forest > Protected forest
"Protected Area" under WPA = NP, sanctuary, conservation reserve, community reserve (4 only)
Biosphere zones: core (no human activity), buffer (research, limited use), transition (settlements)

t: REDD+ → what each letter and the "plus" mean
text:
## 1. Expansion
Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and forest Degradation +
A voluntary climate-change mitigation approach developed by Parties to the UNFCCC
Aims to incentivise developing countries (results-based payments) to keep forests standing
## 2. The five REDD+ activities
Activity | Part of
Reducing emissions from deforestation | RED (original)
Reducing emissions from forest degradation | REDD
Conservation of forest carbon stocks | +
Sustainable management of forests | +
Enhancement of forest carbon stocks | +
⚠ The "plus" = conservation, sustainable management and enhancement; REDD+ is for developing countries, not developed ones
⚠ REDD+ is a framework under UNFCCC; UN-REDD is a UN programme that helps countries implement it

t: REDD+ → origin and milestones in the UNFCCC
text:
## 1. Timeline
Year | COP | REDD+ step
2005 | COP11 Montreal | "RED" proposed by Papua New Guinea and Costa Rica
2007 | COP13 Bali | Bali Action Plan: REDD and the "plus" enter talks
2008 | - | UN-REDD created; World Bank FCPF operational
2010 | COP16 Cancun | Five activities and safeguards agreed
2013 | COP19 Warsaw | Warsaw Framework for REDD+ (rulebook for results-based finance)
2015 | COP21 Paris | Article 5 of the Paris Agreement encourages REDD+
## Beyond your notes
Montreal 2005, Cancun 2010, Warsaw Framework 2013 and Paris Article 5 are from standard UNFCCC records; the Bali link and 2008 dates are in PMF
India released its National REDD+ Strategy in 2018 (MoEFCC)

HQ | Geneva, Switzerland

## 1. FLR
Term coined in 2000 by IUCN and WWF; applied across landscapes, not single sites
Global attention since 2011 (Bonn Challenge)
## 2. Seven FLR principles
No. | Principle
1 | Maintain natural ecosystems
2 | Focus on landscapes, not sites
3 | Conserve, recover, sustainably manage forests

Global Partnership on Forest and Landscape Restoration: network initiated by IUCN; responds directly to the Bonn Challenge

text:
## 1. What it is
Developed by Japanese botanist Akira Miyawaki in the 1970s to restore degraded land
Ultra-dense, rapid afforestation creating self-sustaining native mini/micro-forests; widely used in urban areas
Also called the "Pot Plantation Method"
## 2. Four core principles (PMF 2026)
Principle | Detail
Native species only | Species that would naturally grow there
High density | 3-5 saplings per sq m
Multi-layered canopy | Shrub, sub-tree, tree, canopy layers
Random arrangement | No rows
⚠ PMF March 2025 gives 2-4 types per sq m; PMF Aug 2026 gives 3-5 saplings per sq m
⚠ Not GM gardens, not arid commercial farming, not coastal wind farming

Grows up to 10x faster | High initial cost (soil enhancement)
30x denser; more oxygen, less dust | Manpower intensive early on

Cuts urban heat island, noise, dust | Needs green city planning alongside

t: Ape or monkey → the classification trap
text:
## 1. Apes vs monkeys
Feature | Apes | Monkeys
Tail | No tail | Tail present
Examples | Gibbon, gorilla, orangutan, chimpanzee, bonobo | Langur, macaque, spider monkey
In India | Only hoolock gibbon | Many (langurs, macaques)
## 2. Great apes vs lesser apes
Lesser apes = gibbons: smallest and fastest apes; ~20 species of apes on Earth
Great apes = orangutan, gorilla, chimpanzee, bonobo (none in India)
Old World monkeys: Africa, Asia (all Indian monkeys); New World monkeys: Central and South America (spider monkey)
⚠ Langur is a monkey, not an ape: it has a tail
⚠ "Slow loris" and "slender loris" are primates but neither monkeys nor apes (lorises, family Loridae)
PYQ 2008: "which is not an ape?" (gibbon, gorilla, langur, orangutan); trap: langur

t: Western hoolock gibbon → India's only ape
text:
## 1. Key facts
Attribute | Western hoolock | Eastern hoolock
IUCN | Endangered | Vulnerable
WPA | Schedule I | -
Range | NE India, Bangladesh, Myanmar west of Chindwin | Myanmar east of Chindwin
Separated by the Chindwin (Myanmar) and Lohit-Dibang rivers (India)
India's hoolock: south of the Brahmaputra in NE India
## 2. Biology
Diurnal, arboreal; moves by brachiation (swinging with long arms); no tail
Small, light-bodied; male and female same size, colour differs (male black, white brows; female grey-brown)
Monogamous pairs, defend territory with loud morning duets; eats fruits, insects, leaves; ~25 yr in wild
Habitats: Hollongapar Gibbon WLS (Jorhat, Assam), Namdapha, Nokrek BR, Dibru-Saikhowa
⚠ Gibbons are not gorilla-like: they are the lightest apes
PYQ 2026: sanctuary in NE + Endangered + brachiation correct; "heavy build like gorillas" wrong

t: Lion, cheetah, leopard → behaviour statements
text:
## 1. What UPSC tested
Statement | Verdict | Why
Lions have no particular breeding season | Correct | Breed year-round
Unlike other big cats, cheetahs do not roar | Correct | Growl, chirp, bark instead
Male leopards do not scent-mark | Wrong | Male leopards roar and scent-mark territory
## 2. Other behaviour facts
Leopard: solitary, arboreal, nocturnal; rosettes without central spot (jaguar has one)

Honeybees perform the waggle dance to tell nestmates the direction, distance and quality of food, water or nest sites

text:
## 1. The 2023 statements - all correct
Statement | Organism | Example
Grow above 100 °C | Hyperthermophiles (archaea) | Pyrolobus fumarii at 113 °C; hot springs, hydrothermal vents

Form | Survives | Example

Anoxybiosis | No oxygen | Nematodes

Microscopic (0.3-0.5 mm), eight legs; survive -272 °C to 150 °C, radiation, vacuum

## 1. Gases and solids from a coal plant (PMF)
Output | Pollutants
Gases | CO₂, SO₂, NOₓ, PM, CH₄, CO (incomplete combustion), VOCs
Solid | Fly ash (ESP ash, dry fly ash, pond ash, mound ash)
Toxic metals in ash | Mercury, cadmium, arsenic, lead, nickel, boron, zinc, copper
Water | Acid mine drainage, cooling-tower blowdown, ash-pond wastewater
Process: coal → heat → high-pressure steam → turbine → generator; efficiency only 20-45%

Coal also emits mercury: coal plants and gold mining are major mercury sources (2023 PYQ)

t: Fly ash → composition, uses and rules
text:
## 1. What it is made of
Part | Content
Main oxides | Aluminium silicate, SiO₂, CaO; also Fe, Mg oxides
Toxic elements | Lead, mercury, cadmium, chromium, arsenic, nickel, cobalt, selenium, boron, barium, copper
Size | Mixed; airborne part falls in PM₁₀ and PM₂.₅
## 2. Uses
Cement replacement up to 35% (Portland cement in concrete)
Fly ash bricks: lightweight, durable (Preview: stronger than clay bricks)
Road embankments, concrete roads, mine filling, wasteland reclamation, soil conditioner (water-holding capacity)
## 3. MoEF rule
Fly ash products mandatory in construction, road embankments and low-lying landfill within 100 km of a thermal plant; mine filling within 50 km
⚠ Statement "fly ash is SiO₂ and CaO only, no toxic elements" is false
PYQ 2015: bricks and cement replacement correct (1 and 2)

## 1. Assertion-Reason logic
Gas from coal | Causes acid rain?
SO₂ / SO₃ | Yes → sulphuric acid
NOₓ (NO₂, N₂O₃, N₂O₅) | Yes → nitric / nitrous acid
CO₂ | Makes normal rain mildly acidic (pH ~5.6) only
CO | No
Coal plants do cause acid rain (A true) and do emit carbon oxides (R true), but R does not explain A
⚠ Answer pattern: "Both true, R is not the correct explanation"

## 1. Process and emissions
Limestone (75%) + clay (25%) → kiln at ~1,400 °C (coal fired) → clinker → ground with 3-5% gypsum → Portland cement
Emission route | Detail
Calcination | Carbon in limestone released as CO₂: 1 t cement → at least 0.5 t CO₂
Fuel | Coal in kilns: same pollutants as a thermal plant
Cut CO₂ by | Replacing part of limestone/clinker with fly ash or blast-furnace slag

Feature | Black carbon (soot) | Brown carbon
Source | Incomplete burning of fossil fuel, diesel, biomass | Biomass, impure organic burning

text:
## 1. Quick facts
Gas | Property UPSC asks
CO | Colourless, odourless; binds haemoglobin 200-300x more than O₂ → carboxyhaemoglobin; toxic above 35 ppm; not a direct GHG
CO₂ | Asphyxiant (7% suffocates); GHG; ocean acidification

text:
## 1. Tropospheric ozone
Not emitted directly: forms when NOₓ + VOCs (and CO) react in sunlight; some comes down from the stratosphere
Feature | Fact
Peak time | Hot, sunny days; afternoon
Season | Summer (Delhi summer ozone as serious as winter smog)
Health | Triggers asthma, eye irritation, lower lung function
Plants | Reduces photosynthesis and crop yield
Climate | Short-lived GHG
Biogenic VOCs from plants rise in heat and add to ozone
⚠ Ozone peaks in sunny weather, not "inclement weather" (2022 statement 2 false)
## In news 2025-26
Study (2004-2024 data): heatwaves worsen ozone; levels stay high 3-4 days after; ~800 deaths from ozone in 2024 heatwaves; hotspots NW India, IGP, western Himalayas
CAQM reimposed GRAP Stage-I in May 2026 (summer dust and ozone)

Item | Detail
Inputs | NOₓ + VOCs + sunlight (vehicle-heavy cities)
Products (photo-oxidants) | Ozone, PAN (peroxyacetyl nitrate), H₂O₂, aldehydes

## 1. London / classical smog
Feature | Sulphurous smog | Photochemical smog
Cause | Coal (SO₂ + smoke) + fog | NOₓ + VOCs + sunlight
Weather | Cold, humid, inversion | Warm, sunny
Colour | Grey/black | Brownish

Made of | Water droplets / ice | Dry SPM (dust, smoke, salt) | SPM + toxic gases + secondary pollutants

## 1. Cause list
Gas | Cause of acid rain?
Sulphur dioxide | Yes (H₂SO₄)
Nitrogen oxides | Yes (HNO₃)
Carbon monoxide | No
Ozone | No (only helps oxidise SO₂/NOₓ)

Acid rain = precipitation with pH < 5.6; wet (rain, snow, fog) or dry deposition
Sources: coal power plants, industries, vehicles; also volcanoes (HCl, HF)

t: Acid rain → chemistry, effects and control
text:
## 1. Chemistry
2SO₂ + O₂ → 2SO₃; SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄; acidic N₂O₃, NO₂, N₂O₅ → HNO₂, HNO₃
Sunlight makes photo-oxidants (ozone) that speed the oxidation; nitrate in acid rain is a plant nutrient
pH is logarithmic: pH 4 is 10x more acidic than pH 5, 100x more than pH 6
## 2. Effects and control
Effect | Control
Lake and soil acidification | Liming (CaO / CaCO₃) of water
Marble cancer (Taj Mahal) | Low-sulphur fuel, coal washing
Forest and crop damage | FGD for SO₂; low-NOₓ burners, SCR, SNCR for NOₓ
Taj Trapezium Zone: ~10,400 sq km around the Taj, UP and Rajasthan, set up to protect the Taj from air pollution (2021 PYQ)
CLRTAP (1979) protocols: Helsinki 1985 (sulphur, -30%), Gothenburg 1999 (SO₂, NOₓ, NH₃, VOCs); India is not a party

topic: Ozone layer and the Antarctic ozone hole
t: Antarctic ozone hole → why it forms (polar vortex + PSCs + CFCs)
text:
## 1. The three ingredients
Ingredient | Role
Inflow of CFCs/halons (ODS) | Supply chlorine and bromine to the stratosphere
Polar vortex (kept in place by a prominent polar front) | Lifts long-lived ODS into the lower stratosphere; isolates and chills polar air
Polar stratospheric clouds (PSCs) | Surfaces that turn inactive chlorine into reactive chlorine
Spring sunlight (Sept-Oct) | Splits reactive chlorine into Cl radicals → rapid ozone loss
## 2. Why the wrong options fail (PYQ 2011)
Tropospheric turbulence does not reach the stratosphere
Absence of polar front → vortex slips into temperate zone and weakens (no hole)
Methane is not an ODS: no halogen; it only forms reservoir compounds with halogens
Global warming heating the poles has no direct role in polar ozone loss
Only two weather phenomena reach the lower stratosphere: polar vortex and towering cumulus (cumulus do not occur at the poles)
⚠ The answer needs presence of polar front and stratospheric clouds plus CFC inflow
PYQ 2011: asked the reason for the Antarctic ozone hole; trap: "tropospheric turbulence" and "methane" sound plausible but neither reaches/destroys stratospheric ozone

topic: Ozone layer and the Antarctic ozone hole
t: Polar stratospheric clouds → composition, height, chemistry
text:
## 1. Facts
Feature | PSCs
Other name | Nacreous (iridescent) clouds, rare
Height | 12-22 km (PMF Environment); 15-25 km (PMF Physical Geography)
Contain | Water, nitric acid, sulphuric acid
When | Polar winter, inside the vortex; more intense at the South Pole
Seen | High latitudes, up to 2 hours after sunset / before dawn
## 2. What they do
Convert reservoir halogens (HCl, ClONO₂) into reactive forms (Cl₂, HOCl)
In spring sunlight these release Cl radicals and ClO → accelerated ozone loss
Nitric acid in PSCs reacts with CFC-derived chlorine (Preview)
⚠ The stratosphere is very dry and nearly cloudless; PSCs are the exception
⚠ Two PMF books give different heights (12-22 km vs 15-25 km): both mean the lower stratosphere

topic: Ozone layer and the Antarctic ozone hole
t: Antarctica vs Arctic, and other causes of polar ozone loss
text:
## 1. Why mostly the South Pole
 | Antarctic | Arctic
Vortex | Colder, more stable, longer-lived | Warmer, less stable
PSC formation | Extensive | Limited
Ozone loss | Large, regular ozone hole | Smaller, variable; big loss only in unusually cold years (2020)
## 2. Minor and contested factors
Mesosphere NOₓ descending in the polar winter vortex affects the upper stratosphere; not the primary cause of the hole
Nanoparticles bind the hydroxyl radical (•OH), the atmosphere's cleanser that removes ODS → indirectly aid depletion
Tropical ozone hole claim (year-round, larger than Antarctic): strongly contested; tropics naturally have less ozone
Ozone formation is very slow over the poles (Preview)
Ozone hole is not a true hole: a region of exceptionally depleted ozone; discovered by the British Antarctic Survey (Farman, Gardiner, Shanklin), published in Nature, May 1985
⚠ "Ozone hole is maximum over Antarctica", not Arctic, India or Europe

topic: Ozone layer and the Antarctic ozone hole
t: Halogens and the chlorine chain reaction
text:
## 1. Halogens (Group 17)
Halogen | Symbol | Ozone role
Fluorine | F | No ozone destruction (HFCs have zero ODP)
Chlorine | Cl | Main destroyer (CFCs, HCFCs, CCl₄, methyl chloroform)
Bromine | Br | Destroyer (halons, methyl bromide)
Iodine, Astatine, Tennessine | I, At, Ts | Not regulated ODS
Highly reactive: seven valence electrons
## 2. Mechanism
CFCs/halons photodissociate under UV in the stratosphere → release Cl/Br radicals
Each radical starts a catalytic chain: one chlorine atom can break over 100,000 ozone molecules before removal
ODS take 2-5 years to reach the stratosphere (Preview)
## Beyond your notes
Cl + O₃ → ClO + O₂; ClO + O → Cl + O₂ (chlorine is regenerated, hence "catalytic")
⚠ A halogen-free gas (methane, CO₂, CO) cannot catalyse ozone destruction directly

topic: Ozone layer and the Antarctic ozone hole
t: Ozone layer → altitude, UV absorbed, measurement
text:
## 1. Numbers (sources differ)
Item | Value | Source
Stratospheric ozone | 15-35 km; layer of peak concentration 20-25 km | PMF Environment
Ozonosphere | 20-55 km, peak 20-30 km | PMF Physical Geography
Ozone layer | 10-40 km | LENS (World Ozone Day 2026)
Share of atmospheric ozone in stratosphere | ~90% (troposphere ~10%) | LENS, Rocket Sheets
Unit | Dobson Unit: 1 DU = 0.01 mm of pure ozone at 0°C, 1 atm | Rocket Sheets
## 2. UV filtering
Band | Wavelength | Ozone layer
UV-C | 100-280 nm | Absorbs nearly all
UV-B | 280-315 nm | Absorbs most
UV-A | 315-400 nm | Passes through
Chapman cycle: UV splits O₂ → O; O + O₂ → O₃; UV splits O₃ again (ozone-oxygen cycle); ozonosphere is also called chemosphere
Ozone absorption warms the stratosphere: temperature rises with height (inversion)
⚠ Good ozone = stratospheric; bad ozone = tropospheric (secondary pollutant, a GHG)
⚠ NCERT Physics puts the absorbing ozone at 40-50 km; follow PMF (15-35 km, peak 20-25 km)

topic: Ozone layer and the Antarctic ozone hole
t: Effects of ozone depletion and the size of the loss
text:
## 1. Effects of more UV-B (NCERT)
Affected | Effect
Humans | Skin cancer, eye damage (cataract)
Oceans | Lower phytoplankton production → hits aquatic food chain
Land | Affects growth of terrestrial plants
## 2. Scale
About 5% reduction in the ozone layer detected 1979-1990 (NCERT)
CAMS defines the ozone hole as total column ozone below 220 DU
## Beyond your notes
Normal global average column ozone is about 300 DU; the Antarctic hole peaks in September-October
Likely next: a "how many" on UV effects, or which UV band reaches the surface (UV-A)

topic: Ozone layer and the Antarctic ozone hole
t: Ozone hole and stratosphere → news 2025-26
text:
## In news 2025-26
Event | Date | What it says
Antarctic ozone hole expansion (CAMS) | Sept 2026 | Grew to ~25 million sq km, ~5 million above seasonal average; extreme cold → more PSCs; short-term vortex variability, not failure of ODS phase-out
Dense ozone pocket over North Bay of Bengal (PIB) | Aug 2026 | At 21-23 km, below the normal 25-30 km peak; strong horizontal currents and downward winds compressed air; no day-night variation
Sudden Stratospheric Warming warning | Dec 2025 | Up to 50°C rise in days; Rossby waves weaken the polar vortex, can reverse westerlies to easterlies
Antarctic sea-ice collapse cause | May 2026 | GHGs and the ozone hole strengthened westerlies, lifting warm Circumpolar Deep Water
Stratospheric Aerosol Injection study | June 2025 | SO₂ geoengineering may delay ozone recovery
CAMS = Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service, part of the EU Space Programme, run by ECMWF
Hunga Tonga eruption sent water vapour to the stratosphere: aids ozone-destroying reactions; linked to the very large 2023 ozone hole (P-MCA 2025)
⚠ A bigger hole in one year does not mean recovery has reversed

topic: Ozone-depleting substances, HFCs and their uses
t: CFCs → what they are used in (and not)
text:
## 1. Uses (PYQ 2012 list + likely-next)
Use | CFC used?
Blowing agent for plastic foams | Yes
Cleaning electronic components (solvent; trichlorofluoromethane dissolves grease) | Yes
Pressurising agent / propellant in aerosol cans | Yes
Refrigerant in refrigerators and ACs (Freon-11, CFC-12) | Yes
Dry-cleaning and industrial solvents | Yes
Tubeless tyres | No (carbon black + vulcanisation with sulphur)
## 2. Properties
Non-toxic, non-flammable, colourless, odourless, highly stable: last 80-100 years
Inert in the lower atmosphere; break down only under stratospheric UV
Also potent GHGs with very high GWP
⚠ Stability is why CFCs were useful and why they reach the stratosphere
PYQ 2012: CFC uses, answer 1, 3 and 4; trap: tubeless tyres (rubber industry uses carbon black, not CFCs)

topic: Ozone-depleting substances, HFCs and their uses
t: HFCs → uses, properties, why phased down
text:
## 1. Uses (PYQ 2023)
Use | HFC used?
Aerosol propellants | Yes
Foam-blowing agents | Yes
Fire retardants / suppression (clean agents) | Yes
Refrigerants in ACs, refrigerators, cooling | Yes (main use)
Lubricants | No: HFCs and ODS have no lubricating property
## 2. Properties
Entirely human-made; introduced to replace CFCs and HCFCs
Zero ODP: contain no chlorine or bromine
Very high GWP: hundreds to thousands of times CO₂; long-lived
Counted as a short-lived climate pollutant / super pollutant
⚠ HFCs are "ozone-friendly" but climate-unfriendly: controlled by the Kigali Amendment, not because they deplete ozone

text:
## 1. PMF table
ODS | Example | Typical use | ODP | GWP
CFCs | Freon-11 | Refrigerants, aerosols, foam, solvents | High | High
Halons | Halon-1211, 1301 | Fire extinguishers | High | High
HBFCs | HBFC-12B1 | Fire suppression | Medium | High
HCFCs | R-22 | Refrigerants, some foams | Medium | High
Carbon tetrachloride | CCl₄ | Solvent, cleaning | High | High
Methyl chloroform | CH₃CCl₃ | Metal/electronics cleaning | Medium | Medium
Methyl bromide | CH₃Br | Soil fumigation, pest control | High | Low
Chlorobromomethane | CH₂BrCl | Fire extinguishing (not an HBFC) | Medium | NA
Nitrous oxide | N₂O | Anaesthetic, rocket oxidiser | Low | High
ODP is relative to CFC; GWP relative to CO₂, usually over 100 years

text:
## 1. Comparison

Year | 1985 | 1987 (signed 16 Sept); in force 1 Jan 1989 | 2016 (15 Oct, Kigali, Rwanda); in force 1 Jan 2019
Nature | Framework: monitoring, reporting, research | Action treaty under Vienna: time-bound phase-out of ODS | Adds HFCs to controlled list: phase-down

Secretariat: Ozone Secretariat (UNEP), Nairobi

t: Montreal Protocol → provisions and controlled substances
text:
## 1. Key provisions
Controls production and consumption of listed ODS; nearly 100 man-made chemicals
Controlled: CFCs, halons, CCl₄, methyl chloroform, HCFCs, HBFCs, methyl bromide, bromochloromethane; HFCs since Kigali
Differentiated timelines: developing countries get longer periods
Multilateral Fund (MLF): set up by the London Amendment, 1990; funds developing-country compliance
Article 5 countries: per capita ODS consumption < 0.3 kg/year (India is one)
UNEP is an implementing agency of the MLF and GEF
## 2. Achievements
Phased out nearly 99% of controlled ODS
Climate co-benefit: many ODS are potent GHGs
## Beyond your notes
Other MLF implementing agencies: UNDP, UNIDO, World Bank
India joined the Montreal Protocol in 1992 (verify)
⚠ Montreal does not cover N₂O, methane or CO₂

topic: Measuring water pollution: DO, BOD, COD
t: BOD → what it measures and what a high value means
text:
## 1. Definition
BOD (Biological/Biochemical Oxygen Demand) = amount of dissolved oxygen needed by aerobic microorganisms to decompose biodegradable organic matter (sewage, food waste, decaying plants)
Unit mg/L; standard test = BOD₅ (5 days at 20°C)
High BOD = high organic pollution → microbes use up oxygen → low DO, fish kills, foul anaerobic conditions
BOD (mg/L) | Water quality
1-2 | Very good: little organic matter
3-5 | Fair: moderately clean
6-9 | Poor: somewhat polluted
10 and above | Very poor: very polluted
## 2. Limitation
Measures only biodegradable matter → "not a reliable method" alone (misses heavy metals, plastics, non-biodegradable organics)
⚠ BOD and DO move in opposite directions: more organic waste → higher BOD, lower DO
PYQ 2017: BOD is a standard criterion for pollution assay in aquatic ecosystems; traps: blood oxygen, forest ecosystems, high-altitude oxygen

topic: Measuring water pollution: DO, BOD, COD
t: DO → indicator of river health
text:
## 1. What DO is
Free oxygen dissolved in water (mg/L); needed by fish, aquatic insects, aerobic microbes → key indicator of self-purifying capacity
DO level | Meaning (PMF)
Below 8.0 mg/L | May be considered contaminated
Below 4.0 mg/L | Highly polluted
5 mg/L minimum | Bathing class (GAP)
## 2. What lowers DO
Microbes decomposing sewage, decaying plants, organic waste
Thermal pollution / hot weather: warm water holds less oxygen
Stagnant / slow flow: less mixing
Algal blooms: lower DO at night and during decomposition
DO also depends on surface turbulence and photosynthesis
## 3. Indicator species
Tubifex (annelid worm) and some insect larvae survive in low-DO polluted water → indicator species of contaminated water
PYQ 1998: river pollution is measured by the dissolved amount of oxygen; traps: chlorine, ozone, nitrogen

topic: Measuring water pollution: DO, BOD, COD
t: COD vs BOD → which is higher and why
text:
Feature | BOD | COD
Oxidised by | Microbes (biological) | Chemical oxidant
Substances counted | Biodegradable organics only | Biodegradable + non-biodegradable organics + oxidisable inorganics
Time | 5 days | Few hours (beyond your notes)
Value | Lower | Always higher than BOD
As pollution measure | Less reliable | "Slightly better" (PMF)
COD is expressed in ppm of oxygen (PMF)
⚠ COD is never lower than BOD: everything microbes can oxidise, chemicals can too, plus more
## Beyond your notes
BOD/COD ratio indicates biodegradability: a high ratio means waste is easily treated biologically
TDS, turbidity, pH, total and faecal coliform are other water-quality parameters; coliform = indicator of faecal contamination

topic: Measuring water pollution: DO, BOD, COD
t: CPCB designated best use → DO and BOD limits by class
text:
CPCB with SPCBs classifies water bodies A to E by pH, DO, BOD, total coliforms, free ammonia
Class | Best use | DO (min) | BOD (max)
A | Drinking source without conventional treatment, after disinfection | 6 mg/L | 2 mg/L
B | Outdoor bathing (organised) | 5 mg/L | 3 mg/L
C | Drinking source after conventional treatment | 4 mg/L | 3 mg/L
D | Wildlife and fisheries | 4 mg/L | free ammonia max 1.2 mg/L
E | Irrigation, industrial cooling, waste disposal | n.a. | limits on EC, SAR, boron
Total coliform (MPN/100 mL): A 50, B 500, C 5000
⚠ Class C (treated drinking) is looser than B (bathing) on coliform: B is 500, C is 5000
Basis of the Ganga Action Plan and the National River Action Plan

text:

CPCB assesses rivers biannually using BOD
BOD above 3 mg/L breaches the outdoor bathing standard
Polluted River Stretch (PRS) = two adjacent monitoring sites with BOD > 3 mg/L
Priority | BOD (mg/L)
Priority-1 (worst) | above 30
Priority-5 (least) | 3-6
Improvement = stretch moving from Priority 1 towards 5

text:
Substance | In Indian drinking water? | What it is
Arsenic | Yes: Ganga-Brahmaputra delta, WB, Assam | Geogenic + mining, fly ash
Fluoride | Yes: Rajasthan, Gujarat, arid states | Geogenic (fluorspar, cryolite, fluorapatite, granite)

Nitrate | Yes: exceeds limit in ~20% samples (CGWB 2024) | Fertilisers, septic tanks

Sorbitol | No | Sugar alcohol in fruits/berries; sweetener
Formaldehyde | No (as water pollutant) | VOC, indoor air pollutant, carcinogen

t: Arsenic and fluoride → source, disease, limit
text:
Feature | Arsenic | Fluoride
Nature | Tasteless, odourless carcinogen | Natural mineral; good in trace amounts
Hotspot | Ganges delta (India, Bangladesh), WB | Rajasthan, Gujarat; 230 districts
Disease | Black foot disease (peripheral vascular disease, gangrene), skin and lung cancer | Dental fluorosis (children below 8), skeletal fluorosis, knock-knee
Early signs | Melanosis (dark spots) → keratosis (palms) | White streaks → brown stains → pitting
BIS limit | 0.01 mg/L acceptable (beyond your notes); PMF gives 0.05 mg/L | 1.0 desirable, 1.5 permissible mg/L
Removal | Bleaching powder + alum | Nalgonda technique, activated alumina
WHO fluoride limit = 1.5 mg/L; up to 8.2 mg/L found in some groundwater
⚠ PMF gives arsenic removal "to BIS limit 0.05 mg/L"; current BIS IS 10500 acceptable limit is 0.01 mg/L (verify)

t: Uranium, radon and nitrate → limits and effects
text:
## 1. Uranium
Weakly radioactive; half-life ~4.5 billion years (U-238); biological half-life ~15 days
Limit: 0.03 mg/L (30 µg/L) in BIS IS 10500:2012 = WHO provisional value
Effect: kidney toxicity; CKD in Srikakulam (AP) linked; inquiry into UCIL, Kadapa
## 2. Radon
From radioactive granites; uranium → radium → radon; Bengaluru groundwater 50-100x limit
Radon → lung cancer; uranium → kidney cancer
## 3. Nitrate
Forms methaemoglobin (cannot bind oxygen) → methaemoglobinemia = blue baby syndrome
Only 33% of fertiliser nitrogen is used by plants
Contaminant | Health effect
Nitrate | Blue baby syndrome
Uranium | Kidney damage
Radon | Lung cancer
Radioactive iodine | Thyroid cancer
## In news 2025-26
CGWB 2024 report (Aug 2025 CA): nitrate, fluoride, arsenic, uranium widespread; 56% districts exceed nitrate limit (CARE)
Indore, Jan 2026: sewage leak into drinking lines → deaths, hundreds ill (PMF)

t: Heavy metals → disease they cause
text:
Heavy metal = density above 5 g/cm³ (Hg, Cd, Cu, Pb, As)
Metal | Disease / effect
Mercury | Minamata disease (via methylmercury): numb limbs, deafness, blurred vision
Cadmium | Itai-itai ("ouch-ouch"): painful bones and joints; lung, liver cancer

Arsenic | Black foot disease, skin cancer
Fluoride (not a metal) | Fluorosis, knock-knee
Nitrate | Blue baby syndrome

t: Sources → point vs non-point, thermal, mining
text:
Type | Examples
Point source | Drainpipe of industrial effluent, STP outfall
Non-point source | Agricultural runoff, grazing land, construction sites, abandoned mines
Geogenic | Rock-water leaching: fluoride, arsenic, iron, manganese, salinity
Thermal | Power plant cooling water raises temp 5-15 °C → lower DO
Radiation | e.g., Fukushima 2011
## Mining
Acid Rock Drainage: sulphides + water → sulphuric acid (natural)
Acid Mine Drainage: magnified ARD from excavation; Thiobacillus ferrooxidans (acidophilic, pH 1.5-2) speeds acidification
Mining chemicals: cyanide, sulphuric acid, mercury
## Other

Freshwater Salinisation Syndrome: road de-icing salt, oil and gas extraction, saltwater intrusion
Microplastics: found in Ganga, Delhi groundwater, salt and sugar (Toxics Link); details in plastics topic

t: Eutrophication → stages and lake types
text:
## 1. Meaning
Response to added nutrients (nitrates and phosphates) → phytoplankton explosion → algal bloom → death and decay → oxygen depletion
Type | Cause | Speed
Natural eutrophication | Slow nutrient enrichment | Millennia
Cultural eutrophication | Human sewage, fertiliser, detergents | Accelerated
## 2. Lake categories by nutrients
Lake type | Nutrients
Oligotrophic | Very low
Mesotrophic | Moderate
Eutrophic | Very high
Most Indian lakes: eutrophic or mesotrophic
## 3. Effects
Collapsing food chains, species invasion, lake → marsh → land (ageing of lakes), coral loss (turbidity), colour and smell, gelatinous zooplankton
Sequence of dead zone: eutrophication → algal bloom → hypoxia
⚠ Phosphorus is usually the limiting nutrient in freshwater, nitrogen in seas (beyond your notes)

t: Algal bloom → why oxygen crashes
text:
Time | What phytoplankton do
Day | Photosynthesise, add oxygen
Night | Respire heavily, consume oxygen
After death | Decomposers use more oxygen
Dense bloom blocks sunlight → submerged plants die
Anaerobic water favours Clostridium botulinum (toxins kill fish, birds, mammals)
Warm water favours blooms; climate change worsens them
Phytoplankton: diatoms, dinoflagellates, cryptomonads, green and blue-green algae; give over half of oxygen we breathe
## In news 2025-26
Thames (UK): bloom risk rising with climate change despite 40-year fall in phosphorus (LENS Mar 2025)
Lake Victoria turned green (CA 360 Feb 2026): nutrient runoff, sewage; largest lake in Africa, source of White Nile
Red-tide events listed as a risk to seaweed farming (LENS Jul 2025)

t: Harmful algal blooms → causes in Indian seas
text:
Most blooms are harmless; HABs release neurotoxins and hepatotoxins → shellfish poisoning, fish kills, hit tourism and fisheries
Cause | How it feeds blooms
Nutrients from estuaries | Rivers carry N and P from sewage, farms, industry
Monsoon land runoff | Pulse of fertilisers and organic matter
Upwelling | Brings nutrient-rich deep water to surface (natural)
Warm water | Faster growth
Ocean stratification | Reduces upwelling → fewer nutrients (opposite effect)
⚠ Upwelling is a natural cause; questions treat it as correct along with human ones
PYQ 2011: causes of HABs in Indian seas = all three (estuary nutrients, monsoon runoff, upwelling); trap: picking only the man-made ones

t: Red, brown and blue tides → which organism
text:
Tide | Organism / cause
Red tide | Blooms of pigmented dinoflagellates (estuaries, coasts)
Brown tide | Brown algal blooms (most blooms are red or brown)
Blue tide | Bioluminescent dinoflagellates (e.g., Noctiluca, beyond your notes); low DO + high nitrogen
Green water | Green algae / cyanobacteria
## Chlorophyll types
Chlorophyll | Found in
a | All higher plants, algae, cyanobacteria
b | Higher plants, green algae
c | Diatoms, dinoflagellates, brown algae
d | Only red algae
Bioluminescence: anti-predator response; higher in deep-living and planktonic species
PYQ 1998: estuarine blooms of pigmented dinoflagellates = red tides; traps: sea tides, black tides, sea flowers

t: Dead zones → where and why
text:
Hypoxic zones: very low oxygen, usually 200-800 m below surface
Natural (upwelling) or human-made (fertiliser runoff → bloom → decay)
Dead zone | Note
Gulf of Mexico | One of the largest; forms every spring (Mississippi fertiliser)
Gulf of Oman | Growing
Baltic Sea | Large (beyond your notes)
Ocean oxygen fell ~2% (1960-2010) (IUCN): eutrophication, nitrogen deposition from fossil fuels, warming
Warming → less oxygen solubility + stratification (meltwater layer blocks upwelling)
Excess nitrogen from ammonia runoff also drives dead zones

t: Invasive aquatic weeds → feature
text:
Weed | Key facts
Water hyacinth | Native to Amazon; "Terror of Bengal"; world's worst aquatic weed; thrives in eutrophic water; also absorbs heavy metals (phytoremediation)
Forked fanwort | Turned Kerala waters pink; from Central/South America; needs much oxygen
Water lettuce (Nile cabbage) | Free-floating; mats block light, deplete oxygen; hyperaccumulator used in phytoremediation (LENS Nov 2025)
Other names of hyacinth: "German weed" (Bangladesh), "Florida devil" (South Africa), "Japanese trouble" (Sri Lanka)
⚠ Same weed is a pollution indicator and a remediation tool: hyacinth/lettuce take up heavy metals

t: Bioremediation → what it can and cannot do
text:
## 1. Meaning
Use of microorganisms (bacteria, fungi), algae or plants to degrade contaminants into less toxic forms
Enhances the same biodegradation that occurs in nature
Microbes can be genetically engineered for the job
Statement | True?
Enhances natural biodegradation | Yes
GM microbes can be designed for it | Yes
Any heavy metal (Cd, Pb) readily and completely removed | No
Limited to biodegradable compounds | Yes
Slower than other treatments | Yes
Cheaper, eco-friendly | Yes
⚠ Metals cannot be destroyed; microbes only bind, accumulate or change them to safer forms (biosorption, bioaccumulation)
PYQ 2017: advantages = 1 and 3; trap: "any heavy metal readily and completely treated"

t: In-situ bioremediation → technique and example
text:
Technique | What is done | Example
Bioventing | Air/nutrients into unsaturated soil (vadose zone) | Pseudomonas on petroleum soil
Biosparging | Air injected below the water table (saturated zone) | Benzene/BTEX from aquifers
Biostimulation | Add nutrients (N, P) or electron acceptors to native microbes | Oil-spill sites

topic: Mercury: sources, uses and the Minamata Convention
t: Mercury pollution → its sources
text:
## 1. Largest human-made source
Artisanal and Small-Scale Gold Mining (ASGM): about 38%, the largest human-made source
Mercury binds gold into an amalgam; the amalgam is heated and mercury evaporates, leaving gold
ASGM releases more than 1,000 tonnes of mercury a year (tailings + vapour)
## 2. Other sources
Type | Sources
Natural | Volcanic eruptions, fossil fuels, metal ores, other minerals
Combustion | Coal-based thermal power plants (mercury in coal released as gas; also in fly ash), waste incineration
Industry | Mining and refining of copper, gold, lead, zinc; cement (mercury in limestone and coal); caustic soda production
Products | CFL and fluorescent lamps, batteries, thermometers, dental amalgam, PVC, pesticides
Coal TPPs give about 80% of mercury emitted by industry (with 60% PM, 45% SO₂, 30% NO₂)
PYQ 2023: how many of three statements are correct (gold mining, coal TPPs, "no known safe level"); key: only two
⚠ The official key treated "no known safe level of mercury" as incorrect; PMF's own solution calls all three correct. "No safe level" is WHO's line for lead, the trap to remember

topic: Mercury: sources, uses and the Minamata Convention
t: Fluorescent lamps → why mercury is used
text:
## 1. How a fluorescent tube works
Electric current excites mercury vapour → mercury emits ultraviolet (UV) radiation
UV strikes the phosphor coating on the inner wall → phosphor fluoresces → visible light
Part | Job
Mercury vapour | Emits UV when current passes
Phosphor coating | Converts UV → visible light
Glass tube | Holds the gas; blocks most UV
⚠ Mercury does not convert UV into visible light, and there is no mercury coating that makes light white; the phosphor does the conversion
## 2. Compared with other lamps
Incandescent: heats a filament until it glows; low cost, low efficiency (most energy lost as heat)
Fluorescent / CFL: higher efficiency, longer life, but mercury makes broken or dumped lamps a hazard
LED: no mercury; but LEDs contain arsenic (PMF lists LEDs as an arsenic source)
PYQ 2010: asked why mercury is used in fluorescent lamps; answer: mercury emits UV; trap: the option saying mercury converts UV to visible light

topic: Mercury: sources, uses and the Minamata Convention
t: Mercury in products and e-waste → where it hides
text:
## 1. Product and e-waste sources (PMF list)
Product | Note
CFL bulbs, lamps, LCD screens, CRT monitors | Mercury vapour or backlights
Switches, thermostats, sensors | Mercury switches
Thermometers, medical equipment | Liquid metallic mercury
Batteries, mobile phones | Button and older batteries
Printed solders | Alloy with tin
Dental amalgam fillings | Mercury + silver alloy
Skin-lightening cosmetics | Mercury blocks melanin
Pesticides, PVC | Older uses
## 2. Behaviour of spilled mercury
High surface tension → forms tiny spherical droplets
High vapour pressure → evaporates fast; indoors it quickly becomes an inhalation hazard
⚠ Inhaling mercury vapour is more dangerous than swallowing liquid mercury
State PCS 2020 (Chhattisgarh): pesticides, dental amalgam, fluorescent lamps and coal TPPs are all four sources of mercury
## In news 2025-26
July 2026: study found mercury up to 20 times the permissible 1 ppm in some cosmetics; mercury inhibits the enzyme behind melanin and lightens skin within days

topic: Mercury: sources, uses and the Minamata Convention
t: Methylmercury and Minamata disease → health impacts
text:
## 1. Forms of mercury
Form | Key fact
Elemental (metallic) | Vapour reaches the brain easily
Methylmercury | Formed by bacteria acting on mercury in water, soil, plants; most toxic at low doses
Inorganic salts | Older use in cosmetics and medicines
Methylmercury bioaccumulates and biomagnifies in fish → highest in top predators
Methylmercury crosses the placenta → impaired foetal brain development
## 2. Health effects
Damage to central nervous system, kidneys, lungs; tremors, memory loss, poor coordination
Depression, paralysis; possible cardiovascular risk
WHO ranks mercury among the top 10 chemicals of major public health concern
## 3. Minamata disease
Japan, 1950s: people ate fish from Minamata Bay contaminated with methylmercury from industrial wastewater
Symptoms: numbness in hands and feet, stumbling, problems in seeing, hearing, swallowing; many died
⚠ Minamata disease = mercury; Itai-itai = cadmium; do not swap them
## Beyond your notes
WHO's top 10 list: air pollution, arsenic, asbestos, benzene, cadmium, dioxins, inadequate or excess fluoride, lead, mercury, highly hazardous pesticides

topic: Mercury: sources, uses and the Minamata Convention
t: Minamata Convention → what it regulates
text:
## 1. Basics
Item | Fact
Nature | Legally binding treaty on mercury and its compounds
Adopted | 2013 (signed by 92 countries)
In force | 2017
India | Ratified 2018
Secretariat / implementer | UNEP
Scope | Entire life-cycle: mining, trade, use in products and processes, emissions, safe disposal
## 2. Key provisions
Annex A products: phase-out of manufacture, import, export of mercury-added products (lamps, batteries, thermometers, cosmetics)
Cosmetics with over 1 ppm mercury phased out by 2020; later COP amendments removed the 1 ppm threshold → total ban on mercury-added cosmetics
Dental amalgam: earlier "phase-down"; now a phase-out
## In news 2025-26
Nov 2025: parties agreed to phase out mercury-based dental amalgams by 2034
Sep 2025: a Parliamentary Committee called for eliminating mercury-based medical devices in line with the Convention
## Beyond your notes
Parties with significant ASGM must prepare National Action Plans to reduce mercury use in gold mining
Likely next: year of adoption vs entry into force (2013 vs 2017), India's ratification (2018), and which products are banned

topic: Other heavy metals: lead, cadmium, chromium, arsenic
t: Lead → sources and health effects
text:
Type | Sources
Major | Mining, lead-acid batteries, battery scrap recycling, paints (quick drying), fly ash, plastic toys (lead softens plastic), smelting
Minor | Lead-soldered food cans, lip products, leaded water pipes, glass, ayurvedic medicines (Rasa Shastra)
E-waste | Batteries, solar panels, PVC, solder in PCBs, CRT glass
Household | Old aluminium pressure cookers (news 2025), cookware, cosmetics, ceramics
Recycling of lead-acid batteries is a leading cause of child lead poisoning in low-income countries
## 2. Health effects
Neurotoxic: irreversible behavioural and neurological damage in children; anaemia, kidney damage
Carcinogen of lungs and kidneys; stillbirths, miscarriages; maternal exposure linked to early Alzheimer's
Particle-bound air pollutant; was used as tetraethyl lead (TEL) anti-knock additive in petrol
IAS 2012: after leaded petrol was banned, lead still comes from smelting units and paints; pens and pencils (graphite) and hair oils were the distractors

topic: Other heavy metals: lead, cadmium, chromium, arsenic
t: Lead → control measures and limits in India
text:
## 1. Measures
Measure | Year | What it does
Leaded petrol ban | 2000 | Removed the main exposure source
Lead Paint Rules | 2016 | Decorative paint lead capped at 90 ppm
FSSAI food limits | 2011 | Bans lead chromate in turmeric; ≤10 ppm in packaged food
Insecticides Act amendment | 2019 | Bans lead arsenate in farming
PVC stabiliser rules | 2021 | Regulates lead stabilisers in PVC pipes
NAAQS | 2009 | Ambient lead standard (CPCB)
GAELP (Global Alliance to Eliminate Lead Paint), 2011: UNEP + WHO partnership
## 2. Burden
One-third of the world's children have blood lead ≥5 µg/dL; India is the worst affected
Lead exposure costs India nearly 5% of GDP

18-24 Oct 2026: 14th International Lead Poisoning Prevention Week, theme "From Detection to Prevention" (first week held 2012)

topic: Smelters and coal plants: industrial toxic emissions
t: Copper smelting → the pollutants it releases
text:
## 1. What is released
Pollutant | Why
Sulphur dioxide (SO₂) | Most copper ores (chalcopyrite, copper iron sulphide) are sulphur-based; roasting removes 20-50% sulphur as SO₂
Sulphuric acid | High SO₂ is converted to H₂SO₄, itself an irritant and water contaminant
Slag | Waste of iron oxide and heavy metals → leaches arsenic, cadmium, lead, mercury, nickel into groundwater
Particulate matter | Air pollutant from the process
Radon | From radioactive decay in uranium and copper ores
## 2. Not a concern
Carbon monoxide is not released in lethal quantities: CO formed in the furnace reacts with the ore to give CO₂
⚠ Lethal CO comes from incomplete combustion; copper smelters are known for SO₂ + slag, not CO
PYQ 2021: concerns about copper smelters; answer slag leaching + SO₂ (2 and 3 only); trap: "lethal quantities of CO"

topic: Smelters and coal plants: industrial toxic emissions
t: Copper smelting → process steps and by-products
text:
Step | Output
Mining chalcopyrite | Ore with <1% Cu
Concentration (crushing, flotation) | ~34.5% Cu
Roasting in smelter (near ports) | Removes sulphur as SO₂ → sulphuric acid
Smelting | Matte (~65% Cu) + slag
Converting | Blister copper (~99%)
Anode furnace, then electrolytic refining | 99.99% copper
Slime from refining | Gold, silver, selenium, tellurium recovered
## Uses of copper slag
Abrasive blast-cleaning, road construction, cement, mortar, concrete aggregates
PYQ 2020: copper slag is a preferred material in rural road construction (with cold mix asphalt and geotextiles) to cut the carbon footprint

topic: Smelters and coal plants: industrial toxic emissions
t: Sterlite copper plant, Thoothukudi → case facts
text:
Vedanta's Sterlite smelter at Thoothukudi (Tuticorin), Tamil Nadu
Sterlite and Hindalco's smelter in coastal Gujarat made over 80% of India's copper; Sterlite met 36% of India's refined copper demand
## 1. Why it was closed (2018)
Issue | Fact
Trigger | 2018 protests against doubling capacity (4 lakh → 8 lakh t/yr)
Location | 14 km from Gulf of Mannar Marine National Park; norm for hazardous industry: >25 km from an eco-sensitive zone
Pollution | SO₂ fumes; effluents with heavy metals in water bodies
Units | Sulphuric acid plant, phosphoric acid plant, 160 MW coal power plant
Closure since 2018 → India depends more on imported refined copper (PMF May 2025)
## Beyond your notes
Supreme Court in 2024 refused to allow the plant to reopen, upholding the closure (verify)

topic: Smelters and coal plants: industrial toxic emissions
t: Coal thermal power plants → toxic metals and gases
text:
## 1. Fly ash
Ash ponds (fly ash + water) collapse → contaminate farms, water bodies, groundwater
Toxic metals in fly ash: mercury, cadmium, arsenic, lead, lithium, zinc, copper, nickel, boron, aluminium; also fluoride, sulphur
## 2. Gases and effluents
Output | Pollutants
Stack gases | CO₂, SO₂, NOx, PM, methane, CO (incomplete combustion), VOCs, mercury
Water | Acid mine drainage from coal mines; cooling-tower blowdown; ash-handling and wet FGD wastewater
Indian coal has high ash (25-45%) vs imported coal (10-20%)
FGD (flue gas desulphurisation): limestone or ammonia slurry turns SO₂ into gypsum; removes up to 95% of SO₂
PYQ 2020: coal ash contains arsenic, lead and mercury; TPPs release SO₂ and NOx; Indian coal is high-ash: all three correct
## In news 2025-26
2025: a high-powered committee recommended dropping mandatory FGD for most coal plants; only about 22 GW (~8%) of coal capacity had FGD
India was the largest SO₂ emitter in 2022 (over 20% of anthropogenic emissions)
⚠ PMF figures differ by issue: 39 of 537 coal plants with FGD (Magnum Q3) vs 22 GW (~8%) of capacity (LENS June 2025); both describe very low coverage

t: PFAS → what they are, where they occur
text:
## 1. Definition
Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances: a large group of human-made chemicals with very strong carbon-fluorine (C-F) bonds
C-F bond → resistant to heat, water, oil and chemical degradation
Best known: PFOA (perfluorooctanoic acid) and PFOS (perfluorooctane sulfonic acid)
## 2. Uses (make things grease-proof, water-proof, stick-proof, stain-resistant)
Use | Example
Cookware | Non-stick (Teflon): PFOA used in making Teflon
Textiles | Water-repellent clothing, stain-resistant fabrics, carpets
Packaging | Food packaging, paper straws
Safety | Fire-fighting foams
Others | Cosmetics, industrial coatings, electroplating

## 1. Three properties UPSC tested
Property | Fact

Persistent | Break down extremely slowly ("forever chemicals")

Cancer, thyroid disorders, infertility, developmental problems, liver damage, raised cholesterol, immune effects

PIBO = Producer, Importer, Brand Owner; must collect packaging waste they put on market

PIBO category | 2025-26 | 2026-27 | 2027-28 | 2028-29
Category I (rigid) | 30% | 40% | 50% | 60%
Category II | 10% | 10% | 20% | 20%
Category III | 5% | 5% | 10% | 10%
