topic: Land degradation: meaning, types and causes
t: Land degradation → types and definitions
text:
## 1. Meaning
Soil/land degradation = decline in soil quality from improper use (agricultural, pastoral, industrial, urban)
UNCCD/PMF: a negative trend in land condition from direct or indirect human-induced processes; long-term loss of biological productivity, ecological integrity or value to humans
Type | What it covers
Physical | Soil erosion by water and wind, compaction, waterlogging
Chemical | Salinity, alkalinity, acidification, nutrient loss
Biological | Pollution, loss of vegetative cover and soil organisms
## 2. Related terms
Desertification = land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas; not the natural expansion of existing deserts
Sustainable land management (SLM): using soil, water, plants to meet needs while keeping long-term productive potential
Land Degradation Neutrality (LDN): amount and quality of land resources remain stable or increase (UNCCD)
⚠ Desertification can occur in cold deserts too (Ladakh, Lahaul-Spiti): it has no climatic boundary (Mains 2020)

topic: Land degradation: meaning, types and causes
t: Land degradation → causes (complete list)
text:
Cause | How it degrades land
Deforestation | Roots no longer bind soil; e.g. Shiwaliks, Chos of Punjab, Chambal ravines
Shifting cultivation (jhum) | Slash-and-burn; topsoil lost on hill slopes (Nagaland)
Overgrazing | Grass torn out by roots; hooves pulverise soil
Faulty farming | Ploughing along the slope, monocropping, no crop rotation
Over-irrigation | Waterlogging and salinisation
Fertiliser imbalance | Urea gets over 80% subsidy; N:P:K skewed
Mining | Opencast mining (Goa, Jharkhand, Odisha, Aravallis)
Urbanisation | Fertile cropland lost: 1.6-3.3 Mha/yr globally (2000-2030, GLO)
NCERT: India loses 5.3 billion tonnes of soil a year to erosion, with 0.8 Mt N, 1.8 Mt P, 26.3 Mt K
India supports 16% of world population and 20% of livestock on 2.5% of land; per capita forest land 0.08 ha vs 0.47 ha needed
Soil organic carbon fell from about 1% to 0.3% over 70 years; deficiencies of zinc, boron, iron widespread
⚠ Ploughing across the slope (contour ploughing) conserves soil; ploughing along the slope erodes it
Likely next: "how many of the following cause land degradation" lists: all of deforestation, overgrazing, shifting cultivation, over-irrigation are correct

topic: Land degradation: meaning, types and causes
t: Land degradation → impacts and land restoration
text:
Impact | Mechanism
Climate change | Degraded land absorbs less CO2; carbon sinks become sources
Food and water security | Lower yields, less groundwater recharge
Biodiversity | Habitat degradation and fragmentation
Drought | No vegetation cover worsens drought and the hydrological regime
Water bodies | Sand and silt deposition cuts reservoir capacity
Land restoration: ecological process of restoring a natural, safe landscape for humans, wildlife and plants
UNEP: half of world GDP depends on nature; every $1 in restoration returns up to $30
Almost 80% of carbon in terrestrial ecosystems is stored in soils
Globally, desertification pace is 30-35 times the historical rate; about 1,500 million people depend on degrading land
## In news 2025-26
World Environment Day 2024 (5 June, host Saudi Arabia): theme "Land restoration, desertification and drought resilience"
World Soil Day (5 December): 2025 theme "Healthy Soils for Healthy Cities"; proposed 2002 by IUSS, backed by FAO and Thailand; UNGA adopted 2013, first observed 2014

topic: Soil erosion by water and wind
t: Water erosion → order of the stages
text:
## 1. The sequence
Stage | What happens
1. Splash (raindrop) | Raindrop (about 5 mm, hits at about 32 km/h) acts like a tiny bomb; breaks crumb structure
2. Sheet | Displaced particles clog pores; water runs off as a sheet, removing a thin uniform layer
3. Rill | Finger-like channels a few cm deep; removable by normal tillage
4. Gully | Rills deepen and widen into gullies; grow by headward erosion
5. Ravine → canyon | Gully bed deepens (ravine 30 m or more); canyon a few hundred metres (Grand Canyon)
Other water erosion: streambank, landslides, coastal, glacial
Vegetation stops raindrops hitting soil directly: the first defence against splash erosion
⚠ Order is splash → sheet → rill → gully; sheet erosion is "scarcely perceptible" yet comes before rills
PYQ 2001: arrange splash, sheet, rill, gully erosion; answer splash, sheet, rill, gully

topic: Soil erosion by water and wind
t: Gully erosion → ravines and badlands
text:
Gullies over a large area give badland topography: Chambal ravines (Morena, Bhind, Gwalior, Shivpuri in MP)
Gully erosion (not splash, sheet or rill) forms the Chambal ravines (IAS 1994)
Landform | Size
Rill | Narrow, shallow channel
Gully | Metres to tens of metres deep
Ravine | Larger than gully, narrower than canyon
Canyon / gorge | Deep, steep-sided; gorge steeper and narrower
Most erosion-affected areas: Chambal-Yamuna ravines, Shiwalik foothills, Chotanagpur, Malwa (Tapti-Sabarmati), black-soil Maharashtra, arid Haryana-Rajasthan-Gujarat
## In news 2025-26
2025 Nature study: gully erosion in 77 high-risk districts, mainly eastern and southern India; worst states Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan
Eastern India: more severe gully erosion; western India: mainly badlands; Jharkhand = top priority; threatens LDN by 2030
⚠ Policy gap: no clear legal distinction between gullies and badlands
Soil piping (tunnel erosion): sub-surface tunnels whose roofs collapse; lateritic Western Ghats; Kerala declared it a state-specific disaster (2017)

topic: Soil erosion by water and wind
t: Wind erosion → saltation, suspension, creep
text:
Process | Particle size | Movement
Saltation | Fine and medium sand | Bounds and leaps
Suspension | Small sand and dust | Carried long distances in air
Surface creep | Coarse sand | Rolled along the surface
Left behind | Very coarse sand, gravel | Desert pavement
Significant in arid and semi-arid regions with no physical obstruction
Deflation leaves depressions: first step in oasis formation
Fine-particle soils (silt, clay) and bare, dry land are most susceptible
Impacts: topsoil and nutrient loss, broken aggregates, dust air pollution, sedimentation, land abandonment
⚠ Wind erosion is controlled by shelterbelts, windbreaks, sand fences, mulching, conservation tillage: not by contour bunding

topic: Soil erosion by water and wind
t: Coastal and sea erosion → India's coastline
text:
NCCR (attached office of Ministry of Earth Sciences) monitors shoreline change
32% of India's coastline eroded and 27% expanded (accretion) between 1990 and 2018 (NCCR)
Coast | Finding
West Bengal | 60% of coastline eroded: most vulnerable
Odisha | Erosion expanded 51%
Andhra Pradesh | 28.7% eroding; 28 km at Visakhapatnam (since port, 1930s)
East vs west | East coast erodes more: rougher Bay of Bengal, cyclones, NE monsoon
Measure | How it works
Groyne | Built perpendicular to shore; traps longshore drift
Beach nourishment | Dredged sand deposited on eroding beach
Submerged breakwater | About 500 m offshore; breaks wave energy
Seawalls, revetments | Hard protection
NCSCM: research institute under MoEFCC for sustainable coastal management
⚠ Groynes run perpendicular to the coast, seawalls run parallel

t: Salinisation → causes and effects
text:
## 1. How it forms
Over-irrigation in canal command areas raises the water table; salts (Na, Ca, Mg) rise by capillary action and remain as white efflorescence when water evaporates
High evaporation in dry climates; seawater intrusion; mineral-rich parent rock
Effect | Detail
Soil becomes impermeable | Salts bind particles, cutting porosity and permeability
Lower fertility and yield | Cultivation needs heavy leaching with irrigation water
Limited crops | Only salt-tolerant: cotton, barley
Poor fodder and food quality | -
Flooding | Reduced percolation
Construction damage | Roads and buildings
⚠ Salinisation does not raise crop production, raise the water table or fill air spaces with water (2011 distractors); the rising water table is its cause, not its effect
PYQ 2011: effect of salinisation on irrigated land → "It makes some soils impermeable"

t: Salt-affected soils in India → where and how much
text:
India: about 6.7-6.75 million ha salt-affected (PMF)
Region | Driver
Indo-Gangetic plains: UP, Punjab, Haryana | Canal over-irrigation
Rajasthan arid zone | Indira Gandhi Canal boosted farming but spread salinity
Semi-arid Gujarat, Maharashtra, AP, Telangana, Karnataka | Poor drainage, high evaporation
Coastal belts | Seawater intrusion
Saline and alkaline soils are deficient in calcium and nitrogen
In ISRO's atlas, salinity accounts for only 1.12% of desertification (mainly irrigated cropland)
⚠ PMF names Uttar Pradesh as most affected; CSSRI estimates give Gujarat the largest salt-affected area (Beyond your notes, verify)
Usar / reh / kallar: local names for saline-alkaline patches in UP, Punjab (Beyond your notes)

t: Saline and alkaline soils → reclamation
text:
Method | Purpose
Drainage outlets | Drain excess water, lower the water table
Canal and tank lining | Seal seepage
Gypsum (liberal application) | Converts alkali (sodium) into soluble compounds that leach out
Sulphur, pyrite, sulphuric acid | Acid-forming: neutralise alkali
Rice husk, rice straw | Decompose to form mild acid
Salt-tolerant vegetation | Improves cover
Crop rotation, judicious irrigation | Prevents build-up
⚠ Gypsum treats alkaline (sodic) soils; lime treats acidic soils: do not swap them
Beyond your notes: CSSRI, Karnal (ICAR) is the research institute for salt-affected soils

t: Waterlogging → extent and remedies
text:
Waterlogged soils are saturated by monsoon accumulation or leaks
India: about 12 million ha waterlogged, half coastal, half inland (PMF)
Over-irrigation affects 6-7 million ha through waterlogging and salinisation (Mains Magnum)
Waterlogging is one of the chief causes of salinity
Remedy | How
Surface drainage | Open drains to an outlet
Vertical drainage | Pump groundwater from wells/bores; works in Indo-Gangetic plain
Subsurface drains | Pipes below root zone
Land levelling, tolerant crops | Avoid pooling
Green Revolution side effects: waterlogging, malaria breeding, soil fertility loss, water table depletion in tubewell areas
⚠ Drainage is the only real cure for waterlogging (PMF)

t: Riverbed sand mining → consequences
text:
Consequence | Correct? | Why
Lowering of the water table | Yes | Removes the sand aquifer and capillary network
Pollution of groundwater | Yes | Exposes deeper layers; contaminants seep in
Decreased salinity in river | No | Sand loss raises salinity (seawater intrusion in coastal stretches; exposed surfaces evaporate and concentrate salts)
Riverbank erosion, bed incision | Yes | Sediment balance broken
Habitat loss, turbidity | Yes | Spawning grounds lost
Bridge and infrastructure damage | Yes | Undermined foundations
Capillary rise is stronger in clay (fine pores) than sand
⚠ The "decreased salinity" option is the trap: sand mining increases salinity risk
PYQ 2018: consequences of heavy sand mining in riverbeds → 2 and 3 only (groundwater pollution, lower water table)

t: Sand mining → law and alternatives
text:
## 1. Legal status
Sand is a minor mineral under Section 3(e) of the MMDR Act, 1957: states frame rules
Supreme Court (2012): prior environmental clearance mandatory for all minor-mineral mining, including sand
No national ban on river sand mining; restrictions are state-specific (e.g. Kerala ban 2016)
India needs about 1 billion tonnes of sand a year; 1.77 billion tonnes by 2034
## 2. Manufactured sand (M-sand)
Feature | M-sand | River sand
Source | Crushed hard rock | River deposits
Grain | Angular, rough | Rounded, smooth
Impurities | Silt, clay removed | Variable
Drawback | Lower workability; more water/cement | Ecological damage
## In news 2025-26
Study: stone quarries near protected areas expanded after Kerala's 2016 river-sand ban (demand for M-sand): habitat loss, more soil erosion
Ban effects: riverbeds recover, groundwater recharge improves, less saltwater intrusion; but costs rise and illegal mining grows
Beyond your notes: MoEFCC Sustainable Sand Mining Management Guidelines 2016 and Enforcement and Monitoring Guidelines for Sand Mining 2020

t: Conservation method → terrain where it is used
text:
Method | Where used | Erosion agent checked
Contour bunding | Sloping / hilly land | Water
Terracing | Steep slopes | Water
Contour ploughing | Gentle slopes | Water (and wind if across wind)
Strip cropping | Slopes and windy plains | Water and wind
Check dams, gully plugs | Gullies, drainage lines | Water
Shelterbelts / windbreaks | Coastal and dry regions | Wind
Sand fences | Desert margins, dunes, construction sites | Wind
Drainage | Low flat flood-prone land | Waterlogging
⚠ Contour bunding is not for desert margins (wind), low flood plains (drainage) or scrublands (weeds)
PYQ 2013: contour bunding is used in desert margins / flood plains / scrublands / none of the above → none: it is for slopes

t: Contour bunding and terracing → how they work
text:
## 1. Contour bunding
Banks (bunds) built along the contours; divides a slope into many small slopes
Regulates water flow, promotes absorption, reduces runoff and soil loss
## 2. Terrace farming
Steps cut along a steep hill slope give flat surfaces for crops; retaining walls control flow
Harappans also used terracing and crop rotation (Testbook)
## 3. Related structures
Structure | Description
Contour barriers | Stone, grass or soil along contours with trenches; live, dead or mixed; build a terrace effect
Rock dam | Rocks piled across a channel to slow water
Check dams | Across gullies: hold water, prevent erosion, recharge groundwater (NCERT)
Farm ponds, percolation tanks | Watershed structures (IWMP, DPAP)
⚠ Contour = along lines of equal height, i.e. across the slope
Contour ploughing cuts erosion by 10-50% (PMF Agriculture)

t: Agronomic methods → crop rotation, strip cropping, mulching
text:
Method | How it conserves soil
Crop rotation | Different crops draw different nutrients; legumes fix nitrogen
Strip cropping | Alternate parallel strips; land never fully bare; tall crops act as windbreaks
Intercropping | Different crops in alternate rows, sown at different times
Mulching | Straw, grass cover: less erosion, moisture retained, even temperature, no weeds
Early-maturing varieties | Less time on soil
Zero / reduced tillage | Soil undisturbed, moisture conserved
Cover crops, agroforestry | Year-round cover
Potato needs potash, wheat needs nitrate: rotate them
Rotation rule: legume after non-legume, low-water crop after high-water crop
Sorghum fields erode fastest, clover least (IAS 1994)
⚠ Seed modification does not improve soil fertility (MPPSC 1991)

t: Wind erosion control → windbreaks and sand fences
text:
Method | Detail
Shelterbelts / windbreaks | Rows of trees in coastal and dry regions; Casuarina most popular (salt-tolerant, fast, stabilises dunes)
Sand fences | Evenly spaced wooden slats or fabric; cut wind speed and trap blowing sand; also around construction sites
Dune mulching | Plant mulch as a physical barrier to moving sand
Tree plantation in transition zones | China, Sahel
Ploughing perpendicular to wind | Lowers wind velocity at the surface
⚠ Answer-key conflict on PYQ 2010: Preview (Ghatna Chakra) gives 1, 3 and 4 (dropping sand fences); the official reading and PMF treat sand fences as soil conservation, so all four (crop rotation, sand fences, terracing, windbreaks)
PYQ 2010: which of crop rotation, sand fences, terracing, wind breaks are soil conservation → 1, 2, 3 and 4

t: Other measures → afforestation, grazing, geotextiles, biochar
text:
Measure | Fact
Afforestation | Forest target raised to 33% in the 2nd Plan: 20% plains, 60% hills
Checking overgrazing | Separate grazing grounds, more fodder
Checking shifting cultivation | Resettle tribals in settled farming
Dams | Slow floods; but indiscriminate dams cause landslides (Himalaya)
Geotextiles | Permeable fabrics: synthetic (polypropylene, polyester) or natural (jute, coir)
Biochar | Pyrolysis of biomass in low oxygen; raises water-holding 10-25%
2020: GoI allowed coir geotextiles for rural roads under PMGSY
UPSC 2020: copper slag, cold mix asphalt, geotextiles preferred in rural roads (not hot mix asphalt, Portland cement)
## In news 2025-26
Biochar from surplus crop residue could remove up to 450 Mt CO2/yr by 2030; cuts soil N2O 30-50%
Soil Health Card: over 25.55 crore cards (Nov 2025); N:P:K ratio worsened to 10.9:4.1:1 (Economic Survey 2025-26)

topic: Desertification in India and its control
t: ISRO Desertification Atlas → India's figures
text:
Figure | Value
Degraded land (2018-19) | 97.85 Mha = 29.77% of geographical area
Degraded land (2003-05) | 94.53 Mha (28.8%)
Annual addition | about 2.2 lakh ha a year
Drylands | 228.3 Mha (70%) of India
Under desertification | 82.6 Mha (about 25%)

t: Greenhouse effect → how CO₂ traps heat
text:
## 1. Mechanism
Sunlight (visible, near-UV, near-IR) passes through; surface warms and re-emits longer-wave infrared (terrestrial radiation)
GHGs absorb this outgoing infrared and re-radiate part of it back to the surface
Radiation | CO₂ behaviour
Incoming solar (short-wave) | Transparent (lets it pass)
Outgoing terrestrial infrared (long-wave) | Opaque: absorbs and re-radiates
UV | Absorbed by ozone in the stratosphere, not CO₂
Only O₃ and water vapour absorb both incoming and outgoing radiation (PMF)
Natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth at ~15°C; without it about -18°C
Water aerosols (vapour, ice, fog, sea-salt droplets) give >95% of total greenhouse warming
⚠ CO₂ does not absorb UV or "all solar radiation"; it absorbs infrared emitted by Earth
PYQ 2012: rising CO₂ warms the air because it absorbs the infrared part of radiation; traps: UV, all solar radiation, water vapour

t: Atmospheric constituents → which warm the air
text:
Substance | Warms? | How
CO₂, CH₄, N₂O | Yes | GHGs: absorb outgoing IR
Water vapour | Yes | Most abundant and strongest overall GHG; also a feedback
SF₆ | Yes | Synthetic GHG; GWP 23,900; life 3,200 yr
Soot (black carbon) | Yes | Absorbs incoming sunlight; darkens snow and ice
Tropospheric ozone | Yes | Secondary GHG from CO, NO₂, VOCs + sunlight
CFCs, HFCs, PFCs | Yes | Very high GWP
Carbon monoxide | Indirect | Not a direct GHG; prolongs CH₄ via OH, forms O₃
Sulphate aerosols | Cool | Reflect sunlight
Black carbon = short-lived climate forcer, not a GHG; stays days to weeks
⚠ "All three" trap: soot, SF₆ and water vapour all warm the atmosphere
PYQ 2010: soot, sulphur hexafluoride, water vapour → 1, 2 and 3
## Super pollutants
Short-lived climate pollutants: methane, black carbon, HFCs, tropospheric ozone

t: GHGs → GWP and lifetime
text:
GWP = heat absorbed by a gas relative to the same mass of CO₂ (CO₂ = 1); GWP100 over 100 years
Gas | GWP100 | Lifetime (years)
CO₂ | 1 | 50-200 (centuries to millennia, other books)
CH₄ | 28 (GWP20 = 84) | 12
N₂O | 265 | 120
HFCs | 140-11,700 | 1-270
PFCs | 6,500-9,200 | 800-50,000
SF₆ | 23,900 (highest) | 3,200
GWP* (introduced at COP24, 2018): accounts for lifetimes; better for short-lived gases; criticised for greenwashing
CO₂ contributes most to the greenhouse effect: high concentration + long life (PYQ 2003)
⚠ Other books give CH₄ 25-28 and N₂O 298 (older AR4 values); PMF uses 28 and 265
⚠ Methane is more potent but shorter-lived; N₂O is long-lived like CO₂
## Beyond your notes
IPCC AR6 GWP100: fossil CH₄ about 29.8, N₂O about 273 (verify)

t: Other GHGs → water vapour, ozone, fluorinated gases
text:
Gas | Key facts
Water vapour | 0.02-4% of air; 90% within 6 km; falls from equator to poles; rises as world warms (feedback)
Ozone (O₃) | Stratosphere absorbs UV; ground-level O₃ is a secondary pollutant and GHG
CFCs | Phased out under Montreal Protocol (ozone depletion)
HFCs | CFC replacements; potent, long-lived GHGs (Kigali Amendment)
PFCs | By-products of aluminium smelting and semiconductor making
SF₆ | Circuit breakers, transmission equipment, magnesium processing, leak tracer
Carbon footprint: total direct + indirect emissions, in CO₂e
Carbon intensity: emissions per unit of GDP or energy
⚠ Biomass burning releases CO, CH₄, SO₂ directly; O₃ forms from them (UPSC 2019 key: all four)

Forcing by long-lived GHGs | +54% (1990-2024); CO₂ ≈ 81% of the increase

t: Methane → natural and human sources
text:
Source | Type | Process
Wetlands | Natural (largest natural) | Anaerobic decomposition
Termites | Natural | Gut microbes
Oceans, methane hydrates | Natural | Sediments, zooplankton
Rice fields | Human (agriculture) | Flooded, anaerobic soil
Livestock (cud-chewers) | Human (agriculture) | Enteric fermentation, mostly belching
Coal mining, oil and gas | Human (fossil) | Leaks and venting, coal-bed methane
Landfills, sewage | Human (waste) | Anaerobic decay
Biomass burning | Human | Incomplete combustion
Human 55-65% of methane; of human share: agriculture ~40% > fossil fuels ~35% > waste ~20-25%
Natural order: wetlands > termites > oceans > hydrates
Methane = marsh gas; main part of natural gas (80-95%); burns with a blue flame
⚠ All four (rice, coal mining, domestic animals, wetlands) are methane sources

t: Rice paddies → methane and nitrous oxide
text:
Gas | Why rice emits it
Methane (CH₄) | Flooding creates anaerobic soil; methanogens decompose organic matter
Nitrous oxide (N₂O) | Nitrogen fertilisers in soil; more with intermittent wetting
CO₂, black carbon | Stubble burning
Rice is the most important crop source of both CH₄ and N₂O (not cotton, sugarcane, wheat)
Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) cuts methane but can raise N₂O (soil aeration)
Direct-seeded rice (DSR) also saves water and methane
⚠ AWD is a trade-off: less CH₄, more N₂O
PYQ 2010: rice emits methane (anaerobic) and N₂O (N-fertiliser) → both correct

## In news 2025-26

NICRA (ICAR) for climate-resilient rice; India supplies 40% of global rice exports

t: Methane hydrates → where, risk and fate
text:
Clathrates: methane trapped in a cage of water molecules at high pressure, low temperature
Feature | Fact
Where | Arctic tundra / permafrost and under the seafloor (deep oceans, continental margins)
Risk | Warming, ocean acidification destabilise them → massive methane release
Past | Seafloor methane release suggested for the Permian-Triassic extinction (252 mya, "Great Dying")
Fate in air | Methane oxidises to CO₂ (and water) in about a decade or two (lifetime ~12 yr)
Hydrates were sinks; warming turns them into sources
⚠ All three statements true: warming may release them; found in tundra and seafloor; CH₄ → CO₂ in a decade or two
PYQ 2019: methane hydrate statements → 1, 2 and 3
## Beyond your notes
India's gas hydrate potential is studied in the Krishna-Godavari basin (NGHP expeditions) (verify)

t: Methane sinks and cuts → how CH₄ leaves the air
text:
Sink | How
Hydroxyl radical (OH) | Oxidises CH₄ in troposphere and stratosphere; OH = "cleanser of the atmosphere"
Aerated soils | Methanotrophic bacteria eat CH₄
Hydrates (past) | Stored CH₄, now leaking
Isoprene (from oaks, poplars) uses up OH → methane lasts longer
Methane ≈ 30% of warming since pre-industrial (UNEP)
Pledge / target | Detail
Global Methane Pledge (COP26, 2021) | Voluntary 30% cut by 2030 vs 2020
UNEP Global Methane Assessment (2021) | 45% cut by 2030 feasible; avoids ~0.3°C by 2040s
⚠ India has not joined the Global Methane Pledge
## In news 2025-26
India is the 3rd-largest methane emitter after China and USA: 31 Mt (~9%); landfills ~15% of India's methane; satellites show higher landfill emissions (CARE Dec 2025)

t: Nitrous oxide → sources and facts

Fact | Value

topic: CO₂ sources: cement, energy and global emissions
t: Cement → why it emits so much CO₂
text:
## 1. Process (PMF)
Crush limestone (75%) + clay (25%) → burn in kiln ~1,400°C (calcination) → clinker → grind with 3-5% gypsum → Portland cement
Emission source | Explains cement CO₂?
Calcination: limestone (CaCO₃) → lime (CaO) + CO₂ | Yes (process emissions)
Coal burnt to heat the kiln | Yes (fuel emissions)
Clay (silica) mixed with limestone | No: true, but releases no CO₂
1 t cement → at least 0.5 t CO₂
Cement ≈ 8% of global CO₂ (more than 5%)
Cuts: replace clinker with blast-furnace slag, fly ash; gypsum regulates setting
⚠ Statement-II trap: clay mixing is correct but does not explain the emissions; only lime-making does
PYQ 2025: cement >5% of CO₂; clay mixed with limestone; limestone → lime in clinker → both correct, only one (III) explains I
## India
Cement states Rajasthan, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, MP = 57% of output

topic: Carbon sinks, carbon fertilisation and feedbacks
t: Anthropogenic CO₂ → where it goes
text:
Fate | Share / note
Stays in atmosphere | Roughly half
Land sink (plants, soils) | ~31% (2010-19, IPCC AR6)
Ocean sink (dissolution + phytoplankton photosynthesis) | ~23% (AR6); PMF: ocean absorbs 25-30% a year
Escape to stratosphere/space | No
Trapped in polar ice caps | No (ice only records past air)
Phytoplankton fix CO₂; dead organic matter sinks to deep ocean (biological pump)
Ocean = largest active carbon sink; its uptake causes acidification
Blue carbon: carbon in ocean and coastal ecosystems (mangroves, seagrass, salt marsh) (PYQ 2021)
⚠ Polar ice does not remove CO₂; it only traps tiny air bubbles used to study past climate

topic: Carbon sinks, carbon fertilisation and feedbacks
t: Carbon fertilisation → meaning and limits
text:
Carbon fertilisation = increased plant growth (photosynthesis) due to higher atmospheric CO₂
Term | Meaning
Carbon fertilisation | More CO₂ → more plant growth
Greenhouse warming | More CO₂ → higher temperature
Ocean acidification | More CO₂ → lower ocean pH
Adaptation | Living beings adjusting to change
CO₂ fertilisation explains ~70% of global greening; nitrogen ~9%
Limits: nutrients, water, heat; land sink can flip under drought, fire, pests
Moderate warming (1-3°C) may help temperate crop yields; tropics lose
⚠ Carbon fertilisation is not warming, acidification or adaptation
PYQ 2018: carbon fertilisation = increased plant growth from higher CO₂

topic: Carbon sinks, carbon fertilisation and feedbacks
t: Carbon on Earth → reservoirs
text:
Total carbon ≈ 1.85 billion Gt; 1.845 billion Gt below the surface
Above-surface store | Gt | Share
Deep ocean | 37,000 | 85.1%
Marine sediments | 3,000 | 6.9%
Terrestrial biosphere | 2,000 | 4.6%
Surface ocean | 900 | 2%
Atmosphere | 590 | 1.4% (smallest)
Permafrost holds 1,400-1,700 Gt C, about twice the atmosphere's carbon
Boreal forests: up to 80% of carbon in soils (peat); taiga and tundra hold one-third of soil carbon
⚠ The deep ocean, not forests, is the largest above-surface carbon store
## Carbon cycle (PYQ 2011)
Add CO₂: respiration, decay, volcanic action, burning
Remove CO₂: photosynthesis

topic: Carbon sinks, carbon fertilisation and feedbacks
t: Carbon sinks → when they turn into sources
text:
System | Flip
Tundra / permafrost | Sink in the 1970s → source today (thaw releases CO₂, CH₄)
Taiga and temperate forests | Become source at ~3°C (thaw, wildfire)
Amazon | Beyond ~2°C parts may turn savanna (store → source)
Greenland lakes | Turned brown after 2022 rain; CO₂ emissions up 350%
Wildfire-hit forests | Australia 2019-20, California 2025
Positive feedback: warming → thaw/fire → more GHG → more warming
Negative feedback: low thick clouds reflect sunlight (cooling)
Cloud type | Net effect
Thick low clouds | Coolers (high albedo)
Thin high cirrus | Warmers (trap heat)
⚠ Cirrus thinning and stratospheric sulphate injection are geoengineering to cool Earth (UPSC 2019)

topic: Impacts on oceans, ice and the biosphere
t: Ocean acidification → who is harmed
text:
CO₂ + H₂O → carbonic acid → H⁺ rises → carbonate ions fall → pH drops
Surface pH ~8.2 → ~8.1; ocean is still alkaline ("less alkaline", not acidic)
Effect | Harmed?
Calcareous phytoplankton (coccolithophores) | Yes: shells harder to build
Coral reefs | Yes: weaker calcification, lower resilience
Animals with planktonic larvae (molluscs, crustaceans, echinoderms) | Yes
Cloud formation | Less DMS from phytoplankton → fewer cloud seeds (PMF)
Cloud seeding (artificial rain) | No: unrelated human technique
Nicknames: "evil twin of global warming", "the other CO₂ problem"
Acidification does not directly cause bleaching; heat does
⚠ PMF notes acidification may reduce cloud formation via DMS, but the UPSC key excludes "cloud seeding"
PYQ 2012: concern for calcareous phytoplankton, corals, animals with planktonic larvae → 1, 2 and 3 only

topic: Impacts on oceans, ice and the biosphere
t: Ocean warming → heatwaves, oxygen loss, AMOC
text:
Change | Fact
Ocean heat | Holds ~90% of excess heat
Marine heatwaves | Doubled in frequency since 1982; 84-90% human-caused; may rise 20-50 times by 2081
Deoxygenation | Warm water holds less O₂; oxygen minimum zones expand; stratification
AMOC weakening | Less Sahel and South Asian monsoon rain; more North Europe storms; fewer Atlantic cyclones; higher sea level on NE North America
Coral bleaching | 4th global event: ~84% of reefs, 83 countries (earlier: 1998, 2010, 2014-17)
Bleaching: corals expel zooxanthellae; 1°C above normal for weeks can trigger it
GBR: 6th mass bleaching since 2016 in 2025; Ningaloo bleached too
⚠ Bleached corals are not dead; recovery takes >15 years after mass events

topic: Impacts on oceans, ice and the biosphere
t: Warming beyond 3°C → likely impacts
text:
Statement | Verdict | Why
Terrestrial biosphere → net carbon source | Yes | Taiga thaw, dieback, wildfire
Widespread coral mortality | Yes | Corals very heat-sensitive
All wetlands permanently disappear | No | Coastal wetlands (Sundarbans, Chilika) drown; inland (Keoladeo, Kolleru) survive
Cereals impossible anywhere | No | Tropics lose; temperate yields rise short-run
IPCC AR6 WG II: species at very high extinction risk 14% at 1.5°C, 29% at 3°C, 39% at 4°C
Sea level: ~2.3 m per °C over 2,000 years (PMF)
⚠ Absolute words ("all wetlands", "anywhere") mark the false statements
PYQ 2014: impacts beyond 3°C → 1 and 2 only

topic: Impacts on oceans, ice and the biosphere
t: Tipping points and feedbacks → thresholds
text:
Tipping point: threshold beyond which change is self-perpetuating and irreversible on human timescales
Element | Threshold / status (UN brief 2026)
Warm-water coral reefs | 1.2°C threshold already crossed
Amazon | Beyond ~2°C may become savanna
Greenland + West Antarctic ice sheets | Could add 10 m sea level
Permafrost | Thaw releases trapped methane
AMOC | Weakening from meltwater
Climate sensitivity: warming for doubled CO₂ (~260 → ~520 ppm); range 1.5-4.5°C; newer models 3-7°C
Feedbacks: water vapour (+), albedo loss (+), clouds (±), permafrost (+)
## In news 2025-26
UN Secretary-General's Scientific Advisory Board Brief #12 on tipping points (London Climate Action Week): world ~1.3°C above pre-industrial (PMF LENS June 2026)
WMO: 2026-2030 may stay 1.3-1.9°C above pre-industrial; 91% chance of a year above 1.5°C

topic: Impacts on oceans, ice and the biosphere
t: Arctic amplification → why the Arctic warms fastest
text:
Arctic warmed nearly 4 times the global average since 1979 (Nature study)
Cause | Mechanism

topic: Heat stress, India's emissions and climate risk
t: Wet-bulb temperature → meaning and the 35°C limit
text:
Wet-bulb temperature (WBT): lowest temperature air can reach by evaporative cooling; thermometer wrapped in wet cloth
Combines heat and humidity
Condition | WBT vs dry-bulb
100% humidity | WBT = dry-bulb
Lower humidity | WBT < dry-bulb
WBT 30-35°C | Hyperthermia risk to brain, heart
WBT 35°C | Upper limit of human survivability: body cannot shed heat by sweating
World Bank: India could be among the first places where WBT routinely exceeds 35°C
Moist heatwaves in India linked to BSISO (30-90-day monsoon oscillation); NW India in active phases, south and east in break phases

Concept originated in the Kyoto Protocol
1 carbon credit = 1 tonne CO₂ (or CO₂e); tradable certificate
Earned via afforestation, renewables, sequestration, methane capture, or bought on an exchange
Awarded to those who cut below their quota; goal is to limit emission increase
## 2. Trading
Type | How
Emission trading / cap-and-trade | Sell unused units to over-emitters
Offset trading | Invest in carbon projects that cut emissions
MCX launched carbon credit futures in 2009

topic: Carbon sinks, blue carbon and soil carbon
t: Blue carbon → meaning and which ecosystems
text:
## 1. Definition
Blue carbon = carbon captured by the world's ocean and coastal ecosystems
Blue-carbon ecosystems: mangroves + seagrasses + salt marshes
Carbon "colour" | What it means
Blue | Ocean + coastal ecosystems (mangrove, seagrass, salt marsh)
Green | Forest biomass and agricultural soils (terrestrial sinks)
Black | Soot from incomplete combustion (a PM2.5 component, not a sink)
Brown / fossil | Carbon in petroleum, natural gas, coal
## 2. Why it matters
Coastal systems are much smaller than forests but sequester carbon much faster and can keep it for millions of years (in sediments)
When damaged they release large amounts of carbon back to the air
Ocean = planet's largest active carbon sink, absorbing ~25-30% of anthropogenic CO2 each year
⚠ "Carbon in forest biomass and agricultural soils" is the wrong option (that is green/terrestrial carbon); "carbon in the atmosphere" and "carbon in petroleum" are also distractors
PYQ 2021: "What is blue carbon?" Answer: carbon captured by oceans and coastal ecosystems

topic: Carbon sinks, blue carbon and soil carbon
t: Carbon sink vs source → forests, oceans, soils
text:
## 1. Definitions
Carbon sink: absorbs more carbon than it releases; carbon source: releases more than it absorbs
Forests, soils, oceans and atmosphere all store carbon and act as sink or source at different times
Store | Acts as sink when | Becomes a source when
Forest | Density or area increases | Degraded, burnt (CO2), or buried biomass exposed and decomposes (methane)
Ocean | Dissolves CO2; coastal ecosystems bury carbon | Coastal ecosystems damaged; ocean storage lowers pH
Soil | Organic matter builds up (low disturbance) | Ploughing, erosion, burning residue
Boreal (taiga) forest | Up to 80% of carbon in soils as peat | Warming of 3°C turns it into a source (permafrost thaw, wildfires)
Tropical forests absorb about 18% of the CO2 added by fossil fuels
⚠ Kyoto treats absorption by trees and soil as as effective as cutting fossil emissions for meeting commitments
Bhutan = carbon-negative country; net zero = emissions balanced by removals

topic: Carbon sinks, blue carbon and soil carbon
t: Soil carbon → which farm practices sequester carbon
text:
## 1. The 2012 trio
Practice | What it is | Stores soil carbon?
Zero tillage | Seed sown straight into unploughed soil with previous crop residue | Yes: least soil disturbance, organic matter builds up
Contour bunding | Banks along contours on slopes | No (key): soil and moisture conservation
Relay cropping | Second crop sown into a standing first crop before harvest (e.g. wheat into maturing rice, Bihar/UP) | No (key): saves time, raises cropping intensity
## 2. Other carbon-building practices
Conservation agriculture: 3 principles - minimum soil disturbance, permanent soil cover, crop diversification
Cover crops, mulching, residue retention, compost, agroforestry, biochar
⚠ Contour bunding and relay cropping are good practices but not soil-carbon sequestration measures in the UPSC key
PYQ 2012: contour bunding, relay cropping, zero tillage - only zero tillage (answer "3 only")
PYQ 2020 (related): zero tillage lets wheat be sown without burning residue, allows direct seeding of paddy without nursery, and enables soil carbon sequestration - all three correct

topic: Carbon sinks, blue carbon and soil carbon
t: Biochar and soil-carbon credits → features
text:
## 1. Biochar
Porous, charcoal-like, carbon-rich solid made by pyrolysis (heating biomass with zero or limited oxygen)
Climate role: avoids emissions from burning/decay and locks carbon for centuries → a persistent CO2-removal method
Co-products of pyrolysis: syngas and bio-oil
Benefit | Figure (source)
CO2 locked | 1 t biochar ≈ 2.5-3 t CO2e (CARE Jun 2026)
Credits | 1 t certified biochar ≈ 2-2.8 t CO2e credits under VM0042
Soil | Water-holding +10-25%; soil N2O -30-50% (PMF Jun 2026)
Scale | Surplus residue biochar could remove up to 450 Mt CO2/yr by 2030
## In news 2025-26
Sep 2026: India's first soil-carbon payments to 2,550 farmers of Punjab and Haryana under Aadi programme (Grow Indigo, 2019, ICAR guidance): direct seeded rice, reduced tillage, residue management
VM0042 = Verra methodology for agricultural land management credits
Aug 2026: Aaranyak pilots biochar from invasive weeds (Lantana, Chromolaena, Mikania) in Assam's Khalingduar RF
IIT Kharagpur's KISAN kiln for smallholder biochar

topic: Carbon capture, storage and carbon removal
t: CO2 storage sites → where captured carbon can be stored
text:
## 1. Geological storage (the 2017 list: all correct)
Site | Why it works
Abandoned / uneconomic coal seams | Coal absorbs (adsorbs) CO2
Depleted oil and gas reservoirs | Proven traps; CO2 also used for Enhanced Oil Recovery
Deep saline formations (aquifers) | Large porous rock volume under impermeable cap
Basalt formations | CO2 mineralises into carbonate rock (beyond PMF text, standard option)
Below 800 m, CO2 stays supercritical, so it can be injected safely
## 2. Ocean storage
Liquid CO2 injected at 500-3,000 m, dissolves under pressure; early stage
⚠ Ocean storage slightly lowers pH (adds to acidification)
PYQ 2017: coal seams, depleted oil/gas reservoirs, deep saline formations - all three (answer d)

topic: Carbon capture, storage and carbon removal
t: CCS vs CCUS → difference and products
text:
## 1. Stages
Capture (pre-combustion, post-combustion, oxy-fuel) → transport (pipelines/ships) → utilisation or storage
Aspect | CCS | CCUS
Steps | Capture + Storage | Capture + Utilisation + Storage
Purpose | Permanent emission cut | Use CO2 as a resource and/or store it
Revenue | Usually low | Possible
Examples | Saline aquifer, depleted fields | EOR, concrete curing, e-fuels
## 2. CO2 utilisation products
Green urea (2NH3 + CO2 → urea + H2O), methanol, ethanol, ammonia, carbonated concrete, aggregates, bio-plastics, algae-based biofuels
CO2-EOR: net climate effect depends on CO2 trapped vs emissions from the extra oil
Blue hydrogen = fossil hydrogen + carbon capture; green hydrogen = renewable electrolysis
⚠ CCS captures from point sources (power, steel); DAC captures from ambient air

topic: Carbon capture, storage and carbon removal
t: Direct Air Capture → uses
text:
## 1. What DAC is
Machines extract CO2 directly from the atmosphere at any location, unlike point-source capture
DACCS = DAC + storage; geological/mineral storage can keep CO2 for up to 1,000 years
Helps only if carbon negative (absorbs more than its energy use emits)
Use of DAC CO2 | Example
Sequestration | Stored in deep geological formations
Plastics / materials | Polycarbonates, cement, carbon fibres
Food processing | Carbonated beverages, cold storage, packaging
Aviation fuel | CO2 + green hydrogen via Power-to-Liquid (e-fuel) → synthetic low-carbon jet fuel
⚠ All three 2025 statements were correct: no "only" trap; product use still counts as keeping carbon locked
PYQ 2025: DAC for sequestration, plastics and food processing, and aviation synthetic fuel - all (answer c)
E-fuels: renewable power → green H2 (electrolysis) + captured CO2 (or N2 for ammonia) → liquid/gaseous fuels replacing petrol, diesel, jet fuel

topic: Carbon capture, storage and carbon removal
t: Enhanced rock weathering and ocean alkalinity → how they remove CO2
text:
## 1. The 2023 trio (all discussed for CCS)
Activity | Mechanism
Finely ground basalt on farmland (ERW) | Rain carbonic acid + rock → bicarbonate → eventually limestone; crushing raises surface area
Lime added to oceans (ocean alkalinity enhancement) | More carbonate ions → dissolved CO2 stored as bicarbonate; buffers acidity
CO2 as carbonated water into abandoned mines | Underground storage/mineralisation
## 2. ERW: benefits and concerns
Benefits: better soil fertility (alkalinity, nutrients), cheap (basalt is a quarry by-product), neutralises acidic runoff
Concerns: nickel, chromium in some rocks; respiratory hazard from rock dust; carbon-accounting risk if capture overestimated
Effectiveness depends on rock type and size, moisture, heat, soil, land management
## In news 2025-26
Brazil: world's first verified ERW carbon removal credits (2025)
Mati Carbon (Indian startup) won the $50 million XPRIZE Carbon Removal grand prize
PYQ 2023: basalt, lime in oceans, carbonated water in mines - all three (answer c)

topic: Carbon capture, storage and carbon removal
t: Carbon dioxide removal methods → list and risks
text:
## 1. GHG removal (carbon geoengineering) methods
Method | How | Key risk
Afforestation | Global-scale tree planting | Reversible (fire, felling)
Biochar | Char biomass, bury it | Feedstock supply
BECCS | Grow biomass, burn for energy, capture CO2 | Land vs food, water, monoculture plantations
DAC / DACCS | Machines pull CO2 from air | High cost and energy
Ocean fertilisation | Add iron/nutrients → phytoplankton bloom | Food-chain disruption, uncertain storage
Enhanced weathering | Spread silicate/carbonate rock | Dust, local water quality
BECCS can give net removal, unlike CCS on fossil plants
⚠ CDR cannot replace immediate emission cuts: costly, unproven at scale, governance gaps
## In news 2025-26
Sep 2026: overshoot study - every 5 years of high emissions adds 0.1°C peak warming and needs 220 billion t of CO2 removal to reverse
Oct 2026 UNEP Emissions Gap: return to 1.5°C by 2100 requires large-scale CDR alongside cuts

t: Geoengineering → two families
text:
## 1. Definition
Deliberate large-scale intervention in Earth's systems to counter climate change
Family | Aim | Examples
Solar Radiation Management (SRM) | Reflect a small share of sunlight to space | SAI, cirrus thinning, marine cloud brightening, space reflectors, surface albedo
Carbon Dioxide Removal (CDR / GGR) | Take GHGs out of the air | Afforestation, biochar, BECCS, DAC, ocean fertilisation, enhanced weathering
⚠ SRM treats the symptom (temperature), not CO2 levels: ocean acidification continues
⚠ Cloud seeding (artificial rain) is weather modification, not geoengineering
PYQ 2019: cirrus cloud thinning and sulphate aerosol injection into the stratosphere are suggested for reducing global warming - not artificial rain, cyclones or solar wind

t: SRM techniques → what each does
text:
## 1. Methods
Technique | Mechanism
Stratospheric Aerosol Injection (SAI) | SO2 injected into stratosphere → sulphuric acid aerosols raise albedo; mimics volcanic eruptions
Cirrus cloud thinning | Thin high ice clouds (6-13 km) that trap more heat than they reflect → more heat escapes (cooling)
Marine Cloud Brightening (MCB) | Spray sea-salt droplets; aerosols act as cloud condensation nuclei → brighter clouds
Space reflectors | Block some sunlight before it reaches Earth
Albedo enhancement | Make land surface or clouds more reflective
Cirrus clouds reflect little sunlight but absorb heat strongly → "strong warmers"
Venus is brightest planet because of reflective sulphuric acid clouds (~75% albedo)
⚠ Cirrus thinning works on outgoing heat, while SAI and MCB work on incoming sunlight

t: SRM risks → termination shock and side effects
text:
## 1. Stratospheric Aerosol Injection
Termination shock: if stopped suddenly, rapid warming within 10-20 years → dependence
Ineffective in polar winter (no sunlight)
May disrupt monsoons and hydrological cycle, delay ozone recovery, cause acid rain; masks warming and reduces urgency to cut emissions
Cools poles more than tropics (fairness concern)
Study figure (2025) | Value
SO2 for ~0.6°C cooling | 12 Mt/yr at 13 km
SO2 for 1°C cooling | 21 Mt/yr
## 2. Marine Cloud Brightening
Can change regional rainfall, reduce hurricane intensity, minor crop failures
## In news 2025-26
Jul 2026 study: MCB in the tropical Pacific can disrupt Bjerknes feedback (SST and trade winds) and strengthen El Niño

t: Polar geoengineering → five concepts and concerns
text:
## 1. The five (study, 2025)
Concept | What | Concern
SAI | Reflective SO2 aerosols | No sun in polar winter; termination shock
Sea curtains / walls | Buoyant barriers block warm water to ice shelves | Cost > $1 billion per km
Sea-ice management | Glass microbeads; pump seawater onto ice | 360 Mt beads/yr ≈ global plastic output; may absorb heat
Basal water removal | Pump water from under glaciers to slow flow | Disturbs subglacial environment
Ocean fertilisation | Iron to trigger phytoplankton | Food chains, nutrient cycles
Also proposed: artificial snow on the West Antarctic Ice Sheet (seawater pumped 1,500 m up by wind turbines)
⚠ Conclusion of the study: unproven at climate scale; immediate decarbonisation is the proven route

topic: Carbon credits, carbon markets and carbon pricing
t: Carbon credit → what it is, who sets the price
text:
## 1. Basics
1 carbon credit = 1 tonne of CO2 (or CO2-equivalent of another GHG such as methane)
Tradable certificate/permit; earned by afforestation, renewables, sequestration, methane capture, or bought on an exchange
Arose with the Kyoto Protocol (1997) flexible mechanisms
2011 statement | Verdict
Credit system ratified with Kyoto Protocol | Correct
Awarded to those who cut GHGs below quota | Correct
Goal: limit increase of CO2 emissions | Correct
Price fixed by UNEP from time to time | Wrong: price set by supply and demand on exchanges
MCX (India) launched carbon credit futures in 2009

topic: Carbon credits, carbon markets and carbon pricing
t: Kyoto flexible mechanisms → units each creates
text:
## 1. Three mechanisms
Mechanism | Between | Unit (1 unit = 1 t CO2)
Clean Development Mechanism (CDM) | Annex B party funds project in developing country (e.g. India) | CER (Certified Emission Reduction)
Joint Implementation (JI) | Annex B party funds project in another Annex B party | ERU (Emission Reduction Unit)
Emissions Trading (cap-and-trade) | Sell unused allowances (Kyoto quota) | Kyoto units
Land-use sinks | Reforestation | RMU (Removal Unit)
Non-compliance: shortfall + 30% extra in next period; may be barred from trading
Adaptation Fund (Poznan, 2008) is financed partly by a 2% share of CER proceeds
⚠ The Paris Article 6.4 mechanism succeeds the CDM
## Beyond your notes
Kyoto allowance unit = AAU (Assigned Amount Unit); CDM credits come from non-Annex I hosts, JI from Annex I (economies in transition) hosts

topic: Carbon credits, carbon markets and carbon pricing
t: Cap-and-trade vs offset vs carbon tax → how they differ
text:
## 1. Trading types
Type | Principle
Emission trading (cap-and-trade) | Cap set; firms with spare allowances sell to those over the limit
Offset trading (baseline-and-credit) | Credits earned by funding low-emission or carbon-capturing projects
## 2. Tax vs trading
Carbon tax (price instrument) | Carbon trading (quantity instrument)
Fixes the price; emissions vary | Fixes the quantity (cap); price varies
Pay for every tonne | Pay only beyond the quota
Price certainty, stable investment | Quantity certainty, cost uncertainty
India's "sort of carbon tax": Clean Energy Cess on coal (Budget 2010-11) → GST Compensation Cess ₹400/t → abolished by 56th GST Council (Sep 2025), GST on coal raised 5% → 18%
Proposed Differential Global Carbon Tax: high per-capita emitters pay low emitters (India top beneficiary)

topic: Carbon credits, carbon markets and carbon pricing
t: Carbon markets → Statement-I/II verdict and global spread
text:
## 1. The 2023 pair
Statement-I (likely one of the most widespread climate tools): correct - over 21% of world emissions under carbon pricing by end-2021 (15% in 2020); ~28% by 2025 with 43 carbon taxes and 37 ETSs (World Bank)
Statement-II (transfer resources from private sector to State): correct but not the explanation - in the official key, revenue reaches the State via auctions, taxes, tariffs
⚠ Answer key (b): both correct, II does not explain I. Some coaching summaries read II as false: in a market, money mostly moves firm to firm; go with the key
## 2. Criticisms of carbon markets
EU-ETS over-allocated allowances (lobbying); cheap CDM credits from China and India crashed prices
Almost 1 billion unretired credits in 2024 (supply > demand)
Carbon pricing raised > $100 billion for public budgets in 2024
PYQ 2023: Statement-I/II on carbon markets - both correct, II not the explanation

topic: Carbon credits, carbon markets and carbon pricing
t: Social cost of carbon → meaning
text:
## 1. Definition
Social Cost of Carbon (SCC) = monetary value of the long-term damage from emitting one extra tonne of CO2 in a given year
Puts climate impacts into money terms for policy and cost-benefit analysis
Term | Meaning
Social cost of carbon | Damage cost per extra tonne of CO2
Carbon footprint | GHG emitted by a person or product
Carbon intensity | GHG per unit of GDP/output
Carbon price | Price paid per tonne via tax or ETS
India's country-level SCC (2019-20) ≈ $91/t - the highest of any country; US next at ~$50
⚠ Distractors in 2020: fossil-fuel requirement of a country, a climate refugee's adaptation effort, a person's carbon footprint
PYQ 2020: SCC measures long-term damage of a tonne of CO2 in a given year (answer a)

text:

## 1. Basis
Article 4 (para 19) of Paris: Parties should strive to communicate long-term low GHG emission development strategies; COP26 urged submission by COP27

## 2. Four considerations
No. | Consideration

2 | Significant energy needs for development

International accounting tool for governments and business leaders to understand, quantify and manage GHG emissions

topic: Hydrogen: green hydrogen, fuel cells and H-CNG
t: Hydrogen colours → energy source and carbon capture
text:
## 1. The colour code
Colour | Made from | Process | Carbon capture?
Brown | Coal | Gasification | No
Grey | Natural gas / fossil fuels | Steam methane reforming (SMR) | No
Blue | Natural gas / fossil fuels | SMR | Yes (CCS)
Green | Renewable power (solar, wind, hydro) | Electrolysis of water | Not needed
## 2. Key facts
Electrolysis: 2H2O → 2H2 + O2 in an electrolyser (cathode + anode); about 9 litres of demineralised water per kg of H2 (MNRE, IEA)
India's Green Hydrogen Standard (MNRE, 2023): green only if emissions ≤ 2 kg CO2-eq per kg H2, well-to-gate, 12-month average
Green H2 can also come from biomass if it stays within the same 2 kg limit
Most hydrogen in India today is grey (methane reforming), used mainly to make ammonia fertiliser
⚠ Natural gas + CCS = blue, not green; green uses no fossil fuel at all
PYQ 2026: statement "green hydrogen is decarbonised hydrogen from natural gas reforming with CCS" was the trap (that is blue); electrolysis with RE and the Mission's ~50 MMT abatement were correct

text:
## 1. Three uses UPSC tested (all correct)
Use | How
Direct fuel in internal combustion engines | Hydrogen is combustible; burnt alone or blended (H2-ICE vehicles)
Blended with natural gas | For heat or power; city gas networks take H2 in limited proportions
Fuel cells | Hydrogen + oxygen → electricity → electric motor (FCEV)
## 2. Other uses (likely next)
Grid storage: surplus solar/wind → H2 → back to electricity at peak demand
Shipping: converted to green ammonia and green methanol as ship fuel
E-methanol: green H2 + captured CO2; Denmark's Kasso plant is the world's first commercial-scale e-methanol plant
Govt plan: 15% green hydrogen blending in PNG (domestic, commercial, industrial)
⚠ Hydrogen is an energy carrier, not an energy source: it must be made from water, gas or biomass
PYQ 2023 ("how many"): ICE fuel, blending with natural gas, fuel cells: all three correct

text:

Sector | Role of green hydrogen

Petroleum refineries | H2 removes sulphur from petrol and diesel (hydrotreating, hydrocracking)

High-temperature heat and chemical feedstock needs; direct electrification is difficult

topic: Hydrogen: green hydrogen, fuel cells and H-CNG
t: Hydrogen fuel cell vehicles → how they work and what they emit
text:
## 1. Fuel cell working
Electrochemical device: chemical energy → electrical energy directly (no burning)
H2 to anode; catalyst (platinum, palladium, gold) splits H2 into protons + electrons
Electrons flow through external circuit = current; protons cross the electrolyte to the cathode, join oxygen
By-products: water (vapour), heat, air
Item | Fact
Tailpipe emission of FCEV | Only water vapour (and warm air)
Common fuel cell types | Hydrogen and phosphoric acid; also methanol, ethanol, natural gas cells
Advantage | More efficient than thermal plants
Drawback | Costly catalysts (platinum, palladium)
Overall efficiency order: EVs > Hydrogen > Diesel > Petrol vehicles
⚠ Options in 2024: hydrogen peroxide, hydronium, oxygen, water vapour; only water vapour is right
PYQ 2024: exhaust of hydrogen FCEV = water vapour

topic: Hydrogen: green hydrogen, fuel cells and H-CNG
t: Hydrogen as fuel → storage and challenges
text:
## 1. Storage forms
Form | Condition | Issue
Compressed gas | 350-700 bar | Low energy per volume, pressure risk
Liquid hydrogen | -253°C (boils at -252.8°C) | Liquefaction energy, boil-off
Solid-state | Metal hydrides (MgH2), MOFs | Heavy, slow release
## 2. Fuel facts
Highest energy by weight (~3x petrol) but lowest by volume (~4x less as liquid)
Smallest molecule: leaks easily; highly reactive with oxygen
Lack of refuelling stations; EVs are more efficient overall
Palladium hydride absorbs hydrogen at low temperature (UPPCS 2008)
## In news 2025-26
India's first indigenous hydrogen train: Jind-Sonipat (89 km), Haryana, Northern Railway; designed by RDSO, built by ICF Chennai; 10-coach, world's longest and most powerful hydrogen train; emits only water vapour and heat
Hydrogen for Heritage: 35 hydrogen trainsets on heritage/hill routes
NGHM pilots: 37 hydrogen buses and trucks on 10 routes with 9 refuelling stations

topic: Hydrogen: green hydrogen, fuel cells and H-CNG
t: H-CNG → blend share, emissions and cost
text:
## 1. Facts
H-CNG = CNG + hydrogen; 4-9% H2 by energy; flame speed up to 8x CNG
MoRTH allowed 18% H2 blending (by volume) in CNG engines; CMV Rules 1989 amended to add H-CNG as automotive fuel
Delhi: first city to run H-CNG buses
## 2. Emissions and cost
Claim | Correct?
Eliminates carbon monoxide | No: cuts CO by up to 70%
Reduces CO2 and hydrocarbon emissions | Yes
Hydrogen up to one-fifth by volume | Yes (~18-20%)
Cheaper than CNG | No: slightly costlier
Up to 5% fuel savings; higher octane; engines can be tuned for lower NOx; suited to heavy-duty vehicles
⚠ "Reduces" is right, "eliminates" is wrong: the classic H-CNG trap
PYQ 2019: answer 2 and 3 only (reduces CO2/HC; up to one-fifth H2)
## In news 2025-26
MoRTH draft (2026) revises gaseous fuel terms to include H-CNG mixtures in CMV Rules

## 1. Four generations
Gen | Feedstock | Examples | Issue
1G (basic, conventional) | Food crops: sugarcane, maize, edible oils, animal fat | Bioethanol, biodiesel, biogas | Food vs fuel
2G (lignocellulosic) | Non-food biomass: rice/wheat straw, bagasse, corn stover, bamboo, wood waste, MSW, jatropha | Cellulosic ethanol, FT diesel, bio-CNG | High enzyme/pre-treatment cost
3G | Algae (micro, macro/seaweed, cyanobacteria) | Algal biodiesel, ethanol, biohydrogen | Costly harvesting, R&D stage
4G | GM crops/microbes + CCS/CCU | E-fuels, BECCS fuels, drop-ins | Experimental; carbon-negative aim
## 2. Key facts
Ethanol energy = ~65-70% of petrol (~27% less energy-dense); E10-E20 cut mileage up to 7%

t: Algae (3G) biofuels → advantages and limits
text:
## 1. Advantages
Grown in ponds, tanks, photobioreactors on land, open ponds, wastewater, saline/brackish water; uses non-arable land
10-30x more oil per acre than oil crops; biomass doubles in 6-10 hours
No food-vs-fuel clash; absorbs CO2 (even flue gas); one feedstock → biodiesel, ethanol, biogas, hydrogen, jet fuel
## 2. Limits
Limitation | Detail
High expertise/technology | Engineering until construction is complete
Large-scale facilities | Needed for viability; ecological and social concerns (water, land, energy)
High cost | Harvesting, dewatering, lipid extraction
Not commercial | Still R&D/pilot stage
Competing uses | Nutraceuticals, cosmetics pay more
Species: Chlorella, Spirulina, Botryococcus braunii, Dunaliella; seaweeds Sargassum, Gracilaria
⚠ "Algae biofuel possible only in seas, not on continents" is false
PYQ 2017: limits = expertise + large-scale facilities (2 and 3 only)

## 1. Comparison
Feature | Solar PV | Solar thermal
Principle | Photovoltaic effect: light → electricity directly | Sunlight → heat → steam → turbine
Output | DC (inverter makes AC) | AC (via turbine-generator)
Material | Silicon semiconductor, p-n junction | Collectors, mirrors, molten salt
Uses | Rooftop, parks, street lights, pumps | Water heaters, cookers, CSP plants

text:
## 1. Mechanism
Two reservoirs at different heights
Low demand / surplus solar-wind: power pumps water up to the upper reservoir
Peak demand: water flows down through turbines → electricity
Acts as a large "water battery" for the grid: long-duration energy storage
Feature | Fact
Efficiency | ~70-80%
Life | 40-60 years

text:
## 1. Who defined it
Item | Fact
Body | Brundtland Commission = World Commission on Environment and Development (WCED), UN-mandated, early 1980s
Report | Our Common Future (1987)
Definition | "Meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs"
Purpose | Bridge the conflict between economic development and environmental protection
## 2. Key words of the definition
Catch words: "needs" (linked to distribution of resources) and "future generations"
Our Common Future: meet the basic needs of all; redistribution = a moral issue
Edward Barbier: raise the material living standard of the poor at the grassroots
⚠ NCERT writes that UNCED defined it; the definition comes from the 1987 Brundtland report, which UNCED (1992) took up

topic: Sustainable development: concept and carrying capacity
t: Sustainable development → carrying capacity
text:
## 1. Meaning
Carrying capacity = the maximum ecosystem services (or population) an ecosystem can support sustainably; beyond it, the system degrades
Sustainable development is intertwined with carrying capacity: development must stay within ecological limits
## 2. Herman Daly's five conditions (NCERT)
Condition | Rule
Population | Keep it within the carrying capacity (like a ship's plimsoll line)
Technology | Input-efficient, not input-consuming
Renewable resources | Extraction rate not above regeneration rate
Non-renewable resources | Depletion rate not above creation of renewable substitutes
Pollution | Inefficiencies from pollution corrected
⚠ Distractors in the 2010 PYQ: social justice, inclusive growth, globalisation; the answer is carrying capacity
PYQ 2010: Brundtland's definition "is intertwined with" carrying capacity

topic: Sustainable development: concept and carrying capacity

t: CBD → three objectives, parties and non-parties
text:
## 1. Basics
Legally binding; opened for signature at the Rio Earth Summit 1992, in force 29 Dec 1993
Secretariat: Montreal, Canada (hosted under UNEP)
India ratified 1994; implemented by Biological Diversity Act 2002 (NBA Chennai, SBBs, BMCs)
## 2. Three objectives
# | Objective
1 | Conservation of biological diversity
2 | Sustainable use of its components
3 | Fair and equitable sharing of benefits from genetic resources (ABS)
## 3. Parties
196 Parties (195 countries + EU)
Not ratified: USA, Andorra, South Sudan, Holy See
⚠ "All UN members are CBD parties" is false: USA is the big exception
Article 26: each Party submits National Reports (about every 4 years)

t: Nagoya Protocol → access and benefit-sharing (ABS)
text:
## 1. Core facts
Item | Fact
Adopted | COP10, 2010, Nagoya (Japan) (29 Oct)
In force | 12 Oct 2014
Status | Second protocol to CBD (first = Cartagena 2000)
Parties | 142 (141 states + EU)
Subject | Access to genetic resources + fair sharing of benefits (CBD objective 3)
## 2. Key obligations
Prior Informed Consent (PIC) of the provider country before access
Mutually Agreed Terms (MAT) for monetary or non-monetary benefit-sharing
Compliance: users must not use illegally acquired genetic resources
Covers plant, animal, microbial resources + traditional knowledge; human genetic material excluded
⚠ India's date: PMF Environment says India a party "(2014)"; Prelims Magnum 2027-Q3 says since 2012 (India ratified in 2012; the Protocol entered into force in 2014)
