Feature | What the Act does
Schedules | Species get different levels of protection; scheduled animals cannot be hunted
Schedule changes | GoI can add, delete or transfer entries between Schedules
Protected Areas | Sanctuary, National Park, Conservation Reserve, Community Reserve (+ Tiger Reserve)
Trade | Controlled through permits and licences
Authorities | State Govt appoints the Chief Wildlife Warden; Central Govt appoints Directors / Assistant Directors
Penalties | Imprisonment and fines for hunting, trade, commercial exploitation
## Beyond your notes
Wildlife entered the Concurrent List by the 42nd Amendment (1976): Entry 17B "protection of wild animals and birds" (forests = 17A); same amendment added Art 48A (DPSP) and Art 51A(g) (Fundamental Duty)
⚠ Wildlife is Concurrent, not State List: this is why a State (Kerala 2025) needs Presidential assent to amend the WPA for itself

t: Old schedules (1972 Act, six) → protection level
text:
## 1. The six schedules before 2022
Schedule | Species | Protection
I | Critically endangered animals | Hunting and trade prohibited throughout India; highest penalties
II | Less endangered than Sch I | Hunting and trade prohibited throughout India
III | Big game species | Hunting prohibited; penalties less severe
IV | Small game species | Hunting prohibited; penalties less severe
V | Vermin | Hunting without restriction
VI | Plants (specified plants) | Cultivation and planting prohibited without licence
Vermin = small wild animals that carry disease and destroy plants and food
## Beyond your notes
Old Sch V vermin (4): common crow, fruit bats, mice, rats
Old Sch VI specified plants (6): Beddome's cycad, Blue Vanda, Kuth (Saussurea), Ladies' slipper orchids, Pitcher plant (Nepenthes khasiana), Red Vanda
PYQ 2020: Schedule VI plant = licence is required to cultivate it; traps: "cannot be cultivated under any circumstances", "GM crop", "invasive"

t: New schedules (2022 Amendment, four) → what each lists
text:
## 1. Rationalised to four (in force from 1 April 2023)
Schedule | Lists | Protection
I | Animals with the highest protection, incl. critically endangered | Highest
II | Animals with lower protection than Sch I | Close to Sch I
III | Protected plant species (old Sch VI) | Licence for cultivation / dealing
IV | Specimens listed in CITES Appendices ("scheduled specimens") | Penalties less severe
## 2. What changed
Animal schedules 4 → 2 (one for greater protection)
Vermin schedule removed (old Sch V)
New CITES schedule inserted (Sch IV)
⚠ Old Sch VI (plants) = new Sch III; a question naming "Schedule VI" uses the pre-2022 numbering
⚠ New Sch IV is the CITES schedule, not "small game" as in the old Act
Hunting of any scheduled species prohibited, except when the CWLW permits (human life, property, scientific management)

t: Schedule I → what "Schedule I status" implies
text:
## 1. Meaning
Schedule I = same highest level of protection as the tiger; hunting and trade banned all over India; heaviest penalties
Examples (PMF): tiger, clouded leopard, blackbuck, snow leopard; also gharial, Indian wild ass, wild buffalo (2017 PYQ)
Option UPSC gave (2017) | Correct?
Same protection as the tiger | Yes
Extinct in the wild, kept in captivity | No
Endemic to a region of India | No
⚠ Schedule I says nothing about endemism or extinction status; it is a legal protection level
## 2. Criticisms of the 2022 Schedule I
Same schedule for tiger, jackal, great Indian bustard, barn owl - no prioritisation
Chital now Sch I though invasive in Andamans - hinders culling
Wild pig and nilgai raised to Sch I - states cannot do limited culls of crop raiders
PYQ 2017: a tortoise in Schedule I "enjoys the same level of protection as the tiger"

t: Licensing Rules 2024 → which schedules can get trade licences
text:
## 1. Wildlife (Protection) Licensing (Additional Matters for Consideration) Rules, 2024
Notified by MoEFCC; replace the 1983 Rules
New guidelines for licences in snake venom, captive animals, trophy animals, stuffed animals
Rules | Licence bar | Note
1983 | Sch I and Part II of Sch II | Exceptional cases with prior Central approval
2024 | Sch I only | Prior consultation with GoI; Sch II restrictions lifted
New criteria: capacity, source of supplies, implications for hunting or trade
⚠ 2024 Rules lifted the bar on Schedule II; Schedule I licences still barred (except with GoI consultation)

t: Hunting ban → which animals cannot be hunted
text:
## 1. The rule
Wild animals specified in the Schedules cannot be hunted by any person, except as provided by law
Animal (2017 PYQ) | Hunting?
Gharial | Cannot be hunted except as permitted by law
Indian wild ass | Cannot be hunted except as permitted by law
Wild buffalo | Cannot be hunted except as permitted by law
Answer "1, 2 and 3": all three are Schedule I animals
⚠ Do not drop wild buffalo as "domesticated": the wild water buffalo is protected (Kaziranga holds wild water buffaloes)
## Beyond your notes
"Hunting" in the Act is wide: killing, poisoning, capturing, trapping, snaring, baiting, injuring, and taking eggs or nests
PYQ 2017: asked which of three cannot be hunted; trap: thinking only a "famous" animal like the gharial is protected

t: Exceptions → when a protected animal may be killed and by whom
text:
## 1. Section 11 (CWLW's power)
A scheduled animal may be hunted/killed only with permission of the State's Chief Wildlife Warden if it:
Situation | Permitted?
Has become dangerous to human life | Yes
Is diseased beyond recovery | Yes
Is disabled beyond recovery | Yes
Merely apprehended to become dangerous | No
Otherwise hunted normally | No
Also permitted by CWLW: protection of property, scientific management (2022 Amendment wording)
⚠ "Apprehension" of danger is not enough; the animal must actually pose a threat (2022 PYQ)
## Beyond your notes
Section 12: special permits for education, scientific research, scientific management, collection for zoos/museums, and snake venom for life-saving drugs
Self-defence killing is not an offence, but the animal killed becomes Government property

t: Ownership → whose property a wild animal is
text:
## 1. Section 39 (Government property)
Situation | Owner
Wild animal hunted, its parts, hunting tools, captive-bred animals | State Government
Animal hunted in a Sanctuary / National Park declared by the Central Govt | Central Government
2022: a live government-property animal that cannot go back to the wild must be housed in a recognised zoo or rescue centre; hunted parts (incl. meat) disposed of as GoI prescribes, no commercial sale
## 2. Equal protection
The WPA does not discriminate between animals inside and outside Protected Areas: a declared protected animal gets equal protection anywhere
2022 PYQ statement | Verdict
Wild animals are the sole property of the government | Wrong
Protected animal entitled to equal protection inside or outside PAs | Correct
Apprehension of danger is sufficient ground to capture/kill | Wrong
⚠ Only animals hunted, captive or seized become Government property; the Act does not declare all wildlife "sole property" of government
PYQ 2022: answer "2 only"; the trap was the word sole and the word apprehension

t: Vermin → who declares, for how long
text:
## 1. Vermin declaration (Section 62)
Only the Central Government can declare a wild animal vermin (Section 62)
Process: State requests MoEFCC → Centre notifies the species as vermin for a specified region and duration
Status is temporary and area-limited; vermin lose legal protection
Common examples: rats, mice, common crows, fruit bats
⚠ Schedule I animals cannot be declared vermin
## In news 2025-26
Kerala asked the Centre to declare wild boar vermin for six months in conflict-hotspot villages
Kerala proposed moving the s.11(1)(a) power from the CWLW to regional Chief Conservators of Forests (Kerala has five CCFs)
Wild Life Protection (Kerala Amendment) Bill, 2025 passed by the Kerala Assembly (Oct 2025): lets the State declare Schedule II animals vermin for set regions/periods; CWLW may order killing/capture/tranquillising/relocating of animals causing serious injury; regional conservators and panchayats may act
Needs Presidential assent under Art 254(2) (amends a central law on a Concurrent subject)
⚠ Criticism: conflicts with the WPA, which gives the Union exclusive power over schedules

topic: Sanctuary and National Park - legal regime
t: National Park vs Sanctuary → rights, grazing, boundaries
text:
## 1. The core differences
Point | Wildlife Sanctuary | National Park
Declared by | State (or Central) Govt notification | State (or Central) Govt notification
Rights of people | Certain rights may be permitted | No rights permitted
Grazing | Regulated / controlled / prohibited by CWLW | No livestock grazing
Biomass / forest produce | Collection for bona fide needs allowed | Not allowed
Boundaries | Not precisely specified | Clearly demarcated
Human activity | Limited biotic interference | None, except as authorised by CWLW
A sanctuary can be upgraded to a National Park; all sanctuary rules also apply to NPs
Protection order: NP > Sanctuary > Reserved Forest > Protected Forest
⚠ In June 2022 the Supreme Court barred mining inside national parks and wildlife sanctuaries
PYQ 2012: local people cannot collect/use biomass in National Parks; allowed (regulated) in sanctuaries, biosphere reserves, Ramsar wetlands

topic: Sanctuary and National Park - legal regime
t: National Park boundaries → who fixes and who alters them
text:
## 1. Boundaries
NP boundaries are defined (demarcated) by the State through notification; UPSC 2010 accepted "defined by legislation"
State Govt cannot alter NP boundaries without the National Board for Wildlife's recommendation
Alteration is by resolution of the State Legislature on NBWL recommendation (Preview: "except on a resolution passed by the Legislature of the State")
The same NBWL rule covers sanctuaries, conservation and community reserves (Section 26A: prior NBWL approval before altering a PA boundary)
2010 PYQ statement | Verdict
NP boundaries defined by legislation | Correct
Biosphere Reserve declared to conserve a few specific species | Wrong - whole ecosystems
Limited biotic interference permitted in a sanctuary | Correct
## In news 2025-26
Nahargarh WLS (Rajasthan): state altered boundaries, allegedly to benefit hotels in the ESZ; s.26A needs prior NBWL approval
⚠ Answer 2010 = "1 and 3 only"

topic: Sanctuary and National Park - legal regime
t: Sanctuary → who manages and what is allowed inside
text:
## 1. Management
Chief Wildlife Warden controls, manages and maintains all sanctuaries; CWLW appointed by State Govt
2022: CWLW must act per sanctuary management plans made on GoI guidelines; in Scheduled Areas and FRA areas plans need Gram Sabha consultation
State appoints a Collector to settle people's rights
Grazing and firewood by tribals permitted but strictly regulated; settlements not allowed (relocation attempted)
## 2. Non-prohibited activities in a sanctuary
1972 Act | 2022 Amendment adds
Grazing or movement of livestock | Hunting within permit conditions
CWLW permits only for residents' bona fide personal needs, not commercial | Exercise of land rights allowed to continue
- | Bona fide drinking and household water by local people
⚠ Without a CWLW permit nobody may harm wildlife, alter habitat or change water flow in a sanctuary

topic: Sanctuary and National Park - legal regime
t: Protected Area network → how many of each (2026)
text:
## 1. India's PA network (ENVIS, Feb 2026, per Preview)
Category | Number
Total PAs | 1134 (≈1.87 lakh km², 5.69% of geographic area)
National Parks | 106
Wildlife Sanctuaries | 574
Conservation Reserves | 145
Community Reserves | 309
Most NPs: Madhya Pradesh (11), then Assam (7); most sanctuaries: Andaman & Nicobar (96)
First NP: Jim Corbett (1936, as Hailey NP), Uttarakhand; Project Tiger launched there in 1973
⚠ Biosphere reserves and tiger reserves are not counted as separate PA categories in the 4-category ENVIS list
⚠ PMF (Prelims Magnum 2025-06) cites "109 National Parks (2023)"; the 106 figure is the ENVIS 2026 count in Preview

t: Community Reserve → who manages, what is banned and allowed
text:
## 1. Declaration (Section 36C)
State Govt declares any private or community land where an individual/community has volunteered to conserve wildlife
Land must not be within a National Park, Sanctuary or Conservation Reserve
Aim: protect fauna, flora and traditional or cultural conservation values and practices
## 2. Management (Section 36D)
Community Reserve Management Committee = the authority that conserves, maintains and manages it
Members: not less than five nominated by the Village Panchayat (or Gram Sabha where no Panchayat) + one rep of the State Forest/Wildlife Dept
On private land: the committee includes the land owner
Committee elects a Chairman who is also the Honorary Wildlife Warden
2023 PYQ statement | Verdict
CWLW becomes the governing authority | Wrong - Management Committee
Hunting not allowed | Correct
People may collect NTFP | Correct
Traditional agriculture allowed | Wrong - no agriculture, no jhum
⚠ UPSC framed it as "Central Government notifies"; the Act gives the power to the State Government
PYQ 2023: answer "Only two"; trap: CWLW manages sanctuaries, not community reserves

t: Conservation Reserve → who declares, which land, who advises
text:
## 1. Section 36A (added by 2002 Amendment)
State Govt may declare land owned by it, especially adjacent to NPs and sanctuaries and land linking one PA with another
Precondition: consultation with local communities
Conservation Reserve Management Committee (s.36B) advises the CWLW
Regulated low-impact activities; hunting and habitat destruction banned
Point | Conservation Reserve | Community Reserve
Land | Government-owned | Private or community
Typical place | Next to PAs / corridors | Anywhere not in NP/WLS/CR
Who manages | CWLW, advised by CRMC | Management Committee itself
Rights of residents | Not affected | Not affected
⚠ 2022 Amendment also empowers the GoI to notify a conservation reserve
## In news 2025-26
Kumram Bheem CR (Telangana, 1,492 km²): corridor linking Kawal TR with Tadoba-Andhari TR; a nesting site of the long-billed vulture; 240+ bird species
Tsarap Chu CR (Spiti, HP): India's largest high-altitude PA; links Kibber and Chandratal WLS
Greater Hessarghatta Grasslands (Bengaluru) approved as a CR by Karnataka

t: Protected Areas under WPA → which five, declared by whom
text:
## 1. The five PA types (PMF)
PA | Declared by | Key condition
Wildlife Sanctuary | State or Central Govt | Rights determined by Collector
National Park | State or Central Govt | No rights; boundary change needs NBWL
Conservation Reserve | State Govt (now GoI too) | Govt land; consult local people
Community Reserve | State Govt | Private/community land; volunteers
Tiger Reserve | State Govt | On recommendation of NTCA
"Protected Area" is defined in the WPA: NP, Sanctuary, Conservation Reserve, Community Reserve
⚠ Biosphere Reserve, ESZ, Reserved Forest are not PAs under the WPA
## In news 2025-26
Gogabeel (Bihar's first Community Reserve, 2019) became India's 94th Ramsar site
SC (2025) told Rajasthan to map sacred groves as forests and notify them as community reserves

t: Tiger Reserve → core, buffer and notification steps
text:
## 1. Legal regime
Protection status same as a sanctuary; monitored by NTCA (statutory, WPA amended 2006)
Core = Critical Tiger Habitat (CTH): NP or sanctuary, inviolate - no mining, grazing, tourism
Buffer: forest + non-forest land, limited human activity, eases pressure on core
Step | Who
Identify area | State Govt
Proposal review | NTCA, then MoEFCC
Preliminary notification | State Govt under WPA
Final notification | State Govt under Section 38V
Boundary change / de-notification: only on NTCA recommendation + NBWL approval (de-notify only in public interest)
CTH | CWLH
Only tiger reserves, under WPA | Any PA, under FRA 2006 after settling rights
## In news 2025-26
Madhav NP (MP) became India's 58th TR (2025); Ratapani WLS was the 57th (2024)
Sariska: Rajasthan proposed redrawing its CTH; boundary changes need SC-NBWL approval
AP set up a State-Level Steering Committee (s.38U) for Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam TR, India's largest TR
SC (2024): tiger safaris only outside core and buffer

t: Biosphere Reserve → purpose and legal status
text:
## 1. What it is
Large protected terrestrial, marine and coastal ecosystems designated under UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere (MAB) Programme after national nomination
UNESCO: "learning places for sustainable development" - conserve wildlife, plant and animal resources and the traditional life of tribals
No change in legal status: land/forest laws and ownership stay the same; the country keeps sovereignty
May contain one or more NPs or sanctuaries
Body | Role
IN-MAB Committee (MoEF) | Recommends sites to UNESCO
State Govt | Prepares Management Action Plan
IN-MAB | Approves and monitors the plan
GoI funding | 90:10 NE + 3 Himalayan states; 60:40 others
⚠ BR is not created under the WPA; only its core (NP/WLS) is regulated by the WPA
PYQ 2014: conservation of biodiversity together with traditional human life = biosphere reserves; NPs and sanctuaries discourage human activity

t: Biosphere Reserve zones → what each zone allows
text:
## 1. Core-buffer-transition
Zone | Human activity
Core | None; strictly protected; usually NP/WLS under WPA
Buffer | Limited: research, monitoring, training, education, limited recreation
Transition | Sustainable settlements, agriculture, forestry, tourism
## 2. UNESCO criteria
An effectively protected, minimally disturbed core
Core sustains viable populations of all trophic levels
A management authority that secures cooperation of local (tribal) communities
Seville Strategy (1995): added social, cultural, spiritual and economic needs of people
⚠ Preview says "BRs entertain no human activity" - true only of the core; PMF: transition zone has settlements
PYQ 2010: a BR conserves representative ecosystems as a whole, not "a few specific species"

t: Biosphere Reserves in India → how many and the newest
text:
## 1. Counts
India has 13 BRs in UNESCO's World Network of Biosphere Reserves (WNBR)
WNBR: created 1971 under MAB; 785 sites in 142 countries (2025)
## In news 2025-26
Cold Desert BR (Lahaul-Spiti, HP) added to WNBR at the 37th MAB session, Paris (Sept 2025) - India's 13th
India's first high-altitude cold desert BR; covers Pin Valley NP, Kibber WLS, Chandratal WLS
São Tomé and Príncipe: first country with its entire territory a biosphere reserve
## Beyond your notes
India has 18 notified BRs (as of 2026); first: Nilgiri (1986), also India's first in WNBR (2000)
Largest by area: Great Rann of Kachchh BR, Gujarat (verify)
⚠ 18 notified nationally vs 13 in UNESCO's WNBR - "how many" questions turn on this gap

t: Eco-Sensitive Zones → law, width and activities
text:
## 1. Legal basis
Notified by MoEFCC around NPs and sanctuaries as shock absorbers / transition zones
Under Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 (Rule 5), not the WPA; the EPA does not even use the word "ESZ"
National Wildlife Action Plan 2002-2016: land within 10 km of PAs; GoI can go beyond 10 km for corridors
SC, June 2022: minimum 1 km ESZ around every PA unless exempted
Category | Activities
Prohibited | Commercial mining, sawmills, polluting industries, major hydro projects, effluent discharge, commercial firewood, flying over PAs
Regulated | Tree felling, hotels/resorts, commercial groundwater use, drastic farm changes
Permitted | Ongoing farming/horticulture by locals, rainwater harvesting, organic farming, renewables
⚠ UPSC 2014: ESZs are not declared under the WPA and do not ban all activity except agriculture - answer "Neither"
## In news 2025-26
ESZs notified around Barasingha WLS (UP, 408.7 km², Apr 2026) and Parvati-Arga Bird Sanctuary (UP)

topic: Bodies under WPA and the 2022 Amendment
t: Statutory bodies → chair and main power
text:
## 1. Bodies under the WPA
Body | Basis | Chair | Key power
NBWL | s.5A, 2002 Amendment (replaced IBWL 1952) | Prime Minister | Approves projects in PAs; no PA boundary change without it
SBWL | 2002 Amendment | Chief Minister | Advises State on PA selection, schedules, tribal needs
CZA | WPA (1991 Amendment) | Environment Minister | Recognises/derecognises zoos
NTCA | 2006 Amendment | Environment Minister | Recommends tiger reserves; runs Project Tiger
WCCB | 2006 Amendment | - (HQ New Delhi) | Wildlife crime intelligence, data bank
NBWL: 47 members; Vice-Chair = Environment Minister; 3 MPs (2 LS + 1 RS), 5 NGO reps, 10 ecologists, Chief of Army Staff; status report on wildlife every 2 years
SC-NBWL (Standing Committee, chaired by Environment Minister) clears projects in PAs, tiger reserves and corridors
⚠ NBWL chair = PM; NTCA and CZA chair = Environment Minister; SBWL = CM
## In news 2025-26
PM chaired the 7th NBWL meeting at Gir NP (2025): wildlife health referral centre at Junagadh, Project Gharial, human-animal conflict centre at SACON, Coimbatore
## Beyond your notes
CZA set up in 1992 under the 1991 Amendment (verify)

topic: Bodies under WPA and the 2022 Amendment
t: Chief Wildlife Warden → powers under the Act
text:
## 1. CWLW (appointed by the State Govt)
Power | Where
Permit killing of dangerous/diseased/disabled scheduled animals | s.11
Control, manage, maintain sanctuaries (per management plan since 2022) | Sanctuary chapter
Permits to enter sanctuary, alter habitat or water flow | Sanctuary chapter
Regulate/prohibit grazing in sanctuaries | Sanctuary chapter
Authorise activity inside a National Park | NP chapter
Licence to cultivate specified plants (or officer authorised by State) | Plants chapter
Receive voluntary surrender of captive animals (2022) | New provision
Approve captive elephant transfers for welfare | 2024 Rules
⚠ CWLW does not govern a Community Reserve (Management Committee) and is only advised by the Conservation Reserve committee
## In news 2025-26
Tiger Outside Tiger Reserve pilot (CAMPA funding): NTCA + state CWLWs in 80 forest divisions, 10 states

topic: Bodies under WPA and the 2022 Amendment
t: WPA amendments → what each added
text:
## 1. Amendments up to 2021 (seven): 1982, 1986, 1991, 1993, 2002, 2006, 2013
Year | Added
1982 | Capture and transport of wild animals for scientific management
2002 | NBWL, SBWL; Conservation and Community Reserves (s.36A-36D)
2006 | NTCA, WCCB, tiger reserves; inviolate spaces with voluntary relocation
2013 | Protects hunting rights of Scheduled Tribes in Andaman & Nicobar
2022 | Schedules 6 → 4, CITES chapter, invasive species, elephants
⚠ Conservation/Community Reserves came in 2002, not in the original 1972 Act

topic: Bodies under WPA and the 2022 Amendment
t: WPA Amendment 2022 → what changed versus 1972
text:
## 1. Objectives
Give effect to CITES obligations; rationalise schedules; strengthen species protection; better PA management; benefit tribal communities
Aspect | 1972 | 2022
Purpose words | "protection of wild animals, birds and plants" | "protection, conservation and management of wildlife"
Invasive alien species | No provision | Defined; Centre can regulate/ban import, trade, possession
CITES | No provision | GoI designates Management Authority (permits) and Scientific Authority (advice)
Captive elephants | No commercial transfer | Transfer/transport for religious or other purposes allowed
Surrender of captive animals | No provision | Voluntary surrender to CWLW, no compensation; becomes State property
Conservation reserve | Only State declares | GoI can also notify
Possessors of live scheduled animals need registration from the Management Authority; breeders of Appendix I species need a licence; altering a specimen's identification mark is barred
⚠ Criticism: "other purposes" for elephants is vague; more Central power over a Concurrent subject

topic: Bodies under WPA and the 2022 Amendment
t: Captive Elephant Rules 2024 → conditions for transfer
text:
## 1. Captive Elephant (Transfer or Transport) Rules, 2024 (March 2024)
Regulate the 2022 "religious or other purposes" clause
Transfer allowed if the owner cannot maintain the elephant or CWLW finds it needed for the animal's welfare
Transfer only if the elephant's genetic profile is registered on the Ministry's electronic portal
Exempt from the bar on commercial sale (1972) | Status
Peacock tail feathers and articles from them | Exempt
Captive animals moved between recognised zoos / zoos and museums | Exempt
⚠ Commercial trade in elephants is still prohibited; only non-commercial transfer is eased

topic: Bodies under WPA and the 2022 Amendment
t: CITES link → who is India's Management Authority
text:
## 1. CITES and Schedule IV
CITES signed 1973 (Washington DC), India ratified 1976; 185 Parties; Secretariat under UNEP, Geneva
Legally binding but does not override national law - hence the WPA 2022 CITES chapter
Appendix | Species | Trade
I | Threatened with extinction | Only in exceptional cases
II | Not yet endangered but may become so | Regulated
III | Protected in at least one country seeking help | Cooperation
India's Management Authority: ADG (Wildlife), MoEFCC; WCCB also acts as a Management Authority and issues permits
⚠ WPA Schedule IV = CITES-listed specimens; tiger is Sch I of WPA and Appendix I of CITES

t: Major environmental laws → year, purpose, body created
text:
## 1. The core list
Law | Year | Key point
Indian Forest Act | 1927 | Reserved / Protected / Village forests; duty on timber
Wild Life (Protection) Act | 1972 | National parks, sanctuaries notified under it
Water (P&CP) Act | 1974 | Created CPCB and SPCBs
Water Cess Act | 1977 | Cess on industrial water use for the Boards
Forest (Conservation) Act → Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam | 1980 | Central approval to divert forest land
Air (P&CP) Act | 1981 | Air pollution; consent in air pollution control areas
Environment (Protection) Act | 1986 | Umbrella law, after Bhopal (1984)
Public Liability Insurance Act | 1991 | Relief for hazardous-substance accidents
Biological Diversity Act | 2002 | NBA-SBB-BMC; benefit sharing
Forest Rights Act | 2006 | Rights of forest dwellers; Gram Sabha
NGT Act | 2010 | Green tribunal; appeals within 6 months
Compensatory Afforestation Fund Act | 2016 | National and State CAF and CAMPA
⚠ CPCB was created by the Water Act 1974, not the EPA; EPA only uses it for technical services

t: Constitution → Articles on environment
text:
## 1. Provisions
Provision | Content
Art 48A (DPSP) | State shall protect and improve environment, safeguard forests and wildlife
Art 51A(g) (Fundamental Duty) | Every citizen to protect environment incl. forests, lakes, rivers, wildlife; compassion for living creatures
Art 21 | Right to life read to include right to a healthy environment (NGT Act rests on it)
Art 253 | Parliament can legislate to implement international treaties/decisions: basis of EPA 1986 (Stockholm 1972)
42nd Amendment (1976) | Added 48A, 51A(g); moved 'Forests' and 'Protection of wild animals and birds' from State to Concurrent List
'Environment' is in no list → residuary → Centre
Department of Environment 1980 → MoEF 1985 → MoEFCC 2014
⚠ 48A binds the State; 51A(g) binds the citizen

t: Water Act 1974 → boards, consent and amendments
text:
## 1. Provisions
Aim: prevent/control water pollution, maintain wholesomeness of water
Prior consent of SPCB to set up any industry/local body discharging sewage or effluent; then consent to operate
Amended 1978, 1988, 2024; 1988 widened scope to groundwater pollution (Environment & DM book)
## 2. Water (P&CP) Amendment Act, 2024
Change | Detail
Decriminalisation | Minor offences: penalty ₹10,000 to ₹15 lakh instead of jail
Exemption | Centre (with CPCB) may exempt some industrial plants from consent
Guidelines | Centre may issue guidelines on grant/refusal of consent
SPCB chair | Centre prescribes manner of nomination and service terms
Water Cess Act 1977: 70% rebate on cess for installing effluent treatment
PCBs can levy environmental compensation under s.33A Water Act and s.31A Air Act (SC ruling, LENS Aug 2025; polluter pays)
## Beyond your notes
Water Cess Act, 1977 was repealed in 2017 when the cess was subsumed into GST (verify)

t: Air Act 1981 → consent areas and amendments
text:
## 1. Provisions
Enacted to implement Stockholm 1972 decisions
Industries in air pollution control areas need SPCB consent; SPCBs set emission standards for industry and automobiles after consulting CPCB
CPCB acts as SPCB for UTs
## 2. Amendments
Amendment | Change
1987 | Boards can close defaulting plants; citizen suit; noise pollution added
Jan Vishwas 2023 | Penalties ₹10,000-15 lakh + daily fines; adjudicating officers (JS rank); appeal to NGT within 60 days with 10% pre-deposit; money to Environment Protection Fund
Rules 2024 | Inquiry and penalty: notice within 30 days, finish within 6 months
Jail remains for operating without consent (s.21) or not paying penalty within 90 days
⚠ "Noise" came into the Air Act (1987), not the Water Act

t: EPA 1986 → background, basis and definitions
text:
## 1. Background
Enacted under Article 253 after Stockholm 1972 and Bhopal 1984
Umbrella legislation: coordinates authorities under the Water and Air Acts
## 2. Definitions in the Act
Term | Definition
Environment | Water, air, land and their inter-relationship with humans, other living creatures, plants, micro-organisms and property
Environmental pollutant | Solid, liquid or gaseous substance in a concentration that is or may be injurious
Hazardous substance | Any substance that may harm humans, other creatures, plants, micro-organisms, property, environment
⚠ "Property" is part of the definition of environment; "noise" is not named in EPA's definition

t: EPA powers of the Centre → what the Act contains and what it lacks
text:
## 1. The 12 powers (Section 3)
# | Power
1-2 | Coordinate states; plan nationwide programmes
3 | Lay down emission/discharge standards of pollutants
4 | Restrict location of industries (basis of ESZ, CRZ)
5-6 | Close/prohibit/regulate industry; stop electricity, water supply
7-8 | Accident prevention; hazardous substance handling
9-10 | Inspection; set up or recognise laboratories
11-12 | Codes/manuals; any other matter (makes it umbrella)
Section 3(3): Centre may constitute authorities → e.g. CGWA (1997)
## 2. Not in the Act
Public participation requirement and procedure → comes from the EIA Notification (public hearing), not EPA text
⚠ EPA 1986 does not mention Eco-Sensitive Zones or public hearing by name
PYQ 2019: EPA empowers GoI to lay down emission/discharge standards (correct), but not to state public-participation procedure → 2 only

t: EPA enforcement → cognisance, citizen suit, Jan Vishwas
text:
## 1. Original provisions
Provision | Rule
Protection | No suit for acts done in good faith

Jail replaced mainly by monetary penalties; jail only if penalty unpaid in 90 days
Adjudicating officers impose penalties; appeal to NGT, 10% pre-deposit
Heads of government departments liable unless due diligence shown
EP Act now overrides other laws in case of conflict
⚠ Citizen-suit notice under EPA = 60 days; NGT appeal under Jan Vishwas = 60 days (Air Act)

text:
## 1. Categories
Category | Rule | Protection
Reserved Forest | All activities prohibited unless permitted; Forest Settlement Officer (civil court powers) settles claims first | Highest
Protected Forest | All activities permitted unless prohibited; demarcated or undemarcated | Middle
Village Forest | State assigns reserved forest land to a village community | Lowest
Based on IFAs of 1865/1878 and 1894; focus on revenue/duty on timber
2017 amendment: bamboo removed from "tree" → bamboo grown outside forests can be felled/transported without permit

Policies: 1894, 1952, 1988; NFP 1988: 33% area under forest/tree cover; introduced JFM; draft policy 2018 pending

topic: Forest laws: IFA 1927 and Van Adhiniyam 1980
t: Forest (Conservation) Act 1980 → central approval for diversion
text:
## 1. Features
Covers reserved, protected, village and private forests
De-reservation or use for non-forest purpose needs prior Centre approval (non-forest = anything except reafforestation)
Appeal to NGT; Forest Advisory Committee advises Centre; 1992 amendment allowed some non-forest activities with approval
TN Godavarman (1996): Act applies to all forests by dictionary meaning, whatever ownership → deemed forests
## 2. Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam (2023 amendment)
Change | Detail
Name | FCA → Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980
Preamble | Forests for Net Zero 2070; carbon sink 2.5-3 bn t CO2 by 2030; 33% cover
Applies to | Land notified as forest, or recorded as forest on/after 25 Oct 1980
Excluded | Land legally diverted on or before 12 Dec 1996
⚠ The 2023 law narrows coverage to notified/recorded forests, excluding many deemed and unclassed forests

topic: Forest laws: IFA 1927 and Van Adhiniyam 1980
t: Van Adhiniyam exemptions → limits and concerns
text:
## 1. Exemptions
Purpose | Limit
Access along public roads/railways to habitations | 0.10 ha per case
Strategic/security projects within 100 km of international borders | Up to 10 ha
Defence, paramilitary camps, public utilities in LWE areas | Up to 5 ha
Also exempted: zoos, safaris, eco-tourism, silvicultural operations
## 2. Concerns
Community/customary lands diverted without Gram Sabha consent or FRA safeguards
NE: unclassed forests dominate (Nagaland 97.3%, Meghalaya 88.2%, Manipur 76% of RFA); almost all Nagaland lies within 100 km of border; overlaps Indo-Burma hotspot; clash with Art 371 and Sixth Schedule
## In news 2025-26
Van Amendment Rules, 2025: CA land banks on land with canopy up to 0.4; scheme plantations count as CA; no CA for underground mining without surface rights; Stage-I validity 2 → 5 years; critical-mineral mining land-use minimum 20 → 10 years
Forest Conservation Guidelines, 2026: afforestation/restoration by govt or private bodies without CA or NPV, if 10-year working plans followed
FAC recommended uniform penalties: penal CA on equal area + penal NPV (up to 5x NPV, SC Aug 2017)

Item | Detail

## 1. Rights
Type | Content

Use rights | Minor forest produce (ownership, collection, sale), grazing, fishing
Relief and development | Rehabilitation on illegal eviction; basic amenities (schools, health etc.)
Forest management | Protect, regenerate, manage community forest resource (CFR)
First-time recognition of community rights, IPR over traditional knowledge on biodiversity, rights of displaced communities

## 1. Functions
Section | Role
Section 6 | Gram Sabha is the authority to initiate determination of individual and community rights; passes resolutions on claims
Section 5 | Gram Sabha and right-holders to protect wildlife, forest, biodiversity, water sources
CWH | Free informed consent of Gram Sabha needed before relocation (2011 guidelines)
Gram Sabha decisions can be appealed (PMF: before the court)

## 1. Definition (FRA only)
Areas of national parks and sanctuaries to be kept inviolate for wildlife, established case by case on scientific criteria
FRA makes MoEFCC the agency for CWH guidelines
## 2. Guidelines
Guidelines | Process
2011 | State shows right-holders cause irreversible damage; Gram Sabha consent before relocation; rights settled first
2018 | Chief Wildlife Warden sets up 7-member expert committee (chaired by CCF of the PA); 15-day public notice; SC-NBWL decides with MoTA representative; gazette notification
No CWH notified for over a decade after FRA
⚠ 2018 guidelines replaced Gram Sabha consent with stakeholder consultation (dilution)
## 3. CWH vs CTH
Feature | Critical Wildlife Habitat | Critical Tiger Habitat
Law | FRA 2006 | WPA 1972 (2006 amendment)
Applies to | All NPs and sanctuaries | Tiger reserves (core)
Notified by | After SC-NBWL decision | State govt, with NTCA input

t: Compensatory afforestation → rule under the forest law
text:
## 1. Rule
Case | CA required
Forest land diverted | Equal area of non-forest (revenue) land, or
If revenue land unavailable | Twice the area of degraded forest land
Since 2019 notification | CA allowed on forest land with crown density below 40%
Project proponent identifies land, pays CA cost + Net Present Value (NPV); state forest department plants
NPV: value of services lost (timber, fuelwood, carbon, water recharge) until new forest matures
CEC: ~85% of CA target met 2019-20 to 2023-24; Digital APO Portal, National CAMPA Dashboard
## 2. Problems
Greenwashing, unutilised funds, lack of land, fragmented plots, monoculture, biotic pressure, edge effects
⚠ CA flows from the Forest (Conservation) Act 1980; the CAF Act 2016 only manages the money

Item | Detail

CAF Act | 2016: gives CAMPA statutory status at national and state levels
National CAF | In Public Account of India: 10% of payments
State CAF | In Public Account of each State: 90%
Receives | CA money, NPV, project-specific payments
National CAMPA | Advisory council headed by Union Environment Minister

Catchment treatment, assisted natural regeneration, forest and wildlife management, relocation of villages from PAs, human-wildlife conflict, training
Funds Nagar Van Yojana (urban forests)

Item | Rule
Directly affected area | Within radius set by State, max 15 km from mine
Indirectly affected area | Max 25 km, even in adjacent districts
Affected people | 'Affected' and 'displaced' families (LARR Act 2013) + those identified by Gram Sabha

t: NGT Act → constitutional basis (Article 21)
text:
## 1. Which provision the NGT Act rests on
NGT Act 2010 was enacted under Article 21: right to life includes the right to a healthy environment
Purpose: expeditious disposal of environmental cases; appeals to be disposed of within 6 months
## 2. Environment in the Constitution (likely next)
Provision | What it says
Art 21 | Right to life → right to healthy environment (basis of NGT Act)
Art 48A (DPSP) | State shall protect and improve environment, forests, wildlife
Art 51A(g) (FD) | Citizen's duty to protect environment, compassion for living creatures
Art 253 | Parliament legislates to implement treaties → basis of EPA 1986
42nd Amendment 1976 | Added 48A, 51A(g); moved Forests and Wild animals and birds from State to Concurrent List
⚠ Art 275(1) (grants for Scheduled Areas/ST welfare) and Art 243A (Gram Sabha powers) have nothing to do with the NGT Act
⚠ EPA 1986 rests on Art 253, the NGT Act on Art 21: do not swap them
PYQ 2012: asked which provisions the NGT Act is "in consonance with" among Art 21, Art 275(1), Art 243A; only Art 21

t: NGT → establishment, benches and members
text:
## 1. Establishment
Established 18 October 2010 under the NGT Act 2010; replaced the National Environment Appellate Authority (NEAA, 1997), which was dissolved
First Chairperson: Justice Lokeshwar Singh Panta; current Chairperson: Justice Prakash Shrivastava (2026)
⚠ Testbook says NGT started functioning on 1 July 2011; PMF and ROCKET give only the establishment date (18 Oct 2010)
## 2. Benches (5 zones)
Zone | Bench
North (Principal Bench) | New Delhi
West | Pune
Central | Bhopal
South | Chennai
East | Kolkata
## 3. Members
Sanctioned strength: 10 judicial + 10 expert members; Act allows up to 20 of each
Each bench: at least one judicial and one expert member
Chairperson: serving/retired Chief Justice of a High Court or a Supreme Court judge; also a judicial member
## Beyond your notes
Chairperson is appointed by the Central Government in consultation with the Chief Justice of India

t: NGT jurisdiction → the seven Schedule I Acts
text:
## 1. Original jurisdiction
Civil cases on a "substantial question relating to environment" and damage due to a specific activity (e.g. pollution); "substantial" is not defined
## 2. Laws in Schedule I (complete list: 7)
# | Act
1 | Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1974
2 | Water Cess Act 1977
3 | Forest (Conservation) Act 1980
4 | Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1981
5 | Environment (Protection) Act 1986
6 | Public Liability Insurance Act 1991
7 | Biological Diversity Act 2002
## 3. Outside NGT's jurisdiction
Wild Life (Protection) Act 1972
Indian Forest Act 1927
State laws on forests and tree preservation
⚠ A WPA 1972 or Indian Forest Act 1927 dispute does not go to NGT; the Forest (Conservation) Act 1980 does
⚠ NGT has civil jurisdiction only: it cannot prosecute criminal offences (e.g. "ecocide")

t: NGT → powers, principles and appeal
text:
## 1. Powers
Orders are binding; can grant relief, compensation and damages
Can review its own decisions (Rule 22, NGT Rules)
Appeal against an NGT order lies to the Supreme Court within 90 days
## 2. Procedure and principles
Feature | NGT position
Civil Procedure Code 1908 | Not bound; follows natural justice
Indian Evidence Act 1872 | Not bound
Principles it must apply | Sustainable development, precautionary principle, polluter pays
## 3. NGT as appellate forum under other laws
Appeals against penalty orders of adjudicating officers under the Air Act (Jan Vishwas 2023) go to NGT within 60 days with 10% pre-deposit
Appeals under the Water Amendment Act 2024 and the Biological Diversity Rules 2024 also lie to the NGT
⚠ Appeal from NGT goes to the Supreme Court, not to a High Court
## Issues
Tribunalisation: government appoints members; attempts to dilute appointment criteria

t: NGT vs CPCB → how they differ
text:
Point | NGT | CPCB
Created by | NGT Act 2010 | Water Act 1974 (statutory)
Nature | Specialised judicial (quasi-judicial) body | Statutory organisation under MoEFCC
Core role | Environmental justice; reduces litigation burden on higher courts | Prevent, control, abate pollution
Signature phrase | Expeditious disposal of environmental cases | Cleanliness of streams and wells; improve air quality
Headquarters | Principal Bench New Delhi | New Delhi
⚠ CPCB was not created by executive order: it is statutory (Water Act 1974); both bodies are statutory
⚠ Bodies created by executive order/resolution in this topic: NMCG is a society; IREDA is a company: neither is a CPCB-type statutory board

topic: Pollution control boards and EPA bodies
t: CPCB → legal basis and functions
text:
## 1. Legal basis
Constituted 1974 under the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1974
Given powers and functions under the Air Act 1981
Offers technical services to MoEFCC under the EPA 1986

text:
## 1. The Act
Enacted to meet CBD 1992 commitments; passed December 2002, President's assent February 2003
Aims: conserve biodiversity, sustainable use, fair and equitable benefit sharing, check biopiracy
## 2. Three tiers
Tier | Body | Key role
National | National Biodiversity Authority (NBA), Chennai, 2003 | Approvals for foreigners, IPR, transfer of results abroad; NBF
State | State Biodiversity Boards (SBBs) / UT Biodiversity Councils | Approvals/terms for Indian entities; advise state govt

topic: EIA: meaning, legal basis and history
t: EIA → what it is and which law it comes from
text:
## 1. Meaning
Environmental Impact Assessment: systematic process to identify, predict, evaluate and mitigate environmental and social impacts of a proposed project before approval
Essential aspects (PMF): risk assessment, environmental management, post-product monitoring
## 2. Legal basis
Item | Fact
Parent Act | Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 (umbrella law)
Instrument | EIA Notification, 2006 (a notification under EPA, not a separate Act)
Output | Environmental Clearance (EC), the "go-ahead"
Who grants | MoEFCC (Category A); SEIAA (Category B)
Scope | 39+ types of activities: mining, infrastructure, industry, thermal power, river valley
⚠ India has no standalone EIA law; China passed one in 2002 (PMF way-forward)
⚠ EIA is ex ante (before the project); "prior" EC is the rule
Expect: "EIA in India is mandated by a separate Act of Parliament" → false; it is a notification under EPA 1986

topic: EIA: meaning, legal basis and history
t: History of EIA in India → 1976-77 to 2006
text:
Year | Step
1976-77 | Planning Commission asks Department of Science and Technology to examine river-valley projects environmentally
Till 1994 | EC was an administrative decision without legal backing
27 Jan 1994 | First EIA Notification under EPA 1986: EC mandatory for new projects, expansion or modernisation (Schedule 1 projects)
14 Sept 2006 | EIA Notification 2006 replaces 1994: decentralises EC (Category A centre, Category B states); makes prior EC explicit
1994 notification required clearance before start but did not use the word "prior"; 2006 made prior EC mandatory
2006 put the onus of clearing smaller projects on state bodies (by size/capacity)
⚠ The first EIA concern was river-valley projects, not mining or industry
## Beyond your notes
Exact date of the 2006 notification: 14 September 2006 (Indian Geography gives only "September 2006")

topic: EIA: meaning, legal basis and history

text:

No. | Class
1 | Mining
2 | Industrial
3 | Thermal power
4 | River valley, multipurpose, irrigation, hydro-electric
5 | Infrastructure development and miscellaneous
6 | Nuclear power
## 2. Participants (5)
Project proponent; environmental consultant (paid by the proponent); State PCB / Pollution Control Committee; the public; Impact Assessment Agency (MoEFCC)
Indian Geography also lists the regional office of MoEFCC
## 3. Linked clearances
Single window: a project needing both EC and forest clearance (Forest (Conservation) Act 1980, now Van Adhiniyam) files both together; processed concurrently
Coasts: states/UTs prepare Coastal Zone Management Plans under the CRZ notification, approved by MoEFCC
⚠ Forest clearance and EC are different approvals under different laws

topic: EIA Notification 2006: categories, stages and clearance
t: Category A, B1, B2 → who appraises and who clears
text:
Category | Level | Appraised by | EC granted by | Screening? | EIA report?
A | National (large projects) | Expert Appraisal Committee (EAC) | MoEFCC | No (EC automatic requirement) | Yes
B1 | State | State Expert Appraisal Committee (SEAC) | SEIAA | Yes | Yes (mandatory)
B2 | State | SEAC | SEIAA | Yes | No EIA, no public hearing
Category A skips screening because EC is mandatory anyway
Only Category B is screened, then split into B1 and B2
A and B1 go through the full EIA cycle; B2 is out of the full process
⚠ SEIAA grants, SEAC appraises/recommends: SEAC is advisory, SEIAA is the regulator
⚠ EAC = central technical body; SEAC = state technical body
## Beyond your notes
General condition: a Category B project within 10 km of a protected area, critically polluted area, eco-sensitive area, or inter-state / international boundary is treated as Category A

topic: EIA Notification 2006: categories, stages and clearance
t: EIA Notification 2006 → the four stages
text:
Stage | What happens | Applies to
1. Screening | Decide whether EIA is needed (B1 or B2) | Category B only
2. Scoping | Fix Terms of Reference (ToR): key issues, impact zone, studies needed | A and B1
3. Public consultation | Public hearing + written responses | A and B1 (with exemptions)
4. Appraisal | EAC/SEAC scrutinises final EIA report and hearing outcome; recommends grant or rejection | A and B1
Order: Screening → Scoping → Public hearing → Appraisal (PMF)
⚠ Public hearing comes after the draft EIA report and before appraisal; it is not the first step
Decision within 90 days if the proponent gives complete information (PMF)
Expect a sequence question: correct order is screening, scoping, public consultation, appraisal

topic: EIA Notification 2006: categories, stages and clearance
t: Full EIA cycle → steps inside the report
text:
## 1. Steps (PMF; the process is cyclical)
Screening → Scoping → Baseline data (environmental status of the study area) → Impact prediction (positive/negative, reversible/irreversible, temporary/permanent)
→ Risk assessment (inventory analysis, hazard probability and index) → Assessment of alternatives (location and technology) → Mitigation measures
→ EIA report → Public hearing → Decision making (Impact Assessment Authority with experts, using EIA + EMP) → Monitoring and implementation of EMP
## 2. Environmental Management Plan (EMP)
EMP contains | Note
Mitigation for each component | Prevention and control
Rehabilitation and resettlement plan | Part of EMP
Monitoring plan | Post-clearance
⚠ Alternatives must cover both site and process technology
## Beyond your notes
EIA consultants must be accredited by QCI-NABET (Quality Council of India) (verify)

Other projects (industry, infrastructure) | 7 years | 
Post-clearance monitoring checks EC conditions and EMP implementation

Proponents file six-monthly compliance reports on EC conditions (verify)

Exempt from public hearing
All Category B2 projects

t: Public hearing and EIA → shortcomings
text:
Problem | Detail (PMF)
Late consultation | Public comments not taken early → conflict later
Exclusions | Many high-impact projects kept out of hearings
Documents | Not available on time; not in local languages (e.g. Vizhinjam Port)

text:
Body | Takes over from | Does
SAEIA (Standing Authority on EIA) | SEIAA | Grants or refuses EC
SCEIA (Standing Committee on Environment Impact Appraisal) | SEAC | Appraises and recommends

topic: Ex-post facto clearance and court rulings
t: Vanashakti judgment (May 2025) and its recall (Nov 2025)
text:
## 1. Vanashakti, May 2025
SC struck down the 2017 notification (one-time six-month window for violators) and the 2021 Office Memorandum/SOP for retrospective EC
Called ex-post facto EC a "gross illegality", "anathema" and "alien to environmental jurisprudence"
Violated Article 14 (preference to violators) and Article 21 (right to healthy environment); barred future such notifications
## 2. Recall, 18 November 2025 (3-judge bench, 2:1)
Ground | Detail
Earlier rulings | D Swamy v Karnataka SPCB (2021), Pahwa Plastics (2022) allowed post-facto EC in exceptional cases
Cost | ~₹20,000 crore of projects faced demolition
Public interest | Hospitals, airports, medical colleges would stall
Dissent: Vanashakti was not per incuriam; ex-post facto EC breaks the precautionary principle
⚠ After the recall, retrospective EC is litigable again; it is not settled law

t: Temperature scales → fixed points and conversion
text:
Scale | Water freezes | Water boils | Absolute zero
Celsius | 0°C | 100°C | −273.15°C
Fahrenheit | 32°F | 212°F | −459.67°F
Kelvin | 273.15 K | 373.15 K | 0 K
K = °C + 273.15; °F = (°C x 9/5) + 32; C/5 = (F−32)/9 = (K−273)/5
−40°C = −40°F: the two scales meet (beyond your notes)
Kelvin has no negative values; at 0 K molecular motion stops
Triple point of water: 273.16 K (0.01°C), 611.657 Pa; earlier used to define the kelvin

## Heat vs temperature
Feature | Heat | Temperature
Nature | Energy in transit | Average kinetic energy of particles

Depends on mass? | Yes | No

t: Ball bearings → why they reduce friction
text:
## 1. What they do
Replace sliding friction with much smaller rolling friction
Balls touch wheel and axle only at tiny points → effective area of contact is reduced
Option (2013) | Status
Actual area of contact increased | Wrong
Effectiveness of contact increased | Wrong
Effective area of contact reduced | Correct
## 2. Other ways to reduce friction (beyond your notes)
Lubricants: oil, grease, graphite (PMF lists graphite as a lubricant)
Polishing surfaces, streamlining (cuts fluid drag)
Wheels and rollers, air cushions (hovercraft), magnetic levitation
⚠ Friction is not removed by bearings; it is changed from sliding to rolling
PYQ 2013: ball bearings reduce the effective area of contact; trap: "actual area increased"

t: Types of friction → feature and example
text:
Type | Feature | Example
Static | Object at rest; self-adjusting up to limiting friction | Book on table, car on hill, ladder on wall
Limiting | Maximum static friction just before motion | 
Kinetic (sliding) | Object moving; roughly constant, independent of speed | Braking car tyres, sliding book
Rolling | Much smaller than sliding | Ball rolling, ball bearings
Fluid (drag) | Rises with speed, fluid density and viscosity | Swimmer, skydiver
Order: static > sliding > rolling
Coefficient depends on nature of surfaces (rubber on asphalt > metal on metal)
Friction is a non-conservative force (work depends on path)
## Uses vs harms
Useful friction | Harmful friction
Walking, tyre grip, brakes | Wear and tear of shoes, tyres, machine parts
Matchstick lighting, writing | Wasted heat, lower efficiency, extra fuel
Nails and screws hold | Noise; needs lubrication
⚠ Static friction is larger than kinetic friction: starting a push is harder than keeping it going

t: Washing machine and centrifuge → working principle
text:
## 1. Centripetal vs centrifugal
Force | Direction | Nature
Centripetal | Towards centre | Real (tension, gravity, friction supply it)
Centrifugal | Outward | Apparent/pseudo, in a rotating frame
Uniform circular motion: speed constant but velocity changes (direction) → centripetal acceleration
## 2. Machines using spinning
Device | Principle
Washing machine dryer | Centrifugation: fast spin throws water out through drum holes
Cream separator | Centrifugation: lighter cream collects at centre (beyond your notes)
Laboratory centrifuge | Separates by density (blood plasma, cells) (beyond your notes)
Banking of roads | Supplies centripetal force on curves (beyond your notes)
⚠ Not dialysis, reverse osmosis or diffusion: those are membrane/concentration processes
Pseudo forces: centrifugal and Coriolis (rotating Earth)
PYQ 1997: working principle of a washing machine = centrifugation

t: Newton's laws and inertia → everyday example
text:
Law / idea | Statement | Example
1st law (inertia) | Body keeps rest or uniform motion unless an unbalanced force acts | Passengers lurch forward when bus stops
2nd law | F = m x a | Heavier box needs more push
3rd law | Equal and opposite reaction, simultaneous, on different bodies | Walking, rocket propulsion
Inertia of rest |  | Dust leaves a shaken carpet
Inertia of direction |  | Objects slide sideways when a car turns
Impulse | Force x time = change in momentum | Airbags lengthen impact time
Conservation of momentum | Total momentum fixed with no external force | Gun recoil, rockets, collisions
Inertia is proportional to mass; moment of inertia resists rotation
## Collisions
Type | Momentum | Kinetic energy
Elastic | Conserved | Conserved
Inelastic | Conserved | Not conserved
Perfectly inelastic | Conserved | Maximum loss; bodies stick
⚠ Momentum is conserved in all collisions; only KE differs

t: Gravity, mass and weight → what changes where
text:
Feature | Mass | Weight
Meaning | Amount of matter | Force of gravity on it
Type | Scalar | Vector
Unit | kg | Newton
Changes with place? | No | Yes (Moon, poles, altitude)
## What changes g (~9.8 m/s²)
Factor | Effect on g
Altitude rises | g decreases
Depth into Earth | g decreases
Poles vs equator | g higher at poles (less centrifugal effect, closer to centre)
Dense rock below | Slightly higher
In vacuum all bodies fall with the same acceleration, whatever their mass
Weightlessness: gravity still acts; no normal (support) force (free fall, orbit)
Four fundamental forces: strong > electromagnetic > weak > gravity; gravity and EM have infinite range

topic: Fluids: pressure, buoyancy, surface tension, capillarity
t: Capillarity → what it explains and what it does not
text:
## 1. Mechanism
Liquid rises or falls in narrow spaces due to adhesion (liquid-solid) vs cohesion (liquid-liquid)
Higher surface tension → greater capillary rise; rise is greater in narrower tubes (beyond your notes)
Case | Condition | Example
Capillary rise | Adhesion > cohesion | Water in thin glass tube
Capillary fall | Cohesion > adhesion | Mercury in glass
## 2. Explained by capillarity
Phenomenon | Capillarity?
Kerosene rising in lamp wick | Yes
Blotting paper absorbing ink | Yes
Sap/water rising in tall trees | Yes (UPSC key)
Towel soaking water, ink in fountain-pen nib, soil moisture | Yes
Drinking through a straw | No: atmospheric pressure
⚠ Preview: in tall trees water rises mainly by cohesion-adhesion and transpiration pull; capillarity alone cannot lift it to great heights; UPSC 2012 still counted trees as capillarity
PYQ 2012: without capillarity, lamp, blotting paper and trees fail (1, 3, 4); trap: the straw

topic: Fluids: pressure, buoyancy, surface tension, capillarity
t: Surface tension and viscosity → cause and temperature effect
text:
Feature | Surface tension | Viscosity
Meaning | Surface acts like a stretched membrane | Resistance to flow (internal friction between layers)
Cause | Cohesion; net inward pull on surface molecules | Intermolecular forces between layers
Rise in temperature | Decreases | Liquids: decreases; gases: increases
Lowered by | Soap, detergents (surfactants) | Heating (liquids)
Examples | Spherical drops, insects walking on water, bubbles | Honey, glycerine slow; water, alcohol fast
Drops are spherical: a sphere has the least surface area for a volume
Water has high surface tension due to hydrogen bonding
## Fluid types
Type | Viscosity | Example
Newtonian | Constant | Water, air
Non-Newtonian | Changes with stress | Blood, ketchup
Laminar (smooth layers, low speed) vs turbulent (eddies); switch set by Reynolds number at critical velocity
⚠ Gas viscosity rises with temperature: opposite of liquids

topic: Fluids: pressure, buoyancy, surface tension, capillarity
t: Pressure → Pascal's law and atmospheric pressure
text:
## 1. Fluid pressure
P = ρgh + P₀: rises with depth, density, g, external pressure; acts equally in all directions
Pressure = force / area: smaller area, more pressure (sharp knife, pointed nail; beyond your notes)
## 2. Pascal's law
Pressure on a confined fluid is transmitted undiminished in all directions
Uses: hydraulic lifts, brakes, presses; pneumatic systems
## 3. Atmospheric pressure
Measure | Value at sea level
1 atm | 101,325 Pa
Mercury column | 760 mm Hg
psi | 14.7
Measured by barometer; manometer = pressure of a fluid column
Effect of atmospheric pressure | Example
Liquid pushed up a straw | Sucking lowers pressure inside
Syringe draws liquid | Boyle's law
Boiling point lower on hills | Less pressure
Fountain pen leaks in aircraft | Lower cabin pressure (beyond your notes)
⚠ Straw and syringe = air pressure, not capillarity

topic: Fluids: pressure, buoyancy, surface tension, capillarity
t: Buoyancy and Archimedes → float or sink
text:
Buoyant force = weight of fluid displaced (Archimedes); acts at centre of buoyancy
Condition | Result
Weight > buoyant force | Sinks
Weight = buoyant force | Floats / neutral buoyancy
Weight < buoyant force | Rises
Relative density below 1 | Floats on water
Denser fluid → more buoyancy: easier to float in sea water than fresh water
Uses: ships, submarines, helium balloons, icebergs
Relative density = density / density of water at 4°C (1000 kg/m³); dimensionless
Fraction submerged = density of solid / density of liquid
Ice melting in a glass: water level stays the same
⚠ A floating ship displaces water equal to its own weight, not its volume

topic: Fluids: pressure, buoyancy, surface tension, capillarity
t: Bernoulli and gas laws → application
text:
## 1. Bernoulli's theorem
For steady, non-viscous flow: pressure + kinetic + potential energy = constant → faster flow, lower pressure
Application | How
Aeroplane wing lift | Faster air above, lower pressure
Venturi meter | Measures flow rate
Roofs blown off in storms | Fast wind lowers pressure above (beyond your notes)
Torricelli's law | Efflux speed ∝ √height
## 2. Gas laws
Law | Holds constant | Relation | Example
Boyle | Temperature | P ∝ 1/V | Breathing, syringe
Charles | Pressure | V ∝ T | Hot-air balloon
Gay-Lussac | Volume | P ∝ T | Tyre pressure on hot day, pressure cooker
Avogadro | P and T | V ∝ moles | Inflating balloon
Ideal gas law PV = nRT; real gases deviate at high pressure, low temperature

topic: Fluids: pressure, buoyancy, surface tension, capillarity
t: Properties of solids → term and example
text:
Property | Meaning | Example
Elasticity | Regains shape within elastic limit | Rubber band
Plasticity | Permanent deformation | Clay
Ductility | Drawn into wires | Gold, copper
Malleability | Beaten into sheets | Aluminium, gold
Brittleness | Breaks without bending | Glass, ceramic
Hardness | Resists scratching | Diamond
Fatigue | Weakening by repeated loading | Aircraft wings
Creep | Slow deformation under constant load, high heat | Hot metal parts
Hooke's law: stress ∝ strain within elastic limit; stress unit = Pascal; strain has no unit
Steel is more elastic than rubber in the physics sense (resists deformation more; beyond your notes)
⚠ Stiffness: steel stiffer than rubber; toughness: steel tougher than glass

topic: Heat, latent heat and the behaviour of water
t: Latent heat → steam burns, ice and the AC statement
text:
## 1. Types of heat
Heat | Effect
Sensible | Changes temperature, no phase change
Latent | Changes state, temperature constant
Latent heat of fusion | Solid ↔ liquid at melting point (ice ~80 cal/g, beyond your notes)
Latent heat of vaporisation | Liquid ↔ gas at boiling point (water ~540 cal/g)
## 2. The 2003 statements
Statement | Status
Steam at 100°C and water at 100°C hold same heat | Wrong: steam holds 540 cal/g more
Latent heat of fusion = latent heat of vaporisation | Wrong: vaporisation much greater
AC extracts room heat at evaporator, rejects at condenser | Correct
Steam burns are worse than boiling-water burns: steam releases latent heat on condensing on skin
⚠ Released heat on condensation = latent heat of vaporisation; on freezing = latent heat of fusion
PYQ 2003: only statement 3 correct (answer d)

topic: Heat, latent heat and the behaviour of water
t: Phase changes → heat absorbed or released
text:
Process | Change | Heat
Melting | Solid → liquid | Absorbed
Freezing | Liquid → solid | Released
Vaporisation | Liquid → gas | Absorbed (endothermic)
Condensation | Gas → liquid | Released (exothermic)
Sublimation | Solid → gas | Absorbed: dry ice, naphthalene
Deposition | Gas → solid | Released: frost, snowflakes
Ionisation | Gas → plasma | Absorbed: neon lights
## Evaporation vs boiling
Feature | Evaporation | Boiling
Where | Surface only | Throughout liquid
Temperature | Any below boiling point | At boiling point
Speed | Slow | Fast, bubbles
Effect | Cooling | Temperature stays constant
Evaporation rises with temperature, surface area, wind, low humidity; sweating and earthen pots cool by evaporation (beyond your notes for pots)
Impurities (salt) lower the freezing point of water and raise the boiling point (latter beyond your notes)
Latent heat of condensation drives convectional rain and cyclones (Physical Geography)

topic: Heat, latent heat and the behaviour of water
t: Pressure cooker → what sets its temperature
text:
## 1. Boiling point and pressure
Boiling = when vapour pressure equals outside pressure
Pressure | Boiling point | Example
Higher | Rises | Pressure cooker ~120°C; autoclave (beyond your notes)
Lower | Falls | Hills: food cooks slowly
Ice: higher pressure lowers its melting point (regelation; beyond your notes); PMF: most substances' melting point rises
## 2. Cooking temperature depends on
Factor | Matters?
Area of vent hole | Yes: smaller hole, more pressure
Weight on the lid (whistle) | Yes: heavier weight, more pressure
Flame temperature | No: extra heat only makes more steam escape
Food being cooked | No
Handle made of ebonite/bakelite: poor conductor of heat
⚠ Bigger flame = faster reaching pressure, not higher cooking temperature
PYQ 2021: area of hole and weight of lid (answer c); trap: flame temperature

topic: Heat, latent heat and the behaviour of water
t: Anomalous expansion of water → why lakes freeze from the top
text:
## 1. The anomaly
Most liquids contract on cooling; water contracts down to 4°C, then expands from 4°C to 0°C
Maximum density at 4°C (1000 kg/m³); ice is less dense than water → floats
## 2. Frozen lake
Layer | Temperature
Ice (top) | 0°C and below
Water just below ice | 0-4°C, lighter
Bottom water | 4°C, densest, stays liquid
Ice is a poor conductor and insulates water below (helps, but not the main answer)
Aquatic life survives winter
## 3. Consequences
Water pipes and corked bottles burst in freezing weather: water expands on freezing
Icebergs and ice cubes float; ice melting in a glass leaves level unchanged
⚠ Main reason for liquid lake bottom = maximum density at 4°C, not "ice is a bad conductor"
PYQ 2011: answer (c) density of water maximum at 4°C

topic: Heat, latent heat and the behaviour of water
t: Specific heat and thermal expansion → example
text:
## 1. Specific heat
Heat to raise 1 unit mass by 1°C; water has very high specific heat
Consequence of water's high specific heat | 
Sea heats and cools slowly → maritime climate mild | 
Sea and land breezes | 
Water used as coolant in car radiators, hot-water bottles | (beyond your notes)
## 2. Thermal expansion
Type | Meaning
Linear / area / volume | Rise in length / area / volume
Apparent | Liquid expansion seen in a container
Real | True liquid expansion, ignoring container
Gaps in rails and bridges, sagging power lines in summer (beyond your notes)
Newton's law of cooling: rate of heat loss ∝ temperature difference (small difference)
## 3. Thermodynamic processes
Process | Constant
Isothermal | Temperature (ice melting at 0°C)
Isobaric | Pressure (open-pot heating)
Isochoric | Volume (rigid container)
Adiabatic | No heat exchange (insulated compression)

t: Conduction, convection, radiation → medium and example
text:
Feature | Conduction | Convection | Radiation
Medium | Needed, direct contact | Fluid (liquid, gas) | None (works in vacuum)
Mechanism | Molecular collisions | Bulk movement of fluid: warm rises, cool sinks | Electromagnetic waves (infrared)
Speed | Slow | Moderate | Fastest
Common in | Solids, metals | Liquids, gases | Space
Example | Metal rod, hot stove | Boiling water, sea breeze, radiator | Sunlight, warmth of fire
⚠ Convection is impossible in solids and vacuum; radiation is the only mode through vacuum
Black body: perfect absorber and emitter; dark, rough surfaces absorb and emit more

t: Car radiator → working principle
text:
## 1. How it works
Engine heats coolant (water/antifreeze) → hot coolant circulates to radiator → heat lost to air → cooled coolant returns
Circulation of heated fluid = convection; conduction only at metal surfaces
Option (2010) | Status
Conduction only | Wrong
Convection | Correct
Radiation only | Wrong
Conduction and radiation | Wrong
Water is the coolant because of high specific heat (beyond your notes)
Despite the name, a car radiator loses little heat by radiation (beyond your notes)
PYQ 2010: car radiator works on convection; trap: the word "radiator" suggests radiation

t: Thermos flask, clouds, greenhouse → which mode is blocked
text:
Device / effect | Heat mode involved
Thermos (vacuum) flask | Vacuum gap stops conduction and convection; silvered walls stop radiation
Cloudy nights warmer | Clouds reflect back Earth's outgoing heat
Greenhouse | Glass passes sunlight, blocks outgoing infrared; closed space stops convection
Woollen clothes | Trapped air = poor conductor (beyond your notes)
Ebonite cooker handle | Poor conductor
Ice box / thermocol | Poor conductor (beyond your notes)
Natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth at ~15°C; without it −18°C
GHGs: CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, water vapour, CFCs
⚠ Thermos stops heat flow by all three modes (Preview: "conduction, convection and radiation")

t: Sea breeze and land breeze → direction and cause
text:
Breeze | Time | Blows from | Why
Sea breeze | Day | Sea → land | Land heats faster, low pressure over land
Land breeze | Night | Land → sea | Land cools faster, sea warmer
Valley breeze | Day | Valley → up slope | Slopes heat (beyond your notes)
Mountain breeze | Night | Slope → valley | Cold dense air drains down
Cause: land has lower specific heat than water; driven by convection

text:
## 1. Characteristics of light
Property | Fact
Nature | Dual: wave (reflection, refraction, diffraction, interference) + particle (photon, photoelectric effect)
Wave type | Transverse EM wave: electric and magnetic fields perpendicular to each other and to motion
Speed in vacuum | 3 × 10^8 m/s; slower in denser media (glass, water)
Relation | Speed = wavelength × frequency
Visible range | 400 nm (violet) to 700 nm (red)
Needs no medium: travels through vacuum (unlike sound)

topic: Nature of Light, Reflection and Mirrors
t: Reflection → laws and types
text:
## 1. Laws of reflection
Angle of incidence = angle of reflection (measured from the normal)
Incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in the same plane
## 2. Types
Type | Surface | Result
Regular (specular) | Smooth, shiny (mirror, still water) | Parallel rays, clear image
Irregular (diffuse) | Rough (wall, paper) | Rays scatter, no image; lets us see objects
Sound obeys the same laws of reflection (echo)
⚠ In total internal reflection no light is transmitted; ordinary reflection always loses some light (NCERT)

topic: Nature of Light, Reflection and Mirrors
t: Mirrors → image formed and uses
text:
## 1. Three mirrors
Mirror | Image | Uses
Plane | Virtual, upright, laterally inverted, same size, as far behind as object in front | Dressing mirror, periscope
Concave (converging) | Real-inverted or virtual-magnified (object between F and pole) | Shaving mirror, torch / headlight reflector, reflecting telescope, satellite dish
Convex (diverging) | Always virtual, upright, diminished | Vehicle rear-view, security / traffic mirrors (wide field)
Mirror formula: 1/f = 1/v + 1/u; magnification m = image height / object height
m > 1 magnified; m < 1 diminished; m = 1 same size
⚠ Real images are inverted and can be taken on a screen; virtual images are upright and cannot
⚠ Concave mirror gives a virtual, magnified image only when object is between F and pole

topic: Refraction, Total Internal Reflection and Lenses
t: Refraction → bending rules
text:
## 1. What changes and what does not
Quantity | On refraction
Speed | Changes (slower in denser medium)
Wavelength | Changes
Frequency | Unchanged
Direction | Bends towards normal entering denser; away entering rarer
Along the normal | No bending
Snell's law: sin i / sin r = constant (refractive index of medium 2 w.r.t. 1)
Refractive index = speed in vacuum / speed in medium
Applications: lenses, prism, mirage, optical fibre
⚠ Frequency (hence colour) stays the same; only speed and wavelength change

topic: Refraction, Total Internal Reflection and Lenses
t: Refractive index → ranking of media
text:
## 1. Values (PMF, NCERT)
Medium | Refractive index | Critical angle (to air)
Vacuum | 1.000 | none
Air | 1.0003 | none
Water | 1.33 | 48.75°
Crown glass | 1.52 | 41.14°
Dense flint glass | 1.62 | 37.31°
Diamond | 2.42 | 24.41° (smallest)
Order of optical density: Diamond > Glass > Water > Air
Higher refractive index = smaller critical angle = easier TIR
⚠ "Optically denser" is about refractive index, not mass density

topic: Refraction, Total Internal Reflection and Lenses
t: Total internal reflection → when it can happen
text:
## 1. Two conditions
Light goes from denser to rarer medium
Angle of incidence greater than the critical angle
Critical angle: angle in denser medium for which refraction angle = 90°
Pair | TIR possible?
Diamond → glass | Yes (denser to rarer)
Glass → air, water → air | Yes
Water → glass | No (rarer to denser)
Air → water, air → glass | No
⚠ Air to anything denser can never give TIR

text:
## 1. Types
Type | Condition | Image
Inferior | Ground hotter than air above (deserts, roads) | Below object, looks like water
Superior | Cold surface, warm air above (temperature inversion), over water / polar seas | Above object
Looming | Type of superior mirage | Object appears raised / floating

topic: Refraction, Total Internal Reflection and Lenses
t: Air bubble in water → why it acts as a concave lens
text:
## 1. The reversal rule
Lens behaviour depends on lens medium relative to surroundings
Object | Surrounding | Shape | Acts as
Glass bead | Air | Convex | Converging
Air bubble | Water (denser) | Convex (spherical) | Diverging = concave lens
Water drop | Air | Convex | Converging
Rays go denser → rarer → denser, so they spread out
⚠ A convex-shaped bubble behaves as a concave lens because it is rarer than the water

t: Dispersion → which colour bends most
text:
## 1. Splitting of white light
Refractive index depends on wavelength: shorter wavelength = higher refractive index
Colour | Wavelength | Bending in prism | Speed in glass
Violet | Shortest (~400 nm) | Most | Slowest
Red | Longest (~700 nm) | Least | Fastest
Order: VIBGYOR; Newton: second inverted prism recombines to white light
Flint glass disperses more than crown glass

t: Rainbow → three processes in a raindrop

Step | Process
1 | Refraction on entering the drop
2 | Dispersion into colours
3 | Internal reflection at back of drop
4 | Refraction again on leaving
## 2. Primary vs secondary
Rainbow | Primary | Secondary
Internal reflections | One | Two
Colour order | Red outside, violet inside | Reversed
Brightness | Brighter | Fainter
Seen only with back to the Sun, rain in opposite sky

Type | Particle size vs wavelength | Wavelength dependence | Example

Mie | Comparable | Weak; mostly forward | Haze, fog, halos
Non-selective | Much larger (droplets, dust) | None | White clouds, fog, mist
