t: Fuse → how it works and what it must have
text:
## 1. Principle and connection
Works on the heating effect of current: excess current heats the wire, it melts ("blows") and breaks the circuit
Connected in series with the circuit/appliance (never parallel)
Protects against overload and short circuit
## 2. Fuse wire properties
Property | Fuse wire | Why
Melting point | Low | Must melt quickly on overcurrent
Connection | Series | All current must pass through it
Material | Tin-lead alloy (~63% Sn, 37% Pb) | Melts ~183°C vs copper ~1085°C, aluminium ~660°C
Rating | Sn-Pb for low current (up to ~15 A); copper fuse wire above 15 A | Household vs heavy circuits
⚠ UPSC 1998 answer: fuse must have a low melting point. Wrong options: connected in parallel with main switch, made mainly from silver alloys, must have very high resistance
⚠ State PSC keys say fuse wire has "high resistance / high resistivity"; UPSC rejected "very high resistance". Safe line: low melting point + series is always right
⚠ Assertion "Sn-Pb alloy is used for fuse" is true; reason "it has a higher melting point than Cu and Al" is false (UPPCS 2025)
PYQ 1998: four statements on the main-supply fuse; only "low melting point" correct

t: Joule heating → why a current-carrying wire gets hot
text:
## 1. Mechanism
Moving (drifting) electrons collide with the ions/atoms of the lattice and hand over energy → lattice vibrates more → temperature rises
It is not metal atoms colliding with each other
Electrical energy → heat = heating effect of current (one of 3 effects: heating, magnetic, chemical)
## 2. Speeds to remember (NCERT)
Quantity | Order of value
Drift speed of electrons in Cu wire | ~1 mm/s (1.1 × 10⁻³ m/s)
Thermal speed of Cu atoms (300 K) | ~2 × 10² m/s
Speed of the electric field (signal) along wire | 3 × 10⁸ m/s (speed of EM wave)
⚠ A bulb glows instantly not because electrons race at light speed (drift is ~mm/s) but because the field travels at ~light speed
PYQ 1998 (A-R): A "wire heats when current passes" true; R "collision of metal atoms with each other releases heat" false → answer A true, R false
## Beyond your notes
Joule's law: H = I²Rt (heat ∝ square of current, resistance, time); applications: heater, iron, toaster, filament bulb, fuse

t: Current, voltage, resistance → definitions and units
text:
Quantity | Meaning | Formula | SI unit
Charge | Property of matter; + on protons, − on electrons | - | coulomb (C)
Current | Rate of flow of charge | I = Q / t | ampere (1 A = 1 C/s)
Voltage (potential difference) | Work done per unit charge | V = W / Q | volt (1 V = 1 J/C)
Resistance | Opposition to current | R = V / I | ohm (1 Ω = 1 V/A)
Resistivity | Material property | ρ = R × A / L | ohm-metre
Power | Rate of energy use | P = V × I | watt (1 W = 1 J/s); 1 HP ≈ 746 W
Energy | Work done by current | E = P × t | joule; bills in kWh ("unit")
Ohm's law: V = I × R; holds only for ohmic (linear) materials
Coulomb's law: force ∝ q₁q₂ / r² (inverse square, like gravity)
Current flows only when there is a potential difference; two bodies at the same potential exchange no current
⚠ Distribution companies bill in kWh; India's grid runs at 50 Hz, not 60 Hz (MPPSC A-R trap)

t: Resistance → what it depends on (conductor vs semiconductor)
text:
## 1. Factors (PMF)
Factor | Effect on resistance
Length | Directly proportional (longer → more R)
Cross-section area | Inversely proportional (thicker → less R)
Material | Cu, Ag low; rubber, glass high
Temperature | Conductors: R rises with T; semiconductors: R falls with T
Resistivity depends only on material and temperature, not on shape/size; resistance depends on dimensions too
## 2. Three classes of material
Class | Examples | Band gap | Use
Conductors | Cu, Ag, Al, Au, graphite (non-metal), salt water | None | Wiring
Insulators | Rubber, plastic, wood, glass, ceramic, dry air | Large | Insulation
Semiconductors | Silicon, germanium | Small | Diodes, transistors, solar cells
⚠ Graphite is the non-metal conductor; silver is the best metallic conductor but copper is used for cost
## Beyond your notes
Human body (dry) resistance is high (order of 10⁴-10⁵ Ω); wet skin lowers it sharply, so shocks are worse with wet hands

t: Domestic wiring → series or parallel, earthing, short circuit
text:
## 1. House circuit
Domestic wiring is a parallel connection: each appliance gets full voltage; one failing does not cut the others (UPSC 1996)
Short circuit: live touches neutral, resistance ≈ 0 → current rises very high (I = V/R) → heat, fire; fuse/MCB cuts it
Overloading: too many appliances on one socket → excess current
## 2. Three wires (Preview)
Wire | Old Indian colour | Role
Live (phase) | Red | Carries supply voltage
Neutral | Black | Return path
Earth | Green | Leaks fault current to ground; protects user from shock on metal bodies
Earthing: metal body of appliance connected to earth so a fault current flows to ground, not through the user
⚠ Old code: red live, black neutral, green earth. Black is neutral, not earth (CGPSC 2014)
## Beyond your notes
New IEC/BIS colours (verify): brown live, blue neutral, green-yellow earth
MCB (miniature circuit breaker): trips on overload (bimetal strip) and short circuit (electromagnet); reset by a switch, not replaced
Fuse vs MCB: fuse is cheap but one-time (must be rewired); MCB is reusable and faster to restore
RCCB/ELCB: trips on earth leakage current (protects people from shock); MCB/fuse protect wiring from overcurrent

t: AC vs DC → sources and conversion devices
text:
Feature | DC | AC
Direction | One direction only | Reverses periodically
Sources | Batteries, solar cells/panels | Power grid, AC generator (alternator)
Use | Charging batteries, electronics | Household supply, long-distance transmission
India frequency | - | 50 Hz (±0.5 Hz tolerated)
## Conversion devices
Device | Does what
Rectifier | AC → DC
Inverter | DC → AC
Transformer | Steps AC voltage up/down
Commutator (in DC dynamo) | Makes generator output DC
Slip rings | Used in AC generator
A simple dynamo produces AC; DC generator uses a commutator, AC generator uses slip rings (CGPSC 2018)
⚠ AC is not preferable for charging a storage battery (needs DC via rectifier)
## Beyond your notes
A transformer does not work on DC (needs a changing magnetic field; Faraday's law of induction)
AC is preferred for transmission because transformers raise voltage, cutting I²R losses

t: Semiconductors and superconductors → key properties
text:
## 1. Semiconductors (PMF S&T)
Type | Doped with | Majority carrier
Intrinsic | Pure Si, Ge | Electrons = holes
n-type | Phosphorus, arsenic (donors, 5 valence e⁻) | Electrons
p-type | Boron, gallium (acceptors) | Holes
Conductivity increases with temperature (opposite to metals)
## 2. Superconductors
Zero resistance + expel magnetic field (Meissner effect, perfect diamagnetism) below critical temperature (Tc)
Electrons pair as Cooper pairs that move without scattering
Type I (mercury, lead): abrupt loss above critical field; Type II: partial field penetration, practical use
Uses: MRI, maglev, particle-accelerator magnets (LHC at 1.9 K), superconducting qubits, fusion tokamaks
⚠ Superconductors lose superconductivity above Tc, critical magnetic field or critical current
## In news 2025-26
Nobel Physics 2025: Clarke, Devoret, Martinis for macroscopic quantum tunnelling and energy quantisation in a superconducting Josephson junction circuit → base of superconducting qubits
China tested the world's largest fusion reactor magnet (582 tonnes, superconducting) to confine tokamak plasma (2026)

t: Four forces → relative strength, range, carrier
text:
Force | Strength rank | Range | Acts on | Carrier
Strong nuclear | 1 (strongest) | Very short (nucleus) | Quarks, nucleons | Gluons
Electromagnetic | 2 | Infinite | Charged particles only | Photons
Weak nuclear | 3 | Very short | Subatomic particles | W and Z bosons
Gravitational | 4 (weakest) | Infinite | All masses | Graviton (hypothetical)
Order: strong > electromagnetic > weak > gravity
Two infinite-range forces: gravity, electromagnetism; two short-range: strong, weak
⚠ Gravity is the weakest, though it dominates at cosmic scale; it is not in the Standard Model (Standard Model explains only 3 forces)
⚠ Weak force is weaker than EM but stronger than gravity
PYQ 2013: "which is NOT correct" → "Gravity is the strongest of the four". True statements: EM acts only on charged particles; weak force causes radioactivity; strong force holds protons and neutrons in nucleus

t: Each force → what it explains (examples)
text:
## 1. Gravitational
Attraction between masses; Einstein: curvature of space-time; ∝ 1/distance²
Holds Moon in orbit, structure of stars and galaxies
## 2. Electromagnetic (Lorentz force)
Attractive or repulsive; governed by Coulomb's law
Explains electricity, magnetism, light, chemistry, all atomic-molecular phenomena; e.g., comb and hair
## 3. Strong nuclear
Binds protons and neutrons, overcoming proton-proton repulsion; binds quarks into hadrons
Force increases with distance within its tiny range (quark confinement); powers fusion and fission
## 4. Weak nuclear
Causes beta decay → radioactivity; neutron → proton + electron + antineutrino
Drives nuclear reactions in stars and produces neutrinos
Phenomenon | Force responsible
Radioactive (beta) decay | Weak
Stability of nucleus | Strong
Chemical bonding, friction, light | Electromagnetic
Planetary orbits, tides | Gravity
## Beyond your notes
Electroweak unification: EM and weak forces unify at high energy (Glashow, Salam, Weinberg, Nobel 1979); W and Z bosons found at CERN in 1983
A theory of quantum gravity (string theory, loop quantum gravity) is still unproven

t: Alpha particle → what it is
text:
## 1. Identity
Alpha particle = nucleus of helium (He⁴⁺⁺): 2 protons + 2 neutrons, no electrons
Charge +2e; mass ≈ 4 u, i.e., very nearly the mass of a helium atom (electrons negligible)
Discovered by Rutherford (he discovered both alpha and beta rays)
Option in 1996 PYQ | Correct?
Two protons | No (misses 2 neutrons)
An atom of helium | Yes
Two positrons + two neutrons | No
Two positrons | No (positron mass = electron mass)
⚠ Mass is that of a helium nucleus/atom, not of two protons; charge is +2 because of 2 protons
PYQ 1996: "alpha carries two positive charges; its mass is very nearly that of" → an atom of helium

t: Alpha, beta, gamma → nature, speed, penetration
text:
Feature | Alpha (α) | Beta (β) | Gamma (γ)
Nature | Helium nuclei | Fast electrons (β⁻) or positrons (β⁺) | EM radiation (photons)
Charge | +2 | −1 or +1 | Neutral
Mass | 4 u | ~0.00055 u | Zero
Speed | ~1/10 of light | Close to light | = light
Penetration (Al) | Lowest (~0.002 cm) | ~0.5 cm | Highest (>5 cm)
Ionising power | Highest | ~100× less than α | ~100× less than β
Gamma emission usually follows alpha or beta emission (nucleus drops from excited state)
⚠ Penetration: γ > β > α; ionisation: α > β > γ (reverse orders)
⚠ Only beta (β⁻) of the three carries negative charge (BPSC 2002); neutron and neutrino carry zero charge

t: Nucleus → discovery, composition, decay
text:
## 1. Milestones
Discovery | By | Note
Nucleus (gold-foil α scattering, 1911) | Rutherford (Geiger & Marsden did experiment) | Atom mostly empty space
Neutron (1932) | Chadwick | Nobel 1935; mass ≈ proton
Nucleus size 10⁻¹⁵ to 10⁻¹⁴ m; atom ~10⁻¹⁰ m (10,000-100,000× bigger)
A = Z + N (mass number = protons + neutrons); nucleons = protons + neutrons
## 2. Decay facts (NCERT)
Free neutron is unstable: n → p + e⁻ + antineutrino, mean life ~1000 s; stable inside nucleus
β⁻ decay emits an antineutrino; β⁺ decay emits a neutrino
Stable nuclei: n/p ≈ 1:1 (light), ~3:2 (heavy); only ~10% of known isotopes are stable
Fusion of hydrogen into helium powers all stars; fission splits heavy nuclei (U-235)
⚠ Electron-positron pair: identical mass, equal and opposite charge; they annihilate into gamma photons
## Beyond your notes
Positron (first antiparticle) discovered by Carl Anderson, 1932, in cosmic rays

topic: Standard Model: quarks, leptons, bosons, Higgs and antimatter
t: Standard Model → 17 particles, fermions vs bosons
text:
Group | Spin | Members | Role
Fermions (Enrico Fermi) | Half-integer (1/2) | 6 quarks + 6 leptons = 12 | Matter
Gauge bosons (S.N. Bose) | 1 | Photon, gluon, W, Z | Force carriers
Scalar boson | 0 | Higgs (only one known) | Mass
Total 17 fundamental particles; explains 3 forces (strong, weak, EM), not gravity
Fermions obey Pauli exclusion (Fermi-Dirac statistics); bosons do not (Bose-Einstein statistics)
⚠ Protons and neutrons are NOT fundamental (made of quarks) and are not among the 17
⚠ "Which is a fundamental particle: neutron, proton, pi-meson, quark?" → quark (UPRO 2017)
## Beyond your notes
Graviton (gravity carrier) is hypothetical; it appears in string theory, not in the Standard Model

topic: Standard Model: quarks, leptons, bosons, Higgs and antimatter
t: Quarks and hadrons → types and combinations
text:
## 1. Quarks
Six flavours: up, down, charm, strange, top, bottom; up lightest, top heaviest (most massive known particle)
Fractional charges: +2/3 e (u, c, t), −1/3 e (d, s, b)
Carry colour charge (red, green, blue); feel all four forces; confined, never free
## 2. Hadrons (quarks bound by gluons)
Hadron | Made of | Example
Baryon | 3 quarks | Proton (uud), neutron (udd)
Meson | Quark + antiquark | Pions, kaons, B mesons
Exotic | 4 or 5 quarks | Tetraquarks, pentaquarks (found at LHC)
Quark-gluon plasma recreated at LHC (and RHIC, USA)
## In news 2025-26
LHC discovered Xi-cc-plus: two charm + one down quark, ~4× heavier than a proton (2026)

topic: Standard Model: quarks, leptons, bosons, Higgs and antimatter
t: Leptons → six types and the electron family
text:
Charged lepton (−1) | Neutral partner | Note
Electron | Electron neutrino | Lightest, stable; chemical bonding, current
Muon | Muon neutrino | ~200× electron mass; decays to e + neutrinos; cosmic rays
Tau | Tau neutrino | Heaviest (~3500× electron); very short-lived
Leptons do not feel the strong force; can exist independently
Charged leptons feel EM + weak; neutrinos only weak + gravity
⚠ Electron, muon, tau are leptons, not quarks; muons reaching the ground come from cosmic rays

topic: Standard Model: quarks, leptons, bosons, Higgs and antimatter
t: Bosons → which force each carries
text:
Boson | Force / role | Mass | Antiparticle
Photon (γ) | Electromagnetic; light | Massless, chargeless | Own antiparticle
Gluon (g) | Strong; binds quarks | Massless; has colour | -
W⁺, W⁻ | Weak (radioactive decay) | Heavy | W⁺ ↔ W⁻
Z⁰ | Weak | Heavy | Own antiparticle
Higgs (H) | Gives mass (not a force carrier) | Heavy | -
W and Z discovered 1983; gluons studied at RHIC (Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider)
⚠ Higgs is a boson but not a gauge/force carrier in the strict sense; it is the only scalar (spin-0) fundamental particle

topic: Standard Model: quarks, leptons, bosons, Higgs and antimatter
t: Higgs boson → why its discovery matters
text:
## 1. Facts
Proposed 1964 by Peter Higgs and five others; found 2012 by ATLAS and CMS at LHC, CERN
Nobel Physics 2013: Peter Higgs and François Englert
Quantum excitation of the Higgs field, which fills all space (even vacuum) with a non-zero value
Spin 0, no electric charge, no colour charge; lifetime ~10⁻²² s
"God particle" is a media term from Leon Lederman's 1993 book
## 2. Mass generation
Interaction with Higgs field | Result | Example
Strong | Heavy | W, Z bosons
Moderate | Has mass | Electrons, quarks
None | Massless | Photon
Without it: all particles massless, no atoms, stars, planets, life
⚠ Explains why elementary particles have mass; it does not enable teleportation or better fission fuel
⚠ Preview dates confirmation 14 March 2013; PMF says 2012 (announcement July 2012): answer 2012
PYQ 2013: three "importances" of Higgs; only "understand why elementary particles have mass" → 1 only
## In news 2025-26
Peter Higgs died (April 2024); LHC to produce 380 million Higgs bosons after HL-LHC upgrade (vs 55 million so far)

topic: Standard Model: quarks, leptons, bosons, Higgs and antimatter
t: Antimatter → what it is and what creating it implies
text:
## 1. Basics
Antiparticle: same mass, opposite charge and quantum numbers
Particle | Antiparticle
Electron | Positron
Proton | Antiproton
Neutron | Antineutron
Neutrino | Antineutrino
Particle + antiparticle → annihilation → energy (E = mc²); e⁻ + e⁺ → gamma rays
Sources: cosmic rays, radioactive decay; made in accelerators (CERN); use: PET scans
Matter-antimatter asymmetry: Big Bang made equal amounts, universe is matter-dominated (unsolved); explained by CP violation (a Sakharov condition)
## 2. The 2012 PYQ
Brookhaven National Laboratory (USA, RHIC), with Indian scientists, created anti-helium-4 nucleus, the heaviest antimatter
⚠ Implications: probe antimatter stars/galaxies and evolution of the universe; not mineral prospecting or oil exploration
PYQ 2012: answer 2 and 3 only

topic: Standard Model: quarks, leptons, bosons, Higgs and antimatter
t: Antimatter experiments → in news 2025-26
text:
Experiment | Where | What
BASE-STEP | CERN | First road transport of antimatter (antiprotons) (2026)
LHCb | CERN | First CP violation in baryons (Λb⁰: u, d, b quarks), ~2.45% asymmetry, 5.2 sigma (2025)
AEgIS | CERN, with India | Measure gravity on antihydrogen; first pulsed antihydrogen (2018); laser cooling of positronium
Positronium: hydrogen-like atom of electron + positron; half-life 142 ns
Before 2025, CP violation was seen only in mesons (kaons, B mesons)
⚠ 5 sigma is the discovery threshold in particle physics
⚠ Antimatter is extremely rare in nature; mostly made artificially

t: Beyond the Standard Model → dark matter, dark energy, SUSY, strings
text:
Feature | Dark matter | Dark energy
Nature | Invisible matter (no EM emission/absorption) | Unknown energy
Effect | Gravitational pull | Repulsive (anti-gravity)
Role | Holds galaxies together | Drives accelerated expansion
Share | ~27% | ~68%
Ordinary matter ~5%; dark matter detected only by gravitational effects
Supersymmetry: every particle has a heavier superpartner differing by ½ spin (selectron, squark, photino, gluino)
String theory: particles are vibrating 1-D strings; includes graviton; aims at a "theory of everything"
Neutrino mass and oscillation already point beyond the Standard Model
⚠ Dark energy (68%) > dark matter (27%) > ordinary matter (5%)

t: Neutrino → properties (the "ghost particle")
text:
## 1. Properties
Property | Neutrino
Family | Lepton (fundamental fermion)
Charge | Zero (not deflected by magnetic fields)
Mass | Tiny but non-zero; lightest particle with mass
Speed | Close to light
Forces felt | Only weak + gravity
Flavours | 3: electron, muon, tau
Abundance | 2nd most abundant particle after photons; most abundant particle with mass
Pass through matter almost untouched: ~100 billion through a fingertip every second (PMF); "trillions through the body every second" (UPSC 2010)
Natural: Sun's fusion (main source reaching Earth), supernovae, cosmic rays in atmosphere, beta decay, Big Bang relics, Earth's interior (geoneutrinos)
Artificial: nuclear reactors, particle accelerators; even bananas (K-40 beta decay)
⚠ PMF S&T says "billions" pass through the body; other PMF pages say 100 billion through a finger: the 2010 key accepts "trillions"
PYQ 2010 (INO context): all four true: chargeless, near light speed; created in beta decay; negligible but non-zero mass; trillions pass through the body each second
## Beyond your notes
Neutrino proposed by Wolfgang Pauli (1930) to save energy conservation in beta decay; named by Fermi

t: Neutrino oscillation and mass → why it matters
text:
## 1. Oscillation
A neutrino changes flavour in flight (e.g., solar electron neutrino detected as muon/tau neutrino)
Possible only if neutrinos have mass → evidence for physics beyond the Standard Model
Nobel Physics 2015: Takaaki Kajita (Super-Kamiokande) and Arthur McDonald (SNO) for discovering oscillations
## 2. Uses of neutrinos
Use | How
Solar studies | Monitor fusion in Sun's core
Supernova early warning | Neutrinos escape before light
Geophysics | Geoneutrinos map Earth's interior
Nuclear safeguards | Detect reactor/spent-fuel antineutrinos from a distance
⚠ Neutrinos are the only fundamental particles whose mass is still uncertain

t: Neutrino mass experiments → in news 2025-26
text:
Experiment | Country | Finding
KATRIN (Karlsruhe Tritium Neutrino) | Germany (12 institutions: Germany, UK, Czech Rep., USA) | Neutrino mass < 0.45 eV, nearly halving earlier limit; from 36 million electrons of tritium beta decay
AMoRE | South Korea | No evidence of neutrinoless double beta decay, using molybdenum-100; pilot since 2015
Double Chooz | France | First measurement of antineutrinos from spent nuclear fuel
Double beta decay: 2 neutrons → 2 protons + 2 electrons + 2 antineutrinos
Neutrinoless (0νββ): only 2 electrons emitted → would prove neutrino is a Majorana particle (its own antiparticle)
KATRIN measures electron antineutrino mass directly, independent of cosmological models
⚠ Spent-fuel antineutrino detection helps check if fuel is secretly diverted for weapons
⚠ Majorana 1 is a quantum-computing chip using Majorana particles (do not confuse with AMoRE)

t: IceCube → location and features
text:
## 1. Facts
IceCube Neutrino Observatory, at the geographic South Pole, near Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station
World's largest neutrino detector; first gigaton detector; one cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice
Buried deep in the ice (shields background); 5,160 optical sensors; completed 2010, operating since 2011
Detects blue Cherenkov light from charged particles made when a neutrino hits a nucleus in ice
Studies high-energy cosmic neutrinos, supernovae, black holes, gamma-ray bursts, cosmic-ray origin; also dark matter searches and glaciology
Founded neutrino astronomy and multi-messenger astronomy
⚠ All three 2015 statements true: largest (km³), dark matter telescope, buried deep → 1, 2 and 3
PYQ 2015: IceCube statements; trap is doubting "dark matter search": it is correct
## In news 2025-26
Nobel Physics 2026: Francis Halzen (Belgian-American) for conceptualising and leading IceCube and discovering neutrinos of astrophysical origin

t: Physical vs chemical change → which is which
text:
## 1. The test
Feature | Physical change | Chemical change
New substance | Not formed | Formed
Composition | Same | Changes (bonds broken and made)
Reversibility | Usually reversible | Usually irreversible
Energy | Little | Significant heat/light
Mass | Conserved | Conserved
## 2. Examples UPSC-type options use
Physical | Chemical
Melting of ice, freezing, boiling | Souring of milk (lactose → lactic acid)
Crystallisation of NaCl, dissolving salt or sugar | Curd formation, digestion, cooking
Sublimation of camphor, NH₄Cl | Rusting of iron, burning, fireworks
Breaking glass, cutting paper, stretching rubber | Photosynthesis, respiration
Magnetisation of iron, expansion on heating | Electrolysis of water, neutralisation
⚠ Irreversible is not the test: breaking glass is irreversible but physical; only a new substance makes it chemical
⚠ Dissolving and crystallisation are physical (salt is recovered unchanged)
PYQ 2014: of crystallisation of NaCl, melting of ice, souring of milk, only souring of milk is chemical (3 only)

t: Pure substances and mixtures → classification
text:
Category | Type | Meaning | Examples
Pure substance | Element | One kind of atom; cannot be broken chemically | H, O, gold
Pure substance | Compound | Two or more elements chemically bonded in fixed ratio | Water, NaCl, CO₂
Mixture | Homogeneous | Uniform composition | Salt water, air, alloys (brass, bronze)
Mixture | Heterogeneous | Components distinguishable | Oil and water, sand and water
Compound: properties differ from its elements; separated only chemically (e.g. electrolysis)
Mixture: variable composition; components keep their properties; no fixed melting/boiling point; separated physically
⚠ Alloys and air are mixtures (homogeneous), not compounds
⚠ Organic compounds have C-H bonds (glucose, methane); CO₂ and NaCl are inorganic
## 2. Matter terms
Extensive property depends on amount (mass, volume); intensive does not (density, colour, boiling point)
States: solid, liquid, gas, plasma (Sun, lightning, aurora), Bose-Einstein condensate (near absolute zero)

t: Chemical reactions → type and example
text:
Type | Pattern | Example
Combination | A + B → AB | 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O
Decomposition | AB → A + B | Electrolysis of water
Displacement | A + BC → AC + B | Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu
Double displacement | AB + CD → AD + CB | NaCl + AgNO₃ → AgCl + NaNO₃
Precipitation | Insoluble solid forms | BaCl₂ + Na₂SO₄ → BaSO₄↓
Neutralisation | Acid + base → salt + water | HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O
Redox | Oxidation = loss of electrons; reduction = gain | 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO
Combustion | With O₂, heat + light | CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
Endothermic absorbs energy (photosynthesis); exothermic releases (combustion, respiration)
Catalyst lowers activation energy, not consumed, does not shift equilibrium; e.g. nickel in hydrogenation of oils (vanaspati), enzymes as biocatalysts
⚠ Oxidising agent is itself reduced (gains electrons); reducing agent (H₂, CO, Na) is oxidised

t: Corrosion, fermentation, rancidity → process and prevention
text:
Feature | Corrosion | Fermentation | Rancidity
Type | Chemical (oxidation of metal) | Biological (enzymes, anaerobic) | Chemical (oxidation/hydrolysis of fats)
Example | Rusting of iron, tarnishing of silver | Ethanol by yeast (zymase); lactic acid in curd | Rancid butter, stale fried snacks
Needs | Oxygen + moisture (acids, salt speed it) | Sugar + microbes | Air, light, heat, moisture
Prevention | Paint, galvanisation (Zn), chromium plating, alloying | (useful process) | Airtight packing, antioxidants (BHT, vitamin E), refrigeration, nitrogen flushing
⚠ Rusting needs both O₂ and water: iron in dry air or in boiled (air-free) water does not rust
⚠ Silver tarnishes black due to H₂S (Ag₂S), not oxygen
## Beyond your notes
Chips packets are flushed with nitrogen to delay rancidity

t: Elements of life → C, H, N, O (+ P, S)
text:
Element | Role
Carbon | Backbone of all organic molecules (catenation)
Hydrogen | In water and all organic compounds
Nitrogen | Amino acids, proteins, nucleic acids
Oxygen | Water, respiration, organic groups
Phosphorus | DNA/RNA backbone, ATP, phospholipids
Sulfur | Some amino acids (cysteine, methionine)
Preview: six elements (H, O, C, N, P, S) make up the matter of living things
Oparin-Haldane hypothesis: life arose by chemical evolution from simple gases (CH₄, NH₃, H₂O, H₂) on early Earth
⚠ 2012 traps: sodium, calcium, potassium are needed by life but were not the "origin of life" set
PYQ 2012: elements primarily responsible for the origin of life → carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen
## Beyond your notes
Miller-Urey experiment (1953) made amino acids from CH₄, NH₃, H₂, water vapour with electric sparks
Most abundant element in human body by mass: oxygen; in Earth's crust: oxygen, then silicon; most abundant metal in crust: aluminium

t: Water → why it is the universal solvent
text:
## 1. Reason: polarity (dipole)
Water is polar (dipolar): partial negative near oxygen, partial positive near hydrogens; bent shape
Its ends attract oppositely charged parts of other substances, surround ions and pull them apart → dissolves salts, sugars, acids, bases, gases
PMF: polarity also makes water amphoteric (acts as acid and base) and lets it form hydrates
Rocket Sheets: water dissolves ionic salts best due to high dipole moment; ionic compounds are generally insoluble in alcohol
⚠ 2021 traps: "good conductor of heat", "high specific heat", "oxide of hydrogen" are not the reason; pure water is in fact a poor conductor
PYQ 2021: water dissolves more substances than any other liquid because it is dipolar
## Beyond your notes
Hydrogen bonding (also due to polarity) gives water its high specific heat and high boiling point, and makes ice less dense than water (ice floats)

t: Polar vs non-polar molecules → solubility rule
text:
Feature | Polar | Non-polar
Electron sharing | Unequal | Equal
Dipole moment | Present | Absent
Geometry | Asymmetrical | Symmetrical
Forces | Dipole-dipole, hydrogen bonds | Weak London (van der Waals)
Boiling point | Higher | Lower
Dissolves in | Polar solvents (water) | Non-polar solvents (oil, benzene)
Examples | H₂O, NH₃, HCl | CH₄, CO₂, O₂
Rule: like dissolves like
⚠ CO₂ is non-polar (linear, dipoles cancel) though its bonds are polar; H₂O is polar because it is bent

Solvent | Solute | Example
Solid | Solid | Alloys (brass)
Solid | Liquid | Mercury in gold (amalgam)
Solid | Gas | Hydrogen in palladium
Liquid | Solid | Sugar in water
Liquid | Liquid | Alcohol in water
Liquid | Gas | Carbonated water
Gas | Solid | Camphor in air
Gas | Liquid | Water vapour in air
Gas | Gas | Air
True solution: particles < 1 nm, transparent, no Tyndall effect, cannot be filtered, does not settle

⚠ Salt water conducts (electrolyte); sugar water does not

Temporary hardness (bicarbonates) is removed by boiling; permanent hardness (chlorides, sulphates) needs washing soda or ion exchange

text:
Metal | Density (g/cm³) | Note

Potassium | 0.86 | Most reactive in series
Sodium | 0.97 | Street lights, liquid coolant in fast reactors

Lithium carbonate (Li₂CO₃): commercial form of lithium, raw material for Li-ion batteries, also used in bipolar disorder medicine; fall in its price cuts battery-storage costs (PMF Prelims Magnum Sept 2026); lithium called "white gold"

t: Reactivity series → order and consequences
text:
Order | Metals | Behaviour
Most reactive | K > Na > Ca | React vigorously with cold water
 | Mg > Al > Zn > Fe | Mg reacts with hot water; Zn, Fe with acids/steam
 | Pb | Slow with acids
(Hydrogen) | H | Metals above it displace H₂ from dilute acids
Least reactive | Cu > Hg > Ag > Au | No reaction with dilute acids; found native
A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from its salt: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu
Top metals (K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al) are never free in nature; extracted by electrolysis of molten salts (Al: Hall-Héroult with cryolite)
Aluminium resists corrosion despite high reactivity: protective oxide layer (anodising)
⚠ Food cans are tin-plated, not zinc-coated: zinc is more reactive and would react with food acids
## Beyond your notes
Caesium/francium are more reactive than potassium; school series start at K

t: Amalgam → which metals form it
text:

Zinc | Yes (zinc amalgam)
Copper | Yes
Magnesium | Yes
Silver, tin, gold, sodium | Yes
Iron | No

⚠ Because iron does not amalgamate, mercury is stored and shipped in iron flasks
PYQ 1998: metal that does not form amalgam → iron (traps zinc, copper, magnesium)
## Beyond your notes
Sodium amalgam is used as a reducing agent; gold mining uses mercury amalgamation (a pollution issue)

topic: Non-metals, Metalloids, Noble Gases and Allotropes
t: Selenium and metalloids → semiconductors
text:
## 1. Selenium (Se, Z = 34)
Non-metal, photoconductive: conductivity rises when it absorbs light; shows photovoltaic action
Grey selenium is a semiconductor; several allotropes
Discovered by Berzelius (1817)
PYQ 2007: non-metal that is not a poor conductor → selenium (traps sulfur, bromine, phosphorus)
## 2. The six metalloids (PMF)
Metalloid | Note
Boron, silicon, germanium | Semiconductors
Arsenic, antimony, tellurium | Amphoteric oxides
Metalloids: shiny like metals, brittle like non-metals; conduct better than non-metals, worse than metals
Silicon: about 28% of crust, from silica (sand, quartz); most used semiconductor; germanium was used in the first transistor (Bell Labs, 1947) (CARE Apr 2026)
⚠ Selenium is not one of the six metalloids in PMF's list; it is a non-metal that conducts
## Beyond your notes
Selenium was used in photocopiers (xerography), light meters and early solar cells

t: Acid strength → formic vs acetic (assertion-reason)
text:
Point | Formic acid | Acetic acid
Formula | HCOOH | CH₃COOH

t: Lead → health effects and India's control measures
text:
## 1. The metal and the disease
Bluish-white, soft, malleable, ductile, poor conductor, low melting point, usually found with zinc, silver, copper ores
Lead poisoning = plumbism (also saturnism); harm above 5 µg/dL blood lead
Causes anaemia, cognitive decline, kidney damage, foetal harm; neurological, cardiovascular damage
One-third of the world's children burdened; India the worst-affected
## 2. Control measures in India
Measure | Year | Provision
Leaded petrol ban | 2000 | Leaded petrol phased out
Lead Paint Rules | 2016 | Decorative paint lead capped at 90 ppm
FSSAI food limits | 2011 | Bans lead chromate in turmeric; ≤10 ppm in packaged food
Insecticides Act amendment | 2019 | Bans lead arsenate in farming
GAELP (global) | 2011 | UNEP + WHO alliance to eliminate lead paint
## In news 2025-26
Lead poisoning from cookware (Aug 2025): old aluminium pressure cookers leach lead; cast iron cookware gives natural iron fortification

t: Bisphenol A and other endocrine disruptors → where found
text:
## 1. Bisphenol A (BPA)
Industrial chemical for polycarbonate plastics and epoxy resins (inner lining of metal food cans)
Found in food containers, water bottles, thermal-paper receipts; substitute BPS is similar
Mimics oestrogen: linked to infertility, obesity, heart disease, type II diabetes, cancer
⚠ BPA is not a cancer test, a doping test or an alloy steel (the 2008 distractors): it is a food-packaging chemical
## 2. Endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs): the full set
EDC | Found in | Effect
BPA and BPS | Food containers, bottles, thermal paper | Mimics oestrogen
Phthalates (DEHP, DBP) | Cosmetics, toys, medical (IV) tubing; make plastics flexible | Lower testosterone
PFAS | Non-stick cookware, food packaging | Cancer, thyroid issues
Dioxins | By-product of plastic making; burning PVC | Carcinogen; passes into breast milk
EDCs mimic or block oestrogen, testosterone, thyroid hormones
PYQ 2008: "What is Bisphenol A?" → a chemical used for food-packaging materials

t: PFAS and microplastics → what they are, why in news
text:
## 1. PFAS ("forever chemicals")
Human-made compounds with very strong carbon-fluorine (C-F) bonds: resist heat, water, oil, degradation
Uses: non-stick cookware, waterproof and stain-resistant textiles, food packaging, firefighting foams
PFOS is one PFAS; it suppresses the antiviral protein IRF3
## 2. Micro- and nanoplastics
Type | Size | Note
Microplastics | < 5 mm | Primary (microbeads in cosmetics) or secondary (breakdown of bottles, bags)
Inhalable microplastics | < 10 µm | Not covered by PM2.5/PM10 standards
Nanoplastics | 1-1000 nm | Make E. coli more virulent
Carry heavy metals (lead, cadmium) and phthalates ("Trojan-horse effect"); microbeads banned in cosmetics under PWM Rules
## In news 2025-26
PFAS in India's water (Oct 2026): India has no PFAS limit under IS 10500:2012
Stockholm Convention COP, Geneva (2025): chlorpyrifos, LC-PFCAs (forever chemicals in cookware), MCCPs added to Annex A (elimination); UV-328 allowed in aerospace and defence
Inhalable microplastics study (Dec 2025): ~8.8 µg/m³; urban resident inhales ~132 µg a day
Toxics Link: microplastics in all 10 salt and sugar samples; FSSAI project (2024) to set standards

t: Fruit ripening and formaldehyde → hazards in daily use
text:
## 1. Calcium carbide (banned ripener)
Greyish-black welding chemical; reacts with moisture to release acetylene, which imitates ethylene (natural ripening hormone)
Commercial grade contains arsenic and phosphorus: vomiting, ulcers, neurological disorders, cancer
Banned for ripening under FSS (Prohibition and Restriction on Sales) Regulations, 2011
## 2. Formaldehyde
Colourless, strong-smelling; used in resins (urea-formaldehyde), building materials, preservative
Released from preservatives (DMDM hydantoin, imidazolidinyl urea, quaternium-15) in shampoos, lotions, eyelash glue
IARC: human carcinogen
## In news 2025-26
Calcium carbide (Apr 2026): Hyderabad police and municipal inspections on carbide-ripened mangoes
## Beyond your notes
FSSAI permits ethylene gas for artificial ripening (verify the ppm limit)

topic: Food additives, sweeteners and food acids
t: Aspartame → why it is a low-calorie sweetener
text:
## 1. The 2011 logic
Aspartame = aspartic acid + phenylalanine (a dipeptide); it is metabolised and gives 4 kcal/g, like protein
But it is ~200 times sweeter than sugar, so the amount needed is tiny → negligible calories
Broken down into phenylalanine, aspartic acid and methanol, all handled by the body normally
Option in 2011 | Verdict
As sweet as sugar, not oxidised (no enzymes) | Wrong
Becomes resistant to oxidation in processing | Wrong
Converted into metabolites that yield no calories | Wrong
Several times sweeter, so small quantity gives fewer calories | Correct
⚠ Aspartame is not calorie-free and not unmetabolised: the low calorie count comes only from the tiny dose
## In news 2025-26
Study on artificial sweeteners and cognitive decline (Sep 2025): WHO (IARC) classified aspartame "possibly carcinogenic" in 2023; erythritol (sugar alcohol) linked to blood clotting
## Beyond your notes
Products with aspartame carry a warning for phenylketonurics (cannot metabolise phenylalanine)

Caffeine (tea, coffee) is a diuretic | Correct | Mild diuretic: increases urine output

text:
## 1. What they are
Unsaturated fat with a double bond in the trans configuration
Natural trans fat: small amounts in dairy and meat of ruminants (safe in moderation)
Industrial trans fat: partial hydrogenation of liquid oils → vanaspati, margarine, bakery and fried foods
## 2. Fats compared
Fat | Examples | Effect
Monounsaturated (MUFA) | Olive oil, nuts | Healthy
Polyunsaturated (PUFA, omega-3, omega-6) | Sunflower oil, fish, flaxseed | Healthy; essential fatty acids
Saturated | Butter, ghee, cheese | Unhealthy in excess

FSSAI caps industrial trans fat at 2% of total fat in oils and fats (from Jan 2022)

Item | Mandatory on label?
List of ingredients, including additives | Yes
Nutrition information | Yes

Medical recommendations about possible allergic reactions | No

text:

Statutory body under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
FSSAI sets national standards; State Food Safety Authorities enforce (98% of food businesses are under states)
## 2. FSS regulations that UPSC-style questions cite
Regulation | Covers

topic: Food safety law: FSSAI, labelling and fortification

text:
## 1. Front-of-Package Labelling (FOPL)
Simple visible label flagging high sugar, salt, saturated fat (HFSS) on packaged food
Supreme Court (Feb 2026) directed FSSAI to consider mandatory FOPL for HFSS foods (Right to Health under Art 21)
FSSAI proposed Indian Nutrition Rating (INR): a star rating like BEE energy labels
Health advocates prefer warning labels ("High in Sugar"), judged more effective
## 2. Other labelling news
Issue | Date | What changed
"ORS" label | Oct 2025 | No product may use "ORS" unless the formula is WHO-approved; stops sugary drinks posing as ORS
Added sugar in Nestlé baby food | 2024 | Daily Value for added sugar 50 g/day (2,000 kcal diet)
ICMR-INDIAB 2023 | 2023 | Diabetes 101 million (11.4%): the case for FOPL
⚠ Added sugars include white and brown sugar, honey added in processing and high-fructose corn syrup; sugar naturally in milk (lactose) and fruit (fructose) is not "added"

topic: Food safety law: FSSAI, labelling and fortification
t: Food fortification → nutrient added to each staple
text:
## 1. Fortified rice
Fortified Rice Kernels (FRK): rice flour enriched and re-shaped into grains, blended 1:100 with normal rice
FSSAI mandates iron, folic acid, vitamin B12; zinc, vitamin A and other B-vitamins optional
Aim: "hidden hunger", anaemia; supplied through PDS and PM POSHAN school meals
## 2. Staples and their nutrients
Staple | Added nutrient
Rice | Iron, folic acid, vitamin B12
Edible oil | Vitamins A and D
Salt | Iodine (double-fortified: iodine + iron)
Wheat flour (atta) | Iron, folic acid, vitamin B12
Milk | Vitamins A and D
PMF: mandatory fortification of rice, edible oil and salt
## In news 2025-26
First FRK export (Nov 2025): Chhattisgarh → Costa Rica, facilitated by APEDA
## Beyond your notes
Fortified food carries the "+F" logo; oil, milk and atta rows above are FSSAI fortification standards (2018)

topic: Alcohols and glycols: hooch, antifreeze, cough syrup
t: Methyl alcohol → cause of hooch tragedies and blindness
text:
## 1. Why methanol blinds and kills
Spurious/illicit liquor contains methanol (CH3OH) in place of ethanol
Liver enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase converts it to formaldehyde (methanal) and formic acid
Methanal coagulates protoplasm and damages the optic nerve → blindness, then death
Ethanol competes for the same enzyme → acts as a temporary antidote
Option (1996) | Hooch culprit?
Ethyl alcohol | No: the drinking alcohol
Amyl alcohol | No
Benzyl alcohol | No
Methyl alcohol | Yes
## 2. Regulation
FSS (Alcoholic Beverages) Regulations, 2018 fix maximum methanol in each liquor
Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers: mandatory certification of methanol; quality standard IS 517
⚠ Liquor strength: beer ~5%, wine ~12%, distilled spirits ~40% ethanol
## Beyond your notes
Denatured spirit = ethanol made undrinkable by adding methanol; fomepizole is the medical antidote

topic: Alcohols and glycols: hooch, antifreeze, cough syrup
t: Methanol vs ethanol → properties and uses
text:
## 1. Side by side (PMF)
Feature | Methanol (methyl alcohol) | Ethanol (ethyl alcohol)
Formula | CH3OH | C2H5OH
Toxicity | Poisonous even in small doses | Drinking alcohol; harmful only in excess
Main use | Feedstock for formaldehyde, acetic acid; solvent; biodiesel making | Beverages, sanitisers, perfumes, antiseptic
Made from | Coal and natural gas (via syngas CO + H2) | Fermentation of biomass, food crops
Flame | Bright white | Bright blue
Calorific value | ~23 MJ/kg | ~29 MJ/kg (more range)
Both are cleaner fuels with high octane; ethanol is preferred for blending
## 2. Methanol economy (NITI Aayog)
M15 (15% methanol in petrol) can cut fuel imports by 15% and GHG by ~20%
20% DME (dimethyl ether) in LPG may save Rs 6,000 crore a year
Isopropyl alcohol = rubbing alcohol (disinfectant)

topic: Alcohols and glycols: hooch, antifreeze, cough syrup
t: Ethylene glycol → antifreeze and other glycols
text:
## 1. Antifreeze
Ethylene glycol is the automobile antifreeze: mixed with radiator water it lowers the freezing point and raises the boiling point
Also a raw material: ethylene glycol + terephthalic acid → PET/terylene; + phthalic acid → glyptal
⚠ Not methanol, ethanol or propyl alcohol (1997 options); PMF lists ethylene among antifreeze raw materials because glycol is made from it
## 2. The glycol family
Glycol | Use | Safe to swallow?
Ethylene glycol | Antifreeze, coolant, PET | No: toxic
Diethylene glycol (DEG) | Antifreeze, brake fluid, solvent | No: kidney failure
Propylene glycol | Solvent in syrups, food | Yes (pharma grade)
Glycerin (glycerol) | Solvent in syrups, cosmetics | Yes
## In news 2025-26
DEG in cough syrup (Oct 2025): at least 20 children died in Madhya Pradesh; DEG is metabolised into toxins causing acute kidney injury and anuria
Drugs Rules amended (June 2026): village-sale exemptions removed from Schedule K to curb codeine misuse and DEG deaths
Exam angle: a syrup should use glycerin or propylene glycol; DEG and ethylene glycol are industrial poisons

Fuel gas | Major constituents | How obtained
CNG | Methane + ethane | Natural gas compressed

text:
## 1. Comparison
Fuel | Gas | Form | Key fact
LPG | Propane + butane | Liquid under moderate pressure, ~1/260 volume | Heavier than air: settles near floor
CNG | Methane | Gas at 200-250 kg/cm2 | Lighter than air; auto-ignition ~540°C

## 2. Natural gas types
Associated (wet) gas with oil; non-associated (dry); sour gas has H2S; coalbed methane = "sweet gas"

West Asia crisis, Strait of Hormuz (Mar 2026): India imports ~50% of its gas, 55-60% of that from West Asia; refiners maximised LPG; domestic LPG share 40% → 55%; cylinder booking gap 25 days urban, 45 days rural

t: Mine explosions → methane mixed with air
text:
## 1. Firedamp
Methane (firedamp) seeps from coal seams; explodes when it forms 5-15% of the air and meets a spark or flame

Hydrogen and oxygen | No

Methane and air | Yes

## 2. Methane facts

Coalbed methane is extracted from coal seams as fuel

t: Chlorination → why chlorine disinfects
text:
## 1. The chemistry
Cl2 + H2O → HOCl (hypochlorous acid) + HCl
HOCl is a weak acid but a strong oxidising agent: penetrates microbial cells and oxidises enzymes and proteins
WHO: HOCl is the principal disinfecting agent; its share depends on pH (more HOCl at lower pH)
Option (2010) | Verdict
Formation of hydrochloric acid | Wrong
Formation of hypochlorous acid | Correct
Formation of nascent oxygen | Wrong (old textbook explanation)
Formation of hydrogen | Wrong
⚠ Trap: nascent oxygen is the old bleaching explanation; UPSC's answer is HOCl
## 2. Practice
Chlorine leaves a residual that guards the distribution network; bleaching powder (calcium hypochlorite, CaOCl2) is the household form
Chlorine + natural organics → chloroform and other by-products; minimised by chlorinating after coagulation, sedimentation, filtration
BIS limit for chloramines: 4.0 mg/L

t: UV, RO, ozone and chlorine → what each removes
text:
## 1. Purification methods compared
Method | Kills microbes | Removes dissolved salts | Removes turbidity / odour | Residual effect
UV | Yes (DNA damage) | No | No | No
RO | Yes (membrane) | Yes | Yes | No
Ozone | Yes | No | Removes taste/odour | No residue
Chlorine | Yes | No | No | Yes
## 2. UV (PYQ 2012)
UV at 254 nm damages microbial DNA: bacteria, viruses, Cryptosporidium, Giardia cannot reproduce
Does not remove odour, does not speed sedimentation or clear turbidity
⚠ Answer 1 only: UV only inactivates/kills microbes
## 3. RO and ozone
RO: pressure forces water through a semipermeable membrane against osmosis; removes salts, bacteria, viruses, softens water; but wastes water, uses energy, strips useful minerals
Ozone: no taste/odour, no residue, cannot be stored (made on-site), costlier than chlorine
## Beyond your notes
UV needs clear water: turbidity shields microbes, so filtration comes first

t: Municipal water treatment → sequence and chemicals
text:
## 1. Steps
Step | What happens | Chemical / medium
Coagulation / flocculation | Fine dirt clumps into flocs | Alum (aluminium sulphate), ferric sulphate, sodium aluminate
Sedimentation | Flocs settle as sludge | Slow-moving basins
Filtration | Suspended impurities removed | Sand, gravel, crushed anthracite
Disinfection | Microbes killed | Chlorine, ozone, UV
pH correction | Reduce pipe corrosion | Lime
## 2. Removing specific contaminants
Iron: aeration and oxidation → insoluble ferric hydroxide, then filtration (BIS iron 0.3 mg/L; problem in North-East)
Arsenic: bleaching powder + alum bring it to the BIS limit of 0.05 mg/L
Fluoride: Nalgonda technique (alum/aluminium salts, lime, bleaching powder); activated alumina filters

text:
## 1. Contaminant → disease
Contaminant | Source | Disease
Fluoride | Geogenic: fluorspar, cryolite, fluorapatite, granite | Dental and skeletal fluorosis
Arsenic | Geogenic, worsened by over-pumping | Skin lesions, cancer

CGWB Annual Groundwater Quality Report 2024 (Aug 2025): 440 districts; Ballia (UP) arsenic 200 µg/L (20x WHO); 56% of districts exceed nitrate limits

t: Effluents → change in water's physico-chemical character
text:
## 1. The 1996 question
Option | Changes physico-chemical characteristics?
Aquatic macrophytes | No (biological part of the water body)
Aquatic fungi | No
Effluents | Yes: alter pH, turbidity, dissolved oxygen, chemistry
Evapotranspiration | No (water loss, not pollution)
## 2. Effluents and their effects
Industrial and domestic effluents add chemicals, heavy metals, nutrients
Phosphates and nitrates (detergents, fertilisers) → eutrophication: algal bloom, oxygen depletion
Only 30% of India's urban sewage is treated; 70% goes untreated into rivers (CPCB)
Thermal plant effluents and acid mine drainage add heavy metals; fly ash holds mercury, arsenic, lead, cadmium

topic: Acid rain and air pollutants from fuels
t: Acid rain → which oxides cause it
text:
## 1. Definition
Wet (rain, snow, fog) or dry deposition more acidic than pH 5.6
Normal rain is ~pH 5.6 because dissolved CO2 forms weak carbonic acid: not acid rain
## 2. Gas → role in acid rain
Gas | Causes acid rain? | How
SO2, SO3 | Yes (main historic driver) | → sulphuric acid
NO2, N2O3, N2O5 | Yes | → nitric and nitrous acid
NO, N2O | Indirectly | Neutral; oxidise to NO2
Ozone | Catalyst only | Speeds SO2/NOx → acids via OH radicals
CO, CO2 | No | Cannot push pH below 5.6
"Oxides of hydrogen" (water) | No | Not acid-forming
⚠ 2010 answer 2 and 3 only (N and S oxides); 2022 repeat: NO2 and SO2 cause it, CO and ozone do not
PYQ 2010, 2013, 2022: the same angle three times; always N and S oxides, never CO, CO2 or O3

topic: Acid rain and air pollutants from fuels
t: Acid rain → sources, chemistry and effects
text:
Coal-based power plants, industries (smelting, cement, steel), vehicles
Natural: volcanoes (SO2, HCl, HF), lightning (NOx); fertiliser nitrogen also forms nitric acid
## 2. Chemistry
2SO2 + O2 + 2H2O → 2H2SO4; N2O5 + H2O → 2HNO3
About half the atmospheric acidity falls as dry deposition
pH 4 is 10x more acidic than pH 5 and 100x more than pH 6
## 3. Effects
Acidifies lakes and soils; acid rain also brings nitrate (plant nutrient) to soil
## Beyond your notes
Corrodes marble and limestone (Taj Mahal "marble cancer" from Mathura refinery); leaches aluminium from soil; kills fish and forests

topic: Acid rain and air pollutants from fuels
t: Flue gas desulphurisation → SO2 control in news
text:
## 1. FGD
Flue gas from coal plants holds CO2, CO, NOx, SO2, PM
FGD passes it through limestone (or ammonia) slurry: SO2 → gypsum; removes up to 95% SO2
Other SO2 controls: fuel switching, coal washing, fluidised bed combustion
## 2. Status
Fact | Figure
FGD mandate for coal plants | 2015 (deadlines extended to 2027-30)
Capacity with FGD | 22 GW (~8%)
Plants with FGD | 39 of 537
India's share of global SO2 (2022) | Largest emitter, >20%
## In news 2025-26
High-powered committee under PSA Ajay Sood (Apr 2025): drop the blanket FGD mandate; argued SO2 aerosol health impact <5% and sulphate aerosols cool the climate
Most coal plants are no longer required to install FGD (2025)
Delhi tests titanium dioxide "smog-eating" coatings that break down NO2 and VOCs
⚠ CARE: 92% of 600 units lacked FGD; PMF: only 8% of capacity had it: same picture

text:
## 1. Differences (PMF table)
Feature | Animal cell | Plant cell
Cell wall | Absent | Present, made of cellulose
Shape | Irregular | Fixed, rectangular
Vacuole | Many small | One large central (up to 90% of volume)
Chloroplasts | Absent | Present
Centrioles | Present | Absent
Lysosomes | Present | Rare
Cilia | Present | Rare
## 2. Common to both
Plasma membrane, nucleus, cytoplasm, ER, ribosomes, mitochondria, Golgi complex

t: Cell wall → which organism, made of what

Organism | Cell wall material
Plants | Cellulose, hemicellulose, pectins, proteins
Fungi | Chitin, glucans, glycoproteins
Bacteria | Peptidoglycan (murein)
Algae | Cellulose, galactans, mannans, CaCO3

Organelle | Own DNA? | Notes
Mitochondrion | Yes (circular) + own ribosomes | Double membrane; inner folds = cristae; divides by fission

t: Mitochondrial disease and MRT → how it works
text:
## 1. Mitochondrial disease (two kinds)
Cause | Inherited from
Faulty genes in nuclear DNA | Both parents
Faulty genes in mtDNA | Mother only
## 2. Mitochondrial Replacement Therapy (MRT / MDT, "three-parent baby")
Technique | When | What moves
Maternal Spindle Transfer (MST) | Before fertilisation | Mother's chromosome spindle → donor egg
Pronuclear Transfer (PNT) | After fertilisation | Parents' pronuclei → donor zygote
Embryo: nuclear DNA of mother and father + mtDNA of donor; both methods use IVF
UK first to regulate and approve (2015), then Australia (2021)
⚠ MRT cannot cure existing disease or prevent disease from nuclear DNA mutations
## In news 2025-26
New clinical trial: eight babies born free of mitochondrial disease through MRT
PYQ 2021: both statements correct (MRT before or after IVF fertilisation; mito disease entirely from mother)

Bases | A, T, G, C | A, U, G, C

t: Glucose breakdown → name of each stage
text:
## 1. Stages
Stage | Where | Oxygen? | Product
Glycolysis | Cytoplasm | Not needed | Glucose (6C) → 2 pyruvate (3C)
Krebs cycle | Mitochondria | Needed | CO2
Oxidative phosphorylation | Mitochondria | Needed | Most ATP
Aerobic respiration = complete oxidation of glucose with O2 → CO2 + H2O + energy
⚠ Glycolysis is only the first step, common to all organisms; in anaerobes it is the only step
⚠ Hydrolysis = breakdown using water, not respiration
PYQ 1998: "complete conversion of glucose in presence of oxygen into CO2 and water" = aerobic respiration; traps glycolysis and hydrolysis

Feature | Aerobic | Anaerobic
Oxygen | Required | Not required
Site | Cytoplasm + mitochondria | Cytoplasm only
ATP per glucose | 36-38 | 2
End products | CO2 + water | Lactic acid (muscle) or ethanol + CO2 (yeast)
Oxidation | Complete | Partial
## 2. Examples
Yeast fermentation → ethanol + CO2
Muscle in intense exercise → lactic acid → fatigue, cramps
⚠ Anaerobic in muscle gives lactic acid, no CO2; in yeast gives ethanol and CO2

t: Mendel's laws → ratios
text:
## 1. Laws
Law | Shown by
Dominance | F1 all tall (Tt)
Segregation | F2 3:1 phenotype, 1:2:1 genotype
Independent assortment | Dihybrid F2 9:3:3:1
## 2. Exceptions
Pattern | Example | Ratio / result
Incomplete dominance | Snapdragon: red x white → pink | F2 1:2:1
Co-dominance | AB blood group | Both expressed
Polygenic | Skin colour, height | Continuous range
Pleiotropy | Phenylketonuria | One gene, many traits
Linkage | Genes close on a chromosome | Breaks independent assortment
Mendel used pea, 7 traits; Sutton and Boveri: chromosomal theory; Morgan: fruit fly; Sturtevant: first genetic map (centimorgan)

Disorder | Feature
Haemophilia | Clotting fails; mainly males

Type | Examples
Physical | UV radiation (PMF), X-rays, gamma rays, radioactive isotopes (C-14)
Chemical | PAHs (mutagenic and carcinogenic; incomplete combustion, cigarette smoke), benzene, formaldehyde (from paint)

t: Mutation → types and examples
text:
## 1. Table (PMF)
Type | Change | Example
Point mutation | One base pair | Sickle-cell anaemia
Frame-shift | Insertion/deletion of bases | Changes every codon after it
Chromosomal | Deletion/duplication of segments | Cancer cells
Nonsense | Premature stop codon | ~25% of disease mutations
Aneuploidy | Gain/loss of whole chromosome | Down, Turner
Polyploidy | Extra full set | Common in plants
Mutations are the key source of genetic variation; they disprove Lamarck's acquired-trait idea

PERT (prime-editing-mediated readthrough): edited tRNAs read through premature stop codons
Helicase gene mutations → Bloom and Werner syndromes (genome instability)

t: Spiders → behaviour (female kills male) and silk
text:
## 1. Sexual cannibalism
In many spiders (e.g., black widow) the female kills and eats the male after (or during) mating
PYQ 2008 option | Female kills male after copulation?
Dragonfly | No
Honeybee | No (drone dies after mating; queen does not kill it)
Spider | Yes
Pit viper | No
## 2. Other spider facts
All spiders are predators; many eat each other; found on every continent except Antarctica
Spider silk = gossamer silk: protein fibre, both strong and elastic; used for webs, egg sacs, nests, ballooning
Not all spin webs: wolf spiders ambush on the ground; jumping spiders hunt by sight
⚠ Pirate (cannibal) spiders (Mimetidae) kill other spiders by mimicking prey or mate vibrations

Praying mantis females also often eat males during mating (another likely option)
