t: Arthropoda → phylum features and useful members
text:
Feature | Arthropoda
Body | Segmented, bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic, coelomate
Skeleton | Chitinous exoskeleton; jointed appendages (arthros = joint)
Circulation | Open (blood-filled coelom)
Excretion | Malpighian tubules
Breathing | Gills, book gills, book lungs, tracheae
Reproduction | Mostly dioecious, oviparous
Useful/harmful members: Apis (honeybee), Bombyx (silkworm), Laccifer (lac insect); vectors Anopheles, Culex, Aedes; gregarious pest Locusta; living fossil Limulus
Silk of commerce is taken at the pupa (cocoon) stage (UPSC 2000)
⚠ Female Anopheles rests at an angle to the surface; Culex rests parallel

topic: Animal kingdom: phyla and vertebrate classes
t: Non-chordate phyla → key feature and examples
text:
Phylum | Key feature | Examples
Porifera | Pores, canal system; cellular level | Sycon, Spongilla, bath sponge
Cnidaria | Cnidoblasts (stinging cells); polyp/medusa | Hydra, jellyfish, sea anemone, corals, Portuguese man-of-war
Ctenophora | 8 comb plates; bioluminescence | Comb jellies
Platyhelminthes | Flat; acoelomate; flame cells | Tapeworm, liver fluke, Planaria
Aschelminthes | Round; pseudocoelom | Ascaris, filaria worm, hookworm, guinea worm
Annelida | Ring segments (metamerism) | Earthworm, leech, Nereis
Arthropoda | Jointed legs, exoskeleton | Insects, arachnids, crustaceans
Mollusca | Shell, muscular foot, radula | Snail, octopus, squid, pearl oyster
Echinodermata | Water vascular system, spiny skin | Starfish, sea urchin, sea cucumber
Mollusca is the second-largest phylum; colossal squid is the largest invertebrate
⚠ Tapeworm hermaphrodite; roundworm separate sexes; guinea worm is a nematode, not an annelid (UPSC 2001)
⚠ Octopus is a mollusc (UPSC 2003); starfish, jellyfish are not fish

topic: Animal kingdom: phyla and vertebrate classes
t: Vertebrate classes → heart, body temperature, eggs
text:
Class | Heart chambers | Blood | Reproduction | Examples
Cyclostomata | 2 | Cold | Jawless; ectoparasites | Lamprey, hagfish
Chondrichthyes | 2 | Cold | Many viviparous | Shark, dogfish (Scoliodon), stingray, sawfish
Osteichthyes | 2 | Cold | Mostly oviparous | Rohu, catla, seahorse, flying fish
Amphibia | 3 | Cold | External fertilisation | Frog, toad, salamander, Ichthyophis
Reptilia | 3 (crocodile 4) | Cold | Shelled eggs | Turtle, tortoise, python, lizard
Aves | 4 | Warm | Oviparous | Crow, ostrich, penguin
Mammalia | 4 | Warm | Mostly viviparous | Otter, kangaroo, whale, bat
Sharks lack an air bladder and must keep swimming; bony fish have an air bladder
⚠ Crocodile is the reptile with a 4-chambered heart; frog 3; fish 2 (UPSC-style A-R trap)
⚠ Seahorse is a true fish; hagfish is a jawless cyclostome; whale, dolphin, bat are mammals

topic: Animal kingdom: phyla and vertebrate classes
t: Mammals → egg-layers, pouch-bearers and placentals
text:
Group | Birth | Examples | Range
Monotremes | Lay eggs | Platypus, 4 species of echidna | Australia, New Guinea
Marsupials | Tiny young finish growth in pouch | Kangaroo, koala, wombat, wallaby, Tasmanian devil, opossum | Australasia, Americas
Placentals | Placenta, live birth | Most mammals | Worldwide
Monotremes: no nipples (milk from skin patches), cloaca, low body temperature (~30-32°C); transitional link reptiles → mammals
Platypus: carnivore with electroreception, IUCN Near Threatened; echidna: insectivore, rolls into spiny ball
⚠ Marsupials are not naturally found in India (UPSC 2023); kangaroo is a marsupial, Australia's national animal
⚠ Opossum is an American marsupial: marsupials are not only Australian
## In news 2025-26
AMHY gene found as the sex-determining gene of monotremes: hormone-based, unlike SRY in other mammals; evolved ~100 mya
Australia approved the first single-dose chlamydia vaccine for koalas (cuts mortality ~65%); koala IUCN Vulnerable

topic: Animal kingdom: phyla and vertebrate classes
t: Animal traits → odd-one-out and trait questions
text:
Question | Answer
Not an ape: gibbon, gorilla, langur, orangutan | Langur (a tailed monkey) (UPSC 2008)
Panda belongs to the family of | Bear (Ursidae) (UPSC 2009)
Roll up to protect: hedgehog, marmot, pangolin | Hedgehog and pangolin (UPSC 2021)
Uses stick tools to scrape insects | Orangutan (UPSC 2023)
Herbivores among turtles, fish, marine mammals; viviparous snakes | All exist (green sea turtle, parrotfish, dugong, green anaconda) (UPSC 2019)
Poisonous species among butterflies, fish, frogs | All three (UPSC 2024)
Detritivores | Earthworms, millipedes, woodlice (not jellyfish, seahorses) (UPSC 2024)
Only snake that builds a nest; eats other snakes | King cobra (UPSC 1995, 2008)
Vampire bats are the only mammals living solely on blood
⚠ Gibbon is the smallest ape (lesser ape); great apes: gorilla, chimpanzee, orangutan, bonobo, humans
## Beyond your notes
Bat is the only mammal capable of true flight; flying squirrels only glide

topic: Evolutionary sequences and the history of life
t: Vertebrate sequence → which group came first
text:
## 1. Order of appearance
Order | Group | Example in PYQs
1 | Fish (jawless first, then jawed) | Shark
2 | Amphibians (from lobe-finned fish) | Salamander, frog
3 | Reptiles | Tortoise, python
4 | Birds and mammals (both from reptiles) | Otter, kangaroo, hawk
Rule: fish → amphibian → reptile → mammal/bird; invertebrates (octopus, crab, prawn) come before all vertebrates
## 2. Approximate ages (Preview)
Salamander lineage ~360 mya; python lineage ~300 mya; kangaroo (marsupial) ~145 mya
⚠ An option is right only if every step goes "older → newer"; check each organism's class, not its size or habitat
PYQ 2010: Shark - Tortoise - Otter (fish, reptile, mammal)
PYQ 2009: Salamander - Python - Kangaroo; wrong: Octopus-Dolphin-Shark (mammal before fish), Pangolin-Tortoise-Hawk (mammal first), Frog-Crab-Prawn (invertebrates after amphibian)

topic: Evolutionary sequences and the history of life
t: Sequence options → class of each organism
text:
Organism | Class / group
Octopus | Mollusc (invertebrate)
Crab, prawn | Crustacean (invertebrate)
Shark | Cartilaginous fish
Frog, salamander | Amphibian
Tortoise, python | Reptile
Hawk | Bird
Pangolin, otter, dolphin, kangaroo | Mammal
Otter is an aquatic mammal (family Mustelidae); dolphin a marine mammal; neither is a fish
⚠ Pangolin ("scaly anteater") is a mammal despite its scales; dolphin breathes through a blowhole

topic: Evolutionary sequences and the history of life
t: History of life → milestones (PMF brief account)
text:
Stage | When (PMF) | Note
First cellular life | ~2000 mya | Early cells may have produced oxygen
Invertebrates dominate | ~500 mya | Cambrian explosion of hard-bodied life
Jawless fish | ~350 mya | First vertebrates
Plants invade land | ~320 mya | Plants first, then animals
Amphibians | From lobefins | Ancestors of frogs, salamanders
Reptiles | Shelled eggs for dry land | Dominated for 200+ million years
Dinosaurs extinct | ~65 mya | Climate change, or evolved into birds
Mammals radiate | After dinosaurs | Viviparous, small shrew-like first
Mesozoic (~252-66 mya) = age of reptiles/dinosaurs: Triassic → Jurassic → Cretaceous
Primitive atmosphere was reducing, with no free oxygen; cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) are among the oldest organisms and added oxygen (UPSC 2018)
⚠ Preview: life existed by ~3.5 billion years ago (perhaps 3.77); PMF gives ~2000 mya for first cells: follow PMF, note the gap
⚠ Cenozoic epochs, oldest first: Paleocene, Eocene, Oligocene, Miocene, Pliocene, Pleistocene, Holocene

topic: Evolutionary sequences and the history of life
t: Connecting links and living fossils → between which groups
text:
Organism | Link / status
Archaeopteryx | Reptiles → birds (feathers + reptile teeth and tail); Jurassic, ~150 mya; Solnhofen, Germany
Monotremes (platypus, echidna) | Reptiles → mammals
Lobe-finned fish | Fish → amphibians
Limulus (horseshoe/king crab) | Living fossil
Tardigrades | Emerged ~600 mya; survived all five mass extinctions
Mammoth is related to the elephant (common ancestor ~6 mya)
⚠ Archaeopteryx links Reptilia and Aves, not reptiles and mammals
## Beyond your notes
Peripatus links annelids and arthropods; coelacanth is a living-fossil lobe-finned fish (rediscovered 1938)

topic: Evolutionary sequences and the history of life
t: Human evolution → order and features
text:
Hominin | When | Key fact
Dryopithecus, Ramapithecus | ~15 mya | Ape-like / more man-like; Ramapithecus fossils in Siwalik hills
Australopithecus | 3-4 mya, Africa | Bipedal, small brain
Homo habilis | ~2 mya | "Handy man", first human-like
Homo erectus | ~1.5 mya | First out of Africa; first to control fire
Neanderthals | 100,000-40,000 years ago | Europe-Asia; larger brain; buried dead; interbred with sapiens
Homo sapiens | ~200,000 years ago, Africa | Farming ~10,000 years ago
Cro-Magnon: early European Homo sapiens, brain ~1600 cc, considered the latest direct ancestor of modern man (BPSC)
Denisovans: extinct archaic human species from Asia (Altai, Siberia), found 2010 from a finger bone (UPSC 2019)
Closest living relatives: chimpanzees and bonobos
⚠ Hominoid = all apes; hominid = great apes + humans; hominin = humans and extinct ancestors

topic: Theories of evolution and genetics: who proposed what
t: Theory → proponent (match-the-list table)
text:
Theory / concept | Proponent
Mutation theory | Hugo de Vries (Dutch)
Natural selection (Origin of Species, 1859) | Charles Darwin
One gene - one enzyme | Beadle and Tatum
Operon concept (lac operon) | Jacob and Monod
Inheritance of acquired characters | Lamarck (Philosophie Zoologique, 1809)
Laws of inheritance | Gregor Mendel (father of genetics, peas)
Chromosomal theory of inheritance | Sutton and Boveri
Central dogma (DNA → RNA → protein) | Francis Crick
"Survival of the fittest" phrase | Herbert Spencer
Germ-plasm; disproved acquired traits (mouse tails) | August Weismann
Binomial nomenclature | Linnaeus (father of taxonomy)
Five-kingdom classification (1969) | R.H. Whittaker
Chemical origin of life ("primordial soup") | Oparin and Haldane
Spark-discharge experiment (1953) | Stanley Miller (with Harold Urey)
PYQ 1998: Mutation - de Vries; Evolution - Darwin; one gene one enzyme - Beadle and Tatum; operon - Jacob and Monod (code I-D, II-C, III-A, IV-B)
⚠ Swap trap: Beadle-Tatum ↔ Jacob-Monod; Darwin ↔ de Vries

topic: Theories of evolution and genetics: who proposed what
t: Lamarckism → use and disuse, acquired characters
text:
## 1. Two laws (Lamarck, French, 1809)
Law | Example
Use and disuse of organs | Giraffe neck lengthened by stretching; snakes lost limbs by disuse
Inheritance of acquired characters | Blacksmith's strong arms passed to children
Other Lamarck examples: webbed feet of aquatic birds, long legs of wading birds, whales lost hind limbs
First broad theory of organic evolution; supplanted by Darwin (1859) and Mendel; Weismann cut mouse tails for 5 generations: no tailless young
⚠ Loss of limbs in snakes, as explained by Lamarck = use and disuse of organs (UPSC 2002)
## In news 2025-26
Rice inherits cold tolerance epigenetically (Cell, May 2025): ACT1 gene kept active (no DNA methylation) for 5 generations with no DNA mutation → limited support for Lamarck via epigenetics
Epigenetics: heritable change in gene expression without change in DNA sequence (e.g., methyl tags)

topic: Theories of evolution and genetics: who proposed what
t: Darwinism → natural selection, its components
text:
## 1. Components (PMF)
Step | Meaning
Variation | Individuals differ
Overproduction | More offspring than can survive
Struggle for existence | Competition for limited resources
Survival of the fittest | Best adapted, not strongest
Inheritance | Useful traits passed on
Speciation | Changes accumulate into new species
Book: On the Origin of Species (1859); also The Descent of Man (human origins)
Inspired by the voyage of HMS Beagle and Galapagos finches (beak shapes → adaptive radiation)
Darwin saw speciation as gradual; de Vries as sudden (saltation)
⚠ "Survival of the fittest" was coined by Spencer, adopted by Darwin later
⚠ Natural selection in action: industrial melanism (dark moths in polluted England), pesticide and antibiotic resistance
## Beyond your notes
Alfred Russel Wallace reached natural selection independently; joint Darwin-Wallace paper, 1858

topic: Theories of evolution and genetics: who proposed what
t: Mutation theory → de Vries and the 2002 key
text:
## 1. De Vries (The Mutation Theory, 1901-03)
Worked on evening primrose, Oenothera lamarckiana
Evolution is jerky: new species arise by sudden mutations (discontinuous variations), even in a single step (saltation)
Only germline mutations are inherited; somatic are not; nature selects useful ones
## 2. Mutation types (PMF)
Type | Change | Example
Point | Single base pair | Sickle-cell anaemia
Frame-shift | Insertion/deletion of bases | -
Chromosomal | Large segments lost/added | Cancer cells
Mutagens: chemicals, UV radiation
⚠ UPSC 2002 key: most responsible factor for the origin of a new species = Mutation (ultimate source of variation); BPSC 1994 key for "main factor of evolution" = natural selection: read the exact wording
PYQ 2002: options isolation, mutation, natural selection, sexual reproduction → mutation

topic: Theories of evolution and genetics: who proposed what
t: Modern synthesis and Hardy-Weinberg → factors of evolution
text:
## 1. Modern synthetic theory (Neo-Darwinism)
Natural selection + Mendelian/population genetics; Dobzhansky, Fisher, Haldane, Sewall Wright, Ernst Mayr, Stebbins
Five factors: mutation, recombination, gene flow and genetic drift, natural selection, reproductive isolation
## 2. Hardy-Weinberg principle
Allele and genotype frequencies stay constant if there are no evolutionary forces
Condition for equilibrium | Force it removes
No mutation | Mutation
Random mating | Sexual selection
No natural selection | Selection
Large population | Genetic drift
No migration | Gene flow
⚠ A small population faces greater extinction risk: less variation, more drift

topic: Theories of evolution and genetics: who proposed what
t: Evidences of evolution → homologous vs analogous
text:
Evidence | Example
Fossils | Deeper layers = older (extinct dinosaurs)
Homologous organs (same origin, different use) | Forelimbs of whale, bat, cheetah, human → divergent evolution
Analogous organs (different origin, same use) | Bird and butterfly wings → convergent evolution
Biochemical | Similar genes/proteins; near-universal genetic code
Artificial selection | Dog breeds
Industrial melanism | Peppered moth
Adaptive radiation: one ancestor → many forms (Galapagos finches, Australian marsupials)
Convergent evolution: placental wolf and Tasmanian wolf (marsupial) look alike
⚠ Wings of bird and bat are homologous as forelimbs but analogous as wings; venom glands of snakes are homologous to salivary glands (UPSC 1993)

topic: Theories of evolution and genetics: who proposed what
t: Origin of life → hypotheses and Miller's experiment
text:
Idea | Who | Gist
Spontaneous generation | Disproved by Louis Pasteur | Life only from life
Panspermia | - | Life came from space (comets, meteorites)
Chemical evolution | Oparin (book "Origin of Life"), Haldane ("hot dilute soup") | Organic molecules formed in a reducing early atmosphere
Spark-discharge experiment | Stanley Miller, 1953 (Urey's lab, Chicago) | CH₄, NH₃, H₂, water vapour + electric sparks → amino acids (glycine, alanine)
Miller ran the apparatus for one week; energy sources on early Earth: UV, lightning, radioactivity (little ozone)
Coacervates: membrane-bound droplets that concentrate molecules
⚠ Gas absent from the primitive atmosphere: oxygen (UPRO 2016)

topic: Theories of evolution and genetics: who proposed what
t: Gene-level discoveries → what each explained
text:
Discovery | Who | What it shows
One gene - one enzyme | Beadle & Tatum | Each gene controls one specific enzyme
Operon (lac operon in E. coli) | Jacob & Monod | Genes switched on/off: beta-galactosidase made only when lactose is present
Genetic code | - | 64 codons: 61 amino acids, 3 stop (UAA, UAG, UGA); AUG start
Sex by XY | - | Sperm decides sex: X → girl, Y → boy
Temperature-dependent sex | - | Turtles, crocodiles: low incubation temperature → males
Prokaryotic genes are regulated mainly at transcription by activators and repressors
⚠ The code is universal (minor exceptions in mitochondria), which is itself evidence of common descent
## Beyond your notes
Beadle and Tatum used the bread mould Neurospora; Jacob and Monod (with Lwoff) won the 1965 Nobel; T.H. Morgan (fruit fly) showed linkage

topic: Viruses: nature, hosts and the "no virus can" traps
t: Viruses → what they lack, and why they need a living host
text:
## 1. Acellular, inert outside a host
Non-cellular pathogens; inert outside host cells: "dormant life", metabolically inactive outside a host
Obligate (intracellular) parasites: cannot live or reproduce independently; take over the host cell's machinery to replicate
Not placed in Whittaker's five kingdoms (with viroids, prions and lichens)
## 2. What a virus does not have
Missing | Consequence
Energy-generating enzymes (no ATP-making metabolism) | Uses the host's energy
Ribosomes / own protein synthesis | Uses host ribosomes
Cell, cytoplasm, membrane-bound organelles | Not a cell, not "truly living"
Ability to grow on a non-living medium | Cannot be cultured on synthetic media
⚠ PYQ 2013 answer was "1 only": lack energy enzymes = true; culturable "in any synthetic medium" = false; spread "by biological vectors only" = false
PYQ 2013: three virus statements; trap: the words "any" and "only" make statements 2 and 3 false

topic: Viruses: nature, hosts and the "no virus can" traps
t: Viruses → which hosts they infect
text:
## 1. Every group of life has its viruses
Virus type | Host | Example
Bacteriophage (phage) | Bacteria (also archaea) | ΦX174, T4 (on E. coli)
Mycovirus | Fungi | Viruses of mushrooms and moulds
Plant virus | Plants | TMV, Cucumber Mosaic Virus, rice tungro (RTSV + RTBV)
Animal / human virus | Animals, humans | HIV, influenza, SARS-CoV-2, rabies
Insect virus | Insects | HpNPV (teak defoliator moth larva)
Plant virus symptoms: mosaic, leaf rolling and curling, yellowing, vein clearing, dwarfing, stunting
Human virus diseases: mumps, smallpox, herpes, influenza, AIDS
⚠ PYQ 2016: viruses infect bacteria, fungi and plants: answer all three (1, 2 and 3)
PYQ 2016 and 2025 both turn on bacteriophages; know mycovirus = fungi as the next twist

topic: Viruses: nature, hosts and the "no virus can" traps
t: "No virus can..." → why every absolute statement is false
text:
## 1. The 2025 statements (all three false, answer "None")
Statement | Truth
No virus can survive in ocean waters | False: viruses are the most abundant biological entities in the ocean, mostly phages of marine bacteria; they regulate microbes and nutrient cycling
No virus can infect bacteria | False: bacteriophages infect and replicate in bacteria
No virus can change transcriptional activity of host cells | False: viruses hijack host transcription; HIV (a retrovirus) integrates its DNA copy into host DNA
## 2. Other absolute claims that fail
"Viruses are spread only by vectors": false (droplets, contact, water/food, blood, sexual route, mother to child)
"Viruses contain both DNA and RNA": false (either, never both)
"Antibiotics kill viruses": false (antibiotics act on bacteria)
⚠ Phages are the most abundant biological entities on Earth and are harmless to human cells (PMF)
PYQ 2025: "How many are correct" with three "No virus can" lines; trap: an absolute "no/only/all" in microbiology is almost always false

topic: Viruses: nature, hosts and the "no virus can" traps
t: Viruses → structure and genome
text:
## 1. Build
Nucleoprotein: infectious nucleic acid inside a protein coat, the capsid, made of subunits called capsomeres
Some viruses add an outer envelope (CARE May 2026)
Smaller than bacteria; pass through bacterial filters; not visible under an ordinary light microscope
## 2. Genome by host
Group | Usual genome
Plant viruses | Single-stranded RNA
Animal viruses | ss or ds RNA, or ds DNA
Bacteriophages | Usually double-stranded DNA
Retroviruses (HIV) | RNA, copied to DNA by reverse transcriptase
⚠ DNA viruses are usually double-stranded, not single-stranded (CGPSC 2021 trap); RNA viruses mutate faster than DNA viruses
## 3. Discovery
M.W. Beijerinck discovered/named viruses ("virus" = venom/poisonous fluid) (PMF)
⚠ Dmitri Ivanovsky first showed the tobacco mosaic agent passes bacterial filters (Rocket Sheets); PMF credits Beijerinck: both names appear in options
## 4. Reverse transcriptase
Temin and Baltimore: information can flow RNA → DNA, against the old central dogma
Used in RT-PCR to measure viral load; human genome carries retroelements of viral origin

topic: Viruses: nature, hosts and the "no virus can" traps
t: Viruses → how they spread and what they cause
text:
## 1. Routes (not "vectors only")
Route | Examples
Biological vector (mosquito) | Dengue, chikungunya, Zika, yellow fever (Aedes); Japanese encephalitis
Droplet / respiratory | Influenza, COVID-19, measles, mumps
Bite / saliva of animal | Rabies
Blood, sexual, mother to child | HIV, Hepatitis B
Faecal-oral (food, water) | Polio, Hepatitis A
Insect vector in plants | CMV by aphids
Bats / pigs / date-palm sap | Nipah (RNA virus; first seen 1998, Malaysia)
## 2. Why HIV is hard to cure
Integrates into host DNA; latent reservoirs invisible to ART; mutates extremely fast; destroys CD4+ T cells
No vaccine, no functional cure; ART suppresses viral load to undetectable levels
## In news 2025-26
Zoonotic spillover concern (Nipah, Ebola, hantavirus-like outbreaks): viruses can infect humans, animals, plants and even bacteria (CARE May 2026)

topic: Viruses: nature, hosts and the "no virus can" traps
t: Bacteriophages → phage therapy and AI-designed phages
text:
## 1. "Good viruses"
Infect and destroy specific bacteria; found in soil, water and the human microbiome
High specificity: spare beneficial microbiota, unlike broad-spectrum antibiotics
Self-limiting: multiply only while target bacteria exist; degrade after
Co-evolve with bacteria, overcoming resistance
## 2. Therapy
Strategy | How
Natural phage therapy | Patient's bacteria tested against a phage library/bank, matched phage cultured and given
Engineered phages | Broader host range, attack dormant bacteria, enzymes to break biofilms
Uses: burns, diabetic foot ulcers, UTIs, respiratory and GI infections, MDR infections
⚠ Limitation: each phage is strain-specific, so treatment must be matched/personalised
## In news 2025-26
Stanford used genome AI models Evo (Evo 1, Evo 2) to design the first AI-designed viral (phage) genomes; template ΦX174 (first genome sequenced 1977, synthesised 2003); killed antibiotic-resistant E. coli
Klebsiella pneumoniae makes protein "Neo" via reverse transcriptase and non-coding RNA to stop phage infection (PMF S&T CA 2025)
Phages re-emerging as alternatives to antibiotics (LENS June 2025)

topic: Viruses: nature, hosts and the "no virus can" traps
t: Viroids, prions, obelisks, giant viruses → how they differ from viruses
text:
## 1. Sub-viral agents
Agent | Made of | Protein coat | Disease / note
Virus | DNA or RNA + capsid | Yes | AIDS, flu, TMV
Viroid (T.O. Diener) | Free, short circular RNA (250-400 nt) | No | Plants only: potato spindle tuber, coconut cadang-cadang
Prion | Abnormally folded protein, no nucleic acid | n.a. | BSE (mad cow), human CJD
Obelisk | Circular ssRNA, 1-2 genes, ~1,000 nt, rod-like | No | In gut/oral microbiome bacteria
Viroids do not encode proteins; viruses do encode proteins but cannot make them alone
Obelisks sit between viruses and viroids: coatless like viroids, protein genes like viruses; found by next-generation sequencing
⚠ Viroids are smaller than viruses; prions are similar in size to viruses
## In news 2025-26
Giant viruses about 1.5 billion years old found in Yellowstone hot springs; "giant" = very large genomes; no risk to humans (PMF Misc CA 2025)
## Beyond your notes
Prions discovered by Stanley Prusiner; giant viruses (e.g. Mimivirus) can exceed small bacteria in size

t: Bacteria, fungi, viruses → which grow on artificial/synthetic media
text:
## 1. The 2021 answer: bacteria and fungi only ("1 and 2 only")
Organism | Synthetic medium? | Why / media
Bacteria | Yes | Simple nutrient needs; nutrient agar, nutrient broth, selective media
Fungi (yeasts, moulds) | Yes | Sabouraud Dextrose Agar, Potato Dextrose Agar, Czapek-Dox Agar
Viruses | No | Obligate intracellular parasites: need living host cells
Medium supplies carbon, nitrogen, vitamins, minerals (and water)
⚠ Even the smallest free-living cell, mycoplasma, grows on a cell-free medium; a virus never does
PYQ 2021: three organisms, which can be cultured; trap: viruses (also tested 2013 "any synthetic medium")
## Beyond your notes
Viruses are grown in living systems: embryonated chicken eggs, cell/tissue cultures, live animals; phages on bacterial lawns
Some bacteria still resist lab culture (e.g. Mycobacterium leprae); "culturable" is the rule for the group, not every species

t: Fermentation culture → how microbes are grown at scale
text:
## 1. Fermentation technology
Microbes (bacteria, yeast, fungi) convert substrates (sugars) into products in a bioreactor (fermenter) under controlled conditions
Step | What happens
Strain selection | Saccharomyces cerevisiae for alcohol, Lactobacillus for curd
Culture medium | Carbon (sugar), nitrogen, salts, vitamins, water
Fermentation | Controlled pH, temperature, aeration
Downstream | Filtration, centrifugation, distillation, purification
## 2. Products
Sector | Products
Pharma | Penicillin, streptomycin, erythromycin; insulin, HGH, Hepatitis B vaccine; vitamin B12, riboflavin; probiotics
Food | Curd, yogurt, cheese (lactic acid); beer, wine (alcoholic); bread (yeast CO2); idli, dosa, pickles
Agriculture | Rhizobium, Azospirillum biofertilisers; Bt biopesticide
⚠ Virus-based products (vaccines) need cell culture, not plain fermentation media

t: Bacteria → defining traits
text:
## 1. Prokaryotes of Kingdom Monera
Feature | Bacteria
Nucleus | Absent: DNA in a nucleoid
DNA | Circular, no histones; extra plasmids (e.g. antibiotic resistance)
Organelles | No membrane-bound organelles; small (70S) ribosomes
Cell wall | Present in most: peptidoglycan (non-cellulosic)
Respiration | Aerobic and anaerobic
Reproduction | Binary fission; spores in bad conditions; primitive sexual DNA transfer
Most abundant microorganisms; live in hot springs, deserts, snow, deep oceans, soil, gut
## 2. Shapes
Shape | Name
Spherical | Coccus
Rod | Bacillus
Comma | Vibrio
Spiral | Spirillum
⚠ Bacteria are unicellular (PMF also notes some multicellular forms); cyanobacteria are bacteria, not true algae
Likely next: "Bacteria have no DNA outside the nucleoid" (false: plasmids)

t: Eubacteria → groups and examples
text:
## 1. Four groups (PMF)
Group | Feature | Examples
Cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) | Chlorophyll, photosynthetic, oxygen-producing; heterocysts fix N2; bloom in polluted water | Nostoc, Anabaena
Chemosynthetic autotrophs | Oxidise nitrates, nitrites, ammonia for ATP; recycle N, P, Fe, S | Nitrifying bacteria
Heterotrophic bacteria | Most abundant; decomposers; curd, antibiotics, N-fixation in legumes | Rhizobium, Lactobacillus
Mycoplasma | No cell wall; smallest living cells; survive without O2 | M. pneumoniae
Anabaena lives in the fern Azolla: biofertiliser for rice
⚠ Mycoplasma has no cell wall, so it is naturally resistant to penicillin and other cell-wall antibiotics

t: Unicellular organisms → mode of asexual reproduction
text:
## 1. Methods with examples
Method | How | Examples
Binary fission | One cell → two identical cells | Amoeba, Paramecium, Leishmania (kala-azar), bacteria
Multiple fission | One cell → many at once | Plasmodium; encysted Amoeba
Budding | Bud grows and separates | Yeast (also multicellular Hydra)
Spore formation | Hardy spores in sporangia | Rhizopus (bread mould), bacteria under stress
Fragmentation | Body breaks, pieces regrow | Spirogyra (multicellular alga)
In bad conditions Amoeba forms a cyst (encystation), then multiple fission releases many amoebae
Asexual = one parent, clones, fast, no variation

t: Photosynthesis → what energy change takes place
text:
## 1. The process
Green plants make food from CO2 + water + sunlight, releasing O2 and storing glucose → plants are autotrophs
Energy change: light (free) energy → chemical (potential) energy stored in food
Process | Energy change | Gas exchange
Photosynthesis | Free energy converted into potential energy and stored | CO2 in, O2 out
Respiration | Potential energy of food released as usable (free) energy, ATP | O2 in, CO2 + H2O out
Equation: 6CO2 + 6H2O + light → C6H12O6 + 6O2 (chlorophyll)
⚠ Options describing food oxidised to CO2 and water or O2 taken in, CO2 given out describe respiration, not photosynthesis
PYQ 2014: photosynthesis = free energy converted into potential energy and stored (answer b)

t: Light absorption → which colours plants use
text:
## 1. Colours
Chlorophyll a absorbs most strongly in the blue and red parts of the spectrum; green is reflected → leaves look green
Red and blue = most effective for photosynthesis; green used least efficiently
Light | Effect on plants
Blue | Strongly absorbed; plants small but robust
Red | Strongly absorbed; red alone causes stem elongation
Green | Reflected / poorly used
Ultraviolet | Causes dwarfing
High light → shoot growth over root growth, small thick sun leaves; low light → tall weak stems, thin shade leaves, delayed flowering
Below minimum light: respiration exceeds photosynthesis → plant releases more CO2 than it fixes and stops growing
⚠ Distractor pairs in 2007: violet-orange, indigo-yellow, yellow-violet
PYQ 2007: light strongly absorbed by plants = blue and red (answer b)

t: Photosynthetic pigments → colour and role
text:
## 1. Pigments
Pigment | Colour | Note
Chlorophyll a | Blue-green | Primary, most abundant; in all higher plants, algae, cyanobacteria
Chlorophyll b | Yellow-green | Accessory; higher plants and green algae
Xanthophylls | Yellow | Accessory; in chromoplasts
Carotenoids | Yellow-orange | Accessory; protect chlorophyll from photo-oxidation
Accessory pigments absorb other wavelengths and pass energy to chlorophyll a
Chlorophyll c: diatoms, dinoflagellates, brown algae; chlorophyll d: red algae (PMF)
Pigments can be separated by paper chromatography
Red/purple leaves (anthocyanins) still contain chlorophyll and photosynthesise
⚠ Chlorophyll molecule has magnesium at its centre (Mg and N are its base elements)

t: Light and dark reactions → where and what
text:
## 1. Two stages
Stage | Site | Needs | Products
Light reactions | Thylakoid membranes (grana) | Light, water | O2 (from splitting water), ATP, NADPH
Dark reactions (Calvin cycle) | Stroma | ATP + NADPH, CO2 | Glucose
O2 released in photosynthesis comes from water, not from CO2
Dark reactions do not need direct light but are enzyme-driven → temperature-sensitive
## 2. Where photosynthesis happens
Not only leaves: green stems, green fruits, cactus stems (leaves reduced to spines), Opuntia flattened stems, Australian acacia phyllodes (green petioles)
Also algae and cyanobacteria
## In news 2025-26
Sep 2026: Ghost Flower orchid (*Gastrodia keyiensis*), Keyi Panyor, Arunachal: achlorophyllous, leafless, lives on soil fungi (holomycotrophy) - a plant that does not photosynthesise

t: Factors affecting photosynthesis → limiting factors
text:
## 1. Law of limiting factors
The most deficient factor sets the rate (ample light and water but low CO2 → CO2 limits)
Factor | Effect
Light | Rate rises to saturation at ~10% of full sunlight; excess damages chlorophyll
CO2 | Major limiting factor (only 0.03-0.04% of air); 0.05% boosts rate, higher harms
Temperature | Affects enzyme-driven dark reactions more than light reactions
Water | Mainly indirect: water stress closes stomata, cutting CO2 uptake
Internal factors: number, size, age, orientation of leaves; chloroplasts; chlorophyll content

t: C3, C4 and CAM plants → differences
text:
## 1. Pathways
Type | First stable product | Examples | Feature
C3 | 3-carbon (PGA) | Rice, wheat, most plants | Normal Calvin cycle
C4 | Oxaloacetic acid (4-C) | Sugarcane, maize, sorghum (jowar), Cyperus | Better photosynthesisers in heat and high light
CAM | Organic acids at night | Cactus, Opuntia, succulents | Stomata open at night, closed by day to save water
Jowar is a short-day C4 plant (PMF Indian Agriculture)
## Beyond your notes
C4 leaves show Kranz anatomy (bundle-sheath cells); C4 plants have little photorespiration
Pineapple is a CAM crop; CAM = Crassulacean Acid Metabolism
⚠ The Preview book labels CAM as "C-2"; standard usage: C2 = photorespiration, CAM is a separate pathway

t: Respiration in plants → features
text:
## 1. Gas exchange
Plants respire day and night; by day the CO2 from respiration is used in photosynthesis, so net O2 is released; at night they release CO2
No special respiratory organs: gases move by diffusion through stomata (leaves) and lenticels (stems)
Reason plants need no lungs | Explanation
Each part serves itself | Leaves, stems, roots exchange gases directly
Low demand | Respiration needs lower than animals; photosynthesis supplies O2
Short distances | Cells near surface; air spaces in stems and roots
Glucose for respiration comes from sucrose (split by invertase into glucose + fructose) or stored starch
Swamp plants like Rhizophora have pneumatophores (upward roots) to get oxygen for root respiration

t: Aerobic vs anaerobic respiration → comparison
text:
## 1. Table
Feature | Aerobic | Anaerobic
Oxygen | Required | Not required
Site | Cytoplasm + mitochondria | Cytoplasm only
ATP per glucose | 36-38 | 2
End products | CO2 + water | Ethanol + CO2 (yeast, plants) or lactic acid (animal muscle)
Oxidation | Complete | Partial
Waterlogged roots switch to anaerobic respiration → ethanol builds up, roots suffer
⚠ In plants and yeast anaerobic respiration gives alcohol, not lactic acid
ATP = energy currency of the cell; aerobic respiration yields ~18-19 times more ATP per glucose than anaerobic
Algal blooms: phytoplankton release O2 by day but consume far more at night → oxygen depletion of water bodies

t: Cold storage of fruits → why it works
text:
## 1. Mechanism
Low temperature slows metabolism, especially the rate of respiration → delays ripening and ageing → longer storage life
2013 option | Verdict
Sunlight exposure prevented | Wrong: not the main reason
CO2 concentration increased | Wrong (that is controlled-atmosphere storage, not cold)
Rate of respiration decreased | Correct
Humidity increased | Wrong
## 2. Ripening and its control
Ethylene (C2H4) = gaseous plant hormone for fruit ripening
GM Flavr Savr tomato = delayed ripening (first commercial GM food)
## Beyond your notes
Fruits like banana, mango, tomato, apple are climacteric: a burst of respiration and ethylene at ripening; cold storage suppresses this burst
Calcium carbide (releases acetylene) is a banned artificial ripening agent in India; ethylene/ethephon is permitted (verify current FSSAI norms)
PYQ 2013: cold chamber extends storage life because respiration rate falls (answer c)

t: Plant hormones → main role of each
text:
## 1. Hormones
Hormone | Main role
Auxins | Cell elongation, phototropism, root development (rooting of cuttings)
Gibberellins | Stem elongation, seed germination, fruit development
Cytokinins | Cell division, delay ageing
Abscisic acid (ABA) | Inhibits growth, seed dormancy, leaf senescence; stress hormone
Ethylene | Fruit ripening
Zinc is needed to synthesise auxin
Tissue culture media: cytokinin-dominant → shoots, auxin-dominant → roots
## Beyond your notes
ABA closes stomata during water stress; gibberellins cause bolting and break dormancy; auxin (2,4-D) is used as a weedicide

t: Plant movements → tropisms and nastic responses
text:
## 1. Types
Plants have no nervous system or muscles but respond to stimuli
Movement | Stimulus | Example
Phototropism | Light | Shoots bend toward light
Geotropism | Gravity | Roots grow down
Hydrotropism | Water | Roots grow toward water
Chemotropism | Chemicals | Pollen tube grows to ovule
Thigmotropism | Touch | Tendrils coil around support
Mimosa (touch-me-not) folds leaves without growth: cells change shape by losing/gaining water (turgor change), signal is electrical-chemical
⚠ Tropisms are growth movements; Mimosa folding is a non-growth (turgor) movement

topic: Transport in plants: xylem, phloem and root hairs
t: Xylem vs phloem → what each carries
text:
## 1. Comparison
Feature | Xylem | Phloem
Carries | Water and minerals, roots → leaves | Food (sugars) from leaves → other parts (translocation)
Direction | Unidirectional (upward) | Bidirectional
Cells | Mostly dead | Mostly living
Mechanism | Passive (transpiration pull) | Active (energy-dependent)
Components | Tracheids, vessels (only in angiosperms), xylem parenchyma (only living), xylem fibres | Sieve tubes (no nucleus), companion cells, phloem parenchyma, phloem fibres (dead)
Both are complex permanent tissues (vascular tissues)
In woody stems the phloem lies just inside the bark; xylem forms the inner wood
⚠ Sieve tubes are alive but lack a nucleus; they are controlled by companion cells

topic: Transport in plants: xylem, phloem and root hairs
t: Girdling (ring-barking) → why the tree dies
text:
## 1. Sequence
Bark removed in a ring near the base → phloem removed (xylem/wood left intact)
Food from leaves cannot reach roots → roots starve of energy and die → root water uptake stops → whole tree dries and dies
2011 option | Verdict
Water cannot rise to aerial parts | Wrong: xylem is inside, still intact (water rises at first)
Roots are starved of energy | Correct
Infected by soil microbes | Wrong
Roots get no oxygen | Wrong
Classic ringing experiment proves phloem carries food downward
⚠ Death is gradual: leaves stay green until starving roots fail
PYQ 2011: tree dies after bark-ring removal because roots are starved of energy (answer b)

topic: Transport in plants: xylem, phloem and root hairs
t: Root hairs and transplanting → why seedlings fail
text:
## 1. Root hairs
Formed in the maturation zone; tiny extensions of root epidermal cells that greatly increase absorptive surface area
Root regions from tip: root cap → meristematic → elongation → maturation (root hairs)
During transplanting most root hairs are lost → water and mineral uptake falls → seedling wilts (transplant shock)
2013 option | Verdict
New soil lacks minerals | Wrong
Root hairs grip new soil too hard | Wrong
Root hairs lost in transplantation | Correct
Leaves damaged | Wrong
## 2. Practice links
SRI (System of Rice Intensification): transplant young, single seedlings at wider spacing with care for roots
Aeroponically grown plants do not suffer transplant shock when moved to soil (PMF)
PYQ 2013: transplanted seedlings do not grow because root hairs are lost (answer c)

topic: Transport in plants: xylem, phloem and root hairs
t: Water absorption by roots → pathways
text:
## 1. Two routes
Pathway | Route | Feature
Apoplast | Cell walls and intercellular spaces | Faster, no membranes; blocked by Casparian strip in endodermis
Symplast | Cytoplasm via plasmodesmata | Slower, selective (crosses membranes)
Mycorrhiza: root-fungus symbiosis; fungal hyphae supply water and minerals (esp. phosphorus), root gives sugars; Pinus needs mycorrhiza
Membrane transport: simple diffusion (no protein, no ATP), facilitated diffusion (protein, no ATP; aquaporins for water), active transport (pumps, ATP, uphill)
⚠ Only active transport moves substances against a concentration gradient and uses ATP

topic: Transport in plants: xylem, phloem and root hairs
t: Ascent of sap → root pressure and transpiration pull
text:
## 1. Forces
Force | Feature
Root pressure | Positive pressure from active ion uptake; pushes water only a small height; seen as guttation
Transpiration pull | Main force; evaporation from leaves pulls water up, up to 15 m per hour
Water column held by cohesion (water-water), adhesion (water-wall) and surface tension
Guttation: water droplets at leaf tips when water is plentiful and transpiration low (night, early morning)
## 2. Stomata
Two guard cells (bean-shaped; dumbbell-shaped in grasses) with chloroplasts; turgid → open, flaccid → close
Usually open by day, closed at night (CAM plants reverse this)
Dicots: more stomata on lower leaf surface; monocots: equal on both
Potassium controls stomatal opening

topic: Transport in plants: xylem, phloem and root hairs
t: Plant-water relations → osmosis, plasmolysis, imbibition
text:
## 1. Terms
Term | Meaning
Water potential | Water moves from higher to lower potential; pure water = zero (highest)
Hypertonic solution | Cell loses water → plasmolysis (membrane shrinks from wall)
Hypotonic solution | Cell gains water → turgid
Isotonic solution | No net movement → flaccid
Imbibition | Solids (seeds, dry wood) absorb water without forming a solution and swell
Plasmolysis is reversible in hypotonic solution
Imbibition lets seeds swell and break through soil; swelling wood was used to split rocks
Frost: frozen soil water cannot be absorbed while transpiration continues → desiccation

t: Essential elements → macro vs micro list
text:
## 1. The 17 essential elements
Group | Elements | Amount
Macronutrients (9) | C, H, O, N, P, K, Ca, Mg, S | > 10 mmol/kg dry matter
Micronutrients (8) | Fe, Mn, Cu, Mo, Zn, B, Cl, Ni | < 10 mmol/kg dry matter
Beneficial (not essential) | Sodium, silicon, cobalt, selenium | Needed by some higher plants
C, H, O come from air and water; the rest from soil as minerals
NPK = most significant macronutrients; N needed in the largest amount
⚠ Sodium is not an essential micronutrient (only "beneficial", e.g. for some halophytes and C4 plants); boron, zinc, copper are essential

text:
## 1. Roles
Nutrient | Key role
Nitrogen | Proteins, nucleic acids, hormones, chlorophyll; vegetative growth
Phosphorus | ATP, membranes, nucleic acids; early root growth; legume N-fixation; hastens maturity
Potassium | Stomatal movement, enzyme activation, turgor; disease resistance; deficiency → lodging
Calcium | Cell wall (calcium pectate), cell division, root hairs; collects in older leaves
Magnesium | Centre of chlorophyll; enzymes of respiration/photosynthesis; ribosomes
Sulphur | Amino acids cysteine, methionine; vitamins thiamine (B1), biotin; odour compounds
Sources: urea (highest N of solid fertilisers), superphosphate (P), KCl / potash (K), lime, gypsum, dolomite (Ca), dolomite/Epsom salt (Mg), gypsum (S)

Micronutrient | Key role
Iron | Needed in largest amount among micronutrients; chlorophyll formation, electron transfer
Manganese | Splits water in photosynthesis; enzyme activation
Zinc | Enzymes; synthesis of auxin; regulates legume N-fixation

Element type | Examples | Symptoms appear first in
Mobile | N, K, Mg | Older leaves
Immobile | S, Ca | Younger leaves

Symptom | Caused by lack of
Chlorosis (yellowing) | N, K, Mg, S, Fe, Mn, Zn, Mo
Necrosis (tissue death) | Ca, Mg, Cu, K
Stunted growth | N, K, S, Mo
Delayed flowering | N, S, Mo

Method | How | Example
Cutting | Plant a stem/leaf/root piece | Rose

Grafting | Join scion onto rooted stock | Apple, mango

Based on totipotency; steps: explant → sterilisation → medium → callus → shoots/roots → hardening → field

t: Insectivorous plants → why they eat insects
text:
## 1. Reason
They grow in nitrogen-deficient soils (marshy, acidic, bogs) and trap insects for nitrogen (and other minerals)
They do photosynthesise normally; insects are a mineral supplement, not the energy source
2010 option | Verdict
Shady places, poor photosynthesis | Wrong
Nitrogen-deficient soils; insects give nitrogen | Correct
Cannot make vitamins | Wrong
Living fossils between autotrophs and heterotrophs | Wrong
## 2. Examples
Pitcher plant and Venus flytrap: leaves modified to catch and digest insects; sundew also cited
Utricularia kumtensis: new bladderwort (lithophytic, grows on rocks), Karnataka (Oct 2025)
## Beyond your notes
Genera: pitcher = Nepenthes (*N. khasiana*, Meghalaya, India's only native pitcher plant), sundew = Drosera, Venus flytrap = Dionaea, bladderwort = Utricularia (aquatic, bladder traps)
PYQ 2008 (related): insectivorous plant = pitcher plant (not passion flower, night queen, flame of the forest)

text:
## 1. Night blooming
Most desert plants bloom at night because their pollinators (insects, bats) are active at night, avoiding daytime heat
Night flowers: pale/white, strongly fragrant, nectar-rich; bat flowers large (baobab, agave)
1995 option | Verdict
Controlled by low temperature | Wrong
Sensitive to moon phases | Wrong
Insects eat flowers by day | Wrong
Desert insects active at night | Correct
## 2. Xerophyte adaptations
Thick cuticle (thicker in desert plants), leaves reduced to spines (cactus)
Stem photosynthesis: flattened Opuntia, fleshy Euphorbia
CAM: stomata open only at night
PYQ 1995: desert plants bloom at night because desert insects are active at night (answer d)

Group | Body | Vascular tissue | Example
Algae (thallophyta) | Thallus | Absent | Spirogyra, Chara (green); Laminaria, Sargassum (brown); Porphyra, Gracilaria (red)

t: ABO blood groups → antigen, antibody, donor
text:
## 1. ABO table
Group | Antigen on RBC | Antibody in plasma | Can receive from
A | A | anti-B | A, O
B | B | anti-A | B, O
AB | A and B | none | AB, A, B, O
O | none | anti-A and anti-B | O only
Universal recipient = AB: plasma has no anti-A or anti-B antibodies
Universal donor = O: RBCs carry no A or B antigen
Antigen = triggers immune response; antibody = protein made against a foreign antigen
⚠ AB has both antigens, so "lack of antigen" and "lack of both" are wrong; the hinge is lack of antibodies
PYQ 1995: AB is universal recipient because of lack of antibodies
## Beyond your notes
Safest universal red-cell donor is O negative; universal plasma donor is AB (no antibodies)

t: Rh factor → incompatibility and anti-D
text:
## 1. Rh system
Rh antigen (a protein) on RBCs of about 80% of people → Rh+; absent → Rh-
Named after the rhesus monkey, where it was first found
Situation | Result
Rh- person gets Rh+ blood | Makes anti-Rh antibodies (problem on a repeat transfusion)
Rh- mother, Rh+ baby, 1st pregnancy | Usually safe (placenta separates blood); mixing at delivery sensitises mother
Next Rh+ pregnancy | Antibodies cross placenta → erythroblastosis fetalis (HDFN): anaemia, jaundice, death
Prevention | Anti-D (anti-Rh) antibodies to mother right after first birth
⚠ Danger is Rh- mother + Rh+ baby, not the reverse
## In news 2025-26
Mar 2025: James Harrison ("man with the golden arm", Australia) died; his rare anti-D plasma protected millions of babies; before anti-D (1960s) ~50% of HDFN babies died
Jun 2025: France identified a new blood group system, EMM-negative ("Gwada negative"), reported as the 48th blood group system

text:
## 1. Plasma (about 55%)
Straw-coloured; 90-92% water, 6-8% proteins
Plasma protein | Role
Fibrinogen | Clotting
Globulins | Immunity
Albumin | Osmotic balance
Serum = plasma without clotting factors
## 2. Formed elements (about 45%)
Cell | Count | Key fact
RBC | 5-5.5 million/mm3 (men) | No nucleus, biconcave, live 120 days, destroyed in spleen
WBC | 6,000-8,000/mm3 | Nucleated; neutrophils most abundant, basophils rarest, monocytes largest
Platelets | 1.5-3.5 lakh/mm3 | From megakaryocytes; clotting
Haemoglobin: 12-16 g per 100 ml blood
⚠ Spleen = graveyard of RBCs; RBCs are made in red bone marrow

## 1. Steps
Step | Change
Injury | Platelet and tissue factors released
Thrombokinase | Converts prothrombin → thrombin
Thrombin | Converts fibrinogen → fibrin
Fibrin threads | Trap cells → clot
Calcium ions are essential for clotting
Vitamin K is needed for clotting factors; deficiency → bleeding tendency
Heparin (from basophils) is an anticoagulant

Four chambers: 2 atria (upper), 2 ventricles (lower, thicker walls); covered by pericardium
Valve | Between
Tricuspid | Right atrium → right ventricle
Bicuspid (mitral) | Left atrium → left ventricle
Semilunar | Ventricles → pulmonary artery / aorta

Heart is myogenic; sympathetic nerves speed it, parasympathetic slow it
Fact | Value

Normal BP | 120/80 mm Hg
Cardiac output | ~5 litres/min

Feature | Arteries | Veins | Capillaries
Direction | Away from heart | Towards heart | Link arterioles and venules

Walls | Thick, elastic | Thin | One cell thick

t: Double circulation and heart diseases
text:
## 1. Circuits
Circuit | Path
Pulmonary | Right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium
Systemic | Left ventricle → aorta → body → vena cava → right atrium
Hepatic portal | Intestine → liver, before systemic circulation
Coronary | Exclusively heart muscle
Single circulation: fish (2 chambers); incomplete double: amphibians, most reptiles (3); complete double: crocodiles, birds, mammals (4)
## 2. Disorders

Angina: chest pain from too little oxygen to heart muscle
Heart failure ≠ cardiac arrest (heart stops) ≠ heart attack (muscle damage)

First heart transplant: Christiaan Barnard, 1967

Nitrous oxide (N2O) | Laughing gas; anaesthesia
Nitrogen dioxide (NO2) | Air pollutant
Nitrogen pentoxide | Strong oxidiser

t: Carbon monoxide → why it starves the body of oxygen
text:
## 1. Mechanism
CO combines with haemoglobin → carboxyhaemoglobin, occupying sites that carry oxygen
CO has about 200-250 times higher affinity for haemoglobin than oxygen (PMF PYQ book)
Toxic above 35 ppm; most common fatal air poisoning (poor ventilation, geysers, heaters)
Option (2010) | Verdict
CO converted to CO2 in body | Wrong
Much higher affinity for haemoglobin than O2 | Correct
Destroys haemoglobin's structure | Wrong: binding is reversible
Affects respiratory centre | Wrong
⚠ CO does not destroy haemoglobin; it out-competes oxygen
PYQ 2010: CO lowers oxygen supply because of its much higher affinity for haemoglobin
## Beyond your notes
Treatment: fresh air, 100% or hyperbaric oxygen; CO is colourless and odourless

t: Retroviruses → how HIV copies itself
text:
## 1. Steps
Genetic material is RNA; enzyme reverse transcriptase converts RNA → DNA
Integrase inserts viral DNA into host DNA; protease cuts proteins to build new virions
Host cell is tricked into following viral instructions
Term | Meaning
Antiretroviral | Drug that blocks retrovirus replication (e.g., ART for HIV)
Viral capsid | Protein shell around viral genome (target of lenacapavir)
Reverse transcription | RNA → DNA (reverse of normal DNA → RNA)
## 2. Why HIV is hard to cure (CARE Dec 2025)
Integration: viral DNA indistinguishable from human DNA
Latency: dormant reservoir cells invisible to immunity and ART
High mutation rate: no stable vaccine target
Attacks CD4+ T cells, the coordinators of immunity
⚠ "Retro" refers to the reverse flow of information, not to age; HIV-1 subtype C dominates in India

So ACE2 = the cell receptor / doorway for the COVID virus
Option set in 2021 | Right?
Genes in GM plants | No
Indian satellite navigation | No
Radio collars for wildlife | No
Spread of viral diseases | Yes

t: HIV transmission → routes and relative risk
text:
## 1. Routes (PMF)
Unprotected sex: most common route
Blood: contaminated needles, instruments, infected blood or products
Mother-to-child: pregnancy, childbirth, breastfeeding
Fluids: blood, semen, vaginal/rectal fluids, breast milk
## 2. Not spread by
Casual contact, hugging, kissing, shaking hands, sharing utensils or food, insect bites, coughing; HIV is fragile outside the body

Female → male twice as likely as male → female | Wrong: male → female is more likely
Other STIs raise the risk | Correct
Mother → baby in pregnancy, birth, breastfeeding | Correct
Transfusion riskier than contaminated needle | Correct

topic: HIV and hepatitis: blood and sexual spread
t: HIV → stages, tests and treatment
text:
Stage | Feature
Acute HIV | Flu-like 2-4 weeks after infection; highly transmissible
Chronic HIV | Slow replication, no symptoms; can last 10+ years untreated
AIDS | Opportunistic infections (TB, herpes, pneumonia) and cancers (Kaposi's sarcoma, lymphoma); survival 1-3 years untreated
HIV destroys CD4 T cells; WHO Advanced HIV Disease: CD4 < 200 cells/mm³ or stage 3/4; all HIV+ children under 5
Tests: ELISA and rapid tests (antibodies), antigen/antibody tests, NAT (viral load); Western blot confirms ELISA
Window period: antibodies take ~28 days; infants need virological tests (antibody tests unreliable)
ART: lifelong, stops replication; undetectable viral load = does not transmit (TasP)
⚠ HIV is incurable and has no preventive vaccine; ART manages, it does not cure
⚠ World AIDS Day: 1 December (since 1988)

text:
2019 statement | Verdict
HBV is transmitted much like HIV | Correct
HBV, unlike HCV, has no vaccine | Wrong: B has a vaccine, C does not
HBV+HCV infections several times HIV | Correct (~254 m HBV, ~50 m HCV vs ~40 m living with HIV)
Some HBV/HCV carriers are symptomless for years | Correct
HBV vaccine: birth dose within 24 hours, then 6, 10, 14 weeks in the pentavalent (DPT + HepB + Hib)
HCV: pan-genotypic direct-acting antivirals cure in 12-24 weeks
PYQ 2019: "not correct" was the vaccine statement reversed; easy to fall for because HCV is the curable one
## In news 2025-26
India: 2nd-highest viral hepatitis burden; 29.8 million chronic HBV + 5.5 million HCV, ~11.6% of global cases (LENS CA 28 July 2026)
NVHCP (2018): free screening and treatment; 21 crore screened, 6.12 lakh treated; universal HBV screening of pregnant women
Havisure: India's first indigenous hepatitis A vaccine (Indian Immunologicals); hepatitis A vaccine to enter UIP (Nov 2025)

Mosquito | Diseases | Note
Aedes (aegypti; albopictus = tiger mosquito) | Dengue, chikungunya, Zika, yellow fever | Bites by day
Anopheles (female) | Malaria | Also filariasis
Culex | Japanese encephalitis, West Nile, filariasis | JE reservoir: pigs, aquatic birds
⚠ Filariasis has three mosquito vectors (Culex, Anopheles, Aedes); dengue, Zika, chikungunya share one (Aedes)

Trap pattern: a mosquito-borne disease offered as blood/tattoo-borne (2013) or as sexually transmitted (Zika 2017: it is both)

t: Zika → vector, routes, complications
text:
Item | Fact
Virus | Mosquito-borne flavivirus; found Zika Forest, Uganda, 1947
Vector | Aedes (same as dengue), daytime biter
Other routes | Mother-to-foetus, sexual, possibly blood transfusion
Symptoms | Rash, fever, conjunctivitis, joint pain; most infections asymptomatic
Complications | Microcephaly in babies, Guillain-Barré syndrome, myelitis, peripheral neuropathy
Vaccine / cure | None (DNA vaccines under trial)

PYQ 2017: "Both 1 and 2"; trap: assuming a mosquito disease cannot spread sexually
Flavivirus family members: dengue, Zika, yellow fever, JE, West Nile

t: Eradicated vs eliminated → which disease is which
text:
Term | Meaning | Example
Eradication | Zero cases worldwide, permanently | Smallpox (only human disease)
Elimination | Zero / below-threshold cases in a region | Polio in India, trachoma in India
Control | Reduced, still present | Diphtheria, chickenpox
Smallpox (variola virus): eradicated globally 1980 by WHO vaccination; India declared smallpox-free in 1979 (PMF)
First and only human disease eradicated by vaccines; rinderpest is the animal one
2014 option | Eradicated in India?
Diphtheria | No (toxoid vaccine, still occurs)
Chickenpox | No
Smallpox | Yes
PYQ 2014: "3 only"; trap: diseases prevented by routine vaccines (diphtheria) are not eradicated

t: Tuberculosis → types, drug resistance, vaccine
text:
Item | Fact
Pathogen | Mycobacterium tuberculosis; airborne
Types | Latent (no symptoms, not infectious) vs active (infectious)

World TB Day: 24 March

t: Antigen vs antibody → meaning
text:
Term | Meaning
Antigen | Foreign substance (on bacteria, viruses, toxins, pollen) that triggers the immune system and stimulates antibody formation
Antibody (immunoglobulin, Ig) | Protein made by B cells (plasma cells) that binds a specific antigen
Allergen | Harmless antigen that provokes an overreaction (pollen, dander)
Antitoxin / antivenom | Ready-made antibodies (passive immunity)
⚠ Antigen does not destroy bacteria, lower temperature or act as an antidote: those were the 1997/2001 distractors
PYQ 2001 and 1997: antigen "stimulates formation of antibody" / "triggers the immune system"
Vaccine = antigen in safe form (weakened, killed, part, toxoid, mRNA or vector-delivered gene)

t: Innate vs adaptive immunity → features
text:
Feature | Innate | Adaptive (acquired)
Present | From birth | Develops after exposure
Target | Non-specific | Specific antigen
Speed | Immediate | Slow at first
Memory | None | Yes (faster second response)
Cells | Neutrophils, macrophages, NK cells, mast cells, eosinophils, basophils, dendritic cells | B and T lymphocytes
## Innate barriers
Physical: skin, mucous membranes; physiological: stomach acid, saliva, tears
Cellular: phagocytes, NK cells; cytokine: interferons from virus-infected cells protect neighbours
Cell | Job
Basophils | Histamine (blood flow), heparin (anti-clot)
Eosinophils | Kill parasites
Dendritic cells | Present antigens, alert immunity
⚠ NK cells are innate, despite killing infected cells like cytotoxic T cells

t: B cells and T cells → role
text:
Feature | B cells | T cells
Formed / mature | Bone marrow / bone marrow | Bone marrow / thymus
Immunity | Humoral (antibodies in body fluids) | Cell-mediated (no antibodies)
Effector | Become plasma cells → antibodies | Helper, cytotoxic (killer), regulatory
Helper T (CD4): activate B and cytotoxic T cells, release cytokines (HIV's target)
Cytotoxic T: kill infected cells by apoptosis
Regulatory T (T-reg, FOXP3): prevent overreaction; weak T-reg → autoimmunity (type 1 diabetes, RA, lupus, IPEX)
⚠ T cells do not secrete antibodies; they help B cells make them
PYQ 2022: B and T cells "protect the body from diseases caused by pathogens"; distractors: allergens, pain relief, immunosuppression
## In news 2025-26
2025 Nobel (Medicine) context on peripheral tolerance and T-regs (CARE Oct 2025): boosting T-regs for autoimmunity and transplants, cutting them in cancer

t: Active vs passive immunity → examples
text:
Type | Natural | Artificial
Active (own antibodies, memory, long-lasting) | Recovery from chickenpox | Vaccine (e.g., measles)
Passive (ready-made antibodies, immediate, short) | Mother → child via placenta, breast milk | Antivenom, rabies immunoglobulin, monoclonal antibodies
Herd immunity: enough people immune that infection cannot spread; protects unvaccinated
Vaccine types: live attenuated (BCG, MMR, OPV), inactivated (IPV, hepatitis A, rabies), subunit (hepatitis B, HPV), toxoid (diphtheria, tetanus), mRNA, viral vector
⚠ Passive immunity has no memory cells; a vaccine gives active immunity
Snakebite antivenom and rabies immunoglobulin act at once, so they are given after exposure; vaccines need weeks to build memory

t: Antibody classes → where found and role
text:
Class | Where / role
IgG | Most common (70-75%); blood; long-term immunity; only one crossing the placenta
IgA | Second most abundant; tears, saliva, breast milk; guards mucosa
IgM | First antibody made in infection; blood and lymph
IgE | Skin, lungs, mucosa; allergy (histamine release, anaphylaxis) and parasites
IgD | On B-cell surface; B-cell maturation
⚠ High IgE signals allergy or parasitic infection; IgM (early) vs IgG (later/past) is used to date an infection
## Beyond your notes
IgM is the largest antibody (pentamer); IgA in colostrum gives newborn gut protection

t: Immune disorders and monoclonal antibodies
text:
Disorder | Meaning | Example
Autoimmune | Immune system attacks self | Type 1 diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, MS, psoriasis, Graves', Hashimoto's, celiac, vitiligo, myasthenia gravis, GBS
Immunodeficiency | Weak or absent immunity | AIDS
Allergy | Overreaction to harmless allergens | Hay fever, food allergy
Monoclonal antibodies (mAbs): lab-made identical copies of one antibody (hybridoma or recombinant DNA); used for cancer (rituximab, trastuzumab), autoimmunity (adalimumab), infection (palivizumab for RSV, Ebola's Inmazeb, Ebanga), diagnosis (pregnancy tests)
Guillain-Barré syndrome: triggered by Campylobacter jejuni, Zika, rarely vaccines
⚠ mAbs are man-made proteins and give passive, not active, immunity (2025 PYQ on mAbs for Nipah: all three statements true)

t: Haemophilia → cause, factor and inheritance
text:
Item | Fact
Effect | Non-clotting of blood: excessive bleeding into joints, muscles
Haemophilia A | Lacks factor VIII (F8 gene)
Haemophilia B | Lacks factor IX (F9 gene)
Inheritance | X-linked recessive: mostly males; females usually carriers

PYQ 1998: haemophilia leads to non-clotting of blood
Clotting chain: liver makes fibrinogen (soluble) → thrombin converts it to fibrin (insoluble mesh)
## In news 2025-26
India's first human gene therapy trial for haemophilia A at CMC Vellore: lentiviral vector inserts a working FVIII gene into haematopoietic stem cells (DBT, with Emory University)

t: Vaccine types → what each contains, examples
text:
## 1. The main classes
Type | Contains | Examples | Key point
Live attenuated | Weakened pathogen that replicates | BCG, MMR, OPV, Rotavac | Strong, long immunity; not for immunocompromised or pregnant
Inactivated (killed) | Pathogen killed by heat or chemicals | IPV, Hepatitis A, Rabies, Covaxin | Safe; weaker, needs boosters
Subunit / recombinant / polysaccharide / conjugate | Pieces: protein or sugar | Hepatitis B (recombinant), HPV (VLP), Pneumococcal, Meningococcal (conjugate) | Fewer side effects; may need many doses
Toxoid | Inactivated bacterial toxin | Diphtheria, Tetanus | Periodic boosters
mRNA / DNA | Genetic code for an antigen | Pfizer, Moderna; ZyCoV-D (DNA) | Fast to design; mRNA needs ultra-cold storage
Viral vector | Harmless virus carrying the gene | Covishield, Sputnik V, J&J | Antibody + T-cell response; pre-existing immunity to vector cuts effect
⚠ OPV is live, IPV is inactivated
⚠ Toxoid vaccines act against the toxin, not the bacterium

t: Recombinant vector vaccines → how they are made
text:
## 1. Mechanism
Genetic engineering: the gene for a pathogen's antigen is isolated and inserted into a vector
The vector (a harmless or weakened microbe) carries the gene into host cells, which then make the antigen
Both bacteria and viruses serve as vectors (adenovirus in Covishield; Lactococcus lactis bacterium in AdFalciVax)
Vector is modified so it does not cause disease
## 2. Related recombinant products
Product | Recombinant feature
Hepatitis B vaccine | Viral gene expressed in yeast; first recombinant vaccine (1986)
AdFalciVax (malaria) | Recombinant chimeric, built in Lactococcus lactis
Insulin, growth hormone | Therapeutic proteins by rDNA
PYQ 2021: genetic engineering used, bacteria and viruses as vectors: both correct

t: mRNA vaccines → mechanism and Indian firsts
text:
## 1. How mRNA vaccines work
Step | What happens
Delivery | Lipid nanoparticles carry synthetic mRNA into cells
Expression | Ribosomes translate mRNA into the antigen (e.g. spike protein)
Activation | Antigen on cell surface triggers antibodies and T-cells
Memory | Memory cells give faster response on re-exposure
No live pathogen, so no infection risk; mRNA does not enter the nucleus or change DNA (Beyond your notes)
GEMCOVAC-19 (Gennova, Pune): India's first indigenous mRNA vaccine; does not need ultra-cold storage
Rare adverse event: myocarditis with mRNA vaccines
## In news 2025-26
Enteromix (Russia): mRNA cancer vaccine, reported 100% trial efficacy; first target colorectal cancer
⚠ Pfizer's vaccine came from German start-up BioNTech

t: Vaccine basics → components, immunity, challenges
text:
## 1. Components
Component | Role | Example
Antigen | Triggers immunity | Killed/weakened pathogen, protein, mRNA
Adjuvant | Boosts response | Aluminium salts
Stabiliser | Keeps potency | Sugars, gelatin
Preservative | Stops contamination in multi-dose vials | 2-phenoxyethanol
## 2. Key ideas
Vaccines give active acquired immunity; antibodies or mAbs given directly give passive immunity
Herd immunity: enough people immune that infection cannot spread
Smallpox eradicated 1980: the only human disease eradicated by vaccines
Hard targets: fast-mutating HIV, influenza, SARS-CoV-2; complex immunity for malaria, dengue, TB
Edward Jenner: smallpox vaccine; Pasteur: rabies; Salk: polio
⚠ No vaccine is free of side effects: rare events are tracked by post-marketing surveillance

text:
## 1. PCV facts
Item | Fact
Pathogen | Streptococcus pneumoniae (bacterium)
Protects against | Pneumonia, meningitis, sepsis (bacteraemia)
Type | Conjugate: weak polysaccharide antigen joined to a strong carrier protein
Why conjugate | Children under 2 respond poorly to plain sugar antigens
Indian PCV | Pneumosil (Serum Institute)
UIP status | Sub-national UIP vaccine (with JE, rotavirus)
Leading cause of bacterial pneumonia in children under five
Fewer infections means less antibiotic use, so it helps fight drug-resistant bacteria
⚠ "No side effects and no allergic reactions" is false: fever, swelling and rare allergy occur

t: Malaria vaccine → why it is hard
text:
## 1. Reasons
Malaria is caused by several species of Plasmodium, each with different antigens
Parasite has many life stages (sporozoite, liver, blood, sexual), each with different antigens
Immune response to malaria is complex and not fully understood
## 2. Plasmodium species in humans (5)
Species | Note
P. falciparum | Deadliest; cerebral malaria; common in Africa and India
P. vivax | Most common in India and Asia
P. malariae, P. ovale | Less common
P. knowlesi | Monkey malaria that infects humans
Malaria is a protozoan disease spread by female Anopheles; man is the intermediate host, mosquito the definitive host
⚠ Wrong options in PYQ 2010: "man develops no immunity", "vaccines only against bacteria"
PYQ 2010: answer "several species of Plasmodium"

Product | Maker | Fact
RTS,S/AS01 (Mosquirix) | GSK | First WHO-recommended malaria vaccine (2021, Beyond your notes)
R21/Matrix-M | Oxford, made by Serum Institute | WHO-recommended; Cote d'Ivoire first to roll it out (2024)
AdFalciVax | ICMR | India's first indigenous multi-stage malaria vaccine
MAM01 (mAb) | Univ. of Maryland | Complete protection in a trial
RTS,S and R21 target P. falciparum circumsporozoite protein; WHO-recommended for children
AdFalciVax: recombinant chimeric; built in food-grade bacterium Lactococcus lactis; targets pre-erythrocytic (liver) and sexual stages; stops infection and transmission to mosquitoes; stable 9 months at room temperature
Licensed (2025) to Indian Immunologicals, Techinvention, Panacea, Biological E, Zydus
MAM01 binds the CSP of P. falciparum, neutralising sporozoites before they reach the liver
⚠ Neither RTS,S nor R21 is in use in India (PMF General Science)

t: Monoclonal antibodies → what they are, how they act
text:
## 1. Definition
Man-made (laboratory) proteins that act like the body's antibodies
Monoclonal: all copies come from a single clone of immune cells, so all are identical
Each binds one specific antigen (on a virus, cancer cell or toxin)
Made by hybridoma technology or recombinant DNA technology
## 2. How they act
Action | Effect
Neutralise | Block virus entry or toxin
Mark | Tag infected or cancer cells for immune destruction
Block receptors | Stop signalling
Carry drugs | Deliver toxins or radioactive molecules to target cells
Give instant (passive) immunity, unlike vaccines that need time and doses; one shot can last months
⚠ They stimulate or assist immunity by binding antigens: PYQ 2025 statement 2 was correct
PYQ 2025: all three statements correct (man-made, bind specific antigens, used against Nipah)

Use | Example mAb

## 2. Nipah virus
Single-stranded RNA virus; zoonotic; natural host fruit bats (flying foxes)
Spread by contact with infected animals, contaminated food, and human to human
No approved vaccine or cure; m102.4 mAb showed promise; IAV made HiBiT-tagged virus-like particles to aid antibody development
⚠ VLPs are non-infectious: no viral genetic material

t: Biofilms → where they form, why they resist drugs
text:
## 1. What a biofilm is
A community of microbes (bacteria, fungi, protists) stuck to a surface inside a slimy matrix of sugars (polysaccharides), proteins, fats and DNA
Common example: dental plaque
## 2. Where they form
Surface | Example
Medical implants | Catheters, pacemakers, dental implants, prosthetics
Living tissue | Teeth, coronary artery plaques
Food and food-processing surfaces | Dairy (e.g. cheese plants), meat units
Water systems | Pipes
## 3. Why they matter
Matrix blocks drugs and immune cells: biofilms show antibiotic resistance
Spread through quorum sensing (signal molecules called autoinducers)
⚠ All three PYQ statements were correct: implants, food surfaces, antibiotic resistance
PYQ 2022: answer "1, 2 and 3"

t: Solar storm → which effects on Earth are possible
text:
## 1. What a solar storm is
Solar flare (burst of radiation) + CME (cloud of plasma and magnetic field) hit Earth's magnetosphere and ionosphere → geomagnetic storm
## 2. Effects: the 2022 list sorted
Possible effect | Yes/No | Why
GPS and navigation fail | Yes | Ionosphere disturbed, signals bend/scintillate
Power grids damaged | Yes | Geomagnetically induced currents overload transformers, blackouts
Intense auroras over much of Earth | Yes | Charged particles reach lower latitudes in big storms
Satellite orbits disturbed | Yes | Upper atmosphere heats, expands → drag on LEO satellites
Shortwave (HF) radio of aircraft over poles cut | Yes | Polar cap absorption, radio blackout
Tsunamis at equator | No | Tsunamis are seismic (earthquakes, volcanoes, landslides)
Forest fires over the planet | No | Storm energy is deposited in the upper atmosphere
Other effects in CA: astronaut radiation, high-altitude polar flights, pipeline corrosion, communication and banking networks
⚠ Answer 2022: 1, 3, 4, 6, 7; the two traps are the "ground" disasters (tsunami, forest fire)
PYQ 2022: seven-item list; every space-weather effect is electromagnetic or upper-atmospheric, never geological

t: Solar flares, CMEs, solar wind, prominences → how they differ
text:
Phenomenon | What it is | Key number
Solar flare | Magnetic storm, very bright spot with gaseous eruption; heats corona gas | 10-20 million °C; classes A, B, C, M, X (X strongest)
CME | Massive expulsion of plasma + magnetic field from the corona | 250-3000 km/s; 1-3 days to reach Earth
Solar wind | Continuous outflow of plasma (electrons, protons) from the corona | Up to 900 km/s, about 1 million °C
Prominence | Arc of gas held above the surface by magnetic fields | Loops hundreds of thousands of miles; lasts months
Flares travel at light speed (radiation); CMEs are slower than flares
Flares and CMEs occur more at solar maximum, when the Sun's magnetic polarity flips
⚠ A flare is light/radiation; a CME is matter. Radio blackouts start within minutes (flare); geomagnetic storms come a day or more later (CME)
Plasma = 4th state of matter (ionised gas): lightning, electric sparks, neon ("plasma") lights

text:
## 1. Inside out
Layer | Feature
Core | Fusion; 16 million °C
Radiative zone | Energy moves out as radiation
Convective zone | Energy moves by convection
Photosphere | Visible bright surface; emits most radiation; 6000 °C; sunspots here
Chromosphere | Thin layer above, a bit cooler (4,320 °C)
Corona | Outer plasma atmosphere, millions of km; seen best in a total solar eclipse; source of solar wind
⚠ The corona is far hotter than the photosphere (millions of °C): the "coronal heating problem" studied by Aditya-L1 and Solar Orbiter
## 2. Heliosphere
The solar wind blows a bubble in the interstellar medium: heliosphere; its edge heliopause; the shock ahead of it bow shock
Voyager 1 and 2 are now in interstellar space

text:
Term | Meaning
Sunspot | Dark patch on the photosphere, 500-1500 °C cooler; strong magnetic field blocks convection
Umbra / penumbra | Dark centre / lighter rim
Lifetime | Few days to few months
Solar cycle | About 11 years, tracked by sunspot counts
Solar maximum | Mid-cycle: most sunspots, flares, CMEs
Solar minimum | Start/end: few or no sunspots
Hale cycle | Magnetic poles flip every ~11 yrs, flip back in another 11 → 22-year magnetic cycle
Driven by differential rotation (equator faster than poles) twisting magnetic field lines
Sun is about 1% cooler with no sunspots; may affect Earth's climate
Impacts: satellites, radio, GPS, power grids, cosmic-ray flux, ozone, auroras
⚠ Sunspots are cooler, not hotter, than their surroundings, yet more sunspots = a more active Sun

Point | Fact

Where | High latitudes: Arctic and Antarctic, guided by Earth's magnetic field lines
Names | Aurora borealis (north), aurora australis (south)
In big storms | Seen at much lower latitudes (the 2022 PYQ statement)

## In news 2025-26
MAVEN (NASA, 2013) detected the Zwaan-Wolf effect in the Martian atmosphere for the first time (2026): solar wind in magnetic flux tubes is squeezed and pushed sideways; explains gradual atmosphere loss

t: Moon → why we see only one face
text:
Point | Fact
Cause | Tidal locking (synchronous rotation)
Rotation period | About 27.3 days
Revolution period | About 27.3 days (same)
Result | The same face always turns to Earth
Visible share | About 59% of the surface over time (libration)
Far side | Not dark: it gets sunlight; only unseen from Earth
⚠ PYQ 2005 A-R: A (same face) and R (rotation ≈ revolution, 27.3 days) both true and R explains A
## Beyond your notes
Sidereal month 27.3 days (relative to stars); synodic month 29.5 days (new moon to new moon, the phase cycle)
⚠ "Dark side of the Moon" is a misnomer: it is the far side

t: Moon → key numbers and effects on Earth
text:
Property | Value
Diameter | 3,474 km, about one-quarter of Earth; 5th largest moon
Mean distance | 3,84,400 km (perigee 3,63,300, apogee 4,05,500 km)
Gravity | 1.62 m/s² (about 1/6 Earth)
Origin | Giant impact ("big splat"): a body 1-3 × Mars hit early Earth; Moon formed about 4.44 billion years ago
Stabiliser | Keeps Earth's tilt steady (without it tilt could swing up to 85°)
Tides | Tidal friction slows Earth's spin (1.4 ms per 100 years); Moon recedes 4 cm per year
Early Earth | Day only about 6 hours long
Moon is depleted in carbon and volatiles (nitrogen, hydrogen); lunar night 350+ hours (about 14 Earth days); poles avoid long nights
⚠ Light from the Moon is reflected sunlight; the Moon has no atmosphere, so no sound, no twilight, big temperature swings

t: Eclipses and special moons → when and why
text:
Event | Condition
Solar eclipse | Moon between Sun and Earth; only at new moon
Lunar eclipse | Earth between Sun and Moon; only at full moon; safe to view with naked eye
Blood Moon | Moon turns coppery red in a total lunar eclipse: Earth's atmosphere scatters blue (Rayleigh scattering) and bends red light onto the Moon
Supermoon | Full or new moon at perigee in syzygy; about 14% larger, 30% brighter; 3-4 times a year; perigean spring tides
Blue Moon | 2nd full moon in a calendar month (or extra full moon in a season)
Micromoon | Full moon at apogee
Not every new/full moon gives an eclipse: the Moon's orbit is tilted about 5° to the ecliptic (Beyond your notes)

Total lunar eclipse ("Blood Moon") seen across India, Sept 2025 (LENS Sept 2025)
Supermoon (Oct 2025) and Wolf Supermoon (January's first full moon at perigee), peak 2-3 January 2026
Total lunar eclipse visible across India, March 2026 (LENS March 2026)

topic: Asteroids, comets, meteors and dwarf planets
t: Asteroids → where they lie and what they are
text:
Point | Fact
What | Rocky and metallic remnants of planet formation (some ice); also called planetoids
Why not a planet | Jupiter's gravity stopped them from coalescing
Where | Asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, 2.3-3.3 AU
Size | Microscopic to hundreds of km
Largest | Ceres (946 km, 2.77 AU): also a dwarf planet
2nd largest | Vesta (525 km)
Other groups | Trojans at Jupiter's L4/L5; near-Earth asteroids (Apollo type)
All asteroids except Ceres are small solar system bodies
⚠ The belt is between Mars and Jupiter: traps say Jupiter-Saturn (1998) or Venus-Mercury (2011)
PYQ 1997: small rocks revolving between Mars and Jupiter = asteroids (not meteors, comets or meteorites)
PYQ 1998: statements 1 (rocky debris) and 2 (some ~1000 km) correct; 3 (Jupiter-Saturn) wrong → answer 1 and 2

topic: Asteroids, comets, meteors and dwarf planets
t: Asteroids vs comets → the 2011 differences
text:
Feature | Asteroid | Comet
Made of | Rock and metal | Frozen gases (water, ammonia, methane, CO2) holding rocky/metallic bits ("dirty snowball")
Where found | Mostly between Mars and Jupiter | Kuiper belt (short-period), Oort cloud (long-period)
Orbit | Mostly near-circular | Highly elliptical
Tail | None | Glowing coma and tail near the Sun
Size | Up to ~950 km | Nucleus often about 10 km
⚠ PYQ 2011 statement 2 wrong: comets are not found mostly between Venus and Mercury; answer 1 and 3 only
Both are primitive remnants of the early solar system, so missions sample them
## Missions
Hayabusa / Hayabusa-2 (Japan): asteroid sample return
OSIRIS-REx (NASA, Bennu samples), DART (NASA, deflected Dimorphos 2022), Rosetta (ESA, comet 67P) (Beyond your notes)

topic: Asteroids, comets, meteors and dwarf planets
t: Comets → tail, origin and famous ones
text:
## 1. Why the tail points away from the Sun
Near the Sun the ice outgasses → coma (gas cloud) and tail
Solar radiation pressure and the solar wind push gas and dust away from the Sun
So the tail points away from the Sun whatever the comet's direction; going outward, the tail leads
⚠ PYQ 1997 traps: not centrifugal force, not attraction by a star, not a fixed orientation
## 2. Origin
Type | Period | Source
Short-period | Few hundred years or less | Kuiper belt (30-50 AU)
Long-period | Thousands of years | Oort cloud (5,000-100,000 AU)
## 3. Famous comets
Comet | Fact
Halley's | Returns every 76 years; last 1986 (next 2061, Beyond your notes); parent of Eta Aquariids (May) and Orionids (Oct)
NASA count | 3,910 known comets
## Beyond your notes
Two tails: ion tail (blue, straight, pushed by solar wind) and dust tail (curved, pushed by radiation pressure)

topic: Asteroids, comets, meteors and dwarf planets
t: Meteoroid, meteor, meteorite → which is which
text:
Term | Meaning
Meteoroid | Solid debris from asteroids/comets floating in space
Meteor | Streak of light (shooting/falling star) when a meteoroid enters the atmosphere and burns up
Meteorite | The chunk that survives and reaches the ground
Meteor shower | Many meteors when Earth crosses a comet's (or asteroid's) debris trail
Fireball | Very bright meteor
Meteors burn in the mesosphere (start around 200 km, high speed, friction)
⚠ PYQ 1995: meteor = piece of matter from outer space entering Earth's atmosphere; not a moving star, not part of a constellation, not a tailless comet
PYQ 1995 and 1997: the four names (asteroid, comet, meteor, meteorite) are swapped as options; fix each by location

topic: Asteroids, comets, meteors and dwarf planets

text:
## 1. IAU definitions (2006)
Criterion | Planet | Dwarf planet
Orbits the Sun | Yes | Yes
Round (hydrostatic equilibrium) | Yes | Yes
Not a moon | Yes | Yes
Cleared its orbit | Yes | No
## 2. Members
Body | Where | Fact
Pluto | Kuiper belt, 39 AU | 2,377 km; discovered 1930; demoted 2006; 5 moons: Charon (largest), Nix, Hydra, Kerberos, Styx
Eris | Kuiper belt / scattered disc | 2,326 km; its discovery forced the 2006 decision

Zone | Distance | Made of

Oort cloud | 5,000-100,000 AU | Spherical shell of icy bodies; long-period comets
New Horizons (NASA, 2006): first Pluto flyby (2015): nitrogen-ice plains (Sputnik Planitia); then Arrokoth (2019)
