Object | Fact
1I/'Oumuamua | 2017, first interstellar object
2I/Borisov | 2019, first interstellar comet

t: Pole star → finding north and other directions
text:
Point | Fact
Pole star | Star in line with Earth's axis; at present Polaris (North Star), a system of 3 stars
Seen from | Northern hemisphere only
Movement | Does not appear to move; all stars seem to revolve around it
Shows | True north
Facing the polestar: north ahead, east on the right, west on the left, south behind
## Walking with the polestar
To go | Keep the polestar
North | In front
South | Behind
East | On the left
West | On the right
⚠ PYQ 2012: village east → walk keeping the polestar to the left; trap: "to the right" gives west
Ursa Major (Saptarishi, Big Dipper): its two pointer stars point to Polaris
## Beyond your notes
Altitude of Polaris above the horizon ≈ observer's latitude: 0° at the equator, 90° at the North Pole
There is no bright south pole star; the Southern Cross (Crux) is used instead

t: Star paths → what they show about latitude
text:
Observer at | Stars rise and set
Equator | Perpendicular (vertical) to the horizon; celestial poles lie on the horizon
Mid-latitudes | At a slant to the horizon
Poles | Do not rise or set: circle parallel to the horizon
Stars move parallel to the celestial equator (projection of Earth's equator into space)
⚠ PYQ 2001: stars rising perpendicular to the horizon → observer at the Equator; North/South Pole options are traps (there, stars move parallel to the horizon)
PYQ 2001 and 2012: both use the sky as a compass; the logic is Earth's axis, not memorised facts

topic: Big Bang and the expanding universe
t: Expanding universe → what counts as evidence (2012)
text:
## 1. The four 2012 items
Item | Evidence of expansion?
Detection of microwaves in space (CMB) | Yes
Redshift of distant galaxies | Yes
Movement of asteroids | No: solar-system motion
Supernova explosions | Official key: No (answer 1 and 2)
⚠ PMF argues supernovae (gravitational waves) also count and marks "none of the above"; the official key and Preview give (a) 1 and 2: write 1 and 2
⚠ Distant Type Ia supernovae dimmer than expected showed accelerating expansion (1998; Nobel 2011: Perlmutter, Riess, Schmidt), so the trap is real
## 2. The three classic proofs of the Big Bang (PMF)
Cosmological redshift, CMB, gravitational waves
PYQ 2012: "evidence for continued expansion" = CMB + redshift; asteroids are a distractor from the solar system

topic: Big Bang and the expanding universe
t: Big Bang → timeline and fate
text:
Time after Big Bang | Event
10^-43 s | Inflation: atom-size to grapefruit-size
10^-6 s | Quarks clump into protons and neutrons
3 min | Too hot for atoms; light cannot shine
3,00,000 years | Atoms form (H, He; traces of Li, Be): light shines (source of CMB)
~1 billion years | First galaxies and stars
Universe age 13.8 billion years; ~100 billion galaxies of ~100 billion stars each
Big Crunch: one possible end: expansion stops, universe collapses to a dense point
Accelerated expansion began ~5 billion years ago (dark-energy era)
⚠ The Big Bang was not an explosion in space: all of space was one hot, dense point

topic: Big Bang and the expanding universe
t: Redshift, Hubble's law and the CMB
text:
## 1. Redshift and blueshift
Shift | Meaning
Redshift | Source moving away: wavelength stretched
Blueshift | Source approaching
Edwin Hubble first tied galactic redshift to an expanding universe (1920s)
Hubble's law: the farther a galaxy, the faster it recedes
Expanding universe rests on the Doppler effect (not Raman, Zeeman or Stark)
## 2. Cosmic Microwave Background
Faint glow seen by radio telescopes, strongest in the microwave band
Relic radiation of the Big Bang: oldest light, comes from all directions
## 3. Hubble constant
Rate of expansion; methods disagree ("Hubble tension")
Gravitational waves as "standard sirens": wave gives distance, light gives velocity
Type Ia supernovae and Cepheids are "standard candles"

topic: Big Bang and the expanding universe
t: Dark matter and dark energy → shares and evidence
text:
Component | Share | Key fact
Dark energy | ~68% of mass-energy | Drives accelerating expansion
Dark matter | ~27% of mass-energy; ~85% of all matter | No light emitted or absorbed; felt only by gravity
Ordinary matter | ~5% | Stars, gas, planets
Dark energy + dark matter = 95.1% of the universe (PMF)
Evidence for dark matter: fast rotation of galaxies' outer arms, gravitational lensing, structure formation
Vera Rubin gave the first evidence (1970s)
## In news 2025-26
Gamma-ray glow near the Milky Way's centre studied as possible dark-matter annihilation; Cherenkov Telescope Array (Chile) can test it (LENS Oct 2025)
Vera C. Rubin Observatory (Cerro Pachon, Chile; Simonyi Survey Telescope) began imaging (LENS Jul 2025)
Missing ordinary matter located as diffuse intergalactic gas using Fast Radio Bursts (76% in the intergalactic medium)

Centre | Supermassive black hole Sagittarius A*

Spiral galaxies: gas-rich, new stars form in the arms

topic: Astronomical distances and the nearest stars
t: Light-year → why astronomers use it (2021)
text:
## 1. The 2021 options
Option | Verdict
Distances among stellar bodies do not change | Wrong: they change
Gravity of stellar bodies does not change | Wrong
Light always travels in a straight line | Wrong: gravity bends light
Speed of light is always the same | Correct
## 2. The unit
Light-year = distance light travels in vacuum in one (Julian) year: a unit of distance, not time
Speed of light ~3,00,000 km/s (299,792 km/s)
1 ly = 9.46 x 10^12 km (9.46 trillion km)
Sunlight takes ~8.3 minutes (8 min 19 s) to reach Earth
⚠ "Straight line" is the tempting wrong option: general relativity says light bends near mass
PYQ 2021: the hinge is constancy of light's speed, which makes time a reliable ruler

topic: Astronomical distances and the nearest stars
t: Astronomical units → AU, light-year, parsec
text:
Unit | Definition | Value
Astronomical Unit (AU) | Mean Earth-Sun distance | ~149.6 million km
Light-year | Distance light covers in a Julian year (365.25 days) | 9.46 x 10^15 m
Parsec | Distance at which 1 AU subtends 1 arc-second | ~3.26 light-years
Order: parsec > light-year > AU
AU suits the solar system; light-year and parsec suit stars and galaxies; megaparsec for galaxy clusters
Voyager 1 crossed the termination shock at 94 AU, Voyager 2 at 84 AU
## Beyond your notes
1 parsec ≈ 3.26 ly ≈ 2,06,265 AU
⚠ A light-year is never a measure of time; nor is a parsec

topic: Stellar life cycle and the Chandrasekhar limit
t: Life cycle → small star versus massive star
text:
Stage | Small star (Sun-like) | Massive star
1 | Nebula (gas + dust): birthplace | Nebula
2 | Protostar: no fusion yet, glows by contraction | Protostar
3 | T Tauri star | -
4 | Main sequence (H → He fusion) | Main sequence
5 | Red giant | Red supergiant
6 | Planetary nebula | Supernova (Type II)
7 | White dwarf → black dwarf | Neutron star or black hole
~90% of stars, including the Sun, are main-sequence stars
Fusion needs millions of degrees: H nuclei fuse to helium, releasing energy
⚠ Planetary nebula has nothing to do with planets: it is the shed outer layer of a dying small star

topic: Stellar life cycle and the Chandrasekhar limit
t: Giant versus dwarf stars → lifespan (2024)
text:
## 1. The 2024 Statement-I/II
Statement | Verdict
I: Giant stars live much longer than dwarf stars | Incorrect
II: Giant stars have a greater rate of nuclear reactions | Correct
Answer (d): I incorrect, II correct
## 2. The rule
Property | Massive / giant star | Dwarf star
Core temperature, pressure | Higher | Lower
Fusion rate | Faster | Slower
Luminosity | Higher | Lower
Lifespan | Shorter | Longer
End | Supernova → neutron star / black hole | White dwarf
Red dwarfs: faintest main-sequence stars (<1/1000 Sun's brightness), ~4000 °C, about three-quarters of Milky Way stars, long lifespans
⚠ More fuel does not mean longer life: burn rate rises much faster than mass
PYQ 2024: Statement-II is true and is the reason Statement-I is false

topic: Stellar life cycle and the Chandrasekhar limit
t: Objects in space → correct descriptions (2023)
text:
## 1. The 2023 pairs
Object | Given description | Correct?
Cepheids | Giant clouds of dust and gas | No: they brighten and dim periodically
Nebulae | Stars that brighten and dim periodically | No: clouds of gas and dust
Pulsars | Neutron stars formed when massive stars collapse | Yes
Answer only one (descriptions of 1 and 2 were swapped)
## 2. Likely-next objects
Object | Description
Cepheid variable | Regular period-luminosity relation: a cosmic yardstick
Quasar | Extremely bright core of a distant galaxy, powered by a supermassive black hole
Magnetar | Highly magnetised neutron star, X-ray and radio flares
Brown dwarf | "Failed star": too small for H fusion (up to ~70 Jupiter masses)
Nova | Flare on a white dwarf taking gas from a companion
Hubble identified 800+ Cepheids in 24 galaxies to fix the universe's age at 13.8 billion years

topic: Stellar life cycle and the Chandrasekhar limit
t: Red giant, white dwarf, black dwarf → the end of a Sun-like star
text:
Stage | Fact
Red giant | 10-100 x Sun's diameter; very bright but cooler surface; H burns in a shell around a helium core; helium → carbon
Red supergiant | Enormous red giant of a massive star
Planetary nebula | Ejected shell, lasts a few tens of thousands of years
White dwarf | Small, hot, degenerate matter: a spoonful weighs several tonnes
Black dwarf | Cooled white dwarf: none exists yet (takes longer than 13.8 billion years)
The Sun will swell into a red giant beyond Venus's orbit, then end as a white dwarf
Degenerate matter: electrons pushed close to nuclei after fusion stops and gravity wins
⚠ Brown dwarf ≠ black dwarf: a brown dwarf never ignited; a black dwarf is a dead, cooled white dwarf

topic: Stellar life cycle and the Chandrasekhar limit
t: Supernova → Type Ia versus Type II, and nova
text:
Feature | Nova | Type Ia supernova | Type II supernova
Star | White dwarf in a binary | White dwarf in a binary | Massive star (red supergiant)
Cause | Surface fusion of gas taken from companion | Runaway carbon fusion destroys the star | Core collapse (iron core)

topic: Orbits and why satellites stay up
t: Geostationary orbit → the three conditions
text:
## 1. What makes an orbit geostationary
Condition | Value | In the 2011 PYQ
Geosynchronous | period = Earth's rotation, 23 h 56 m 4 s | correct
Circular | eccentricity 0 | correct
Equatorial | inclination 0°, in the plane of the equator | correct
Direction | west to east (prograde) | not asked
Altitude | ~35,786 km above the surface | 22,236 km = wrong
Satellite appears fixed over one point on the equator → ground antennas stay fixed, no tracking
3 GEO satellites cover nearly the whole Earth except the polar regions; one covers ~1/3 of the surface
⚠ 22,236 is the altitude in miles, not km; 35,786 km (~36,000 km) is the answer
⚠ Every GEO is a GSO, but a GSO is GEO only if circular and at 0° inclination
PYQ 2011: telecom relay satellites; answer "1, 2 and 3 only"; trap: the 22,236 km altitude statement

topic: Orbits and why satellites stay up
t: GSO vs GEO → how they differ
text:
Feature | Geosynchronous (GSO) | Geostationary (GEO)
Period | 24 h (sidereal) | 24 h (sidereal)
Altitude | ~35,786 km | ~35,786 km
Inclination | can be inclined | 0°
Shape | circular or elliptical | always circular
Ground track | figure-of-eight (drifts N-S) | a fixed point
Ground antenna | tracking needed if inclined | fixed antenna
Indian users | NavIC IGSO satellites (29°) | INSAT, GSAT, NavIC GEO satellites
## 2. Uses of GSO/GEO (PMF list)
Communication: GSAT, INSAT; weather: INSAT-3D/3DR, GOES; navigation: NavIC, QZSS
Problems: latency, poor polar coverage, crowded GEO belt, end-of-life move to a graveyard orbit
⚠ INSAT-3D/3DR give weather updates every 15 minutes from GEO; polar satellites cannot do continuous watch

topic: Orbits and why satellites stay up
t: Orbits by altitude → LEO, MEO, HEO
text:
Orbit | Altitude | Period | Speed | Uses and examples
LEO | 160 (180)-2,000 km | 90-120 min | ~7.8 km/s | Earth observation, ISS (~400 km), Cartosat, RISAT, Starlink, OneWeb, Kuiper
MEO | 2,000-35,500 km | 2-12 h | 3.9-7.3 km/s | GNSS: GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou; O3b
HEO / GEO band | ≥ 35,500 km | 24 h and more | ~3 km/s | GEO comsats; deep-space (Aditya-L1, JWST, Chandra)
## 3. Hinge facts
Lower orbit = faster speed, lower latency, better resolution, faster orbital decay (drag)
MEO satellites pass through the Van Allen belts → need radiation shielding
Satellite-internet constellations sit at 500-2,000 km; latency below 50 ms vs GEO's ~36,000 km
⚠ NavIC is not in MEO: its 7 satellites are at ~36,000 km (GEO + inclined GSO); GPS/Galileo/GLONASS are MEO

topic: Orbits and why satellites stay up
t: Orbits by inclination and direction → which satellites use them
text:
Orbit | Inclination | Feature | Examples
Equatorial | 0° | over equator | INSAT, GSAT, GOES
Polar | ~90° | passes over poles, global coverage | IRS, NOAA, RISAT
Sun-synchronous (SSO) | ~98° | same local solar time daily | Cartosat, Resourcesat, Landsat, Sentinel
Inclined | between 0° and 90° (or 90°-180°) | regional, mid-latitudes | NavIC IGSO (29°), GLONASS
Prograde | 0°-90° | west to east, uses Earth's spin | most satellites, ISS, GPS
Retrograde | 90°-180° | east to west, needs more fuel | some spy satellites
## 4. Why launch eastward from near the equator
Earth's surface moves ~1,600 km/h (~460 m/s) at the equator → free boost for eastward launches
Benefit applies to GEO and equatorial orbits only; polar satellites are launched north/south and get no boost
⚠ SSO is near-polar and retrograde (~98°), not exactly polar

topic: Orbits and why satellites stay up
t: Sun-synchronous, semi-synchronous and transfer orbits → features
text:
Orbit | Altitude | Period | Key fact | Users
SSO | 600-800 km | 90-120 min | plane precesses ~1°/day; constant lighting | remote sensing, spy satellites, SCATSAT
Semi-synchronous | ~20,200 km | ~12 h | 2 orbits/day; GPS at 55° | GPS, Galileo, GLONASS
Molniya / Tundra | highly elliptical | 12 h / 24 h | long dwell over high latitudes | Russian polar comms
GTO | perigee in LEO, apogee at GEO | 6-12 h | satellite circularises with own motor | GSAT, INSAT, NVS
Hohmann transfer | ellipse between 2 circles | half an orbit | 2 burns, most fuel-efficient | LEO→GEO, Mangalyaan
Bi-elliptic transfer: 3 burns; better only when target orbit > ~11.94× the initial one
Shapes: circular e = 0, elliptical 0 < e < 1, parabolic e = 1 (exactly escape speed), hyperbolic e > 1 (Voyager, 'Oumuamua)
⚠ Rockets do not take comsats straight to GEO: they drop them in GTO; the satellite's apogee motor does the rest

topic: Orbits and why satellites stay up
t: Why a satellite does not fall → gravity and orbital speed
text:
## 5. The physics UPSC asked
Earth's gravity still acts at orbital height; it supplies the centripetal acceleration for circular motion
The rocket gives a large sideways (tangential) speed: the satellite keeps "falling" but the curved Earth falls away beneath it → free fall
Option in 2011 PYQ | Verdict | Why
gravity does not exist there | wrong | gravity acts at all heights
neutralised by Moon's pull | wrong | Moon does not cancel Earth's pull
gravity provides the speed | wrong | rocket provides the speed
gravity provides the acceleration | correct | centripetal acceleration
## 6. Related velocities and laws
Orbital velocity: ~7.8 km/s in LEO, ~3.07 km/s at GEO; lower orbit needs higher speed
Escape velocity of Earth: ~11.2 km/s (~25,000 mph)
Kepler's 2nd law: fastest at perigee, slowest at apogee; 3rd law: T² ∝ a³
Astronauts feel weightless because they and the craft fall together (apparent weight 0), not because g = 0
⚠ PMF explains stability as gravity balanced by "centrifugal force"; in exam language choose centripetal acceleration provided by gravity
PYQ 2011: "attraction of Earth provides the necessary acceleration"; trap: "provides the necessary speed"

topic: Satellite navigation: GNSS, NavIC and GPS
t: How satellite navigation works → atomic clocks, trilateration, jamming
text:
## 1. Steps
Each satellite carries atomic clocks and broadcasts its position + exact time
Receiver measures signal delay: distance = time delay × speed of light
Trilateration (distances, spheres) not triangulation (angles): 4 satellites minimum = 3 for position + 1 to fix receiver clock error
Clock | Feature
Caesium | most accurate
Rubidium | smaller, cheaper, slightly less accurate; used on NavIC
Atomic principle | microwave frequency emitted when electrons change energy levels
## 2. Threats
Threat | What happens
Jamming | strong radio signal blocks GNSS signals; receiver loses position
Spoofing | fake signals mimic real ones; receiver shows wrong location
## In news 2025-26
West Asia conflict raised GPS jamming/spoofing near the Strait of Hormuz, hitting shipping (Mar 2026); dark-fleet ships use GPS spoofing and switch off AIS
⚠ Triangulation is used in land surveying; GNSS uses trilateration

text:
Item | Fact
Full form | GPS Aided GEO Augmented Navigation
Type | SBAS (Satellite-Based Augmentation System): augments GPS, not an independent system
Developers | ISRO + Airports Authority of India (AAI)
Operational | since 2015; first SBAS certified for the equatorial region
Space segment | hosted payloads on GEO satellites GSAT-8, GSAT-10, GSAT-15 (no dedicated satellites)
Accuracy | GPS ~5-15 m → GAGAN horizontal ≤ 3 m, vertical ≤ 4-5 m
Integrity | alert within ~6 seconds if a GPS signal is unsafe
Coverage | entire Indian Flight Information Region + adjoining oceans
## 1. What it adds (2025 PYQ statements)
Accuracy + integrity + availability of GPS → correct
Uniform, high-quality air traffic management → correct
Benefits only aviation → wrong: also maritime, highways, railways, surveying, tolling, GEMINI for fishermen

topic: GAGAN, aviation navigation and aircraft black boxes
t: SBAS → how it works and the world's systems
text:
## 1. Steps
Surveyed ground reference stations compare GPS position with true position → error
Master Control Centre computes corrections and integrity messages
Corrections uplinked to GEO satellites → broadcast → receiver applies them in real time
SBAS | Country/region
GAGAN | India
WAAS | USA
EGNOS | Europe
MSAS | Japan
BDSBAS | China
India lies in the Equatorial Ionisation Anomaly: plasma bubbles distort GPS; GAGAN uses ISRO's IGM-MLDF ionospheric model
GPS alone fails ICAO Safety-of-Life needs: weak vertical accuracy, no instant integrity alert
⚠ SBAS does not replace GPS; NavIC is the independent system, GAGAN the augmentation layer

text:

text:
## 1. Profile
India's first dedicated solar mission; launched 2 Sept 2023 on PSLV-C57 (XL)
Placed in a halo orbit around Sun-Earth L1 (~1.5 million km from Earth) on 6 Jan 2024
Why L1: no eclipse, 24x7 Sun view; warns of CMEs ~30-60 min ahead; low station-keeping fuel
Has released >27 TB of solar data
## 2. Seven payloads
Remote sensing (4, view the Sun) | In situ (3, particles and fields at L1)
VELC (coronagraph, IIA Bengaluru) | ASPEX
SUIT (UV imager) | PAPA
SoLEXS (soft X-ray) | Magnetometer
HEL1OS (hard X-ray) | -
⚠ 7 payloads: 4 remote + 3 in situ; L1 is dynamically unstable, hence a halo orbit
## In news 2025-26
VELC recorded its first significant CME onset; maiden data set released 6 Jan 2025
USA's SOLAR-1 (NOAA, earlier SWFO-L1, launched Sept 2025) also watches the Sun from L1

t: Nuclear fission → what happens and what is released
text:
## 1. The process
A slow (thermal) neutron strikes a fissile nucleus (U-235, Pu-239, U-233) → it splits into two fission fragments
Releases energy (mostly heat), 2-3 neutrons and gamma radiation; NCERT: on average 2½ neutrons per U-235 fission
Energy ≈ 200 MeV per fissioning nucleus; mass lost becomes energy (E = mc²)
Fragments vary: Ba + Kr, Sb + Nb, Xe + Sr - all neutron-rich, radioactive (emit beta)
Condition for fission | Meaning
Fissile nucleus | U-235, Pu-239, U-233
Slow neutron | Thermal neutrons (~0.025 eV) are captured easily
Critical mass | Minimum mass; below it too many neutrons escape and the reaction dies
1 kg uranium by fission ≈ 10¹⁴ J; 1 kg coal ≈ 10⁷ J (NCERT) - a million times more
## 2. History
Fission discovered 1938 by Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann; explained by Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch; neutron discovered by Chadwick (1932); chain reaction suggested by Enrico Fermi (1939)

t: Chain reaction → why it is self-sustaining
text:
## 1. The two reasons (UPSC 2001)
Each fission releases more neutrons than it consumes (2-3)
Fast neutrons are slowed by a moderator (graphite, heavy water, water) so they cause further fission
2001 PYQ statement | Verdict
More neutrons released in each fission | Correct
Neutrons immediately take part in fission | Wrong - they must first be slowed
Fast neutrons slowed down by graphite | Correct
Every neutron released starts a further fission | Wrong - many escape or are absorbed
⚠ Unslowed fast neutrons mostly escape from the reactor (NCERT); slow neutrons have a much higher probability of fissioning U-235
PYQ 2001: answer "I and III"; trap words: "immediately" and "every"

t: Multiplication factor k → critical, subcritical, supercritical
text:
## 1. k = fissions in one generation ÷ fissions in the previous one
State | k | What happens
Subcritical | < 1 | Reaction dies out
Critical | = 1 | Each fission causes exactly one more; steady power - normal reactor state
Supercritical | > 1 | Power rises exponentially; used briefly at start-up; uncontrolled → explosion
Criticality = enough neutrons from fission to make up for those lost by leakage or absorption; "attaining criticality" = first self-sustaining chain reaction
Control rods (cadmium) regulate k; safety rods drop in to cut k below 1 fast
⚠ Chernobyl (1986): reactor went supercritical (NCERT example)
## In news 2025-26
PFBR, Kalpakkam attained first criticality (reported April 2026) - India formally entered Stage II

t: Nuclear reactor vs atom bomb → controlled vs uncontrolled
text:
## 1. The difference (UPSC 1995)
Point | Nuclear reactor | Atom (fission) bomb
Chain reaction | Controlled, steady | Uncontrolled, rapid
k | Held at 1 | Far above 1 (supercritical)
Control | Moderator + control rods | None
Neutrons | Mostly slow (thermal reactors) | Fast neutrons
Fuel | Natural / low-enriched U (3-5%) | Highly enriched U-235 (~90%) or Pu-239
Output | Steady heat → electricity | Instant blast, heat, radiation
⚠ Both have a chain reaction; the difference is only control - options "no chain reaction in reactor/bomb" are wrong
PYQ 1995: "chain reaction in a nuclear reactor is controlled"

text:
## 1. Types by design
Type | Principle | Example
Gun-type fission | Two subcritical U-235 masses fired together | Little Boy, Hiroshima, 6 Aug 1945 (~15 kt)
Implosion fission | Pu-239 core compressed by explosives | Fat Man, Nagasaki, 9 Aug 1945 (~21 kt)
Boosted fission | D-T gas in core adds fusion neutrons | Higher yield, compact warheads
Thermonuclear (H-bomb) | Fission primary ignites fusion secondary | Ivy Mike (US, 1952); Tsar Bomba (USSR 1961, ~50 Mt, largest)
Trinity test (July 1945, New Mexico): first nuclear explosion, Pu implosion device
India: Pokhran-I "Smiling Buddha" (1974); Pokhran-II "Operation Shakti" (1998) included a thermonuclear test
⚠ A hydrogen bomb needs a fission bomb as its trigger; pure fusion weapons are only theoretical

text:
## 1. Key terms
Term | Meaning | Examples
Fissile | Fissions with a slow neutron | U-235, U-233, Pu-239 (Pu-241)
Fertile | Becomes fissile by neutron capture | U-238 → Pu-239; Th-232 → U-233
Natural uranium | U-238 99.3%, U-235 0.7%, U-234 <0.01% | Used in PHWRs
LEU | < 20% U-235 (power reactors 3-5%) | PWR, BWR
HEU | ≥ 20% U-235 | Research/naval reactors up to 20%
Weapons-grade | ~90% U-235 | Bombs
U-235 is the only naturally occurring fissile isotope
Enrichment: uranium → gas UF₆; gas centrifuge (most used), gaseous diffusion (older), laser separation (developing)
Yellowcake = refined uranium ore concentrate
⚠ Thorium-232 is not fissile - it must be bred into U-233 first
⚠ All plutonium isotopes fission with fast neutrons, but only Pu-239 and Pu-241 are fissile with slow ones

t: Reactor components → function and material
text:
## 1. Parts of a nuclear reactor
Component | Function | Materials
Fuel | Fissile material that splits | U-235, Pu-239, U-233
Moderator | Slows fast neutrons to thermal | Heavy water, graphite, light water (beryllium oxide)
Control rods | Absorb excess neutrons, regulate/stop reaction | Cadmium, boron, hafnium
Coolant | Carries heat away from core | Light/heavy water, CO₂, liquid sodium, helium
Cladding | Seals fuel pellets | Zirconium alloys (Zircaloy)
Pressure vessel | Encloses core at high pressure | Thick steel alloy
Shielding | Stops radiation leakage | Concrete, lead, water
⚠ Moderator slows neutrons; control rods absorb them - the two are swapped in trap options
⚠ Without control rods the chain reaction "goes out of bounds" (state PSC PYQ)

t: Moderator → what heavy water does
text:
## 1. Moderation
Moderators are light nuclei: a neutron loses energy by elastic collision (like a marble hitting an identical marble)
Common moderators: water, heavy water (D₂O), graphite (NCERT); Preview adds beryllium oxide; light water is most common
Moderator | Absorbs neutrons? | Fuel it allows | Reactor
Heavy water (D₂O) | Very few - best neutron economy | Natural uranium | PHWR (CANDU)
Light water (H₂O) | Some | Enriched uranium needed | PWR, BWR
Graphite | Few | Natural/enriched | Magnox (UK), RBMK (USSR, Chernobyl type)
None | - | MOX (Pu + U) | Fast breeder
In PHWRs heavy water is both moderator and coolant
⚠ UPSC 2011 options were slow / speed up / cool down / stop: answer "slow down neutrons"; PMF prints a version with "(d) Both (a) and (c)" as answer - in a PHWR it also cools, but its principal role is moderation
⚠ Heavy water = D₂O (deuterium: 1 proton + 1 neutron); it is not radioactive, but neutron capture in it makes radioactive tritium
PYQ 2011: function of heavy water = slow down neutrons

t: Zirconium → why it is essential in reactors
text:
## 1. Fuel cladding
Zirconium alloys (Zircaloy) clad the fuel rods
Property | Why it matters
Very low neutron absorption (cross-section) | Does not "steal" neutrons from the chain reaction
High corrosion resistance | Survives hot water/steam for years
High melting point, strength | Holds fuel pellets safely
Listed as an associated (prescribed) material under the Atomic Energy Act 1962 with heavy water, nuclear-grade graphite, beryllium, lithium-6
⚠ In severe overheating, zirconium reacts with steam → hydrogen gas → explosion risk (Fukushima-type)
⚠ Zirconium is not radioactive (UPSC 2001 asked which is not radioactive: zirconium, not astatine/francium/tritium)
## Beyond your notes
Hafnium (always found with zirconium) absorbs neutrons strongly, so it is removed from cladding-grade zirconium and used in control rods
PYQ 1998: element essential for building reactors = zirconium; distractors cobalt, nickel, tungsten

## 1. Comparison
Reactor | Fuel | Moderator / coolant | Loops | India example
PWR | LEU 3-5% | Light water / light water (~150 atm) | Two | Kudankulam (Russian VVER)
BWR | LEU 3-5% | Light water; boils in core | One (steam to turbine) | Tarapur units 1-2 (US)

t: Three stages → reactor, fuel, output
text:
## 1. Bhabha's plan (presented 1954, adopted 1958)
Stage | Reactor | Fuel | Moderator / coolant | Output
I | PHWR | Natural uranium | Heavy water / heavy water | Power + Pu-239 in spent fuel
II | Fast Breeder | MOX: Pu-239 + U-238 | None / liquid sodium | Power + more Pu-239; U-233 from Th-232 blanket
III | Thorium reactors (AHWR) | Th-232 + U-233 | Heavy water / boiling light water | Power + U-233 (self-sustaining)
Logic: India has ~1-2% of world uranium but ~25% of world thorium (monazite sands of Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Odisha)
Thorium is fertile, not fissile: needs U-233 bred in Stage II first
⚠ Stage II uses fast neutrons (no moderator); Stages I and III use slow neutrons
⚠ India follows a closed fuel cycle: spent fuel reprocessed (Trombay, Tarapur, Kalpakkam) to recover Pu and U

t: Nuclear fusion → conditions and fuel
text:
## 1. Fusion
Two light nuclei (usually deuterium + tritium) fuse into helium-4 + a fast neutron; lost mass becomes energy; D-T releases 17.6 MeV
Powers the Sun and stars (Sun's core ~15 million K)
Condition | Why
10⁷-10⁸ K (over 100 million °C in reactors) | Overcome Coulomb repulsion; matter becomes plasma
High density/pressure | More collisions
Confinement time (Lawson criterion) | Density × time must exceed a minimum
Confinement method | Magnetic (tokamak) or inertial (lasers)
Fuel: deuterium from seawater; tritium bred from lithium inside the reactor
Also called thermonuclear reactions (they need very high temperature)
⚠ Fusion cannot run away: if conditions fail the plasma cools and the reaction stops - no meltdown

t: Fusion vs fission → the comparison table
text:
## 1. Side by side
Point | Fission | Fusion
Nuclei | Heavy split | Light join
Fuel | U-235, Pu-239 | Deuterium, tritium
Chain reaction | Yes | No
Energy per unit mass | High | 3-4 times higher (PMF)
Waste | Long-lived radioactive | Only short-lived activation products
Status | Commercial since 1950s | Experimental; no net-gain power plant yet
Weapon | Atom bomb | Hydrogen bomb
Fusion's problems: plasma confinement, tritium scarcity (radioactive), neutron damage to walls, cost
⚠ "Fusion produces no radioactivity at all" is wrong: tritium is radioactive and neutrons activate wall materials

Soviet design of the 1950s (Igor Tamm, Andrei Sakharov); doughnut-shaped (toroidal) vacuum chamber

Approach | Method | Example

## 1. Spontaneous decay of unstable nuclei
Ray | Nature | Stopped by
Alpha (α) | Helium nucleus | Paper, skin, few cm of air
Beta (β) | Fast electron | Thin aluminium sheet
Gamma (γ) | High-energy photons | Thick lead or concrete
Discovered by Henri Becquerel (1896); Curies found radium and polonium; all three shared Physics Nobel 1903
Half-life = time for half the atoms to decay (T½ = 0.693/λ); decay rate unaffected by temperature, pressure or chemical state

Electrochemical device: converts chemical energy of hydrogen directly into electricity, with water + heat as the only by-products

t: Fuel cell → working and components
text:
## 1. Steps of a hydrogen fuel cell
Part | Role
Anode (negative) | H2 supplied; splits into protons (H+) and electrons; oxidation
Electrolyte / membrane | Lets only protons pass; blocks electrons
External circuit | Electrons flow anode → cathode = electric current
Cathode (positive) | O2 (air) + protons + electrons → water
Catalyst | Usually platinum: speeds reactions at both electrodes (main cost)
Bipolar plates, gas diffusion layer | Connect cells in a stack, spread gases, remove water
Fuel cell stack: many cells joined to raise voltage and power
Efficiency ~60%, higher than thermal plants (no combustion loss)
## 2. Pros and cons
Pros: zero carbon (if H2 green), quiet (no moving parts), fast refuelling, low maintenance
Cons: platinum cost, H2 storage (high pressure/cryogenic), few refuelling stations, flammability, durability
⚠ Fuel cell = generator (needs continuous fuel); battery = store (needs recharging)

text:
Energy source (exists naturally) | Energy carrier (made using other energy)
Solar, wind, coal, hydropower | Electricity, hydrogen, batteries
Free H2 is rare on Earth; it is locked in water and hydrocarbons
Getting it needs energy: electrolysis (electricity) or steam methane reforming (natural gas)
Value: stores surplus renewable power for seasonal use (batteries are short-duration)
Hard-to-abate users: steel (replaces coke, DRI route), fertiliser (ammonia), refineries (desulphurisation), heavy transport, shipping
⚠ Ammonia carries 17.6% hydrogen by weight: a leading carrier for shipping hydrogen

text:
## 1. The 2025 question
Element | Where in a Li-ion cell | Cathode?
Lithium | Core of the cathode (lithium metal oxide) | Yes
Cobalt | LCO, NMC, NCA cathodes | Yes
Nickel | NMC, NCA (high-energy) cathodes | Yes

⚠ Answer: only three; graphite is the most common anode, never the cathode
⚠ Lithium is also in the electrolyte (lithium salt), but UPSC counted it as a cathode element
## 2. Likely-next elements

topic: EV batteries, cells and battery chemistry
t: Lithium-ion cell → components and ion movement
text:
Component | Material
Anode (negative) | Graphite (carbon) on copper foil
Cathode (positive) | Lithium metal oxide (LiCoO2, LiFePO4, NMC) on aluminium foil
Electrolyte | Lithium salt (LiPF6) in an organic solvent (flammable)
Separator | Permeable membrane: passes Li+, prevents short circuit
Battery management system | Temperature sensor, voltage regulator, state-of-charge monitor
Charging: Li+ moves cathode → anode; discharging: anode → cathode (current produced)
First prototype 1985, Akira Yoshino
Pros: high energy density, ~90-95% efficiency, light, low self-discharge
Cons: cost (Li, Co), thermal runaway, recycling, no fast charge at 0 °C, degrades in heat
⚠ Discharge = ions go to the cathode; a statement reversing charge/discharge direction is the classic trap

Nobel Chemistry 2019: John Goodenough, Stanley Whittingham, Akira Yoshino (Li-ion battery)

t: Dry cell (Leclanche) → electrolyte and parts
text:
## 1. The 2009 question
Option | Correct?
Ammonium chloride + zinc chloride | Yes
Sodium chloride + calcium chloride | No
Magnesium chloride + zinc chloride | No
Ammonium chloride + calcium chloride | No
## 2. Parts
Zinc container = anode (negative); carbon (graphite) rod = cathode (positive)
Manganese dioxide (MnO2) around the carbon rod: depolariser (reduces polarisation)
Electrolyte is a moist paste of NH4Cl (sal ammoniac) + ZnCl2, not a liquid: works in any orientation
Primary cell: reaction not reversible, so it cannot be recharged; converts chemical → electrical energy
⚠ Each wrong option keeps one right salt (NH4Cl or ZnCl2) and adds a wrong partner; learn the pair
## Beyond your notes
Leclanche dry cell gives about 1.5 V; the alkaline cell swaps NH4Cl for potassium hydroxide
Primary cells: dry, alkaline, button (mercury, silver oxide); secondary (rechargeable): lead-acid, NiCd, NiMH, Li-ion

Need | What storage does
Intermittency of solar/wind | Time-shifts energy
Grid stability | Holds frequency and voltage
Peak demand | Charges off-peak, discharges at peak
EV mobility; off-grid access | Batteries
Storage families and examples:
Family | Examples
Electrochemical | Li-ion, Na-ion, solid-state, flow batteries

text:
Technology | Working | Efficiency / life
Pumped hydro (PHS) | Pump water uphill off-peak, release through turbines at peak | 70-80%, 40-60 years; most widely used large storage

t: Biodiesel → making, properties, pros and cons
text:
Made by transesterification of vegetable oil, animal fat or used cooking oil with methanol/ethanol
Chemically Fatty Acid Methyl Esters (FAMEs); used pure (B100) or blended (B5, B10, B20)
Property | Biodiesel vs fossil diesel
Calorific value | 37-40 MJ/kg vs 42-46: ~10-12% less energy
Cetane number | 46-65: higher, better ignition
Flash point | ~130 °C vs ~60 °C: safer
Oxygen | 10-12%: fuller combustion
Sulphur | Negligible: near-zero SO2
Viscosity | Higher: better lubricity
NOx | Slightly higher
Cons: cold-flow problems, hygroscopic, oxidises in storage
⚠ Biodiesel cuts CO, SO2, PM, hydrocarbons but can raise NOx

topic: Coal gasification, syngas and gaseous fuels
t: Coal gasification → which products it can make
text:
## 1. Process
Thermochemical (~700 °C+): coal + oxygen + steam (partial oxidation) → syngas = CO + H2 (+ CO2, CH4, water vapour)
C + H2O → CO + H2; then water-gas shift: CO + H2O → CO2 + H2
## 2. Product check (UPSC 2025)
Substance | From coal syngas? | Route
Urea | Yes | H2 → ammonia (Haber-Bosch) + CO2 from the same plant → urea
Ethanol | Yes | Syngas via Fischer-Tropsch / catalytic conversion
Nitroglycerine | No | Glycerol (from fats/oils) + nitric acid
Methanol, DME | Yes | Syngas over catalysts
Synthetic natural gas | Yes | Methanation (CO + H2 → CH4 + H2O)
Hydrogen, electricity | Yes | Shift reaction; gas turbines
⚠ Answer (official key): only two; PMF S&T book p.859 marks "all three" (nitroglycerine via intermediates); PMF Environment and the key say two: follow two
Nitroglycerine also: a vasodilator for angina (chest pain)

topic: Coal gasification, syngas and gaseous fuels

Feature | Gasification | Liquefaction
Product | Syngas (CO + H2) | Liquid hydrocarbons (synthetic crude)
End products | H2, ammonia, methanol, SNG, power | Petrol, diesel, kerosene, waxes, lubricants
Cuts imports of | Natural gas (and fertiliser) | Crude oil
Emissions | Lower; can add CCS | Higher CO2
Types of gasifiers: fixed bed, fluidised bed, entrained flow
Biomass gasification: partial oxidation of coconut shells, groundnut shells, rice husk → producer gas (CO, H2, CH4, CO2, N2)
Pyrolysis (no oxygen) → biochar (solid), bio-oil (liquid), syngas
Gas | Composition
Water gas | CO + H2
Producer gas | CO + H2 + N2

t: Methanol and DME → coal and gas-based fuels
text:
Methanol (CH3OH): from natural gas, coal, biomass, or CO2 + green H2 (e-methanol) via syngas
Pros: high octane, liquid at room temperature, very low PM, negligible SOx; cons: toxic, corrosive, lower energy per litre
Initiative | Fact
Methanol Economy | NITI Aayog; M15 (15% methanol in petrol) notified
Projected gain | 20% DME in LPG → ~₹6,000 crore saved/year
E-methanol | World's first commercial plant at Kasso, Denmark
Research | DST's Methanol Economy Research Programme
DME (dimethyl ether): made from methanol/syngas; LPG-like cooking fuel India can make entirely at home
## In news 2025-26
India's first port-based green methanol plant (May 2026); SC struck down Maharashtra's methanol denaturing rules (Sep 2026)
⚠ Methanol (wood alcohol) is far more toxic than ethanol

topic: Genetic engineering basics: rDNA, PCR and lab feats
t: Genetic engineering tools → what each does
text:
## 1. The toolkit
Tool | Nickname | Job
Restriction enzymes (restriction endonucleases) | DNA scissors | Cut DNA at specific sequences ("sticky" or "blunt" ends)
DNA ligase | DNA glue | Joins gene and vector → recombinant DNA
Vectors (plasmids, viruses) | DNA carriers | Carry the gene into the host and replicate
PCR | DNA copier | Makes millions of copies of a DNA piece
Marker genes (antibiotic resistance, reporter) | Selectors | Pick out transformed cells
## 2. Two principles of modern biotech
Genetic engineering (changing DNA) + bioprocess engineering (large-scale production in bioreactors, sterile, downstream processing)
⚠ In older biotech the restriction enzyme is the "molecular scissors"; in genome editing the term is used for Cas9: read the context

topic: Genetic engineering basics: rDNA, PCR and lab feats
t: Recombinant DNA technology → steps and products
text:
## 1. Steps
Step | What happens
1. Isolation | Donor DNA and vector DNA extracted
2. Cutting | Restriction enzymes cut both
3. Insertion | Gene put into vector (usually plasmid)
4. Ligation | DNA ligase seals → rDNA
5. Transformation | rDNA enters host (often bacterium) → GMO
6. Selection | Antibiotic-resistance markers / reporter genes
7. Expression | Host makes the protein (e.g. insulin), purified
## 2. Products and uses
Therapeutic proteins: insulin, growth hormone, clotting factor VIII (haemophilia), erythropoietin
Monoclonal antibodies, vaccines, gene therapy, bioremediation, de-extinction research
Concerns: ecological risk, allergy, patenting and biopiracy, unknown long-term effects
rDNA is precise, faster, controlled compared with conventional breeding

topic: Genetic engineering basics: rDNA, PCR and lab feats
t: Recombinant DNA → which gene transfers are possible
text:
## 1. All three are possible
Transfer | Example
Across plant species | Pest-resistance genes moved between plants
Animal → plant | Animal genes put into plants for specific proteins
Microbe → higher organism | Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) gene into cotton, brinjal
Human → bacterium | Human insulin gene in E. coli
## 2. Why
rDNA isolates a gene from one organism and inserts it into another even across species or kingdoms
The genetic code is universal, so the host can read the foreign gene
⚠ "Only within plants" is wrong: rDNA crosses kingdoms
PYQ 2013: across plant species, animals to plants, microbes to higher organisms: all three (1, 2 and 3)

topic: Genetic engineering basics: rDNA, PCR and lab feats
t: Lab feats → what science can and cannot do yet
text:
## 1. UPSC 2019 statements
Claim | Status
Artificial functional DNA made in labs | Possible (gene synthesis)
DNA from an animal cell replicated outside a living cell | Possible (PCR)
Cells from plants/animals divide in petri dishes | Possible (cell/tissue culture)
Functional chromosomes by joining DNA segments of different species | Not possible (per key)
## 2. Synthetic biology (likely next)
Gene synthesis, DNA assembly, metabolic engineering, synthetic genomes
Synthetic cell: *Mycoplasma mycoides* with a lab-made genome; minimal cells
Yeast engineered to make artemisinin (anti-malarial); BioBricks = standard parts
India has no specific law for synthetic organisms beyond EPA-based biosafety rules
⚠ Gene transfer across species (GMOs) is routine; building a whole functional chromosome from mixed species is not
PYQ 2019: the "not correct" option was functional chromosomes from different species

topic: Genetic engineering basics: rDNA, PCR and lab feats
t: PCR → steps, types and uses
text:
## 1. Three steps (repeated cycles)
Step | Temperature | Event
Denaturation | 94-98°C | Double strand separates
Annealing | 50-65°C | Primers bind target
Extension | 72°C | Taq polymerase (heat-stable) builds new strands
## 2. Types
Type | Use
RT-PCR | RNA → DNA first; RNA viruses (HIV, SARS-CoV-2)
qPCR / real-time | Fluorescent dyes, measures as it goes (COVID tests)
Multiplex | Several targets at once
Nested | Two rounds, higher specificity
Digital PCR | Counts molecules; cancer mutations
Uses: infection diagnosis, sickle cell/thalassaemia detection, DNA fingerprinting, GM crop detection
Reverse transcriptase (Temin, Baltimore) showed RNA → DNA flow is possible
⚠ PCR copies DNA outside the cell: that is why the 2019 option "replicate outside a living cell" was correct

topic: Genetic engineering basics: rDNA, PCR and lab feats
t: Biotechnology colours → field of use
text:
## 1. Branches
Colour | Field | Examples
Green | Agriculture | GM crops, biofertilisers
Red | Medicine | Vaccines, gene therapy, mAbs
Blue | Marine | Algae biofuels, marine drugs
White | Industry | Enzymes, bioplastics
Grey | Environment | Bioremediation
Yellow | Food | Probiotics, fermented foods
Gold | Bioinformatics | Genome sequencing, drug design
## 2. Policy
BioE3 Policy (2024): Biotechnology for Economy, Environment, Employment; biomanufacturing, biofoundries
India's bioeconomy $10 bn (2014) → $165.7 bn (2024); target $300 bn by 2030
## In news 2025-26
India's first publicly funded DST-ICGEB Bio-Foundry (ICGEB: 1983 under UNIDO; HQ Trieste, centres New Delhi and Cape Town)
One year of BioE3: BioE3 Challenge for Youth and National Biofoundry Network; DBT-ISRO MoU for space biotech

topic: Genome editing: CRISPR, base and prime editing, RNAi
t: CRISPR-Cas9 → components and their roles
text:
## 1. Components
Part | Role
CRISPR (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats) | Bacterial DNA "memory" of past viruses
Cas9 (CRISPR-associated protein 9) | Molecular scissors: nuclease making a double-strand cut
Guide RNA (gRNA) | Navigator: leads Cas9 to the target by base pairing
## 2. Steps
Design gRNA → deliver (microinjection, electroporation, viral vectors) → target recognition → cut → cell repairs: switches gene off (errors) or inserts a new one (template)
Origin: natural defence of bacteria and archaea against viruses
Doudna and Charpentier (2012 demo) → Nobel Chemistry 2020
Better than ZFNs/TALENs: simpler, faster, cheaper, multiplex
⚠ Cas9 is not a biosensor, a pest-resistance gene or a herbicide
PYQ 2019: Cas9 = molecular scissors used in targeted gene editing

topic: Genome editing: CRISPR, base and prime editing, RNAi
t: CRISPR-Cas9 → uses and concerns
text:
## 1. Uses
Field | Example
Medicine | Sickle cell, cystic fibrosis, HIV/HPV DNA, CAR-T, disease models
Agriculture | Bacterial-blight-resistant rice; no foreign DNA → may escape GMO rules
Animals | Disease-resistant livestock; gene drive mosquitoes (malaria, dengue)
Conservation | De-extinction (dire wolf)
Diagnostics | FELUDA paper-strip COVID test
## 2. Concerns
Off-target cuts, immune reaction to bacterial Cas9, unpredictable repair, delivery difficulty
Designer babies with embryo editing; no clear Indian law yet
## Beyond your notes
He Jiankui (China, 2018): twins Lulu and Nana, first germline-edited babies (claimed): global condemnation (in Preview source)

topic: Genome editing: CRISPR, base and prime editing, RNAi
t: CRISPR vs base editing vs prime editing → mechanism
text:
## 1. Comparison
Feature | CRISPR-Cas9 | Base editing | Prime editing
Cut | Double-strand break | No DSB; deaminase converts one base | No DSB; Cas9 nickase + reverse transcriptase
Edits | Insertions, deletions, knockouts | Single base swaps (C→T, A→G) | Insertions, deletions, all 12 base swaps
Guide | gRNA | gRNA | pegRNA
Precision | Moderate | High | Very high
Off-target | Significant | Lower | Lowest
Limit | Unpredictable repair | No insertions/deletions | Complex, slower
## In news 2025-26
PERT (Prime-Editing-mediated Readthrough of premature stop codons): rewrites a human tRNA gene to read through nonsense mutations (~25% of disease mutations); worked in mice (Batten, Tay-Sachs, Niemann-Pick C1) via AAV9; enzyme PE6c
⚠ Base editing cannot insert or delete; prime editing can

topic: Genome editing: CRISPR, base and prime editing, RNAi
t: Other genome editors → features
text:
## 1. Tools
Tool | Feature
ZFNs, TALENs | Older protein-guided nucleases; costlier, slower
TnpB (transposon-associated) | Indian (ICAR-CRRI Cuttack); 400-500 amino acids vs Cas9 1,000-1,400 → fits viral vectors; patent-free
dCas9 | "Dead" Cas9: gene switch, turns genes on/off without cutting (heat-tolerant tomato, potato)
enFnCas9 | Indian engineered Cas9 (IGIB) used for sickle cell therapy
GlowCas9 | Fluorescent Cas9 to watch editing in live cells
Cas12a, GeoCas9, CasLambda | Other nucleases (IGI supplied to IARI, 2025)
## 2. Gene editing vs GM
GM: foreign gene from another species (transgenic) → strict GEAC route
Genome-edited (SDN-1/2, no foreign DNA): simpler route; IBSC certifies no foreign DNA (DBT guidelines 2022)
## In news 2025-26
India's first genome-edited rice: DRR Dhan 100 (Kamala) and Pusa DST Rice 1; CRISPR-edited mustard (Varuna)
India's first gene-edited sheep (Kashmir University + ICAR, CRISPR-Cas9)

topic: Genome editing: CRISPR, base and prime editing, RNAi
t: RNA interference → mechanism and uses
text:
## 1. Mechanism
Natural process: small RNAs block or destroy specific mRNA → protein not made → gene silenced
Virus brings double-stranded RNA → Dicer (Dicer-like enzymes in plants) chops it into siRNAs → siRNA guides destruction of matching RNA
## 2. Uses (UPSC 2019)
Claim | Correct?
Gene-silencing therapies | Yes
Cancer therapy (silence oncogenes) | Yes
Virus-resistant crops (e.g. papaya) | Yes
Hormone replacement therapy | No: RNAi only suppresses genes, does not supply hormones
Also explored for HIV, hepatitis, Huntington's disease
## In news 2025-26
RNA-based antiviral protects plants against Cucumber Mosaic Virus (aphid-spread, 1,200+ hosts; 25-30% banana losses)
## Beyond your notes
RNAi discovered by Andrew Fire and Craig Mello (Nobel Medicine 2006)
PYQ 2019: answer 1, 2 and 4; trap = hormone replacement

topic: Genome editing: CRISPR, base and prime editing, RNAi
t: RNA editing vs DNA editing → permanence and risk
text:
## 1. Comparison
Basis | RNA editing | DNA editing
Permanence | Temporary; effect fades | Permanent change to genome
Enzyme | ADAR (already in human body) + guide RNA | Bacterial proteins (Cas9)
Immune risk | Lower | Can trigger immune reaction
Error risk | Reversible | Irreversible errors possible
## 2. Related terms
Epigenetic marks: chemical changes regulating genes without altering DNA sequence; reversible
Genomic imprinting: only one parent's allele expressed (DNA methylation)
mRNA = messenger RNA: carries code to ribosomes; basis of mRNA vaccines (GEMCOVAC-19, India's first)
⚠ RNA editing fixes the message, not the gene: it is not inherited

topic: Genome editing: CRISPR, base and prime editing, RNAi
t: Somatic vs germline editing → who inherits the change
text:
## 1. Comparison
Feature | Somatic | Germline
Cells | Body cells: skin, liver, blood | Eggs, sperm, their precursor cells, early embryos
Spread | Only treated tissue | Every cell of the organism
Heritable? | No | Yes: passes to future generations
Status | Most used, ethically accepted (e.g. sickle cell) | Generally prohibited in humans
## 2. UPSC 2020 statements (all possible)
Editing cells that produce eggs or sperm of a prospective parent: possible
Editing a genome before birth at the early embryo stage: possible
Injecting human iPS cells into a pig embryo (human-animal chimera): possible; aim: human-compatible organs
⚠ "Possible" is not "permitted": technically feasible, ethically restricted
PYQ 2020: 1, 2 and 3

topic: Genome editing: CRISPR, base and prime editing, RNAi
t: Gene editing therapies in news → disease and delivery
text:
## 1. Cases
Therapy | Fact
First personalised CRISPR therapy (US, 2025) | Infant with CPS-1 deficiency (urea cycle, toxic ammonia); delivered in vivo to liver by lipid nanoparticles
Casgevy | CRISPR therapy for thalassaemia/sickle cell; FDA approval 2023
BIRSA-101 | India's first indigenous CRISPR therapy for sickle cell disease; CSIR-IGIB; named after Birsa Munda
Gene-edited banana | Stays yellow 12 h after peeling: PPO gene disabled (like Arctic apple, 2017)
## 2. India context
National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission (2023-2047); SCD is among 21 disabilities (RPwD Act 2016)
Sickle cell = HBB gene defect; RBCs become crescent-shaped
⚠ CPS-1 therapy was in vivo; earlier CRISPR treatments edited stem cells outside the body

topic: Gene therapy, genetic medicines and CAR-T
t: Genetic medicines → what they do and how they are delivered
text:
## 1. UPSC 2026 statements
Claim | Correct?
Correct or compensate faulty genes behind disease | Yes
Carried by engineered viruses and lipid nanoparticles | Yes
Alter the entire DNA sequence | No: target a specific gene, segment or RNA pathway
## 2. How genetic medicines act
Replace a defective gene, repair it, silence a harmful gene (siRNA, RNAi), or supply missing function
Formats: gene therapy (DNA), mRNA drugs, siRNA, CRISPR editors, AAV vectors
Aim: treat root cause, not symptoms (precision biotherapeutics, BioE3)
⚠ Nothing in medicine rewrites the whole genome; edits are targeted
PYQ 2026: answer 1 and 2 only

topic: Gene therapy, genetic medicines and CAR-T
t: Gene therapy → methods and vectors
text:
## 1. Methods
Method | What it does
Gene replacement | Adds a working copy of a defective gene
Gene inactivation | Silences a harmful/overactive gene
Gene editing | Corrects the gene (CRISPR-Cas9)
## 2. Delivery vectors
Type | Examples
Viral (disease genes removed) | Adenovirus, retrovirus, lentivirus, AAV
Non-viral | Liposomes, nanoparticles (LNPs), naked DNA injection, electroporation
## 3. Uses
Genetic disorders (sickle cell, cystic fibrosis, haemophilia), cancers (CAR-T), viral diseases, spinal muscular atrophy, inherited blindness (Leber congenital amaurosis)
India: National Guidelines for Gene Therapy Product Development and Clinical Trials (2019)
⚠ Somatic gene therapy is accepted; germline therapy is generally prohibited in humans

topic: Gene therapy, genetic medicines and CAR-T
t: CAR-T cell therapy → steps and India's NexCAR19
text:
## 1. Steps
Step | Detail
1. Collect | T-cells drawn (leukapheresis)
2. Engineer | CAR gene added by lentivirus/retrovirus or CRISPR
3. Expand | Grown to millions-billions in lab
4. Infuse | Back into patient
5. Kill | Bind antigen (e.g. CD19 on B-cells) and destroy cancer
## 2. Facts
Best for blood (B-cell) cancers; weak against solid tumours
Side effects: Cytokine Release Syndrome, neurotoxicity
NexCAR19: India's first indigenous CAR-T; ImmunoACT (IIT Bombay) + Tata Memorial; CD19 target; CDSCO-approved; ~Rs 30-40 lakh vs Rs 3-4 crore abroad
⚠ CAR-T uses the patient's own T-cells (autologous): low rejection

topic: Gene therapy, genetic medicines and CAR-T
t: In vivo CAR-T → how it differs
text:
## 1. Comparison
Feature | Traditional CAR-T | In vivo CAR-T
Where T-cells are changed | Ex vivo (lab) | Inside the body
Genetic tool | Viral vector (permanent) | mRNA in CD8-targeted LNPs (transient)
Chemotherapy before | Yes (lymphodepletion) | No
Manufacturing | Custom per patient | Standard, scalable
Scope | B-cell cancers | Cancers and autoimmune diseases
## 2. Terms
LNP: tiny fat particle carrying genes/mRNA; CD8: marker on cytotoxic T-cells
Ex vivo = outside the body; in vivo = inside the body
⚠ In vivo CAR-T uses no viral vector and makes no permanent gene change

topic: Gene therapy, genetic medicines and CAR-T
t: Advanced therapies in news → regulation and cases
text:
## 1. Advanced Therapeutic Products (ATPs)
Type | Examples
Gene therapies | CRISPR therapies for haemophilia, sickle cell
Cell-derived products | Stem-cell regenerative therapies, CAR-T
Xenografts | Pig heart valves
Drugs Rules 1945 amended: ATPs under Central Licence Approving Authority; CDSCO approves trials/marketing; DBT oversees genetic manipulation
## 2. Haemophilia
Haemophilia A = lack of Factor VIII (X-linked recessive; F8 gene); Haemophilia B = F9
Indian scientists reported success with gene therapy for severe haemophilia A (one-time; body makes its own factor)
US-approved Roctavian uses adenovirus vector and needs corticosteroids
## Beyond your notes
Casgevy was first approved by the UK (Nov 2023), then the US FDA (Dec 2023) (verify)

topic: Mitochondrial replacement, cloning and stem cells
t: Mitochondrial disease → how it is inherited
text:
## 1. Two kinds
Faulty genes in | Inherited from
Nuclear DNA (codes some mitochondrial parts) | Both parents
Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) | Mother only (egg cytoplasm carries mitochondria)
## 2. Facts
Mitochondria = "powerhouse" of the cell; own circular DNA, many copies per cell
Effects: muscular dystrophy, heart, liver, brain disorders; no cure, only symptom care
mtDNA is used to trace maternal lineage and identify old remains
⚠ Some individuals inherited mtDNA from both parents (2018 paper): Preview marks the 2021 statement "entirely from mother" false; the official key says both statements correct
PYQ 2021: MRT before or after IVF prevents transmission; mitochondrial disease from mother: key both 1 and 2

topic: Mitochondrial replacement, cloning and stem cells
t: Mitochondrial replacement therapy → techniques
text:
## 1. MRT / Mitochondrial Donation Treatment
IVF-based "three-parent baby" method: nuclear DNA of mother + father, healthy mitochondria from a donor
Baby has ~99.8% DNA from parents, 0.1-0.2% donor mtDNA
## 2. Techniques
Technique | When | What moves
Maternal Spindle Transfer (MST) | Before fertilisation | Mother's spindle (chromosomes) into enucleated donor egg, then fertilised
Pronuclear Transfer (PNT) | After fertilisation | Pronuclei of both parents from the zygote into enucleated donor zygote
Polar Body Transfer (PBT) | Newest | Polar body genome
## 3. Law
UK first to regulate and approve MRT (2015); Australia (2021)
## In news 2025-26
Eight babies born in the UK using MDT to avoid mitochondrial disease
⚠ MRT cannot cure existing disease or stop disease from nuclear DNA mutations
PYQ 2020: pronuclear transfer → prevention of mitochondrial diseases in offspring

topic: Mitochondrial replacement, cloning and stem cells
t: Somatic cell nuclear transfer → steps and cloning types
text:
## 1. SCNT steps
Take a somatic (body) cell → remove nucleus of a donor egg (enucleation) → insert somatic nucleus → activate (electric/chemical) → blastocyst
## 2. Cloning types
Type | Method | Use
Gene (molecular) cloning | Gene in plasmid copied in E. coli | Insulin, vaccines
Cellular cloning | One cell cultured in vitro | Drug testing, mAbs
Reproductive cloning | SCNT + embryo into surrogate | Dolly, livestock
Therapeutic cloning | SCNT, embryo not implanted; stem cells harvested | Regenerative medicine
Concerns: low success, health defects, genetic uniformity, ethics
⚠ SCNT is for cloning, not biolarvicides, bioplastics or disease-free organisms
PYQ 2017: SCNT → reproductive cloning of animals

topic: Mitochondrial replacement, cloning and stem cells
t: Cloning milestones → animal, place, method
text:
## 1. Firsts
Clone | Fact
Dolly (sheep, 1996) | First mammal cloned from an adult somatic cell; SCNT; Roslin Institute, Scotland; udder cell; 434 attempts; died 2003
Zhong Zhong, Hua Hua (2017) | First primates cloned by SCNT (macaques, China)
Samrupa (2009) | First cloned buffalo calf, NDRI Karnal; lived 6 days
Garima (2009) | Female cloned buffalo
Deepasha (2014) | Cloned wild buffalo of Chhattisgarh
Ganga (2023) | India's first cloned Gir cow calf, NDRI
Inzaj | First cloned camel, Dubai
## 2. De-extinction
Dire wolf (2025, Colossal Biosciences): ancient DNA + CRISPR-edited gray wolf cells + nuclear transfer; dog surrogates; pups Romulus, Remus, Khaleesi
Dire wolf (*Aenocyon dirus*) extinct ~12,500 years; shares 99.5% DNA with gray wolf
First "revived" species: bucardo (Pyrenean ibex)
⚠ Dolly was not made by IVF
PYQ 1999: A (first cloned mammal) true, R (made by IVF) false

topic: Mitochondrial replacement, cloning and stem cells
t: Stem cell types → potency and source
text:
## 1. Two properties
Self-renewal (divide to make more stem cells; can renew in vitro virtually forever) and differentiation
## 2. Types
Type | Source | Potency
Embryonic (ESC) | Blastocyst, 5-7 day embryo | Pluripotent
Adult (somatic) | Bone marrow, fat, skin | Multipotent
iPSC | Adult cells reprogrammed | Pluripotent
Perinatal | Umbilical cord blood, placenta | Multipotent
Totipotent (zygote) | Fertilised egg | Can form whole organism + placenta
Stem cells exist in plants, fish, amphibians too (zebrafish, frogs): not mammals only
## Beyond your notes
iPSCs: Shinya Yamanaka (2006); Nobel Medicine 2012 with John Gurdon
⚠ Embryos are not the only source; extracting ESCs destroys the blastocyst
PYQ 2002: correct = self-renew in vitro + Indian centres made cell lines (3 and 4)

topic: Mitochondrial replacement, cloning and stem cells
t: Stem cell therapy → uses, risks and rules
text:
## 1. Uses
Area | Use
Blood disorders | Bone marrow (haematopoietic) transplant: leukaemia, thalassaemia, sickle cell
Drug screening | Stem-cell-derived tissues test drugs and model disease
Research | Parkinson's, spinal injury, heart repair, type 1 diabetes, cornea/retina, cartilage (MSCs)
Skin | Cultured grafts for burns
## 2. Risks
Teratomas (pluripotent cells), immune rejection, ethics (embryo destruction), genetic instability, cost
## 3. Rules
National Guidelines for Stem Cell Research (2017): commercial stem cell therapy prohibited except bone marrow transplant; gene editing in stem cells only for in vitro research
## In news 2025-26
India's first Animal Stem Cell Biobank at NIAB (National Biopharma Mission, DBT)
PYQ 2012: drug screening + medical therapy (2 and 3); "mammals only" false

topic: Mitochondrial replacement, cloning and stem cells
t: Chimeras and xenotransplantation → what and why pigs
text:
## 1. Terms
Term | Meaning
Chimera | Organism with cells of two species (human iPSC in pig embryo)
Xenotransplantation | Cells/tissues/organs from animal to human
Organoid | Lab-grown mini-organ from stem cells
Organ-on-chip | Microchip with living cells mimicking an organ (drug testing)
## 2. Xenotransplant facts
Types: cell (pig islets, experimental), tissue (pig heart valves, common), whole organ (pig kidney/heart, experimental)
Why pigs: similar organ size, fast breeding, gene-editable, lower zoonotic risk than primates
Risks: hyperacute rejection (human antibodies against a pig sugar moiety), porcine endogenous retroviruses, lifelong immunosuppression
## In news 2025-26
First recipient of a gene-edited pig kidney died about two months after surgery
⚠ Xenotransplantation is still experimental, except tissue grafts like heart valves

topic: DNA fingerprinting, omics and genome projects
t: DNA fingerprinting → basis and what it proves
text:
## 1. Basis
Uses DNA polymorphisms: individual-specific variations
Based on Short Tandem Repeats (STRs): 2-6 bp repeats; repeat number varies; unique to each person except identical twins; also VNTRs and SNPs
## 2. Steps
Step | Detail
Extraction | From blood, saliva, semen, hair (with root), bone, skin
PCR | Amplifies tiny traces
Electrophoresis | Separates fragments → band profile
## 3. Uses
Paternity, criminal identity (rape, assault), disaster victims, transplant matching
Child gets half DNA from each parent, so profiles reveal parentage
⚠ Paternity is fixed by DNA fingerprinting, not protein analysis, chromosome counting or DNA quantity
PYQ 2000: A and R true, R explains A (trace hair, saliva, semen suffice); PYQ 1997: paternity → DNA fingerprinting

topic: DNA fingerprinting, omics and genome projects
t: DNA analysis methods → when each is used
text:
## 1. Methods
Method | Used when
STR analysis | Standard profiling
mtDNA analysis | Nuclear DNA degraded (old remains); matches maternal relatives
Y-STR analysis | Matches male relatives (paternal line)
SNP analysis | Single-base variation; compare with toothbrush/hairbrush DNA
Gel electrophoresis | DNA moves to positive pole; small fragments travel farther; ethidium bromide + UV
## 2. Law (DNA evidence)
SC, Devakar v. State of TN (2025): uniform DNA guidelines; sealed samples to FSL within 48 hours; chain-of-custody register
Art 20(3) does not cover DNA (not self-incrimination); BNSS Sec 53, 53A; BSA Sec 39 (expert opinion); Criminal Procedure (Identification) Act 2022
## Beyond your notes
DNA fingerprinting devised by Alec Jeffreys (UK, 1984); in India by Lalji Singh at CDFD Hyderabad / CCMB
DNA Technology (Use and Application) Regulation Bill 2019 was withdrawn in 2023 (verify)

topic: DNA fingerprinting, omics and genome projects
t: Omics terms → what each catalogues
text:
## 1. The "-omes"
Term | Full set of
Genome | All DNA (genes + non-coding) of an organism
Exome | Protein-coding exons (~1-2% of genome)
Transcriptome | All RNA transcripts, mainly mRNA, expressed at a given time
Proteome | All proteins
Metabolome | All small-molecule metabolites
Pangenome | Genomes of many individuals of a species (core + accessory genes)
Epigenome | Chemical marks on DNA/histones
## 2. Facts
Transcriptome shows which genes are active; differs between cells and times
Bioinformatics = computers + statistics on DNA, RNA, protein data
## In news 2025-26
First pangenome of Asian cultivated rice (China, 144 varieties)
⚠ Transcriptome is not genome-editing enzymes, mutation mechanism or the description of gene expression
PYQ 2016: transcriptome = full range of mRNA molecules expressed by an organism

topic: DNA fingerprinting, omics and genome projects
t: Gene mapping and genome sequencing → benefits
text:
## 1. Gene mapping (UPSC 2011)
Claim | Correct?
Know the pedigree of livestock | Yes
Develop disease-resistant animal breeds | Yes
Understand causes of all human diseases | No: environment and lifestyle also matter
## 2. Genome sequencing in agriculture (UPSC 2011, all correct)
Find markers for disease resistance and drought tolerance; cut breeding time (10-15 years normally); decode host-pathogen relationships
## 3. Medical uses
Diagnose genetic disorders; BRCA1/2 cancer risk; pharmacogenomics (right drug, right dose); carrier screening; pathogen surveillance; AMR genes
⚠ "All diseases" is the extreme-word trap
PYQ 2011: gene mapping → 1 and 3 only

topic: DNA fingerprinting, omics and genome projects
t: DNA sequencing → types and technologies
text:
## 1. Scope
Type | Covers
Whole Genome Sequencing (WGS) | Entire DNA, coding + non-coding
Whole Exome Sequencing (WES) | Only exons (~1-2%); cheaper
Targeted | Chosen gene panels
Mitochondrial | mtDNA; maternal ancestry
## 2. Technology generations
Generation | Example | Feature
First: Sanger (1977) | ddNTP chain termination | Accurate, slow, one fragment
Next-Gen (NGS) | Illumina, Roche 454, SOLiD | Millions of fragments in parallel; short reads
Third | Oxford Nanopore, PacBio | Single molecule, long reads, no amplification
Other diagnostics: DNA microarray (thousands of genes at once), FISH (fluorescent probes on chromosomes)
Digital Sequence Information (DSI): CBD COP16 (Cali, 2024) set up the Cali Fund

topic: DNA fingerprinting, omics and genome projects
t: Genome India Project → facts
text:
## 1. Basics
Item | Fact
Started | January 2020
Funding | Department of Biotechnology (DBT)
Aim | Catalogue genetic diversity of Indians; precision medicine, health planning
Target | Whole genomes of 10,000 healthy, unrelated Indians
Institutions | 20; sequencing at IISc, CCMB, IGIB, NIBMG, GBRC
## 2. Findings (Nature Genetics)
9,772 genomes analysed; 180 million variants; most in non-coding DNA
Covers Indo-European, Dravidian, Austro-Asiatic, Tibeto-Burman groups (tribal + non-tribal)
Endogamy → population-specific mutations; ancient Andamanese groups not included
⚠ Genome India is independent, not part of the Human Genome Project
PYQ 2026: DBT-funded + diversity catalogue correct (2 and 3 only)

topic: DNA fingerprinting, omics and genome projects
t: Human Genome Project and other genome missions → facts
text:
## 1. Human Genome Project
Item | Fact
Launched / completed | 1990 / 2003
Nature | Publicly funded international collaboration
Aim | Sequence human base pairs; map all genes

text:
## 1. Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt)
A soil bacterium that naturally makes Cry (crystal) proteins toxic to certain insect larvae
Toxin disrupts the gut of the feeding larva → death; harmless to other forms of life (humans, mammals)
Bt itself is used as a natural insecticide in organic farming
Bt strain targets | Insect order | Examples
Lepidoptera | Butterflies, moths, skippers | Bollworms, fruit and shoot borer
Diptera | Flies | Mosquito larvae
Coleoptera | Beetles | Beetle larvae
## 2. History
1901: Shigetane Ishiwatari (Japan) found it killing silkworms (Bacillus sotto)
1911: Ernst Berliner (Germany) isolated it from a flour moth and named it B. thuringiensis
⚠ The Bt gene comes from a bacterium: not a virus, insect, plant or fungus

t: Barnase, barstar, bar → what each gene does
text:
## 1. The three genes
Gene | Protein action | Role in DMH-11
Barnase | Ribonuclease (RNA-degrading) | Male sterility: no pollen; female parent line
Barstar | Binds and blocks barnase | Restores fertility in hybrid; male parent line
Bar | Herbicide resistance | Glufosinate tolerance; used as marker
## 2. Why needed
Mustard is self-pollinating (flowers have both sexes) → hybrids need one parent made male sterile
Conventional route: cytoplasmic male sterility (CMS) → found inadequate for large-scale hybrid seed
Hybrid seed = barnase line × barstar line → fertile, vigorous F1
⚠ Transgenic = carries external DNA; a hybrid carries only DNA of the two parents
⚠ Bar gene makes DMH-11 effectively herbicide tolerant: a key objection

t: Making a GM crop → steps and gene-delivery methods
text:
## 1. Steps
1. Identify and isolate the gene (e.g., Cry gene from Bt)
2. Cut with restriction enzymes; insert into a vector (plasmid); join with DNA ligase
3. Insert into plant cells
4. Select transformed cells (antibiotic/herbicide markers)
5. Regenerate whole plants by tissue culture
6. Lab/greenhouse → confined field trials → large-scale trials → approval
## 2. Delivery methods
Method | How | Mainly for
Agrobacterium tumefaciens | Soil bacterium transfers DNA | Dicots (soybean, tomato); now also rice, maize
Gene gun (biolistics) | Gold or tungsten particles coated with DNA | Monocots (corn, wheat, rice)
rDNA can move genes across plant species, animals → plants, microbes → higher organisms (PYQ 2013: all three)

t: Bioremediation → definition and in-situ techniques
text:
## 1. What it is
Use of living organisms (bacteria, fungi, algae, plants) to break down, neutralise or remove pollutants from soil, water or air
Microbes treat pollutants as food → CO₂, water, organic acids, safer metal forms
In-situ = treated at the site; ex-situ = material removed and treated elsewhere
## 2. In-situ techniques
Technique | What is done | Example
Bioventing | Air/nutrients into unsaturated soil (vadose zone) | Pseudomonas removing petroleum
Biosparging | Air injected below the water table (saturated zone) | Benzene/BTEX in aquifers
Biostimulation | Add nutrients (N, P) or electron acceptors (O₂, nitrate) to native microbes | Nitrate removal from groundwater
Bioaugmentation | Import specialised microbes | Dehalococcoides for TCE (chlorinated solvents)
Constructed wetlands | Plant-microbe beds filter sewage | Reed beds, Kerala
Anaerobic digestion | No oxygen → biogas (CH₄ + CO₂) + slurry | Community biogas plant
Bioelectrochemical | Microbial fuel cells treat wastewater + power | Geobacter MFCs
⚠ Bioventing = unsaturated soil; biosparging = saturated zone/groundwater
⚠ Biostimulation boosts native microbes; bioaugmentation adds new ones
⚠ PMF Environment calls bioventing "nutrients through wells"; PMF S&T says air + nutrients into vadose zone (follow S&T)

t: Bioremediation → ex-situ techniques and metal recovery
text:
## 1. Soil treatment off-site
Technique | Key process | Example
Landfarming | Soil spread thin, periodically tilled | Oil-refinery sludge
Composting | Thermophilic microbes, aerobic | Indore municipal plants (Bacillus, Aspergillus)
Biopiling | Soil heaped into piles, aeration/moisture controlled | Diesel-contaminated soil
Vermicomposting | Earthworms + microbes → vermicast | Eisenia fetida (red wiggler)
Slurry-phase bioreactor | Soil + water in closed tank, fastest | Pesticide soil
## 2. Metal recovery and value addition
Bioleaching: acidophilic bacteria/archaea dissolve metals from ores, tailings, e-waste
Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans: Cu, Au, rare earths; Aspergillus niger, Penicillium: organic acids leach gold, silver, cobalt, nickel, copper
Bioplastic production, waste-to-energy (2G ethanol from rice straw, algae biodiesel, CBG)
Arsenic removal from soil: Bacillus flexus (arsenate) and Acinetobacter junii (arsenite)
⚠ Vermicomposting is less suited to heavy-metal-contaminated soil
## 3. Indore green-waste plant
India's first PPP green waste processing plant (Bicholi Hapsi, Indore), under SBM-Urban: dried, pulverised → eco-fuel, furniture composite, organic fertiliser, biodegradable plates

## 1. Plant-based (phytoremediation)
Type | What plants do | Example

Phytostabilisation | Immobilise metals in root zone | Vetiver grass on mine tailings

## 2. Fungus and microbe based
Mycoremediation: fungi secrete lignin peroxidase, manganese peroxidase, laccase → break hydrocarbons, dyes, pesticides

Strengths | Limits

## 1. How it works (PYQ 2022)
Mineral accretion / electro-accumulation of minerals on steel structures on the seabed

t: Wolbachia → how it curbs mosquito-borne viruses
text:
## 1. The bacterium
Naturally occurring intracellular Gram-negative bacterium; harmless to humans and animals
Found in 40-60% of insect species (PMF)
Does not naturally infect Aedes aegypti (dengue vector) or Anopheles (malaria vector)
## 2. Two mechanisms
Mechanism | What happens
Cytoplasmic incompatibility | Infected males × uninfected/incompatible females → eggs fail to hatch
Pathogen blocking | Reduces viral replication inside mosquitoes (dengue, Zika, chikungunya)
## 3. Two strategies
Strategy | Release | Result
Population suppression | Males only | Mosquito numbers fall
Population replacement | Males + females | Wild population replaced by low-transmission one
⚠ Prevalence: PMF says 40-60%; Preview says 50-60%; PYQ key says 50% of insects (follow PMF)
⚠ No genetic modification and no pesticides: Wolbachia mosquitoes are not GMOs
PYQ 2023: Wolbachia = controlling viral diseases spread by mosquitoes; traps: biochar, bioplastics, crop residues

t: Mosquito-control methods → mechanism compared
text:
Method | How it works | GM?
Wolbachia | Bacterium: incompatibility + virus blocking | No
Oxitec 'friendly' mosquito | GM male Aedes aegypti with self-limiting gene: offspring die before adulthood | Yes
Gene drive | CRISPR biases inheritance to >90% (vs normal 50%) | Yes
Sterile Insect Technique | Males sterilised by radiation, mass-released | No
## 1. Gene drive details
Approaches: population suppression (disrupt fertility genes) and population modification (block parasite, mosquito survives)
Anopheles gambiae trials: ~94% inheritance, big fall in malaria parasite survival
## 2. Watch-outs
⚠ Oxitec Brazil releases (2013-2015): some offspring survived and passed genes into wild populations (PMF concern)
⚠ Male mosquitoes do not bite → cannot transmit malaria; hence only males are released
⚠ SIT eradicated the screwworm fly in the USA (1966): females mate only once
Aedes → viral diseases (dengue, Zika, chikungunya, yellow fever); Anopheles → malaria; Culex → West Nile, Japanese encephalitis

text:
## 1. Definition (PYQ 2022)
Identifies a specimen using a short, standardised DNA segment; every species has its own barcode, like a fingerprint
Sequence is compared with a reference library
Statement in PYQ 2022 | Verdict
Assess the age of a plant or animal | Wrong
Distinguish species that look alike | Correct
Find undesirable plant/animal material in processed food | Correct

## 2. Uses
Cryptic species (genetically distinct, visually identical)
Food authenticity, adulteration, mislabelling
Identifying larval/juvenile stages, describing new species
Tracking illegal wildlife trade, monitoring endangered species
## 3. Steps
Choose region (varies between species, conserved within) → extract DNA → PCR → sequencing → compare with database

t: Optical fibre → works on total internal reflection
text:
## 1. Principle (1995)
Optical fibre works on total internal reflection (TIR), not refraction, scattering or interference
Each fibre = core + cladding; refractive index of core > cladding
Light enters at a suitable angle, strikes the core-cladding boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle, and is reflected again and again (zig-zag) to the far end
Works even when the fibre is bent: acts as a "light pipe"
Condition for TIR | Meaning
Denser to rarer medium | Light must travel from higher to lower refractive index
Angle > critical angle | Angle of incidence must exceed the critical angle
Made of high-purity silica glass/quartz or plastic; silica fibre transmits >95% of light over 1 km
⚠ Other TIR examples (NCERT): sparkle of diamond (critical angle ~24.4°), totally reflecting prisms (bend rays 90°/180°), mirage
PYQ 1995: one-word principle; it reappears in 2020s statements on fibre broadband and undersea cables

t: Optical fibre → why it is fast and reliable

Advantage | Reason
Very high bandwidth | Many wavelengths at once (Wavelength Division Multiplexing, WDM); NCERT: >100 GHz
Low attenuation | Tens of km without boosting; copper needs frequent amplification
Immune to EMI | Carries light, not electricity: no cross-talk
Secure | Does not radiate; tapping causes detectable interruption
Light, durable | Resists corrosion, moisture, lightning
Light in glass travels at about 2 lakh km/s (two-thirds of c); fibre uses laser or LED pulses, mostly in the infrared
NCERT: optical communication uses 1 THz to 1000 THz
## 2. Uses
Field | Use
Telecom | Backbone of broadband (FTTH), 4G/5G backhaul, international internet
Medicine | Endoscopes (view oesophagus, stomach, intestines)
Defence, industry | Sensors, secure military links
Data centres | Server-storage links
⚠ Fibre is not wireless: in "how many are wireless" lists it is the odd one out

Bluetooth 2.4 GHz, Wi-Fi 2.4 or 5 GHz | Correct (Wi-Fi 6E/7 also 6 GHz)
Bluetooth for WLAN only, Wi-Fi for WWAN only | Wrong: Bluetooth = PAN, Wi-Fi = WLAN
Bluetooth needs line of sight, Wi-Fi does not | Wrong: neither needs line of sight
(a) and (b) both correct | Wrong
Feature | Bluetooth | Wi-Fi
Standard | IEEE 802.15.1 | IEEE 802.11
Network | PAN (~10-100 m) | WLAN (~20-100 m)
Speed, power | Low-moderate speed, low power | Higher speed, more power
Use | Earphones, wearables, file transfer | Internet in home, office
Bluetooth developed 1994 by Jaap Haartsen (Ericsson)
⚠ Wi-Fi does not create internet: it only distributes an existing connection wirelessly

t: Visible Light Communication → the 2020 statements
text:
## 1. Answer 2020: statements 1, 3 and 4 correct
Statement (2020) | Verdict | Why
Uses wavelengths 375-780 nm | Correct | Visible band, between UV and IR
Long-range optical wireless | Wrong | Short-range: light cannot pass walls
Faster than Bluetooth | Correct | Visible spectrum offers far more bandwidth
No electromagnetic interference | Correct | Uses light, not radio
Data sent by modulating the intensity of a light source; received by a photodiode
Fluorescent lamps ~10 kbit/s; LEDs up to 500 Mbit/s (Preview); Li-Fi exceeds 1 Gbps

t: Li-Fi → how it works
text:
## 1. Working
Li-Fi (Light Fidelity): term by Harald Haas (2011, beyond notes); uses LED light to carry data
Step | What happens
Transmitter | LED flickers very fast (invisible to eye)
Encoding | Binary 1/0 by intensity changes (On-Off Keying)
Receiver | Photodiode converts light pulses to electrical signals
Processor | Decodes to text, audio, video
Uses visible light (400-800 THz); PMF also says visible, infrared and ultraviolet can be used
Works only while the light is ON, but can be dimmed without losing link
## 2. Answer 2016: both correct
Uses light as medium for high-speed transmission; is wireless and several times faster than Wi-Fi
PYQ 2016: both statements true; no trap

t: Li-Fi vs Wi-Fi → advantages and limits
text:
## 1. Comparison
Feature | Li-Fi | Wi-Fi
Medium | Light (LED) | Radio waves
Speed | Very high (>1 Gbps; up to 100 Gbps claimed) | Moderate to high
Range | Short, room-based | Wider
Walls | Cannot pass | Passes
Security | High (no snooping from outside) | Moderate
Interference | No RF interference: hospitals, aircraft | RF interference possible
Spectrum | Visible spectrum ~10,000 times broader than radio, unlicensed | Crowded ISM bands
## 2. Limits
Needs line of sight or reflected light; each room needs its own transmitter
Disturbed by sunlight/ambient light, obstacles, shadows
Early-stage commercial adoption
## 3. Uses
Hospitals, aircraft cabins, underwater communication, smart lighting, IoT, factories
## In news 2025-26
Oct 2025: Gujarat-based Nav Wireless Technologies deployed the United States' first commercial Li-Fi internet system in New York City (PMF LENS)

text:
## 1. Comparison (PMF)
Gen | Decade | Technology | Speed | Service
1G | 1980s | Analog (FM) | 2.4 kbps | Voice only, no encryption
2G | 1990s | Digital GSM/CDMA | GPRS 56-114 kbps, EDGE ~384 kbps | SMS, MMS, SIM cards
3G | 2000s | WCDMA, HSPA | ~2 Mbps (HSPA+ 40-60) | Mobile internet, video calls
4G | 2010s | LTE, all-IP | 10-100 Mbps (LTE-A >1 Gbps) | HD streaming, VoLTE, UPI
5G | 2020s | 5G NR (3GPP) | 1-10 Gbps | IoT, ultra-low latency
India skipped wide 1G; began with 2G GSM in 1995
4G latency 30-50 ms; 5G below 1 ms
Cellular idea: area split into cells, each with a base station; handover/handoff when moving; frequency reuse in distant cells (NCERT: MTSO)
Mobile phones use UHF (~800-950 MHz in NCERT)
