t: Blockchain → features UPSC tests
text:
## 1. What it is
A decentralised, distributed, immutable digital ledger; records transactions across many computers (nodes) without a central authority
Every node keeps a copy of the entire ledger; copies sync through consensus
Feature | What it means
Decentralisation | No single user/entity controls it; no single point of failure
Transparency | Shared ledger visible to participants; "everyone can inspect" (public chains)
Immutability | Once recorded and accepted, data cannot be altered or deleted (hash-linked)
Security | Cryptography: hashing + digital signatures
Permissionless innovation | Apps (dApps, smart contracts) can be built without anybody's permission (e.g., Ethereum)
Not crypto-only | Land records, supply chains, health records, voting, identity, IP
⚠ PYQ 2020 trap: "all the data in it are about cryptocurrency only" is wrong
PYQ 2026: four features; 1 (visible without risk of alteration), 2 (copies on many computers, syncing within seconds) and 4 (immutable once accepted) correct; 3 ("consortium = blend of public and private") wrong; answer 1, 2 and 4
PYQ 2020: 1 and 3 correct (public ledger no one controls; permissionless apps)

t: Blockchain → structure, types and consensus
text:
## 1. A block holds
Data, its own hash (digital fingerprint), previous block's hash, timestamp, nonce (PoW); first block = Genesis Block
Changing one block changes its hash and breaks all later blocks, so tampering is detectable
## 2. Types
Type | Who controls | Example
Public | Open to anyone | Bitcoin, Ethereum
Private | One organisation | Hyperledger; NPCI's Drunix
Consortium | Group of organisations jointly | Bank/industry consortia
Hybrid | Blend of public and private features, selective access | Enterprise chains
⚠ Sources differ: Oct 2025 CA lumps "Consortium/Hybrid" together; the UPSC 2026 key treats hybrid = public+private blend and consortium = joint control by many organisations. Go with the key
## 3. Consensus mechanisms
Mechanism | How
Proof of Work | Miners solve puzzles; secure but energy-intensive
Proof of Stake | Validators chosen by coins staked; energy-efficient
DPoS / PoA / PBFT | Elected delegates / pre-approved nodes / voting rounds
Consensus prevents double-spending
## Beyond your notes
Bitcoin: Satoshi Nakamoto (2008 paper, launched 2009), SHA-256, cap 21 million; Ethereum PoW → PoS, Sept 2022

t: Encryption → symmetric vs asymmetric, TLS, E2EE
text:
Point | Symmetric (secret key) | Asymmetric (public key)
Keys | One shared key encrypts and decrypts | Key pair: public + private, mathematically related
Examples | DES, AES | RSA, ECC
Strength | Fast, bulk data | Solves key distribution; enables digital signatures
Weakness | Key distribution problem | Slower
Hash function: fixed-length message digest; any change alters it (integrity, not secrecy)
Use | How
SSL/TLS (HTTPS) | Server's certificate checked against a CA; asymmetric for key exchange, then symmetric for speed; hash for integrity
E2EE | Encrypted on sender's device, decrypted only on receiver's; not even the platform reads it (WhatsApp, Signal)
⚠ TLS uses both symmetric and asymmetric; "only public-key" is wrong
⚠ Traceability rule (IT Rules 2021, first originator) is contested as breaking E2EE (WhatsApp LLC v. Union of India, pending)
Quantum answer | Basis
Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) | New maths algorithms resistant to quantum computers; runs on classical systems
Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) | Physics: photons; eavesdropping disturbs the state; no-cloning theorem
## In news 2025-26
IITM-C-DOT Samgnya (National Hub for Quantum Communication, IIT Madras Research Park, Dec 2025) signed an MoU with Q-Clairvoyance on post-quantum cybersecurity (Sept 2026) (Praveen CA 360 Sep 2026)
## Beyond your notes
US NIST finalised the first PQC standards in Aug 2024 (ML-KEM/Kyber, ML-DSA/Dilithium) (verify)

t: Digital signature vs Digital Signature Certificate
text:

What | Electronic method of signing an e-document | Electronic record issued by a Certifying Authority
Job | Proves who signed + content unchanged | Identifies the CA issuing it; holds subscriber details and public key
Use | Integrity, authentication, non-repudiation | Presented to prove identity online
Built on hash (message digest) + asymmetric keys: sign with private key, verify with public key; any change invalidates it
PYQ 2019: only 3 correct ("signing an e-document and ensuring content is unchanged"); answer 3 only
⚠ Statements 1 ("identifies the certifying authority") and 2 ("proof of identity to access a server") describe the DSC, not the signature
DSC classes: 1 basic (email); 2 tax e-filing; 3 highest (high-value transactions)
IT Act 2000: CA licensed under Sec 24; Sec 66C punishes fraudulent use of another's digital signature (LENS Aug 2026)
## In news 2025-26

## Beyond your notes

t: PKI → meaning, components, uses
text:

Component | Role
Public / private key | Public shared, private secret
Digital certificate | Binds a public key to an identity
Certificate Authority | Issues, signs, verifies certificates
Registration Authority | Verifies identity before CA issues
Revocation List | Invalid/compromised certificates
Functions: authentication, encryption, integrity, non-repudiation; uses: HTTPS, e-mail, banking, VPNs, Aadhaar, DigiLocker, GST

⚠ Quantum computers may break RSA/ECC: hence post-quantum cryptography (PQC)

topic: Quantum basics: qubits and core principles
t: Qubit → what it means
text:
## 1. Definition
Qubit = quantum bit, the fundamental unit of quantum information / quantum computation
A classical bit is 0 or 1; a qubit can be 0, 1, or both at once (superposition)
Measurement collapses the superposition into a definite 0 or 1
Feature | Bit | Qubit
States | 0 or 1 | 0, 1 or superposition
Link with others | Independent | Can be entangled
n units represent | One value at a time | 2ⁿ states simultaneously
Stability | Stable | Fragile (decoherence)
## 2. Where the word appears
Quantum computing, quantum communication (photonic qubits in QKD), quantum processors (QPU)
⚠ Not a term of cloud services, Li-Fi / visible light communication or ordinary wireless communication
PYQ 2022: "qubit" is mentioned in the context of quantum computing; distractors were cloud services, VLC and wireless
## Beyond your notes
A logical qubit is an error-corrected qubit built from many physical qubits (PMF: over 1,000 physical qubits per logical qubit)

topic: Quantum basics: qubits and core principles
t: Quantum principles → what each means and enables
text:
Principle | Meaning | Used in
Superposition | System exists in many states at once until measured | Parallel computation
Entanglement | Two particles share one quantum state; measuring one fixes the other, at any distance | QKD, teleportation, linked qubits
Interference | Probability amplitudes add or cancel | Amplifies correct answers
Tunnelling | Particle crosses an energy barrier it classically cannot | Tunnel diodes, STM, flash memory, fusion in stars
Decoherence | Qubit loses quantum state through heat, noise, radiation | The main problem: limits coherence time
No-cloning | An unknown quantum state cannot be copied | Eavesdropping-proof communication
Uncertainty | Position and momentum cannot both be known exactly | Limits of quantum sensing
Entanglement gives instant correlation, but no information travels faster than light
Entanglement first described by Einstein, Podolsky, Rosen (EPR paradox, 1935)
2022 Nobel Physics: Clauser, Aspect, Zeilinger for experiments with entangled photons
⚠ Fixes for decoherence: cryogenic cooling near absolute zero (~10 millikelvin), isolation, error correction, topological qubits

topic: Quantum basics: qubits and core principles
t: Qubit types → strength and limitation
text:
Qubit type | How | Strength | Limitation | Used for
Superconducting | Circuits (Josephson junctions) near absolute zero | Fast gates | Short coherence, extreme cooling | Computing (IBM, Google)
Trapped ion | Charged atoms held by EM fields, moved by lasers | Accurate, long coherence | Slow | Precision computation
Photonic | Photons: polarisation or phase | Travel at light speed, resist decoherence | Hard to store | Communication, QKD
Spin | Electron or nuclear spin up/down | Fits semiconductor tech, scalable | Sensitive to disturbance | Future chips, quantum dots
Topological | Information stored in shape-based properties (Majorana) | Resistant to errors | Research stage | Microsoft Majorana chips
NQM: computers on multiple platforms, chiefly superconducting and photonic
Likely next: which qubit suits communication (photonic) vs computing (superconducting)

topic: Quantum basics: qubits and core principles
t: Classical vs quantum computing → the differences
text:
Feature | Classical | Quantum
Unit | Bit | Qubit
Processing | Sequential | Parallel via superposition
Gates | AND, OR, NOT | Hadamard, CNOT (reversible)
Output | Deterministic | Probabilistic (needs repeated runs)
Error sensitivity | Stable | Highly sensitive
Best at | General tasks | Specific problems: simulation, optimisation, factoring
## 1. How a quantum computation runs
Initialise (qubits at 0) → superposition (gates) → gate sequence → interference → measurement
## 2. Uses
Drug discovery and molecular simulation, materials, optimisation (logistics, finance), AI, climate models
Can break RSA encryption (Shor's algorithm, 1994)
⚠ Quantum computers do not beat classical ones at all tasks; the advantage is domain-specific
⚠ PMF (P-MCA 2025): "fully operational quantum computers do not yet exist"

topic: Quantum basics: qubits and core principles
t: Quantum advantage and Q-Day → milestones in news
text:
Term | Meaning
Quantum advantage | Quantum computer does a useful task faster than any classical computer
Verifiable quantum advantage | Result can be independently checked, not just fast
Quantum Echoes | Google algorithm (2025) running operations forward and backward in time, based on OTOC (out-of-time-order correlator)
Q-Day | Day quantum computers can break public-key cryptography such as RSA-2048

topic: Quantum communication, sensing and Nobel links
t: Quantum Key Distribution → how it works
text:
## 1. Steps
Sender encodes bits in photon states (e.g. polarisation) → sends over optical fibre or free space (satellite) → receiver measures → both compare a sample → any eavesdropping disturbs the states and shows up as errors → clean key used for classical encryption (e.g. AES)
## 2. Basis of security
Classical cryptography | Quantum cryptography
Mathematical complexity | Laws of physics
Eavesdropping may go unnoticed | Always detectable
Data can be copied | No-cloning theorem
Vulnerable to quantum computers | Resistant
QKD distributes keys, not the message itself
Entangled photon pairs come from parametric down-conversion in a crystal
QBER (quantum bit error rate) = % of mismatched photon measurements
⚠ QKD is limited by signal loss and decoherence over distance → needs satellites or quantum repeaters
## In news 2025-26
China built the first 4,600 km space-to-ground quantum network (2021, Micius satellite)

t: CFL vs LED → how each makes light
text:
## 1. Working principle
CFL: current excites mercury vapour → UV radiation → phosphor coating turns it into visible light; a miniaturised fluorescent lamp
LED: current through a semiconductor; electrons recombine with holes and release light = electroluminescence
Feature | CFL | LED
Light source | Mercury vapour + phosphor | Semiconductor (p-n junction)
Efficiency | Moderate | Very high (less heat)
Lifespan | Longer than incandescent | Much longer (~3 times CFL)
Start | Warm-up of a few seconds | Instant
Toxic content | Mercury (disposal problem) | No mercury
Weakness | Sensitive to frequent switching | Higher initial cost; needs heat sink and good driver

t: Sodium lamp vs LED → street-lighting differences
text:

Gas-discharge lamp: current through ionised sodium vapour → yellow-orange light (high-pressure sodium, HPS, common on roads)
Omnidirectional (360°): at least half the light must be reflected and redirected → system inefficiency
Light is almost monochromatic (especially low-pressure sodium) → worst colour rendering; objects look shadowy black
Feature | Sodium lamp | LED
Direction | 360° | Directional (~180° or less)
Spectrum | Nearly monochromatic yellow | Broad; warm to cool white, high CRI
Lifespan | Shorter | 50,000-100,000 h, 2-3 times sodium
Warm-up | Longer | Instant
Light pollution | More (spill) | Less (aimed downward)
⚠ 2021 trap: "sodium lamps have longer life than LED" is false; statements 1 and 3 are true

text:
## 1. What a drone is
Drone = Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV): aircraft with no onboard human pilot
Flown remotely from the ground or autonomously (onboard AI + GPS)
UAV + ground station + data link = UAS (Unmanned Aircraft System)
## 2. Design decides capability
Design | Vertical take-off/landing | Hover | Typical use
Multirotor (quadcopter, hexacopter) | Yes | Yes | Spraying, photography, short-range ISR (e.g. Netra)
Single-rotor (helicopter type) | Yes | Yes | Heavier payloads
Fixed-wing | No: needs runway, catapult or net | No: must keep moving forward for lift | Long-range, long-endurance ISR (Heron, TAPAS)
Hybrid VTOL (fixed-wing + rotors) | Yes | Yes | Endurance + VTOL (e.g. ideaForge SWITCH)
⚠ Only VTOL types (rotary-wing, hybrid) land vertically; only rotary-wing types hover
⚠ DRDO Nishant was catapult-launched: a fixed-wing UAV cannot take off vertically

t: 3D printing → meaning and how it works
text:
## 1. Definition
3D printing = additive manufacturing: object built layer by layer from a digital CAD design
Opposite of subtractive manufacturing (cutting/milling material away) → minimal wastage
## 2. Four steps
Step | What happens
1 | 3D model made in CAD software
2 | Model sliced into thin layers by slicing software
3 | Printer deposits material layer by layer
4 | Layers fuse/solidify into the final object
⚠ Additive = adds material; "3D printing removes material from a block" is the swap trap
One of the physical technologies of the Fourth Industrial Revolution (with autonomous vehicles, advanced robotics)

t: AR vs VR → which keeps the real world
text:
## 1. Core difference
Feature | Augmented Reality (AR) | Virtual Reality (VR)
Real world | Stays visible; digital overlay added | Shut out; fully computer-generated
Immersion | Partial | Full, user transposed
Device | Smartphone/PC camera, tablet, AR glasses (HoloLens, Google Glass) | Headset + controllers + motion sensors (Oculus/Meta Quest, HTC Vive, Google Cardboard)
Examples | Pokémon GO, navigation arrows on roads, virtual try-on, furniture placement | Flight simulators, VR games, virtual tourism, combat training
Cost | Cheaper (works on phones) | Costly hardware
Health issue | Distraction, eye strain | Motion sickness, disorientation
⚠ "AR shuts out the physical world" and "VR projects images onto real objects" are swapped definitions: both false

topic: Missile basics: ballistic, cruise, propulsion and delivery concepts
t: Ballistic vs cruise missile → propulsion and flight path
text:
## 1. The core contrast
Feature | Ballistic missile | Cruise missile
Power | Rocket, powered and guided only in boost phase | Jet engine (turbofan, turbojet, ramjet, scramjet), powered throughout
Path | High parabolic arc, leaves atmosphere for long range | Low altitude (20-100 m), stays inside atmosphere
Speed | Usually hypersonic (Mach 5+) on re-entry | Subsonic, supersonic or hypersonic
Guidance | Inertial (jam-resistant) | GPS + INS + TERCOM, DSMAC; can re-target mid-flight
Payload | Large, MIRV possible | Smaller
Indian examples | Agni, Prithvi, K-series, Shaurya | BrahMos, Nirbhay
## 2. Phases of a ballistic missile
Boost (powered) → mid-course (coasts in space) → terminal (re-entry)
⚠ 2023 statement reversed the two: ballistic missiles are not jet-propelled subsonic; cruise missiles are not rocket-powered only at launch
PYQ 2023: answer "Neither 1 nor 2"; Agni-V is a ballistic missile, BrahMos a supersonic cruise missile

## 1. By nature of explosion

topic: Patents Act 1970: what cannot be patented
t: Patents Act → what is NOT an invention (Section 3)
text:
## 1. The rule
Section 2(j): invention = new product or process + inventive step + industrial application
Section 3 lists what is not an invention (based on TRIPS Art 27.3(b) for life forms)
Clause | Not patentable
3(b) | Contrary to public order or morality
3(c) | Mere discovery, scientific theory, natural substance
3(d) | New form of a known substance without enhanced efficacy
3(h) | Method of agriculture or horticulture
3(i) | Medical, surgical, curative, diagnostic treatment of humans or animals
3(j) | Plants and animals, seeds, varieties, species, essentially biological processes (micro-organisms excepted)
3(k) | Mathematical / business method, algorithm, computer programme per se
3(p) | Traditional knowledge
⚠ Micro-organisms ARE patentable: the only living things outside 3(j)
PYQ 2019: "a biological process to create a seed can be patented" is false; "plant varieties are not patentable" is true
## Beyond your notes
Clause numbers 3(b), 3(e) (mere admixture), 3(h), 3(i), 3(k), 3(p): standard text of Section 3

topic: Patents Act 1970: what cannot be patented
t: Plants, seeds and varieties → Patents Act or PPV&FR Act?
text:
## 1. Where each living thing is protected
Subject | Patentable? | Protected under
Plant variety (new, extant, essentially derived) | No | PPV&FR Act, 2001
Seeds, plants, animals (whole or parts) | No (3(j)) | PPV&FR (varieties)
Biological process to produce seeds/plants | No (3(j)) | none
Micro-organisms | Yes | Patents Act
Microbiological process | Yes | Patents Act
## 2. Why
TRIPS Art 27.3(b) lets members exclude plants/animals but requires plant varieties be protected by patents OR an effective sui generis system: India chose the sui generis PPV&FR Act
Budapest Treaty (1977): micro-organism deposits in an International Depositary Authority count across countries; India has recognised depositories (CSIR/DBT system)
⚠ "Not patentable" does not mean "unprotected": varieties get breeders' rights for 15 years (crops) / 18 years (trees and vines)
PYQ 2019: options mixed seed process (false) with plant varieties (true); answer "3 only"

text:

Feature | Fact
Law | Patents Act, 1970, amended 2005

Term | 20 years from date of filing

Made the Act TRIPS-compliant
Introduced product patents in pharmaceuticals and chemicals (earlier only process patents)
Added safeguards: Section 3(d), pre- and post-grant opposition (Section 25), compulsory licensing

topic: Patents Act 1970: what cannot be patented
t: Section 3(d) → what it bars and why the US objects
text:
## 1. What 3(d) says
New forms of a known substance are not patentable unless they show significantly enhanced efficacy
Covers salts, esters, polymorphs, metabolites, pure forms, isomers, combinations and derivatives
Aim: stop evergreening (extending monopoly by minor modification)
## 2. Who said what
Party | Position
USTR Special 301 | 3(d) "overly restrictive", stifles incremental innovation
India | TRIPS-compliant; protects public health and generic medicine
Doha Declaration 2001 | TRIPS should not stop members protecting public health
## In news 2025-26
Special 301 Report 2025: India again on the Priority Watch List with China, Russia, Indonesia, Chile, Argentina, Mexico, Venezuela; 3(d) cited (LENS Oct 2026 repeats it)
Two lists: Watch List (serious issues, making efforts) and Priority Watch List (significant ongoing problems)
2025: Indian Patent Office revoked Novartis' patent on Vymada (Entresto), a cardiac drug, under 3(d): generics may cut cost >70%
## Beyond your notes
Novartis v Union of India (2013): Supreme Court upheld 3(d) and refused a patent for Glivec (cancer)
Trap: Special 301 is a unilateral US review, not a WTO mechanism

topic: Patents Act 1970: what cannot be patented
t: Compulsory licensing → Section 84 and its grounds
text:
## 1. Section 84
Licence to a third party without the patent holder's consent
Can be sought 3 years after grant of the patent if:
Ground | Meaning
1 | Reasonable requirements of the public not met
2 | Not available at a reasonably affordable price
3 | Patent not worked (commercially used) in India
A TRIPS flexibility for developing countries; reaffirmed by Doha Declaration on TRIPS and Public Health (2001), which India helped secure
## 2. Case
2012: first Indian compulsory licence to Natco Pharma for Bayer's cancer drug Sorafenib Tosylate: price fell from over ₹2.8 lakh/month to about ₹8,800 (over 90% cut)
⚠ Voluntary licence = patent holder agrees (e.g. Cipla's Remdesivir from Gilead, COVID-19); compulsory = government authorises
## In news 2025-26
India-UK CETA (Chapter 13, IPR) reaffirms the India-EFTA dilution: patent working statement now once every 3 years instead of annually, limiting data for compulsory licences
## Beyond your notes
Section 92: national emergency / extreme urgency; Section 92A: export to countries lacking capacity; Section 100: government use

t: Types of IPR → law and term
text:
IPR | Protects | Term | Indian law
Patent | Invention (product/process) | 20 years | Patents Act 1970
Copyright | Literary, artistic, musical works | Life + 60 years | Copyright Act 1957
Trade mark | Brand name, logo | 10 years, renewable | Trade Marks Act 1999
GI | Origin-linked product | 10 years, renewable | GI Act 1999
Industrial design | Appearance, not function | 10 + 5 = 15 years | Designs Act 2000

text:

Automatic once fixed in a tangible medium; protects expression, not the idea
Work | Term
Literary, dramatic, musical, artistic | Author's life + 60 years
Films, sound recordings | 60 years from publication

Berne Convention: Indian works protected in 182 member states
2012 amendment: digital content, performers' rights, access for persons with disabilities, royalties for authors

Not protected: ideas, facts, data

All 193 members, one vote each; chief deliberative organ; resolutions are recommendatory (non-binding)

## 1. The fundamental conventions
Theme | Convention | India ratified?
Forced labour | 29 (1930), 105 (Abolition, 1957) | Yes, Yes
Association | 87 (Freedom of Association), 98 (Collective Bargaining) | No, No
Discrimination | 100 (Equal Remuneration), 111 (Employment and Occupation) | Yes, Yes

t: UN Monetary and Financial Conference → what it created
text:
## 1. The conference
Official name: United Nations Monetary and Financial Conference = Bretton Woods Conference
1-22 July 1944, Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, USA; delegates of 44 nations
Created the IMF and the IBRD (World Bank): the "Bretton Woods twins"
## 2. What came out, and when it began
Body | Agreed | Formally created | Began work
IMF | July 1944 | 27 Dec 1945 | 1 March 1947
IBRD | July 1944 | 27 Dec 1945 | June 1946
GATT | Only recommended (ITO idea) | Signed Geneva, 30 Oct 1947 by 23 nations | 1948
The planned third leg, the International Trade Organization (ITO), never came up; GATT filled the gap until the WTO (1995)
⚠ GATT was not signed at Bretton Woods: UPSC's 2008 question said IBRD, GATT and IMF; the answer was still Bretton Woods
⚠ The UN itself and the WTO did not come out of Bretton Woods (a state PSC 2012 question)
PYQ 2008: name of the conference → Bretton Woods; trap options Bandung, Versailles, Yalta

t: Bretton Woods system → fixed exchange rates and their collapse
text:
## 1. How it worked
Fixed (pegged) exchange rates: currencies pegged to the US dollar, dollar pegged to gold
The US dollar became the main reserve currency; members intervened to keep rates in narrow bands
IMF had to approve exchange rate changes; it gave temporary help for external imbalances
Aim: stop the competitive devaluations and currency wars of the Great Depression
## 2. End of the system
Event | Year | Effect
System collapses | Early 1970s | Floating exchange rates adopted
SDR redefined | 1973 onward | From gold to a basket of currencies
Reserve tranche no longer paid in gold | 1978 | "Gold tranche" renamed reserve tranche
## Beyond your notes
Dollar fixed at $35 per ounce of gold; US ended convertibility in 1971 ("Nixon shock")
Architects: J.M. Keynes (UK) and Harry Dexter White (US)

## 1. Quotas
Denominated in SDRs; decide a member's subscription, voting power, access to IMF resources, and SDR allocation
Formula: GDP 50%, openness 30%, economic variability 15%, reserves 5%
IMF funds come from quotas plus multilateral and bilateral borrowing
## 2. Voting
Rule | Fact
Major decisions | 85% of votes
US vote share | ~16.5% → de facto veto
Vote options | Only "yes" or "abstain"; no formal "no"
Practice | Most decisions by consensus
14th General Review of Quotas: agreed 2010, effective 2016; shifted quota to emerging economies; India became 8th largest holder
⚠ Voting is by economic size, not one-country-one-vote as in the UN General Assembly
## In news 2025-26
India abstained (May 2025) on the IMF Executive Board vote on a loan to Pakistan because IMF rules have no "no" vote

## 1. What it is
The part of a member's quota paid in foreign exchange (earlier gold), normally 25% of quota

Credit system granted by IMF to its members | Correct

Component | Note

Gold | Last-resort asset

text:
## 1. RFI and RCF (PYQ 2022: both are IMF)
Facility | For whom | Key feature
Rapid Financing Instrument (RFI) | All members with urgent BoP need | Quick, low conditionality; no full programme
Rapid Credit Facility (RCF) | Low-income countries | Concessional, no ex-post conditionality; under PRGT
## 2. Other IMF facilities
Facility | Purpose
Stand-By Arrangement (SBA) | Short-term BoP stress, usually 12-24 months
Extended Fund Facility (EFF) | Medium-term BoP problems from structural weakness; longer repayment
Extended Credit Facility (ECF) | Long-term concessional help to low-income countries
Standby Credit Facility (SCF) | Short-term concessional help to low-income countries
Resilience and Sustainability Facility (RSF) | Low-cost long-term finance for climate change, pandemics
CCRT | Debt-service relief to poorest (COVID-19)
RSF eligibility: PRGT-eligible LICs, small states with GNI < 25x IDA cutoff, middle-income with GNI < 10x IDA cutoff
⚠ RFI and RCF are not ADB, World Bank or UNEP-FI windows; RCF is the concessional twin of RFI

## Beyond your notes
Flexible Credit Line (FCL): precautionary line for countries with very strong fundamentals (e.g., Mexico, Chile, Colombia)

topic: IMF instruments: reserve tranche, lending windows and SDR
t: Special Drawing Rights → what the SDR is
text:
## 1. Nature
International reserve asset created by the IMF in 1969 to supplement members' official reserves
First defined in gold; after Bretton Woods collapsed (1973) it became a basket of currencies
Allocated in proportion to quota; exchanged for hard currencies in crises (e.g., 2009)
The IMF's unit of account; nicknamed "paper gold"
⚠ The SDR is not a currency and not a World Bank instrument; "paper gold" = SDR (state PSC repeats)
## 2. Use
Step | What happens
1 | IMF allocates SDRs to Country A by its quota
2 | Country A trades SDRs with Country B for foreign currency
3 | Country A uses that currency to buy goods and services
## Beyond your notes
2021 general allocation of about SDR 456 billion (~$650 billion) to fight the COVID shock

Successor to GATT (1947); created by the Uruguay Round (1986-94)

Decision-making | Consensus, one country one vote

Organ | Role

t: WTO principles → MFN, national treatment, exceptions
text:
Principle | Meaning
Most-Favoured-Nation (GATT Art I) | Any advantage to one member must go to all members
National Treatment (GATT Art III) | Imported goods treated like domestic goods after entry
Special and Differential Treatment | Extra rights and longer timelines for developing countries
Countervailing measures (GATT Art VI) | Allowed against trade-distorting subsidies
No quantitative restrictions (GATT Art XI) | Quotas banned in principle
## 1. MFN exceptions
GATT Art XXIV permits FTAs and Customs Unions – must cover "substantially all trade" and be notified to WTO
Developing countries self-designate status – contested (China claims S&DT)
## 2. Plurilateral vs multilateral
Multilateral agreements bind all members (GATT, GATS, TRIPS, AoA, SPS, TRIMs, TFA)
Plurilateral bind only signatories ("coalition of the willing"); adding one to the rulebook needs explicit consensus (Marrakesh Annex 4)
Joint Statement Initiatives (JSI): introduced at Buenos Aires 2017 – groups of members negotiate without initial consensus
⚠ India's stand: JSIs and plurilaterals violate the consensus rule

t: Dispute settlement → stages and Appellate Body crisis
text:
## 1. Stages (Articles 4-17, DSU)
Stage | What happens
Consultations | Bilateral talks first (Art 4)
Panel | Examines the case and rules
Appellate Body | Appeal on law – not functioning
Implementation | Rulings binding; non-compliance → authorised retaliation
## 2. Crisis
Appellate Body paralysed since 2019 – US blocks appointments of members
Effect: appeals "into the void"; WTO shifts from "rules-based" to "power-based"
642 disputes since 1995; 350+ rulings
## 3. India's cases
Case | Outcome
India-US poultry (2012, bird flu; SPS) | AB ruled for US; later settled by "litigotiation" – India cut tariffs on turkey, duck, berries
India-US solar panels | Domestic-content rules challenged
China vs India EV/battery subsidies (2025) | Alleges violation of National Treatment and ASCM Art 3
## Beyond your notes

topic: Agreement on Agriculture: boxes, de minimis, Peace Clause
t: AoA → three pillars and market access
text:
## 1. Basics
Negotiated in the Uruguay Round; in force 1 Jan 1995
Covers agricultural products but excludes fish and fish products, and forestry products
Three pillars: Market Access, Domestic Support, Export Competition
## 2. Market access rules
Rule | Content
Tariffication | Quotas, variable levies, minimum import prices, discretionary licensing, VERs → converted to tariffs
Tariff cuts – developed | 36% average over 6 years; at least 15% per line
Tariff cuts – developing | 24% over 10 years
BoP-constrained developing | Ceiling bindings instead of tariffication
Minimum access | 3% of domestic consumption (1986-88) in 1995 → 5%
Tariff Rate Quotas | Set quantity at lower tariff
Special Safeguard | Extra duty on import surges or very low prices
⚠ Fish and forestry are outside AoA (fish subsidies are dealt with by the separate Fisheries Subsidies Agreement)

topic: Agreement on Agriculture: boxes, de minimis, Peace Clause
t: Domestic support boxes → what goes in each
text:
Box | Nature | Examples | Limit
Green | Non- or minimally trade-distorting; not product-specific | Research, disease/pest control, rural infrastructure, environment, decoupled income support (PM-KISAN) | No limit
Amber | Trade-distorting | MSP / price support, input subsidies (fertiliser, seeds, power, irrigation) | Reduce; measured by AMS
Blue | Amber with production-limiting conditions (quotas, land set-aside, acreage reduction) | EU-style payments | Exempt from AMS
Development (S&D) box | Developing-country flexibility | Input subsidies to low-income, resource-poor farmers | Exempt
⚠ India's MSP procurement = Amber Box; it cannot shift to Blue because it raises production
⚠ India wants public stockholding moved to the Green Box
⚠ Testbook describes the S&D Box as capped at 5% of output; PMF does not give a cap

t: SPS Agreement → provisions
text:
In force with the WTO, 1995; covers food safety, animal and plant health regulations
Provision | Content
Science | Measures must be based on science
Non-discrimination | No arbitrary discrimination between countries with similar conditions
Harmonisation | Encourages national measures consistent with international standards

Standard-setting | WTO itself does not and will not develop standards

Full name: Common Framework for Debt Treatments beyond the DSSI

National Authority | NACWC: statutory, in the Cabinet Secretariat; liaison with OPCW
⚠ NCERT dates the CWC as "1992" (text adopted); PMF gives signature 1993 and force 1997; use 1993/1997 for "opened/entered into force"
## Beyond your notes
Israel has signed but not ratified the CWC; the US completed destruction of its declared stockpile in 2023

topic: Chemical and biological weapons: OPCW, CWC, BWC
t: Biological Weapons Convention → provisions and gaps
text:
## 1. Facts
Negotiated in Geneva 1969-71; opened 1972; in force 1975
First multilateral treaty to ban an entire category of WMD
188 parties; India ratified 1974
Signed, not ratified: Egypt, Haiti, Somalia, Syria; neither: Israel, Chad, Djibouti, Eritrea, Kiribati
Review Conferences every 5 years; no formal verification regime (unlike CWC/OPCW)
Feature | CWC | BWC
In force | 1997 | 1975
Verification body | OPCW | None
India | Party (1996) | Party (1974)
## 2. India's BWC compliance tools
National Biosecurity Rules, 1989; WMD Act, 2005; SCOMET Category 2
## In news 2025-26
50 years of the BWC (2025): EAM warned that bioterrorism is no longer a distant threat
⚠ "BWC has an inspection agency like OPCW" is wrong

topic: US-Russia arms control and New START
t: New START → parties, limits and expiry
text:
## 1. Facts
Bilateral US-Russia strategic nuclear arms reduction treaty: the last remaining US-Russia arms control pact
Signed in Prague, 2010 by Obama and Medvedev; in force Feb 2011
Replaced START I (1991), superseded SORT (2002)
Caps 1,550 deployed strategic warheads each; covers long-range (strategic) delivery systems
Event | Date
Extended once for 5 years | 2021
Russia suspends participation (no inspections) | Feb 2023
Expiry | 4-5 February 2026
⚠ It is not an East Asia Summit, BRICS or Russia-EU energy treaty (2011 options)
PYQ 2011: New START = bilateral US-Russia strategic arms reduction treaty
## In news 2025-26
Expired without replacement: no binding limits, inspections or data exchange remain
Talks stalled by the Ukraine war and the US demand to include China (China refuses)
## Beyond your notes
Other caps: 700 deployed ICBMs/SLBMs/heavy bombers, 800 deployed + non-deployed launchers

topic: US-Russia arms control and New START
t: US-Soviet arms control treaties → year and content (chronology)
text:
## 1. Chronology
Treaty | Year | Content
LTBT/PTBT | 1963 | No tests in air, space, underwater (US, UK, USSR)
SALT I | 1972 (Nixon-Brezhnev, Moscow) | ABM Treaty + interim agreement on offensive arms
SALT II | 1979 (Carter-Brezhnev, Vienna) | Limits strategic arms; never ratified (Afghanistan invasion)
INF | 1987 | Eliminated ground-launched missiles of 500-5,500 km
START I | 1991 (Gorbachev-Bush Sr) | Big cuts in strategic warheads
START II | 1993 (Yeltsin-Bush Sr) | Further cuts
SORT (Moscow Treaty) | 2002 | Superseded by New START
New START | 2010 | 1,550 deployed warheads
Arms control regulates weapons (ABM, SALT, START, NPT); disarmament gives up a category (BWC, CWC) (NCERT)
## In news 2025-26
INF is dead: US withdrew earlier and Russia ended its commitment
SIPRI: deployed strategic warheads may rise after New START's expiry; China has more than doubled warheads since 2020 (~600)
⚠ INF covered intermediate ranges (500-5,500 km), New START covers strategic (long-range) arms

topic: Law of the Sea (UNCLOS, BBNJ, Polar Code)
t: UNCLOS maritime zones → limits and rights of the coastal state
text:
## 1. The five zones (all measured from the baseline = low-water line)
Zone | Limit | Coastal state's rights
Internal waters | Landward of baseline | Full sovereignty; no innocent passage
Territorial sea | 12 nm (Art 3) | Sovereignty over water, airspace, seabed, subsoil; foreign ships have innocent passage
Contiguous zone | 24 nm | Control only to punish customs, fiscal, immigration, sanitary breaches
EEZ | 200 nm (Art 57) | Sovereign rights over resources, artificial islands, research; no sovereignty
High seas | Beyond EEZ | No state; common heritage of mankind
## 2. Continental shelf
Seabed rights beyond 200 nm "under certain conditions"; claims examined by the CLCS (New York)
EEZ excludes the territorial sea and the shelf beyond 200 nm
⚠ The EEZ gives resource rights, not sovereignty: other states keep freedom of navigation and overflight
⚠ 1 nautical mile = 1,852 m = one minute of latitude
PYQ 2022: three statements (12 nm territorial sea, innocent passage for landlocked states, EEZ not beyond 200 nm), all correct

topic: Law of the Sea (UNCLOS, BBNJ, Polar Code)
t: Passage regimes → which zone, which ships
text:
## 1. Innocent passage (territorial sea)
Art 17: ships of all states, coastal or landlocked, enjoy innocent passage
Innocent = not prejudicial to peace, good order or security of the coastal state
Not available in internal waters (rivers, harbours, lagoons, some bays, the Great Lakes)
## 2. Other regimes
Regime | Where | Note
Transit passage | Straits used for international navigation (Hormuz, Malacca) | Wider than innocent passage
Freedom of navigation | EEZ and high seas | Overflight too
Access to and from the sea | Through transit states | For landlocked states, without taxation of traffic
FONOPs: US Navy passages through waters claimed by coastal states as exclusive
⚠ Landlocked states are not excluded from innocent passage: UNCLOS gives them rights, not fewer rights
## Beyond your notes
Archipelagic sea-lanes passage applies in archipelagic waters (Indonesia, Philippines)

topic: Law of the Sea (UNCLOS, BBNJ, Polar Code)
t: UNCLOS → adoption, parties and three institutions
text:
## 1. Basic facts
Adopted 10 Dec 1982, Montego Bay, Jamaica; in force 16 Nov 1994; "Constitution of the Oceans"
Replaced the 1958 Geneva conventions (incl. Convention on the High Seas)
India: signed 1982, ratified 1995
Uses consensus, not majority vote; UN supports meetings but does not implement it (IMO, IWC do)
## 2. Institutions
Body | Seat | Job
ITLOS | Hamburg | Settles law-of-the-sea disputes
ISA | Kingston, Jamaica | Controls deep-seabed mining beyond national jurisdiction (171 members, India a member)
CLCS | New York | Examines continental shelf extension claims
## 3. Non-parties
USA (signed, not ratified), Colombia, Israel, Peru, Turkey, Venezuela
⚠ Party count differs: PMF Geography 167 countries + EU; Praveen Sir 168 UN members + EU; Environment & DM 168 parties
⚠ Three agreements under UNCLOS: 1994 (ISA/Part XI), 1995 (Fish Stocks), 2023 BBNJ

topic: Law of the Sea (UNCLOS, BBNJ, Polar Code)
t: BBNJ High Seas Treaty → provisions and status
text:
## 1. What it is
Agreement on Marine Biological Diversity of Areas Beyond National Jurisdiction, adopted 2023 under UNCLOS; "Paris Agreement for the Ocean"
Covers 2/3 of the oceans, nearly 1/2 of Earth's surface
First legally binding framework on overfishing, deep-sea mining, benefit sharing, MPAs in international waters
## 2. Key provisions
Pillar | Provision
MPAs | Parties can designate protected zones in the high seas
Marine genetic resources | Benefits = common heritage, shared fairly
EIAs | Mandatory for activities with transboundary/cumulative harm
Capacity building | Technology transfer, finance for developing states
## 3. Bodies and exceptions
COP (main body), Clearing House Mechanism, Scientific and Technical Body, 4 subject committees
Does not apply to warships, military aircraft, naval auxiliaries, or fishing regulated elsewhere
## In news 2025-26
Morocco became the 60th ratifier; treaty entered into force January 2026 (85 parties)
India signed (2024), not ratified as of Feb 2026; USA, China, Russia, Japan not ratified
3rd UN Ocean Conference, Nice (June 2025), France and Costa Rica: Nice Ocean Agreements; India did not sign the "Nice Wake-up Call"

topic: Law of the Sea (UNCLOS, BBNJ, Polar Code)
t: Polar Code → what it is and who made it
text:
## 1. The code
International Code for Ships Operating in Polar Waters, adopted by the IMO, in force 2017
Safety rules for ships and crews, and protection of indigenous communities and wildlife of the fragile polar seas
Mandatory under both SOLAS and MARPOL
## 2. Eliminate the distractors
Distractor | Real instrument
Demarcation of Arctic territories | None: claims go to CLCS under UNCLOS
Norms for polar research | Antarctic Treaty system (Antarctic)
Trade/security pact of Arctic states | Arctic Council is a forum, not a pact
⚠ The Polar Code covers both poles (Arctic and Antarctic), not just the North Pole
PYQ 2022: "best describes the Polar Code" = safety code for ships in polar waters

topic: Law of the Sea (UNCLOS, BBNJ, Polar Code)
t: UNCLOS in news 2025-26 → zones applied
text:
## 1. Events
Event | UNCLOS point
IRIS Dena (Iranian frigate) sank off Galle, March 2026 | Outside Sri Lanka's 12 nm, inside its SAR region: Sri Lanka rescued under UNCLOS; debate on warship immunity
Strait of Hormuz seizures (Iran-US, 2026) | Straits governed by transit passage; high seas free

Right | Article

topic: Human rights instruments (UDHR, CRC, CEDAW, Refugees)
t: UDHR → adoption, status and India
text:
## 1. Facts
Adopted by UNGA 10 Dec 1948 (Human Rights Day), Paris, resolution 217A
Preamble + 30 Articles; first universal list of fundamental rights
Prepared after World War II atrocities; dignity at its core
## 2. Legal status
Instrument | Binding?
UDHR 1948 | No (declaration)
ICCPR 1966 | Yes (civil, political)
ICESCR 1966 | Yes (economic, social, cultural)
UDHR + ICCPR + ICESCR = International Bill of Human Rights
## 3. India
Indian Constitution reflects UDHR in FRs, Preamble, DPSPs, Fundamental Duties (PYQ 2020)
Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 created NHRC and SHRCs
## Beyond your notes
48 for, 0 against, 8 abstentions; Hansa Mehta (India) got "all human beings" in place of "all men"; Eleanor Roosevelt chaired drafting
India acceded to ICCPR and ICESCR in 1979

topic: Human rights instruments (UDHR, CRC, CEDAW, Refugees)
t: CRC 1989 → rights of the child
text:
## 1. Facts
Adopted by UNGA 20 Nov 1989 (World Children's Day); India ratified 11 Dec 1992
Child = person below 18 (Art 1); covers civil, political, economic, social, health, cultural rights
UNICEF is guided by the CRC
## 2. Rights asked and likely next
Right | Article
Best interests of the child | Art 3
Life, survival and development | Art 6
Right to be heard (views) | Art 12
Expression | Art 13
Association | Art 15
Rest, leisure, play, recreation, culture | Art 31
⚠ Right to development, expression and recreation: all three are CRC rights
PYQ 2010: asked which of development, expression, recreation are child rights; answer all three
## Beyond your notes
3 Optional Protocols: children in armed conflict (2000), sale/sexual exploitation (2000), communications procedure (2011); India ratified the first two (2005)
Most widely ratified treaty; USA is the only UN member not party (as of 2026)

Only amendment; removed the pre-1951 and European limits

Objective | Content

Red | Locate and arrest a person wanted for prosecution or to serve a sentence
Blue | Collect additional information on a person's identity, location or activities in a criminal investigation
Green | Warn about a person's criminal activities (habitual offender, threat to public safety)
Yellow | Locate missing persons, especially minors / identify people unable to identify themselves
Black | Seek information on unidentified bodies
Orange | Warn of an imminent threat: event, person, object or process
Purple | Information on modus operandi, objects, devices, concealment methods of criminals
Silver | Identify and trace criminal assets
INTERPOL-UNSC Special Notice | Groups and individuals subject to UN Security Council sanctions

## 1. Confusable pairs
Pair | Hinge
Red vs Blue | Red = arrest; Blue = only information (no arrest)

## 1. The five principles (India-China, 1954)
No. | Principle
1 | Mutual respect for each other's territorial integrity and sovereignty
2 | Mutual non-aggression
3 | Mutual non-interference in each other's internal affairs
4 | Equality and mutual benefit
5 | Peaceful co-existence
⚠ Non-alignment is NOT a Panchsheel principle; it is a separate Nehruvian policy of not joining Cold War blocs
⚠ "Disarmament", "anti-colonialism" and "non-alignment" are distractors; "non-aggression" and "non-interference" are both in

Word from early Buddhist texts: "five taboos" for monks' conduct, adapted by Nehru to inter-state relations

t: Panchsheel → origin, document and spread
text:
## 1. The document
First written into the Agreement on Trade and Intercourse between the Tibet region of China and India (1954)
Negotiated in Beijing, 1953-54; in substance a trade pact on Tibet
India gave up the military, postal and communication rights it held in Tibet (from the 1904 Anglo-Tibetan treaty) and asked nothing in return
## 2. How it spread
Year | Step
1954 | India-China agreement (Nehru era; "Hindi-Chini Bhai-Bhai")
1955 | Bandung Conference folded it into its Ten Principles of International Peace and Cooperation
1957 | UNGA resolution endorsed it as a principle of international law
1961 | Belgrade NAM summit adopted it as a core principle of NAM
⚠ Panchsheel failed to stop the 1962 war; PMF calls 1946-62 "Optimistic Non-Alignment", ending in idealism's limits
## In news 2025-26

## Beyond your notes
Signed 29 April 1954; Nehru and Zhou Enlai associated with it; 70th anniversary marked in 2024

## 1. NCERT definitions
Term | Meaning | Is NAM this?
Isolationism | Staying aloof from world affairs (US 1787-WWI) | No
Neutrality | Staying out of war, taking no position | No
Non-alignment | Not joining either military bloc, active mediation | Yes
India mediated in the Korean War (1950s), the Congo crisis, and on Suez 1956
Non-aligned states fought wars too (India 1962, 1965, 1971)

## 2. From non-alignment to multi-alignment

Strategic autonomy: independent choices across blocs; e.g., balanced stand on the Russia-Ukraine war
Against NAM today: 120 members lack cohesion; rise of G20, Quad, BRICS; Cold War legacy

No reciprocity asked of Nepal, Bangladesh, Bhutan, Maldives, Sri Lanka

text:
## 1. Steps (PMF)
Step | Output
Mine chalcopyrite (copper iron sulphide; under 1% Cu) | Ore
Crush, grind, froth flotation (oils) | Concentrate ~34.5% Cu
Roasting in smelter (mostly near ports) | Removes 20-50% sulphur as SO2 → sulphuric acid
Smelting | Matte (~65% Cu: Cu2S + FeS) + slag
Converter furnace | Blister copper (~99%)
Anode furnace | ~99.5% Cu
Electrolytic refining | 99.99% cathode copper
Slime from refining → gold, silver, selenium, tellurium
Copper slag: abrasive blast-cleaning, roads, cement and concrete
Lead from galena (PbS); zinc from sphalerite (ZnS); nickel matte from nickel sulphide
⚠ Smelting needs a reducing agent (carbon) and a flux; aluminium is the exception (electrolysis)
## 2. Metallurgy routes
Route | Means | Example
Pyrometallurgy | High heat (roast, smelt) | Iron in blast furnace
Hydrometallurgy | Dissolve in acid, then recover | Zinc roast-leach-electrowin
Electrometallurgy | Electricity | Aluminium (Hall-Heroult)
Reactivity series (top → bottom): K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Pb, Cu, Ag, Au

Iron ore (haematite, magnetite) | Source of iron
Limestone | Flux: removes silica as slag
Hot air blast | Burns coke
Reactions: Fe2O3 → Fe3O4 → FeO → Fe, each reduced by CO; exhaust CO and CO2
Coke, not coal: coal has impurities, especially sulphur (makes steel brittle); coke ~90% carbon
Coke ovens emit naphthalene (carcinogenic)
⚠ Coke does not remove silica (limestone does) and is not an oxidising agent

## 1. Facts
Yellowcake = uranium oxide concentrate (U3O8): refined powder from uranium ore

Fertile | Becomes fissile by capturing neutrons: U-238, Pu-240 (and Th-232)
Becquerel | SI unit of radioactivity
Heavy water | Water with deuterium; moderator in PHWRs

Unrestricted display by citizens as long as dignity is kept; three parts: description, display by public/private bodies, display by governments

t: Longitude and time → the 15°-per-hour rule
text:
## 1. The rule
Earth rotates 360° in 24 hours → 15° per hour → 1° in 4 minutes
Rotation is west to east: going east every 15° local time is advanced 1 hour; going west it is retarded 1 hour
Places east of Greenwich gain time; places west lose time
Time difference from GMT | Longitude difference | Example direction
4 minutes | 1° | —
1 hour | 15° | —
5 h 30 min | 82.5° | IST meridian, east (ahead)
6 hours behind | 90° | 90° W
12 hours | 180° | 180° E = GMT+12, 180° W = GMT-12

t: 6 hours behind GMT → 90° W (the 1998 question)
text:
## 1. Solving it
Noon at GMT, 6 a.m. tea elsewhere → place is 6 hours behind → 6 × 15 = 90° → west → 90° W
⚠ "Behind" (earlier clock) = west; "ahead" = east. Do not add 90° to the east
⚠ PMF prints the same 1998 question with noon at the IST meridian: then the place is 90° west of 82.5° E = 7.5° W (also an option). Read which meridian the question names
PYQ 1998: asked the longitude of a place 6 hours behind; trap: options 7°30' W and 90° W are both there, one for the IST version and one for the GMT version

t: Time-difference problems → how to solve
text:
## 1. Steps
Step 1: find the time difference in hours (and minutes)
Step 2: multiply by 15° (or minutes ÷ 4 = degrees)
Step 3: clock later = east, clock earlier = west
Step 4: if a reference meridian other than 0° is given (IST 82.5° E), count from it
## 2. Worked PYQ patterns
PYQ | Asked | Key
1995 | Order Cuba, Greece, Iraq, Costa Rica, Japan from ahead to behind GMT | Japan (+9) > Iraq (+3) > Greece (+2) > Cuba (-5) > Costa Rica (-6)
1997 | IST at noon at IDL if rotation reversed | Normal: IST is 17.5 h ahead of IDL; reversed: 17.5 h behind → 18:30 hrs previous day
2000 | Meridian of India's first millennium sunrise | Only 82°30' E and 92°30' E pass through India → 92°30' E (easternmost)
2007 | City not sharing clock time with others | London, Lisbon, Accra on GMT; Addis Ababa (GMT+3) differs
⚠ Japan is the "land of the rising sun", 9 hours ahead of GMT (PMF hint)

## 1. Standard time
Time of a central meridian chosen by a country; most use the central meridian of their territory

## 2. Indian Standard Time
IST = time at 82.5° E, passing close to the east of Prayagraj → GMT + 5:30
India's east-west extent ~30° → about 2 hours of local-time difference between Gujarat and Arunachal
Fact | Value
Western limit | 68° 7' E
Eastern limit | 97° 25' E (Physical Geography) / 97° 39' E (Indian Physical Geography)
Standard meridian | 82° 30' E

⚠ The two PMF books differ on the eastern limit (97° 25' E vs 97° 39' E); both lie east of 92° 30' E
## 3. Chaibagaan time

t: International Date Line → crossing and date change
text:
## 1. What it is
Imaginary line through the Pacific Ocean, mostly along 180°; bends to keep land groups on one date
180° E = GMT+12, 180° W = GMT-12 → 24-hour difference across it
Crossing | Date effect
East to west (America → Asia) | Lose a day (date goes forward)
West to east (Asia → America) | Gain a day (date repeats)
IST is 17.5 hours ahead of the IDL (GMT-12) time on the western-hemisphere side
⚠ Strait nearest the IDL: Bering Strait (PYQ 2008), not Malacca, Florida or Gibraltar
## Beyond your notes
Countries such as Kiribati shifted the line eastward so all their islands share one date (verify)
PYQ 2008: nearest strait to the IDL; trap: Bering Strait separates Asia and North America at about 169° W

topic: Tides, tidal currents and tidal ports
t: Gulf shape → tidal range (funnelling)
text:
## 1. What raises a tide
At the surface, horizontal tide-generating forces (barrier and funnelling effects) matter more than the vertical pull of moon and sun
Wide continental shelves → higher tidal bulges (barrier effect); mid-ocean islands → low tides
Funnel-shaped bays magnify tides
Gulf shape | Tide
Wide front, narrow rear (funnel) | High tidal range
Narrow front, wide rear | Low tidal range
## 2. Bay of Fundy
Nova Scotia, Canada: highest tidal range in the world, bulge 15-16 m
⚠ 2004 trap: "gulfs with narrow fronts and wider rears experience high tides" is the wrong statement; it is the reverse
PYQ 2004: pick the incorrect statement on tides; trap: the funnel is wide at the mouth, narrow inside

topic: Tides, tidal currents and tidal ports
t: Tidal currents and tidal bores → where and when
text:
## 1. Tidal current
In-and-out movement of water when the tide is channelled between islands or into bays, gulfs, estuaries; a gulf joined to the sea by a narrow channel has strong tidal currents
## 2. Tidal bore
A strong tide entering a narrow and shallow estuary: river water piles up against it, front becomes a vertical wall rushing upstream
Fact | Detail
When | Flood tide only; never ebb tide; almost never neap tides
Needs | Large tidal range, typically > 6 m
India | Common in the Hooghly
Most powerful | Qiantang River, China
Exception | Amazon: mouth not narrow, but shallow with islands and sand bars → strong bore
⚠ A bore needs a shallow, narrow estuary; the Amazon is the textbook exception to "narrow"
PYQ 2004: statements on tidal currents and bores were correct; only the gulf-shape statement was wrong

Whole 280 km of the Bhagirathi-Hooghly from Saugor to Nabadwip is tide-influenced

Tidal currents flush pollutants and desilt estuaries; high tide helps fishing
