t: Ashokan inscriptions
text:
## 1. Classification and sites
Ashokan inscriptions are classified into rock, pillar and cave inscriptions
Major rock edict sites: Shahbazgarhi, Mansehra, Kalsi, Girnar, Dhauli, Jaugada, Yerragudi, Sopara
## 2. Language and script
Most Ashokan inscriptions: Prakrit language; Brahmi script (most use Brahmi)
Site | Script
Shahbazgarhi, Mansehra | Kharosthi — major Ashokan examples
Taxila | Aramaic
Kandahar or Shar-i-Kuna | Greek and Aramaic
Laghman | Aramaic
Kharosthi: Written from right to left — used in north-western India
James Prinsep: Deciphered Brahmi — the first scholar to read Ashoka's edicts
## 3. Ashoka's names
Generally referred to as Priyadarshi or Piyadasi; also Devanampiya Piyadasi — Beloved of the Gods
Personal name occurs at Maski (important for this reason), Gujarra, Nettur, Udagolam
## 4. Important Ashokan inscriptions
Rummindei or Lumbini Pillar: At Lumbini — marks the birthplace of Buddha; Lumbini is identified as Buddha's birthplace
Ashoka visited Lumbini after the twentieth year of his coronation
Exempted Lumbini from the Bali tax; land revenue reduced from one-sixth to one-eighth
Bhabru or Bairat Inscription: Shows (associates) Ashoka's association with Buddhism — his title Piyadasi Raja; associated with the King of Magadha
Kanganahalli Inscription: Karnataka near the Bhima River — a stone portrait of Ashoka and a queen; the phrase "Ranyo Ashoka" — King Ashoka
Kalsi Rock Edicts: Dehradun, Uttarakhand
## 5. Rock Edicts
Edict | Concerns
Rock Edict I | Animal slaughter and sacrifice — the gradual reduction and eventual stopping of animal killing in the royal kitchen
Rock Edict II | South India and medical care — mentions the Cholas, Pandyas, Satiyaputtas, Keralaputtas, Tamraparni or Sri Lanka; medical treatment for humans and animals
Rock Edict XII | Religious tolerance — respect for different religious sects; religious harmony
Rock Edict XIII | Kalinga, remorse, Greeks and Dhamma — the Kalinga War (the eighth year after coronation; dated 261 BC); Ashoka's remorse; shift from military conquest to Dhamma conquest; Greek or Yavana rulers

t: Early and post-Mauryan inscriptions
text:
## 1. Inscriptions
Inscription | Location | Associated with | Key facts
Boghaz-Koi | Asia Minor — present-day Turkey | — | Fourteenth century BC — mentions Indra, Varuna, Mitra, Nasatya
Sohgaura Copper Plate | Gorakhpur, Uttar Pradesh | The Mauryan period | The earliest known copper plate; food-grain preservation — grain preservation during a famine or crisis
Mahasthan Inscription | Bogura in Bangladesh | — | Famine relief
Junagadh Inscription | Girnar or Junagadh, Gujarat | Rudradaman I | Approximately 150 AD; Sanskrit in Brahmi script; the earliest perfect Sanskrit inscription; an early specimen of the Kavya style
Hathigumpha Inscription | The Udayagiri caves of Odisha | Kharavela — Chedi or Mahameghavahana dynasty; ruled Kalinga; followed Jainism | A major source for Kharavela's history — thirteen years of his reign; mentions a Nanda ruler — Mahapadmananda (evidence for a Nanda ruler); canal activity; donations to Jain monks; southern victories
Ayodhya Inscription | — | Pushyamitra Shunga | Pushyamitra performed two Ashvamedha Yajnas
Nanaghat Inscription | — | The Satavahana dynasty | Important for Satakarni I's governance — Satavahana administration
Nashik Inscription | — | Gautami Balashri and Gautamiputra Satakarni | Gautamiputra — the title Ekabrahmana: Unrivalled Brahmana
Sarnath Buddhist Image Inscription | Sarnath | Kanishka | 81 AD — three years after Kanishka's coronation
Rabatak Inscription | Found in Afghanistan — discovered 1993 | Kanishka | Bactrian language in the Greek script; mentions Saket, Kaushambi, Pataliputra and Sri Champa — ⚠ not Shravasti
## 2. Sudarshan Lake
The Junagadh Inscription is important for the history of Sudarshan Lake
Originally constructed by Pushyagupta — governor of Chandragupta Maurya
Canals constructed by Tushasp — governor of Ashoka
Repaired by Rudradaman — without forced labour

t: Gupta and early-medieval inscriptions
text:
## 1. Gupta inscriptions
Inscription | Associated with | Key facts
Prayag Prashasti — the Allahabad Pillar inscription | Samudragupta — authored (composed) by Harisena | Sanskrit in Brahmi script; a panegyric or eulogy — Samudragupta's political and military achievements; southern expeditions; rulers of Dakshinapatha; Mahendra as a Koshala ruler
Mehrauli Iron Pillar | A king named Chandra — identified as Chandragupta II | Devoted to Vishnu — established as a Vishnu Dhvaja; associated with Vishnupada
Bhitari Pillar | Skandagupta | Ghazipur, Uttar Pradesh — the Huna invasion or war
Eran Inscription | The wife of the military commander Gopraj | The first inscriptional evidence of Sati — 510 AD
Mandsaur or Dashpur Inscription | Kumaragupta I — governor Bandhuvarman; composed by Vatsabhatti | Mandsaur or Dashpur in Malwa — a silk-weavers guild (Tantuwayas) from the Lata region or Gujarat built a Sun Temple
## 2. Allahabad Pillar
Originally associated with Ashoka; originally located at Kaushambi; Akbar shifted it to Allahabad or Prayagraj
Contains: An Ashokan inscription; the Queen's Edict of Karuvaki; Samudragupta's inscription composed by Harisena; a Persian inscription of Jahangir
## 3. Early-medieval north
Gwalior Inscription: Records the territory of Mihirakula; Nagabhata I (Gurjara-Pratiharas) destroyed the army of a Mlechcha ruler — interpreted in the source as probably the Arab ruler of Sindh
Sondani Inscription: Yashodharman — composed by Vasula Kavi
Maukhari Copper-Seal: Sarvavarman — found at Asirgarh Fort, Madhya Pradesh; gives the Maukhari genealogy, beginning with Harivarman
Chausath Yogini Temple Inscription: Morena, Madhya Pradesh — 1323 CE; the Kachchhapaghata dynasty; records that Devapala built the temple

t: Deccan, South Indian and Pala inscriptions
text:
## 1. Chalukya inscriptions
Aihole Inscription: Pulakeshin II — at Aihole, Karnataka; composed by Ravikirti; Sanskrit in Southern Brahmi
Records the conflict between Pulakeshin II and Harshavardhana — Harsha's southward expansion stopped at the Narmada
Mentions Kalidasa, Bharavi, the Gurjaras and Harsha
Badami Rock Inscription: Pulakeshin I — Saka 465
Lohnara Inscription: Pulakeshin II — 630 AD; ⚠ does not mention Harsha — associated with the absence of Harsha
## 2. Chola inscriptions
Uttaramerur Inscription: Chola dynasty — famous for village administration; mentions the Sabha, village assemblies and local committees — committee selection and working; Chola local self-government
Thanjavur Inscription: Rajaraja I — military achievements; the defeat of the Chera naval force at Kandallur; Chola overseas expansion
Rajaraja I and Rajendra I commissioned temple-wall inscriptions recording victories and achievements — extensive temple inscriptions are a major reason Chola history is well documented
## 3. Pala and Rashtrakuta
Khalimpur Inscription: Dharmapala — mentions the selection or election of Gopala to end Matsya Nyaya (the Law of the Jungle)
Dharmapala: The title Param Saugat — Buddhist affiliation
Sanjan and Radhanpur Copper Plates: Govinda III (Rashtrakuta dynasty) — his victory over Nagabhata II; he defeated the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty
## 4. Motupalli Epigraph
Concerns trade and tariff rates — imports and exports through Motupalli port; port trade and commodity tariffs
Commodities listed: Sandal, camphor, rose water, ivory, pearls, corals, copper, zinc, lead, silk, pepper, areca nuts

t: Sultanate inscriptions and coins
text:
## 1. Inscriptions and coins
Garhmukteshwar Inscription: Balban — at the Garhmukteshwar Mosque; Balban called himself "Helper of a Caliph"
Mahmud Ghazni: Silver coins with Arabic on one side and Sanskrit — in Devanagari — on the other
Muhammad Ghori: Coins with Goddess Lakshmi on one side and the Kalma in Arabic on the other
Iltutmish: Placed the Caliph's name on coins after recognition by the Caliph
Alauddin Khalji: Used the title Sikandar-i-Sani — inscribed it on coins
Muhammad bin Tughluq: The coin legend "Al Sultan Zilli Allah" — Sultan as Shadow of God

t: Archaeological administration
text:
## 1. Milestones
Year | Event
1784 | William Jones founded the Asiatic Society
1861 | Cunningham became Archaeological Surveyor
1871 | Department of Archaeological Survey established
1901 | Curzon appointed Marshall as Director-General
1902 | Marshall took charge
1904 | Ancient Monuments Preservation Act — enacted during the viceroyalty of Lord Curzon

t: Oldest and earliest in Indian history
text:
## 1. Agriculture and settlement
Mehrgarh: The oldest evidence of settled life; earlier accepted as the oldest evidence of agriculture (the earlier accepted agricultural site); the earliest evidence of wheat
Lahuradeva — Lahuradewa: Currently the oldest evidence of paddy cultivation — the earliest evidence of agriculture in the Indian subcontinent and of rice cultivation
Koldihwa: Earlier considered the oldest site for paddy
Belan Valley (the Prayagraj region): Earliest evidence of rice near the Belan River
Barley and paddy: Among the oldest cultivated food grains — barley was the first cereal used by humans
Narmada Valley: The first human fossil in India
Atranjikhera: The earliest evidence of iron in India
Indus Valley Civilization: The earliest known urban civilization
Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro: The earliest public water tank; Lothal: the earliest known tidal dockyard
## 2. Inscriptions, coins and texts
Sohgaura Copper Plate: The earliest known copper plate (copper-plate record) — the earliest royal (famine-related) order related to famine relief
Satavahana inscriptions: The earliest (religious) land-grant epigraphic record
Rudradaman's Junagadh inscription: The earliest specimen of the Kavya style; the earliest perfect Sanskrit inscription
Prakrit: The language of the earliest stone inscription
Silver punch-marked coins: The earliest extant coins of India
Ashtadhyayi of Panini: The earliest known Sanskrit grammar
Arthashastra: One of the oldest political books
Fourteen Purvas: The earliest Jain holy book; Ardha-Magadhi — the language of the earliest Jain literature
Panchraksha: The oldest paper evidence in India — 1105 CE; at the Ashutosh Museum in Kolkata
Dashpur inscription: The oldest advertisement tradition in India
Dastan-i-Amir Hamza: The earliest Mughal illustrated manuscript
Annamacharya: The earliest known Indian musician
## 3. Temples, buildings and roads
Gudimallam Shiva Linga: The earliest Shiva Linga
Lad Khan Temple at Aihole: One of the earliest temples
Gupta period: The earliest freestanding temples — ⚠ Kailasanatha at Kanchi is not the earliest Dravida-style freestanding temple
Lingaraja Temple: One of the oldest temples in Bhubaneswar
Balban's Tomb: The first purely Indo-Islamic tomb; Alai Darwaza: one of the first Indo-Islamic buildings
Grand Trunk Road — also Sadak-e-Azam: One of Asia's oldest major roads

t: Discovery and excavation timeline
text:
## 1. Timeline
Year | Site | Person | Significance
1826 | Harappa mounds reported | Charles Masson | The first large mounds reported
1853 and 1856 | Harappa visited and excavated | Alexander Cunningham — saw pottery, tools and a seal | ⚠ The significance was not recognized
1921 | Harappa excavation began systematically | Daya Ram Sahni | The beginning of systematic excavation
1922 | Mohenjo-daro investigated | R.D. Banerjee | A major Indus city
1926–27 to 1933–34 | Harappa excavated | M.S. Vats — continued excavation | —
1931 | Chanhudaro discovered | N.G. Majumdar | Later extensively excavated
1935–36 | Chanhudaro excavated | E.J.H. Mackay | A bead-making factory; a furnace
1950 | Ropar discovered | B.B. Lal | A Sutlej site
1953 to 1955 — 1953–55 | Ropar excavated | Yagyadatt Sharma | A major excavation phase
1954 | Lothal discovered | S.R. Rao | A dockyard or port
1958 | Daimabad discovered | B.P. Bopardikar | Bronze objects
1960–61 | Kalibangan excavated | B.B. Lal and B.K. Thapar | A ploughed field; fire altars
1982 | Manda excavated | J.P. Joshi and Madhubala | On the Chenab; Himalayan wood
1990–91 | Dholavira excavated | R.S. Bisht and his colleagues | Reservoirs; water-management systems

t: Harappa, Mohenjo-daro and Chanhudaro
text:
## 1. Harappa
Situated on the Ravi River — Punjab, Pakistan
Granary: Twelve rooms in two rows of six rooms each
Burials: Cemetery R-37; Cemetery H; coffin burial; a graveyard
Religion: The Mother Goddess; phallus and Lingam-Yoni worship
Finds: Wheat and barley in a wooden mortar; dice; a copper scale; a copper mirror; a unicorn seal
The first artefact at Harappa: a stone seal with a unicorn and an inscription — the Harappan script is undeciphered
## 2. Mohenjo-daro
The Great Bath — ritual bathing; the Great Granary; a citadel
A large building — possibly for a high official, a high priest or a college of priests
Excellent road planning — the main road about 9.15 metres wide; roads intersected at right angles
Finds: The Dancing Girl; the Priest-King; the Pashupati seal; the Mother Goddess; a humped bull seal; horse teeth; cotton cloth; skeletons in wells; an ivory weight balance
## 3. Chanhudaro
A bead-making factory — a bead industry; a furnace
Crafts: Bangle-making, shell-working, bead-making
Finds: Lipsticks; an ornamented elephant; toys; an ink pot; carts with seated drivers; phase-cut bricks
⚠ No citadel — the only major Harappan city without a citadel

t: Harappan sites of Gujarat and Maharashtra
text:
## 1. Lothal
Gujarat — situated on the Bhogava River
Famous for its dockyard — a brick basin; a port and trading centre (trade association); traded with West Asia
Rice — rice husk found
Craftsmen: Metal workers, shell ornament makers, bead makers
Finds: Fire altars; a horse figurine; a ship model; a Persian seal; painted jars; a shop; a graveyard; an ivory weight balance; a copper dog
Three double burials
## 2. Dholavira
The Rann of Kachchh, Gujarat — associated with water management and urban planning
A three-part city — three urban divisions: the Citadel, Middle Town and Lower Town
Water: Huge reservoirs; water storage facilities; dams; embankments; an advanced water-harnessing system; rock-cut reservoirs
A Great Bath; a stadium-like structure; special cemetery structures
A ten-sign inscription — ten large-sized Harappan signs
## 3. Other Gujarat sites
Surkotada: Kachchh, Gujarat — a Harappan site; horse bones (horse-related evidence whose interpretation is debated); pot burials
Rangpur: The Saurashtra region of Gujarat — a Late Harappan site; rice, bajra, sorghum
Kerala-no-dhoro: Gujarat — a salt production centre
Nageshwar: Shell
## 4. Daimabad
Maharashtra — on the Pravara River; Chalcolithic, with a later Harappan-associated cultural horizon
Bronze objects: A bronze chariot, a bronze buffalo, bronze sculptures

t: Harappan sites of the north and the frontiers
text:
## 1. Rajasthan, Haryana and Punjab
Kalibangan: Hanumangarh, Rajasthan — on the Ghaggar River; a Harappan association
The earliest excavated evidence of a ploughed agricultural field
Finds: A terracotta plough; fire altars; Mesopotamian seals; toy-cart wheels; a wooden plough; a copper ox; camel bones; wooden drainage
Evidence of an earthquake
Rakhigarhi: Hisar, Haryana — the largest IVC site in India; a major Harappan urban site; the Ghaggar-Hakra river system
A granary; a cemetery; drains; terracotta bricks; double burials; a provincial-capital character in its material
Banawali: Fatehabad, Haryana — a Harappan settlement
A terracotta plough — a terracotta replica of a plough; a toy plough; Mother Goddess figurines; a large quantity of barley grains
An oval settlement; a radial street pattern
Bhagwanpura: Kurukshetra, Haryana — on the Saraswati River; excavated by J.P. Joshi
An important Harappan and Late Harappan site — a Late Harappan and Painted Grey Ware association
⚠ No distinctive artefact is identified for it in the supplied passage
Balu: Haryana — plant remains; the earliest evidence of garlic
Ropar — also known as Rupnagar: On the Sutlej River
The first Harappan site excavated in independent India
Stone and soil buildings; a dog burial — a dog buried with humans; an inscribed steatite seal; Indus pictographs; oval pit burials
## 2. Uttar Pradesh
Alamgirpur: Meerut — on the Hindon River; the eastern boundary of Harappan culture
A terracotta bead-like object coated with gold; evidence of cloth; utensils with triangle, peacock and squirrel impressions
Hulas: Saharanpur — handmade and wheel-made pottery with geometric and naturalistic black-painted designs; chert blades; bone points
Sinauli: Baghpat — 125 graves; mostly primary human burials; north–south orientation; some graves contained animal bones, gold, copper and bangles
Mandi: Muzaffarnagar — a jewellery or treasure hoard; the Late Harappan period; discovered in June 2000
## 3. Jammu and Kashmir
Manda: On the Chenab River — the procurement of Himalayan wood, transported downstream to other Harappan towns
## 4. Frontier sites
Shortughai: Afghanistan — a Harappan trade outpost; lapis lazuli
Sutkagendor: Baluchistan, Pakistan — the western boundary of Harappan culture; clay bangles
Kot Bala: The earliest evidence of a furnace
Amri: Rhinoceros remains

t: Chalcolithic cultures
text:
## 1. Sites and cultures
Culture / site | Location | Association
Ahar/Banas culture — Ahar | Rajasthan | A copper-using Chalcolithic culture
Kayatha culture — Kayatha | Madhya Pradesh | An Early Chalcolithic culture
Malwa culture | Madhya Pradesh | A pottery and cultural complex — Navdatoli (a Chalcolithic settlement)
Jorwe culture | Maharashtra | Village and agricultural settlements — Inamgaon (settlement archaeology)
Savalda culture | Maharashtra | A Chalcolithic tradition

t: Vedic rituals and officials
text:
## 1. Rituals and their associations
Ritual | Associated with
Yajna or sacrifice | The Yajurveda — it describes Vedic ritual procedures
Purushamedha | The Shatapatha Brahmana
Chanting in ceremonies | The Samaveda
Fire or Yagya rituals; burial rituals | The Indus Valley Civilization
Burial and post-burial rituals | The Megalithic culture
Ashvamedha — a Vedic royal ritual | Pravarasena I
Opposition to ritualism | Certain Bhakti and Sant traditions
Number of Sanskaras: 16
## 2. Vedic officials
Official | Function
Purohita | The chief priest — religious adviser to the king
Senani | Commander of the army
Gramani | Head of the village — a village-level authority
Bhagadugha | Revenue collector
Suta | Charioteer — associated with the royal court
Hotri / Hota | A Rigvedic priest who recited hymns
Adhvaryu | The priest responsible for the practical and manual aspects of sacrifice
Upadhyaya | A teacher who taught the Veda and Vedanga as a profession

t: Upanishads and Vedanta
text:
## 1. Upanishadic philosophy
Philosophical literature — philosophy for all times and for all
Universal approach — does not oppose any school of thought, religion or scriptural interpretation
Moksha: Liberation — part of Upanishadic philosophy; first discussed in the Upanishads
Atman: The concept — the core — of the self; not the body or mind
The human soul is associated with the life–death cycle — the continuous cycle of life and death is not the actual aim of the human soul
Katha Upanishad: A conversation between Yama and Nachiketa — on death and what lies beyond it
## 2. Upanishads and maxims
Upanishad | Maxim | Meaning
Mundakopanishad | The national motto — Satyameva Jayate | Truth alone triumphs
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad | The spiritual maxim Tamasoma Jyotirgamaya | Lead from darkness to light; from ignorance to truth
## 3. Vedanta
A philosophical system — literally Vedic philosophy; the end of the Vedas or the climax of Vedic ideology
Prasthanatrayi: The foundations of Vedanta — the Upanishads, Brahma Sutra and Bhagavad Gita
The Prime Prasthan: The Upanishads; the Bhagavata Prasthan is also associated with Vedanta
## 4. Yoga
A philosophical tradition — described in the Upanishads, Mahabharata, Bhagavad Gita, Jain texts and Buddhist texts
Patanjali later explained Yoga as a compact philosophical theory — Patanjali Darshan

t: Smriti texts and legal traditions
text:
## 1. Legal texts
Text | Associated with | Deals with
Manusmriti | Authored by Manu | Dharma and social/legal rules
Yajnavalkya Smriti | Yajnavalkya | The basis for Mitakshara
Mitakshara | Vijnanesvara | A commentary on inheritance
Dayabhaga | Jimutavahana | Inheritance
Smriti Chandrika | Devana Bhatta | Hindu law
Chaturvarga Chintamani | Hemadri | Dharma/legal literature
Parashar Madhav | Madhvacharya | Dharma/legal literature
Daan Sagar | Ballal Sena | Dharma/legal literature

t: Vedic religion and the Vedas
text:
## 1. Early Vedic religion
Nature worship and yajnas — Rigvedic religion was polytheistic
Deity | Key facts
Indra | The most powerful deity — called Purandara, destroyer of forts
Agni | Around 200 hymns dedicated to him
Soma | Associated with the ninth Mandala of the Rigveda
Varuna | Upheld Rita — called Ritasyagopa
All four were Rigvedic deities
Rita: A Vedic concept — cosmic order; natural order
Aghanya: A cow — not worthy of being killed
The Boghaz-Koi inscription mentioned Indra, Varuna, Mitra and Nasatya
## 2. The four Vedas
Veda | Association
Rigveda | The oldest Veda — contains hymns
Yajurveda | Rituals — sacrificial formulas and procedures
Samaveda | Ritual chanting — its verses were chanted during ceremonies
Atharvaveda | Religious and magical practices — spells and charms
## 3. Upanishadic concepts
Concept | Meaning
Brahman | Ultimate reality
Atman | The self
Karma | Connects action with consequence
Moksha | Liberation

t: Philosophical schools
text:
## 1. Six orthodox systems — Shad Darshana
Sankhya, Yoga, Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Mimamsa, Vedanta
⚠ Lokayata and Kapalika are not among the six orthodox systems
## 2. Schools in detail
Sankhya: Kapila — its earliest exponent; associated with Satkaryavada
Yoga: Patanjali — eight limbs:
Limb | Name
First | Yama
Second | Niyama
Third | Asana
Fourth | Pranayama
Fifth | Pratyahara
Sixth | Dharana
Seventh | Dhyana
Eighth | Samadhi
Mimamsa: A Vedic philosophy — Purva Mimamsa with Karmakanda; Uttara Mimamsa with Jnanakanda
Apurva — belongs to Mimamsa: an unseen force linking karma with its result
## 3. Vedanta schools and others
School | Associated with
Advaita Vedanta | Adi Shankaracharya
Vishishtadvaita | Ramanujacharya
Dvaita | Madhvacharya
Lokayata | Charvaka
Shunyavada | Nagarjuna
Pashupata | Lakulisha
Ajivika | Niyativada or determinism (fate)
Bauddha and Jain are Nastika schools
## 4. Charvaka
Also called Lokayata — materialism; direct perception
Dehatmavada: A Charvaka doctrine — closely identifies the body with consciousness

t: Buddhism
text:
## 1. Teachings and places
Four Noble Truths: Suffering; the cause of suffering; the cessation of suffering; the path
Dharmachakrapravartana Sutta: The first sermon at Sarnath
Place | Event in Buddha's life
Lumbini | Birth
Bodh Gaya | Enlightenment
Sarnath | First sermon
Kushinagar | Mahaparinirvana
## 2. The Sangha
A monastic order — women were admitted as Bhikshunis at Vaishali; Mahaprajapati was the first woman to enter the Sangha
Donors: Anathapindika donated Jetavana Vihara; Vishakha built Pubharama; Bimbisara built Venuvana
Chaitya: A place of worship and prayer; Vihara: a residence of monks; Stupa: relics and burial tradition
## 3. Texts and sects
Tripitaka: A Buddhist scripture — the Vinaya Pitaka (monastic rules); the Sutta Pitaka (Buddha's teachings, discourses); the Abhidhamma Pitaka (a philosophical exposition of Dhamma)
Digha Nikaya: Long Suttas; Mahavamsa: regional Buddhist history
Sarvastivada: A Buddhist sect — associated dharmas with the past, present and future
Vajrayana: Flourished particularly from the eighth century — Guhyasamaja is an important text

t: Jainism and the Ajivikas
text:
## 1. Tirthankaras
Jina: Conqueror — victor; Jainism recognizes 24 Tirthankaras
Tirthankara | Key facts
Rishabhdev — also called Adinath | The first Tirthankara
Parshvanath | The twenty-third — taught four restraints; Nirvana at Sammed Shikhar
Mahavira | The twenty-fourth — the last Tirthankara; born at Kundagram near Vaishali; Kaivalya at Jrimbhik village near the Rijupalika River; Nirvana at Pavapuri in 527 BCE
## 2. Doctrines
Five Mahavratas: Ahimsa, Satya, Brahmacharya, Asteya, Aparigraha
Triratna: Right Faith, Right Knowledge, Right Conduct
Samvara: Stoppage of karmic inflow; Nirjara: elimination of karma
Syadvada: Relativity of knowledge — associated with Saptabhanginaya
Sallekhana — also called Samadhi Maran: The last vow — gradual reduction of food and liquid
## 3. Sects and councils
Digambara: Sky-clad; Shwetambara: white-clad
First Jain Sabha: Pataliputra — Sthulabhadra; produced twelve Angas
Second Jain Sabha: Vallabhi — Devardhigani Kshamashraman
Jain literature includes the Agam
## 4. Ajivikas
Makkhali Gosala: A founder or leader of the Ajivikas — the Ajivika tradition
Niyativada: An Ajivika doctrine — fate; determinism
Patronised by Ashoka and Dasharatha; Barabar and Nagarjuni Caves were associated with Ajivika monks

t: Shaivism, Shaktism, Vaishnavism and Bhakti
text:
## 1. Shaiva sects
Sect | Key facts
Pashupata | Lakulisha
Kapalika | Bhairava; skull symbolism; cremation ashes
Lingayat | Basav
Nathpanth | Matsyendranath and Gorakhnath; regarded Shiva as Adinath
Mattamayura | Mentioned in Chedi inscriptions
All are associated with Shaivism
## 2. Shaktism
Associated with Hinduism — worship of Goddess Shakti
The Goddess Mahatmya: Belongs to the Markandeya Purana
Ardhanarishvara: Shaivism and Shaktism — the union of Shiva and Parvati
## 3. Vaishnavism
Associated with the Bhagavata tradition — developed from the Bhagavata religion
Heliodorus and the Besnagar Garuda Pillar: Associated with the Bhagavata religion
Vasudeva: Called Devadevas
The Guptas: Vaishnavism — called Parambhagavatas; Garuda symbolism
## 4. Bhakti
A religious movement — loving devotion towards God; originated in South India — the Dravida or Tamil region
Alvars: Devotees of Vishnu; Nayanars: devotees of Shiva
Saint | Key facts
Shankaracharya | Bhakti and philosophy — propounded Advaitavada
Ramanuja | Bhakti and philosophy — propounded Vishishtadvaita
Chaitanya Mahaprabhu | Vaishnava Bhakti — a devotee of Krishna; Bengal
Tulsidas | Wrote the Ramcharitmanas — in Awadhi
Kabir | Works: Sakhi, Sabad, Ramaini
Mirabai | A devotee of Krishna
Raskhan | A Muslim devotee of Krishna — wrote Prem Vatika

t: Sufism and Sikhism
text:
## 1. Sufism
Islamic mysticism — an ascetic and mystical tradition
Khanqah: A residence of Sufi saints; Sama: a musical and spiritual assembly; Auliya: saints — friends of God
## 2. Chishti saints
Muinuddin Chishti: Established or promoted the Chishti order in India — Ajmer
Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki: A Chishti saint — a disciple of Muinuddin Chishti
Baba Farid: Chishti order — the teacher of Nizamuddin Auliya
Nizamuddin Auliya: Chishti order — called Mehboob-i-Ilahi and Sultan-ul-Mashaikh
## 3. Sufi Silsilahs
Silsilah | Associated with
Chishti | Muinuddin Chishti; Ajmer
Suhrawardi | Bahauddin Zakariya; Multan, Punjab, Sindh
Firdausia | Sharfuddin Yahya Maneri; Bihar
Naqshbandi | Opposed Sama; emphasized Shariat; Ahmad Sirhindi
Qadiri | Followed the tradition of Abdul Qadir Jilani
## 4. Sikhism
Guru Nanak: Founded Sikhism — taught Ik Onkar and monotheism
Guru Arjan Dev: The fifth Sikh Guru — the Adi Granth, also called the Guru Granth Sahib
It included the compositions of Kabir, Baba Farid, Namdev and Raidas
Guru Tegh Bahadur: The ninth Sikh Guru — executed in Delhi in 1675
Guru Gobind Singh: The tenth — the last Sikh Guru; established the Khalsa in 1699
Five Ks of the Khalsa: Kesh, Kangha, Kachha, Kripan, Kada

t: Mughal religious policy and modern reform
text:
## 1. Akbar
Religious policy: Tolerance; accommodation; inter-religious discussions
Abolished the pilgrimage tax and jizya
Ibadat Khana: Established 1575 — for religious discussions; opened to different schools of religion in 1578
Mahzarnama: Dates to 1579 — a religious authority controversy
Din-i-Ilahi — also called Tauhid-i-Ilahi: Established 1582 — an ideology incorporating different traditions; Birbal was a Hindu associated with its acceptance
Aurangzeb: Reimposed jizya in 1679
## 2. Modern reform movements
Raja Ram Mohan Roy: Founded the Brahmo Sabha in 1828 — a modern reform movement
The Brahmo Samaj opposed idol worship, Sati and child marriage

topic: Mahajanapadas and the rise of Magadha
t: Rise of Magadha
text:
## 1. Early Magadha
Initial capital: Rajgriha — also called Girivraj — the first capital; Pataliputra the later capital
First dynasty according to the Puranas: The Brihadratha dynasty — Jarasandha, with his capital at Girivraj; associated with the Sabha Parva of the Mahabharata
## 2. Haryanka dynasty
Bimbisara:
Founded the Haryanka dynasty — the real (actual) founder of the (first) Magadhan Empire
The first great ruler according to Buddhist texts
A major role in the expansion of Magadha — conquered Anga; marriage alliances as an important diplomatic strategy
Died in 492 BCE
Ajatashatru — Ajathasatru, also known as Kunika:
The son and successor of Bimbisara — the next major ruler; killed Bimbisara
Ruled approximately 492 to 460 BCE
Founded Pataliputra; defeated and annexed Vajji; patronized the First Buddhist Council
Udayin: The son of Ajatashatru — succeeded him; the shift of the capital from Rajgriha to Pataliputra is attributed to him
## 3. Places
Place | Significance

Pataliputra — modern Patna | Hosted the Third Buddhist Council
Champa | The capital of Anga — annexed by Magadha
Varanasi — also Kashi | A marriage or diplomatic settlement

t: Alexander's Indian campaign
text:
## 1. Campaign
Indian campaign: 326 BC — left India in 325 BC
Contemporary ruler of Magadha: Dhanananda — Nanda dynasty; Greek name Agrammese; his commander Bhaddasala
## 2. Porus
Porus — also known as Puru: Territory between the Jhelum and Chenab rivers
Alexander fought Porus at the Jhelum River — known as the Hydaspes
After his defeat, Porus's kingdom was restored and he received additional territory
## 3. Others
Ashvaka: A frontier republic — capital Massaga; women took up arms during the resistance
Ambhi: The Indian ruler who supported Alexander
Return point: Paatal
## 4. Reasons for success
Political disunity — the notes cite 28 independent powers in India; a superior army; Indian allies
⚠ Chandragupta did not defeat Alexander

t: Foreign invaders
text:
## 1. Invaders in order
Invader | Period | Target / opponent | Result
Darius I — listed first | Approximately 522–486 BCE | Northwestern India | The first Persian invasion — the first ruler stated to have invaded parts of India
Alexander — listed second | Approximately 326 BCE | Punjab and northwestern India; opposed Porus | Defeated Porus at the Jhelum
Sakas — also called Scythians | Approximately the 1st century BCE | Western India | Later defeated by Chandragupta II
Kushanas | Approximately the 1st century CE | Northwestern India | Kanishka
Hunas | Approximately the 5th century CE — the Gupta period | The Gupta Empire | Skandagupta defeated the first Huna invasion; Toramana led the second Huna attack; Yashodharman defeated Mihirakula
Muhammad bin Qasim | 712 CE | Sindh — opposed Dahir | The Arab conquest of Sindh
Mahmud Ghazni | — | Northern India | 17 attacks — plunder
Muhammad Ghori | Began approximately 1175 CE and continued onward | Opposed Prithviraj and Jayachandra — fought at Tarain and Chandawar | Contributed to the foundation of Turkish power
Genghis Khan | The 13th century | The northwestern frontier | Reached the Indus during Iltutmish's reign
Timur | 1398 — the reign of Nasiruddin Mahmud Shah | Delhi | Invaded Delhi

Ahmad Shah Abdali | Began approximately 1748 and continued onward | Opposed the Marathas | Panipat in 1761 — the Third Battle of Panipat
Toramana and Mihirakula targeted India
## 2. Coinage of foreign rulers

Strato II: Lead coins
Kushanas: Extensively used gold and copper coins — promoted them on a wider scale
Rudradaman and the Saka-Kshatrapas: Silver and copper coinage
Chandragupta II: Silver Rupaka coins after his victory over the Sakas
Mahmud Ghazni: Silver coins with Arabic and Sanskrit legends
Muhammad Ghori: Coins bearing Lakshmi; some bore the Arabic Kalma

t: Shunga and Kanva dynasties
text:
## 1. Founding
Brihadratha: The last Mauryan ruler — assassinated by his commander Pushyamitra Shunga in 185 BCE
Pushyamitra Shunga: Founded the Shunga dynasty after killing Brihadratha — the transition from Maurya to Shunga
Shunga dynasty: Approximately 185 BCE to 73 BCE
Dynastic sequence: Maurya, Shunga, Kanva, Kushan
Magadha: A region associated with the Shungas; the ancestors of the Shungas originated from Ujjain
Pushyamitra was described as a Brahmin — the succeeding Kanvas were also described as Brahmins
## 2. Rituals and literature
Pushyamitra performed two Ashwamedha Yajnas — information from the Ayodhya Inscription
Patanjali: Belonged to the Shunga period — author of Mahabhashya; supervised the organization of the two Ashwamedha ceremonies; a contemporary of Pushyamitra
Agnimitra: The son of Pushyamitra — a Shunga ruler of Vidisha
Malavikagnimitram: Written by Kalidasa — his first play; the love story of Agnimitra of Vidisha and Malavika — Agnimitra is the protagonist
Mrichchhakatikam: Written by Sudraka
## 3. End of the Shungas
Devabhuti: The last Shunga ruler — killed by his minister, Amatya Vasudeva Kanva
The Kanva dynasty succeeded the Shungas — founded by Vasudeva Kanva

t: Kushanas
text:
## 1. Dynasty
The Kushana period: The 1st–3rd century CE — placed after the Mauryas, Shungas and Kanvas
Chronological order: Greeks (326 BCE), Sakas (1st century BCE), Kushanas (1st century CE)
The ruling house: The Kushana dynasty — the Kushana Empire extended beyond India
## 2. Rulers and coins
Kujula Kadphises: Circulated copper coins
Vima Kadphises: The father of Kanishka I
Title: Sarvalokeshvara — Sarvalokeshwar: "Lord of the Whole World"
The first Kushana ruler to issue gold coins — introduced them for regular use in India; the first to issue them on a large scale
Kanishka I: A major Kushana ruler — son of Vima Kadphises
Buddha was depicted on his coins
Chinese texts identify him as Yue-tche; he requested marriage with a Han princess — refused
The Kushanas marched against Pan Chao in 86 AD with 70,000 troops — defeated by a smaller Chinese force
Coronation: 78 AD — many historians consider 78 AD the origin of the Saka Samvat; the Saka–Vikrama difference was 135 years
## 3. Trade and art
Evidence of ports and trading centres: The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea; the Arikamedu excavation
Kushana trade operated through the Persian Bay and the Red Sea
Gandhara school: Developed and flourished during the Kushana period — based on the Indo-Greek style; influenced by Greek art; Kanishka encouraged and protected it
Gandhara and Mathura developed distinct sculptural styles
## 4. Fourth Buddhist Council
Held at Kundalvana in Kashmir in the 1st century AD, during Kanishka's reign
President: Vasumitra (a Buddhist scholar who headed it); vice-president: Ashvaghosha
Resulted in the division of Buddhism into Hinayana and Mahayana — Mahayana treated the Buddha as God; idol worship became associated with it
## 5. Kanishka's court
Scholars: Parshva, Ashvaghosha, Nagarjuna, Charaka — ⚠ Patanjali was not — he belonged to the Shunga period and authored Mahabhashya
Ashvaghosha: The poet laureate — authored Saundarananda, Buddhacharita and Sariputrapakaran
Charaka: The court physician
## 6. Inscriptions
Sarnath Buddhist image inscription: Dated 81 AD — three years after Kanishka's coronation
Rabatak inscription: Found in 1993 near Surkh Kotal in Afghanistan — Greek script, Bactrian language; names Kanishka; mentions Saket, Kaushambi, Pataliputra and Sri Champa
## 7. Yaudheyas and "Fallen Kshatriyas"
Yaudheya copper coins: Six-headed Kartikeya with a peacock — associated with the Kushana period; the Yaudheyas are mentioned in the Puranas and the Ashtadhyayi
The Manusmriti described Shakas, Kushans, Hunas and Pratiharas who did not follow priestly customs or local traditions as "Fallen Kshatriyas"

t: Maukharis and Harsha
text:
## 1. Maukharis
Capital: Kannauj; originated in Gaya
Maukhari rulers: Harivarma, Adityavarma, Ishvaravarma, Sharvavarma, Grahavarma
## 2. Harsha
Original base: Thanesar — shifted his capital to Kannauj (his capital after Thanesar)
Kannauj Assembly: A religious assembly presided over by Harshavardhana — attended by rulers of 20 countries, Brahmins, Shramanas and courtiers
Mahamoksha Council: At the Prayagraj Sangam — every fifth year
Defeated by Pulakesin II on the Narmada — sources: the Aihole Inscription and Hiuen Tsang's account
## 3. Sources
Harshacharita: A main source — authored by Banabhatta
Hiuen Tsang: A Chinese traveller of Harsha's reign — arrived in India in 629 AD

t: Kannauj and the Tripartite Struggle
text:
## 1. Kannauj
After Harsha, Kannauj became a centre of attraction for competing powers — also known as Mahodaya and Mahodayashri
## 2. Tripartite Struggle
Objective: Control of Kannauj — 8th–9th century CE
Participants: The Pala, Gurjara-Pratihara and Rashtrakuta dynasties
## 3. Pratiharas
Founded by Nagabhata I; first capital Ujjain, later capital Kannauj
Chronology: Vatsaraja → Nagabhata II → Mahendrapala I → Mahipala
Mihir Bhoja: Captured Kannauj around 836 AD and made it his capital
Titles: Adivaraha; Prabhasa — followed Vaishnavism
Suleman identified him as the ruler; Al-Masudi called the kingdom Al-Juzr and Bhoja Baura

topic: Dynasties of the Deccan and South India
t: Badami Chalukyas
text:
## 1. Dynasty
Also called the Chalukyas of Badami or Vatapi Chalukyas — c. 543 to 753 CE
Capital: Vatapi — present-day Badami in Bagalkot, Karnataka; Badami and Vatapi were associated with the Chalukyas
Chalukya rule was mainly confined to the Deccan and Southern India — ⚠ not mainly in North India
## 2. Rulers
Ruler | Ruled — reign | Key facts
Pulakeshin I | c. 543 to 566 CE | Founded — the real founder of — the Vatapi Chalukya dynasty; the Ashvamedha
Kirtivarman I | c. 566 to 598 CE | Annexed the Kadambas, Gangas and Mauryas of Konkan
Mangalesha | — | An important ruler between Kirtivarman I and Pulakeshin II
Pulakeshin II | 610 to 642 CE | The most capable and most powerful Chalukya ruler
Vikramaditya I | c. 655 to 680 CE | Restored Chalukya power after the Pallava invasion
Vikramaditya II | c. 733 to 746 CE | Defeated the Pallavas three times; captured Kanchi
Kirtivarman II | c. 746 to 753 CE | The last ruler — overthrown by Rashtrakuta Dantidurga
## 3. Pulakeshin II
Defeated or stopped Harshavardhana on the Narmada — 630–634 CE; Pulakeshin II and Harsha were an important enemy pair
Title: Dakshinapatheshwara — "Lord of the Deccan"
Received a Persian embassy from Khusrau II around 626 CE
Pallava king Narasimhavarman I captured and destroyed Vatapi in 642 CE — assumed the title Vatapikonda; Narasimhavarman I and Pulakeshin II were an important enemy pair
Aihole Inscription: A key source — composed by Ravikirti; Sanskrit and Southern Brahmi; dated 634 CE according to the Saka era; preserved at the Meguti Jain Temple
Mentions Kalidasa and Bharavi — Ravikirti compared his fame with theirs
Lohnara inscription: 630 CE — does not mention Harsha among the defeated enemies
## 4. Other records
A seventh-century inscription concerning Vikramaditya I — discovered at Madapura Lake in Davangere; concerns land-grant practices
## 5. Women
The Chalukyas frequently gave high-ranking administrative positions to women
Vijaya Bhattarika: Queen of Chandraditya — issued two copper plates in her own name; a poetess; administered the kingdom after her husband's death
Kumkumdevi: Sister of Vikramaditya I — her recommendation led to the grant of a village to a Jain monastery
## 6. Architecture
Badami: Rock-cut caves — four rock-cut temples; Caves 1–3 are Hindu temples; Cave 4 a Jain temple
Aihole: Experimental or early temples
Pattadakal: A Chalukya architectural centre — a synthesis of Nagara and Dravida styles
Vesara: A hybrid of Nagara and Dravida styles — associated with the Chalukya style
Ma-Twa-Lin — also called Matwalin: A Chinese traveller — an account of China–India relations during Chalukya rule
Associations: Kanchi with the Pallavas; Tanjore with the Cholas

topic: Dynasties of the Deccan and South India
t: Eastern Chalukyas, Rashtrakutas and Kalyani Chalukyas
text:
## 1. Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi
Also known as the Chalukyas of Vengi — originated as a branch of the Badami Chalukyas
Founded by Kubja Vishnuvardhana — brother of Pulakeshin II
Core region and capital: Vengi in present-day Andhra Pradesh; Rajamahendravaram — also Rajahmundry — later an important centre
An important power in Andhra–Deccan politics — repeated political interaction and conflict with the Cholas
Rajaraja Narendra: A major ruler — connected with the Chola royal family through marriage; associated with Rajamahendravaram; patronised Nannaya
Nannaya began the translation of the Telugu Mahabharata — the Andhra Mahabharatam
The period was an important phase in the development of Telugu literary tradition
Succession became intertwined with the Chola dynasty — Rajendra Chalukya, also known as Kulottunga I, emerged from the Eastern Chalukya–Chola line and united the two political traditions
Region map: Badami — Karnataka; Vengi — Andhra Pradesh
Matwalin: A traveller associated with an account of China–India relations during Chalukya rule
## 2. Rashtrakutas
Dantidurga established the Rashtrakuta dynasty — Empire — in 753 AD; performed the Hiranyagarbha ritual at Ujjayini
Capital: Manyakheta
Amoghavarsha I: An important ruler — born in 800 AD at Shribhavan (on or near the Narmada) in a military camp
Participated in the Tripartite Struggle for Kannauj — Govind III defeated Gurjara-Pratihara ruler Nagabhata II during a North Indian campaign
Religion: Patronized Shaiva, Vaishnava and Shakta traditions; an inclination toward Jainism — Jinasena, a Jain scholar, authored the Adipurana
Kailasa Temple at Ellora: Built by Krishna I — Cave 16; Dravidian architecture; designed to recall Mount Kailasa — Shiva's abode
Ellora: Buddhist, Hindu and Jain rock-cut caves coexist
The Elephanta Caves were built by the Rashtrakutas
Stated chronology: Mahendravarman I → Gopala → Mihir Bhoja
## 3. Kalyani Chalukyas
Also known as the Western Chalukyas — approximately 973 to 1195 CE; a distinctive Deccan cultural tradition
Overthrew the Rashtrakutas in 973 CE — led by Tailapa II
Kalyani Chalukya style: Dravida influences with Deccan innovation — ornate pillars; stepped superstructures; decorated doorways; intricate wall motifs; balanced proportions
Temples: Kasivisvesvara at Lakkundi; Mahadeva at Itagi; Doddabasappa at Dambal — the Lakkundi–Gadag–Itagi tradition was a regional tradition
Sculptures: Deities, dancers, musicians, mythical figures; floral and geometric motifs — increasing ornamentation and dynamism; fine detailing
A precursor to the Hoysala tradition
Literature: Royal patronage enabled Sanskrit and Kannada to flourish
Author | Work
Someshvara III | Manasollasa
Bilhana | Vikramankadeva Charita
Vijnaneshwara | Mitakshara
Nagavarma II | Kavyavalokana; Karnataka Bhashabhushana

topic: Dynasties of the Deccan and South India
t: Imperial Cholas
text:
## 1. Rulers
Imperial Chola period: Approximately the 9th to the 13th century CE
Ruler | Ruled — reign | Key facts
Vijayalaya Chola | — | Founded the Imperial Chola dynasty; captured Tanjavur
Aditya I | — | Defeated the Pallava ruler Aparajita; expanded northward
Parantaka I | — | Defeated the Pandyas and Sri Lanka; lost the Battle of Thakkolam to the Rashtrakutas in 949 CE
Rajaraja I | 985 to 1014 CE | Major imperial expansion; captured northern Sri Lanka; destroyed Anuradhapura; the first Chola king to create a naval army (as credited in the source); conquered the Maldives
Rajendra I | 1014 to 1044 CE | Captured the southern part of Sri Lanka — completed the conquest of Ceylon; defeated Mahinda V; conquered the Ganga valley; built Gangaikonda Cholapuram around 1035 CE and the Chola Gangam (a huge artificial lake); naval expedition against Kadaram and Srivijaya in 1025 CE
Kulottunga I | 1070 to 1122 CE | Abolished tolls; gave complete freedom to Sri Lanka; married his daughter to a Sinhala prince
Rajendra III | 1246 to 1279 CE | —
The Battle of Thakkolam (949 CE) was fought between the Cholas and the Rashtrakutas
## 2. Maritime network and trade
Extended from Sri Lanka to the Malay Peninsula, from the Malay Peninsula to Sumatra, and from Sumatra to Southeast Asia
Merchant guilds: Ayyavole 500; Manigramam
## 3. Administration
Ur: Ordinary villages; Sabha: Brahmana villages; Nagaram: merchant towns
Uttaramerur: Village self-government — the Kudavolai system; Variyams — specialized village committees
Hierarchy: Mandalam → Kottam or Valanadu → Nadu → Ur
Extensive temple-wall inscriptions — an unusually rich historical record; the Thanjavur inscription records Rajaraja I's military achievements and the defeat of a Chera naval force at Kandallur
## 4. Temples and art
Dravida style; monumental temples that served as cultural centres
Brihadeeswara Temple — also the Peruvudaiyar Temple: Thanjavur; Rajaraja I; completed 1010 CE; a granite vimana approximately 66 metres high
Great Living Chola Temples: The Brihadeeswara Temple; Gangaikondacholapuram (Rajendra I); the Airavatesvara Temple at Darasuram (Rajaraja II)
Chola bronzes: The lost-wax technique — Nataraja
Literature: Patronized Tamil and Sanskrit literature — Kamban wrote Ramavataram
Religious life: Emphasized Shaivism — temple institutions supported music, dance and festivals

topic: Dynasties of the Deccan and South India
t: Hoysalas, Yadavas and Kakatiyas
text:
## 1. Hoysalas
Karnataka — capital Dwarasamudra, present-day Halebidu (Hassan district) — famous for Hoysala architectural heritage
Hoysaleshwara Temple: Halebidu — dedicated to Shiva; 12th–13th century; architect Kedroz; construction associated with Narasimha I's reign
Chennakeshava Temple: Belur — built by Vishnuvardhana; dedicated to Vishnu
Halebidu and Belur are Hoysala monuments
Architecture: A distinctive style — star-shaped or stellate plans; soft chlorite-schist stone; lathe-turned pillars; mantapas, kalyanis, pushkaranis; blends Nagara and Dravidian styles
Sculpture: Highly detailed friezes; mythological depictions
After Ballala III's death (1343 CE), Hoysala territories were absorbed into the emerging Vijayanagara sphere
## 2. Yadavas of Devagiri
A medieval South Indian dynasty — the 12th century to the mid-14th century; ruled around 1187–1317 AD in western India
Initially feudatories of the Western Chalukyas; also known as the Seuna rulers of Devagiri
Capital: Devagiri — the realm was in western India and the Deccan, centred on Devagiri
## 3. Kakatiyas
The Eastern Deccan — 12th–14th centuries CE; capital Warangal
Rulers: Rudradeva — also Pratap Rudradeva I; Mahadeva (after Rudradeva); Ganapati Dev — father of Rudrama Devi
Rudrama Devi: Daughter of Ganapati Dev — the fourth independent ruler; a female ruler
Defeated the Pandyas (of South Tamil Nadu), the Eastern Gangas (rulers of Orissa) and the Seuna rulers of Devagiri
The Kakatiyas had a conflict with the Seuna, or Yadava, rulers of Devagiri

t: Ancient battles and conquests
text:
## 1. Battles
Battle — fought / occurred | Year | Between — leaders | Result and significance
Battle of 10 Kings — also called Dasharajnya | — | Sudas — the leader — and a confederacy of 10 kings | Sudas won a decisive victory; mentioned in the Rigveda
Battle of Hydaspes — the ancient period | 326 BCE | Alexander and Porus — the leaders | Alexander defeated Porus — part of Alexander's Indian campaign; an Alexander–India linkage; Hydaspes is the ancient name of the Jhelum
Mauryan–Seleucid conflict | 305 BC | Chandragupta Maurya and Seleucus | Chandragupta Maurya defeated Seleucus
Kalinga War — Battle of Kalinga; the ancient period | 261 BC — 261 BCE | The Mauryas — Ashoka, the leader — and Kalinga | Ashoka conquered Kalinga — a turning point in his life; transformed him; strengthened his association with Buddhism and Dhamma; strategically important for eastern sea routes, overseas trade and Deccan routes
## 2. Persian and Greek invasions
Darius-I (ruled 522–486 BC): Targeted — conquered parts of — northwestern India: the Indus region, Punjab and Rajputana
Part of Persian expansion — the first Persian ruler associated with capturing parts of India; the Persian invasion led to Persian influence in north-western India
Alexander: The Greek invasion — targeted northwestern India; invaded India in 326 BC — 326 BCE; defeated Porus at the Hydaspes; his army was stopped at the Beas
## 3. Gupta-period conflicts
Saka conflict: Chandragupta-II Vikramaditya defeated Rudrasimha-III — the last Saka ruler — during the Gupta period; a Western India campaign; Chandragupta-II assumed the Sakari title and defeated the Sakas
Gupta–Huna conflict: Skandagupta defeated the Hunas — the first Huna invasion occurred during his reign — recorded in the Bhitari Pillar Inscription
Toramana led the second Huna invasion; Mihirakula was defeated by Yashodharman
## 4. Early medieval
Battle of Takkolam — the early medieval period: 949 CE — the Cholas (led by Rajaditya) and a Rashtrakuta-led confederacy (Western Gangas and Vaidumbas, led by Krishna III) — Rajaditya and Krishna III were the leaders; the Rashtrakuta side won; a major Chola–Rashtrakuta conflict

t: Arab, Turkish and Mongol invasions
text:
## 1. Arab invasion of Sindh
Muhammad-bin-Qasim: Targeted and conquered Sindh in 712 AD — also given as 711–12 CE; an Arab invasion (conquest)
Dahir was defeated and killed by him
Arab expansion — his conquest — remained largely limited (confined) to Sindh and Multan
## 2. Mahmud Ghazni
Invaded India during 1000–1027 — repeated invasions: 17 times
Main objective: Wealth and plunder
Attacked Mathura, Thanesar and the famous Somnath temple — the Somnath campaign 1025–1026
## 3. Muhammad Ghori
Campaign — occurred / took place | Year | Result
First invasion of India — his first attack | 1175 | —
Gujarat campaign — the Gujarat conflict | 1178 | Defeated by Mularaja-II/Bhimdev-II — his first defeat in India; Naika Devi acted as regent; associated with Mount Abu
First Battle of Tarain | 1191 | Prithviraj Chauhan — who led it — won; Ghori defeated
Second Battle of Tarain | 1192 | Muhammad Ghori — who led the victorious side — defeated Prithviraj Chauhan; it reversed the result of the 1st Battle
Battle of Chandawar | 1194 | Ghori defeated Jayachandra — also known as Jaichand — near the Yamuna
His invasion had a major impact — it led to the foundation of the Delhi Sultanate
Both battles of Tarain were fought between Prithviraj Chauhan and Muhammad Ghori
## 4. Mongols and Timur
Genghis Khan: Reached the Indus during Iltutmish's reign — his threat or entry into Indian history in 1221 CE
Alauddin Khalji's reign: Repeated Mongol invasions — contributed to a large standing army, military reforms and revenue reforms
Ghazi Malik: Defeated the Mongols in 1320 — chased them 29 times; later became Ghiyasuddin Tughluq
Timur — also known as Taimur: Invaded Delhi in 1398 — "Timur's invasion"; severely weakened the Delhi Sultanate; associated with Nasiruddin Mahmud Tughlaq
## 5. Nadir Shah and Abdali
Nadir Shah: Targeted North India and Delhi — invaded in 1739; defeated the Mughals at the Battle of Karnal (1739); sacked Delhi; took the Koh-i-Noor and the Peacock Throne
Ahmad Shah Abdali — also known as Ahmad Shah Durrani: Invaded North India — defeated the Marathas at the Third Battle of Panipat (1761) — a major setback to Maratha expansion

t: Sultanate-era and Vijayanagara campaigns
text:

Bakhtiyar Khalji:
Conquered Bihar during 1193–1203 — part of Ghurid expansion; destroyed Nalanda and Vikramshila; captured Odantpur
Conquered Bengal during 1198–1203 — captured or entered Nadiya; Lakshman Sen fled to East Bengal; captured Lakhnauti
## 2. Delhi succession
Khizr Khan: Defeated Daulat Khan — took Delhi in 1414; connected with the Delhi succession; founded the Sayyid Khan Dynasty
## 3. Vijayanagara expansion
Kumara Kampana: Conquered Madurai during 1352–53 — annexed to Vijayanagara; Madhura Vijayam is associated with Ganga Devi
Harihara-II: Captured Goa and Belgaum from the Bahamani in 1380 — the Vijayanagara–Bahamani conflict; expanded into Kanara, Mysore, Kanchi and Trichinapalli
## 4. Rajput resistance
Rao Jaitsi: The ruler of Bikaner — defeated Kamran Mirza in the Bikaner conflict

Battle of Kannauj / Kanauj — also called the Battle of Bilgram | 1540 | Sher Shah defeated Humayun — Humayun lost effective control over North India
Battle of Sirhind | 1555 | Humayun defeated Afghan forces — reoccupied Delhi
Chausa preceded Bilgram in the sequence of battles
## 3. Akbar-era battles
Second Battle of Panipat (1556): Akbar's forces — led by him — and Hemu's forces; Akbar's side won — consolidated Mughal power
Battle of Talikota (1565): The combined Deccan Sultanates — Bijapur, Ahmadnagar and Golconda (major opposing forces) — defeated Vijayanagara; a watershed battle that weakened Vijayanagara
Battle of Haldighati (1576): Mughal forces (Akbar's, led by Man Singh) and Rana Pratap's forces (Maharana Pratap) — a Mughal victory; associated with Akbar and Rana Pratap; ⚠ the result is treated with nuance

t: Carnatic Wars, Plassey and Buxar
text:
## 1. Carnatic Wars
War / battle | Years | Between | Result
First Carnatic War | 1746 to 1748 | The English and the French | The British regained Madras; the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748)
Battle of Ambur — part of the Second Carnatic War | 1749 | Muzaffar Jang (Jung), Chanda Sahib and the French against Anwar-ud-din | Anwar-ud-din was defeated and killed; Chanda Sahib gained control of the Carnatic
Second Carnatic War | 1749 to 1754 | English- and French-backed Indian factions | Inconclusive
Third Carnatic War | 1758 to 1763 | The British and the French — Count Lally led the French | The British defeated the French — ended French power in India; the Treaty of Paris (1763)
Battle of Wandiwash — decisive in the Third Carnatic War | 1760 | British forces under Sir Eyre Coote and Count Lally's (Count de Lally's) French forces | The British won — defeated the French
## 2. Bengal
Battle | Year | Between | Result
Battle of Plassey | 1757 | The British (led by Robert Clive) and Siraj-ud-daula (Siraj-ud-Daulah) | Established British control over Bengal — associated with treachery; the beginning of British supremacy
Battle of Buxar | 1764 | The British (led by Hector Munro) and the allied forces of Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daula and Shah Alam II | A major British victory — further consolidation of British supremacy; the Treaty of Allahabad — concluded in 1765

t: Mysore, Maratha and Sikh wars; 1857
text:
## 1. Anglo-Mysore Wars
War / battle — fought / occurred / took place | Year | Key facts
First Anglo-Mysore War | 1767 to 1769 | The British and Mysore — Haidar Ali led Mysore and was victorious; the Treaty of Madras — concluded in 1769
Battle of Pollilur | 10 September 1780 | Haidar Ali and Tipu Sultan (who led the Mysore side) defeated Colonel Baillie — a major British defeat
Second Anglo-Mysore War | 1780 to 1784 | The British and Mysore — Haidar Ali and Tipu Sultan; a major Anglo-Mysore conflict; Haidar Ali allied with the Nizam and the Marathas
Battle of Porto Novo | July 1781 | British forces under Sir Eyre Coote defeated Haidar Ali — a British victory that reversed the British defeat at Pollilur in 1780; part of the Second Anglo-Mysore War
Fourth Anglo-Mysore War | 1799 | The British fought Tipu Sultan — Tipu Sultan died in 1799
## 2. Anglo-Maratha Wars and Kharda
First Anglo-Maratha War (1775 to 1782): The British and the Marathas — the British suffered defeat; the Treaty of Salbai (1782)
Second Anglo-Maratha War: Lord Wellesley and Peshwa Baji Rao II — associated with the Subsidiary Alliance
Third Anglo-Maratha War: Lord Hastings led the British — established British supremacy over the Marathas; ended in 1818
Battle of Kharda — also called Khurda (1795): The Marathas defeated the Nizam — a Maratha victory
## 3. Sikhs
Battle of Chillianwala (13 January 1849): The British (Lord Gough) and the Sikhs — Sher Singh; undecided — ⚠ not a simple decisive British victory
Punjab was annexed by the British in 1849 — the British conquered Punjab and defeated the Sikh Empire after the Second Anglo-Sikh War; associated with Lord Dalhousie; Duleep Singh — the last Sikh ruler

topic: Coins, revenue and the agrarian economy
t: Metals and early coinage
text:
## 1. Metals
The first metal used by humans: copper
Indus Valley: Copper and bronze — Harappan evidence includes gold, silver, copper and brass; ⚠ iron was not found at Harappan sites
Rigvedic Aryans: Gold, silver, copper
Iron: Spread in North India during 1000–600 BC — the Iron Age in India during the Later Vedic period, around 1000 BC
## 2. Punch-marked coins
Also called Aahat coins — early India; mainly silver; the earliest extant coins
Date from the 7th–6th century BC to the Mauryan period
## 3. Indo-Greek coins
Introduced the circulation of gold coins in north-western India — issued gold coins in the 2nd century BC
Strato II: Important Indo-Greek lead coins
Agathocles: Silver coins featuring Sankarshana and Vasudeva — bilingual legends in Greek and Brahmi
Sixteen coins of Menander were discovered at Bairat — a site of coin discovery

topic: Coins, revenue and the agrarian economy
t: Coinage of later dynasties
text:
## 1. Kushanas
Associated with the first gold coins — gold coins had wider, regular and large-scale circulation; copper coins circulated extensively; Kushana coins contained gold and copper
Vima Kadphises: The first Kushana ruler to issue gold coins — used them regularly on a large scale
Kujula Kadphises: Early Kushana copper coinage
Kanishka: Gold and copper coins bearing Buddha
Yaudheya coins: Standing Kartikeya with a peacock
## 2. Saka-Kshatrapas
Gold-to-silver ratio: 1:35 (the Saka-Kshatrpa ratio)
Chastana: Karddamaka dynasty — silver and copper coins; his coins were rare — the copper coins relatively rare
## 3. Satavahanas
Coinage used — coins contained — lead, copper, bronze, silver and potin — ⚠ not gold: gold was absent
Lead and copper were major metals
Potin: An alloy of copper, silver and lead
## 4. Guptas and Kalachuris
Gupta gold coins: Dinara or Dinar; silver coins: Rupaka — Gupta coins contained gold and silver
Chandragupta I: The first Gupta ruler to issue coins — the first Gupta coin issuer
Chandragupta II: Silver Rupaka coins — associated with his victory over the Sakas; known as Sakari
The maximum number of Gupta coins was found at Bayana in Bharatpur, Rajasthan — a major Gupta coin hoard site
Kalachuri coins: Gold, silver and copper
## 5. Sultanate and Sur
Muhammad Ghori: A Muslim ruler's coins bearing Lakshmi — and the Arabic Kalma
Iltutmish: Introduced regular Sultanate coinage — silver and copper coins; made Delhi the capital
His silver coin was mentioned as weighing 175 grams
Placed the Khalifa's name on his coins after recognition by the Abbasid Caliph
Tanka: A silver coin introduced by him; Jital: a copper coin associated with him
Sher Shah currency: Pure gold, silver and copper
Coin | Weight
Sher Shah Rupiya | 178 grains — 173 grains of pure silver
Copper Daam | 380 grains
Exchange ratio: Rupiya to Daam — 1:64

topic: Coins, revenue and the agrarian economy
t: Ancient and medieval revenue terms
text:
## 1. Ancient taxes
Term | Meaning
Bhaga / Bhag | The share of agricultural produce paid as tax — under the Guptas the cultivator paid one-sixth of production
Bali | An important source of revenue in ancient India
Sita | Revenue from crown or state land
Hiranya | A cash tax under the Mauryans — a cash payment instead of payment in produce
Udrang / Udranga | Land revenue under the Guptas
Udakabhog | An irrigation tax under the Guptas
Uparnika | A tax on farmers living on border land under the Guptas
Vishti | Forced labour under the Guptas — treated as a source of state income or tax; associated with Junagadh inscriptions and Gupta copper inscriptions
Irai and Vari | General Chola terms for tax or revenue
Uppayam | The salt tax under the Cholas
Valiam | A tax on specific commodities
Gupta tax-free land grants: Agrarian land given to Brahmins and religious functionaries
## 2. Medieval terms
Term | Meaning
Iqta | A revenue assignment in the Delhi Sultanate
Khalisa | Land under direct state control
Jagir | A revenue assignment to a Mansabdar or Jagirdar
Zabt | A Mughal land-revenue assessment system
Maal | Land revenue under the Mughals
Madad-i-Mash | A revenue-free land grant under the Mughals — to learned, pious and worthy persons; associated with saints, religious institutions and mashaikhs
Jizya | A tax imposed on non-Muslims
Zakat | A religious tax on Muslims
Chauth | A Maratha levy — generally one-fourth; an important Maratha revenue claim
Sardeshmukhi | A Maratha levy — generally 10%; an important Maratha revenue claim
Hundi | A credit or bill-of-exchange instrument
Dagh | The branding of horses in Sultanate military administration

topic: Coins, revenue and the agrarian economy
t: Sultanate and Mughal revenue policy
text:
## 1. Alauddin Khalji
Based revenue collection on measuring land — the first Sultan associated with systematic land measurement
Diwan-i-Mustakharaj: A revenue administration and recovery department
Abolished the traditional tax-collection privileges of Khutts, Mukaddams and Chaudharys — collected revenue more directly; weakened intermediary tax collectors
Reclaimed Milq and Waqf lands — expanded Khalisa land
Taxes: Kharaj — a land tax fixed at 50% of the yield; Ghari — a house tax; Charai — a grazing tax on milch animals
## 2. Firuz Tughlaq
Haqq-e-Sharb: An irrigation tax — 10% of the crop yield
## 3. Akbar
Dahsala or Zabti system: Average produce and prices calculated over ten years
State share: One-third of the produce; cultivator's share: two-thirds
## 4. Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb
Shah Jahan: Levied a pilgrim tax at Banaras and Allahabad — Kavindracharya and Banaras pandits sought its abolition
Aurangzeb: Imposed Jizya on non-Muslims — income-based rates
Exempt: Women, slaves, children below 14, beggars, unemployed persons
Income | Jizya rate per year
Below 200 dirhams | 12 dirhams
200 to 10,000 dirhams | 24 dirhams
Above 10,000 dirhams | 48 dirhams
## 5. Abolitions
Ruler | Abolished
Akbar | Jizya; the pilgrimage tax; his reign abolished child marriage and Sati
Sikandar Lodi | The tax on grains — also described as several grain levies
Alauddin Khalji | The privileges of the Khutt, Mukaddam and Chaudhary
Zain-ul-Abidin of Kashmir | Jizya; cow slaughter
Shah Jahan | Sijda — an Iranian court tradition

topic: Coins, revenue and the agrarian economy
t: Revenue in the national movement
text:
## 1. Salt
The Salt Tax was a major target of Gandhian protest — associated with the Civil Disobedience Movement
Gandhi broke the Salt Law through salt-making at Dandi
C. Rajagopalachari: Led the Vedaranyam Satyagraha — collected salt from the sea
## 2. Champaran
Plantation owners increased taxes on peasants and imposed other illegal exactions — associated with indigo exploitation; Gandhi led the Champaran movement against it
Teen Kathiya: Forced indigo cultivation on three-twentieths of the land — associated with indigo cultivation in Champaran
## 3. Kheda
Crop failure led to revenue demands — Kheda farmers faced them despite crop failure and sought relief from land revenue
The Kheda revenue demand led to the Kheda Satyagraha

topic: Coins, revenue and the agrarian economy

text:
## 1. Crops through history
Barley: The first cereal cultivated by humans — around 8000 BC; Mahagara provides early evidence
Paddy: Lahuradeva — the oldest evidence; Koldihwa was earlier considered the oldest site
Harappan crops: Wheat, barley and rice; cotton agriculture — textiles and trade
Uraiyur: Associated with cotton trade
Ibn Battuta: Rice (in suitable regions), wheat, sugarcane and cotton could be cultivated thrice a year in medieval India
Spices were cultivated in southern India during the medieval period
Maize: ⚠ Not cultivated in India during the 13th–14th centuries — the Portuguese brought or introduced it

Sangam society | Agriculture, fishing, hunting, crafts, trade

All were associated with Firoz Shah Tughlaq

## 4. South Indian irrigation
Kallanai — also the Grand Anicut: Karikala Chola — irrigation and agricultural development
Tank irrigation: The Cholas — a major feature of the agricultural economy
Tanks and reservoirs: The Vijayanagara rulers — irrigation and water management

t: Mughal painting
text:
## 1. Humayun and Akbar
Humayun laid the foundation of Mughal painting
Mir Sayyid Ali: A Persian painter — associated with early Mughal painting
Khwaja Abdus Samad: A Persian painter — helped establish the Mughal atelier
Atelier — Tasvir Khana: Associated with Akbar — an imperial painting workshop; also called a Painting Karkhana
Akbar established Painting Karkhanas at Agra, Fatehpur Sikri and Lahore
European painting: Introduced at the Mughal court by Akbar through the Portuguese — European influence included portraiture and the depiction of smaller distant objects for spatial depth
Daswant and Basawan: Major Mughal painters during Akbar's period
Dastan-i-Amir Hamza: Begun under Humayun and continued under Akbar — supervised by Mir Sayyid Ali and Khwaja Abdus Samad; approximately 100 artists worked on it; approximately 1,400 paintings
## 2. Jahangir — the zenith
Mughal painting reached its zenith — the Golden Age of Mughal painting — during Jahangir's period
Themes included: Portraits, birds, flowers, animals and nature
Shift from manuscripts toward albums; a rise in individual portraits
Jahangir patronised European and Persian arts
Painter | Speciality | Title — received
Abul Hasan | A portrait painter | Nadir-ul-Zaman
Ustad Mansur | Painted birds, animals, plants and nature | Nadir-ul-Asra
Other major painters: Farrukh Beg, Bishan Das, Aqa Reza, Muhammad Nadir, Muhammad Murad, Manohar, Govardhan and Madhav
## 3. Decline
Mughal painting declined during Aurangzeb's period

t: Colonial land revenue systems
text:
## 1. Three settlements compared
Basis | Permanent Settlement | Ryotwari Settlement | Mahalwari Settlement
Associated with | Lord Cornwallis | Thomas Munro and Alexander Read | The mahal or village community
Introduced | 1793 | Began in the early 19th century | The 19th century
Mainly covered | Bengal, Bihar, Odisha, Varanasi | Madras, parts of Bombay, Assam, Coorg; also Eastern Bengal | Uttar Pradesh, the Central Provinces, Punjab; North-Western Provinces included
Revenue relationship — established | Government–zamindar | Government–ryot | Government–village or mahal
Landholder | The zamindar | The peasant or ryot | The village community or collective
Revenue | Permanently fixed | Periodically assessed | Periodically revised
Share of British-occupied area — covered approximately | 19% | 51% | 30%
## 2. Permanent Settlement
Also known as the Zamindari system — recognised zamindars as proprietors or landowners
Zamindari rights: Hereditary; transferable or saleable
Sunset Clause: Required revenue payment by a prescribed sunset deadline — failure to pay led to the auction of the zamindari
Strengthened landlords; increased pressure on peasants
Bengal Tenancy Act: Enacted in 1885 — applied to Bengal and Bihar; dealt with the rights of landlords and tenants
## 3. Ryotwari Settlement
First Ryotwari association: Began in 1792 onward in Baramahal, Tamil Nadu — Alexander Read, assisted by Thomas Munro
Initial revenue demand: 50% of the estimated produce
The ryot or peasant recognised as the proprietor — directly paid revenue to the Government
Thomas Munro: Governor of Madras from 1820 to 1827 — extended it to almost all parts of Madras except permanently settled areas; known as the Father of Ryotwari
⚠ No automatic general exemption after a bad harvest — occasional remission or reduction of revenue was possible
## 4. Mahalwari and Taluqdari
Mahalwari: Revenue assessment based on the village or community
Taluqdari System: Associated with Awadh or Oudh — ⚠ not with Bombay

t: Caste and anti-caste reform

## 1. Varna and Jati
Varna: A four-fold social classification — the four Varnas are Brahmana, Kshatriya, Vaishya and Shudra
Varna | Functions — associated with

Kshatriya | Warrior and ruling functions

Mahavira: Belonged to the Kshatriya class — Kshatriya-Kundagrama; Jamali was his first disciple — warrior-caste followers
Guru Nanak: Rejected caste discrimination — emphasized virtues over caste

Bhakti Movement: Emphasized devotion over birth and status — challenged caste hierarchy

Savitribai Phule: Headed the women's section — worked for lower-caste girls

t: Congress resolutions
text:
## 1. Lucknow — 1916
The Congress–League Agreement — the Congress and the Muslim League reached an agreement at Lucknow in 1916 — the Lucknow Session; Ambika Charan Majumdar
## 2. Nehru Report and ultimatum — 1928
Nehru Report: Issued in 1928 — the All-Parties Convention; Motilal Nehru; provided a constitutional framework for India
Ultimatum on the Nehru Report: Occurred in 1928 at the Calcutta Session — demanded acceptance within the year; failure to accept would lead to a mass movement
## 3. Purna Swaraj — 1929
Purna Swaraj Resolution: Adopted in 1929 at the Lahore Session — Jawaharlal Nehru; adopted Complete Independence as the Congress goal
Flag-hoisting and Complete Independence declaration: 31 December 1929 at Lahore — Jawaharlal Nehru; the national flag was hoisted on the Ravi
Purna Swaraj Day: Observed on 26 January 1930 following the Lahore decision
## 4. Karachi — 1931
Fundamental Rights and National Economic Programme resolution: Adopted in 1931 at the Karachi Session — Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel presided; Jawaharlal Nehru drafted it — associated with Patel and Nehru
Karachi Resolution on Fundamental Rights: Addressed civil liberties, equality, freedom and citizens' rights
Karachi Resolution on the Economic Programme: Addressed labour welfare, economic justice and worker protection — assigned responsibility to the state
## 5. Movements
Swadeshi and Boycott movement: Occurred during the period of the Partition of Bengal — the Congress and the nationalist movement; promoted the boycott of foreign goods, indigenous goods and national education
Home Rule Movement: Occurred in 1917 — Annie Besant, who became INC President at Calcutta in 1917

topic: National movement - Swadeshi to Quit India
t: Partition of Bengal
text:
## 1. Partition — 1905
Announced in 1905 — Viceroy Lord Curzon; became effective on 16 October 1905
Bengal was the main province divided — the new province: Eastern Bengal and Assam
Province | Capital
Eastern Bengal and Assam | Dacca (Dhaka)
Western Bengal | Calcutta
Nationalists interpreted it as a "Divide and Rule" policy — the Swadeshi Movement was the major response
## 2. Annulment — 1911
The Partition was annulled in 1911 — the capital shifted from Calcutta to Delhi in 1911

topic: National movement - Swadeshi to Quit India
t: Extremists — Assertive Nationalists
text:
## 1. Nature
Extremists: Also called Assertive Nationalists — the aggressive nationalist wing; influence increased after 1906
Main objective: Swaraj — complete independence from English rule
Methods: Self-sacrifice, mass movements, aggressive resistance — opposed Moderate methods; rejected Prayer, Petition and Protest
Supported Swadeshi and Boycott — wanted to extend the movement (a wider and extended Swadeshi–Boycott movement); lacked faith in Moderate negotiations with the British
## 2. Moderates vs Extremists
Basis | Moderates | Extremists
Goal | Gradual self-government | Swaraj or complete independence
Method | Prayer, Petition and Protest | Self-sacrifice and resistance
Strategy | Constitutional agitation | Mass movement
View of British | Initially had faith in British liberalism | Increasing distrust of British rule
Swadeshi–Boycott | Less willing to extend it | Wanted it wider and extended
Representative leaders | Dadabhai Naoroji, Gokhale | Tilak, Lajpat Rai, Bipin Chandra Pal, Aurobindo Ghosh
## 3. Surat Split — 1907
A conflict between the Moderates and the Extremists — major issues: Leadership, methods, Congress strategy and Swadeshi–Boycott
## 4. Lal–Bal–Pal–Ghosh
Lal–Bal–Pal: Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Bipin Chandra Pal — a famous Extremist trio
Lal–Bal–Pal–Ghosh: Adds Aurobindo Ghosh — represented four major Extremist leaders (the Extremists or Assertive Nationalists)
Leader | Belonged to | Associated with
Bal Gangadhar Tilak | Maharashtra | Swaraj — gave the slogan "Swaraj is my birthright…"; the Shivaji Festival and Ganpati Festival — used for mass mobilisation; published Kesari and Mahratta; wrote the book Gita Rahasya — Swaraj, festivals and newspapers
Lala Lajpat Rai | Punjab | Known as Sher-e-Punjab and Punjab Kesari; the safety-valve theory — represented Punjab and the safety-valve issue; the Simon Commission protest
Bipin Chandra Pal | Bengal | Lal–Bal–Pal; the Swadeshi Movement; New India; the Brahmo Samaj — Swadeshi and New India
Aurobindo Ghosh | Bengal | The main leader of the Swadeshi Movement during the Partition of Bengal; the Maniktalla Garden raid; Pondicherry — Swadeshi, Maniktalla and Pondicherry
## 5. Key events
Tilak: An Extremist leader — imprisoned in 1908 for six years in Mandalay; Sir Valentine Chirol called him the "Father of Indian unrest"
Lajpat Rai: An Extremist — a member of Lal–Bal–Pal along with Tilak and Bipin Chandra Pal; suffered a lathi-charge injury during the Simon Commission protest; died on 17 November 1928
Young India was the source of the safety-valve theory
Aurobindo Ghosh: An Extremist — arrested in 1908 during the Maniktalla Garden raid; the Maniktalla case involved him — sentenced to one year, later released for lack of evidence
Later moved to Pondicherry — withdrew from revolutionary political activity

topic: National movement - Swadeshi to Quit India
t: Jallianwala Bagh
text:
## 1. Background — Rowlatt Satyagraha
Rowlatt Act: March 1919 — popularly described as "No Vakil, No Appeal, No Daleel"; Gandhi responded through the Rowlatt Satyagraha (the immediate context)
Country-wide strike: 6 April 1919
Dr. Saifuddin Kitchlew and Dr. Satyapal: The Punjab leaders arrested on 9 April 1919
## 2. The incident
Place: Amritsar, Punjab — date: 13 April 1919; occasion: Baisakhi
Viceroy: Lord Chelmsford
The crowd gathered for a protest and to celebrate Baisakhi
Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer ordered the firing — ordered troops to open fire
Michael O'Dwyer: The Lieutenant Governor of Punjab — Dyer was associated with the firing, O'Dwyer with Punjab administration
British supporters described Dyer as the "Lion of British Empire" — he received the Sword of Honour
## 3. Inquiries
Official inquiry: The Hunter Committee — also called the Disorders Inquiry Committee; chairman Lord William Hunter
Seven members — four British and three Indian: C.H. Setalvad, Pandit Jagat Narayan, Sultan Ahmad Khan
Criticised Dyer's actions — described them as an "Error in judgement"
Congress investigation: Conducted by the Congress Inquiry Committee — Gandhi was associated with drafting the report
## 4. Reactions
Rabindranath Tagore renounced or returned his Knighthood on 31 May 1919
Shankaran Nair resigned from the Viceroy's Executive Council
Montagu described the action as "Preventive Murder"
Udham Singh killed Michael O'Dwyer — assassinated on 13 March 1940 at Caxton Hall in London
## 5. Impact
Deepened hostility towards British rule; faith in British justice declined; strengthened the nationalist movement
A major turning point in Gandhi's political career — an important background to the Non-Cooperation Movement
The Amritsar Congress Session took place in December 1919

topic: National movement - Swadeshi to Quit India
t: Gandhi — early life and first campaigns
text:
## 1. Early life and South Africa
Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi: Born on 2 October 1869 in Porbandar — a barrister; legal training at the Inner Temple in London
1894: Founded the Natal Indian Congress in South Africa
1903: Indian Opinion — a newspaper established in South Africa; published in English, Gujarati, Hindi and Tamil; first issue in June 1903
1904: Established Phoenix Ashram in Durban — Gandhi's first ashram
1910: Gandhi and his colleagues established Tolstoy Farm
1915: Returned to India
February 1916: First major public speech in India at BHU, Varanasi
## 2. Early Satyagrahas in India
Campaign | Year | Issue | Associates / result
Champaran Satyagraha | 1917 | Indigo cultivation — the Tinkathia system | Raj Kumar Shukla invited Gandhi to Champaran — the site of Gandhi's first Satyagraha in India
Ahmedabad Mill Strike | 1918 | Industrial workers — a plague bonus and a wage dispute | Lasted 21 days; workers received a 35% bonus as a result; Ambalal Sarabhai and Anasuya Behn were important associates
Kheda Satyagraha | 1918 | Peasants affected by crop failure — demanded revenue remission or suspension | Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel
Ahmedabad fast: Gandhi used a fast unto death in Ahmedabad in 1918 — his first hunger strike used as a weapon; the strike produced a result in 1918

topic: National movement - Swadeshi to Quit India
t: Gandhi — mass movements
text:
## 1. Non-Cooperation and Civil Disobedience
Non-Cooperation Movement: Began in 1920 — involved boycott and non-cooperation; withdrawn after the Chauri Chaura incident (1922)
Civil Disobedience Movement: Began in 1930 — Gandhi led the Dandi March, which began on 12 March 1930 and violated the Salt Law
## 2. Gandhi–Irwin Pact — 1931
Signed on 5 March 1931 — Gandhi and Lord Irwin; associated with Congress in 1931; Congress withdrew the Civil Disobedience Movement
The 1931 Pact provided for:
Release of non-violent political prisoners
Salt-making in coastal areas without salt tax
Peaceful picketing
Congress agreed to participate in the Second Round Table Conference
Sarojini Naidu called Gandhi and Irwin "Two Mahatmas" — associated with the Gandhi–Irwin discussions
## 3. Second Round Table Conference — 1931
Gandhi was the sole Congress representative — travelled to London on the S.S. Rajputana in 1931; stayed at Kingsley Hall
B. R. Ambedkar demanded separate electorates for the Depressed Classes
## 4. Communal Award and Poona Pact — 1932
Communal Award: Announced in 1932 — the background to Gandhi's fast
Poona Pact: Concluded in 1932 — Gandhi and Ambedkar; joint electorates and reserved seats for the Depressed Classes
⚠ The representatives or followers signed it — the PDF states that Gandhi himself did not sign the Poona Pact
Gandhi founded the All India Anti-Untouchability League; Harijan — his weekly newspaper (1933)
Gandhi resigned from Congress in 1934 — ⚠ not a formal Congress member at the time of Independence
## 5. Quit India — 1942
Quit India Resolution: Passed on 8 August 1942 — represented Gandhi's call — "Do or Die"
Important associates: Jayaprakash Narayan, Ram Manohar Lohia, Aruna Asaf Ali, Matangini Hazra, Kanaklata Barua
## 6. Death
Assassinated by Nathuram Godse on 30 January 1948
Jawaharlal Nehru: "The light has gone out of our lives"

t: Ports of ancient and medieval Andhra
text:
## 1. Motupalli
Also called Desiyakondapattanam — the most important port

In Krishna district — an important port during the Ikshvaku period

## 4. Visakhapatnam
A port in the 19th century — facilitated the transportation and trade of agricultural products
