t: Company rule — Regulating Act 1773 to Charter Act 1853
text:
## 1. Regulating Act, 1773
Governor of Bengal → Governor-General of Bengal: Warren Hastings became the Governor-General of Bengal
Supreme Court at Calcutta (Fort William): Provided for by the Act; established in 1774 — the first Supreme Court
First Chief Justice: Sir Elijah Impey
Banned: Private trade and bribes
## 2. Pitt's India Act, 1784 and the Act of 1786
Pitt's India Act (1784): Established Dual Control
Board of Control → political affairs
Court of Directors → commercial affairs (commerce)
Act of 1786: Governor-General could override his Council and assume the powers of Commander-in-Chief
First to exercise these powers: Lord Cornwallis
## 3. Charter Act, 1813
Trade monopoly in India: Ended (partially abolished) — except the tea trade and trade with China (both monopolies retained)
Christian missionaries: Permitted to operate in India
Education: Annual grant of at least ₹1 lakh for the education of Indians — first such provision
## 4. Charter Act, 1833
Governor-General of Bengal → Governor-General of India (office created): Lord William Bentinck was the first Governor-General of India
Law Member: A fourth member added to the Governor-General's Council — Macaulay, the first Law Member
Commercial status: The Company's commercial role ended entirely — trade monopoly completely abolished in 1833
Section 87: Opened Company service to Indians for the first time — no discrimination based on religion, colour or other such distinctions
## 5. Charter Act, 1853
Legislative and executive functions of the Governor-General's Council clearly separated for the first time
Civil Services: Open competition introduced

t: Crown rule — Act of 1858 and the Indian Councils Acts
text:
## 1. Government of India Act, 1858
Transfer of power: From the Company to the British Crown
Viceroy: Governor-General designated as Viceroy — Lord Canning was the first Viceroy of India
Abolished: Board of Control and Court of Directors
Secretary of State for India: Created, assisted by a 15-member Council
## 2. Indian Councils Act, 1861
Decentralisation: Restored the legislative powers of Bombay and Madras
Indian participation in law-making began
Portfolio System introduced
Viceroy's Ordinance Power: Introduced (origin of the ordinance power) — an ordinance could last at most six months
High Courts Act, 1861: High Courts of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras established in 1862
## 3. Indian Councils Act, 1892
Budget: Discussion permitted — but no voting on the Budget
Questions to the executive: Permitted, with six days' prior notice — no supplementary questions
Principle of (limited) indirect election introduced
## 4. Indian Councils Act, 1909 — Morley-Minto Reforms
Separate electorates for Muslims introduced — Lord Minto: "Father of Communal Electorate"
Indians in Executive Councils: First associated with the Executive Councils of the Viceroy and Governors
Satyendra Prasad (S.P.) Sinha: First Indian in the Viceroy's Executive Council, as Law Member
Supplementary questions allowed
Central Legislature: Enlarged but still unicameral
⚠ Trap: The 1909 Act did not introduce dyarchy and gave no Provincial Autonomy; existing High Courts continued

t: Government of India Acts, 1919 and 1935
text:
## 1. Government of India Act, 1919 — Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms
Dyarchy in the provinces: Introduced for the first time (Provincial Dyarchy, 1919)
Bicameral Central Legislature: First time (bicameralism at the Centre)
Direct elections: First time (at the Centre)
"Responsible government": Term used for the first time
Budgets: Central and Provincial budgets separated; initial separation of subjects
Communal representation: Extended
Chamber of Princes: Established — 120 members; first Chancellor: Maharaja Ganga Singh of Bikaner
Public Accounts Committee: Set up under this Act in 1921
Public Service Commission: Provided by this Act; established on 1 October 1926
## 2. Government of India Act, 1935
All-India Federation: Provided for the first time — never came into existence (not implemented)
Dyarchy: Abolished in the provinces; Central Dyarchy proposed (1935) — never implemented
Provincial Autonomy: Introduced in full
Federal Legislature: Bicameral, proposed
Communal representation: Retained or extended
Federal Court: Established; inaugurated on 1 October 1937 — first Chief Justice: Sir Maurice Gwyer
Territory: Burma separated from India; Sindh and Orissa created as new provinces
Residuary powers: Vested in the Governor-General
Ordinance: Section 42 of this Act is the model for Article 123 (President's Ordinance Power)
## 3. Comparison of the Acts
Feature | Indian Councils Act 1909 | GoI Act 1919 | GoI Act 1935
Dyarchy | Not introduced | Introduced in the provinces | Abolished in provinces; proposed at the Centre
Provincial Autonomy | None | Initial separation of subjects | Full Provincial Autonomy
Communal representation | Separate electorates for Muslims | Extended | Retained or extended
Central Legislature | Enlarged, unicameral | Bicameral | Bicameral Federal Legislature proposed
Courts | Existing High Courts continued | Existing High Courts continued | Federal Court (1937)

t: Independence and the making of the Constitution
text:
## 1. Demand for a Constituent Assembly
Idea first put forward: M.N. Roy, 1934
First formal demand: Swaraj Party, Ranchi conference, May 1934
Constituted under: Cabinet Mission Plan, 1946
First explicit demand for Fundamental Rights: Constitution of India Bill, 1895
## 2. Interim Government
Announced: 24 August 1946; took charge 2 September 1946
Vice-President of the Executive Council: Jawaharlal Nehru
## 3. Constituent Assembly — timeline
9 December 1946: First meeting — temporary President Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha
11 December 1946: Dr. Rajendra Prasad — first permanent elected Chairman/President
13 December 1946: Jawaharlal Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution (at the fifth meeting of the first session)
22 January 1947: Objectives Resolution unanimously adopted
22 July 1947: National Flag adopted
29 August 1947: Drafting Committee constituted, headed by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
26 November 1949: Constitution adopted and enacted — observed as Constitution Day
24 January 1950: Final meeting; National Anthem adopted
26 January 1950: Constitution fully came into force; Republic of India established
Office-bearers: Frank Anthony — first nominated temporary Deputy Chairman; H.C. Mukherjee — first permanent Vice-President
First draft: B.N. Rau, as Constitutional Advisor
Women members: 15
## 4. Indian Independence Act, 1947
Ended: British rule (British sovereignty)
Created: Two independent Dominions — India and Pakistan
Constituent Assemblies: Given dual powers — constitution-making and legislative

t: Landmark constitutional amendments
text:
1st Amendment (1951): Added the Ninth Schedule, Articles 31A and 31B and Article 15(4) (clause (4) to Article 15); restricted the rights under Article 19; addressed agrarian reforms
42nd Amendment (1976) — "Mini-Constitution":
Added the terms Socialist, Secular and Integrity to the Preamble
Inserted Fundamental Duties as Part IVA (Article 51A)
44th Amendment (1978): Nullified emergency-era distortions; restored fundamental safeguards
Removed the Right to Property from Fundamental Rights → now Article 300A
Inserted the term "armed rebellion"
52nd Amendment (1985): Anti-Defection Law — inserted the Tenth Schedule; amended Articles 101, 102, 190 and 191; gave political parties constitutional recognition for the first time
61st Amendment (1988/89): Voting age 21 → 18; effective 28 March 1989; first exercised in the 1989 General Election
73rd and 74th Amendments (1992):
73rd: Constitutional status to Panchayati Raj — Part IX, Articles 243 to 243O, Eleventh Schedule, three-tier system; enforced 24 April 1993
74th: Municipalities — Part IXA, Articles 243P to 243ZG, Twelfth Schedule; enforced 1 June 1993
84th Amendment (2001): Seat-allocation freeze — Lok Sabha seat allocations based on the 1971 Census, continued up to 2026
86th Amendment (2002): Article 21A — Right to Education for children of 6–14 years; Article 51A(k) — the eleventh Fundamental Duty (education of children)
91st Amendment (2003): Strengthened anti-defection provisions; limited the size of the Council of Ministers — capped at 15% of the strength of the House
99th Amendment (2014): National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC) — struck down by the Supreme Court as unconstitutional in 2015
101st Amendment (2016): Goods and Services Tax — effective 1 July 2017
103rd and 104th Amendments (2019):
103rd: 10% reservation for Economically Weaker Sections
104th: Ended Anglo-Indian nominations — effective January 2020
106th Amendment (2023): About one-third reservation for women in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies

t: Important statutes
text:
## 1. Representation of the People Acts
RPA, 1950: Framework for seat allocation, electoral rolls and Legislative Council composition — associated with Section 10, Schedule 3 and Article 171
RPA, 1951: Registration of political parties by the Election Commission of India; conduct of elections; disqualification on conviction
Convicted and sentenced to at least two years → disqualified during the imprisonment and for six years after release
## 2. Rights and accountability laws
Protection of Civil Rights Act: 1955
Maintenance of Internal Security Act (MISA): 1971 — an internal security statute, not a social welfare act
Child Labour (Prohibition & Regulation) Act: 1986
Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act: 1989 — 23 sections; effective 1990 (enforced 30 January 1990)
Protection of Human Rights Act: 1993 — enforced 28 September 1993; concerns life, liberty, equality and dignity
Established the NHRC (on 12 October 1993), State Human Rights Commissions and Human Rights Courts
PESA — Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act: 1996
Right to Information Act (2005): Assent 15 June 2005; enforced/effective 12 October 2005
A legal right supporting transparency and accountability; rooted in the MKSS movement
Namit Sharma Case (2012) related to the RTI Act
Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act: 2005 — enforced 26 October 2006
National Green Tribunal Act: 2010
## 3. Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 (in effect 2014)
Selection Committee — five members:
Prime Minister (Chair)
Speaker of the Lok Sabha
Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha
Chief Justice of India or a Supreme Court nominee
An eminent jurist
⚠ Trap: The Rajya Sabha Chairman is not a member
Minimum age of the Lokpal: 45 years
Covers: The Prime Minister and public servants inside and outside India
## 4. Panchayati Raj milestones
Community Development Programme (1952): First major rural development programme after independence
National Extension Service: 1953
Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957): Recommended a three-tier model
Panchayati Raj first launched: 2 October 1959, Nagaur (Rajasthan), inaugurated by Jawaharlal Nehru
Committees: Ashok Mehta (1977), G.V.K. Rao (1985), L.M. Singhvi (1986)

t: Polity firsts — persons and offices
text:
## 1. Heads of State and Government
First President: Dr. Rajendra Prasad (from Bihar)
First woman President: Pratibha Patil; first tribal woman President: Droupadi Murmu

Leader of the Opposition first recognised in the Lok Sabha: 1969
First actress nominated to the Rajya Sabha: Nargis Dutt, 1980
## 3. Judiciary, states and parties

First woman Governor: Sarojini Naidu (Uttar Pradesh)
First woman Chief Minister: Sucheta Kripalani (Uttar Pradesh)
First President of the Bharatiya Jana Sangh: Dr. Shyama Prasad Mukherjee
First President of the BJP: Atal Bihari Vajpayee, 1980

t: Polity firsts — institutions, bodies and events
text:
## 1. Forms of government and doctrines
Parliamentary form of government: First introduced in Great Britain
Presidential form of government: First formed in the USA
Judicial Review: First propounded in the USA — Marbury v. Madison (1803)
Basic Structure doctrine: First propounded in Kesavananda Bharati (1973)
Fundamental Rights amendable: First held in the Shankari Prasad case

Finance Commission: First Chairman K.C. Neogy; constituted in 1951 (some sources: set up in 1952)
Planning Commission: First Chairman (ex officio) Pt. Jawaharlal Nehru; first Deputy Chairman Gulzarilal Nanda

First Official Language Commission: 1955, headed by B.G. Kher
First Classical Language: Tamil
## 3. Ombudsman, Lokpal and Lokayukta
Ombudsman: First created in Sweden, 1809
First Administrative Reforms Commission (1966): Recommended Lokpal and Lokayuktas — interim report submitted by Morarji Desai
First Lokpal Bill: 1968; first Lokpal of India: Justice Pinaki Chandra Ghose
First state with a Lokayukta: Maharashtra (1971 or 1972); first to pass a Lokayukta Act: Odisha
## 4. Emergency and local government
President's Rule (Article 356) first imposed: PEPSU, 1953 — some sources say Punjab, 1951
First Municipal Corporation: Madras, 1688
Panchayati Raj: Rajasthan the first state, Andhra Pradesh the second; Madhya Pradesh first to implement the 73rd Amendment in its true spirit

t: Demand for a Constituent Assembly and its composition
text:
## 1. Demand — 1934 to 1946
1934: M.N. Roy — first idea of a Constituent Assembly
May 1934: Swaraj Party — first formal demand, Ranchi Conference; the Congress officially demanded it at Patna
1938: Jawaharlal Nehru — clear statement supporting a Constituent Assembly
1940: August Offer — accepted the principle
1942: Cripps Mission — final proposal for an elected Constituent Assembly
1946: Constituted under the Cabinet Mission Plan
## 2. Seats and representation
Planned seats: 389
British India: 296 — 292 from Governor's provinces + 4 from Chief Commissioners' provinces
Princely States: 93

t: Sources of the Constitution — borrowed features
text:
## 1. Government of India Act, 1935 — the main blueprint
Structural and administrative backbone: Federal scheme, Governor, judiciary, Emergency provisions, Public Service Commission
## 2. Borrowed from other constitutions
Source | Features borrowed
Britain | Parliamentary form of government; Rule of Law; Cabinet system; single citizenship; bicameral legislature; parliamentary privileges; prerogative writs
USA | Fundamental Rights; judicial review; independence of the judiciary; idea of the Preamble; post of Vice-President; impeachment of the President; removal of judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts

South Africa | Procedure for constitutional amendment; election of members of the Rajya Sabha
USSR | Fundamental Duties; ideals of social, economic and political justice in the Preamble
France | Ideal of a republic; ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity in the Preamble

t: Seventh Schedule — distribution of legislative powers
text:
## 1. Framework
Governed by: Part XI (Articles 245 to 255) and the Seventh Schedule (Union List, State List, Concurrent List)
Article 246: Operationalises the subject distribution
246(1): Parliament — exclusive competence over List I (Union List)
246(3): State Legislatures — exclusive competence over List II (State List)
246(2): Both — concurrent competence over List III (Concurrent List)
Article 246A: Special provision for GST — by the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016
Parliament and State Legislatures get simultaneous power to frame GST laws — breaks the strict exclusive-list dichotomy of Article 246
Article 248: Residuary powers (subjects in none of the three Lists) vested exclusively in Parliament — e.g. space research, cyber law
Residuary powers lie with the States in the USA and Australia; with the Centre in Canada and India
Article 254 — repugnancy: On a Concurrent subject, Central law prevails over conflicting State law
Exception 254(2): A State law reserved for the President's assent and assented can prevail
## 2. Examples of subjects
Union List | State List | Concurrent List
Defence, armed forces | Public order (Entry 1) | Education
Foreign affairs, treaties | Police (incl. Railway Police) | Forests
Railways | Prisons, reformatories | Electricity
Banking, insurance | Public health, sanitation | Criminal law
Census (decennial enumerations) | Local government / Panchayati Raj / Municipalities (Entry 5) | Criminal procedure (Code of Criminal Procedure)
Corporation tax | Agriculture, agricultural education | Civil procedure (Code of Civil Procedure)
Radio and television broadcasting | Land, land reforms, land revenue, land assessment | Marriage, divorce, adoption
Inter-State Trade and Commerce (Entry 42) | Tolls, capitation taxes | Economic and social planning (Entry 20)
Inter-State migration, quarantine (Entry 81) | Fisheries | Population control and family planning (Entry 20A)
Atomic energy, mineral resources | Markets and fairs | Adulteration of foodstuffs and goods
Stock exchanges, futures markets | Trade and Commerce within a State (Entry 26 — subject to List III, Entry 33) | Price control; prevention of cruelty to animals
⚠ Traps: Railways → Union, but Railway Police → State (police); Economic and Social Planning → Concurrent, not Union
## 3. 42nd Amendment (1976) — State List → Concurrent List
Transferred: Education, forests, weights and measures, protection of wild animals and birds, administration of justice
Administration of justice: constitution and organisation of all courts except the Supreme Court and High Courts
Entry 20A inserted into the Concurrent List — population control and family planning
## 4. When Parliament can legislate on State List subjects
Article 249 — national interest: Rajya Sabha resolution by at least two-thirds of members present and voting
The law remains in force for one year; ceases six months after the resolution lapses
Article 250 — National Emergency (Article 352): Law can extend to the whole or any part of India; ceases six months after the Emergency ends
Article 252 — consent of States: Requests by at least two State Legislatures through resolutions
Applies only to the consenting States; can be amended or repealed only by Parliament
Article 253 — international agreements: Plenary power to implement international treaties, conventions and accords
Article 356 — President's Rule: Parliament exercises the legislative powers of the State Legislature

t: Preamble — origin, text and key words
text:
## 1. Origin and sources
Basis: The Objectives Resolution
Moved by Pt. Jawaharlal Nehru on 13 December 1946
Adopted on 22 January 1947
Idea borrowed from: Constitution of the USA
Language influenced by: Australian Constitution
## 2. Nature of the State
People of India resolved to constitute India into a: Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic
Sovereign: Supreme authority; freedom from external control
Socialist: Aims at reducing inequality
Secular: Equal respect for all religions
Democratic: Government of the people, by the people and for the people
Republic: Elected head of state — not a hereditary head of state
⚠ Trap: "Socialist" and "Secular" were not in the original Preamble; the word "Federal" is not mentioned in the Preamble at all
## 3. Objectives secured for all citizens
Justice: Social, economic and political
Liberty: Of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship
Equality: Of status and opportunity
Fraternity (promoted among all citizens), assuring:
The dignity of the individual
The unity and integrity of the Nation
## 4. Date in the Preamble
26 November 1949: The Constituent Assembly adopted, enacted and gave to itself the Constitution
The date mentioned is the date of: Adoption

t: Preamble — amendment, cases and status
text:
## 1. The only amendment — 42nd Amendment Act, 1976
42nd Constitutional Amendment Act (1976): Known as the Mini Constitution
Words added: Socialist, Secular and Integrity
Change: "Unity of the Nation" → "Unity and Integrity of the Nation"
Times amended: Only once so far
Amendable under: Article 368 — but the basic structure cannot be altered
## 2. Is the Preamble part of the Constitution? — landmark cases
Case | Year | Held
Berubari Union Case | 1960 | Preamble is not a part of the Constitution
Golaknath Case | 1967 | Preamble is a part of the Constitution
Kesavananda Bharati Case | 1973 | Preamble is a part of the Constitution (settled); it can be amended; the basic structure cannot be destroyed
LIC of India Case | 1995 | Reaffirmed: Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution
## 3. Status and descriptions
Called: Key to the Constitution; Soul of the Constitution
K. M. Munshi: Called it the Political Horoscope
Reflects: The philosophy, ideals and objectives of the Constitution
Non-justiciable: Cannot be enforced in a court of law
Powers and rights: Does not confer any power and does not create any right by itself

t: Citizenship — Part II, Articles 5 to 11
text:
## 1. Constitutional framework
Part II: Articles 5 to 11 — primarily identifies citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution (26 January 1950)
Who regulates citizenship: Parliament alone, by law, under Article 11 — acquisition, termination and all related matters
No power to make citizenship laws: State Legislatures, the President, the Election Commission
Citizenship Act: 1955 — Citizenship Rules made under Section 18
Single citizenship and a single domicile across India — unitary features of the federal structure
Contrast: the USA has dual (federal and state) citizenship
## 2. Articles 5 to 11
Article 5 — citizenship at commencement: Domicile in India plus any one of:
Birth in India
Either parent born in India
Residence in India for at least five years before 1950
Article 6: Rights of persons who migrated from Pakistan to India — migration before and after the permit cut-off date, 19 July 1948
Article 7: Certain migrants to Pakistan — those who went after 1 March 1947; covers those who later returned under a resettlement permit
Article 8: Persons of Indian Origin residing abroad — registration as a citizen by an Indian diplomatic or consular representative
Article 9: Voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship → automatic loss of Indian citizenship (the single citizenship rule)
Article 10: Continuance of the rights of citizenship — subject to laws made by Parliament
Article 11: Parliament's comprehensive power to regulate citizenship by law

t: Citizenship Act, 1955 — acquisition, loss, OCI and CAA
text:
## 1. Five modes of acquiring citizenship — mnemonic B-D-R-N-I
Birth: Depends on the place of birth — jus soli with modified criteria
Descent: Born outside India to Indian citizen parents — jus sanguinis
Registration (Section 5):
Person of Indian Origin ordinarily resident in India for seven years before applying
Persons married to Indian citizens
Naturalization (Section 6): Foreigners meeting residency and character criteria
Incorporation of territory: India acquires a new territory — e.g. Goa, Pondicherry, Sikkim
## 2. Three modes of losing citizenship — mnemonic R-T-D
Renunciation: Voluntary surrender by an Indian national
Termination: Automatic loss when a citizen voluntarily acquires another country's citizenship — linked to Article 9
Deprivation (Section 10): Compulsory termination by the Central Government for:
Fraud
Disloyalty to the Constitution
Unlawful trading with an enemy during war
Imprisonment of at least two years within five years of naturalization or registration
## 3. Common traps
President (Article 58): In India both a citizen by birth and a naturalized citizen are eligible; in the USA only a natural-born citizen can become President
Do not confer citizenship: Depositing money in Indian banks; purchasing property in India
Do not by themselves end citizenship: Marrying a foreign citizen; criticising the government or its policies
⚠ Trap: "A naturalized citizen can never be deprived of citizenship" is false — deprivation under Section 10
## 4. Overseas Citizen of India (OCI)
Provision: Section 7A
Strictly ineligible: Persons who were citizens of Pakistan or Bangladesh, or whose parents or grandparents belonged to Pakistan or Bangladesh
## 5. Citizenship Amendment Act, 2019
Passed: Lok Sabha 9 December 2019; Rajya Sabha 11 December 2019; Presidential Assent 12 December 2019
Applies to: Six non-Muslim persecuted minorities from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan
Cut-off: Entered India on or before 31 December 2014

t: Fundamental Rights — features and history
text:
## 1. Basics
Location: Part III — Articles 12 to 35 (24 Articles)
Borrowed from: Mainly the Bill of Rights of the USA
Number: Originally seven; presently six
Right to Property removed by the 44th Amendment (1978) — Article 19(1)(f) deleted; now a legal right under Article 300-A
Available against the State — Article 12 defines the State
Justiciable: Enforceable by courts — the judiciary (Supreme Court and High Courts) is the guardian of Fundamental Rights
## 2. Milestones in the demand
1895: First demand — Swaraj Bill
1928: Motilal Nehru Report
1931: Karachi Session of the Congress
## 3. Citizens only vs everyone
Only citizens (five rights): Articles 15, 16, 19, 29 and 30
Citizens and foreigners: The remaining rights — Articles 14, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27 and 28
## 4. Amendment and suspension
Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights but cannot destroy the Basic Structure — Kesavananda Bharati (1973)
During a National Emergency Fundamental Rights can be suspended:
Article 358: Article 19 suspended automatically — only in case of war or external aggression
Article 359: President (by order) suspends the enforcement of other Fundamental Rights — except Articles 20 and 21 (after the 44th Amendment)

t: The six Fundamental Rights
text:
## 1. Right to Equality — Articles 14 to 18 (five Articles)
Article 14: Equality before law

Article 17: Abolishes untouchability

t: Writs — Article 32 and Article 226
text:
## 1. Writ jurisdiction
Origin: Prerogative remedies borrowed from English common law
Supreme Court — Article 32: Narrower — only for Fundamental Rights (Part III); a direct and effective Fundamental Right to constitutional remedies
High Courts — Article 226: Wider — can be approached for Fundamental Rights and any other purpose, including ordinary statutory or legal rights
Article 32(3): Parliament may by law empower any other court to exercise these powers within its local jurisdiction
Five writs: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo-Warranto
## 2. The five writs
Writ | Literal meaning | Issued against | Purpose
Habeas Corpus | "To have the body" / "Let us have the body" | Public authorities and private individuals | Release from unlawful or illegal detention — safeguards individual liberty (bodily freedom)
Mandamus | "We command" | Public officials, statutory bodies, inferior courts, tribunals | Compels performance of a mandatory public or legal duty refused or neglected
Prohibition | "To forbid" / "To restrain" | Judicial and quasi-judicial bodies only | A higher court stops a lower court or tribunal from exceeding or usurping jurisdiction — while the proceeding is pending
Certiorari | "To be certified" / "To be informed" | Judicial, quasi-judicial and administrative bodies | Quashes an illegal order already passed — lack or excess of jurisdiction, or error of law on the face of the record (postmortem review)
Quo-Warranto | "By what authority?" / "By what warrant?" | A person holding or claiming a substantive public office | Prevents illegal usurpation of a permanent public office created by statute or the Constitution
## 3. Key distinctions
Habeas Corpus: Applies whenever detention (custody) is illegal — the only writ directly against private individuals in cases of illegal confinement
Mandamus:
Does not lie against purely private bodies unless they discharge a public duty
Does not lie against the President or Governors
Can lie against a government company or statutory corporation performing a public function
Prohibition vs Certiorari:
Prohibition: Before the order — halts a pending proceeding to prevent excess of jurisdiction
Certiorari: After the order — corrects or quashes decisions with jurisdictional error
Quo-Warranto: Challenges the legal qualification or title of a person holding public office
Any public-minded citizen (any member of the public) can move a petition — no aggrieved-party status needed (the petitioner need not be personally aggrieved); the traditional locus standi requirement is relaxed

t: Directive Principles of State Policy — nature and classification
text:
## 1. Basics
Location: Part IV — Articles 36 to 51 (16 articles)
Inspired by (borrowed from): The Irish Constitution (Ireland)
Non-justiciable (Article 37): Cannot be enforced by any court — yet fundamental in the governance of the country
Aim: Social and economic democracy; a welfare state
Called: Instrument of Instructions; Conscience of the Constitution
Article 36: Defines the State; Article 37: Application of the Directive Principles
## 2. Classification
Group | Articles (number) | Key articles
Socialistic | 8–9 articles | 38, 39, 39A, 41, 42, 43, 43A, 47
Gandhian | 6 articles | 40, 43, 43B, 46, 47, 48
Liberal-Intellectual | 7 articles | 44, 45, 48, 48A, 49, 50, 51

t: Articles 38 to 51
text:
## 1. Socialistic principles
Article 38: Social order — promote the welfare of the people and minimise inequalities (made more comprehensive/strengthened by the 44th Amendment)
Article 39 — principles of policy: Adequate means of livelihood; equal pay for equal work; protection of children
Article 39A: Equal justice and free legal aid — added by the 42nd Amendment
Article 41: Right to work, right to education, public assistance
Article 42: Just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief
Article 43: Living wage and a decent standard of life; also promote cottage industries (Gandhian)
Article 43A: Workers' participation in management of industries — added by the 42nd Amendment
## 2. Gandhian principles
Article 40: Organisation of village panchayats
Article 43B: Promotion of cooperative societies — added by the 97th Amendment
Article 46: Educational and economic interests of Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and other weaker sections
Article 47: Raise the level of nutrition and the standard of living; improve public health; prohibit consumption of intoxicating drinks and drugs
Article 48: Prohibit slaughter of cows, calves and other milch animals
## 3. Liberal-intellectual principles
Article 44: Uniform Civil Code — still not fully implemented
Article 45: Early childhood care and education — originally free and compulsory education up to 14 years; changed by the 86th Amendment to education for children below 6 years
Article 48: Organisation of agriculture and animal husbandry
Article 48A: Protect and improve the environment; safeguard forests and wildlife — added by the 42nd Amendment
Environmental protection: Article 48A as a Directive Principle; Article 51A(g) as a Fundamental Duty
Article 49: Protection of monuments and places of national importance
Article 50: Separation of the Judiciary from the Executive
Article 51: Promotion of international peace and security
## 4. Amendments
42nd (1976): Added 39A, 43A, 48A
44th (1978): Strengthened Article 38
86th (2002): Amended Article 45
97th (2011): Added Article 43B

t: Fundamental Rights vs Directive Principles
text:
Basis | Fundamental Rights | Directive Principles
Justiciability | Justiciable — enforced in courts | Non-justiciable — cannot be enforced in courts
Aim | Political democracy | Social and economic democracy
Sanction | Legal | Moral and political
In a conflict | Generally prevail — except Articles 39(b) and 39(c) in some cases | Subordinate, with exceptions
## 1. Landmark cases
Champakam Dorairajan (1951): Fundamental Rights superior to Directive Principles
Golaknath (1967): Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights
Kesavananda Bharati (1973): Established the Basic Structure principle
Minerva Mills (1980): Balance — Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles are equally important

t: Fundamental Duties — Article 51-A
text:
## 1. Basics
Location: Part IV-A — contains only one Article, Article 51-A
Added by: 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 (came into force 3 January 1977)
Recommended by: Swaran Singh Committee (1976)
Inspired by: Constitution of the erstwhile USSR (Soviet Union)
Number: Originally 10; presently 11 — the 11th added by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002
## 2. The eleven duties — every citizen shall
51-A(a): Abide by the Constitution; respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem
51-A(b): Cherish and follow the noble ideals that inspired the national struggle for freedom
51-A(c): Uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India
51-A(d): Defend the country and render national service when called upon
51-A(e): Promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood among all the people of India
Transcending religious, linguistic, regional and sectional diversities
Renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women
51-A(f): Value and preserve the rich heritage of India's composite culture
51-A(g): Protect and improve the natural environment — forests, lakes, rivers and wild life; have compassion for living creatures
51-A(h): Develop scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform
51-A(i): Safeguard public property and abjure violence
51-A(j): Strive towards excellence in every sphere of individual and collective activity — so the nation constantly rises to higher levels of endeavour and achievement
51-A(k): A parent or guardian shall provide opportunities for education to their child or ward aged 6 to 14 years (six to fourteen) — the 11th duty, 86th Amendment (2002)
## 3. Nature
Non-justiciable: Cannot be enforced directly by courts; no legal sanction for violating them — moral obligations on citizens
Apply only to citizens — not to foreigners
Parliament can make laws to enforce them
Use in courts: Help in interpreting ambiguous laws and in determining the constitutionality of laws
Contrast: Fundamental Rights are justiciable and available against the State

t: President — position, election and tenure
text:
## 1. Position
Article 52: There shall be a President of India
Article 53: Executive power of the Union vested in the President — exercised directly or through subordinate officers
Nominal / constitutional head of the State (Head of the State, not Head of the Government)
Real executive: The Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister
First Citizen of India; symbol of the unity, integrity and solidarity of the nation; Rank 1 in the Order of Precedence
Supreme Commander of the Defence (Armed) Forces — Article 53(2)
Integral part of Parliament — Article 79
## 2. Election — indirect (not directly elected)
Electoral College — elected members of:
Both Houses of Parliament
Legislative Assemblies of the States
Legislative Assemblies of Delhi and Puducherry — added by the 70th Amendment
Do not vote: Nominated members of Parliament; members of State Legislative Councils
Method: Proportional representation by Single Transferable Vote; secret ballot
Vote value: MLA votes → uniformity among the states; MP votes → parity between the Union and the states
Disputes: Decided by the Supreme Court — its decision is final
## 3. Qualifications (Article 58), term and removal
Qualifications (of a candidate): Citizen of India; completed 35 years of age; qualified for election to the Lok Sabha; holds no office of profit
Term: Five years (Article 56); eligible for re-election any number of times (Article 57)
Oath: Administered by the Chief Justice of India
Emoluments: Charged on the Consolidated Fund of India
Resignation: Addressed to the Vice-President
Impeachment (Article 61): For violation of the Constitution
Charge can be preferred by either House; needs a special majority in both Houses
⚠ Elected MLAs take part in the election but not in the impeachment
## 4. Vacancy
Death, resignation, removal or other vacancy: Vice-President acts as President (Article 65)
Both offices vacant: Chief Justice of India acts — or the senior-most Supreme Court Judge — under the President's Succession Act
## 5. Presidents — firsts
Dr. Rajendra Prasad: First President; longest-serving — two terms
Pratibha Patil: First woman President — 12th or 14th by the stated tenure counts
Droupadi Murmu: First tribal President — the 15th President

t: President — powers
text:
## 1. Executive and appointment powers
Appoints:
Prime Minister — normally the leader of the majority party — and other Ministers
Governors
Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts
Comptroller and Auditor General; Attorney General
Chairman and members of the UPSC; Election Commissioners; members of the Finance Commission
Ambassadors and High Commissioners
Article 78: Can seek information from the Prime Minister
## 2. Legislative powers
Summons and prorogues Parliament; dissolves the Lok Sabha
Addresses Parliament — Article 87
Assent to Bills (Article 111): Absolute, suspensive and pocket vetoes
Can return a Bill only once — except a Money Bill
Nominates 12 members to the Rajya Sabha
Ordinances (Article 123): When Parliament is not in session — co-extensive with Parliament's legislative power
## 3. Judicial, emergency and military powers
Article 72: Pardons, reprieves, respites, remissions; suspend or commute sentences
Article 143: Advisory opinion of the Supreme Court — not binding
Emergencies:
National Emergency — Article 352
President's Rule / State Emergency — Article 356
Financial Emergency — Article 360
War and peace: Declares war and concludes peace on the advice of the Council of Ministers
## 4. Limited discretion
Hung Parliament: May appoint a Prime Minister
Lost majority: May dismiss the government
Dissolving the Lok Sabha; the pocket veto
Return advice of the Council of Ministers for reconsideration once — added by the 44th Amendment

t: Vice-President
text:
## 1. Position and election
Article 63: There shall be a Vice-President — second-highest office in the Order of Precedence; modelled on the American Vice-President
Article 64: Ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha — presides over its sittings; casting vote in a tie
Does not preside while a resolution for his own removal is under consideration
Not a member of either House — not a part of Parliament (the President is)
Elected (not appointed): Indirectly, by members of both Houses — elected and nominated MPs
State Legislative Assemblies do not take part — the key difference from the Presidential election
Method: Proportional representation by Single Transferable Vote; secret ballot
Disputes (Article 71): All doubts and disputes decided by the Supreme Court — final
## 2. Qualifications, term and removal
Qualifications: Citizen; completed 35 years; qualified for election to the Rajya Sabha; no office of profit
Term: Five years (Article 67); re-election any number of times
Oath: Administered by the President
Resignation: Addressed to the President
Removal: Rajya Sabha resolution passed by a majority of all the then members of the Council of States — the Lok Sabha must agree to it
Fourteen-day notice; no formal impeachment like the President's
## 3. Acting as President (Article 65)
When: Presidential vacancy — death, resignation, removal; or the President is unable to discharge functions — absence, illness
Maximum period: Six months — a new President must be elected within six months
Pay: As Chairman of the Rajya Sabha draws salary and allowances — not charged on the Consolidated Fund of India
When acting as President: the President's salary, allowances and privileges
As a nominated member: Does not take part in the Presidential election
## 4. Vice-Presidents — firsts
Dr. S. Radhakrishnan: First and longest-serving — two terms
Mohammad Hamid Ansari: Only person to serve two full terms
## 5. President vs Vice-President
Basis | President | Vice-President
Electoral College | MPs and MLAs of States and Union Territories (elected only) | Only MPs — elected and nominated
Qualification linked to | Lok Sabha | Rajya Sabha
Removal | Impeachment by both Houses | Rajya Sabha resolution agreed to by the Lok Sabha
Resignation to | Vice-President | President
Part of Parliament | Yes | No

t: Ordinance-making power
text:
## 1. Basis
President: Article 123 (Part V); Governor: Article 213 (Part VI)
Nature: A legislative power of the Executive — not an executive or administrative function
When: Only when the Legislature is in recess — not when both Houses (or the single House of a unicameral state) are in session
President: when either or both Houses of Parliament are not in session; Governor: when either or both Houses of the State Legislature are not in session
Satisfaction: Circumstances exist requiring immediate action
Force: Same force and effect as an Act — and subject to the same limitations
## 2. President vs Governor
Basis | President | Governor
Subjects | Union List and Concurrent List | State List and Concurrent List
Approval | By Parliament | By the State Legislature — not the President or the Union Council of Ministers
Prior Presidential instruction | Not applicable | Mandatory in three cases — Bills needing prior sanction, reservation or Presidential assent
Lapse | Six weeks after Parliament reassembles | Six weeks after the State Legislature reassembles
Withdrawal | Any time — Article 123(2)(b) | Any time
## 3. Scope and limits
Can: Amend an ordinary Act; modify or repeal existing Central or State laws within legislative competence; operate retrospectively (like an ordinary statute); introduce or amend tax provisions
Cannot: Amend the Constitution under Article 368 (limited to ordinary legislative power); violate Fundamental Rights — subject to Article 13(2), void if it takes away or abridges Part III rights
Laying: Must be laid before the Legislature on reassembly; ceases six weeks after reassembly unless approved earlier
Houses reassembling on different dates → six weeks from the later date
Maximum life: Six months and six weeks — maximum gap between sessions is six months (Articles 85 and 174) + the six-week approval window
⚠ Trap: "The President cannot repeal or withdraw an ordinance once issued" is false
## 4. Judicial review
Subject to judicial review: D.C. Wadhwa (1987); Krishna Kumar Singh (2017)
Re-promulgation without legislative ratification is a subversion of the Constitution

topic: Prime Minister and Council of Ministers
t: Prime Minister — position, appointment and role
text:
## 1. Position
Real executive head of the Union — Head of Government; the President is the nominal/constitutional head (Head of State)
Heads the Council of Ministers; leader of the majority party or coalition in the Lok Sabha
Leader of the Lok Sabha (Leader of the House); chief spokesperson of the Government
## 2. Appointment, oath and membership
Appointed by the President (Article 75(1)) — normally the leader of the majority party in the Lok Sabha
Oath: Administered by the President; resignation addressed to the President
Member of either House: Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha
Rajya Sabha PMs: Indira Gandhi (initially), Manmohan Singh
Need not be an MP when appointed — must become one within six months (Article 75(5))
Responsible only to the Lok Sabha — not to the Rajya Sabha
## 3. Powers and functions
Ministers: Selects Ministers, allocates portfolios, can ask any Minister to resign; advises the President on appointing other Ministers
Link between President and Council of Ministers (Article 78):
Communicates all decisions and administrative proposals of the Council to the President
Furnishes information required by the President
Submits for the Council's reconsideration any matter decided by an individual Minister, if the President requires
Advises the President on: summoning and prorogation of Parliament; dissolution of the Lok Sabha; Emergency (through the Cabinet's recommendation)
Chairman of: NITI Aayog (earlier the Planning Commission), National Development Council, National Integration Council, Inter-State Council, National Disaster Management Authority
## 4. Prime Ministers — firsts
Jawaharlal Nehru: First and longest-serving PM
Indira Gandhi: First woman PM
Morarji Desai: First non-Congress PM
Deputy Prime Minister: Not a constitutional post — a political, extra-constitutional post created for political convenience
Carries the status of a Cabinet Minister; no superior powers over the PM
First: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel (1947 to 1950)

topic: Prime Minister and Council of Ministers
t: Council of Ministers and the Cabinet
text:
## 1. Constitutional provisions — Part V
Articles 74, 75, 77 and 78
Article 74: Council of Ministers headed by the PM to aid and advise the President
Article 75: Appointment, tenure, responsibility and other provisions on Ministers
Article 78: Duties of the Prime Minister
Executive power: Constitutionally vested in the President — Article 53
## 2. Union Ministers
Appointed by the President on the PM's advice; hold office during the pleasure of the President (Article 75(2)) — not legally the pleasure of the PM
Oath of Office and Oath of Secrecy: Administered by the President — forms in the Third Schedule
Membership: Either House (need not be the Lok Sabha); a non-member must become a member within six consecutive months or ceases to be a Minister
In Parliament: Can speak and participate in the proceedings of both Houses and joint sittings; can vote only in the House of which he is a member
## 3. Council of Ministers vs Cabinet
Basis | Council of Ministers | Union Cabinet
Nature | Wider collective constitutional body | Smaller, compact inner core — apex policy-formulation and core decision-making body
Size | 60–80 members | 15–20 members
Composition | PM, Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State (independent charge), Ministers of State, Deputy Ministers | PM and Cabinet-rank Ministers only
Powers | Broad powers under Articles 74 and 75 | Highest executive category in the ranking
Word "Cabinet": Not in the original text — inserted into Article 352(3) by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978
Four-tier classification of Ministers: a convention (tradition) — the Constitution does not classify Ministers into tiers
## 4. Responsibility
Collective responsibility — Article 75(3): Only to the Lok Sabha — not to the Rajya Sabha, Parliament as a whole or the President
"Sink or swim together": The entire Council, including the PM, resigns if a No-Confidence Motion is passed or the government loses a confidence vote / its majority in the Lok Sabha
Individual responsibility: Each Minister answerable to Parliament for administrative and bureaucratic lapses in his portfolio
## 5. Confidence and No-Confidence Motions
Confidence Motion: Moved by the Government (Council of Ministers) to demonstrate its majority
No-Confidence Motion: Moved by the Opposition in the Lok Sabha — Rule 198
## 6. Size limit — 91st Amendment Act, 2003 (a 15% ceiling on the number of Ministers)
Union — Article 75(1A): Total Ministers, including the PM, not more than 15% of the total strength of the Lok Sabha
States — Article 164(1A): The number of Ministers cannot exceed 15% of the strength of the Legislative Assembly (including the Chief Minister); minimum 12 Ministers

t: Attorney General of India — Article 76
text:
## 1. Office and appointment
Highest law officer of the Government of India — a constitutional post under Part V, Article 76
Appointed by: The President; holds office during the pleasure of the President
No fixed tenure in the Constitution; the President can remove him at any time
Resignation to the President; traditionally resigns when the Council of Ministers changes
Remuneration: Determined by the President — not fixed by Parliament or the Constitution
## 2. Qualifications — equal to a Supreme Court judge
Citizen of India, and one of:
High Court judge for at least five years
Advocate of a High Court for at least ten years
A distinguished jurist in the opinion of the President
## 3. Duties and rights
Duties: Advises the Government of India on legal matters; performs other legal duties referred by the President
Right of audience in all courts in India while on official duty
Article 88 (rights in respect of the Houses of Parliament): Can speak and take part in the proceedings of either House (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha), joint sittings, and any Parliamentary Committee of which he is named a member
⚠ Cannot vote on any motion or bill
Article 105(4): Privileges and immunities of a Member of Parliament
Not a member of the Central Cabinet; not a full-time government servant — private practice not completely debarred, but subject to government restrictions
## 4. Attorney General vs Advocate General vs Solicitor General
Basis | Attorney General | Advocate General | Solicitor General
Basis | Constitutional — Article 76 | Constitutional — Article 165 | Non-constitutional / statutory
Serves | Union Government (national level) | State Government | Union Government — assists the Attorney General
Appointed by | President | Governor | Appointments Committee of the Cabinet
Tenure | Pleasure of the President | Pleasure of the Governor | Fixed statutory term
Legislative floor | Can speak in Parliament | Can speak in the State Legislature — Article 177 | No floor rights
Additional Solicitors General: Also non-constitutional — the SG and ASGs were created to assist the Attorney General

t: Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) — Articles 148 to 151
text:
## 1. Status
Part V, Chapter V — Articles 148 to 151; an independent constitutional authority
Guardian of the Public Purse / Guardian of Public Finance; head of the Indian Audit and Accounts Department
Dr. B.R. Ambedkar: The most important officer under the Constitution
Four bulwarks of democracy: CAG, Supreme Court, UPSC, Election Commission of India
CAG (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act: 1971
1976 departmentalisation: Accounting separated from auditing — CAG relieved of preparing Union accounts from 1 March 1976
Union accounts now compiled by the Central Government Accounts authority under the Ministry of Finance; CAG still compiles and maintains the accounts of most States
## 2. Appointment, tenure and removal — Article 148
Appointed by: The President — Article 148(1), by warrant under his hand and seal
⚠ Not the Prime Minister, the Finance Minister or the Public Accounts Committee
Tenure: Six years or 65 years of age, whichever is earlier — a dual tenure cap under the CAG Act, 1971 and Article 148(3) (⚠ not five years / 62 years)
Removal: By the President through the parliamentary removal process — Article 148(1) read with Article 124(4): same grounds and manner as a Supreme Court Judge
Address by both Houses, passed by a special majority, on proved misbehaviour or incapacity
After retirement — Article 148(4): Complete bar — no further office under the Government of India or of any State
Contrast: the UPSC Chairman also cannot take another job; judges can head commissions after retirement
Salary and service conditions: Fixed by Parliament by law — Article 148(3) and the Second Schedule; cannot be varied to his disadvantage after appointment
Administrative expenses — Article 148(6): Charged on the Consolidated Fund of India — salaries, allowances and pensions of the CAG and staff (non-votable)
## 3. Duties and powers — Articles 149 to 151
Article 148: Appointment, oath, tenure, removal, post-retirement ban, salary and charged expenses
Article 149: Duties and powers — audits the receipts, expenditures, stores and accounts of the Union and the States
Article 150: Form of accounts — prescribed by the President on the advice of the CAG (the CAG does not prescribe it unilaterally)
Article 151(1): Union audit reports → President → laid before both Houses of Parliament
Article 151(2): State audit reports → Governor → laid before the State Legislature
Ultimate responsibility for taking action on the findings rests with Parliament (Union reports) / the State Legislature (State reports)
## 4. What the CAG audits
All expenditure from the Consolidated Funds of India, the States and Union Territories with Legislative Assemblies
All transactions of the Contingency Funds and Public Accounts of the Union and the States
Manufacturing, trading and profit and loss accounts of government entities; stores and stocks; public sector undertakings
Performance audits: Economy, efficiency and effectiveness
Audit timing: Post-expenditure (ex-post facto)
## 5. Limits — an Auditor General, not a Comptroller
No day-to-day control over the exchequer; does not control the issue or drawal of money from the treasury — unlike the British CAG
No power to disallow expenditure, enforce recovery or initiate criminal prosecutions
Public Accounts Committee: Friend, Philosopher and Guide — attends its meetings; assists its line-by-line examination of audit reports
⚠ False claims:
"CAG submits audit reports directly to the PAC / Parliament" — reports go first to the President or Governor
"CAG ensures no money is drawn from the Consolidated Fund of India without prior sanction"

topic: Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha and Legislative Councils
t: Lok Sabha — composition, membership and term
text:
## 1. Composition — Article 81
Maximum strength: 552 — up to 530 directly elected from the States + up to 20 from the Union Territories
Present strength: 543 elected — 530 from States + 13 from Union Territories
Anglo-Indians: Two nominated members under Article 331 — discontinued by the 104th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2019 (abolished after 25 January 2020); no nominated members now
First Lok Sabha: 489 elected members
Most seats: Uttar Pradesh — 80
Elected directly on adult suffrage — Article 326
## 2. Qualifications — Article 84
Citizen of India; at least 25 years old
Registered as a voter in a parliamentary constituency
Not holding an office of profit; not of unsound mind; not an undischarged insolvent
Other qualifications: prescribed by the Representation of the People Act
## 3. Disqualification
Article 102 and the Representation of the People Act, 1951
Tenth Schedule (Anti-Defection Law) — decided by the Speaker
Member of both Houses: Must choose one within 10 days
Contesting: From at most two constituencies
## 4. Term (duration) — Article 83
Five years from the date of its first sitting; can be dissolved earlier by the President
National Emergency: Parliament can extend the term one year at a time
## 5. Seat becomes vacant on
Resignation — addressed to the Speaker
Disqualification
Absence for 60 days without permission
Becoming a member of the other House
## 6. Reservation — Article 330
Seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in proportion to their population
Initially for 10 years; repeatedly extended — the 104th Amendment extended it until 2030
## 7. Quorum and ministers
Quorum: One-tenth of the total membership
Non-member Minister: Must get elected within six months
Council of Ministers: Limited to 15 percent of the total membership of the Lok Sabha — 91st Amendment

topic: Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha and Legislative Councils
t: Rajya Sabha — composition and special powers
text:
## 1. Composition — Article 80
Maximum strength: 250 — up to 238 elected representatives of States and Union Territories + 12 nominated by the President
Present strength: 245 — 233 elected + 12 nominated
Nominated for special knowledge or practical experience in literature, science, art and social service
Union Territories represented: Only three — Delhi, Puducherry, Jammu and Kashmir
Election: Indirect — by the elected members of State Legislative Assemblies, by proportional representation through the Single Transferable Vote
Seat allocation: Based on population — Fourth Schedule; most seats: Uttar Pradesh — 31
First nominated woman member: Nargis Dutt, 1980
## 2. Membership and term
Qualifications (Article 84): Citizen; minimum age 30 years; registered voter in any parliamentary constituency; no office of profit
Disqualifications: Same as the Lok Sabha — Article 102, the RPA 1951 and the Tenth Schedule; anti-defection questions decided by the Chairman
Term of a member: Six years; one-third retire every two years
Permanent House: Not subject to dissolution — Article 83(1)
Casual vacancy: Filled for the remainder of the term
Resignation addressed to the Chairman — the Vice-President
Quorum: One-tenth of total membership
## 3. Special powers
Article 249: Authorise Parliament to legislate on a State List subject in the national interest — two-thirds of members present and voting
Article 312: Initiate creation of new All-India Services — two-thirds majority
Equal powers with the Lok Sabha on Constitutional Amendment Bills; can introduce Ordinary and Constitutional Amendment Bills
Money Bills: Can only recommend changes within 14 days — the Lok Sabha introduces them and has the final say
## 4. Lok Sabha vs Rajya Sabha
Basis | Lok Sabha | Rajya Sabha
Maximum strength | 552 | 250
Election | Direct | Indirect
Minimum age | 25 years | 30 years
Term | Five years; can be dissolved | Member six years; permanent House
Nominated members | None (Anglo-Indian nomination abolished) | 12

topic: Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha and Legislative Councils
t: The three "Councils" and the State Legislative Council
text:
## 1. Three "Councils" in Indian Polity
Council of Ministers: An executive body aiding and advising the President (Union — Article 74) or the Governor (State — Article 163)
Council of States: The Rajya Sabha — Upper House of Parliament, Article 80
State Legislative Council: The Vidhan Parishad — Upper House of bicameral State Legislatures, Articles 168, 169 and 171
Parliament = President + Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha; the Vice-President is ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha but not a member of Parliament (not a member of the Council of States)
## 2. Union vs State Council of Ministers
Basis | Union | State
Aids and advises | President — Article 74 | Governor — Article 163
Collectively responsible to | Lok Sabha — Article 75(3) | Legislative Assembly — Article 164(2)
Ministers hold office during the pleasure of | President (not the PM) | Governor (not the CM)
Maximum size (91st Amendment, 2003) | 15% of the Lok Sabha | 15% of the Assembly; minimum 12
Non-member Minister — maximum | Six consecutive months — Article 75(5) | Six consecutive months — Article 164(4)
Cabinet (smaller inner core) | Prime Minister + Cabinet Ministers | Chief Minister + Cabinet Ministers
Responsibility: Only to the Lower House — not to the Rajya Sabha, Parliament as a whole, or the President/Governor
"Cabinet": Inserted into Article 352 by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978 — which also lets the President return the Council's advice once; he is bound after reconsideration
Governor: Bound by ministerial advice except in discretionary areas
## 3. State legislatures — Part VI
Part VI: Articles 168 to 212
Bicameral: Governor + Legislative Assembly (Lower House) + Legislative Council (Upper House); unicameral: Governor + Legislative Assembly
Bicameral States — 6: Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Bihar, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Uttar Pradesh — largest Council: Uttar Pradesh, 100 seats
Bicameralism first introduced at the Central level by the GoI Act, 1919 — Council of State and Central Legislative Assembly
## 4. Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad) — Article 171
Size: Maximum one-third of the Assembly; minimum 40 members
Composition:
One-third elected by MLAs — from among non-MLAs
One-third elected by local authorities — municipalities and district boards
One-twelfth elected by graduates — at least 3 years of standing, residing in the State
One-twelfth elected by teachers — at least 3 years of standing, in institutions of at least secondary-school level
One-sixth nominated by the Governor — literature, science, art, the co-operative movement, social service (five fields)
Election: Proportional representation by single transferable vote, by secret ballot
⚠ Traps: The co-operative movement is a ground under Article 171 but not for the Rajya Sabha (Article 80); industrialists and commerce are not valid categories
Permanent body: Cannot be dissolved (not even on the Governor's recommendation) — member's term six years; one-third retire every two years
Chairman: Elected by the Council from among its members — Article 182 (not nominated by the Governor)
Called: The Upper House / House of Elders
## 5. Creation or abolition of a Council — Article 169
State Assembly initiates it by passing a resolution by special majority — a majority (at least 50 percent) of the total membership and at least two-thirds of members present and voting
The resolution is recommendatory — it does not legally compel the Union to introduce a bill
Parliament then enacts the law creating or abolishing the Council by simple majority, like an ordinary bill — not an amendment of the Constitution under Article 368
## 6. Council vs Assembly — powers
Basis | Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha) | Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad)
Basis | Article 170 | Article 171
House | Lower / Popular House | Upper House
Life | Five-year term; dissolvable; cannot be abolished | Permanent; can be abolished (Article 169)
Minimum age | 25 years | 30 years
Size | Maximum 500; minimum 60 | Maximum one-third of the Assembly; minimum 40
Presiding officer | Speaker — elected from its members; decides Money Bill status | Chairman
Money Bill | Originates only here; final authority | Only recommends; must return within 14 days — else deemed passed
Ordinary Bill | Originating and overriding chamber — can re-pass a bill | Can delay 3 months after the first passage + 1 month after re-passage = 4 months maximum; no veto, cannot permanently block
Council of States (Rajya Sabha) compared: also permanent (cannot be dissolved or abolished); members six years, one-third retire every two years; minimum age 30; maximum 250

t: Speaker of the Lok Sabha
text:
## 1. Constitutional basis
Part V — Articles 93, 94, 95, 96, 100, 110 and 118
Election (Article 93): By the Lok Sabha from among its sitting members — must already be an elected MP (a non-member cannot be chosen under the six-month relaxation rule)
Date of election: Fixed by the President
Oath: No separate oath as presiding officer — only the oath as an ordinary Member of Parliament
Lok Sabha Secretariat: Functions under the Speaker's control and guidance
## 2. Normal sittings vs own removal resolution
Situation | Presides | Speaks / takes part | Votes in the first instance | Casting vote
Normal sittings | Yes | Yes | No | Yes — on an equality of votes (Article 100)
Own removal resolution (Article 96) | No — even if present | Yes | Yes — like an ordinary member | No — not in a tie
## 3. Resignation, dissolution and removal
Resignation: In writing to the Deputy Speaker — Article 94(b) (laterally, not upward to the President)
On dissolution: Does not vacate office immediately — continues until just before the first meeting of the new Lok Sabha
Removal — Article 94(c): Resolution passed by a majority of all the then members (effective majority), after at least 14 days' written notice
## 4. Powers
Money Bill — Article 110(4): Sole and final authority to certify a Money Bill — the endorsement is final when the Bill goes to the Rajya Sabha and to the President
Joint sitting — Article 118(4): Presides; in his absence the Deputy Speaker, before the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
Quorum (Article 100): One-tenth of the House — adjourns or suspends the sitting when there is no quorum
Adjournment sine die
Anti-defection (Tenth Schedule): Decides disqualification — subject to judicial review (Kihoto Hollohan)
Rule 8(1): Fixes the date for the election of the Deputy Speaker
## 5. Regular Speaker vs Pro-Tem Speaker
Basis | Regular Speaker | Pro-Tem Speaker
Basis | Article 93 | Article 95(1)
Chosen by | Elected by Lok Sabha members | Appointed by the President — selection follows a convention (practice): usually the senior-most elected MP of the new House
Role | Regular presiding officer; enforces rules and business | Administers the oath to newly elected MPs; enables the election of the regular Speaker
Tenure | Continues through dissolution until the next House meets | Temporary — ceases the moment the regular Speaker is elected
## 6. Speakers — firsts
G. V. Mavalankar: First Speaker — 1952 to 1956
Meira Kumar: First woman Speaker — 15th Lok Sabha, 2009 to 2014
Sumitra Mahajan: Second woman Speaker — 16th Lok Sabha, 2014 to 2019

t: Deputy Speaker and the Rajya Sabha presiding officers
text:
## 1. Deputy Speaker — Articles 93 to 96
Elected by the Lok Sabha from its sitting members (Article 93)
Date fixed by the Speaker (Rule 8(1)); communicated to members by the Secretary-General
From the Opposition: Only a convention (practice) — not a constitutional requirement
Oath: No separate oath — only as an ordinary MP
Resignation: To the Speaker — Article 94(b) (not to the President or the Prime Minister)
Removal: Effective majority — a majority of all the then members of the Lok Sabha (not a simple or two-thirds majority); fourteen days' notice
On dissolution: Vacates office immediately — the protection of continuing after dissolution applies only to the Speaker
## 2. Deputy Speaker — powers and position
In the Chair: Same powers as the Speaker — no appeal to the Speaker against his ruling
Joint sittings: Presides when the Speaker is absent — Article 118(4)
Parliamentary Committee: Automatically becomes its chairman when appointed to it
When not in the Chair (normal proceedings): Sits as an ordinary member of the House — can participate in debates, move motions, vote in the first instance
Own removal resolution (Article 96): Cannot preside even if present; can speak, participate and vote in the first instance; no casting vote when votes are equally divided
## 3. Rajya Sabha
Chairman: The Vice-President — ex officio, Articles 64 and 89(1); not a member of the Rajya Sabha
Deputy Chairman: Chosen from among the sitting members of the Rajya Sabha — Article 89(2)

text:

## 2. Financial committees of Parliament
Committee | Members | Chairman
Public Accounts Committee | 22 — 15 Lok Sabha + 7 Rajya Sabha | Appointed by the Speaker — from the Opposition by convention since 1967
Estimates Committee | 30 — Lok Sabha only; the largest committee | Appointed by the Speaker — traditionally from the ruling party
Committee on Public Undertakings | 22 — 15 Lok Sabha + 7 Rajya Sabha | Appointed by the Speaker
## 3. Constitutional and statutory bodies
UPSC Chairperson: Appointed and removed by the President (Article 315)
Removal for misbehaviour needs a binding Supreme Court inquiry (Article 317) — Parliament has no role
State PSC Chairperson: Appointed by the Governor — but only the President can remove the Chairperson or a member
Finance Commission (Article 280): Chairperson appointed by the President; fixed statutory term
Five members — one Chairperson + four others

First Chairperson: K.C. Neogy
