t: Sessions — summoning, adjournment, prorogation and dissolution
text:
## 1. Summoning — Article 85 (Part V)
The President summons each House at such time and place as he thinks fit
Maximum gap between two sessions: six months — between the last sitting of one session and the first sitting of the next
So Parliament must meet at least twice a year
⚠ Not in the Constitution:
A fixed number of sessions — Budget, Monsoon and Winter sessions are a convention
A minimum number of sitting days — not 60, 90 or 100 per year
## 2. Ending a sitting or session
Device | By whom | Effect
Adjournment | Presiding Officer (Speaker or Chairman) | Suspends the sitting for a specified time — hours, days or weeks; session unaffected; pending business stays active
Adjournment sine die | Presiding Officer | Ends the sitting indefinitely — no day named for reassembly; precedes prorogation
Prorogation — Article 85(2)(a) | President, on the advice of the Council of Ministers | Terminates the session; pending bills unaffected; notices lapse unless re-introduced
Dissolution — Article 85(2)(b) | President | Ends the very life of the Lok Sabha — pending bills, motions and resolutions lapse (subject to Article 107 rules); the Rajya Sabha is permanent
## 3. Linked time limits
Ordinance (Article 123): Valid six weeks after reassembly; maximum life without approval six months plus six weeks
Absence of an MP (Article 101(4)): Unexcused absence for 60 days can lead to vacation of the seat — the calculation excludes periods of prorogation and adjournments of more than four consecutive days

t: Question Hour and Zero Hour
text:
## 1. Purpose
Executive accountability: Parliamentary hours and procedural motions are the main means of enforcing executive accountability, scrutinising government policies and actions, and controlling the Council of Ministers
Accountability triangle: Question Hour + Supplementary Questions + Adjournment Motions — directly ensure cabinet (executive) responsibility to the legislature
Indigenous Indian contributions: Zero Hour and the Calling Attention Motion
## 2. Question Hour vs Zero Hour
Basis | Question Hour | Zero Hour
Timing — Lok Sabha | First hour of every sitting — 11:00 AM to 12:00 Noon | Immediately follows Question Hour — 12:00 Noon to 1:00 PM
Timing — Rajya Sabha | 12:00 Noon to 1:00 PM (shifted after 2014) | 11:00 AM to 12:00 Noon
Nature | Formal procedure — codified in the Rules | Informal convention — an Indian innovation of the early 1960s
Purpose | Asking and answering questions addressed to Ministers on administrative actions | Raising urgent matters of public importance without prior notice
Duration | Maximum one hour | Generally up to one hour — some notes say it is not fixed
## 3. Types of questions — the three primary categories
Basis | Starred Question | Unstarred Question | Short Notice Question
Mark | Asterisk | No asterisk | Identified by a shorter notice period
Answer | Oral — on the floor of the House | Written — laid on the Table (purely written; no oral answer) | Oral
Supplementary questions | Allowed — after the oral answer | Not allowed | Allowed
Subject | General / ordinary public importance | General / ordinary public importance | Urgent public importance
Daily limit | At most 20 listed for oral answer | No strict limit of 20 | At the discretion of the Speaker or Chairman
All three are taken up during Question Hour

t: Motions and other procedural devices
text:
## 1. Motions on the Government's survival
Motion | Moved by / where | Key points
No-Confidence Motion | Opposition — Lok Sabha only — Rule 198 | Tests the Council of Ministers' majority; needs the support of 50 members; if passed, the Government must resign; first moved by J. B. Kripalani in 1963 against Jawaharlal Nehru
Confidence Motion | Government (Council of Ministers) — Lok Sabha only | Proves majority floor support; if defeated, the Government falls
Censure Motion | Lok Sabha only | Strong disapproval / criticism of specific policies; reasons must be stated; does not force resignation — shows political weakness
## 2. Calling Attention vs Adjournment Motion
Basis | Calling Attention Motion | Adjournment Motion
Origin | Indian parliamentary innovation | Traditional parliamentary device
House | Either House | Lok Sabha only
Permission | Presiding Officer's permission | Presiding Officer's consent
Objective | Draw a Minister's attention to an urgent public matter | Discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance
Business | Does not disrupt the daily agenda | Interrupts / suspends normal business
Censure | No element of condemnation | Involves censure or condemnation of the Government
Adjournment Motion conditions: A single, definite, specific matter of recent occurrence; cannot raise a question of privilege; only one per sitting; admissible only when other tools (e.g. Short Duration discussions) are too late
Restriction: Calling Attention notices restricted the scope of the Adjournment Motion — not of Question Hour or Zero Hour
## 3. Other motions
Privilege Motion: Against a Minister for withholding or distorting facts — either House; Presiding Officer's consent; referred to the Committee of Privileges
Closure / Guillotine Motion: Lok Sabha only — when the allotted debate time expires, debate closes immediately and all undiscussed financial demands and clauses are put to the vote
## 4. Cut Motions — on a demand for grant
Cut Motion | Reduction | Purpose
Policy Cut | Reduce to ₹1 | Complete disapproval of the underlying policy
Economy Cut | By a specified amount | Administrative economy
Token Cut | By ₹100 | Ventilate a specific grievance within government responsibility
Passing any Cut Motion in the Lok Sabha signals loss of financial control — the Government must resign
## 5. Rules and conventions
Rule 184 (Lok Sabha): Discussion on a matter of public interest with a formal motion and voting — defeat can mean potential collapse of the ruling party
Rule 377 (Lok Sabha): Raise urgent matters not covered under Questions, Calling Attention or other motions
Written notice to the Secretary-General
Number of matters raised daily increased from 20 to 30 in 2015
Interpellation: The formal right of asking questions of the Executive — demanding explanations of government actions or policies
Yielding the Floor: Convention — the Speaker orders a speaking member to yield (stop) so that another member can speak

t: Kinds of Bills
text:
## 1. Basics
Bill: Proposed legislation — becomes an Act only after the President's assent (Article 111)
Parliament = President + Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha — the President is an integral part of Parliament but not a member of either House
Private Member's Bill: Introduced by an MP who is not a Minister — not necessarily a nominated member
## 2. Money Bill — Articles 109 and 110
Introduced: Only in the Lok Sabha, with the President's prior recommendation
Contents: Provisions on taxes, borrowings, custody of and withdrawal from the Consolidated Fund of India
A Bill dealing merely with fines or penalties is not a Money Bill
Rajya Sabha: Only a recommendatory role — recommendations within 14 days; cannot amend or reject it
Certification: The Speaker's decision (Article 110(3)) is final
Joint Sitting: Not possible
Every Money Bill is a Financial Bill — but not every Financial Bill is a Money Bill
## 3. Financial Bills — Article 117
Financial Bill (I) — Article 117(1): Contains Article 110 matters plus general legislation
Only in the Lok Sabha; needs the President's recommendation for introduction
The Rajya Sabha can reject or amend it fully; Joint Sitting possible
Financial Bill (II) — Article 117(3): Involves expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India; no Article 110 matters
In either House; President's recommendation needed before consideration; Joint Sitting possible
## 4. Comparison — Ordinary, Money and Constitution Amendment Bills
Basis | Ordinary Bill | Money Bill | Constitution Amendment Bill
Articles | 107 and 108 | 109 and 110 | 368
House of origin | Either House | Lok Sabha only | Either House — not a State Legislature
President's prior recommendation | Not required | Required | Not required
Rajya Sabha's power | Equal — may amend or reject; no fixed time limit | Only recommendations within 14 days | Equal — passed separately by each House
Majority | Simple | Simple | Special — a majority of the total membership + two-thirds of members present and voting
Joint Sitting (Article 108) | Yes — in a deadlock | No | No
President's options | Assent, withhold, or return once | Assent or withhold — cannot return | Must give assent — no veto
Federal provisions in an Amendment Bill also need ratification by at least one-half of the State Legislatures

t: Passing a Bill — readings, joint sittings, assent and lapse
text:
## 1. Readings
General discussion on a Bill: Second Reading — not the First or Third Reading
## 2. Joint Sitting — Article 108
Summoned by the President (who expresses the intention to summon it)
Presided over by the Lok Sabha Speaker → in his absence the Deputy Speaker → then the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
Quorum: One-tenth of the total membership; questions decided by simple majority
Three Joint Sittings so far:
1961: Dowry Prohibition Bill
1978: Banking Service Commission Repeal Bill
2002: Prevention of Terrorism Act (POTA)
## 3. Vetoes used
Pocket Veto: President Giani Zail Singh — Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, 1986
Absolute Veto: President Dr. Rajendra Prasad — PEPSU Appropriation Bill, 1954
## 4. Lapse of Bills on dissolution of the Lok Sabha
Lapses: A Bill pending in the Lok Sabha; a Bill passed by the Lok Sabha but pending in the Rajya Sabha
Does not lapse: A Bill pending in the Rajya Sabha not yet passed by the Lok Sabha; a Bill for which a Joint Sitting has been notified
Prorogation does not cause a Bill to lapse
## 5. State Bills
Legislative Council can delay an Ordinary Bill three months the first time and one month the second time — maximum four months
State Money Bill: Originates in the Legislative Assembly with the Governor's recommendation; the Council gets 14 days
Reservation: The Governor can reserve a State Bill for the President — Article 200; the President considers it — Article 201
## 6. Articles at a glance
Article 108: Joint Sittings; Articles 109 and 110: Money Bills; Article 111: Presidential Assent
Articles 112 to 114: Budget, Demands for Grants, Appropriation Bill; Article 116: Vote-on-Account; Article 117: Financial Bills
Articles 200 and 201: Governor's and President's assent to State Bills; Article 368: Constitutional amendment

t: Budget and financial terms
text:
Annual Financial Statement (Article 112): The constitutional name for the Union Budget
Appropriation Bill (Article 114): Authorises withdrawal from the Consolidated Fund of India — for voted grants and charged expenditure
Vote on Account (Article 116): An advance grant by the Lok Sabha for estimated expenditure for part of the financial year, pending passage of the budget
Vote of Credit: An unexpected, blank-check grant — for an emergency or indefinite demand whose details cannot be stated in a budget
Charged Expenditure: Non-votable — paid directly out of the Consolidated Fund of India; can only be discussed
Cut Motions:
Policy Cut: Reduce a demand to ₹1 — complete disapproval of the underlying policy
Economy Cut: Reduce by a specified amount — demands economy in expenditure
Token Cut: Reduce by ₹100 — ventilates a specific grievance within the Government's responsibility

t: Rules of procedure in the Lok Sabha — quick recap
text:
## 1. Rules vs Constitution
Constitution: Gives the broad institutional framework; day-to-day proceedings follow the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha
Not in the Constitution — derive from parliamentary rules or conventions: No-Confidence Motion, Zero Hour, Rule 377
Primary mechanisms for executive accountability: Question Hour, Supplementary Questions, Adjournment Motions
## 2. Motions
No-Confidence Motion (Rule 198): Lok Sabha only; against the entire Council of Ministers — not an individual minister
Written notice to the Secretary-General; support of at least 50 members for leave; no reasons need be stated
Tests the majority support of the Council of Ministers
Confidence Motion: Moved by the Government (Council of Ministers) — demonstrates majority on the floor
Censure Motion: Strong disapproval of specific policies — against an individual minister or the entire Council; reasons must be stated
Rule 184: A substantive motion — discussion on a specific matter of public interest followed by voting; significant political consequences
Rule 377: Raise matters of general public importance that cannot be raised under Questions, Calling Attention or other Motions
Written notice + the Speaker's consent; daily limit 20 → 30 in 2015
Adjournment Motion: Interrupts / suspends normal business — a definite matter of urgent public importance and recent occurrence; element of censure or condemnation
Calling Attention Motion: Indian innovation — draws a Minister's attention to an urgent matter; resembles an Adjournment Motion but has no censure element
Closure Motion: Cuts short debate and puts the matter to vote
Guillotine: A form of closure when the allotted time expires — all remaining discussed and undiscussed clauses or demands for grants go to vote immediately
## 3. Question Hour, Zero Hour and questions
Question Hour: First hour of every sitting — 11 AM to 12 Noon; a formal procedure under the Rules of Procedure; for asking and answering classified questions; lasts one hour
Zero Hour: Follows Question Hour — 12 Noon to 1 PM; Indian innovation of the early 1960s; informal convention; urgent matters of great public importance without prior formal notice; generally up to one hour
Starred: Oral answer on the floor; supplementaries allowed; at most 20 per day
Unstarred: Written answer laid on the table; no supplementaries
Short Notice: Urgent matter of public importance; notice shorter than 10 clear days; oral answer; supplementaries allowed
## 4. Other rules and constitutional basis
Rule 8(1): Election of the Deputy Speaker — date fixed by the Speaker, notified by the Secretary-General
Money Bill: Article 110; Joint Sitting: Article 108

t: Parliamentary and constitutional glossary
text:
## 1. Sessions and sittings
Summoning: By the President — Article 85; maximum gap between two sessions six months
Session: From the first sitting of a House to its prorogation or dissolution — standard sessions: Budget, Monsoon, Winter
Sitting: A daily meeting of a House during a session — morning and post-lunch sittings
Adjournment: Ends a daily sitting for a specified time — hours, days or weeks — by the Presiding Officer (Speaker or Chairman)
Adjournment sine die: Ends a sitting without assigning a day for reassembly
Prorogation (Article 85(2)): By the President (or Governor) — terminates a session, not the House itself
Dissolution: By the President (or Governor) — ends the life of the House; applies only to the Lok Sabha (the Rajya Sabha is permanent)
Recess: Period between prorogation and the start of a new session — the President may issue ordinances (Article 123) during recess
Quorum (Article 100): Minimum members needed to conduct business — one-tenth of the total membership
## 2. Writs — recap
Writ | Meaning | Purpose
Habeas Corpus | "To have the body" | Quashes illegal or unlawful physical detention
Mandamus | "We Command" | Directs a public official, inferior court or statutory authority to perform a mandatory public or legal duty
Prohibition | "To Forbid" | Preventive — a higher court stops an inferior court or tribunal from exceeding its jurisdiction
Certiorari | "To be Certified" | A higher court quashes an order already passed — for lack of jurisdiction or an error of law; curative and preventive
Quo-Warranto | "By what warrant/authority" | Inquires into the legality of a claim to a public office — prevents illegal usurpation
## 3. Judicial review and basic structure
Judicial Review: An inherent power of constitutional courts — examines legislative enactments and executive actions against constitutional validity
Basic Structure Doctrine: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) — core structural features cannot be abrogated or destroyed, even through Article 368
## 4. Pardoning terms
Pardon: Completely absorbs and removes both the sentence and the conviction — the offender is in the same position as if the offence had never been committed
Commutation: Substitutes a lighter form of punishment for a heavier one — e.g. death sentence → rigorous life imprisonment
Remission: Reduces the period of a sentence without changing its character — e.g. two years of rigorous imprisonment → one year
Respite: Awards a lesser sentence in place of the original penalty, due to special personal circumstances — pregnancy, mental or physical disability
Reprieve: A temporary stay / postponement of execution — especially for the death penalty — giving time to seek a Presidential pardon
## 5. Elections and representation
First-Past-the-Post: A plurality system — the candidate with the highest number of valid votes wins; no absolute majority (over 50 percent) needed
PR-STV (Proportional Representation by Single Transferable Vote): Multi-preference, quota-based, indirect — to ensure proportional representation
Used to elect the President, Vice-President, Rajya Sabha and Legislative Councils
Delimitation: Statutory process of redrawing constituency boundaries on recent census figures — enforces equal representation
Right to vote: A legal / statutory right — not a Fundamental Right
## 6. Other terms
Dyarchy: "Double Rule" — introduced in the provinces by the GoI Act, 1919
Reserved subjects: Governor and Executive Council; Transferred subjects: Governor and popular Ministers
Collective Responsibility (Article 75(3)): The Council of Ministers is collectively answerable to the Lok Sabha (the popular House) — all ministers sink or swim together
Panchayati Raj: Three-tier system everywhere — intermediate tier Panchayat Samiti is optional in States with a population of 20 lakh or less

t: Parliamentary committees — types and financial committees
text:
## 1. Role and types
Role: A primary mechanism of parliamentary control over administration — detailed and complex legislative scrutiny
Broadly classified into two types:
Standing Committees: Permanent and continuous; reconstituted annually or periodically — e.g. Financial Committees, Department-Related Standing Committees
Ad-hoc Committees: Temporary — for a specific inquiry or task; cease to exist after their reports — e.g. Joint Parliamentary Committees, Inquiry Committees
Department-Related Standing Committees: 24 — 16 of the Lok Sabha + 8 of the Rajya Sabha (joint ratio about 2:1)
## 2. The three financial committees
Basis | Public Accounts Committee | Estimates Committee | Committee on Public Undertakings
Members | 22 — 15 Lok Sabha + 7 Rajya Sabha | 30 — Lok Sabha only (zero Rajya Sabha) | 22 — 15 Lok Sabha + 7 Rajya Sabha
Size | — | The single largest committee | —
Election | PR-STV | PR-STV | PR-STV
Tenure | One year | One year | One year
Chairman | Appointed by the Speaker — from the Opposition since 1967 | Appointed by the Speaker — from the ruling party | Appointed by the Speaker
Work | Primarily examines CAG audit reports, appropriation accounts, wasteful expenditure | Examines budget estimates; suggests economy and efficiency in administration | Scrutinises PSU accounts, commercial soundness and PSU-related CAG reports (PSU audits)
Election of members: All three by proportional representation through the single transferable vote
Ministers cannot be elected or nominated to the PAC, the Estimates Committee or the Committee on Public Undertakings
## 3. A Joint Parliamentary Committee — 2G Spectrum
Constituted: 2011 — an Ad-hoc Joint Committee
Members: 30 — 20 Lok Sabha + 10 Rajya Sabha
Chairman: P.C. Chacko

t: Other parliamentary committees
text:
Committee on Subordinate Legislation: Checks that delegated executive rule-making — regulations, bye-laws and sub-rules — stays within statutory limits
15 members in each House; Ministers cannot be members
Committee on Government Assurances: Tracks and reports on the fulfilment of promises, undertakings and assurances given by Ministers on the floor of the House
Committee on Petitions: Examines petitions and representations submitted to the House
Lok Sabha: 15 members; Rajya Sabha: 10 members; Ministers cannot be members
Business Advisory Committee: Regulates the official parliamentary timetable and the programme of House business
Rules Committee: Recommends amendments, additions and procedural adjustments to the Rules of Procedure
Lok Sabha Ethics Committee:
First constituted as an Ad-hoc Committee on 16 May 2000; became permanent in 2015
Oversees the moral and ethical conduct of members; cannot take up sub-judice matters
Consultative Committees: Constituted by the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs — not parliamentary committees per se; MPs from specific zones or ministries

t: Constituent Assembly committees — recap
text:
Drafting Committee: Chaired by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar — 7 members in total
B.L. Mitter (original member) → replaced by N. Madhava Rau
D.P. Khaitan (original member) → replaced by T.T. Krishnamachari

t: The three funds of the Union
text:
## 1. Constitutional basis
Part XII: Articles 265 to 267 — funds and taxation
Article 265: No tax shall be levied or collected except by authority of law
Article 266: Consolidated Funds and Public Accounts of the Union and the States
Article 267: Contingency Funds of the Union and the States
Part V: Articles 112 to 116 — budget procedure
## 2. Consolidated Fund vs Public Account vs Contingency Fund
Basis | Consolidated Fund of India | Public Account of India | Contingency Fund of India
Article | 266(1) | 266(2) | 267(1)
Contents | All revenues (taxes, duties, non-tax revenue), all loans (treasury bills, market loans, foreign loans) and repayments of loans | Money held in trust or custody — provident funds, judicial deposits, savings bank deposits | An imprest at the disposal of the President for unforeseen expenses
Controlled by | Parliament | Executive (Government) | President — administered by the Finance Secretary on his behalf
Nature | Dynamic main treasury account | Operational banking account — operates as a banker | Fixed statutory corpus
Withdrawal | Only under an Appropriation Act (Article 114) passed by Parliament | Executive disbursements — no prior parliamentary voting | Advances — no prior voting; ex-post facto approval later
⚠ Cannot authorise withdrawals from the Consolidated Fund on their own authority: the President, Prime Minister, Finance Minister, CAG
## 3. Budget Articles 112 to 116
Article 112: Annual Financial Statement (Union Budget) — 112(3) lists the charged items
Article 113: Procedure for estimates — Demands for Grants
Article 114: Appropriation Bills — authority for withdrawal from the Consolidated Fund (114(3): every withdrawal needs an Appropriation Act)
Article 115: Supplementary, additional and excess grants
Article 116: Vote on Account, Votes of Credit and Exceptional Grants

t: Charged expenditure and constitutional salaries
text:
## 1. Charged expenditure
Non-votable: Not submitted to the vote of Parliament (or a State Legislature) — but can be discussed by both Houses
Purpose: Guarantees the financial independence of constitutional offices
Three separate questions: The authority that determines the salary (Parliament or a State Legislature, by law) is distinct from the fund that pays it, which is distinct from whether it is charged or voted
Schedules: Second Schedule — salaries (emoluments, allowances and privileges) of the President, Governors, Presiding Officers, Supreme Court and High Court Judges, CAG; Third Schedule — forms of oaths
## 2. Charged on the Consolidated Fund of India
President: Emoluments, allowances and office expenses
Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha; Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha — salaries, allowances and pensions
Supreme Court judges — salaries, allowances and pensions
High Court judges — only their pensions — Article 112(3)(d)(iii)
CAG — salary, allowances, pension and administrative expenses
Debt charges of the Government of India — interest and sinking fund charges
Any sum to satisfy a judgment, decree or arbitral award against the Government of India
## 3. Who fixes, who pays, charged or voted
Office | Fixed by law under | Salary paid from | Pension paid from | Charged or voted
President | Article 59(3) | Consolidated Fund of India | CFI | Charged (non-votable)
Prime Minister and Ministers | Article 75(6) | CFI | CFI | Voted — not charged; fully votable through annual Demands for Grants
Speaker and Deputy Speaker | Article 97 | CFI | — | Charged
Chairman and Deputy Chairman (Rajya Sabha) | Article 97 | CFI | — | Charged
Supreme Court Judges (incl. CJI) | Article 125 | CFI | CFI | Charged
High Court Judges (incl. Chief Justice) | Article 221 | Consolidated Fund of the State — Article 202(3) | CFI | Salary charged on the State fund; pension charged on the CFI
CAG | Article 148(3) | CFI | CFI | Charged — Articles 148(3) and 148(6)
Governor | Article 158(3) | Consolidated Fund of the State | State fund | Charged on the State fund (non-votable)
Election Commission (CEC and ECs) | — | CFI (salaries and administrative expenses) | CFI | Voted — not among the charged items of Article 112(3)
## 4. Special cases
Vice-President: No salary as Vice-President — no separate fund and not charged as VP; draws salary solely in the capacity of Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (charged on the CFI)
One individual appointed Governor of two or more States: Emoluments and allowances payable allocated among the States in the proportion the President fixes by order (Article 158)
Article 125: Salaries, allowances and rights of Supreme Court Judges; Article 221: High Court Judges

t: Supreme Court — establishment, Chief Justice and judges
text:
## 1. Establishment
Part V, Chapter IV: Articles 124 to 147
Inaugurated: 28 January 1950 — succeeded the Federal Court (set up under the GoI Act, 1935) and the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council
Article 124: Establishment and constitution of the Supreme Court; appointment of judges
124(1): Parliament alone can increase the number of judges by law
124(2): Judges retire at 65 years
Article 130 — seat: Delhi — the Chief Justice may decide other places for sittings with the President's approval
## 2. Chief Justice of India
Heads the Union Judiciary
Appointed by the President — Article 124(2); by convention, the senior-most SC judge
Term: No fixed term in years — holds office until 65 years of age
Oath: By the President (or a person he appoints) — form in the Third Schedule
Resignation: In writing to the President
## 3. Acting, ad hoc and retired judges
Acting Chief Justice — Article 126: Appointed by the President when the CJI's office is vacant, the CJI is absent or unable to perform duties
Ad hoc judges — Article 127: Appointed by the Chief Justice, with the previous consent of the President and after consulting the concerned High Court Chief Justice — to meet a lack of quorum
Retired judges — Article 128: The Chief Justice may request them to attend sittings, with the President's prior consent
## 4. Court of Record — Article 129
Judgments have evidentiary value and cannot be questioned when produced before a subordinate court
Power to punish for contempt of itself — an inherent power
High Courts have parallel status — Article 215
## 5. Removal of judges — Article 124(4)
By order of the President after an Address by Parliament
Grounds: Proved misbehaviour or incapacity
Special majority in each House, in the same session: a majority of the total membership + at least two-thirds of members present and voting
Statutory inquiry: Procedure under the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968

t: Jurisdiction and powers of the Supreme Court
text:
## 1. Original jurisdiction — Article 131 (exclusive)
Federal disputes involving a legal right:
Centre vs one or more States
Centre and one or more States vs other States
One State vs another State
Excludes:
Political questions that involve no legal right
Treaties and agreements made before the Constitution (pre-Constitution treaties)
Inter-State water disputes — Article 262
Finance Commission matters — Article 280
Recovery of damages by a private party against the Union
## 2. Writ jurisdiction — Article 32
A Fundamental Right to approach the SC directly for enforcement of Part III rights — the SC cannot refuse an Article 32 petition
Writs: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo Warranto
Narrower than the High Courts' — Article 226 covers Fundamental Rights and legal rights
## 3. Appellate jurisdiction
Article 132 — constitutional: High Court judgments involving a substantial question of law on interpreting the Constitution — needs a High Court certificate (Article 134A)
Article 133 — civil: Civil proceedings with a substantial question of law of general importance — the High Court certifies under Article 134A that the SC must decide it
Article 134 — criminal: Where a High Court reversed an acquittal into a death sentence, or withdrew a trial to itself — capital-punishment reversals appealable as of right, without a certificate
Article 136 — Special Leave Petition: Discretionary, plenary and residual power — special leave to appeal from any judgment or order of any court or tribunal
Article 136(2): Not against courts-martial / Military Tribunals / Armed Forces Courts
## 4. Review, advice and complete justice
Article 137 — review: The SC reviews its own judgments, orders and pronouncements — distinct from judicial review of statutes; subject to Parliamentary law and court rules
Article 143 — advisory: The President refers questions of law or fact of public importance
143(1): SC may tender (or refuse) its opinion on matters of public importance
143(2): SC must (is bound to) tender its opinion on pre-constitutional disputes
Opinions are strictly advisory — not binding on the President
Article 141: Law declared by the SC is binding on all courts in India
Article 142: Pass any decree or order for complete justice in any cause pending before it — unhindered by ordinary statutory limitations
Curative petition: Evolved in Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002) — from the SC's inherent powers anchored in Article 142
Available after a review petition (Article 137) is dismissed; prevents abuse of process and cures gross miscarriage of justice
## 5. Constitution Bench — Article 145(3)
At least five judges — for cases with a substantial question of law on interpreting the Constitution, and for Article 143 references

t: Collegium system, the Judges Cases and the NJAC
text:
## 1. The Collegium
Governs: Appointment and transfer of Supreme Court and High Court judges
Not a constitutional body — not expressly in the Constitution, not created by an Act of Parliament — judicially evolved through the Judges Cases (Supreme Court rulings)
Formal appointment: By the President — SC judges under Article 124(2), HC judges under Article 217(1) — on the Collegium's binding recommendations ("consultation" with the prescribed collegium = concurrence)
Executive representation: Zero
## 2. The Judges Cases
Case | Year | Held
First Judges Case — S.P. Gupta v. Union of India | 1981 | Consultation does not mean concurrence — executive primacy (supremacy)
Second Judges Case — SCAORA v. Union of India | 1993 | Reversed the first: consultation means concurrence — judicial primacy; the Collegium was born — CJI + two senior-most judges
Third Judges Case — from a Presidential Reference | 1998 | Clarified the Collegium's working; the CJI's opinion must reflect plural consultation; expanded the SC Collegium to CJI + four senior-most judges
Fourth Judges Case | 2015 | NJAC struck down as unconstitutional — violated the independence of the judiciary; the Collegium restored and operational from 2015
## 3. Collegium compositions
SC appointments and elevations: CJI + four senior-most SC judges — five members
High Court appointments: Initiated by the HC Chief Justice + two senior-most HC judges → forwarded to the SC Collegium of the CJI + two senior-most SC judges
High Court transfers: CJI + four senior-most SC judges, consulting the Chief Justices of the transferring and receiving High Courts
## 4. National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC)
Created by: The 99th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2014 and the NJAC Act, 2014 (2014–15)
Six members (total strength):
Chief Justice of India — Chairperson
Two senior SC judges
Union Law Minister — a permanent member
Two eminent persons — nominated by the Prime Minister, the CJI and the Leader of the Opposition
Struck down (2015): Executive involvement infringed the independence of the judiciary — part of the basic structure of the Constitution

t: Supreme Court judges vs High Court judges
text:
## 1. Comparison
Basis | Supreme Court Judge | High Court Judge
Provisions | Part V, Chapter IV — Articles 124–147 (Article 124) | Part VI, Chapter V — Articles 214–231 (Article 217)
Appointed by | President — by warrant under his hand and seal | President — by warrant; the Governor has no power to appoint
Oath | President — Article 124(6) | Governor — Article 219
Resignation to | President — Article 124(2)(a) | President — Article 217(1)(a)
Retirement age | 65 | 62 — raised from 60 by the 15th Amendment Act, 1963
Distinguished jurist | Eligible — Article 124(3)(c) | Not eligible — no such provision
Transfer | Not applicable | Article 222 — by the President on the advice of the collegium led by the CJI
Pleading after retirement | Completely barred — no court or authority in India (Article 124(7)) | Only in the Supreme Court and other High Courts where not a permanent judge (Article 220)
Salary charged on | Consolidated Fund of India | Consolidated Fund of the State — Article 202(3)
Pension charged on | Consolidated Fund of India | Consolidated Fund of India (not the State) — Article 112(3)(d)(iii)
Court of record | Article 129 | Article 215
Removal of both: By the President's order after a parliamentary Address passed by each House by special majority — at least 50% of the total strength and two-thirds of members present and voting — for proved misbehaviour or incapacity
## 2. Other High Court judges
Acting Chief Justice — Article 223: Appointed by the President from among the HC judges — when the Chief Justice's office is vacant, or he is temporarily absent or unable to perform duties
Additional Judges — Article 224(1): By the President — for a temporary increase in business or arrears of work; for a period not exceeding two years, and not beyond 62 years of age
Acting Judges — Article 224(2): By the President — when a permanent judge is temporarily absent or acting as Chief Justice; ceases at 62
Retired judges — Article 224A: The HC Chief Justice may request a retired HC or SC judge to sit and act as an HC judge — with the President's prior consent
## 3. High Court Chief Justice — administrative capacity
Administrative acts (e.g. staff appointments, disciplinary actions) are subject to writ jurisdiction under Article 226 — another judge of the same High Court may exercise it
No absolute immunity from judicial review of administrative decisions

t: High Courts — establishment, judges and jurisdiction
text:
## 1. Framework and history
Part VI, Chapter V: Articles 214 to 231 (the Supreme Court: Articles 124 to 147, Part V)
Article 214: A High Court for each State
Indian High Courts Act, 1861: First three High Courts in 1862 — Calcutta, Bombay, Madras
North-Western Provinces High Court: Set up at Agra in 1866 → shifted to Allahabad in 1869
## 2. Key Articles
Article 215: Court of Record — evidentiary value; power to punish for contempt
Article 216: Composition — a Chief Justice and other judges appointed by the President; the President fixes each High Court's strength
⚠ Not Parliament, the Governor or the Chief Minister — contrast: Parliament fixes the Supreme Court's strength by law (Article 124(1))
Article 217: Appointment and conditions of office — removal under Article 217(1)(b) read with Article 124(4)
Article 218: Applies certain Supreme Court removal provisions to High Courts
Article 219: Oath — by the Governor of the State
Article 220: Restriction on practice after being a permanent judge
Article 221: Salaries, allowances and pensions
Article 222: Transfer of a judge from one High Court to another — by the President
Article 223: Acting Chief Justice; Article 224: Additional and Acting Judges; Article 224A: Retired judges attending
Article 226: Writs; Article 227: Superintendence
Article 230: Extending jurisdiction to Union Territories; Article 231: Common High Court for two or more States or UTs — established by Parliament
## 3. Appointment, qualifications and removal
Chief Justice: Appointed by the President after consulting the CJI and the Governor
Other judges: After consulting the CJI, the Governor and the Chief Justice of that High Court
Qualifications: Citizen of India, and at least 10 years in judicial office in India or 10 years as an advocate of a High Court — no provision for a distinguished jurist
Removal: By the President alone — after an Address by each House by special majority, only for proved misbehaviour or incapacity
After retirement: A permanent judge cannot plead or act before any court or authority in India — except the Supreme Court and a High Court where he was not a permanent judge
## 4. High Court vs Supreme Court
Basis | High Court | Supreme Court
Strength fixed by | President — Article 216 | Parliament by law — Article 124(1)
Appointment | President by warrant — Article 217 | President by warrant — Article 124
Oath | Governor — Article 219 | President — Article 124(6)
Resignation to | President — Article 217(1)(a) | President — Article 124(2)(a)
Retirement | 62 years | 65 years
Court of Record | Article 215 | Article 129
Writs | Fundamental Rights and ordinary legal rights — Article 226 | Fundamental Rights only — Article 32
Advisory jurisdiction | None | Article 143
Salary / pension | Salary on the State Fund; pension on the Consolidated Fund of India | Both on the Consolidated Fund of India
## 5. Writs and superintendence
Article 226: Broader than the Supreme Court's writ jurisdiction — Fundamental Rights and any other legal purpose or right; the writ power is discretionary
Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right
Article 227: Administrative and judicial superintendence over all subordinate courts and tribunals in its territory
⚠ Exception — Article 227(4): Not over courts or tribunals under laws relating to the Armed Forces
## 6. High Courts with more than one State or UT
High Court | Jurisdiction
Bombay | Maharashtra, Goa, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu
Calcutta | West Bengal, Andaman and Nicobar Islands
Kerala | Kerala, Lakshadweep
Madras | Tamil Nadu, Puducherry
Punjab and Haryana | Punjab, Haryana, Chandigarh
Gauhati | Assam, Nagaland, Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh

t: Tribunals — Part XIV-A
text:
## 1. Basics
Part XIV-A: Articles 323-A and 323-B — inserted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendations
Nature: Quasi-judicial, specialised dispute-resolution bodies — to reduce pendency in regular courts and provide domain expertise
⚠ Tribunals are not placed in Part XI (Union–State relations) or Part X (Scheduled and Tribal Areas)
Related Parts: Part IX Panchayats (243 to 243-O); Part IX-A Municipalities (243-P to 243-ZG); Part IX-B Co-operative Societies (243-ZH to 243-ZT); Part XIV Services (308 to 323)
## 2. Article 323-A vs Article 323-B
Basis | Article 323-A | Article 323-B
Subjects | Exclusively public service matters — recruitment and conditions of service of Union, State, local-authority and statutory-authority employees | Taxation, foreign exchange, industrial disputes, land reforms, ceiling on property, foodstuffs, elections to Parliament and State Legislatures
Who can create | Only Parliament by law — Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985; State Legislatures have no power | Parliament and State Legislatures — States only within their legislative competence
Structure | One Central Administrative Tribunal + State Administrative Tribunals (separate or joint for States) | A hierarchy of tribunals can be created
## 3. L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997)
Judicial review by the High Courts (Articles 226 and 227) and the Supreme Court (Article 32) is an integral part of the Basic Structure
Clauses in Articles 323-A and 323-B excluding the jurisdiction of the High Courts and Supreme Court — declared unconstitutional
Tribunal decisions (e.g. CAT) face scrutiny first before a Division Bench of the concerned High Court; the Supreme Court may be approached after that
## 4. Important tribunals
Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT): 1985 under the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 (Article 323-A) — original jurisdiction over service matters of Union civil servants; appeals to the Division Bench of the jurisdictional High Court
TDSAT: Set up by the TRAI (Amendment) Act, 2000 (parent: TRAI Act, 1997) — disputes in telecommunications, broadcasting and airport tariffs
Telecom, broadcasting and tariff appeals go directly to the Supreme Court on substantial questions of law; cyber appellate orders go to the High Court
National Green Tribunal: Statutory — NGT Act, 2010; guided by natural justice, not bound by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908; appeals directly to the Supreme Court within 90 days
Armed Forces Tribunal Act: 2007
## 5. IMDT Act case
Illegal Migrants (Determination by Tribunals) Act, 1983 (IMDT Act): Struck down in Sarbananda Sonowal v. Union of India (2005)
Reason: It violated Article 355 — the Union's duty to protect States against external aggression and internal disturbance

topic: Judicial review, doctrines and landmark cases
t: Judicial review
text:
## 1. Meaning
Inherent constitutional power of the higher judiciary to examine the constitutionality of legislative enactments and executive orders (actions) — and declare them void when they contravene the Constitution
Vested jointly in the Supreme Court (Article 32) and the High Courts (Article 226) — not in the Supreme Court alone
Origin: USA — Marbury v. Madison (1803), Chief Justice John Marshall
India: Constitutional supremacy with judicial review of primary legislation
UK: Parliamentary sovereignty — no traditional judicial review; primary statutes cannot be struck down
Associated Articles: 13, 32, 136, 137, 226 and 227
## 2. Textual basis
Article 13(2): The primary textual foundation — laws abridging Fundamental Rights are void pro tanto; an express basis for striking down ultra vires laws
Article 32: SC writ jurisdiction for Fundamental Rights — a constitutional remedy and part of the Basic Structure
Article 226: HC writ jurisdiction — Fundamental Rights and any other legal right; wider than Article 32
Article 137: SC reviews its own judgments or orders
Article 142: Complete Justice decrees — inherent equitable jurisdiction, distinct from judicial review
## 3. Basic Structure status
Kesavananda Bharati (1973), Minerva Mills (1980) and L. Chandra Kumar (1997): Judicial review under Articles 32 and 226 is an integral, inviolable part of the Basic Structure
Parliament cannot abrogate it even through Article 368; constitutional amendments are themselves subject to judicial review on the Basic Structure touchstone
## 4. Ninth Schedule
First Amendment Act (1951): Added Articles 31A and 31B and the Ninth Schedule — to insulate agrarian and land-reform laws from judicial review on Fundamental Rights grounds
Enacted largely to overcome early judicial interpretations restricting state welfare and land acquisition measures
## 5. What judicial review is not
Not questioning the political wisdom, policy merits or advisability of legislation
Not automatic pre-assent scrutiny of Bills; not an ordinary appellate proceeding
Federal role: Reinforces the federal principle, preserves the distribution of powers, enforces constitutional limits — it is not a unitary element
Unitary elements: All India Services, the Governor's appointment, Emergency provisions

topic: Judicial review, doctrines and landmark cases
t: The amendment battle and the Basic Structure
text:
## 1. Can Parliament amend Fundamental Rights?
Case | Year | Held
Shankari Prasad v. Union of India | 1951 | Yes — upheld Parliament's power under Article 368 and the First Amendment; "law" in Article 13(2) does not include constitutional amendments (Article 13 vs Article 368)
Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan | 1965 | Yes — reaffirmed the power to amend any part of the Constitution; upheld the First Amendment (Article 368)
Golaknath v. State of Punjab | 1967 | No — reversed (overruled) the earlier cases; a constitutional amendment is law under Article 13(2); Parliament cannot abridge or take away any Fundamental Right — the first case to limit the amending power
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala | 1973 | Yes, but — Parliament can amend any part, including Fundamental Rights, but cannot alter, damage or destroy the Basic Structure
Minerva Mills v. Union of India | 1980 | Reaffirmed the Basic Structure — a limited amending power is itself a basic feature
## 2. Kesavananda Bharati (24 April 1973)
Largest bench: 13 judges; decided by a 7:6 majority
Propounded the Basic Structure Doctrine — linked to Article 368 (Part XX) and the 24th Amendment
Recognised the Preamble as part of the Constitution
Parliament's constituent power is plenary but limited — it cannot abrogate the essential foundation or basic features
## 3. Minerva Mills (1980)
Struck down clauses of the 42nd Amendment — clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368, and clauses giving absolute precedence to DPSP over Fundamental Rights
Restored the balance between Part III and Part IV
## 4. Traps
⚠ "Basic Structure is explicitly defined in Part XX" — false: it was judicially formulated
⚠ "Fundamental Rights can never be amended after Kesavananda" — false: they can be, if the amendment does not violate the Basic Structure

topic: Judicial review, doctrines and landmark cases
t: Constitutional doctrines
text:
Nature: Most doctrines are judicially evolved — not expressly defined or written in the Constitution
Doctrine | Origin | Articles | Meaning
Basic Structure | Kesavananda Bharati (1973) | Article 368 (Part XX) | Parliament cannot destroy the basic features
Judicial Review | Marbury v. Madison (1803) — John Marshall (USA) | 13, 32, 136, 137, 226, 227 | The higher judiciary (SC and HCs) adjudicates the validity of legislative acts and executive actions
Severability | A.K. Gopalan (1950) and State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951) | 13(1) and 13(2) | Only the offending portion of a statute is void; the valid portion survives if it can be separated
Eclipse | Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of M.P. (1955) | 13(1) | Pre-constitutional laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are not dead ab initio — they stay overshadowed (dormant) and revive if the Fundamental Right is amended
Pith and Substance | Prafulla Kumar v. Bank of Commerce (1947) and State of Rajasthan v. G. Chawla (1959) | Article 246 and the Seventh Schedule | Resolves overlaps between legislative fields by the law's true nature and essence; incidental encroachment on another List does not decide validity
Colorable Legislation | Kameshwar Singh v. State of Bihar (1952) | Article 246 | "What cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly" — transgression of legislative competence under a permissible guise

topic: Judicial review, doctrines and landmark cases
t: Landmark cases
text:
## 1. Cases in chronological order
Order — each preceded the next: A.K. Gopalan → Shankari Prasad → Champakam Dorairajan → Berubari Union → Sajjan Singh → Golaknath → Kesavananda Bharati → Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain → Maneka Gandhi → Minerva Mills → Kihoto Hollohan → S.R. Bommai
Case | Year | Held | Linked to
A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras | 1950 | Narrow interpretation of Article 21 — "procedure established by law"; preventive detention | Article 21
Champakam Dorairajan | 1951 | Fundamental Rights prevail over DPSP in a conflict — directly led to the First Amendment, 1951 inserting Article 15(4) (reservations) | Articles 15, 29, 37, 46
Berubari Union | 1960 | Preamble not an integral part of the Constitution — later overturned by Kesavananda Bharati and S.R. Bommai | Article 3; the Preamble
Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain | 1975 | Struck down parts of the 39th Amendment that barred judicial review of election disputes of the Prime Minister and the Speaker; free and fair elections are part of the Basic Structure | 39th Amendment (later nullified by the 44th); Article 329A
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India | 1978 | Widened Article 21 — right to travel abroad; procedure must be just, fair and reasonable; the golden triangle of Articles 14, 19 and 21 (mutually inclusive) | Articles 14, 19, 21
P. Sambamurthy v. State of A.P. | 1987 | Struck down portions of the 32nd Amendment (special provisions for Andhra Pradesh) — judicial review | 32nd Amendment
Indra Sawhney | 1992 | Upheld 27% OBC reservation (quota), excluded the creamy layer; 50% (vertical) cap on total reservations | Articles 15(4), 16(4)
Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillu | 1992–93 | Upheld the 52nd Amendment (Tenth Schedule, Anti-Defection Law); the Speaker's ruling on defection is subject to judicial review | 52nd Amendment; Tenth Schedule
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India | 1994 | Guidelines against arbitrary use of Article 356 (President's Rule) — proclamations subject to judicial review; secularism and federalism are basic features; reaffirmed the Preamble as integral | Articles 356, 355
Vishaka | 1997 | Guidelines against sexual harassment at the workplace | Articles 14, 19(1)(g), 21
M. Nagaraj | 2006 | Validated reservation in promotions — subject to quantifiable backwardness and efficiency data | Article 335
K.S. Puttaswamy | 2017 | 9-judge Bench — right to privacy is a Fundamental Right | Article 21; Part III
Shayara Bano | 2017 | Talaq-e-Biddat (instant Triple Talaq) unconstitutional and arbitrary | Articles 14, 21
Navtej Singh Johar | 2018 | Decriminalised consensual same-sex acts between adults — read down (invalidated) Section 377 of the IPC (⚠ not Article 377 of the Constitution) | Articles 14, 15, 19, 21
## 2. Rights read into Article 21
Right | Case and year
Travel abroad | Satwant Singh (1967); Maneka Gandhi (1978)
Privacy | Govind (1975); developed in Malak Singh (1980); K.S. Puttaswamy (2017)
Shelter and livelihood | Olga Tellis (1985); Chameli Singh (1995)
Emergency medical aid | Parmanand Katara (1989)
Clean environment and clean air | Subhash Kumar (1991)
Marry a person of one's choice | Lata Singh (2006)
## 3. Other cases
Randhir Singh (1982): Equal pay for equal work — read Articles 14, 16 and 39(d) with the Preamble
Bachan Singh: Death penalty in the "rarest of rare cases" is not unconstitutional under Article 21
Coal Allocation Scam Case (2013): The SC coined "Caged Parrot"
Sarbananda Sonowal (2005): Struck down the IMDT Act (Illegal Migrants (Determination by Tribunals) Act) under Article 355 — the Union's duty to protect States against external aggression and internal disturbance

topic: Judicial review, doctrines and landmark cases
t: Rule of Law and constitutional government
text:
## 1. Origin
A.V. Dicey (British jurist) — Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution (1885)
Borrowed from Britain with: Parliamentary Government, Single Citizenship, Cabinet System, Prerogative Writs
In India: Anchored mainly in Article 14 — equality before law and equal protection of the laws, for citizens and foreigners
Basic Structure: Affirmed in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and Indira Nehru Gandhi (1975)
## 2. Dicey's three elements
1. Absence of arbitrary power (limitation of powers): Supremacy of regular law over arbitrary power — no punishment except for a distinct breach of law proved in the ordinary legal manner
⚠ "The State has inherent unlimited police powers" — false
2. Equality before the law: All classes equally subject to the ordinary law, administered by ordinary courts — no one above the law
Dicey opposed the French Droit Administratif; ⚠ "executive officials are subject only to special administrative tribunals" — false
3. Primacy of individual rights (liberty and civil rights): The Constitution is the result of individual rights defined and enforced by courts — rights come from judicial decisions, not from the Constitution
UK: Constitution results from judicial decisions; India: the Constitution is the source of rights — India reverses the third premise and adopts the first two intact
⚠ "People's responsibility to the Government" is not a pillar — delete it from the framework; the Rule of Law restrains the government and does not expand citizens' obedience
## 3. Rule of Law vs Rule by Law
Rule of Law | Rule by Law
Government under law — the government itself is subordinate to law | Government above law — law as an instrument (weapon) of state control; the ruler stays above the law
Laws must be just, fair and non-arbitrary | Governs citizens only
## 4. Equality before law vs equal protection of laws
Equality before law | Equal protection of the laws
British origin | American origin
Negative concept — no special privilege for anyone | Positive concept — equal treatment in equal circumstances; permits reasonable classification
## 5. Procedure and discretion
"Procedure established by law" (text of Article 21): A law is valid if made by the correct legislative procedure — A.K. Gopalan (1950)
Due process after Maneka Gandhi (1978): Law must be just, fair and reasonable and free from procedural arbitrariness
Unguided, uncontrolled or uncanalised discretion given to an executive authority violates non-arbitrariness under Article 14 and subverts the Rule of Law — discretion without objective standards or judicial safeguards is ultra vires Article 14
## 6. Constitutional government and PIL
Constitutional Government = Limited Government: Defines, restrains and checks power — provisions prevent executive tyranny
Public Interest Litigation: Promotes and strengthens access to justice for disadvantaged persons — but is not indispensable for the Rule of Law, which existed before PIL through Articles 14, 32 and 226

t: Governor — appointment, position and powers
text:
## 1. Position
Nominal / constitutional head of the State — the Chief Minister and the Council of Ministers are the real executive
Article 153: A Governor for each State — the same person can be Governor of two or more States (Seventh Amendment)
Article 154: Executive power of the State vested in the Governor
Integral part of the State Legislature — Article 168
## 2. Appointment and tenure
Not elected — appointed (nominated) by the President by warrant under his hand and seal (Article 155)
Article 156: Holds office during the pleasure of the President — not the Chief Minister
Normal term: Five years — can be removed earlier or continue beyond it
Qualifications: Citizen of India; completed 35 years of age; not an MP or MLA (must vacate any such seat); no office of profit
Oath (Article 159): By the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court
Emoluments (Article 202): Charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State — for a Governor of two or more States, the President decides how the salary is shared
## 3. Powers
Executive:
Appoints the Chief Minister, other Ministers (on the CM's advice), the Advocate-General, the State Election Commissioner, the Chairman and members of the State Public Service Commission
Appoints District Judges in consultation with the High Court
Article 167: Can seek information from the Chief Minister
Operates the Contingency Fund of the State
Legislative:
Summons and prorogues the State Legislature; dissolves the Legislative Assembly
Addresses the Legislature — Article 176
Bills (Article 200): Assent, withhold assent, or reserve for the President
Ordinances (Article 213): When the Legislature is not in session
Nominates one-sixth of the Legislative Council (where the State has one)
Anti-defection: Decides disqualification of MLAs on the advice of the Election Commission
Pardoning (Article 161): Pardons, reprieves, respites, remissions; suspend or commute sentences — only for offences against State laws
Emergency: Can recommend President's Rule — Article 356
## 4. Discretion and special responsibilities
Discretionary powers: Appoint a CM in a hung Assembly; dismiss a Council that has lost its majority; dissolve the Assembly; reserve a Bill for the President (even against the Council's advice); recommend President's Rule
Not bound by the Council of Ministers' advice in all matters
Fifth Schedule: Special responsibility for Scheduled Areas — report to the President
Sixth Schedule: Special powers over Autonomous District Councils; special responsibility in certain States and tribal areas
## 5. Immunity — Article 361
No criminal proceedings during the term of office
Civil proceedings only after two months' notice
## 6. President vs Governor
Basis | President | Governor
Chosen by | Electoral College | Appointed by the President
Term | Five years | Five years, subject to the pleasure of the President
Removal | Impeachment | At the pleasure of the President
Ordinances | Article 123 | Article 213
Pardon | Article 72 — all cases | Article 161 — State laws only
Discretion | Very limited | Comparatively more
## 7. Firsts
Sarojini Naidu: First woman Governor — Uttar Pradesh
Padmaja Naidu: First woman Governor of an independent State — West Bengal
Jammu and Kashmir: Governor earlier called Sadr-e-Riyasat — changed to Governor in 1965

t: Chief Minister
text:
## 1. Position
Real executive head of the State and head of the Government; heads the State Council of Ministers
Leader of the majority party or coalition in the Legislative Assembly; leader of the Assembly; chief spokesperson of the State Government
Article 163: Council of Ministers headed by the CM to aid and advise the Governor
Article 164: Appointment, tenure, responsibility and size limit of Ministers
## 2. Appointment
Appointed by the Governor — normally the leader of the majority party; in a hung Assembly the Governor has discretion
Member of the Legislative Assembly or the Legislative Council (if any) — need not be a member when appointed, but must become one within six months
Oath by the Governor; resignation addressed to the Governor
Delhi and Puducherry: CM appointed by the President — Article 239AA
## 3. Powers and duties
Ministers: Selects them; allocates portfolios; can recommend the removal of any Minister; advises the Governor on appointing other Ministers
Article 167 — link between the Governor and the Council of Ministers:
Communicates all decisions on administration and proposals for legislation
Furnishes information required by the Governor
Submits for the Council's consideration any matter decided by a single Minister
Advises the Governor on: summoning and prorogation of the Legislature; dissolution of the Assembly
## 4. Responsibility and size
Collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly — Article 164(2) — not to the Legislative Council
A passed No-Confidence Motion → the entire Council, including the CM, must resign
91st Constitutional Amendment Act (2003): Total Ministers including the CM ≤ 15% of the Assembly's total strength; minimum 12 (including the CM) in smaller States
## 5. Firsts
Sucheta Kripalani: First woman CM — Uttar Pradesh
E. M. S. Namboodiripad: First non-Congress CM — Kerala, 1957

t: State Legislative Assembly — composition and elections
text:
## 1. Framework
Part VI: Articles 168 to 212
Article 168 — composition: Unicameral = Governor + Legislative Assembly; bicameral = Governor + Legislative Assembly + Legislative Council
Constitutional basis: Assembly — Article 170; Council — Article 171
Bicameral States — six (with Legislative Councils): Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Bihar, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Uttar Pradesh
## 2. Election
Lower / popular house — directly elected by citizens from single-member territorial constituencies
Universal adult suffrage — Article 326; First-Past-the-Post — the candidate with the highest number of valid votes wins (no absolute majority of more than 50 percent needed)
Conducted by the Election Commission of India (Article 324) — not the State Election Commission
## 3. Strength — Article 170
Maximum: 500; minimum: 60 (standard; subject to statutory exceptions)
Assembly | Seats
Uttar Pradesh — largest | 403
Sikkim — smallest State (a special constitutional exception) | 32
Goa | 40
Mizoram | 40
Puducherry — smallest UT Assembly | 33 — 30 elected + 3 nominated
## 4. Membership and reservation
Minimum age (Article 173): Assembly 25 years; Council 30 years
Reservation (Article 332): Seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in every Assembly, in proportion to their population in the State
104th Amendment Act (2020): Ended Anglo-Indian nomination — Article 333
106th Amendment Act (2023): About one-third reservation for women in directly elected seats — effective after post-census delimitation
Disqualification (Article 191): Office of profit, unsoundness of mind, undischarged insolvent, loss of citizenship
Decided by the Governor (Article 192) — who must obtain and act on the binding opinion of the Election Commission of India
Defection (Tenth Schedule anti-defection provisions): Decided exclusively by the Speaker (Council: Chairman) — subject to judicial review
## 5. Term — Article 172
Five years; dissolvable (temporary); cannot be abolished
National Emergency (Article 352): Parliament may extend it by law one year at a time — at most up to six months after the Emergency ceases
Council of Ministers: Collectively responsible to the Assembly — Article 164(2); capped at 15 percent of the Assembly (Article 164, 91st Amendment Act, 2003); minimum 12 ministers including the Chief Minister (minimum size); a non-member minister for at most six consecutive months

t: State Legislature — working and procedure
text:
## 1. Presiding officers
Speaker and Deputy Speaker (Article 178): Elected by the Assembly from among its sitting members
Resignation (Article 179): Speaker → Deputy Speaker; Deputy Speaker → Speaker
On dissolution: The Speaker does not vacate office immediately — continues until just before the first meeting of the new Assembly
Voting: The Speaker cannot vote in the first instance — has a casting vote when votes are equally divided
Council: The Chairman presides — Article 182
## 2. Governor's role — sessions and address
Article 174: Summons, prorogues and dissolves the Assembly; maximum gap between sessions six months
Article 176: Addresses the Assembly at the commencement of the first session after each general election and the first session of each year
## 3. Money Bills — Articles 198, 199 and 207
Introduced only in the Assembly, on the Governor's prior recommendation (Article 207)
Speaker's certification of a Money Bill is sole and final
Council: Only recommends; must return it within 14 days — cannot amend or reject it; the Assembly may accept or reject its recommendations; the Assembly has final authority
## 4. Ordinary Bills — Article 197
The Assembly is the originating and overriding chamber
Council's delay: Up to three months the first time; after the Assembly re-passes it, one month the second time — four months in all
No veto — the Council cannot permanently block ordinary legislation
## 5. Assent and ordinances
Articles 200 and 201: The Governor can give assent, withhold assent, return an ordinary Bill (no fixed time limit to act on a returned Bill), or reserve it for the President
Article 213: Ordinance during recess — ceases six weeks after the Legislature reassembles unless approved earlier
## 6. Creating or abolishing a Council — Article 169
The Assembly must initiate it by passing a resolution — the base House for creation or abolition
Special majority: A majority (at least 50 percent) of the total membership + at least two-thirds of members present and voting
The resolution does not compel the Union to introduce a Bill in Parliament
Parliament enacts the resolution into law by simple majority
## 7. Assembly vs Council
Basis | Legislative Assembly | Legislative Council
House | Lower / popular house | Upper house / House of Elders
Election | Directly — First-Past-the-Post | Indirectly — PR by single transferable vote and nomination
Minimum age | 25 | 30
Strength | 60 to 500 | Minimum 40; maximum one-third of the Assembly
Life | Five-year tenure; subject to dissolution; cannot be abolished | Permanent; one-third retire every two years; member's term six years; can be created or abolished (Article 169)
Money Bill | Sole house of introduction; final authority | Delay only 14 days
Ordinary Bill | Originating and overriding | Delay up to four months
## 8. Articles at a glance
170: Composition; 173: Membership age (25); 174: Prorogation and dissolution; 178 and 179: Speaker's election and resignation
192: Disqualification by the Governor; 198 and 199: State Money Bill; 200 and 201: Assent and reservation; 213: Ordinances

t: Advocate General of the State — Article 165
text:
## 1. Office
Highest law officer of the State — the official legal adviser to the State Government; Part VI, Article 165
Appointed by: The Governor — Article 165(1) (not the President)
Qualification: Must be qualified to be a High Court Judge (Article 217)
Tenure: No fixed tenure — holds office during the pleasure of the Governor (Article 165(3))
⚠ False claims: "During the pleasure of the State Cabinet" or "of the Chief Minister"
Duties (Article 165(2)): Advises the State Government on legal matters; other legal duties assigned by the Governor or the Constitution
## 2. Rights in the Legislature — Article 177
May speak and participate in the proceedings of both Houses (Legislative Assembly and Legislative Council), joint sittings, and any State Legislative Committee of which he is named a member
Not a member of the State Legislature — may not vote on any motion or bill
## 3. Advocate General vs Attorney General vs Solicitor General
Basis | Advocate General | Attorney General of India | Solicitor General of India
Basis | Article 165 — Part VI | Article 76 — Part V | No constitutional basis — statutory
Serves | State Government | Union Government | Assists the Attorney General
Appointed by | Governor | President | Appointments Committee of the Cabinet
Qualification | Of a High Court Judge (Article 217) | Of a Supreme Court Judge (Article 124(3)) | A distinguished senior advocate
Tenure | Pleasure of the Governor | Pleasure of the President | Fixed statutory term
Floor rights | State Legislature — Article 177 | Parliament — Article 88 | None in Parliament
Pairings to remember: Article 76 / 165 — Attorney General / Advocate General; Article 88 / 177 — rights in Parliament / State Legislature; Article 124(3) / 217 — qualifications of a SC / HC Judge
High Court Judges are appointed by the President; the Advocate General by the Governor

t: Commissions on Centre–State relations and the Inter-State Council
text:
## 1. Commissions and committees
Rajamannar Committee: Appointed by the Tamil Nadu Government — examined Centre–State Relations; a state-level initiative for federal autonomy
Sarkaria Commission: Landmark commission — recommended a permanent Inter-State Council (Inter-Governmental Council) — exam focus: Article 263
Punchhi Commission: The second major commission on Centre–State Relations — Indian federalism
Reviewed the working, conventions, judicial interpretations and dialogue mechanisms of Centre–State Relations
Exam focus: federal dialogue and coordination mechanisms (federalism, Centre–State Relations)
⚠ The permanent Inter-State Council recommendation belongs to Sarkaria, not Punchhi
Indrajit Gupta Committee: State funding of elections / electoral reforms — not Centre–State Relations; a classic elimination option
## 2. Inter-State Council — Article 263
A constitutional body (not a purely non-constitutional or extra-statutory one)
Established by the President — not enacted by Parliament
Set up on 28 May 1990, following the Sarkaria Commission

t: Special provisions for some States — Article 371 series
text:
Location: Part XXI of the Constitution
Article | State | Special provision
371 | Maharashtra and Gujarat | Separate development boards — Vidarbha, Marathwada, Saurashtra, Kutch
371-A | Nagaland | Protects Naga customary laws, religious and social practices, administration of justice, ownership and transfer of land and resources
371-B | Assam | A committee of the Assembly of members from tribal areas
371-C | Manipur | A committee of the Assembly of members elected from the Hill areas
371-D | Andhra Pradesh and Telangana | Equitable opportunities and facilities in public employment and education across regions
371-E | Andhra Pradesh only | A Central University by parliamentary law
371-F | Sikkim | Special provisions on its incorporation, assembly size and governance
371-G | Mizoram | Protects Mizo religious and social practices, customary law, ownership and transfer of land
371-H | Arunachal Pradesh | Governor's special responsibility for law and order
371-I | Goa | Special minimum size of the Assembly — 30 members
371-J | Karnataka | Hyderabad–Karnataka region — a special development board; reservations in education and employment; inserted by the 98th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2012
371-J targets the socio-economic development of the Hyderabad–Karnataka region — six backward districts

t: Scheduled Areas and Tribal Areas — Fifth and Sixth Schedules
text:
## 1. Fifth Schedule — Scheduled Areas
Part X, Article 244(1) — administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes
Declared / notified by: The President (the authority for area notification)
Does not make the area a Union Territory or a separate state; does not end the State Government's executive power — it continues, subject to the Fifth Schedule
Tribal Advisory Council: Mandatory in each State having Scheduled Areas — Paragraph 4 of the Fifth Schedule; advises on the welfare and advancement of Scheduled Tribes (the key governance body)
Governor:
Submits a report on the administration of Scheduled Areas directly to the President — annually and whenever the President requires (⚠ not the Chief Minister to the Union Home Ministry)
May make regulations prohibiting or restricting transfer of tribal land to non-tribals, and regulating money-lending to Scheduled Tribes
Oversees land transfers and the applicability of central and state laws
Samatha v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1997): Landmark ruling — transfer of tribal land in Scheduled Areas to private parties for mining is null, void and inoperative under the Fifth Schedule
Covers 10 States: Andhra Pradesh (AP), Telangana (TS), Jharkhand (JH), Chhattisgarh (CG), Gujarat (GJ), Himachal Pradesh (HP), Madhya Pradesh (MP), Maharashtra (MH), Odisha (OD), Rajasthan (RJ)
## 2. Sixth Schedule — Tribal Areas
Article 244(2); associated with Article 275(1) — administration of Tribal Areas
Covers four North-Eastern States only: Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram — ⚠ not Manipur or Nagaland
Bodies: Autonomous District Councils and Autonomous Regional Councils — significant legislative, administrative and judicial powers
## 3. Fifth vs Sixth Schedule
Basis | Fifth Schedule | Sixth Schedule
Relates to | Scheduled Areas | Tribal Areas
Article | 244(1) | 244(2)
States | 10 | 4 North-Eastern
Key body | Tribal Advisory Council | Autonomous District and Regional Councils

t: Local self-government — evolution and committees
text:
## 1. Meaning
Democratic decentralisation — community participation and local accountability; not central control or mere administration
Functions include: Public health, sanitation, water supply, rural development — ⚠ not maintenance of public order or judicial review
Article 40 (DPSP): The State shall organise Village Panchayats as units of self-government
## 2. History
Charles Metcalfe: Called Indian village communities "Little Republics"
Lord Ripon's Resolution (1882): Ripon — the Father of Local Self-Government in India
GoI Act, 1919: Local self-government a Transferred Subject under provincial dyarchy
First Municipal Corporation: Madras, 1688
First Panchayati Raj State: Rajasthan — Nagaur district, 2 October 1959; Andhra Pradesh the second
## 3. Committees
Committee | Year | Recommended
Balwant Rai Mehta — "Architect of Panchayati Raj" | 1957 | Three-tier system — Gram Panchayat, Panchayat Samiti, Zila Parishad
Ashok Mehta | 1977–78 | Two-tier model; separate Nyaya Panchayats
Hanumantha Rao | 1983 | Decentralisation of powers and finance; district planning bodies
G.V.K. Rao | 1985 | Revitalisation and a representative character for Panchayats
L.M. Singhvi | 1986 | Constitutional status and greater financial resources for local bodies

t: 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendment Acts (1992)
text:
## 1. At a glance
Basis | 73rd Amendment | 74th Amendment
Concerns | Rural local self-government — Panchayats | Urban local self-government — Municipalities
In force | 24 April 1993 — observed as National Panchayati Raj Day | 1 June 1993
Part inserted | Part IX — Articles 243 to 243-O | Part IX-A — Articles 243P to 243ZG
Schedule | 11th Schedule — 29 functional subjects | 12th Schedule — 18 functional subjects
Institutions | Gram Panchayat (village), Panchayat Samiti (block), Zila Parishad (district) | Nagar Panchayat (transitional area), Municipal Council (smaller urban area), Municipal Corporation (larger urban area)
Planning: Both systems are interlinked with district planning bodies — District Planning Committee (Article 243ZD); Metropolitan Planning Committee (Article 243ZE)
## 2. Gram Sabha and the three tiers
Gram Sabha (Article 243A): Village-level general assembly — the entire electorate (registered voters) of a village
Gram Panchayat: The elected executive body
Article 243B: Three-tier system is mandatory — the intermediate tier is optional for States with a population of 20 lakh or less
## 3. Paired Articles — Panchayats and Municipalities
Subject | Panchayats | Municipalities | Key rule
Composition | 243C | 243R | Regulated by the State Legislature; minimum age 21 years
Reservation | 243D | 243T | Women: not less than one-third (at least 33 percent) of total seats and of chairperson positions
Tenure | 243E | 243U | Five years; if dissolved early, elections within six months — not needed if less than six months remain
Powers and responsibilities | 243G | 243W | Economic development, social justice, sanitation, public health, local utilities, roads and bridges
State Finance Commission | 243-I | 243-Y | Constituted by the Governor every five years; reviews the distribution of local finances
Accounts and audit | 243J | 243Z | Audit laws provided for by the State Legislature — ⚠ not enacted by the Union Parliament, the CAG or the District Collector
State Election Commission | 243K | 243ZA | Superintendence, direction and conduct of local elections

t: Emergency provisions — the three emergencies
text:
## 1. Framework
Part XVIII: Articles 352 to 360
K.M. Nambiar: Called the President's emergency powers a "fraud on the Constitution"
## 2. Comparison
Basis | National Emergency — Article 352 | President's Rule — Article 356 | Financial Emergency — Article 360
Ground | War, external aggression or armed rebellion | Failure of constitutional machinery in a State | Threat to the financial stability or credit of India or any part
Approval by Parliament | Within 1 month (was 2 months — reduced by the 44th Amendment) | Within 2 months | Within 2 months
Majority | Special majority in both Houses | Simple majority | Simple majority
Duration | 6 months at a time — no maximum limit | 6 months at a time — maximum 3 years | Until revoked by the President
Lok Sabha dissolved | Survives 30 days from the first sitting of the new Lok Sabha | 30 days | 30 days
Effect | Parliament legislates on the State List; Articles 358 and 359 operate | State Assembly dissolved or suspended; Parliament passes the State Budget | Executive gives financial directions; salaries may be cut — including Supreme Court and High Court judges
Fundamental Rights | Articles 20 and 21 can never be suspended | Not directly suspended | Not directly suspended
Used | 3 times — 1962, 1971, 1975 | Over 100 times across States | Never invoked since independence
## 3. President's Rule — Article 356
When: The government of a State cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution
How: On the Governor's report or otherwise (suo motu)
Beyond 1 year only if:
A National Emergency is in operation in all of India or any part of the State, and
The Election Commission of India certifies that Assembly elections cannot be held

t: National Emergency — effects and the 44th Amendment
text:
## 1. Proclamation
Only on the written advice of the Union Cabinet
1975 Emergency: Proclaimed 25 June 1975 on the ground of Internal Disturbance; withdrawn 21 March 1977
## 2. Effects on legislation and finance
State List: Parliament gets overriding jurisdiction — such laws cease 6 months after the Emergency is revoked
Terms of the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies: Parliament may extend them by law 1 year at a time — at most 6 months after the Emergency ceases
Article 354: The President may modify the distribution of revenues between the Union and the States — valid until the end of the financial year in which the proclamation ceases
## 3. Article 358 vs Article 359
Basis | Article 358 | Article 359
What | Automatically suspends the 6 freedoms of Article 19 | Suspends the right to approach courts for enforcement of specified Fundamental Rights
How | Automatic on proclamation | Needs a separate Presidential Order
Ground | Only war or external aggression (external emergency) — not armed rebellion | Both external and internal (armed rebellion) emergencies
Exception | — | Articles 20 and 21 can never be suspended under any circumstances
## 4. 44th Amendment Act, 1978
Replaced "Internal Disturbance" with "Armed Rebellion" in Article 352
Cut the parliamentary approval time for a National Emergency from 2 months to 1 month
Established the non-suspendability of Articles 20 and 21 — they can never be suspended under Article 359

t: Amendment procedure — Article 368
text:
## 1. Three kinds of amendment
Article 368 (Part XX): The amendment power and procedure — the Constitution balances flexibility and rigidity
Simple majority — outside Article 368:
Creation or alteration of States — Article 3
Creation or abolition of State Legislative Councils — Article 169
Salaries of judges and officials
Special majority: Passed by each House separately — a majority of the total membership + two-thirds of members present and voting
Special majority + State ratification: Federal provisions — ratified by at least half of the State Legislatures, by simple majority (not all States)
## 2. Federal provisions needing State ratification
Election of the President — but not his qualifications, conditions of office or tenure
Union-State executive and legislative relations
Supreme Court and High Courts provisions
Seventh Schedule Lists
Article 368 itself
GST Council provisions
First amendment needing ratification: The 3rd Amendment (1954) — Entry 33 of the Concurrent List
## 3. Procedure
Introduction: In either the Lok Sabha or the Rajya Sabha — not in a State Legislature; no prior recommendation of the President
Passage: Each House independently by special majority — no joint sitting; the Bill fails completely if one House rejects it
Assent: The President must give assent — no veto, no power to return — made mandatory by the 24th Amendment (1971)

text:
