t: Election Commission of India — status, composition and powers
text:
## 1. Constitutional status
Nature: A permanent, independent, constitutional body — Part XV, Articles 324 to 329 relate to it; constitutional basis Article 324 (Part XV)
Established: 25 January 1950 — celebrated annually as National Voters' Day since 2011
Article 324(1): Vests the superintendence, direction and control of elections in the Election Commission of India
## 2. ECI vs State Election Commission
Basis | Election Commission of India | State Election Commission
Constitutional basis | Article 324 — Part XV | Articles 243K and 243ZA — Parts IX and IX-A
Conducts elections to | Parliament — Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha; State Legislatures — Legislative Assemblies and Legislative Councils; the President and Vice-President | Local bodies — Panchayats (Gram Panchayats, Panchayat Samitis, Zilla Parishads) and Municipalities / Municipal Corporations
Head removed like | A Supreme Court Judge | A High Court Judge
Operates under | The Constitution | The respective State Panchayati and State Municipal legislation
⚠ Trap: The ECI does not conduct local body elections
⚠ Trap: The ECI does not conduct elections of presiding officers chosen internally by the respective Houses:
Lok Sabha — Speaker and Deputy Speaker — Article 93
Legislative Assembly — Speaker and Deputy Speaker — Article 178
Rajya Sabha — Deputy Chairman — Article 89(2)
Legislative Council — Chairman — Article 182
## 3. Composition
One Chief Election Commissioner + two Election Commissioners — a multi-member body continuously since 1 October 1993
Equal powers; matters decided by majority; salary equivalent to that of Supreme Court Judges
Appointed by: The President of India
Tenure: Six years or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier
Removal:
CEC: Only in the same manner and on the same grounds as a Supreme Court Judge — removal safeguard in Article 324(5)
Other Election Commissioners and Regional Commissioners: Removed by the President on the recommendation of the CEC
First CEC: Sukumar Sen (1950 to 1958); first woman CEC: V. S. Ramadevi
## 4. Advisory role — disqualification of legislators
Basis | Members of Parliament | State legislators (Assembly and Council)
Article | 103 | 192
Decided by | The President | The Governor
Based on | The opinion of the ECI — binding | The opinion of the ECI — binding
## 5. Election schedule and Model Code of Conduct
Notifications: Issued by the President for Parliament elections and the Governor for State Legislature elections — ⚠ the ECI does not issue election notifications
ECI: Recommends election dates; determines and administers the election schedule
Model Code of Conduct: Formulated and enforced by the ECI — an Election Commission-formulated guideline, not an Act of Parliament
Operates — comes into force immediately — from the date of the ECI's formal announcement of the election schedule
## 6. Voters' rights — Articles 325 and 326
Article 325: A single general electoral roll — no discrimination in electoral rolls on the basis of religion, race, caste or sex
Article 326: Universal adult suffrage for Lok Sabha and Legislative Assembly elections
Voting age: Reduced from 21 to 18 years — 61st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1988; the change became effective in 1989
Right to vote and right to be elected / contest: Legal or statutory rights — not Fundamental Rights
Established by the Supreme Court in Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India (2006)
Election disputes: Handled exclusively by the judiciary through election petitions
President and Vice-President election disputes — exclusively the Supreme Court, Article 71
Simultaneous elections: May require amendment of Articles 83, 85, 172, 174 and 356

t: Electoral systems — President, Vice-President, Parliament and State Legislatures
text:
## 1. At a glance
Office / House | Article | Electorate | Method
President | 54 | Elected Members of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) + elected Members of State Legislative Assemblies, including Delhi and Puducherry (70th Constitutional Amendment Act) | Indirect; proportional representation by single transferable vote; secret ballot
Vice-President | 66 | All Members of Parliament — elected and nominated | Indirect; PR by single transferable vote; secret ballot
Lok Sabha | 81 | Citizens directly from territorial electoral rolls | Direct; first-past-the-post
Rajya Sabha | 80 | Elected Members of the Legislative Assemblies of the respective States | Indirect; PR by single transferable vote
Legislative Assembly | 170 | Citizens of the State — universal adult suffrage (Article 326) | Direct; first-past-the-post
Legislative Council | 171 | Indirect election categories + gubernatorial nomination | PR by single transferable vote; secret ballot
Panchayats and Municipalities | — | Ward members and Panchs — directly elected by local voters | Local-body framework; minimum age 21
## 2. President
Cannot vote: Nominated Members of Parliament, nominated Members of State Legislative Assemblies and Members of State Legislative Councils — the Councils are excluded from the electoral college
Nomination: 50 proposers and 50 seconders
Vote value: An MLA's vote varies from State to State — based on population ratios; an MP's vote is uniform across all Members of Parliament
Article 71(4): The election cannot be challenged or delayed because vacancies exist in the electoral college
## 3. Vice-President
State Legislatures — Assembly and Council members — are completely excluded; no role in the election
The Vice-President is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha — but not a member of it
## 4. Rajya Sabha
Nominated MLAs and Members of Legislative Councils cannot vote
Seat allocation: Based on population — not allocated equally among the States
## 5. Legislative Council — composition
Elected / nominated by | Share
Legislative Assembly members | One-third
Local bodies | One-third
Graduates | One-twelfth
Teachers | One-twelfth
Nominated by the Governor | One-sixth
⚠ Trap: Industrialists are not an electoral category
Minimum age for membership: 30 years
## 6. First-past-the-post
The candidate with the highest number of votes — only the highest vote count among contestants — wins
No need for more than 50 percent — no absolute majority of 50 percent plus one vote required

t: Representation of the People Acts, parties, delimitation and reforms
text:
## 1. RPA 1950 vs RPA 1951
Basis | Representation of the People Act, 1950 | Representation of the People Act, 1951
Nature | Pre-election framework — voter rolls | Operational conduct of elections and candidature
Deals with | Allocation of seats — seat quotas for the Lok Sabha, Assemblies and Councils; delimitation of constituencies (framework); voter qualifications; registration of electors; preparation of electoral rolls; the detailed composition of State Legislative Councils | Actual conduct of elections; nomination, scrutiny and counting procedures; qualifications and disqualifications of candidates (for holding membership); registration of political parties (Section 29A); corrupt practices; election petitions and disputes
Linked Articles | 81, 82, 170, 171, 325, 326 | 84, 102, 173, 191, 324, 329
Council composition in detail: Article 171(2), Section 10 and the Third Schedule of the RPA 1950
## 2. Political parties
Registration: By the Election Commission of India under Section 29A of the RPA 1951
⚠ Trap: Not the Ministry of Law and Justice, not Parliament
Recognition (National or State party) and allotment of symbols: Decided by the ECI under the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968
⚠ Trap: The Order is not issued by Parliament, the Law Ministry or the President
Disputes: The ECI adjudicates disputes concerning party mergers and splits
## 3. National Party — any one criterion
Seats: At least 2% of the total Lok Sabha seats (= 11 seats), from at least three different States
Votes + seats: At least 6% of the total valid votes polled in four or more States in a Lok Sabha general election or a State Legislative Assembly election — and at least four Lok Sabha seats from any State or States
State recognition: Officially recognized as a State Party in at least four different States
## 4. Candidates
Seat limit — Section 33 / 33(7), RPA 1951: A maximum of two constituencies at a time — Lok Sabha / Parliamentary or State Assembly
The RPA 1951 was amended in 1996 to cap the number of constituencies at two — Devi Lal had contested from three Lok Sabha seats in the 1991 elections
Security deposit: Forfeited if the candidate fails to secure more than one-sixth of the total valid votes polled
Rajya Sabha domicile: Before 2003, a candidate had to be an elector in the particular State of contest — the 2003 amendment removed this; any registered elector in India can contest from any State
Upheld by the Supreme Court in Kuldip Nayar (2006) — removal of the domicile or voter requirement
Death of a contesting candidate: Before the 1996 amendment, elections were automatically countermanded — after it, no longer; a recognized political party may nominate a replacement within a set timeframe
Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990) on electoral reforms: State funding of elections; use of electronic voting machines — measures later enacted in the 1996 amendment to the RPA 1951
## 5. Delimitation Commission
Constituted by the Central Government under an Act of Parliament (parliamentary law) — an independent body that executes constituency delimitation
Headed by a retired Supreme Court Judge; members include the Chief Election Commissioner and State Election Commissioners
Orders: Have the force of law; cannot be called in question in any court (Article 329); cannot be modified when laid before Parliament or State Legislative Assemblies
Four Commissions so far — 1952, 1963, 1973, 2002

t: EVMs, EPIC, VVPAT and NOTA
text:
## 1. Timeline
Date | Milestone
19 May 1982 | First experimental use of EVMs — Parur Assembly constituency, Kerala — associated with A.C. Jose v. Sivan Pillai
1989 | Section 61A added to the Representation of the People Act, 1951 — statutory backing for EVMs
1993 | Electors Photo Identity Card (EPIC / Voter ID) — nationwide rollout initiated under CEC T. N. Seshan
June 1999 | Goa — the first State to conduct an entire General Assembly election using EVMs across all constituencies
2004 | 14th Lok Sabha General Election — the first nationwide general election entirely using EVMs
4 September 2013 | VVPAT first used — Noksen Assembly by-election, Nagaland
27 September 2013 | NOTA implemented — Supreme Court judgment in PUCL v. Union of India
⚠ Order: VVPAT was introduced before NOTA in 2013 — NOTA was mandated later in September 2013
## 2. EVM
An electronic vote-recording and vote-counting apparatus — ⚠ not an electoral system
Deployed under the superintendence, direction and control of the Election Commission of India (ECI)
Used for Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assembly elections
India conducts direct general elections using the First-Past-the-Post (FPTP) system — the candidate with the highest valid votes wins; need not cross 50% of the votes
## 3. EPIC and VVPAT
EPIC: Established voter photo-identification — introduced to prevent bogus voting and impersonation
VVPAT — Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail: Generates an independent paper slip for verification — visible to the voter for 7 seconds
## 4. NOTA — None of the Above
An electoral option on ballot papers and Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) — a negative voting choice button on ballot units
Enables voters to exercise a negative vote — formally reject all contesting candidates in secret
PUCL v. Union of India — landmark Supreme Court judgment dated 27 September 2013 — directed the mandatory introduction of the NOTA button on EVMs
Linked the right to register a negative vote in secrecy with the Freedom of Speech and Expression — Article 19(1)(a)
How: The voter attends the polling booth and presses the NOTA button on the EVM — secrecy fully preserved
Effect: A symbolic expression only — does not determine the election outcome by itself; the candidate with the highest valid votes among the contestants is declared elected
⚠ Trap: "Election cancelled and a fresh poll held if NOTA gets the majority or highest votes" — false; under First-Past-the-Post the election is not cancelled merely because NOTA receives the maximum votes
Not abstention: Exercising NOTA is not non-voting or abstaining — it is the active exercise of the statutory right to vote, registering a neutral or negative choice
Scope: Limited to direct Lok Sabha and Assembly elections — not applicable in Rajya Sabha or Legislative Council elections (Supreme Court struck down NOTA for them in 2018)
## 5. NOTA vs Rule 49-O vs the right to reject
Basis | NOTA | Old Rule 49-O (abstention) | Full international right to reject
How | Press the NOTA button on the EVM | The voter entered the polling booth and refused to vote before the Presiding Officer — recorded in Form 17-A | Voters reject all candidates via the ballot or EVM
Secrecy | Preserved | Violated | Preserved
Effect | Symbolic — highest valid votes wins | Did not affect the winning tally; struck down as ultra vires | Re-election mandated if rejection crosses more than 50% — threshold not applicable in India

t: Women's political representation and reservation
text:
## 1. Baseline
First constitutionally institutionalized through the 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendment Acts, 1992 — not less than one-third (33.33%) of directly elected seats and Chairperson offices in rural and urban local bodies
106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023 — Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam — extends not less than one-third reservation to the Lok Sabha, State Legislative Assemblies and the Legislative Assembly of the National Capital Territory of Delhi
## 2. Where reservation applies
Body | Article | Enabled by | Covers — not less than one-third
Panchayati Raj Institutions | 243D | 73rd Amendment, 1992 | Total seats and offices — directly elected seats (243D(3)); Chairperson posts at all three tiers (243D(4))
Municipalities | 243T | 74th Amendment, 1992 | Total seats and offices — directly elected seats (243T(3)); Chairperson posts (243T(4))
House of the People (Lok Sabha) | 330A | 106th Amendment, 2023 | Total seats — general seats and seats reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes
State Legislative Assemblies | 332A | 106th Amendment, 2023 | Total seats — general seats and seats reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes
Delhi Legislative Assembly (NCT) | 239AA(2)(ba) | 106th Amendment, 2023 | Total seats — directly elected seats and Scheduled Caste-reserved seats
Rajya Sabha and State Legislative Councils | — | No provision | Nil — strictly excluded from the scope of the 106th Amendment
⚠ Trap: The 106th Amendment applies to the Lok Sabha, State Legislative Assemblies and the Delhi Legislative Assembly — it does not provide 33% reservation in the Rajya Sabha or State Legislative Councils
## 3. Panchayats in detail — Article 243D
243D(2): Within seats reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, not less than one-third are reserved for SC and ST women — the mandatory sub-quota is one-third, ⚠ not 50%
243D(3): Not less than one-third of the total directly elected seats in every Panchayat — including SC and ST women
243D(4): Not less than one-third of Chairperson offices — at the village, intermediate and district levels
Baseline: One-third (33.33%) — States have statutory discretion to increase it
Bihar — the first State to grant 50% reservation for women in Panchayats (2006); followed by Madhya Pradesh, Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh
Minimum age to contest Panchayat and Municipality elections: 21 years — Articles 243F and 243V — ⚠ not 25 years
## 4. Commencement — Article 334A
The pre-condition for the 106th Amendment reservation — does not come into force immediately
Takes effect only after a delimitation exercise, following publication of the relevant figures of the first decennial Census conducted after the Act
Duration: An initial 15 years from commencement — Parliament may extend it by law
Rotation: Reserved seats rotated after every subsequent delimitation — as determined by parliamentary law
## 5. Women in the Lok Sabha — milestones
Lok Sabha | Year | Women MPs
6th — lowest among the stated milestones | 1977 | 19
17th — highest up to that point | 2019 | 78 — approximately 14.36% of total strength

t: Political parties in India
text:
## 1. Formation of major parties
Party | Formed | Key facts
Indian National Congress | 1885 | First president — W.C. Banerjee
Communist Party of India | 1925 | Split in 1964 — led to the formation of the Communist Party of India (Marxist)
Bharatiya Jana Sangh | 1951 | Founded by Dr. Syama Prasad Mookerjee
Bharatiya Janata Party | 1980 | Succeeded the Bharatiya Jana Sangh; first president — Atal Bihari Vajpayee
Bahujan Samaj Party | 1984 | —
Samajwadi Party | 1992 | —
All India Trinamool Congress | 1998 | Abbreviated AITC; also known as TMC
Nationalist Congress Party | 1999 | Split from the Indian National Congress — associated with Sharad Pawar, P.A. Sangma and Tariq Anwar
## 2. Party system
Rajni Kothari: Coined the terms "One-Party Dominant System" and "Congress System"
The Congress party dominated India's democratic, multi-party electoral landscape after independence — the Congress System
1989 General Election: Marked the end of the Congress System — ushered in an era of minority and coalition governments
V.P. Singh led the National Front — with outside support from the Bharatiya Janata Party and the Left
## 3. Leader of Opposition
First formally recognized: 1969
Threshold: The largest opposition party must hold at least 10% of the total House strength — approximately 55 seats in the Lok Sabha
## 4. Constitutional recognition
Political parties were not included in the original 1950 constitutional text
Introduced — explicitly recognized for the first time — through the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985, which introduced the Tenth Schedule
## 5. National Party — Route 2
At least 6% of votes in four states and four Lok Sabha seats — the two recognition conditions under Route 2 are both mandatory

t: Anti-defection law — Tenth Schedule
text:
## 1. Origin and amendment
52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985: Introduced the Anti-Defection Law — added the 10th Schedule; amended Articles 101, 102, 190 and 191
Bill passed: 15 February 1985; in force: 1 March 1985
Jammu and Kashmir: Enacted its own state Anti-Defection legislation in 1979
91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003: Strengthened the law
Deleted — omitted — the original one-third split exception; the one-third split protection is completely abolished (obsolete threshold)
Capped the Council of Ministers at 15% of the Lower House
## 2. Grounds of disqualification
Member | Disqualified for | Protected / exception
Party-elected member — an MP or MLA | Voluntarily giving up party membership; voting or abstaining from voting contrary to the party whip without prior permission | Prior permission obtained, or the party condones the action within 15 days
Independent elected member | Joining any political party after election — including joining the government as an independent minister without taking party membership | —
Nominated member | Joining a political party after the expiry of six months from taking a seat | May join a party within six months of taking a seat
Presiding officer — Speaker or Chairman | Joining another political party while holding office or after vacating office | May voluntarily give up party membership upon election to the Chair and rejoin the original party after demitting office
Voluntarily giving up membership: Broader than formal resignation — includes conduct; e.g. publicly campaigning for an opposition party, even without a formal resignation letter
## 3. Merger exception
No disqualification when a member's original political party merges with another party and at least two-thirds of the legislature (legislative) party members agree to the merger
⚠ Trap: Protection requires two-thirds, not one-third
## 4. Who decides — defection vs general disqualification
Basis | Defection — 10th Schedule | General disqualification — Union MP | General disqualification — State MLA / MLC
Provisions | 10th Schedule; Articles 102(2) and 191(2) | Articles 102(1) and 103 | Articles 191(1) and 192
Decided by | The Presiding Officer of the concerned House — the Speaker or Chairman alone, acting as a tribunal | The President of India | The Governor of the State
ECI's role | Not consulted | Opinion must be obtained — mandatory and binding | Opinion must be obtained — mandatory and binding
Review | Judicial review — Kihoto Hollohan (1992), Supreme Court | — | —
⚠ Trap: The President and the Governor have no jurisdiction over 10th Schedule defection matters
Time limit: The 10th Schedule prescribes no statutory time limit for the Presiding Officer to decide a defection petition

t: Constitutional, statutory and extra-constitutional bodies
text:
## 1. Three kinds of body
Type | Basis | Examples
Constitutional | Directly established, empowered and anchored within the text of the Constitution of India | Election Commission, Public Service Commissions, Finance Commission, CAG, Attorney General, Advocate General, National Commissions for SCs, STs and Backward Classes, State Finance and Election Commissions
Statutory | Created by an Act of Parliament or a State Legislature | National Human Rights Commission, Lokpal, National Green Tribunal
Extra-constitutional / non-statutory | Established through an executive order or cabinet resolution | NITI Aayog, Planning Commission, National Development Council
## 2. Constitutional bodies
Body | Article | Appointed by | Key facts
Attorney General of India | 76 | President | Holds office during the pleasure of the President; qualified to be a Supreme Court judge
Advocate General of a State | 165 | Governor | Holds office during the pleasure of the Governor; qualified to be a High Court judge
Comptroller and Auditor General | 148 | President | Removed on the same grounds and in the same manner as a Supreme Court judge; tenure six years or until the age of 65
Finance Commission of India | 280 | President | Five members — one Chairman and four other members; qualifications of members determined by Parliament by law
State Finance Commission | 243-I and 243-Y | Governor | Constituted every five years; reviews the finances of Panchayats and Municipalities
Union / State Public Service Commissions | 315 | President (UPSC); Governor (State PSC) | Members of both removed only by the President — Article 317, after a Supreme Court inquiry
Election Commission of India | 324 | President | Chief Election Commissioner removed in the same manner as a Supreme Court judge
State Election Commission | 243-K and 243-ZA | Governor | Conducts local body elections; State Election Commissioner removed in the same manner as a High Court judge
National Commission for Scheduled Castes | 338 | President | Submits annual reports to the President
National Commission for Scheduled Tribes | 338-A | President | Bifurcated from the National Commission for Scheduled Castes — 89th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003
National Commission for Backward Classes | 338-B | President | Full constitutional status — 102nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2018
Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities | 350-B | President | Office inserted by the 7th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956; submits an annual report to the President
⚠ Trap: The National Commission for Backward Classes is not merely a statutory body under the 1993 Act — constitutional under Article 338-B
Local bodies: Elections conducted solely by the State Election Commission (Article 243-K) — ⚠ the Election Commission of India does not conduct local body elections; financial devolution recommended by the State Finance Commission (Article 243-I) to the Governor
## 3. Statutory bodies
Body | Act
National Human Rights Commission and State Human Rights Commissions | Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993
Zonal Councils | States Reorganisation Act, 1956 — Section 15; the Home Minister is their common Chairman
Lokpal and Lokayuktas | Act of 2013
National Green Tribunal | Act of 2010
Central Information Commission | Right to Information Act, 2005
Central Vigilance Commission | Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003
⚠ Trap: Pairing the National Human Rights Commission with a constitutional Article is false — it is statutory
## 4. Extra-constitutional bodies
Body | Established | Instrument
Planning Commission | 1950 | Cabinet Resolution dated 15 March 1950
National Development Council | 1952 | Executive Order dated 6 August 1952
NITI Aayog | 2015 | Cabinet Resolution dated 1 January 2015
Law Commission of India | — | Constituted periodically by executive order
⚠ Trap: The Planning Commission and NITI Aayog are extra-constitutional bodies — neither constitutional nor statutory
Inter-State Council: Article 263 — set up in May 1990 on the recommendations of the Sarkaria Commission

t: Finance Commission and fiscal federalism
text:
## 1. Nature
Constitutional body under Article 280 — Part XII; a permanent, independent, quasi-judicial body — an anchor of fiscal federalism
Constituted by the President every five years or earlier when necessary — ⚠ not strictly every five years
First Finance Commission: Constituted under a Presidential order in 1951; set up on 6 April 1952 — Chairman K.C. Neogy (1952 to 1957)
## 2. Composition — Article 280(1) and (2)
Five members — one Chairman + four other members — appointed by the President
Qualifications: Determined by Parliament by law — Article 280(2) — ⚠ not by the President or the Union Cabinet
Powers of a civil court: Summoning of persons and production of documents — a quasi-judicial character
## 3. Functions
Distribution of the net (tax) proceeds of divisible Union taxes between the Centre (Union) and the States; allocation among the States
Principles governing grants-in-aid of State revenues from the Consolidated Fund of India — Article 275
Measures to augment the Consolidated Fund of a State — to supplement the resources of Panchayats and Municipalities, on the basis of the recommendations of the State Finance Commission
Any other matter referred by the President in the interest of sound public finance
## 4. Report — Article 281
Submitted to the President, who causes it to be laid before both Houses of Parliament with an explanatory memorandum on action taken
⚠ Trap: The President, not the Finance Minister, lays the report before Parliament
## 5. Union vs State Finance Commission
Basis | Union Finance Commission | State Finance Commission
Article — belongs to | 280 — Part XII | 243-I and 243-Y — Parts IX and IX-A
Appointed by | President of India | Governor of the State
Deals with | Fiscal distribution between the Union and the States | Distribution between the State and local bodies — Panchayats and Municipalities
Constituted | Every five years or earlier | Every five years
Report | To the President, then Parliament (Article 281) | To the Governor, then the State Legislature
## 6. Recent Finance Commissions
Commission | Period | Chairman | Key facts
14th | 2015–20 | Y.V. Reddy | Raised the States' share of net divisible taxes from 32% to 42% — 10 percentage points
15th | 2020–26 | N.K. Singh | Two reports — the first for 2020–21, the second for 2021–26
## 7. Grants and disputes
Article 275: Statutory grants-in-aid to States — principles recommended by the Finance Commission
Article 282: Discretionary grants — by the Union or a State, for any public purpose, even outside its legislative purview
Centre–State legal and constitutional disputes: Resolved by the Supreme Court under its Original Jurisdiction — Article 131 — ⚠ not by the Finance Commission
## 8. Financial Articles at a glance
Article | Concerns
148 | Comptroller and Auditor General
266 | Consolidated Fund
267 | Contingency Fund
269A | IGST — 101st Constitutional Amendment
270 | Taxes shared between the Centre and the States
275 | Grants-in-aid
280 | Finance Commission
281 | Finance Commission report
360 | Financial Emergency

t: National Human Rights Commission
text:
## 1. Status
A statutory and independent body — not constitutional — established under the Protection of Human Rights Act (PHRA), 1993, effective 28 September 1993
Human rights: Rights relating to life, liberty, equality and dignity — guaranteed by the Constitution or embodied in international covenants, and enforceable by courts in India
Three levels: NHRC (national level) and SHRC (state level) under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993; Human Rights Courts — a district- or trial-level mechanism for speedy trials
## 2. Composition and appointment
Chairperson: A former Chief Justice of India or a former Supreme Court judge; plus judicial members, expert members and specified ex-officio representation
Appointed by: The President of India — on the recommendations of a six-member High-Level Selection Committee:
Prime Minister — Chairperson (the selection head)
Speaker of the Lok Sabha
Union Home Minister
Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha
Leader of the Opposition in the Rajya Sabha
Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha — he represents the Rajya Sabha
⚠ Trap: The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha is not a member of the committee
## 3. NHRC vs SHRC
Basis | NHRC | SHRC
Law | Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 | Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993
Nature | Statutory — not constitutional | Statutory — not constitutional
Appointed by | President of India | Governor of the State
Selection head | Prime Minister | Chief Minister
Jurisdiction | Union List and Concurrent List — matters at the national level | State List and Concurrent List
## 4. Powers and functions
All the powers of a civil court while inquiring into complaints:
Summon witnesses and examine them under oath
Discover documents and require their production
Requisition public records
Inquires into human rights violations and negligence by public servants in preventing them
Visits jails and detention centres to study the living conditions of inmates — suggests reforms
Promotes human rights literacy; encourages non-governmental organizations
## 5. Limits
Recommendations: Advisory / recommendatory in nature
⚠ Not a regular court of law; does not directly execute criminal sentencing
Armed forces: No direct or unrestricted investigative powers — under the statutory procedure it calls for an independent report from the Central Government and makes recommendations based on it
Section 2(m) of the Protection of Human Rights Act defines armed forces — naval, military and air forces and other Union armed forces

t: Oaths, resignations and removal
text:
## 1. Executive heads and ministers
Office | Oath — Article | Oath administered by | Resignation addressed to | Removal
President of India | 60 | Chief Justice of India — or the senior-most Supreme Court Judge if the CJI is unavailable | Vice-President — Article 56(1)(a); the VP communicates it to the Lok Sabha Speaker | Impeachment by Parliament — Article 61; 14 days' notice; two-thirds of the total membership
Vice-President of India | 69 | President of India | President of India | Rajya Sabha resolution passed by an effective majority and agreed to by the Lok Sabha — Article 67
Prime Minister and Union Ministers | 75(4) — oath of office and of secrecy | President of India | President of India — Union Ministers route it through the Prime Minister | Dismissed by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister; upon loss of the Lok Sabha majority
Governor of a State | 159 | Chief Justice of the (State) High Court — or the senior-most High Court Judge if the Chief Justice is unavailable | President of India — Article 156(2) | Removed by the President at pleasure — Article 156 — without impeachment
Chief Minister and State Ministers | 164(3) — oath of office and of secrecy | Governor of the State | Governor of the State — State Ministers route it through the Chief Minister | Dismissed by the Governor on the advice of the Chief Minister; upon loss of the Assembly majority
Oath forms: Codified directly in Article 60 (President), Article 69 (Vice-President) and Article 159 (Governor) — ⚠ not contained in the Third Schedule
## 2. Presiding officers
No separate oath of office as presiding officers — the Speaker, Deputy Speaker and Rajya Sabha Deputy Chairman take oath only as ordinary Members of Parliament
Office | Resignation addressed to | Removal
Speaker of the Lok Sabha | Deputy Speaker — Article 94(b) — ⚠ not the President | Lok Sabha resolution by an effective majority — Article 94; 14 days' notice
Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha | Speaker — Article 94(b) — ⚠ not the President | Lok Sabha resolution by an effective majority — Article 94; 14 days' notice
Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha | Chairman of the Rajya Sabha | Rajya Sabha resolution by an effective majority — Article 90; 14 days' notice
14 days' notice: At least 14 days' advance written notice is required for the removal of the President, the Lok Sabha Speaker, the Lok Sabha Deputy Speaker and the Rajya Sabha Deputy Chairman
## 3. Judges
Office | Oath — Article | Oath administered by | Resignation addressed to | Removal
Supreme Court Judge | 124(6) | President of India or a person appointed by the President | President of India | Order of the President following an address by Parliament — Article 124(4)
High Court Judge | 217(1) and 219 | Governor of the State | President of India | Order of the President following an address by Parliament — Article 217(1)

t: Age limits, tenures and retirement
text:
## 1. Minimum ages
Must be at least — years old | Office | Article
18 | Voter — universal adult suffrage | 326 — reduced from 21 to 18 by the 61st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1988; the reduction became effective in 1989
21 | Panchayat member or chairperson; Municipality member or Mayor — election contestant | 243F(1)(a) (Panchayat); 243V(1)(a) (Municipality)
25 | Member of the Lok Sabha and of a State Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha); Prime Minister or Chief Minister heading the lower chamber | 84(b) (Lok Sabha); 173(b) (Vidhan Sabha)
30 | Member of the Rajya Sabha and of a Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad) — the baseline for all Upper Houses / second chambers | 84(b) (Rajya Sabha); 173(b) (Vidhan Parishad)
35 | President, Vice-President and Governor — the constitutional executive heads | 58(1)(b) (President); 66(3)(b) (Vice-President); 157 (Governor)
Disqualification for contesting Panchayat or Municipality elections does not apply at or above 21 years of age
Twenty-five years is the minimum possible age for becoming Prime Minister or Chief Minister when heading the lower chamber
Thirty-five years is the highest entry age required in the Indian Constitution
## 2. Retirement ages and tenures
Office | Tenure / retirement | Basis
High Court Judge | Retires at 62 — raised from 60 to 62 by the 15th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1963; also applies to Additional and Acting judges | 217(1); 224(3)
Supreme Court Judge | No fixed tenure in years — retires upon turning 65 | 124(2)
Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners | 6 years or until 65, whichever is earlier — capped by either — statutory condition | Election Commission Act, 1991/2023
UPSC Chairman and Members | 6 years or until 65, whichever is earlier — retire at 65 | 316(2)
SPSC Chairman and Members | 6 years or until 62, whichever is earlier — retire at 62 | 316(2)
Comptroller and Auditor General | 6 years or until 65, whichever is earlier — retires at 65 | 148(3) and the CAG Act, 1971
## 3. Terms of offices and Houses
Five years: The President, the Lok Sabha, a State Legislative Assembly, a Panchayat and a Municipality — the constitutional tenure
Six years: A Rajya Sabha member and a State Legislative Council member — one-third of members retire every two years
Governor: A five-year term — holds office during the pleasure of the President; continues in office until the successor assumes office

Committee | Members | Composition

t: Constitutional days and time limits
text:
## 1. Fourteen days
Matter | Rule | Basis
Impeachment of the President | Prior notice of fourteen days; notice signed by at least one-fourth of the members | Article 61
Money Bill in the Rajya Sabha | Must be returned within fourteen days — else deemed passed by the Rajya Sabha | Article 109
Simultaneous membership of Parliament and a State Legislature | Resign the State Legislature seat within fourteen days — failure vacates the Parliament seat | Representation of the People Act, 1951
Removal of presiding officers | Fourteen days' notice — the Speaker and the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha | Article 90(c) (Deputy Chairman)
## 2. Thirty and sixty days
Thirty days — Emergency during Lok Sabha dissolution (Article 352): The proclamation survives for thirty days from the first sitting of the reconstituted Lok Sabha, provided the Rajya Sabha has approved it
Sixty days — unauthorised absence (Article 101(4)): An MP's seat may be declared vacant if absent from all House meetings for sixty days without permission
Excluded from the calculation of continuous absence: periods of prorogation and adjournments exceeding four consecutive days
## 3. One, two and six months
Period | Matter | Basis
One month | Parliamentary approval of a National Emergency — by special majority; reduced from two months to one by the Forty-Fourth Amendment of 1978 | Article 352
Two months | Parliamentary approval of President's Rule and of a Financial Emergency | Articles 356 and 360
Six months | Presidential vacancy caused by death, resignation or removal must be filled — the Vice-President acts as President in the interim | Article 62(2)
Six months | Maximum gap between sessions of Parliament — Parliament must meet at least twice a year | Article 85
Six months | An Emergency continues for six months at a time — the extension cycle | Article 352
Six months | State laws on State List subjects — the six-month post-Emergency timeframe | Article 250
## 4. 120 days — Right to Information Act, 2005
Assented to on 15 June 2005; came fully into force after 120 days on 12 October 2005 — the 120-day commencement timeframe governed by its statutory enforcement provision

t: Founders — Comte, Durkheim, Marx and Weber
text:
## 1. Auguste Comte (1798 to 1857)
Known as the Father of Sociology — coined the term Sociology; the founder of Positivism
Motto: "Order and Progress"
Positivism: Knowledge should be based on observation, experimentation and scientific evidence
Law of Three Stages — he proposed it:
Stage | Events explained through | Rain occurs because of
Theological Stage | Divine or supernatural forces | God's will
Metaphysical Stage | Abstract concepts | Nature's force
Positive Stage | Scientific explanation — events explained scientifically | Atmospheric processes
## 2. Emile Durkheim (born 1858, died 1917)
Regarded as the Father of Modern Sociology
Important works: The Division of Labour in Society; Suicide; Rules of Sociological Method
Society is a reality sui generis
Social facts — he developed the concept: External forces that influence individual behaviour — e.g. laws, customs, religion, traditions
Collective conscience: Shared beliefs and values that unite society
Anomie: A condition of normlessness caused by rapid social change — e.g. crime, suicide, social unrest
## 3. Karl Marx (born 1818, died 1883)
Known as the Father of Scientific Socialism — one of the most influential sociologists in conflict theory
Works: Das Kapital (published 1867); the Communist Manifesto with Friedrich Engels (published 1848)
Historical materialism: Economic conditions shape society, politics and culture
History is the history of class conflicts — class struggle
Examples of class conflict: Master and slave; lord and serf; bourgeoisie and proletariat
Surplus value: Workers produce more value than the wages they receive
Alienation: Workers become alienated from the product of their labour, the production process, society and themselves
Predicted that workers would overthrow capitalism and establish a classless society
## 4. Max Weber (1864 to 1920)
Known as the Father of Interpretative Sociology — wrote (studied) The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism
Ideal type — he developed the concept: An analytical model used to understand social reality
Types of social action:
Action | Basis
Instrumentally rational | Goal-oriented behaviour
Value-rational | Values and ethics
Traditional | Customs and traditions
Affective | Emotions
Bureaucracy: Hierarchy; rules and regulations; specialization; a merit system; impersonality
Types of authority: Traditional — customs; charismatic — personality and leadership; legal-rational — laws and rules

t: Other Western sociologists
text:
## 1. C. Wright Mills (1916 to 1962)
An American sociologist — famous for the concept of sociological imagination; wrote The Sociological Imagination (published 1959) — introduced the concept in 1959
Sociological imagination: Understanding the relationship between biography, history and society — the ability to connect personal experiences with larger social forces and historical processes
Individual problems are often reflections of wider social issues
Personal trouble | Public issue
Being unemployed | Large-scale unemployment due to economic slowdown
Student stress | A competitive education system
Power Elite Theory: Power is concentrated among political leaders, military leaders and corporate elites
Highlighted inequality and the concentration of power in modern society
## 2. George Simmel (1858 to 1918)
A German sociologist — studied social interaction and urban life
Formal sociology: Studies patterns of social interaction — society exists because individuals interact
Dyad: A group of two people — e.g. a husband and wife; triad: a group of three people — e.g. a teacher, parent and student
Urbanization increases individualism, competition and social distance
## 3. Herbert Blumer (1900 to 1987)
An American sociologist — founded Symbolic Interactionism (his major contribution)
People act based on the meanings they attach to things
Meaning develops through social interaction, communication and interpretation; language creates meaning; individuals interpret meanings
Symbols: The national flag represents patriotism; a wedding ring — marriage commitment; a uniform — authority
## 4. Others
Sociologist | Contribution
Herbert Spencer | Compared society to a biological organism
Talcott Parsons | Developed Structural Functionalism
Robert K. Merton | Developed the concepts of Manifest Functions and Latent Functions
George Herbert Mead | Developed Symbolic Interactionism

t: Indian sociologists and the Indological approach
text:

The study of Indian society through ancient texts, scriptures, epics, religious literature and historical records
Seeks to understand Indian society through the Vedas, Upanishads, Smritis, Puranas, Ramayana, Mahabharata and Dharmashastras
Features: Text-based; a historical perspective; cultural interpretation; emphasizes continuity
## 2. Indian sociologists and their ideas

A. R. Desai | Nationalism emerged from socio-economic changes under colonialism — Social Background of Indian Nationalism
Yogendra Singh | Studied the modernization of Indian tradition — Modernization of Indian Tradition
Andre Beteille | Studied the relationship among caste, class and power — Caste, Class and Power
N. K. Bose | Change in India occurs through adjustment rather than conflict

A. M. Shah | The joint family is changing, not disappearing — it continues despite modernization; Joint Family Studies

## 3. Features of caste
Segmental division; hierarchy; restrictions on feeding and social intercourse
Caste is a system of social separation

t: Caste and social stratification
text:
## 1. Caste terms
Varna: A four-fold social division; Jati: a birth-based caste group
Sanskritization: The adoption of upper-caste practices; Westernization: the adoption of Western values
Dominant caste: An economically and politically powerful caste
Untouchability: Social exclusion based on caste; casteism: loyalty to one's own caste
## 2. Systems of stratification
System | Features | Examples
Caste system | Birth-based; endogamy; hereditary occupation; restricted mobility; purity and pollution | Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra
Class system | Wealth and occupation; achieved status; an open system — social mobility is possible | Upper, middle and lower class
Estate system | Medieval Europe | Clergy, nobility, commoners
Slavery system | Extreme inequality — a person was treated as property; no freedom | Ancient Greece, Rome, America
G. S. Ghurye: Caste is characterized by hierarchy, endogamy and social restrictions
Karl Marx: The history of all societies is the history of class struggle
## 3. Bases of stratification in India
Traditional: Caste, varna, tribe, religion
Modern: Education, occupation, income, political power, urbanization

t: Status and social mobility
text:
## 1. Caste status
The social position occupied by an individual within the caste hierarchy — determined by birth; a fixed social position
Linked with occupation; determines social prestige
## 2. Ascribed vs achieved status
Basis | Ascribed status | Achieved status
Obtained | By birth | Through personal effort
Examples | Caste, gender, family background | An IAS Officer, a Doctor, a Scientist
Increased achieved status in modern India: Education, urbanization, industrialization, reservation policies, globalization
## 3. Social mobility
Social mobility: The movement of individuals from one social position to another — movement between social positions
Type | Meaning
Vertical | Upward or downward movement
Horizontal | A change with the same status — change without status change
Intergenerational | Between generations
Intragenerational | Within a lifetime
Example of upward mobility: A farmer's son becoming an IAS officer
## 4. Hereditary occupations
Hereditary characteristics, occupations, rights and positions are passed from one generation to another
Hereditary position: Kingship; hereditary right: property ownership
Hereditary occupations: Traditional occupations; family businesses
In the caste system: Potter, carpenter, blacksmith, weaver
Weakened by education, industrialization, urbanization and occupational mobility

t: Kinship, marriage rules and family terms
text:
## 1. Endogamy and exogamy
Endogamy: Marriage within one's own social group — within a caste, tribe or religion
Preserves group identity; maintains caste boundaries; controls property transfer; promotes cultural continuity and social solidarity; preserves traditions
Exogamy: Marriage outside one's own social group
Hypergamy — also known as Anuloma: Marriage into a higher caste
Anuloma: A union between a high-caste male and a low-caste female
Hypogamy — also known as Pratiloma: Marriage into a lower caste
Pratiloma: A union between a low-caste male and a high-caste female
## 2. Forms of marriage
Term | Meaning
Monogamy | One husband and one wife
Polygyny | One man and many wives
Polyandry | One woman and many husbands
Sororal polygyny | Marriage to sisters
Fraternal polyandry | Marriage to brothers
Levirate | A widow marries her husband's brother
Sororate | A widower marries his wife's sister
Child marriage | Marriage below the legal age
Widow remarriage | The marriage of a widow again
## 3. Descent, residence and kin
Term | Meaning
Patrilineal descent | Through the father
Matrilineal descent | Through the mother
Patriarchy | A male-dominated system
Matriarchy | A female-dominated system
Patrilocal residence | A wife lives with her husband's family
Matrilocal residence | A husband lives with his wife's family
Avunculocal residence | Residence with a maternal uncle
Nuclear family | Parents and children
Joint family | Multiple generations together
Consanguineal kin | Blood relatives
Affinal kin | Relatives by marriage
Clan | A group with a common ancestor
Lineage | A direct descent group
Gotra | A common male ancestor group
Sapinda | A blood relationship group

t: Tribal and cultural terms; social stability
text:
## 1. Tribal terms
Animism: The worship of nature spirits; totemism: the worship of an animal or plant symbol
Shifting cultivation: Slash-and-burn agriculture — Jhum cultivation in Northeast India
Ghotul: A youth dormitory among Muria tribes
Tribe: A community with common territory and culture
## 2. Cultural terms
Term | Meaning
Ethnocentrism | Viewing one's own culture as superior
Acculturation | Cultural exchange between groups
Assimilation | Absorption into a dominant culture
Integration | Participation while retaining identity
Ethnicity | Shared cultural identity; an ethnic group shares a common culture
Cultural pluralism | The coexistence of different cultures
Cultural lag | Delay in adjustment to change
Cultural diffusion | The spread of culture
Cultural relativism | Understanding a culture on its own terms
Multiculturalism | The coexistence of multiple cultures
Xenophobia | Fear of foreigners
Regionalism | Loyalty to a region
Communalism | Loyalty to a religious group
## 3. Social stability
A condition in which society maintains peace, order, harmony, continuity and the effective functioning of institutions — persists despite social changes
Key features: Social cohesion; social harmony; the rule of law; economic security; political stability; inclusive development
Promoted by:
The family — the primary agent of socialization
Education and value inculcation; constitutional values; democratic institutions
Welfare schemes and social justice measures; religious and cultural tolerance
Threatened by: Poverty and unemployment; casteism; communalism; regionalism; extremism and terrorism; social inequality; gender discrimination

t: Functions of the family
text:
## 1. Family as an institution
A basic and primary social institution
Functions: Reproduction; socialization; emotional support; economic security; cultural transmission
Important scholars of family: George Peter Murdock, Talcott Parsons, Irawati Karve
## 2. Biological and protective functions
Ensures the continuity of society through reproduction — produces the next generation
Provides socially approved sexual relations — prevents social disorder by regulating sexual behaviour
Protects infants, children, elderly and sick members
Protects members from social and economic risks; supports children, women, elderly persons and disabled persons
## 3. Socialization and education
The first school of the child — teaches language, customs, values, traditions and norms
Encourages acceptable behaviour; discourages deviant behaviour
Teaches basic education before school; develops discipline and moral values; encourages learning habits
A child learns language, manners and respect for elders in the family
## 4. Identity and status
Provides caste, religious, language and national identity; provides social status
Transfers traditions from one generation to another
## 5. Economic functions
Provides food, shelter and clothing; members perform different roles
Transfers wealth and property through inheritance; consumes goods and services collectively
## 6. Emotional and religious functions
Provides love, affection and care; builds confidence and self-esteem; helps members cope with stress and crises
Introduces religious beliefs and rituals; celebrates festivals and ceremonies — Diwali, Eid, Christmas, Gurpurab; preserves religious traditions
## 7. Murdock's four universal functions
George Peter Murdock identified four universal functions of the family:
Function | Meaning
Sexual regulation | Regulation of sexual relations
Reproductive | The birth of children
Economic | Economic cooperation
Educational | Socialization of children

t: Social institutions of Indian society
text:
## 1. Marriage and kinship
Marriage: A socially approved union between individuals — regulates sexual behavior; legitimizes children; creates kinship ties; provides social stability
Types: Monogamy, polygyny, polyandry, endogamy, exogamy; important terms: Anuloma, Pratiloma, Levirate, Sororate
Kinship: A system of social relationships based on blood and marriage — consanguineal (blood relations) and affinal (marriage relations)
Important concepts: Gotra, Sapinda, clan, lineage; scholar: Irawati Karve
## 2. Religion
A system of beliefs and practices concerning sacred things — scholar: Emile Durkheim
Promotes social cohesion; provides moral guidance; exercises social control; provides emotional support; strengthens social solidarity
Major religions in India: Hinduism, Islam, Christianity, Sikhism, Buddhism, Jainism, Zoroastrianism
## 3. Education
The process of transmitting knowledge, skills and values — performs socialization; develops skills; promotes social mobility; contributes to nation building
Constitutional provision: Article 21A; the Right to Education Act — enacted 2009
Important institutions: Schools, colleges, universities
## 4. Economy and polity
Economy: Production, distribution and consumption — provides employment; creates wealth; performs resource allocation; sectors — primary, secondary, tertiary
Polity or state: Exercises authority and maintains order — law and order; justice; welfare; governance
Important elements: The legislature, executive and judiciary
## 5. Caste and tribe
Caste: A birth-based social institution unique to Indian society — endogamy, hierarchy, hereditary occupation, social restrictions
Scholars: G. S. Ghurye, M. N. Srinivas; concepts: Sanskritization, Dominant Caste, Westernization
Tribe: A social group sharing common territory, culture, language and ancestry — practices endogamy; political organization
Scholar: Verrier Elwin; terms: Animism, Totemism, Ghotul, Jhum Cultivation
## 6. Media
A modern social institution — disseminates information; creates awareness; forms public opinion
Types: Print, electronic and social media
Contributes to social change; promotes political participation; facilitates cultural diffusion

t: Hindu marriage types — Manu Smriti
text:
## 1. The eight forms
Manu Smriti recognizes eight types of Hindu marriages
Form | Nature | Status in Manusmriti
Brahma | Giving a daughter to a learned and worthy groom | Approved
Daiva | Giving a daughter to a priest performing a sacrifice | Approved
Arsha | Receiving symbolic gifts from the groom | Approved
Prajapatya | Based on duty and family life | Approved
Gandharva | Based on mutual love and consent | Conditionally accepted
Asura | Purchasing the bride by giving wealth to her family | Disapproved
Rakshasa | Forceful abduction after battle | Disapproved
Paisacha | Taking a woman through deceit or exploitation | The most condemned form
Approved or Prashasta: Brahma, Daiva, Arsha, Prajapatya
Disapproved or Aprashasta: Gandharva, Asura, Rakshasa, Paisacha — ⚠ Gandharva is listed among the disapproved or Aprashasta marriages although conditionally accepted
## 2. The forms in detail
Brahma: The father voluntarily gives his daughter to a qualified, educated, virtuous groom knowledgeable in the Vedas
No dowry; no bride price — considered the highest form of marriage
Modern equivalent: An arranged marriage based on qualifications and compatibility
Daiva: The daughter is given to a Ritvik priest who officiates a sacrifice — linked with religious rituals; the groom is a priest
Arsha: Performed after receiving a symbolic gift such as a cow and a bull from the groom — only a symbolic exchange; common among sages and hermits
Prajapatya: Performed with blessings emphasizing duty — emphasizes family welfare and procreation; focuses on Dharma; husband and wife share responsibilities
Gandharva: Mutual love and consent of the couple — no parental approval required; a love marriage; a voluntary union
Example: Shakuntala and Dushyanta; many references occur in epics
Asura: The groom gives wealth to the bride's family — purchasing the bride; a bride price; wealth is the primary consideration
Rakshasa: The forceful abduction of a woman — associated with Kshatriyas; after warfare or conflict; abduction-type marriages are mentioned in epics
Paisacha: Deceit, intoxication, coercion — exploitation of a woman without her consent; the most condemned form; considered immoral and sinful

t: Succession and inheritance
text:
## 1. Succession
The transfer of authority, office, position or property from one person to another
Type | Transfer | Example
Lineal succession | From parent to child | Father-to-son
Collateral succession | Among relatives | Brother-to-brother
Importance: Continuity of institutions; political stability; social order; legitimacy
Examples: Political leadership transition; royal succession; transfer of family property
## 2. Inheritance
The transfer of property, wealth, rights and obligations after death — from one generation to another
Type | Includes
Property inheritance | Land, houses, buildings
Financial inheritance | Money, shares, savings
Cultural inheritance | Language, customs, traditions
Social inheritance | Status, reputation, networks
## 3. Inheritance laws
Law | Provision
Hindu Succession Act, 1956 | Provides inheritance rights to Hindus
Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 | Granted daughters equal coparcenary rights
Indian Succession Act, 1925 | Applies mainly to Christians and others
Muslim inheritance | Governed by Sharia principles
Contemporary issues: Women's property rights; gender equality; family disputes; property fragmentation

t: Social research
text:
## 1. Nature
Systematic and scientific — studies society, social relationships and social problems
Objectives: Discovering facts; explaining social phenomena; testing theories; solving social problems
## 2. Steps — in order
Step 1: Problem identification — precedes literature review
Step 2: Literature review — precedes hypothesis formulation
Step 3: Hypothesis formulation — precedes data collection
Step 4: Data collection — precedes data analysis
Step 5: Data analysis — precedes interpretation
Step 6: Interpretation — precedes report writing
Step 7: Report writing
Each is a step in social research
## 3. Types
Basic, applied, quantitative and qualitative research

t: Social diagnosis
text:
## 1. Nature
The systematic assessment of an individual's or a group's social conditions, social problems and social needs before planning interventions
Introduced by Mary Richmond — social workers diagnose social problems in the same way that doctors diagnose diseases
Objectives: Identifying social problems; understanding root causes; assessing needs; planning interventions
## 2. Steps
Step | Name | Involves
First | Information collection | Gathering facts about the individual or family
Second | Problem identification | Identifying social, economic and psychological issues
Third | Analysis | Determining causes and consequences
Fourth | Planning | Developing intervention strategies
Fifth | Follow-up | Monitoring outcomes
## 3. Applications and importance
Areas of application: Child welfare; family counselling; community development; rehabilitation services; poverty alleviation programmes
Importance: Scientific problem-solving; effective social work; better policy implementation; targeted interventions
## 4. Example — a school dropout
A school dropout may face poverty, family conflict, child labour and a lack of educational support
Interventions for a diagnosed school dropout are designed according to the identified problems

t: Religious fundamentalism and network society
text:
## 1. Religious fundamentalism
Strict adherence to religious beliefs and practices — often rejects modern interpretations
Features: Literal interpretation of scriptures; religious conservatism; resistance to change; group exclusiveness
Causes: Identity crisis; globalization; social insecurity; political mobilization; economic inequalities
## 2. Network society
A society where social, economic, political and cultural activities are organized through digital networks
Propounded by Manuel Castells
Features: Internet-based communication; global connectivity; information economy; digital platforms; virtual communities
Examples: Social media networks; online education; digital governance; e-commerce

t: High-risk families
text:
## 1. Nature
Families facing severe social, economic, health, psychological or environmental challenges
Characteristics: Poverty; unemployment; domestic violence; substance abuse; single-parent households; chronic illness or disability; child neglect and abuse; family conflicts
## 2. Causing factors
Factor | Examples
Economic | Poverty, debt burden, job insecurity
Social | Family breakdown, migration, social exclusion
Psychological | Mental stress, depression, addiction
## 3. Consequences and measures
Consequences: Child labour; school dropouts; juvenile delinquency; malnutrition; crime and deviance
Government measures: Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS); Mission Vatsalya; POSHAN Abhiyaan; National Family Benefit Scheme

t: Social issues — policies and enforcement
text:
## 1. Casteism and atrocities
Protection of Civil Rights (PCR) Act: Enacted 1955
SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Amendment Act: Enacted 2018
National Toll-Free Helpline: 14566
Mechanism: Automatic FIR registration without a preliminary inquiry; central assistance for atrocity victim relief; incentives for inter-caste marriage
## 2. Crimes against women
Nirbhaya Fund projects: Fast Track Special Courts; Cyber Forensic Labs
NDSO: National Database on Sexual Offenders; SHe-Box: Sexual Harassment electronic Box
Mechanism: Speedy trials; an investigation tracking system for sexual offences; streamlined redressal under the POSH Act
## 3. Child labour and abuse
PENCIL: Platform for Effective Enforcement for No Child Labour
POCSO Amendment Act: Stringent punishments
Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Amendment Act: Empowers District Magistrates to issue accelerated adoption orders
Mechanism: Inter-agency coordination to rescue and rehabilitate child labourers
## 4. Youth unrest and agitation
Initiatives: PM-YUVA; Mera Yuva Bharat (MY Bharat); the PM-Vidyalaxmi Scheme; Kaushal Vikas Yojana (PMKVY 4.0)
Mechanism: Channeling the youth demographic dividend through digital youth leadership networks; collateral-free higher education loans; future-ready skilling
## 5. Regionalisation and insurgency
PM-DevINE: Prime Minister's Development Initiative for North East Region
VVP: Vibrant Villages Programme
Peace accords: The Bodo, Bru-Reang and NLFT agreements — made via the Ministry of Home Affairs
Mechanism: Infrastructure saturation and livelihood creation in border villages and the North East — intended to integrate isolated regions

t: Gender mainstreaming and gender audit
text:
## 1. Gender mainstreaming
The process of integrating gender perspectives into policies, programmes, laws and institutions
Promoted globally during the Fourth World Conference on Women — Beijing, 1995
Aims: Achieve gender equality; reduce gender discrimination; promote women's participation; ensure equitable development
Promotes: Women's empowerment; inclusive governance; social justice; sustainable development
## 2. Tools
Tool | Purpose
Gender analysis | Assesses gender impacts
Gender planning | Incorporates gender concerns into policymaking
Gender budgeting | Allocates resources for gender-sensitive programmes
Gender monitoring | Evaluates gender outcomes
Examples: Beti Bachao Beti Padhao; Gender Budget Statements; Mission Shakti; Women Reservation initiatives
## 3. Gender Audit
A systematic assessment of policies, programmes, institutions and budgets
Evaluates gender equality; promotes gender justice; identifies gender gaps; improves women's participation; ensures gender-sensitive governance
Includes: Gender budgeting; equal opportunities; workplace safety; decision-making participation

t: Universal Declaration of Human Rights
text:
## 1. Adoption
A foundational international document — recognizes the fundamental rights and freedoms of all human beings
Adopted by the United Nations General Assembly on 10 December 1948
Prepared after the atrocities of World War II — to safeguard human dignity
## 2. Features
Universal applicability; upholds equality and non-discrimination
Protects civil, political, economic, social and cultural rights
Human dignity is at its core; contains a preamble and 30 articles
## 3. Rights recognized
Right to life; freedom of speech; freedom of religion; equality before law; right to work; right to education; right to health; right to social security
## 4. Influence in India
Influenced Fundamental Rights; inspired the Directive Principles of State Policy; a basis for human rights legislation
Related bodies: The United Nations; the National Human Rights Commission; State Human Rights Commissions

t: Judgements on reservation, tribes and minorities
text:
## 1. SC, ST, OBC and EWS cases
Case | Decided | Concerns | Ruling
Janki Prasad Parimoo v. State of J&K | 1973 | Other Backward Classes | Caste alone cannot be the sole determinant of backwardness under Article 15(4) — backwardness must include social and educational indicators
Indra Sawhney v. Union of India — the Mandal Case | 1992 | Other Backward Classes | Upheld a 27% quota for OBCs; introduced the creamy layer exclusion; fixed the reservation ceiling at 50%; ruled out quotas in promotions
Samatha v. State of Andhra Pradesh | 1997 | Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes | Nullified mining leases to non-tribals in Schedule V areas — tribal land cannot be leased to private parties or corporations
M. Nagaraj v. Union of India | 2006 | Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes | Upheld reservation in promotions — subject to quantifiable data demonstrating backwardness and inadequate representation, and to overall administrative efficiency (Article 335)
Orissa Mining Corporation v. MoEF — the Niyamgiri Case | 2013 | Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes | Affirmed the statutory role of the Gram Sabha under the Forest Rights Act, 2006 — it safeguards the religious and cultural rights of Dongria Kondh tribals
Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta | 2018 | Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes | Removed the requirement to prove backwardness for SCs and STs in promotions; extended the creamy layer principle to SC and ST promotions
Janki Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India | 2022 | Economically Weaker Sections | Upheld the validity of the 103rd Constitutional Amendment Act — a 10% quota for EWS; economic criteria alone can form a valid basis for classification
State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh | 2024 — a 7-judge bench | Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes | Overruled E.V. Chinnaiah (2004); affirmed that states have constitutional power to sub-classify SCs and STs — basis: Articles 15(4) and 16(4); sub-classification must use empirical data; recommended identification of the creamy layer
## 2. Disability and minority cases
Case | Decided | Concerns | Ruling
T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka | 2002 | Minorities | Under Article 30, the unit for determining religious and linguistic minority status is the State — ⚠ not the entire nation
Rajive Raturi v. Union of India | 2018 | Persons with Disabilities | Framed concrete directions for time-bound visual, auditory and mobility accessibility in public transport and built infrastructure — legal basis: the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act
Vikash Kumar v. UPSC | 2021 | Persons with Disabilities | Scribe facilities cannot be restricted only to persons with benchmark disabilities; recognized reasonable accommodation as an intrinsic component of equality

t: Judgements on women, family, gender and children
text:
## 1. Women and family
Case | Decided | Ruling
Saroj Rani v. Sudarshan Kumar Chadha | 1984 | Upheld the constitutional validity of Restitution of Conjugal Rights — under Section 9 of the Hindu Marriage Act
Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan | 1997 | Laid down binding guidelines against sexual harassment at the workplace — based on Articles 14, 19 and 21; directly led to the POSH Act, 2013
Danial Latifi v. Union of India | 2001 | Upheld the Muslim Women Act, 1986 — maintenance is not limited solely to the iddat period; it must cover reasonable provision for the wife's entire life
Shayara Bano v. Union of India | 2017 | Declared instant Talaq-e-Biddat unconstitutional and arbitrary — violative of Article 14
Joseph Shine v. Union of India | 2018 | Struck down Section 497 of the IPC (adultery) — archaic and patriarchal; violative of Articles 14 and 21
Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma | 2020 | Clarified the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 — daughters have coparcenary rights by birth, not depending on whether the father was alive on the amendment date
X v. Principal Secretary, H&FW, GNCTD | 2022 | All women are entitled to safe and legal abortion up to 24 weeks under the MTP Act — regardless of marital status; included marital rape within medical termination rules
## 2. Gender identity
Case | Decided | Ruling
NALSA v. Union of India | 2014 | Recognized transgender individuals as the Third Gender — affirmed their fundamental right to self-identify their gender identity
Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India | 2018 | Decriminalized consensual same-sex adult relationships by reading down Section 377 of the IPC
## 3. Children
Case | Decided | Ruling
M.C. Mehta v. State of Tamil Nadu | 1996 | Banned child labour in hazardous industries; mandated a Child Labour Rehabilitation-cum-Welfare Fund
Bachpan Bachao Andolan v. Union of India | 2011 | Guidelines against trafficking, child begging and circus child labour; mandated human-rights oversight of all Child Care Institutions
Independent Thought v. Union of India | 2017 | Struck down the marital rape exception for minor wives under Section 375 of the IPC — intercourse with a girl below 18 is statutory rape regardless of marriage

t: Judgements on secularism, elections and public order
text:
## 1. Cases
Case | Decided | Ruling
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India | 1994 | Secularism is a basic feature of the Constitution — state governments acting against secularism can be dismissed under Article 356
In Re: Destruction of Public and Private Properties | 2009 | Leaders and organizers of agitations resulting in property destruction are subject to vicarious civil and criminal liability
Abhiram Singh v. C.D. Commachen | 2017 | Expanded Section 123(3) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 — appeals to religion, race, caste, community or language during election campaigns constitute a corrupt practice
Tehseen S. Poonawalla v. Union of India | 2018 | Preventive, corrective and punitive measures to combat mob lynching and cow vigilantism
Shakti Vahini v. Union of India | 2018 | Declared Khap Panchayat interference and honor killings illegal — the right to choose a life partner is part of Article 21
Amit Sahni v. Commissioner of Police — concerning Shaheen Bagh | 2020 | Recognized the right to protest peacefully under Article 19 — but public ways and public spaces cannot be occupied indefinitely

t: Caste, SC/ST and tribal laws
text:
## 1. Caste Disabilities Removal Act, 1850
Enacted 1850 — removed legal disabilities due to caste conversion
## 2. Protection of Civil Rights Act (PCR), 1955
Enacted (passed) in 1955; came into force on June 1, 1955
Renamed in 1976 from the Untouchability Offences Act
Enforces Article 17 of the Constitution — punishes the practice of untouchability; prescribes penalties for practicing untouchability and for enforcing religious and social disabilities arising from it
## 3. SC and ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989
Enacted (passed) in 1989; came into force on January 30, 1990; amended in 2018 — on August 20, 2018
Prevents atrocities against Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes; contains an explicit list of atrocities
Does not allow anticipatory bail — Section 18A bars anticipatory bail
Section 18A removes the requirement of a preliminary inquiry and of prior sanction before arrest
## 4. Manual Scavengers Act, 2013
The Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers and their Rehabilitation Act — enacted (passed) in 2013; came into force on December 6, 2013
Eliminates manual scavenging:
Completely prohibits hazardous manual cleaning of sewer and septic tanks
Totally bans manual cleaning of unsanitary latrines, open drains and sewers without protective gear
Mandates mechanization and alternative livelihood rehabilitation
## 5. PESA, 1996
The Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act — also known as PESA; enacted (passed) in 1996; came into force on December 24, 1996
Provides tribal self-governance — extends Part IX of the Constitution to Schedule V areas; empowers traditional Gram Sabhas
Gram Sabhas get authority over natural resources, minor forest produce, dispute resolution and project approvals in Schedule V areas
## 6. Forest Rights Act, 2006
Also known as FRA — enacted (passed) in 2006; came into force on December 31, 2007; rules notified on January 1, 2008
Recognizes tribal forest rights — recognizes and vests individual and community forest rights in forest-dwelling Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers
## 7. Commissions
National Commission for Backward Classes Act: Enacted 1993 — created the National Commission for Backward Classes
National Commission for Minorities Act: Enacted 1992 — establishes the National Commission for Minorities

Act | Enacted | Key provisions

Persons with Disabilities Act | 1995 | The first comprehensive disability law

Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act — the RPwD Act | 2016 (passed); came into force on April 19, 2017 | A rights-based disability framework; replaced the 1995 Act; expanded disability categories from 7 to 21 — recognizes 21 categories; 4% reservation in government jobs (public employment) and 5% in higher education for persons with benchmark disabilities; penalizes discrimination
## 2. Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007

t: Marriage and family laws
text:

Hindu Marriage Act | 1955 | May 18, 1955 | Concerns Hindu marriages — codified conditions of Hindu marriage, divorce and restitution of conjugal rights
Prohibition of Child Marriage Act — PCMA | 2006 | November 1, 2007 | Prevents child marriage; replaced the 1929 Sarda Act; marriageable (minimum) age — 18 years for females, 21 years for males; child marriages are voidable at the child's option
Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act | 2019 (passed) | September 19, 2018 — date of enforcement, with retrospective effect; Royal Assent on July 31, 2019 | Criminalized (criminalizes) instant triple talaq — Talaq-e-Biddat is void, illegal and a criminal offense; imprisonment of up to 3 years
The Hindu Marriage Act and personal laws: Statutory codified personal laws — cover conditions of marriage, divorce and restitution of conjugal rights
## 2. Hindu family laws
Act | Enacted | Provides

Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act | 1956 | Adoption
Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act | 1956 | Guardianship
Family Courts Act | 1984 | Family dispute resolution

t: Women's protection laws
text:

Maternity Benefit Act | 1961 | — | Maternity protection
Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act | 2017 (passed) | — | Enhanced paid maternity leave from 12 weeks to 26 weeks; a crèche facility for establishments with at least 50 employees
Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act | 1971 | April 1, 1972; amended on September 24, 2021 | Legalized abortion up to 24 weeks on specified therapeutic and vulnerable-group grounds

t: Child rights laws
text:
## 1. Child laws
Act | Enacted | Came into force / amended | Key provisions
Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act | 1986 (passed) | Came into force on December 23, 1986; amended (majorly) in 2016 — on September 1, 2016 | Completely bans — prohibits — employing children below 14 in all occupations; regulates — restricts — adolescents aged 14 to 18 working in hazardous conditions (processes)
Commissions for Protection of Child Rights (CPCR) Act | 2005 (passed) | February 15, 2006 | Established — constituted — the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) and State Commissions (SCPCRs) as statutory bodies — statutory watchdogs for children's legal and constitutional rights; they monitor child welfare
Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act | 2009 (passed) | April 1, 2010 | Enforces Article 21A — free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14 (6–14 years); 25% reservation — quota — for disadvantaged groups in private unaided schools; universal elementary education; protects minority educational rights under Article 30
Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act | 2012 (passed) | Came into force on November 14, 2012; amended in 2019 — on August 16, 2019 | Gender-neutral; punishes child sexual abuse — stringent punishments; the 2019 amendment added capital punishment for aggravated penetrative (sexual) assault; child-friendly special courts; mandates reporting
Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act | 2015 (passed) | Came into force on January 15, 2016; amended in 2021 — also given as September 1, 2022 | Juveniles aged 16 to 18 (16–18 years) may be tried as adults for heinous offenses (crimes); the 2021/2022 amendment empowered District Magistrates (DMs) and Additional District Magistrates to issue adoption orders
