t: Religion, public order and criminal laws
text:
## 1. Religion
Places of Worship (Special Provisions) Act: Enacted 1991; came into force on July 11, 1991
Maintains — freezes — the religious character of places of worship as it existed on 15 August 1947 (August 15, 1947)
Has specific statutory exceptions to its freeze
Religious Institutions (Prevention of Misuse) Act: Enacted 1988 — prohibits the use of religious premises for political activities, harboring criminals and harboring arms
## 2. Security and examinations
Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act: Enacted 1967 — UAPA; a national security framework — addresses disruptive activities, unlawful associations and terror funding
Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act: Enacted 2024; came into force on June 21, 2024
Curbs paper leaks and organized cheating in central competitive examinations — central recruitment and entrance tests
The offense is non-bailable; severe fines and imprisonment
## 3. New criminal laws
Law | Enacted | Came into force | Replaced | Key provisions
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) | 2023 | July 1, 2024 | The IPC — IPC 1860 | Dedicated chapters (provisions) prioritizing offenses against women and children; defines organized crime; penalizes mob lynching
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) | 2023 | July 1, 2024 | The CrPC — CrPC 1973 | Integrates timelines for charge sheets; strict investigation timeframes; mandates video recording of searches and seizures; digital forensics; a statutory Zero FIR

t: Commissions on backward classes and Scheduled Castes
text:
## 1. Backward Classes Commissions
Commission | Established / constituted | Chair | Purpose and key facts
First Backward Classes Commission — the Kaka Kalelkar Commission | 1953 — by the President under Article 340 | Kaka Kalelkar | Concerned Other Backward Classes (OBCs) — to identify backward classes; the first commission to use social and educational criteria to identify backward classes; recommended a caste-based census and reservations for backward classes
Second Backward Classes Commission — also called the Mandal Commission (the B.P. Mandal Commission) | 1979 — by the Ministry of Home Affairs | B. P. Mandal | Concerned OBCs — OBC reservation; identified 3,743 backward castes; formulated 11 social, educational and economic indicators; recommended 27% reservation for OBCs
Rohini Commission — the Justice G. Rohini Commission | Established 2017 — by the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment under Article 340; submitted its report in 2023 | G. Rohini | Concerned OBCs — OBC sub-categorization; examined sub-categorization within OBCs in the Central List; aimed to ensure equitable distribution of reservation benefits among underrepresented groups
## 2. Scheduled Castes and De-Notified Tribes
Commission | Constituted | By | Key facts
Bhikhu Ramji Idate Commission | 2017 | The Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment | Concerned Scheduled Castes and De-Notified Tribes (DNTs) — surveyed De-Notified, Nomadic and Semi-Nomadic Tribes; led directly to the formulation of the SEED Scheme
Justice K.G. Balakrishnan Commission | 2022 | The Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment | Concerned Scheduled Castes (SCs) — examined the legal feasibility of according Scheduled Caste status to Dalits who converted to religions other than Hinduism, Sikhism and Buddhism
Rajiv Gauba Committee | A Cabinet Secretary panel formed in 2024 | The Central Government through the Department of Personnel and Training | Concerned SCs — explored equitable administrative mechanisms and alternative interventions for the most backward sub-castes among SCs; Madigas were cited as an example

t: Commissions on minorities, women and disability
text:

Committee | Established / constituted | Chair / by | Key facts
Gopal Singh Committee | 1983 | Gopal Singh | Minority welfare
Ranganath Misra Commission — the National Commission for Religious and Linguistic Minorities | Established 2004 — also given as constituted 2007 — by the Ministry of Minority Affairs | Ranganath Misra | Concerned — studied — religious and linguistic minorities; recommended 15% reservation for minorities and 10% for Muslims in education and government jobs
Sachar Committee — the Justice Rajindar Sachar Committee | Established 2005 — also given as constituted 2006; a Prime Minister's High-Level Committee | Rajinder Sachar | Concerned minorities — studied (assessed) the socio-economic and educational status of the Muslim community in India; highlighted severe under-representation of Muslims in public employment and higher education

t: Firsts — sociology, kinship, caste and marriage law
text:
## 1. Sociology
Auguste Comte: The father of Sociology
G. S. Ghurye: The father of Indian Sociology; the first Indian sociologist
M. N. Srinivas: The father of Modern Indian Sociology
First Sociology Department in India: University of Bombay — 1919
## 2. Kinship and family
Irawati Karve:
The first woman sociologist of India; the first sociologist to study the Indian family systematically
The first Indian scholar of kinship studies; the first scholar to classify Indian family regions
The first anthropologist to classify Indian kinship zones; the first scholar to highlight North-South kinship differences
Wrote Kinship Organization in India (1953) — the first major book on Indian kinship and family; the first landmark work on kinship in India
G. S. Ghurye: The first sociologist to explain the linkage between kinship and caste
Directive Principles, particularly Articles 39 and 42: The first constitutional recognition of family welfare
National Family Planning Programme: India launched the first in the world — 1952; the first Asian country to launch a Family Planning Programme
## 3. Caste
Herbert Risley: The first scholar to define caste scientifically
G. S. Ghurye: The first Indian sociologist to study caste systematically — Caste and Race in India (1932), the first major book on caste
M. N. Srinivas: The first sociologist to coin the term Sanskritization and to explain Dominant Caste
Article 17: The first Constitutional provision against — abolishing — untouchability
## 4. Marriage laws
Age of Consent Act: The first legal measure against child marriage — 1891
Sharda Act — the Child Marriage Restraint Act: The first Child Marriage Restraint Law — the first comprehensive child marriage law — 1929
Special Marriage Act: The first Special Marriage Law — 1872
Hindu Marriage Act: The first codified Hindu Marriage Law after Independence — 1955

t: Firsts — reservation, tribes, minorities and integration
text:
## 1. Reservation and backward classes
Kolhapur State — under Shahu Maharaj — the first State to implement reservation: the first reservation policy in India (1902); Shahu Maharaj was the first ruler to introduce reservation

1st Amendment Act of 1951: The first Constitutional Amendment — enacted 1951 — related to reservations; the first Constitutional recognition of OBC reservation
Kaka Kalelkar Commission: The first Backward Class Commission — 1953; Kaka Kalelkar — its first Chairman
Mandal Commission: The first Commission to recommend 27% reservation — B. P. Mandal, the first Mandal Commission Chairman

National Commission for Scheduled Castes: Established under Article 338 — constitutional status under the 65th Amendment; the first (separate) NCSC — 2004
National Commission for Scheduled Tribes: The first (separate) — 2004

Tilka Manjhi: The first tribal freedom fighter against the British

7th Constitutional Amendment of 1956: The first Constitutional Amendment addressing regional imbalance indirectly
G. S. Ghurye: The first sociologist to study ethnicity and culture in India
## 5. Minorities and integration

Articles 29 and 30: The first Constitutional provisions for minority rights; Article 30 — the first Minority Educational Rights provision
Prime Minister's New 15-Point Programme for Minorities: First introduced 1983
Sachar Committee: The first national data-based committee on minorities — 2005
Ranganath Misra Commission: The first Commission on Religious and Linguistic Minorities — 2004
Communal Award: The first Communal Award — 1932
National Integration Council: First established 1961 — first Chairman: Jawaharlal Nehru
National Foundation for Communal Harmony: First established 1992
Article 51A(e): The first Constitutional Duty promoting harmony
National Human Rights Commission: First established 1993
Right to Equality: The first Fundamental Right enforced

t: Firsts — children, youth, disability and welfare policy

First | Year

MGNREGA — the first rights-based welfare legislation | 2005
Public Distribution System: The first Food Security Programme

text:
## 1. Scheduled Castes
Scheduled Castes are a target group of welfare mechanisms — nodal ministry for all three schemes: Social Justice and Empowerment
Scheme | Key facts
PM-AJAY — Pradhan Mantri Anusuchit Jaati Abhyuday Yojana | Merges the Adarsh Gram scheme, the Special Central Assistance to Scheduled Caste Sub Plan scheme and the Babu Jagjivan Ram Chhatrawas Yojana; supports village development, socio-economic infrastructure and hostels

Scheduled Tribes are a target group of welfare mechanisms
Scheme | Nodal ministry | Key facts

text:

t: GDP, GNP and national income aggregates
text:
## 1. GDP
GDP: The value of final goods and services produced within domestic territory
Gross: Before deducting depreciation
Domestic production: Within the country irrespective of nationality
## 2. GNP
Gross National Product (GNP): The total monetary value of final goods and services produced by the normal residents of a country during a given period
Includes production occurring inside and outside the country's boundaries
⚠ GDP is not equal to GNP — GNP considers nationality or factor income
## 3. GDP vs GNP
Basis | GDP | GNP
Based on | The domestic territory of a country | The normal residents or nationals of a country
Measures | Production within the country | Production by residents within the country and outside the country
Nature | Location-based | Residence-based
## 4. Formulae
Aggregate | Formula
NDP | GDP minus (subtracting) depreciation
GNP | GDP plus (adding) Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA); also NNP plus depreciation
NNP — Net National Product | NDP plus NFIA; also GNP minus depreciation
NNP at market price | GNP at market price minus depreciation
National Income | NNP at factor cost = GNP at market price minus depreciation minus indirect taxes plus subsidies
## 5. Nominal vs real
Nominal GDP: Measured at current-year prices
Real GDP: Measured at constant or base-year prices — base-year prices are used to calculate it; real GDP growth is a better indicator of actual output growth

t: Growth vs development
text:
## 1. Concepts
Economic growth: A quantitative increase in output — GDP measures economic growth
Economic development: A broader qualitative and structural improvement — ⚠ GDP alone is not sufficient to measure it
HDI includes life expectancy, education and income
## 2. Trap — real GNP and development
An increase in absolute real GNP — or in per-capita real GNP — does not necessarily mean higher economic development
Rising poverty or rising unemployment can prevent an increase in real GNP from indicating higher economic development

t: National Statistical Office and IIP
text:
## 1. NSO
NSO: National Statistical Office — functions under the Ministry of Statistics & Programme Implementation (MoSPI)
Created 2019 — formed by merging the Central Statistical Office (CSO) and the National Sample Survey Office (NSSO)
Main role: Collection, compilation and dissemination of official statistics
## 2. Functions
Estimates and releases National Income — National Income estimates include GDP, GNI, NNI, Per Capita Income and other National Accounts estimates
Computes and releases the Index of Industrial Production (IIP)
Compiles Energy Statistics and labour and employment statistics; conducts statistical surveys
## 3. IIP
Released monthly
Covers the mining, manufacturing and electricity sectors

t: Gross Value Added
text:
## 1. GVA
Gross Value Added (GVA): Measures the value added by producers and by sectors to the economy — a production-side measure
GDP: A broader measure of domestic production after accounting for net taxes on products
Real GVA: Calculated at constant prices using a base year — the base year removes the effect of price changes
Nominal GVA: Calculated at current prices
## 2. GVA sectors
Sector group | Components
Agriculture and allied activities | Agriculture, livestock, forestry, fishing
Industry | Mining and quarrying; manufacturing; electricity, gas, water supply and other utilities; construction
Services | Trade, hotels, transport and communication; financial, real estate and professional services; public administration, defence and other services

t: Economic sectors
text:
## 1. Primary, secondary and tertiary
Sector | Nature | Major activities / examples
Primary | Directly uses or extracts natural resources | Agriculture, forestry, fishing, dairy (dairy farming), mining; mineral exploration — classified as primary in the source's classification
Secondary | Converts raw materials or natural products into finished or other forms | Manufacturing (textile manufacturing), processing (raw materials), weaving (cloth), industrial activity, construction, electricity, gas, water and utilities
Tertiary | Provides services rather than producing physical goods | Transport, communication, trade (commerce), banking, education, health, administration, hotels, finance, real estate, professional services, marketing, social work, business services, personal services
Disguised unemployment: Mainly associated with the primary sector or agriculture
## 2. Other classifications
Public sector: Government ownership or control; private sector: private ownership or control
Mixed economy: The coexistence of public and private sectors
## 3. Real vs financial sector
Basis | Real sector | Financial sector
Involves | The production of goods and services; the purchase or flow of goods and services; physical economic activity | Financial transactions; money and financial assets
Parts | Agriculture, manufacturing | Banking, lending, bonds and securities
Example | A farmer harvesting crops | A bank lending money

topic: Economic development, HDI and inclusive growth
t: Human development, HDI and MPI
text:
## 1. Human development approach
Focuses on people, opportunities and choices
Developed by Mahbub-ul-Haq; Amartya Sen provided the intellectual foundation through the capability approach
First Human Development Report: Published 1990 — by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)
## 2. GDP vs human development
Basis | GDP or per-capita income | Human development
Nature | Primarily an economic measure | A broader, people-centred approach
Focus | Income and output | Capabilities and well-being
Dimensions | A one-dimensional income measure | Multidimensional
## 3. HDI vs MPI
Basis | Human Development Index (HDI) | Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI)
Measures | Human development | Multidimensional poverty
Considers | Health, education and standard of living | Health, education and living standards
Associated with | The UNDP; the Human Development Report (HDR) | OPHI and UNDP — first included in the Human Development Report in 2010

topic: Economic development, HDI and inclusive growth
t: Inclusive growth and governance
text:
## 1. Requirements of inclusive growth
Requirement | Why
Infrastructure development | Expands access and economic opportunities
Agricultural development or revival | Benefits the rural population
Education | Improves capabilities
Health | Improves human capital
Employment opportunities | Enable participation in growth
Access to credit | Enables productive activity
SHGs | Enable financial and economic participation
MSMEs | Provide employment and entrepreneurship
Right to Education | Brings disadvantaged children into the mainstream
## 2. Inclusive growth vs inclusive governance
Basis | Inclusive growth | Inclusive governance
Involves | Economic development | Governance and service delivery
Provides | Shared economic benefits | Ensures equal access to government facilities
Aim | Reduces poverty and inequality | Promotes participation and inclusion
Includes | Employment, credit and infrastructure | Public health, planning and welfare services

t: Origins of planning and early policy
text:
## 1. Plans before the First Five Year Plan
Plan | Year

First Five Year Plan: Started — began — on 1 April 1951; period 1951–56 — the first planned-development model was adopted on 1 April 1951

## 3. Industrial policy
First Industrial Policy of independent India: 1948 — announced by Dr. Shyama Prasad Mukherjee
Second Industrial Policy Resolution: 1956 — introduced the Joint Sector concept
Liberalisation began in 1991 — the New Economic Policy introduced liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation

The cottage industry was the first industry to develop in India

t: Planning Commission and NITI Aayog
text:
## 1. Planning Commission
Established on March 15, 1950 — created by a Cabinet Resolution
Non-constitutional and non-statutory in nature; an advisory body — characterized as a quasi-political body
## 2. Planning Commission vs Finance Commission
Basis | Planning Commission | Finance Commission
Nature | Non-constitutional | Constitutional — Article 280 of the Constitution
Dealt with | Planning and resource allocation | Tax devolution and grants
Old framework | Plan resources | Non-Plan resources
Permanence | A permanent body | Constituted periodically
## 3. NITI Aayog
NITI: National Institution for Transforming India
Established on January 1, 2015 through a (Union) Cabinet Resolution — replaced the Planning Commission
A public policy think tank — a policy think tank
Chairperson: The Prime Minister; first Vice-Chairman: Arvind Panagariya
Core approach / model: Cooperative federalism and a bottom-up approach — promotes greater involvement of States in policy-making
## 4. Governing Council
Brings together the Prime Minister, Chief Ministers and Union Territory leadership — Chairperson: the Prime Minister
Includes:
The Chief Ministers of all States
The Chief Ministers of Union Territories with legislatures — Delhi and Puducherry
The Lieutenant Governors of other Union Territories
A Vice-Chairperson; full-time members; ex-officio members; special invitees
## 5. DMEO
DMEO: Development, Monitoring and Evaluation Office — established on September 18, 2015
An attached office of NITI Aayog
Created by merging the Programme Evaluation Organization and the Independent Evaluation Office
Monitors and evaluates the implementation of government programmes and initiatives

topic: Economic reforms, industrial policy and CPSEs
t: The 1991 reforms — LPG
text:
## 1. Background
The 1991 New Economic Policy was introduced to address the severe 1991 Balance of Payments crisis
LPG model: Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation — the New Industrial Policy was associated with LPG; LPG reforms were associated with multinational corporations
## 2. Stabilisation vs structural adjustment
Basis | Stabilisation | Structural Adjustment
Term | Short-term — strictly short-term | Long-term
Nature | Demand-side | Supply-side
Addresses | Inflation and macroeconomic imbalances | Industrial, trade, financial and investment structures
## 3. Liberalisation vs globalisation
Liberalisation | Globalisation
Removes or reduces domestic controls — reduces restrictions; focuses on removing state controls | Integrates the domestic economy with the world economy
De-licensing | Associated: international trade
Deregulation | Associated: foreign investment
Import liberalisation | Associated: multinational corporation participation
Promotes greater market orientation | Promotes greater global integration; facilitates technology flows
## 4. Liberalisation
Instruments: Industrial de-licensing; import deregulation; a decrease in import duty on capital goods
Private-sector expansion is an aspect of Liberalisation
New Industrial Policy — announced on 24 July 1991 — the primary starting anchor of Liberalisation
Instruments lower the cost of technology and capital equipment — this boosts domestic manufacturing competitiveness
## 5. Globalisation
Involves the reduction of import duties on capital goods
Facilitates expanded entry and participation of Multinational Corporations
Occurs through trade, foreign direct investment capital and cross-border technology
Free trade: The reduction or removal of trade barriers
## 6. Outcomes after 1991
Foreign Direct Investment inflows increased; foreign-exchange reserves expanded; India's share in global exports grew
⚠ Agriculture's share in GDP did not increase enormously — it declined after the 1991 reforms

topic: Economic reforms, industrial policy and CPSEs
t: Industrial policy and SEZ policy
text:
## 1. Milestones
Year | Policy | Key feature
1948 | Industrial Policy Resolution | Associated with a mixed economic model
1951 | Industrial Development and Regulation Act | Established the licensing framework — introduced industrial licensing
1956 | Industrial Policy Resolution | Promoted industrialisation, the public sector and the joint sector — established public-sector and joint-sector dominance
1991 | New Industrial Policy — the Liberal Industrial Policy (July 24, 1991) | Associated with liberalisation — massive de-licensing and deregulation
2000 | Special Economic Zone Policy — announced on 1 April 2000 (April 1, 2000) | Under the Globalisation framework
## 2. SEZ Policy objectives
Primary objective: Boost export competitiveness — promote exports; export promotion
Attract foreign direct investment — foreign investment
Create — provide — an internationally competitive trade environment
Create a level playing field for exports
## 3. Fiscal policy
Includes taxation, expenditure and public debt
Objectives: Growth, employment, price stability and equity
V. P. Singh: Associated with the Long-Term Fiscal Policy of 1985–86

topic: Economic reforms, industrial policy and CPSEs
t: Capital productivity, growth and corridors
text:
## 1. Capital Output Ratio (COR)
Basis | High COR | Low COR
Meaning | More capital is needed for each unit of output — investment produces relatively less output | A given amount of capital produces greater output
Capital productivity | Lower | Higher
⚠ High COR combined with high savings may still result in slow output growth
## 2. Hindu Rate of Growth
Coined by economist Raj Krishna
Refers to India's slow rate of growth of national income or GDP — around 3.5%
Associated with the period from the 1950s to the early 1980s — the relatively slow growth of the pre-reform planning era
## 3. Corridors and zones
Industrial corridor: Combines industrial development with connectivity
Economic corridor: Connectivity that facilitates the movement of goods, services and economic activity
Dedicated Freight Corridor: Dedicated railway freight transportation infrastructure
National Investment and Manufacturing Zone (NIMZ): A large developed area with an ecosystem for world-class manufacturing
Instruments of the National Manufacturing Policy, 2011 — envisaged as large areas of developed land with the required ecosystem

topic: Economic reforms, industrial policy and CPSEs
t: Navratna and Maharatna CPSEs
text:
## 1. CPSE categories
CPSEs are classified as Miniratna, Navratna and Maharatna
Categorisation is based on factors such as turnover, net worth and net profit
## 2. Navratna
Associated with selected Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs)
The Navratna scheme: Introduced 1997 — initially covered 9 CPSEs (the key PYQ association: 9 CPSEs were initially selected)
Main purpose: Give selected CPSEs greater autonomy and powers; objective — to compete more effectively in the global market
Examples: Bharat Electronics Ltd. (BEL), NALCO, MTNL, RINL
## 3. Maharatna
A status or category given to selected Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) — introduced (originated) in 2010
Administered by the Department of Public Enterprises (DPE)
Purpose: Greater autonomy, greater financial and managerial powers to large, high-performing CPSEs — still greater autonomy and power to expand
Introduced to give greater autonomy to selected Navratna CPSEs and enable them to compete globally
Factors in categorisation: Turnover, net worth, net profit
Maharatna CPSEs:
BHEL — received Maharatna status in 2013
GAIL, Coal India Ltd., Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. (IOCL), NTPC, SAIL, ONGC
BPCL, HPCL, Power Grid Corporation, Power Finance Corporation, REC
Oil India Ltd. — later upgraded from Navratna to Maharatna; HAL — later upgraded to Maharatna

## 1. Committees
Committee | Chaired by | Focus

t: Minimum Support Price and CACP
text:
## 1. MSP
MSP: Minimum Support Price — a government-announced minimum price for selected agricultural commodities
Purpose: Protect farmers against a sharp fall in market prices
A market intervention by the government — a price support mechanism; provides a remunerative and stable price environment
MSP-based procurement helps build food stocks, which support the Public Distribution System (PDS)
MSP chain: MSP promotes price stability → price stability protects farmer income → farmer income protection creates a production incentive → production incentives support food security
## 2. APC to CACP
Agricultural Prices Commission (APC): Established 1965 (January 1965) — renamed the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP)
CACP recommends MSP; the Government of India fixes MSP
Main objective of the CACP: Incentivise farmers
Incentivising farmers promotes the adoption of modern technology → modern technology increases productivity → increased productivity leads to increased production
## 3. MSP vs FRP
Basis | MSP | FRP — Fair & Remunerative Price
Applies to | MSP commodities | Sugarcane
Recommended by | CACP | CACP
Fixed / approved by | The government | The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA)
## 4. Cost concepts
Concept | Meaning
A2 | The actual paid-out costs incurred by the farmer
FL | The imputed value of family labour
A2 + FL | Paid-out cost plus family labour
C2 | A2 + FL + land rent + fixed capital costs and other costs

t: Unemployment — measures and types
text:
## 1. Measures of unemployment
Measure | Reference period
Usual Status (US) | 1 year or 365 days
Current Weekly Status (CWS) | 1 week
Current Daily Status (CDS) | Each day of the reference week
## 2. Employment elasticity
High: Growth generates relatively more employment; low: growth generates relatively less employment
## 3. Types of unemployment
Type | Cause | Nature | Example
Frictional | Transitions between jobs | Voluntary, short-term — a normal part of labour churn | A recent graduate searching for a first job
Structural | A mismatch of skills or geography | Long-term — driven by technology or industry shifts | Factory workers displaced by industrial automation
Cyclical | A deficiency in aggregate demand | Directly tied to business cycles — recessions and downturns | Layoffs across sectors during an economic recession
Seasonal | Predictable demand shifts by season | Annual, periodic and anticipated fluctuations | Agricultural labourers or resort staff unemployed during the off-season
Disguised | Surplus labour with zero marginal productivity — more workers than required | Employed on paper — output remains unchanged if they are removed | Five family members working on a farm plot that needs only two workers
Underemployment | Underutilization of worker capacity | Working below one's skill level or involuntary part-time work | An engineer working part-time as a cashier
Institutional | Regulatory and policy barriers | Arises from labour laws, high minimum wages or union rules | Employers halting hiring because of rigid layoff regulations
Vulnerable | A lack of formal contracts and social security — daily-wage work | High job insecurity — common in informal sectors | Construction labour or unorganized street vending

t: Labour concepts and P-Notes
text:
## 1. Labour and work concepts
WPR: Employed population divided by total population
LFPR: The labour force divided by the working-age population
Gig economy work: Task- or assignment-based
Platform economy: Uses a digital platform to connect participants
Marketplace model: A platform to connect buyers and sellers; inventory model: an entity owning or controlling inventory
Casual worker: Non-regular or casual employment; fixed-term employment: for a predetermined period
Microfinance: Financial services to low-income groups
Real sector: Goods and services; financial sector: money and financial assets
## 2. P-Notes vs FDI
Basis | Participatory Notes (P-Notes) | Foreign direct investment
Exposure | Portfolio-type exposure — linked to Indian securities; enable an overseas investor to obtain market exposure | Direct investment — in an enterprise or business; gives the foreign investor a direct investment
Stability | Relatively more mobile and volatile | Relatively more stable and long-term
Regulation | The ultimate P-Note investor does not directly register with SEBI | Subject to the applicable FDI framework

t: Reserve Bank of India — structure and functions
text:
## 1. Basics
RBI: Reserve Bank of India — the central bank of India; a statutory body
RBI Act: 1934; established on 1 April 1935
Nationalised: 1949 — fully owned by the Government of India after nationalisation
Headquarters: Original — Kolkata; permanent — Mumbai, since 1937
## 2. Functions
Currency issue: Issues currency notes except the ₹1 note
Banker to banks:
Commercial banks keep deposits and reserves with the RBI
Lends to banks when required; advises banks on monetary matters
Lender of Last Resort — provides emergency liquidity to banks
Banker to the Government — of India (the Central Government) and State Governments:
Conducts banking transactions for the government
Manages public debt — government borrowing and public debt
Advises the government on monetary and financial matters
Acts as the government's agent for India's IMF membership
Monetary policy: Responsible for conducting monetary policy — controls credit; controls money and credit through monetary policy
Others: Manages foreign exchange reserves; regulates and supervises the banking system; oversees payment and settlement systems; supports financial and economic development
## 3. Who issues what
Item | Issued by
₹1 note | The Government of India, through the Ministry of Finance
Other currency notes | The Reserve Bank of India
Coins | The Government of India

t: Monetary policy instruments
text:
## 1. Instruments at a glance
Instrument | Meaning
Bank Rate | The RBI's lending or discount rate — a traditional rate associated with RBI lending or rediscounting; involves bills of exchange or commercial paper
Repo Rate | Lending by the RBI to banks against securities — the rate at which the RBI lends to banks
Reverse Repo | Enables the RBI to absorb liquidity from banks — the rate at which the RBI borrows from banks
CRR — Cash Reserve Ratio | A cash reserve maintained with the RBI
SLR — Statutory Liquidity Ratio | Liquid assets maintained by banks themselves
OMO | The RBI buying or selling government securities
MSF | An emergency overnight borrowing facility
Monetary policy instruments: Repo Rate, Reverse Repo Rate, Bank Rate, Cash Reserve Ratio, Statutory Liquidity Ratio — ⚠ fiscal deficit is associated with fiscal policy
## 2. Repo vs reverse repo
Basis | Repo Rate | Reverse Repo Rate
Use | Liquidity injection; regulate money supply | Liquidity absorption — absorb surplus liquidity
Mechanism | A bank borrows from the RBI | A bank parks money with the RBI
## 3. Repo vs Bank Rate
Basis | Repo Rate | Bank Rate
Nature | Short-term lending by the RBI | A traditional rate
Against | Eligible securities | Bills of exchange or commercial paper
Use | Liquidity management | Monetary policy
Associated with | Repo transactions | Bank lending or rediscounting
## 4. MSF vs repo
Basis | Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) | Repo
Nature | An overnight borrowing facility | A short-term borrowing mechanism
Borrower | Banks borrow from the RBI | Banks borrow from the RBI
Use | Marginal or short-term liquidity needs | Regular liquidity management
Collateral | Can involve dipping into the Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) portfolio | Against eligible securities
Cost | ⚠ Traditionally a higher cost than the repo rate | Principal policy lending rate in the source framework
## 5. Bank rate and stance
Lower bank rate: Borrowing cheaper; expands liquidity — an expansionary stance
Higher bank rate: Borrowing costlier; contracts liquidity — a tight stance
Central bank policy rates directly regulate the capacity for credit creation

t: CRR and SLR
text:
## 1. CRR vs SLR
Basis | CRR | SLR
Kept | Deposited with the RBI — an RBI-held reserve | Maintained by the bank itself — not deposited with the RBI; the bank's own holdings
Form | Only cash | Cash, gold and approved securities or other liquid assets
Returns | Do not earn interest | Can earn returns
Role | Controls liquidity and credit — regulates credit and liquidity | Controls liquidity; a liquidity buffer — regulates credit and liquidity
## 2. SLR in detail
The minimum percentage of Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL) that commercial banks must maintain in liquid assets before lending
Eligible assets: Liquid cash, gold and other unencumbered approved securities
Government securities are commonly used — most commonly held in Government Securities (G-Secs), which earn interest income while meeting SLR requirements
## 3. Changing the SLR
Basis | SLR increase | SLR decrease
Funds | Banks lock a higher percentage of funds in liquid assets — reduces investible loan funds | Banks hold fewer funds in mandatory liquid assets — frees up capital for loans; expands lending capacity
Credit creation | Decreases | Increases
Effect | Money supply contracts; controls inflationary pressures | Stimulates broader economic activity
Raising the SLR: A direct contractionary quantitative credit control tool — the central bank uses a higher SLR during inflation; it reins in excessive commercial bank credit growth
An increase in the cash reserve ratio decreases credit creation

t: Money supply
text:
## 1. M1 and M3
M1 — narrow money: Currency with the public + demand deposits + other deposits with the RBI
High liquidity — directly spendable transaction money
M3 — broad money: M1 plus time deposits with banks — the most commonly used measure of broad aggregate money supply
M3 minus M1 equals time deposits with banks
## 2. Components
Component | In M1 | In M3 | Nature
Currency with the public | Included | Included | Immediate cash in hand
Demand deposits with banks | Included | Included | Can be withdrawn instantly on demand
Other deposits with the RBI | Included | Included | Highly liquid balances
Time deposits with banks | ⚠ Not included — excluded | Included | Locked for a fixed period — the least liquid deposits
## 3. Liquidity
Liquidity order: Currency, savings deposits, demand deposits, time deposits
Cash: The most liquid form of money; fixed or time deposits: the least liquid
## 4. Withdrawal and the multiplier
⚠ A cash withdrawal does not change the aggregate money supply — withdrawing ₹1 lakh from demand deposits reduces demand deposits by ₹1 lakh and increases currency with the public by ₹1 lakh
Money multiplier: Total money supply divided by base money — expressed as M3 divided by M0
An increase in banking habits increases the money multiplier

t: Basel norms
text:
## 1. Basel Committee
Originally named the Committee on Banking Regulations and Supervisory Practices — established at the end of 1974
Background: International currency and banking disturbances; the failure of Bankhaus Herstatt was an important trigger
Secretariat and headquarters: At the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) in Basel
Purpose: Improve banking supervision; promote financial stability
## 2. Basel accords
Accord | Year | Key associations

## 3. Growth vs development

Concept | Quantitative | Broader and normative

Associated with | Mainly production and income — measures: GDP and GNP growth | Overall socio-economic well-being — health, education, employment and poverty reduction

t: Financial inclusion and FSDC
text:
## 1. Financial inclusion
Extends financial services to the poor population; expands banking infrastructure in underserved and rural areas
Provides access to credit for weaker sections
Promotes financial literacy through awareness and informed use
Facilitates payments and remittances through the formal financial system
Promotes access to insurance for financial security
## 2. Inclusion vs exclusion
Financial inclusion | Financial exclusion
Access to formal financial services | A lack of access to formal financial services
Access to a bank account | No or limited banking access
Access to credit | Credit constraints
Access to insurance | A lack of insurance access
Payments and remittances | Limited payment facilities
Financial literacy | A lack of awareness
## 3. Committee on Financial Inclusion
Chairman: Dr. C. Rangarajan — constituted on 26 June 2006; final report on 4 January 2008
Focus: A strategy for financial inclusion
## 4. Small Financing Banks
Provide credit to small business units, small and marginal farmers and entrepreneurs, particularly in rural areas
## 5. Financial Stability and Development Council
An apex-level forum for financial stability and development — chairman: the Union Finance Minister
Members: Include financial-sector regulators
Role: Macroprudential supervision; also financial literacy and financial inclusion

t: Inflation — concepts and types
text:
## 1. Basics
Inflation: An increase in the general price level — decreases the purchasing power of money
Deflation: A decrease in the price level; ⚠ disinflation: a decrease in the inflation rate
## 2. Headline vs core inflation
Basis | Headline inflation | Core inflation
Represents | Total inflation | The underlying inflation trend
Food | Includes food | Excludes volatile food
Fuel and energy | Includes fuel and energy — food and energy | Excludes volatile fuel and energy — food and fuel
Stability | More volatile | Relatively more stable
## 3. Types
Type | Cause
Demand-pull | Demand increases
Cost-push | Production costs increase
Bottleneck | A supply constraint
Stagflation | Combines inflation, slow growth and unemployment
## 4. Policy links
A decrease in the Bank Rate increases liquidity; an increase is contractionary
OMO: A monetary policy instrument; ⚠ public revenue is associated with fiscal policy

t: The Budget and its accounts
text:
## 1. Constitutional basis
Article 112: The estimated receipts and estimated expenditure of the Government of India for every financial year are laid before both Houses of Parliament
Annual Financial Statement: The main Budget document
Gender budgeting: Introduced in the Union Budget of 2005–06
## 2. Revenue vs Capital Account
Item | Account
Tax receipts | Revenue Account
Interest receipts | Revenue Account
Dividends and profits | Revenue Account
Revenue expenditure | Revenue Account — does not create a liability
Borrowings | Capital Account
Disinvestment | Capital Account
Recovery of loans | Capital Account
Asset creation expenditure | Capital Account — may create a liability or reduce assets
## 3. Capital Budget
Capital receipts and capital payments
Capital receipts: Market borrowings, Treasury Bills, foreign loans
Capital payments: Acquisition of land, buildings and machinery; investments in shares; loans and advances to States, Union Territories and others

t: Revenue and capital receipts
text:
## 1. The test
Basis | Revenue receipts | Capital receipts
Liability | Do not create a liability — create no new liability | Create a liability
Assets | Do not reduce government assets | Or reduce (financial) assets
A revenue receipt neither creates a liability nor reduces assets; a capital receipt creates a liability or reduces assets
Borrowings create a liability; disinvestment reduces assets
## 2. Revenue receipts
Consist of tax revenue and non-tax revenue
Tax revenue: Income tax, corporation tax, customs duties, union excise duties, GST
Non-tax revenue: Interest receipts; dividends and profits from public (government) enterprises; fees and other receipts
## 3. Capital receipts
Borrowings — market borrowings; disinvestment; recovery of loans; foreign loans — loans from the World Bank; Treasury Bills
## 4. Capital-Output Ratio
COR: The capital required to produce one unit of output
Decrease: Increases the productivity of capital and growth potential
Increase: More capital is needed per unit of output — growth may be slower

t: Revenue and capital expenditure
text:
## 1. Revenue expenditure
Does not create assets
Includes: Salaries (and allowances), pensions, subsidies, interest payments, administrative expenses
## 2. Capital expenditure
Directed toward acquiring, creating, upgrading and extending the life of assets — asset creation or acquisition
Strengthens long-term productive capacity — long-term productive investment
Examples: Land, buildings (land and buildings), equipment, computers, software, new technology, infrastructure or asset creation
## 3. Non-plan expenditure
Includes: Subsidies, interest payments, defence services, maintenance of infrastructure, salaries, pensions, statutory transfers

t: FRBM Act and deficits
text:
## 1. FRBM Act
Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act (FRBM Act) — enacted in August 2003; effective on 5 July 2004
Aim: Fiscal discipline and fiscal prudence
Main focus: Reduce the fiscal deficit, the revenue deficit and public debt
Objectives:
Deficit reduction; debt management
Discipline in public finances; transparency in fiscal operations
Improving the management of public funds; strengthening fiscal prudence
Improving macroeconomic management; moving towards a balanced budget
## 2. Deficits
Deficit | Formula
Revenue deficit | Revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts
Fiscal deficit | Total expenditure minus total non-debt receipts
Primary deficit | Fiscal deficit minus interest payments
## 3. FRBM Review Committee
The N.K. Singh Committee — chairman N.K. Singh; formed in May 2016; report in January 2017
Key recommendation: Limit combined Centre and State debt to 60% of GDP — Centre 40%; States 20%

t: Types of taxes
text:
## 1. By rate structure
Tax | Feature
Progressive | The average tax burden increases with income
Regressive | The relative burden tends to be higher on lower-income groups
Proportional | The same tax rate regardless of income level
Degressive | The rate initially rises with income and then becomes flat
## 2. Direct vs indirect taxes
Basis | Direct tax | Indirect tax
Burden | Cannot be shifted to another person — incidence and impact fall on the same taxpayer | Can be shifted to another person — generally through prices
Examples | Income Tax, Corporation Tax, Wealth Tax, Capital Gains Tax, Property Tax, Gift Tax | Customs Duty, Excise Duty, Service Tax, Sales Tax, VAT, GST
## 3. Taxes and their base
Tax | Associated with
Income Tax | Income
Corporation Tax | Company income or profit
Capital Gains Tax | Gains from the sale of a capital asset
Wealth Tax — a historical tax | Wealth
Customs Duty | The import or export of goods
Excise Duty | The production, sale or licensing of specified goods
GST | Goods and services
VAT | Value added at stages
Service Tax — a historical indirect tax | Services

t: Goods and Services Tax
text:
## 1. Basics
GST: Goods and Services Tax — an indirect tax; a multi-stage, destination-based tax
Introduced through the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016; implemented on 1 July 2017
Basic principle: Taxation on the supply of goods and services
Major objectives: A common or unified national market; reduce cascading of taxes
Destination principle: Revenue ultimately accrues to the jurisdiction where goods or services are consumed — ⚠ not where they are produced
## 2. Components
Component | Full form | Administered by
CGST | Central Goods and Services Tax | The Centre — administers and collects
SGST | State Goods and Services Tax | States
IGST | Integrated Goods and Services Tax | The Centre — administers and collects
UTGST | Union Territory Goods and Services Tax | —
## 3. Taxes subsumed
Central Excise Duty, Service Tax, State VAT and various other Central and State indirect taxes
## 4. Revenue Neutral Rate
RNR: Revenue Neutral Rate — a rate or structure intended to generate approximately the same revenue under GST as under the earlier tax system
Its calculation is subject to the assumptions used

## 1. GST Council
A constitutional body — Article 279A
Chairperson: The Union Finance Minister
Members: The Union Minister of State in charge of Revenue or Finance; the Minister in charge of Finance or Taxation from each State
Makes recommendations on tax rates, exemptions, threshold limits and other GST-related matters
Legislative powers: Parliament and State Legislatures have GST legislative powers; the GST Council makes recommendations
## 2. Articles

t: Public debt
text:
## 1. Concepts
Debt: An amount borrowed that creates an obligation to repay
Public debt: Government borrowings or liabilities — classified into internal debt and external debt
## 2. Internal vs external debt
Basis | Internal debt | External debt
Meaning | Raised within the domestic economy | Raised from external or foreign sources
Creditors | Domestic lenders, institutions or investors | Foreign creditors or institutions
Currency | Generally domestic currency | May involve foreign currency or foreign-denominated obligations
Major conceptual instruments | G-Secs, T-Bills and others | External assistance and foreign borrowings
Key idea | Domestic borrowing | Foreign borrowing
## 3. Securities
Government dated securities — G-Secs: Long-term government securities
Treasury bills: Short-term government debt instruments
Market-based securities: Issued through auctions

t: Treasury Bills and government securities
text:
## 1. Types
Security | Issued by | Maturity
Treasury Bills | The Central Government | Short-term — less than one year
Government Bonds or Dated Securities | The Central Government | Long-term — at least one year
State Development Loans | State Governments — state government bonds or dated securities | —
## 2. Treasury Bills
Short-term debt instruments — money-market instruments
Zero-coupon securities — do not pay periodic interest; issued at a discount to face value and redeemed at face value on maturity
Tenors: 91 days, 182 days, 364 days
Sold by the Reserve Bank of India through auction
First issued in India in 1917
## 3. Government Bonds
Maturity of at least one year; interest-bearing securities
Issued by the Central Government or State Governments
Returns through coupon payments and principal repayment

t: Bonds — key terms
text:
## 1. Terms
Term | Meaning
Bond | A debt instrument through which the issuer borrows money from investors
Bondholder | A creditor or lender to the issuer — receives interest or returns according to the bond's terms
Issuer | A government, company or other eligible entity raising funds
Maturity | The date when the principal or face value becomes repayable
Face value / par value | The nominal value of a bond
Coupon / interest | The stated interest payment on a bond
Yield | The return earned by an investor
⚠ Market yield and bond price generally move in opposite directions

t: Government funds
text:
## 1. The three funds
Fund | Nature
Consolidated Fund of India | The main government account — the main government fund; credited with government revenues, loans raised by the government and loan recoveries
Contingency Fund of India | Urgent and unforeseen expenditure
Public Account of India | Holds money in trust for the government — a government-held trust or liability account; the government is liable to repay or use the money according to applicable rules
The State Provident Fund is part of the Public Account
## 2. National Investment Fund
Established in November 2005 — receives and channelises proceeds from the disinvestment of Central Public Sector Enterprises
Corpus intended to be permanent; professionally managed
Government objective: Generate returns without depleting its corpus
Classified under the Public Account
## 3. Rural Infrastructure Development Fund
RIDF — created in 1995–96; associated with and administered by NABARD
Initial corpus: ₹2,000 crore
Broad areas: Agriculture and related sectors; the social sector; rural connectivity
Examples: Rural roads, rural water supply, rural electrification
## 4. Other funds and regulators
Mutual funds: Regulated by SEBI
Pension funds and NPS: Associated with PFRDA
Provident fund: Contractual retirement savings

t: SEBI
text:
## 1. Basics
SEBI: Securities and Exchange Board of India — the stock exchange regulator in India
Initially established in 1988 as a non-statutory body; statutory status on 12 April 1992 under the SEBI Act, 1992 — its parent law
Headquarters: Mumbai
## 2. Purpose and objectives
Core purposes / main objectives: Investor protection — protect investors; promote, develop and regulate the securities market
## 3. Functions
Regulates stock exchange operations
Regulates and monitors mutual funds
Prevents irregularities and scams in the capital market
Regulates the primary and secondary markets — secondary market institutions: stock exchanges, brokers, depositories
Regulates credit rating agencies

t: Primary and secondary markets
text:
## 1. Comparison
Basis | Primary market | Secondary market
Deals in | New securities | Existing securities
Transactions | From companies to investors | Between investors
Examples | IPOs, FPOs, rights issues | Stock-exchange trading
## 2. Stock exchanges
A stock exchange: An organized market for trading securities and shares — part of the securities market and the capital market
Government securities can be traded through securities-market platforms

t: Stock exchanges and indices
text:
## 1. National Stock Exchange
Established in November 1992 on the recommendation of the Manohar J. Pherwani Committee — headquarters Mumbai
Recognized by SEBI in April 1993; began operations in 1994
First segment: The Wholesale Debt Market; the Cash Market was subsequently launched
Original promoters: IDBI, SBI, IFCI, LIC, GIC, IDFC
## 2. Bombay Stock Exchange
BSE: Bombay Stock Exchange — moved to Dalal Street (Mumbai) in 1874; Dalal Street is associated with the BSE and the share market
Sensex: A popular index of the BSE — a free-float market-capitalization-weighted index
Represents the overall movement of the selected 30 companies
A rise in Sensex indicates an overall rise in the prices of the group of 30 companies — ⚠ not a rise in the prices of all BSE shares
CDSL: A depository — initially promoted by BSE
## 3. Market terms
Bull, Bear, Stag and Lame Duck: Associated with the share market
Bull: Expects prices to rise — a bull market has generally rising prices
Bear: Expects prices to fall — a bear market has generally declining prices
Blue-chip shares: Large, well-established, financially sound companies
Beta: Measures a security's fluctuations — systematic risk — relative to the overall market
STT: Securities Transaction Tax — applies to specified securities transactions on domestic exchanges

t: Mutual funds and financial regulators
text:
## 1. Mutual fund milestones
Year | Milestone
1964 | UTI established
1987 | Non-UTI public-sector mutual funds established
1993 | Private-sector mutual funds permitted; the first SEBI Mutual Funds Regulations
1996 | The revised SEBI Mutual Funds Regulations
## 2. Regulators and institutions
Body | Associated with
SEBI | The capital and securities market
RBI | The money and banking system
NABARD | Agricultural credit
SIDBI | Small-scale and MSME finance
IRDAI | The insurance sector
PFRDA | The pension sector
Forward Markets Commission: The regulator of commodity futures markets — established 1953; merged with SEBI in 2015
## 3. Alternative Investment Funds
Venture capital funds: Category I
Hedge funds: Category III

t: National Payments Corporation of India
text:
## 1. Basics
NPCI: National Payments Corporation of India — incorporated in December 2008
A not-for-profit company — incorporated as a Section 25 company under the Companies Act, 1956
Section 8 of the Companies Act, 2013 corresponds to Section 25 of the Companies Act, 1956
An initiative of the Reserve Bank of India and the Indian Banks' Association
RBI: The central bank and regulator; IBA: a banking-industry association
Operates under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007
The umbrella organisation for retail payment and settlement systems — a payment-system infrastructure and operations organisation
## 2. NPCI products
Product | Purpose
UPI | Instant account-to-account payments
IMPS | Immediate interbank electronic fund transfers
RuPay | A domestic card-payment network
AePS | Aadhaar-enabled banking transactions
NACH | High-volume recurring electronic transactions
NETC | Electronic toll collection through FASTag
BHIM | A UPI-based payment app
Bharat BillPay | An interoperable bill-payment system
## 3. Milestones
Year | Milestone
2007 | Payment and Settlement Systems Act enacted
2008 | NPCI incorporated
2009 | Authorisation for retail payment systems and NFS operations
2010 | IMPS and AePS introduced
2012 | RuPay launched; NACH implemented
2016 | UPI pilot; BHIM launched; NETC FASTag launched

t: UPI, AePS and financial inclusion
text:
## 1. UPI
Unified Payments Interface — developed by NPCI
An instant payment system — enables bank-to-bank payments using interoperable payment infrastructure
## 2. AePS
Enables basic banking transactions through Aadhaar authentication
Designed to support financial inclusion and interoperable banking
## 3. Payments and inclusion
NPCI's payment infrastructure supports digital payments — digital payments provide wider access, which contributes to financial inclusion
Particularly relevant to AePS, UPI, IMPS, RuPay and NACH

topic: External sector - BoP, forex and exchange rate
t: Balance of Payments
text:
## 1. BoP vs BoT
Basis | Balance of Trade | Balance of Payments
Coverage | Goods only — visible trade; records only goods | All international economic transactions — goods, services, transfers and capital transactions
Formula / scope | Exports of goods minus imports of goods | The broader external account
Place | Part of the Current Account | Current Account and Capital/financial Account transactions
Balance of Payments: A systematic and complete record of all economic transactions between the residents of a country and the rest of the world during a specified period — normally one year
BoT surplus: Goods exports greater than goods imports; BoT deficit: goods imports greater than goods exports
## 2. Current Account
Includes goods, services, income and transfers
Visible trade: Exports and imports of goods
Invisible transactions: Services, transfer payments and net income
Private remittances: Included in the Current Account
Current Account Deficit: Payments exceed receipts — from goods, services, transfers and net income
## 3. Capital Account
Cross-border capital movements — foreign loans, Foreign Direct Investment (FDI), portfolio investment, international purchases and sales of assets
## 4. Convertibility
Current Account Convertibility: Freedom to convert domestic currency into foreign currency — for current international transactions
Capital Account Convertibility: Freedom to conduct investment and financial-asset transactions without capital controls

topic: External sector - BoP, forex and exchange rate
t: Foreign trade
text:
## 1. Basic terms
Exports: Goods and services sold to the rest of the world; imports: purchased from the rest of the world
Net exports: X − M — positive net exports: a trade surplus; negative: a trade deficit
Trade surplus: Exports greater than imports; trade deficit: imports greater than exports
Closed economy: Neither exports nor imports
## 2. Invisible exports
Services are invisible exports — invisible exports mainly consist of services
Examples of services exports: IT/software, tourism, banking, insurance, financial services, advertising
Foreign tourist spending in India is an export of services — an invisible export
## 3. Imports
Major-import hierarchy: Fuel > Petroleum, Oil & Lubricants > Capital Goods > Chemicals > Gold/Silver

topic: External sector - BoP, forex and exchange rate
t: Foreign exchange reserves and SDRs
text:
## 1. Components of India's reserves
Foreign Currency Assets (FCA); gold; Special Drawing Rights (SDRs); the Reserve Tranche Position (RTP) with the IMF
## 2. SDR
Special Drawing Rights — an international reserve asset created by the IMF in 1969 (an IMF-created reserve asset)
Created to supplement member countries' official reserves — known as paper gold
Defined in terms of gold; redefined in terms of a basket of currencies after the collapse of the Bretton Woods System in 1973
## 3. Reserve Tranche Position
A reserve position with the IMF — a member's unconditional drawing position
Historically called the gold tranche

topic: External sector - BoP, forex and exchange rate
t: Exchange rate
text:
## 1. Concepts
Exchange rate: The price or value of one currency expressed in terms of another currency
Flexible or floating exchange rate: The market determines the currency value
## 2. Four terms
Term | System | Meaning
Devaluation | Fixed | An official reduction — an officially reduced currency value
Revaluation | Fixed | An officially increased currency value
Appreciation | Flexible | A market-driven rise in currency value
Depreciation | Flexible | A market-driven fall in currency value
A change from $1 = ₹60 to $1 = ₹58 represents rupee appreciation; a change from $1 = ₹60 to $1 = ₹65 represents rupee depreciation
## 3. Devaluation
Makes the domestic currency cheaper — domestic exports relatively cheaper abroad; imports relatively expensive
May improve export competitiveness — ⚠ does not necessarily improve the trade balance
Rupee devaluations: 1949 (the first), 1966, 1991
The 1991 devaluation — devalued twice — in two steps: on July 1 and July 3
## 4. NEER and REER
Nominal Effective Exchange Rate (NEER): A weighted average of bilateral nominal exchange rates — against a basket of trading-partner currencies
Real Effective Exchange Rate (REER): The NEER adjusted for relative price or inflation differentials — considers differences between domestic and foreign economies
⚠ An increase in NEER does not indicate appreciation in the cited convention; an increase in REER does not automatically mean better competitiveness
## 5. Influences
Demand and supply influence the exchange rate; inflation and a fiscal deficit can affect the exchange value
⚠ The World Bank does not determine the currency price

topic: Foreign investment - FDI, FII and P-Notes
t: Foreign direct investment
text:
## 1. Nature
FDI: Foreign direct investment — a largely non-debt-creating capital flow; generally longer-term foreign investment in Indian enterprises
Associated with capital, technology transfer, management skills, innovation, competition, employment and export competitiveness
## 2. What counts as FDI
Subsidiaries of foreign companies in India
Majority foreign equity holdings in Indian companies
Companies exclusively financed by foreign companies
⚠ Portfolio investment does not automatically constitute FDI
## 3. Instruments — FDI can be made through
Equity shares, debentures, preference shares, share warrants
## 4. Routes — FDI can enter through
Route | Approval
Automatic Route | Does not require prior government approval — subject to applicable conditions
Government Route | Requires prior government approval
## 5. E-commerce models
FDI is permitted under the marketplace model; ⚠ not permitted under the inventory-based model

topic: Foreign investment - FDI, FII and P-Notes
t: FDI vs FPI and FII
text:
## 1. FDI vs FPI
Basis | FDI | FPI
Type | Direct investment | Portfolio investment
Stability | Relatively stable and long-term | More volatile than FDI
Brings | Can bring technology and management skills | Primarily financial capital
Target | Specific sectors and enterprises | Primarily investment in securities
Control | Greater involvement and control | No comparable direct managerial involvement
## 2. FDI vs FII
Basis | FII — Foreign Institutional Investor | FDI
Type | Portfolio investment | Direct investment
Brings | Primarily financial capital | Capital along with technology and management
Term | More short-term; buoyant | Long-term; relatively stable
Market | Primarily securities markets | Investment in enterprises or sectors
Volatility | More volatile | Less volatile than FII, according to the source
## 3. SEBI FPI Regulations, 2019
Issued 2019 — unified FIIs, sub-accounts and QFIs under the FPI framework
## 4. P-Notes
An instrument issued by a registered FII or FPI to an overseas investor
Enables the overseas investor to obtain exposure to Indian stocks
⚠ An overseas investor using a P-Note does not directly register with SEBI

topic: Foreign investment - FDI, FII and P-Notes
t: IFC, IDA and Masala Bonds
text:
## 1. IFC vs IDA
Basis | International Finance Corporation (IFC) | International Development Association (IDA)
Group | An institution — a member — of the World Bank Group | A member of the World Bank Group
Established | 1956 | 1960
Focus | The private sector — private-sector development; private enterprise; private investment and development | The poorest countries
Nature | An international development institution | Provides concessional loans and grants
## 2. First Masala Bond
Issued in November 2014 by the World Bank-backed IFC
Issued outside India but denominated in Indian rupees
Used to fund infrastructure projects in India

topic: Trade policy - SEZs and export promotion
t: Special Economic Zones
text:
## 1. Nature
SEZ: Special Economic Zone — a designated area created to promote exports, investment, employment, infrastructure and additional economic activity
Simplified procedures; a business-friendly environment
A major export-promotion instrument — objectives include exports, investment, employment and infrastructure
## 2. SEZ milestones
Date | Milestone
April 1, 2000 | India's first SEZ policy announced — the SEZ policy introduced in 2000
2005 | SEZ Act passed by Parliament (enacted) — President's assent on June 23, 2005
February 10, 2006 | The SEZ Act and Rules came into effect
## 3. Export Processing Zones
Kandla, Gujarat: India's first and Asia's first — the first Asian EPZ — Export Processing Zone (EPZ) — established 1965; later associated with Kandla SEZ
Surat: India's first private-sector EPZ — established 1997; converted into an SEZ on November 1, 2000

topic: Trade policy - SEZs and export promotion
t: Export promotion institutions
text:
## 1. Institutions
Body | Full form / role
EXIM Bank | Export-Import Bank of India — established 1982
ECGC | Export Credit Guarantee Corporation of India — export credit-risk insurance
MMTC | Minerals and Metals Trading Corporation of India Limited — a foreign trade and trading organisation
STC | State Trading Corporation of India Limited — engaged in foreign trade
IBEF | India Brand Equity Foundation — established 1996; promotes the India Brand internationally
## 2. Schemes and terms
EXIM Policy 2000: Announced on March 31, 2000 — part of the 1997–2002 framework
EPCG: Export Promotion Capital Goods
Duty drawback: The refund of duties on inputs used for export production
NIRVIK: Niryat Rin Vikas Yojana — export credit insurance; enhanced insurance cover

topic: Trade policy - SEZs and export promotion
t: Trade terms and regional integration
text:
## 1. Trade barriers and terms
Term | Meaning
Tariff | A tax on imports
Import quota | A quantity restriction on imports
Anti-dumping measures | Protect against goods exported below normal value
Free trade | Little or no tariff and little or no quantitative restriction
Import licensing | An administrative restriction on imports
Rules of origin | Determine the country of origin for trade-policy purposes
Entrepot trade | Importing goods, storing or trading imported goods and re-exporting them
## 2. Trade agreements
FTA: Free Trade Agreement
CEPA: Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement
CECA: Comprehensive Economic Cooperation Agreement
## 3. Stages of integration
Stage | Features
Customs union | A common external tariff; free internal trade
Common market | A customs union with free movement of factors
Economic union | A common market with coordinated economic policies

t: GATT and WTO
text:
## 1. WTO
World Trade Organization — established on 1 January 1995; an international trade organization
Agreement: The Marrakesh Agreement of 1994
Replaced GATT; originated from the Uruguay Round of GATT
Headquarters: Geneva, Switzerland
## 2. GATT
General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade — signed on 30 October 1947 at Geneva; 23 founding contracting parties
Came into effect in 1948
Main focus: Reduction of tariffs and quantitative restrictions
## 3. GATT vs WTO
Basis | GATT | WTO
Established | 1947 | 1995
Nature | An agreement | An international organization
Coverage | Mainly goods | Goods, services, intellectual property rights and investment measures
Framework | A framework for trade | A broader multilateral trade framework

t: Uruguay Round and agricultural subsidy boxes
text:
## 1. Uruguay Round
1986 to 1993 — expanded the trade framework beyond goods to include:
GATS — Trade in Services
TRIPS — Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights
TRIMS — Trade-Related Investment Measures
## 2. Subsidy boxes
Box | Nature | Examples
Green Box | Minimal or no trade distortion — permitted | Decoupled income support; environmental programmes; regional development; agricultural research; farmer training; pest and disease control
Amber Box | Distorts trade or production — subject to limits | Price support; production-linked subsidies
Blue Box | Amber-type support with production-limiting conditions — combines Amber Box support with production limitation | —

t: IMF and World Bank
text:
## 1. IMF
Conceived at the Bretton Woods Conference in 1944; formally established on 27 December 1945
An international monetary institution — a Bretton Woods institution; headquarters Washington, D.C.
Main objective: International monetary stability — promotes it; associated with monetary stability
Major lending focus: Balance of payments problems — addresses them; provides lending
India: A founding member — joined on 27 December 1945
## 2. IMF functions
Monitors global economies and member economies
Provides financial assistance to members facing balance of payments difficulties
Provides practical and technical assistance
## 3. IMF facilities
Reserve tranche: A member's unconditional drawing right on IMF resources — arises from a member's quota subscription and subsequent changes
Rapid Financing Instrument: Rapid financial assistance through the IMF for urgent balance of payments needs — available to IMF members
Rapid Credit Facility: Concessional assistance through the IMF for urgent balance of payments needs — available to low-income countries
## 4. IMF vs World Bank
Basis | IMF | World Bank
Associated with | Monetary stability | Development
Provides | Lending for balance of payments problems | Development and project financing; development assistance
Origin | A Bretton Woods institution | A Bretton Woods institution
Headquarters | Washington, D.C. | Washington, D.C.
