t: The Solar System and the planets
text:
## 1. Basics
The Solar System is centred on the Sun — 4.6 billion years old
Main components: The Sun, eight planets, dwarf planets, satellites, asteroids, comets, meteoroids and cosmic dust
Gravity keeps bodies in orbit
Number of planets: Current — eight; former — nine, before Pluto's reclassification
Pluto reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006 by the IAU
## 2. Groups of planets
Terrestrial rocky planets — the inner planets, in order: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars
Jovian giant planets — the outer planets, in order: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune
Gas giants: Jupiter and Saturn; ice giants: Uranus and Neptune
## 3. Planet data
Planet | Distance from the Sun (million km) | Diameter (km) | Revolution around the Sun
Mercury | 57.9 | 4,879 | 88 days
Venus | 108.2 | 12,104 | 224.7 days
Earth | 149.6 | 12,756 | 365.25 days
Mars | 228 | 6,792 | 687 days
Jupiter | 778.5 | 142,984 | 11.86 years
Saturn | 1,432 | 120,536 | 29.4 years
Uranus | 2,867 | 51,118 | 84.07 years
Neptune | 4,515 | 49,528 | 164.9 years
## 4. Superlatives
Feature | Planet
Nearest planet to the Sun; smallest planet; fastest orbital velocity | Mercury
Farthest planet from the Sun; coldest planet; slowest orbital velocity; longest revolution period — 165 years | Neptune
Largest planet; highest gravitational acceleration | Jupiter
Brightest planet; hottest planet | Venus
Densest planet — density 5.5 g/cm³ | Earth
## 5. Nicknames and features
Venus: The Earth-twin; the Morning and Evening Star
Mars: The Red Planet
Saturn: Prominent rings
No natural satellites: Mercury and Venus
Earth: Third from the Sun; neighbours — Venus and Mars

t: The Earth
text:
## 1. Shape and size
Shape: A geoid or oblate spheroid — wider at the equator and flatter at the poles
Equatorial diameter: 12,756 km; polar diameter: 12,714 km; equatorial circumference: 40,090 km
Axial tilt: 23.5°
Aristotle: The first stated source for Earth's spherical shape
Weight variation: Caused by rotation and its non-spherical shape
Centrifugal force: Maximum at the equator
An object's weight: Minimum at the equator; maximum at the poles
## 2. Rotation and revolution
Motion | Meaning | Time | Produces
Rotation | The spinning of Earth on its axis — from west to east | 24 hours | Day and night — the daily cycle
Revolution | The movement of Earth around the Sun (direction: around the Sun) | 365.25 days | A year and seasons — with axial tilt
Orbital speed: 29.8 km/s
Aryabhatta: Explained the apparent daily motion of the Sun through Earth's rotation
## 3. Distance from the Sun
Mean distance: 149.6 million km = one astronomical unit (the mean Earth–Sun distance) — approximately 149.6 × 10⁹ m
Sunlight takes 8 minutes 19 seconds to reach Earth — to travel one astronomical unit
Perihelion: Earth closest to the Sun — early January; orbital speed higher
Aphelion: Earth farthest from the Sun — early July; orbital speed lower
## 4. Sun's position through the year
Date | Sun overhead at | Northern Hemisphere | Southern Hemisphere
21 March | Equator — equinox | Spring begins | Autumn begins
21 June | Tropic of Cancer | Summer solstice | Winter
23 September | Equator — equinox | Autumn begins | Spring begins
22 December | Tropic of Capricorn | Winter solstice | Summer
Equinoxes (21 March and 23 September): Day and night approximately equal
## 5. Composition
Crust: Oxygen 46.6%; silicon 27.72%; aluminium 8.13%; iron 5%
Mantle: Lies below the crust
Core: Begins at a depth of 2,900 km — outer core of liquid iron and nickel; inner core of solid iron
NIFE: Nickel and ferrum — iron
## 6. Other facts
Habitable zone: The Goldilocks Zone — Earth is the only known life-supporting planet
Geomagnetic equator location tested at Thumba
Earth Day: Observed on 22 April; the first Earth Day was observed in 1970

t: The Sun
text:
## 1. Nature
A star at the centre of the Solar System — the closest star to Earth; Alpha Centauri is the next closest star mentioned
Contains 99.8% of the Solar System's mass; diameter 109 times Earth's diameter
Interior: A plasma state; core temperature 15 million°C
Photosphere: The visible bright layer — about 5,500°C
Energy: Nuclear fusion — converts hydrogen into helium and releases energy
## 2. Solar phenomena
Sunspot: A dark patch on the photosphere
Aurora: Produced by solar particles interacting with the atmosphere — Aurora Borealis in the north; Aurora Australis in the south
Corona: Visible during a (total) solar eclipse

t: The Moon and eclipses
text:
## 1. The Moon
Earth's natural satellite — diameter 3,475 km
Distance from Earth: Average 384,400 km; minimum 363,300 km; maximum 405,500 km
Orbital and rotation period: 27 days 7 hours 43 minutes — shows the same face toward Earth
Atmosphere: Essentially absent; gravity: one-sixth of Earth's gravity
Lunar month: 29.5 days
Apollo 11 (1969): The first human landing on the Moon — in the Sea of Tranquility
## 2. Perigee and apogee
Perigee: The Moon's closest position to Earth — stronger gravity and higher tides; a full moon near / at perigee is a supermoon
Apogee: The Moon's farthest position from Earth — weaker gravity
## 3. Phases
Full moon: Earth approximately between the Sun and Moon
New moon: The Moon between the Sun and Earth
Half moon: The Sun–Earth–Moon angle is 90°
Blue moon: Two full moons in one calendar month (the calendar definition); alternatively an extra full moon in an astronomical season; stated frequency — 2.7154 years
## 4. Eclipses
Basis | Solar eclipse | Lunar eclipse
Position | The Moon is between the Sun and Earth | Earth is between the Sun and Moon
Phase | New moon | Full moon
Shadow | The Moon's shadow falls on Earth | Earth's shadow falls on the Moon
Visibility | A limited region | A larger part of the night side
Feature | The corona is visible | The Moon may appear reddish

t: Asteroids, comets, meteors and astronomers
text:
## 1. Asteroids vs comets
Basis | Asteroids | Comets
Composition | Rock and metal | Ice, dust and rock
Location | The main asteroid belt — between Mars and Jupiter | The outer system — the Kuiper and Oort regions
Tails | Generally do not have tails | Develop tails near the Sun
Orbits | Less eccentric | Highly elliptical
## 2. Comets
Near the Sun: A comet develops a coma and tail — the tail contains dust and ionised material and points away from the Sun, directed by radiation pressure and solar wind
Comet | Key facts
Halley's Comet | A short-period comet — period about 76 years; last appeared 1986; next expected 2061
Hale-Bopp | A long-period comet — period 2,534 years; discovered 1995
Shoemaker–Levy 9 | Collided with Jupiter in July 1994
67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko | Targeted by Rosetta
## 3. Meteoroid, meteor, meteorite
Meteoroid: A small rocky or metallic body in space
Meteor: A bright streak produced when a meteoroid enters the atmosphere and heats up — popularly a shooting star; atmospheric friction and heating cause it to glow
Meteorite: A meteoroid that survives and reaches the surface
## 4. Astronomers
Astronomer | Contribution
Copernicus | Proposed the heliocentric model
Kepler | Formulated the three laws of planetary motion
Galileo | Studied the Galilean moons and falling bodies
Newton | Formulated the laws of gravity
William Herschel | Discovered Uranus — 1781
Clyde Tombaugh | Discovered Pluto — 1930
Johann Galle | Associated with Neptune

t: Rotation — day, night and time
text:
## 1. Two primary motions
Earth has two primary motions: rotation and revolution
Rotation: Earth spins on its own axis — movement on Earth's axis
Earth's axis: An imaginary line joining — through — the North and South Poles
## 2. Rotation facts
Direction: From west to east — appears counter-clockwise when viewed from the North Pole
Period: Completes one rotation — a full rotation of 360° — in 24 hours
Angular speed: 15° per hour — 1° every 4 minutes
Linear rotational speed: Maximum at the Equator; zero at the Poles
Results: Day and night (the main result); time differences and time zones; the Coriolis effect (force); a centrifugal effect
## 3. Day and night
Day: The part of Earth facing the Sun; night: the part turned away from the Sun
Circle of illumination: Divides the illuminated and dark portions of Earth
Caused by Earth's rotation on its axis — ⚠ revolution does not cause day and night; axial tilt alone does not either
## 4. Longitude and time
Longitude difference | Time
1° | 4 minutes
15° | 1 hour
180° | 12 hours
Longitude difference produces local-time difference
Eastward movement: Local time advances; westward movement: local time retards (decreases)
24 theoretical world time zones — each covering 15°
180° meridian: Associated with the International Date Line — the date changes across it
## 5. Coriolis effect
Caused by Earth's rotation — the apparent deflection of moving objects or air
Deflected to the right in the Northern Hemisphere; to the left in the Southern Hemisphere
Zero or absent at the Equator; maximum at the Poles — increases with latitude and velocity
Applies to winds, ocean currents and cyclones
## 6. Centrifugal effect
Caused by Earth's rotation — the centrifugal force is maximum at the Equator; minimum or zero at the Poles
Causes equatorial bulging and polar flattening — Earth's shape resulting from this is an oblate spheroid
Weight: Minimum at the Equator; increases toward the Poles; maximum at the Poles — rotation makes it so
## 7. Changes in rotation
Earth's rotation axis has shifted slightly over time; the length of day has changed by a very small measurable amount
Ice-sheet melting redistributes mass and water toward lower latitudes — this redistribution can influence Earth's rotation and axis
Solar flares and coronal mass ejections affect the upper atmosphere — ⚠ not the primary explanation in the relevant question

t: Revolution, orbit and the calendar
text:
## 1. Revolution
Revolution: Earth's movement around the Sun in an elliptical orbit — revolution changes Earth's position around the Sun
Period: 365.25 days — also given as 365 days, 6 hours, 9 minutes and 9.51 seconds
Average orbital speed: 29.78 km/s
Results: A year — the annual cycle (the major result); seasons along with axial tilt
## 2. Axial tilt and parallelism
Axial inclination: 23.5° (23½°) from the perpendicular to the orbital plane — the axis makes an angle of 66.5° (66½°) with — is inclined to — the orbital plane
A major factor in seasons — changes the angle and duration of solar illumination
Parallelism: Earth's axis maintains approximately the same orientation — remains approximately parallel — as Earth revolves
Produces opposite seasons — seasonal reversal — between the two hemispheres
⚠ The correct statement is that there is parallelism of Earth's axis
## 3. Perihelion and aphelion
Basis | Perihelion | Aphelion
Meaning | Earth nearest to the Sun — minimum Earth–Sun distance | Earth farthest from the Sun — maximum Earth–Sun distance
Date | Early January — approximately 4 January | Early July — approximately 4 July
Distance | Approximately 147 million km | Approximately 152 million km
Orbital speed | Greater / faster — maximum | Lower / slower — minimum
Northern Hemisphere | During its winter period | During its summer period
Kepler's Second Law explains Earth's maximum speed at perihelion and minimum speed at aphelion
⚠ Distance from the Sun does not primarily cause seasons — only a minor or slight role
## 4. Leap year
A normal calendar year: 365 days — the extra fraction is one-fourth of a day, which accumulates to one day in four years
Leap year: 366 days — the extra day is 29 February
## 5. Rotation vs revolution
Basis | Rotation | Revolution
Movement | On Earth's axis | Around the Sun
Period | 24 hours | 365.25 days
Direction / path | West-to-east | An elliptical orbit
Main result | Day and night | A year
Seasonal role | Indirect | Direct — combined with axial tilt
Coriolis effect | Has a role | No primary role
Centrifugal effect | Has a role | —
Time zones | Produces | Does not produce
Solstices and equinoxes | ⚠ Not the direct cause | Causes them along with axial tilt
Perihelion and aphelion | Does not cause | Associated

t: Seasons — causes and solar angle
text:
## 1. Why seasons occur
Earth revolves around the Sun (in 365.25 days) and has an axial tilt of 23½° — Earth is tilted by 23½° as it revolves
Main consequence of revolution and axial tilt: A changing angle of insolation during the year — revolution and axial tilt produce the seasonal cycle
⚠ Earth's rotation causes day and night, not seasons; revolution alone is not sufficient — it needs axial tilt
Axial tilt combined with revolution causes: Changing day length; solstices and equinoxes; opposite seasons in the hemispheres; six-month polar day and night
## 2. Mechanism
Earth's position relative to the Sun changes during revolution; the axial tilt remains approximately parallel
The hemispheres alternately tilt toward and away from the Sun
The angle of solar rays — the angle of insolation — and the length of day change during the year; one hemisphere receives longer illumination at a time
Changes in heating produce seasons; the seasons in opposite hemispheres are opposite
## 3. Summer vs winter
Basis | Summer | Winter
Hemisphere tilt | Tilted toward the Sun | Tilted away from the Sun
Solar rays / angle | More direct | More oblique — more slanting
Energy | Greater concentration — Earth receives greater solar energy | Lower concentration — lower solar energy
Days | Longer | Shorter
Sun's apparent altitude | Higher | Lower
Heating | Greater | Lower
More vertical or direct rays: Concentrated energy and greater heating; more oblique or slanting rays spread energy over a larger area — lower heating
The summer hemisphere receives more direct rays and longer days; the winter hemisphere more oblique rays and shorter days
Seasonal temperature depends on insolation and day length
## 4. Shadows
A higher Sun in the sky: a smaller shadow; a lower Sun: a longer shadow; a vertically overhead Sun: no shadow — a vertical Sun produces no noon shadow
Noon shadow at the Tropic of Cancer: Minimum or absent on 21 June
Noon shadow at the Equator: Absent in March and September

t: Solstices and equinoxes
text:
## 1. Solstices
Basis | June solstice | December solstice
Date | 20 or 21 June (approximately 21 June) | 21 or 22 December
Northern Hemisphere | Summer solstice — summer, longest day, shortest night | Winter solstice — winter, shortest day, longest night
Southern Hemisphere | Winter, shortest day, longest night | Summer solstice — summer, longest day, shortest night
Sun's direct rays — vertically overhead | Tropic of Cancer (23.5°N / 23½°N) | Tropic of Capricorn (23.5°S / 23½°S)
Pole tilted toward the Sun | North Pole — the Arctic Circle and regions beyond it can experience continuous daylight (lasting six months) | South Pole — the Antarctic region experiences continuous daylight
At the June solstice the Equator has approximately a 12-hour day
Two solstices per year — the Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer or Tropic of Capricorn; seasonal contrast is maximum; ⚠ day and night are not equal
## 2. Equinoxes
Equinox: Approximately equal day and night — occurs twice a year (two equinoxes per year) — a transition point between seasons
Dates: March equinox approximately 20 or 21 March; September equinox approximately 22 or 23 September — the equinoxes occur in March and September
The direct rays of the Sun fall on the Equator; both hemispheres have approximately equal day and night
March equinox: Spring begins in the Northern Hemisphere; autumn begins in the Southern Hemisphere
September equinox: Autumn begins in the Northern Hemisphere; spring begins in the Southern Hemisphere
## 3. The year at a glance
Date | Vertical Sun overhead at | Northern Hemisphere | Southern Hemisphere | Sun then
21 March | Equator | Spring | Autumn | Starts moving northward
21 June | Tropic of Cancer | Summer — longest day and shortest night | Winter — shortest day and longest night | Starts moving southward
23 September | Equator | Autumn | Spring | Continues moving southward after it
21 or 22 December | Tropic of Capricorn | Winter — shortest day and longest night | Summer — longest day and shortest night | —
## 4. Day length through the year
Period | Northern Hemisphere days | Southern Hemisphere days
21 March to 21 June | Progressively lengthen | Progressively shorten
21 June to 23 September | Progressively shorten | Progressively lengthen
23 September to 21 December | Progressively shorten | Progressively lengthen
21 December to 21 March | Progressively lengthen | Progressively shorten
Northern Hemisphere longest day on 21 June — in the second half of June, usually on 20 or 21 June; shortest day on 21 December
Southern Hemisphere longest day on 21 December — in the second half of December; shortest day on 21 June
## 5. Christmas in Australia
December is winter in the Northern Hemisphere and summer in the Southern Hemisphere — Christmas is summer in Australia, which is in the Southern Hemisphere

t: Latitudes, the Equator and the poles
text:
## 1. Key latitudes
Latitude | Value | Association
Equator | 0° | The Sun is overhead near the equinoxes
Tropic of Cancer | 23.5°N | The Sun is overhead near the June solstice
Tropic of Capricorn | 23.5°S | The Sun is overhead near the December solstice
Arctic Circle | 66.5°N | Polar day and night effects
Antarctic Circle | 66.5°S | Polar day and night effects
Angular distance from the Tropic of Cancer to the Tropic of Capricorn: 47° = 23½° plus 23½°
Noon altitude at the Tropic of Cancer at the December solstice: 43° — calculated as 90° − 47° = 43°
## 2. The Equator
Day and night approximately equal throughout the year — about 12 hours of day and 12 hours of night; seasonal variation in day length is very small
The Sun is overhead at the Equator during an equinox
No distinct winter or summer — generally wet and dry seasons instead
## 3. The poles
North Pole: Six months of continuous daylight (around June) and six months of darkness (around December)
South Pole: The opposite daylight and darkness pattern — continuous darkness around June, continuous daylight around December
Polar day and polar night each last approximately six months
Main reason: Axial inclination combined with revolution — the 23½° axial tilt and revolution tilt a pole toward the Sun; during polar day the Sun remains above the horizon
Continuous daylight: Beyond the Arctic Circle during Northern Hemisphere summer; beyond the Antarctic Circle during Southern Hemisphere summer
## 4. Midnight Sun
The Sun remains visible around midnight — north of the Arctic Circle and south of the Antarctic Circle
Strongest around the respective summer solstice — can produce 24-hour daylight
Example: Norway

t: Monsoons and Indian seasons
text:
## 1. Monsoon
A seasonal reversal of wind pattern — from the Arabic word Mausim, meaning season
Main mechanism: Differential heating and cooling of land and sea
Summer heating produces low pressure; winter cooling produces high pressure — seasonal pressure reversal produces monsoons
Monsoonal winds reverse direction according to the season — seasonal wind reversal produces monsoons
Summer: From sea to land; winter: from land to sea
⚠ Land and sea breezes are daily or diurnal, rather than annual; mountain and valley breezes are periodic
Monsoonal climate: Wet and dry seasons; seasonal rainfall is associated with the Indian monsoon
## 2. Indian monsoon seasons
Southwest monsoon: June to September
Retreating monsoon: October to November
Northeast monsoon: Important for southeastern India
## 3. Indian traditional seasons
Season | Months
Spring | March to April
Summer | May to June
Rainy | July to August
Autumn | September to October
Pre-winter | November to December
Winter | January to February
## 4. Seasonal crop cycles
Crop | Sown | Harvested
Rabi | October or November | March or April — or in summer
Kharif | June or July | October or November
Zaid | Grown between Rabi and Kharif — a short summer season | —
Seasonal vegetation: Includes tropical deciduous forests

t: Layers of the earth
text:
## 1. Compositional layers
Layer | Position | Composition | State
Crust | The outermost layer | Oxygen, silicon, aluminium, iron and other elements — oxygen is the most abundant | Solid
Mantle | Below the crust — between the crust and the core; its base at approximately 2,900 km depth | Mainly magnesium–iron silicates | Predominantly solid — behaves plastically over geological time
Outer core | Below the mantle | Mainly iron and nickel | Liquid — S-waves stop here
Inner core | Central | Mainly iron and nickel | Solid — called the NIFE or solid core
The core begins at approximately 2,900 km depth
Core: Main constituent — iron; nickel is another major constituent; the traditional term NIFE means nickel plus iron
Compositional layering: Crust, mantle, core; mechanical layering: lithosphere, asthenosphere, deeper mantle, outer core, inner core
## 2. Elements of the crust — by weight
Rank | Element | Share
First | Oxygen | 46.60%
Second | Silicon | 27.72%
Third | Aluminium | 8.13%
Fourth | Iron | 5.00%
Fifth | Calcium | 3.63%
Sixth | Sodium | 2.83%
Seventh | Potassium | 2.59%
Eighth | Magnesium | 2.09%
## 3. Continental vs oceanic crust
Basis | Continental crust | Oceanic crust
Thickness | Thicker | Thinner
Main rock | Granite | Basalt
Density | Lower | Higher
Age | Generally older | Generally younger
Composition | More silicon and aluminium | More iron and magnesium
Forms | The continents | The ocean floors
## 4. Lithosphere vs asthenosphere
Basis | Lithosphere | Asthenosphere
Nature | Rigid — relatively strong — the rigid upper zone associated with the mantle | Weak and ductile — mechanically weaker; an important upper zone of the mantle
Made of / position | The crust and uppermost mantle | Underlies — the upper mantle portion below the lithosphere
Plates | Broken into plates | Allows plate movement — lets lithospheric plates move
Association | An earthquake-generating shell | Mantle flow
## 5. Role of the mantle
Mantle movement drives plate movement — a major role in plate tectonics, volcanism and endogenic activity
The major source region for magma; the layer below the crust is the mantle
## 6. Density
Earth's average density: approximately 5.5 g/cm³ — Earth is the densest planet
Density generally increases inward — heavier materials are concentrated in Earth's core
## 7. Geodynamo
Movement and convection of conducting material in the liquid outer core produce the geodynamo, which generates Earth's magnetic field
Magnetic-field reversals: Linked to changes in molten-core movement

t: Seismic waves and discontinuities
text:
## 1. Seismic waves as evidence
Earthquakes generate seismic waves, which travel through different materials and undergo reflection and refraction
Velocity changes reveal differences in materials; shadow zones help infer internal boundaries
Seismic-wave evidence identifies the crust, mantle and core
## 2. P, S and surface waves
Basis | P-waves | S-waves | Surface waves
Name | Primary — compressional or longitudinal push-pull waves | Secondary — transverse or shear shake waves | Surface waves — L-waves
Speed | The fastest — arrive first | Slower than P-waves — S-waves travel more slowly; P-waves travel faster than S-waves — do not arrive first | The slowest — do not arrive first
Medium | Solids, liquids and gases | Solids only — not through liquids or gases | —
Through Earth's interior | Yes | Yes | No
Particle vibration | Parallel to the direction of propagation | Perpendicular to the direction of propagation | —
Destructive power | Lower than surface waves | — | The highest
## 3. Evidence for the liquid outer core
S-waves cannot cross the liquid outer core — they disappear because it is liquid; S-wave behaviour establishes the existence of a liquid outer core
P-waves: Strongly refracted at the mantle–core boundary
P-wave shadow zone: Standard — approximately 103°–142°; also given as approximately 105°–140°
S-waves do not reappear beyond the core-related shadow zone
## 4. Discontinuities
Discontinuity | Separates | Seismic clue
Conrad | Upper and lower continental crust | A crustal velocity change
Mohorovicic / Moho | Crust and mantle | A sudden velocity increase
410 km and 660 km | Mark mantle mineralogical zones | Phase changes
Gutenberg | Mantle and outer core | S-waves disappear; P-wave velocity changes
Lehmann | Outer core and inner core | Linked to the solid inner core

t: Internal processes, magma and rocks
text:
## 1. Endogenic processes
Internal heat produces endogenic processes, which drive mantle dynamics; mantle dynamics drive plate movement
Mantle heat causes convection or thermal movement
Plate movement produces folding, faulting, earthquakes, volcanism and mountain building — plate movement causes earthquakes
## 2. Plate boundaries
Convergence: Mountains and subduction
Divergence: New crust
Subduction: Destruction and recycling of crust — old crust is destroyed by subduction
New crust is added by seafloor spreading
## 3. Magma and lava
Magma: Molten rock or material below Earth's surface — produces volcanism
Lava: Magma after it reaches Earth's surface — molten material that reaches the surface; dominated by silica
Volcano: An outlet for magma, lava and gases — releases lava, ash and gases
Water vapour: The most abundant volcanic gas
## 4. Rock types
Rock | Formation | Examples
Igneous | Cooling or solidification of magma or lava | Granite — intrusive; basalt — extrusive
Sedimentary | Surface deposition | —
Metamorphic | Existing rock altered by heat or pressure | —

t: Landform types at a glance
text:
## 1. Major landforms and their formation
Landform | Formed by | Examples
Mountains | Folding, erosion, faulting and volcanism | Major mountains: the Himalayas, Andes, Alps, Rockies, Sierra Nevada, Aravallis
Plateaus | Uplift, volcanism, erosion and deposition | Major plateaus: the Tibetan Plateau, Deccan Plateau, Pamir Plateau, Patagonia Plateau, the Meseta
Plains | Deposition, erosion and marine processes | Major plains: the Indo-Gangetic Plain, the Great Plains
Valleys | Rivers, glaciers, tectonic processes and karst processes | V-shaped, U-shaped, rift, hanging and blind valleys — listed as river landforms
River landforms | Erosion, transportation and deposition processes | Gorges, canyons, waterfalls, meanders, deltas, alluvial fans
Glacial landforms | — | Cirques, arêtes, horns, moraine
Desert landforms | Wind erosion and deposition | Dunes, yardangs, mushroom rocks, playas, loess
Karst landforms | The solution of limestone | Sinkholes, dolines, caves, stalactites, stalagmites, blind valleys
Coastal landforms | Waves, currents and tides | Cliffs, caves, arches, stacks, beaches, spits, lagoons
Tectonic landforms | Faulting, folding and crustal movement | Rift valleys, horsts, grabens, fold mountains
## 2. Agents and landforms
Agent | Landforms
Running water | Deltas, V-shaped valleys, gorges, meanders, alluvial fans
Glaciers | Cirques, arêtes, horns, U-shaped valleys, hanging valleys; with marine submergence — fjords
Wind | Sand dunes, yardangs, mushroom rocks
Karst or groundwater | Sinkholes, stalactites
Waves | Sea caves, sea arches, sea stacks
Longshore drift | Spits
Tectonic faulting | Rift valleys, horsts, grabens
## 3. Key contrasts
Mountains are steep or pointed, whereas plateaus are elevated and flat-topped
Young fold mountains are high and rugged, whereas old fold mountains are low and rounded
Fold mountains result from compression, whereas block mountains result from faulting
A canyon is a more extensive and deeply eroded gorge
V-shaped valleys are formed by rivers, whereas U-shaped valleys are formed by glaciers
A hanging valley is glacial, whereas a rift valley is tectonic
A delta is dominated by deposition, whereas an estuary is associated with tidal or drowned-mouth processes
A stalactite hangs from a roof, whereas a stalagmite rises from a floor
A horst is an uplifted block, whereas a graben is a down-faulted block
A barchan is crescent-shaped, whereas a seif dune is longitudinal
A spit projects from the coast, whereas a tombolo connects an island to the mainland

t: Mountains
text:
## 1. Types of mountains
Type | Formation | Features | Examples
Young fold mountains | Compression and folding | Very high; rugged terrain; steep slopes; sharp peaks | The Himalayas, Alps, Andes, Rockies
Old fold mountains | Ancient folding and prolonged denudation | Lower than young fold mountains; rounded; highly eroded | The Aravallis, Appalachians, Urals, Pennines
Block mountains | Faulting | Uplifted blocks; steep fault scarps; linked with rift valleys | The Sierra Nevada, Vosges, Black Forest, Salt Range
Volcanic mountains | Accumulation of lava and volcanic material | Conical peaks | Kilimanjaro, Fuji
Residual mountains | Erosion leaves resistant rocks — remnants of older elevated surfaces | — | The Aravallis, Appalachians, Pennines
Dome mountains | Magma pushes upward without erupting through the crust | Dome-shaped uplifts | The Black Hills, Bighorns
## 2. Fold vs block vs volcanic
Basis | Fold mountains | Block mountains | Volcanic mountains
Main force | Compression | Faulting | Volcanism
Basic process | Folding | Uplift and downthrow | Lava accumulation
Common form | Rugged, parallel ranges | Fault scarps | A cone shape
Associated with | Fold belts | Horsts and grabens | Craters
Examples | The Himalaya, Alps, Andes | The Sierra Nevada, Vosges | Fuji, Kilimanjaro
## 3. Key facts
The world's highest peaks mostly occur in young fold mountains — the Andes and the Himalayas are young fold mountains
The Appalachians and the Aravallis are old fold or residual mountains
The Rhine Valley and the Vosges form a block mountain–rift valley system
Mount Kilimanjaro: A volcanic mountain
The Andes (South America): The longest major mountain range

t: Plateaus
text:
## 1. Types of plateau
Type | Nature | Examples
Intermontane | Enclosed or surrounded by mountains | The Tibetan, Pamir, Bolivia, Peru and Colombia Plateaus
Piedmont | At foothills or mountain margins | The Piedmont Plateau of the USA; the Patagonia Plateau
Continental | Broad elevated continental surfaces | The Peninsular, African, Arabian, Australian and South American Plateaus
Volcanic or lava | Extensive lava or pyroclastic accumulation | The Deccan Plateau; the Columbia Plateau; parts of Brazil and Siberia
Fluvial | River deposition | The Panna, Bhander, Rewa and Rohtas Plateaus
Domed | Broad dome-like uplift | The Ozark Plateau
## 2. Notable plateaus
Tibetan Plateau: The highest plateau — average elevation 4,500 metres; covers 2.5 million square kilometres
Pamir: Known as the Roof of the World
Meseta: Located in the Iberian Peninsula — in Spain
## 3. Indian plateaus
Peninsular Plateau: An ancient, relatively stable crystalline landmass — includes the Deccan, Malwa and Chotanagpur regions
Central Highlands: North of the Narmada; Bundelkhand and Baghelkhand are eastern extensions
Malwa Plateau: Between the Aravalli and Vindhya ranges
Bhander Plateau: The southern part of the Vindhyan scarpland
Chotanagpur Plateau: Mineral-rich; drained by the Damodar — Damodar drainage
Deccan Plateau: South of the Narmada — a predominantly basaltic volcanic origin; associated with the Deccan Trap — a basaltic lava plateau
Meghalaya Plateau: A detached extension of the Peninsular Plateau
Dandakaranya: A central-eastern — central or eastern Peninsular — highland region

t: Valleys and river landforms
text:
## 1. Valleys
Valley | Formed by | Notes
V-shaped | River erosion | Upper and middle river courses; narrow — in youthful rivers
U-shaped | Glacial erosion — glaciers | Glaciers widen and deepen V-shaped valleys — glacially modified valleys have U-shaped cross-sections
Hanging | A tributary glacier — less erosive — left above a main valley | A waterfall occurs at the junction of a hanging valley
Rift | Crustal faulting or divergence | Death Valley, the Narmada Valley
Blind | — | In karst or limestone regions; end abruptly
## 2. Rift valleys
Formation: Divergence or tension causes faulting; faulting causes the central block to subside
An elongated depression associated with faulting
Horst: An uplifted fault block; graben: a down-faulted block
Examples: Death Valley (USA); the Rhine Rift Valley; the Narmada Valley; the Tapi Valley — the Narmada and Tapi are rift valleys
## 3. Gorges and canyons
Basis | Gorge | Canyon
Nature | A deep, narrow, steep-sided river valley | A very deeply eroded gorge — more deeply or widely eroded; very deep and steep-sided
Sides | Steep or near-vertical | Very steep
Formed by | River erosion — vertical erosion | Prolonged river erosion — intense prolonged erosion
Example | Chisapani Gorge | The Grand Canyon
## 4. River landforms by process
Landform | Process | Description
Waterfall | Differential erosion | A sudden vertical fall
Meander | Lateral erosion and deposition | A sinuous river course
Oxbow lake | Meander cut-off | Crescent-shaped
Floodplain | Deposition | A flat depositional valley floor
Natural levees | Deposition | Raised banks along rivers
Alluvial fan | Deposition | A cone or fan at a mountain foot
Delta | Deposition at river mouths | Accumulates sediment into the sea
Estuary | — | A drowned river mouth — a funnel-shaped tidal mouth
## 5. Delta vs estuary
Basis | Delta | Estuary
Dominant process | Deposition | Erosion or tidal flushing
Rivers / tides | Sediment-rich rivers | Strong tidal action
Mouth | A deltaic river divides into distributaries | Usually a single funnel-shaped opening
Coast / channels | Shallow coasts | Deeper navigable channels
Example | The Ganga-Brahmaputra | Many Western Ghats rivers

t: Glacial, desert, karst and coastal landforms
text:
## 1. Glacial landforms
Landform | Formed by | Description
Cirque / corrie | Glacial erosion | A bowl-shaped hollow
Arête | Two cirques eroding a ridge | A knife-edged ridge
Horn | Several cirques eroding a mountain | A sharp pyramidal peak
Fjord | A drowned glacial U-shaped valley | A deep, narrow sea inlet
Moraine | Glacial deposition | Accumulated debris
Drumlin | Glacial deposition | A streamlined oval hill
Esker | Meltwater deposition | A long winding ridge
## 2. Desert (wind) landforms
Landform | Formed by | Description
Sand dunes | Wind deposition | Accumulations of sand
Barchans | Wind deposition | Crescent-shaped dunes
Seif / longitudinal dunes | Wind deposition | Long, narrow ridges
Yardangs | Wind erosion | Streamlined ridges
Mushroom rocks | Wind abrasion | Narrow bases and wider tops
Deflation hollows | Wind removal | Depressions
Playa | Evaporation or deposition | A dry lake bed
Loess | Wind deposition | A fine silt deposit
## 3. Karst landforms
Lapiaz or karren: Grooved limestone
Sinkhole or doline: A closed depression; uvala: coalesced dolines; polje: a large enclosed karst depression
Caves or caverns: Underground dissolution features
Stalactite: Hangs from a cave roof; stalagmite: rises from a cave floor
Blind valley: Terminates abruptly; swallow hole: a place where a stream disappears underground
## 4. Coastal landforms
Landform | Formation
Sea cliffs | Wave erosion
Wave-cut platforms | Cliff retreat
Sea caves | Weak zones are eroded
Sea arches | Caves enlarge through a headland
Sea stacks | Arches collapse
Sea stumps | Stacks are further eroded
Beaches | Sand or shingle accumulation
Spits | Longshore deposition
Bars | Depositional ridges across bays
Lagoon | A water body separated by a bar or spit
Tombolo | A bar connecting an island to the mainland

t: Plains and India's physiographic divisions
text:
## 1. Types of plains
Plain | Formation | Examples
Alluvial plains | River deposition | The Indo-Gangetic Plain
Flood plains | Repeated flood deposition | Along river valleys
Deltaic plains | Deposition at river mouths | The Ganga-Brahmaputra Delta
Coastal plains | Marine and fluvial deposition | The Eastern and Western Coastal Plains
Loess plains | Wind-blown silt deposition | China; other dry regions
Outwash plains | Glacial meltwater deposition | At glacial margins
## 2. India's physiographic divisions
Division | Key features
Himalayas | Young fold mountains; high relief; landslides, glaciers and valleys
Northern Plains | Vast alluvial depositional plains — contain Bhabar, Terai, Bhangar and Khadar
Peninsular Plateau | An ancient stable crystalline landmass — the Deccan, Malwa and Chotanagpur regions
Indian Desert | An arid western region — includes the Thar, dunes and the Rann
Coastal plains | Narrow in the west and broader in the east — the Konkan, Malabar, Northern Circars, Coromandel
Islands | The Andaman–Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep — volcanic, coral or tectonic origins
## 3. Indian landform facts
Chambal: Ravines and badland topography
Western Ghats rivers: Short and swift; generally estuarine mouths
Ganga-Brahmaputra: The world's major delta system
Rann of Kutch: A salt marsh — a seasonal marshy desert
Lakshadweep: Coral islands or atolls
Barren Island: An active volcano; Narcondam: volcanic and inactive-dormant

t: Composition of the atmosphere
text:
## 1. Gases
Gas | Share | Type | Role
Nitrogen (N₂) | Approximately 78% — the most abundant atmospheric gas | Permanent | An essential nutrient; a major atmospheric constituent
Oxygen (O₂) | Approximately 21% — the second most abundant | Permanent | Supports respiration and combustion
Argon (Ar) | Approximately 0.93% — a major inert gas | Permanent | An inert gas
Carbon dioxide (CO₂) | Approximately 0.04% | Variable | Supports photosynthesis; contributes to the greenhouse effect
Water vapour | Approximately 0–4% — highly variable | Variable | Humidity, clouds, precipitation, the greenhouse effect
Ozone (O₃) | Trace quantities | Variable | Absorbs (harmful) ultraviolet radiation
Dry-air composition sequence: N₂ > O₂ > Ar > CO₂
Permanent gases — nitrogen, oxygen and argon — have relatively constant proportions; variable gases vary spatially and temporally
Minor trace gases: Neon, helium, xenon, hydrogen and krypton
Greenhouse gases: Also methane and nitrous oxide (N₂O)
## 2. Vertical distribution
Carbon dioxide: Concentrated relatively low — up to approximately 20 km
Oxygen and nitrogen extend much higher than the lower atmosphere; hydrogen extends higher than nitrogen and oxygen
Water vapour: Decreases with altitude — strongly concentrated near the surface or in the troposphere; more abundant in the tropics than at the poles
Ozone: Concentrated mainly in the stratosphere
## 3. Dust and aerosols
Dust particles act as condensation nuclei; dust and moisture contribute to cloud formation
Aerosols scatter or absorb radiation; dust concentration influences atmospheric transparency and radiation
## 4. Evolution of the atmosphere
Basis | Early atmosphere | Modern atmosphere
Character | Reducing | Oxygen-rich
Oxygen | Little or no free oxygen | Significant oxygen
Gases | Carbon dioxide, methane, ammonia and water vapour among other gases | Nitrogen and oxygen dominate
Biological evolution altered the atmosphere; the biosphere and atmosphere interact

t: Layers of the atmosphere
text:
## 1. Layers at a glance
Layer | Extent | Temperature with height | Keyword / most important association
Troposphere | Surface to approximately 8 km at the poles and 18 km at the equator (0 to 8 or 18 km); average upper limit approximately 13 km | Decreases | Weather — its major identity
Stratosphere | Approximately 13 or 18 km to 50 km | Increases | Ozone — its major identity
Mesosphere | Approximately 50 km to 80 km | Decreases | Meteors — meteors burn here
Thermosphere | Begins at approximately 80 km and extends upward | Rises sharply | Ionisation and aurora; high temperatures
Exosphere | The outermost atmospheric layer — an outer limit rather than a definite height | — | Space — the outer atmospheric region and satellites
Ionosphere: Radio waves and aurora are its most important associations
## 2. Troposphere
The lowest atmospheric layer — average thickness 13 km; 8 km thick at the poles, 18 km at the equator
Normal lapse rate: 6.5°C per kilometre — approximately 1°C per 165 metres; temperature is higher near the surface than at higher altitudes and very low near the tropopause
Most atmospheric mass is concentrated here; water vapour and dust (particles) are concentrated here
Strong vertical convection and condensation occur here — almost all weather phenomena occur in the troposphere
Clouds, rainfall, storms and weather result from tropospheric water vapour, dust, convection and condensation
The most important layer for biological activity
Thicker at the equator than at the poles — the chain:
Strong solar heating causes strong convection, which transports heat upward at the equator
Strong convection causes air to rise higher; rising air causes the tropopause to rise
A higher tropopause produces a thicker troposphere
## 3. Tropopause
The upper boundary of the troposphere — the boundary between the troposphere and the stratosphere
Higher at the equator (stronger convection there) and lower at the poles
Separates the weather-dominated troposphere from the relatively stable stratosphere
## 4. Stratosphere and the ozone layer
Lies above the troposphere; extends up to 50 km
Temperature increases with altitude — ⚠ upward in the stratosphere, whereas it decreases upward in the troposphere
Ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation; this absorption converts solar energy into heat, which causes temperature to increase upward
Very little water vapour; clouds and weather very limited; relatively stable — suitable for jet aircraft
Ozone layer: Ozone gas (O₃) — an ozone molecule contains three oxygen atoms
Located mainly in the stratosphere — present mainly in the lower stratosphere; maximum concentration roughly between 15 km and 35 km
Absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation — protects life from excessive ultraviolet radiation
## 5. Mesosphere
Lies above the stratosphere — approximately 50 km to 80 km
Temperature decreases with altitude — very cold
Meteors burn or ablate here; upper boundary: the mesopause
## 6. Thermosphere and ionosphere
Thermosphere: Lies above the mesosphere — temperature rises sharply with altitude; air density extremely low; ionisation significant
Ionosphere: Electrically charged or ionised particles — traditional approximate region 80–640 km
Reflects radio waves — supports long-distance radio communication; radio communication and telecommunications are closely associated with it
Associated with auroral phenomena — aurora occurs in the upper atmosphere or ionospheric region
## 7. Aurora
Caused by solar charged particles that interact with Earth's upper atmosphere or magnetic environment
The interaction excites atmospheric particles; excited atmospheric particles produce a light display
Aurora Borealis: Northern Hemisphere; Aurora Australis: Southern Hemisphere
## 8. Exosphere
The outermost atmospheric region — very high and rarefied conditions; density extremely low
Contains predominantly very light gases; gradually merges with — transitions into — outer space
Communication satellites operate in its outer region; satellites are associated with the outer or exospheric region

t: Elements and controls of climate
text:
## 1. Elements vs factors
Elements of climate | Factors or controls of climate
Temperature | Latitude
Atmospheric pressure | Altitude
Wind | Distance from the sea or continentality
Humidity | Pressure and wind systems
Cloudiness | Relief or topography
Precipitation | Ocean currents
Sunshine or insolation | Vegetation or land cover
Temperature range | Jet streams and atmospheric circulation
## 2. The elements defined
Temperature: Measures the degree of heat — includes daily and annual ranges; controlled by latitude and altitude
Atmospheric pressure: The force exerted by air — varies with temperature and altitude
Wind: The horizontal movement of air — moves from high pressure toward low pressure
Humidity: The water vapour present in the atmosphere
Cloudiness: Condensed water or ice particles in the atmosphere
Precipitation: Water falling from the atmosphere — rain, snow, sleet and hail
Sunshine or insolation: Incoming solar energy — controls heating
Temperature range: The difference between maximum and minimum temperature

t: Temperature, pressure and wind
text:
## 1. Controls of temperature
Latitude: Temperature generally decreases from the equator toward the poles — through the solar angle
The equator receives more direct rays — greater heating; the poles receive oblique rays — lower heating
Seasonal variation increases with latitude; the annual temperature range is generally greater toward higher latitudes
Altitude: Temperature generally decreases with increasing altitude — lower temperature at higher altitude produces a cooler climate
The Himalayas are cooler despite having a lower latitude
Sea: Moderates temperature — the sea heats and cools slowly; land heats and cools rapidly
Basis | Coastal regions | Interior regions
Temperatures | Moderated | More extreme
Annual temperature range | Smaller | Larger
Climate | Equable | Extreme — continental
Ocean currents: Warm currents raise coastal temperatures; cold currents lower them
Relief: Alters temperature and air movement; mountain slopes and aspects affect temperature
## 2. Clouds and temperature
Cloud cover modifies heating and cooling — affects day and night temperature
Sky | Day | Night
Cloudy | Reduces incoming solar radiation — cooler daytime temperatures | Reduces terrestrial heat loss — warmer nights
Clear | Greater solar heating | Greater terrestrial cooling
## 3. Temperature and pressure
Increasing temperature → air expands → air density decreases → low pressure
Decreasing temperature → air contracts → air density increases → high pressure
Increasing — higher — altitude decreases atmospheric pressure — lower atmospheric pressure occurs at higher altitude
Temperature differences create pressure differences
## 4. Wind
Horizontal pressure differences produce wind — the pressure gradient initiates wind; a greater pressure gradient produces stronger winds
Earth's rotation deflects wind — the Coriolis force; latitude changes the Coriolis effect
Relief channels and blocks winds; mountain relief modifies rainfall and wind
Pressure belts control major global circulation
Seasonal heating causes seasonal wind reversal

t: Humidity and precipitation
text:
## 1. Humidity
Absolute humidity: The actual mass of water vapour per unit volume
Relative humidity: Actual moisture divided by moisture-holding capacity, multiplied by 100
Warm air can hold more water vapour; cold air can hold less
Dew point: The temperature at which air becomes saturated
Condensation: Changes water vapour into liquid or solid form; clouds form through condensation around nuclei at altitude
## 2. Types of precipitation
Type | Mechanism | Typical location
Convectional | Strong heating, rising air, cooling and condensation | The Western Ghats — the example location given
Cyclonic or frontal | Convergence or frontal uplift, rising air, cooling and condensation | Temperate regions
Relief-induced | Topography modifies rainfall distribution | Differs between windward and leeward locations
## 3. Relief and rainfall
Mountains block or redirect air masses
Windward slopes receive orographic rainfall; leeward slopes form rain shadows
The Western Ghats produce a strong rainfall contrast across their slopes
The Himalayas block cold continental winds and influence the monsoon

t: Monsoon, ocean currents and jet streams
text:
## 1. Monsoon mechanism
Summer heating produces low pressure over heated land; a pressure gradient draws moisture-bearing winds
The ITCZ shifts northward during summer — this northward shift helps monsoon circulation
Winter cooling reverses the pressure pattern — seasonal pressure reversal, which causes seasonal wind reversal
## 2. Ocean currents and climate
Warm currents: Warm adjoining coastal air; increase moisture availability; can moderate cold coastal climates
Cold currents: Cool adjoining coasts; can suppress convection
Cold currents combined with subtropical highs are often associated with arid west-coast climates
## 3. Jet streams and teleconnections
Subtropical Westerly Jet: Connected with winter weather and Western Disturbances
Western Disturbances: Winter precipitation over northwestern India
Tropical Easterly Jet: Supports summer monsoon circulation
ENSO or El Niño: Generally weakens the Indian monsoon
IOD: Modulates monsoon variability — a positive IOD can partly offset the effect of El Niño
SST anomalies: Influence atmospheric circulation and rainfall

t: Air masses
text:
## 1. Nature
An air mass: A large body of air with relatively uniform temperature and humidity
Forms over a source region with uniform surface properties — the source region may be land or ocean
Classified on the basis of the temperature and moisture content of their source regions
Control temperature, humidity, stability and precipitation
## 2. Types
Source region | Properties | Designation
Tropical oceans | Warm and moist | mT — maritime Tropical
Tropical land areas | Warm and dry | cT — continental Tropical
Polar oceans | Cold and moist | mP — maritime Polar
Polar land areas | Cold and dry | cP — continental Polar
Arctic and Antarctic | Extremely cold and dry | cA or cAA
## 3. Modification
An air mass travels away from its source region and gets modified — it loses its original characteristics
Passes over | Change
A warm surface | Warmer and more unstable
A cold surface | Cooler and more stable
An ocean | Gains moisture
Land | Loses moisture — becomes drier
Vertical mixing alters the temperature and humidity profile
## 4. Climatic effects
A new air mass can cause a sudden rise or fall in temperature
Seasonal shifts in air masses produce seasonal climatic changes — e.g. monsoon winds
Persistent air-mass influence creates characteristic regional climates — e.g. maritime and continental climates
Air masses and fronts can produce cold waves, heat waves, thunderstorms and blizzards

t: Fronts
text:
## 1. Nature
A front: A boundary zone between two contrasting air masses — forms when two air masses with different temperatures and humidity meet
Lighter, warmer air is forced to rise over denser, colder air
Mid-latitude cyclones form along fronts; frontal uplift produces cyclonic or frontal rainfall
## 2. Types of front
Front | Formation | Uplift | Weather
Warm front | Warm air advances over cold air | Gradual | Widespread light to moderate rain
Cold front | Cold air undercuts warm air | Steep | Intense short-duration rain and thunderstorms
Occluded front | A cold front overtakes a warm front | — | Complex weather — often prolonged precipitation
Stationary front | Neither air mass advances | — | Prolonged cloudy and rainy conditions
## 3. The uplift chain
Uplift at a front forces air to rise — the uplift of warm air produces cooling
Adiabatic cooling causes temperature to fall to the dew point — condensation begins when air cools to the dew point
Condensation changes water vapour into liquid or ice particles — cloud formation results — clouds and precipitation
Precipitation occurs when droplets grow and fall — rain, snow or sleet
Final impact: Changes in wind, temperature, humidity and pressure; in weather systems and climatic patterns

t: Atmospheric disturbances at a glance
text:
## 1. Types and scale
Disturbance | Nature | Scale
Tropical cyclone | A low-pressure system over warm tropical oceans | Large-scale
Temperate or extratropical cyclone | A mid-latitude cyclone associated with air-mass interaction | Large-scale
Anticyclone | A high-pressure centre; outward-moving air | Large-scale
Thunderstorm | A violent convective storm with lightning and thunder | Local
Tornado or twister | A violently rotating, funnel-shaped disturbance | Very local
Western Disturbance | An extratropical storm affecting northwest India | Regional
Cloudburst | Intense localized rainfall | Local
Local squall or local storm | Sudden, violent, gusty wind associated with a storm | —
## 2. Comparison
Basis | Tropical cyclone | Temperate cyclone | Anticyclone | Thunderstorm | Tornado
Occur mainly | The tropics | The mid-latitudes | Various regions | Many regions | Severe-storm regions
Major mechanism | Warm ocean plus convection | Air-mass interaction and fronts | Subsidence | Strong convection | Severe rotating convection
Fronts | ⚠ Not characteristic | Characteristic | Not characteristic | Not characteristic | Not characteristic
Clouds | Cumulonimbus and rainbands — the major cloud | Stratiform and cumuliform | Generally clear skies | Cumulonimbus | Cumulonimbus supercell
## 3. Clouds
Cumulus: Convective development
Cumulonimbus: Thunderstorms, heavy rain and hail
Nimbostratus: Prolonged precipitation
Cirrostratus: A high-altitude cloud

t: Tropical cyclones
text:
## 1. Conditions for formation
Condition | Role
Warm sea-surface temperature — a warm tropical ocean | Supplies heat and moisture — the energy source
Warm, moist air | Provides latent-heat energy; moisture fuels convection
Coriolis force | Provides and maintains rotational circulation
An unstable troposphere — instability | Supports vigorous vertical convection
Low vertical wind shear | Lets the vertical structure remain organised — maintains vertical organisation
A pre-existing disturbance — an initial disturbance | The initial low-pressure or convergence centre — the seed
Sufficient distance from the Equator | Lets the Coriolis force become effective
⚠ The Coriolis force is too weak near the Equator for tropical cyclones to form exactly there
## 2. Structure
Centre: The region of lowest pressure
Eye: The central region of comparatively light winds and fair weather; higher temperature
Eyewall: The most intense zone — strong winds, heavy rainfall and thunderstorms
Spiral rainbands: Curved cloud bands that produce rain and wind
Rotation: Anticlockwise in the Northern Hemisphere; clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere
## 3. Regional names
Region | Name
USA and the Atlantic region | Hurricane
China and the western Pacific; the South China Sea | Typhoon
Northern and northwestern Australia | Willy-Willy
India | Cyclone
Nargis: An example in Myanmar

t: Cyclones vs anticyclones
text:
## 1. Comparison
Basis | Cyclone | Anticyclone
Centre | Low-pressure | High-pressure
Air movement | Inward; air rises | Outward; air descends
Weather | Cloudier and stormier | Generally clearer
Northern Hemisphere rotation | Anticlockwise | Clockwise
Southern Hemisphere rotation | Clockwise | Anticlockwise

t: Temperate cyclones, Western Disturbances and tornadoes
text:
## 1. Temperate or extratropical cyclones
Occur mainly in the mid-latitudes — approximately 35°–65° in both hemispheres
Main wind influence: Westerlies — generally move from west to east
Key mechanism: Interaction of contrasting air masses; associated with fronts
Indian example: The Western Disturbance
## 2. Western Disturbances
An extratropical or cyclonic disturbance — originates in the Mediterranean region
Steered by the westerlies and the Subtropical Westerly Jet
Occur mainly in winter; main region affected: northwestern India
Bring winter rainfall and snowfall to mountains — agriculturally important for Rabi crops
Rainfall decreases from west to east across the northwestern plain
## 3. Tornadoes in the tornado-prone USA
The Gulf of Mexico supplies warm, moisture-rich air
Cold, drier continental air and atmospheric instability contribute to tornado formation
Strong wind shear produces severe thunderstorms or supercells, which create tornado potential

t: Ocean temperature and density
text:
## 1. Temperature
Ocean surface temperature: Mainly controlled by latitude and insolation
Generally decreases with depth
Basis | Surface ocean water | Deep ocean water
Temperature | Relatively warm | Colder
Density | Less dense | Denser
Ocean temperature influences ocean density, ocean circulation and marine life
## 2. Density
Depends mainly on temperature and salinity
Higher salinity generally produces higher density; lower temperature generally produces higher density
## 3. "-cline" layers
Layer | Indicates | Prefix
Thermocline | A layer where temperature changes rapidly with depth | "thermo" — temperature
Halocline | Rapid salinity change with depth | "halo" — salt
Pycnocline | Rapid density change with depth — a density-gradient layer; drives deep-ocean circulation | "pycno" — density

t: Ocean salinity
text:
## 1. Basics
Average ocean salinity: Approximately 35‰ — approximately 35 grams of dissolved salts per 1 kilogram of seawater
Main source of ocean salts: Land; rivers are the major carriers of salts to the ocean
Controls of salinity: Evaporation, precipitation, river water, winds, ocean currents, volcanoes
Isohalines: Represent salinity on maps
## 2. Dissolved salts
Salt | Share of dissolved salts
Sodium chloride — the major contribution | Approximately 77.8%
Magnesium chloride | Approximately 10.9%
Magnesium sulphate | Approximately 4.7%
Calcium sulphate | Approximately 3.6%
Potassium sulphate | Approximately 2.5%
Calcium carbonate | Approximately 0.3%
Magnesium bromide | Approximately 0.2%
## 3. Distribution of salinity
Region | Salinity | Reason
Equatorial regions | Relatively lower | Heavy rainfall
Subtropical and desert belts — the 20°–40° N/S belts | Higher — generally high | High / strong evaporation; low humidity
Polar regions | Relatively lower | Low evaporation; freshwater from ice melt; rivers
## 4. Seas
Sea | Salinity | Reason
Arabian Sea | Approximately 36‰ — higher | Higher evaporation
Bay of Bengal | Approximately 30‰ — lower | Large freshwater input
Red Sea | Very high — extremely saline water | High evaporation; very low precipitation; river input is very limited; a narrow connection through Bab-el-Mandeb

t: Waves, tides and tsunamis
text:
## 1. Waves vs tides vs currents
Basis | Waves | Tides | Ocean currents
Nature | Oscillatory movements of water — mainly transfer energy | Vertical and periodic changes in water level — periodic changes in sea level | Continuous directed movements of water — horizontal movement of water
Driver | Wind — the main driver | Moon-, Sun- and Earth-related forces | Winds, density differences, the Coriolis force, pressure differences; influenced by coastline and ocean-floor configuration
Timing | Variable | Highly periodic | Relatively continuous
Effect | Coastal erosion and deposition — coastal erosion is a key effect | Tidal energy; key patterns — spring and neap tides | Climate, fisheries and navigation; direction and warm- or cold-water characteristics
## 2. Spring vs neap tides
Basis | Spring tide | Neap tide
Sun, Earth and Moon | Aligned | At right angles
Moon phase | New moon or full moon | First quarter or third quarter
Gravitational effects | Reinforce each other | Partially opposing
Tidal range | Maximum | Minimum
## 3. Tsunamis
Long-wavelength destructive sea disturbances — ⚠ different causes from ordinary wind-driven waves

t: Ocean currents
text:
## 1. Drivers
Surface currents: Driven mainly by prevailing winds and Earth's rotation — winds drive surface water
Trade winds drive major surface currents; westerlies drive mid-latitude currents
Deep-ocean currents: Driven by density differences caused (produced) by temperature and salinity — temperature and salinity each change water density
Coriolis effect: Earth's rotation deflects moving water — deflects ocean currents
Differential heating: Creates temperature and density differences
Coastline configuration: Controls, deflects or redirects currents; ocean-floor configuration / relief modifies current direction — influences current pathways
Others: Tides (control currents; cause water movement; contribute to ocean-water movement); gravity; air pressure (influences surface-water movement); seasonal winds — seasonal current changes
## 2. Warm vs cold currents
Basis | Warm currents | Cold currents
Water | Relatively warmer — generally moved toward higher latitudes | Relatively colder — generally moved toward lower latitudes
Origin | Often lower latitudes | Often higher-latitude or cold-water regions
Coastal effect | Can warm adjacent coastal areas | Can cool adjacent coastal areas
Ocean currents redistribute heat and influence climate
## 3. Major currents
Current | Type | Ocean / region
Gulf Stream | Warm | North Atlantic
North Atlantic Drift | Warm | North Atlantic Ocean — flows toward Europe
Norwegian Current | Warm | North Atlantic Ocean — the Norwegian coast
Kuroshio | Warm | —
Brazil Current | Warm | South Atlantic Ocean — the east coast of Brazil
Agulhas Current | Warm | The Indian Ocean and southeastern Africa — or the South Indian Ocean
Mozambique Current | Warm | Indian Ocean — the Mozambique Channel
Labrador Current | Cold | —
Falkland Current | Cold | —
Canary Current | Cold | North Atlantic Ocean — northwestern Africa
Benguela Current | Cold | South Atlantic Ocean — southwestern Africa
Humboldt or Peru Current | Cold | Pacific Ocean — the west coast of South America
California Current | Cold | Pacific Ocean — the west coast of North America

t: Marine life, coral reefs and acidification
text:
## 1. Marine organisms
Plankton: Organisms that drift with water
Phytoplankton: Primary producers; zooplankton: animal plankton — part of the food chain
Nekton: Actively swimming organisms
Benthos: Organisms associated with the ocean bottom
## 2. Coral reefs
Highly diverse marine ecosystems — extremely rich marine habitats
Form through consolidation of the skeletons of marine organisms and coral polyps
Distribution: Mainly tropical and semi-tropical waters — typically around 25°N–25°S; some extend to approximately 30° latitude
Major concentrations: Australia, Indonesia, the Philippines
Great Barrier Reef: The largest coral reef system — in Australia (the largest coral reef is near Australia), in the Pacific Ocean, near the Queensland coast
Addu Atoll: In the Indian Ocean
Atoll: A ring-shaped coral island or reef structure surrounding a lagoon — a circular or horseshoe shape; in a tropical or subtropical marine setting
## 3. Ocean acidification
Atmospheric carbon dioxide increases; the ocean absorbs more carbon dioxide
Carbonic acid formation → ocean pH falls → carbonate availability decreases
Decreased carbonate availability affects calcareous organisms — calcareous phytoplankton, coral reefs and some marine organisms
⚠ Does not necessarily affect cloud formation

t: Types of hydrological disaster
text:
## 1. Types and effects
Disaster | Nature | Effects
River flood | River discharge exceeds channel capacity | Inundation; crop damage; property damage
Flash flood | Sudden high-intensity runoff or discharge | Very rapid destruction
Urban flood | Rainfall combined with inadequate urban drainage | Waterlogging; disrupts infrastructure
Cloudburst | Extremely intense localized rainfall | Flash floods; landslides
Dam failure | Structural or operational failure followed by sudden water release | Catastrophic downstream flooding
Coastal flooding | Storm surge, tidal action or wave action affecting a low-lying coast | Inundation; salinity
Drought | A prolonged water deficit | Affects agriculture, water supply and ecosystems
## 2. Causes of flooding
Cause | Effect
Heavy rainfall | Discharge rises rapidly
Cloudburst | Very intense rainfall over a small area
Snowmelt | A sudden increase in river flow
Siltation | Reduces channel depth or capacity
Embankment failure | Water escapes the channel
Deforestation | Increases runoff
Urbanisation | Increases runoff through impervious surfaces
Floodplain encroachment | Increases human exposure
Poor drainage | Water accumulates
Dam failure | Sudden downstream discharge
## 3. Secondary hazards
Primary | Secondary hazard
Cloudburst | Flash flood
Flash flood | Landslide
River flood | Bank erosion
Flood | Water contamination; disease risk; crop or livelihood loss
Coastal flood | Salinity intrusion
Dam failure | Downstream flash flooding
Urban flood | Traffic or infrastructure collapse

t: Flash floods, cloudbursts, urban floods and dam failure
text:
## 1. Flash floods
Very rapid onset; very short warning time
Triggers: Intense rainfall or a cloudburst; sudden water release; steep terrain
Vulnerable: Mountains; steep catchments; urban areas — highly vulnerable
Main dangers: High flow velocity; debris
Associated with landslides, erosion and infrastructure damage
## 2. Cloudburst vs ordinary heavy rainfall
Basis | Cloudburst | Ordinary heavy rainfall
Area | Highly localized | May cover a larger area
Intensity | Extremely intense | Can have varying intensity
Timing | Sudden | Can be prolonged
Runoff | Rapid runoff | Depends on duration and intensity
Flood potential | Strong flash-flood potential | Depends on basin conditions
## 3. Causes of urban flooding
Intense rainfall; cloudbursts; cyclone rainfall
Encroachment of drains; wetland destruction; impervious surfaces; poor storm-water drainage
High river discharge; high tides or storm surge
Unplanned urbanisation; low-lying terrain; floodplain construction
## 4. Causes of dam failure
Structural: A weak foundation; foundation instability; material failure; design failure
Natural: An extreme flood exceeding design capacity; landslides; earthquakes; extreme rainfall
Management: Improper reservoir management; poor inspection; poor maintenance
Overtopping: Water exceeds the dam crest
Sedimentation: Reduces dam storage capacity
## 5. Coastal flooding
A cyclone produces a storm surge; a high tide produces a higher baseline water level
Heavy coastal rainfall causes drainage congestion
Sea-level rise increases coastal exposure; a low-lying delta experiences greater inundation
Salinity intrusion: Agricultural and water impacts

t: Flood management
text:
## 1. Risk-reduction measures
Measure | Purpose
Hazard mapping | Identifies risk zones
Flood forecasting | Provides early warning
Drainage planning | Reduces urban waterlogging
Wetland protection | Preserves natural storage
Floodplain zoning | Prevents exposure
Dam safety | Prevents catastrophic release
Embankment maintenance | Reduces breach risk
Community preparedness | Improves response
## 2. Structural vs non-structural measures
Structural | Non-structural
Dams and reservoirs | Flood forecasting
Embankments | Early warning
Drainage systems | Floodplain zoning
Retention basins | Building regulations
Channel improvement | Awareness
Storm-water infrastructure | Insurance or risk transfer
Coastal protection | Disaster preparedness
## 3. Disaster sequence
During a disaster: Early warning → evacuation → rescue → shelters → emergency medical or water supply
After a disaster: Relief → restoration → reconstruction → resilient rebuilding
## 4. Nature-based buffers
Wetlands: Store excess water; floodplains: temporary water storage
Mangroves: Buffer coastal hazards
Forests: Increase infiltration and interception
Riparian vegetation: Stabilises banks
Urban green infrastructure: Increases infiltration; reduces runoff

t: Aravalli and Central Indian ranges
text:
## 1. Aravalli Range
Located in Rajasthan, Haryana and Delhi — its northern extension reaches Delhi
One of the oldest mountain ranges — geological age about 570 million years; a residual mountain range
Highest peak: Guru Shikhar — 1,722 metres; Sirohi district, Rajasthan
## 2. Vindhyan and Satpura
Vindhyan Range: Central India — north of the Narmada Valley; part of the central Indian highlands
Mukandara Hills: An extension of the Vindhyan Range — southeastern Rajasthan
Satpura Range: Central India — between the Narmada and Tapi valleys (flanked by the Narmada River and the Tapti River); part of the Deccan Plateau
A major Central Indian range — an important physiographic range
The Vindhya and Satpura converge at Amarkantak
## 3. Satpura system
Mahadeo Range (Hills): Central India — Madhya Pradesh; part of the Satpura system; associated with the Maikal Range
Maikal Range: The Madhya Pradesh–Chhattisgarh region — the eastern part of the Satpura system; part of the central Indian highlands
Kaimur Range: Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar
## 4. Maharashtra and Gujarat
Satmala Hills, Harishchandra Range, Balaghat Range: Maharashtra
Mandav Hills: Gujarat
## 5. Eastern India
Dalma Hills: Jharkhand — the Chotanagpur region; the Eastern Indian hill system
Parasnath Hill: Giridih district, Jharkhand — 1,365 metres; associated with Shikharji — the Shikharji Jain Temple

text:

Karnataka | Karnataka

## 2. Deccan Plateau
Peninsular India — extends across Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu
Extensive basaltic and lava formations; forms a major part of the Peninsular Plateau; associated with Peninsular India
## 3. Malwa and Bundelkhand
Malwa Plateau: Extends across Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan — lies (is situated) between the Aravalli Range and the Vindhya Range
The Aravalli lies north; the Vindhya lies south; Bundelkhand lies east — it extends eastward to Bundelkhand
Bundelkhand Plateau: Central India — mainly Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh; east of the Malwa Plateau, forming its eastern border (the Malwa lies west of it)
## 4. Chota Nagpur Plateau
Mainly in Jharkhand — the maximum part lies there; extends into Odisha, West Bengal, Bihar and Chhattisgarh
Mineral-rich; includes the Patland region
Ranchi, Hazaribagh and Palamu Plateaus: Jharkhand — belong to the Chota Nagpur region; each is a Patland Plateau — an important component of the Patland region
## 5. Meghalaya Plateau
A northeastern extension of the Peninsular Plateau — includes the Garo, Khasi and Jaintia Hills
⚠ The Bhuban Hills are distinct from the Meghalaya Plateau
## 6. Dandakaranya
Extends across Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Telangana, Maharashtra and Andhra Pradesh — the central-eastern Peninsular region
Covers approximately 89,078 square kilometres; extends approximately 480 kilometres from east to west
## 7. Other plateaus
Bhander Plateau: Madhya Pradesh — belongs to the Vindhyan region; the southern part of the Vindhyan Scarpland; associated with the Vindhya Mountains
Amarkantak Plateau: A Central Indian highland — belongs to the Vindhyan–Satpura complex; an important highland of the Vindhya–Satpura region; a Central Indian physiographic association
Karnataka Plateau: Karnataka — the interior of Peninsular India; includes Malnad — also called Malenadu — mountainous and densely forested in western Karnataka
Coimbatore Plateau: Tamil Nadu — around Coimbatore; the southern Peninsular region — part of the southern Peninsular plateau system

t: The Ganga system
text:
## 1. Course of the Ganga
Bhagirathi: Originates at Gomukh in Uttarkashi district, Uttarakhand — Uttarkashi is situated on it
Alaknanda: Originates at Satopanth Glacier above Badrinath
Alaknanda and Bhagirathi meet at Devprayag, Uttarakhand, to form the Ganga
Enters the plains at Haridwar; flows through Farakka in West Bengal before entering Bangladesh — known as Padma in Bangladesh
## 2. Tributaries of the Ganga
Bank | Tributaries
Left-bank | Ramganga, Gomati, Ghaghara, Gandak, Kosi, Mahananda
Right-bank | Yamuna — the longest tributary of the Ganga; Son
## 3. Left-bank tributaries in detail
Ramganga: Joins Ganga near Kannauj, Uttar Pradesh
Ghaghra (Ghaghara): Originates at Mapchachungo Glacier; meets Ganga at Revilganj in Saran district, Bihar
Sharda — also called Kali — joins the Ghaghra in the plains, before the Ghaghara meets the Ganga
Gandak: Originates in the Nepal Himalayas; joins Ganga at Sonpur near Patna, Bihar
Kosi: Tributaries — Sun Kosi, Arun Kosi, Tamur Kosi
Mahananda: The last left-bank tributary of Ganga — joins Ganga in West Bengal
## 4. Son and Damodar
Son: Originates at Amarkantak Hill; joins Ganga near Patna, Bihar
Tributaries: Johilla, Mahanadi, Banas, Gopad, Rihand, Ghogher, Kanhar, North Koel
Damodar: Originates at Khamarpat Hill in the Chota Nagpur Plateau; flows through a rift valley; joins — flows into — the Hugli
Tributaries: Barakar — the main tributary; Konar, Jamunia, Barki
Chain: Barakar flows into the Damodar → Damodar flows into the Hugli — the Barakar–Damodar–Hugli chain

Bank | Tributaries of the Yamuna
Right-bank | Chambal, Sindh, Betwa, Ken
Left-bank | Tons, Hanuman Ganga, Sasur Khaderi
Tributary chain: Chambal, then Sindh, then Betwa, then Ken — Sindh is shown in the tributary chain of Chambal; Betwa is shown after Sindh; Ken is shown after Betwa
## 2. Chambal
Originates near Dr. Ambedkar Nagar (Mhow) in Madhya Pradesh
Flows through Sawai Madhopur and Dholpur in Rajasthan before joining Yamuna — Chambal joins Yamuna
Tributaries: Kali Sindh, Parvati, Kshipra

## 2. Major tributaries
Major tributaries of the Brahmaputra: Dibang, Lohit, Subansiri, Kameng (also called Jia Bharali), Sankosh, Manas, Burhi Dihing, Dhansiri, Kopili (or Kapili), Teesta
Tributary | Key facts
Dibang | Flows across Dibang Valley and Lower Dibang Valley districts of Arunachal Pradesh
Kameng | Flows through Arunachal Pradesh and Assam
Lohit | Originates in eastern Tibet; flows through Arunachal Pradesh and Assam
Subansiri | Originates in Tibet; flows through Arunachal Pradesh and Assam
Sankosh | Originates in northern Bhutan; joins Brahmaputra near the Assam–West Bengal border — forms the boundary between Assam and West Bengal
Teesta | Flows through Sikkim and West Bengal; joins Brahmaputra in Bangladesh
Rangeet | Originates in Sikkim — a tributary of the Teesta
Manas and Kopili are tributaries of the Brahmaputra

t: The Indus system
text:
## 1. Tributaries
Major tributaries of the Indus: Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, Sutlej — Chenab is the largest tributary
Chain: Chenab receives Jhelum and Ravi (Ravi joins Chenab in Pakistan); Sutlej receives Chenab; Sutlej joins Indus
## 2. Rivers in detail
River | Key facts
Jhelum | Originates at Verinag at the foot of the Pir Panjal; flows through Srinagar and Wular Lake; enters Pakistan through a deep and narrow gorge
Kishanganga | A tributary of the Jhelum — called (known as) Neelum in Pakistan
Sutlej | Tributaries: Beas, Spiti, Baspa; Ludhiana and Firozpur lie on its old bank
Spiti | Originates at Kunzam La; joins Sutlej near Khab in Kinnaur district, Himachal Pradesh
Zanskar | Lies near Sarchu on the border of Himachal Pradesh and Ladakh; joins Indus at Nimu
Indus | Leh lies on its right bank

t: Peninsular rivers
text:
## 1. Godavari
Originates at Nasik, or Nashik, in Maharashtra — flows from Nashik through Maharashtra, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh; forms a delta on the eastern coast
Towns: Nanded, Nashik, Rajamahendravaram
Principal tributaries: Pravara, Purna, Manjra (also called Manjira), Penganga, Wardha, Wainganga, Pranhita, Indravati, Maner, Sabari
## 2. Krishna
Originates at Mahabaleshwar in Maharashtra — Vijayawada and Srisailam are situated on it
Major tributaries: Koyna, Yerla, Varna, Panchganga, Ghataprabha, Bhima, Tungabhadra
Tungabhadra flows into the Krishna; Hagari — also called Vedavathi — joins the Tungabhadra, flowing from the Western Ghats through Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh
Musi: A tributary of Krishna — associated with Hyderabad
## 3. Mahanadi
Origin: Sihawa; flows through Cuttack
Kuakhai: Part of the Mahanadi delta — associated with Bhubaneswar
Bank | Tributaries of the Mahanadi
Left-bank | Seonath (also called Shivnath), Hasdeo, Mand, Ib
Right-bank | Ong, Tel, Jonk
## 4. Cauvery
Tiruchirappalli is situated on it; Shivasamudram is associated with it
Tributaries: Bhavani, Hemavathi
## 5. Narmada and Tapi
Narmada: Originates at Amarkantak in the Maikal Range — flows west through a rift valley to the Arabian Sea; the Narmada Valley lies between the Vindhya and Satpura ranges
Jabalpur and Bhedaghat are situated on it; Dhuandhar Falls and Kapildhara Falls (Anuppur district, Madhya Pradesh) are associated with it
Tributary: Tawa
Tapi: Originates at Multai in Betul district, Madhya Pradesh — flows through Surat, Gujarat; flows westward to the Arabian Sea
## 6. Other rivers
Mahi: Originates in Rajasthan's Banswara district — enters Madhya Pradesh and enters Rajasthan; flows southwest into the Gulf of Khambhat; crosses the Tropic of Cancer twice
Luni: Originates southwest of Ajmer in Rajasthan in the Aravalli region — flows through the south-eastern Thar to the Rann of Kutch in Gujarat
Kali: Rises near Diggi village in Uttara Kannada, Karnataka — flows westward to the Arabian Sea
Mithi: Originates at Vihar Lake in Mumbai — Powai Lake water joins it; joins the Arabian Sea near the Bay of Mahim
Subarnarekha: Tributary — Kharkai

t: Rainfall zones of India
text:
## 1. Zones
Zone | Areas
Very heavy | The Western Coast and Northeast India
Heavy | The Western Ghats and Meghalaya
Moderate | Most of the Northern Plains and parts of Central India
Scanty | Western Rajasthan, Gujarat, Punjab, Haryana and the rain-shadow Deccan
Very scanty | Western Rajasthan and the Thar region
## 2. Heaviest rainfall
The Western Coast receives the heaviest rainfall — the Western Ghats and the west coast
Key regions: Kerala; coastal Karnataka; the Konkan coast and Maharashtra
## 3. Low-rainfall areas
Important rain-shadow areas: The interior of Maharashtra and Karnataka; Telangana; Andhra Pradesh; Tamil Nadu
The eastern and Deccan Ghats side of the Western Ghats has rain-shadow and low-rainfall conditions
Western Rajasthan: Scanty — very low annual rainfall, as in the Thar Desert

t: Causes of rainfall patterns
text:
## 1. Western Coast
The Arabian Sea branch of the Southwest Monsoon causes heavy rainfall — moist winds strike the Western Ghats, which produce (heavy) orographic rainfall
The Western Coast receives rainfall from the Arabian Sea branch in association with the Western Ghats
## 2. Meghalaya
Very heavy rainfall — extremely heavy from the Meghalaya Hills; the Garo, Khasi and Jaintia Hills
Caused by the Bay of Bengal branch and orographic uplift — Meghalaya receives rainfall from the Bay of Bengal branch in association with its hills
Famous locations: Mawsynram and Cherrapunji — orographic uplift causes rainfall at both
## 3. Barriers
Himalayas: An orographic barrier — help confine the monsoon
Aravallis: Little orographic rainfall in Rajasthan because the winds run roughly parallel to them — Western Rajasthan has scanty rainfall because the Aravallis do not provide an effective barrier
Interior Deccan: Low rainfall because of the Western Ghats rain shadow
## 4. Other sources
Tamil Nadu coast: Rainfall from the Northeast or retreating monsoon
Northwestern India: Winter rainfall from Western Disturbances — important areas: Jammu and Kashmir; Punjab; Haryana and the adjoining plains
