t: Alluvial soil
text:
## 1. Nature
Deposited by rivers — highly fertile; the largest and most widespread soil group
Generally rich in potash, phosphoric acid and lime; generally poor in nitrogen and humus
## 2. Where it occurs
States: Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal, Assam — the Northern Plains contain alluvial soil
Deltas — deltaic alluvium: The Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Cauvery Deltas
Valleys: The Narmada and Tapi Valleys
## 3. Khadar, Bhangar, Bhabar and Tarai
Term | Nature
Khadar | New alluvium — deposited by floods; renewed frequently; generally more fertile than older alluvium
Bhangar | Old alluvium — on higher ground, beyond normal flood reach; contains calcareous concretions called kankar
Bhabar | A coarse alluvial belt below the Shiwalik Hills — streams disappear into its permeable sediments
Tarai | A marshy lowland — south of Bhabar

t: Black, red and laterite soils
text:
## 1. Black soil
Mainly across the Deccan Plateau — Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Karnataka, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu
Developed largely from basaltic or lava rocks
Very high water retention; clayey; develops cracks on drying
Black because of its mineral composition — particularly iron- and titanium-related constituents
## 2. Red soil
Mainly across Peninsular India — Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, parts of Maharashtra
Forms through the weathering of ancient crystalline igneous and metamorphic rocks
Red colour because of iron — the iron concentration is associated with its colour
## 3. Laterite soil
Develops in the Western Ghats, Eastern Ghats, South Maharashtra, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, West Bengal, Kerala, Jharkhand, Assam, Meghalaya
Forms under high temperature and heavy rainfall, where wet and dry seasons alternate
Formation: Intense leaching — removal of silica and lime; accumulation of iron and aluminium oxides
Generally of low fertility

t: Desert and saline soils
text:
## 1. Desert or arid soil
Western Rajasthan; the Thar Desert; parts of Gujarat
Sandy; low organic matter; low moisture retention; often affected by salinity or alkalinity
## 2. Saline or alkaline soil
Saline soil: Contains excess soluble salts
Occurs in Gujarat, Rajasthan, Punjab and Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and other irrigated or arid regions
Largest area of saline soil: Gujarat; maximum alkali area: Uttar Pradesh

t: Rivers of Africa and the Americas
text:
## 1. Africa
Nile:
The White Nile originates in Lake Victoria; the Blue Nile in Lake Tana (Ethiopia)
They meet at Khartoum (Sudan); the Nile flows into the Mediterranean Sea
The Nile basin has 11 countries — ⚠ Chad is not in the Nile basin
Egypt: Known as the "Gift of the Nile"
Congo: Drains into the Atlantic Ocean — the Congo Basin is the world's second-largest tropical rainforest and the world's largest tropical peatland
Zambezi: Africa — has (associated with) Victoria Falls; Kariba Dam; forms part of the Zambia–Zimbabwe boundary; drains into the Indian Ocean
Niger: West Africa — the "Oil River" of West Africa; associated with the historical palm-oil trade; an inland delta; the Niger Delta is a major petroleum region; drains into the Atlantic Ocean
## 2. South America
Amazon: Originates in the Andes, in Peru — flows mainly through Brazil; drains into the Atlantic Ocean
Orinoco: Flows through Venezuela and Colombia
Paraná–Paraguay river system: Important for the Southern Cone
## 3. North America
Mississippi: A bird's-foot delta; originates in Lake Itasca; drains into the Atlantic Ocean
The Mississippi–Missouri is a combined river system — very long
Colorado: USA — cuts (carved) the Grand Canyon; Lake Mead and Hoover Dam; ⚠ not on the Mississippi
St. Lawrence: Connects the Great Lakes to the Atlantic Ocean
Rio Grande: A major section of the USA–Mexico international boundary — called Río Bravo in Mexico

t: Rivers of Asia and Europe
text:
## 1. Asia
Yangtze: The Three Gorges Dam — the world's largest hydroelectric power project; associated with the Pacific / East China Sea category
Huang He — also known (called) as the Yellow River:
Called the "Sorrow of China" — "China's sorrow"
A high sediment load — heavy silt — due to erosion of the Loess Plateau
Drains into the Bohai Sea
Mekong: The "Danube of the East" — flows through China, Myanmar, Laos, Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam
⚠ Does not flow through Malaysia; drains into the South China Sea — not the Andaman Sea; associated with the Pacific / East China Sea category
Amur: The Far East of Russia and China
Ob, Yenisei and Lena: Siberian rivers — flow north across Siberia into the Arctic Ocean; spring ice blockage contributes to flooding
Amu Darya and Syr Darya: Central Asia — drain into the Aral Sea; their diversion for irrigation contributed to the shrinkage of the Aral Sea
Tigris and Euphrates: The twin rivers of Mesopotamia — meet to form the Shatt al-Arab; ultimately drain into the Persian Gulf
## 2. Europe
Volga: Drains into the landlocked Caspian Sea — the Caspian Sea is endorheic
Rhine: Flows through Europe — Switzerland, Germany and the Netherlands; enters the North Sea near Rotterdam; associated with a rift valley; an important waterway
Danube: Drains into the Black Sea
Dnieper: Drains into the Black Sea
Thames: Drains into the North Sea — ⚠ not the Irish Sea

Asian (AH1) Highway | 20,557 km | Tokyo (Japan) to the Turkey–Bulgaria border | The longest route in the Asian Highway Network
Highway 1 | 14,500 km | Australia — circles the entire Australian continent | The longest continuous national highway
Trans-Siberian Highway | 11,000 km | St. Petersburg to Vladivostok in Russia — extends across Russia | The longest highway network within a single country after Australia's Highway 1
## 2. Networks and routes
Asian Highway Network: Extends across Asia — an international road network promoted by UNESCAP
Trans-African Highways: Extend across Africa — a network of planned major roads; e.g. the Tripoli–Cape Town route
Silk Road or Silk Route: From China through Central Asia to Europe — a historic trade route involving land and sea routes; ⚠ not a single modern highway
Golden Quadrilateral: India — connects Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata

t: Sea routes and chokepoints
text:
## 1. Major sea routes
Route | Connects | Features
North Atlantic Route — the Big Trunk Route | The northeastern United States and northwestern Europe — two major industrial regions | The busiest sea route — the busiest ocean trade route — in the world
Mediterranean–Indian Ocean Route — the Suez Route | Europe and Asia, and Europe and East Africa, via the Suez Canal | The shortest route between Europe and Asia; high traffic
Cape of Good Hope Route | Europe and Asia via southern Africa | A longer alternative when the Suez Canal is blocked
Panama Canal Route | The Atlantic Ocean and the Pacific Ocean | Shortens the voyage between the eastern and western coasts of the Americas
Trans-Pacific Route | East Asia and the west coast of the Americas | Growing container traffic
## 2. Chokepoints
Chokepoint | Connects | Features
Strait of Malacca | The Indian Ocean and the South China Sea | The world's busiest strait — about one-third of global trade; a major oil route to East Asia; alternatives: the Lombok and Sunda Straits
Strait of Hormuz | The Persian Gulf and the Arabian Sea | The most critical oil chokepoint — about 20% of global oil
Suez Canal | The Mediterranean Sea and the Red Sea | Shortens the Europe–Asia route — about 12–15% of global seaborne trade
Panama Canal | The Atlantic Ocean and the Pacific Ocean | Vital for trade between the Americas and Asia and the United States
Bab-el-Mandeb | The Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden | A gateway to the Suez Canal — critical for Europe–Asia traffic
Strait of Gibraltar | The Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea | The entrance to the Mediterranean Sea
Turkish Straits — the Bosphorus and the Dardanelles | The Black Sea and the Mediterranean Sea | Russia's warm-water access
## 3. Historic routes
Silk Route: A historic land trade route; Spice Routes: historic sea trade routes

t: Boundaries and border rivers
text:
## 1. Size
Area: 1,62,970 square kilometres — the 8th largest state by area
Population: The 10th largest state by population — 2011 Census figures
Largest district: YSR Kadapa; smallest district: Visakhapatnam
## 2. Boundaries
Direction | Andhra Pradesh bounded by | Rayalaseema bordered by
North | Chhattisgarh and Odisha | Telangana
East | Bay of Bengal | —
South | Tamil Nadu | Tamil Nadu
West | Karnataka | Karnataka
## 3. Border rivers
Sileru River: At the tri-junction of Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and Odisha
A tributary of the Sabari River — originates in Andhra Pradesh, flows through Odisha, joins the Sabari at the tri-junction boundary
Known as Machkand in its upper reaches
Tammileru River: Forms the boundary between Krishna and West Godavari districts — subsequently drains into Kolleru Lake; the Tammileru Dam is built on it

Tamil Nadu received a large part of Tiruttani Taluka of Chittoor district

2014: Seven mandals of Khammam transferred to Andhra Pradesh

t: Godavari, Krishna and Penna
text:
## 1. Godavari
Origin: Triyambakeswar
Tributaries: Manjeera, Pranahita, Indravathi, Kinnerasani, Sabari (the main tributary) and Sileru
Width: 2.7 km wide at Rajahmundry
Sir Arthur Cotton's dam: At Dhawaleswaram
Seven branches: Divides in the erstwhile East Godavari and West Godavari districts
Branch | Location / mouth
Gowthami | Yanam — joins the Bay of Bengal
Vashista | Antarvedi — joins the Bay of Bengal
Vinateya | Mouth at Komarigiripatnam
Tulya | Bendamoorlanka
Bharadwaja | Bendamoorlanka
Koushika | Kakinada or Coringa delta region
Athreya | Coringa village
## 2. Krishna and Tungabhadra
Krishna — origin: Mahabaleshwar in Maharashtra
Flows through Kurnool, Guntur and Krishna districts — enters the Bay of Bengal at Hamsaladeevi
Nagarjuna Sagar — near Nandikonda; the Srisailam Hydroelectric Power Station is on the Krishna
Splits into two branches at Puligada — 64 km below Vijayawada; Diviseema lies between the two branches
Tungabhadra: The biggest and most important tributary of the Krishna — 531 km long
Origin: Varaha Mountains of the Western Ghats
Joins the Krishna at Sangameswaram (Sangam) in Kurnool district
Hagari (= Vedavathi) — the biggest tributary of the Tungabhadra — joins it near Siruguppa
## 3. Penna
Other names: Pinakini; Penneru
Origin: Nandidurga Hills; enters AP in Anantapur district
Course: Forms a gorge at Gandikota in Kadapa district; a small delta in Nellore district
Mouth: Joins the Bay of Bengal at Vutukuru in Palnadu district; meets the sea at Pulicat Lake
Somasila Dam: On the Penna near Nellore
Tributary | Joins the Penna at
Cheyyeru — formed by the confluence of Bahuda and Pancha | Gundlamada, Kadapa
Chitravathi | Gandikota, Kadapa
Kundu | Adinimmayapalli
Papagni | Near Kamalapuram

t: Other rivers of Andhra Pradesh
text:
## 1. North-coastal rivers
River | Origin | Course and mouth | Tributaries / projects
Vamsadhara — the biggest river born in the Eastern Ghats | Jayapur Hills, Odisha | Enters AP at Pathapatnam, Srikakulam district; joins the Bay of Bengal at Kalingapatnam | Mahendratanaya — an important tributary
Nagavali — also called Langulya | Rayagarh Hills, Odisha | Enters AP in Srikakulam district; joins the Bay of Bengal at Mopasu Bandar | Janjavathi — an important tributary — Asia's first rubber dam
Champavathi | Near Andra village | Joins the Bay of Bengal near Konada | Eduvampula Gedda, Chitti Gedda, Pothula Gedda, Gadi Gedda; Denkada check dam near Saripalli, Vizianagaram; Tarakarama Thirtha Sagaram; Kumili Dam
Gosthani — an east-flowing river, 120 km long | Anantagiri Hills of the Eastern Ghats | Joins the Bay of Bengal through an estuary near Bheemunipatnam | Three percent of Visakhapatnam district lies in its basin
## 2. Machkhand, Sileru and Sabari
Machkhand — also called Matsya Kundala: Originates in the Madugula Hills of Anakapalli district — initially flows northward, then eastward, and enters Odisha; Duduma Waterfalls are on it
Sileru: A major tributary of the Sabari (and so of the Godavari) — originates in Andhra Pradesh, flows through Odisha, joins the Sabari at the tri-junction of Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, and Odisha; its upper reaches are called Machkand
Sabari — also called the Kolab River: The main tributary of the Godavari — originates in the Sinkaram Hill ranges of Odisha
## 3. South and central rivers
Gundlakamma: Originates in the Nallamala forests of Kurnool district — joins the sea at Devarampadu village
Arani — also called Araniyar — 108 km long:
Originates at Sadasivakonda in the Narayanavanam Protected Forest of Chittoor district
Flows southward, then eastward — joins the south-western tip of Pulicat Lake
Swarnamukhi: The Tirumala and Srikalahasthi temples are in its basin
Historical name: Mogaleru — in the works of Dhurjati
Kalyani — a tributary; the Kalyani Dam is constructed on it
Tammileru: Forms the boundary between Krishna and West Godavari districts — drains into Kolleru Lake; the Tammileru Dam is constructed on it

t: Force and its types
text:
## 1. Balanced and unbalanced force
Unbalanced force: Changes an object's state of motion — can accelerate, decelerate or change its direction
Balanced force: No change in the state of motion — the object remains at rest or moves with uniform velocity
## 2. Types of force
Force | Nature
Frictional | Opposes relative motion or the tendency of motion
Gravitational | Attracts objects towards each other — weight is a gravitational force
Centripetal | Keeps an object in a circular path — acts towards the centre
Tension | Pulls along a string or rope
Normal | A perpendicular push by a surface
Spring | A restoring force — follows Hooke's law
## 3. Units of force and weight
SI unit of force: The newton (N) — one newton = one kilogram metre per second squared = 10⁵ dynes; other units: dyne, kilogram-force (kgf), poundal
SI unit of weight: The newton (N); also kilogram-force (kgf) — one kgf is about 9.8 newtons

t: Newton's laws and momentum
text:
## 1. Newton's laws
Law | Applications / examples
First law | Seat belts; sudden braking effects; objects at rest staying at rest — a passenger lurches forward when a bus stops suddenly; a book remains on a table until pushed
Second law — F = ma | Designing vehicles; calculating the acceleration of rockets and lifts; a heavier suitcase needs more force to accelerate; pushing an empty vs a loaded cart
Third law | Rocket propulsion, walking, swimming, gun recoil, jet engines
## 2. Action and reaction pairs
Action | Reaction
A walking foot pushes the ground backward | The ground pushes the foot forward
A rocket expels gases downward (rocket gases push down) | The gases push the rocket upward — the rocket moves up
A gun pushes a bullet forward | The bullet pushes the gun backward — gun recoil (a gun recoils when a bullet is fired)
A bird pushes air downward | The air pushes the bird upward
A swimmer pushes water backward | The water pushes the swimmer forward
A hammer hits a nail | The nail hits the hammer with equal force
The Earth pulls an apple downward | The apple pulls the Earth upward — giving the Earth a very small acceleration
## 3. Conservation of momentum
The total linear momentum of an isolated system is conserved when no external force acts
Collision: Total momentum before = total momentum after
Explosion: Total momentum remains zero if the system was initially at rest
Gun recoil: The gun and bullet system's momentum is conserved — the bullet's forward momentum = the gun's backward momentum
Rocket: The rocket and exhaust gases momentum is conserved — exhaust gases gain backward momentum; the rocket gains forward momentum
Jet engines: High-speed exhaust produces a large momentum change
Impulse in daily life: Vehicle safety design uses collision principles; airbags increase the time of impact and decrease force; catching a ball by drawing the hands back increases the time interval

t: Work, energy and power
text:
## 1. Units
Work: SI unit the joule (J) — one joule = one newton metre = one kilogram metre squared per second squared = 10⁷ ergs; each another unit of work: erg, electronvolt (eV), calorie, kilowatt-hour (kWh)
One electronvolt = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ joules
Power: SI unit the watt (W) — one watt = one joule per second; other units: horsepower (hp), kilowatt (kW), megawatt (MW); one horsepower = 746 watts
## 2. Forms of energy
Kinetic energy: Translational or rotational
Potential energy: Gravitational, elastic / spring, electric, chemical, nuclear
Mechanical energy equals kinetic energy plus potential energy
Thermal / heat energy: Internal energy due to molecular motion
Other types: Sound, light, electrical, magnetic, nuclear
## 3. Energy conversion
Device / process | Converts
Generator / dynamo | Mechanical → electrical
Electric motor | Electrical → mechanical
Battery / cell | Chemical → electrical
LED / bulb | Electrical → light
Solar cell | Light → electrical
Nuclear power plant | Nuclear → heat → electrical
Free fall, pendulum, roller coaster | Potential → kinetic
Friction in brakes | Kinetic → heat
## 4. Conservation of energy
Energy can neither be created nor destroyed — it can only be transformed
Mechanical energy conservation: KE + PE = constant — when only conservative forces act
Applications: Pendulum, free fall, spring-mass system, ideal collisions

text:
## 1. Types
Type | Fact
Static friction | Opposes the tendency of motion — self-adjusting; maximum = μₛN
Kinetic / sliding friction | Opposes actual sliding motion — μₖN
Rolling friction | Opposes rolling — much smaller than sliding friction
Fluid friction / viscous drag | Opposes motion in fluids
## 2. Friction is useful
Walking and running: The forward push — friction enables walking; without friction, people slip
Writing: Grip between a pen and paper — friction helps in writing and holding
Vehicles: Move and stop — braking converts kinetic energy to heat; traction and braking are advantages
Grip: Prevents objects slipping
Useful heat: Ignites a matchstick; drilling
Belts and pulleys: Power transmission — belt drives
## 3. Friction is harmful
Wear and tear in machine parts and tyres; surfaces become rough over time
Unwanted heat — overheating of engines and brakes
Reduces efficiency — energy loss in machines; opposes motion; extra fuel consumption in vehicles

t: Circular motion and simple machines
text:
## 1. Centripetal vs centrifugal
Basis | Centripetal force | Centrifugal force
Nature | A real force towards the centre — provides the acceleration for circular motion | A pseudo force in a rotating frame — acts away from the centre
Provided by / examples | Tension, gravity, friction, electrostatic and magnetic force | Clothes and water thrown outward in a washing machine; mud flies off a rotating wheel; particles move outward in a rotating frame
## 2. What provides centripetal force
Situation | Provided by
Vehicle on a level circular road | Friction
Vehicle on a banked road | The component of normal force and friction
Satellite and planetary motion | Gravitational force
Stone tied to a string | Tension
Electron around a nucleus | Electrostatic attraction
Loop-the-loop | Gravity and normal force
## 3. Outward effects
Merry-go-round: A feeling of being pushed outward — a pseudo force
Centrifuge: Separates cream or blood — denser particles move outward
Planetary rings and the shape of Earth — Earth bulges at the equator
## 4. Simple machines
Machine | Used in
Lever | Scissors, see-saw, crowbar, bottle opener, the human forearm
Inclined plane | Ramps, slopes, screws, wedges
Pulley | Lifting heavy loads — cranes, flagpoles, elevators
Wheel and axle | Steering wheel, door knobs, screwdrivers
Screw jack | Lifts cars or heavy vehicles
Gears | Bicycles, clocks, automobiles — convert speed and torque

t: Gravity and the value of g
text:
## 1. Effects of gravity
Weight: The force with which Earth attracts a body
Free fall: The acceleration of a freely falling body — equals g when air resistance is neglected; in a vacuum all bodies fall with the same acceleration, independent of mass
Orbital motion: Keeps planets and satellites in orbit
Tides: The differential gravitational pull of the Moon and the Sun
Earth's shape: Slightly oblate — a bulge at the equator, due to rotation and gravity
Atmosphere: Gravity prevents it from escaping
Direction: Gravitational acceleration is always towards the centre of Earth
## 2. Variation of g
Maximum at the poles, minimum at the equator — the poles are closer to Earth's centre
Decreases with altitude and with depth; g = 0 at the centre of Earth; approaches zero at very large height
Earth's rotation slightly reduces g — the centrifugal effect
Place | Distance from centre | Centrifugal effect | Weight
Poles | Minimum | Zero | Maximum on the surface — greater than at the equator
Equator | Maximum | Maximum reduction | Slightly less than at the poles

t: Mass, weight and weightlessness
text:
## 1. Mass vs weight
Basis | Mass | Weight
Meaning | Inertia — the amount of matter | A force — given by the formula W = mg
Nature | A scalar quantity | A force vector
Varies? | Remains constant | Depends on location
SI unit | Kilogram (kg) | Newton (N)
In weightlessness | Unchanged | Zero
## 2. Weight at different places
Earth's surface: Maximum under normal conditions — maximum at the poles
Height / depth: Weight decreases with height above and depth below the surface; zero at the centre of Earth; approaches zero at very large height and in far space
Moon: About one-sixth of a person's weight on Earth
## 3. Weightlessness
Apparent weight is zero inside a freely falling elevator and an orbiting satellite — in free fall the normal force becomes zero; apparent weight N is zero when effective gravity is zero
An orbiting satellite and its astronaut both accelerate towards Earth with the same g
Astronauts in space stations experience continuous free fall
Zero-g training: Aircraft parabolic flights
Microgravity experiments: Fluid behaviour, crystal growth, human physiology; satellite instruments are designed for a weightless environment

t: Satellite orbits
text:
Orbit | Fact
Low Earth orbit | 160 km to 2000 km — the International Space Station about 400 km above Earth
Geostationary | About 36,000 km above the equator — a period of 24 hours
Polar | Passes over the poles
Elliptical | Different apogee and perigee distances
Circular | Centripetal force equals gravitational force

t: Density, buoyancy and Pascal's law
text:
## 1. Density
An object floats when its density is less than the liquid's density
Hydrometer and lactometer: Measure the relative density of liquids — the lactometer checks the purity of milk
Centrifugation: Separates mixtures — denser particles settle
Ships and submarines: Control average density using ballast — submarines control buoyancy using ballast tanks
Atmospheric density: Decreases with height
## 2. Pascal's law — hydraulics
Hydraulic lift and press: Multiply force
Hydraulic brakes: Transmit pressure equally to all wheels
Hydraulic jack: Lifts heavy vehicles
Syringe: Pressure applied at one end is transmitted to the other end
Excavators and bulldozers: Hydraulic systems for force amplification
## 3. Buoyancy — Archimedes' principle
Cause: Higher hydrostatic pressure at greater depth — pressure at the bottom of a submerged object is greater than at the top; the net upward buoyant force acts vertically upward through the centre of buoyancy
Ships and boats: Float when their weight equals the buoyant force
Hot-air balloons and airships: Rise when buoyant force is greater than weight — heated air has lower density, producing a net upward force
Life jackets: Increase the buoyant force; buoyancy helps swimmers stay afloat
Iceberg: Only a small part remains above water — ice is less dense than water
Fish bladder: Controls buoyancy for depth regulation

t: Surface tension and capillarity
text:
## 1. Surface tension
Water strider / insect walking on water: The surface acts like an elastic membrane
Small liquid drops: Spherical — minimises surface area; molten metals form a spherical shape in space and in powder metallurgy
Floating needle / razor blade: Surface tension supports the weight
Soap bubbles: Two surfaces — higher excess pressure
Contact angle: In wetting, depends on surface tension — waterproofing fabrics increases the contact angle
Detergents and soaps: Reduce surface tension — better cleaning action
Lung surfactants: Reduce surface tension in alveoli
Drops: Medicine droppers and ink pens — the formation of drops
## 2. Capillarity
Capillary rise or fall — meniscus formation
Liquid in a glass tube | Behaviour | Meniscus
Water (narrow tube) | Rises | Concave
Mercury | Falls — the level is depressed | Convex
Examples of capillary action:
Water rises in plants and trees — xylem (against gravity)
Ink absorbed by blotting paper — its pores
Oil rises in a lamp wick
Moisture rises in walls — bricks

t: Viscosity, elasticity and compressibility
text:
## 1. Viscosity
Viscous oils: Reduce friction and wear — machine lubrication
Streamlined shapes: Reduce viscous drag on ships and aeroplanes
Blood: Viscosity affects blood pressure and blood flow
Hydraulic shock absorbers: Viscous damping
High-viscosity liquids — paint, honey — flow slowly
Terminal velocity: Raindrops and parachutes reach a constant speed
## 2. Elasticity
Springs and shock absorbers: Store and release elastic energy
Bridges and buildings: Materials selected for high elasticity or strength
Rubber bands and tyres: A high elastic limit and resilience
Cranes and lifting machines: Steel cables with high Young's modulus
Musical instrument strings: Remain under tension — elastic property
Railway tracks: Expansion gaps in spans to handle thermal stress
## 3. Compressibility — bulk modulus
Bulk modulus applications: The incompressibility of liquids and the compressibility of gases
Hydraulic systems: Liquids with low compressibility transmit force
Submarine hulls: Must withstand high pressure — materials with low compressibility
Speed of sound: Depends on the compressibility of the medium
Gas storage cylinders: High-pressure gases — gases have high compressibility
Pneumatic shock absorbers: Air compressibility for cushioning

t: Heat, temperature and scales
text:
## 1. Heat vs temperature
Heat: A form of energy that flows due to a temperature difference — from higher to lower temperature
Depends on mass, specific heat and temperature change
Temperature: Measures the hotness or coldness of a body — related to the average kinetic energy of molecules
Thermal equilibrium: Bodies at the same temperature — no net heat flow
## 2. Units
SI unit of heat or energy: The joule (J)
One calorie = 4.186 joules (about 4.2 joules); one kilocalorie = 4186 joules
Mechanical equivalent of heat: 4.186 joules per calorie
## 3. Temperature scales
Scale | Symbol | Ice point | Steam point | Note
Celsius | °C | 0°C | 100°C | —
Kelvin | K | 273.15 K | — | An absolute scale — starts at absolute zero
Fahrenheit | °F | 32°F | 212°F | —
Rankine | °R | — | — | An absolute Fahrenheit scale
Conversion: Kelvin temperature equals the Celsius temperature plus 273.15 — approximately K = °C + 273
27°C ≈ 300 K; 0°C ≈ 273 K; –273°C ≈ 0 K
## 4. Absolute zero
0 K = –273.15°C = –459.67°F — the lowest possible temperature
Molecular motion is minimum; unattainable according to the Third Law of Thermodynamics
For an ideal gas, volume and pressure theoretically become zero
The starting point of the Kelvin scale

t: Transfer of heat
text:
## 1. Modes
Mode | How | Medium
Conduction | Direct contact — no bulk motion | Requires a material medium — best in solids
Convection | Actual movement of fluid particles | Requires a fluid medium — liquids and gases
Radiation | Electromagnetic waves | No medium needed — occurs in a vacuum
## 2. Examples
Conduction:
A metal spoon in hot tea becomes hot
Heating one end of a metal rod makes the other end hot
Metal bases of cooking utensils conduct heat to food
Wood and plastic — poor conductors, used for insulation
Convection:
Boiling water — hot water rises, cold water sinks — convection currents
Sea breeze and land breeze — air movement due to a temperature difference
Room heaters and air conditioners circulate air
Hot air balloons rise — hot air rises
Radiation:
Heat from the Sun reaches Earth through a vacuum
Feeling heat from a fire or heater without touching it
A black body — a perfect absorber and perfect emitter of radiation
Shiny walls in a thermos flask minimize radiation loss

t: Thermal expansion and the anomaly of water
text:
## 1. Applications of expansion
Railway tracks: Gaps left for thermal expansion
Bridges: Rollers or expansion joints
Thermometers: Liquid expansion measures temperature
Bimetallic strips: Thermostats, electric irons, fire alarms
Hot rivets: Contract on cooling — a tight joint
Overflow pipes in tanks: Allow for the expansion of liquid
## 2. Anomalous expansion of water
Water contracts when heated from 0°C to 4°C
Maximum density — minimum volume — at 4°C; density decreases below and above 4°C
Lakes and ponds freeze from the top — aquatic life survives

t: Specific heat and latent heat
text:
## 1. High specific heat of water
Coolant: Water absorbs large heat with a small temperature change
Coastal areas: A moderate climate
Hot water bottles: Retain heat for a longer time
Land vs sea: Land has a lower specific heat than sea water — heats and cools faster
Substances with high specific heat cook more slowly
## 2. Latent heat
Change | Latent heat | Note
Fusion of ice | 3.34 × 10⁵ J/kg — 80 cal/g | Melting point 0°C at 1 atmosphere; temperature constant during melting
Vaporisation of water | 2.26 × 10⁶ J/kg — 540 cal/g | Boiling point 100°C at 1 atmosphere; temperature constant during boiling; boiling point increases with pressure
Ice cools: Its high latent heat of fusion absorbs a large amount of heat
Steam burns more severely than boiling water: High latent heat of vaporisation
Refrigeration: Uses latent heat absorbed during evaporation
Perspiration: Its evaporation cools the body
Clouds and rain: Latent heat released during condensation

t: Evaporation, refrigeration and heat engines
text:
## 1. Evaporation
Faster molecules escape from a liquid — the average kinetic energy of the remaining molecules decreases → cooling
Examples: Sweating; water in an earthen pot; desert coolers
Increased by: Higher temperature, larger surface area, lower humidity, wind
A surface phenomenon occurring at all temperatures — this is how it differs from boiling
## 2. Refrigerator
Extracts heat from the cold body inside and rejects it to the hot surroundings — based on the Second Law of Thermodynamics; external work is required
Cycle: Evaporation → compression → condensation → expansion
Liquid refrigerant evaporates at low pressure — absorbs latent heat; it absorbs heat during evaporation and releases heat during condensation
Refrigerants:
Earlier: Ammonia; Freon — Freons are CFCs, now phased out
Modern: HFCs, HCs, R-134a, R-600a
Desirable: Low boiling point, high latent heat, non-toxic, non-flammable, stable
## 3. Heat engine
Converts heat energy into mechanical work — absorbs heat from a source, does work, and rejects heat to a sink
Requires: A hot source, a cold sink and a working substance
Based on the First Law and Second Law of Thermodynamics

t: Types of waves
text:
## 1. Classification
Basis | Types
Medium | Mechanical and electromagnetic waves
Direction of vibration | Transverse and longitudinal waves
Energy propagation | Progressive and stationary waves
Dimension | One-, two- and three-dimensional waves
Others | Matter waves — de Broglie; shock waves
## 2. Medium
Mechanical waves: Require a material medium — a solid, liquid or gas; e.g. sound, waves on a string, water surface waves
Electromagnetic waves: No medium — travel in a vacuum; e.g. light; all electromagnetic waves are transverse
Matter waves: Associated with moving particles — no medium needed
## 3. Transverse or longitudinal
Wave | Type
Sound in air | Longitudinal — travels through gas
Waves on a string; water surface waves | Transverse
Seismic waves | P-waves (primary — travel through solids, liquids and gases) and S-waves (secondary) — both longitudinal and transverse
Spring / slinky | Longitudinal or transverse — compression waves in a solid
Ultrasonic waves | Longitudinal — in various media
Pressure waves | Travel through fluids
## 4. Electromagnetic wavelengths
Wave | Wavelength
Radio waves | Greater than 1 metre
Microwaves | 1 millimetre to 1 metre
Infrared | 700 nanometres to 1 millimetre
Visible light | 400 to 700 nanometres
Ultraviolet | 10 to 400 nanometres
X-rays | 0.01 to 10 nanometres
Gamma rays | Less than 0.01 nanometre

t: Wave properties, energy and uses
text:
## 1. Amplitude, velocity and wavelength
Higher amplitude: Louder sound; brighter light — energy and intensity proportional to the square of amplitude; ⚠ no effect on wave speed, frequency or wavelength
Velocity: Independent of frequency in the same medium — changes with the properties of different media; the speed of light is the same for all frequencies in a vacuum
Wavelength: At the same frequency, higher velocity gives a longer wavelength (so faster sound has a longer wavelength); in the same medium, velocity is constant and wavelength is inversely proportional to frequency
Sound travels faster in solids than in the other listed media
## 2. Energy
Waves transfer energy without transferring matter
Wave energy ∝ the square of amplitude multiplied by the square of frequency
Intensity: Power per unit area — ∝ square of amplitude
Mechanical waves: Energy from particle oscillation; electromagnetic waves: from oscillating electric and magnetic fields
## 3. Uses
Wave | Uses
Sound | Communication, sonar, medical ultrasound
Light | Vision, optical fibres, lasers
Radio waves | Broadcasting; mobile communication
Microwaves | Cooking, radar, satellite communication
X-rays | Medical imaging; security scanning
Ultrasonic waves | Cleaning, echocardiography, ranging

t: Interference, diffraction, polarization and Doppler effect
text:
## 1. Interference
Young's double-slit experiment: Constructive and destructive interference of light
Thin-film interference: Colours in soap bubbles and oil films
Beats: Interference of two close frequencies of sound
Destructive interference: Anti-reflective coatings; noise-cancelling headphones
## 2. Diffraction
Bending of light around an obstacle — light enters the geometrical shadow
Sound is heard around corners — sound waves diffract easily because of their long wavelengths; ⚠ light cannot be seen clearly around corners — very small wavelength
Single-slit pattern: A central bright fringe and secondary fringes
Diffraction grating: Produces spectra
Fresnel diffraction: Near-field patterns; Fraunhofer diffraction: far-field patterns
## 3. Polarization
Polaroid sunglasses: Reduce glare — cut reflected light; photography uses glare-reduction filters
Three-dimensional (3D) movies: Use separate images for each eye
LCD screens: Control light transmission
Stress analysis: Photoelasticity shows stress patterns
Optical activity: Measures the concentration of solutions
Communication: Polarization multiplexing in optical fibres
## 4. Doppler effect
The apparent change in frequency due to relative motion between a source and an observer
Approaching source: Higher apparent frequency and pitch
Receding source: Lower apparent frequency and pitch
Applications:
Radar speed guns (police radar): Vehicle / traffic speed
Medical Doppler ultrasound: Blood-flow velocity
Astronomy: Red shift and blue shift — the expanding universe and star motion (Doppler effect for light)
SONAR: Speed of submarines and underwater objects
Weather radar: Storms and wind speed
Bats: Echolocation with frequency shifts
Sirens demonstrate it

t: Sound — nature, speed and characteristics
text:
## 1. Nature
A mechanical, longitudinal wave — compressions and rarefactions
Requires a material medium — solids, liquids and gases; cannot travel through a vacuum (speed zero — no medium)
## 2. Speed of sound
Medium (20–25°C) | Approximate speed
Air | 340–343 m/s
Water | 1480–1500 m/s
Steel / iron | 5000–6000 m/s
Glass | 5000–6000 m/s
Vacuum | Zero
Order: Solid > liquid > gas in general
Solids: Fastest — high elasticity / bulk modulus; molecules closely packed — a train sound is heard better through rails than air
Liquids: Intermediate — less elastic than solids
Gases: Slowest — low elasticity; molecules far apart
Temperature: Speed increases with temperature — about 0.61 m/s per 1°C; about 331 m/s at 0°C and 343 m/s at 20°C
## 3. Frequency, wavelength and amplitude
Frequency: The number of vibrations (compressions) per second — unit hertz (Hz); determines pitch
Audible range: 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz)
Wavelength: The distance between two successive compressions or rarefactions — higher frequency, smaller wavelength
At 340 m/s in air: 20 Hz → 17 m; 20 kHz → 1.7 cm
Amplitude: The maximum displacement of particles from their mean position — unit metre (m); determines loudness and intensity; energy ∝ square of amplitude; ⚠ no effect on speed, frequency or pitch
## 4. Pitch, loudness and quality
Characteristic | Depends on | Notes
Pitch | Frequency — directly proportional | The sensation of frequency in the brain; independent of amplitude and loudness; low frequency — bass / deep sound (male voice); high frequency — shrill (female voice, whistle)
Loudness | Amplitude — directly related | The sensation of intensity or amplitude; unit decibel (dB); independent of frequency and pitch
Quality / timbre | The waveform — overtones and harmonics present; the shape of the periodic waveform | Distinguishes two sounds of the same pitch and loudness — the same note on a flute, violin and piano sounds different; more overtones → richer quality

t: Ultrasound, infrasound, SONAR and echo
text:
## 1. Ranges
Infrasonic: Below 20 Hz; ultrasonic: above 20 kHz
Human hearing: Most sensitive around 2000–4000 Hz; the limit decreases with age — age-related hearing loss especially affects higher frequencies
## 2. Uses of ultrasound
Medical imaging — sonography; echocardiography — images the heart
Cleaning delicate parts and jewellery
Industry: Detects cracks or flaws in metals; welding and drilling in precision machining
SONAR: Underwater detection
Pest control: Drives away insects and rodents
## 3. Infrasound
Elephants and whales: Communication
Seismic waves contain infrasonic frequencies — earthquake detection
Weather: Monitoring; detects storms and tornadoes; study of the atmosphere
Military: Detects nuclear explosions and missiles
Animals can sense it before natural disasters; it propagates over long distances
## 4. SONAR — Sound Navigation And Ranging
Echo method — reflection of ultrasonic waves: sends ultrasonic pulses toward an object, which reflects them; measures the time interval between sending and receiving
Why ultrasound: High frequency, less diffraction, greater directionality
Uses: Detecting submarines (a military use); ocean depth; mapping the seabed; locating fish (fishing industry); underwater navigation by ships and submarines; locating wrecks and sunken ships or objects; limited use in underwater communication
## 5. Echo
Uses: SONAR — distance and depth measurement; medical ultrasound — imaging internal organs; measuring the speed of sound (echo time); architectural acoustics — designing halls for reverberation control
Echolocation: Bats and dolphins — navigation; radar uses a similar principle with electromagnetic waves
Minimum distance for an echo: 17.2 m — based on the ear's persistence of hearing of 0.1 s

t: Musical instruments
text:
Type | Examples | Sound from
String | Guitar, sitar, violin | Vibration of strings — transverse standing waves
Wind | Flute, clarinet, shehnai | Vibration of an air column — a longitudinal standing wave
Membrane | Tabla, drum | A stretched membrane
Plate | Cymbals, bells | Plates or solids
Electronic | Electronic oscillators and speakers | —
Pitch: Controlled by the frequency of vibration
String: Length, tension and thickness of the string
Wind: Length of its air column
Loudness: The amplitude of vibration — depends on the force of striking or blowing
Quality / timbre: Overtones or harmonics — depend on the shape and material of the instrument
Pipes: A closed pipe produces only odd harmonics; an open pipe produces all harmonics

t: Nature of light and media
text:
## 1. Dual nature
Light has a dual nature:
Wave nature — explains interference, diffraction, polarisation
Particle nature — photons — explains the photoelectric effect and the Compton effect
Electromagnetic waves: Transverse; no medium needed — light travels freely through vacuum, at its maximum speed there, denoted c
## 2. Media
Medium | Light | Examples
Transparent | Passes through | Glass, water, air
Translucent | Partially passes | Frosted glass, butter paper
Opaque | Does not pass | Wood, metal, stone
A medium with a higher refractive index is optically denser

t: Reflection and mirrors
text:
## 1. Laws of reflection
First law: The incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in the same plane
Second law: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection
Normal: Perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence
Reflection | Surface | Image | Example
Regular / specular | Smooth | Clear | Mirror
Irregular / diffused | Rough | Not clear | Wall, paper
## 2. Images formed
Mirror | Image
Plane | Virtual, erect, same size — laterally inverted (left and right reversed); image distance = object distance; magnification m = +1
Concave | Real and inverted when the object is beyond C; virtual and erect when within F
Convex | Always virtual and erect; diminished
## 3. Uses of mirrors
Mirror | Uses
Plane | Looking glass, periscope, kaleidoscope
Concave | Shaving / makeup mirror — magnified erect image (object within F); headlights — a parallel beam with the bulb at the focus; solar cooker / furnace — converges sun rays at the focus; torch / searchlight — a strong parallel beam; dentist mirror — magnified image of teeth; reflecting telescope — a large aperture, no chromatic aberration
Convex | Rear-view mirror — a wide field of view, erect diminished image; security / shop mirror — large-area coverage; street lamps — the reflector diverges light over a larger area; ATM or parking area — a wider view for safety

t: Refraction, total internal reflection and optical fibres
text:
## 1. Refraction
Cause: A change in the speed of light — light travels at different speeds in different media (an optical-density difference)
Frequency stays the same; wavelength changes
Applications: Lenses converge or diverge light; prisms — deviation and dispersion; optical fibres — transmit signals; spectacles — correct eye defects; cameras and microscopes — form images
Apparent depth: Objects in water appear raised
## 2. Critical angle and total internal reflection (TIR)
Critical angle — denoted by C: The angle of incidence in a denser medium for which the angle of refraction in the rarer medium is 90° — depends on the pair of media, and slightly on wavelength
Conditions for TIR: Light travels from an optically denser to a rarer medium; the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle (i > C)
Result: The entire light is reflected back into the denser medium — no refraction, 100% reflection in the ideal case
Based on TIR (TIR devices):
Optical fibres — keep light inside the core; communication and endoscopy
Diamond brilliance / sparkle — multiple TIRs; a very small critical angle of about 24.4°
Porro prism / binoculars — image inversion without loss; prisms in binoculars or periscopes reflect light without silvering
Endoscope — medical viewing
Mirage — atmospheric TIR
Reflectors in road signs — high visibility
Dew drops sparkle — optical reflection effects
## 3. Optical fibres
Structure: The core has a higher refractive index than the cladding (which has a lower one); the angle of incidence at the core-cladding interface must satisfy i > C
Advantages: Low loss; high bandwidth; immune to interference
Uses:
Telecommunication — internet, telephone and cable-TV signals
Medical endoscopy — viewing internal organs; precise laser delivery in surgery
Sensors — temperature, pressure, strain
Military and aircraft — lightweight data transmission
Decorative and medical illumination
Endoscope: A bundle of optical fibres using TIR — one bundle for illumination, one for image transmission; flexible enough for body cavities; non-invasive or minimally invasive viewing
## 4. Mirage
Caused by a continuous decrease or increase of refractive index with height — can appear as an inverted image of a distant object
Inferior mirage: In a desert — TIR due to hot air near the ground (lower refractive index); a water-like appearance
Superior mirage: TIR due to cold air layers
## 5. Diamond
A very high refractive index — about 2.42; a very small critical angle — about 24.4°
Most light undergoes TIR — multiple internal reflections; facets designed to maximise TIR
Brilliance and fire: TIR and dispersion

t: Lenses
text:
## 1. Types
Lens | Shape | Types
Convex | Thicker at the centre | Double-convex, plano-convex, concavo-convex
Concave | Thicker at the edges | Double-concave, plano-concave, convexo-concave
Cylindrical | — | Corrects astigmatism
Bifocal / progressive | — | Combines two powers
## 2. Images by a convex lens
Object position | Image
Beyond 2F | Real, inverted, diminished
At 2F | Real, inverted, same-sized
Between F and 2F | Real, inverted, magnified
At F | Real, inverted, highly magnified — at infinity
Within F | Virtual, erect, magnified
Concave lens: Virtual, erect, diminished for any object position
## 3. Uses
Lens | Uses
Convex | Magnifying glass — a virtual magnified image (object within F); camera — a real inverted image on film or a sensor; microscope and telescope objectives — a real image; projector — a magnified real image on a screen; the eye lens — a real image on the retina; burning glass — converges sun rays
Concave | Spectacles for myopia — diverges rays so the image forms on the retina; peephole / door viewers — a wide field of view; some Galileo telescopes — an eyepiece
Combination | Microscopes, telescopes, binoculars — can correct certain aberrations
## 4. Power of a lens
The reciprocal of its focal length in metres — unit dioptre — symbol D
Convex: Positive power; concave: negative power

t: The human eye and its defects
text:
## 1. Parts of the eye
Part | Function
Cornea | The main refraction — about 70% of the focusing
Iris | Controls pupil size — the amount of light entering
Pupil | The aperture for light entry
Eye lens | Fine focusing through accommodation
Ciliary muscles | Change the curvature of the eye lens
Retina | The screen where the image is formed — rods and cones
Optic nerve | Carries signals to the brain
Aqueous and vitreous humour | Maintain the shape of the eye; contribute to refraction
## 2. Accommodation
The ability of the eye to focus objects at different distances — ciliary muscles change the lens curvature
Near vision: The lens becomes thicker — more converging; distant vision: thinner
Range: From the near point (25 cm) to the far point (infinity); loss of accommodation causes presbyopia
Near point: The closest distance the eye sees clearly — normal 25 cm, the least distance of distinct vision
Far point: The farthest distance seen clearly — normal infinity
## 3. Defects of vision
Defect | Meaning / cause | Image | Correction | Near / far point
Myopia — short-sightedness | Distant objects blurred — an elongated eyeball or excessive converging power | In front of the retina | Concave (diverging) lens — negative power, e.g. –2 D — diverges rays onto the retina | Near point closer than 25 cm; far point finite — closer than infinity
Hypermetropia — long-sightedness | Nearby objects blurred — a shortened eyeball or insufficient converging power | Behind the retina | Convex (converging) lens — positive power, e.g. +2 D — converges rays onto the retina | Near point farther than 25 cm; far point infinity — affects near vision despite it
Presbyopia | Age-related loss of accommodation — weakening of the ciliary muscles; loss of lens flexibility | The near point recedes (farther than 25 cm) | Bifocal or progressive lenses — the near portion convex | Can involve a combination of myopia and hypermetropia in old age
Astigmatism | A distorted image — irregular curvature of the cornea or lens; different powers in different meridians | Blurred or distorted vision at all distances | Cylindrical lens; toric contact lenses; surgery | —
Cataract | Clouding of the eye lens | — | — | —
Colour blindness | A genetic defect in cones | — | — | —

t: Dispersion, scattering and atmospheric optics
text:
## 1. Dispersion
Cause: Different wavelengths have different refractive indices
Violet: Maximum deviation — the highest refractive index in the visible spectrum
Red: Minimum deviation — the lowest refractive index
Visible spectrum: Continuous — VIBGYOR; a prism spectrometer gives a pure spectrum; a rainbow is a natural spectrum
Chromatic aberration: A defect in lenses — minimised by an achromatic doublet
Spectroscopy: Analyses light from stars and elements
Diamond fire: Dispersion of white light
## 2. Rainbow
Phenomena: Dispersion, total internal reflection and refraction in water drops
Sunlight enters a water drop and disperses → TIR at the back of the drop → the dispersed light refracts out
Primary rainbow: One TIR — red outermost (outer side), violet innermost (inner side)
Secondary rainbow: Two TIRs — reversed colours; fainter
The Sun is behind the observer; water drops in front
## 3. Scattering
Type | Particles | Examples
Rayleigh | Much smaller than the wavelength — varies as 1/λ⁴ | Blue sky; red sunset
Mie | Larger particles | Clouds (white clouds); milk
Shorter wavelengths scatter more strongly — by dust and air molecules
Blue sky: Blue and violet are scattered the most — the highest frequencies among the relevant visible colours; the eye is more sensitive to blue than violet, so the sky therefore appears blue to the human eye; scattered light reaches the eye from all directions
Red sunset: Sunlight travels a greater distance through the atmosphere — blue is scattered away; the remaining red or orange light reaches the eye; pollution and dust enhance the red colour
## 4. Atmospheric refraction
Twinkling stars: Air-density variations cause continuous changes in refractive index — starlight is bent randomly: random apparent positions and fluctuating apparent intensity
Planets do not twinkle: They appear as discs — an averaging effect
Advance sunrise and delayed sunset: About two minutes each
The apparent position of stars is affected
## 5. Summary of phenomena
Phenomenon | Cause
Rainbow | Dispersion and total internal reflection in water drops
Blue sky, red sunset | Rayleigh scattering
Mirage | Total internal reflection
Twinkling of stars | Atmospheric refraction
Eclipse | Shadow formation — the rectilinear propagation of light

t: Effects of current and electrical safety
text:
## 1. Heating effect
Uses: Electric iron, heater, geyser, toaster; incandescent bulbs — old-style lighting; electric stoves — cooking (induction devices partly); electric fuses — protection; electric furnaces — industrial heating; welding
## 2. Magnetic effect
Motors, fans, pumps; electric vehicles
Generators — power stations
Electromagnets — cranes, relays, MRI devices
Measuring instruments — galvanometers, ammeters, voltmeters
Communication — loudspeakers, microphones; storage — magnetic tapes, older hard disks
## 3. Electric fuse
Principle: The heating effect of current
Material: A low-melting-point alloy — tin-lead
Melts when current exceeds its rated value — breaks the circuit; melts immediately during a short circuit
Placed in series with the device or circuit — overcurrent protection prevents damage due to excess current
Household wiring: A main fuse and individual circuit fuses; some appliances have built-in fuses
## 4. Earthing
Protects against electric shock — a low-resistance path to ground for leakage current
Keeps the metal body of an appliance at zero potential — during a fault, excess current flows to earth and the fuse blows
Colour code: Green or green-yellow
## 5. Short circuit and overloading
Short circuit: Live and neutral wires touch each other directly; also insulation failure
Overloading: Too many high-power devices — very high current → heating and a fire hazard
Prevention: A fuse or MCB; proper earthing

t: Temperature behaviour and doping
text:
## 1. Effect of temperature
When temperature rises, a semiconductor's conductivity increases and its resistivity / resistance decreases (falls)
More covalent bonds break — more free electrons and holes
The intrinsic carrier concentration increases exponentially with temperature
Opposite to metals — a semiconductor has a negative temperature coefficient of resistance; metals a positive one
At 0 K: A pure semiconductor has high resistance — acts as an insulator
A doped semiconductor has lower resistance than an intrinsic one
## 2. Doping
The controlled addition of impurity atoms to a pure semiconductor — to increase conductivity in a controlled manner
Dopant concentration: Very small — one impurity atom in 10⁶ to 10⁸ atoms
Produces an extrinsic semiconductor — donor doping = n-type; acceptor doping = p-type
## 3. n-type vs p-type
Basis | n-type | p-type
Dopant | Pentavalent — Group 15: phosphorus, arsenic, antimony — a donor | Trivalent — Group 13: boron, aluminium, gallium, indium — an acceptor
Effect | The extra electron becomes a free electron | The deficiency creates a hole
Majority carriers | Electrons — provide the main conduction | Holes
Minority carriers | Holes | Electrons
Charge | Overall neutral — positive ions balance the extra electrons | Overall neutral — negative ions balance the holes
## 4. Charge carriers
Intrinsic semiconductor: Equal numbers of electrons and holes
Electron: Negative charge — conduction by free electrons in the conduction band
Hole: A vacancy of an electron in a covalent bond — a positive charge carrier; its apparent movement is opposite to that of electrons

text:

Emitter: Heavily doped; base: thin and lightly doped; collector: moderately doped
Biasing: Emitter-base junction forward biased; collector-base junction reverse biased
A small input current controls a large output current
Uses:
Amplifier — increases the strength of weak signals
Switch — ON/OFF control in digital circuits
Oscillator — generates oscillating signals
Building blocks of integrated circuits in computers and mobile devices
Signal processing in radio and television; switching high-power loads

t: Superconductors
text:
Zero electrical resistance below its critical temperature — the temperature below which superconductivity appears
Perfect diamagnetism — the Meissner effect expels the magnetic field
Destroyed above the critical magnetic field; the critical current density is the maximum current it can carry
Examples: Mercury (critical temperature 4.2 K); niobium alloys; high-Tc cuprates — YBCO
Uses: MRI magnets; Maglev trains; lossless power transmission in the future; SQUIDs

topic: Physical and chemical changes, solutions and colloids
t: Physical vs chemical change
text:
## 1. Comparison
Basis | Physical change | Chemical change
New substance | Not formed | Formed
Composition | Remains the same | Changes
Reversibility | Usually reversible | Usually irreversible
Energy | Little or no energy change | Significant energy absorbed or released as heat or light
Mass | Conserved | Conserved — Law of Conservation of Mass
## 2. Examples of physical change
Example | Change
Melting of ice and wax | Solid → liquid — same substance, no new substance
Boiling / evaporation of water | Liquid → gas
Freezing of water | Liquid → solid
Dissolving salt / sugar in water | Forms a solution — the solute can be recovered from salt-water and sugar-water solutions
Breaking glass / chalk | Size or shape only
Stretching a rubber band | Temporarily changes shape
Cutting paper / wood | Size only
Magnetisation of iron | Temporarily changes its property
Expansion of metals on heating | Changes volume
Sublimation of camphor / ammonium chloride | Solid → gas — same substance
## 3. Examples of chemical change
Example | Products / process
Burning paper, wood, a candle | Ash, carbon dioxide and water
Cooking / baking food | New compounds
Digestion of food | Breaks down complex molecules
Curd from milk | Lactic acid bacteria (Lactobacillus) convert lactose — microbial action
Souring of milk | Lactic acid
Photosynthesis | Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen
Respiration | Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy
Fireworks explosion | New gases and compounds
Electrolysis of water | Hydrogen and oxygen gases
Acid + base | Salt and water

Change | Type | Example

topic: Physical and chemical changes, solutions and colloids
t: Solutions
text:
## 1. Terms
Solute: The substance dissolved; solvent: dissolves the solute — a solid, liquid or gas
Solution: A homogeneous mixture of a solute and a solvent
## 2. Types of solution
Type | Solute | Solvent | Example
Gaseous | Gas | Gas | Air — oxygen in nitrogen
Gas-in-liquid | Gas | Liquid | Oxygen in water
Liquid-in-liquid | Liquid | Liquid | Ethanol in water
Solid-in-liquid | Solid | Liquid | Sodium chloride / sucrose in water
Gas-in-solid | Gas | Solid | Hydrogen in palladium
Liquid-in-solid | Liquid | Solid | Mercury in gold — an amalgam
Solid-in-solid | Solid | Solid | Alloys — brass (copper + zinc), bronze (copper + tin)
## 3. Concentration
Unsaturated: Can dissolve more solute
Saturated: The maximum amount of solute dissolved at a given temperature and pressure — excess solute remains undissolved
Concentrated: A large amount of solute relative to the solvent; dilute: a small amount
Ideal solution: Zero enthalpy of mixing; identical intermolecular forces
## 4. True solution
Particles invisible to the naked eye; no Tyndall effect — does not scatter light; stable; the solute cannot be separated by filtration
## 5. Solubility
Defined under specified temperature and pressure; affected by the nature of the solute and solvent — "like dissolves like"
Expressed as: Grams of solute per 100 grams or per 100 millilitres of solvent; molarity; molality; mole fraction

topic: Physical and chemical changes, solutions and colloids
t: Colloids and osmosis
text:
## 1. Types of colloid
Colloid | Dispersed phase | Dispersion medium | Examples
Solid aerosol | Solid | Gas | Smoke, dust
Liquid aerosol | Liquid | Gas | Cloud, mist, fog
Emulsion | Liquid | Liquid | Milk (an oil-in-water emulsion), cream, mayonnaise
Gel | Liquid | Solid | Jelly, butter, cheese
Sol | Solid | Liquid | Gold sol, sulfur sol
Solid sol | Solid | Solid | Coloured glass, gems (gems are solid sols), ruby glass
Foam — gas dispersed in liquid | Gas | Liquid | Whipped cream, soap lather
Solid foam — gas dispersed in solid | Gas | Solid | Pumice stone, foam rubber
Aerosols are classified as solid or liquid aerosols
⚠ Honey: Not a colloid — a supercooled liquid
## 2. Osmosis and reverse osmosis
Osmosis: Movement of solvent (water) through a semipermeable membrane — from low to high solute concentration; plant roots absorb water by osmosis
Reverse osmosis: External pressure on the concentrated side — solvent moves from high to low concentration
Uses: Desalination of seawater; purification of water — removes ions and bacteria

K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > H > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au
Potassium above sodium; sodium above calcium; calcium above magnesium; magnesium above aluminium; aluminium above zinc; zinc above iron; iron above lead; lead above hydrogen; hydrogen above copper; copper above mercury; mercury above silver; silver above gold
Sodium, potassium and calcium react vigorously with cold water
Storage: Sodium and potassium are stored under kerosene — it prevents them reacting with air or moisture
## 3. Corrosion
Rust: Hydrated Fe₂O₃ — formation involves iron, oxygen and moisture (requires both oxygen and water); the weight increases
Silver tarnish: Silver reacts with hydrogen sulphide → black silver sulphide (Ag₂S)
Prevention:
Galvanizing: Coats iron or steel with zinc
Anodizing: An aluminium oxide layer on aluminium
Tin plating: For food cans — coated with tin rather than zinc, since zinc is more reactive than tin (tin is less reactive)
Painting and oiling

t: Hydrogen — colours, production and uses
text:
## 1. Colours of hydrogen
Type | Produced by | CO₂ emissions | Notes
Grey | Steam methane reforming (SMR) of natural gas, or coal gasification | High — released | About 95% of current global production; the cheapest
Blue | SMR with carbon capture and storage (CCS) | Low — captured | Transitional — not fully zero-carbon
Green | Electrolysis of water using renewable electricity — solar, wind or hydroelectricity | Zero | The cleanest — a focus of India's Mission
Pink / purple | Electrolysis using nuclear electricity | Near-zero | —
Turquoise | Methane pyrolysis — produces solid carbon | Near-zero | An emerging route
Brown / black | Coal gasification without CCS | Very high | The dirtiest
## 2. Production routes
Route | Source / process | Produces
Steam methane reforming | Natural gas and steam | Grey — or blue when CCS is used
Coal / biomass gasification | Coal or biomass | Grey or brown
Water electrolysis | Water and electricity | Green — with renewable electricity
Methane pyrolysis | Natural gas at high temperature without oxygen | Turquoise
Nuclear-powered electrolysis | Water and nuclear electricity | Pink
Biological / photobiological | Microbes or algae | Emerging green routes
## 3. Properties
A colourless, odourless, tasteless gas — the lightest element; the lowest density among gases
The highest calorific value among common fuels — about 150,000 kJ/kg
Highly flammable — pale blue flame; combustion produces only water (H₂O) — a clean fuel
An energy carrier — not a primary energy source; stores and transports energy
## 4. Uses
Industry: Petroleum refining — desulphurisation; ammonia for fertilisers; methanol; steel through the direct reduced iron (DRI) process; a chemical feedstock
Transport: Fuel-cell vehicles — buses, trucks, trains and ships; rocket fuel; blended in compressed natural gas (CNG)
Power: Fuel cells generate electricity; backup power; grid balancing — storing excess renewable energy; may be used for heating in the future
Fuel cell: An electrochemical device — converts H₂ and O₂ into electricity and H₂O; high efficiency; zero emissions at the point of use
## 5. Green hydrogen applications
Hard-to-abate industries: Green steel — replacing coking coal; fertiliser through green ammonia; refineries
Transport: Heavy-duty vehicles, shipping, aviation (synthetic fuels), railways
Energy: Long-duration energy storage; peak power
Chemicals: Green methanol and other chemical derivatives; exported as green ammonia or green methanol energy carriers
## 6. Why hydrogen matters
Enables the storage and transport of renewable energy
Decarbonises steel, cement, fertilisers, heavy transport, shipping and aviation — useful for hard-to-abate sectors where direct electrification is difficult
Green hydrogen produces only water and replaces fossil-based hydrogen and fuels; reduces dependence on imported fossil fuels
Critical for India's 2070 net-zero target; important for global climate goals

Hydrogen | Pure H₂ | Electrolysis of water or steam reforming | Gaseous clean / future fuel

Water gas | CO and H₂ | — | —
Wood, cow-dung | — | Biomass | Solid renewable

Fuel | kJ/kg | Level

## 2. Uses
Fuel | Uses
Petrol | Spark-ignition engines — car and bike engines
Diesel | Compression-ignition engines — truck, bus and generator engines
CNG | Public transport and cars — a cleaner alternative to petrol and diesel
LPG | Domestic cooking and heating; some vehicles
Kerosene | Domestic lighting and cooking in rural areas; aviation jet fuel

t: Pollution and fuel quality
text:
## 1. Emissions
Fuel | Emissions
Coal | High CO₂; SO₂, NOₓ, particulate matter, ash — severe air pollution; especially high pollution among petrol, diesel and coal
Petrol and diesel | CO₂, CO, NOₓ, unburnt hydrocarbons, particulate matter — diesel produces more particulate matter than petrol; higher pollution levels
LPG and CNG | Lower CO, (unburnt) hydrocarbons and particulate emissions than petrol and diesel — cleaner, but still produce CO₂
Biogas | Low emissions — mainly CO₂ and traces of H₂S when untreated; renewable and relatively clean when purified
Hydrogen | The cleanest fuel — zero carbon emissions; only water (vapour) when burned or used in fuel cells (pure combustion); zero CO₂, CO, SO₂ and particulate emissions
Wood and cow-dung | Smoke, CO and particulate matter — indoor air pollution
## 2. Octane and cetane numbers
Measure | What it measures | Reference
Octane number | The anti-knock quality of petrol in spark-ignition engines — higher = better resistance to knocking | Iso-octane = 100; n-heptane = 0
Cetane number | The ignition quality of diesel in compression-ignition engines — higher = shorter ignition delay and smoother combustion | Cetane (n-hexadecane) = 100
## 3. Knocking
Abnormal combustion or auto-ignition in petrol engines — a metallic knock sound; reduces engine efficiency; can cause engine damage
Anti-knocking agents increase the octane number: Tetraethyl lead (TEL) — phased out because of its toxicity; MTBE; ethanol; toluene

t: Soaps and detergents
text:
## 1. Soap — composition and making
Soap: Sodium or potassium salts of higher fatty acids — 12–18 carbon atoms (C₁₂–C₁₈)
Palmitic acid: C₁₅H₃₁COOH; stearic acid: C₁₇H₃₅COOH
Hard soap: Saturated fats + sodium hydroxide (NaOH) — caustic soda produces hard soap
Soft soap: Unsaturated vegetable oils + potassium hydroxide (KOH) — caustic potash produces soft soap
Structure: A long hydrocarbon chain — hydrophobic; a hydrophilic –COO⁻Na⁺ group
Saponification: The soap-making process — fat or oil reacts with an alkali → soap and glycerol
Raw materials: Vegetable and animal fats and oils — peanut, mahua, castor, coconut, olive and palm kernel oils
Additives:
Sodium rosinate: More foam
Glycerol: Shaving soap — prevents drying
Sodium silicate: Hardness and durability
Sulfur: Anti-acne effect
## 2. Cleansing action
The hydrophobic tail dissolves in grease or oil — forms micelles; the hydrophilic head dissolves in water
Soap suspends grease or oil in water as tiny droplets — washed away with water
Soap decreases the surface tension of water
## 3. Soap in hard water
Insoluble scum — calcium and magnesium salts of fatty acids
No lather (poor lather); wastage of soap; poor cleaning — soap is suitable only for soft water
## 4. Detergents
Synthetic surfactants — ionic, non-ionic or zwitterionic
Common detergents: Alkylbenzene sulfonates; sodium lauryl sulphate — anionic, a 12-carbon chain
Structure: A long carbon chain of 12–18 carbon atoms + a polar group such as sulfonate
Calcium and magnesium salts of detergents are soluble in water — lather even in hard water; no scum; better cleaning power in hard water than soap
## 5. Soap vs detergent
Basis | Soap | Detergent
Source | Natural fats or oils and alkali | Synthetic
Solution | Alkaline — because of hydrolysis | Usually neutral
Delicate fabrics / clothes | Not suitable — harmful | Suitable — safe
Hard water | Poor lather | Excellent lather
Biodegradability | Generally biodegradable | Some older detergents non-biodegradable

Basis | Antiseptics | Disinfectants
Used on | Living tissue — safe for it | Non-living objects — toxic to tissue

## 4. Antibiotics
Alexander Fleming: Discovered penicillin in 1928 from Penicillium notatum
Main sources: Fungi and bacteria — Streptomyces and Bacillus are important bacterial sources

Selman Waksman: Coined the term antibiotic in 1942
## 5. Anaesthesia and sedatives
General anaesthesia: Reversible loss of consciousness
Local anaesthesia: Reversible loss of sensation in a limited area — retains consciousness
The effect is reversible — sensation returns after it wears off
Barbiturates: Reduce anxiety; induce sleep

t: Production, uses and environmental impact
text:
## 1. Production
Urea: Made from ammonia and CO₂ — the Haber process and CO₂
Natural gas (methane): The raw material for ammonia used in nitrogen fertilizers
Phosphatic fertilizers: Rock phosphate + sulfuric acid — the sulfur comes from oil refineries; superphosphate = rock phosphate + H₂SO₄
## 2. Uses
Fertilizer | Effect
Urea | Vegetative growth — wheat and most crops
Phosphatic | Root development, flowering, fruiting
Potassic | Disease resistance, drought tolerance, quality
DAP | A balanced nitrogen and phosphorus supply
Green manure and biofertilizers | Soil health — organic matter; green manure contributes to nitrogen fixation
Neem-coated urea | Slow release — increases nitrogen-use efficiency
## 3. Environmental impact
Excess nitrogen fertilizers: Soil acidification; nitrate leaching to groundwater; eutrophication
Continuous chemical fertilizer use: Decline in soil organic matter; reduced microbial activity; lower nutrient density in food
Solutions: Organic manure, vermicompost, biofertilizers; neem-coated urea — slows fertilizer release
## 4. Green manure
A cover crop grown and ploughed in while green or just after flowering
Plants: Mainly legumes — clover, vetch, sesbania
Benefits: Adds organic matter and humus; fixes atmospheric nitrogen through root nodules; improves soil structure, water retention and microbial activity

topic: Chemistry in daily life and industry
t: Properties of common substances — extremes
text:
## 1. Hardness
Substance | Fact
Diamond (C) | The hardest natural substance — Mohs 10
Tungsten (W) | The hardest metal among metals
Talc (Mg₃Si₄O₁₀(OH)₂) | The softest mineral — Mohs 1; used as baby powder
Graphite | A very soft allotrope of carbon — Mohs 1–2
Sodium (Na) and potassium (K) | Soft alkali metals — cut with a knife
## 2. Lightness and density
Hydrogen (H): The lightest element — atomic weight about 1.008
Lithium (Li): The lightest metal — density 0.534 g/cm³ (about 0.53)
Lighter than water — float on water, densities below 1 g/cm³: lithium (0.53) < potassium (about 0.86) < sodium (about 0.97)
Osmium (Os): The densest metal — 22.61 g/cm³
Uranium (U): The heaviest natural element — atomic number 92; density 19.05 g/cm³
Platinum: 21.09 g/cm³ — platinum is denser than gold, and gold denser than mercury: platinum > gold > mercury
Common densities: Gold about 19.3; mercury about 13.6; steel about 7.8 g/cm³ — gold > mercury > steel
## 3. Reactivity
Potassium (K): The most reactive metal — top of the reactivity series
Fluorine (F): The most reactive non-metal and halogen — the highest electronegativity
Gold (Au): The least reactive metal — occurs in the native state; gold, platinum and silver — noble metals, among the least reactive
Reactivity series as given in the source: K > Na > Ca > Hg > Ag > Au > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > H > Cu
## 4. Abundance
Where | Abundance
Universe | Hydrogen about 75%; helium next
Earth's crust (by mass) | Oxygen 46.6%; silicon 27.7%; aluminium 8.1% — aluminium the third most abundant element
Atmosphere (by volume) | Nitrogen 78%; oxygen 21%; argon 0.93%; carbon dioxide about 0.03%
Human body | Oxygen — mainly as H₂O
Organic compound on Earth | Cellulose
## 5. Melting and boiling points
Among the given options: Boron 2453 K > iron 1808 K > silicon 1693 K > aluminium 933 K — boron has the highest melting point
Tungsten: A very high melting point — about 3422 °C (used in filaments); boiling point about 5555 °C — the highest among metals
Solder: A low-melting alloy of tin and lead — melts at about 183 °C
Teflon: Melts at about 327 °C
Boiling points: Hydrogen peroxide 150.2 °C; acetic acid 117.9 °C; ethanol 78.2–78.5 °C; liquid hydrogen –252.9 °C — cryogenic
Hydrogen: A pure and clean fuel — burns only to form H₂O
## 6. Conductivity
Silver (Ag): The best electrical and thermal conductor
Mercury: The best heat conductor among the given liquids — but the poorest (heat) conductor among metals; thermal conductivity 8.3 W/mK — lower than lead
Sulfur (S), phosphorus (P), bromine (Br): Poor electrical conductors among non-metals
Selenium: A photoconductor
Mica: A good heat conductor but a poor electrical conductor
## 7. Acids, bases and solubility
Strong acids: Hydrochloric, sulfuric and nitric acids — completely ionised
Aqua regia: 3 parts hydrochloric acid + 1 part nitric acid — dissolves gold and platinum
Strong bases: Sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide — used in soap making
Weak bases used as antacids: Magnesium hydroxide (milk of magnesia) and aluminium hydroxide
Ammonia (NH₃): Highly soluble in water — hydrogen bonding and polarity
Water: A solvent with a high dipole moment — dissolves ionic salts best; ionic compounds are generally insoluble in alcohol
Hard water: High Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions — does not lather with soap

t: Firsts — evolution, cells and genetics
text:
## 1. Earliest life and evolution

Barbara McClintock: First identified transposable elements
Yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae): The first organism with a complete eukaryotic genome sequenced — 1996
Schizosaccharomyces pombe: The yeast cited for the first microbial semiconductor-diode fabrication

t: Photosynthesis and chlorophyll
text:
## 1. Photosynthesis
Converts light energy into chemical energy — and carbon dioxide into organic compounds
Main food product: Glucose — stored as starch or sucrose; by-product: oxygen
Level | Site
Plant part | The green parts — the leaf is the main organ
Tissue | Mesophyll
Organelle | Chloroplast
Light reaction | Thylakoid membrane
Dark reaction — Calvin cycle | Stroma
## 2. Chlorophyll
The main / essential light-capturing photosynthetic pigment — green; located in chloroplasts — in the grana or thylakoid system
Absorbs light (energy) — strongly absorbs red and blue light; red light is the most effective for photosynthesis
Green light is largely reflected — giving plants their green appearance
## 3. Metal elements in biomolecules
Molecule | Element
Chlorophyll | Magnesium — symbol Mg
Haemoglobin | Iron (Fe)
Vitamin B12 | Cobalt (Co)

t: Respiration, stomata and transpiration
text:
## 1. Respiration
Cellular respiration: Occurs primarily in mitochondria
Glycolysis: In the cytoplasm
Aerobic respiration: Includes mitochondrial stages
Anaerobic respiration: Through a cytoplasmic pathway or fermentation
## 2. Stomata
Located in the leaf epidermis — a stoma = a pore + guard cells
Functions: Gas exchange — carbon dioxide entry, oxygen exit; transpiration
Opening and closing: Controlled by guard-cell turgidity — potassium is important
Abscisic acid (ABA): Promotes stomatal closure under water stress
## 3. Transpiration
The loss of water vapour from a plant — stomata are the major route
Roles: Water movement creates transpiration pull; cooling regulates leaf temperature; mineral movement with upward water transport
Excessive transpiration: Water loss — reduced by ABA (stomatal closure) and xerophyte adaptations

t: Plant nutrients — functions and deficiency symptoms
text:
## 1. Nutrient table
Nutrient — symbol | Functions | Deficiency causes
Nitrogen — N | Amino acids and proteins (an amino-acid component of proteins); an essential component of chlorophyll; nucleic acids — the nitrogen-containing bases of DNA and RNA; growth and development | Chlorosis / yellowing; stunted growth (stunting)
Phosphorus — P | ATP — energy transfer; a structural component of DNA and RNA (nucleic acids); phospholipids — membrane development; root development; early plant growth; hastens maturity; early flowering | Poor root development; dark or intensely green leaves; reddish / reddening leaves
Potassium — K | Enzyme activation (activates enzymes); regulates stomatal opening and closing; water balance; helps plants withstand stress | Necrosis; interveinal chlorosis; wilting
Sulphur — S | Cysteine and methionine (amino acids); vitamins; chloroplast function (chloroplasts); nitrogen fixation (N₂ fixation) | Yellowing; stunted growth
Calcium — Ca | Cell and plant structure; enzyme activation; nutrient transport | Stunting; blossom-end rot
Magnesium — Mg | A constituent of chlorophyll; enzyme activation | Chlorophyll-related
Iron — Fe | Chlorophyll synthesis; electron transport; an enzyme cofactor | Interveinal chlorosis; necrosis
Boron — B | Meristem and cell development (meristem growth); sugar transport; nodule formation | Growth and meristem problems / abnormalities; poor meristem and cell development; nodule-related effects
Molybdenum — Mo | Nitrogen metabolism; an enzyme cofactor | Affects / impairs nitrogen metabolism
Zinc — Zn | Enzyme and growth functions | —
Copper — Cu | Enzyme functions | —
Manganese — Mn | Enzyme and photosynthetic functions | —
Cl, Ni | Micronutrients | —
## 2. Uptake and fertilizers
Nitrogen uptake: Plants mainly take up nitrogen as nitrate (NO₃⁻); nitrogen fixation converts atmospheric N₂ into usable nitrogen compounds
Nitrogen fertilizer: Supports wheat growth and development
Phosphorus fertilizer: Supports early plant and root growth
Potassium fertilizer: Regulates stomata; promotes plant vigor
NPK: Provides the major plant nutrients
Organic manure: Supplies nutrients — has relatively limited phosphorus in its source
Chemical fertilizer: An important source of concentrated nutrients

t: Biofertilizers and root symbioses

Mycorrhiza: A fungus–(plant) root association — improves nutrient and water acquisition, especially phosphorus uptake; provides better plant growth

Biofertilizers in general: Add nutrients; promote growth
## 3. Legume root nodule and leg-haemoglobin
A legume root nodule has a symbiotic relationship with Rhizobium
Leg-haemoglobin: Located in legume root nodules — associated with Rhizobium symbiosis
Red or pink
Helps maintain suitable oxygen conditions for nitrogen fixation — supports an efficient nitrogen-fixing environment

t: Blood — components and clotting
text:
## 1. Components

t: Kidneys and excretion
text:
## 1. Kidney functions
Location: Either side of the vertebral column
Main function: Filter blood and form urine — the main nitrogenous waste removed is urea (formed in the liver, filtered by the kidneys)
Balance: Extracellular fluid volume (water balance); ionic balance; acid–base balance (pH regulation)
Long-term regulation of blood pressure; removes metabolic wastes and toxins
Urine pathway: Kidney → ureter → bladder → urethra
Urine: About 1.5 litres per day (average normal volume); pH about 6.0

Distal convoluted tubule | Regulation, reabsorption and secretion
Collecting duct | Final urine concentration
Renal artery / renal vein | Carries blood to the kidney / carries filtered blood to the circulation
## 3. Nitrogenous wastes
Waste | Excretion | Animals
Ammonia | Ammonotelic | —
Urea | Ureotelic | Humans
Uric acid | Uricotelic | Birds, reptiles, insects
## 4. Kidney disorders
Kidney stones: Calcium oxalate emphasized
Renal failure: The kidney cannot adequately filter — dialysis is artificial filtration
Diabetes insipidus: ADH deficiency — excessive urine production
Kidney damage: Affects filtration and excretion
