t: Immune system, antibodies and antigens
text:
## 1. Immune cells
WBCs: Defend against disease; lymphocytes — the major cells of immunity
B cells: Antibody-mediated responses — antibody-producing cells belong to the lymphocyte / B-cell lineage
T cells: Cell-mediated immunity
Natural Killer cells: Immune defence
## 2. Antigen and antibody
Antigen: A substance that triggers the immune system — induces the formation of antibodies
Antibody: A blood protein — a globulin; produced in response to an antigen
Combines / binds specifically with its inducing antigen — the binding produces an immune response
Helps neutralize or remove a foreign antigen; can trigger or modulate immune functions
Immunoglobulin: A major antibody class; IgM — the first immunoglobulin produced during an infection
Monoclonal antibody: Binds a specific antigen — discussed as therapeutic antibodies for Nipah
Basic relationship: Antigen → antibody → immune response
## 3. Immunity in disease
Infectious disease: The immune system defends against pathogens; COVID-19 — a vaccine-induced immune response
Autoimmune disease: The immune system reacts against self
Allergy: An abnormal or excessive immune response

t: Biotechnology — applications, rDNA and GMOs
text:
## 1. Applications
Field | Uses
Agriculture | Improved crops; transgenic / genetically modified crops — transgenic crops an agricultural application
Medicine | Drugs, vaccines, diagnostics, gene therapy — genetic diagnostics identify genetic diseases
Industry | Microbial production of useful products
Genetics | Genetic libraries; gene manipulation
Biochips: Drug discovery — DNA-, RNA- and protein-based biochips used in basic research
Human insulin: Produced using genetically engineered / recombinant bacteria — a human insulin gene transferred to bacteria
## 2. Recombinant DNA technology
Recombinant DNA: Formed by combining genetic material — the technology transfers genes between organisms, even microbial genes to higher organisms
Gene cloning: Amplifies or copies a desired gene
Recombinant plasmid: A desired DNA fragment or gene inserted into a plasmid — introduced into a bacterium through transformation
Bacteria multiply rapidly — producing large quantities of DNA or product
## 3. GMOs and transgenic organisms
GMO — genetically modified organism: Genetic makeup (genome) altered / changed through genetic engineering
Transfers a gene from one organism to another — in ways that would not naturally occur; to produce desired traits or products
Approximately synonymous with transgenic organism in the relevant context
Transgenic organism: A foreign gene introduced — receives a gene from another organism through genetic engineering, for a desired characteristic or product; biotechnology produces transgenic organisms carrying introduced genes

t: DNA fingerprinting, sequencing and the genome
text:
## 1. DNA fingerprinting
Basis: DNA polymorphism — fingerprinting is possible because DNA polymorphisms vary among individuals; most human DNA is similar, but variable DNA regions differ among individuals (polymorphism)
Tissues from the same person show the same degree and pattern of polymorphism
Polymorphisms are inheritable / inherited from parents to offspring (parent to child)
A biotechnological method for identifying humans
Uses: Individual identification; biological parentage / paternity (establishing and proving it — parentage testing, paternity disputes); criminal identification and forensic cases — rape and assault cases; conservation of endangered living beings
Samples: Blood, saliva, skin, bone, hair follicles, sperm; DNA evidence from hair, saliva and dried semen
## 2. DNA sequencing
Determines the nucleotide or base sequence — genetic information depends on the order of bases; DNA bases: A, G, C and T
Uses: Genetics — to study genes and genomes; genetic variation — to detect sequence differences; biotechnology — molecular and genomic analysis
## 3. Genome and transcriptome
Genome: Complete genetic information (genetic makeup) — contains the genetic information required to form an individual; roughly fixed for a line except for mutations
Zygote genome: A combination of DNA from two gametes
Human genome: About 3 billion DNA bases — more than 99% are the same among humans
Genome sequencing: Analyzes the DNA sequence of a genome
Transcriptome: The sum total of expressed mRNA molecules — can change with environmental conditions
## 4. Gene therapy
A biotechnology and genetic-engineering application — targets genetic abnormalities or diseases
Basic idea: Alter, replace or correct defective genetic function — genetic engineering is used; CRISPR has the potential to correct genetic defects

t: Genetic engineering tools
text:
## 1. CRISPR-Cas9 — genome editing
CRISPR: Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats — specialized stretches of DNA; originated as a natural defence mechanism of bacteria and archaea
Cas9: An enzyme that cuts DNA strands — nicknamed molecular scissors; guide RNA guides Cas9 to the desired genomic location
Gene editing: Alters DNA sequences; modifies gene function; can remove existing or add new genes
Uses: Correct genetic defects; treat or prevent disease; improve crops — ⚠ raises ethical concerns
## 2. RNAi and restriction enzymes
RNAi — RNA interference: Based on gene silencing — targets gene expression; reduces or prevents the expression of the target gene
Restriction enzyme (restriction endonuclease): Cleaves DNA into fragments — cuts at or near specific recognition sites (restriction sites); a role in genetic engineering by cutting DNA — popularly molecular scissors
## 3. DNA ligase
Joins DNA fragments — forms or seals DNA linkages; joins desired DNA with vector DNA in genetic engineering
Described as a molecular stitcher and molecular glue
## 4. Plasmids and vectors
Plasmid: A small DNA molecule within a cell, separate from chromosomal DNA — replicates independently; commonly circular, double-stranded DNA
Found in bacteria — also in some archaea and eukaryotes; natural plasmid genes may confer advantages such as antibiotic resistance
Biotechnology: To clone, transfer and manipulate genes — an experimental plasmid is a vector
Plasmid + gene = a recombinant plasmid; its entry into bacteria = transformation; bacteria act as factories to copy recombinant DNA
pBR322: A classic vector — an early widely used Escherichia coli cloning vector; the letter p denotes plasmid; the letters BR refer to Bolivar and Rodriguez
## 5. PCR — Polymerase Chain Reaction
Core purpose: Amplification of DNA — many copies of a selected DNA sequence
Uses: Molecular and genetic analysis; detection and diagnostic testing; DNA-based research; analysis of small quantities of DNA
## 6. Stem cells and cloning
Stem cells: Key property — the ability to differentiate into other cell types; can be isolated and grown in the laboratory
Gene transfer: Embryonic stem cells — genetic engineering inserts a desired gene; the modified stem cells are returned to an organism or embryonic system
Gene cloning: The copying / amplification of a desired gene or DNA fragment — plasmid cloning inserts a gene into a plasmid vector; bacteria in a bacterial cloning system rapidly copy recombinant DNA
Whole-animal cloning: Produces a complete organism
Cloning technology: A genetic and biotechnological technique

t: mRNA, vaccines, personalised medicine and biofilms
text:
## 1. mRNA and microRNA
mRNA — messenger RNA: Carries the genetic message for protein production
A vaccine platform — instructs cells to produce a target antigen; the immune system recognises the antigen and produces an immune response
microRNA: A small non-coding RNA — regulates gene expression, typically through post-transcriptional regulation; suppresses or reduces target gene expression — linked to gene silencing
## 2. Vaccine types
Vaccine | Uses
Live-attenuated | A weakened pathogen
Inactivated | A killed or inactivated pathogen
Subunit | A selected antigen or protein
Recombinant | A recombinant antigen
Viral-vector | A vector to deliver genetic instructions
DNA | DNA
mRNA | mRNA
Toxoid | An inactivated bacterial toxin
## 3. Personalised (precision) medicine
Adapts treatment using individual biological or genetic information — goal: more individually tailored prevention, diagnosis and treatment
Tools: Genome sequencing — genomic information; DNA sequencing — sequence or variant information; genetic testing — identifies relevant variants; pharmacogenomics — links genetics to drug response
## 4. Biofilms
A microbial sessile community — cells adhere to a surface or interface and to each other; matrix of extracellular polymeric substances
Form on / in: Medical implants, human tissues, food, food-processing surfaces
Antibiotic resistance; greater tolerance to host defence and external stress — the matrix gives additional resistance or protection; difficult-to-eradicate infections
Resistance progression in bacteria: MDR → XDR → TDR

text:
## 1. Basic terms
Term | Meaning
Ecology | The study of relationships between organisms and the environment

## 2. Levels of biodiversity

Type | Where | Examples

t: Ecosystem structure and energy flow
text:
## 1. Ecosystem
An open system — components: abiotic components, producers, consumers, decomposers
Main decomposers: Bacteria and fungi
Energy flow: Unidirectional — energy transfer upward in a food chain decreases (Lindeman's 10% law — energy transfer between trophic levels)
Productivity: Primary — at the autotroph level; secondary — at the heterotroph level; mangroves — the highest among the listed ecosystems; oceans — the lowest
Carrying capacity: The maximum sustainable population
Biosphere: All ecosystems together
## 2. Trophic levels
Level | Organisms
First | Producers
Second | Primary consumers — herbivores
Third | Secondary consumers
Fourth / highest | Tertiary consumers — top carnivores
Energy decreases upward mainly due to heat loss
## 3. Ecological pyramids
An ecological pyramid represents trophic-level relationships in an ecosystem
Pyramid | Represents | Shape
Numbers | The number of organisms | Upright or inverted
Biomass | The biomass at each trophic level | Upright or inverted — upright in a forest and grassland; inverted in a pond and marine ecosystem
Energy | The energy at each trophic level | Always upright

t: Biogeochemical cycles
text:
Biogeochemical cycle: The movement of chemical elements — nutrient movement through biotic and abiotic components; another term is the nutritional cycle
Biotic components: Living organisms; abiotic: the non-living environment
Carbon cycle: CO₂ exchange through biological processes
Takes up / removes CO₂: Photosynthesis
Releases CO₂: Respiration, decay, fossil-fuel combustion
Water cycle: Driven by solar energy
Phosphorus cycle: Involves rock weathering

t: Wildlife Protection Act and protected areas
text:
## 1. The Act
The first comprehensive legislation for wildlife protection in India — passed by Parliament; Presidential assent on 9 September 1972
A legal framework for protecting wild animals, birds and plants
Protected areas under it: National Parks, Wildlife Sanctuaries, Conservation Reserves, Community Reserves
## 2. Ownership and hunting
Section 39(1): Every wild animal is owned by the State Government — an animal hunted in a Sanctuary or National Park declared by the Central Government is owned by the Central Government
Gharial, Indian wild ass, wild buffalo: Cannot be hunted except as permitted by law
A protected animal may not be hunted normally — but may be captured or killed when it poses a danger to human life, is diseased, or disabled beyond recovery
## 3. Community Reserve — Section 36C
Formed on private land or community land — ⚠ not on land already a National Park, Wildlife Sanctuary or Conservation Reserve
Declared by the State Government — for the conservation of fauna and flora and traditional and cultural values
## 4. Sanctuary vs National Park
Basis | Wildlife Sanctuary | National Park
Hunting | Prohibited without permission | Completely prohibited
Cattle grazing | Regular / allowed | Completely prohibited
Human activity | Some permitted — restricted activities | None — except as permitted by the Chief Wildlife Warden
Legal framework | Wildlife Protection Act, 1972 | Wildlife Protection Act, 1972

t: Air pollution — sources and pollutants
text:
## 1. Sources
Natural: Forest fires; volcanic eruptions
Anthropogenic: Fuel combustion (a major source); automobiles; industries; fossil-fuel burning
## 2. Pollutants and their sources
Pollutant | Sources / association
Carbon monoxide (CO) | Vehicle exhaust — transport; combustion
Sulfur dioxide (SO₂) | Burning fossil fuels (fuel combustion); power stations; industries; diesel vehicles — acid rain
Nitrogen oxides (NOx) | Combustion and vehicles (transport); power stations; industries — air pollution and acid rain
PM2.5 and PM10 | Combustion and vehicles; construction; diesel exhaust; road dust; biomass and domestic burning

O₃ | A secondary pollutant — photochemical reactions
Benzene | Petrol combustion; petrol stations
PAH | Fuel combustion; industrial emissions
VOC | Transport, solvents, industrial and domestic sources
## 3. Effects
Carbon monoxide: Combines with haemoglobin → carboxyhaemoglobin — reacts with haemoglobin more readily than oxygen; a dangerous air pollutant
Smog: Smoke + fog; photochemical smog — from nitrogen oxides, hydrocarbons and sunlight; PAN (peroxyacyl nitrate) is associated with it
Lichen: An indicator of air pollution
## 4. Pollutant codes and AQI
Codes: PM10 (particulate matter), PM2.5 (fine particulate matter), NO₂, CO, O₃, SO₂, NH₃ (ammonia), Pb (lead)
AQI | Category

## 2. Water Act

A statutory organization — constituted in September 1974 under the Water Act, 1974
The national-level pollution-control board — functions at the central level; deals with water and air pollution
State Pollution Control Boards (SPCBs): Implement pollution-control functions at the state level
CPCB and SPCBs: Monitor water bodies and industrial discharges; can take action against violators

t: Solid waste — methods and terms
text:
## 1. Basics
Solid waste requires collection, processing and disposal
Biodegradable waste: Decomposes naturally by microorganisms — includes sewage and domestic organic waste; biodegradable municipal solid waste includes food, organic and yard waste
Non-biodegradable waste: Plastic, DDT, asbestos
SWM Rules, 2016: The key provision — criteria for landfill and waste-processing sites
## 2. Methods
Method | Meaning
Compost | Decomposed (biodegradable) organic waste — a nutrient-rich material with organic matter and nutrients; made in pits from e.g. livestock excreta and vegetable waste — composting is the decomposition of biodegradable waste
Vermicompost | Worm compost — produced using earthworms, which speed up decomposition (vermicomposting)
Landfill | Disposal of solid waste in a designated land area
Incineration | The controlled burning of waste — an incinerator burns waste
Recycling | Processing waste into usable material
Pyrolysis, plasma gasification | Waste-to-energy processes
## 3. Producer responsibility and e-waste
Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR): A producer's responsibility for the environmentally sound management of a product or waste throughout its life cycle — at the end of its life (end-of-life products / management)
Introduced under the Plastic Waste Management and Handling Rules, 2011
R2 Code of Practices: The electronics recycling industry — responsible electronics recycling; promotes environmentally responsible practices; a company following them can become R2 Certified

t: Biomass, microbial fuel cells and carbon
text:
## 1. Biomass from waste
Agricultural waste, food-processing residues, animal manure, human sewage, biogenic municipal solid waste — biomass sources relevant to waste; biogenic MSW serves as biomass feedstock — a biomass energy source
## 2. Microbial fuel cell (MFC)
Microorganisms act as catalysts — converts the chemical energy of organic substrates into electricity
Used in wastewater treatment — can clean wastewater and generate electricity simultaneously
## 3. Carbon emissions and sinks
Sources: Fossil-fuel burning — a major source; automobiles use petrol and diesel; thermal power uses coal — coal combustion produces CO₂, NOx and SO₂
Sinks: Forests; blue carbon — oceans and coastal ecosystems: mangroves, seagrass, salt marshes
Carbon sequestration: Capture and long-term storage — geological storage in coal seams, depleted oil and gas reservoirs, deep saline formations
Common Carbon Metric: Building operations
Carbon fertilization: Increased plant growth due to CO₂
Photosynthesis removes CO₂; respiration and decay release it
Bhutan: A carbon-negative country; net zero — emissions balanced by removals

t: Ozone and the ozone layer
text:
## 1. Ozone
Formula O₃ — three oxygen atoms; forms through the reaction UV radiation + O₂ → O₃
Measured in Dobson Units (DU) — one DU = 0.01 mm of pure ozone (O₃) at 0°C and 1 atm
## 2. Location
The ozone layer is mainly in the stratosphere — which extends from about 10 km to 50 km — the main ozone layer about 15 km to 30 km
About 90% of ozone in the stratosphere and 10% in the troposphere (per the source)
Basis | Stratospheric ozone | Tropospheric ozone
Nature | Protective — absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation; protects life on Earth | A pollutant — harmful to living organisms
Main function: Absorbing harmful ultraviolet radiation — the layer protects from UV radiation
## 3. Ultraviolet bands

UV-A | 315–400 nm
UV-B | 280–315 nm
UV-C | 100–280 nm

World Ozone Day: 16 September — the International Day for the Preservation of the Ozone Layer; declared by the UN General Assembly in 1994; commemorates the signing date of the Montreal Protocol

t: Greenhouse effect and greenhouse gases
text:
## 1. Greenhouse effect
Natural warming caused by the absorption and re-radiation of heat by greenhouse gases

Without it, Earth's average temperature would be about −18°C
## 2. Greenhouse gases

t: Climate agreements and India's commitments
text:
## 1. Clean Development Mechanism (CDM)
Article 12 of the Kyoto Protocol — one of Kyoto's flexible mechanisms
Emission-reduction projects by developed countries in developing countries — generates Certified Emission Reductions (CERs); one CER = one tonne of carbon-dioxide equivalent
## 2. Paris Agreement
2015 — COP21 in Paris
Aims: Keep warming well below 2°C above the pre-industrial level; pursue efforts toward 1.5°C
INDC: Intended Nationally Determined Contributions
## 3. Green India Mission
One of the eight NAPCC missions — to protect, restore and enhance forest cover
Responds to climate change through adaptation and mitigation
Focus: Biodiversity, water, biomass, mangroves, wetlands, critical habitats
## 4. Panchamrit — COP26, Glasgow
Five targets for India:
500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030
50% of energy requirements from renewable energy by 2030
Reduce projected cumulative carbon emissions by 1 billion tonnes by 2030
Reduce carbon intensity by 45% by 2030
Net Zero by 2070

t: Crisis life cycle and disaster management phases
text:
## 1. Crisis management life cycle — three phases
Phase | Focus
Pre-crisis | Prevention and mitigation; preparedness; risk reduction
During crisis | Immediate response; rescue; relief; crisis handling
Post-crisis | Recovery → rehabilitation → reconstruction
## 2. The phases in detail
Disaster management has four phases
Phase | When | Aim | Includes
Prevention | Before a disaster | Stop a hazard from becoming a disaster — proactive and long-term | Land-use zoning; regulating deforestation; controlling industrial siting
Mitigation | Before a disaster | Reduce disaster risk and the severity / impact; minimise future losses — the most cost-effective phase | Earthquake-resistant buildings, embankments, building codes, afforestation, insurance, hazard mapping
Preparedness / preparation | Before a disaster | Readiness — ensures a ready and effective response; capacity building; the first and critical step | Preparedness planning, (Early) Warning Systems, evacuation arrangements, community preparedness, emergency resources, coordination, mock drills, stockpiling, training through Aapda Mitra, Emergency Operation Centres, contingency plans
Response | During or immediately / just after | Immediate action — save lives; meet basic needs; time-critical | Search and rescue, evacuation, first aid, temporary shelters, food and water, law and order
Recovery | After a disaster | Restore normal life / normalcy; reduce future vulnerability; Build Back Better — long-term; builds resilience | Rehabilitation, reconstruction, livelihood support, psycho-social care, resilient infrastructure
Risk assessment leads to mitigation
Non-structural mitigation: Community awareness and education programmes
Cyclone mitigation: Planting trees along coastal areas; earthquake mitigation: reframing and implementing building-construction guidelines
## 3. Response
The community is usually the first responder
Urban response: Civic authorities, the fire brigade, local police — the district administration has the basic responsibility; the Collector plays a pivotal role
Search and Rescue: A major role in the post-disaster scenario
## 4. Stages
Stage | Covers | Focus
Pre-disaster | Prevention, mitigation, preparedness | Risk reduction and readiness
During-disaster | Response | Immediate life-saving action
Post-disaster (post-crisis) | Recovery, rehabilitation, reconstruction | Rebuild better and reduce future risk

t: Shift in approach — 3Rs to 3Ps
text:
Basis | Pre-2005 | Post-DM Act 2005
Approach | The three Rs — rescue, relief, rehabilitation | The three Ps — prevention, preparedness, proofing / mitigation

The disaster management cycle is continuous — lessons from recovery lead to better prevention
Sendai Framework (2015–2030): Global alignment for disaster management

text:
## 1. Broad classes
Class | Hazards
Geological | Earthquake, landslide, tsunami
Hydro-meteorological / atmospheric | Cyclone, flood, drought, thunderstorm-related hazards, hailstorm
Man-made / human-induced | Fire, industrial or chemical, nuclear, biological disasters
## 2. Natural hazard subtypes
Subtype | Examples
Geophysical | Earthquake, tsunami, landslide, volcanic eruption
Hydrological | Flood, flash flood, avalanche
Meteorological | Cyclone, hurricane, tornado, thunderstorm, hailstorm
Climatological | Drought, heat wave, cold wave, forest fire
Biological | Epidemics, pest attacks
## 3. Man-made / anthropogenic subtypes
Subtype | Examples
Technological | Industrial accidents, chemical leaks, nuclear accidents, dam failure
Transport | Air, rail, road and ship accidents
Social / complex | Terrorism, riots, war, civil strife
Socio-natural hazards: A combination of natural and human factors — floods worsened by deforestation; landslides caused by unscientific construction
## 4. Institutional notes
Ministry of Home Affairs: The nodal ministry for overall coordination
Key approach: Shifted from hazard-centric management to multi-hazard risk reduction
Sendai's first priority: Understanding disaster risk, including hazards

t: Vulnerability and vulnerable groups
text:
## 1. Types of vulnerability
Type | Meaning | Examples
Physical | Susceptibility of buildings, infrastructure and physical assets | Weak houses in earthquake zones; settlements in floodplains
Social | Based on age, gender, caste, disability, social status | Women, children, elderly, SC/ST communities, persons with disabilities
Economic | Poverty; lack of livelihood options; low income | Daily wage workers, small farmers, informal sector workers
Environmental | Degradation of natural systems that increases risk | Deforestation → landslides; loss of mangroves → greater cyclone impact
Systemic / institutional | Weak governance; poor coordination; lack of preparedness | Inadequate early warning systems; delayed response
## 2. Vulnerable groups in India
Basis | Groups
Age | Children — especially unaccompanied children; elderly people
Gender | Women — pregnant, lactating, single women, widows; transgender persons
Disability | Persons with Disabilities (PwD)
Socio-economic | Poor people, SC/ST communities, informal sector workers, homeless people
Location | People in high-risk zones — coastal areas, Seismic Zone V, flood plains, hilly areas
Others | Migrants, refugees, remote tribal communities
## 3. NDMA focus areas
Disability-inclusive DRR: The NDMA Guidelines on Disability Inclusive Disaster Risk Reduction (2019)
School safety: A special focus on children
Gender mainstreaming: Women's leadership and participation in DRR — part of the PM's 10-Point Agenda
Minimum standards of relief: Special provisions for vulnerable groups
Community-based DRR: Including the most vulnerable in planning

t: UNISDR to UNDRR
text:
## 1. Names and history
Old: UNISDR — United Nations International Strategy for Disaster Reduction; established 1999 as the secretariat for — and to implement — the International Strategy for Disaster Reduction
Current: UNDRR — United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction; rebranded on 1 May 2019
Headquarters: Geneva, Switzerland
Led by the Special Representative of the UN Secretary-General for Disaster Risk Reduction
Period | Milestone
1989–1999 | The International Decade for Natural Disaster Reduction
1999 | UNISDR established
2005–2015 | UNISDR supported the Hyogo Framework for Action
2015 | Supported adoption of the Sendai Framework (2015–2030)
2019 | Rebranded as UNDRR
## 2. Role of UNDRR
The focal point within the UN system for coordination of DRR — coordinates DRR across the UN system
The custodian of the Sendai Framework — supports its implementation, monitoring and review
Promotes a global culture of DRR; provides tools, guidelines, data and best practices
Convenes the Global Platform for Disaster Risk Reduction

t: Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015–2030
text:
## 1. Adoption and nature
Adopted on 18 March 2015 at the Third UN World Conference on Disaster Risk Reduction — Sendai, Japan; duration 2015–2030
Succeeded the Hyogo Framework for Action (HFA) 2005–2015
Custodian: UNDRR
A voluntary, non-binding global agreement
Expected outcome: A substantial reduction of disaster risk and of losses in lives, livelihoods, health and in economic, physical, social, cultural and environmental assets
## 2. Four priorities
Priority | Emphasizes
1. Understanding disaster risk | Risk assessment in all dimensions — hazard, vulnerability, exposure, capacity
2. Strengthening disaster risk governance | Laws, institutions, policies and coordination at all levels
3. Investing in DRR for resilience | Public and private investment in prevention and mitigation
4. Enhancing disaster preparedness for effective response and to "Build Back Better" | Preparedness, recovery, rehabilitation, reconstruction
## 3. Seven global targets
Target | Aim
A | Substantially reduce global disaster mortality by 2030
B | Substantially reduce the number of affected people globally by 2030
C | Reduce direct economic loss in relation to global GDP by 2030
D | Substantially reduce disaster damage to critical infrastructure and disruption of basic services by 2030
E | Substantially increase the number of countries with national and local DRR strategies by 2020
F | Substantially enhance international cooperation to developing countries by 2030
G | Substantially increase the availability of and access to multi-hazard early warning systems and disaster risk information by 2030
In short, the global targets: reducing disaster mortality, the number of affected people, economic loss and damage to infrastructure; increasing DRR strategies, international cooperation and early warning systems
## 4. Guiding principles
States have the primary role in reducing disaster risk
All-of-society engagement: Government, private sector, civil society, academia, media
Multi-hazard approach: Natural and man-made hazards
Build Back Better: Recovery as an opportunity to reduce future risk
Inclusive and people-centred: Special attention to vulnerable groups

t: World Conferences on Disaster Risk Reduction
text:
WCDRR — World Conference on Disaster Risk Reduction: Organised by the United Nations — to discuss and adopt international frameworks for DRR
Three WCDRRs held — all hosted by Japan; UNDRR (formerly UNISDR) coordinated the 2nd and 3rd
WCDRR | Year | Venue | Outcome document
1st | 1994 | Yokohama, Japan | Yokohama World Strategy and Plan of Action for a Safer World
2nd | 2005 | Kobe, Japan (Hyogo) | Hyogo Framework for Action (HFA) 2005–2015
3rd | 2015 | Sendai, Japan | Sendai Framework for DRR 2015–2030
## 1. Frameworks compared
Framework | Adopted | Period | Features
Yokohama Strategy | 1994 | 1994 onwards | The first global guidelines on disaster prevention, preparedness and mitigation
Hyogo Framework for Action | 2005 | 2005–2015 | Building the resilience of nations and communities — five priorities for action
Sendai Framework | 2015 | 2015–2030 | The current global framework — four priorities, seven global targets; Build Back Better

t: Background — HPC and the road to the DM Act
text:
High Powered Committee (HPC): Constituted in August 1999 for a systematic, comprehensive and holistic approach to disasters — first Chairman J.C. Pant
Original mandate: Plans for natural disasters only — later expanded to man-made disasters
Report: Submitted 2001 — theme "building a culture of prevention"; a shift from relief-centric approaches to prevention, mitigation and preparedness
Bhuj earthquake, Gujarat (2001): Influenced institutional reforms
Nodal ministry: The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) — subjects shifted from the Department / Ministry of Agriculture to MHA after the Gujarat earthquake of 2001 (in 2002); MHA is nodal at the Central level after 2002
Indian Ocean Tsunami (2004): A major catalyst — it exposed gaps in India's disaster response system
First responder: The community — neighbours and local people
Uttarakhand: The first state to establish a dedicated Ministry of Disaster Management

t: Disaster Management Act, 2005
text:
## 1. The Act
Full name of the law: The Disaster Management Act, 2005 — Act No. 53 of 2005; enacted 2005
Enacted after the 2004 Indian Ocean Tsunami exposed gaps in India's disaster response system — the tsunami acted as a major catalyst for the Act
Passed / Presidential assent: December 23, 2005; came into force progressively from 2006 onwards
National-level legislation — a legal and institutional framework for effective disaster management; extends to the whole of India
11 Chapters; 79 Sections
## 2. Key sections
Section | Provides for
3 | National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) — the legal basis
8 | National Executive Committee (NEC)
14 | State Disaster Management Authority (SDMA) — established by the Governor of a State
25 | District Disaster Management Authority (DDMA)
14 and 25 | State- and district-level planning and coordination
42 | National Institute of Disaster Management (NIDM)
44 | National Disaster Response Force (NDRF)
46 | National Disaster Response Fund (NDRF)
47 | National Disaster Mitigation Fund (NDMF)
48 | State Disaster Response Fund (SDRF)
## 3. Bodies and funds under the Act
Body / fund | Role
NDMA | The national-level authority — the apex body for policies, plans and guidelines
SDMA / DDMA | State-level / district-level authority
NEC | Assists the NDMA
NIDM | Capacity building, training and research
NDRF (force) | A specialised disaster response force
SDRF (force) | A state-level response force
National Disaster Response Fund | A central fund for severe disasters
State Disaster Response Fund | The primary fund with States for immediate relief
NDMF | Mitigation measures — later operationalised
SDMF | State-level mitigation
## 4. 2025 amendment
Urban Disaster Management Authorities (UDMA) for State Capitals and cities with Municipal Corporations
Statutory status to the NCMC and the High-Level Committee — greater legal backing
Disaster databases — better data-driven planning
Aligns with the Sendai Framework; updates definitions of risk and resilience

text:

## 3. Funds and schemes

NIDM: A premier institute for capacity building, training and research
Aapda Mitra: An NDMA scheme — trains community volunteers as first responders; search and rescue and first aid

t: National policy, plan and frameworks
text:
## 1. National Policy on Disaster Management (NPDM)
Issued 2009 — approved by the Union Cabinet on 22 October 2009; prepared by the NDMA; formulated in pursuance of the DM Act, 2005
Vision: A safe and disaster-resilient India — holistic, proactive, multi-disaster oriented and technology-driven
Core approach: Shifted from relief-centric response to prevention, mitigation and preparedness
## 2. Other frameworks
Framework | Year | Facts
Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction | Covers the period 2015 to 2030 | A global blueprint — four priorities, seven targets; guides India's DM policy; succeeded the Hyogo Framework (2005–2015)
PM's 10-Point Agenda on DRR | 2016 | Announced at the Asian Ministerial Conference on DRR in New Delhi — India's action-oriented roadmap aligned with Sendai
National Disaster Management Plan | 2016 — the first; revised 2019 | An operational plan implementing the NPDM and Sendai
Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure | 2019 | An international initiative led by India

t: National institutions
text:
Institution | Location | Role
NDMA — National Disaster Management Authority | New Delhi | The apex policy body for disaster management in India — chaired by the Prime Minister
NIDM — National Institute of Disaster Management | New Delhi, Rohini — Southern Campus in Vijayawada, Andhra Pradesh | A premier, statutory institute for capacity building, training, research and policy advocacy — established under Section 42 of the Disaster Management Act, 2005; founded as the National Centre for Disaster Management (NCDM) in 1995, upgraded to NIDM in 2003; President — the Union Home Minister
NDRF — National Disaster Response Force | HQ New Delhi | A specialist / specialised response force for natural and man-made disasters — including CBRN; raised 2006 — established under Section 44 of the Disaster Management Act, 2005
NDRF Academy | Nagpur | Training for NDRF, SDRF and Civil Defence personnel
NDRF Regional HQ for AP, Telangana and Karnataka | Vijayawada | Disaster response
INCOIS — Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services | Hyderabad | Houses the Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre (ITEWC) — India's official tsunami warning centre, issuing tsunami early warnings
NRSC — National Remote Sensing Centre | Hyderabad | Remote-sensing support for disaster monitoring and mapping
IMD — India (Indian) Meteorological Department | New Delhi (Delhi) | Cyclone forecasting — the cyclone forecasting agency; weather forecasts and warnings (cyclone and rainfall warnings); early-warning systems
GSI — Geological Survey of India | HQ Kolkata | Landslide forecasting (the landslide forecasting agency) and studies; seismic and geological hazard assessment; hazard mapping
CWC — Central Water Commission | New Delhi | Forecasts floods
National Fire Service College (NFSC) | Nagpur | Firefighting, rescue and disaster response training
Centre for Disaster Management (CDM) | LBSNAA, Mussoorie | Trains civil servants in disaster management
National Cyclone Risk Mitigation Project | HQ New Delhi | Cyclone-risk mitigation
APSDMA | Andhra Pradesh | State-level alerts — systems such as Vajrapath, Varuna and Red Message
State Administrative Training Institutes (ATIs) | Across states | State-level centres for capacity building and training
IUINDRR-NIDM | Under NIDM | A network of universities for DRR research, curriculum and capacity building
India Disaster Resource Network (IDRN) | Under NIDM and the MHA | An online inventory of resources for disaster response
NCMC: Headed by the Cabinet Secretary — coordinates the response during major crises
CCS: Handles nuclear, biological and chemical emergencies
Tsunami warning: Hyderabad — operated through INCOIS

t: International and regional centres
text:
Centre | Location | Role
ITIC — International Tsunami Information Centre | Honolulu, Hawaii, USA | Tsunami information and capacity building; supports global tsunami warning and preparedness — supported by UNESCO-IOC and NOAA
PTWC — Pacific Tsunami Warning Center | Honolulu, Hawaii, USA | Tsunami warnings for the Pacific Ocean
IOC — UNESCO Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission | Paris, France | Coordinates global tsunami-warning systems
United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction — abbreviated UNDRR | Geneva, Switzerland | The focal point for the Sendai Framework — focuses on global disaster-risk reduction
ADPC — Asian Disaster Preparedness Centre / Asian Disaster Center | Bangkok, Thailand | Disaster awareness and local capabilities; regional capacity building in Asia
ADRC — Asian Disaster Reduction Center | Kobe, Japan | Information sharing and research on disasters
SDMC — SAARC Disaster Management Centre | Earlier New Delhi, India — since restructured | Regional cooperation among SAARC countries
Indian Ocean Tsunami Warning System: Coordinated through the IOC — regional centres in India, Indonesia, Australia and other countries; established after the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami

t: Ministry of Home Affairs and roles of governments
text:
## 1. Ministry of Home Affairs
The nodal ministry for disaster management — at the Union level (except drought, pest attack and epidemics)
Shifted from the Department of Agriculture after the Gujarat Earthquake of 2001
Overall coordination at the national level; provides support, coordination and resources to the State Governments
Primary responsibility lies with the State Governments
## 2. Disaster Management Division of the MHA
Mobilises resources and coordinates central assistance to states for response and relief
Operates the National Emergency Operations Centre and the national Control Room
Handles NDRF, SDRF, NDMF and SDMF (fund) matters; administers the DM Act, 2005
Concerned with prevention, mitigation, preparedness and long-term rehabilitation
Coordinates international assistance and HADR (humanitarian assistance and disaster relief) operations
Administrative and budgetary matters of the NDMA, NDRF and NIDM
Strengthens Fire Services, Civil Defence and Home Guards
## 3. Bodies under the MHA
NDMA: Under the MHA's administrative control — a policy body chaired by the Prime Minister
NDRF: Under the MHA — operational control through the NDMA
NIDM: A capacity-building institute under the MHA
NEC: Chaired by the Union Home Secretary; High Level Committee: Union Home Minister — financial approvals
## 4. Roles of each level
Union Government: Physical and financial resources; early warning; coordination
NCMC — Cabinet Secretary: coordinates and directs responses to national crises; CCS — nuclear, biological and chemical emergencies
State Government: Post-disaster relief and rehabilitation — the State Crisis Management Committee (chaired by the Chief Secretary) handles state-level crises
District: The Collector / District Magistrate — overall disaster management
Community: Usually the first responder at the ground level

t: Nodal ministries and technical agencies by hazard
text:
## 1. Nodal ministries
Hazard | Nodal ministry
Earthquakes, cyclones and tornadoes, tsunamis | Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES) — with IMD, responsible for cyclone and earthquake forecasting
Floods, GLOFs | Ministry of Jal Shakti — with the CWC for technical aspects of floods
Urban floods | Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs
Droughts, hailstorms, frost and cold waves, pest attacks | Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare
Landslides | Ministry of Mines
Avalanches | Ministry of Defence
Forest fires; industrial and chemical disasters | Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
Nuclear and radiological emergencies | Department of Atomic Energy (DAE)
Biological disasters and epidemics | Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
Oil spills | Ministry of Defence (Indian Coast Guard)
Civil aviation accidents | Ministry of Civil Aviation
Rail accidents | Ministry of Railways
Road accidents | Ministry of Road Transport and Highways
## 2. Technical agencies
Hazard | Technical agency
Cyclones | India Meteorological Department (IMD)
Tsunamis | INCOIS (Hyderabad)
Floods | Central Water Commission (CWC)
Earthquakes | National Centre for Seismology — under MoES
Landslides | Geological Survey of India (GSI)

t: National Disaster Response Force (NDRF)
text:
## 1. Establishment and control
NDRF — National Disaster Response Force: A disaster response force — response force operations
Established 2006 — legal basis Section 44 of the DM Act, 2005; Raising Day 19 January
Parent ministry: Ministry of Home Affairs; controlling authority: the NDMA
Headquarters: New Delhi; regional HQ for AP, Telangana and Karnataka — Vijayawada; NDRF Academy — Nagpur
Motto: "Aapada Seva Sadaiv Sarvatra" — "Disaster Service Always Everywhere"
Director General: A senior IPS officer — rank of ADG
## 2. Strength and composition
The world's largest dedicated disaster response force
16 battalions — expanded from an initial 8; about 1,149 personnel per battalion; a total strength of more than 18,000
Each battalion: 18 self-contained Search and Rescue teams — engineers, technicians, electricians, dog squads, medical and paramedic personnel
Parent forces (on deputation): BSF, CRPF, CISF, ITBP, SSB, Assam Rifles
## 3. Roles and skills
Responds to: Floods, earthquakes, cyclones, landslides, avalanches, building collapses, industrial accidents, and chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear emergencies
Skills: Collapsed Structure Search and Rescue (CSSR), flood rescue, mountain rescue, Medical First Response
Pre-positions teams before disasters — strategic placement based on the vulnerability profile across India; multiple Regional Response Centres for faster response
## 4. International deployments
Country | Year
Japan | 2011
Nepal | 2015
Turkey | 2023 — Operation Dost
Myanmar | —
## 5. Related roles
The community is the first responder; the District Magistrate / Collector has overall responsibility at the district level (district disaster management)
NCMC: Crisis coordination; State Crisis Management Committee: headed by the Chief Secretary

t: State Disaster Response Force
text:
SDRF — State Disaster Response Force: A state-level specialised response force — the counterpart of the NDRF
Legal basis: The DM Act, 2005 — including Section 44 and related rules
Raised by the respective State or Union Territory Governments — the first responder within the state, during the first 24–48 hours
Trained by the NDRF or the NDRF Academy — similar training standards
Drawn mainly from the State Police; also Armed Police, Fire Services, Home Guards, Civil Defence
Organisation: A battalion model — similar to the NDRF; multi-disciplinary teams
Specialises in search and rescue, flood rescue, collapsed-structure rescue, and CBRN response in some states

t: State Disaster Response Fund
text:
## 1. The fund
SDRF — State Disaster Response Fund: Legal basis Section 48(1)(a) of the DM Act, 2005
The primary fund with states for immediate relief — to victims of notified disasters
Administered by the State Executive Committee — headed by the Chief Secretary
## 2. Contributions
States | Centre | State
General-category | 75% | 25%
Special-category — Northeastern and Himalayan states | 90% | 10%
## 3. Notified disasters
Cyclone, drought, earthquake, fire, flood, tsunami, hailstorm, landslide, avalanche, cloudburst, pest attack, frost and cold wave
State-specific disasters — not in the notified list: up to 10% of the fund can be used
## 4. Limits
Used only for immediate relief — ⚠ not for compensation for individual losses or long-term reconstruction

t: Mitigation measures and mitigation funds
text:
## 1. Mitigation
Definition (in the DM Act, 2005): Measures aimed at reducing the risk, impact or effects of a disaster or threatening disaster situation
Belongs to the pre-disaster phase — with prevention and preparedness; the most cost-effective phase of the Disaster Management Cycle
Goal: Reduce vulnerability; lessen the impact of hazards
Paradigm shift: From relief-centric (the 3Rs) to mitigation-centric (prevention, mitigation and preparedness)
General measures: Risk assessment; non-structural mitigation — community awareness and education programmes
## 2. Structural vs non-structural
Basis | Structural | Non-structural
Meaning | Physical or engineering constructions | Policies, laws, awareness and planning
Examples in India | Embankments, dams, cyclone shelters, earthquake-resistant buildings, retrofitting, sea walls, check dams | Building codes (IS 1893, the National Building Code), Flood Plain Zoning, land-use planning, insurance, public awareness, early warning systems, training
## 3. Hazard-wise mitigation
Hazard | Structural | Non-structural
Flood | Embankments, dams, channel improvement | Flood Plain Zoning; flood forecasting (CWC); watershed management; flood-plain management, flood-proofing, forecasting and warning
Earthquake | Retrofitting; earthquake-resistant design (IS 1893) | Seismic microzonation; building codes; awareness; reframing and implementing building-construction guidelines
Cyclone | Multi-purpose coastal embankments | Early warning systems; coastal regulation zones; community training; planting many trees along coastal areas
Drought | Check dams, farm ponds, irrigation | Drought-resistant crops; water conservation; insurance under PMFBY
Landslide | Retaining walls (against steep slopes); slope stabilisation | Land-use regulation; afforestation; early warning; regulating settlements in hazard-prone areas
## 4. Andhra Pradesh
Vulnerable cyclone stretch: Ongole to Machilipatnam
Maximum human-life loss: The 1977 cyclone
## 5. Mitigation funds
NDMF (National Disaster Mitigation Fund) and SDMF (State Disaster Mitigation Fund) — the key mitigation funds
Provided for in the DM Act, 2005; operationalised after the 15th Finance Commission recommendations
DRR to be integrated into all development sectors — mainstreaming DRR is part of the PM's 10-Point Agenda

t: Earthquakes — basics and seismic zones
text:
## 1. Basics
An earthquake is a geological disaster — ⚠ not an atmospheric natural disaster
Focus: The origin point inside Earth; epicentre: the point directly above the focus on the surface
Intensity: Measured on the Mercalli Scale; a seismograph measures earthquakes
Seismology: The study of earthquakes — John Milne, the father of modern seismology
## 2. Seismic zones of India — four
Zone | Risk | Expected intensity (MSK) | Zone factor | Covers
V | Very high | IX and above | 0.36 | The entire North-East, Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, parts of Bihar, Kutch (Gujarat), the Andaman and Nicobar Islands
IV | High | VIII | 0.24 | Delhi, parts of J&K and Himachal Pradesh, North Bihar, parts of Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Rajasthan, Maharashtra
III | Moderate | VII | 0.16 | The remaining Indo-Gangetic plains, coastal areas, Kerala, Goa, parts of Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan
II | Low | VI or less | 0.10 | Most of Peninsular India — a stable region
Andhra Pradesh: Lies in Seismic Zones II and III

t: Major Indian earthquakes and seismic management
text:
## 1. Major earthquakes
Earthquake | Year | Magnitude | Facts
Assam | 1897 | 8.1 | One of the earliest well-studied great earthquakes
Kangra | 1905 | 7.8 | About 20,000 deaths
Bihar-Nepal | 1934 | 8.1 | Massive damage in the Gangetic plains
Assam-Tibet | 1950 | 8.6 | One of the largest ever recorded
Koyna | 1967 | 6.3 | Reservoir-induced seismicity
Latur / Killari | 1993 | 6.2 | About 10,000 deaths in peninsular India
Bhuj, Gujarat | 2001 | 7.7 | A major turning point — led to the DM Act of 2005
Sikkim | 2011 | 6.9 | The Himalayan region
Nepal-India / Gorkha | 2015 | 7.8 | Significant impact in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh
## 2. Seismic management
National Centre for Seismology (NCS): Real-time monitoring and earthquake information — under the Ministry of Earth Sciences
NDMA: Policy guidelines; the National Earthquake Risk Mitigation Project
BIS Code IS 1893: Earthquake-resistant design of structures; the National Building Code incorporates seismic provisions
Seismic microzonation: Detailed risk mapping of cities such as Delhi and Guwahati
National Disaster Response Force (NDRF): Conducts specialised search and rescue — Collapsed Structure Search and Rescue (CSSR)

t: Tsunamis
text:
## 1. Nature and causes
Large waves generated by sudden movements of the ocean floor — displacing a large volume of water; a natural disaster; the term is Japanese in origin
Most commonly associated with earthquakes — an earthquake beneath the sea
Other triggers: Submarine and terrestrial impacts, landslides, volcanic eruptions, explosions, bolide impacts
Can occur at any time of day or night; slows down as it approaches the shore
Sequence: An undersea disturbance → sudden displacement of the ocean floor → displaces a large volume of water → generates tsunami waves → waves reach coastal areas → inundation and destruction of life and property
Effects: Strips beaches; uproots plantations; inundates large inland areas; damages life and property
## 2. 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami
December 2004 — severe damage in Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Pondicherry, Kerala and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands
More than 12,000 confirmed deaths in India; 5,640 unaccounted
Estimated damage: More than ₹11,000 crore — about US$2.56 billion
## 3. Warning
Tsunami Warning Centre in India: Hyderabad — the Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre (ITEWC), established in INCOIS (Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services, Hyderabad)
International Tsunami Information Centre: Honolulu
Remote sensing, GIS and satellite data address tsunami and coastal disaster vulnerability — GIS is spatial data, a disaster-management tool
## 4. Related dates
World Tsunami Awareness Day: November 5
International Day for DRR: October 13 — began 1989
World Conference on Disaster Management: Yokohama, 1994
IDNDR: Covered the period 1990 to 2000
Sendai Framework: Disaster risk reduction — adopted 2015

t: Disaster scales and intensity measures
text:
Scale | Used for | Measures | Range / facts
Richter Scale | Earthquakes | Magnitude — the energy released | Logarithmic; usually 1 to 10 or higher; developed by Charles Richter in 1935
Moment Magnitude Scale (Mw) | Earthquakes | Magnitude | Logarithmic; the modern standard — preferred over Richter for large earthquakes
Modified Mercalli Intensity (MMI) | Earthquakes | Intensity — observed effects and damage | I to XII — based on human observation and damage
MSK-64 | Earthquakes | Intensity | I to XII — used in India and many European countries
Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale | Hurricanes and tropical cyclones in the Atlantic and Pacific | Wind speed | Category 1 to Category 5
Fujita / Enhanced Fujita (F/EF) | Tornadoes | Wind speed and damage — tornado intensity | F0/EF0 to F5/EF5
Beaufort Scale | Wind and storms | Wind force — general wind strength | 0 to 12
International Nuclear Event Scale | Nuclear and radiological events | Severity of a nuclear event | Level 0 to Level 7 — IAEA (1990)
Indian Cyclone Intensity Scale | Cyclones in India — used by the IMD | Wind speed | Depression → Cyclonic Storm → Severe → Very Severe → Extremely Severe → Super Cyclonic Storm

t: Tropical cyclones and hurricanes
text:
## 1. What a cyclone is
A cyclone is a low-pressure area — a large-scale rotating low-pressure system over warm tropical oceans; scientific name tropical cyclone; a rapid-onset disaster
Produces strong winds, heavy rainfall and storm surge
## 2. Hurricane
A regional name for a tropical cyclone — North Atlantic cyclones are called hurricanes
A large, rotating tropical storm system forming over warm ocean waters — sustained winds of at least 119 km/h (74 mph), the minimum for a hurricane, typhoon or cyclone
A low-pressure centre — the eye; spiral rain bands; produces strong winds, heavy rainfall, storm surge
Rotation: Counter-clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere; clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere
Measured by the Saffir–Simpson Wind Scale
## 3. Regional names
Name | Region
Hurricanes | North and Central Atlantic, Caribbean Sea, Gulf of Mexico, Northeast Pacific
Typhoons | Northwest Pacific — East Asia, the Philippines, Japan
Cyclones | Indian Ocean, Bay of Bengal, Arabian Sea, South Pacific
## 4. Saffir–Simpson categories
Category | Wind speed | Damage
1 | 119–153 km/h | Minimal
2 | 154–177 km/h | Moderate
3 | 178–208 km/h | Extensive
4 | 209–251 km/h | Extreme
5 | At least 252 km/h | Catastrophic
## 5. India
⚠ India does not get hurricanes — it gets tropical cyclones in the Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea; "cyclone" is the common name
Major threats: High winds, storm surge, heavy rainfall, flooding, coastal inundation
The East Coast — Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, West Bengal, Tamil Nadu — is more vulnerable than the West Coast; the Bay of Bengal : Arabian Sea ratio is about 4:1

t: IMD cyclone classification
text:
The IMD officially classifies low-pressure systems over the North Indian Ocean (Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea) — based on the maximum sustained (surface) wind speed, a 3-minute average
Category | km/h | Knots
Low Pressure Area — the weakest | Less than 31 | Less than 17
Depression | 31–49 | 17–27
Deep Depression | 50–61 | 28–33
Cyclonic Storm — naming begins (62 km/h and above) | 62–88 | 34–47
Severe Cyclonic Storm | 89–117 | 48–63
Very Severe Cyclonic Storm | 118–166 | 64–89
Extremely Severe Cyclonic Storm — introduced 2015 | 167–221 | 90–119
Super Cyclonic Storm — the highest category | 222 or more | 120 or more
⚠ The IMD classification differs from the Saffir–Simpson Scale — which is used for hurricanes

t: Cyclone agencies, projects and major cyclones
text:
## 1. Agencies
India Meteorological Department (IMD): Forecasting, tracking, naming and early warning of cyclones — HQ Delhi
RSMC New Delhi: The Regional Specialised Meteorological Centre for the North Indian Ocean
INCOIS: Storm-surge and high-wave warnings
NDMA: Policy guidelines and overall coordination — Guidelines on Management of Cyclones (2008)
NDRF and SDRF: Pre-positioning, evacuation, search and rescue
APSDMA: Disaster mitigation and response in Andhra Pradesh
## 2. Projects and technology
NCRMP — National Cyclone Risk Mitigation Project: World Bank-assisted — cyclone risk mitigation; cyclone shelters (a key project), early warning, last-mile connectivity
Doppler Radar Network: Forecasts heavy rainfall and thunderstorms
SCATSAT-1: Weather forecasting, cyclone prediction and tracking for India
GIS, remote sensing and satellite data: Disaster mapping — GIS supports spatial analysis
## 3. Andhra Pradesh
Most vulnerable stretch: Ongole to Machilipatnam
1977 cyclone: The maximum loss of human life
Hudhud (2014): Devastated Visakhapatnam
Phethai: Landfall in December 2018 — from the Bay of Bengal to Andhra Pradesh
## 4. Major cyclones
Cyclone | Year | Place | Facts
Bhola | 1970 | The Indian sub-continent | —
Super Cyclone | 1999 | Odisha | About 10,000 deaths — a major push for a modern disaster-management system
Phailin | 2013 | Odisha | Massive evacuation — very low casualties
Hudhud | 2014 | Andhra Pradesh | Severe damage to Visakhapatnam
Fani | 2019 | Odisha | Gold-standard evacuation of about 1.2 million people
Amphan | 2020 | West Bengal | A super cyclonic storm
Tauktae | 2021 | The Arabian Sea | A rare intense west-coast cyclone

t: Tornadoes
text:
## 1. Nature
A violently rotating column of air extending from a thunderstorm to the ground — very strong rotating winds; a localised, short-duration atmospheric hazard
Wind speeds: 105 to 322 km/h — can exceed 300 km/h in severe cases
A funnel-shaped cloud — narrow or wide
Lasts a few minutes — rarely more than 15–20 minutes; can remain stationary or travel up to about 90–100 km/h
Measured on the Fujita Scale / Enhanced Fujita Scale — 6 categories
## 2. Tornadoes in India
Rare compared with the USA — but increasing in recent years
Most prone: Eastern and North-Eastern India — West Bengal, Odisha, Jharkhand, Bihar, Assam
Season: Pre-monsoon — March to May — especially with Nor'westers (Kal Baisakhi)
Deadliest: 24 March 1998 at Belda (West Bengal–Odisha border) — about 250 deaths
Other events: New Delhi (1978); Berhampore (1993); Kendrapara, Odisha (2009); recent cases in Odisha, Punjab, Haryana, Jammu and Kashmir

t: Floods — nature, types and extent
text:
## 1. Nature
A flood is the overflow of water onto normally dry land — water in rivers, streams and other water bodies that cannot be contained
Causes: Excess rainfall; river overflow; other causes
A rapid-onset disaster — the most frequent natural disaster in India
Aggravated by poor drainage, urbanization and poor planning (urban flooding); prolonged rainfall can cause heavy landslides, which can block rivers and cause downstream havoc
## 2. Extent in India
Flood-affected areas: About 10% of India
Flood-prone area: About 40 million hectares (Rashtriya Barh Ayog estimate); recent estimates up to about 49 million hectares
Worst-affected states: Assam and Bihar; next: Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal
Annual losses: Damage worth thousands of crores; significant loss of life and of crops
## 3. Types of flood
Type | Cause | Commonly affected
Riverine / fluvial | Overflow of rivers due to heavy monsoon rainfall | The Ganga, Brahmaputra, Kosi and Godavari basins
Flash floods | Sudden intense rainfall or cloudbursts | Himalayan regions; urban areas
Urban floods | Poor drainage, heavy rain, encroachment on wetlands | Mumbai, Chennai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Delhi
Coastal floods | Storm surges, cyclones, high tides | The east and west coasts
Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs) | Bursting of glacial lakes | Himalayan states — Uttarakhand, Sikkim

t: Flood management and major floods
text:
## 1. Institutions
National Flood Commission — Rashtriya Barh Ayog: Established 1980 — recommended comprehensive flood management
Central Water Commission: A flood forecasting network across India
NDMA: Policy guidelines and coordination — Guidelines on Management of Floods (2008); Guidelines on Urban Flooding (2010)
Brahmaputra Board: Flood and erosion control in North-East India
State Irrigation / Water Resources Departments: Implement structural flood-control works
NDRF and SDRF: Search, rescue and relief during floods
Flood management: Flood forecasting, warnings and disaster preparedness
## 2. Odisha Flood Hazard Atlas
A unique flood hazard atlas — based on historical flood inundation captured through satellite imagery (2000 to 2018) — to manage floods more efficiently
GIS: Deals with spatial data — can model, analyse and display community vulnerability
## 3. Major floods
Flood | Year | Cause / impact
Mumbai | 2005 | 944 millimetres of rain in 24 hours — drainage failure
Bihar | 2008 | An embankment breach in the Kosi region
Uttarakhand | 2013 | Kedarnath — a cloudburst and a Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) contributed
Chennai | 2015 | Extreme rain; wetland destruction
Kerala | 2018 | Heavy rain; dam releases

t: Cloudbursts
text:
## 1. Definition
IMD: Extremely intense rainfall over about 20–30 square kilometres — at least 100 mm (10 cm) in one hour
A highly localised, short-duration extreme weather event — often with thunderstorms; conceptually a rapid-onset disaster
Triggers flash floods and landslides — the major secondary hazards
Mostly at altitudes of 1,000 to 2,500 metres in mountainous regions
## 2. Mechanism
Orographic lifting: Warm, moist air forced to rise rapidly over steep mountain slopes — the main trigger mechanism
Atmospheric instability: Strong convection and towering cumulonimbus clouds
High moisture in monsoon air masses
Sudden release: Updrafts weaken and the accumulated water falls intensively
## 3. Vulnerable areas
Region | Areas | Why
Himalayan region | Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh, Sikkim | Steep slopes; the orographic effect; the monsoon
Western Ghats | Parts of Kerala, Karnataka, Maharashtra | Intense monsoon rainfall on the windward side
Plains | Occasionally — rare | Localised convection
## 4. Forecasting and events
Extremely difficult to forecast — highly localised; tools: Doppler Weather Radar, nowcasting
Famous events: Leh (2010); Kedarnath (2013); recent Himalayan events

t: Hailstorms
text:
## 1. Nature
Precipitation as ice pellets — hailstones — formed in strong thunderstorms
A localised, short-duration, high-intensity weather hazard — ⚠ not a biological disaster
Formation: Strong updrafts in cumulonimbus clouds freeze raindrops; repeated layering increases hailstone size
## 2. Season and regions
Season: Mainly the pre-monsoon (March to May); also winter; rare during the monsoon
India has a high frequency — among countries with frequent moderate to severe hail events
Highest probability: Maharashtra — especially Vidarbha and Marathwada
Central India: Madhya Pradesh; parts of Chhattisgarh
North and Northwest India: Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh
Others: Bihar, parts of Karnataka, Uttarakhand
## 3. Factors
Atmospheric: Strong convective instability; abundant moisture; strong updrafts
Synoptic: Western Disturbances; wind discontinuity lines
Terrain: Plateaus and hilly regions enhance convection
Climate change: Increasing frequency and intensity of extreme convective events
## 4. Onset of disasters
Rapid-onset: Cyclone, flood, tsunami
Slow-onset: Drought — a creeping emergency
An earthquake is a geological disaster

t: Drought — nature, causes and history
text:
## 1. Nature
Drought: A serious shortfall in the availability of water — a prolonged deficiency of rainfall or moisture leading to water scarcity
A slow-onset natural disaster — also called a creeping emergency or creeping hazard
Mainly affects: Agriculture, drinking-water supply and industry
## 2. Causes in India
Mainly the inadequacy and uneven distribution of rainfall
More than 80% of India's rainfall is received in less than 100 days during the southwest monsoon
Large parts of India depend on rain-fed agriculture — vulnerable to drought
Excess withdrawal of groundwater over replenishment aggravates drought in the long run
Peninsular India: Surface-water availability itself becomes scarce in years of insufficient rainfall
## 3. Extent
Category | Rainfall | Share of India's area
Total drought-prone | — | About 68% of the geographical area
Chronically drought-prone | Less than 750 mm | About 33%
Drought-prone | 750–1125 mm | About 35%
## 4. History of drought management
Arthashastra (4th century B.C.): Devoted a section to mitigation measures for combating famines
After Independence: Drought-relief works undertaken in severely affected areas
Green Revolution (late 1960s): Reduced the necessity for famine-relief work
Drought Prone Areas Programme: Taken up as a holistic drought-management programme
Disaster Management Act, 2005: Provided national-level disaster-management legislation

t: Drought — types, indicators and management
text:
## 1. Types of drought
Type | Indicator | Time lag
Meteorological | Rainfall deficiency of at least 25% from the long-period average | Immediate
Agricultural | Soil moisture insufficient for crop growth | Intermediate
Hydrological | Depletion of reservoirs, rivers, aquifers and other surface-water and groundwater sources | Delayed — weeks to months
Socio-economic | Demand for water exceeds supply — causes social and economic stress | Long-term
## 2. Guidelines and declaration
NDMA Guidelines on Drought: Issued 2010
Manual for Drought Management: Revised 2016 by the Ministry of Agriculture
Adopted a multi-indicator approach — rather than relying only on rainfall
At least three triggers are required for drought declaration
Monitoring indicators: Rainfall deviation, dry spells, NDVI, soil moisture, reservoir and groundwater levels
## 3. Relief and support
State Disaster Response Fund: The primary fund for drought relief
National Disaster Response Fund: Used in severe drought cases
MGNREGA: Employment support
PMFBY: Crop insurance

t: Heatwaves
text:
## 1. Nature
Heatwave: A period of abnormally high temperatures exceeding the normal maximum temperature during the summer season
Season in India: Mainly March to June; sometimes extends to July
Nodal agency for forecasting heatwaves: India Meteorological Department — early warning through colour-coded alerts
NDMA Guidelines for Preparation of Action Plan – Prevention and Management of Heat Wave: Key guidelines; updated 2019
A notified disaster: Included in the list of notified disasters eligible for SDRF and NDRF assistance — as per the latest updates
## 2. Declaration criteria
Region | Minimum threshold | Heatwave — departure from normal | Severe heatwave
Plains | 40°C | 4.5°C to 6.4°C | More than 6.4°C
Coastal areas | 37°C | 4.5°C or more | —
Hilly regions | 30°C | 4.5°C to 6.4°C | More than 6.4°C
Plains — by actual maximum temperature: Heatwave also identified at at least 45°C; severe heatwave at at least 47°C
## 3. Colour alert levels
Colour | Indicates | Action
Green | Normal conditions | No action
Yellow | Heat alert | Be updated and monitor conditions
Orange | Severe heat alert | Preparedness
Red | Extreme heat alert | Action
## 4. Management
Heat Action Plans: Prepared by states and cities with support from NDMA and IMD
Cool roofs: Reflective coatings or white painting of roofs
Public awareness measures: Communicating do's and don'ts; ORS distribution; establishing cooling centres
Structural measures: Shade structures; drinking water points; adjusted working hours

t: Cold waves
text:
## 1. Nature
Cold wave: A significant drop in minimum temperature below the normal climatological average during the winter season
Main season in India: November to March; peak impact December to February
Nodal agency for forecasting cold waves: India Meteorological Department — issues colour-coded cold-wave alerts: Yellow, Orange and Red
NDMA Guidelines on Cold Wave and Frost: Issued 2021 — focus on preparedness, vulnerability mapping and community awareness
A notified disaster eligible for assistance under the SDRF and NDRF
## 2. Declaration criteria — minimum temperature
Region | Threshold | Cold wave — negative departure | Severe cold wave — negative departure
Plains | 10°C or below | 4.5°C to 6.4°C | Greater than 6.4°C
Hilly regions | 0°C or below | 4.5°C to 6.4°C | Greater than 6.4°C
Coastal stations | 15°C or below | 4.5°C or more | —
Plains — based on actual temperature: Cold wave when the actual minimum temperature is 4°C or below; severe cold wave at 2°C or below
## 3. Cold day
Cold day: Maximum temperature departure of –4.5°C to –6.4°C while the minimum temperature is already low
Severe cold day: Maximum temperature departure less than –6.4°C
## 4. Impacts
Health: Hypothermia; respiratory diseases; frostbite; increased mortality among elderly people and children
Groups most vulnerable: Homeless people, elderly people, children, outdoor workers, street vendors, poor households
Agriculture: Crop damage due to frost; affects livestock
Power demand: Increases
## 5. Measures
Protective measures: Distributing warm clothing; providing night shelters; establishing community kitchens; medical preparedness
Agricultural measures: Frost-protection techniques for crops

t: Landslides — nature, triggers and regions
text:
## 1. Nature
Landslide: The mass movement of rocks, debris or earth down mountain slopes or riverbanks — a rapid downward movement of rock, soil, debris or vegetation, influenced by gravity
May occur gradually or suddenly without warning; common terrain: hilly regions
Both a geological hazard and a hydro-meteorological hazard
Associated with earthquakes, floods and volcanic eruptions
Prolonged rainfall: A major rainfall trigger; heavy rainfall is the main trigger for landslides in India
## 2. Extent and institutions
Landslide-prone: About 12.6% of India's land area — about 0.42 million square kilometres
Most vulnerable regions: The Himalayas, the Northeast and the Western Ghats
Geological Survey of India (GSI): Associated with landslide forecasting; conducts the National Landslide Susceptibility Mapping programme
National Landslide Forecasting Centre: A key landslide initiative
NDMA — Guidelines on Management of Landslides and Snow Avalanches: Issued 2009
National Landslide Risk Management Strategy: Issued 2019
Recent major event: Wayanad, Kerala — 2024
## 3. Landslide-prone regions
Region | Areas | Triggers
Northwest Himalayas | Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand | Earthquakes, heavy rainfall, road cutting
Northeast Himalayas | Sikkim, Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Mizoram, Nagaland, Meghalaya | Heavy rainfall, Jhum cultivation
Western Ghats and Konkan region | Kerala, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Goa, Tamil Nadu's Nilgiris | Intense monsoon rainfall, deforestation
Eastern Ghats | The Araku region | Localised heavy rainfall
## 4. Mitigation
Structural measures: Retaining walls (against steep slopes); rock bolting; wire mesh; drainage improvement; slope grading
Non-structural measures: Landslide Hazard Zonation mapping; Early Warning Systems; land-use regulation; awareness
Regulating settlements in hazard-prone areas; construction in high-risk zones should be restricted; mountain-specific building codes should be enforced

t: Avalanches
text:
## 1. Nature
Avalanche: A rapid flow of snow, ice and debris down a mountain slope — a geological and snow-related natural hazard
Occur in India mainly in the Himalayan region — in high-altitude areas
## 2. Institutions
Nodal ministry: Ministry of Defence
Key technical agency: Defence Geoinformatics Research Establishment (DGRE) — earlier known as the Snow and Avalanche Study Establishment (SASE); functions under the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO)
Conducts avalanche forecasting and research; undertakes hazard mapping; develops mitigation technologies
Issues daily avalanche warning bulletins during the winter season
Border Roads Organisation (BRO): Constructs and maintains roads and installs protection structures in avalanche-prone areas
NDMA guidelines: Risk zonation, early warning, structural and non-structural mitigation measures
## 3. Types
Type | Description
Slab avalanche | A large cohesive slab of snow breaks off and slides — ⚠ the most dangerous type
Loose snow avalanche — sluff | Small slides of dry, powdery snow
Ice avalanche | Ice masses from glaciers
Rock / debris avalanche | A mixture of rock, soil and snow
## 4. Causes
Natural: Heavy snowfall; weak snow layers caused by a temperature gradient; steep slopes of 30°–45°; earthquakes and seismic activity; wind loading; a rapid temperature rise; rain falling on snow
Human / other: Skiing; mountaineering; road construction; artificial triggering using explosives; deforestation; climate change effects
## 5. Avalanche-prone areas of India
State / UT | Areas
Jammu and Kashmir | The most affected region
Ladakh | High-altitude zones
Himachal Pradesh | Lahaul-Spiti, Kinnaur, Rohtang Pass, Chamba
Uttarakhand | Higher reaches of the Garhwal and Kumaon Himalaya
Sikkim, Arunachal Pradesh | High-altitude Himalayan stretches
## 6. Management measures
Structural: Snow bridges; snow nets; retaining walls; galleries
Non-structural: Hazard zonation mapping; restricted movement; training; awareness

t: Nuclear and radiological disasters
text:
## 1. Nature
Nuclear disaster: An uncontrolled release of radioactive material causing significant harm to life, health, property or the environment
A man-made or technological disaster in the CBRN category — ⚠ a nuclear explosion is not a natural disaster
Nuclear disasters: Include nuclear accidents involving reactors
Radiological disasters: Include orphan-source incidents, transport accidents and dirty-bomb incidents
Key threat: Ionising radiation — alpha radiation, beta radiation, gamma radiation and neutrons
Long-term impacts: Cancer; genetic damage; environmental contamination for decades or centuries
## 2. Major nuclear and radiological events
Event | Year | Place | Key facts
Three Mile Island accident | 1979 | USA | A partial core meltdown; no major release
Chernobyl disaster | 26 April 1986 | Ukraine — formerly the USSR | The worst nuclear accident; Level 7 on the INES scale
Fukushima Daiichi disaster | 2011 | Japan | Tsunami-triggered; Level 7 on the INES scale
Mayapuri incident | 2010 | Delhi, India | An orphan Cobalt-60 source — a radiological emergency

t: Nuclear emergency management in India
text:
## 1. Institutions
Department of Atomic Energy (DAE): The nodal agency for man-made radiological emergencies in the public domain — the nodal technical agency
Crisis Management Group (CMG): Associated with the Department of Atomic Energy
Cabinet Committee on Security (CCS): Handles nuclear, biological and chemical emergencies
Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB): An independent regulator for nuclear and radiation safety
National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA): Issued the National Guidelines on Management of Nuclear and Radiological Emergencies (2009)
BARC/DAE Emergency Response Centres: A network of specialised centres for detection and response
National Disaster Response Force (NDRF): Specially trained CBRN battalions for response
District Administration: Leads the off-site emergency — the District Collector is the Incident Commander
## 2. Zones
Exclusion zone: A radius of 1–1.5 km around a reactor — public habitation is prohibited
Emergency Planning Zone (EPZ): Concentric zones for protective actions
## 3. Protective actions
Iodine prophylaxis: Potassium iodide (KI) or potassium iodate tablets — protects the thyroid
Others: Sheltering, evacuation, food and water control, decontamination

t: GIS in disaster management
text:
## 1. What GIS is
GIS: Geographic Information System — a tool for disaster management that deals with spatial data
Stores, manipulates, analyses and presents geographical data
Supports modelling and analysing spatial data and displaying community vulnerability
Disaster mapping: Uses remote sensing, GIS and satellite data
## 2. GIS across the disaster cycle
Phase | GIS uses
Prevention / mitigation | Hazard zonation mapping; vulnerability assessment; risk mapping; land-use planning
Preparedness | Evacuation route planning; resource mapping; early warning systems
Response | Real-time damage assessment; search and rescue coordination; resource allocation
Recovery / reconstruction | Damage assessment; "Build Back Better" planning; monitoring reconstruction
## 3. GIS by hazard
Hazard | GIS uses | Associated agency / programme
Flood | Flood inundation mapping; floodplain zoning; real-time flood monitoring | —
Cyclone | Cyclone track monitoring; storm surge modelling; cyclone evacuation planning | —
Earthquake | Seismic hazard zonation; earthquake damage assessment using pre-event and post-event images | —
Landslide | Landslide susceptibility mapping | The Geological Survey of India's NLSM programme
Drought | Agricultural drought assessment | NADAMS
Forest fire | Forest fire detection and monitoring | —
Tsunami | Tsunami inundation modelling; tsunami evacuation planning | INCOIS
## 4. Institutions
National Remote Sensing Centre: A Decision Support Centre in GIS-based disaster management — provides satellite-based inputs
ISRO: Disaster Management Support Programme (DMSP); Bhuvan — ISRO's geoportal for visualisation and analysis
NDMA and SDMAs: Use GIS for planning, decision support and developing guidelines
National Database for Emergency Management: Abbreviated NDEM
